It was the first game built around climbing ladders between walkable platforms, before Donkey Kong, in what were first called "climbing games" and later platform games.
trivia: It did well in Japan but was an obscure, unsuccessful release in North America.
Apple Panic (1981), an unauthorised clone, outsold the original in North America, and Lode Runner (1983) took inspiration from its digging.
Chuckie Egg's creator, Nigel Alderton, cited it as an inspiration, down to its colour scheme.
Over a dozen clones appeared, many with "panic" in the title.
Michael Thomasson called it the foundation of platformers.
devStory: Universal developed it, with Kazutoshi Ueda, later designer of Lady Bug and Mr. Do!, on the team, taking the digging and trapping of Heiankyo Alien (1979) and turning it side-on with platforms and ladders. It came out in November 1980 and did well in Japan, where it tied as the 14th-highest-grossing arcade game of 1981, but flopped in North America; Electronic Games blamed the novelty of the idea and reported an average play time of 30 seconds. Casio and Coleco published home versions in 1983, after an unauthorised clone, Apple Panic, had already become an Apple II best seller.

title: Pac-Man
description: Pac-Man (1980) is Namco's maze game in which a yellow disc eats dots while four ghosts give chase — designed by Toru Iwatani to draw women and couples into arcades, and the best-selling arcade game of all time.
longDescription: Pac-Man eats the dots in a maze while the ghosts Blinky, Pinky, Inky and Clyde hunt him; power pellets briefly turn the tables so he can eat them. Blinky chases him directly, Pinky and Inky try to get ahead and corner him, and Clyde switches between chasing and fleeing. Within a year more than 100,000 cabinets had sold, taking over $1 billion in quarters.
trivia: Iwatani often said a pizza with a slice missing inspired the shape; in 1986 he said that was only partly true, and that he also rounded off the Japanese character for "mouth".
The ghosts' Japanese names mean chaser, ambusher, fickle and playing dumb.
An integer overflow garbles level 256, making it impossible to finish.
Billy Mitchell scored a perfect 3,333,360 in 1999; Guinness reinstated the record in 2020.
devStory: Iwatani's team began in early 1979 and took one year and five months, then the longest development of any video game. Namco released it in Japan in May 1980, and Midway in North America later that year. It led to a Hanna-Barbera cartoon and the No. 9 hit "Pac-Man Fever".

title: Centipede
description: Centipede (1981) is Atari's trackball shooter, designed by Ed Logg and Dona Bailey, in which a centipede winds down through a mushroom field — one of the first arcade games with a large female audience.
longDescription: The player's Bug Blaster, moved with a trackball along the bottom of the screen, fires darts at a centipede that enters at the top and drops a row and reverses each time it touches a mushroom or the edge. Each segment hit becomes another mushroom, and shooting a middle segment splits the centipede in two, the rear piece growing a new head. Mushrooms take four shots to clear, and a crowded field brings the centipede down faster. Once it reaches the bottom, extra heads keep arriving from the sides. Fleas drop straight down leaving mushrooms, spiders zig-zag across eating mushrooms and score more the closer they are shot, and scorpions poison the mushrooms they touch, sending any centipede that hits one diving straight at the player. Each new centipede is one segment shorter, with a faster detached head.
trivia: One estimate put half its players as women.
The Atari 2600 version sold 1,475,240 cartridges in 1982–83.
Its sequel, Millipede, followed in 1982.
It was used in the final round of the 1981 Atari World Championships.
Jim Schneider's 1984 score of 16,389,547 is the arcade record.
devStory: Ed Logg, who said he did the design, and Dona Bailey, who wrote about half the programming and was one of the few women programming games at the time, developed it at Atari; Bailey wanted it to look visually arresting and liked pastel colours. It reached North American arcades in August 1981 and was the third-highest-grossing arcade game of 1982 in the US, tied with Donkey Kong. One estimate put half its players as women. Atari and Atarisoft ported it widely, and the 2600 version sold 1,475,240 cartridges in 1982 and 1983. It was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2020.

title: Warlords
description: Warlords (1981) is Atari's castle battle for up to four players, each guarding a corner fortress with a paddle-controlled shield and deflecting fireballs at the others.
longDescription: Combining ideas from Atari's Quadrapong and Breakout, it gives each player a castle in a corner of the screen: an L-shaped wall around a Warlord, crowned for a human King and helmeted for a computer-controlled Black Knight. A paddle moves the shield around the castle to deflect fireballs, which bounce off everything and knock chunks out of the walls, and a "Power stone" button lets the shield catch and hurl a fireball harder at the cost of slowly wearing down the player's own walls. A dragon launches the first fireball, always at a human, up to four can be in play, and a destroyed Warlord releases a fireball in the opposite direction of the killing shot. The last player standing gets a bonus.
trivia: It won an Arkie Award for Best 'Pong' Variant in 1982.
Atari built 1,014 upright and 1,253 cocktail cabinets.
Game Informer ranked it the 25th best video game of all time in 2009.
An eight-player remake, Lords of Lunar, is hidden on the making-of disc of Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete.
On the upright cabinet, the players team up against the computer.
devStory: Roger Hector, an Atari graphic artist, pitched it as Kings in the Corner at a brainstorming session; it became Castles & Kings, an Atari 2600 game programmed by Carla Meninsky, while Norm Avellar and Greg Rivera programmed the arcade version. After a four-player prototype cabinet proved too big to produce, Atari made a colour cocktail cabinet for up to four players and a black-and-white upright for two, which reflects the picture off a mirror over a castle backdrop. Field-tested in September 1980, it shipped in April 1981, the 2600 version in May, and Sega released it in Japan in July.

title: Defender
description: Defender (1981) is Williams' side-scrolling shooter: protect humanoids on a wraparound planet from alien abductors, using five buttons and a joystick.
longDescription: Defender flies the player over a mountainous planet wider than the screen, with a scanner at the top showing the whole world and brackets marking the visible part. Landers try to carry ten astronauts up the screen and turn into mutants, which chase the ship and fire; shooting a Lander frees its captive, who must be caught and set down. After the first stage come Baiters, fast discs that shoot or ram, Bombers that drop floating mines, and Pods that burst into homing Swarmers. If every astronaut is lost, the planet explodes and mutants swarm the level until surviving waves restore it. The controls — a two-way joystick plus thrust, reverse, fire, smart bomb and hyperspace buttons — were unusually complex, combining Space Invaders' joystick with Asteroids' buttons. Three smart bombs clear the screen in an emergency, and hyperspace teleports the ship at random, sometimes destroying it.
trivia: It was the second-highest-grossing US arcade game of 1981, behind Pac-Man.
About 70,000 machines were sold worldwide.
The team took the idea of a wraparound world from Asteroids and made the play area wider than the screen.
Its title was inspired by the 1960s TV series The Defenders.
A 2000 US postage stamp showed it, which Guinness recognised as the first video game on a stamp.
devStory: Eugene Jarvis led development at Williams, a pinball maker, from around October 1979, with Larry DeMar, Sam Dicker and Paul Dussault assisting and Steve Ritchie advising; early prototypes based on Space Invaders and Asteroids were abandoned, and Ritchie argued for scrolling in both directions. It ran on a Motorola 6809 with a 6800 for sound, with a 16-colour display and animation handled in software written in assembly language. The game was unfinished in September 1980, when Williams unveiled it at the AMOA show; the attract mode and high-score table were added the night before, and a prototype board caught fire from a wrongly fitted EPROM. It reached Japan in February 1981 and North America in March, and became Williams' best-selling arcade game.

title: Galaga
description: Namco's 1981 sequel to Galaxian, in which diving alien formations can capture your ship with a tractor beam — and rescuing it gives you a double-barrelled fighter.
longDescription: The player's ship, Gyaraga, moves along the bottom of the screen and must clear each stage of the Galaga aliens, which fly into formation from the top and sides and then dive while firing. Four Boss Galaga at the top of the formation take two shots, and can use a tractor beam to capture the player's ship, costing a life. If a life remains, shooting the captor as it dives frees the ship and joins it to the new one as a dual fighter, with twice the firepower but a larger target; shooting the captor while it sits in formation turns the captured ship into an enemy. Some aliens morph into new types, and later stages bring more shots and faster dives. Stage 3 and every fourth stage after it is a Challenging Stage, where aliens fly a set pattern without firing.
trivia: Its Challenging Stages were added after a bug that sent enemies flying off the screen gave the team the idea.
The tractor beam was inspired by a film in which a ship was captured by a circling laser.
Clearing stage 255 announces stage zero and a kill screen.
The NES version was released in North America in 1988 as Galaga: Demons of Death.
An extinct shark, Galagadon nordquistae, was named after it in 2019 because its teeth resemble the aliens.
devStory: Shigeru Yokoyama led its development at Namco as a follow-up to Galaxian, with Toru Ogawa as lead programmer, Hiroshi Ono on graphics and Nobuyuki Ohnogi on music. Meant for the Galaxian board, it moved to a new Namco Galaga board, and because sprite limits stopped the dual fighter from firing, Yokoyama made the ship and bullet sprites 16 by 16 pixels. Early location tests did poorly because players could go too far on one coin, so executives asked for more difficulty. Namco released it in Japan in September 1981 and Midway in North America that November. It was Japan's sixth-highest-grossing arcade game of 1981 and third of 1982, and it was still in the US top ten earners in 1983.

title: Ms. Pac-Man
description: Ms. Pac-Man (1982) grew from a Pac-Man enhancement kit into an official sequel, with four mazes, bouncing fruit and less predictable ghosts.
longDescription: Ms. Pac-Man began as Crazy Otto, an enhancement kit for Pac-Man made by programmers at General Computer Corporation, whose rights Midway bought. It keeps the original's dots and energizers but rotates through four mazes — pink, light blue, brown and dark blue — most with two sets of warp tunnels instead of one, and solid-coloured walls. Bonus fruit bounces in through the tunnels rather than appearing in the centre, in random order from round eight. The ghosts gain semi-random movement, so fixed patterns stop working, and the orange ghost is called Sue instead of Clyde. Ms. Pac-Man spins and falls when she dies, the sound effects and music are all new, and three intermissions follow Pac-Man and Ms. Pac-Man's relationship, ending with a stork delivering a baby.
trivia: The cabinet and title screen say 1981, but it debuted in February 1982.
Development began without Namco's consent, but Namco's president gave feedback on the character and Namco took the same royalties per cabinet as for Pac-Man.
About 125,000 cabinets had sold by 1988, and Cash Box and the AMOA named it 1982's highest-grossing arcade game.
Namco president Masaya Nakamura's reported verdict on the character was "Love the concept, get rid of the hair."
It was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2022.
devStory: A 1981 settlement with Atari barred GCC from selling conversion kits without the manufacturer's consent, so GCC showed the finished game to Midway, which agreed to take the rights in exchange for royalties on 29 October 1981. The name went from Super Pac-Man through Pac-Woman, Miss Pac-Man and Mrs. Pac-Man before settling on Ms. Pac-Man, and Midway's Stan Jarocki said the game partly responded to how many Pac-Man players were women. It debuted at a press conference in Sherman Oaks, California, on 3 February 1982. Midway and GCC later fought over merchandise royalties, settling in 1983. Bandai Namco still owns the rights.

title: Scramble
description: Scramble (1981) is Konami's side-scrolling shooter, the first with forced scrolling and distinct levels: fly through six sections, bombing fuel tanks to stay airborne.
longDescription: The player flies a jet through six sections of scrolling terrain, each with different obstacles and no break between them, with one button to fire forward and another to drop bombs. Fuel drains constantly and is topped up by destroying fuel tanks on the ground, and touching the terrain or an enemy destroys the jet. Destroying the base at the end of the final section raises a flag, and the game loops back to the start with faster fuel depletion. Survival scores 10 points a second, rockets 50 on the ground and 80 in the air, fuel tanks 150, mystery targets up to 300 and the base 800, and a single extra jet is awarded at 10,000. Defender came earlier as a horizontally scrolling shooter, but Scramble was the first with forced scrolling and multiple distinct levels.
trivia: Stern sold about 10,000 cabinets in its first two months in the US, and over 15,000 in five, making it Stern's second-best seller after Berzerk.
Gradius (1985) began as a follow-up, under the working title Scramble 2.
Its harder sequel, Super Cobra, came out the same year.
Computer and Video Games wrote that it "was the first arcade game to send you on a mission".
A Konami Code unlocks three extra ships in the Game Boy Advance version.
devStory: Konami developed it in late 1980 and released it in Japan on 8 January 1981, with Leijac distributing; Stern saw it at a London trade exhibit that month and took an exclusive licence for the Americas, starting US sales on 17 March. It sold 15,136 US cabinets by 4 August, topped RePlay's monthly chart that June and was Konami's first major worldwide hit. In Stern Electronics v. Kaufman (1982), a court held that Stern could copyright the game's images and sounds, not just its code, in a case over a near-identical knock-off. Konami founder Kagemasa Kōzuki later called it the company's most important game.

title: Tempest
description: Tempest (1981) is Dave Theurer's colour vector tube shooter for Atari: spin a rotary knob to move around the rim of a 3D web and blast enemies climbing towards you.
longDescription: The player's claw-shaped blaster moves around the rim of a tube drawn in colour vector graphics, steered with a rotary knob, and fires down its lanes at enemies climbing from the far end. Flippers drag the blaster down the tube, Pulsars electrify their lane, Fuseballs jump along lane edges, Spikers leave spikes behind them, and Tankers split into two Flippers when destroyed, with Fuseball and Pulsar Tankers in later levels. A Superzapper destroys every enemy on the field once per level, and a second use kills one at random. Once a level is cleared the player warps down the tube, dying on any spike left in the way. There are sixteen level shapes, some closed tubes and some open; after all sixteen they repeat in new colours and at higher difficulty. It was the first game to let players choose their starting level, a feature Atari called SkillStep.
trivia: Theurer said its design came from a nightmare in which monsters crawled out of a hole in the ground.
It was the first game to let players choose their starting level, a feature Atari called SkillStep.
Theurer also designed Missile Command.
Jeff Minter made the authorised sequels Tempest 2000, Tempest 3000 and Tempest 4000.
Nolan Bushnell said it is his favourite game Atari published.
devStory: Dave Theurer designed and programmed it at Atari. It began as a first-person remake of Space Invaders, but early versions had many problems, so he changed the design; its prototypes were named Aliens, then Vortex, before Tempest. It used Atari's Color-QuadraScan vector display and a dial controller like Pong's, and came in upright, cabaret and cocktail cabinets, the cocktail version flipping the screen for each player. Atari released it in North America in October 1981. Early units had ROM glitches that let certain end scores unlock tricks, including 40 free credits, and Atari shipped fixed chips to operators.

title: Gorf
description: A 1981 Midway shooter that packed five different games into one cabinet — including takes on Space Invaders and Galaxian — and taunted players with a synthesised robot voice.
longDescription: The player's starship, from the Interstellar Space Force, must stop the Empire of Gorf from conquering Earth. Unlike Space Invaders and Galaxian, the ship can move in every direction within the lower third of the screen, and its single "quark laser" can be fired at any time, cancelling the previous shot. The game cycles through five missions: Astro Battles, a Space Invaders clone behind a parabolic force field; Laser Attack, with two formations of dive-bombers, a laser gunner and a miniature Gorf robot; Galaxians; Space Warp, with enemies spiralling out of a wormhole; and Flag Ship, whose force field must be broken to reach its core. Destroying the core raises the player's rank, from Space Cadet up to Space Avenger, and restarts the cycle faster. A speech chip gives voice to a Gorfian robot that taunts the player, and players could buy up to seven lives with credits before starting.
trivia: Its speech includes "Long live Gorf!" and "Prepare for annihilation, Space Cadet!"
Home versions dropped the Galaxians stage because Namco owns the rights to Galaxian.
Play Meter ranked it number one on its arcade chart in September 1981.
Its fire button is built into the pistol grip, derived from a B-1 bomber control design.
A sequel, Ms. Gorf, was cancelled; its surviving disks are labelled "RIP Ms. GORF 6/82 - 8/83".
devStory: Jamie Fenton developed it at Dave Nutting Associates, Midway's long-time research consultants, reusing custom chips from the Bally Astrocade, whose team Fenton had led. It began as an adaptation of Star Trek: The Motion Picture, abandoned after Fenton read the script, which is why the boss flagship resembles the Enterprise; the boss fight drew on the trench run in Star Wars. Three missions were original and two borrowed from Space Invaders and Galaxian, which Midway distributed in the US. Fenton spent over a year on it, mostly at home. Field-tested alongside Pac-Man, it reached US arcades in February 1981.

title: Wizard of Wor
description: Wizard of Wor (1981) is Midway's dungeon shooter for one or two players, who cooperate or compete while the Wizard mocks them in synthesised speech.
longDescription: One or two Worriors must clear enclosed mazes of monsters — blue Burwors, yellow Garwors and red Thorwors — cooperating or competing for points, with a radar at the bottom of the screen showing where the monsters are. Tunnels at the sides lead to the opposite edge of the maze, though each closes briefly after use. Once every monster is dead a Worluk appears, and destroying it before it flees doubles the points in the next maze; after that the Wizard of Wor himself may appear, staying until he is killed or kills a Worrior. Each maze opens with the first five notes of Dragnet, the fifth missing if the Worluk escaped, and the Wizard taunts the player in synthesised speech. Later mazes are more open and the monsters harder to avoid.
trivia: Its early working title was Invisible Monsters.
It was moderately successful in arcades.
Each maze opens with the start of the Dragnet theme.
Electronic Games called its two-player cooperation a "unique playing experience".
It appears in the 1983 film Joysticks.
devStory: Tom McHugh and Dave Nutting designed it at Dave Nutting Associates, and Midway released it on 5 June 1981, where it was moderately successful. An earlier prototype, Invisible Monsters, dated 1980, plays much like the final game but without speech; it surfaced on Craigslist around 2016. Home versions followed for the Bally Astrocade as The Incredible Wizard in 1982, which won Best Multi-Player Video Game at the Arkie Awards, the Atari 2600 and 5200 through CBS Electronics, and the Commodore 64.

title: Qix
description: Qix (1981) is Taito's abstract territory game, designed by Randy and Sandy Pfeiffer: draw lines to claim the screen while dodging the swirling Qix.
longDescription: The player's diamond-shaped marker moves along the edges of the playfield, and holding the Slow Draw or Fast Draw button extends a line, a Stix, into empty territory; closing off an area claims it and fills it with colour, with areas drawn entirely in Slow Draw worth double. The Qix, a tangle of moving lines that drifts at random rather than hunting the marker, costs a life if it touches an unfinished Stix. Stopping mid-line lights a fuse that burns towards the marker, and Sparx patrol the edges and completed lines, later mutating into Super Sparx that can chase along unfinished ones. Claiming 75% of the playfield, adjustable from 50% to 90%, wins a level, with a bonus for each percent above it. From level three there are two Qixes, and splitting them into separate regions ends the level and raises a scoring multiplier, up to nine.
trivia: It was the fifth-highest-grossing arcade game of 1981 in Japan.
Volfied (1989) was among its sequels, and imitators such as Gals Panic started a subgenre of uncovering a picture.
The attract mode calls a dead end that triggers the fuse a "Spiral Death Trap".
Den of Geek put it on its 2011 list of the ten most cloned video games.
Mario's desert outfit from the Game Boy version later became a costume in Super Mario Odyssey.
devStory: Husband and wife Randy and Sandy Pfeiffer designed it for Taito's American division, one of the few games that division made, and it came out in North America in October 1981 and in Japan that November. It was a commercial hit, and the fifth-highest-grossing arcade game of 1981 in Japan, but its popularity faded about a year later; Taito's Keith Egging said the concept was too mystifying. Ports followed on the Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit computers and Commodore 64, then the Amiga, Game Boy, NES and Lynx, and the Game Boy version has cameos by Mario, Luigi and Princess Peach.

title: Donkey Kong
description: Donkey Kong (1981) is Shigeru Miyamoto's first game for Nintendo, in which a carpenter called Jumpman — later Mario — climbs girders to rescue Pauline from a giant ape.
longDescription: Jumpman — later Mario — climbs a construction site to rescue Pauline while Donkey Kong hurls barrels and other hazards down at him. He jumps to dodge obstacles and cross gaps, climbs ladders, and can smash obstacles after picking up a hammer. Points come from dodging or destroying obstacles, collecting items and finishing stages quickly. The player starts with three lives, losing one on touching an obstacle or falling. The four stages — sloping girders, a conveyor-belt structure, elevators and rivets — each call for a different approach. Miyamoto put the emphasis on jumping and designed it as a multi-stage game told like a comic strip, which was uncommon for arcade games then; it is called one of the earliest platform games. Converted from about 2,000 unsold Radar Scope cabinets, it was the top-grossing US arcade game of 1982 and pulled Nintendo out of financial trouble.
trivia: The heroine was first called "Lady" before being renamed Pauline.
Universal sued, saying it infringed King Kong; Nintendo won, and its lawyer John Kirby is honoured in the name of the character Kirby.
The documentary The King of Kong (2007) followed Steve Wiebe and Billy Mitchell's high-score rivalry.
The Game & Watch version sold 8 million units and Coleco's cartridges 6 million.
It began as a Popeye game, until a licensing deal with King Features fell through.
devStory: After Radar Scope failed in 1980, Minoru Arakawa asked Nintendo president Hiroshi Yamauchi for a game that could reuse the unsold cabinets, and Miyamoto, a first-time designer, created Donkey Kong under Gunpei Yokoi's supervision. The original idea used Popeye characters, but a licensing deal with King Features fell through, so Bluto became a gorilla, Popeye became Mario and Olive Oyl became Pauline. Miyamoto cited Beauty and the Beast and the 1933 King Kong as influences, and the name was meant to suggest a stubborn gorilla. Four programmers from Ikegami Tsushinki spent three months turning his design into a finished game, and Yukio Kaneoka composed the music. It was released in July 1981, though the team had been told it would fail.

title: Frogger
description: Frogger (1981) is Konami's arcade game of guiding frogs across a busy road and a river of logs and turtles to five homes at the top of the screen.
longDescription: With a four-direction joystick, the player hops each frog one space at a time across a road of race cars, dune buggies, trucks and bulldozers, then over a river by riding logs, alligators and turtles moving in opposite directions, to reach one of five homes at the top. Riding off-screen, landing on diving turtles, snakes, otters or alligator jaws, jumping into an occupied home or the bush, or running out of the 30 seconds each frog has all cost a life. A fly in a home is worth 200 points, as is carrying a female frog home from a log; each forward step scores 10 points and filling all five homes 1,000. Filling them completes a level and raises the difficulty. The opening tune is the first verse of the Japanese children's song "Inu no Omawarisan", with "Yankee Doodle" added in the American release.
trivia: Sega/Gremlin's US cabinets earned $135 million.
Home versions had sold 20 million copies worldwide by 2005.
The 1998 Seinfeld episode "The Frogger" features the machine and George's old high score.
A 1982 Softline article called it "the arcade game with the most ways to die".
Michael Smith's 1,404,570 points, scored on 21 September 2024, is the record.
devStory: Konami developed it, with Takeshi Hara directing, Takahide Harima designing and Keiichi Miyoshi programming, and on 22 July 1981 Sega gained exclusive worldwide manufacturing rights. It came out in Japan in August 1981 and North America in September. Sega/Gremlin doubted it would sell there, but Elizabeth Falconer found it in Gremlin's library and pushed for licensing; the company paid Konami $3,500 a day for a 60-day window, and distributors signed up after a prototype was playtested in a San Diego bar. It earned over $135 million in US cabinet sales, Sega/Gremlin's most successful release, and Parker Brothers sold 4 million Atari 2600 cartridges by the end of 1982.

title: Ultima I
description: Ultima I (1981) is Richard Garriott's Apple II role-playing game, the first commercial Ultima, mixing dungeon crawling with a trip into space.
longDescription: Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness is set in Sosaria, whose four continents are each ruled by two of eight lords. The overworld is seen from above and the dungeons in first person. Each continent has two castles offering quests: one kind sends the player to a place on the map for a stat boost, the other to kill a particular monster in a dungeon for an item needed in the endgame. Characters are Human, Elf, Dwarf or Bobbit, and fighter, cleric, wizard or thief, with points spread across statistics such as Strength and Charisma; food runs down every two steps outside towns, and each level takes 1,000 experience points. Spells are bought in shops and used once. A first-person space section asks for 20 enemy ships to be destroyed, and a time machine, powered by four lords' gems, carries the player back to kill the wizard Mondain before he creates his Gem of Immortality.
trivia: The game includes a first-person space section where the player shoots down enemy ships.
Ken W. Arnold co-developed it, and it introduced the characters Iolo and Shamino.
It sold about 20,000 copies by mid-1982 and about 50,000 in all; Origin re-coded it in assembly language in 1986.
Its working title was Ultimatum.
It has been described as the first open-world computer game.
devStory: Richard Garriott began it after the unexpected success of Akalabeth, reusing much of that game's code for the dungeons and adding towns, quests, a plot and Star Wars touches such as spaceships and lightsabers. He made it in his freshman year at the University of Texas with his friend Ken W. Arnold, who wrote the assembly code for its tile graphics, in under a year and in Applesoft BASIC. The working title, Ultimatum, was shortened because a board game company already used it. California Pacific Computer Company released it for the Apple II in June 1981, and Origin re-coded it in assembly language in 1986.

sources.title: Ultima I: The First Age of Darkness

title: Stargate
description: Stargate (1981) is the sequel to Defender, adding an invisibility cloak and a warp gate to Williams' demanding side-scrolling shooter.
longDescription: Stargate keeps Defender's wraparound, mountainous planet, its scanner and its humanoids, which Landers try to capture and fuse with into Mutants, and adds a new button: Inviso, which makes the ship invisible and destroys any ship it touches, while its energy lasts. The controls are a joystick for up and down plus buttons for reverse, thrust, fire, smart bomb, Inviso and hyperspace. The enemies grow to include Baiters, Bombers, Pods, Swarmers, Firebombers, Yllabian Space Guppies, Phreds, Big Reds, Munchies and Dynamos. Flying into the Stargate teleports the ship to a humanoid being captured or falling, or to the far side of the planet, and carrying at least four humanoids into it warps the player ahead three levels during the first ten. Ten humanoids start on the planet, which is restored every five waves. Special stages, the Yllabian Dogfight and the Firebomber Showdown, arrive at waves 5 and 10 and recur every ten waves.
trivia: Some home versions were renamed Defender II for legal reasons, so Williams could secure the Defender trademark.
It was the first of only three games by Vid Kidz, the studio Jarvis and DeMar formed.
GamesMaster ranked it 82nd in its 1996 list of the best games.
A cabinet appears in the NewsRadio episode "Arcade", where Eugene Jarvis has a cameo.
Once the score reaches 9,990,000, every enemy destroyed awards an extra life, smart bomb and Inviso energy.
devStory: Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar designed it at their own studio, Vid Kidz, and Williams released it in October 1981 as the sequel to Defender, which had come out earlier that year. Atarisoft published ports for the Apple II, Commodore 64 and IBM PC, and Atari the Atari 2600 version in 1984; HAL Laboratory made the NES version, released in Japan in 1987, and Jeff Minter the Amiga and Atari ST ports of 1990.

title: Wizardry
description: Wizardry (1981) is Sir-Tech's first-person party dungeon crawler for the Apple II, whose rules later shaped Japanese RPGs such as Dragon Quest.
longDescription: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord has players build a party of up to six characters from five races — Human, Elf, Dwarf, Gnome and Hobbit — and three alignments, Good, Neutral and Evil, with good and evil characters normally unable to share a party. They start in four basic classes, Fighter, Priest, Mage and Thief, and can later reach the elite Bishop, Samurai, Lord and Ninja. The party descends a ten-level maze beneath Trebor's castle, seen in first person, to defeat the arch-wizard Werdna on the bottom level and retrieve his amulet. Each level is a 20×20 grid with no automap, so players map it on the graph paper included in the box, while darkness squares and teleport traps make that harder. Combat pits the party against one to four groups of monsters, shown as a picture in place of the maze, and spellcasters learn spells from seven tiers. Progress can only be saved outside the dungeon, and if a whole party dies, a new one must go down to recover the bodies and their gear.
trivia: It sold 24,000 copies by mid-1982 and 200,000 in its first three years.
Together with Ultima, it inspired Japanese RPG series such as Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy, and it became popular in Japan on computers like the PC-8801.
A beta version was shown at the 1980 Boston Computer Convention.
Werdna and Trebor are the designers' first names spelled backwards.
Computer Gaming World readers rated it the top adventure for five years, until Ultima IV replaced it in 1986.
devStory: Andrew Greenberg began it in 1978 as a Cornell University student and developed it with Robert Woodhead, drawing on the 1977 PLATO game Oubliette; it was playable by fall 1979. First written in Applesoft BASIC, it was rewritten in UCSD Pascal because BASIC was too slow, and publication waited for a run-time system that arrived in early 1981. Development took two and a half man-years, almost one of them spent on playtesting and balancing. Norman Sirotek, who founded Sir-Tech in 1980, showed a beta at that year's Boston Computer Convention, and Sir-Tech released it for the Apple II in September 1981. It was the most popular Apple II game of 1981 and had sold well over 500,000 copies by 1989.

sources.title: Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord

title: Tron
description: Tron (1982) is Midway's arcade tie-in to the Disney film, four sub-games in one — including the light cycles that inspired countless snake games.
longDescription: Tron gathers four short games, each drawn from the film: light cycle duels in which trails become walls, a tank battle, a fight against grid bugs, and a run at the I/O Tower through a shield of spinning blocks. Players choose the order and must clear all four to advance. Built to launch alongside Disney's 1982 film, it was one of the first major movie tie-in arcade games and one of the best-selling cabinets of its year.
trivia: Tron was a four-in-one game — players cycled through four distinct mini-games, each tied to a scene from the film.
The light cycle section became the most iconic, inspiring dozens of snake-style games in its wake.
It was one of the first major film tie-in arcade games, establishing the pattern of synchronising game and film releases.
The game used synthesised dialogue from the film, creating an immersive connection to the movie unusual for its era.
devStory: Tron was developed by Midway in 1982 to tie in with Disney's film of the same name. The game was designed by Bill Adams and comprised four sub-games: a light cycle race, a tank battle, a grid bug shooter, and an I/O Tower level. It was one of the first major licensed games and one of the first to use speech synthesis matched to a film property. Tron became one of the best-selling arcade games of 1982.

title: Robotron: 2084
description: Robotron: 2084 (1982) is Williams' frantic arena shooter, the game that introduced twin-stick controls: one stick to move, one to fire.
longDescription: Robotron drops the player into a single screen swarming with robots, with one joystick for movement and a second for shooting in any direction — the layout every later twin-stick shooter inherits. Each wave also scatters members of 'the last human family' across the arena to rescue for escalating bonuses. Designed by Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar, it is deliberately overwhelming, and remains one of the most intense games of the golden age.
trivia: Robotron introduced the twin-stick shooter control scheme: one joystick moves, the other aims independently — a format used by Geometry Wars, Halo, and countless modern games.
The game is deliberately overwhelming — the screen fills with hundreds of enemies and the player cannot win, only delay defeat.
Jarvis designed the twin-stick layout after a hand injury forced him to think about both hands having equal roles.
The instruction to save the "last human family" gave the chaos a moral dimension — players felt guilt when the family was killed.
devStory: Robotron: 2084 was designed by Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar at Williams Electronics in 1982. Jarvis designed the twin-stick control scheme — one stick for movement, one for aiming — after suffering a hand injury and wanting to create a game where both hands were equally engaged. The game's frantic pace and the directive to save human survivors added moral weight to the shooting. It remains one of the most intense arcade games ever made.

title: Joust
description: Joust (1982) is Williams' flapping-combat game: ride an ostrich, flap to gain height and strike enemy riders from above to unseat them.
longDescription: In Joust a knight on an ostrich battles buzzard-riding enemies across floating platforms; in any collision, the higher lance wins. Unseated enemies leave eggs that hatch into tougher foes if not collected in time, and an indestructible pterodactyl hunts players who linger. A second player rides a stork, and the two can work together or knock each other off. John Newcomer's flap-based physics make it one of the most skill-driven games of its era.
trivia: The physics system required players to flap the button to gain altitude — whoever was higher in a collision won, creating a genuinely skill-based mechanic.
Joust's two-player mode was co-operative but friendly fire was always on — accidental kills were common, and deliberate betrayal was possible.
The Buzzard Riders regenerated as faster pterodactyls if their eggs weren't collected quickly — time pressure was constant.
A pterodactyl could occasionally appear and was indestructible, forcing players to avoid rather than fight it.
Joust was ported to the NES and Atari 2600, with both versions being notable for faithfully capturing the original's feel.
devStory: Joust was designed by John Newcomer at Williams Electronics in 1982. The concept of a knight riding an ostrich and jousting against buzzard-mounted enemies was entirely original. The physics — flapping to gain altitude, collisions decided by height — required genuine skill to master. Joust also featured a co-operative two-player mode where the second player rode a stork, but friendly fire was always enabled.

title: Moon Patrol
description: Moon Patrol (1982) is Irem's scrolling lunar buggy game, an early showcase of parallax scrolling: jump craters and shoot forward and upward at once.
longDescription: Moon Patrol puts the player in a six-wheeled buggy crossing the lunar surface, jumping craters and mines while firing ahead at rocks and upward at attacking craft. Layers of scenery scroll at different speeds behind the action, one of the earliest arcade uses of parallax scrolling to suggest depth. A progress bar tracks the buggy through lettered checkpoints, giving the run a clear structure. Irem developed it and Williams distributed it in North America.
trivia: Moon Patrol was one of the first arcade games to use parallax scrolling — background layers moving at different speeds to suggest depth, a technique used in countless side-scrollers since.
Players could fire both forward (at ground obstacles) and upward (at aircraft) simultaneously — requiring two-directional threat management.
A progress map at the bottom of the screen showed players exactly where they were in the level — an early HUD navigation element.
The game's checkpoint system divided levels into named sections, giving players a sense of structured progression unusual for 1982.
devStory: Moon Patrol was developed by Irem in 1982. It introduced two simultaneous scrolling axes — horizontal ground movement and a parallax background — making it one of the first games to use parallax scrolling to create depth. Players drove a lunar rover and could fire both forward and upward simultaneously. It was also one of the first games to display level progress with a map showing the player's position.

title: Pole Position
description: Pole Position (1982) is Namco's behind-the-car racer set at Fuji Speedway, with a qualifying lap before the race — the template for arcade driving games.
longDescription: Pole Position puts the camera behind the car on a recreation of Japan's Fuji Speedway. Players first run a qualifying lap to earn a grid position, then race against computer cars, with sprites that scale up as they approach to create convincing depth from 2D graphics. Released in North America by Atari, it was the highest-grossing arcade game in the US in 1983 and set the pattern for racing games that followed.
trivia: Pole Position was based on Fuji Speedway — one of the first arcade games to use a real-world circuit.
The behind-the-car perspective was new to racing games, creating a sense of speed and immersion that top-down games couldn't match.
A qualifying lap determined starting grid position — a faithful recreation of real Formula One procedure.
The game's sprite-scaling technique (enlarging car sprites as they approached) created convincing 3D depth using 2D graphics.
Pole Position was the highest-grossing arcade game in the US in 1983, beating Pac-Man and Donkey Kong.
devStory: Pole Position was developed by Namco in 1982 and brought genuine racing game immersion to arcades. Players drove in a third-person perspective behind the car — unprecedented in arcade racing. The game included a qualifying lap, a grid start, and an actual race against computer opponents on a real circuit (Fuji Speedway). It became one of the highest-grossing arcade games of 1982 and established the modern racing game template.

title: Time Pilot
description: Konami's 1982 shooter of aerial dogfights across the ages: your fighter flies through endlessly scrolling skies, and each stage moves forward in time to a new era of aircraft.
longDescription:
Time Pilot was developed and published by Konami for arcades in 1982, distributed in the United States by Centuri and in PAL regions by Atari. It was designed by Yoshiki Okamoto.

The player's jet stays at the centre of the screen while open sky scrolls in every direction around it, and enemy aircraft attack from all sides. Each level is set in a different period, from early biplanes through to more modern aircraft, giving the game its time-travel theme. Konami and Coleco released home versions for the Atari 2600, MSX and ColecoVision in 1983.
trivia: Okamoto designed Time Pilot against his employer's explicit instructions — he was supposed to be making a mahjong game.
The time travel mechanic — fighting enemies from WWI biplanes to UFOs across five historical eras — was a completely original concept.
Konami released the game despite their initial anger, and it became a hit that justified Okamoto's defiance.
The scrolling in all eight directions simultaneously was technically demanding for 1982 hardware.
devStory: Time Pilot was designed by Yoshiki Okamoto at Konami in 1982. The game was Okamoto's first — he had been assigned to design a mahjong game but instead secretly built Time Pilot. Konami was initially furious but released the game when they saw its quality. Okamoto moved to Capcom soon afterwards, where he designed 1942 and later produced Street Fighter II.

title: Dig Dug
description: Dig Dug (1982) is Namco's arcade digging game: tunnel through the earth and defeat monsters by pumping them up until they pop, or by dropping rocks.
longDescription: Dig Dug tunnels through layered soil, and the underground map is whatever the player carves out. His weapon is an air pump: harpoon a Pooka or a fire-breathing Fygar and pump until it bursts. Loosening a rock onto enemies below scores more, and crushing several at once pays escalating bonuses, so every round rewards planning. Namco published it with Atari in North America, and it became one of the company's most successful arcade games.
trivia: The pump mechanic — inflating enemies until they explode — was entirely original and has never been convincingly replicated in another game.
Fygar the dragon could breathe fire horizontally, but only if the player was on the same level — vertical positioning provided safety.
Dropping a rock on multiple enemies scored escalating bonus points — risk-reward planning was built into every level.
The underground map was entirely carved by the player — no two playthroughs looked the same.
devStory: Dig Dug was developed by Namco in 1982. The game mechanic — pumping enemies to inflate and pop them, or dropping rocks on them — was unique. The underground landscape the player carved out persisted through the level, creating a dynamic environment. Dig Dug became one of Namco's most successful arcade games.

title: Donkey Kong Jr.
description: Donkey Kong Jr. (1982) is Nintendo's sequel with the roles reversed: play as Donkey Kong's son, climbing vines to free his father from Mario.
longDescription: Donkey Kong Jr. flips the original's story — Donkey Kong is caged, and Mario is the captor. The son climbs vines and chains, moving faster with a hand on each, while dodging Snapjaws and birds and dropping fruit on enemies below. Designed under Shigeru Miyamoto, it is the only game in which Mario appears as the villain.
trivia: Donkey Kong Jr. is one of the only games where Mario is the villain — he has imprisoned Donkey Kong and must be defeated.
The vine-climbing mechanic required holding two vine controls to move faster — a genuinely innovative control design.
Like the original Donkey Kong, it has four distinct stages, each with its own layout and hazards.
Nintendo designed the game to counter the perception that Donkey Kong was a one-trick arcade hit.
devStory: Donkey Kong Jr. was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and released by Nintendo in 1982. For the first time in arcade history, the villain of the previous game — Donkey Kong — became the character to be rescued, while the hero of the original (Mario) became the antagonist. Miyamoto reversed the roles as a creative experiment. The game was also notable for requiring players to climb vines using both hands, a more nuanced control mechanic than the original's joystick.

title: Pengo
description: Pengo (1982) is Sega's puzzle-action maze game: a penguin pushes and slides ice blocks to crush the Sno-Bees that hunt him.
longDescription: Pengo, a penguin controlled with a four-way joystick and one button, pushes ice blocks to slide them across a maze, or crushes a block when something is behind it. The goal is to destroy every Sno-Bee by crushing it with a sliding block, by crushing the blocks that hold unhatched eggs, or by stunning it against a wall, which happens when Pengo pushes the wall it is touching, and then walking over it. Sno-Bees can crush blocks too, and new ones hatch to replace those destroyed. Each round has three diamond blocks that cannot be crushed; lining them up scores 10,000 points, or 5,000 if any touches a wall, and briefly stuns every Sno-Bee. After two minutes the remaining Sno-Bees turn into faster Blobs that head for a corner and escape, and finishing a round in under 60 seconds earns a time bonus. The 16 rounds are punctuated by intermission animations.
trivia: The first arcade version uses "Popcorn" as its theme music.
Lining up the three diamond blocks scores up to 10,000 points.
Zero magazine reported that Hudson Soft's Bomberman series borrowed gameplay from it.
It was Japan's fourth-highest-grossing arcade game of 1982.
A widescreen remake for up to eight players was location-tested in Japan from 2010.
devStory: Coreland developed it for Sega, with Nobuo Kodera, Tsutomu Iwane and Akira Nakakuma among its designers. It was released in Japan in September 1982, in North America that October and in Europe in December. The first arcade version used "Popcorn" as its theme, while a second version had original music. It was Japan's fourth-highest-grossing arcade game of 1982 and a commercial success for Sega in the US, with an estimated 2,000 cabinets sold. Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit and Atari 2600 versions followed in 1983 and 1984, and a Game Gear version in 1990.

title: BurgerTime
description: BurgerTime (1982) is Data East's arcade game of giant burgers: walk across buns, patties and lettuce to drop them onto plates while dodging living food.
longDescription: Chef Peter Pepper builds burgers by walking across each ingredient until it drops a level, eventually stacking complete burgers on the plates below. Mr. Hot Dog, Mr. Egg and Mr. Pickle chase him around the ladders and girders; a limited supply of pepper stuns them briefly, and dropping an ingredient on top of enemies — or while they ride it — scores big. Its absurd food theme made it one of the most recognisable and widely ported games of the early 1980s.
trivia: BurgerTime's enemies — Mr. Hot Dog, Mr. Egg, and Mr. Pickle — were the ingredients that chef Peter Pepper was using, rebelling against their own consumption.
The pepper weapon was limited — players had a finite supply, making each use a meaningful decision.
Walking over ingredient strips caused them to fall — timing drops to crush multiple enemies simultaneously was the core skill.
The game's food theme made it one of the most distinctive and recognisable arcade games of 1982.
devStory: BurgerTime was developed by Data East in 1982. Players controlled chef Peter Pepper who built burgers by walking over ingredients to drop them onto lower levels, while being chased by living food enemies. The game's absurdist food-based theme and the mechanic of using pepper spray as a weapon gave it a distinct personality. It was one of the most ported games of the early 1980s.

title: Mr. Do!
description: Mr. Do! (1982) is Universal's digging game: a clown tunnels through a garden, collects cherries and defeats monsters with a bouncing power ball.
longDescription: Mr. Do, a circus clown (a snowman in the original Japanese version), digs tunnels through the playfield, collecting cherries in groups of eight, with a bonus for clearing a group without pausing. Monsters called creeps chase him, and he fights back with a bouncing power ball, which must come back before it can be thrown again and takes longer to re-form each time, or by dropping apples on them; an apple that falls too far breaks, and a falling apple can crush Mr. Do too. Every 5,000 points, the highlighted letter of EXTRA enters as an Alphamonster, and collecting all five letters ends the level with a cut scene set to the Astro Boy theme and an extra life. Dropping an apple can reveal a diamond, which completes the level and awards a credit. A level also ends when all cherries are gone or all creeps destroyed.
trivia: In the original Japanese version, Mr. Do is a snowman.
The power ball was inspired by a Super Ball stuck on a roof near Universal's Japanese office.
It is considered the first arcade game released as a conversion kit.
Its sequels are Mr. Do's Castle (1983), Mr. Do's Wild Ride (1984) and Do! Run Run (1984).
Spelling EXTRA plays a cut scene set to the Astro Boy theme.
devStory: Kazutoshi Ueda created it at Universal, inspired by Namco's Dig Dug, released earlier in 1982; the power ball came from a Super Ball stuck on a roof near Universal's Japanese office. It came out in Japan in October 1982, distributed by Taito, and in North America in February 1983. About 30,000 arcade units sold in the US, and it was the best-selling conversion kit until 1984, topping RePlay's conversion kit chart for five months of 1983. Ueda later worked at Tecmo and co-founded Atlus.

title: Popeye
description: Popeye (1982) is Nintendo's arcade game of the cartoon sailor: catch Olive Oyl's falling hearts and notes while Bluto and the Sea Hag attack.
longDescription: Popeye climbs between the floors of each scene collecting the hearts, notes or letters Olive Oyl throws down before they sink into the sea, while Bluto chases him and the Sea Hag hurls bottles. A can of spinach briefly lets Popeye knock Bluto away. Nintendo had first wanted the Popeye licence for the game that became Donkey Kong; once it secured the rights, it built an arcade game around the characters. It was one of Nintendo's last major coin-ops before the Famicom took over the company's focus.
trivia: Donkey Kong was originally designed as a Popeye game — Miyamoto adapted the concept when the licence fell through, making Mario a substitute for Popeye.
The game arrived as Nintendo was preparing the Famicom, and a home version was one of the console's three launch titles in Japan in 1983.
Bluto throws objects at Popeye from above — a structure directly mirroring Donkey Kong's barrel-throwing.
Spinach cans temporarily made Popeye invincible and able to attack Bluto directly — matching the character's established cartoon behaviour.
devStory: Popeye was developed by Nintendo in 1982. Shigeru Miyamoto had originally pitched the Popeye licence for what became Donkey Kong, but could not secure it in time. When Nintendo finally got the licence, Miyamoto built the game around the same structural ideas. Its Famicom conversion was one of the console's launch titles in Japan.

title: Millipede
description: Millipede (1982) is Atari's sequel to Centipede, in which an elf archer defends a mushroom forest from a millipede, bees, earwigs, inchworms and other insects, using DDT bombs for big scores.
longDescription: Played with a trackball and a fire button that can be held for rapid fire, it puts an elf archer at the foot of a mushroom forest as a millipede winds down from the top, dropping a row and reversing whenever it hits an obstacle; shooting a body segment splits it, and the rear section grows a head of its own. The millipede is faster than Centipede's and its head harder to hit. Earwigs replace scorpions, bees replace fleas and take two shots, inchworms briefly slow every enemy when hit, ladybugs turn mushrooms into indestructible flowers, and dragonflies and mosquitoes drop mushrooms or shift them up a row. DDT bombs, up to four at a time, explode when shot and destroy everything in their cloud for triple points. Bonus waves replace the millipede with swarms worth up to 1,000 points each, and the mushrooms grow and vanish in a pattern like Conway's Game of Life.
trivia: Its DDT bombs destroy everything in their cloud, and enemies killed by them score triple.
Ladybugs turn mushrooms into flowers that cannot be destroyed.
The "ED" and "FXL" on its default high-score table stand for Ed Logg and Franz Lanzinger.
Players can start at an advanced level, depending on the previous player's score.
Donald Hayes scored a record 10,627,331 points in 2004.
devStory: Ed Logg designed it and programmed it with Mark Cerny, with music by Brad Fuller, and Atari released it in North America in November 1982; Cash Box ranked it America's fourth highest-grossing arcade game of 1983, behind Ms. Pac-Man, Pole Position and Dragon's Lair. Namco released it in Japan in 1984. Versions followed for the Atari 2600 and 8-bit computers in 1984, the Atari ST, the Famicom, made by HAL Laboratory in 1987, and the Game Boy, paired with Centipede, in 1995.

title: Sinistar
description: Williams Electronics' notoriously hard space shooter, famous for its giant talking skull-faced enemy and its digitised threats — "Beware, I live!"
longDescription:
Sinistar was developed and manufactured by Williams Electronics, and its arcade release came in 1983. It was made by a team of Sam Dicker, Jack Haeger, Noah Falstein, RJ Mical, Python Anghelo and Richard Witt.

The player pilots a small ship through open space, mining planetoids for crystals that can be turned into "Sinibombs" — the only weapon able to harm the Sinistar, a huge spacecraft with a menacing face that worker ships are steadily assembling. Once complete, it hunts the player while shouting digitised speech. That use of speech and its punishing difficulty are what the game is best remembered for.
trivia: "BEWARE, I LIVE!" — Sinistar's taunting speech was delivered in a deep, synthesised voice that players found genuinely intimidating.
Sinistar was built by worker ships in real time — if players didn't destroy workers fast enough, the boss completed construction sooner.
Players had to mine asteroids for crystals, then craft sinibombs — a resource-gathering loop inside an action game.
The game featured a zoom effect as Sinistar approached — the closer the boss, the more screen space it occupied.
"RUN, COWARD!" was another Sinistar voice line, equally memorable and panic-inducing.
devStory: Sinistar was designed by Sam Dicker, Jack Haeger, Noah Falstein, and RJ Mical at Williams Electronics in 1982. The game featured an enormous boss character — Sinistar — that players had to defeat using bombs collected by mining asteroids, while the boss was simultaneously being constructed by worker ships. The booming synthesised voice of Sinistar ("BEWARE, I LIVE!") became one of gaming's most memorable audio moments.

title: Xevious
description: Xevious (1982) is Namco's vertically scrolling shooter with separate air and ground weapons, hidden secrets and a world built out behind the scenes.
longDescription: Xevious flies the Solvalou fighter over forests, roads and alien bases, firing a zapper at aircraft and aiming bombs at ground targets through a sight ahead of the ship — two layers of threat to track at once. Bombing certain empty spots reveals hidden bonuses, one of the first secrets in an arcade game. Designer Masanobu Endoh wrote an extensive history for its world, most of which never appeared on screen. Atari released it in North America, and it later came to the Famicom.
trivia: Endoh created an entire mythology and history for the Xevious world, writing detailed backstory that was never shown in the game itself.
The split targeting system — one button for aircraft, one for ground targets — required two layers of simultaneous spatial awareness.
Hidden "Solvalou" symbols were embedded in the terrain, invisible until players bombed specific ground locations — one of gaming's earliest secrets.
Its 1984 Famicom conversion was a major hit in Japan, selling more than a million copies.
devStory: Xevious was designed by Masanobu Endoh at Namco and released in 1982. Endoh spent over a year developing an elaborate fictional world — Xevious — complete with its own history, mythology, and geography, most of which never appeared in the game. The split-plane shooting mechanic (gun for air targets, bomb for ground targets) was new. Endoh embedded hidden "Solvalou" symbols throughout the levels as a mystery for players to discover.

title: River Raid
description: River Raid (1982) is Carol Shaw's Atari 2600 shooter for Activision: fly up a river, destroying ships, helicopters and bridges while refuelling on the way.
longDescription: River Raid flies a jet up a vertically scrolling river, shooting tankers, helicopters, jets and bridges while avoiding the banks. Fuel runs down constantly and is replenished by flying over fuel depots — which can also be shot for points, a choice the player makes over and over. Carol Shaw generated the river with an algorithm rather than storing it, producing a long, varied course within the 2600's tiny memory. It was one of Activision's best-sellers and among the most acclaimed games on the system.
trivia: Carol Shaw was one of the first female professional game programmers — River Raid was her masterpiece and one of the best-reviewed 2600 games ever made.
The river was procedurally generated using a seed algorithm — each section was different but the game always remained playable.
Fuel management was core to the design — players had to weigh speed (reaching fuel depots faster) against caution (avoiding being shot).
River Raid was banned in West Germany for supposedly training children in military strategy and war skills.
Shaw programmed the 2600's limited hardware so efficiently that the game ran at a smooth framerate other developers struggled to achieve.
devStory: River Raid was programmed by Carol Shaw at Activision in 1982. Shaw was one of the very few women working as a game programmer in the early 1980s and had previously worked at Atari. She designed the procedurally generated river using a clever algorithm that produced different terrain every game while maintaining playable structure. River Raid was one of Activision's best-selling titles and demonstrated that procedural generation could create compelling replayable content.

title: Pitfall!
description: David Crane's 1982 Atari 2600 jungle adventure, in which Pitfall Harry swings on vines and dodges crocodiles hunting for treasure against a 20-minute clock.
longDescription:
Pitfall! was designed by David Crane and published by Activision for the Atari 2600 in 1982. The player guides Pitfall Harry through a jungle in search of treasure, with 20 minutes to collect as much as possible.

The jungle is full of hazards — pits, quicksand, rolling logs, crocodiles and scorpions — some costing points and others a life, and Harry jumps, climbs ladders and swings across gaps on vines. Its large world, smooth animation and run-and-jump design were remarkable for the 2600 and made it one of the most influential games on the console. It was later ported to the Atari 5200, Atari 8-bit computers, ColecoVision, Commodore 64 and MSX.
trivia: Crane hand-animated every frame of Pitfall Harry's movement to create fluid, expressive motion unusual for the Atari 2600.
The game had 255 screens connected in a loop — players could complete it left-to-right or take a shortcut through underground tunnels.
Pitfall! sold over 4 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of the entire Atari 2600 era.
The underground tunnels let players skip above-ground screens — finding the optimal route was a speedrunning puzzle built into the design.
As an Activision game, Pitfall! credited Crane by name — Activision had been founded by programmers who left Atari partly because it refused to credit them.
devStory: Pitfall! was designed by David Crane at Activision in 1982. Crane wrote the game in five and a half months and achieved a 16-bit-quality look on the Atari 2600 through expert hardware manipulation. Pitfall Harry was one of the first platformer protagonists with consistent visual personality — his animation was expressive and fluid. Pitfall! sold over 4 million copies, making it one of the best-selling games of the Atari era.

title: Gravitar
description: Atari's 1982 vector shooter of planets with gravity: the Asteroids-style rotate-and-thrust controls are fighting a constant pull, which made it one of the hardest games of its day.
longDescription:
Gravitar was developed and published by Atari for arcades in 1982. It uses the same rotate-and-thrust controls as Asteroids and Space Duel, but adds gravity: the player's ship is drawn towards planets and stars, so every move has to account for the pull.

The game became known above all for its difficulty. It was the first of more than twenty games that Mike Hally designed and produced for Atari; Rich Adam was its main programmer and Brad Chaboya designed the cabinet art. An Atari 2600 version, programmed by Dan Hitchens, followed in 1983.
trivia: Gravitar featured one of the most realistic gravity simulations in any arcade game — the pull from the central star was always present and had to be counteracted.
The game was so difficult that Atari created a "Novice" version by adding more fuel — even the easy mode was considered hard.
Cave walls were instant death — a single touch destroyed the ship regardless of speed.
The reactor explosion sequence, after successfully destroying a base's reactor, gave a brief respite of satisfaction before the next challenge.
devStory: Gravitar was developed by Atari in 1982. Players navigated a spacecraft with realistic physics through cave systems, rescuing humanoids and destroying reactors while managing both fuel and gravity from a central star. The game was notoriously difficult — the physics simulation was unforgiving and the cave walls were instant death. It was admired by programmers for its physics engine and by masochists for its difficulty.

title: Zaxxon
description: Zaxxon is a groundbreaking 1982 Sega arcade game that introduced the isometric perspective to arcade gaming, giving the shooter a three-dimensional feel years before 3D graphics became standard. Players pilot a spacecraft through a fortress filled with missiles, cannons, walls with altitude-gated gaps, and fighter planes, adjusting altitude with a shadow beneath the ship as the only depth reference. The game's isometric projection created a visual style unlike anything seen before in arcades, and its challenging altitude-based gameplay required a new kind of spatial thinking. Zaxxon was a major commercial success and its visual style influenced countless games that followed.
longDescription: Zaxxon was designed by Sega and was one of the first arcade games to use an isometric axonometric view — a technique that creates the illusion of 3D by rotating the viewpoint 45 degrees. The name 'Zaxxon' derives from 'axonometric.' The ship's altitude was shown by a shadow on the ground, requiring players to judge depth to navigate through wall gaps at precise heights. Players had to manage fuel by shooting fuel tanks throughout levels. Enemy fighters attacked in 3D space, requiring players to match their altitude to hit them. Coleco's ColecoVision port was a major selling point for that console. The game's technical innovation and visual distinctiveness made it a landmark in the history of game graphics, directly influencing the isometric perspective games that flourished throughout the 1980s.
trivia: Zaxxon was the first arcade game to use isometric perspective, creating the illusion of 3D space using a fixed diagonal viewpoint.
A shadow beneath the player's ship showed its altitude — essential information for navigating barriers that required flying at specific heights.
The name "Zaxxon" is derived from "axis" and "isometric" — coined by the game's marketing team.
Coleco's tabletop version of Zaxxon used a clever mirror trick to create a genuine 3D effect from a 2D screen.
devStory: Zaxxon was developed by Sega in 1982 and was the first arcade game to use isometric perspective — an angled overhead view suggesting three-dimensional space. The name came from a portmanteau of "axis" and "isometric." Designers had to solve novel problems: players needed to understand their altitude to avoid obstacles and hit targets accurately. A shadow under the ship showed its height relative to the ground.

title: Q*bert
description: Q*bert is a 1982 arcade game by Gottlieb in which a spherical, orange, long-nosed character hops around a pyramid of cubes from an isometric perspective, changing each cube's colour by landing on it while being pursued by various enemies. Players must change every cube to the target colour without being caught by Coily the snake, Slick and Sam who reverse colour changes, and other hazards. Q*bert's distinctive character design, gibberish speech bubbles when he falls off the pyramid, and challenging puzzle mechanics made it one of the most beloved games of the golden age of arcade gaming. It sold over 25,000 cabinets and became one of Gottlieb's biggest hits.
longDescription: Q*bert was designed by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee, who originally envisioned the character as '@!#?@!' (a placeholder name that became part of the game's identity). The pyramid of cubes created a three-dimensional puzzle challenge on a two-dimensional screen, with later levels requiring multiple hops on each cube to reach the target colour and introducing enemies that revert cubes already changed. Q*bert could hop off the edge of the pyramid and catch floating discs that teleported him back to the top — a mechanic that added both escape routes and strategic traps when players lured Coily off the edge with them. The character appeared on TV shows, lunch boxes, and countless licensed products. Q*bert was later included in the 2015 film Pixels and remains one of the most recognizable characters of the arcade era.
trivia: Q*bert's speech — "@!#?@!" — was synthesised dialogue; the character's curse words became a cultural touchstone of early gaming.
The "Coily" snake enemy homed in on Q*bert and could only be defeated by luring it off the pyramid onto a floating disc.
The colour-changing mechanic required covering every cube, with later rounds requiring cubes to be hopped multiple times.
Q*bert appeared on Saturday morning cartoons, lunchboxes, and T-shirts — one of the most heavily licensed characters of the early gaming era.
devStory: Q*bert was designed by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee at Gottlieb in 1982. Lee drew the character as a doodle and Davis built mechanics around it — changing pyramid cube colours by hopping on them. The gibberish speech (rendered as "@!#?@!" in cartoons and advertising) was synthesised dialogue that varied depending on the situation. Q*bert became an enormous cultural phenomenon and one of the most licensed game characters of the 1980s.

title: Mario Bros.
description: Mario Bros. (1983) is Nintendo's two-player arcade game set in the sewers: bump enemies from below to flip them, then kick them off the platform.
longDescription: Mario and Luigi work a series of sewer platforms as turtles, crabs and flies emerge from the pipes. Hitting a platform from underneath flips the enemy standing on it, and a quick kick finishes it off; the POW block shakes every platform at once. The two players can help each other or knock each other's enemies back to life. Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Gunpei Yokoi, it was the first game to name Luigi, and its turtles led to the Koopa Troopas of Super Mario Bros.
trivia: Mario Bros. was the first game to feature Luigi as a named character alongside Mario — establishing the sibling partnership that defines Nintendo's most beloved franchise.
Mario's profession changed from carpenter (Donkey Kong) to plumber here — the sewer setting made the occupation change logical.
The turtle enemies in Mario Bros. were the direct ancestors of the Koopa Troopas in Super Mario Bros.
The two-player mode allowed players to accidentally or deliberately knock each other off platforms — a source of both co-operation and rivalry.
devStory: Mario Bros. was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and released by Nintendo in 1983. It was the first game to name both Mario and his brother Luigi, establishing them as a pair. The plumber setting was introduced here — the action took place in a sewer. The co-operative/competitive mechanic where both players shared a screen and could interfere with each other was novel and made it a favourite for two-player sessions.

title: Star Wars
description: Star Wars (1983) is Atari's 3D colour vector arcade game, in which the player flies an X-wing through a dogfight, over the Death Star and down the trench.
longDescription: Each wave has three phases: fighting TIE fighters in space, flying over the Death Star's surface, and the trench run that ends with a torpedo into the exhaust port. The X-wing has six shields, and every collision costs one. The Death Star regenerates and each wave gets harder. Speech synthesis recreates lines from the film.
trivia: It began in 1981 as a project called Warp Speed before Atari licensed Star Wars.
A conversion kit turned the cabinet into its 1985 sequel, The Empire Strikes Back.
devStory: Mike Hally designed it, with programming by Greg Rivera and Norm Avellar and sound by Earl Vickers. Released in May 1983 in upright and cockpit cabinets, it was Atari's best-selling arcade game of the year, with 12,695 built.

title: Spy Hunter
description: Bally Midway's 1983 spy-car game, conceived as a James Bond tie-in: drive the gadget-laden Interceptor down an endless road, destroying enemy vehicles with an arsenal of weapons.
longDescription:
Spy Hunter was developed and published by Bally Midway for arcades in 1983. It drew on the James Bond films and had originally been intended to carry the Bond licence.

The player drives the "Interceptor", a heavily armed spy car, down a vertically scrolling road and must destroy enemy vehicles using onboard weapons while sparing civilian traffic. The cabinet came in both sit-down and upright versions, with the upright more common, and its controls were unusually elaborate: a steering yoke styled like an aircraft control with special-purpose buttons, a two-position gear stick and an accelerator pedal.
trivia: Spy Hunter used the Peter Gunn Theme by Henry Mancini — one of the first arcade games to license a recognisable music track.
A weaponised truck appeared periodically to resupply the player with new weapons — a unique mid-mission mechanic.
Hitting civilian vehicles cost points, adding a moral dimension to the driving action.
The boat sequences — triggered by driving into the water — used completely different vehicle mechanics from the car sections.
devStory: Spy Hunter was designed by Bally Midway in 1983, inspired by the James Bond film series. Players drove a sports car armed with machine guns, oil slicks, and smoke screens, protecting civilians while destroying enemy vehicles. The game used the Peter Gunn Theme as background music — one of the first games to license a recognisable pop music track.

title: Crystal Castles
description: Crystal Castles (1983) is Atari's trackball maze game: guide Bentley Bear through 3D-looking castles, collecting gems before the enemies do.
longDescription: Bentley Bear, steered with a trackball, collects gems scattered through castles drawn in a three-dimensional projection, with ramps, stairs and hidden passages; collecting the last gem on a board earns a bonus, and honeypots appear for extra points. Bentley can jump to avoid obstacles. Some enemies eat gems, trees chase him by the quickest path and can be stunned by jumping over them, and a Gem Eater can be defeated by running into it while a gem is rising through its body. Each level has four waves, the fourth featuring Berthilda the Witch, who can only be beaten after Bentley picks up the magic hat in the maze; otherwise the hat makes him briefly invincible. Warps lead to higher levels. Unusually for its time, the game has a proper ending: a congratulatory message, a ranking by lives remaining and a bonus for speed of play.
trivia: Bentley Bear was originally called Bear Braveheart.
Its warps predate those in Super Mario Bros. (1985).
It is among the earliest arcade games with a distinct ending.
It won a Certificate of Merit at the 1985 Arkie Awards.
Lanzinger later left Atari over a dispute about residuals for home conversions.
devStory: Franz Lanzinger programmed it and wrote all of its code, his first game at Atari, with Barbara Singh creating most of the moving objects and Dave Ralston helping design some of the more complicated mazes; the game first had 12 mazes. Lanzinger chose the trackball because he liked Centipede and Millipede, and kept it despite management encouraging a joystick, and he spent $2,000 playing arcade games as research. The hero was first named Bear Braveheart, until marketing changed it and an engineering competition picked Bentley. Atari released it on 8 July 1983, and an Atari 2600 version followed in March 1984.

title: Lode Runner
description: Lode Runner (1983) is Douglas E. Smith's puzzle platformer for Broderbund: dig temporary holes to trap guards and collect all the gold, with 150 levels and an editor.
longDescription: Lode Runner's hero cannot fight. He collects gold across a screen of bricks, ladders and ropes, digging holes that trap pursuing guards before the bricks refill; once all the gold is taken, an escape ladder appears. The guards follow predictable rules, so skilled players steer them precisely. Douglas E. Smith built 150 levels and shipped the level editor he used to make them, one of the first commercial games to let players design their own stages. It was ported to many platforms.
trivia: Lode Runner included a level editor, making it one of the first commercial games with built-in tools for user-created content.
Smith designed all 150 levels himself over many months, testing each for difficulty and flow.
The enemy AI followed a specific hierarchical pathfinding algorithm — knowledgeable players could manipulate enemy movement precisely.
The game was ported to over 20 platforms, making it one of the most-ported games of the early computing era.
A sequel, Championship Lode Runner, featured only the hardest levels, aimed at players who found the original too easy.
devStory: Lode Runner was designed by Douglas E. Smith in 1983. Smith created the game on an Apple II and sold it to Broderbund after demonstrating it at a computer show. The mechanic of digging temporary holes to trap enemies — rather than shooting them — was original. Smith also included a level editor, making Lode Runner one of the first commercial games with user-created content tools. Over 150 levels were included, plus infinite custom ones.

title: M.U.L.E.
description: M.U.L.E. (1983) is a four-player economic strategy game by Dan Bunten Berry: settle a planet, farm resources and trade in real-time auctions.
longDescription: In M.U.L.E. four colonists claim plots on the planet Irata and outfit their robotic M.U.L.E.s to produce food, energy and smithore. Every turn ends with a real-time auction in which players physically walk their buyers and sellers towards a price, so supply and demand — and bluffing — decide the market. Designed by Dan Bunten Berry at Ozark Softscape and published by Electronic Arts, it was built to be played together around one screen and is often named among the greatest games ever made.
trivia: M.U.L.E. was designed by Dan Bunten Berry, who later transitioned and reflected on her game designs from a new perspective — calling M.U.L.E. her masterpiece.
All four players played simultaneously, with decisions made in parallel — real-time negotiation and betrayal were built into the structure.
The game simulated a complete economy: supply and demand affected prices dynamically based on player actions.
Berry designed the game to be played at a party, around a TV, with friends — social gaming as a deliberate design goal in 1983.
M.U.L.E. appeared on multiple "greatest games ever made" lists decades after its release, particularly praised by game designers.
devStory: M.U.L.E. was designed by Dan Bunten Berry (then credited as Dan Bunten) at Electronic Arts in 1983. Berry designed the game specifically around social interaction — four players simultaneously bid, trade, and compete in real time. Berry later said it was their favourite of all their games, and in interviews after transitioning in the 1990s, expressed regret that her pioneering multiplayer designs had not received more recognition. M.U.L.E. is considered one of the greatest games ever made.

title: Track & Field
description: Track & Field (1983) is Konami's Olympic arcade game of six events, won by hammering run buttons as fast as possible — hard on fingers and machines alike.
longDescription: Track & Field covers the 100m dash, long jump, javelin, 110m hurdles, hammer throw and high jump. Speed comes from alternately hammering two run buttons, while a third button handles the jump or throw at the right moment and angle, and each event has a qualifying mark to beat.
