longDescription: Sonic the Hedgehog was developed by Sonic Team — Yuji Naka on programming, Naoto Ohshima on character and world design, Hirokazu Yasuhara on level design. The character emerged from a design brief requiring a mascot that communicated attitude and speed. Naka's momentum physics engine — in which Sonic's speed built and carried through curved surfaces using trigonometric angle tracking — was the technical achievement that made the game's feel unique. The game was bundled with the Genesis from 1991, replacing Altered Beast as the pack-in, and sold over 15 million copies.
trivia: Sonic's speed was designed to showcase the Genesis's hardware scrolling capability — the fast horizontal scrolling was a deliberate competitive demonstration against the SNES.
Yuji Naka wrote the Sonic engine in 68000 assembly language and optimised it to run at a locked 60 frames per second.
The iconic Green Hill Zone music was composed by Masato Nakamura, bassist for Japanese pop group Dreams Come True.
Early Sonic designs included a human girlfriend character and a band; Naoto Ohshima's final hedgehog design was chosen after multiple character concepts were rejected.
devStory: Sonic the Hedgehog was developed by a team of approximately fifteen people at Sega over approximately ten months. Yuji Naka led programming, Naoto Ohshima led character and art design, and Hirokazu Yasuhara designed the levels. The game launched in Japan in July 1991 and became the Genesis's defining title.

title: Streets of Rage
description: Streets of Rage was Sega's beat 'em up for the Genesis — three playable characters, responsive combat, and a celebrated Yuzo Koshiro soundtrack that applied house and techno music to a video game for the first time. The game established a franchise and demonstrated what Genesis hardware could produce in the genre.
longDescription: Streets of Rage was developed internally at Sega as a response to Capcom's Final Fight, which had arrived on SNES but not Genesis. The game's music — composed by Yuzo Koshiro using FM synthesis to produce house and techno tracks — was technically remarkable for 1991 game music and remains one of the most distinctive soundtracks of the era. The three characters — Axel, Blaze, and Adam — had different speed and power characteristics that made character selection a meaningful choice.
trivia: Streets of Rage's soundtrack by Yuzo Koshiro applied house and techno music production techniques to FM synthesis, producing music that contemporary DJs played in clubs without knowing it was from a video game.
The game includes a special police attack — calling in a police car that fires a rocket at all enemies on screen — that could be used once per level.
Streets of Rage was released on Genesis because Sega couldn't port Final Fight, which had launched as a SNES exclusive.
Yuzo Koshiro composed the Streets of Rage soundtrack using a custom music sequencer he had written himself.
devStory: Streets of Rage was developed by Sega's internal development team as a direct competitor to Capcom's Final Fight. The game launched in Japan in August 1991. Yuzo Koshiro's music became the game's most celebrated element.

title: Sonic the Hedgehog 2
description: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 introduced Tails — a two-tailed fox who followed Sonic and could be controlled by a second player — and the spin dash, a move that allowed Sonic to accelerate from a standstill. The game outsold its predecessor and introduced the Emerald Hill Zone aesthetic that remained the franchise's visual identity for years.
longDescription: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was co-developed between Sonic Team in Japan and Sega Technical Institute in San Francisco. The spin dash — spinning in place to build speed before launching — addressed a design problem in the first game: the need to run to build speed before slopes. The game introduced the two-player competitive mode and the Super Sonic transformation achieved by collecting all seven Chaos Emeralds.
trivia: 'Sonic 2sday' — the November 24, 1992 simultaneous worldwide release — was one of the first coordinated global game launches.
Several levels were cut from Sonic 2 during development, including Hidden Palace Zone, which was restored in the 2013 remaster based on remnant code found in the original cartridge.
Tails was designed by an artist who won an internal Sega design competition — the character's full name, Miles 'Tails' Prower, is a pun on 'miles per hour.'
Sonic 2 introduced the Super Sonic transformation as a reference to Dragon Ball Z's Super Saiyan form, complete with golden palette swap and invincibility.
devStory: Sonic the Hedgehog 2 was developed jointly by Sonic Team in Japan and Sega Technical Institute in the United States under significant deadline pressure. The collaborative arrangement was contentious but produced a game that outsold the original.

title: Streets of Rage 2
description: Streets of Rage 2 (1992) is Ancient's Mega Drive beat 'em up, in which Axel, Blaze, Max and Skate fight through Wood Oak City to rescue Adam from Mr. X, scored by Yuzo Koshiro.
longDescription: A year after the first game, Mr. X and the Syndicate return for revenge. Skate comes home to find his house wrecked and his brother Adam missing, with a photo of Adam chained at Mr. X's feet, and Axel and Blaze set out to rescue him, joined by Skate and the wrestler Max, as crime spreads through Wood Oak City. One or two players fight waves of enemies and pick up weapons and items. Max is slow but powerful, and Skate, Adam's younger brother, gets around on rollerblades. Standard attacks were expanded from the first game, each character has a Blitz Attack performed by double-tapping a direction, and Special Attacks, which cost health but hit enemies on all sides, replace the first game's police car. A Duel mode lets two players fight each other. The trail ends on Mr. X's island, against him and his bodyguard Shiva.
trivia: In Japan it is Bare Knuckle II, and Skate is called Sammy.
Sega Force said it was the first 2 MB cartridge on the Mega Drive.
Yuzo Koshiro was invited to DJ its music in nightclubs.
Mr. X's cigar was removed outside Japan.
M2's 3D Streets of Rage 2 for the 3DS added a Rage Relay mode and stereoscopic 3D.
devStory:
Ayano Koshiro was the lead graphic designer, designing the graphics, characters and combat, and Yuzo Koshiro wrote most of the music, with three tracks by Motohiro Kawashima; the team was inspired by Street Fighter II, which had a cabinet in Ancient's office. Yuzo composed on a PC-8801 in his own music language, drawing on house, techno and breakbeat, and critics called the soundtrack "revolutionary". Sega released it in North America in 1992 and in Japan in January 1993 as Bare Knuckle II.

It was the top-selling Mega Drive game in Japan in January 1993 and entered the UK chart at number one. Computer and Video Games called it the finest scrolling arcade beat 'em up on any format, and GamePro the "side-scrolling street fighter to beat".

title: Gunstar Heroes
description: Gunstar Heroes was the debut game from Treasure — a studio founded by ex-Konami developers — and demonstrated technical ambitions the Genesis had not previously been pushed to achieve. A run-and-gun with combinable weapon types, enormous bosses, and combat that filled the screen with projectiles and enemies, it established Treasure's reputation for hardware-pushing action design.
longDescription: Gunstar Heroes was developed by Treasure, founded in 1992 by developers who had left Konami. The game pushed the Genesis hardware to display more simultaneous objects and projectiles than previous Genesis games had managed. The weapon combination system — four base weapons that could be combined into ten distinct weapon types — created varied play styles. The game's bosses, some occupying most of the screen, required different strategies for each encounter.
trivia: Treasure was founded by developers who had worked on Contra and other Konami games and wanted to create more technically ambitious action games than Konami's production process allowed.
Gunstar Heroes uses techniques Sega had marketed as a Genesis advantage — Treasure's game is one of the few that genuinely exploited them.
The dice game boss — a board game in which landing on certain squares triggers different bosses — was a self-contained game within the game.
Gunstar Heroes sold modestly on release but became a collector's item, with original cartridges selling for high prices decades later.
devStory: Gunstar Heroes was developed by Treasure in approximately one year as the studio's debut title. The small team of approximately ten developers, all ex-Konami, designed the game to showcase Genesis hardware capabilities they felt hadn't been fully exploited. Sega published the game in Japan in September 1993.

title: Shinobi III: Return of the Master Ninja
description: Shinobi III (1993) is Sega's Mega Drive ninja platformer, delayed a year so its gameplay and graphics could be reworked, and one of the system's most praised action games.
longDescription: Two years after its defeat, the crime syndicate Neo Zeed rises again under the Shadow Master. Joe Musashi senses its return and leaves his mountain home in Japan to face his old enemy. It is a hack-and-slash platformer that reviewers found faster than its predecessor and, Power Unlimited said, a little easier; MegaTech singled out its new attacks and moves. Mega thought it far too easy apart from its tricky bosses, while Complex called the last level "freaking impossible".
trivia: Previews showed levels and moves that never made the final game; a beta later leaked as a ROM.
In Japan it was called The Super Shinobi II.
Sega producer Yosuke Okunari called it the most refined 2D Shinobi game when M2 chose it for the Sega 3D Classics series.
Lizardcube said Shinobi: Art of Vengeance (2025) was directly inspired by it and The Revenge of Shinobi.
Retro Gamer included it in its top ten Mega Drive games.
devStory:
Tomoyuki Ito and Takeshi Matsuhashi directed it, Naohisa Nakazawa designed it, and Hirofumi Murasaki, Morihiko Akiyama and Masayuki Nagao composed the music. It was set for 1992, and previews in GamePro, Mean Machines and Computer and Video Games showed levels, enemies and moves that never made the final game; Sega delayed it to 1993 to improve the gameplay and visuals, cutting many features and adding new ones. It came out in Japan as The Super Shinobi II on 23 July 1993 and in the West that September.

MegaTech gave it 93% and a Hyper Game award, IGN's Levi Buchanan called it "a legit Genesis great", and Complex later ranked it the third-best Genesis game.

sources.title: Shinobi III: Return of the Ninja Master

title: Comix Zone
description: Comix Zone (1995) is Sega Technical Institute's Mega Drive beat 'em up set inside the panels of a comic book, in which artist Sketch Turner is trapped in his own creation by the villain Mortus.
longDescription: While Sketch Turner works on his comic during a thunderstorm, lightning strikes the page and frees its villain, the mutant Mortus, who sends Sketch into the comic, meaning to kill him and take his body. Inside a post-apocalyptic world of ruined New York, the Himalayas and the atolls of Zealand, Sketch joins General Alissa Cyan against Mortus. Every screen is a comic panel with speech balloons. Six pages in three episodes hold enemies or simple puzzles, sometimes with branching panels, and Sketch can use the art itself, tearing a page into a paper plane to attack. He carries up to three items, his pet rat Roadkill peels back parts of the page to reveal them, and iced tea is the only thing that restores health. Losing all health or falling into a pit ends the game unless a continue has been earned.
trivia: The game is notoriously hard: health items are rare, and punching through scenery to find a path drains Sketch's own health.
Sega of Japan reportedly called it a symbol of American culture's flaws; the team took it as a compliment.
It and The Ooze were the only games to carry the S.T.I. logo.
Morawiec later regretted following the testers' advice to make it harder.
A film adaptation was announced in 2022.
devStory:
Peter Morawiec conceived it after a trip to a comic shop in Palo Alto with Sega Technical Institute colleagues, taking the story from a-ha's "Take On Me" video, and pitched a demo, "Joe Pencil Trapped in the Comix Zone", in December 1992. It was delayed for Sonic Spinball, and work began in late 1993 with Morawiec, Adrian Stephens and Dean Lester. Marketing disliked Joe Pencil, who became the grunge-styled Sketch Turner, and asked for a sidekick, so Morawiec created Roadkill because a rat took up little screen space. Stephens fitted the game into 2 megabytes while decompressing large pages during play, and Howard Drossin wrote the rock soundtrack.

Sega released it in North America in July 1995, late in the Genesis's life, and it failed to break even, though it has since gained a cult following.

title: Super Mario Land
description: Super Mario Land (1989) is Nintendo R&D1's Game Boy launch platformer, in which Mario crosses the four kingdoms of Sarasaland to rescue Princess Daisy from Tatanga; it sold over 25 million copies.
longDescription: Mario travels to Sarasaland, not the Mushroom Kingdom, to rescue Princess Daisy, in her first appearance, from the alien Tatanga. The 12 levels span four worlds of three levels, against 32 in Super Mario Bros., and the screen scrolls only to the right. Two levels are scrolling shooters in which Mario pilots a submarine and a plane. He throws bouncing Superballs instead of fireballs, Koopa shells explode after a delay, hearts give extra lives, and enemies include sphinxes, seahorses and Moai heads. Instead of a flagpole, each level ends with a climb to an upper exit leading to a bonus game for extra lives or a Superball Flower. Finishing the game unlocks a harder mode with more enemies.
trivia: It introduced Princess Daisy.
Two of its levels are scrolling shooters, piloting a submarine and a plane.
Mario is just 12 pixels tall on the Game Boy screen.
Ambassadors of Funk's 1992 single "Supermarioland", which samples its music, reached the UK top ten.
It sold more than 25 million copies, the fourth best-selling Game Boy game.
devStory: Nintendo president Hiroshi Yamauchi wanted a fun Mario game to sell the Game Boy, and R&D1 began it in the second half of 1988, over six to nine months, with Gunpei Yokoi producing, Satoru Okada directing and Hirokazu Tanaka composing; it was the first mainline Mario not designed by Shigeru Miyamoto. It was meant as the Game Boy's showcase until Tetris was bundled instead. Launched with the system in Japan on 21 April 1989, it was North America's second best-selling release of 1989 after Tetris, and it went on to sell more than 25 million copies, outselling Super Mario Bros. 3. Computer and Video Games called it "an arcade machine in your pocket".

title: The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening
description: Link's Awakening was developed largely by junior Nintendo staff in their spare time and became one of the finest Zelda games. Set on a mysterious island rather than Hyrule, with no Ganon, no Triforce, and a story involving music and a sleeping whale deity, it was distinctly strange — and distinctly beloved. The island of Koholint was later revealed to be a dream.
longDescription: Link's Awakening began as an unofficial Game Boy port of A Link to the Past, developed by junior Nintendo staff member Takashi Tezuka outside official development time. When Nintendo management discovered the project and played it, they directed resources to complete it as an official release. The game's story — in which Link is trapped on an island that turns out to exist only as a dream — was unusually melancholy and sophisticated for a Game Boy game.
trivia: It began as an after-hours experiment to see whether A Link to the Past could work on the Game Boy, and grew into an official project.
Mario enemies — Goombas, Piranha Plants, a Chain Chomp — turn up in the game, fitting its dreamlike setting.
Link's Awakening was the first Zelda game in which Princess Zelda does not appear — she is not a character in the story at all.
The 2019 Nintendo Switch remake recreated the original with a toy-like art style and added a Chamber Dungeon mode for arranging dungeon rooms.
devStory: Link's Awakening grew out of an after-hours experiment on Game Boy hardware and was directed by Takashi Tezuka. The game launched in Japan in June 1993.

sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening

title: Kirby's Dream Land
description: Kirby's Dream Land introduced Kirby — a round, pink character with the ability to inhale enemies and use their air to fly — in a short, accessible Game Boy platformer. Designed intentionally to be beatable by players of any skill level, it was Masahiro Sakurai's first commercial design credit at age 19, establishing a franchise that continued for over thirty years.
longDescription: Kirby's Dream Land was designed by Masahiro Sakurai, who joined HAL Laboratory as a designer at 18. Sakurai's design philosophy was that games should be accessible to players without extensive gaming experience. Kirby's ability to float indefinitely was designed to ensure that no player would fail from a missed jump. The game was explicitly designed to be short and completable, with a harder extra mode for experienced players.
trivia: Masahiro Sakurai designed Kirby's Dream Land at age 19 while a full-time HAL Laboratory employee, creating the game in approximately one year.
Kirby was named after John Kirby, the Nintendo of America lawyer who successfully defended Nintendo in the Donkey Kong copyright lawsuit against Universal Studios.
The game was intentionally short — approximately 30 minutes to complete — with a harder 'Extra Game' mode offering significantly more challenge.
Sakurai always imagined Kirby as pink, while Miyamoto thought he should be yellow — and since the Game Boy was monochrome, the American box art showed him white.
devStory: Kirby's Dream Land was designed by Masahiro Sakurai, then 19, at HAL Laboratory. Sakurai designed it deliberately for beginners, as a game almost anyone could finish. The game launched in Japan in April 1992.

title: Pokémon Red and Blue
description: Pokémon Red and Blue launched the highest-grossing entertainment franchise in history. Players captured, trained, and battled creatures called Pokémon across two versions with slight differences in available species, requiring trading between versions to complete the 151-creature Pokédex. The Game Boy Link Cable was built into the game's design from the beginning.
longDescription: Pokémon was designed by Satoshi Tajiri and developed over six years at Game Freak. Tajiri's concept — creatures that could be captured and traded between Game Boys via the Link Cable — was inspired by his childhood insect collecting in rural Japan. The version duality — Red and Blue with different exclusive Pokémon — made the Link Cable essential for completionists. The game launched in Japan in February 1996 and in North America in September 1998, simultaneously with the anime series.
trivia: Pokémon's six-year development nearly bankrupted Game Freak — the team worked without salaries for extended periods and some members took outside work to survive.
The version duality — Red versus Blue — was intentional from the beginning of design: Tajiri's concept required trading to be necessary for completion, not optional.
MissingNo — a glitch Pokémon that appeared through a specific sequence of actions — became one of gaming's most famous bugs, immortalised in player folklore.
Ken Sugimori finalised the artwork for all 151 Pokémon, working from designs by a small team of artists including Atsuko Nishida and Motofumi Fujiwara.
devStory: Pokémon was designed by Satoshi Tajiri and developed by Game Freak over six years. Shigeru Miyamoto acted as a mentor to the project during its long development. The game launched in Japan in February 1996.

title: Civilization
description: Sid Meier's Civilization put players in command of a civilisation from 4000 BC through the space age, making decisions about city building, research, diplomacy, and war. The game's turn-based structure and historical scope created a 'one more turn' engagement that players reported losing entire nights to. It defined the 4X strategy genre: eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate.
longDescription: Civilization was designed by Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley at MicroProse. The game synthesised board game mechanics with computer-managed complexity — hundreds of variables tracking each civilisation's development simultaneously. The technology tree — a branching research path from the wheel through nuclear fission — communicated historical progression while creating strategic choices about which technological paths to prioritise.
trivia: Sid Meier has described Civilization as a game that 'simulates the history of the world' — a description he was initially reluctant to make for fear of overstating its accuracy.
The legend that a programming bug made Gandhi obsessed with nuclear weapons is a myth — Sid Meier and Brian Reynolds have both said it never happened in the original game.
Civilization was inspired partly by Francis Tresham's board game Civilisation, though the computer game expanded far beyond the board game's scope.

The 'one more turn' phenomenon — players intending to stop playing but continuing indefinitely — was documented in player reports from Civilization's first release and became a standard description of the genre's engagement mechanism.
devStory: Civilization was designed by Sid Meier and Bruce Shelley at MicroProse. Meier had previously designed Covert Action, which he felt had failed commercially; Civilization was his attempt to build a historical strategy game with broader appeal. The game launched in September 1991.

title: Doom
description: Doom (1993) is id Software's first-person shooter, in which a space marine fights from the moons of Mars into hell; released as shareware, it named the deathmatch and was modded for decades.
longDescription: An unnamed marine, posted to Mars after assaulting a superior who ordered his unit to fire on civilians, answers a call for help from a Union Aerospace Corporation base on Phobos, where secret teleportation experiments have gone wrong; his team is wiped out, and he goes in with only a pistol. The three episodes, of eight levels each, run from the bases of Phobos and Deimos into hell itself, ending against two Barons of Hell, a cyberdemon and a cybernetic spider-demon. Each level ends at a marked exit, and players manage health, armour and ammunition for weapons from the shotgun and chainsaw to the plasma rifle and BFG 9000, among toxic pits, crushing ceilings and keycard doors. Two to four players can play co-operatively or in deathmatch.
trivia: The BFG 9000's initials famously stand for a profane 'Big F— Gun'; the manual offered the politer 'Big Freaking Gun'.
Romero coined the term "deathmatch", and Kevin Cloud "fragging".
Its working title was Green and Pissed.
Some demons were clay models and latex sculptures, photographed and digitised into sprites.
The Library of Congress chose it in 2007 as one of ten games for preservation.
devStory:
id began it in 1992 as a darker game of fighting demons with technology, built on a new engine by John Carmack and inspired by Evil Dead II, Aliens and the team's Dungeons & Dragons campaign; Carmack took the name from a line in The Color of Money. Tom Hall's story-heavy "Doom Bible" was rejected, and he was replaced in September 1993 by Sandy Petersen, who designed levels alongside John Romero, while Adrian Carmack and Kevin Cloud did the art and Bobby Prince the music. The engine, written mostly in C on NeXT computers, stored levels in separate WAD files, which made modding easy.

The first episode went online at midnight on 10 December 1993, crashing the University of Wisconsin's network, and Doom sold 3.5 million copies by 1999, with an estimated 10 to 20 million people playing it within two years.

title: Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness
description: Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness (1995) is Blizzard's real-time strategy sequel, in which humans and orcs fight the Second War on land, at sea and in the air, with a map editor and eight-player multiplayer.
longDescription: After the fall of Azeroth, its survivors flee by sea to Lordaeron, and the orcs follow in the Second War; separate human and orc campaigns tell the story from each side, through Gul'dan's rebellion, the death of the Alliance commander Anduin Lothar at Blackrock Spire and the destruction of the Dark Portal. Players gather four resources — gold, wood, oil and food — build structures and units and research upgrades. Both sides have melee, ranged, naval and air units and spellcasters; shipyards build warships and oil tankers, which set up offshore platforms, and each farm feeds four units, often doubling as a defensive wall. Fog of war hides unexplored terrain and shows only what friendly units can see, with buildings left in their last-seen state, and units can be selected by clicking or dragging a box. Up to eight players can play together, and a map editor lets players build their own scenarios.
trivia: Its separate human and orc campaigns tell the Second War from both sides.
Clicking a unit repeatedly makes it respond with increasingly exasperated jokes — a gag carried over from the first Warcraft that became a Blizzard tradition.
It was the second best-selling computer game of 1996 in the US, behind Myst.
Next Generation ranked it tenth in its 1996 list of the top 100 games of all time.
It was remastered with Warcraft: Orcs & Humans in 2024.
devStory:
Blizzard began it in February 1995, after the response to Warcraft: Orcs & Humans, and released it in North America on 5 December 1995 through Davidson & Associates, with a Mac version in 1996. Early designs mixed modern and fantasy elements before the team kept to fantasy. The Beyond the Dark Portal expansion, first contracted to Cyberlore, was finished in-house in 1996.

It debuted at number two behind Myst, sold 500,000 copies within three months and passed 2 million by July 1998 and 3 million by 2001. PC Gamer US named it the best game of 1995, and Macworld wrote that it "set the standard for the genre". A Battle.net Edition followed in 1999, and its play and story shaped StarCraft.

title: Command and Conquer
description: Command and Conquer refined the real-time strategy template Westwood had established with Dune II. Two factions — the Global Defense Initiative and the Brotherhood of Nod — fought over Tiberium, an alien resource. Live-action FMV cutscenes between missions gave the game a cinematic register that competitors hadn't attempted.
longDescription: Command and Conquer was developed by Westwood Studios in approximately one year. The game's FMV cutscenes — filmed in Westwood's Las Vegas offices with studio employees as actors — were narratively effective, with Kane becoming one of the most memorable villains in gaming history. The game introduced online multiplayer through the Westwood Online service, predating Xbox Live by seven years. It sold over 3 million copies and established a franchise that continued for two decades.
trivia: Kane was played by Joseph Kucan, who was also directing the game's video sequences — he stepped in front of the camera himself.
The Tiberium resource — an alien mineral that spreads across the map — was designed to create strategic maps that changed over time.
Command and Conquer shipped on two CDs simultaneously containing the GDI and Nod campaigns — players could choose which faction's story to experience first.
devStory: Command and Conquer was developed by Westwood Studios in Las Vegas under producer Brett Sperry. The game was designed as a follow-up to Dune II with more polished production and a contemporary setting. The FMV sequences were shot in-house with a mix of actors and Westwood staff.

title: Quake
description: Quake was the first true 3D first-person shooter — where Doom had used 2D sprites in 3D spaces, Quake rendered everything in genuine 3D polygons. The engine supported full mouse-look, network multiplayer, and the competitive deathmatching that defined online PC gaming for years. The Nine Inch Nails soundtrack by Trent Reznor gave the game an atmosphere unlike any contemporary.
longDescription: Quake was developed by id Software following Doom's commercial success and represented a complete engine rewrite. John Carmack's Quake engine rendered environments and characters in genuine 3D polygons with a BSP tree and portal rendering system. The game's network code supported up to 16 players simultaneously over internet connections, creating the deathmatching culture that competitive gaming descended from. Trent Reznor of Nine Inch Nails provided the ambient soundtrack.
trivia: Quake's client–server networking — refined for internet play in QuakeWorld later in 1996 — set the template for online FPS netcode.
Deathmatch players borrowed 'frag' from military slang for a kill; the term was already used with Doom and became standard with Quake.
Trent Reznor and Nine Inch Nails created the game's ambient soundtrack and sound effects — the nail-gun ammunition boxes carry the NIN logo.
Quake shipped with a software renderer; GLQuake, released early in 1997, added support for 3D accelerator cards such as the 3dfx Voodoo.
devStory: Quake was developed by id Software over approximately two years following Doom's success. John Carmack led engine development while John Romero led level design — the increasing tension between their approaches contributed to Romero's departure from id Software shortly after the game's release. Quake shipped in June 1996.

title: Diablo
description: Diablo combined dungeon-crawling RPG structure with real-time action combat and procedurally generated levels. Players clicked to attack, clicked to move, and clicked to collect the randomised loot that enemies dropped — a game loop of kill, collect, and grow stronger that players sustained for hundreds of hours. Battle.net online play made the loot economy a community phenomenon.
longDescription: Diablo was developed by Condor Inc., which Blizzard acquired and renamed Blizzard North during development. The game's original design was turn-based; Blizzard shifted it to real-time action after playtesting. The loot randomisation system — items with random properties within defined parameter ranges — created the engagement loop that Diablo became known for. The game introduced the Tristram OST composed by Matt Uelmen, widely considered one of the finest game soundtracks of its era.
trivia: Diablo was originally designed as a turn-based game — the real-time action system was adopted after Blizzard playtested the turn-based version and found the real-time alternative more engaging.
The 'Cow Level' — a frequently requested secret level that Blizzard denied existed — was added as a real location in Diablo II as a response to persistent player requests.
The Tristram theme — Diablo's ambient guitar piece — became one of the most recognised pieces of game music in the 1990s.
Battle.net, Blizzard's free online service, launched alongside Diablo — one of the first major free online gaming services.
devStory: Diablo was developed by Condor Inc. in San Mateo, California, which Blizzard acquired partway through development and renamed Blizzard North. The game launched in December 1996 and sold over 2.5 million copies, establishing the action RPG subgenre.

title: StarCraft
description: StarCraft introduced three asymmetric factions — the human Terran, the insectoid Zerg, and the ancient Protoss — each with completely different units, buildings, and strategies. The balance between them was precise enough to sustain professional competitive play in South Korea for over a decade, where StarCraft became a national sport broadcast on dedicated television channels.
longDescription: StarCraft was initially received as a Warcraft reskin. Professional play in South Korea, where dedicated television channels broadcast matches and players achieved celebrity status, revealed that the game's asymmetric design was balanced precisely enough to sustain a competitive scene at a level no other game had achieved. The Korea e-Sports Association regulated professional play from 2000, with player contracts, team salaries, and league structures equivalent to conventional sports.
trivia: StarCraft's South Korean professional scene produced actions-per-minute rates of 300 or more from top players — a physical execution speed comparable to professional musicians.
The game was so popular in South Korea that it helped fuel the boom in PC bangs — internet cafes where people gathered to play.
StarCraft's three factions are completely asymmetric yet achieve competitive balance that has sustained tournament play for over two decades.
Brood War, the 1998 expansion, adjusted faction balance and became the definitive competitive version played in professional tournaments.
devStory: StarCraft was developed by Blizzard Entertainment in approximately two years following Warcraft II. The three-faction design was an ambitious departure from the symmetric-faction approach most RTS games used. The game launched in March 1998 and its adoption in South Korea as a professional esport transformed how the industry understood competitive gaming.

title: Half-Life
description: Half-Life delivered its science fiction horror narrative without a single cutscene — the player was always in control as Gordon Freeman, experiencing the Black Mesa incident from the first person throughout. The game's seamless narrative delivery changed what players expected from FPS storytelling. It sold 8 million copies and earned over 50 Game of the Year awards.
longDescription: Half-Life was developed by Valve Software using a modified Quake engine. The game's central design decision — maintaining the player's first-person perspective and control throughout the narrative without interruption — required every story beat to be delivered in the game environment rather than in cutscenes. The result was a narrative mode that subsequent games including BioShock, Portal, and Halo adopted as a standard approach. Counter-Strike — the multiplayer game that grew from a Half-Life mod — became the most-played online PC game for much of the following decade.
trivia: Valve's first game, Half-Life was built on a heavily modified version of id Software's Quake engine; Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington founded Valve after leaving Microsoft.
The opening tram ride through Black Mesa introduces the world without taking control away from the player — a celebrated piece of environmental storytelling.
Counter-Strike began as a Half-Life mod — Valve recognised its commercial potential and hired both developers.
Half-Life was originally supposed to ship in 1997; after extensive internal playtesting revealed design problems, the team rebuilt much of the game, shipping in November 1998.
devStory: Half-Life was developed by Valve Software, founded by Gabe Newell and Mike Harrington after they left Microsoft. Valve licensed the Quake engine and modified it substantially. The game shipped in November 1998 to universal critical acclaim after an extended development following a difficult internal review.

title: Resident Evil
description: Resident Evil (1996) is Capcom's PlayStation horror game, in which S.T.A.R.S. agents trapped in the Spencer Mansion fight zombies created by Umbrella's t-Virus — the first game labelled "survival horror".
longDescription: On 24 July 1998, in the Arklay forest outside Raccoon City, the S.T.A.R.S. Alpha Team searches for the missing Bravo Team; after dogs attack, Chris Redfield, Jill Valentine, Barry Burton and their captain Albert Wesker take shelter in the Spencer Mansion. It turns out to be an Umbrella research facility, where the t-Virus has turned people and animals into flesh-eating monsters, and Wesker is Umbrella's mole. Seen through fixed camera angles over pre-rendered backgrounds, with tank controls, the player chooses Chris, who is tougher and carries six items, or Jill, who carries eight and has a lockpick. Ammunition is scarce, health shows as an electrocardiogram, herbs can be combined, item boxes store extras, and saving at typewriters uses up ink ribbons. The partners, Rebecca Chambers for Chris and Barry for Jill, and whether they survive, decide the ending.
trivia: It was renamed from Bio Hazard in the West because the name could not be trademarked in the US, where a band called Biohazard already used it.
The opening live-action video, shot in Japan with American actors, became notorious for its acting.
Guinness World Records 2008 listed it for "Worst Game Dialogue Ever".
Fujiwara said he expected it to sell about 200,000 copies.
It was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2024.
devStory:
Tokuro Fujiwara, who created Sweet Home, proposed it, and Shinji Mikami directed, starting in 1993 on the Super NES before moving to the PlayStation in 1994. Mikami adopted fixed cameras after playing Alone in the Dark, the mansion drew partly on The Shining's Overlook Hotel, and a first-person prototype and a co-op mode were dropped. The team peaked at about 80 people. For the West it was renamed from Bio Hazard because the name could not be trademarked in the US, where Bio-Hazard Battle and the band Biohazard already existed.

Capcom released it in Japan on 22 March 1996. Famitsu gave it 38 out of 40, it sold over a million copies in Japan that year, and by Capcom's count the PlayStation versions sold 5.08 million, the best-selling PlayStation game at the time.

title: Crash Bandicoot
description: Crash Bandicoot was the PlayStation's answer to Mario — a platform game with a marsupial protagonist rendered in full 3D with a camera behind the character. The behind-character perspective solved the 3D platformer camera problem by restricting movement to a near-linear axis, concentrating polygon budget on the path ahead. The game sold 6.8 million copies.
longDescription: Crash Bandicoot was developed by Naughty Dog — Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin's team — with Mark Cerny as producer. The camera decision — behind the character, limiting lateral movement — was a technical and design solution simultaneously: by facing the player forward along the level axis, Naughty Dog could render the environment ahead with more detail than a free camera would allow. The game's engine pushed the PlayStation's memory management to its limits.
trivia: Naughty Dog's internal nickname for the project was 'Sonic's Ass Game', because the camera spent so much time behind the character.
The game's designer Andy Gavin wrote a custom memory allocator that reduced memory fragmentation, allowing Naughty Dog to fit significantly more data into the PlayStation's limited RAM.
Crash's design was created after character proposals featuring a wombat, a Tasmanian devil, and a dog were rejected — a marsupial was eventually chosen for personality reasons.
devStory: Crash Bandicoot was developed by Naughty Dog, then a small studio (Andy Gavin and Jason Rubin) who had hired additional engineers. Mark Cerny was brought in as producer to provide mentorship and PlayStation hardware expertise. The game shipped in September 1996 as Sony's platform game answer to Nintendo's Mario.

title: Tomb Raider
description: Tomb Raider introduced Lara Croft — an aristocratic archaeologist exploring ancient tombs — in a 3D action-adventure with environmental puzzle solving and third-person combat. The game's large, navigable 3D environments were technically impressive for 1996 and the character became one of gaming's most recognisable. It sold over 7 million copies across platforms.
longDescription: Tomb Raider was developed by Core Design in Derby, England. Lara Croft was designed as a female protagonist after the lead designer considered and rejected a male character. The game's 3D environments — ancient ruins, Egyptian tombs, Peruvian temples — were navigated through jumping puzzles that required spatial reasoning in three dimensions.
trivia: Lara Croft was originally named Laura Cruz before being anglicised for the Western market.
Lara Croft's exaggerated figure was the result of a design mistake — a developer accidentally scaled the model's measurements by 150% and the team decided they preferred the result.
Tomb Raider sold over 7 million copies across PlayStation, Sega Saturn, and PC — making Lara Croft the most recognisable new character of the 1990s gaming era.

Core Design was pressured by publisher Eidos to produce annual Tomb Raider sequels, a pace that Core's staff described as causing design exhaustion that contributed to later entries' declining quality.
devStory: Tomb Raider was developed by Core Design under Toby Gard, who created the Lara Croft character, and producer Adrian Smith. Gard left Core Design after the first game due to disagreements about the direction of Lara's character in sequels. The game launched in October 1996 on PlayStation and Saturn simultaneously.

title: Final Fantasy VII
description: Final Fantasy VII moved the franchise to 3D and to PlayStation, bringing it to a global mainstream audience. Cloud Strife's story — involving corporate dystopia, environmental collapse, and questions about identity and memory — combined with the death of Aerith Gainsborough, which shocked millions of players, made it the defining JRPG of its era. It sold 9.8 million copies.
longDescription: Final Fantasy VII was directed by Yoshinori Kitase and co-written by Kazushige Nojima and Hironobu Sakaguchi. The game moved from sprite-based visuals to 3D polygon characters on pre-rendered backgrounds. The Materia system replaced traditional character classes with equippable ability gems that any character could use. The death of Aerith — permanent, not reversible later in the story — was a narrative choice that defined a generation's understanding of what game stories could do.
trivia: Final Fantasy VII was originally planned for the Nintendo 64 before Square moved development to PlayStation due to the N64's cartridge storage limitations.
The game's development budget was approximately $45 million — one of the largest ever at the time — and required a 180-person development team.
Cloud Strife's unreliable memory and the revelation about his past — that his remembered history is partially fabricated — was one of the first major narrative twists in mainstream RPG gaming.
devStory: Final Fantasy VII was produced by Hironobu Sakaguchi and directed by Yoshinori Kitase at Square. The decision to move to PlayStation rather than Nintendo 64 was driven by CD-ROM storage capacity — the game used three CDs and would have required multiple cartridges at prohibitive cost. The game launched in Japan in January 1997.

title: Gran Turismo
description: Gran Turismo was a racing simulator of unprecedented depth for a console game. Over 140 real licensed cars with accurate physics modelling, license tests that taught driving technique, and a career mode requiring players to earn money to buy and modify cars created a game that car enthusiasts and casual players could both find compelling. It sold 10.8 million copies.
longDescription: Gran Turismo was developed by Polyphony Digital under Kazunori Yamauchi, who spent five years on the game's development. The game's physics simulation — modelling tire grip, weight transfer, and braking distance for each individual car — was significantly more accurate than any console racing game that preceded it. The license test mode, which required players to demonstrate specific driving techniques before accessing certain race classes, made the game both educational and initially barrier-creating.
trivia: Gran Turismo took five years to develop — Kazunori Yamauchi began work in 1992 and the game shipped in 1997. Sony nearly cancelled the project multiple times due to the extended timeline.
The game's 140+ licensed vehicles required individual licensing agreements with each manufacturer — a legal and administrative undertaking equivalent to the technical development.
Gran Turismo's license test mode — requiring players to demonstrate cornering, braking, and other techniques — was controversial among some players and praised by driving enthusiasts.
The game's replay mode — watching a recorded race from multiple camera angles — was used by racing journalists to demonstrate footage that was visually comparable to broadcast racing coverage.
devStory: Gran Turismo was developed by Polyphony Digital under Kazunori Yamauchi over five years beginning in 1992. Sony nearly cancelled the project on multiple occasions due to the development time and cost. The game launched in Japan in December 1997 and became the best-selling PlayStation game.

title: Castlevania: Symphony of the Night
description: Symphony of the Night combined Metroid's connected-world exploration with RPG character levelling in a massive inverted castle. Alucard — Dracula's dhampir son — acquired equipment, levelled up, and found abilities that opened new areas in a game with a secret second castle doubling its scope. It defined the Metroidvania genre and remained a critical benchmark for decades.
longDescription: Symphony of the Night was directed by Koji Igarashi, who would produce most subsequent Castlevania games. The game was a commercial disappointment on release but its critical reputation grew through the following decade. The inverted castle — a second complete castle mapped upside-down, accessible only after reaching the 'good' ending trigger — doubled the game's content in a way players hadn't anticipated.
trivia: Symphony of the Night sold modestly at first in North America, but it was reissued as a budget 'Greatest Hits' title and grew into one of the most influential games of its generation.
Alucard's name is 'Dracula' spelled backwards — a detail established in his 1989 Castlevania III appearance and carried forward.
The game's famous line — 'What is a man? A miserable little pile of secrets!' — was a localisation enhancement of more straightforward Japanese dialogue.
Symphony of the Night's inverted castle — the game's second half — was kept secret from pre-release coverage and was a genuine surprise that players discovered through play.
devStory: Symphony of the Night was directed by Toru Hagihara at Konami, with Koji Igarashi as assistant director and writer, as a response to perceived player rejection of more linear Castlevania entries. Igarashi wanted to return to exploration-based gameplay and combined it with RPG progression. The game shipped in Japan in March 1997.

title: Metal Gear Solid
description: Metal Gear Solid brought stealth action to a mainstream PlayStation audience with full voice acting, a formalised enemy awareness system, and a cinematic presentation that referenced Hollywood action films. Solid Snake infiltrated Shadow Moses Island to stop nuclear launch. The exclamation mark above detected enemies became one of gaming's most recognisable images.
longDescription: Metal Gear Solid was directed by Hideo Kojima at Konami as the first Metal Gear game with 3D graphics and full voice acting. The game's enemy awareness system — with distinct alert, caution, and normal states communicated through music and enemy behaviour — formalised the stealth game's design vocabulary. The game's use of metatextual breaks — a psychic villain who reads the player's memory card, a boss whose codec frequency is printed on the game's case — created moments that players discussed as singular experiences.
trivia: Psycho Mantis — Metal Gear Solid's psychic villain — read the player's PlayStation memory card and commented on their save files from other Konami games before the boss fight.
The game's codec frequency for Colonel Campbell — 140.85 — became a metric of 1990s gaming cultural knowledge.
Metal Gear Solid's development required Kojima to teach himself film direction theory — he described the game's cinematics as his attempt to apply film grammar to game cutscenes.
The game was one of the first PlayStation games with a full English voice cast of professional actors.
devStory: Metal Gear Solid was directed by Hideo Kojima at Konami in approximately three years following the MSX2 game Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake. Kojima designed the game as a cinematic experience as much as a game, with extended codec conversations and cutscenes that were unusual for PlayStation games of the era. The game launched in Japan in September 1998.

title: Tekken 3
description: Tekken 3 was the definitive fighting game of the PlayStation era — faster, more responsive, and more visually accomplished than any fighting game previously available on home hardware. The roster of 23 characters included series veterans and new additions including Eddie Gordo's capoeira. The game sold 8.3 million copies and is often cited as one of the greatest fighting games ever made.
longDescription: Tekken 3 ran at 60 frames per second with smoother animations and more polygons per character than the previous PlayStation Tekken games. The arcade version had been available for two years before the PlayStation port, which was considered a near-perfect conversion. The game's Tekken Force mode — a side-scrolling beat 'em up — and Tekken Ball mode added content beyond the fighting game itself.
trivia: Tekken 3's PlayStation port was considered by fighting game players to be the most accurate arcade-to-console conversion of its era, running at 60fps with minimal compromises.
Eddie Gordo's capoeira fighting style was so popular with new players that it caused tension in competitive scenes between casual and technical players.
Tekken 3 replaced most of the Tekken 2 roster's main characters with their children or successors — a narrative device that allowed character design refreshes while maintaining story continuity.
The game's Theater Mode — unlocked after completing the game — contained all the game's movies and character-specific bonus content.
devStory: Tekken 3 was released in arcades in 1997, followed by a PlayStation port in 1998. The PlayStation conversion was given sufficient development time to produce what reviewers considered the finest fighting game port on the platform.

title: Spyro the Dragon
description: Spyro the Dragon (1998) is Insomniac Games' PlayStation 3D platformer, in which a young purple dragon frees his crystallised elders from Gnasty Gnorc, with music by The Police's Stewart Copeland.
longDescription:
The Dragon Kingdom's five homeworlds — the Artisans, Peace Keepers, Magic Crafters, Beast Makers and Dream Weavers — lived in harmony until Gnasty Gnorc, a banished gnorc living in a junkyard, took offence at the dragons' comments about him on television. He crystallises every dragon, steals their treasure and turns the gems into minions. Only Spyro, a young purple dragon, escapes, and sets out with his dragonfly friend Sparx.

Each homeworld is a hub with portals to levels, a boss and a hidden flight stage, and a balloonist carries Spyro on once he has collected enough. Stepping on the base of a crystallised dragon frees it, and the freed dragons give advice and save the game. Spyro charges and breathes fire — some armoured enemies can only be charged, and large ones only burned — and glides on his wings. Sparx shows Spyro's health by his colour, collects nearby gems and is restored by butterflies released from defeated sheep. Gems lie in enemies, boxes and chests, and thieves carrying stolen dragon eggs must be chased down.
trivia: Stewart Copeland, former drummer of The Police, composed the soundtrack.
Michael John cited Super Mario 64 as an influence.
Matt Whiting, a NASA engineer, helped program the movement and camera, whose first version caused nausea.
Its marketing included a campaign starring Toasty the Sheep and the website sheepagainstspyro.com.
It was remade in the Spyro Reignited Trilogy in 2018.
devStory:
It was Insomniac Games' second game, after Disruptor (1996), which sold poorly but was praised; artist Craig Stitt proposed the dragon. Early versions were darker, partly inspired by DragonHeart, until producer Mark Cerny pushed for mass-market appeal. The names Pete and Pyro were rejected before "Spyro", and Charles Zembillas designed the character, first green and then purple so he would not blend into the grass. Alex Hastings built its panoramic engine with varying levels of detail, one of the first PlayStation games to use such a system, and about 80% of the code was in assembly. Stewart Copeland composed the music, and Carlos Alazraqui voiced Spyro.

Sony released it in North America on 9 September 1998. Sales started slowly but picked up after the holidays, reaching a million in North America by December 1999 and nearly 5 million worldwide by 2007. Critics praised its graphics, draw distance, music and level design, though some found it easy.

title: Super Mario 64
description: Super Mario 64 was the first fully 3D Mario game and one of the most influential games ever made. Mario's movement — the triple jump, wall jump, long jump, and ground pound — was so responsive and satisfying that subsequent 3D platformers used it as the reference standard. 120 Power Stars hidden across 15 worlds made it the defining 3D collect-a-thon.
longDescription: Super Mario 64 was directed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Yoshiaki Koizumi at Nintendo EAD. The game's movement system was designed before any level was built — Miyamoto's team spent months iterating Mario's physical responses until the movement felt correct, then built levels around what the movement made possible. The camera system — Lakitu following Mario at a distance — attempted the difficult problem of following a player character in three-dimensional space.
trivia: Super Mario 64's development team spent approximately six months perfecting Mario's movement system before designing a single level — Miyamoto's philosophy that the movement had to feel correct before the levels could be built.
The game's camera system was nicknamed 'Lakitu's Camera' — the cloud-riding character was re-canonised as the camera operator.
Super Mario 64's source code was accidentally leaked in 2020, revealing development remnants including incomplete worlds and early versions of the movement system.
The game launched with the N64 in Japan in June 1996 and sold nearly 12 million copies, making it the best-selling Nintendo 64 game.
devStory: Super Mario 64 was directed by Shigeru Miyamoto at Nintendo EAD as the N64 launch title. The game's development focused first on getting Mario's movement right before building any levels. The N64's analogue stick was designed specifically to support the game's three-dimensional movement requirements.

title: GoldenEye 007
description: GoldenEye 007 demonstrated that console first-person shooters could work. The game's single-player campaign across 18 missions adapted the 1995 Bond film with genuine design ambition: objectives beyond simple elimination, stealth options, and difficulty levels that changed mission objectives. The four-player split-screen multiplayer defined university gaming for years.
longDescription: GoldenEye 007 was developed by a team of eight at Rare, most of whom had no prior FPS development experience. The game was originally conceived as a rail shooter before becoming a full free-movement FPS. The mission-based structure — multiple objectives per mission, with additional objectives unlocked on higher difficulties — created replay incentive. The split-screen multiplayer, supporting four players on one console, became the definitive console FPS multiplayer experience until Halo on Xbox.
trivia: GoldenEye's development team had no prior experience making a first-person shooter — the project was led by Martin Hollis, who had previously worked on Killer Instinct.
The game was originally planned as an on-rails shooter in the style of Virtua Cop before the team moved to free movement.
GoldenEye's body part hit detection — enemies reacting differently to shots in different locations — was an innovation that FPS games of the era hadn't implemented.
The multiplayer mode was added late in development and was not in the original design brief — the team added it in approximately two months near the end of the project.
devStory: GoldenEye 007 was developed by a small team at Rare led by Martin Hollis over approximately three years. The project's scope expanded from a rail shooter to a full FPS, extending the development timeline significantly. It launched in August 1997, nearly two years after the film.

title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
description: Ocarina of Time translated the Zelda formula to 3D with innovations including Z-targeting — locking onto enemies for combat — time travel between Link's childhood and adulthood, and the largest open world a Zelda game had contained. It remains the highest-rated game on Metacritic and is consistently cited as one of the greatest games ever made.
longDescription: Ocarina of Time was directed by Eiji Aonuma and Toru Osawa at Nintendo EAD. The game's Z-targeting system — locking the camera and movement relative to an enemy — solved the fundamental problem of 3D action combat. The solution was so effective that subsequent 3D action games adopted it as a standard. The time-travel mechanic — moving between a child and adult version of Hyrule — was used to create puzzles requiring reasoning about both time periods simultaneously.
trivia: Ocarina of Time's Z-targeting system was designed to solve the problem of 3D combat — every 3D action game that followed adopted some version of the lock-on targeting approach.
Ocarina of Time holds the highest Metacritic score of any game — 99 out of 100.
Navi — Link's fairy companion who provides hints — became one of gaming's most memed characters due to her persistent interruptions.
devStory: Ocarina of Time was directed by a team including Toru Osawa, Eiji Aonuma and Yoshiaki Koizumi, with Shigeru Miyamoto as producer. The game took approximately four years to develop and was one of the most anticipated games of the Nintendo 64 era. It launched in Japan in November 1998 and became the fastest-selling game of its year.

sources.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

title: Star Fox 64
description: Star Fox 64 fully realised the rail shooter concept that the SNES Star Fox had introduced. Full voice acting across the entire cast, a branching mission system with multiple routes, and All-Range Mode — free-movement dogfighting — expanded the formula. The game shipped bundled with the Rumble Pak, giving the N64 controller its first vibration feedback.
longDescription: Star Fox 64 was the first game to ship bundled with the Rumble Pak, Nintendo's vibration feedback peripheral. The branching mission structure — taking different routes through the Lylat System based on in-mission success conditions — gave the game substantial replay value. All-Range Mode, available in certain missions, removed the rail and allowed free flight in three dimensions.
trivia: Star Fox 64 was the first game to ship bundled with the Rumble Pak — introducing console controller vibration to a mainstream audience before it became a standard feature.
Slippy Toad's voice was a deliberate design choice to produce an emotional reaction that reinforced his role as the team member most frequently in trouble.
Star Fox 64's branching mission paths can lead to significantly different final boss sequences — the 'true' final boss is accessible only through the game's hardest route.
The game's medal system — earning medals by reaching kill quotas in each mission — unlocked a multiplayer-only ship and extended the game's competitive value.
devStory: Star Fox 64 was developed by Nintendo EAD as a full realisation of the Star Fox concept on N64 hardware, after a cancelled project called Star Fox 2 on SNES. The game launched in Japan in April 1997 and was Nintendo's summer release title.

title: Banjo-Kazooie
description: Banjo-Kazooie (1998) is Rare's Nintendo 64 platformer, in which Banjo the bear and Kazooie the bird cross nine worlds collecting Jiggies to rescue Banjo's sister Tooty from the witch Gruntilda.
longDescription: When the witch Gruntilda's cauldron, Dingpot, names Banjo's sister Tooty the prettiest girl on Spiral Mountain, Gruntilda kidnaps her to steal her beauty. Banjo and Kazooie, the bird riding in his backpack, enter Gruntilda's Lair, the hub linking nine non-linear worlds, each holding 10 Jiggies and 100 musical notes; all 100 Jiggies are needed for the proper ending, and the notes open the lair's doors. Bottles the mole teaches 14 special moves, among them Kazooie's Talon Trot, Beak Bomb and egg shooting, while feather pads allow flight and Wellington boots let Kazooie cross harmful ground. The shaman Mumbo Jumbo, paid in Mumbo Tokens, turns the pair into a termite, an alligator, a walrus, a pumpkin and a bee. Before the final battle, Gruntilda hosts a quiz show, Grunty's Furnace Fun.
trivia: Before the final battle, Grunty's Furnace Fun puts the player through a game-show quiz about the adventure — and about Grunty herself.
Kazooie was named after the kazoo, and Gruntilda was inspired by Grotbags from an ITV series.
Its Stop 'N' Swop feature, meant to unlock content in other games, was dropped after Nintendo objected.
Staff worked weeks of 80 hours or more and earned 50 cents in royalties per copy sold.
It sold over 3 million copies, and Banjo-Tooie followed in 2000.
devStory:
It began as Project Dream, a Super NES role-playing game started after Donkey Kong Country 2, whose hero changed from a boy to a rabbit to a bear. It moved to the Nintendo 64 as a 2.5D platformer before Rare switched to full 3D after seeing an early Super Mario 64. Work on the final game began in March 1997 with ten people, growing to 15, and took 17 months, with Gregg Mayles as head designer, Steve Mayles designing the characters and Chris Sutherland as head programmer. Grant Kirkhope wrote all the music and sound effects, his first full game, and its vertical remixing faded layers of music in and out as the player moved.

Nintendo released it in North America on 29 June 1998. It scored 92 on Metacritic, was the fourth best-selling game of 1998 in the US and won Console Action Game of the Year at the Interactive Achievement Awards.

title: Street Fighter II: The World Warrior
description: Street Fighter II defined the competitive fighting game genre. Eight characters with distinct move sets competed across international stages. The combo system — discovered accidentally by players and left intact by Capcom — became the genre's technical foundation. The game generated an estimated $1.5 billion in quarters.
longDescription: Street Fighter II was directed by Akira Nishitani and designed by Nishitani and Akira Yasuda at Capcom. The game introduced the six-button attack layout that became the standard for fighting games. The combo system — chaining normal moves into special moves before the opponent's hitstun expired — was not designed as a feature but was discovered through player experimentation and left in by Capcom when they recognised its value for competitive play.
trivia: Street Fighter II's combo system was discovered by players rather than designed by Capcom — the developers kept it in after playtesting revealed it created competitive depth they hadn't planned.
The game generated an estimated $1.5 billion in quarters by 1992, making it one of the highest-grossing arcade games ever produced.
Chun-Li was one of the first playable female characters in a competitive fighting game — her design influenced how female characters were written in the genre for decades.
The SNES pad's four face buttons and two shoulder buttons happened to match the arcade game's six attacks, helping make the 1992 SNES port a system-seller.
devStory: Street Fighter II was designed by Akira Nishitani and Akira Yasuda at Capcom after the original Street Fighter's moderate commercial performance. The development team wanted to create a more immediate, accessible fighting game while maintaining competitive depth. The game launched in arcades in February 1991.

title: Mortal Kombat
description: Mortal Kombat was a fighting game built around digitised actor photos rather than hand-drawn sprites, and around Fatalities — finishing moves that killed opponents in graphic ways. The game's violence triggered congressional hearings that led to the ESRB rating system. Despite — or because of — the controversy, it became one of the most commercially successful fighting game franchises.
longDescription: Mortal Kombat was designed by Ed Boon and John Tobias at Midway. The game's digitised graphics — actors photographed performing martial arts moves — gave it a visual realism that hand-drawn characters didn't have. The Fatalities — special finishing moves that killed the defeated opponent graphically — were designed to differentiate the game from Street Fighter II and generate press attention. The attention they generated was more significant than anticipated.
trivia: Mortal Kombat, along with Night Trap, was at the centre of the 1993 US congressional hearings on video game violence, which led to the creation of the Entertainment Software Rating Board in 1994.
The SNES version turned the blood into grey 'sweat' and toned down the Fatalities, while the Genesis version hid the blood behind a code — and outsold it.
Goro — the four-armed boss character — was a physical puppet photographed in stop-motion, then digitised, rather than drawn digitally.
Mortal Kombat began as a planned tie-in with Jean-Claude Van Damme; when the deal fell through, Ed Boon and John Tobias created their own characters — Johnny Cage is a nod to the idea.
devStory: Mortal Kombat was designed by Ed Boon and John Tobias at Midway in under a year. The game was conceived as a fighting game with more graphic violence than Street Fighter II offered, and the Fatality system was designed specifically to differentiate it. The arcade game launched in October 1992.

title: NBA Jam
description: NBA Jam reduced basketball to its most exciting elements: dunks, blocked shots, and turnovers, with two players per side, unlimited dribbling, and boosted jumping. Licensed NBA players with real statistics made it feel authentic; 'He's on fire!' and 'Boom-shakalaka!' made it feel like nothing else. It became the highest-grossing arcade game of 1993.
longDescription: NBA Jam was designed by Mark Turmell at Midway and used digitised player images. The game's exaggerated physics — players could jump three times their height for slam dunks — combined with real NBA licensing created an arcade experience that felt like basketball amplified to its most dramatic moments. The commentary by Tim Kitzrow became culturally pervasive.
trivia: NBA Jam was the highest-grossing arcade game of 1993, earning approximately $1 billion in quarters — Midway produced enough cabinets that the game appeared in almost every arcade in North America.
The game contained hidden unlockable characters including Bill Clinton, Al Gore, and various celebrities — accessible through specific button combinations on the character select screen.
Mark Turmell, the game's designer, programmed the Chicago Bulls' opponent to miss shots at clutch moments — a bias he built in because he was a Detroit Pistons fan.
'He's on fire!' — the commentary line for a player who had made three consecutive baskets — entered mainstream sports broadcasting vocabulary after NBA Jam's cultural saturation.
devStory: NBA Jam was designed by Mark Turmell at Midway and developed in approximately one year. The game used the same hardware as Mortal Kombat and similar digitised actor photography techniques. It launched in arcades in March 1993 and became the fastest-selling arcade game of its year.

title: Metal Slug
description: Metal Slug was a run-and-gun with hand-drawn animation of exceptional quality — hundreds of frames per character, enemies with unique death animations, and environmental detail that made the Neo Geo hardware produce its finest visuals. The game's comedy combined with precise shooting to create a defining arcade experience.
longDescription: Metal Slug was developed by Nazca Corporation — former Irem employees — before SNK acquired Nazca and brought the team in-house. The game's animation quality was unprecedented for a run-and-gun: each enemy character had dozens of frames of animation, drawn by hand at the Neo Geo hardware's sprite capability limits. The tank vehicle — the Metal Slug itself — was controllable by the player and destroyed in dramatic animated sequences.
trivia: Metal Slug's development team at Nazca Corporation were mostly ex-Irem employees who brought the same commitment to detailed sprite animation to SNK's platform.

The game's animation was so detailed that the development team spent more time animating enemy death sequences than designing levels — each enemy had specific death animations for different weapon types.
Metal Slug's POW rescue mechanic — freed prisoners gave players power-ups — was designed to reward players for exploring thoroughly rather than simply moving forward.

The Neo Geo hardware that Metal Slug ran on was significantly more powerful for 2D sprites than contemporary PlayStation or Saturn hardware — SNK's arcade-first business model meant their home hardware matched arcade capability.
devStory: Metal Slug was developed by Nazca Corporation under director Takahiro Nishitani after the team left Irem. SNK published the game on their Neo Geo MVS arcade hardware in 1996 and acquired Nazca Corporation during development. The game was a commercial and critical success that established a franchise still active decades later.

title: Virtua Fighter
description: Virtua Fighter was the first 3D fighting game — replacing the sprite-based characters of Street Fighter II and Mortal Kombat with polygon models in a three-dimensional arena. Yu Suzuki's AM2 team built a game that was visually novel but also mechanically deep, with a three-button control scheme and throw-heavy combat that Japanese players adopted for competitive play.
longDescription: Virtua Fighter was developed by Yu Suzuki's AM2 team at Sega on the Model 1 arcade hardware. The game's polygon characters — blocky by later standards — were genuinely three-dimensional and moved in three-dimensional space, which no fighting game had previously achieved. The game's combat mechanics, while superficially simpler than Street Fighter II's, had significant depth in throw mixups, guard breaks, and position-dependent damage.
trivia: The game ran on Sega's Model 1 hardware — the same board used for Virtua Racing — which was the most powerful arcade hardware available in 1993.
Virtua Fighter became Japan's most competitive fighting game series, with the tournament scene producing technical depth that few Western fighting game communities matched.
Akira Yuki — Virtua Fighter's most technically demanding character — required specific input sequences that were physically difficult enough that mastery became a community status marker.
devStory: Virtua Fighter was designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega AM2 as the team's follow-up to Virtua Racing. Suzuki wanted to apply the 3D polygon technology to a fighting game, reasoning that three-dimensional movement and combat would create depth that 2D fighters couldn't achieve. The game launched in arcades in December 1993.

title: Super Castlevania IV
description: Super Castlevania IV was a near-total reimagining of the original Castlevania for the SNES. Simon Belmont's whip could now be aimed in eight directions and used to latch onto hooks, fundamentally changing the game's navigation. The Mode 7 rotation in the boss room and the Konami soundtrack — using the SNES sound chip for orchestral atmosphere — made it a showpiece for the hardware.
longDescription: Super Castlevania IV was developed by Konami and used the SNES's audio and graphics capabilities more comprehensively than most launch-window titles. The eight-directional whip was the most significant mechanical change to the Castlevania formula since the original — allowing players to clear enemies to the sides and overhead without the strict jump-and-attack timing the NES games required. The game's 11 stages included some of the most elaborate environmental design in the 16-bit era, including a rotating room rendered in Mode 7.
trivia: Super Castlevania IV reused the original Castlevania's stage themes remixed for the SNES sound hardware — the comparison between NES and SNES versions of Vampire Killer became a standard demo of the hardware upgrade.

The eight-directional whip was not carried forward into subsequent Castlevania games — later entries returned to the limited directional attacks of the NES originals, frustrating players who had grown accustomed to the SNES control scheme.
Super Castlevania IV was long considered the definitive entry in the series until Symphony of the Night's reputation grew to surpass it in critical esteem.
devStory: Super Castlevania IV was developed by Konami's internal team as a SNES showcase title. The game was designed to be a reimagining rather than a direct sequel — retelling the original's story with new mechanics and graphics. It launched in Japan in October 1991.

title: Secret of Mana
description: Secret of Mana (1993) is Square's Super NES action RPG, in which a boy who pulls the Mana Sword from a stone joins a girl and a sprite to restore the Mana Temples, for up to three players at once.
longDescription:
An ancient civilisation built the flying Mana Fortress by exploiting mana, and a hero destroyed it with the Mana Sword. Now an empire, manipulated by the sorcerer Thanatos, seeks the eight Mana Seeds to rebuild it. A boy from Potos pulls a rusty sword from a stone, releasing monsters, and is banished; it is the Mana Sword, which must be recharged at the eight Mana Temples. He is joined by a girl searching for the warrior Dyluck and a sprite who has lost its memory.

Up to three players can play together with the Super Multitap, with the computer controlling any character not taken. The hero learns weapons fastest, the girl heals and the sprite casts offensive magic, learned by rescuing eight elemental spirits. Combat runs in real time, with each swing draining a power bar that recharges for a full-strength blow, and each of the eight weapon types, from sword to whip and javelin, can be reforged with Weapon Orbs and trained to unlock special attacks. The Ring Command menu, which pauses the game, handles equipment and spells, and the flying dragon Flammie crosses a Mode 7 world later on.
trivia: It began as a launch game for the planned Super NES CD-ROM, and up to 40% of the planned content was cut when it moved to cartridge.
Multiplayer was added once the developers realised all three characters could be human-controlled.
Ted Woolsey translated it in about 30 days and said much of the script was cut for space.
Its ring menu was widely imitated, according to Edge.
A 3D remake was released in 2018.
devStory:
Koichi Ishii, creator of Final Fantasy Adventure, directed and designed it, with Nasir Gebelli programming and Hiromichi Tanaka producing. It began as an action-oriented Final Fantasy IV, was briefly codenamed "Chrono Trigger", and was planned as a launch title for the Super NES CD-ROM add-on; when that collapsed, Square moved it to cartridge, cutting routes and endings, and Ishii estimated up to 40% of the planned game was dropped. Hiroki Kikuta, in his first game score, created his own instrument samples, inspired by landscapes and Balinese music.

Square released it in Japan on 6 August 1993 and North America that October. It sold 1.83 million copies by 2003, and EGM named it the best RPG of 1993.

title: ActRaiser
description: ActRaiser combined two entirely different gameplay modes in a single game: side-scrolling action sequences in which the player fought as a god-figure, and a city-building simulation in which players guided human civilisation from above. The alternation between them was seamless in design and unique in concept. Yuzo Koshiro's orchestral soundtrack was considered the finest on SNES at launch.
longDescription: ActRaiser was developed by Quintet and published by Enix for the SNES launch window. The action sequences — platforming with combat — were connected to the simulation sequences by narrative: clearing monsters from action stages allowed humans to populate new areas, whose growth funded further action stages. Yuzo Koshiro's soundtrack, composed using FM synthesis techniques he had developed for his earlier work, exploited the SNES sound chip more fully than nearly any other launch-window game.
trivia: An early Super Famicom release in 1990 (1991 in North America), ActRaiser showed that the new console could support ideas beyond sharper graphics.
Yuzo Koshiro composed the ActRaiser soundtrack before Streets of Rage — the orchestral quality caused immediate comparisons to film scoring.
The simulation mode in ActRaiser was significantly simplified in ActRaiser 2, which removed it entirely — a decision that disappointed players who had considered it the game's most original element.

The player character in ActRaiser is never named — the manual refers to them as 'the Master,' establishing an ambiguity about the game's theological setting that Quintet carried through their subsequent games.
devStory: ActRaiser was developed by Quintet in Japan as an early Super Famicom title. The combination of action and simulation genres was Quintet's attempt to create a game that justified the new hardware's capabilities beyond graphical improvements. It launched in Japan in December 1990.

title: Super Punch-Out!!
description: Super Punch-Out!! (1994) is Nintendo's Super NES boxing game, in which a see-through boxer reads the tells of 16 opponents across four circuits, with a Time Attack mode for the fastest knockouts.
longDescription: The player's boxer is seen from behind as a translucent figure, like the wireframe in the arcade game, so the opponent stays visible. Jabs go to the head and body blows to either side, and the boxer can block, dodge left or right and duck, though ducking does not avoid body blows and strong punches cannot be blocked. Opponents guard differently by stance, so players must find openings. Landing punches fills a power meter that unlocks knockout punches such as uppercuts and hooks, and a red background behind the boxer's face marks a Power-Up state with faster, stronger blows. Running out of stamina means a knockdown; failing to rise by ten or being knocked down three times loses the bout, and there are no decisions, only a three-minute limit. Sixteen opponents fill four circuits, the fourth opened only by never losing, and Time Attack records the fastest knockouts.
trivia: The player's boxer is seen from behind as a see-through figure so the opponent stays visible.
A hidden two-player mode, unlocked with a button code, was discovered in 2022.
Its boxer was an unlockable fighter in the GameCube version of EA's Fight Night Round 2.
IGN ranked it 17th among its top 100 SNES games in 2011.
EGM ranked it the 56th best console game of all time in 1997.
devStory: Nintendo's R&D3 team made it, with Makoto Wada and Yasuyuki Oyagi directing and Genyo Takeda producing, alongside StarTropics II, and Mike Shapiro and Charles Martinet voiced the boxers, referee and announcer. It was described as the closest home version of the arcade Punch-Out!! and Super Punch-Out!!, though not a direct port.
