Zzap!64 gave it 97%, a Gold Medal and the verdict "THE classic shoot em up", and in 2002 its readers named it the best Commodore 64 game ever. A faster Competition Edition followed in 1986, Heavy Metal Paradroid in 1987 and Paradroid 90 for the Amiga and Atari ST in 1990.

title: Uridium
description: Uridium (1986) is Andrew Braybrook's Commodore 64 shooter: a Manta fighter skims fifteen giant Dreadnoughts, strafing their defences before landing to destroy each one.
longDescription: Enemy Super-Dreadnoughts orbit fifteen planets, draining their mineral cores, and the player's Manta fighter must destroy each one. Every level is a single huge Dreadnought, named after a metal and ending with the fictional Uridium. The Manta flies at a fixed height over the hull, which scrolls in both directions, and must flip sideways to slip through narrow gaps in later ships. Waves of enemy fighters attack, and flashing ports release homing mines that cannot be shot and eventually burst on their own. Once enough defences are gone, a "Land Now!" signal tells the player to slow down and touch down on the landing strip, after which the reactor self-destructs and the ship crumbles beneath the departing Manta. Players can score more by ignoring the signal to hunt elite fighters.
trivia: The C64 cannot scroll a separate background layer, so the stars are drawn as characters whose pixels shift against the scroll, making them appear to stand still.
It won Best Arcade-style Game of the Year at the 1986 Golden Joystick Awards and reached number one in the British all-formats chart.
A message on the last Dreadnought reads "GOOD ZAPPING... TURKEY.", visible only once the ship is destroyed.
Crash's readers voted it the best shooting game of the year.
Uridium 2 followed on the Amiga.
devStory: Andrew Braybrook designed it at Graftgold, with music by Steve Turner, and Hewson released it for the Commodore 64 on 28 February 1986; Robert Orchard coined the name, saying in the manual, "I really thought it existed". It reached number one in the Commodore 64 and all-formats charts, and Zzap!64 gave it 94%, calling it "visually awesome, sonically sound, technically stunning and a brilliant shoot em up to boot". Dominic Robinson programmed the ZX Spectrum version, and other ports followed for the Amstrad, Atari ST, BBC Micro and PC; in 1990 Mindscape reused it for an NES game licensed from the film The Last Starfighter.

title: The Last Ninja
description: The Last Ninja (1987) is System 3's isometric action-adventure, in which Armakuni crosses the island of Lin-Fen to recover the Koga Scrolls from the shogun Kunitoki.
longDescription: The Fujiwara clan practised Ninjutsu for centuries, and every ten years its ninja gathered on the island of Lin-Fen to honour the White Ninja. The shogun Kunitoki, envious of their art, attacked the gathering to steal the Koga Scrolls and train his own men. Armakuni survived only because he was at the Bunkinkan shrine, and as the last ninja he sets out to reach Kunitoki's palace, kill him and recover the scrolls. The world is seen from an isometric viewpoint with movement in eight directions, and the game mixes exploration, puzzles and combat. Traps and fatal terrain demand precise jumps, kneeling at shrines and fountains reveals the next item, and items hidden in trees and bushes flash briefly as each screen loads. Fights aim blows at the head, body or legs, with a ninjato, nunchaku, staff, shuriken and smoke bombs.
trivia: It was the best-selling Commodore 64 game of its time, with over 750,000 copies sold in Europe; designer Mark Cale has put total sales at about 4 million.
It was runner-up for Game of the Year at the 1988 Golden Joystick Awards and was followed by Last Ninja 2 and Last Ninja 3.
Its fights let players aim at the head, body or legs.
Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum versions were made but never released.
It came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2008.
devStory: Designed by Mark Cale and Tim Best, it was first developed for almost a year by SoftView, a Hungarian team at Novotrade, in a Forth-like language meant to ease porting; when it missed every deadline, the advance was refunded, the team went uncredited, and Cale took the code to London, where John Twiddy rewrote the engine for the Commodore 64. Cale cited the square cursor of Atari's Adventure as an inspiration, Hugh Riley drew the art, and Ben Daglish and Anthony Lees wrote the music. System 3 released it in 1987, and Computer Gaming World said "there is no exaggerating the graphic excellence" of it. Amiga and Atari ST versions followed in 1990 as Last Ninja Remix.

title: Wizball
description: Wizball (1987) is Sensible Software's colour-restoring shooter: a bouncing wizard and his cat collect red, green and blue paint to bring grey Wizworld back to life.
longDescription: The evil Zark has drained the colour from Wizworld, and the wizard Wiz, travelling as a bouncing green ball, sets out with his cat Nifta, as Catellite, to restore it. Each of the eight levels starts in three shades of grey and needs a different colour, mixed from quantities of red, green and blue paint, and portals lead between them; only the first three are open at the start. Wiz bounces at a fixed rate, and the player controls only how fast he spins, which decides how he moves after each landing. He cannot collect paint himself: that is Catellite's job, gathering droplets released by shooting coloured spheres, and holding fire while moving the joystick steers the cat instead of the wizard. Pearls dropped by some enemies buy better control, more firepower and the cat itself. In two-player co-op, the second player controls Catellite.
trivia: Zzap!64 gave it 96%, later rated it 98% as the best C64 shoot 'em up, and in December 1988 named it the best game it had ever reviewed.
Martin Galway composed the music for the Commodore 64 version.
Retro Gamer's readers voted it the second-best C64 game in 2011.
The C64 version sends four or five waves of enemies at once, making it much harder than the Amiga and ST versions.
A sequel, Wizkid, appeared in 1992.
devStory: Jon Hare and Chris Yates, the founders of Sensible Software, made it; Hare said it began as a Nemesis-inspired shooter, with the bouncing ball and its controls coming first and the wizard story last, and work paused while they made Parallax. Martin Galway wrote the Commodore 64 music. Ocean released it for the C64 in 1987, with Spectrum and Amstrad versions that year and Amiga and Atari ST versions in 1988. Zzap!64 gave it 96% and a Sizzler but not a Gold Medal, which its former editor later said it should have had, and in December 1988 named it the best game of all time; Hare blamed Ocean's marketing for disappointing sales.

title: Alex Kidd in Miracle World
description: Alex Kidd in Miracle World (1986) is the Master System's signature platformer, in which Alex punches through 17 stages and plays rock-paper-scissors against Janken the Great's henchmen.
longDescription: Janken the Great has overthrown King Thunder of Radaxian and kidnapped Prince Egle and his fiancée, Princess Lora. Alex, a young martial artist, punches enemies and breaks rocks to open new paths across 17 stages, some scrolling and some single-screen, collecting money to spend in shops on items and vehicles such as a motorbike and a helicopter. Many stages end with a game of rock-paper-scissors against one of Janken's three henchmen, and losing costs a life, just as a single hit does. Alex learns he is King Thunder's lost son, defeats Janken, who is turned to stone, and recovers the crown, and Egle becomes king. There is no save system.
trivia: The game was built into many Master System and Master System II consoles. The built-in version swaps the original's rice-ball map icon for a hamburger and inverts the buttons.
Entering a button code on the Game Over screen continues the game, at a cost of 400 Baums.
It began as a Dragon Ball game before the licence expired.
IGN gave it 9/10 and an Editor's Choice award in 2008.
The 2021 DX remake lets players switch between modern and retro graphics.
devStory: Kotaro Hayashida designed it, with art by Rieko Kodama and music by Tokuhiko Uwabo, and it began in 1984 as a licensed Dragon Ball tie-in; when the licence expired, Sega president Hayao Nakayama had it restarted from scratch. Sega released it in Japan on 1 November 1986 and in North America that December. From 1990 a modified version was built into Master System II consoles in the US, Australia and Europe. Computer and Video Games called it "Sega's answer to Mario", and Power Play named it the best Sega game of 1987. A remake, Alex Kidd in Miracle World DX, followed in 2021.

title: Psycho Fox
description: Psycho Fox (1989) is Vic Tokai's Master System platformer, in which a fox uses a Shinto stick to become a monkey, hippo or tiger on the way to overthrowing the evil deity Madfox Daimyōjin.
longDescription: Fox priests worship Inari Daimyōjin, the fox deity, until Madfox Daimyōjin, an evil fox, rises through the priesthood, seizes the shrine, corrupts the land and fills it with creatures. A young fox, later known as Psycho Fox, is chosen to rid the land of him. Each side-scrolling level runs left to right through crowds of enemies, and AllGame noted that each offers a choice of two routes. A Shinto stick transforms the hero into three other animals: the hippo is slow and jumps low but punches through special blocks, the monkey jumps highest and the tiger runs fastest. The bird ally Bird Fly can act as armour or be thrown like a boomerang, and if the player is hit while carrying it, the bird flies off instead of a life being lost.
trivia: In Brazil, Tec Toy released it as Sapo Xulé: Os Invasores do Brejo, with the fox replaced by a cartoon frog.
Vic Tokai made Kid Kool as an NES counterpart, and Decap Attack on the Mega Drive is regarded as its spiritual successor.
Sega Power and S: The Sega Magazine both scored it 93%.
EGM's four reviewers each gave it 7 out of 10.
Its hero's transformations are triggered by a Shinto stick.
devStory: Toshihisa Hasegawa directed it at Vic Tokai, with Shoji Suzuki programming and music by Fumito Tamayama and Hiroto Kanno, and Sega published it for the Master System in Europe in December 1989 and North America in May 1990. Mean Machines gave it 90%, praising its addictiveness and graphics, and S: The Sega Magazine scored it 93%, calling it "one of the best games for the Master System". AllGame was cooler, calling it "a fun, if largely unoriginal game".

title: Wolfenstein 3D
description: Wolfenstein 3D (1992) is id Software's fast first-person shooter, in which Allied spy B.J. Blazkowicz fights his way out of a Nazi castle — the game that set the template for the genre.
longDescription: B.J. Blazkowicz, a Polish-American Allied spy, is captured while seeking the plans for Operation Eisenfaust and imprisoned in Castle Wolfenstein. Across the first three episodes he escapes, stops a Nazi plan to build undead mutants at Castle Hollehammer, and fights Adolf Hitler in a robotic suit with four chain guns beneath the Reichstag; the second three, The Nocturnal Missions, are a prequel about German chemical warfare. Each level is a flat grid of equal-height walls and doors, drawn in real time with ray casting, while guards, dogs and objects are flat sprites drawn from set angles. Players fight with a knife, pistol, submachine gun and chain gun, reach an elevator or beat a boss to finish each level, and find secret areas behind walls that slide back. Each episode starts with four lives, and points come from kills, treasure and par times.
trivia: Germany banned the game in 1994 over its Nazi symbols; the ban was lifted in 2018 and the game removed from the index in 2019.
For the Super NES version, Nintendo required the Nazi imagery and German voice clips to be cut, the blood removed and the attack dogs replaced with giant rats.
It hides a level modelled on Pac-Man.
It was the first shareware title to win a Codie award.
Carmack's side work on a new engine during its follow-up became the basis for Doom.
devStory:
John Romero proposed remaking Muse Software's 1981 Castle Wolfenstein in 3D, and id began work on 15 December 1991, buying the Wolfenstein trademark for $5,000. John Carmack wrote the ray-casting engine in about a month, Romero and Tom Hall designed it, Adrian Carmack drew the sprites at eight angles and Bobby Prince wrote the music; the graphics moved from 16-colour EGA to 256-colour VGA four months before release. Apogee released the first episode as shareware on 5 May 1992, with Scott Miller persuading id to make six episodes instead of three, and FormGen published Spear of Destiny that September.

The whole game cost about $25,000 in rent and salaries. Apogee's first royalty cheque was $100,000, and it is called the grandfather of 3D shooters.

title: The Lords of Midnight
description: The Lords of Midnight (1984) is Mike Singleton's ZX Spectrum epic: an adventure and a wargame at once, fought across a frozen land seen in first-person panoramas.
longDescription: Doomdark the Witchking has locked the Land of Midnight in endless winter. The player begins with four characters — Luxor the Moonprince, Rorthron the Wise, Corleth the Fey and Morkin — and can recruit up to twenty-eight more lords and their armies. The game can be won in two ways: Morkin can carry out a lone quest to destroy the Ice Crown, or the armies of the Free can march north and capture his citadel, Ushgarak. Doomdark wins by killing Morkin and either killing Luxor or taking the capital, Xajorkith. Every location is drawn as a first-person view that can be turned to any of the eight points of the compass, built from pre-scaled images in a technique known as landscaping.
trivia: The game can be played as a pure adventure, as a wargame, or as the 'Epic', which asks the player to pursue both victories at once.
Crash gave it 10 out of 10 in its adventure column, its readers voted it adventure game of the year, and it won Best Strategy Game at the Golden Joystick Awards.
devStory: Singleton's game was published for the ZX Spectrum by Beyond Software in 1984, with Amstrad CPC and Commodore 64 versions following. A sequel, Doomdark's Revenge, came out the same year; a third part, The Eye of the Moon, was never released. Chris Wild's remake brought the game to modern platforms from 2012.

title: Ant Attack
description: Ant Attack (1983) is Sandy White's ZX Spectrum rescue game, set in a walled isometric city of giant ants — and one of the first games to let the player choose to be a boy or a girl.
longDescription: The player chooses to play as a boy or a girl and enters the walled city of Antescher to rescue the other, who has been captured and left unable to move. Giant ants roam the streets and give chase, and the player's grenades can kill them but can hurt people too. Once the hostage is reached, the pair must escape the city together, and each new rescue places the next captive somewhere harder to reach. The city is drawn in a "Softsolid 3D" isometric view that, unlike Zaxxon or Q*bert, lets the player climb up and down the scenery as well as move across it.
trivia: The city's name, Antescher, is a nod to the artist M. C. Escher.
In 2009 Edge wrote that the game 'marked the very beginnings of the survival horror genre'.
It was among the first games to let players choose their gender.
Your Sinclair ranked the Spectrum version 14th among its top 100 games.
devStory: Sandy White wrote it by hand on paper in assembler mnemonics, assembled it himself and typed the hex code into an EEPROM emulator attached to a ZX Spectrum; the graphics were drawn on squared paper and converted to hex, and the high-score table was added in BASIC. Quicksilva published it for the Spectrum in 1983, with a Commodore 64 version in 1984. Crash gave it 85%, and it came second to Ah Diddums for Best Original Game at the 1983 Golden Joystick Awards. It was possibly the first isometric game on home computers, and White reused its projection for Zombie Zombie.

title: Skool Daze
description: Skool Daze (1984) is Microsphere's ZX Spectrum school simulation, in which Eric must steal his report card from the staff-room safe without collecting 10,000 lines.
longDescription: Eric is a pupil at a British school who needs to get his report card out of the safe in the staff room, which means completing a series of tasks around the school. The computer runs everyone else: the headmaster Mr Wacker, the science master Mr Rockitt, Mr Withit for geography and Mr Creak for history, and fellow pupils such as the tearaway Boy Wander, the bully Angelface and the swot Einstein. Teachers chase Eric when he is out of class or misbehaving and hand out lines — and sometimes when it isn't his fault, such as when he is knocked down or happens to be near a teacher hit by someone else's shot. Reaching 10,000 lines gets Eric expelled. Before the game starts, the player can rename every character.
trivia: It sold about 50,000 copies on release despite very little marketing, and Crash scored it 93%.
It is regarded as an early example of the sandbox game and appears in 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
Its sequel, Back to Skool, added a neighbouring girls' school, stink bombs, mice, water pistols and a long-suffering caretaker.
It is cited as an influence on Little Computer People and The Sims.
devStory:
Skool Daze was a family production: David Reidy designed it on paper and his wife Helen, then a schoolteacher, typed in the code, while family friend Keith Warrington, a graphic design student, drew the characters on squared paper, using tracing paper for the animation frames. The pupils were based on Just William and The Bash Street Kids, and Warrington modelled the teachers on his own, Mr Withit on his favourite; the Spectrum's low resolution pushed him towards cartoon-like figures. Microsphere released it for the ZX Spectrum in 1984 and the Commodore 64 in 1985.

It sold 50,000 copies despite little marketing, and Crash gave it 93% and a Crash Smash award. Reidy later felt a proper campaign could have earned more, and regretted the income lost to piracy.

title: Chuckie Egg
description: Chuckie Egg (1983) is the British home-computer platformer in which Hen-House Harry collects twelve eggs per level while dodging hens and, eventually, a giant freed duck.
longDescription:
Hen-House Harry must collect the twelve eggs on each level before the timer runs out, climbing ladders, jumping between platforms and riding lifts that rise and wrap from the top of the screen to the bottom. Piles of seed score points and briefly stop the clock, but patrolling hens eat them. Touching a hen, falling through a gap at the bottom or being carried into the top of the screen on a lift costs one of Harry's five lives, with an extra life every 10,000 points.

The first eight levels are played beneath a giant caged duck. On the second pass the hens are gone but the duck is free and homes in on Harry; the third brings the hens back alongside it, the fourth adds more, and the fifth makes everything faster. After all forty levels the game carries on with a "level 41" that copies level 33.
trivia: Nigel Alderton was 16 or 17 when he wrote it.
After level 40 the game carries on with level 33's layout, labelled level 41.
Its purple and green colour scheme was chosen in the manner of Space Panic.
A mobile remake, Super Chuckie Egg, came out in 2017.
Chuckie Egg 2 followed in 1985.
devStory:
Nigel Alderton, aged 16 or 17, wrote it, inspired by arcade games including Space Panic, and showed a pre-release ZX Spectrum version to A&F Software, founded two years earlier by Doug Anderson and Mike Fitzgerald, after a month or two's work; Anderson wrote the BBC Micro version at the same time, and Mike Webb finished the Dragon port. The publisher chose the name. It came out in 1983 for the Spectrum, BBC Micro and Dragon, and was later converted to many other computers.

The Spectrum version reached number 12 on a multi-format chart in late 1983, and the BBC version topped the BBC chart in 1984. Your Sinclair later ranked it 13th among the best Spectrum games, and The Telegraph called it a "revelation" on release.

title: Penguin Adventure
description: Penguin Adventure (1986) is Konami's MSX sequel to Antarctic Adventure, sending the penguin Penta on a race for a golden apple to save a dying princess.
longDescription: Penguette, the Penguin Princess, is ill, and only a golden apple can cure her, so Penta sets off to fetch it. It builds on Antarctic Adventure's racing with many more stages and enemies — forest, ice, water and caves, with bonus levels in outer space — along with bosses, minigames and role-playing touches. Three fishermen trade items, including a gun, for the fish Penta collects, and holes in the track, usually hazards, sometimes hide shortcuts. The game has more than one ending: in the bad ending the princess dies, and the good ending is hidden behind a secret.
trivia: Hideo Kojima contributed planning ideas for about a month, including the shop's slot machine and some boss tactics, but is not credited; his directorial debut was Metal Gear the following year.
The good ending is reached by pausing the game a particular number of times.
Some writers trace Metal Gear Solid's multiple endings to it, though Kojima says he only contributed ideas.
Zemina made an unauthorised Master System version, Dreamland, in South Korea.
A digital manga ran in Weekly Konami Magazine in 2006 and 2007.
devStory: Ryouhei Shogaki directed and designed it at Konami with programmer Hiroyuki Fukui, and Yoshinori Sasaki and Kenichi Matsubara composed the music. It was Hideo Kojima's first professional work: he helped plan it for about a month, suggesting the shop's slot machine and ways of beating bosses, though he is not credited. Konami released it for the MSX in Japan on 28 October 1986 and in Europe in 1987, and it was later included in the Konami Antiques MSX Collection on the PlayStation and Saturn.

title: The Maze of Galious
description: The Maze of Galious (1987) is Konami's MSX exploration game, in which Popolon and Aphrodite search Castle Greek and ten hidden worlds to rescue their unborn child from the priest Galious.
longDescription: The second Knightmare game turns the series from a shooter into an exploration game like The Legend of Zelda. Popolon and Princess Aphrodite travel through Castle Greek to free their unborn child, Pampas, from the priest Galious. The castle is an overworld with entrances to ten worlds, each holding items, enemies and power-ups, and new items open new areas. The player switches between the heroes: Popolon pushes stones, opens heavy doors and varies his jump, while Aphrodite fires more shots and lasts longer underwater. Each world's Great Demon can be summoned only by finding its name on a gravestone and typing it at the boss's door, and three hidden items help against it. Enemies drop coins for shops, arrows and keys, and a full experience gauge restores health. If one hero dies, the other can pay to revive them at a shrine, and passwords from Demeter's Shrine save progress.
trivia: Plugging Game Master, Knightmare or Q*bert into the MSX's second cartridge slot unlocks extra content.
It is cited as an influence on La-Mulana, and its exploration design fed into Castlevania II: Simon's Quest.
La-Mulana's creator, Takumi Naramura, won the rights to make a remake through Konami's 2022 contest.
Francisco Téllez de Meneses cited it as an influence on Unepic.
Pampas was later confirmed as a boy in Shalom: Knightmare III.
devStory: Konami's MSX division made it, a team of seven led by director and designer Ryouhei Shogaki, with Kazuhiko Uehara, in his first Konami game, composing for the SCC sound chip; such projects usually took four to six months, and an eleventh world was cut for lack of memory. The team never decided whether Pampas was a boy or a girl. Konami released it in Japan on 18 April 1987, and a reworked Famicom version with redesigned maps followed in August. Input MSX gave it 49 out of 50, though Hardcore Gaming 101 later called it "downright dull" beside Legacy of the Wizard.

title: Mystery House
description: Mystery House (1980) is Roberta and Ken Williams' Apple II murder mystery — the first graphical adventure game and the first release of the company that became Sierra On-Line.
longDescription: The player begins outside an abandoned Victorian mansion and is locked inside with seven others: Tom the plumber, Sam the mechanic, Sally the seamstress, Dr. Green the surgeon, Joe the grave-digger, Bill the butcher and Daisy the cook. The first aim is to find a hidden cache of jewels, but bodies begin to turn up, and the player must work out who the murderer is before becoming the next victim. Commands are typed in, as in the text adventures of the time, but each location is shown as a simple line drawing above the text.
trivia: Roberta Williams drew on Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None and the board game Clue.
Sierra released the game into the public domain in 1987 to mark the company's seventh anniversary.
It was released as Hi-Res Adventure #1.
Computer Gaming World ranked it fourth among the most innovative computer games in 1996.
Its Japanese versions sold about 50,000 copies.
devStory:
Ken Williams wanted to start a company making business software for the Apple II. After he bought Colossal Cave Adventure from a catalogue and played it with Roberta Williams, they decided the market for such games was underdeveloped, and Roberta wrote her own, inspired by Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None and the board game Clue. Ken coded it on his brother's Apple II and suggested adding pictures. Roberta traced seventy scenes on a VersaWriter, and because the images would not fit on a floppy disk, Ken turned them into coordinates and drawing instructions.

On-Line Systems released it on 5 May 1980, sold in Ziploc bags with a floppy disk and an instruction sheet for $24.95. It sold more than 10,000 copies by mail order and about 80,000 including a 1982 re-release, and its follow-up let the couple make games full-time.

title: Choplifter
description: Choplifter (1982) is Dan Gorlin's Apple II rescue game, in which a helicopter pilot carries 64 hostages out of enemy territory sixteen at a time.
longDescription:
The player flies a rescue helicopter into the territory of the Bungeling Empire, where 64 hostages — "delegates to the United Nations Conference on Peace and Child Rearing" — are held in four buildings of sixteen each. The helicopter carries sixteen passengers at a time, so a full rescue takes several trips: shoot open a building, land so the hostages can climb aboard, and fly them back to base. It can turn to face left, right or towards the screen, the last used mainly to shoot tanks.

Care is needed on the ground: landing on hostages or blocking their exit kills them, and in some versions so does a tilted landing. Tanks can attack the grounded helicopter, which can only fire at them in the air, jet fighters use missiles and bombs, and later an alien spacecraft appears. Each trip grows more dangerous as the enemy counterattacks.
trivia: Sega released an arcade version in 1985, which Game Machine listed as the most successful table arcade unit of October 1985.
It won a Certificate of Merit for Best Computer Audiovisual Effects at the 4th Arkie Awards.
Sega's Air Rescue (1991) was a spiritual successor.
inXile released Choplifter HD in 2012.
The Addison-Wesley Book of Atari Software gave it an A+ and called it "a masterpiece".
devStory:
Dan Gorlin, who had worked for the Rand Corporation, wrote it in six months on an Apple II lent by his grandfather. He first planned it in 3D but switched to 2D for technical reasons, building the helicopter's animation first, then the scenery, the tanks and planes, and finally the hostages, an idea inspired by Defender. Broderbund found his flight model too realistic and helped make it easier to fly. Gorlin said it was not a reference to the Iran hostage crisis.

Broderbund published it for the Apple II on 21 May 1982, and it sold 9,000 copies within weeks. Softline called it "the first Interactive Computer-Assisted Animated Movie", and Billboard named it Computer Game of the Year. Versions for the Atari 8-bit computers, Commodore 64, Atari 5200, ColecoVision, Master System and others followed.

title: Karateka
description: Karateka (1984) is Jordan Mechner's rotoscoped Apple II martial-arts game, in which a lone fighter climbs to Akuma's fortress to rescue Princess Mariko.
longDescription:
An unnamed hero climbs a mountain into the fortress of the warlord Akuma, who holds Princess Mariko prisoner, scrolling from left to right and fighting one guard per screen. In a fighting stance he can punch, kick and dodge; each hit knocks a notch off a fighter's health bar, which slowly recovers if he avoids being hit, and losing all of it means starting again from the beginning. Akuma sends a trained hawk, which must be knocked away with well-timed blows, and an open cliff edge and a falling portcullis can kill.

The fighters move with unusually lifelike animation, and the game cuts away to scenes of Mariko and Akuma inside the fortress. After beating Akuma, the hero enters Mariko's cell, and the finale holds a famous trap: approaching her in a fighting stance gets him killed by a single kick, while approaching peacefully completes the rescue.
trivia: Mechner created the animation by drawing over film of his karate teacher, a technique called rotoscoping.
Putting the Apple II disk in upside down made the game play upside down — a deliberate Easter egg.
Reviewers questioned why the hero and heroine had blond hair in a Japanese setting.
Mechner considered Veda Cook's Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit versions the best ports.
A 2012 remake replaced the one-hit deaths with rhythm-based combat.
devStory:
Jordan Mechner made it as a side project at Yale over about two years, submitting it late in his sophomore year. Broderbund had turned down his earlier game, Deathbounce, but sent him a copy of Choplifter, which encouraged him to try original ideas. His influences included his karate lessons, Ukiyo-e prints, Akira Kurosawa's films — he copied screen wipes from Seven Samurai — early Disney animation and silent films. His father, Francis Mechner, composed the music, since the Apple II could not play music and animate at once.

Broderbund released it in December 1984. It reached number two on Billboard's software chart in July 1985, was certified gold for 100,000 sales in January 1986 and passed 500,000 by 2000. Compute! called its animation "by far the best" it had seen in an Apple arcade game. Mechner's next game was Prince of Persia.

title: Star Raiders
description: Star Raiders (1980) is Doug Neubauer's first-person space combat game for the Atari 400 and 800, which made the computers' name and set conventions later used by Elite and Wing Commander.
longDescription: The player captains a starship of the Atarian Federation in a war against the Zylon Empire, protecting starbases and destroying Zylon ships before they destroy the player or the ship runs out of energy. Combat takes place in a first-person 3D cockpit view with front and rear views and a targeting computer, while a 2D galactic chart is used to plot hyperwarp jumps between sectors. Energy drives the engines, shields and photon torpedoes and is restored by docking with a friendly starbase, and subspace radio warns when a starbase is surrounded. Six ship systems can be damaged, shown as PESCLR: photons, engines, shields, computer, long-range scan and radio. Four skill levels run from Novice to Commander, and instead of a score the game ends with a rank such as "Garbage Scow Captain" or "Star Commander".
trivia: Neubauer took the idea of a galactic chart from the 1971 text game Star Trek; the Zylons' name came from Battlestar Galactica's Cylons.
In 2007 it was named to a ten-game video game canon submitted to the Library of Congress.
Joe Decuir linked its success to the decision to give the Atari 400 a keyboard.
The Atari 5200 version was the first game to use all 12 buttons on that console's controller.
Atari paid its developers no royalties for it.
devStory: Doug Neubauer, an engineer who had joined Atari from National Semiconductor and helped develop the POKEY sound chip, wrote it during a slow period in hardware design, with Jay Miner's blessing, over eight to ten months from early 1979. He took the galactic chart from the 1971 text game Star Trek, and with no existing 3D motion code to draw on, spent weeks deriving equations on paper without sine or cosine; a docking feature was cut to fit an 8 KB cartridge. Released in March 1980, it was called the first killer app computer game, and Byte said it was probably the greatest single contributor to sales of the Atari 400 and 800. It established conventions later used by Elite and Wing Commander.

title: Miner 2049er
description: Miner 2049er (1982) is Bill Hogue's Atari 8-bit platformer, in which Mountie Bounty Bob claims every floor of a uranium mine against the clock — ported to 22 systems.
longDescription: Bounty Bob, a Mountie, has chased a wanted criminal into a series of uranium mines. On each level he must walk over every part of every floor, which changes as he surveys it, before the timer at the top of the screen runs out, while avoiding gaps, radioactive waste and slow lifts. Transporters warp him to numbered doors, interconnected slides force him along a path, and a cannon has to be powered with TNT. Collecting prospecting gear such as candles and drills turns the mutants green and vulnerable to his touch, an idea Bill Hogue took from Pac-Man, while the climbing came from Donkey Kong. Bob has five lives, lost to mutants, long falls or the clock. The Atari computer version has ten levels, which needed a custom 16 KB cartridge, twice the size of Star Raiders' or Missile Command's.
trivia: Video magazine named it Electronic Game of the Year at the 5th Arkie Awards in 1984.
Retro Gamer counts 22 platforms that received a version, from the Atari 2600 and ColecoVision to the IBM PC and Game Boy.
Matthew Smith said it influenced Manic Miner.
Mike Livesay reverse-engineered the ColecoVision to build his own development kit for its version.
Video called it "the most widely played home electronic game of all time" in January 1984.
devStory:
Big Five Software in Van Nuys, California, had sold mail-order TRS-80 games, mostly arcade clones, before moving to the Atari for its colours and sound, and because cartridges were harder to pirate. Hogue designed the play first and the mining theme afterwards, named after the miners of the 1849 Gold Rush, and the team built their own circuit boards for the larger ROM. It came out in December 1982, and at least 15 companies were lined up to make versions; it appeared on 22 systems, a mass licensing campaign new to the industry. InfoWorld wrote in 1983 that it was "selling like crazy", and Micro Fun's ColecoVision version was reported as the year's top-selling video game.

Bounty Bob Strikes Back! followed in 1985, after which Big Five closed and Hogue left the industry.

title: Summer Games
description: Summer Games (1984) is Epyx's unofficial Olympics for up to eight players on the Commodore 64, the first in a long line of multi-event sports games.
longDescription: Up to eight players each choose a country and take turns competing for medals in events that vary between versions, among them the pole vault, platform diving, sprinting, gymnastics, freestyle swimming and skeet shooting. Medals score five points for gold, three for silver and one for bronze toward an overall winner, and most versions save world records to disk. Players can run through every event in turn, pick a few or just one, or practise. Without an official licence, the competition is presented as the "Epyx Games".
trivia: It sold more than 250,000 copies by November 1989.
Epyx followed it with Summer Games II, Winter Games, World Games and California Games, and the C64 version can link with Summer Games II.
A historian called the Games series "the most sustainedly popular in the long life of the Commodore 64".
Next Generation ranked the series 89th in its 1996 top 100 games.
It was re-released on the C64 Direct-to-TV in 2004.
devStory:
It grew out of Starpath's Supercharger game Sweat! The Decathlon Game, itself influenced by Microsoft's Olympic Decathlon. Epyx bought the struggling Starpath during development, but the 1983 crash killed all its Supercharger games, and several Starpath staff, including Sweat! programmer Scott Nelson, moved to Epyx and began a new decathlon game for the Commodore 64. Nelson, Stephen Landrum and Randy Glover were among its designers, and Glover wrote the music.

Epyx released it in 1984, the year of the Los Angeles Olympics, and Ahoy! called it "tremendously successful"; it sold more than 250,000 copies by 1989. Versions followed for the Apple II, Atari computers, Atari 2600 and 7800 and Master System, and Quicksilva, then U.S. Gold, published it in Britain.

title: Ghostbusters
description: Ghostbusters (1984) is David Crane's Commodore 64 film tie-in, a business game in which the player runs a ghost-catching franchise while the city's psychokinetic energy rises toward disaster.
longDescription: The player starts a Ghostbusters franchise with a sum of money, buying a car and equipment, then drives around a city map responding to hauntings. At each haunted building two Ghostbusters lay a trap and steer a Slimer into it; a miss slimes one of the team. Ghosts drifting toward Zuul's temple push the city's PK energy higher, and sometimes merge into the Stay Puft Marshmallow Man, who crushes a block of the city. The game ends when PK energy reaches 9999, and it is only won if the player has earned more than was spent on equipment.
trivia: Finishing the game gives an account number that starts a new game with the money already earned.
Crane added digitised speech from the film and a bouncing-ball sing-along to Ray Parker Jr.'s theme song.
devStory: Activision reportedly gave the team six weeks to make the game while the film was in cinemas, so Crane adapted a project he was already working on, a game called Car Wars that already had a resource-management side. It was released on the Commodore 64 on 26 October 1984 and sold over two million copies by 1989; it spent three months at the top of the UK chart in 1985 and remained Activision's best-selling Commodore game.

title: Wonder Boy in Monster Land
description: Wonder Boy in Monster Land (1988) is the Master System version of Westone's arcade sequel, which turned Wonder Boy into a platformer with gold, shops and upgradable equipment.
longDescription:
Eleven years after the first game, the evil King has returned as the MEKA Dragon, raised an army, enslaved Wonder Land's people with mind-controlling bracelets and hired the knights Red and Blue, turning it into Monster Land. Bock Lee Temjin, called Tom-Tom, who earned the title Wonder Boy by rescuing Tanya, sets out across twelve levels of towns, valleys, deserts, islands and castles to defeat it.

He starts with nothing but a sword and a revival potion from the mayor. Defeated enemies and hidden spots in trees and clouds give gold, which buys boots for higher jumps and faster running, armour, shields that repel shots and magic weapons — rolling bombs, fireballs, tornadoes and a thunder flash that hits every enemy on screen. Taverns and fortune tellers give hints, hospitals restore health and time, and boss rooms hold keys, gold or a better sword. Later shops are unmarked or invisible, and some doors hide traps. He has five hearts, and an hourglass drains them when it runs out.
trivia: On the PC Engine the game was turned into Bikkuriman World, and on the Famicom into Jaleco's Saiyūki World, each with different characters.
Computer and Video Games scored the Master System version 9/10.
Saiyūki World's unofficial sequel reached North America as Whomp 'Em.
The ZX Spectrum version uses a candle instead of an hourglass.
Its ending sets up Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap.
devStory:
Ryuichi Nishizawa and Michishito Ishizuka, two of the three founders of Escape, later renamed Westone, created it, aiming to fuse arcade action with role-playing in the manner of The Black Onyx, Wizardry and Dragon Quest; Nishizawa disliked earlier hybrids such as The Tower of Druaga, complaining that there was no one to talk to in their dungeons. Shinichi Sakamoto composed the music. The arcade game, on Sega's System 2 board, came out in Japan in July 1987 and sold slowly at first before becoming a decent seller.

Sega's Master System version came out in Japan on 31 January 1988 and in North America that August. Dragon called it "a good game with a bad name", and IGN later listed it among seven Master System games players need.

title: Donkey Kong
description: The ColecoVision's Donkey Kong (1982) was the first home version of Nintendo's arcade hit, packed in with every console and praised as the most faithful arcade conversion of its day.
longDescription: As in the arcade original, a carpenter — the character who would become Mario — climbs girders and ladders, jumping barrels thrown by Donkey Kong, to rescue a woman held at the top of the screen. Coleco built its new console's launch around the game: every ColecoVision came with the cartridge, and the console was positioned as offering a closer arcade experience than the Atari 2600 or Intellivision. A 1983 Creative Computing review called it 'the most faithful adaptation of the original video game I have seen'.
trivia: Coleco's Eric Bromley negotiated the licence with Nintendo's Hiroshi Yamauchi, who reportedly asked for $200,000 up front that day plus $2 for every unit sold.
After Universal's president threatened to sue over the home version, Coleco agreed to pay Universal royalties of 3% of the game's net sale price.
devStory: The ColecoVision went on sale in August 1982 with Donkey Kong as its pack-in, and Coleco sold more than 500,000 consoles by Christmas, helped by the game. The bundled version eventually sold 2 million units. Coleco also released versions for the Atari 2600 and Intellivision.

title: Smurf: Rescue in Gargamel's Castle
description: Smurf: Rescue in Gargamel's Castle (1982) is Coleco's ColecoVision platformer, in which a Smurf walks and jumps from the village to Gargamel's castle to free Smurfette.
longDescription: Gargamel has kidnapped Smurfette, and the player guides a Smurf from the Smurf village through a forest and a cave to the wizard's castle. Each side-scrolling screen holds obstacles to jump — fences, stalagmites and ledges — and a mistimed jump means instant death. An energy bar slowly runs down throughout, and higher difficulty settings add crows, flying bats and spiders. The background music includes "Simple Gifts" and the first movement of Beethoven's Sixth Symphony, the "Pastoral".
trivia: Moving back and forth between two particular forest screens awards hundreds of thousands of points — one of several Easter eggs in the ColecoVision version.
It won Best Video Game Audiovisual Effects at the 4th Arkie Awards, and Video magazine judged its audiovisuals the best in the ColecoVision line.
Computer Entertainer said the Smurf was "nearly as well animated as the cartoons from which he is drawn".
Initials sometimes appear when moving between screens in the ColecoVision version.
Every missed jump is fatal.
devStory: Coleco based it on the Smurfs television series and released it for the ColecoVision in September 1982, a month after the console's launch, with an Atari 2600 version following in April 1983. Video magazine judged its audiovisuals the best in the ColecoVision line, likening the look to a Saturday-morning cartoon and calling its audio "sophisticated", but warned players to "prepare for frustration" until they learned to judge the leaps. Computer Entertainer gave it four stars for play and graphics and called it "a must" for Smurfs fans, finding the 2600 version less elegant but still an excellent conversion, and Creative Computing called it "truly good fun" for young children and older ones alike.

title: Highly Responsive to Prayers
description: Highly Responsive to Prayers (1997) is the first Touhou Project game: ZUN's PC-98 Arkanoid-style game that introduced the shrine maiden Reimu Hakurei and sold about 30 copies.
longDescription: After her shrine is destroyed, Reimu Hakurei, the shrine maiden of Hakurei Shrine, passes through a gateway into another world to find those responsible. Unlike the shooters that followed, the game plays like Arkanoid: Reimu bounces a Yin-Yang Orb around the screen, swinging her gohei and throwing ofuda, aiming to flip every card on the stage. If time runs out, bullets rain down from above. There are 20 stages with a boss every fifth, and after stage 5 the player chooses between the Makai and Hell routes, each with its own stages, bosses and ending.
trivia: It introduced two Touhou fixtures: the bomb and the four difficulty levels, Easy, Normal, Hard and Lunatic.
According to ZUN, it sold about 30 copies.
Its sequel, Story of Eastern Wonderland, sold about 50.
Japanese fans call the five PC-98 games the "old works".
ZUN still writes, draws, programs and scores the Touhou games himself.
devStory: Jun'ya "ZUN" Ōta made it, handling programming, graphics, writing and music, while studying at Tokyo Denki University, and published it through his student club, Amusement Makers. He began in 1995 and first showed it in November 1996 before its release at Comiket 52. It was the first of five Touhou games on the PC-98, built for its graphics and six-channel FM sound; the second, Story of Eastern Wonderland, introduced the bullet-hell play the series is known for. The series moved to Windows with Embodiment of Scarlet Devil in 2002 and grew to 20 main games, recognised by Guinness in 2010 as the most prolific fan-made shooter series.

title: Princess Maker 2
description: Princess Maker 2 (1993) is Gainax's PC-98 raising simulation, in which the player schedules a daughter's lessons, jobs and adventures from age 10 to 18 — with 74 possible endings.
longDescription:
A nameless warrior defeats the Demon King in single combat and settles in the capital, where a shooting star brings him a ten-year-old girl from the heavens to raise. The player brings her up to eighteen, planning her life one month at a time in three periods, with advice from the butler Cube. Each period goes to classes in academics, art, religion, fighting or magic; to part-time jobs that open up as she grows, with promotions for streaks of success; to adventures across four maps, where defeat is never fatal; or to free time, holidays and rest, which she needs to avoid falling ill.

Rival girls appear at work and in October's festivals — fighting tournaments, dances, art shows and cooking contests — and her star sign, diet, clothes and even her drawings on the bedroom wall change as she grows. At eighteen she chooses a career, from queen or general to barmaid, and the game ends on one of 74 possible outcomes.
trivia: An English MS-DOS version was finished and sent out for review, but cancelled in 1996 when the company making it, IntraCorp, went bankrupt. It later leaked online.
It sold 30,000 copies by September 1993, and Gainax received 10,000 fan letters.
The FM Towns version added voice acting by Hiroko Kasahara.
Wired praised it in 1997 as a departure from violent PC games.
Source code for the PC-9801 version was partly released in 2025.
devStory:
Gainax, also known for Neon Genesis Evangelion, made it as the second Princess Maker. Takami Akai said the sequel answered complaints that the first was repetitive with more events, reactions and ways to succeed; he considered starting with an infant but decided against it, and described it as "a long-term game where you make a commitment and create your own world". It was expected in autumn 1992 and came out for the PC-9801 on 15 June 1993, followed by MS-DOS, FM Towns, PC Engine, Saturn, 3DO and Windows versions; Masahiro Kajihara composed the music.

It sold 30,000 copies by September 1993 and was Comptiq's most popular computer game in January 1994, though some critics objected to its sexual allusions. The 2004 remaster Refine reached English-speaking players on Steam in 2016.

title: Panzer Dragoon Saga
description: Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998) is Team Andromeda's four-disc Saturn role-playing game, in which the mercenary Edge rides a shape-shifting dragon — critically adored, barely printed and never re-released.
longDescription: The series' rail-shooting gives way to a role-playing game. Edge, a young mercenary guarding an Empire excavation of Ancient Age ruins, finds a girl, Azel, buried in a wall, before the mutinous Black Fleet under Craymen attacks, takes her, kills his companions and shoots him. A mysterious dragon rescues him, and he sets out for revenge. Edge is the only playable character, exploring on foot to talk, shop and upgrade his gun, and flying his dragon across canyons, deserts, forests and underground ruins. Random battles mix real time and turns: three action gauges fill continuously, and moving between quadrants around an enemy exposes weak points and avoids danger. The dragon's lasers hit several targets, Edge's gun one, and "berserks" work like magic. The dragon can be reshaped at any time, trading attack, defence, agility and spirit against each other. The game can be finished in under 20 hours.
trivia: Sega initially made 20,000 North American copies, which sold out in two days; Europe got about 1,000. English copies now sell for hundreds of dollars.
Director Yukio Futatsugi has said Sega lost the source code, which is one reason the game has never been re-released.
It is fully voiced, three years before Final Fantasy added voice acting in Final Fantasy X.
The motion-capture actor rode a dragon made of beer crates.
IGN called it the "best game no one played" in 2009.
devStory: Producer Yoji Ishiji proposed an RPG after the first Panzer Dragoon, and Sega told the team to make one that could outsell Final Fantasy VII. Directed by Yukio Futatsugi, who called it the hardest Panzer Dragoon to make, Saga was built by about 40 people — twice the team of Panzer Dragoon II Zwei — who wrote all the graphics code from scratch; Akihiko Mukaiyama designed the quadrant battle system, and Saori Kobayashi and Mariko Nanba composed the music. Development was tense, and two staff members died. Released in Japan on 29 January 1998 on four discs, it sold poorly as Sega moved on to the Dreamcast, but its 92% GameRankings average is the highest of any Saturn game.

title: Radiant Silvergun
description: Radiant Silvergun (1998) is Treasure's vertical shooter with seven weapons that level up permanently through colour-chained kills — the Japan-only Saturn game that became a byword for rare and expensive.
longDescription: The ship starts with three weapons — a forward laser, homing shots and a spread gun — each on its own button. Pressing two at once fires three more attacks: a rear laser, a homing plasma beam and short-range missiles. All three together swing a sword that absorbs certain enemy bullets and charges a screen-clearing attack. Enemies come in red, blue and yellow, and destroying the same colour in a row builds chains that score heavily and level up whichever weapon made the kill, with upgrades kept for the rest of the game. The story, set in 2520 after an ancient robot triggers a catastrophe, is told through animated scenes and loops back on itself.
trivia: Hidden dogs throughout the game give bonus points and unlock options when shot.
Its spiritual successor, Ikaruga (2001), was originally subtitled Radiant Silvergun 2.
devStory: Hiroshi Iuchi directed a team of about ten at Treasure, a studio known for console action games, with music by Hitoshi Sakimoto. It appeared in Japanese arcades on 28 May 1998 and on the Saturn that July, selling around 50,000 copies; it did not get a Western release until the Xbox 360 version in 2011.

title: Burning Rangers
description: Burning Rangers (1998) is Sonic Team's Saturn firefighting game, in which jetpack-equipped rescuers put out fires and save civilians, guided only by a voice on the radio.
longDescription: In a future where fire is the only remaining threat to human life, the Burning Rangers fight blazes and rescue trapped civilians; the player chooses Shou Amabane or Tillis. The four missions take place in a power plant, an underwater habitat, a space station and a spaceship in zero gravity, the last ending with the rescue of Iria Klein, who was sent into space in suspended animation with an incurable disease. Energy crystals dropped by extinguished fires work like the rings in Sonic the Hedgehog: one protects from a hit, and they are spent to teleport civilians to safety, five per rescue, while ten give a shield. There is no map; a navigator gives spoken directions through the building, which can be repeated. The player can jetpack, backflip, roll, swim and dive, each stage ends with a boss and a grade from S to D, and finishing the game unlocks a mode that shuffles the corridors into up to 3,125 routes.
trivia: Producer Yuji Naka wanted to make a game about rescuing people rather than killing them.
It uses the same engine as NiGHTS into Dreams.
Its working title was Firefighter.
The team researched it with a trip to Hong Kong and a visit to Universal Studios' Backdraft attraction, but never consulted real firefighters.
A firefighter at the Tokyo Game Show said the costumes were too thin.
devStory:
Directed by Naoto Ohshima and produced by Yuji Naka, it was made by a team of 31 from about November 1996, after Christmas NiGHTS, over about a year and a half. Naka wanted a game about rescuing people rather than killing them, and the team chose firefighters, whom Ohshima saw as heroes people could identify with; it was first conceived as a four-player online game, an idea later revisited in Phantasy Star Online. It was Sonic Team's first game with spoken dialogue, used no background music during play, and its cut-scenes were made by TMS Entertainment.

Sega released it in Japan on 26 February 1998, in North America on 28 May and in Europe on 19 June, among the last Saturn games. Critics praised its lighting and character designs but criticised its collision detection, glitches and short length.

title: Power Stone
description: Power Stone (1999) is Capcom's 3D arena fighter for the Dreamcast, where tables, chairs and bombs are weapons and collecting three Power Stones transforms a fighter.
longDescription:
In the 19th century, adventurers who believe in legends and myths fight each other for the Power Stone, said to make any dream come true. Ten fighters take part, among them the boxer Edward Falcon, the chef Wang-Tang, the swordsman Ryoma, the kunoichi Ayame, the fortune teller Rouge, the bandaged Jack and the heavyweight Gunrock, with the pirate Kraken and the final boss Valgas unlockable.

Fights take place in fully 3D arenas the fighters can roam freely, picking up and fighting with tables, chairs, rocks and bombs. Gems called Power Stones appear during the fight, and a fighter who gathers three transforms into a powered-up form with two super attacks, one long-range and one close-range or a grab, until the power bar drains. A match ends when one fighter's life runs out.
trivia: Character art was by Akira Yasuda, the artist known as Akiman, and Hideki Ishikawa.
A manga and an anime series followed in 1999, and the sequel Power Stone 2 in 2000.
The footballer Thierry Henry named it his favourite Dreamcast game in a 1999 promotion.
Wang-Tang's powered-up moves resemble a Super Saiyan's.
Both games were included in Capcom Fighting Collection 2 in 2025.
devStory:
Tatsuya Nakae and Hideaki Itsuno directed it at Capcom, with Takeshi Tezuka producing, character art by Akira Yasuda and Hideki Ishikawa and music by Tetsuya Shibata. It ran on Sega's NAOMI arcade board and reached Japanese arcades and the Dreamcast in February 1999, arriving in North America that September.

Famitsu scored the Dreamcast version 34 out of 40, and Next Generation gave it five stars. It sold about 200,000 copies, and Power Stone 2 followed in 2000 with four-player fights.

title: Starglider
description: Starglider (1986) is Jez San's wireframe 3D flight game for the Atari ST and Amiga, fighting Egron invaders on the planet Novenia — the series that led Argonaut to build the Super FX chip.
longDescription: The planet Novenia was protected by a network of defence satellites, until the mechanised Egrons disguised their battleships as Stargliders, a flock of migratory space birds the satellites were programmed not to shoot, and slipped through. The player flies the only prototype fighter left, over the landscape in fast first-person wireframe 3D, to drive them out. It starts armed only with lasers; TV-guided missiles need a large amount of energy to launch and steer, which the fighter collects by skimming low over high-tension power lines. The backstory is told in a science-fiction novella by James Follett packed with the game, and most versions feature sampled speech by Rainbird's Clare Edgeley.
trivia: The Amiga version's title music by Dave Lowe used digitised samples as instruments, before tracker music became common.
Argonaut's work on Starglider led to its partnership with Nintendo on the Super FX chip that powered Star Fox.
An NES prototype, NESGlider, was shown to Nintendo in 1990, which told Argonaut to work on the Super Famicom instead.
Compute! said it was so realistic "you'll duck and squirm in your seat".
The ST and Amiga versions open with a short song with vocals.
devStory:
Jez San designed it with Rick Clucas at Argonaut Software, inspired by his love of Atari's 1983 Star Wars arcade game, and Rainbird published it on the Atari ST in 1986, with versions for many computers in 1987; Realtime Games and Solid Image made several of the conversions. Dave Lowe's Amiga title music used digitised samples as instruments, before tracker music became common.

Crash's readers voted it Game of the Year for 1986, and it sold close to 200,000 copies. Starglider 2, with filled polygons, followed in 1988.

title: Golvellius: Valley of Doom
description: Golvellius: Valley of Doom (1988) is Compile's Master System action-adventure, in which Kelesis fights through eight guarded regions of a valley to rescue Princess Rena.
longDescription: Princess Rena has gone into the Valley of Doom to find a rare herb to cure her father, the king, and the swordsman Kelesis goes in after her. Most of the game is top-down sword combat across eight regions — a valley, desert, graveyard, fields, swamp, beach, woods and forest — each but the fields ruled by a boss who must be defeated to move on. Secret chambers hidden around the valley open to give advice, better weapons and other items, and underground caverns switch between side-scrolling and top-down screens on the way to each boss's lair. The final area opens only once every boss has fallen, its location revealed by clues from the valley's people, though players with the aqua-boots can slip in early through an underground river.
trivia: Golvellius himself turns out to be a good creature possessed by a demon, who joins Kelesis after his defeat; the sequel the ending implies was never made.
Computer and Video Games scored the Master System version 87% in 1989.
A spin-off, Super Cooks, appeared on an MSX2 disk magazine in 1989.
The Master System version was ported to the iPhone in 2009.
devStory: Compile first released Golvellius on the MSX in Japan in April 1987 as Maou Golvellius. Sega licensed it in 1988 and published an enhanced version, with new graphics and different overworld and dungeon layouts, for the Master System in Japan that August and in North America in December as Golvellius: Valley of Doom. An MSX2 remake later that year reused much of the Master System art with different layouts. Computer and Video Games scored the Master System version 87% in 1989, and Computer Entertainer gave it seven stars out of eight.

title: Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic
description: Yume Kōjō: Doki Doki Panic (1987) is Nintendo's Famicom Disk System platformer made for a Fuji Television event — the game that was reworked into the Western Super Mario Bros. 2.
longDescription: Doki Doki Panic was a promotional game built around the mascots of Fuji Television's Yume Kōjō '87 event: Imajin, Lina, Mama and Papa, who enter a storybook world with an Arabian theme. Instead of stomping on enemies, which does not defeat them, the characters pull vegetables out of the ground and pick up and throw enemies and objects. Each of the four plays differently in speed, strength and jumping, and the game has to be finished with every one of them. The music is by Koji Kondo.
trivia: Its design began as a two-player, vertically scrolling prototype by Kensuke Tanabe, which was shelved when Shigeru Miyamoto asked for horizontal scrolling.

Nintendo of America judged the Japanese Super Mario Bros. 2 too hard and too similar to the first game, so Doki Doki Panic was converted instead: Mario, Luigi, Toad and the Princess replaced the four mascots, a run button was added, and the game no longer had to be completed with every character.
devStory: Directed by Kensuke Tanabe and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto at Nintendo R&D4, the game was released for the Famicom Disk System in Japan on 10 July 1987. As Super Mario Bros. 2 it reached North America on 9 October 1988, and Japan eventually received that version too, as Super Mario USA, in 1992.

title: Famicom Detective Club: The Missing Heir
description: Famicom Detective Club: The Missing Heir (1988) is Nintendo's two-part Famicom Disk System mystery, designed by Yoshio Sakamoto, which stayed in Japan for 33 years.
longDescription:
A young man is found unconscious near a cliff by a man named Amachi, with no memory of who he is. He learns from Ayumi Tachibana that he is an assistant detective investigating the death of Kiku Ayashiro, and the case leads him to the Ayashiro estate in the village of Myoujin. A local saying holds that the dead return to kill anyone who steals the family's treasure, and he uncovers its link to a series of murders.

The player chooses commands such as Ask, Examine, Take, Show and Go, which appear only when they can be used; Examine and Take put a cursor over the scene. Dialogue appears in a box at the bottom of the screen, some answers have to be spelled out by scrolling through letters, and progress can be saved from the menu.
trivia: It was released in two parts on separate disks, in April and June 1988.
Its sequel, The Girl Who Stands Behind (1989), is a prequel set three years earlier.
Its composer is credited only as "Hiromi", thought to be a pseudonym.
A Game Boy Advance version came out in 2004 in the Famicom Mini series.
Ayumi Tachibana appears as a trophy in Super Smash Bros. Melee.
devStory:
Gunpei Yokoi asked Yoshio Sakamoto for the game, then called Famicom Shōnen Tanteidan, and it was Sakamoto's first work as a scenario writer; the scenario was first titled Corpse Village. Its inspirations were Enix's The Portopia Serial Murder Case and Seishi Yokomizo's mystery novels, such as The Inugami Clan, and co-writer Toru Osawa wanted packaging like Toho's posters for the Yokomizo films. Satoru Okada directed it at Nintendo R&D1, and Tose worked on it uncredited.

It came out on the Famicom Disk System in two volumes, in April and June 1988, and Famitsu scored the first 29 out of 40. Mages remade both Famicom Detective Club games for the Switch in May 2021, with voiced dialogue, their first release in English.

title: Blue Lightning
description: Blue Lightning (1989) is Epyx's After Burner-style jet combat game and one of the Atari Lynx's North American launch titles, built to show off the handheld's sprite scaling and rotation.
longDescription: A rookie pilot from the US Air Force's Flight Command squadron flies the Blue Lightning, a prototype fighter the Pentagon uses to break through enemy territory and help allies in the war. Seen from behind, as in Sega's After Burner, which inspired it, the game runs across nine missions of increasing difficulty in different places with different tasks. Missiles are limited, with a machine gun to fall back on, and the six planes in reserve serve as lives; losing one restarts the mission. The game leans heavily on the Lynx's hardware sprite scaling and rotation to create its pseudo-3D effect.
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly named it the Lynx's Handheld Game of the Year for 1990.
Attention to Detail remade it for the Atari Jaguar CD, where it was a pack-in game in 1995.
Its name was probably inspired by Blue Thunder.
Its ROM-streaming technique was later reused in Zarlor Mercenary.
IGN's Robert A. Jung called it a "blue-ribbon winner" in 1999.
devStory:
Stephen Landrum and artist Arthur Koch conceived it as a commissioned pseudo-3D flight game for the Handy, as the Lynx was first called, and drew on After Burner after visiting local arcades. Landrum first wanted a first-person cockpit shooter, until Koch made the views third-person. Chuck Sommerville, creator of Chip's Challenge, named it and built an animation engine for the intro, later reused in Electrocop and Todd's Adventures in Slime World, and the game broke a system rule by streaming data straight from ROM.

Shown alongside the system at the Summer 1989 CES, it was a North American launch title. Critics praised its visuals and its showcase of the Lynx's abilities but found the missions repetitive.

title: Gates of Zendocon
description: Gates of Zendocon (1989) is Epyx's Atari Lynx launch shooter: 51 'universes' joined by teleport gates, in search of the evil spider Zendocon.
longDescription: The evil spider Zendocon has trapped an unnamed space fighter in a web of 51 interconnected universes, linked by teleportation gates and full of alien bases, and the player blasts a way through his armies on a horizontally scrolling screen to find and defeat him. The route through the gates is non-linear. Aliens that Zendocon has enslaved can join the ship as allies and help protect it. Damage shows on the ship itself: it loses its laser tip, then its engine, before a final hit destroys it.
trivia: A hidden level awards points for shooting the faces of the game's creators.
Designer Peter Engelbrite began work before working Lynx hardware existed, writing an emulator on an Apple II first.
Alex Rudis made the hidden level's faces with a video camera, rotating his own portrait as it was scanned.
Atari proposed a Jaguar version on Bethesda's cancelled Protector engine, but Bethesda turned it down.
The Games Machine gave it 92.
devStory:
Peter M. Engelbrite wrote, designed and programmed it at Epyx, where he had also converted California Games, Summer Games and Winter Games to the Atari 2600. Work began before any Lynx hardware existed, so he wrote a Lynx emulator on an Apple II that showed sprites as ASCII text; later an early Lynx revision ran it, slowly. Robert Vieira and Alex Rudis composed the music.

Shown with the Lynx at the 1989 Summer CES, it was a North American launch title that year, alongside California Games, Blue Lightning and Electrocop. Reviews were mostly positive, praising its presentation and originality; STart's Clayton Walnum found it shallow, while IGN called it "a good buy".

title: Gex
description: Gex (1995) is Crystal Dynamics' 3DO platformer starring a wisecracking, television-obsessed gecko trapped in the Media Dimension, which sold about 750,000 copies on the 3DO.
longDescription:
Gex, a gecko who has inherited a mansion in Maui and watches far too much television, swallows a fly that turns out to be a drone of Rez, overlord of the Media Dimension. Rez pulls him through the TV to make him his network's mascot, and Gex has to find remotes to destroy the sets blocking his way out. The 24 levels are spread across five worlds themed on TV channels, each ending in a boss, and hidden remotes open more levels; perfect runs earn pieces of a remote for the secret world Planet X.

Gex whips enemies, switches and projectiles with his tail, coils it to bounce, and climbs walls and ceilings with the suction pads on his feet. Power-ups, eaten with his tongue, give speed, invulnerability or projectiles, and 100 golden flies earn an extra life. Comedian Dana Gould voiced Gex and wrote all his one-liners.
trivia: GamePro named it Best 3DO Game at the 1994 Consumer Electronics Show, before release.
Next Generation reported about 750,000 copies of the 3DO version sold worldwide.
A designer was fired after playtesters found hidden messages, including a colleague's phone number, in a level.
The game ends with Gex back home, wondering what is on HBO.
Limited Run Games released the Gex Trilogy in 2025.
devStory:
Lyle Hall conceived it in 1993, soon after Crystal Dynamics was founded, as a 3DO mascot to rival Mario and Sonic. The first idea starred a stunt performer called Gecko X against Karl Chameleon in film-themed levels, before lead programmer Gregg Travers proposed a world of television. With only two artists, each level took about two months, and when the team missed its June 1994 target with less than half the game done, a planned science-fiction world was cut. Development took about 21 months.

It reached the 3DO in North America on 7 April 1995 and was later bundled with some consoles. EGM named it Best 3DO Game of 1995, and Beam Software's PlayStation and Saturn versions followed that December.

title: Cybermorph
description: Cybermorph (1993) was the Atari Jaguar's North American pack-in game: a polygonal flight shooter in which a morphing fighter recovers pods across 40 planets, guided by the AI voice Skylar.
longDescription:
The Pernitia empire has conquered planets across several sectors with self-repairing robot technology, and the resistance's new weapons, supplies and frozen fighters have been seized and sealed in pods. The player flies the TransmoGriffon, a shape-shifting prototype fighter carried between planets by cruisers, to win them back across five sectors of eight planets each. Each planet opens with a briefing, and collecting enough pods opens the exit; pod carriers flying them into antimatter vortex towers destroy them, and losing too many aborts the mission. Each sector ends with a boss, and later ones add teleporters, force fields and spikes guarding the pods.

The game is played in the third person, with a first-person view available. Weapons dropped by enemies and cargo carriers change the ship's shape, crashing into mountains damages it and hitting a building destroys it outright. There is no time limit, and a password records progress. Skylar, the ship's computer, comments in sampled speech voiced by Victoria Lowe.
trivia: Its engine began as a landscape demo that Attention to Detail wrote in 11 days for the never-released Konix Multisystem, based on David Braben's Zarch.
The 1994 reissue shrank the cartridge from 2 MB to 1 MB, dropping the intro animation, the music and some of Skylar's lines.
Fewer than 2,000 copies had been sold separately from the console by April 1995.
One level designer named two levels after his daughters.
It was re-released for the first time in Atari 50 in 2022.
devStory:
Attention to Detail, founded in 1988 by graduates of the University of Birmingham, had built an operating system, tools and demos for the Konix Multisystem, including a 3D landscape demo based on David Braben's Zarch written in 11 days. Atari liked the demo, and it became the basis of Cybermorph; Brian Pollock wrote the 3D engine and a map editor that turned each map into a seed for a fractal algorithm. Atari's testers designed the levels while ATD laid down terrain and enemies, and memory limits turned the planned animated intro and ending into still images. It drew Gouraud-shaded polygons, about 400 to 600 at a time, at 10 to 18 frames per second.

Unveiled in August 1993, it shipped with the Jaguar in North America on 23 November 1993, replacing Trevor McFur as the pack-in. Critics were divided, praising its shading and variety but finding the pod collecting repetitive and comparing it unfavourably with Star Fox.

title: Star Castle
description: Star Castle (1980) is Cinematronics' vector shooter, in which a ship chips away at three rotating shield rings to destroy the cannon at their centre — the game Yars' Revenge was built from.
longDescription:
An enemy cannon sits at the centre of three rotating rings of shields, each of twelve sections that take two hits apiece. The player's ship rotates, thrusts and fires small shots, and must blast a gap through the rings to hit the cannon, which tracks the ship constantly and, once the rings are open, fires a large white-noise blast. Three tiny homing mines chase the ship and destroy it on contact; they are hard to hit and worth no points. Destroying the outer ring prompts the cannon to rebuild: the middle ring moves out, the inner ring takes its place and a new ring emerges from the core.

Destroying the cannon collapses the rings and earns an extra ship, and the next level brings a new gun, faster rings, faster mines and sharper tracking. The game was drawn in black-and-white vector graphics, with a coloured plastic overlay turning the rings yellow, orange and red and the rest of the screen blue.
trivia: Atari's Howard Scott Warshaw, asked to port it to the 2600, reworked its ideas into Yars' Revenge instead.
It was Cinematronics' most successful game, selling more than 10,000 units.
Yars' Revenge, which grew out of it, became Atari's best-selling original 2600 game.
Clones included Ring Raiders for the Apple II and Star Island for the Atari 8-bit.
A hobbyist 2600 version was finally made in 2012.
devStory: Tim Skelly, who also designed Starhawk, Armor Attack and Rip Off, designed it at Cinematronics, and Scott Boden programmed it; Skelly said the background starfield was traced from the outline of a woman in a magazine. It was released in October 1980, and a Vectrex version followed in October 1983. Michael Blanchet's 1982 book How to Beat the Video Games called it "a standout among the wave of free-flight games that emerged after Asteroids", and Flux ranked it 83rd among the top 100 video games in 1995.

title: Jetpac
description: Jetpac (1983) is Ultimate Play the Game's first home computer game: Jetman assembles and fuels a rocket while fighting off aliens, on a 16K ZX Spectrum. It sold over 300,000 copies.
longDescription: Jetman, an astronaut with a jetpack, has to put his rocket back together from parts scattered around the screen, then collect fuel for it, all while waves of aliens attack. The world wraps around horizontally and has three platforms. Once the rocket is fuelled he can board it and fly to the next planet. Falling treasures can be caught for bonus points. The aliens change form every level, each with its own movement pattern, cycling back after eight levels, and every four levels the rocket resets and must be rebuilt, bringing an extra life and a new design with a higher number.
trivia: It won Game of the Year at the 1983 Golden Joystick Awards.
Jetpac reappeared as an unlockable minigame inside Donkey Kong 64 (1999), and in Rare Replay (2015).
A remake, Jetpac Refuelled, came to Xbox Live Arcade in 2007.
Crash ran a Lunar Jetman comic strip from 1984 to 1991.
Retro Gamer's readers ranked it 14th among the best games of all time.
devStory:
Tim and Chris Stamper founded Ultimate Play the Game in Ashby-de-la-Zouch in 1982 with Tim's wife, Carol; Chris programmed Jetpac and Tim drew the graphics, for a 16K ZX Spectrum. It was the company's first game, released in 1983 for the Spectrum and VIC-20 and in 1984 for the BBC Micro, and a ROM version for the ZX Interface 2 loaded almost instantly. It topped the first Spectrum sales chart published by Computer and Video Games, which scored it 9 out of 10, and sold over 300,000 copies, bringing in £1 million.

Ultimate later became Rare. Lunar Jetman followed in 1983 and Solar Jetman on the NES in 1990.

title: Gods
description: Gods (1991) is the Bitmap Brothers' platform game, in which Hercules fights through four guardians to win back the citadel of the gods — with a score by John Foxx as Nation 12.
longDescription: Four guardians have seized the citadel of the gods, who promise any hero who wins it back a single favour; the hero asks for a seat among them, and the gods take comfort in expecting him to fail. Across four levels, each ending with a guardian boss, progress needs precisely timed jumps, and careful planning pays off better than rushing. Puzzles with levers and objects sometimes require backtracking, and the inventory holds four items. Up to three of each weapon can be used at once, with an adjustable spread, alongside bouncing axes and fireballs. The enemies adapt to the player's position and skill, and small thieves dart out of walls to grab out-of-reach items, which can be recovered by shooting them at the right moment. Between levels a trader sells weapons and items for the jewels and bags of treasure collected.
trivia: John Foxx, recording as Nation 12, performed the music, and Simon Bisley painted the box art.
Computer Gaming World named it one of the top four action games of 1992.
Little thieves steal items the player cannot reach, unless shot at the right moment.
The game gives the player bonuses for playing badly, to help them along.
Licensing restrictions ended sales of Gods Remastered in 2022.
devStory:
Eric Matthews and Steve Tall designed it at the Bitmap Brothers, with Tall programming and Mark Coleman drawing the graphics in SpriteFX. As usual for the studio, an outside musician wrote the score: John Foxx, as Nation 12, and the comic artist Simon Bisley painted the box. Renegade released it in Europe and Mindscape in North America in 1991. Computer and Video Games, CU Amiga and The One gave it 93%, and Computer Gaming World named it one of the top four action games of 1992.

Mega Drive, Super NES, Archimedes and PC-98 versions followed, the consoles running noticeably faster and harder. Gods Remastered came out in 2018.

title: Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe
description: Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe (1990) is the Bitmap Brothers' violent future sport, a blend of handball and ice hockey in which the underdog team Brutal Deluxe fights its way up the league.
longDescription: The first Speedball league, founded in 2095, collapsed amid violence and corruption, and the sport went underground until Speedball 2 was set up five years later to win back the public. The game begins in 2105 with a new team, Brutal Deluxe, in a violent sport that mixes handball and ice hockey, with nine players a side instead of the original's five. Matches last 180 seconds in two halves. A goal is worth 10 points, raised to 15 or 20 by lighting the multiplier ramps on the walls, and floor and wall targets give bonuses — but injuring an opponent scores as much as a goal. Injured players are replaced from a bench of three substitutes, and once they are all hurt the injured have to play on. There are knockout, cup, league, practice and two-player modes.
trivia: Its soundtrack, by Simon Rogers with Richard Joseph, won Best Soundtrack at the 1991 Golden Joystick Awards.
Amiga Power ranked it the third-best game of all time, and it has sold more than two million copies.
Injuring an opponent scores as many points as a goal.
Mega ranked it the seventh-best game of all time in 1994.
Jon Hare directed Speedball 2 HD in 2013.
devStory:
