The Bitmap Brothers made it as the sequel to 1988's Speedball, with Eric Matthews designing, Robert Trevellyan programming and Daniel Malone drawing, and music written by Simon Rogers and remixed by Richard Joseph; its concept recalls the 1975 film Rollerball. Michael Burdett voiced the ice cream seller, and Glenn Fabry painted the European cover. It came out for the Amiga and Atari ST in 1990 and was converted to the Mega Drive, Master System, Game Boy, Atari Jaguar and many others.

Amiga Power ranked it the third-best game of all time in 1991, and PC Gamer US the 24th-best computer game in 1994. It sold more than two million copies and was remade several times, including Speedball 2100 for the PlayStation and an Xbox Live Arcade version in 2007.

title: Dragon Quest
description: Dragon Quest (1986) is Yuji Horii's Famicom role-playing game, drawn by Akira Toriyama and scored by Koichi Sugiyama, often credited with setting the template for Japanese console RPGs. North America got it in 1989 as Dragon Warrior.
longDescription: A lone hero sets out across the land of Alefgard to rescue Princess Gwaelin from the Dragonlord, who has stolen the Ball of Light and plunged the land into darkness. Only after the princess is saved does the game reveal its true objective. The world is open to explore, and its monsters grow tougher the further the hero travels from the castle. Battles are turn-based and seen in first person, with four commands: fight, run, spell and item. Nintendo's North American version replaced the Japanese password system with battery-backed saves.
trivia: The North American title changed to Dragon Warrior to avoid a trademark conflict with the tabletop game DragonQuest.
Nintendo Power gave the game away with subscriptions in 1990, bringing in nearly 500,000 new subscribers.
It won several 1986 Famitsu awards, including Game of the Year.
devStory: Chunsoft developed the game for Enix, with Yuji Horii as designer and writer, Koichi Nakamura directing, Akira Toriyama on art and Koichi Sugiyama on music. It was released for the Famicom in Japan on 27 May 1986 and sold about 1.5 million copies there, and more than 2 million worldwide. It was later remade for the Super Famicom, the Game Boy Color and, in 2025, in HD-2D.

title: Mother
description: Mother (1989) is Shigesato Itoi's Famicom role-playing game set in a late-20th-century America, with baseball bats and psychic powers in place of swords and magic. Its finished English version was shelved, and it finally appeared in the West in 2015 as EarthBound Beginnings.
longDescription: In the early 1900s a married couple vanishes; the husband, George, returns two years later, but his wife, Maria, never does. In 1988 a poltergeist attacks the home of Ninten, whose great-grandfather studied psychic powers, and Queen Mary of Magicant asks him to collect the eight melodies of a song. Ninten is joined by Lloyd, a bullied child prodigy, and Ana, a psychic girl, both about 11 or 12, and by Teddy, a gang leader out to avenge his parents. The heroes fight hippies, zombies, possessed objects, robots and aliens with baseball bats, toy guns, frying pans and PSI powers, in first-person battles against random encounters, travel between towns by train and save by phoning Ninten's father. In the end, Mary is revealed to be Maria, who raised the alien Gyiyg, and on Holy Loly Mountain the party sings him a lullaby.
trivia: Itoi took the title partly from John Lennon's song "Mother", and also from "mothership".
An English localisation, Earth Bound, was finished in 1990 but shelved; a prototype cartridge surfaced in 1998 and circulated as EarthBound Zero.
Its 1994 sequel, Mother 2, reached the US in 1995 as EarthBound.
Critical hits display the word "SMAAAASH!!".
Its soundtrack album was recorded in Tokyo, London and Bath.
devStory:
The copywriter Shigesato Itoi became interested in role-playing games after playing Dragon Quest and pitched "ESP1" to Shigeru Miyamoto, who asked him to simplify it; Itoi reportedly cried on the train home. Miyamoto then assembled a team, and Itoi directed and wrote it over about two years, drawing on Poltergeist and Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Keiichi Suzuki and Hirokazu Tanaka wrote the music for the Famicom's three-note sound. Released on 27 July 1989, it sold about 400,000 copies, the sixth best-selling game of 1989 in Japan, and Famitsu awarded it 31 out of 40.

Phil Sandhop led an English version, Earth Bound, finished in September 1990 but shelved, and the game finally reached the West as EarthBound Beginnings in 2015.

title: Lemmings
description: Lemmings (1991) is DMA Design's puzzle game in which green-haired creatures walk straight into danger unless the player assigns them jobs; it sold an estimated 15 million copies.
longDescription:
Trap doors release a steady line of green-haired, blue-robed lemmings, who walk straight ahead whatever lies in their path. The player has to get a required share of them to the exit within a time limit by assigning eight skills in limited numbers: climbers, floaters, bombers, blockers, builders who lay 12-step stairways, bashers, miners and diggers. Lemmings die from long falls, water, lava, traps and walking off the screen, and bombers explode after five seconds. The release rate can be raised but not lowered below the level's setting, and the "nuke" button turns every remaining lemming into a bomber.

The original 120 levels are split into four difficulty ratings, Fun, Tricky, Taxing and Mayhem, and there are 20 two-player levels on a split screen, using the Amiga's ability to run two mice at once, where each player tries to get more of their own lemmings home.
trivia: The game started when Mike Dailly animated tiny 8×8 pixel figures in Deluxe Paint and Russell Kay said, "There's a game in that!"
In 2004 Graham Cormode proved that deciding whether a Lemmings level can be solved is NP-hard.
Blizzard's Bob Fitch said it helped inspire Warcraft: Orcs & Humans.
Bronze lemming statues were installed in Dundee in 2013.
It was one of the games on a 2020 Royal Mail stamp series.
devStory:
The idea came when Mike Dailly, DMA Design's first employee, animated tiny 8×8 pixel figures in Deluxe Paint while working on another game, and Russell Kay said there was a game in it and coined the name. David Jones designed it and programmed it with Kay and Dailly, Gary Timmons smoothed the walking animation and drew the box art, and the team built hundreds of levels with a Deluxe Paint-based editor. Psygnosis had Tim Wright replace the original sampled music with arrangements of classical and traditional tunes.

Psygnosis released it on 14 February 1991, and it sold more than 55,000 copies on its first day on the Amiga. Computer Gaming World named it Action Game of the Year for 1992, and Next Generation ranked it second only to Tetris among puzzle games. Jones stopped counting after porting it to 20 systems.

title: Defender of the Crown
description: Defender of the Crown (1986) is Cinemaware's Amiga strategy game set in 12th-century England, where Saxon lords fight Normans for territory through sieges, jousts and raids, with art by James D. Sachs.
longDescription: England in 1149 is without a king, and rival factions fight over its territory. The player picks one of four Saxon lords — Wilfred of Ivanhoe, Cedric of Rotherwood, Geoffrey Longsword or Wolfric the Wild — and fights the Norman hordes and, eventually, rival Saxons for control of the land. Armies are raised and sent against enemy armies, castles are looted or besieged, and jousting tournaments can win territory outright. The player can also rescue a damsel in distress and call on Robin Hood for help. The strategy is a war of attrition: build bigger armies and strike at the right moment.
trivia: Computer Gaming World gave it an award for Artistic Achievement in a Computer Game in 1987.
In 1989 it became the second game to ship on CD-ROM, after The Manhole.
Some planned features were cut partly because of Cinemaware's financial strain.
Its cover was painted by Ezra Tucker, with hired models in rented costumes.
Rainbow Arts' Joan of Arc (1989) was directly inspired by it.
devStory:
It was Cinemaware's first game, designed by Kellyn Beeck, with graphics by James D. Sachs and music by Jim Cuomo; R.J. Mical said Sachs pushed the Amiga to its full potential. Financial strain made the company ship it without features such as catapult-launched fireballs, more castles and deeper strategy, some of which turned up in later versions, and the Atari ST version added a sword-fighting screen. It was first shown at the Los Angeles Commodore Show in September 1986 and released on 1 November.

Info said its graphics "have set new standards" though its play was the weak link, and Computer Gaming World likewise praised the art while finding the strategy simple. It was a commercial hit, selling more than a million copies by 2001.

title: Marble Madness
description: Marble Madness (1984) is Mark Cerny's isometric arcade game, played with a trackball, in which a marble is steered down six courses against the clock — Atari's first game programmed in C.
longDescription: The player guides a marble through six maze-like isometric courses against the clock, with a trackball in the arcade. Time left at the end of a race carries over, along with a set amount of extra time, and two players can race at once, each with their own clock and the winner earning bonus points and time. Objects, enemies and track surfaces make control harder as the courses progress. The first race, "Practice", is much shorter than the rest, and the fifth, "Silly", has polka-dot patterns and runs in the opposite direction.
trivia: It was among the first games with true stereo sound.
Around 4,000 cabinets were sold, and it briefly became the highest-earning arcade game.
A sequel, Marble Man: Marble Madness II, was planned for 1991 with seventeen courses but cancelled after poor location tests.
A planned motorised trackball was dropped because it did not grip the ball properly.
EGM ranked it the tenth-best arcade game of all time in 1997.
devStory:
Mark Cerny designed it at Atari and programmed it with Bob Flanagan over ten months, after a project based on Michael Jackson's Thriller was cancelled; Sam Comstock co-designed and animated the enemies. Cerny drew on miniature golf, racing games and M. C. Escher, and admired the 3D graphics of Battlezone and I, Robot. Written in C, it ran at 30 frames per second rather than 60, and its courses were stored as heightmaps and rendered by ray tracing, allowing shadows and anti-aliasing; Flanagan wrote a 3D physics model for the marble. It was the first arcade game with a Yamaha FM sound chip, generating music in time with play, composed by Brad Fuller and Hal Canon. Atari's management wanted a smiley face on the marble; the compromise was smiley traces on the cabinet art.

It came out in December 1984, and about 4,000 cabinets were sold. Cerny thought its short length gave it an arcade life of only about six weeks. Rare ported it to the NES.

title: Elevator Action
description: Elevator Action (1983) is Taito's spy game, in which Agent 17 works down a 30-storey building by elevator, collecting secret documents from behind red doors before escaping by car.
longDescription:
Agent 17, codename Otto, enters a 30-storey building at the roof and must reach the ground floor, riding elevators and escalators between floors. Secret documents behind red doors are worth 500 points each, and once all have been taken he escapes in a car waiting in the basement, earning 1,000 points for each level cleared up to 10,000; trying to leave early sends him back to the highest unopened door. Otto can jump, duck and fire up to three pistol shots at once, jump across an empty shaft and ride on an elevator's roof.

Enemy agents can be shot, jump-kicked at close range, crushed by elevators or killed by dropping a light fixture on them, and shooting a light plunges part of the building into darkness. Taking too long sets off an alarm that makes enemies more aggressive and elevators slower. Otto loses a life if he is shot, crushed or falls down an open shaft.
trivia: It was Taito's first game sold as a conversion kit in North America.
It was one of the five highest-grossing arcade games of 1984 in American street locations.
An Atari 2600 version was cancelled.
Elevator Action Returns followed in 1994, and the light-gun Elevator Action Death Parade in 2009.
A first-person spin-off, Spy Games: Elevator Mission, lost its licence after Square Enix bought Taito.
devStory:
Toshio Kono designed it at Taito, with music by Yoshio Imamura. Taito America's Mike Von Kennel called it a "top test piece" during location testing, and it was released in Japan in June 1983 and North America in July, Taito's first game sold as a conversion kit there; kit sales set a record for the company.

It was Game Machine's most successful new table arcade unit of July 1983, topped the table charts from September to November and stayed on them until March 1984. It won a Certificate of Merit at the 1985 Arkie Awards. Micronics converted it to the Famicom in 1985.

title: Rainbow Islands
description: Rainbow Islands (1987) is Taito's sequel to Bubble Bobble, in which Bubby and Bobby climb ten islands using rainbows as weapons and platforms while the sea rises below them.
longDescription:
Bubby and Bobby set out to defeat the Dark Shadow, the villain behind the events of Bubble Bobble, and save the Rainbow Islands. Each of the ten islands has its own theme and four rounds, and the heroes must climb to the top before the rising sea catches them; a map shows the islands before each one, and enemies grow faster on later islands. Rainbows serve as weapons, platforms and a way to collect items, and jumping on one drops it onto the enemies below, leaving a damaging trail. Power-ups make the player and the rainbows faster and add more rainbows.

Collecting seven small diamonds of different colours in a round earns a bonus, and the colour of each diamond depends on where a defeated enemy lands. Taking them in the right order opens a secret room at the end of each island with a permanent power-up, and the game has several endings and hidden scoring tricks.
trivia: The NES version replaced the main theme because it resembled "Over the Rainbow".
Amiga Power ranked it the best game of all time in its 1991 and 1992 top 100 lists.
A tougher Extra Version reshuffled the enemies and bosses and appeared in limited numbers in arcades.
The NES version swaps one island for one based on KiKi KaiKai.
The original arcade version was released outside Japan for the first time in 2024.
devStory:
Fukio Mitsuji designed it at Taito, with music by Hisayoshi Ogura, as the second of four arcade games in the Bubble Bobble series. Taito released it in Japanese arcades in October 1987, and it was Game Machine's second most successful table arcade unit that November and one of the ten highest-grossing arcade games of 1988 in Japan.

Graftgold converted it to the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Amiga and Atari ST for Ocean in 1989 and 1990. The Spectrum version topped the UK charts in May and June 1990 and again after a budget re-release, and Crash's readers voted it the best game of all time in 1991.

title: The Sentinel
description: The Sentinel (1986) is Geoff Crammond's 3D puzzle game for the BBC Micro, in which a Synthoid that cannot walk climbs a landscape by absorbing and creating objects, keeping out of the Sentinel's gaze.
longDescription: The player is a telepathic Synthoid that cannot walk. To climb from the lowest ground to the platform where the Sentinel stands, it absorbs objects for energy and spends it creating trees, boulders and new Synthoid shells, placing a boulder on a visible square, standing a shell on top and transferring its consciousness into it; it can only touch squares it can see. If the Sentinel's slowly turning gaze falls on the player's square, it drains energy, and running out ends the game. Later levels add Sentries, and either can turn a tree into a Meanie that forces a costly hyperspace jump. Every unit absorbed reappears as a tree somewhere on the landscape, so the total energy stays constant. Absorbing the Sentinel ends the level, and the more energy is left when the player hyperspaces away, the more levels are skipped; passwords save progress.
trivia: It won Best Original Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards.
The game has no ending: after the last level it loops back to level 1; Crammond said he never expected anyone to finish it.
A fake sequel, Monolith, was previewed as an April Fool's joke in 1995; the real sequel, Sentinel Returns, came out in 1998.
Your Sinclair ranked it seventh in its official top 100.
PC Format called it "straight out of left field".
devStory: Geoff Crammond created it for the BBC Micro, and Firebird published it in 1986, among the first home computer games with solid-filled 3D graphics. Crammond also did the Commodore 64 and Amstrad versions, Mike Follin converted it to the ZX Spectrum, Steve Bak to the Atari ST and Amiga, whose version has a sampled soundtrack by David Whittaker, and Mark Roll to the PC. In the US it was released as The Sentry. Zzap!64 gave it a Gold Medal without a numbered score, calling it exceptional software in a class of its own, and Next Generation later ranked it the 53rd best game of all time.

title: Exile
description: Exile (1988) is a BBC Micro action-adventure with a physics simulation of gravity, inertia, water and wind, in which a jet-packed explorer roams the caves of planet Phoebus — often cited as one of the earliest Metroidvania games.
longDescription: Mike Finn of the Columbus Force is sent to the planet Phoebus to help Commander David Sprake and the survivors of the disabled ship Pericles against Triax, a renegade genetic engineer known as the Exile, who steals a Destinator from Finn's ship at the start. Finn explores a single huge underground world with an upgradable jet pack and weapons, both powered by energy cells, and a teleport system pulls him back to a safe point he has chosen, or to his ship, when he is close to death. The game simulates gravity, inertia, mass, explosions, shockwaves, water, wind and fire, following Newton's laws, and many puzzles come from that physics: lifting a boulder across a windy shaft, or keeping water in a glass steady while a bird pushes him about. Creatures react to noise, see along lines of sight and remember where they last saw him. Challenges can be tackled in many orders, and some choices make the game impossible to finish.
trivia: To save memory, the BBC version used a reduced 128×128 screen and generated its world procedurally from a fixed seed.
Amiga Power named the Amiga version the best game of 1991.
Its personal teleporter has been described as a predecessor of Portal's.
On the Amiga, the imps in the caves cry out in imitation of Monty Python's "Ni".
It has never been released outside Europe.
devStory:
Peter Irvin, author of Starship Command, and Jeremy Smith, author of Thrust, wrote it for the BBC Micro and Acorn Electron, and Superior Software published it in 1988 with a novella by Mark Cullen. To fit the BBC Micro, they used a custom 128×128 screen mode and generated the world procedurally from a fixed seed, with some hand-designed areas, and the base game has no status display or text, signalling fuel and energy with chimes. It was Smith's last known game before his death in an accident.

Audiogenic published Commodore 64, Atari ST and Amiga versions from 1991, and Edge awarded it 10/10 in 2002. It is often cited as one of the earliest Metroidvania games.

title: Rogue
description: Rogue (1980) is the Unix dungeon crawler of procedurally generated levels, ASCII graphics and permanent death that gave the roguelike genre its name.
longDescription: The player, shown as an @ sign, descends through dungeon levels drawn in ASCII characters to fetch the Amulet of Yendor from the bottom and climb back to the surface, unable to return to earlier levels until the Amulet is found. Each level is a grid of up to three by three rooms, sometimes with dead ends or mazes, generated afresh every game, and the 26 kinds of monster, harder the deeper they lie, are each a capital letter. Movement uses the h, j, k and l keys, as in the vi editor, and play is turn-based. Death is permanent: the save file is erased when it is loaded, so players cannot reload after a mistake, a rule that came out of playtesting to stop save scumming.
trivia: Yendor is "Rodney" spelled backwards.
In 1983 a bot called Rog-O-Matic achieved a higher median score than 15 top Carnegie Mellon players.
Dennis Ritchie reportedly called it "the biggest waste of CPU cycles in history".
Jerry Pournelle named the IBM PC version his game of the month in Byte in 1984.
PC World ranked it sixth among the ten greatest PC games in 2009.
devStory: Michael Toy and Glenn Wichman wrote it as students at UC Santa Cruz, inspired by the 1971 Star Trek game, Colossal Cave Adventure and Dungeons & Dragons; Toy led the programming in C, Wichman named it, and Ken Arnold, whose curses library drew its display, later contributed. It appeared in the 4th BSD manual in 1980 and spread with BSD Unix. Toy and Jon Lane formed A.I. Design to sell an IBM PC version, and Epyx funded Macintosh, Amiga and Atari ST versions, but the commercial releases flopped, partly because they were essentially the free BSD game. Hack and Moria followed, and the roguelike genre is named after it.

title: Montezuma's Revenge
description: Montezuma's Revenge (1984) is Robert Jaeger's platform game in which Panama Joe searches a 99-room Aztec pyramid for treasure. Decades later it became a famous hard case for AI research.
longDescription:
Panama Joe explores the underground pyramid of Montezuma II, nine floors and 99 rooms below the entrance, to reach the Treasure Chamber in the centre of the lowest level. He scores by gathering jewels and killing enemies, collects keys for doors and torches, swords and amulets, and runs, jumps, slides down poles and climbs chains and ladders past skulls, snakes, spiders, laser gates, conveyor belts, vanishing floors and fire pits. The inventory has limited slots. The lowest floors are dark unless he has found a torch. In the Treasure Chamber he has a short time to leap between chains collecting jewels before dropping down a pole to the next level.

The game has nine difficulty levels, which open and block paths, add enemies, move items and darken more rooms, until level 9 is entirely dark; from level 5, an enemy that kills Panama Joe stays in play. Level 1 opens only the left half of the pyramid and level 2 only the right, and from level 3 the whole pyramid is open.
trivia: General game-playing AI algorithms failed at it in 2013; OpenAI made progress in 2018, and Uber's Go-Explore later handled it.
It had sold more than 600,000 copies by 1997.
Its title is slang for traveller's diarrhoea in Mexico.
The prototype used "Spanish Flea" as placeholder music.
A 40th Anniversary Edition in 2025 added a Director's Cut where Montezuma can finally be fought.
devStory: Robert Jaeger, who had already written a Pac-Man clone and other games for the Atari 800, was 16 when a friend, Mark Sunshine, suggested a Meso-American theme and the title, and showed the unfinished game at the 1983 Consumer Electronics Show with his father. That version had a giant King Montezuma who could stomp the player but not be beaten, half its rooms were empty, and it needed 48 KB and a disk drive. Parker Brothers quickly bought the rights, and Bob Halliday and Charlie Sebor of Base Two squeezed it onto 16 KB cartridges, replacing the boss with the treasure room, adding the difficulty levels and cutting the animated title screen. It came out in 1984 for the Atari 2600, Atari 8-bit, ColecoVision, Commodore 64 and other systems, and sold more than 600,000 copies by 1997.

title: Pool of Radiance
description: Pool of Radiance (1988) is SSI's first game based on the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons rules, set in the city of Phlan in the Forgotten Realms — the start of the Gold Box series.
longDescription:
The city of Phlan, on the northern shore of the Moonsea, has fallen into ruin, and its council recruits adventurers to clear out the monsters. The party starts in New Phlan, where three temples heal and resurrect for a price, a hiring hall offers extra companions and tavern gossip may or may not be true; council proclamations hide coded clues that must be read with the printed Adventurer's Journal. The first quests clear a slum block and Sokol Keep on Thorn Island, whose undead fall only to silver and magic, and the adventure widens to the Moonsea region before a final battle with Tyranthraxus, an evil spirit possessing an ancient dragon.

The player builds a party of up to six from six races and four classes — fighter, cleric, magic-user and thief — with non-humans able to multi-class. Exploration is in first person, while combat switches to a top-down view where fighters sweep through weak foes and thieves back-stab. Spells must be memorised each day, levels are bought by training in the city, and characters could be carried into the later Gold Box games.
trivia: It won the 1988 Origins Award for Best Fantasy or Science Fiction Computer Game.
The DOS and Mac versions used a code wheel both as copy protection and for in-game puzzles.
Its scenario was also published as the tabletop module Ruins of Adventure.
The 1992 NES version is the only one with a full soundtrack.
PC Gamer US ranked it the 43rd-best computer game ever in 1994.
devStory:
It was the first official Advanced Dungeons & Dragons computer game, with a scenario by TSR designers Jim Ward, David Cook, Steve Winter and Mike Breault, and was coded by SSI's Special Projects team under Chuck Kroegel. It took 35 people a year, and the main challenge was translating the AD&D rules exactly into a program; it was the first game on what became the Gold Box engine. SSI released it in June 1988 for the Commodore 64, Apple II and IBM PC.

It sold 264,536 copies for computers in North America, three times as many as Heroes of the Lance and SSI's best seller to that point. Computer Gaming World's reviewers were split, Ken St. Andre praising it while others found the combat long.

title: Day of the Tentacle
description: Day of the Tentacle (1993) is LucasArts' time-travel adventure and sequel to Maniac Mansion, in which three friends in three different eras work together to stop Purple Tentacle from taking over the world.
longDescription:
Five years after Maniac Mansion, Purple Tentacle, a mutant lab assistant of Dr. Fred Edison, drinks toxic sludge, grows flipper-like arms and decides to take over the world. His harmless brother Green Tentacle asks Bernard Bernoulli for help, and Dr. Fred sends Bernard and his friends Hoagie and Laverne a day back in time to switch off the Sludge-O-Matic. A fake diamond wrecks the time machine, and they are scattered: Hoagie lands 200 years in the past, where the Founding Fathers are writing the Constitution, Laverne 200 years in the future, where Purple Tentacle rules, and Bernard back in the present.

The player switches between the three and passes items between eras through the "Chron-o-Johns", portable toilets turned into time machines, so that a change in the past solves a puzzle in the future: a tentacle's medical chart becomes the design of the American flag, and the flag returns as a tentacle disguise. Hoagie works with Benjamin Franklin on a superbattery, and figures such as John Hancock, Thomas Jefferson and George Washington appear. It was the last SCUMM game with the classic verb-and-inventory panel, and the complete original Maniac Mansion can be played on a computer inside the game.
trivia: About 4,500 lines of dialogue were recorded for it at Studio 222 in Hollywood.
Adventure Gamers ranked it the best adventure game of all time in 2004.
Its art took inspiration from Chuck Jones's Looney Tunes cartoons.
Hoagie was based on a Megadeth roadie.
Double Fine's 2016 remaster lets players switch between the original and redrawn graphics.
devStory:
Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman, who had both assisted Ron Gilbert on Monkey Island, co-led it, their first time directing, with Gilbert and Gary Winnick helping on the early planning; Gilbert proposed the time travel. A character-selection system was dropped, cutting the playable cast from six to three. Larry Ahern drew concept art and Peter Chan the backgrounds, about two days each, inspired by Chuck Jones's cartoons. Voice work was added late, as CD-ROM sales grew, with about 4,500 lines recorded, and Peter McConnell, Michael Land and Clint Bajakian scored the present, future and past. It cost about $600,000.

LucasArts released it on 25 June 1993. Computer Gaming World named it Adventure Game of the Year, shared with Gabriel Knight, and its Charles Ardai said calling it a sequel to Maniac Mansion was like calling the space shuttle a sequel to the slingshot.

title: Alone in the Dark
description: Alone in the Dark (1992) is Infogrames' Lovecraft-inspired haunted-house game, often called the first 3D survival horror game, whose polygon characters and fixed cameras Resident Evil later adopted.
longDescription:
In 1925 Jeremy Hartwood, an artist and the owner of Derceto, a Louisiana mansion, kills himself. The player chooses Edward Carnby, a private investigator hired to retrieve a piano, or Emily Hartwood, Jeremy's niece, who believes the piano hides a secret note. Doors slam shut behind them and monsters attack in the attic. Derceto was built by the occultist pirate Ezechiel Pregzt, whose spirit lives on in a tree in the caverns beneath the house; Jeremy died so that Pregzt could not take his body, and now Pregzt wants the player's.

Most enemies can be fought with fists, feet and weapons found in the house, but some can only be beaten with a puzzle and others must simply be avoided. Inventory is limited by weight, and dropped items stay where they fall. Books in the library, including the Necronomicon, tell the backstory, though reading one or opening the wrong door can kill. The monsters — Deep Ones, Nightgaunts, Chthonians — each have their own theme. After the attic and third floor, the lower floors open up and can be explored more freely.
trivia: Shinji Mikami adopted its fixed-camera approach for Resident Evil (1996).
Working titles included In the Dark, Screams in the Dark and The Evil Fear.
Bonnell's original idea was a game in which matches gave brief glimpses of a dark environment.
Raynal left after Infogrames required its sequel to keep the same engine.
The final scene shows a zombie driving the player's car back to civilisation.
devStory:
Infogrames acquired the rights to adapt Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu in 1991. Programmer Frédérick Raynal, a fan of Dario Argento and George A. Romero, pitched a 3D horror game and built the engine in his spare time with artist Didier Chanfray; a proof of concept in September 1991 won approval, and the team grew from three to seven. Raynal said Argento and Romero mattered more than Lovecraft, whom he drew on for atmosphere and creatures. Chaosium later withdrew the licence. Bruno Bonnell insisted the credit read "Game created by Infogrames" rather than naming Raynal, which Raynal later called a major personal trauma.

It won Best Graphics, Most Original Game and Best French Game at the 1993 European Computer Trade Show, and was the second best-selling DOS game in March 1993. A CD version that year added voices.

sources.title: Alone in the Dark (1992 video game)

title: Grim Fandango
description: Grim Fandango (1998) is Tim Schafer's film-noir adventure set in the Land of the Dead, where Manny Calavera sells travel packages to departed souls. Critics loved it, but its weak sales helped end LucasArts' adventure games.
longDescription: Manny Calavera works as a travel agent for the Department of Death in the Land of the Dead, a retro-futuristic world styled on the 1950s. The story borrows from the Day of the Dead and from film noir, and was planned as a four-year journey, each year built from branches of puzzles. Its 3D characters move over pre-rendered backgrounds, and the original used tank controls. Players solve puzzles by collecting objects and talking to characters. Peter McConnell's score mixes jazz, big band and Mexican folk music.
trivia: Its GrimE engine was scripted in Lua, one of the first notable uses of the language in games.
The working title was Deeds of the Dead; The Long Siesta and Dirt Nap were also considered.
Adventure Gamers ranked it first in its 2011 list of the top 100 adventure games.
devStory: Tim Schafer directed and wrote the game on a budget of about $3 million, with Bret Mogilefsky programming and Peter Tsacle on art. It was released for Windows on 30 October 1998 and won several Adventure Game of the Year awards, but sold only 58,617 copies in the US by the end of the year. Double Fine released a remastered version in 2015.

title: Full Throttle
description: Full Throttle (1995) is Tim Schafer's biker adventure, in which gang leader Ben is framed for murder — the first LucasArts adventure to sell more than a million copies.
longDescription:
In the near future, Corley Motors is the last motorcycle maker in the country. Its vice president, Adrian Ripburger, murders the founder, Malcolm Corley, and frames Ben, leader of the Polecats biker gang. Ben teams up with Maureen, the mechanic who repairs his sabotaged bike and turns out to be Corley's illegitimate daughter, and with photographer Miranda's pictures of the murder, he jumps Poyahoga Gorge, survives a demolition derby staged by the Vultures and exposes Ripburger at the shareholders' meeting.

The game introduced a contextual pie menu shaped like the gang's emblem, with a skull's mouth to talk, eyes to examine and a hand to pick up, use or pull. Dialogue offers several choices, and between the puzzles come motorcycle fights with rival gangs. Failed action sequences simply reset rather than ending the game.
trivia: Mark Hamill voiced the villain Ripburger, and Roy Conrad voiced Ben.
Its soundtrack licensed songs by the rock band The Gone Jackals.
Two sequels were started, in 2000 and 2002, and both were cancelled.
Computer Gaming World's readers voted it Adventure Game of the Year for 1995.
Double Fine's 2017 remaster lets players switch between the original and remastered graphics.
devStory:
It was Tim Schafer's first project as lead writer and designer, after Day of the Tentacle; he said management hated his first pitch, but a revised one was approved. Inspirations included biker culture, Hunter S. Thompson's Hell's Angels and Kurosawa's Yojimbo, and a cut peyote sequence later became the basis of Psychonauts. Built on SCUMM with the INSANE engine for its video, it cost $1.5 million over a year and a half, and its cast were mostly professional actors, among them Mark Hamill and Kath Soucie.

LucasArts released it on 19 May 1995, its first game sold only on CD-ROM. It sold over a million copies against a target of about 100,000, scored 86 on Metacritic and was praised for its animation, voice acting and music, though many reviewers found it short and its puzzles easy.

title: Sam & Max Hit the Road
description: Sam & Max Hit the Road (1993) is LucasArts' adventure based on Steve Purcell's comics, in which the duo chase a stolen frozen Bigfoot across America's tourist traps.
longDescription:
Sam and Max, the Freelance Police, are sent by their unseen Commissioner to a carnival, where Bruno, a frozen Bigfoot, has escaped along with Trixie the Giraffe-Necked Girl, who turns out to be in love with him. The case takes them across the United States in their 1960 DeSoto, from the World's Largest Ball of Twine to a vortex controlled by giant underground magnets and bungee jumping off Mount Rushmore, and up against Conroy Bumpus, a Liverpudlian country singer who has captured Bruno.

The cursor cycles between walking, talking, looking, picking up and using, and conversation topics appear as icons. Max can be used like an item, usually on characters where violence solves the problem. A map of the US shows new destinations as the story unlocks them, and minigames include a whack-a-mole game with live rats and a car-themed Battleship. Sam and Max cannot die or reach a dead end.
trivia: PC Gamer called it "still the best graphic adventure for the PC, hands down" in 1998.
Snuckey's parodies the Stuckey's roadside chain, and Frog Rock was based on a real attraction.
It was the first LucasArts game to use storyboarding.
A petition of 32,000 signatures followed the cancellation of Sam & Max: Freelance Police in 2004.
Purcell said LucasArts let him stay close to his vision despite its edgier material.
devStory:
Steve Purcell created Sam and Max in 1987 comics, and after joining LucasArts drew them as test material for SCUMM programmers and in the company newsletter; LucasArts offered to make a game in 1992. Sean Clark and Michael Stemmle directed it, with Purcell and Collette Michaud among the designers, adapting Purcell's 1989 comic On The Road on a planned eight-month schedule. It compressed the verbs into the cursor and moved the inventory to a separate screen. Clint Bajakian, Michael Land and Peter McConnell wrote the score using iMUSE, and the CD version added full speech, with Bill Farmer as Sam and Nick Jameson as Max.

It came out for MS-DOS in November 1993. Edge gave it 9/10, praising its humour and puzzles though not its minigames, and Purcell said it sold well, a hit by most standards. Two LucasArts sequels were cancelled, and Telltale Games took over the series in 2005.

title: The 7th Guest
description: The 7th Guest (1993) is Trilobyte's puzzle game set in the haunted Stauf mansion, with pre-rendered 3D rooms and live-action video. It shipped only on CD-ROM and is credited, with Myst, with selling CD-ROM drives.
longDescription:
In 1935 the drifter Henry Stauf kills a woman for her purse, begins carving dolls after strange visions and becomes a successful toymaker, until the children who own his toys fall ill and die. He builds a mansion at the edge of town and vanishes. The player, an amnesiac called Ego, wakes inside it and sees visions of one night when six guests — Martine Burden, Edward and Elinor Knox, Julia Heine, Brian Dutton and Hamilton Temple — were invited, while Stauf waited for a seventh: Tad, a boy who had entered the house on a dare. Ego turns out to be Tad's spirit.

Twenty-one puzzles of increasing difficulty unlock the video scenes, with Stauf taunting the player throughout: dividing a cake into six equal pieces, chess problems, mazes, word puzzles and an Ataxx-like board game. The hint book in the library gives clues twice and solves the puzzle outright on the third use. It was the first graphic adventure at 640×320 in 256 colours.
trivia: Bill Gates called it "the new standard in interactive entertainment".
It won Electronic Entertainment's 1993 Breakthrough Game award.
Its sequel, The 11th Hour, followed in 1995.
The mansion's exterior was based on the Nunan House in Jacksonville, Oregon.
A Kickstarter for The 7th Guest 3: The Collector failed in 2013.
devStory:
Designer Rob Landeros and programmer Graeme Devine pitched it to Virgin Games' Martin Alper and left to found Trilobyte with Virgin's help. Matthew Costello wrote the story from their design, and George "The Fat Man" Sanger composed the score. Devine's GROOVIE engine streamed from CD-ROM — "CD-ROM is bloody slow", he said — and a plan to film the house in live action gave way to pre-rendered 3D; the graphics took over two years and $500,000. The imperfect bluescreen footage left ghostly halos, which were kept. The puzzles came from 19th-century puzzle books.

Virgin published it for DOS on 28 April 1993. It sold 450,000 copies in its first year and over a million by 1995, more than Myst at the time, and with Myst is credited with popularising CD-ROM drives.

title: Syndicate
description: Syndicate (1993) is Bullfrog's isometric real-time tactics game, in which a squad of four cyborg agents carries out assassination, rescue and persuasion missions for a megacorporation in a cyberpunk 2096.
longDescription:
In 2096 the corporation EuroCorp has invented the CHIP, a device inserted in the neck that dulls perception and leaves people open to manipulation, and the megacorporations have become crime syndicates fighting over its manufacture. The player runs one of them, sending teams of one to four cyborg agents — captured civilians, enhanced and reprogrammed — on missions of assassination, rescue and "persuasion" against rivals such as The Tao, Sphinx Inc. and The Castrilos, ending at the Atlantic Accelerator research station.

The Persuadertron recruits targets and civilians to follow the squad, scanners locate people and vehicles, and medikits heal. Players choose their agents' weapons, cybernetic upgrades and behaviour. Taxes from conquered territories pay for research into better weapons, from pistols and Uzis to miniguns, flamethrowers, sniper rifles, lasers and the Gauss gun, but taxing too heavily can provoke a revolt that forces the mission to be replayed.
trivia: PC Gamer UK ranked it the 11th best computer game of all time in 1994.
Computer Gaming World criticised its lack of multiplayer and its repetitive missions.
If all agents are lost, the player's airship self-destructs.
Amiga Power ranked it the 7th-best Amiga game in 1996.
Satellite Reign, by some of its original staff, is a spiritual successor.
devStory:
Sean Cooper designed it and programmed it with Phillip Jones at Bullfrog, with Peter Molyneux producing, art by Chris Hill and Paul McLaughlin and music by Russell Shaw. EA released it for the Amiga and MS-DOS in the UK on 2 July 1993, and the American Revolt expansion followed that year. Versions for the Mega Drive and Super NES had new levels and graphics.

PC Gamer UK ranked it the 11th-best computer game of all time in 1994, and GamePro called the SNES version "a thinking man's shoot-em-up game". Syndicate Wars followed in 1996, and Starbreeze rebooted it as a first-person shooter in 2012.

title: Eye of the Beholder
description: Eye of the Beholder (1991) is Westwood's first-person Advanced Dungeons & Dragons dungeon crawler for SSI, in which a party descends beneath Waterdeep to face the beholder Xanathar.
longDescription:
The Lords of Waterdeep hire a band of adventurers to investigate an evil beneath the city, but a collapse caused by the beholder Xanathar seals the sewer entrance behind them. The party descends through the territory of dwarf and drow clans to Xanathar's lair for the final fight.

In the style of Dungeon Master (1987), the dungeon is seen in pseudo-3D first person and the party is controlled by pointing and clicking. The player starts with four characters and can grow the party to six by recruiting non-player characters or resurrecting the skeletons of dead ones, and the party can be carried over into the sequels. It follows the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons rules closely, including its spells and ranged weapons.
trivia: The original DOS version ended with a small text window; the Amiga version added an animated ending.
In 1991 SSI ran a "Beholder Bonus" contest in which players hunted for 12 hidden easter eggs.
Yuzo Koshiro and Motohiro Kawashima scored the Sega CD version.
Its cover art won Computer Gaming World's reader poll for best advertisement in January 1991.
Fans later remade it as modules for Neverwinter Nights.
devStory:
Brett Sperry directed it at Westwood Associates for SSI, under the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons licence, with design by Phillip W. Gorrow, Eydie Laramore, Paul S. Mudra and Joseph Bostic, music by Mudra and cover art by Jeff Easley. It came out for MS-DOS and the Amiga in 1991, and reached the top of the Software Publishers Association's MS-DOS chart that April, the last SSI D&D game to do so. It sold over 150,000 copies by mid-1991.

Computer and Video Games scored the DOS version 96%, and Computer Gaming World's reviewers praised its graphics and challenge, though Scorpia criticised the spell interface and abrupt ending. Westwood made the sequel, The Legend of Darkmoon, the same year, while SSI developed the third game itself in 1993.

title: The Bard's Tale
description: The Bard's Tale (1985) is Interplay's dungeon-crawling RPG set in Skara Brae, frozen under Mangar the Dark's Eternal Winter, and reportedly the best-selling computer RPG of the 1980s.
longDescription:
The town of Skara Brae lies under Mangar the Dark's spell of Eternal Winter, its west gates blocked by snow and its streets overrun by monsters. The player builds a party of up to six from bards, hunters, monks, paladins, rogues, warriors, magicians and conjurers; experienced spellcasters can become sorcerers and wizards, and one who has learned every spell of all four schools becomes an Archmage. The party descends through six dungeons — a wine cellar, the sewers, the catacombs beneath the Mad God's temple, Harkyn's Castle, Kylearan's Tower and finally Mangar's five-level tower.

Exploration is in first person, and fights are turn-based and described in text. Bards play songs that act as long-lasting spells, some needed to solve puzzles, and most versions have the player cast the 85 magic spells by typing four-letter codes from the manual. Levels can only be raised at the unmarked Review Board. Some versions let players import characters from Wizardry and Ultima III.
trivia: It was originally going to be called Shadow Snare.
Zzap!64 gave the Commodore 64 version 94% and a Sizzler award.
The series was first called Tales of the Unknown, and the original box reads "Volume I".
A planned Bard's Tale IV became the unrelated Dragon Wars because of rights issues.
Baen Books published eight novels set in its world in the 1990s.
devStory:
Michael Cranford designed and programmed it at Interplay, with additional design by Brian Fargo and Roe Adams III, graphics by David Lowery and music by Lawrence Holland. Much of the design drew on Cranford and Fargo's Dungeons & Dragons games, and Cranford said they set out to improve on games such as the Apple version of Wizardry. A consultant suggested the name Skara Brae, which Ultima IV also used. EA released it for the Apple II and Commodore 64 in December 1985.

It sold a reported 407,000 copies, the best-selling computer RPG of the 1980s and the first non-Wizardry RPG to challenge Ultima's sales. Computer Gaming World's Scorpia called it "not to be missed!", and it entered the magazine's Hall of Fame in 1988.

title: Wasteland
description: Wasteland (1988) is Interplay's post-nuclear role-playing game, in which a squad of Desert Rangers explores the ruined American Southwest. Fallout (1997) is widely seen as its spiritual successor.
longDescription:
In 2087, generations after a nuclear war in 1998, the Desert Rangers, a remnant of the US Army, keep the peace in the American Southwest. Exploring the surviving enclaves, including a ruined Las Vegas, they uncover a pre-war artificial intelligence at Base Cochise that is building killer machines and cybernetic humans for "Project Darwin", a plan to replace humanity with genetically pure specimens. With the android Max, the player destroys it by melting down the base's reactor.

The rules come from the tabletop games Tunnels & Trolls and Mercenaries, Spies and Private Eyes. Characters have seven attributes and are promoted through combat and skill use, and the party of four can grow to seven by recruiting people and creatures, who may refuse orders. Changes to the world are saved as the player makes them, one of the first persistent worlds. Story text is printed in a separate paragraph book, which also served as copy protection and included a fake Mars storyline and false passwords to catch cheats. The game is known for its harshness, and its combat messages, such as "reduced to a thin red paste", earned it a PG-13 sticker.
trivia: Computer Gaming World named it Adventure Game of the Year for 1988.
inXile acquired the rights in 2003 and made Wasteland 2 (2014) and Wasteland 3 (2020).
The paragraph book contained a fake storyline set on Mars to mislead anyone reading ahead.
Orson Scott Card's review in Compute! criticised its lack of a meaningful overarching story.
Wasteland Remastered came out for its 30th anniversary in 2020.
devStory:
Brian Fargo, who directed it, said Interplay began in 1986, building it on the Apple II as a hybrid of Ultima and The Bard's Tale in a setting inspired by Mad Max 2. Ken St. Andre and Michael A. Stackpole, creators of the tabletop systems, designed and wrote it with Liz Danforth; St. Andre said the story took over a year, and changed an early plot resembling Red Dawn to killer robots, pitching it as The Terminator meets Daffy Duck. Alan Pavlish wrote it in Apple II machine language.

EA released it for the Apple II in March 1988, and it sold about 250,000 copies. Interplay later called Fallout (1997) its spiritual successor.

title: Raid on Bungeling Bay
description: Raid on Bungeling Bay (1984) is Will Wright's helicopter shooter whose map editor became the start of SimCity.
longDescription: A helicopter launched from an aircraft carrier must bomb six factories on the islands of a small planetoid held by the Bungeling Empire, fighting off gun turrets, fighter jets, guided missiles and a battleship, and reloading at a hidden island. The carrier is the home base and has to be defended too. Supply boats sail between the islands, and the factories grow and develop new technology over time, so if the player takes too long they build enough weapons to overwhelm the helicopter; failure means the Bungeling Empire takes over Earth.
trivia: Wright built a map editor for the game as a personal project, and it grew into City Planner and then SimCity (1989).
The Commodore 64 version sold 20,000 to 30,000 copies in America, while Hudson's Famicom version sold about a million in Japan.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 24th best computer game ever in 1996.
In Japan it is also known simply as Bungeling Bay.
Sony published an MSX version in Japan in 1985.
devStory:
It was Will Wright's first game. He designed it and programmed the Commodore 64 version, which Broderbund released in North America in December 1984 and Ariolasoft in Europe. Hudson Soft made the Famicom version, released in Japan in February 1985, and an arcade conversion that Nintendo distributed in Japan, and Broderbund published the NES version in North America in 1987.

The C64 version sold only 20,000 to 30,000 copies in America, while the Famicom one sold about a million in Japan; Wright credited the cartridge format, which limited piracy, and its being one of the first American games published in Japan. Creative Computing said it "blows Choplifter away!", and its sales gave Wright the freedom to make SimCity.

title: Mappy
description: Mappy (1983) is Namco's arcade game in which a police mouse bounces on trampolines through a mansion of cats to recover stolen goods.
longDescription:
Mappy, a police mouse, has to recover goods stolen by a gang of cats — the small pink Meowkies and their large red leader, Goro — from a mansion of floors linked by trampolines. The ten items come in five pairs: stereos, televisions, Mona Lisa paintings, computers and safes, and collecting a pair in a row multiplies the second item's value, up to six times. Goro can hide behind items, and grabbing one stuns him.

Mappy is safe from the cats while bouncing, but a trampoline breaks after four bounces in a row until he lands. Doors open towards their knobs and knock back anyone nearby, and flashing doors release a microwave that sweeps cats away for points, doubled if Goro is caught. If Mappy lingers, more Meowkies arrive and then a coin with Goro's face that can kill him in mid-air. Bonus rounds have him bouncing to pop balloons, and later rounds add bells, an attic and floors that open into holes.
trivia: Its name probably comes from mappo, mildly derogatory Japanese slang for a policeman.
Its board was a revision of the Super Pac-Man hardware with added horizontal scrolling.
In Japan Goro is called Nyamco.
Sequels included Hopping Mappy (1986) and Mappy-Land on the Famicom.
Hardcore Gamer included it in its 200 best video games of all time in 2015.
devStory: Namco released it in Japan in March 1983 and Bally Midway in North America the following month, with graphics by Hiroshi Ono and music by Nobuyuki Ohnogi. It ran on a revision of the Super Pac-Man hardware that added horizontal scrolling. It was Game Machine's third most successful table arcade unit in May 1983 and topped its new table cabinet chart that June. A Famicom version followed in 1984.

title: River City Ransom
description: River City Ransom (1989) is Technos Japan's open-world beat 'em up, in which Alex and Ryan fight through River City's gangs, buying fighting techniques in shops along the way.
longDescription:
Alex and Ryan cross River City to reach River City High and rescue Ryan's girlfriend Cyndi from a villain called Slick. The city is open to explore in any order, and the fighting resembles Double Dragon, with punches, kicks and jumps, and brass knuckles, steel pipes and rubbish bins to pick up and throw. Nine gangs, from "The Generic Dudes" to the Frat Guys, the Jocks and the Squids, are told apart by their shirt colours, and each has a boss.

Defeated gang members drop money, which buys food and spa treatments that restore health and can permanently raise punching and kicking, and books that teach techniques such as Grand Slam, Stone Hands and Dragon Feet. A password saves stats, skills, items, money and defeated bosses.
trivia: In Japan it is Downtown Nekketsu Monogatari, the third Kunio-kun game on the NES.
A Kickstarter-funded follow-up, River City Ransom: Underground, was released in 2017.
Its Kickstarter raised $217,643 against a goal of CA$180,000.
It was the first console game published by Technōs's North American arm without Taito's involvement.
Kunio and other characters appear as spirits in Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.
devStory:
Technōs Japan made it as the third Kunio-kun game and the first designed specifically for the NES, directed by Mitsuhiro Yoshida and Hiroyuki Sekimoto with music by Kazuo Sawa. It came out in Japan as Downtown Nekketsu Monogatari on 25 April 1989, in North America in January 1990 and in Europe as Street Gangs. Enhanced versions followed on the X68000 and the PC Engine CD, and River City Ransom EX on the Game Boy Advance in 2004.

First reviews were mixed: Famitsu praised its blend of fighting and role-playing, while GamesMaster gave it 32%. Its reputation grew, and IGN later ranked it 15th among the best NES games.

title: Kaboom!
description: Kaboom! (1981) is Larry Kaplan's Activision paddle game, in which the player catches the Mad Bomber's bombs in water buckets. It sold more than a million cartridges.
longDescription: The Mad Bomber drops bombs at rising speed, and the player catches them in a stack of three water buckets with the paddle controller, which had fallen out of regular use by then. Each bomb caught is defused for points. Missing one sets off every bomb on screen and costs a bucket, and reaching 1,000 points restores a lost one. The difficulty switches can halve the buckets' width, and two players can take turns with separate scores. The Mad Bomber's face changes with the play.
trivia: Kaplan based it on Atari's 1978 arcade game Avalanche: "I just ripped off Avalanche."
David Crane drew the Mad Bomber and the buckets, and the bomber's striped shirt came from an unreleased Crane project.
Critics praised the Mad Bomber's changing expressions.
Paul Wilson's Atari 5200 and 8-bit versions added a two-player "Pitch and Catch" mode.
A Super NES follow-up, Kaboom!: The Return of the Mad Bomber, was shown in 1991 but never released.
devStory:
Larry Kaplan, who had followed David Crane and Alan Miller from Atari to Activision, based it openly on Dennis Koble's 1978 arcade game Avalanche, replacing its falling rocks with a single figure dropping bombs. Crane drew the Mad Bomber and the buckets, reusing the striped shirt of a running man from his unpublished 1979 "Cops and Robbers" game, a character later used in Pitfall!, and added the bomber's changing expressions. Activision released it in July 1981 alongside Freeway, and it won Best Audio-Visual Effects at the 1982 Arcade Awards.

It became one of the best-selling 2600 games, over a million copies by 1984. Electronic Games found it "infinitely more enjoyable" than Avalanche, while Softline dismissed it as only a test of paddle controls.

title: Little Big Adventure
description: Little Big Adventure (1994) is Frédérick Raynal's isometric action-adventure, in which Twinsen stands up to the tyrant Dr FunFrock on the planet Twinsun, switching between four behaviour modes.
longDescription:
Twinsun is a planet held between two suns, home to four species: the human-like Quetches, the round Spheros, the elephant-like Grobos and the Rabbibunnies. The tyrant Dr FunFrock has herded everyone into the southern hemisphere and rules through clones that travel by teleporter. Twinsen, a young Quetch, is locked in an asylum for his prophetic dreams, really telepathic messages from the goddess Sendell, and after he escapes, clones arrest his girlfriend Zoe in his place. He sets out to gather artifacts, join the rebels and stop FunFrock from drilling down to the Well of Sendell.

Polygon characters and vehicles move through pre-rendered isometric scenes in real time. Twinsen switches between four behaviour modes — Normal, Athletic, Aggressive and Discreet — each changing what he can do and how the Magic Ball he throws behaves, and Aggressive adds punches and kicks. Islands open up as objectives are met, many tasks are optional, almost everyone speaks and replies, and the game saves automatically.
trivia: In North America Activision released it as Relentless: Twinsen's Adventure, and it sold only 30,000 copies there.
Its source code was released under the GPL in October 2021.
A remake, Little Big Adventure – Twinsen's Quest, came out in 2024.
The floppy disk version replaced its videos with still images and its recorded music with MIDI.
A planned Atari Jaguar CD version was never released.
devStory:
Frédérick Raynal founded Adeline Software after growing frustrated at Infogrames while working on Alone in the Dark. Lead coder Serge Plagnol said Electronic Arts' US division wanted Twinsen to be tougher and "kick ass", which Adeline refused, and Philippe Vachey composed the music. EA released it in Europe in 1994, and Edge gave it 9/10.

It sold 320,000 copies by February 1997 and over 500,000 by 1999, but only about 30,000 in the US, where Activision released it as Relentless: Twinsen's Adventure; Raynal blamed the aggressive name, cover and combat-focused advertising. Little Big Adventure 2 followed in 1997.

title: Ultima Underworld: The Stygian Abyss
description: Ultima Underworld (1992) is the first-person role-playing game from the studio that became Looking Glass, set in a texture-mapped 3D dungeon. It is considered the first immersive sim.
longDescription:
The wizard brothers Garamon and Tyball summoned a demon, the Slasher of Veils; Garamon died sealing it away. Tyball now plans to sacrifice Arial, daughter of Baron Almric, and the Avatar, framed for her kidnapping, is banished into the Great Stygian Abyss, the dungeon beneath the Isle of the Avatar. There the remnants of Cabirus's failed utopian colony — humans, goblins, trolls and others — live in rival factions. The Avatar must rescue Arial, gather Cabirus's eight talismans and cast them into the volcano at the bottom of the Abyss.

The dungeon is a real-time 3D space with texture-mapped walls, floors and ceilings and varying heights, and the player can look up and down, jump and swim; light sources burn down, and an automap records what has been seen and lets the player add notes. Combat is in real time, with longer clicks for harder blows and the cursor position choosing a jab or a slash. Over forty spells are cast by combining runestones, mantras chanted at shrines raise skills, food and rest are needed, weapons wear out and thrown objects bounce. Areas, puzzles and quests can be tackled in any order.
trivia: Its engine became the basis for System Shock.
It is cited as an influence on Deus Ex, Half-Life, BioShock, The Elder Scrolls: Arena and Tomb Raider.
It won the 1992 Origins Award for Best Fantasy or Science Fiction Computer Game.
Origin's rejection of a third Underworld led indirectly to Arkane's Arx Fatalis.
Underworld Ascendant (2018) is a licensed spiritual successor.
devStory:
Paul Neurath conceived it in 1989, after Space Rogue, and Blue Sky Productions, founded in Salem, New Hampshire, began work in May 1990. A prototype built in about a month, using Chris Green's texture-mapping algorithm, impressed Origin at the June 1990 CES. Doug Church programmed it and later led the project, writing the story with Dan Schmidt, and Warren Spector became producer as cancellation rumours spread. Its inspirations included Dungeon Master, Wizardry and Tolkien's Moria. The budget grew from a $30,000 advance to $400,000, and the final four months were spent crunching in a cold basement office in Somerville.

Origin released it on 21 March 1992. Sales were slow at first, growing by word of mouth to nearly 500,000, and Computer Gaming World named it Role-Playing Game of the Year. It is cited as the first immersive sim.

title: Star Wars: X-Wing
description: Star Wars: X-Wing (1993) is Totally Games' space combat simulator, in which the player flies Rebel starfighters from the cockpit in polygonal 3D. Its launch shipment of 100,000 copies sold out in a weekend.
longDescription:
The player is a Rebel pilot in the time before and during the climax of A New Hope, flying the A-wing, X-wing and Y-wing from inside the cockpit. Three tours of duty of 12 to 14 operations each end with Luke Skywalker's attack on the Death Star; tours can be played in any order, but the operations within them run in sequence. Missions range from dogfights and escorts to convoy attacks and strikes on capital ships, and the player can give orders to wingmen. Energy is divided between lasers, shields and engines, so charging weapons or shields slows the ship, lasers can fire singly or linked, and shields can be balanced fore and aft.

The hub is the concourse of the Mon Calamari cruiser Independence, with a proving ground of gates to fly through against the clock, a historical simulator of extra missions, a technical room and a film room for reviewing recorded flights. Dying in combat costs score and medals but not campaign progress, and failed operations can be retried. The limited edition included a novella, The Farlander Papers, that casts the player as Keyan Farlander.
trivia: It was the first game other than an adventure to use LucasArts' iMUSE music system.
A sixth tour, set at Echo Base, was planned but never made.
Computer Gaming World named it Simulation of the Year for 1993.
The floppy version let players assign their own saved pilots as wingmen, a feature later removed.
Composer Clint Bajakian voiced Darth Vader.
devStory:
The Star Wars computer licence reverted from Broderbund to LucasArts in 1992. Lawrence Holland, who had made Second World War air combat simulations, designed it with Edward Kilham at Totally Games, drawing some influence from Star Raiders, and its ships were among the first in games drawn as 3D polygons rather than bitmap sprites. Michael Land, Clint Bajakian and Peter McConnell built its MIDI score from John Williams's themes and original pieces, the first use of iMUSE outside an adventure game.

It came out in February 1993; the launch shipment of 100,000 sold out over the debut weekend, and retailers had ordered nearly 500,000 by December. Computer Gaming World named it Simulation of the Year, shared with World Circuit, and Compute! called it the first authentic space combat simulator, though some found its missions rigid. Two expansions, Imperial Pursuit and B-Wing, followed the same year, carrying the story to the founding of the base seen in The Empire Strikes Back.

title: Star Wars: TIE Fighter
description: Star Wars: TIE Fighter (1994) is Totally Games' follow-up to X-Wing that puts the player in an Imperial cockpit. PC Gamer ranked it the best game of all time in 1997.
longDescription:
Soon after the Empire's victory on Hoth, the player joins the Imperial Navy as a starfighter pilot, fighting Rebels, pirates, combatants in civil wars and traitorous Imperial forces across seven tours of duty, each of four to eight missions. The original campaign ends with the pilot foiling a coup against Emperor Palpatine. A figure from the Emperor's Inner Circle hands out secret objectives that earn extra medals and promotions, while primary objectives advance the story and the pilot's military rank. Missions cover dogfights, escorts, inspections and attacks on capital ships and stations, starting in unshielded TIE fighters and moving up to shielded craft such as the TIE Advanced, TIE Defender and TIE Avenger.

The pilot divides power between weapons, engines and shields, balances shields front and rear, and chooses the order in which damaged systems are repaired. Ion cannons disable targets, tractor beams hold fighters and jamming beams disrupt capital-ship defences, and individual components such as shield generators can be targeted on a 3D model. Between missions, the concourse offers a training simulator, a combat chamber with extra missions and a room for recorded flights. The flight music uses iMUSE, with leitmotifs that react to events.
trivia: Pirated copies leaked in early July 1994, before its release on 20 July.
The novella and strategy guide name the pilot Maarek Stele.
The TIE Defender and TIE Avenger it introduced later became part of Star Wars canon.
PC Gamer ranked it the best game of all time in 1997.
IGN called it the "best Star Wars game ever made" in 2010.
devStory:
Lawrence Holland and Edward Kilham designed it at Totally Games on the X-Wing engine, adding Gouraud shading, and Clint Bajakian and Peter McConnell scored it around John Williams's themes. LucasArts released it for MS-DOS on 20 July 1994, after a two-disk demo bundled with Computer Gaming World. The expansions Defender of the Empire and Enemies of the Empire follow Grand Admiral Thrawn's hunt for an Imperial traitor, and the 1995 Collector's CD-ROM added 640×480 graphics, voiceovers and both expansions.

Computer Gaming World gave it five stars, PC Gamer US named it the top action game of 1994, and Computer Games Strategy Plus its best game of the year. GameSpot called the CD edition "the best space combat game ever made", and White Wolf noted the moral discomfort of flying for the Empire.

title: Star Wars: Dark Forces
description: Star Wars: Dark Forces (1995) is LucasArts' first-person shooter starring mercenary Kyle Katarn. Its Jedi engine added looking up and down, jumping and multi-floor levels.
longDescription:
Kyle Katarn joined the Imperial Academy believing the Rebels had killed his parents, then defected when Jan Ors revealed the Empire was responsible. Now a mercenary for the Rebel Alliance, he first steals the Death Star plans, then, a year later, investigates attacks by a new kind of Imperial soldier and uncovers the Dark Trooper Project led by General Rom Mohc. The trail runs through Anoat City's sewers, a detention centre where he rescues Crix Madine, Jabba the Hutt's ship and Coruscant, with Boba Fett in pursuit, and ends aboard the Executor and Mohc's flagship, the Arc Hammer.

The Jedi engine let the player look up and down, duck, jump and swim through levels with several floors. Missions have story-linked objectives, and alongside fighting there are environmental puzzles, river crossings and switch-controlled mazes. Every weapon except Kyle's fists has a secondary mode, and items such as a headlamp, ice cleats and an air mask draw on batteries.
trivia: Luke Skywalker was first planned as the hero; Kyle Katarn was created to give the team more freedom.
The Dark Troopers later appeared in The Mandalorian.
It shipped more than 300,000 copies before launch and debuted at number one on PC Data's chart.
Skywalker Ranch staff contributed sounds, music and costumes for the cutscenes.
Nightdive Studios released a remaster in 2024.
devStory:
Daron Stinnett led the project, Ray Gresko led programming and Justin Chin handled graphics and story; production began in September 1993, inspired by Doom mods with Death Star levels. Luke Skywalker was the original hero, but the team created Kyle Katarn for more freedom. The Jedi engine was written from scratch, with 3D objects, fog, animated textures and shading, and Lucasfilm rejected two of three Dark Trooper designs. Clint Bajakian composed music based on John Williams's cues using iMUSE.

It came out for MS-DOS on 8 March 1995. PC Gamer gave it 92% and its award for Best Sound Effects, though critics noted its short length and lack of multiplayer. By September 1999 it had sold 952,033 copies in the US. Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II followed in 1997.

title: Dungeon Keeper
description: Dungeon Keeper (1997) is Bullfrog's dungeon-management game, in which the player plays the villain, building a lair, recruiting monsters and fending off invading heroes. It was Peter Molyneux's last project at Bullfrog.
longDescription:
The player is a Dungeon Keeper, building an underground lair around a Dungeon Heart, whose destruction means defeat, and fighting off the heroes who come to steal treasure and kill monsters. Imps dig tunnels, mine gold and gems, claim territory and set traps; the Hand of Evil picks creatures up, drops them where they are needed and slaps them to make them work faster, at the cost of some health. Rooms such as lairs, a hatchery where chickens are raised for food, a treasury and a training room decide which creatures come through the portal — warlocks, vampires, dragons, the Horned Reaper — and each has its own needs, rivals and wages, paid on Payday. Unhappy creatures vandalise the dungeon or desert.

Creatures can also be won by imprisoning and torturing enemies or by sacrifices at the temple. A possession spell gives a first-person view through any creature's eyes. The campaign crosses twenty regions of a fictional country, each ruled by a Lord of the Land, ending with the Avatar, who returns with an army after his first defeat. A sinister mentor, voiced by Richard Ridings, offers advice throughout.
trivia: Computer Gaming World called it "the most unique game in years".
The fan project KeeperFX, begun in 2010, fixes bugs and adds features.
Glenn Corpes said its engine inspired Minecraft.
Healey based the Horned Reaper, the game's mascot, on an ex-girlfriend.
The Deeper Dungeons expansion (1997) added 15 single-player and 15 multiplayer levels.
Theme Hospital's intro shows a doctor playing it, and the Horned Reaper as a patient.
devStory:
Peter Molyneux said the idea came to him in a traffic jam; Bullfrog chairman Les Edgar described it as Dungeons & Dragons with "slightly weird Bullfrog humour", and Molyneux saw the villain's work as a management simulation. Work began in November 1994 under lead programmer Simon Carter, on an engine based on Magic Carpet's built by Glenn Corpes. Mark Healey designed the characters, drew about 90 per cent of the graphics and proposed the slap. Late in development the team started over because the game felt too much like Command & Conquer, moving to imps digging and creatures arriving through portals.

Molyneux, who had decided to leave after EA bought Bullfrog, departed in July 1997 to found Lionhead; the team finished the game in his house. It came out in June 1997 and won PC Role-Playing Game of the Year at the first Interactive Achievement Awards. It sold 700,000 copies by 2003, which Molyneux called a "missed opportunity" next to Theme Park.

title: Theme Hospital
description: Theme Hospital (1997) is Bullfrog's comic hospital-management game, in which the player treats patients with diseases such as Bloaty Head and King Complex. It sold more than 4 million copies.
longDescription:
The player runs a private hospital, building rooms from blueprints — GP's offices, psychiatry, operating theatres, pharmacies, an inflator room, research labs, staff rooms and toilets — and hiring doctors, nurses, handymen and receptionists, each with their own stats. Patients arrive with invented diseases such as Bloaty Head, King Complex, whose sufferers impersonate Elvis, and Alien DNA; a GP diagnoses them or sends them on to specialists. Machines left unmaintained explode.

Emergencies must be cured within a time limit, epidemics can be covered up before the health inspector arrives, and impressed VIPs bring cash and reputation. Rats can be shot with the cursor, and rival hospitals are run by Holly from Red Dwarf and Deep Thought from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. Each level sets goals for money, reputation, cures and the hospital's value, and is lost if the money runs out or too many patients die. A later patch added multiplayer for up to four players.
trivia: The original cover art was recalled because it used a green cross the developers had no right to use.
A Sega Saturn version, Sim Hospital, was cancelled.
Producer Mark Webley and artist Gary Carr later founded Two Point Studios, whose Two Point Hospital came out in 2018.
A disease cut from the game, Animal Magnetism, appears in Two Point Hospital.
Some sound effects came from studio sessions with T'Pau, Prefab Sprout and Seal.
devStory:
Peter Molyneux and James Leach came up with the idea, though Molyneux was busy with Dungeon Keeper. Designer Mark Webley and artist Gary Carr researched it at real hospitals, then swapped real diseases for invented ones, aiming for humour rather than gore; Leach wrote the text and the illnesses. Bloaty Head was based on one of Molyneux's allergic reactions, and King Complex was first called Elvis Impersonator until it emerged Elvis's estate owned the rights. The team borrowed heavily from Theme Park's code, cut a plan for four historical eras, and spent over two years on it. Russell Shaw and Adrian Moore made the music and sound.

EA released it on 28 March 1997. It sold over 4 million copies. Critics praised its graphics, humour and depth, while NHS managers, MPs and The Daily Telegraph, which called it "sick", objected.

title: Duke Nukem 3D
description: Duke Nukem 3D (1996) is 3D Realms' first-person shooter set in an alien-invaded Los Angeles, known for its interactive levels, unusual weapons and Duke's one-liners. Its Build engine was written by Ken Silverman.
longDescription:
Duke Nukem returns from Duke Nukem II, is shot down over Los Angeles and finds that aliens have mutated the LAPD into "Pig Cops". The three episodes, L.A. Meltdown, Lunar Apocalypse and Shrapnel City, take him from the city's streets to the Moon, where captured women are held in incubators, and back, against bosses such as the Alien Battlelord, the Overlord and the Cycloid Emperor. Levels pass through cinemas, strip clubs, military bases, a flooded city and space stations, packed with nods to films such as Aliens, Dirty Harry and Pulp Fiction.

The play resembles Doom, but levels are non-linear and most props can be destroyed or used: air ducts and sewers offer back routes, light switches work, and water fountains and broken hydrants restore health. Weapons include Duke's Mighty Foot, pipe bombs, a freezethrower, a shrink ray, laser trip mines and the Devastator, and items include a jet pack, night-vision goggles, steroids and the HoloDuke decoy. Jon St. John voiced Duke's one-liners. Dukematch offers online multiplayer.
trivia: Next Generation wrote that "Duke Nukem 3D has everything Doom doesn't."
Its sexual content and portrayal of women drew criticism, and it was restricted in Germany and banned in Brazil in 1999.
The source code was released under the GPL on 1 April 2003.
The 20th Anniversary World Tour (2016) added a fifth episode with new music by Lee Jackson.
Its long-delayed sequel, Duke Nukem Forever, came out in 2011.
devStory:
3D Realms began it in 1994 on Ken Silverman's Build engine, with a team of eight that grew to twelve or thirteen and a budget of about $300,000; Scott Miller said they wanted realistic locations such as cinemas and strip clubs. Greg Malone produced, Allen H. Blum III and Richard Gray designed, and Lee Jackson and Robert Prince composed. FormGen published it. The shareware episode came out on 29 January 1996 and the full game on 19 April, followed by the Atomic Edition with a fourth episode that December.

It scored 89 on Metacritic, with praise for its interactivity, level design and humour, and sold about 3.5 million copies. Its sexual content drew criticism: some countries got censored versions, Germany restricted its advertising, and Brazil banned it in 1999.

title: Suikoden
description: Suikoden (1995) is Konami's PlayStation RPG, loosely based on the novel Water Margin, in which a general's son gathers the 108 Stars of Destiny to rebel against the Scarlet Moon Empire.
longDescription:
The hero, son of Teo McDohl, a great general of the Scarlet Moon Empire, serves the corrupt empire until his friend Ted is wounded by a servant of the court and passes him the Soul Eater, one of the 27 True Runes. Fleeing the capital, Gregminster, he is drawn into the rebellion led by Odessa Silverberg, and after her death her brother Mathiu, a former imperial strategist, helps him take command of the Liberation Army. An abandoned castle becomes its headquarters, and the goal is to recruit the 108 Stars of Destiny, a structure loosely based on the novel Water Margin.

Battles are turn-based with six-character parties placed by weapon range. Each character has a unique weapon, sharpened by blacksmiths rather than bought, and magic comes from runes with limited uses per spell level. One-on-one duels use a rock-paper-scissors system — attack beats defend, defend beats special, special beats attack — as do large war battles, where charges, archers and magic beat one another in turn.
trivia: Warren Spector cited it as an influence on Deus Ex.
GameFan named it RPG of the Year in its 1996 Megawards.
Spector said its limited choices inspired him to make more meaningful ones in Deus Ex.
Lower-level characters gain more experience from each battle.
An HD remaster of the first two games came out worldwide in March 2025.
devStory:
Yoshitaka Murayama directed it and wrote the scenario, citing Romance of the Three Kingdoms and The Eternal Champion as inspirations. Kazumi Kitaue produced it, Junko Kawano designed it and drew the art, and Miki Higashino led a team of composers. Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo made it over roughly two years. It came out in Japan on 15 December 1995 and in North America a year later; a Saturn version in 1998 added new locations and a new opening.

IGN called it "one of the best RPGs ever made", and Next Generation "one of the most addictive RPGs to come along", though GameSpot found it short and easy. It began the Suikoden series, and Suikoden II followed in 1998.

title: Chrono Cross
description: Chrono Cross (1999) is Square's PlayStation RPG set in the world of Chrono Trigger, in which Serge moves between two parallel worlds — one where he drowned ten years before.
longDescription: Serge, a 17-year-old from the fishing village of Arni in the El Nido archipelago, slips into a parallel world in which he drowned ten years earlier.
