The original character portraits were modelled on Mel Gibson, Sean Connery, Tom Berenger and Richard Crenna.
Killing one of the children in the fortress costs Snake health.
Its "Theme of Solid Snake" appears in Super Smash Bros. Brawl.
devStory:
After the NES Metal Gear sold over a million copies in North America, Konami began Snake's Revenge for the West without Hideo Kojima. Kojima conceived his own sequel after a junior colleague on that project talked to him on a Tokyo train, and after winning approval despite the first game's poor Famicom sales, Kojima researched it by consulting a former Green Beret and playing survival games in a forest near the office. The ROM grew from 3 to 4 megabits, and the game used Konami's SCC sound chip. Kojima wanted to call it Solid Snake, after Indiana Jones; the sales department added "Metal Gear 2".

It came out on the MSX2 in Japan on 20 July 1990 and reached number one on MSX Magazine's sales chart that October. GameSpy later called it one of the best 8-bit games ever made, and IGN credits it with introducing noise attraction, crawling and enemy view cones.

title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons
description: Commander Keen (1990) is the shareware platformer by the team that became id Software, whose smooth scrolling on the PC came from John Carmack's adaptive tile refresh.
longDescription:
Eight-year-old genius Billy Blaze builds a spaceship and becomes Commander Keen. While his parents are out he flies to Mars, where the Vorticons steal four parts of his ship and hide them in Martian cities. In The Earth Explodes he disables the Tantalus Ray cannons of a Vorticon mothership aimed at eight landmarks on Earth, and in Keen Must Die! he travels to the Vorticon homeworld to defeat the Grand Intellect — his school rival Mortimer McMire, whose IQ is a single point higher than his own.

Keen runs and jumps through side-scrolling levels reached from a top-down map, where he can also save. A pogo stick lets him bounce higher, and a raygun with limited ammunition deals with enemies, some of which cannot be killed. Yorps can be stunned by jumping on them, keycards open locked areas, food gives points, and an extra life comes every 20,000. Secret levels and messages in a Galactic Alphabet are hidden throughout.
trivia: It began after the team recreated the first level of Super Mario Bros. 3 on the PC; Nintendo turned down the demo.
Apogee had been taking about $7,000 a month; Keen brought in over $60,000 a month by June 1991.
Scott Miller sent the team a weekly $100 "pizza bonus".
It won Best Entertainment Software and Best Overall at the 1992 Shareware Industry Awards.
A planned trilogy, The Universe Is Toast!, was cancelled after Wolfenstein 3D's success.
devStory:
In September 1990 John Carmack, working at Softdisk in Shreveport, developed adaptive tile refresh, which allowed smooth scrolling on PCs. He and Tom Hall made a demo copying Super Mario Bros. 3, and the team pitched a PC Mario to Nintendo, which declined. Apogee's Scott Miller gave them a $2,000 advance — the whole budget — to make a game by Christmas, in three parts to suit Apogee's shareware model. Hall designed it, Carmack and John Romero programmed it, and they worked nights and weekends while still at Softdisk.

The first episode went up on bulletin boards on 14 December 1990, and the other two were sold together for $30. Apogee had been making about $7,000 a month; Keen brought in nearly $30,000 by Christmas and over $60,000 a month by June 1991. The royalties let the team leave Softdisk and found id Software.

sources.title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

title: Fire and Ice
description: Fire and Ice (1992) is Andrew Braybrook's Graftgold platformer starring Cool Coyote, who freezes monsters with his shots and defeats them to collect the pieces of each level's key.
longDescription: Cool Coyote has to find each level's exit door and unlock it with a key made of several pieces, which are carried by monsters. His shots do no damage on their own: enough hits freeze a monster for a short time, and touching it while it is frozen kills it and frees its piece of the key. The 1994 Amiga CD32 version added detailed background scenery, 256 on-screen colours and several layers of parallax scrolling.
trivia: A finished Mega Drive version was never released.
A Game Gear version was planned but also never released.
Amiga magazines scored it 90% and above, including 92% from Amiga Mania.
Spain's Super Juegos gave the CD32 version 90.
Its full title is Fire and Ice: The Daring Adventures of Cool Coyote.
devStory:
Andrew Braybrook designed it at Graftgold with Phillip Williams, with music by Jason Page, and Renegade published it on the Amiga and Atari ST in 1992 as Fire and Ice: The Daring Adventures of Cool Coyote. Amiga magazines rated it highly: The One and Amiga Mania gave it 92%, Amiga Mania making it game of the month, Amiga Action 91% and CU Amiga 90%, and critics called it an exceptionally well-made platformer.

An MS-DOS version followed in 1993, the CD32 one in 1994, a RISC OS version in 1995 and a Master System version for Virgin in 1996.

title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame
description: Prince of Persia 2 (1993) is Jordan Mechner's sequel, with bigger fights, richer scenery and a 75-minute limit, ending on a cliffhanger that was never resolved.
longDescription:
Eleven days after the first game, the Prince asks for the Princess's hand, but Jaffar, magically disguised as him, has him thrown out. The Prince flees by ship, is shipwrecked by Jaffar's lightning and wakes on an island of skeletons, while Jaffar seizes the throne and puts the Princess under a slow death spell. In the ruins of Basra the Prince finds his father's dagger and sword, and visions of his mother reveal that he is the royal survivor of a massacre. At a red temple of warrior monks he learns that his shadow can leave his body and claims a magic flame, which he uses to burn Jaffar.

The sequel is heavier on combat than the original, with up to four enemies at once, sometimes from both sides, and reinforcements replacing the fallen. Areas are larger and backdrops more varied, and the Prince escapes on a magic carpet and later rides a magical horse. A 75-minute limit starts partway in and runs in real time. Lives are unlimited, but lost time can only be recovered by loading a save.
trivia: Computer Gaming World named it Action Game of the Year in 1994.
Mechner said the planned sequel to resolve its cliffhanger never came.
The ending shows a witch watching the couple in a crystal ball.
A Genesis port by Microïds was cancelled and leaked in 2006.
The Xbox version of The Sands of Time hides the game in a secret area.
devStory:
Jordan Mechner designed it, but unlike the original did not program it himself; Broderbund developed it, with music by Jonelle Adkisson. It came out for MS-DOS in May 1993, followed by Mac, FM Towns and PC-98 versions, and a 1996 Super NES port by Titus.

Most reviewers considered it an improvement on the original. Computer Gaming World's Charles Ardai called it "in every dimension better" but criticised the save system, and the magazine named it Action Game of the Year in 1994. It had sold 750,000 copies by 2000. The trilogy closed with Prince of Persia 3D in 1999.

sources.title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame

title: Ultima Online
description: Ultima Online (1997) is Origin's online role-playing world, produced by Richard Garriott, with skills instead of levels, player housing and open player-versus-player combat.
longDescription: Characters improve by using skills rather than through levels or classes, keep houses that persist in the world, and craft goods for an economy run by players. At launch any player could attack any other. The original world, later called Felucca, kept those harsh rules, and the Renaissance expansion of 2000 added a mirrored world, Trammel, where fighting was only by consent and more land was open for housing. Richard Garriott's character Lord British was a major figure in the world. A planned artificial-life ecology was removed after players killed all the wildlife before it could spawn.
trivia: During the 1997 beta, a player called Rainz killed Lord British, Garriott's own character, with a fire field spell because his invulnerability had not been reset after a crash.
It reached about 100,000 subscribers within six months and peaked at around 250,000 in 2003.
Guinness listed it as the first MMORPG to reach 100,000 players.
Garriott left Origin in 2000 and took Lord British with him.
The Third Dawn expansion (2001) added a 3D client.
devStory:
Work began in 1995 on a $2.5 million budget, with Garriott, Starr Long, Rick Delashmit and Scott Phillips at the core and Raph Koster later joining as lead designer, writing public "designer letters" as Designer Dragon. It was shown at E3 in May 1996 as Shattered Legacy, and Origin said over 3,000 players took part in early alpha testing. An internal forecast put the ceiling at 15,000 subscribers.

It launched on 24 September 1997 at $65 and sold 65,000 copies by mid-November; in Japan, the first 5,000 sold out in 15 minutes, and EA called it its fastest-selling computer game. It reached 100,000 subscribers within six months, causing severe lag, and won Online Game of the Year at the first Interactive Achievement Awards, though reviewers were harsh: GameSpot gave it 4.9/10.

title: Roc'n Rope
description: Roc'n Rope (1983) is Tokuro Fujiwara's Konami arcade game, described as the first "wire action" game, in which an archaeologist fires a harpoon rope to climb towards a phoenix.
longDescription: An archaeologist armed with a flashlight and a harpoon gun must climb rocky platforms to reach a phoenix. He climbs by firing ropes up to the ledges above. He has no direct way to attack: man-sized dinosaurs and red-haired cavemen can be dazed with the flashlight, or left to get caught on a harpoon rope and fall. Fallen phoenix feathers and phoenix eggs make him invulnerable for a short time.
trivia: It became the basis for Capcom's Bionic Commando (1987), which Fujiwara intended as an expanded version of it.
Coleco made Atari 2600 and ColecoVision versions in 1984.
Its title is also written "Roc 'N Rope", as on the American flyer.
It is described as the first "wire action" game.
The hero cannot attack directly, only stun enemies or trip them on his ropes.
devStory: Tokuro Fujiwara, later known for his career at Capcom, designed it at Konami, which released it in Japan on 3 March 1983 and worldwide in April, with Interlogic publishing it in North America. It is counted among Konami's early arcade hits alongside Scramble, Frogger and Yie Ar Kung-Fu, and is called the first "wire action" game. Coleco released Atari 2600 and ColecoVision versions in 1984. Hamster later added it to its Arcade Archives series, and to Arcade Archives 2 for Switch 2, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series in December 2025.

title: Mikie
description: Mikie (1984) is Konami's school maze game, in which a student dodges staff while collecting hearts that spell out a letter from his girlfriend, to chiptune versions of Beatles songs.
longDescription:
Mikie runs through his school collecting hearts that spell out a letter from his girlfriend, while staff chase him; he can head-butt them or slam doors in their faces. In the classroom he bumps students out of their seats to find the hearts beneath them, then leaves through the corridor, where only the flashing "In" door is safe and others hide a boxing glove or hairy foot. The locker room has basketballs to throw and the cafeteria roasts to hurl at the cooks, while in the dance studio dancing girls stun him. In the last stage, the garden, footballers guard the hearts on his way to his girlfriend, Mandy.

A later revision, High School Graffiti Mikie, swapped the head-butt for a paralysing shout, made him sob instead of rolling on the floor when caught, and sped enemies up after each loop.
trivia: In Japan it was set in an office and titled Shinnyū Shain Tōru-kun, because of concerns about school violence.
Its music includes versions of "A Hard Day's Night" and "Twist and Shout", licensed through JASRAC.
One corridor door hides a girl worth 5,000 points.
The revised version changed the blackboard text from "E=MC2" to "Failure Teaches Success".
Crash gave the Spectrum version a Smash award.
devStory: Konami location-tested it in Japan with its high-school theme, but did not release it there as it was because its premise of sneaking out of school came during a period of school violence. The Japanese version, Shinnyū Shain Tōru-kun, "Freshman Employee Toru", moved it to an office, with a manager for the teacher and security guards for the footballers, and was Japan's second most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's 1 December 1984 issue. Centuri released it in North America, it was a major success in European arcades in 1985, and Imagine Software made the home computer versions. Computer and Video Games called it "a weird game".

title: TwinBee
description: TwinBee (1985) is Konami's two-player "cute 'em up", in which bells shot out of clouds change colour to give different power-ups.
longDescription: Player one flies TwinBee and player two WinBee, with an eight-way joystick and separate buttons for shooting air enemies and bombing ground ones, as in Xevious. Bells hidden in floating clouds change colour as they are shot: yellow is worth points, white gives a twin cannon, blue adds speed up to five levels, green makes copies of the ship and red gives a barrier, though green and red cannot be combined. Ground enemies also drop a three-way gun and a star that clears the screen. A bullet to the body costs a life, but one to the side knocks off an arm, and with both arms gone the ship cannot bomb until it reaches an ambulance; lose them a second time and no ambulance comes. The two ships can line up side by side or one above the other for stronger attacks.
trivia: It was the first game on Konami's Bubble System arcade hardware.
It did not come out outside Japan until 2007, on a Nintendo DS compilation, where it was called RainbowBell in North America.
Its ambulance repairs the ship's lost arms only once.
Simultaneous two-player play was uncommon at the time, as Family Computer Magazine noted.
A 3D Classics version came to the 3DS in 2011.
devStory: Konami released it in Japanese arcades in February 1985, the first game on its Bubble System hardware, with music by Shigeru Fukutake and Yoshinori Sasaki, and Game Machine ranked it the third most successful table arcade unit that March. Famicom and MSX versions followed in 1986. It is credited with Sega's Fantasy Zone as an early "cute 'em up" and began the TwinBee series, which spawned audio dramas and anime in Japan. Gamest's reviewer praised its co-operative attacks and suggested the green bell's copies were a forerunner of Gradius's options.

title: Konami's Ping Pong
description: Konami's Ping Pong (1985) is an arcade table tennis game, described as the first to play like the real sport, with players shown as floating hands.
longDescription: Described as the first video game to play like real table tennis, rather than like Pong, it shows the table from an isometric angle with the players as floating hands. Games go to 11 with a two-point lead, but at 14–14 the next point wins, and matches are the best of three. Players hit forehands, backhands, lobs and smashes. Hitting from the far side of the table is harder, so in single-player games the player is always on the near side. Penta, the penguin from Antarctic Adventure, appears on the title screen, where a bouncing ball knocks him out, and in the crowd.
trivia: The penguin from Antarctic Adventure, later known as Penta, appears on the title screen and in the crowd.
Nintendo published it on the Famicom Disk System in 1987 as Smash Ping Pong, with Donkey Kong Jr. in the crowd.
In Europe it reached the Wii Virtual Console as Smash Table Tennis.
Hamster re-released it in 2024 as Konami's Table Tennis.
Its players are shown only as disembodied hands.
devStory: Konami released it in Japanese arcades in May 1985, and Game Machine listed it as the 19th most successful table arcade unit in its 1 September issue. An MSX version followed that year, and in 1986 Imagine Software and Doug Burns, credited as "Bernie Duggs", released Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad versions as Ping Pong, with scaled-down graphics and sound but the arcade play intact; Crash gave the Spectrum one a Smash award. Nintendo published a Famicom Disk System version in 1987 as Smash Ping Pong.

title: Shao-lin's Road
description: Shao-lin's Road (1985) is Konami's arcade beat 'em up, released in North America as Kicker and sold in Europe as a follow-up to Yie Ar Kung-Fu.
longDescription:
Wanpyou, called Kicker in the arcade version and Lee in other ports, has just mastered Chin-style Shaolin martial arts when the Triad Yamucha Gang kills his master, Raochuu, and traps him in their Jaken Temple. He fights his way out for revenge. With a four-way joystick and two buttons he moves left and right, jumps between floors and attacks with jumping kicks, while enemies come out of doorways to fight hand to hand or throw things.

Each level, or "step", needs a set number of enemies defeated, shown on a meter. Green-clad enemies release a coloured sphere that, if caught, gives a few seconds of a meteor hammer, fireballs or an orbiting ball, and food drifting across the screen is worth bonus points. Wanpyou can take three hits, and a fourth costs a life. Each step has two halves, the second ending with a boss who takes five hits, and finishing a half restores the damage meter and pays a bonus based on hits taken. The five step designs repeat in a cycle, growing harder each time.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Shōrinji E No Michi.
Taito's The Legend of Kage (1985) was influenced by it.
Estel Goffinet scored 50,000,000 points in 2014 in just under 32 hours of play.
It came to Microsoft's Game Room on Xbox 360 and Windows in 2010.
It was a commercial success in European arcades.
devStory: Konami released it in Japanese arcades in April 1985 and in North America that August as Kicker, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's 22nd most successful table arcade unit of mid-June 1985. In Europe it was marketed as a follow-up to Yie Ar Kung-Fu and was a commercial success in arcades, followed by Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum versions in 1986 and an Amstrad CPC version in 1987. It was later included in Konami Arcade Classics on the PlayStation in 1998 and Konami Classics Series: Arcade Hits on the DS in 2007, and Hamster added it to its Arcade Archives series in 2023.

title: Haunted Castle
description: Haunted Castle (1987) is Konami's arcade Castlevania, in which Simon Belmont faces Dracula to rescue his wife Selena, with a difficulty Time Extension called brutal.
longDescription: Simon Belmont sets out to rescue his wife Selena from Dracula across six linear stages. His whip can be upgraded by defeating certain enemies, first to a spiked morning star and then to a sword. Hearts pay for one sub-weapon at a time: bombs for a powerful ground attack, boomerangs, a stopwatch that freezes enemies, crosses or torches that burn along the ground. Skeletons, zombies, mermen and hunchbacks fill the stages, and each ends with a boss, among them Medusa, Frankenstein's monster and Dracula himself. Several board versions exist, with Version M the hardest and K and J easier.
trivia: It was the second arcade Castlevania after VS. Castlevania, and the first not ported from a console.
M2 remade it as Haunted Castle Revisited for the 2024 Castlevania Dominus Collection.
Its first-stage theme, "Cross Your Heart", returned in Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin.
Its last stage's theme was remixed for Julius in Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow.
Micom BASIC Magazine gave it 1.5 out of 6.
devStory:
Masaaki Kukino designed it at Konami for a custom JAMMA board, the second arcade Castlevania after VS. Castlevania and the first not ported from a console. Kenichi Matsubara, who had worked on Castlevania II, composed the music with Masahiro Ikariko, and "Bloody Tears" from Castlevania II returns as the third stage's theme. Konami released it in the West on 26 December 1987 and in Japan on 22 February 1988 as Akumajō Dracula, and Game Machine listed it as the sixth most popular arcade game in Japan that April.

Time Extension ranked it last among the Castlevania games, blaming difficulty it said was designed to draw coins and stiff controls.

title: Thunder Cross
description: Thunder Cross (1988) is Konami's horizontal shooter, in which the Thunder fighter lines up to four option pods and switches between Vulcan, Laser and ricocheting Boomerang shots.
longDescription: In a future of space colonisation, an unknown force called Black Impulse attacks the planet Haniamu IV, and Earth's strongest ships against it are the Blue Thunder M-45, flown by player one, and its earlier model, the Red Thunder M-24, flown by player two. Across seven stages, each ending with a boss, the player switches between three weapons: the Vulcan shot, the Laser and the Boomerang shot, which also ricochets. Up to four options can be collected; they line up vertically and fire on command. After the seventh stage the game loops into a harder version of the same seven, so it must be beaten twice.
trivia: Its sequel, Thunder Cross II, came out in 1991.
Space Manbow (1989) is sometimes considered a spin-off because of their similarities.
The two players fly different models, the Blue Thunder M-45 and the older Red Thunder M-24.
The Boomerang shot doubles as a ricochet weapon.
Its 2007 PlayStation 2 release was part of Hamster's Oretachi Geasen Zoku budget series.
devStory: Konami released it in Japanese arcades in October 1988, in North America in January 1989 and in Europe later that year, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit in its 1 December 1988 issue. Hamster re-released it in Japan on the PlayStation 2 in 2007, then in its Arcade Archives series on PlayStation 4 in 2017 and Switch in 2021, and it was added to Konami's Arcade Classics Anniversary Collection in 2019.

title: Parodius! From Myth to Laughter
description: Parodius (1990) is Konami's comic send-up of Gradius, flown as Vic Viper, an octopus, TwinBee or Pentarou to remixes of classical music.
longDescription:
The Great Octopus threatens Earth, and four heroes set out to stop it. It plays like Gradius, but each character has its own weapons: Vic Viper the classic Gradius set, the Octopus Salamander's ripple laser, TwinBee (coloured as WinBee) a rocket punch and 3-way laser, and Pentarou Gradius II's piercing "Poton" torpedo. TwinBee's bells give one-off effects such as clearing the screen or firing huge beams. Gradius and TwinBee enemies mix with anime-style opponents, including scantily clad women.

The ten arcade stages range from a pirate planet and a Las Vegas circus to a candy fortress, a moai battleship whose boss Yoshiko spits moai, a pinball planet with the neon "Viva Core", and a graveyard of Japanese and Egyptian ghosts. Most music remixes classical pieces, from Strauss's "Thunder and Lightning" polka to Tchaikovsky's "Waltz of the Flowers", Khachaturian's "Sabre Dance" and "Flight of the Bumblebee". The final boss is unarmed.
trivia: The soundtrack remixes works by Strauss, Tchaikovsky, Beethoven and Rossini.
Super Play described the SNES version as "Gradius on hallucinogens".
Its Gradius-style Big Core boss becomes the neon "Viva Core".
In Europe the SNES, Saturn and PlayStation versions were called Parodius: Non-Sense Fantasy.
The Game Boy version shows each character's age.
devStory:
It was Konami's second Parodius, after the MSX game Parodius: The Octopus Saves the Earth, and is often mistaken for the first; the name is a play on "Parody Gradius". Konami released it in arcades in February 1990 as Parodius Da! Shinwa kara Owarai e. It was one of Japan's five highest-grossing arcade games that year and won Gamest's awards for Best Production and Best Shooting Game.

Famicom, Game Boy, X68000, PC Engine and Super Famicom versions followed in 1990–92, the SNES one adding a bath house stage and an "Omake" stage, then PlayStation and Saturn versions paired with Fantastic Parodius. Mean Machines gave the SNES version 93%.

title: The Simpsons
description: The Simpsons (1991) is Konami's four-player arcade beat 'em up, in which the family chase Smithers after he kidnaps Maggie.
longDescription:
Smithers steals a huge diamond for Mr. Burns, it ends up in Maggie's mouth as a pacifier, and he kidnaps her too. The family chases him through Springfield to the nuclear plant, fighting Burns's hired goons across eight stages that each end in a boss fight, and finally Smithers and Burns himself in a battle suit. Homer punches and kicks, Marge swings a vacuum cleaner, Bart uses his skateboard and Lisa her jump rope.

Pairs of characters have team attacks: Homer and Marge roll along holding each other's ankles, Homer carries a child on his shoulders, Marge throws one, and Bart and Lisa clothesline enemies together. Hammers, bowling balls and mailboxes can be picked up as weapons, two players together can throw police cars, and food restores health. Between stages, two minigames test how fast players can hammer the buttons. Binky and Bongo from Life in Hell make brief appearances.
trivia: The Japanese version supports only two players.
It mixes first-season recordings with new lines from Dan Castellaneta, Julie Kavner, Nancy Cartwright and Yeardley Smith.
The Japanese version adds throwable small nuclear bombs and hidden items.
ScrewAttack ranked it the best cartoon-based game.
Arcade1Up released a 30th-anniversary cabinet in 2021.
devStory:
Kengo Nakamura directed it at Konami, with music by Norio Hanzawa. It mixes archive recordings from the show's first season with new lines from Dan Castellaneta, Julie Kavner, Nancy Cartwright and Yeardley Smith. Thousands of cabinets were ordered at its March 1991 debut, and it came out in two-player and four-player cabinets; the Japanese release that August supported only two.

It won an AAMA Platinum award for 1991 sales, among the top three arcade machines of the year. Novotrade ported it to the Commodore 64 and MS-DOS, and it came to Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network in 2012 with online play and the Japanese version as an unlockable.

title: Vendetta
description: Vendetta (1991) is Konami's street-gang beat 'em up, known in Japan as Crime Fighters 2, in which four Cobras fight the Dead End Gang to rescue Kate.
longDescription: Dead End City is run by the Dead End Gang under Faust, who wants control of every street gang, and the only opposition is the Cobras. When the gang kidnaps Kate, Hawk's protégé and the fifth Cobra, the other four go into enemy territory after her: Blood, a former prizefighter; Hawk, a former pro wrestler; Boomer, a martial artist; and Sledge, a former military convict. Controls use separate punch and kick buttons, and punch and kick together give the only aerial attack, costing a bar of energy. Players can grab shotguns, baseball bats, knives and bottles from enemies or boxes, double-team enemies as enemies double-team them, and hit them while they are down, which was new to the genre. After the last boss, all the bosses return together, and then the game loops at a higher difficulty.
trivia: Outside Asia, an enemy's sexual grabbing attacks were cut, most heavily in the US.
Sinclair User named it Best Beat 'Em Up of 1991, jointly with WWF WrestleFest.
In Japan it was called Crime Fighters 2.
Time Extension listed it among the best beat 'em ups of all time in 2023.
It was shown at the 1991 Las Vegas Amusement Expo.
devStory: Satoru Okamoto directed it at Konami as a sequel to Crime Fighters (1989), though it was marketed abroad as a standalone game, with music by Michiru Yamane and Hideaki Shikama. It came out in Japan in July 1991, ranking third among table arcade units that month, and was RePlay's top-grossing new video game in North America that September. The One called it "quite excellent", praising its moody, imaginative graphics, and Nintendo Life gave Hamster's 2021 re-release 9/10.

title: X-Men
description: X-Men (1992) is Konami's arcade beat 'em up for up to six players, whose deluxe cabinet joined two screens into one wide display.
longDescription:
Magneto has kidnapped Professor X and Kitty Pryde, and Cyclops, Colossus, Wolverine, Storm, Nightcrawler and Dazzler fight their way to Island M and then Asteroid M to stop him. On the way they face hundreds of Sentinels, mutant crocodiles and the Reavers, along with Pyro, the Blob, Wendigo, Nimrod, the White Queen, the Juggernaut, the Living Monolith and Mystique.

Each X-Man has punches, kicks and close attacks, and a mutant power that hits every enemy on screen at a cost of three health points; below four points the power cannot normally be used, though bonus powers can be stored like items. Depending on the cabinet, two to six can play at once. The six-player version joins two screens into one wide display, one of them reflected by a mirror.
trivia: Its script is remembered for lines such as "Welcome to die!" and "I am Magneto, master of magnet!"
At MAGFest, crowds have taken to imitating Colossus's roar; Nobuo Uematsu led one in 2012.
The original MAGFest cabinet was donated in 2008 and still carries a memorial to its donor.
GameSpot included it in its greatest games of all time in 2004.
The Japanese version adds power-ups and health packs to the levels.
devStory:
Konami made it, with C. Lee and Hideki Ohyama directing, basing the character designs on the 1989 TV pilot Pryde of the X-Men. It came out in North America in March 1992 and in Japan that June. It topped RePlay's deluxe cabinet chart from May to October 1992, was one of the five highest-grossing dedicated arcade games in the US that year, and was nominated at the AMOA awards for most innovative new technology.

Backbone Entertainment brought it to the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2010 with online play for six; the voices were re-recorded for licensing reasons, but the script's famous lines stayed.

title: Asterix
description: Asterix (1992) is Konami's two-player arcade beat 'em up based on the French comics, in which Asterix and Obelix fight side by side.
longDescription:
Asterix and Obelix fight the Roman Empire side by side, in a horizontally scrolling beat 'em up drawn to look and feel like the French comics, with all its text in English or French. Asterix is small and agile and Obelix big and strong, each with his own animations, though their powers in the game are equal, unlike in the comics. Both punch, kick and clap. Holding the attack button until a hero's face turns red charges a fast rotating-arm attack that, released on an enemy, sends him flying; it is the only way to beat the strongest bosses.

Knocked-down enemies can be picked up: Asterix twirls them overhead, Obelix slams them back and forth into the ground, and either can use them to knock down others nearby. At certain points Dogmatix brings a Magic Potion for Asterix or a roast boar for Obelix, giving brief invincibility. Defeated legionnaires crawl away, and bonus levels break up the fighting, the first level ending with a chariot race.
trivia: The first level ends with a bonus chariot race.
Although Obelix is the stronger in the comics, the two heroes are equally powerful in the game.
Though made in Japan, all its text is in English or French.
The attract mode shows off its comic fighting moves.
Game Zone gave it 4 out of 5 in May 1992.
devStory: Masaaki Kukino, who had designed Haunted Castle, directed it at Konami, with Hitoshi Akamatsu and Yuko Ito programming, Hideto Murata designing the hardware, and a music team including Michiru Yamane and Junya Nakano. The board ran a 12 MHz Motorola 68000 with an 8 MHz Z80 for sound, driving a Yamaha YM2151 and Konami's K053260. Konami released it in 1992, the same year as a separate Asterix game for the Master System, and Game Zone gave it 4 out of 5 that May.

title: Lethal Enforcers
description: Lethal Enforcers (1992) is Konami's light gun game built from digitised photographs, whose realistic violence drew attention in the 1993 US Senate hearings that helped prompt the ESRB.
longDescription:
Chicago police officer Don Marshall, on a break at a donut shop, learns that a major crime organisation has invaded the city and that he is one of two survivors of an elite unit; a second player can join him. Everything on screen is digitised photographs. Armed enemies wear sunglasses, ski masks or gas masks, while police and civilians are barefaced, and one shot kills most enemies. The player starts with a .38 revolver, reloaded by pointing the gun off-screen, and can pick up a .357 Magnum, a shotgun, an assault rifle and single-use weapons such as a grenade launcher, all lost with a life.

The six stages, from a training stage and a bank robbery to Chinatown and a chemical plant, each end with a boss. The player rises through six ranks, from Patrolman to Commander, after each stage with no civilians killed, and is demoted for shooting them.
trivia: Home versions came with the Konami Justifier, a revolver-shaped light gun that Toys "R" Us pulled from sale.
The Genesis version was among the first games rated MA-17, alongside Night Trap and Mortal Kombat.
A pink second-player Justifier was sold only by mail order.
It was the top-selling Sega CD game in the US in November 1993.
Western versions cut an enemy's taunt of "Die, pigs!".
devStory:
Yoshiaki Hatano directed and designed it at Konami, with music by Kenichiro Fukui, and it reached North American arcades in September 1992, where RePlay listed it as the top-grossing upright arcade game from December 1992 to January 1993; it was one of the five highest-grossing dedicated arcade games of 1993 in the US. Genesis, Sega CD and Super NES versions followed in 1993 and 1994, packaged with the Konami Justifier light gun.

Its photorealistic violence made it one of the games discussed at the 1993 US Senate hearings led by Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl, where Lieberman said the Justifier looked too much like a real revolver. The SNES version removed the blood, and EGM said the toned-down violence lost the game's spirit.

title: Sparkster: Rocket Knight Adventures 2
description: Sparkster (1994) is Konami's Genesis sequel to Rocket Knight Adventures, in which Sparkster sets out to rescue Princess Cherry from Axel Gear and King Gedol.
longDescription:
After the fall of the Devontidos Empire, the reptile Gedol Empire rises under King Gedol and sends Axel Gear to kidnap Princess Cherry, cousin of Princess Sherry, to lure Sparkster into a trap. Sparkster's sword now hits only at close range rather than firing projectiles, and his maximum health falls from eight hearts to five. The rocket button launches him in any of eight directions, or spins him on the spot, and the pack recharges itself; a red gauge gives a rocket attack and a white one a longer screw attack that turns screws. Ten blue gems or one red gem start a slot machine that pays out items or bombs.

The six stages each end with a boss, and Sparkster fights Axel's mech in his own SparkRobo at the start and in the fifth stage. Seven Keys to the Seal, five hidden in the stages and two won from Axel, turn him into the stronger Gold Sparkster, and the true ending needs Hard or Very Hard difficulty.
trivia: A separate SNES game, also called Sparkster, came out the same year but does not continue this story.
Akira Yamaoka and Michiru Yamane composed the music.
Sonic the Comic ran a Sparkster strip by Nigel Kitching and Keith Page; a second story was cancelled when Konami's permission could not be obtained.
Harder difficulty settings add new sections rather than just more enemies.
The 2010 Rocket Knight is set 15 years after it.
devStory: Yasushi Takano directed it at Konami, with Tomikazu Kirita producing, Shiori Satoh and Noboru Shirasu designing and Akira Yamaoka and Michiru Yamane composing. It came out in Japan on 23 September 1994 and abroad that autumn. Reviews were positive but less enthusiastic than for the first game: EGM scored it 7.2 out of 10, calling it "overall a good action title", while GamePro called it "a good progression from the original" but noted slowdown in later levels.

title: Congo Bongo
description: Congo Bongo (1983) is Sega's isometric platform game, in which a safari hunter climbs after Bongo, a gorilla who set fire to his tent.
longDescription: A safari hunter climbs after Bongo, a gorilla who set fire to his tent, using an eight-way joystick and one jump button against a falling bonus counter. On Steep Peak he dodges coconuts and monkeys; on Snake Lake he crosses bridges and islands guarded by snakes and scorpions, with a hippopotamus helping him over part of the water; on Rhino Ridge he jumps charging rhinoceroses or hides in holes; and on Lazy Lagoon he crosses on lily pads, hippos and fish, then dodges more rhinos to reach Bongo. After the fourth stage the game returns to the first at a higher difficulty. One or two players take turns.
trivia: Ikegami Tsushinki, credited with its development, had earlier done programming work on Donkey Kong.
A planned sequel was abandoned in the early-1980s market downturn.
Readers of ST. Game voted the Atari version the worst Atari program of 1983.
Sega's marketing executive Bob Rosenbaum said it did strongly in a four-week location test.
The arcade original is unlockable in Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection.
devStory:
Sega released it in Japan on 14 February 1983, also as Tip Top, and in North America and Europe that March, using hardware related to Zaxxon's; Ken Horowitz credits Ikegami Tsushinki with its development. Computer and Video Games described it as "Donkey Kong presented in three dimensions" and said its last stage resembles Frogger. Game Machine ranked it Japan's fifth most successful table arcade game in mid-June 1983, but reception in the US was mixed, and Time reported a Los Angeles distributor selling off its cabinets at a discount during that year's downturn.

Versions followed on a dozen home systems. The ColecoVision, Atari 5200 and Intellivision ones won an Arkie Award for audio-visual effects, but Computer Games gave the 2600 version a C−.

title: Flicky
description: Flicky (1984) is Sega's arcade game about a flightless blue bird leading yellow Chirps to the exit while cats and lizards try to scatter them.
longDescription: Flicky, a blue bird who cannot fly, runs and jumps around each stage gathering the yellow Chirps, which follow her in a chain until they reach the exit; bringing several home at once scores a bonus. If the chain touches an enemy the Chirps scatter, and those wearing sunglasses wander off less predictably. The enemies are Tigers, house cats, and Iggys, green iguanas, and Flicky can throw items such as telephones, flower pots, cups and bottles at them by walking into them and jumping. Each of the 48 stages is a single screen that wraps around horizontally with Flicky always centred, bonus rounds have her catching falling Chirps in a net, and after the last stage the game loops at a higher difficulty.
trivia: It began as a maze game inspired by Namco's Mappy and was called "Busty", then "Flippy".
Kawasaki drew all its graphics with a poorly calibrated graphics tablet.
Iggy was added after testing.
Computer and Video Games and Mean Machines both reported staff leaving their desks to play it.
Flicky became a Sega mascot and appears in Sonic games, notably Sonic 3D Blast, whose mechanics it inspired.
devStory:
Sega wanted to beat Namco's Mappy, popular in Japanese arcades, and Yoji Ishii's boss asked him for a better game of that kind. Ishii, who later designed Fantasy Zone, spent a year on it with artist Yoshiki Kawasaki. Kawasaki's first idea was catching dots in a maze, and a song about sparrows on power lines made the hero a sparrow and the platforms wires, before he swapped the background for an apartment block outside his office window. The dots became Chirps that trail the player, and the team wanted it to carry the message "protect the children".

Sega released it in Japan in May 1984, and Game Machine ranked it the second most popular table arcade unit that July; Bally Midway distributed it in the US. SG-1000 and Japanese computer versions followed, then a Mega Drive version in 1991, which Mean Machines gave 92%.

title: Enduro Racer
description: Enduro Racer (1986) is Yu Suzuki's dirt-bike racer for Sega, the off-road counterpart to Hang-On, with a full-size bike cabinet.
longDescription: Riders race five stages of hills, turns and other riders, with logs and boulders in the way, against a timer. The handlebars steer and work the throttle and brake, and pulling them up pops a wheelie; logs can be jumped, but the bike has to land on a wheelie or it crashes. The timer stops during a crash, but getting going again is slow and eats time. It came in two cabinets: a stand-up version with handlebars and a full-size dirt bike.
trivia: Its ZX Spectrum version reached No. 2 in the UK chart in August 1987, and topped the budget chart in June 1988.
The Japanese Master System version has ten levels; other regions got half, on a 128 KB cartridge instead of 256 KB.
The Commodore 64 version has four levels, the last two harder versions of the first two.
It was London's eighth highest-grossing arcade game of 1986.
Your Sinclair ranked the Spectrum version 50th in its top 100 games in 1993.
devStory:
Yu Suzuki, a fan of dirt bikes, motocross and enduro, had made Hang-On as a road racer because Sega's research found GP 500 racing more popular worldwide; Enduro Racer, on a similar engine and board, gave him his dirt-bike game. Hiroshi Kawaguchi wrote the music. Sega released it in Japan on 16 July 1986, and Game Machine listed it as the most successful upright arcade unit from mid-August through October; it was Japan's sixth highest-grossing upright game of 1986. Clare Edgeley of Computer and Video Games called it "brilliant".

Activision handled the home computer versions. Sinclair User gave the Spectrum one 5 out of 5, saying it "puts other top software houses to shame", while Zzap!64 gave the Commodore 64 version 16%.

title: Super Hang-On
description: Super Hang-On (1987) is Yu Suzuki's sequel to Hang-On, a motorbike racer across four continents with a turbo button and a choice of music.
longDescription: Riders sit on a motorbike cabinet, as in Hang-On, and race across four continents: Africa with 6 stages, Asia with 10, the Americas with 14 and Europe with 18, each stage about half as long as one in the original. The normal top speed is 280 km/h, and reaching it switches on a turbo that pushes the bike to 324 km/h. As in Out Run, the player picks one of four songs before setting off.
trivia: The Mega Drive version added a mode for recruiting sponsors and buying bike upgrades, saved by password.
Sinclair User gave the ZX Spectrum version 10/10 and its SU Classic award.
The Mega Drive box shows a bike and rider in the colours of Shinichi Ito's Rothmans Honda NSR500.
The 3DS version adds stereoscopic 3D and tilt controls that mimic the arcade bike.
It is playable in the arcades of Yakuza 0 and Yakuza 6.
devStory:
Yu Suzuki designed it at Sega R&D1, with music by Katsuhiro Hayashi and Koichi Namiki, and Sega released it in Japan in April 1987 and North America that June. Game Machine listed it as the most successful upright arcade unit of May 1987, and it was Japan's second highest-grossing upright game of the year, behind Out Run, and its seventh highest-grossing arcade game of 1988. Your Sinclair's Peter Shaw called the arcade game "brilliant, fast and the most accurate simulation of riding a motorbike" he had played.

Spectrum, Amstrad and Commodore 64 versions followed in 1987, then Mega Drive, Amiga, Atari ST and other versions in 1989 and 1990. The Mega Drive version added an original mode in which the player recruits sponsors, earns money and buys better parts, saved with a password.

title: Alien Syndrome
description: Alien Syndrome (1987) is Sega's two-player shooter in which Ricky and Mary rescue hostages from alien-infested ships before a time bomb goes off.
longDescription: Ricky and Mary, soldiers hunting aliens, must rescue comrades held hostage aboard alien-infested ships. One or two players move through large levels that scroll in eight directions, and at the start of each a time bomb is set: if it runs out, the ship is destroyed. Rescuing a set number of hostages opens the exit, and the guardian waiting at the end must be defeated before time runs out. After seven levels the game starts again with more aggressive aliens and less time.
trivia: Critics praised its horror atmosphere and sound.
Tengen's NES version was released in North America without a Nintendo license.
A Sega Ages remake for the PlayStation 2 added twin-stick controls.
The arcade original is unlockable in Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection.
A sequel came out on the Game Gear, and a new Alien Syndrome followed on PSP and Wii in 2007.
devStory:
Sega R&D1 made it on the Pre System 16 and System 16B boards, with music by Tohru Nakabayashi, and released it in Japan in April 1987 and North America that June; Game Machine ranked it Japan's third most successful table arcade unit that April. Clare Edgeley of Computer and Video Games called it "one of the most gripping games" she had played in months, praising its Aliens-like horror atmosphere.

Sanritsu made the Master System version, one of that console's best sellers, and the NES one, which Tengen published in North America without a Nintendo license. Softek made the Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64 and Spectrum versions, with David Whittaker scoring the Amiga music.

title: Power Drift
description: Power Drift (1988) is Yu Suzuki's kart racer for Sega, built entirely from scaling sprites on a cabinet that tilted and shook, recognised by Guinness as the first kart racing game.
longDescription: Its world and tracks are built entirely from sprites, which the Sega Y Board could rotate and scale along with the background, and the tracks climb and drop steeply, with cars able to fall off the higher sections. The sit-down cabinet sat on a raised hydraulic platform that tilted and shook. Five courses, A to E, each with a theme such as cities, deserts or beaches, have five tracks of four laps, and players must finish third or better to go on; continuing after a worse finish stops the score rising. Winning every race on a course unlocks an extra stage flown in After Burner II's F-14 or ridden on Super Hang-On's motorbike, and pressing Start switches to a rear view.
trivia: Sinclair User called it "the single most spectacular game ever to arrive in an arcade".
Its ZX Spectrum version knocked RoboCop off the top of the UK chart in 1989.
Guinness World Records recognises it as the first kart racing video game, before Super Mario Kart.
A 3DS version, 3D Power Drift, came out in 2015.
Its track names include Bum Beach and Curry De Parl.
devStory:
Yu Suzuki directed, produced and designed it at Sega AM2, with music by Hiroshi Kawaguchi, and Sega released it in Japan on 5 August 1988; it was the fourth highest-grossing arcade game of 1989 in Japan. Sinclair User gave it 10 out of 10, calling it technically "a breakthrough", and Andy Smith of ACE said it combined the best of Out Run and Buggy Boy.

Activision's 1989 computer versions lacked the tilting cabinet, but the Spectrum one went to the top of the UK chart, and Amstrad Action gave its version a Mastergame award. A Japan-only PC Engine version followed in 1990, while Mega Drive, 32X and Sega CD versions were never released.

title: Shadow Dancer
description: Shadow Dancer (1989) is Sega's arcade sequel to Shinobi, in which the ninja fights alongside a dog he can set on enemies.
longDescription:
A young ninja and his dog fight a terrorist group that has planted time bombs across a city. The play closely follows the arcade Shinobi, with unlimited shuriken and a sword at close range. When the dog barks at an enemy, crouching and attacking sets it on that enemy, but if the player is slow to follow up or the enemy is well defended, the dog shrinks to a harmless pup until the next time bomb is collected or the stage ends. Collecting half a stage's bombs unlocks stronger weapons, and one of three randomly assigned ninpo techniques can clear the screen once per stage.

The four missions have three or four stages each and end with bosses such as an armoured giant throwing energy balls and a female ninja with a naginata. Between missions, a bonus game has the player throwing shuriken at ninjas dropping from a building, for an extra life. The arcade version never names the hero.
trivia: It was the first game made for Sega's System 18 board.
Shadow Dancer: The Secret of Shinobi on the Genesis is a loose adaptation, not a port.
The hero is unnamed in the arcade game; the Master System manual calls him Takashi and the U.S. Gold manual Joe Musashi.
Finishing a stage without shuriken or ninpo earns a bonus.
The dog sits out the boss fights.
devStory: Motoshige Hokoyama directed it as Sega's first game for its System 18 board, and it reached North American arcades in May 1989 and Japan that September. Zero called it derivative of Shinobi and Dragon Ninja but "good fun", and GamePro praised its graphics, animation and audio. Images made the home computer versions, which U.S. Gold released in Europe in 1991, and Your Sinclair called the Spectrum version an "impressive arcade conversion". It sold about 300,000 copies.

title: The Revenge of Shinobi
description: The Revenge of Shinobi (1989) is Sega's Genesis ninja game scored by Yuzo Koshiro, whose enemies looked so like Spider-Man, Batman and Godzilla that it went through several revisions.
longDescription:
Three years after the first game, the syndicate Zeed has re-formed as Neo Zeed, killed Joe Musashi's master and kidnapped his bride, Naoko. Joe reaches the Oboro clan too late, learns of the plot from his dying master and sets out across the world for revenge. He crosses eight districts, each with two platforming scenes and a boss, some with layers he can jump between, such as a military base and a freeway.

A somersault raises his jump and lets him throw eight shuriken in mid-air. Four ninjutsu techniques, among them Mijin and Ikazuchi, can be used once per life unless more are found. Crates hold shuriken, health, lives, ninjutsu and sometimes time bombs. There are four difficulty levels — on the hardest Joe takes double damage and starts with one life instead of ten — and two endings, depending on whether he saves Naoko.
trivia: Spider-Man was licensed only in some versions, and later re-releases replaced him with a recoloured character.
In Japan it was called The Super Shinobi.
One revision replaced the Batman lookalike with a Devilman-like creature.
A Master System version was advertised in 1990 but never released.
EGM ranked it 83rd among the best console games of all time in 1997.
devStory:
Noriyoshi Ohba directed it to show off the new Genesis hardware and adapt the series for home play, making it more story-driven, with one hostage at the end rather than several per level, and adding a life bar. Yuzo Koshiro composed the score, a turning point in his career and the origin of his house-influenced dance style; Ohba was impressed enough to ask him to score Streets of Rage. Some enemies resembled Rambo, Batman, Spider-Man, the Terminator and Godzilla, which Ohba put down to his own lack of creativity, and they were changed over several revisions.

It came out in Japan as The Super Shinobi on 2 December 1989. MegaTech gave it 94% and a Hyper Game award, and Dragon called it a "masterpiece", though it found the final boss too hard.

sources.title: The Revenge of Shinobi (1989 video game)

title: Phantasy Star II
description: Phantasy Star II (1989) is Sega's science-fantasy role-playing game for the Mega Drive, on a 6-megabit cartridge described as the largest console game of its time.
longDescription:
A thousand years after the first Phantasy Star, the planet Mota has been terraformed into a green world of domed farms by Mother Brain, the giant computer that rules it. When biologically engineered biomonsters begin to plague Mota, the government agent Rolf is sent from Paseo to retrieve a recorder from the BioSystem lab. The story takes in the death of Nei, a half-human, half-biomonster girl who falls fighting her vengeful predecessor Neifirst, and the destruction of the planet Palm, and ends with the revelation that Mother Brain was created by surviving Earthlings aboard the spaceship Noah.

Rolf leads a party of up to four from eight characters, each with their own weapons, armour and techniques: Nei; the gun-wielding hunter Rudolf Steiner; the medic Amy Sage; the biologist Hugh Thompson; the mercenary Anna Zirski; the junk dealer Josh Kain, who is good against machines; and the thief Shir Gold. It drops the first game's first-person view for top-down exploration and third-person, turn-based battles.
trivia: Dragon called it "one of the best role-playing games yet to be released for any video game system".
It was remade for the PlayStation 2 in Japan as Phantasy Star Generation 2 in 2005.
RePlay estimated its length at about 250 hours.
It reverses the alien-invasion trope by making Earthlings the invaders.
An Atari Jaguar version was approved in 1994 but never released.
devStory:
Chieko Aoki directed and wrote it, with Yuji Naka producing and programming, Rieko Kodama on art and music by Tokuhiko Uwabo. It was the first video game on a 6-megabit cartridge, the largest console game of its time. Sega released it in Japan on 21 March 1989 and in North America in March 1990, four months before Final Fantasy on the NES, as the Mega Drive's first RPG.

Computer Gaming World's Roe R. Adams called it a system seller for the Genesis, and EGM later ranked it the 30th-best console game of all time in 1997. It is credited as a forerunner of character-driven stories and science-fiction RPG settings.

title: Bonanza Bros.
description: Bonanza Bros. (1990) is Sega's split-screen stealth game, in which brothers Robo and Mobo sneak past guards to grab loot and escape by blimp.
longDescription: Robo and Mobo — called Mike and Spike in some PAL versions — sneak through a bank, a millionaire's mansion, a casino, a mint, an art gallery and a treasury, collecting the loot against a time limit and climbing to the roof where a blimp waits. Two can play together on a screen that is always split in two. The brothers walk, jump, shoot and hide behind columns and furniture. Guards are stunned briefly by a shot or a slammed door, and react to noise or a sighting by hiding, calling for help or firing; some carry riot shields and can only be hit from behind. A life is lost to bullets, dogs, doors or a botched jump, with all the loot dropped. In Japan the brothers are thieves; in the West the police chief of Badville recruits them to test security and recover evidence from crooked businesses.
trivia: In Japan the brothers are thieves; in the West a police chief recruits them to test security.
Several reviewers found it too easy.
It was removed from Western versions of Sonic Gems Collection to keep a universal age rating.
Its spin-offs, Tant-R and Ichidant-R, are puzzle games.
Robo and Mobo are playable in Sonic & Sega All-Stars Racing.
devStory: Sega released it in Japanese arcades in June 1990, one of the earliest games on its System 24 board, with music by Koichi Namiki, and Game Machine listed it as the third most popular arcade game in Japan in mid-July. Computer and Video Games' Julian Rignall praised its originality and "stunning" graphics, calling it a "rather nerve-wracking game of hide and seek". The Mega Drive version followed in 1991, and U.S. Gold published versions for home computers, though several reviewers found it too easy.

title: Kid Chameleon
description: Kid Chameleon (1992) is Sega Technical Institute's Genesis platformer of more than 100 levels, in which masks turn the hero into forms with different powers — with no way to save.
longDescription: Kid Chameleon tries to save his friends from a rogue artificial intelligence inside a virtual reality video game. The game runs to over 100 levels, most ending at a flag, and teleporters warp the player within a level, to other levels or onto alternate paths. Masks turn the hero into different forms, each with its own abilities and hit points — some can climb walls, for instance — and each form has Diamond Powers fuelled by collected diamonds. Most enemies can be beaten by jumping on them. There is no password or save system.
trivia: MegaTech thought it lacked challenge.
Mega ranked it 35th among its top Mega Drive games of all time.
Sonic the Comic ran a Kid Chameleon strip in issues 7–12, and a sequel story in 1995.
It was included in the Sega Genesis Collection and Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection.
devStory:
Graeme Bayless directed it at Sega Technical Institute, with Mark Cerny among the programmers, Yasushi Yamaguchi among the artists and music by Mark Miller. Sega released it in North America in March 1992 and in Japan, as Chameleon Kid, that May.

Reviews were mixed to positive. Sega Force praised its graphics and music and noted similarities to Mario and Sonic, and Console XS liked the variety of forms, while MegaTech found it too easy and others criticised the lack of saves. It averaged 68% on GameRankings.

title: Sonic CD
description: Sonic CD (1993) is the Sega CD's best-selling game, in which Sonic travels between the past, present and future of each stage, and the debut of Amy Rose and Metal Sonic.
longDescription:
Little Planet appears over Never Lake in the last month of each year, and Dr. Robotnik has chained it to a mountain and turned it into a fortress, hunting for the seven Time Stones that control time. Amy Rose follows Sonic there and is kidnapped by Metal Sonic, whom Sonic races in Stardust Speedway before facing Robotnik in Metallic Madness.

Each of the seven rounds has three zones, the third a boss fight. Signs marked "past" and "future" send Sonic through time, and the music changes with each period. Futures are bad by default; destroying a hidden robot generator in the past creates a good one, and good futures in every zone — or all seven Time Stones — earn the best ending. Finishing a zone with 50 rings opens a pseudo-3D special stage where Sonic must destroy six UFOs against the clock to win a Time Stone. Extras include time attack, a music room called D.A. Garden and the animated cutscenes.
trivia: Sega of America delayed the North American release two months to replace the house- and techno-influenced Japanese score with a new one by Spencer Nilsen and others.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it the best Sega CD game of 1993.
Its game data takes 21 MB, against 1 MB for Sonic 2.
Christian Whitehead's 2011 remake includes both soundtracks.
Its US theme song, "Sonic Boom", returned in Super Smash Bros. Brawl.
devStory:
Sega wanted a Sonic game to show off the Sega CD while Yuji Naka and part of Sonic Team were in the US making Sonic 2. Naoto Ohshima directed it, with staff from The Revenge of Shinobi, Golden Axe II and Streets of Rage, building on the original Sonic's code; it began as an enhanced port called CD Sonic the Hedgehog. Kazuyuki Hoshino designed Amy and Metal Sonic, Ohshima cited Back to the Future as an influence, and each stage was built in four variants. Naofumi Hataya and Masafumi Ogata wrote the house- and techno-inspired Japanese score.

It came out in Japan on 23 September 1993 and abroad in November with a new soundtrack. It sold over 1.5 million copies, the Sega CD's best seller, and won Best Sega CD Game of 1993 from EGM and Best CD Game from GamePro.

title: Virtua Striker
description: Virtua Striker (1994) is Sega AM2's arcade football game on the Model 2 board, the first football game with 3D computer graphics.
longDescription: Sixteen teams play a single-elimination knockout tournament modelled on the World Cup's knockout stage, chosen from 18 national sides, each with a preset formation that cannot be changed: Denmark's 5-3-2, Brazil's 4-4-2 and Argentina's diamond among them. Three buttons handle everything. Pass also slides into tackles without the ball; long ball crosses automatically when running parallel to the box; and shoot can be charged, or tapped for a header or volley when meeting a cross. The camera zooms to frame the play.
trivia: A hidden team, FC Sega, made up of the developers, faces players who win the final and can be unlocked with a code.
Sega advertised it as "the first three-dimensional computer graphic soccer game".
Its team selection music can be heard in Virtua Striker 2 with a special code.
It came to Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network in Japan in 2013.
The Argentina side includes Diego Maradona and Gabriel Batistuta.
devStory:
Yu Suzuki proposed it to Satoshi Mifune, a football fan with whom he had worked on Space Harrier and After Burner, and Sega AM2 developed it on the Model 2 board. Mifune doubted it would work and said he would never make another football game if it failed. The three-button layout came from a wish for accessibility and from the lack of any established standard to follow. Released in 1994, it was the first football game with 3D computer graphics, and an early user of texture mapping alongside Daytona USA.

Game Machine ranked it the most successful dedicated arcade game in Japan in its 15 July 1995 issue. Next Generation gave it four stars, calling it "excellent to play and watch" and praising its controls, realistic movement, camera and "gorgeous" texture-mapped players.

title: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei
description: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei (1996) is Team Andromeda's Saturn rail shooter, in which the rider's dragon evolves through several forms depending on the player's scores.
longDescription:
A prequel to the first game, it is set during a war between the Empire and Meccania over the remnants of the Ancient Age. In Jean-Jacques Lundi's village, where people ride pack animals called coolias and glowing mutant coolias are killed as bad omens, Lundi shelters one with a green throat and wings, Lagi. While they are out riding, an automated Ancient Age airship, Shelcoof, destroys the village, and Lagi turns out to fire lasers from its mouth, like the dragons of old.

Enemies come from any direction and show on a radar. Lundi fires his gun while the dragon locks on with lasers, and a Berserk attack, charged by shooting enemies down, sends homing lasers at everything on screen. Levels two to four branch into routes with different scenery and enemies, and each level is scored on kills, damage, route, continues and boss time. Those scores decide which of six forms the dragon evolves into, with a seventh for the final boss, and finishing the game opens the Pandora's Box extras menu.
trivia: A system called ADEC adjusted enemy behaviour to how well the player was doing.
Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it 90th in its 1997 list of the best games of all time.
Programmers kept segmented wooden fish on their desks to study lifelike movement.
The Emperor's design was inspired by the Harkonnens of Dune.
Sega Saturn Magazine gave it 95%.
devStory:
Team Andromeda began it in mid-1995, months after the first game, with a team of 15 to 20 reusing the original engine, and finished in under a year; Tomohiro Kondo produced and directed it, and Katsuhiko Yamada took over the story. Responding to criticism of the first game, the team made it easier and more story-driven, adding branching routes for replay, the evolving dragon (Yukio Futatsugi's idea) and ADEC, Kondo's system for adjusting enemies to the player's performance. With no help from Sega's technical division, they built their own tools.

Yayoi Wachi led the music, mostly generated by the Saturn's PCM hardware because the branching routes made precise scoring impossible. Sega released it in Japan on 22 March 1996, and it averaged 88% on GameRankings; GamePro said it "blows away anything resembling a shooter on the PlayStation thus far".

title: Athena
description: Athena (1986) is SNK's platformer about a princess who falls into Emperor Dante's world with nothing, described as one of the first games with a playable female lead.
longDescription:
Princess Athena of the heavenly Kingdom of Victory, bored with palace life, opens the "Door Which Shouldn't Be Opened" in the basement of Castle Victory and falls into Fantasy World, ruled by the evil Emperor Dante. She loses her dress in the fall and lands in a wilderness of beast-like warriors, armed only with kicks.

She picks up weapons dropped by defeated enemies and finds shields, headgear and armour, which break after a few hits. A hammer smashes stone blocks to reveal armour or magic items, such as Mercury's sandals for great leaps. Across eight worlds of leaping and climbing, each ending with an oversized boss, the mythological weapons and equipment become the means of defeating enemies, and some items are needed to finish the game. Its weapons, items and enemies draw on Greek mythology and ancient Roman culture.
trivia: Athena later appears in SNK fighting games, as a secret character or helping her descendant Athena Asamiya.
It has been described as one of the first games with a playable female character.
Its sequel, Psycho Soldier, followed in 1987.
The NES version was released in North America only, until the arcade original reached the PlayStation Network in 2011.
Your Sinclair gave the Spectrum version a Megagame award.
devStory: Koji Obata designed it at SNK, which released it in Japanese arcades in July 1986; Game Machine listed it as the ninth most successful table arcade game in its 1 September issue. Micronics made the Famicom version, released in Japan in June 1987 and in North America that August, and Ocean released ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 versions under its Imagine label the same year, the Spectrum one earning a Your Sinclair Megagame. The arcade and NES versions are included in SNK 40th Anniversary Collection.

title: Kiki Kaikai
description: Kiki Kaikai (1986) is Taito's overhead shooter set in feudal Japan, in which the shrine maiden Sayo-chan fights yokai with paper charms and a purification rod.
longDescription:
While Sayo-chan, a young Shinto shrine maiden, tends a ceremonial fire, the Seven Lucky Gods appear to warn her of coming danger, and then yōkai kidnap them and carry them off to a distant mountain range. She sets out across the countryside to rescue them, fighting obake and yūrei. Seen from above, she moves freely rather than being pushed forward by the scrolling, throws o-fuda charms in eight directions or swings a purification rod in front of her, and slips of paper dropped by defeated enemies power up either attack's strength or range.

One hit kills Sayo-chan, sending her back to a continuation point, and each level ends with a boss that takes several hits. Striking objects with the rod can reveal hidden items. When the last life is lost, a "number match" screen draws a random three-digit number, and if it matches the last three digits of the score, the player gets a free game.
trivia: It began the series Natsume continued with Pocky & Rocky (1992).
Hisayoshi Ogura's music gives Japanese folk tunes a chiptune sound.
The Famicom Disk System box featured idol singer Miki Ito, who recorded the song "Sayo Carnival".
The NES and Master System versions of Rainbow Islands replace one island with one based on it.
Its heroine and ghosts influenced Reimu Hakurei and the ghost enemies of the Touhou Project games.
devStory:
Hisaya Yabusaki created it at Taito in 1986, drawing on Japanese mythology and the top-down shooters of the day, with Mikio Hatano directing and Hisayoshi Ogura composing music that mixes Japanese folk instruments such as the shamisen with an electronic beat. Taito released it in Japan in October 1986, and Game Machine listed it as the second most successful table arcade unit that November; it was Japan's tenth highest-grossing table arcade game of 1987.

Versions followed on the MSX2 and the Famicom Disk System, whose 1987 edition added levels, enemies and a second shrine maiden, Miki-chan, then the PC Engine in 1990. GameSpot later called it one of Taito's sleepier titles.

title: Heavy Barrel
description: Heavy Barrel (1987) is Data East's overhead run and gun with rotary joysticks, in which players collect six pieces to build a superweapon.
longDescription: Terrorists have seized the underground control complex of a nuclear missile site, and one or two players fight their way in to kill the leader. Players start with an unlimited gun and a few grenades. Better weapons and grenade upgrades lie in the open or in crates opened with keys, which may also hold orbs or one of the six pieces of the Heavy Barrel. Assembled, it is an energy cannon with a wide arc of fire that shoots as fast as the trigger is pressed and destroys any enemy in one hit, apart from the final boss and perhaps one other; it lasts 30 seconds. There are enough pieces to build it three times in a game, and in two-player games whoever picks up the sixth piece gets it. Like SNK's Ikari Warriors, it used eight-way rotary joysticks.
trivia: A Commodore 64 version was contracted but never finished because its developer closed.
It was included in Data East Arcade Classics on the Wii in 2010.
The Heavy Barrel lasts 30 seconds once assembled.
Data East developed the NES version itself.
Its rotary joystick was like the one in SNK's Ikari Warriors.
devStory: Koji Akibayashi designed it at Data East, with music by Azusa Hara and Hiroaki Yoshida, and it reached arcades in 1987; Game Machine listed it as the sixth most successful table arcade unit in mid-January 1988. Quicksilver Software made Apple II and MS-DOS versions in 1989, and Data East made the NES version in 1990, which EGM's four reviewers each gave 7 out of 10.

title: Psycho Soldier
description: Psycho Soldier (1987) is SNK's distant sequel to Athena and the first appearance of Athena Asamiya, who with Sie Kensou was among the first game characters to have a theme song.
longDescription:
Many years after the events of Athena, Athena Asamiya, a girl with psychic powers who hopes to become a pop idol, defends her Japanese hometown from evil beings with her friend and fellow psychic Sie Kensou. Both play the same way. A shield of rotating spheres surrounds the character, and an energy bar beside it measures Psycho Energy, raised by collecting items; each sphere can be launched at enemies or destructible objects, at the cost of that sphere. At low energy the spheres bounce around the screen, while at full energy they swirl faster and spread out, destroying everything in their path. Rocks and other objects sometimes hide power-ups.

Collecting a green egg-like item with a full bar turns the character into a Psycho Creature — a phoenix for Athena, a green dragon for Kensou — with a fire breath and a ramming attack, until the stage boss falls or too many hits drain the energy.
trivia: Athena Asamiya is a descendant of the heroine of Athena (1986).
Athena and Kensou were among the first game characters with their own theme songs, later remixed many times in The King of Fighters.
Athena went on to appear in The King of Fighters, SNK vs. Capcom and Super Smash Bros. Ultimate.
A Crash reviewer found its play boring and Athena slow to react.
devStory: SNK released it in Japan on 3 March 1987, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's seventh most successful table arcade unit in mid-April. Ocean's Imagine label released ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC versions the same year, the Spectrum one converted by Ross Harris. Your Sinclair's Jonathan Davies gave the Spectrum version 8/10, liking its smooth sprites but not its monochrome graphics or weak sound effects, while Crash scored it 69% and 75%.

title: The NewZealand Story
description: The NewZealand Story (1988) is Taito's platformer about Tiki the kiwi rescuing his girlfriend and friends from a leopard seal, inspired by a Taito programmer's holiday in New Zealand.
longDescription:
Tiki the kiwi must rescue his girlfriend and other kiwi chicks kidnapped by a large blue leopard seal, freeing one caged chick at the end of each stage. Tiki dies from one hit. He starts with endless arrows, and pickups swap them for bombs, lasers or bouncing fireballs. He can ride balloons, blimps and UFOs, found lying about or taken from enemies. Levels scroll in every direction, much larger than a single screen, with a mini-map in the corner showing Tiki and the caged kiwi that marks the exit.

Four zones of four rounds each end with a boss, and hidden warps lead to secret areas and shortcuts. Each stage has a hidden time limit: a "Hurry Up!" warning plays when it runs out, and after more time an invincible red devil comes after Tiki. On some later levels, losing a last life to a projectile sends the player to a "Heaven" round with a special ending or a secret way back. Collecting letters to spell EXTEND is borrowed from Bubble Bobble.
trivia: Home computer boxes call the villain a walrus, but the arcade credits say leopard seal.
The NES version was released in North America as Kiwi Kraze.
Amiga Power ranked it the 19th best game of all time.
The Mega Drive version, Japan-only, used levels from an arcade prototype.
Tiki makes cameos in Liquid Kids, Bubble Symphony and Pop'n Pop.
devStory:
A Taito programmer's holiday in New Zealand inspired its concept and setting. Taito released it in arcades in Europe in August 1988 and worldwide that September, with music by Yasuko Yamada and Yasuhisa Watanabe, and Game Machine ranked it Japan's ninth most successful table arcade unit in mid-November.

Ocean published the home computer versions in 1989 with Bob Wakelin's cover art, and it was bundled with the Amiga 500 Batman Pack, which sold over 2 million units. The Spectrum version reached number two in the full-price chart, and Crash called it "an arcade conversion masterpiece". Software Creations made the NES version, with music by Tim and Geoff Follin.

title: Vigilante
description: Vigilante (1988) is Irem's side-scrolling beat 'em up, a spiritual sequel to Kung-Fu Master moved to an American setting.
longDescription: In downtown New York a lone martial artist turns vigilante to fight the Skinheads, a gang ruled by the "Giant Devil", who have kidnapped a woman named Madonna. The player punches and kicks through five stages: a street, a junkyard, the Brooklyn Bridge, a back street and a building under construction. Skinheads with mohawks or spiked hair come at him with knives, chains, motorbikes and guns, and choke him if they get too close. Nunchaku can be picked up and used, but getting hurt while holding them leaves the player unarmed again.
trivia: It began as a Kung-Fu Master sequel, Beyond Kung-Fu: Return of the Master, which was tested in 1987 and shelved.
The Master System version renames Madonna as Maria and the Skinheads as the Rogues, and has an FM sound switch.
Your Sinclair gave the arcade version 8/10 but called the Spectrum version a "pretty standard beat 'em up".
The TurboGrafx-16 version is the closest to the arcade.
Hamster released the arcade version in its Arcade Archives series in 2019.
devStory:
Irem had made an arcade sequel to Kung-Fu Master called Beyond Kung-Fu: Return of the Master, which was location-tested in 1987 and shelved after it underperformed. Irem reworked it with a more American setting as Vigilante, with music by Masato Ishizaki, and released it in North America through Data East in February 1988 and in Japan and Europe in March. Game Machine ranked it Japan's second most successful table arcade unit that April.

Arc System Works made the Master System version, which renamed Madonna as Maria and the Skinheads as the Rogues, and Emerald Software made the home computer versions for U.S. Gold. Irem's own TurboGrafx-16 version, released in Japan in January 1989 and by NEC in North America that October, is the closest to the arcade.

title: Chase H.Q.
description: Chase H.Q. (1988) is Taito's police driving game, in which the player catches fleeing criminals and rams their cars until they stop.
longDescription: Officer Tony Gibson and his partner Raymond Broady drive a black Porsche 928 for the Chase Special Investigation Department. Each of the five levels opens with Nancy at Chase HQ radioing in to say which criminal they are chasing, and the car pulls away into the distance under a time limit. Crashing or driving slowly lets it escape, and where the road forks the wrong turn lengthens the chase. Catching up extends the time, and the criminal's car then has to be rammed repeatedly until it stops. The targets run from Ralph, "the Idaho Slasher", in a white Lotus Esprit to a spy in a red Porsche 928.
trivia: Nancy's radio frequencies are mostly in the 2-metre amateur radio band.
Ocean's home computer versions topped the UK chart at Christmas 1989.
Your Sinclair's readers voted the Spectrum version number one in their 1993 top 100.
Saint Etienne's song "Chase HQ" samples the game.
Its ramming has been cited as a forerunner of Driver and Burnout.
devStory:
Taito made it on its Z System board, with music by Takami Asano, and released it in Japan in September 1988, in Europe in October and in North America in November. It was Japan's highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1989 and at one point the top coin-op in the UK. Arcade History called it arguably the first sprite-scaled racer since Out Run to capture the public's imagination.

Ocean's home computer versions topped the UK chart at Christmas 1989. All three Spectrum magazines scored it 94% or more, and the 8-bit versions won Golden Joysticks for best 8-bit coin-op conversion and soundtrack. Taito made versions for the Famicom, Game Boy, Master System, PC Engine and Game Gear.

title: Midnight Resistance
description: Midnight Resistance (1989) is Data East's Contra-like run and gun, aimed in eight directions with a rotating joystick, in which brothers fight to rescue their family from King Crimson.
longDescription:
Two brothers set out to rescue their family from King Crimson; in the Mega Drive version the hero is Johnny Ford, whose father Malcolm was developing a serum to cure addiction to all narcotics. Up to two players fight through nine stages, aiming in eight directions with a rotating joystick like Ikari Warriors' alongside shoot and jump buttons.

Certain soldiers drop keys, up to six of which can be carried, and at the end of each stage a weapons room hands out guns and power-ups according to the number of keys held. Special guns replace the default rifle until their ammunition runs out, backpack weapons are fired by pushing up while shooting, and a supercharge boosts the current weapon until a life is lost. Dying drops all weapons and keys, which can be picked up again if they stay on screen. Keys from the penultimate stage free relatives before the last fight, and the ending depends on how many were saved.
trivia: Sinclair User ranked the ZX Spectrum version 10th among the 100 best Spectrum games.
Your Sinclair's readers ranked it 11th in their top 100 games of all time.
The Genesis version was on the Sega Genesis Mini 2.
Its rotating joystick was borrowed from Ikari Warriors.
The ending changes with how many family members are rescued.
devStory:
