Koji Akibayashi designed it at Data East, with a power-up system resembling the company's earlier Heavy Barrel, and it reached arcades in 1989; Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most successful table arcade unit in mid-December. The Mega Drive version, Data East's first game for the console, was made with ISCO and Opera House, scored by Shogo Sakai and Hitoshi Sakimoto and released in Japan in April 1991, with Sega publishing it in North America that June; it is one player only.

Special FX made the home computer versions for Ocean, with music by Keith Tinman. The ZX Spectrum version scored 93% in Crash, 92% in Your Sinclair and 90% in Sinclair User.

title: Joe & Mac
description: Joe & Mac (1991), also called Caveman Ninja, is Data East's two-player prehistoric platformer in which two cavemen rescue women kidnapped by a rival tribe.
longDescription: Green-haired Joe and blue-haired Mac are cavemen out to rescue women kidnapped by a rival tribe. They fight with boomerangs, bones, fire, flints, electricity, stone wheels and clubs, and their health drains steadily except during boss fights. Two can play together, and in some versions the players can hurt each other. In the arcade version players pick their route after each boss, and after the final boss they choose one of three exits, each with its own ending.
trivia: A sequel, Joe & Mac 2: Lost in the Tropics, followed with light role-playing elements.
The Japanese version opens with cavemen dragging cavewomen by the hair, a scene Data East removed in the US so children would not see it.
Joe reappeared in the Game Boy puzzle game Franky, Joe & Dirk: On the Tiles, alongside Dragon's Lair's Dirk.
Complex ranked it 69th among the best SNES games in 2018.
Microids released a remake, New Joe & Mac – Caveman Ninja, in 2022.
devStory:
Makoto Kikuchi directed it at Data East, which released it in Japanese arcades in February 1991 and in North America in March; it is also known as Caveman Ninja. The Super NES version, released in Japan that December, was reworked with an overworld map, longer levels, bonus stages, a different final boss and only two endings. Elite Systems made the NES and MS-DOS versions, Motivetime the Amiga and Game Boy ones, and Eden Entertainment Software the Genesis version of 1994, considered the closest to the arcade.

Critics generally praised the graphics and sound but criticised the controls; the Genesis version averaged 75% on GameRankings, while Amiga Power gave the Amiga version 22%.

title: Metal Black
description: Metal Black (1991) is Taito's horizontal shooter that began as a third Darius game, with no extra weapons or bombs, only a beam powered by collecting Newalone molecules.
longDescription:
In 2042 a companion star of Jupiter pushes asteroids towards Earth, and aliens from a distant star, called the Nemesis, use the meteorite wave as cover to invade in search of inorganic materials. Scientists identify the molecule powering their beams as Newalone and launch Project Metal Black to build human ships. Ten years later, a treaty with the Nemesis promises peaceful surrender and bans the CF-345 Black Fly fighters, and the rogue pilot John Ford steals one and heads for Jupiter.

The ship has no extra weapons or bombs; Newalone molecules dropped by the Nemesis raise its beam level and are its only defence. At mid or full level it can fire a huge beam with a screen-shaking lightning effect. Bosses collect Newalone for their own beams, and when beams clash the stronger one wins while the player taps fire to hold the other back. Bonus rounds follow the first and third of the six rounds, and there are two endings.
trivia: It was developed as "Darius Part 22" and reworked as an original game because its tone was considered too dark.
Its beam system inspired G.rev's Border Down, according to Hiroyuki Maruyama.
G-Darius has a similar beam duel system.
Its first boss is called Apartheid.
The Black Fly is a downloadable ship in Dariusburst: Chronicle Saviours.
devStory:
Takatsuna Senba designed it, with Takamasa Hori producing and Yasuhisa Watanabe composing, on Taito's F1 System board, whose expansion chips allowed special graphical effects. It began as Darius 3 under the internal name "Darius Part 22", was reworked as an original game because Taito judged its atmosphere too dark, and had the working title "Project Gun Frontier 2"; Senba said the plan had been a two-screen cabinet like Darius II.

Taito released it in November 1991, and Micom BASIC Magazine gave it an award at its 1992 Video Game Grand Prix. Reviews were mixed, and Ving's Japan-only Saturn version of 1996 sold 7,839 copies in its first week.

title: Undercover Cops
description: Undercover Cops (1992) is Irem's Final Fight-inspired beat 'em up, set in New York in 2043, whose team later went on to form Nazca and make Metal Slug.
longDescription:
In New York in 2043, three "city sweepers" clean the streets of thugs: Zan Takahara, a karate master banned from tournaments after killing a man in self-defence; Matt Gables, a former American football player falsely accused of murder; and Rosa Felmonde, a British vigilante whose lover was killed by thugs. Zan is the all-rounder, Matt the strongest and slowest, and Rosa the fastest. Enemies range from human thugs to mole creatures and mutants with jet packs and blade hands, and the bosses include a Terminator-like cyborg and a carnival freak with a metal claw, before Dr. Crayborn turns into a giant monster.

Players cannot use enemies' weapons but can pick up objects such as burning oil drums, steel girders, concrete columns and fish, and restore health by eating mice, frogs, birds and snails. The game is known for its detailed, grimy backgrounds and was gory for its time, with skeletons pecked by crows and a first boss who can crush the player in a garbage compactor. The Japanese arcade version adds dash-jump attacks, extra throws and an airborne special.
trivia: The Super Famicom version has no two-player mode; its American release was cancelled, though Nintendo Power reviewed it in 1994, until Retro-Bit published 3,000 copies in 2021.
The police car at the end works like the tank in Irem's Moon Patrol.
R-Type's first boss appears on some of its red TV screens.
In the US the heroes were renamed Claude, Bubba and Flame.
It spawned a manga by Waita Uziga and a Game Boy spin-off.
devStory: It was Irem's first attempt at the modern beat 'em up, inspired by Final Fight, and ran on its M-92 board with music by Takushi Hiyamuta. Irem released it in North America in March 1992 and Japan in July, and it ranked sixth among Japan's table arcade units and tenth in RePlay's US chart that August. Varie made the Super Famicom version, released in Japan on 3 March 1995. Members of the team later formed Nazca, which created Metal Slug.

title: In the Hunt
description: In the Hunt (1993) is Irem's submarine shooter, whose designers went on to found Nazca and create Metal Slug.
longDescription: On a post-apocalyptic Earth, the Dark Anarchy Society plans to launch a doomsday superweapon, and the submarine Granvia sets out to stop it. The screen does not scroll by itself: the player steers freely through each level, destroying enemies and dodging projectiles on the way to a boss. The Granvia starts with forward missiles that kill most enemies in one hit, and missiles fired upwards to bring down helicopters and planes. Certain enemies give power-ups unlocking a machine gun, a wave cannon and a "cracker" spread shot, others drop red star-marked orbs worth bonus points, and there are several endings.
trivia: Its Japanese title, Kaitei Daisensō, means Undersea War.
A Super NES version was playable at CES 1994 but never released.
Kujo got the submarine idea from the sound of water near a fountain.
It has been described as a cross between Metal Slug and R-Type.
Hamster re-released it in its Arcade Archives series in 2019.
devStory:
Irem's management had already decided on a shoot 'em up, and Kazuma Kujo, who conceived and designed it, built it for co-op play. He disliked forced scrolling and wanted something other than the usual space theme, and the submarine idea came to him hearing water near a fountain. Akio Oyabu was the graphic designer, and it ran on Irem's M-92 board.

Irem released it in April 1993, and Game Machine ranked it Japan's sixth most popular arcade game that May. PlayStation and Saturn versions followed in 1995 and 1996, released abroad by THQ, and reviews were mixed: EGM praised the number of enemies on screen, while Next Generation found the submarine slow and the game unoriginal. Its designers later founded Nazca, which created Metal Slug.

title: Fighting Vipers
description: Fighting Vipers (1995) is Sega AM2's 3D fighting game on the Virtua Fighter 2 engine, with armour that breaks off and walled arenas instead of ring-outs.
longDescription:
The Vipers compete in the Nutcrack tournament in Armstone City, organised at the behest of the mayor, B.M. Fights use guard, punch and kick buttons with an emphasis on combos, as in Virtua Fighter 2, but each of the nine fighters wears armour that can be broken off, leaving them more vulnerable, with a human-shaped meter showing the damage. Walls enclose every arena: there are no ring-outs, fighters can be bounced off the walls, and strong knockout blows send them over, onto or through them.

The cast has a freeform, Western style: Bahn, a 17-year-old seeking revenge on his absent father; Candy, a fashion student in a plastic fairy costume of her own design; the model Grace; Raxel, lead singer of the hair metal band Death Crunch; Tokio, a former gang leader; the mysterious Sanman; Jane, a construction worker rejected by the Marines; Picky, a skateboarding 14-year-old; and the unlockable masked wrestler Mahler.
trivia: The Saturn version added Pepsiman as a guest fighter, in Japan only.
Sonic the Fighters started when a programmer put Sonic and Tails into this game.
Candy is called Honey in Japan.
The Saturn version also has a hidden bear fighter, Kumachan, based on a balloon in one of the stages.
It is playable in the arcades of Judgment and Lost Judgment.
devStory:
Sega AM2 built it on the Virtua Fighter 2 engine and a nearly identical Model 2 board, aiming at Western players; producer Yu Suzuki dropped ring-outs because he wanted fights to continue. It came out in November 1995, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's most popular arcade game in mid-December, but it was much less popular in North American arcades.

A 15-person AM2 team spent eight months on the 1996 Saturn version, adding Gouraud-shaded lighting to make up for fewer polygons and new training and playback modes. Famitsu scored it 37 out of 40, and Next Generation said that Virtua Fighter 2 is among the best games ever but Fighting Vipers "nearly eclipses it". All its fighters joined Fighters Megamix, and Fighting Vipers 2 followed in 1998.

title: Virtual On: Cyber Troopers
description: Virtual On (1996) is Sega AM3's twin-stick mech battle game, in which two Virtuaroids fight one-on-one.
longDescription:
On a colony world, the syndicate DN reverse-engineered the technology of an extinct race to build battle robots called Virtuaroids, until the test complex's central computer became self-aware and turned the Sun Cannon on civilisation. Two Virtuaroids fight in an arena, over one battle or the best of three rounds.

It is built for twin sticks, each with a trigger and a top button, which drive the robot like a bulldozer: both sticks forward or back to move, one forward and one back to turn. Pulling the sticks apart jumps and turns to face the opponent, and the top Turbo buttons dash for a few seconds while still allowing fire. Each Virtuaroid has three weapons that differ between machines: a left weapon, usually explosive; a right weapon, usually its main gun; and a centre weapon fired with both triggers, powerful but limited by energy. Weapons change with movement, so a standing Temjin's rifle fires a single shot while a dashing one fires a burst.
trivia: Its name combines the Japanese title Virtual-On and the original North American title Cyber Troopers.
The Saturn version supported online play through NetLink in North America and XBAND in Japan.
A twin-stick controller was made for the Saturn version.
The sequel, Oratorio Tangram, followed in 1998.
A PlayStation 4 version came out in Japan in 2019.
devStory:
Sega AM3 built it on the Model 2 board, and it reached Japanese arcades in January 1996; Game Machine named it the most successful dedicated arcade game in its 1 March 1996 issue, though it was not popular in US arcades. The Saturn version, made by a different AM3 team in response to player feedback, came out that November. Producer Juro Watari said converting its large arenas and many projectiles was harder than a typical fighting game, the team wrote a custom operating system rather than using Sega's graphics library, and the polygon backgrounds became scrolling images.

Next Generation called the arcade game "phenomenally intriguing", and Sega Saturn Magazine gave the Saturn version 93%, but GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann found it too shallow for consoles.

title: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders
description: Zak McKracken (1988) is Lucasfilm Games' second SCUMM adventure, in which a tabloid writer and three allies stop aliens from dumbing down humanity with a 60 Hz hum.
longDescription:
In 1997 — nine years after the game was made — Zak McKracken, who writes for the tabloid National Inquisitor, the freelance scientist Annie Larris and two Yale students, Melissa China and Leslie Bennett, take on the Caponians. These aliens have taken over "The Phone Company" and emit a 60 Hz hum from their Mind Bending Machine that is slowly lowering everyone's intelligence. To stop them, the heroes must rebuild the Skolarian Device, left behind by another alien race, whose parts are scattered across Earth and Mars.

The travels take in the Egyptian pyramids, Mexico, Lima, Stonehenge, the Bermuda Triangle and the Face on Mars. The Caponians, modelled on the Men in Black and named after Al Capone, fly Cadillac-shaped spaceships and are led by an Elvis figure known as "The King", while the Skolarians are based on the Greys. Critics noted its many mazes.
trivia: Players had to enter copy-protection codes every time they flew out of the US.
New Age writer David Spangler consulted on the game's materials.
Fox said it was more popular in Germany and Europe than in the US.
The Japanese FM Towns version can swap the characters' eyes for anime eyes.
German fans released a full sequel, Zak McKracken: Between Time and Space, in 2008.
devStory:
David Fox led it at Lucasfilm Games, co-designing and programming it with Matthew Alan Kane on the SCUMM engine first used for Maniac Mansion, which needed major updates for its scope. It was meant to be more serious, in the vein of Indiana Jones, until Ron Gilbert persuaded Fox to add humour, and New Age writer David Spangler consulted on its materials. It came out for the Commodore 64 in October 1988, followed by MS-DOS, Amiga and Atari ST versions and a 256-colour FM Towns version in Japan in 1990.

Computer Gaming World's Charles Ardai called it good but thought it could have been better, while Zzap!, Power Play and ST Action each gave it 90 out of 100.

sources.title: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders

title: Xenon 2: Megablast
description: Xenon 2: Megablast (1989) is the Bitmap Brothers' vertical shooter, named after and scored to Bomb the Bass's "Megablast", with a shop the player can visit twice per level.
longDescription:
A millennium after Xenon, the Xenites have planted five bombs throughout history, and the Megablaster must destroy them across five levels, which range from the Cambrian era to futuristic metal spaceways, with enemies mutated by the bombs' radiation. Each level ends with a boss whose defeat defuses that level's bomb, and levels two to five also have a midpoint boss. Hits drain the shield, a hit with no shield left costs one of three lives, and the scenery can crush the ship. Each level has six restart points, and pulling back at the bottom of the screen reverses the scrolling a little.

Capsules release tokens that upgrade weapons or speed, restore the shield or let the ship dive into the background for a while. Destroyed enemies drop "Real Cash", more for bigger ones, which can be spent or traded for tokens at Crispin's Swop Shop, open twice per level.
trivia: David Whittaker arranged Bomb the Bass's "Megablast (Hip Hop on Precinct 13)" as the main theme.
The Master System version was cut from five levels to three.
The CDTV version added a remix of "Megablast" and voice acting for Crispin by Richard Joseph.
A Super NES version was announced in 1992 but never released.
An Atari Jaguar version came out in 2016.
devStory:
Mike Montgomery, Steve Kelly and Eric Matthews designed it, influenced by Scramble, Gradius and R-Type and aiming for less predictable enemies; Matthews said players wanted destruction and extra weapons, and Xenon's tank transformation was dropped for simplicity. The Assembly Line programmed it, writing on an IBM PC and porting to the ST, and Mark Coleman drew the graphics in DEGAS Elite. Rhythm King's Martin Heath and Bomb the Bass's Tim Simenon were fans, so "Megablast" was licensed for the music.

Image Works released it for the Amiga and Atari ST in September 1989, and both versions topped the Gallup charts for their formats in their first month. Computer and Video Games gave the Amiga version 96% and Zzap!64 97%, though some critics found the scrolling slow and the genre crowded, and ST Format named it the best shoot 'em up of 1990.

title: Stunt Car Racer
description: Stunt Car Racer (1989) is Geoff Crammond's racer on elevated tracks with no barriers and gaps to jump, Your Sinclair's game of 1989.
longDescription:
Two cars race on elevated tracks with no barriers to stop them driving off the side, and ramps they must launch off are the main obstacle. Most tracks have gaps, and falling into one brings a crane to lift the car back, at the cost of time. Turbo is rationed per race. Damage from landing too hard over a crest, hitting a wall, falling or colliding with the other car shows as a crack spreading across the frame at the top of the screen, and once it grows far enough the car is wrecked and the race is over; hard crashes punch holes that stay for the rest of the season and make the crack grow faster.

The single-player league has four divisions of three drivers, with two tracks each, harder in every division. Races run three laps, winning scores two points and the fastest lap one, and at the end of a season the top driver in each division goes up and the bottom one down, the goal being to win division one.
trivia: Two Amigas or Atari STs — or one of each — could be linked by cable for head-to-head races.
In the US it was called Stunt Track Racer.
Your Sinclair named it its game of the year for 1989.
A sequel, Stunt Car Racer Pro, was announced in 2003 but never released.
Edge ranked it the 54th best game in 2000.
devStory:
Geoff Crammond spent three years on it, his second driving game after Revs. It began as a Commodore 64 driving simulator over randomly rolling ground; adding suspension physics, he found driving off ramps the most enjoyable part, and, struggling to place ramps on open ground, put them on an elevated track with banked corners. He said he saw Hard Drivin' only in the final months and it had no influence. MicroProse considered up to eight racers and a track editor but dropped both because of stuttering.

It came out in 1989 on the MicroStyle label for the Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, MS-DOS and ZX Spectrum, with Pete Cooke programming the Spectrum and Amstrad versions. Zzap!64 gave the C64 version 94% and called it the most remarkable C64 program one reviewer had seen, and Amstrad Action called it a "truly stunning racing sim".

title: Kick Off
description: Kick Off (1989) is Dino Dini's football game for Anco, in which the ball is not stuck to the player's feet but knocked ahead, so control takes skill.
longDescription: Instead of sticking to whoever has it, the ball is knocked ahead as the player runs, so keeping it takes skill. The pitch is seen from above, and the game has action replays, players with different characteristics, tactics, fouls, yellow and red cards, injuries, injury time and referees in different moods. It was developed first for the Atari ST and then ported to the Amiga, followed by the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, MS-DOS and others.
trivia: It won a 1989 Golden Joystick Award for Best 16-bit Product.
Amiga User International gave it 97% and called it the "best computer game ever".
Player Manager (1990) was described as the first game to combine football management with a playable match engine.
Dino Dini returned to the series with Kick Off Revival in 2016.
Amiga Power's Stuart Campbell disliked the series.
devStory:
Dino Dini created it, and Anco Software, Anil Gupta's publishing house, released it in 1989. Reviews were outstanding: Amiga User International gave it 97% and called it the "best computer game ever", Zzap!64 and The One 96%, C&VG 95% and Amiga Format 94%. It won the 1989 Golden Joystick for Best 16-bit Product, and Amiga Power ranked it the seventh best game of all time in 1991. The Extra Time expansion disk came out the same year.

Player Manager followed in 1990, combining management with a Kick Off match engine, and then Kick Off 2, with a larger scrolling pitch and league and cup play. Dini left Anco in 1992 for Virgin, where he made Goal! in 1993.

title: Loom
description: Loom (1990) is Brian Moriarty's adventure for Lucasfilm Games, in which Bobbin Threadbare solves puzzles by playing four-note tunes instead of using items.
longDescription:
In the year 8021, on the island of Loom, lives the Guild of Weavers. Bobbin Threadbare, a boy pulled from the Great Loom as an infant and secretly taught to weave, is left alone on his seventeenth birthday when the Weavers are turned into swans. His journey goes on as the Bishop Mandible lets the entity Chaos into the world, and it ends with Bobbin destroying the Great Loom.

Instead of collecting items, Bobbin plays four-note tunes called drafts on his distaff. He learns each one by watching an object with the matching quality — seeing a blade sharpened teaches Sharpening — and starts with only the notes C, D and E. Many drafts can be played backwards to reverse their effect, turning Dye into Bleach, though palindromes such as Terror cannot. On Expert difficulty the notes are not labelled, so drafts must be played by ear. Bobbin cannot die and the game cannot be lost.
trivia: Its music adapts Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, arranged for MIDI by George Sanger.
Computer Gaming World gave it a Special Award for Artistic Achievement.
Two planned sequels, Forge and The Fold, were never made.
In The Secret of Monkey Island, a pirate in the Scumm Bar advertises Loom.
Orson Scott Card is in the credits, but says he only gave minor feedback.
devStory:
Brian Moriarty, formerly of Infocom and the author of Wishbringer and Trinity, led it at Lucasfilm Games, with Mark Ferrari, Gary Winnick and Steve Purcell among the artists. It was the fourth game on the SCUMM engine and the first to drop the verb-and-object interface of Maniac Mansion. Its music adapts Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, arranged for MIDI by George Sanger. The box included a 30-minute audio drama on cassette that sets up the story, and The Book of Patterns, a notebook that doubled as copy protection.

It came out for MS-DOS in 1990, with later Amiga, Atari ST, Mac, FM Towns and TurboGrafx-CD versions and a voiced CD release in 1992. It was a critical success but did not sell well enough to justify sequels; Computer Gaming World's Scorpia praised its graphics but found it "too lightweight".

title: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis
description: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis (1992) is LucasArts' SCUMM adventure in which Indy races Nazis to Atlantis, playable by one of three paths: team, wits or fists.
longDescription:
In 1939, on the eve of the Second World War, Indy is tricked by the Nazi agent Klaus Kerner and teams up with Sophia Hapgood, a former colleague turned psychic, whose bead of orichalcum summons the spirit of the Atlantean king Nur-Ab-Sal. Plato's lost dialogue Hermocrates reveals that Atlantis lies in the Mediterranean, 300 miles from Greece rather than 3,000, and that reaching it takes three stones. The search runs through Monte Carlo, a dig in Algiers, the labyrinth at Knossos, a colony on Thera, a hydrogen balloon and a Nazi submarine to the sunken city, where the scientist Hans Ubermann hopes to use its power for war.

It uses LucasArts' SCUMM verbs and branching conversations. Early on the player picks one of three paths with their own puzzles, scenes and locations: Team, with Sophia at Indy's side; Wits, with harder puzzles; or Fists, with more fighting, which is optional on the other two. Unusually for LucasArts, Indy can die, and the Indy Quotient score tracks puzzles solved and objects found.
trivia: A CD-ROM "talkie" edition with full voice acting followed in 1993.
Falstein said in 2009 that it had sold over a million copies, LucasArts' most successful adventure, with about 30% of its players women.
A sequel, Indiana Jones and the Iron Phoenix, was cancelled, and became a Dark Horse comic.
A Sega CD port was cancelled because Monkey Island had sold poorly on that system.
PC Gamer UK ranked it the 13th-best computer game in 1994.
devStory:
The project began from a rejected Chris Columbus script for the third film, but project leader Hal Barwood, a former film writer and producer, asked to write an original story; Noah Falstein co-designed it and proposed the three paths, which added about six months to a two-year development. Lead artist William L. Eaken based the architecture on Minoan civilisation, and the animation was rotoscoped from footage of Steve Purcell as Indy and Collette Michaud as Sophia. Clint Bajakian, Peter McConnell and Michael Land arranged John Williams's "Raiders March".

It came out in June 1992, and several magazines named it the best adventure game of the year. The CD edition of 1993 recorded about 8,000 lines, with Doug Lee as Indy because Harrison Ford was unavailable.

sources.title: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis

title: Star Control II
description: Star Control II (1992) is Toys for Bob's space adventure across more than 500 stars, with branching conversations with 25 alien races and real-time ship battles.
longDescription:
After the Alliance loses its war with the Ur-Quan Hierarchy, a starship built from Precursor technology and captained by a genius who grew up on the colony Vela returns to Earth to find it enslaved beneath a slave shield, with only a skeleton crew on the starbase in orbit. The captain sets out to build a New Alliance of Free Stars from races that have been destroyed, shielded or forced into service, while the Ur-Quan fight a war with the Kohr-Ah for the right to the Sa-Matra, an ancient Precursor battle platform.

The galaxy holds over 500 stars and 3,800 planets. Dangerous worlds tend to carry the most valuable resources, which pay for upgrades to the flagship and its fleet. Conversations with 25 alien races branch and gradually reveal the galaxy's secrets, and each species even has its own font. Combat is the real-time, one-on-one ship duelling of the first Star Control, and the two-player Super Melee includes every ship from both games.
trivia: The developers ran a soundtrack contest on an Amiga newsgroup, the home of MOD tracker musicians.
The 3DO version's source code was released in 2002 and became the open-source The Ur-Quan Masters.
Its asteroids were made by digitising photographs of pumice.
The 3DO version added 11 hours of voice acting.
Reiche and Ford's spiritual successor, Free Stars: Children of Infinity, raised over $650,000 on Kickstarter in 2024.
devStory:
Toys for Bob, Paul Reiche III and Fred Ford, designed it as a science-fiction adventure role-playing game and played down its scale when pitching it to Accolade; it ran over schedule, and Ford paid for the team's final months himself. Reiche planned it on hand-drawn flowcharts, Greg Johnson wrote dialogue for several races and drew most of the alien ships, and the stars and planets mixed procedural generation with handcrafted art. Accolade released it for MS-DOS in 1992.

Computer Gaming World named it 1993's Adventure Game of the Year, and Pelit its Game of the Year. Tim Cain cited it as an influence on Fallout, and BioWare's Ray Muzyka on Mass Effect.

title: Master of Orion
description: Master of Orion (1993) is Steve Barcia's turn-based space strategy game for MicroProse, the first game described as "4X".
longDescription:
The player leads one of ten races through a randomly generated galaxy, starting with one homeworld, a colony ship and two scouts. Each race has its strengths: Humans are good at trade and diplomacy, the Bulrathi at ground combat, and the Silicoids ignore pollution and can settle hostile worlds but grow slowly. Planets range from seven normal types to six hostile ones that need more advanced technology to colonise, and terraforming and soil enrichment can eventually make any of them a Gaia world. Sliders split each colony's output between ships, defences, factories, ecology and research.

Research runs in six independent fields — computers, construction, force fields, planetary science, propulsion and weapons — and as a field advances its components shrink and get cheaper. Ships are designed from four hull sizes, and battles are decided mostly by numbers and technology. Computer rulers have personalities, remember broken treaties and can be pushed into revolt by spies. Orion, the throne-world of the Ancients, holds the most valuable research in the galaxy, guarded by a warship called the Guardian. Victory comes by wiping out rivals or winning a galactic vote for peaceful unification.
trivia: Alan Emrich's preview in Computer Gaming World summed it up as "4X": explore, expand, exploit, exterminate.
Star Lords, the unreleased prototype, was made freeware in 2001.
Three sequels followed: Battle at Antares, Master of Orion III and the 2016 reimagining Conquer the Stars.
Wargaming bought the franchise out of Atari's bankruptcy in 2013.
The Stellaris developers partly based their game on the series.
devStory:
Master of Orion grew out of Star Lords, a prototype by SimTex's Steve Barcia that he demonstrated to MicroProse and to journalist Alan Emrich; Emrich and Tom Hughes helped refine the design and are credited in the manual. Jeff Johannigman produced it and David Govett wrote the music. MicroProse released it for MS-DOS in September 1993, and a Mac version followed in 1995.

It sold over 100,000 copies, was named best strategy game of 1993 by Computer Games Strategy Plus and won Computer Gaming World's Strategy Game of the Year. CGW later ranked it 33rd among the best games of all time (1996), and PC Gamer 45th (1998).

title: The Settlers
description: The Settlers (1993) is Volker Wertich's Blue Byte economy game, in which carriers move goods along roads to build a working settlement and an army.
longDescription:
On each map the player builds a working settlement around a castle, produces an army and conquers rivals. Serfs carry materials, tools and food and staff the buildings, but are never controlled directly: the player gives general orders and the game assigns the work. Goods travel only by road, built by placing flags, and each stretch between flags gets one carrier, so more flags mean more carriers and less congestion. Every building needs raw materials and a worker with the right tool, so production runs in chains: weapons need iron ore and coal, and the miners need bread from a farm, a mill and a well.

Territory grows only by building military buildings near the border and garrisoning them with at least one knight, made from a serf with a sword and shield. Gold raises knights' morale, they train through five ranks, and attacks are launched by clicking an enemy building and choosing how many to send. There are 30 missions and a free mode for two to four sides, with two-player split screen.
trivia: In North America it was sold as Serf City: Life is Feudal.
About 70,000 lines of 68000 assembly were written before the graphics work began.
A 16-bit counter caps the total at 65,536 settlers.
Each settler's head is just 5×5 pixels.
Free-play maps use a 16-digit code, giving about 270 billion combinations.
devStory:
Volker Wertich designed and programmed it at Blue Byte, inspired by Little Computer People, Populous and SimCity, and scrapped his original Populous-like god game for a simulation of supply and demand. Producer Thomas Hertzler said the aim was "to create an economy simulation without it being boring". Development took over two years, and Wertich wrote about 70,000 lines of 68000 assembly before work on the graphics began.

It came out on the Amiga in Germany on 30 June 1993 and on MS-DOS in 1994. Amiga User International gave it 97% and called it "a true masterpiece", while Computer Gaming World and PC Player found the combat limited. It sold over 400,000 copies by May 1998 and led to nine further games.

title: Frontier: Elite II
description: Frontier: Elite II (1993) is David Braben's sequel to Elite, a plotless space game with Newtonian flight and planets and star systems at true scale.
longDescription:
The player starts in 3200 as a grandchild of Commander Jameson, with 100 credits and an Eagle Long Range Fighter, amid a Cold War-like ceasefire between the Federation, based at Sol, and the Empire, based at Achenar. With no plot, no scripted missions and no way to win, players trade legally or illegally, take military missions for either side, ferry passengers or turn pirate; narcotics, nerve gas, weapons and slaves fetch high prices on black markets but bring fines or police attacks.

Ships obey Newtonian physics, so momentum has to be cancelled to stop, and planets and star systems are at true scale, with a time-acceleration control up to 10,000 times for long trips. Players can land on planets seamlessly, and most stars have planetary systems, including real ones such as Sirius and Betelgeuse. Hyperspace jumps take up to a week, and kills count towards a combat rating running from "Harmless" to "Elite".
trivia: It was the first game to use procedurally generated star systems.
Manual-based copy protection came as police spot-checks: three wrong answers meant arrest.
A bug allowed "wormhole" jumps of 655.36 light years and its multiples.
"The Blue Danube" plays while docking, as in 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Its successors were Frontier: First Encounters (1995) and Elite Dangerous (2014).
devStory:
David Braben wrote it in about 250,000 lines of 68000 assembly, with Chris Sawyer porting the code to 80286 assembly, and the whole game fit on a single floppy disk. It was the first game with procedurally generated star systems, forming planets from the mass of each early solar system. The music arranges Wagner, Mussorgsky and Grieg, with "The Blue Danube" playing during docking as a nod to 2001: A Space Odyssey, plus two pieces by David Lowe.

GameTek and Konami published it in October 1993 for the Amiga, Atari ST and MS-DOS, nine years after Elite, and CU Amiga, which gave it 97%, called it "the longest-awaited sequel of the decade". It sold about 500,000 copies.

title: Transport Tycoon
description: Transport Tycoon (1994) is Chris Sawyer's business simulation, written entirely in assembly language, in which the player builds a transport empire by road, rail, sea and air.
longDescription:
The player borrows money to start a transport company on a randomly generated map and competes in real time against up to seven computer rivals from 1930 to 2030, carrying passengers, mail and cargo by road, rail, sea and air. Routes are built from stations, and one route can mix modes — truck to ship to train. Stations only take cargo from nearby industries and towns, and well-run stations attract more of it; revenue depends on speed, distance and quantity, so mail loses value quickly while coal keeps it.

Technology moves from steam to diesel and electric, with monorails arriving in 1999, and manufacturers offer new models as prototypes that may prove unreliable. Each town's council rates the company by its service and how many trees it cuts down, and a poor rating blocks new stations. Advertising draws custom from rivals, the first company to deliver a requested resource earns a subsidy, and unserved industries can close.
trivia: OpenTTD, a free reverse-engineered recreation of Transport Tycoon Deluxe, was first released in 2004.
Reviewers compared it favourably with Railroad Tycoon and SimCity 2000.
Sawyer finished it in four to five months after MicroProse signed it, against a planned two years.
Part of the soundtrack draws on Herbie Hancock's "Cantaloupe Island".
Sawyer made RollerCoaster Tycoon while working on its spiritual successor, Chris Sawyer's Locomotion (2004).
devStory:
Chris Sawyer began prototyping it in October 1992, funded by years of conversion work on games such as Frontier: Elite II, and wrote it entirely in x86 assembly. It was influenced by Railroad Tycoon and A-Train. The hardest part was the AI, which Sawyer wanted to follow the same rules as the player. Simon Foster drew the art, basing some buildings on Glasgow landmarks, and MicroProse's John Broomhall composed more than 20 blues, funk and jazz pieces. MicroProse signed it in 1994, renamed it Transport Tycoon and released it in November.

Critics praised its depth, graphics and music, though the manual was widely criticised; PC Gamer gave it 91/100, and Next Generation called it "the best economic sim since Civilization". Transport Tycoon Deluxe (1995) added new climates, diagonal track and network play.

title: Hexen: Beyond Heretic
description: Hexen (1995) is Raven Software's sequel to Heretic, a fantasy shooter with three character classes and hub levels full of switch and item puzzles.
longDescription:
After D'Sparil's defeat in Heretic, the realm of Cronos is besieged by Korax, the second of three Serpent Riders, and three heroes set out to destroy him. The player picks one: the Fighter Baratus, tougher and faster, who fights up close; the Mage Daedolon, slowest and most fragile, with long-range spells; or the Cleric Parias, who mixes melee and ranged attacks. Some items work differently for each class — the flechette, a poison-gas bomb, is one — and new ones include the Disc of Repulsion, which pushes enemies and projectiles away, and the Icon of the Defender, a class-specific invincibility.

The journey runs through elemental dungeons, a wilderness, a mountainside seminary, a castle and a necropolis to a showdown with Korax. Instead of a string of separate levels, central hubs link to side levels, and the player shuttles between them solving puzzles with items and switches before moving on to the next hub. On the PC up to eight players can play over a network.
trivia: Its modified Doom engine added jumping, looking up and down, and a scripting system.
The PC version sold over 250,000 copies, but the console ports were poorly received.
The title draws on the German word for "witches" and the verb "to cast a spell".
John Romero said the unreleased third game was to be called Hecatomb.
EGM named it 1997's "Game that Should've Stayed on the PC".
It was re-released with Heretic in 2025, remastered by id Software and Nightdive Studios.
devStory:
Raven Software developed it on NeXTSTEP, as it had Heretic, using a modified Doom engine that added jumping, looking up and down, class selection, CD audio, moving walls and a level scripting language, Action Code Script. Kevin Schilder composed the score. id Software published it for MS-DOS on 30 October 1995, and the Deathkings of the Dark Citadel expansion followed in 1996 with three more hubs.

PC reviews were highly positive, praising the non-linear levels and the three classes; Edge gave it 9/10, and Computer Games Strategy Plus named it the best first-person action game of 1995. The 1997 console ports by Probe and Software Creations fared far worse. It popularised the hub system in first-person shooters, and its source code was released in 1999.

title: Total Annihilation
description: Total Annihilation (1997) is Chris Taylor's real-time strategy game for Cavedog, with height-mapped terrain, streaming resources and an orchestral score by Jeremy Soule.
longDescription:
Each side starts with a lone Commander, a walking war machine that can cloak, cross water and build structures three times faster than a construction vehicle. Metal and Energy are unlimited, flowing in at a constant rate, and running short of either slows every build in proportion; without energy, radar and laser towers shut down. Destroyed units leave wrecks that can be reclaimed for metal.

The terrain is height-mapped, so hills block artillery and high ground extends sight and range, and a physics engine governs shots, explosions and wreckage. Maps vary wind, tides and gravity across desert, ice, lava and Martian worlds, and units include bots, tanks, ships, hovercraft and aircraft. Two factions fight a war that has lasted four thousand years: the Core, which transferred human minds into machines, and the Arm, which rebelled against it. Each has a 25-mission campaign. Jeremy Soule's score, played by the 95-piece Northwest Sinfonia, changes with combat and construction.
trivia: GameSpot named it 1997's Game of the Year, and also gave it Best Strategy Game, Best Multiplayer Game and Best Music.
Each side's unit cap was 250 at launch, later patched to 500.
GameSpy ranked it the best real-time strategy game of all time in 2004, ahead of StarCraft.
The creators of the XTA mod went on to build the open-source Spring engine.
Taylor's later studio, Gas Powered Games, made Supreme Commander (2007), a spiritual successor.
devStory: Chris Taylor designed it at Cavedog, a division of Humongous Entertainment, with Ron Gilbert producing and Clayton Kauzlaric as artist. It launched in September 1997 in 14 countries at once, with English, French and German versions, and from that year Cavedog released free downloadable units, maps and scenarios. Two expansions followed in 1998, The Core Contingency and Battle Tactics, and a medieval spin-off, Kingdoms, in 1999. It had shipped 250,000 copies by the end of October 1997 and sold over 1.5 million by 2002.

title: Unreal
description: Unreal (1998) is Epic MegaGames and Digital Extremes' first-person shooter, the debut of the Unreal Engine, set on the alien world of Na Pali.
longDescription:
The player is Prisoner 849, aboard the prison ship Vortex Rikers when it is pulled down to the uncharted planet Na Pali and crash-lands at the edge of a canyon. The Skaarj, a reptilian race that has enslaved the four-armed native Nali, kill the other survivors, and the prisoner escapes into a world of mines, a water temple and an arena where a Titan must be killed. No other living human is met; the dead leave journals warning of what lies ahead.

The Skaarj have come for Tarydium, a blue crystal with a high energy yield. The game ends with the prisoner destroying the reactor of the Skaarj mothership, killing the Skaarj Queen and escaping in her pod, left drifting in space. Besides the campaign it has multiplayer, and critics singled out its computer-controlled bots.
trivia: Epic made it freeware in 2024.
Critics praised its graphics, music and bots but criticised its laggy online play; it averaged 89% on GameRankings.
PC Gamer US ranked it the 13th-best game ever in 1998.
Ports to the Nintendo 64DD and the Dreamcast were started and cancelled.
Legend Entertainment's expansion, Return to Na Pali (1999), added 17 single-player missions.
The player character was originally female; the released game lets the player choose.
devStory:
Unreal was funded mainly by the proceeds of Epic Pinball, Epic's best-selling shareware title. Lead designer James Schmalz said it began as terrain inspired by Magic Carpet, moving from caverns to the outdoors, while Tim Sweeney led the engine and built an editor for its structures, with Cliff Bleszinski joining as co-designer. GT Interactive secured exclusive worldwide publishing rights in late 1996. The game shipped with UnrealScript and the UnrealEd editor, whose maps could be edited and viewed as they would appear in play, which fostered a large mod community.

It was among the first games to use detail texturing, and its software renderer handled coloured lighting. The tracker-module soundtrack is by Alexander Brandon and Michiel van den Bos, with tracks by Dan Gardopée and Andrew Sega. GT Interactive released it in May 1998; it reached number one on PC Data's US chart, trading the top spot with StarCraft through June, passed a million copies worldwide by September 1999 and about 1.5 million by 2002. Its engine went on to power the Unreal series.

title: Thunder Force IV
description: Thunder Force IV (1992) is Technosoft's Mega Drive shooter, released in North America as Lightening Force, with playfields that scroll vertically as well as sideways.
longDescription:
Two years after Thunder Force III, the Orn Empire plans to wipe out humanity, and the player flies the Fire LEO-04 Rynex against it. The first four of the ten stages can be played in any order. The screen scrolls sideways on its own, but moving up or down scrolls vertically over much larger playfields, revealing enemy waves and hidden power-ups, and the ship's speed can be changed at any time. Each stage ends with a boss, and some have mid-stage bosses.

Some enemies drop new weapons, missiles and lasers firing in different patterns, each with strengths and weaknesses; the player carries several and switches between them. Shields and orbiting satellite ships add protection and firepower, and halfway through the game the player gains the Thunder Sword, a heavy-damage attack that needs two satellites.
trivia: The sound team, led by Naosuke Arai, used distortion effects on the Mega Drive's FM chip to imitate an electric guitar.
IGN ranked it fourth among classic shoot 'em ups and called it Technosoft's best shooter.
Its development team had previously ported Devil's Crush to the Mega Drive.
The 1996 Saturn version fixed slowdown and made the Thunder Force III ship playable.
It came to the Switch in 2018 in the Sega Ages line.
devStory:
Apart from its sound department, the team had not made the earlier Thunder Force games: they had ported Devil's Crush to the Mega Drive and chose this project when offered an original game, reusing code from earlier titles. The sound team, led by Naosuke Arai, were heavy metal fans who tried to make an electric guitar on the Mega Drive's FM chip and settled on its distortion effects.

Technosoft released it in Japan on 24 July 1992, the third and last Thunder Force on the Mega Drive, and Sega released it in Europe that December and in North America in January 1993 as Lightening Force: Quest for the Darkstar. Critics praised its graphics and vertical scrolling; Mean Machines called the graphics "state of the art", while Mega found the play "decidedly average".

title: Heroes of Might and Magic
description: Heroes of Might and Magic (1995) is Jon Van Caneghem's turn-based strategy spin-off from the Might and Magic role-playing series, and the start of its own long series.
longDescription:
Lord Morglin Ironfist flees his homeworld through a magic portal after his cousin seizes the throne, and arrives in Enroth, a land contested by three warlords: the barbarian Lord Slayer, the sorceress Queen Lamanda and the warlock Lord Alamar. In the series' canon Ironfist, a knight, wins and founds a kingdom there.

Players lead generals called heroes, whose armies of creatures from myth and legend explore the map, fight and capture territory, usually until every enemy castle and hero has fallen; some scenarios instead ask for a set amount of gold or a particular artifact. There are four hero and castle types: the Knight and Barbarian favour might, gaining attack and defence, and the Sorceress and Warlock favour magic, gaining spell power and knowledge. Neutral creatures — Rogues, Nomads, Ghosts and Genies — wander the map. It can be played alone or with others.
trivia: The Windows CD included King's Bounty as a bonus.
Next Generation called it "easy to learn, but difficult to master".
Ghosts are the only wandering creatures that cannot be hired.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 133rd-best computer game in 1996.
Inside Mac Games named it Role-Playing Game of the Year for 1996.
devStory:
Jon Van Caneghem designed it at New World Computing as a spin-off of the Might and Magic role-playing series, with Phil Steinmeyer programming, Julia Ulano on art and music by Paul Romero and Rob King. It came out for DOS in September 1995, and by mid-November 100,000 copies had shipped to shops. A Windows 95 version in 1996 added a map editor, a random map generator and new scenarios.

Computer Gaming World gave it 5/5 and named it joint Strategy Game of the Year, though GameSpot found the story thin. It began a series that had sold 1.5 million copies by 1999.

sources.title: Heroes of Might and Magic: A Strategic Quest

title: Twisted Metal
description: Twisted Metal (1995) is SingleTrac's PlayStation car-combat game, in which drivers fight in Calypso's tournament for the prize of a wish.
longDescription:
On Christmas Eve 2005, in the tenth annual Twisted Metal contest, drivers invited by an email reading "WILL YOU DRIVE?" battle through Los Angeles for Calypso, who lives beneath its streets and grants the last survivor a single wish, with no limit on its price or size. Twelve vehicles fight across six arenas that grow larger and more crowded: an underground arena, a warehouse district, a freeway, River Park in Beverly Hills, the suburbs of Cyburbia and the skyscraper rooftops, before a final boss, Minion.

Every vehicle carries twin machine guns with unlimited ammunition that can overheat, and picks up missiles, land mines, tyre spikes and oil slicks, up to 30 weapons at once. Players have three lives, and blue Health Stations restore damage. A two-player Duel mode is included.
trivia: It is set on Christmas Eve 2005, during the tournament's tenth running in Los Angeles.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it its 1995 Game of the Year.
Titles considered included Urban Assault, Cars and Rockets and High Octane.
Its cut live-action endings later appeared in Twisted Metal: Head-On – Extra Twisted Edition on the PS2.
The PC version was used to show off Nvidia's NV1 chip in 1996.
devStory:
SingleTrac formed in spring 1994, with former members of Evans & Sutherland among its founders, after Sony contracted that company to build a 3D game. The idea of car combat came during a traffic jam on Interstate 405; director Michael D. Jackson had suggested a pizza delivery game instead. David Jaffe, a former tester at Sony Imagesoft, led the design with Mike Giam. Codenamed Firestorm, it began on the same codebase as Warhawk, with a deadline of under twelve months and a budget of $850,000. Live-action endings were filmed but cut as too offensive.

Sony showed it at the first E3 in May 1995 and released it in North America that November. Critics liked its variety and two-player mode but found the single-player mode short. It sold over a million copies in North America and began the Twisted Metal series, with Twisted Metal 2 following in 1996.

title: Blast Corps
description: Blast Corps (1997) is Rare's Nintendo 64 demolition game, in which the player smashes buildings out of the path of a runaway nuclear missile carrier.
longDescription:
A runaway carrier loaded with nuclear missiles rolls along a fixed path, and the player has to demolish every building and obstacle in its way before it arrives; if it hits anything, the level is lost. Eight vehicles do the work in different ways: a bulldozer rams, a dump truck slides sideways into walls, a buggy crashes down from high ground, a motorcycle fires missiles, and three robot mechs tumble and stomp. Some levels also call for moving explosive crates against a timer or bridging gaps.

There are 57 levels, seen from a three-quarter overhead view. Once the carrier is safe, the player can keep exploring without a time limit, earning medals for flattening what is left, finding secrets and switching on lights. Hidden communication points open secret levels with their own timed goals, finishing every stage unlocks time trials, and earning every gold medal unlocks harder platinum targets.
trivia: It sold close to a million copies.
Titles considered before release included Heavy Duty Heroes, Blast Radius and Power Dozer.
Nintendo Power ran a three-part comic based on it in issues 97 to 99.
It was among Rare's first Nintendo 64 games.
It was included in Rare Replay in 2015, and on Nintendo's classics service in 2024.
devStory:
Production began in 1995 with a team of four recent graduates, at times growing to seven, led by designer Martin Wakeley. Rare co-founder Chris Stamper wanted a game about destroying buildings, and the idea of a constantly moving object turned into the missile carrier. Mario Kart 64's power slide inspired the dump truck's drift, which Wakeley defended over the team's objections, and the 1995 Super Mario 64 demo showed him how analog 3D control could work. One robot has no arm because the team ran out of memory. Paul Mountain and George Andreas directed it, and Graeme Norgate composed the music.

Shown at a 1995 trade show as Blast Dozer, it came out in Japan and North America in March 1997. It scored 90% on Metacritic, was EGM's Game of the Month for May 1997 and its runner-up for Most Original Game of the Year, but sold below the team's hopes.

title: Mischief Makers
description: Mischief Makers (1997) is Treasure's Nintendo 64 platformer, in which the robot maid Marina Liteyears grabs, shakes and throws objects.
longDescription:
Marina Liteyears, a robot maid, sets out to rescue her creator, the robotics genius Professor Theo, who has been kidnapped by the Emperor of Planet Clancer, a world on the brink of civil war. Marina grabs, shakes and throws almost everything: shaking can turn objects into projectiles, shake loot out of them or change what they do, turning some into homing missiles or multi-directional guns. She can also run, jump, slide and boost with a jetpack in eight directions.

Five worlds of about a dozen levels each, 52 in all, are reached from a stage select, each world with mid-bosses and a final boss. Red, blue and green gems restore health, and yellow gems hidden in each level lengthen the final cutscene. It plays in 2D with pre-rendered 3D graphics, and was described as the Nintendo 64's first single-player 2D side-scrolling platformer.
trivia: GamesRadar called it "possibly the most underrated and widely ignored" Nintendo 64 game.
In Japan it was called Yuke Yuke!! Trouble Makers.
Nintendo Power called it the best side-scroller since Super Mario World.
It was the only game at Enix's booth at the April 1997 Tokyo Game Show.
Marina returned as an unlockable character in Treasure's Rakugaki Showtime (1999).
devStory:
Treasure began work in mid-1995, before the Nintendo 64 launched, with a team averaging 12 people. It was the studio's first game for a Nintendo console after working only on Sega's, chosen because cartridges loaded instantly, though CEO Masato Maegawa found the machine harder to learn than the Saturn. The grabbing mechanic was the hardest part to build.

Enix published it in Japan in June 1997, and Nintendo, which proposed a Western release, published it abroad that October. Critics praised its invention, personality and bosses but criticised its short length, low difficulty and sound; it scored 70 on Metacritic, while Famitsu placed it in its Gold Hall of Fame.

title: Croc: Legend of the Gobbos
description: Croc (1997) is Argonaut's 3D platformer that grew from a Yoshi prototype Nintendo turned down, in which a crocodile rescues the Gobbos from Baron Dante.
longDescription:
King Rufus of the Gobbos finds a baby crocodile floating down a river in a basket, and the Gobbos raise him until he grows far bigger than they are. When Baron Dante and his Dantinis invade Gobbo Valley and lock the Gobbos in steel cages, the yellow bird Beany carries Croc to safety just before Rufus is caught, and Croc sets out to free them.

Levels on the valley's islands are chosen from a world map and mix above-ground, underground and occasional underwater sections, each ending at a gong. Every stage hides six caged Gobbos: five in the level and a sixth in a bonus room opened by collecting five coloured crystals. Croc runs, jumps, climbs, swims and sidesteps, attacks with a full-circle tail swipe and breaks crates with a hip drop. Grey crystals act as health, scattering when he is hit, and a hit with none left costs a life. Rescuing every Gobbo before a world's boss opens a secret level with a jigsaw piece, and saving them all is needed for the final boss and the true ending.
trivia: It sold over 3 million copies on the PlayStation, one of Argonaut's best sellers.
Croc's single fang was based on designer Simon Keating's house cat.
The Gobbos were originally pink until animator Pete Day made them brown.
Snowboarding levels were cut for time.
A remaster came out in 2025.
devStory:
Argonaut, which had made the Super FX chip for Star Fox, began it in 1994 as "Yoshi Racing" and pitched a Yoshi prototype to Nintendo. Shigeru Miyamoto reportedly showed interest, but Nintendo turned it down, citing a similar project of its own, and the rejection along with the cancellation of Star Fox 2 ended Argonaut's relationship with the company. Simon Keating, in his first industry job, designed Croc to look marginally like Yoshi and gave him a single fang based on his house cat, and Jonathan Aris voiced him. The music was by Justin Scharvona, Karin Griffin and Martin Gwynn Jones, and the audio was compressed 4:1 to fit on one disc.

Fox Interactive, chosen from several publishers in 1996, released it in September 1997 for the PlayStation, Saturn and Windows. Critics praised the visuals and music but criticised the camera, and the PlayStation version averaged 79% on GameRankings.

title: Carmageddon
description: Carmageddon (1997) is Stainless Games' racing game in which wrecking every rival or running down every pedestrian wins as well as finishing first — and was censored or banned in several countries.
longDescription: Across 36 tracks in 11 locations, including cities, mines and industrial areas, a race can be won three ways: by finishing the course, by wrecking all the other cars, or by killing every pedestrian on the level. Each race runs against a time limit, and time is won back by collecting bonuses, damaging rivals' cars and running people over. Single-player and multiplayer races are both included, and the soundtrack features three instrumental remixes from Fear Factory's album Demanufacture.
trivia: In Germany and briefly the UK, pedestrians became green-blooded zombies or robots; the BBFC later passed the original after a ten-month appeal.
SCi tried for the Mad Max licence before securing Death Race 2000.
It was passed uncut in Australia with an MA15+ rating.
The Splat Pack expansion (1997) added tracks, cars and 3Dfx support.
Sequels include Carmageddon II: Carpocalypse Now (1998) and the Kickstarter-funded Carmageddon: Reincarnation (2015).
devStory:
Stainless Software began it as a banger-racing prototype called 3D Destruction Derby. SCi signed it in 1995 on condition that it carry a licence; unable to work out who owned the Mad Max rights, it licensed Death Race 2000 instead, though SCi later backed Stainless's own name, Carmageddon. Running down pedestrians, suggested by SCi's Rob Henderson, was added to set it apart from Psygnosis's Destruction Derby and to provoke controversy. Patrick Buckland programmed it on the BRender engine, and Neil Barnden designed it with him.

It came out in June 1997 and was censored in Germany and briefly in the UK, and banned outright in Brazil. Reviews were generally positive: GameSpot gave it 8.8/10, and Next Generation called it "an absolute blast" for players willing to set their morals aside, while GamePro criticised its focus on gore. The series went on to sell about two million copies.

title: Einhänder
description: Einhänder (1997) is Square's PlayStation shooter, in which the player's fighter uses a mechanical arm to grab guns dropped by destroyed enemies.
longDescription:
A scrolling shooter in the tradition of Gradius, it draws its world in 3D while keeping movement on a flat plane. Each fighter carries a machine gun and a manipulator arm that grabs gunpods left by destroyed enemies — cannons, guided missiles, aircraft-sized blades and more — each with its own power, ammunition and range. Empty pods are thrown away, and a pod can be held above or below the ship. Most stages have a mid-boss and an end boss with separately destructible parts, and the scoring multiplies kills by a hit counter that decays as soon as the player stops destroying cores.

The story is set in a future war between Earth and its Moon colony, Selene, which sends one-man Einhänder fighters on suicide missions against the Earth's capital. The pilot comes to question the war and ends up fighting Hyperion, the satellite that relays the military's orders. Three fighters can be chosen, with two more hidden.
trivia: It was never released in Europe.
Kenichiro Fukui's soundtrack is mostly techno and trance.
Working Designs wanted to publish it in North America, but Sony's partnership with Square ruled that out.
IGN ranked it first among 2D space shooters in 2007.
Its team worked on the Gummi Ship sections of Kingdom Hearts III, which include an Einhänder ship and boss as nods.
devStory:
It was Square's first 3D shooter, made by a company known for role-playing games. Tatsuo Fujii, who had programmed Gradius II and Xexex at Konami, directed it, with Yusuke Hirata producing and Kenichiro Fukui composing; the team drew many names from German and from Greek myth. Square released it in Japan on 20 November 1997, where it sold 50,000 copies in three days. Sony published it in North America in May 1998 as the last game in its deal with Square, with faster arm switching and Japan's unlimited-continue "Free" mode removed.

Critics praised its gameplay, graphics and soundtrack, and the main complaints were its length — GameSpot reckoned just over an hour — and the lack of a two-player mode. It scored 89 on Metacritic, and EGM's Kraig Kujawa called it "the best shooter ever".

title: Bust a Groove
description: Bust a Groove (1998) is Metro's PlayStation dance game, in which rival dancers match button prompts to the beat and knock each other off rhythm.
longDescription:
Arrows matching the directional pad and the circle and X symbols appear in time with the beat, and on every fourth beat the player must enter them to perform a dance move or it counts as a miss. Chaining eight moves opens advanced paths with more complex, higher-scoring moves. Each dancer has a "Jammer" attack to interrupt a rival, dodged with a somersault on the Square button.

The ten dancers each have a song and a style: Heat, a former racer with fire powers, breakdances; Frida, an artist, does West Coast hip-hop; Hamm, a former great dancer now working at a burger restaurant, wants to diet; Shorty, 12, does candy hip-hop with her pet mouse Columbo; Gas-O, 15, is a young scientist; and Kitty-N is a TV star. Four more, including the giant Robo-Z and the alien Capoeira duo, are hidden.
trivia: In Japan it was called Bust a Move, renamed abroad to avoid a trademark clash with Bust-A-Move, the Western name of Puzzle Bobble.
The Western release removed Hiro's cigarette and changed Strike's hip flask into a soda can.
The arcade version uses big floor pads, a foot pedal and a giant "Dance!" button.
A third game, Dance Summit 2001, came out only in Japan.
Shorty's English song is sung by Crystal Kay.
devStory: Metro developed it, with art by Hideyuki Tanaka and Makiko Morioka, and Enix released it in Japan on 29 January 1998 as Bust a Move: Dance & Rhythm Action, one of the first rhythm games after PaRappa the Rapper, adding fighting-game touches like attacks and head-to-head play. Sony released it in Europe and 989 Studios in North America that November, with four songs re-recorded in English. Next Generation gave it four stars, praising its music, secret dancers and stage animations, and an arcade version became the third most successful dedicated arcade game in Game Machine's 1 April 1999 issue.

title: Vigilante 8
description: Vigilante 8 (1998) is Luxoflux's car-combat game set in an alternate 1975, where trucker Convoy's Vigilantes fight an oil cartel's gang across the American West.
longDescription:
In an alternate 1975, the oil cartel OMAR (Oil Monopoly Alliance Regime) hires the Australian terrorist Sid Burn to wipe out its American rivals, and his Coyotes use weapons stolen from the secret Site-4 base in Nevada. The trucker Convoy forms the Vigilantes to fight back. Each side has six drivers, from Convoy's niece Sheila and the FBI agent Chassey Blue to the disco-loving Boogie and the beekeeper Beezwax, each with a 1960s or 1970s vehicle and an ending, most Coyote endings showing a setback.

Battles take place across the western United States in Story or Arcade mode, on stages with features such as missiles and aircraft launched at Area 51. Every vehicle has a machine gun and can carry up to three of five weapons — mines, auto-cannons, rocket pods, mortars and homing missiles — plus its own special weapon. Each standard weapon has three special attacks entered with fighting-game-style button inputs, combos of up to six hits are called "Whammies", and wrench icons repair damage.
trivia: The PlayStation version can play ordinary music CDs during matches.
The N64 version adds a Story Mode for the secret character Y The Alien and four-player modes.
The school bus was a favourite with focus groups.
Luxoflux reused its engine for Star Wars: Demolition.
A remake, Vigilante 8 Arcade, came to Xbox Live Arcade in 2008.
devStory:
Activision commissioned a PlayStation port of its 1997 PC game Interstate '76, and because its own team lacked the time it hired Luxoflux, a five-person team of Peter Morawiec, Adrian Stephens, David Goodrich, Jeremy Engleman and Edvard Toth. Activision provided no code or technical help, the levels were shrunk to make fights more frequent, and Luxoflux asked to make it its own game, keeping Interstate '76's vehicles, character models and 1970s style. Jeehun Hwang and Howard Drossin scored the PlayStation version.

It came out on the PlayStation on 4 June 1998, followed by Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions in 1999. Edge called it "a competent and interesting game for anyone who enjoys trashing automobiles".

title: Space Station Silicon Valley
description: Space Station Silicon Valley (1998) is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 platformer, in which a robot reduced to a microchip takes over animals to use their abilities.
longDescription:
In 2001 the space station Silicon Valley launches with robotic animals aboard and vanishes seven minutes later. It reappears a thousand years on, and the expeditions sent after it vanish too. Dan Danger and his robot Evo crash-land on it, and Evo's body is destroyed, leaving only a microchip that can take over the station's animals. Dan, stuck in the wrecked ship, gives out missions and comments on how Evo is doing.

Each animal has its own abilities and survives some environments but not others: bears can smash ice blocks that other animals cannot, so Evo has to switch bodies to get through. The station has four zones, Euro Eden, Arctic Kingdom, Jungle Safari and Desert Adventure, each with six to ten sub-levels built around goals such as hitting switches, shutting off electric fences or gathering objects. Evo collects power cells to keep his energy up and reassembles his protective suit piece by piece for the final level, and every level hides a secret objective worth a gold trophy.
trivia: IGN named it Game of the Month for October 1998 and its Most Innovative Game.
A PlayStation version was released in Europe as Evo's Space Adventures.
A glitch on the N64 version stops players collecting the souvenir in Fat Bear Mountain, so the bonus level cannot normally be reached.
Programmer Obbe Vermeij said there was no push to finish until 18 months into development.
IGN ranked it fifth in a 2007 list of underrated games.
devStory:
DMA Design began it in September 1995 under a three-game deal with BMG Interactive that also produced Grand Theft Auto and Tanktics. It was planned for Windows, PlayStation and Saturn, but the team moved to the Nintendo 64 when Windows could not handle the models and environments they wanted. Lead programmer Leslie Benzies and artist Aaron Garbut compared it with Super Mario 64, the team aimed for a soft-focus, Plasticine look like Wallace and Gromit's, and an early idea of eating robots to grow bigger was dropped. Take-Two bought BMG Interactive in March 1998, and with it the game.

It came out in North America on 22 October 1998 and scored 83 on Metacritic; IGN's Matt Casamassina called it "maybe the most original game to hit Nintendo 64". It did not meet sales expectations, which the team blamed on launching alongside The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

title: Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver
description: Soul Reaver (1999) is Amy Hennig's Crystal Dynamics action-adventure, in which the wraith Raziel shifts between material and spectral realms to take revenge on Kain, with no loading times.
longDescription:
In Nosgoth, whose health is bound to nine Pillars, Kain refused to sacrifice himself as the last guardian and left the land to decay. Kain casts his lieutenant Raziel into the Lake of the Dead. Raziel is revived by the Elder God as a wraith and sets out for revenge, hunting his vampire brothers — Melchiah, Zephon, Rahab and Dumah — before facing Kain, on a journey that ends on a cliffhanger leading into Soul Reaver 2.

Raziel can enter the spectral realm at will, but returns to the material world only through portals; in the material realm his health drains away, while in the spectral one it refills and water has no substance, so he can walk along lakebeds. Blocks, doors and switches work only in the material realm. Vampires must be stunned and then impaled, burned or thrown into sunlight or water, and their souls restore health. Each brother's defeat grants a power — phasing through gates, climbing walls, swimming — and glyphs learned at altars strike groups of enemies.
trivia: Hennig said the team had "over-designed the game" and split the story in two, which explains its cliffhanger.
It is set 1,500 years after Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain.
Eidos spent US$4 million on advertising before release, including a Top Cow comic tie-in.
Its Dreamcast port by Nixxes ran at a higher frame rate.
1UP.com ranked it second among "Games That Ended Halfway Through".
devStory:
Crystal Dynamics began it in 1997, with Amy Hennig directing and co-writing, on an upgraded Gex 3 engine with custom streaming to avoid loading screens. The goals were Tomb Raider-style play and Zelda-like storytelling. Hennig said the team "over-designed the game" and split it in two; a third battle with Kain, more powers and a fuller glyph system were cut, and the fifth brother, Turel, was dropped for lack of time. Kurt Harland wrote most of the music, and the cast included Michael Bell as Raziel, Simon Templeman as Kain and Tony Jay as the Elder God.

Shown at E3 1998, it slipped to August 1999. It scored 91 on Metacritic; critics praised its gothic atmosphere, voice acting and realm-shifting but found its objectives unclear and its play repetitive. It sold about 1.4 million copies by late 2001.

title: Homeworld
description: Homeworld (1999) is Relic's first game, a real-time strategy game fought in full 3D space, whose fleet carries over from mission to mission.
longDescription:
A century before the game, the Kushan of the desert planet Kharak found a buried starship holding a stone map that marked Kharak and a world called Hiigara — "home". They built a mothership to carry 600,000 people there, with the neuroscientist Karan S'jet wired into it as Fleet Command. On its first hyperspace jump the ship meets a hostile carrier; Kharak is razed, and only the frozen migrants aboard survive. A captured captain reveals that the planet was punished for breaking a 4,000-year-old treaty with the Taiidan Empire, and the journey home runs through asteroid fields, a nebula, a ship graveyard and imperial outposts to a final battle over Hiigara.

Each level is a sphere of space in which ships move in full 3D, and the camera can follow any ship from any angle, while a Sensors Manager shows the whole map. Ships fly in formations such as wedges and spheres, harvesters gather resources from rocks, gas and dust clouds, fighters must refuel by docking, and salvage corvettes can capture enemy ships and tow them home. The fleet carries over between the campaign's 16 missions, with difficulty adjusting slightly to its size. Hand-drawn black-and-white cutscenes with narration link the levels.
trivia: Its music includes Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings and a closing song by Yes, "Homeworld (The Ladder)".
Metacritic lists it as the highest-rated computer game of 1999.
The script writers, Martin Cirulis and Arinn Dembo, were credited jointly under a pen name chosen by Sierra, "Marcus Skyler".
Choosing the Kushan or the Taiidan changes only the ship designs, not the story.
Gearbox bought the series from THQ in 2013 for US$1.35 million and released Homeworld Remastered Collection in 2015.
devStory:
It was the first game from Relic Entertainment, founded in Vancouver on 1 June 1997 by Alex Garden, its 22-year-old director, and lead programmer Luke Moloney. Erin Daly designed it, and its inspirations included the original Star Wars trilogy and the 1978 Battlestar Galactica; the working title was Spaghetti Ball. Development took over two years, with most of the gameplay systems finished in the last eight months, and features such as ship customisation were cut. Paul Ruskay scored it.

Sierra released it on 28 September 1999. It sold over 250,000 copies in its first weeks and over 500,000 in six months. Critics praised its graphics, 3D play, sound and multiplayer, and were mixed on the story, the difficulty and the initially disorienting controls. IGN and PC Gamer named it Game of the Year, and Computer Gaming World its Strategy Game of the Year.

title: Medal of Honor
description: Medal of Honor (1999) is the Steven Spielberg-created PlayStation shooter that popularised World War II first-person shooters, with a score by Michael Giacchino.
longDescription: Set from mid-1944 to mid-1945, it sends the player on Office of Strategic Services missions: rescuing a downed American pilot, going undercover to board and destroy a U-boat, recovering stolen art and sabotaging the Nazi war effort. In one sequence the player has to show forged identity papers rather than draw a gun. There is also a two-player split-screen deathmatch, with secret characters — among them William Shakespeare, a German Shepherd and a dinosaur — unlocked by finishing the game or with cheats.
trivia: Spielberg was partly inspired by watching his son play GoldenEye 007.
The Congressional Medal of Honor Society objected at first, until producer Peter Hirschmann persuaded its president the project was serious.
The Official UK PlayStation Magazine ranked it the eighth-best game of all time in its final issue.
Its direct sequel was Medal of Honor: Underground.
José Rizal is one of its secret multiplayer characters.
devStory:
Steven Spielberg, who co-founded DreamWorks Interactive with Microsoft in 1995, conceived it while working on Saving Private Ryan, partly after watching his son play GoldenEye 007. Work began on 11 November 1997, against doubts from management that the Second World War was dated, and the military adviser Dale Dye at first called the demo exploitative. After the Columbine massacre in 1999 the team removed a gory death animation, and when Congressional Medal of Honor Society president Paul Bucha criticised the project, producer Peter Hirschmann won his endorsement with a demo. Michael Giacchino wrote a full orchestral score.

EA released it on 10 November 1999. It scored 92 on Metacritic, won the AIAS award for sound design, and IGN credited it with popularising Second World War shooters. The studio, which had suffered heavy losses, was sold to EA before the game became highly profitable.

title: Balloon Fight
description: Balloon Fight (1984) is Nintendo's Joust-like balloon battle game, programmed by Satoru Iwata, which gained a Balloon Trip mode on the NES.
longDescription:
The Balloon Fighter floats on two balloons, flapping upwards with repeated button presses. In the main mode, one or two players clear each screen of enemy Balloon Fighters by bursting their balloons from above, and enemies that fall into the water or are eaten by the fish are beaten too. Losing one balloon makes it harder to rise, and a life is lost if both are popped, if the fighter falls into the water, is hit by lightning, or is eaten by the giant fish lurking below. Every three stages there is a bonus stage of bursting balloons that float up from chimneys.

The NES version adds Balloon Trip, a scrolling endless stage played on one life, in which the player dodges lightning sparks and collects balloons to climb the rankings. The arcade original has no Balloon Trip and uses different, vertically scrolling level layouts.
trivia: Its gameplay is similar to Williams' Joust (1982).
A sequel, Balloon Kid, came out on the Game Boy in 1990.
The Balloon Fighter was considered for Super Smash Bros. Melee, but the Ice Climbers were chosen instead.
Super Smash Bros. for 3DS has a stage based on it in 8-bit graphics, and Villager uses the Balloon Fighter's helmet.
A Club Nintendo exclusive, Tingle's Balloon Fight, came out on the DS in 2007.
devStory:
Yoshio Sakamoto designed it and drew its art under producer Gunpei Yokoi at Nintendo R&D1, with Satoru Iwata of HAL Laboratory programming and Hirokazu Tanaka composing. VS. Balloon Fight reached arcades in North America in September 1984, and the Famicom version came out in Japan on 22 January 1985, reaching North America in 1986. Hudson Soft ported it to the PC-8801 and Sharp X1.

It later became the first Virtual Console title on the Wii U, and one of the 30 games on the NES Classic Edition.

title: Wrecking Crew
description: Wrecking Crew (1984) is Nintendo's demolition puzzle game, in which Mario, too weighed down by his hammer to jump, must knock down every target in 100 levels.
longDescription:
Mario, or Luigi for a second player in the arcade version, must destroy every target on each of 100 levels with a big hammer whose weight stops him jumping. Each playfield is an invisible grid holding walls, pillars and ladders that can be smashed, indestructible barrels and ladders, and bombs that destroy whatever destructible objects they connect to. The order matters: knocking out a ladder too early can leave a wall out of reach, and chaining destruction, often with bombs, earns bonus points. Doors can be opened to send enemies harmlessly into the background.
