PC Magazine included it among the ten best Game Boy games in 2019.
It was re-released on the 3DS Virtual Console in 2012.
devStory:
Takehiko Hosokawa directed it at Nintendo R&D1, with Takehiro Izushi producing, Masani Ueda designing, Hiroji Kiyotake on art and Kozue Ishikawa composing. It came out in North America on 9 March 1998, and a colour version followed as a Japanese launch title for the Game Boy Color that October.

EGM made it Game of the Month in May 1998, and the colour version averaged 88% on GameRankings. Its approach without time limits carried over to later games in the series.

title: Dragon Warrior Monsters
description: Dragon Warrior Monsters (1998) is the Game Boy Dragon Quest spin-off in which Terry recruits monsters with meat and breeds them into stronger ones.
longDescription:
Before the events of Dragon Quest VI, a monster kidnaps Milly from her brother Terry's home at night. A monster called Watabou tells Terry that the evil Warubou has taken her and brings him to the Kingdom of GreatTree, whose King gives him a slime, Slib, as his first monster. Winning the Starry Night Tournament grants a wish, so Terry sets out to win it and rescue his sister.

Instead of fighting alone, Terry recruits monsters: setting out meat in a battle may persuade one to join afterwards. Spare monsters live on the Farm, where those kept awake grow wilder and less willing to fight, and those put to sleep stop growing. Gates beneath the throne room lead to other worlds, each with a boss in its last area, and are opened by climbing the arena's ranks from G to S, three wins each. From Class F onwards, Terry can breed a male and a female monster at the Shrine of Starry Night into an egg that inherits traits, skills and stats from both, though the parents leave the party. Some monsters can only be bred.
trivia: Terry and Milly appear as children; both come from Dragon Quest VI.
A hidden gate opens after befriending over 100 monsters.
It was the first Dragon Quest game released in Europe.
A 3DS remake, Terry no Wonderland 3D, sold 513,000 copies in its first week in Japan in 2012.
It sold about 2.35 million copies in Japan, but only about 60,000 in North America by April 2000.
devStory:
Tose developed it, with Yuji Horii designing and writing, Akira Toriyama drawing the monsters and Koichi Sugiyama composing, and Enix released it in Japan on 25 September 1998 as Dragon Quest Monsters: Terry no Wonderland. It sold 1.22 million copies that year, the fourth best-selling game of 1998 in Japan, and 2.35 million in all. Eidos co-published it in North America and Europe in January 2000, where it was the first Dragon Quest game released in Europe; it sold 60,000 copies in North America by April.

It averaged about 80% on GameRankings. IGN said it had many of Pokémon's mechanics "but better", though it preferred Pokémon's capture system, and GameSpot said its "rock-solid gameplay makes it a worthwhile endeavor".

title: Pokémon Pinball
description: Pokémon Pinball (1999) is the Game Boy Color pinball game in which the ball is a Poké Ball and players catch all 151 Pokémon across two tables.
longDescription:
The ball is a Poké Ball, and the Red and Blue tables are covered in Pokémon. Each table has locations that decide which Pokémon can appear; a slot machine picks the first one at the start of a game, and each table has its own way of moving to the next, including locations not offered at first. The main goal is score, and the secondary one is to catch all 151 Pokémon, with the Pokédex saved between games.

In Catch Mode, which lasts two minutes, each of six hits on the pop bumpers reveals a sixth of a Pokémon's picture; then it appears and must be hit four times to be caught. Evolution Mode, also two minutes, is the only way to record evolved forms: of the evolution targets on the table, three hold evolution items, and collecting all three opens the centre hole, where sinking the ball evolves the Pokémon.
trivia: It sold 262,000 copies in 20 days, the fastest-selling Game Boy game at the time.
It was the fourth best-selling US video game of 1999.
GameSpot called its rumble "a waste [...] of an AAA battery".
CNET called it "more than a shameless cash-in on the Pokémon phenomenon".
Its sequel, Pokémon Pinball: Ruby & Sapphire, came out on the Game Boy Advance in 2003.
devStory:
Jupiter and HAL Laboratory developed it, with Tsunekazu Ishihara producing and Go Ichinose composing. Nintendo released it in Japan on 14 April 1999 and in North America that June, on a cartridge with a built-in rumble.

It sold 262,000 copies in its first 20 days and was the fourth best-selling game in the US in 1999, behind only Pokémon Red, Blue and Yellow. GameSpot gave it 8.7/10, praising its presentation but criticising its physics, and called the rumble "a nice novelty". It averaged about 82% on GameRankings.

title: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium
description: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium (1999) is SNK's Neo Geo Pocket Color crossover fighter, with 26 characters from both companies and the best seller on the system in Japan.
longDescription:
Fighters battle one-on-one, in tag teams of two or in teams of three that take turns. Players choose between three power gauges: an Average mode with a Capcom-style level gauge, a Counter mode with an SNK-style charge gauge, and a Rush mode whose meter boosts super attacks when full. Each character has a rival, fought between the fourth and fifth stages, and the last two stages bring a tag team of Geese and Bison, then Orochi Iori or Evil Ryu, depending on the player's side and whether the rival was beaten. Only clearing the final stage unlocks a character's ending; otherwise a bad ending plays.

The Olympic mode adds minigames, including a Martian-shooting game taken from Metal Slug 2's final boss and one in which Arthur from Ghosts 'n Goblins hops pits for treasure, along with time-attack, first-strike and survival events. Points earned there unlock a special attack for each character and, over a link cable, extras in Card Fighters' Clash, The King of Fighters: Dream Match 1999 and Capcom vs. SNK on the Dreamcast.
trivia: IGN gave it 10/10.
It sold 75,000 copies in Japan, the best seller there on the Neo Geo Pocket.
It lost a GamePro Readers' Choice Award for best handheld game to Pokémon Yellow.
Its Japanese title translates roughly as "Final Great Battle of the Strongest Fighters".
The 2021 Switch version added local multiplayer and TV play for the first time.
devStory:
It began after SNK's Takashi Nishiyama met Capcom's head of development Yoshiki Okamoto about working together, and the two won over their companies' presidents, Eikichi Kawasaki and Kenzo Tsujimoto. Art director Toyohisa Tanabe said the project was meant to help bring games to the struggling Neo Geo Pocket Color. The roster has 26 fighters, 13 from each company, from Terry Bogard and Kyo Kusanagi to Ryu and Morrigan.

SNK released it in December 1999 in Japan and North America, the first game in the SNK vs. Capcom series. IGN gave it 10/10 and called it "the finest fighting game ever to grace a portable screen". It sold about 75,000 copies in Japan, the most of any Neo Geo Pocket game there, and was re-released on Switch and Windows in 2021.

sources.title: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium

title: Final Fantasy Tactics
description: Final Fantasy Tactics (1997) is Square's PlayStation tactical role-playing game, Yasumi Matsuno's tale of class conflict and suppressed history in the kingdom of Ivalice during the Lion War.
longDescription:
Battles play out on compact three-dimensional isometric maps made of square tiles, where terrain and weather affect the fight and the camera can be rotated and zoomed. Turns are not taken in strict rotation: each unit acts when its Charge Time reaches 100, and it fills at a rate set by the unit's speed. Every successful action earns experience and job points. Between battles the player moves along fixed paths on a world map, visiting towns to take side jobs at the bar, buy equipment and recruit soldiers, while random encounters wait on marked spots.

The job system borrows the series' classic roles, including Wizards, Priests, Monks, Lancers and Thieves. Recruits start as Squires or Chemists, and reaching a set level in one job unlocks others, for twenty in all. Job points buy abilities within each class, and a unit can equip a second job's skills and separate reaction, support and movement abilities on top of its current class.

The story is framed as a historian's account of a long-buried report. After the Fifty Years War, Ivalice is split between Duke Goltana's Black Lion and Duke Larg's White Lion over who will act as regent for an infant heir. Ramza Beoulve, a cadet from a noble family of knights, and his commoner friend Delita Hyral break with the nobility after Delita's sister is killed, and Ramza uncovers how the Glabados Church engineered the war using the Zodiac Stones.
trivia: Hironobu Sakaguchi conceived the game in 1993 but was too busy with the main series to make it.
Matsuno said the Dead Sea Scrolls and The Name of the Rose inspired its story of a suppressed account of history.
Translator Michael Baskett began writing the script in an "Olde English style" but toned it down because characters started to sound alike.
In Japan it came bundled with a demo disc for SaGa Frontier.
Its 2025 remaster, The Ivalice Chronicles, had to rebuild the code from commercial copies because the original source data had not been preserved.
devStory:
Production began at the end of 1995 under Yasumi Matsuno, who had left Quest Corporation after Tactics Ogre and brought several of its staff to Square, including artists Hiroshi Minagawa and Akihiko Yoshida and composers Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata. Sakaguchi produced, Taku Murata led programming, and Hiroyuki Ito designed the battle system, aiming to make it fast and exciting because he found tactical RPGs of the time boring. Matsuno wanted an accessible game focused on individual characters rather than the army simulation of Tactics Ogre, and the small diorama-like maps let it run at 60 frames per second. He said the class-based themes came from watching the hierarchy inside game companies and from Japan's Lost Decades. Against Final Fantasy VII's polished CGI, the team chose a hand-drawn look.

It was released in Japan on 20 June 1997 and in North America on 28 January 1998 by Sony Computer Entertainment. It sold almost 1.24 million copies in Japan in 1997 and over 2.4 million worldwide by August 2011. Critics praised its strategic depth, visuals and story, though some wanted larger battles and RPGFan criticised the English translation. It created the world of Ivalice, later used in Vagrant Story and Final Fantasy XII, and was remade for the PSP as The War of the Lions in 2007.

title: The Legend of Dragoon
description: The Legend of Dragoon (1999) is Sony's own four-disc PlayStation role-playing game, a $16 million production whose timed "addition" attacks and dragon-armoured transformations set it apart from Final Fantasy.
longDescription:
Play moves between a linear 3D area map with fixed routes, fully scaled field locations over pre-rendered backgrounds, and a battle screen. Up to three characters fight in turn-based battles, but attacking triggers an "addition": two blue squares converge on screen, and pressing a button as they overlap continues the combo for more damage. Longer additions are learned over the game, and enemies can counter them, forcing a different button press to keep going.

Each playable character eventually gains a Dragoon Spirit. Spirit points earned from normal attacks let a character transform into Dragoon form for a few turns, taking to the air with wings and swapping the usual commands for Dragoon Attack, a timed circle-and-line button prompt, and Dragoon Magic. Because the team wanted a realistic tone, magic is otherwise available only through items.

On the medieval world of Endiness, the warrior Dart is hunting the Black Monster that killed his parents when he finds his village destroyed and his childhood friend Shana taken prisoner. Rescuing her draws him into a war, the theft of ancient royal artifacts by the Wingly swordsman Lloyd, and a 10,000-year-old plot to revive the God of Destruction.
trivia: The development team grew to over 100 people, many of them recent college or game-school graduates.
Its CGI cutscenes were made with help from Polyphony Digital, which had been spun off from the studio a year earlier.
The team named its characters by writing down 100 names and picking their favourites.
Rose originally had bright green hair, dropped as the setting became more realistic.
On release in Japan it was second only to Pokémon Gold and Silver, selling over 160,000 copies that week.
devStory:
Inspired by the success of Final Fantasy, Sony Computer Entertainment Japan began the game in 1996 with a small team while it was also making Ape Escape. Yasuyuki Hasebe, a battle designer on Super Mario RPG, directed and wrote the story outline, and Shuhei Yoshida produced; Kenichi Iwata was art director and designed the Dragoon armour. The addition system was meant to make players feel they were taking part in battles rather than waiting for commands. The team first planned no CGI movies, then added them for key events, and those films and pre-rendered backgrounds pushed the game onto four CDs. Dennis Martin and Takeo Miratsu composed the music, and Elsa Raven sang the theme, "If You Still Believe".

It was released in Japan on 2 December 1999, in North America in June 2000 in an easier version Yoshida called "complete", and in Europe in January 2001. Reviews were mixed (74 on Metacritic) and often compared it unfavourably with Final Fantasy, while praising its cinematics. It sold over 280,000 copies in Japan and 823,000 in North America by 2007, and Yoshida said US sales recouped its budget.

title: F-Zero X
description: F-Zero X (1998) is Nintendo's first 3D F-Zero, a Nintendo 64 racer that keeps 30 hovercars on screen at 60 frames per second by stripping back its graphics.
longDescription:
Thirty plasma-powered hovercars race on high-altitude circuits full of hills, loops, tunnels, corkscrews and pipes. There are 26 new vehicles plus the four from the original F-Zero, each graded A to E for grip, boost and durability, and before a race the player sets a balance between acceleration and top speed. Drifting holds momentum through corners. A single energy meter serves as both health and boost: it drains when the machine hits rivals or walls and when the player boosts, usually from the second lap, and refills on recharge strips. For the first time racers can attack each other with side and spin attacks, and every five opponents eliminated earns a spare machine.

The Grand Prix runs three-lap races across the Jack, Queen and King cups, six tracks each, on four difficulty levels, with the Joker Cup and the X Cup to unlock. The X Cup generates six random tracks on every playthrough. Death Race sets the player loose on a special course to wipe out the other 29 racers as fast as possible, Time Attack adds ghost racers, and up to four players can race in VS Battle, where eliminated players can drain the leaders' energy on a slot machine.
trivia: It was first known as "F-Zero 64".
According to GameSpot it was the first racing game to run at 60 frames per second with up to 30 vehicles on screen.
Voice actor Jim Wornell based the announcer Mr. Zero's voice on the announcer in Ridge Racer.
To fit on the cartridge, its soundtrack is half-size and mono, with ambient effects added in stereo in real time.
Its 64DD Expansion Kit, released only in Japan in 2000, was the 64DD's only expansion disk and added a track editor and machine creator.
devStory:
Shigeru Miyamoto mentioned a Nintendo 64 F-Zero sequel in mid-1996 while Mario Kart 64 was in development. Nintendo EAD built it with several key Wave Race 64 programmers, including the lead programmer; Tadashi Sugiyama directed, Miyamoto produced, and Taro Bando and Hajime Wakai composed a soundtrack that remixes the original's tunes. Holding 60 frames per second meant cutting background, texture and vehicle detail, with the bulky tracks blocking most of the scenery and fog hiding the horizon. It was first playable at Nintendo Space World in November 1997.

It came out in Japan on 14 July 1998, and in North America on 27 October after a delay under Nintendo's policy of spacing out first-party releases. Critics praised its speed, track design and frame rate but criticised its sparse visuals; it averaged 85 on Metacritic and was EGM's Game of the Month for November 1998. It sold 383,642 copies in North America and 97,684 in Japan.

title: Pilotwings 64
description: Pilotwings 64 (1996) is the Nintendo 64 launch flight game built with Texas simulator firm Paradigm, in which six pilots earn licences by hang glider, rocket belt and gyrocopter over four islands, one a miniature United States.
longDescription:
Before each mission the player picks one of six pilots, whose weight and other traits change how they handle, then takes licence tests scored on time, damage, fuel, accuracy and the softness of the landing, earning bronze, silver or gold. Each of the three main events has its own controls on the Nintendo 64's single analogue stick. Hang gliding means flying through rings or photographing scenery before landing on a target, riding wind currents and climbing in thermals. The Rocket Belt is a jet pack that can hover, tilt and rotate, used to pass through rings, land on floating platforms and pop balloons. The gyrocopter takes off and lands on a runway after flying a course of rings or destroying targets with missiles.

Good results unlock bonus events: skydiving, a human cannonball and the Jumble Hopper, spring-loaded boots for bouncing across the landscape. Birdman mode puts the pilot in a bird suit to explore the four islands freely. One is a miniature United States with the Statue of Liberty, Los Angeles, Chicago, New York and a Mount Rushmore on which Mario's face replaces George Washington's.
trivia: Mario's face replaces George Washington's on the game's Mount Rushmore.
The pilot Lark is modelled on Nester, mascot of Nintendo Power; the character Robin is called "Hooter" in Japan.
Paradigm had made military vehicle and flight simulators but never a video game before.
Composer Dan Hess said Akito Nakatsuka, credited for "sound arrangement", did not arrange any of the music.
Esquire called it the "cheapest game in Nintendo's frighteningly-priced opening range of titles" in the UK.
devStory:
Nintendo approached Paradigm Simulation in 1994 because of its experience with Silicon Graphics workstations, making it one of the Nintendo 64's "Dream Team" developers. Paradigm spent nine months building a technology base with Silicon Graphics, and work on the game began in June 1995, with Nintendo designing it and Paradigm handling the technical side. Makoto Wada directed, Genyo Takeda was the technical contact, and Shigeru Miyamoto produced from Japan, though less closely than on the SNES original because he was making Super Mario 64. Paradigm started from a physics-based approach but aimed for "a more arcade feel", building the islands in its own Vega UltraVision tool and leaning on the console's level of detail, mipmapping, z-buffering and anti-aliasing.

It launched with the Nintendo 64 in Japan on 23 June 1996 and was one of two launch games in North America that September, selling about 90,000 copies in its first few days there. Critics praised its 3D visuals and flying, though some called it a mere tech demo and mocked its lounge-music soundtrack. EGM named it Flying Game of the Year, and it had sold over a million copies worldwide by early 1998. A Nintendo 64 sequel Paradigm announced in 1997 was cancelled.

title: Mario Party
description: Mario Party (1998) is Hudson Soft's Nintendo 64 board game with 50 mini-games, the first in Nintendo's long-running party series and the game whose stick-spinning mini-games led to a glove settlement.
longDescription:
Mario, Luigi, Peach, Yoshi, Wario and Donkey Kong compete to be the "Super Star" on boards themed after each of them, with two more unlocked later. Four characters play each game, any not taken by humans run by the computer at three skill levels, over 20, 35 or 50 turns. Players roll a dice block to move one to ten spaces. Blue spaces give three coins and red ones take three, doubling in the last five turns; others trigger single-player mini-games, Chance Time coin and star swaps, board events, Bowser's interference or a mushroom that grants or costs a turn. Stars are bought from Toad with coins. Boo steals coins for free or a star for 50 coins, Koopa Troopa hands out ten coins at the start, and Bowser forces useless items on passers-by.

After each round of moves, one of 50 mini-games starts, chosen by roulette and set as four-player, one-versus-three or two-versus-two by the colour of the spaces players landed on. At the end three bonus stars go to the top mini-game earner, the richest player and whoever landed on the most "?" spaces. Coins saved in the Mushroom Bank buy mini-games for free play and items in the Mushroom Shop, and Mini-Game Island is a single-player run through every mini-game with four lives.
trivia: Some players got blisters and friction burns from spinning the analogue stick with their palms, a method shown in a Japanese commercial for the game.
Nintendo of America settled about 90 complaints to New York's attorney general by offering gloves to injured players and paying $75,000 in legal fees.
It was left off the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console, where Mario Party 2 was released instead, and returned only in 2022 on Nintendo Classics with a warning about stick rotation.
Hudson Soft, its developer, was best known for Bomberman.
It lost the Interactive Achievement Award for console family title to Pokémon Snap.
devStory: Hudson Soft developed the game for a young audience, with Shigeru Miyamoto supervising, and Nintendo released it in Japan on 18 December 1998, North America on 8 February 1999 and Europe on 9 March 1999. Reviews were generally favourable but said its fun depended on playing with friends: GameSpot's Joe Fielder noted that the mini-games were "nowhere near as good in the single player mode", and critics found the computer players' turns painfully slow and the luck excessive. Its music was praised and its graphics drew mixed views. It was among the five most rented games in its first two months in the US and the fourth best-selling Nintendo 64 game there in 1999, and it began a series that continued with Mario Party 2 later that year.

title: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron
description: Star Wars: Rogue Squadron (1998) is Factor 5 and LucasArts' arcade flight game for the Nintendo 64 and PC, 16 missions of Luke Skywalker's X-wing pilots fighting the Empire between the first two films.
longDescription:
Unlike the simulation-minded X-Wing series, this is fast arcade flight action seen from behind the craft, with a cockpit view available. Each of the 16 levels sets objectives in four kinds: search and destroy, reconnaissance, rescue and protect. Against TIE fighters, bombers and interceptors, walkers, turrets, tanks, probe droids and speeder bikes, the player flies the X-wing, A-wing, Y-wing, snowspeeder and V-wing, each with its own weapons, speed and handling. A level first has to be flown in a set craft but can then be replayed in any. Nine hidden power-ups permanently upgrade weapons or durability.

After each level the player's time, kills, accuracy, friendly craft saved and bonuses collected are measured against bronze, silver and gold benchmarks, and medals raise the player's rank and unlock secrets. These include bonus levels based on the films, Beggar's Canyon, the Death Star trench run and the Battle of Hoth, and extra craft such as the Millennium Falcon and a TIE interceptor. The story runs six months after the Battle of Yavin, with a final level six years after Return of the Jedi.
trivia: A playable 1969 Buick Electra 225, based on a car owned by sound designer Rudolph Stember, is hidden in the game.
Factor 5 secretly included the Naboo Starfighter from the unreleased Phantom Menace, hiding its code with a scrambling system; LucasArts revealed it more than six months after release.
At E3 1998 the game was so unfinished that the TIE fighters flew fixed paths and Brett Tosti followed a set route to make it look like he was fighting them.
Lucasfilm first gave the sound designer Star Wars effects sampled at only 22 kHz.
Producer Julian Eggebrecht said it sold "about 100 times better than anybody expected".
devStory:
After Shadows of the Empire, LucasArts planned a follow-up, and Factor 5 turned the terrain engine it was building for a sequel to Rescue on Fractalus! into a Star Wars game. Its focus on flight came from Shadows of the Empire's snowspeeder level at Hoth; the plan was to combine Fractalus's free roaming with the on-rails play of Atari's Star Wars arcade game. Factor 5 made the engine, the music and its own MOsys FX Surround sound drivers, which fit about 40 minutes each of speech and music, while LucasArts wrote the content. Late on, the team realised it had always been running the game with extra memory; it compressed the game to run on a standard console and persuaded Nintendo to sell the Expansion Pak, which raises the resolution from 320 × 240 to 640 × 480.

It was released for Nintendo 64 and Windows in December 1998, the first game in a three-game Star Wars deal with Nintendo. Critics praised its high-resolution visuals and sound but disliked its distance fog and lack of multiplayer, and it scored 85% on Metacritic. More than a million copies were sold worldwide by August 1999. Two GameCube sequels and Battle for Naboo followed.

title: Shining Force III
description: Shining Force III (1997) is Camelot's Saturn tactical RPG, released in Japan as three scenario discs that tell one war from three sides and carry save data forward, of which only the first was translated.
longDescription:
Battles are turn-based on square grids. Each unit moves a set number of squares and then takes one action, such as attacking, casting a spell, using an item or searching, and turn order comes from agility plus a random factor. Units gain experience from fighting and healing, and each character's class sets its spells and equipment; promotion to a new class is possible between levels 10 and 20 and resets the level to 1. Characters who fight side by side build friendships that raise their stats when they stand near each other. Objectives are simple, such as routing the enemy, killing its leader or reaching a landmark. There is no game over: if the player's leader falls, the Force keeps its experience and loses half its money.

Between battles the game becomes a traditional Japanese role-playing game without dungeons, in which the leader walks around towns, talks to people, finds treasure, shops and picks the army for the next fight. In Japan the story came on three discs, Scenarios 1 to 3, following Synbios of the Republic of Aspinia, Prince Medion of the Empire of Destonia and the mercenary Julian. A peace conference in the city of Saraband collapses into war through the manipulation of the Bulzome Sect, a religious cult. Saves could be carried into later scenarios to change events and earn rewards, which Sega marketed as the "Synchronicity system".
trivia: In the English release of Scenario 1 the script was edited to resolve its original cliffhanger ending.
Japanese players who sent proof of purchase for all three scenarios received a Premium Disk with concept art, a model viewer and bonus battles.
Sega of America mentioned it in 2001 as a good candidate for a PlayStation port, but none was made.
Scenarios 2 and 3 were never officially translated; fans later produced unofficial English translations.
Retro Gamer's Ashley Day named it his favourite game of all time.
devStory: Work began while Shining the Holy Ark (1996) was still being made and took nearly two years, with over thirty people in-house. Sega announced the game as a Saturn exclusive in August 1997 and released it in Japan in three separate parts across late 1997 and 1998. IGN reported rumours that all three had once been planned for English release, but as Saturn sales fell only Scenario 1 was localised, released in North America and Europe in mid-1998 as Shining Force III. Critics praised its fully polygonal graphics, rotating camera, soundtrack and translation, and its simple, fast play compared with more complicated tactical RPGs. Next Generation wrote that like the Saturn itself it was "underproduced, underrated, but fun as hell". Released late in the Saturn's life, it sold in limited numbers. It was Camelot's last Shining game, the series' last on Sega hardware, and the last Camelot game not made only for Nintendo hardware, and it has never been re-released.

title: Castlevania: Bloodlines
description: Castlevania: Bloodlines (1994) is Konami's only Castlevania for the Sega Genesis, set around the First World War with two playable hunters and the series debut of composer Michiru Yamane.
longDescription:
As in earlier Castlevania games, the player fights through each stage, collecting gems to power the axe, boomerang and holy water sub-weapons and powering up the main weapon. Each stage is split into sections, with a sub-boss halfway through and a main boss at the end. There are two characters: John Morris, who whips like a Belmont and can swing across gaps on his whip, and Eric Lecarde, who wields a spear and can make high jumps with it, so some stages split into different routes depending on who is playing.

The story picks up after Quincey Morris, a distant descendant of the Belmonts, put Dracula to rest in 1897. Dracula's niece Elizabeth Bartley is behind the assassination at Sarajevo in June 1914, using the war it starts to collect human souls for her uncle's revival. In 1917 John, Quincey's son, and Eric, whose girlfriend became a vampire when Elizabeth was revived, follow her and the witch Drolta Tzuentes across Europe.
trivia: In PAL regions it was renamed Castlevania: The New Generation, and blood and violent imagery were cut, to keep the word "blood" out of the title.
The Western version is harder than the Japanese one.
Writer Toshiki Yamamura took inspiration from novelist Hideyuki Kikuchi and saw the game as the second act of a three-part Castlevania saga.
Michiru Yamane had studied Bach at university and programmed her own music into the game.
Its story was continued in Castlevania: Portrait of Ruin (2006) on the Nintendo DS.
devStory:
Konami developed Bloodlines in Tokyo as a Castlevania built for the Genesis, faster and more action-led than earlier games while keeping their strategy, and added Eric as a second playable character. Set in a different era from previous games, it is a spin-off from the main series. The team worked within the Genesis's colour palette and an 8-megabit cartridge but felt it still achieved a distinctive atmosphere with detailed character animation. It was Michiru Yamane's first Castlevania score. She felt pressure because the series was known for its music, blended her classical training with the series' rock themes and became a regular series composer.

It was released in March 1994 and sold 9,354 copies in Japan, according to Famitsu. Critics were generally positive, giving it an 81.88% GameRankings average. GamePro said in 1997 that it was not as impressive as Super Castlevania IV but was strong by Genesis standards, and Game Informer later called it "one of the most overlooked treasures in the franchise". It was re-released in the Castlevania Anniversary Collection and on the Genesis Mini in 2019.

title: Contra: Hard Corps
description: Contra: Hard Corps (1994) is Konami's first Contra on a Sega console, a Genesis run-and-gun with four commandos, branching routes and multiple endings.
longDescription:
The player shoots through each side-scrolling stage to a boss, sometimes riding the Motoroid, a hoverbike that turns into an ostrich-like robot. Unlike earlier Contra games, there are no overhead stages, and the player chooses one of four characters, the commandos Ray Poward and Sheena Etranzi, the cyborg Brad Fang and the robot Browny, each with their own set of weapons. Two can play at once but not as the same character. The controls follow Contra III, adapted for the Genesis pad: a button toggles between running while firing and standing still to aim in eight directions, the player can climb walls and ceilings, and a new slide makes the character briefly invulnerable. Up to four weapons, lettered A to D, can be carried, and the current one is lost with a life.

Set five years after Contra III, the story follows the Hard Corps task force against Colonel Bahamut, who has stolen an alien cell to make weapons. Cutscenes advance the plot, and decisions at key moments send the player down different routes to several endings, including joining Bahamut.
trivia: The Japanese version is much easier, with a life gauge that takes three hits and unlimited continues; the US version allows five continues.
In Europe it became Probotector, with robot heroes, Bahamut redrawn as a humanoid alien, the alien cell replaced by an "X-Drive" and one ending removed.
The alien lair stage was inspired by the team's visit to the Meguro Parasite Museum in Tokyo.
A hidden stage added late in development surprised Konami's management, which approved it.
Animator Yasuomi Umetsu drew the Japanese cover and manual art.
devStory:
Development leader Nobuya Nakazato told BEEP! magazine in 1994 that the game was made for the Japanese Mega Drive market, against the idea that Konami had shifted its focus to the West. The team wanted replayability through branching routes, varied stages and little reuse of enemies; the first stage was packed with set pieces so it would stay interesting on repeat plays, and each character changes the tone, from serious with Ray to comic with Browny. Nakazato said it was made from the team's passion as longtime Contra fans rather than for commercial reasons alone.

Famitsu recorded 23,365 copies sold in Japan, where Micom BASIC Magazine ranked it first in popularity in December 1994. Critics praised its bosses, graphics and intense action, though EGM found the difficulty frustrating, and Next Generation called it "the ultimate side-scrolling shooter". It led to its own spin-offs, including Hard Corps: Uprising, and was re-released in the Contra Anniversary Collection and on the Genesis Mini in 2019.

title: Beatmania
description: Beatmania (1997) is Konami's arcade DJ game of five keys and a turntable, which set off Japan's 1998 music-game boom and gave the Bemani line its name.
longDescription:
The player is a club DJ trying to keep a crowd happy. The controls are five keys arranged in a zigzag like piano keys, white on the lower row and black on the top, plus a turntable to the right that is scratched. Each key and the turntable has its own column on screen, and notes fall down them toward a line near the bottom; hitting the right key or scratching as a note reaches the line plays a sound sample that rebuilds the song. Each hit is judged from great to poor, and stray presses and misses drain the audience's satisfaction bar. Each song has to satisfy the crowd to move on to the next stage, and depending on the machine's settings the game can end early if the bar empties.

The score is counted in "money", but the final letter grade reflects overall accuracy. Modes ranged from practice, with a voice-over tutor called DJ Konami in the early versions, to expert courses of set songs. Konami built a standard cabinet with a 29-inch screen and ten speakers and a smaller mini cabinet with a 20-inch screen, six speakers and a turntable about half the size.
trivia: By May 1999 it had sold 6,700 arcade units and earned a Guinness World Record as the most popular DJ-simulation arcade game.
In North America it was released as HipHopMania, and in South Korea as Beatstage.
Konami sued the makers of the South Korean EZ2DJ for copyright infringement over its similar gameplay.
The Japanese PlayStation version used a key disc: later "append" discs were played by swapping discs in.
Its popularity produced unofficial simulators, the best known being BM98.
devStory: Konami released Beatmania in arcades on 31 December 1997, and it contributed largely to the boom in music games in 1998. Game Machine listed it as Japan's most successful dedicated arcade game in its 1 March 1998 issue, and by 2000 it had sold 25,000 arcade machines. A run of mixes followed, from 2ndMix in March 1998 to Beatmania The Final in July 2002, and from 3rdMix Konami used the name Bemani for its whole line of music games. The 1998 PlayStation version, a port of 2ndMix, sold 1.1 million copies in Japan; ASCII made controllers for it, and versions also appeared on the Game Boy Color and WonderSwan. The seven-key Beatmania IIDX spin-off was still receiving new versions long after the original series ended.

title: Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes
description: Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes (1998) is Capcom's CP System II tag-team fighter that first opened the crossover to its whole back catalogue, pitting Mega Man, Strider and Morrigan against Marvel's heroes.
longDescription:
Each player picks a team of two and can swap between them at any time; the resting partner slowly recovers health off-screen. A team wins by knocking out both opponents, or by having more health left when time runs out. In place of the previous game's Variable Assist, a randomly assigned Special Partner can be called in a few times per round, from 22 characters such as Colossus, Cyclops, Jubilee, Arthur from Ghosts 'n Goblins and the Unknown Soldier from Forgotten Worlds. The new Variable Cross, or Duo Team Attack, puts both fighters on screen together for a limited time with unlimited use of the Hyper Combo Gauge, letting the player chain several Hyper Combos in quick succession.

There are 15 regular fighters, drawn from Capcom series such as Darkstalkers, Mega Man and Strider rather than only Street Fighter as in Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter. Codes unlock six secret characters, mostly palette swaps with changed moves, such as Shadow Lady from Chun-Li; Mega Man's sister Roll is the exception, with her own sprites. The arcade mode ends with Onslaught, the villain of Marvel's crossover comics storyline of a year before.
trivia: In the US it sold an estimated 3,000 arcade units, reportedly outperforming Street Fighter III to become Capcom's most successful US arcade game of the period.
The PlayStation port dropped tag-team battles because of the console's limited RAM, keeping them only in a Cross Over mode in which both players use identical teams.
The Dreamcast version added Cross Fever, a four-player two-on-two mode.
Toy Biz made four two-packs of action figures pairing a Marvel and a Capcom character, such as War Machine and Mega Man.
The Marvel vs. Capcom Origins re-release was pulled from online stores in December 2014 after Capcom's Marvel licence apparently expired.
devStory: Capcom built the game for its CP System II arcade board and showed it at the AOU Show in February 1998, releasing it in Japan that month and in North America in March. Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful arcade game of March 1998. The Dreamcast port followed in 1999 and was praised by Game Informer as a "flawless" translation of the arcade game, while GameRevolution felt it lacked depth. The PlayStation port, released as the EX Edition in Japan in November 1999, also lost animation frames to fit in memory; GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann faulted the loss of tag battles, though GamePro accepted the trade-off for speed. Capcom announced Marvel vs. Capcom 2: New Age of Heroes, with three-on-three teams, on 1 December 1999.

sources.title: Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes

title: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams
description: Street Fighter Alpha: Warriors' Dreams (1995), Street Fighter Zero in Japan, is Capcom's first all-new Street Fighter since 1991, a prequel to Street Fighter II with younger fighters, a three-level super gauge and Alpha Counters.
longDescription:
Alpha expands the Super Combo system of Super Street Fighter II Turbo into a three-level gauge that fills as the player attacks; how many punch or kick buttons are pressed decides how much of it a Super Combo spends. After blocking, the player can spend one level on an Alpha Counter. An Auto mode blocks a limited number of attacks automatically and allows instant Super Combos, at the cost of limiting the gauge to one level. New techniques include blocking in mid-air, Chain Combos that cancel one basic move into another of equal or greater strength, and rolling on landing after a knockdown.

The ten regular fighters are Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li and Sagat; Birdie and Adon from the original Street Fighter, playable for the first time; Guy and Sodom from Final Fight; and two newcomers, Guile's combat buddy Charlie and the fortune teller Rose. M. Bison is the final opponent for half the cast, and Akuma and the new Dan, Capcom's parody of SNK's Ryo Sakazaki and Robert Garcia, can appear as hidden challengers. A secret Dramatic Battle lets two players team up as Ryu and Ken against Bison, recreating the climax of Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie.
trivia: Its prototype name was Street Fighter Classic, because it was set between Street Fighter and Street Fighter II.
Capcom of America disliked "Zero" as sounding negative; it was announced as Street Fighter Legends before becoming Alpha, to suggest a new beginning.
The Japanese arcade version plays an instrumental of the film's song "Itoshisa to Setsunasa to Kokoro Zuyosa to" in Dramatic Battle, replaced abroad for licensing reasons.
Its PlayStation and Saturn ports were the first console Street Fighter games with a Training Mode.
It was Japan's second highest-grossing arcade game of 1995, behind Virtua Fighter 2.
devStory:
Production started in October 1994, after Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors. The team was given three months to make a game from scratch and took six. Capcom had been buying back CPS-1 boards from arcades to help sell CPS-2, so Alpha was developed for both boards at once; the CPS-1 version had a different-sounding soundtrack and fewer sound effects, and could be sold to arcades that could not afford to upgrade. Its art followed the style of Darkstalkers and X-Men: Children of the Atom.

RePlay reported it as North America's most popular arcade game of August 1995. Critics praised its sprites, the revamped Super Combos and Alpha Counters, though Next Generation noted that the changes were small. Because it had relatively little animation data, the PlayStation and Saturn ports reused the arcade source code; EGM made the PlayStation version its Game of the Month, and Maximum gave the Saturn version its Game of the Month award. Street Fighter Alpha 2 followed in 1996 and Alpha 3 in 1998.

title: Street Fighter III: New Generation
description: Street Fighter III: New Generation (1997) is Capcom's CP System III sequel to Street Fighter II, which kept only Ryu and Ken, introduced parrying and stayed in 2D when rivals had moved to 3D.
longDescription:
Two fighters trade attacks and special moves to knock each other out, with moves borrowed from other Capcom fighters: dashes and retreats from Darkstalkers, super jumps and quick recovery from X-Men: Children of the Atom, and new leap attacks against crouching opponents. Air blocking from the Alpha games is gone, replaced by parrying: tapping forward or down at the exact moment an attack lands deflects it without damage, even from special moves and Super Arts, and leaves the attacker open to a counter. It demands precise timing.

After choosing a character, the player picks one of three Super Arts, each with its own gauge length and number of stocks, and special moves can be cancelled into them. Characters can be hit into a turned-around state, which lets throws be comboed. The new cast is led by the American grappler Alex, joined by the British boxer Dudley, the Kenyan capoeira fighter Elena, the ninja Ibuki, the Russian Necro, an escaped test subject of Gill's organisation, the hermit Oro, Ken's would-be apprentice Sean and the twins Yun and Yang. Gill, leader of a secret organisation, replaces M. Bison as the boss.
trivia: On the arcade cabinet it is titled "Three: A New Generation of Street Fighters".
It began as an original fighting game; character designer Akira Yasuda suggested adding Ryu, expecting Capcom to turn it into a Street Fighter game, as it did.
Yasuda later told Polygon that if he could change the past, he would "rather just not have worked on that game at all".
Each character has roughly 700 to 1,200 hand-drawn frames of animation.
It cost about 1 billion yen ($8 million) but sold only around 1,000 cabinets in Japan and struggled to break even there.
devStory:
Production began in 1994. Street Fighter II producer Noritaka Funamizu, tired of the series and watching 3D fighters like Virtua Fighter rise, wanted a new game, but Capcom stayed with 2D sprites and built the CPS-3 board to show more colours. Producer Tomoshi Sadamoto worked on a game called New Generation, and Yasuda suggested Ryu; Ken was added later, while Ken and Chun-Li were passed over in favour of an original cast. Yasuda proposed a ninja, who became Ibuki, and Elena grew from an idea of "Yuki in Africa", after model Yuki Uchida. Each developer tuned their own character, leaving the balance uneven, and Hugo slipped to the follow-up, 2nd Impact. Funamizu explained that 3D was "not really suitable" for head-to-head fighting and that Capcom lacked the techniques for good 3D graphics.

Capcom announced the game in March 1996 and showed it that September. Game Machine named it Japan's most successful arcade game of March 1997, but critics such as Next Generation and GamePro praised its graphics while finding little innovation, and it did not become a hit like its predecessor. 2nd Impact followed in 1997, 3rd Strike in 1999, and the Dreamcast compilation Double Impact the same year.

title: Raiden
description: Raiden (1990) is Seibu Kaihatsu's vertical shoot 'em up, built on cheap hardware after a flop and turned by word of mouth into a 17,000-unit arcade hit and a long-running series.
longDescription:
In 2090 the alien Crystals have invaded Earth and seized most of its military hardware. The Vanquish Crystal Defense answers with the Fighting Thunder, an attack craft built on Crystal technology, and one or two players fly it through eight stages of rising difficulty. After the eighth stage the game loops back to the first, harder than before. In co-operative play, each player can fire at the other's craft to generate special projectiles that damage enemies.

Pick-ups include bombs, which wipe out enemy fire and hit a wide area, weapon power-ups and score medals. Two hidden bonuses appear: the Miclus, a boss from Seibu's 1985 game Wiz, and a fairy that releases power-ups when the player dies. A destroyed fighter's shrapnel damages nearby enemies, and continuing restarts the player at the last checkpoint.
trivia: Seibu made a shoot 'em up because it was "relatively inexpensive to produce", after its previous game, Dynamite Duke, sold poorly.
Its designers took notes from 1942, Xevious and Twin Cobra.
The Miclus bonus item is a boss from Seibu's 1985 game Wiz.
In North America, weekly coin earnings in November and December 1990 averaged $194.25 per machine.
Telegames released an Atari Lynx version in 1997, long after the Lynx's commercial life had ended.
devStory:
According to graphic designer Toshinobu Komazawa, later head of MOSS, Seibu Kaihatsu chose a shoot 'em up instead of a Dynamite Duke sequel to recoup that game's costs, and money was so tight that it used less powerful arcade hardware than its earlier titles. President Hitoshi Hamada led production, Tetsuya Kawaguchi was designer and programmer, and Akira Sato composed the music. Tecmo released it in Japan in April 1990, with Fabtek handling North America.

Komazawa said it earned little at first because the modest hardware lacked flashy visuals, but word of mouth built demand, and steady orders over a year took sales to about 17,000 units. Game Machine listed it as Japan's most successful table arcade unit in July 1990, and it was the country's sixth highest-grossing arcade game of 1990 and fifth of 1991. Ports followed on the PC Engine, Jaguar, MS-DOS, Lynx, Mega Drive and SNES (as Raiden Trad), and in The Raiden Project on the PlayStation. Seibu made sequels until its 2005 bankruptcy, after which MOSS, founded by its staff, took over the series.

title: DoDonPachi
description: DoDonPachi (1997) is Cave's second game, an arcade bullet-hell shooter built around combo chains and a laser that slows the ship, with a hidden second loop and a twist about who the enemy really is.
longDescription:
The player picks one of three craft, a red fighter with a narrow stream, a green helicopter whose side guns turn with its movement, or a blue fighter with a three-way spread, and plays it in Shot or Laser mode. Tapping fire shoots normally; holding it merges the two option guns into a powerful laser that slows the ship and damages enemies it touches. Bombs act differently depending on the firing style: a screen-clearing explosion that cancels bullets, or a short-range, high-powered beam. Bomb slots start at three and rise by one with each life lost, up to six.

Scoring rests on combos. Destroying enemies or parts of them adds to a hit count and a draining gauge, and keeping the laser on an enemy holds the chain. Thirteen golden bees are hidden in each stage, worth more with each one found as long as the player does not die. Collecting a bomb with every slot full starts MAXIMUM mode, which adds points constantly and raises a multiplier. Clearing six areas on one credit while meeting conditions such as losing no more than two lives or scoring 50 million opens a far harder second loop, ending with the giant mechanical bees Hachi and Hibachi.
trivia: Like DonPachi, its name joins a Japanese sound for gunfire with a term for bees; here it means roughly "angry leader bee".
Meeting the second-loop conditions reveals that the "aliens" were the pilot's own comrades, and the true ending shows that the commander Longhener wanted to wipe out humanity.
A harder Campaign Version was given as first prize in a Cave score contest; only one board is confirmed to exist and Cave said it lost the source code.
The Saturn port added a new stage and boss in its exclusive Saturn mode.
Players who finish without unlocking the second loop get no staff credits.
devStory:
Atlus released DoDonPachi in Japanese arcades on 5 February 1997 on Cave's CAVE 68000 board, the sixth game on Cave's first-generation hardware. It builds on DonPachi's Get Point System, which it improved, and added MAXIMUM mode. A Saturn conversion followed in September 1997 and a PlayStation version by SPS in September 1998 with optional slowdown, both able to display in horizontal or vertical orientation. Cave later made mobile versions and its own sequel, DoDonPachi DaiOuJou, in 2002, after a DoDonPachi II from another developer in 2001.

Readers of Sega Saturn Magazine in Japan gave the Saturn version 8.9766 out of 10, and the game was included in 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die. Time Extension called it "one of the series most beloved entries".

title: Battle Garegga
description: Battle Garegga (1996) is Raizing's vertical arcade shooter whose hidden rank system makes it harder the more the player shoots, powers up and survives, so experts play it by holding back and dying on purpose.
longDescription:
Green Option pick-ups add up to four support pods to the player's craft, arranged in one of five formations, with secret formations reached by dropping a set number of power-ups before collecting the next. Shooting ground enemies drops red Small Bomber tokens that combine into Large Bombers, up to five in stock, and a partial bomb can be used for a weaker or shorter blast. Power-ups and medals drop from small enemies in a fixed order; each medal collected makes the next worth more, from 100 up to 10,000 points, but letting one fall off the screen resets the value.

The game's difficulty, or rank, rises as the player fires, powers up the main weapon and collects items, and falls when a life is lost, and more so when the player has few lives left. Uncontrolled, rank turns the final stages into a frantic bullet storm, so players keep themselves powered down, conserve shots and lose lives deliberately; finishing on one life requires detailed knowledge of the system. Bullets are realistically coloured rather than bright, and debris from explosions hides them further. The story follows Brian and Jason Wayne, engineers whose weapons are turned on their home by the Federation, flying planes they never handed over.
trivia: Programmer Shinobu Yagawa had earlier worked on Recca (1992) and later made Ibara and Pink Sweets.
A Type 2 version replaced most of the hard-to-see bullets with yellow dots.
The 1998 Saturn version is rare; in 2014 it was listed at £100 in the UK.
It was the last game Electronic Arts published in any capacity on a Sega console.
Hardcore Gaming 101 called it "an absolute classic" in 2012.
devStory: Eighting released Raizing's game in arcades on 3 February 1996, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's eighth most successful arcade game in its 15 March 1996 issue. The Saturn port followed on 26 February 1998 and was rated 8/10 by each of Sega Saturn Magazine's three reviewers in Japan. Raizing's spiritual successor, Battle Bakraid, came out in 1999. In December 2016 M2 released Battle Garegga Rev.2016 for the PlayStation 4 under its M2 Shot Triggers label, with Xbox One and English versions the following year. Eurogamer wrote that "for all its routine, slightly drab looks, this is a game of exquisite artistic intention", and Push Square called it "a defining release in the shmup canon".

title: Adventures of Lolo
description: Adventures of Lolo (1989) is HAL Laboratory's NES block-pushing puzzle game, 50 rooms of hearts, eggs and monsters drawn from the Japanese Eggerland series and the first of them released in North America.
longDescription:
Lolo, a round creature, sets out to rescue Princess Lala from King Egger, whose castle has 50 rooms across ten floors of five. In each room Lolo must collect every heart to open a treasure chest, and the gem inside unlocks the exit and makes all the enemies vanish. Some hearts grant items that help trap or defeat the creatures roaming the maze, such as Skull, Medusa and Rocky, each with its own movement and attack pattern.

Lolo can walk, push certain blocks and fire a limited number of shots. A shot enemy is briefly sealed in an egg, which can be pushed elsewhere, used as a bridge across water, or shot again to remove it for a while. On certain screens Lolo gains powers such as smashing rocks or building a bridge, and some enemies are immune to his shots. Being shot or touched by certain enemies costs a life, while others only block his path by standing still or freezing when touched. A room can be restarted at any time at the cost of a life.
trivia: It is the fifth Eggerland game but the first released in North America, assembled from puzzles in two Japanese Eggerland titles.
A Nintendo representative said Nintendo was "trying to stretch the kids' imaginations" with it.
Its success surprised HAL Laboratory.
Lolo and Lala later turned up as Lololo and Lalala in Kirby's Dream Land and other Kirby games.
The developers of Professor Fizzwizzle and LIT both named it as an inspiration.
devStory: HAL Laboratory developed and published Adventures of Lolo for the NES in North America in April 1989, compiling puzzles from Eggerland: Meikyū no Fukkatsu and Eggerland: Sōzō he no Tabidachi. It found a cult following: Game, Set, Watch's Todd Ciolek called it the "leader of the [block-shoving] movement", the Chicago Tribune called it "a challenge of logic, not brute force", and IGN later named it one of Satoru Iwata's successes, "all about fun, appeal and simplicity". Some critics found its looping music grating and its graphics simple. Sequels followed on the Famicom and NES, including the American Adventures of Lolo 2 and 3, and a separate Game Boy Adventures of Lolo appeared in 1994. The original was re-released on the Wii, Wii U and 3DS Virtual Console and on Nintendo Switch Online.

title: Sorcerian
description: Sorcerian (1987) is Nihon Falcom's fifth Dragon Slayer game, a side-scrolling action RPG for the PC-8801 in which a party of four ages, works and dies across fifteen self-contained quests and add-on scenario packs.
longDescription:
The player creates up to ten characters and takes up to four at a time into a party. Each can be a fighter, wizard, elf or dwarf, and can take one of over 60 jobs, from clown to exorcist, each changing strength, intelligence, protection, magic resistance, vitality, dexterity and karma and what equipment can be used. The fifteen scenarios that come with the game can be played in any order. The whole party is controlled at once: the members run in a line, jump in sequence and attack together, trailing the leader like the Options in Gradius, and some puzzles need a particular class, such as a strong character to force open a door.

Time matters. Characters start at 16, a year passes with each new scenario, and more passes in town while they train or enchant items. Humans grow old at 60, dwarves at 100 and elves at 200, and once old a character may die permanently at any time. The aging system was designed with add-on scenario packs in mind, and Falcom, Amorphous and Quasar Soft all released extra scenarios for the PC-8801 version.
trivia: Its soundtrack was composed by Yuzo Koshiro, Mieko Ishikawa, Reiko Takebayashi, Hideya Nagata and Takahito Abe.
Kenji Kawai arranged the music for the PC Engine CD version.
Sierra published an English MS-DOS version in 1990 with an MT-32 arrangement of the score; Atari ST, Amiga, Apple IIGS and Macintosh ports were announced but never released.
Hideki Kamiya named Sorcerian, along with Hydlide 3, as an inspiration for Scalebound.
Games International called it "a well-preserved museum piece" and gave it 6 out of 10.
devStory:
Nihon Falcom released Sorcerian for the NEC PC-8801 in 1987 as the fifth game in its Dragon Slayer line, then ported it to the PC-9801, PC-88VA, Sharp X1 Turbo and MSX2, where it was titled Dragon Slayer V: Sorcerian. Its episodic format, extended through scenario packs, was new. Console versions with different content followed on the Mega Drive by Sega, the PC Engine CD by Victor Musical Industries and later the Dreamcast, and Falcom released Sorcerian Forever (1997) and Sorcerian Original (2000) for Windows.

In Computer Gaming World, Scorpia liked its fifteen separate small quests for their variety and noted that "this is not just hack-and-slash, as there are puzzles to be solved along the way", though she disliked the magic system and warned that some would find the arcade-style action irksome. Games International thought it was more an arcade game than an RPG.

title: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light
description: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light (1990) is Intelligent Systems' Famicom original of the Fire Emblem series, the tactical RPG with permanent death that popularised the genre in Japan.
longDescription:
Prince Marth of Altea leads a growing army across the continent of Archanea in a linear run of maps unlocked by the story. Each character has a fixed class that sets movement and strength: mounted and flying units move further, archers attack from range and armoured knights take hits. Player and enemy units take turns moving on a grid, and a map is won by defeating key enemies such as commanders. Fights cut to a battle screen that plays out in real time. Every action earns experience, and at 100 points a unit levels up and its stats rise at random.

Towns and secret vendors sell items such as healing potions and weapons, which break after a set number of uses, and money comes only from set events and arena bets. Fallen characters die permanently and leave the story, and the game ends if Marth falls. Over the game 52 characters can be recruited. The story begins when Altea's ally Gra betrays it to the Dolhr Empire of the revived Shadow Dragon Medeus and the sorcerer Gharnef; Marth's father is killed and the sword Falchion stolen, and Marth returns from exile on the island of Talys to win it back with the help of the Fire Emblem shield.
trivia: It was first called "Battle Fantasy Fire Emblem"; designer Shouzou Kaga described it as a dōjin project made on a whim.
To fit the game, Intelligent Systems used part of the save memory, and Nintendo helped make a new cartridge chip to display Japanese text.
A planned Water Dragon boss, Neptune, was cut for hardware reasons, while the Earth Dragon Gaia became Medeus.
Its live-action TV commercial took twenty retakes because the actors overheated and the horse was skittish.
It was officially released outside Japan only in 2020, as a limited-time Switch release for the series' 30th anniversary.
devStory:
Shouzou Kaga proposed the game to Nintendo in 1987 after Intelligent Systems finished Famicom Wars, wanting to join that game's strategy with the story and characters of a role-playing game; he cited Kure Software Koubou's First Queen as an influence. Keisuke Terasaki directed, Gunpei Yokoi produced, and Yuka Tsujiyoko, then Intelligent Systems' only composer, wrote the music. Kaga avoided emphasising numbers to keep it accessible and spread attention across the whole cast. Planned story illustrations, such as Marth kneeling beside Jagen in a pool of blood, were cut when the MMC3 chip proved to have too little memory, and Kaga later regretted the plain graphics.

Released on 20 April 1990, it was criticised by Japanese magazines as hard to understand and poor-looking, and sales were flat for two months until word of mouth and a Famitsu column lifted them. It had sold 329,087 copies by 2002. It led to Fire Emblem Gaiden and a series built on its mechanics, and it is credited with popularising the tactical RPG in Japan and indirectly influencing Tactics Ogre, Final Fantasy Tactics and Disgaea.

sources.title: Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon and the Blade of Light

title: Valkyrie Profile
description: Valkyrie Profile (1999) is tri-Ace's Norse-mythology PlayStation RPG in which the valkyrie Lenneth gathers the souls of the dead for Ragnarok, mixing side-scrolling dungeons, a strict time budget and button-per-character combat.
longDescription:
Lenneth flies over Midgard in 3D and uses Spiritual Concentration to find dungeons, towns and the einherjar, souls of dying warriors whose death scenes are shown as she recruits them. Dungeons play like a platform game: she jumps, slides, swings her sword and shoots ice crystals that freeze enemies or make temporary steps for puzzles. Striking a visible enemy first gives her the advantage in the battle that follows. In towns the view turns to 2D and she disguises herself as a human.

Each of the eight chapters is split into periods, 16 on Easy, 24 on Normal and 28 on Hard, which visits and recruiting use up, so time has to be budgeted. At the end of each chapter at least one einherjar must be sent to Valhalla to meet the gods' requirements, and offering artifacts rather than keeping them raises Lenneth's Evaluation; let it fall to zero and the worst ending follows. In battle the party shares one turn, each member mapped to a face button. Chaining attacks fills a Hit Gauge, and at 100% a character can unleash a special Purify Weird Soul attack, while mages are limited by Charge Time instead of magic points. There are three endings, and the true A ending, revealing Lenneth's human past as the girl Platina, is only reachable on Normal or Hard.
trivia: Its cast includes 21 recruitable einherjar, some only on Normal or Hard difficulty.
Lenneth is one of three valkyrie sisters who share one body, with Hrist and Silmeria.
The English release cut the character Badrach's cigarette but kept his post-battle smoking animation.
Because of its strong reviews and rarity, used copies have sold for $300.
Famitsu readers voted it the 27th best video game of all time in 2006.
devStory: tri-Ace developed the game and Enix published it in Japan on 22 December 1999 and in North America on 29 August 2000. The English release added more cinematics and let players adjust the armour of every character rather than only the active party. It sold over 310,000 copies in Japan by the end of 1999 and over 709,000 worldwide by September 2005, 636,000 of them in Japan. Famitsu gave it 35 out of 40 and it scored 81 on Metacritic; IGN praised its deep if complicated systems and its writing, while Next Generation found it ambitious but more management-heavy than other RPGs. Tose ported it to the PSP as Valkyrie Profile: Lenneth in 2006, and two prequels followed, Valkyrie Profile 2: Silmeria and Covenant of the Plume.

title: Destruction Derby
description: Destruction Derby (1995) is Reflections Interactive's demolition-derby racer for Psygnosis, an early PlayStation showpiece that put 20 cars on screen and modelled their damage in real time.
longDescription:
Based on the sport of demolition derby, the game has the player racing and wrecking cars for points. Collisions change how a car handles, limiting its steering and top speed, and head-on hits risk damaging the radiator, which makes the car overheat and stop. In Destruction Derby mode the player scores by wrecking rivals in a trackless arena called The Bowl. Stock Car Racing is about finishing first with no points for destruction, Wreckin' Racing rewards both, and Time Trial is a solo time attack. The PlayStation version supports two players over a system link, and the MS-DOS version has online multiplayer.

Damage is calculated in real time from the speed and angle of each impact, and the engine could show up to twenty cars on screen at once, which only Daytona USA had managed among console racers at the time. To keep the pack dense enough for big pile-ups, the team made the tracks small.
trivia: It was reported under the working titles Demolition Derby and Demolish 'em Derby.
Director Martin Edmondson said that without simulated physics the game would be "completely unplayable", like "pool when the collisions are all off".
Every car uses the same wire-frame model, told apart only by its textures.
The Saturn version, ported by Perfect Entertainment without transparency effects, was released only in Europe and Japan in August 1996.
It sold more than a million copies by August 1996.
devStory:
The British studio Reflections began the game for the PlayStation in late 1994. Because its publisher Psygnosis belonged to Sony, Reflections received development kits long before the console's release. Producer Tony Parks said the physics were simplified for performance and to suit the PlayStation's digital controller, balancing "realism and playability", and distant objects were drawn with less detail. It debuted at E3 in May 1995, where Edge and Next Generation suggested it could "trounce" Ridge Racer, and was released on 20 October 1995 for PlayStation and then MS-DOS.

GamePro called it "the most raucous racing experience of the fall" while regretting its limited options, and PC Gamer praised it as "thinking man's destruction". The Saturn port was criticised for its inferior graphics. Destruction Derby 2 followed in 1996, and in 2023 IGN named the original one of the PlayStation's "forgotten launch gems".

title: Micro Machines
description: Micro Machines (1991) is Codemasters' unlicensed NES racer of Galoob's toy cars, raced top-down across breakfast tables, desks and pool tables, whose single-screen two-player duels made it a British classic.
longDescription:
Seen from above, toy powerboats, helicopters, Formula One cars and tanks that can shoot their rivals race around household settings: breakfast tables with cereal boxes in the way, desks with pencil sharpeners, pool tables and treehouses. Each course follows a set path, and a racer who strays from it for too long is put back on the track.

In the Micro Machines Challenge the player races three computer opponents and must finish first or second to go on, with three chances before the game ends; every three races a time trial offers an extra chance. Head-to-head pits two vehicles against each other on a single shared screen instead of a split screen. Getting a full screen ahead of the other player, so that the trailing car drops out of view, turns one of eight lights to the leader's colour. The race ends when all eight lights are one colour, or after three laps, when the player with most lights wins; ties go to sudden death. Some characters carry a handicap in two-player games to even things out.
trivia: Its two-player system came from Andrew Graham's prototype California Buggy Boys, based on the 1983 Adventure International game Rally Speedway.
The team worked out the NES hardware by reverse engineering, having no official Nintendo documents.
A crashing bug when reversing in the first race was found too late, so cartridges carried a device like a miniature Game Genie to correct the one wrong bit.
The Game Gear version let two people play on one console, one using the buttons and the other the D-pad.
It is the highest-ranked unlicensed game on IGN's Top 100 NES Games, at 31.
devStory:
At the 1990 Consumer Electronics Show, Codemasters founders David and Richard Darling were struck by the NES's popularity in America and wanted to make games for it without a Nintendo licence. Galoob wanted a game of its Micro Machines toys, so Graham's buggy-racing prototype became the base and Galoob sent Codemasters a selection of toys. Artist Paul Perrot converted the graphics, the team kept the tracks short because they were more fun, and Graham said the multiplayer was the best part of the game and made single-player "boring" by comparison. The game was finished in September 1990.

Camerica released it in 1991, but Nintendo, which had sued Galoob over the Game Genie, wanted it stopped, and the legal dispute hurt NES sales. Ports followed for the Mega Drive in 1993, after Sega's own licensing objections delayed it, and for the Game Gear, Amiga, Master System, SNES, CD-i, PC and Game Boy. Critics praised its originality and two-player mode, Next Generation ranked it 18th on its 1996 list of the greatest games, and The Guardian named it one of the 30 best British video games in 2014. Micro Machines 2: Turbo Tournament followed in 1994.

title: Virtua Tennis
description: Virtua Tennis (1999), Power Smash in Japan, is Sega AM3's NAOMI arcade tennis game, whose 2000 Dreamcast version added the World Circuit career mode and became one of the console's defining games.
longDescription:
In the arcade mode the player has to win five matches on different surfaces and venues to take a tournament, and a strong run brings a challenge from a boss called Master. Exhibition matches can be singles or doubles for up to four human players, lasting from one game to one set, with a choice of court and opponent skill. The licensed players include Jim Courier, Tim Henman, Tommy Haas, Carlos Moyá, Yevgeny Kafelnikov, Cédric Pioline, Thomas Johansson and Mark Philippoussis.

The home versions add World Circuit, in which the player starts ranked 300th and climbs by winning matches and completing training exercises that unlock further events. The exercises were designed to be fun rather than realistic, each with three levels of difficulty, and beating the hardest with time or points to spare unlocks outfits for use in every mode.
trivia: Producer Mie Kumagai's first proposal, a basketball game, was rejected before her tennis pitch was accepted.
The team first built a paddle controller that switched between forehand and backhand when twisted, but dropped it as too difficult to use.
Sega considered stars such as Andre Agassi for the Dreamcast version but found the licence fees could exceed the development budget.
Sega executives feared "Power Smash" would not translate well abroad, so the West got the Virtua label.
NBA player Chris Paul told IGN in 2005 that the game he "really loved" on the Dreamcast was Virtua Tennis.
devStory:
Kumagai wanted a game with broad appeal amid the one-on-one fighting games filling Japanese arcades, hoping to repeat the success of Sega AM2's Virtua Striker, and planned one that could be both casual and competitive. Even after the tennis idea was approved, many inside Sega were sceptical. Her team visited a tennis school for research and, on advice from Virtua Striker director Satoshi Mifune, simplified the controls to a joystick and buttons; location tests went well. The Dreamcast conversion took seven months, doubled the roster to sixteen players and used Japanese tennis players as references for the animation.

Game Machine listed the arcade version as Japan's third most successful arcade game of 1999. The Dreamcast version, released in Europe on 8 September 2000, topped the UK all-formats chart, sold 368,035 copies in North America by 2003 and drew universal acclaim, with a nomination for Game of the Year at the Interactive Achievement Awards. It is credited with popularising tennis games, and Microsoft's Top Spin team cited it as an inspiration.

title: FIFA International Soccer
description: FIFA International Soccer (1993), also known as FIFA 94, is EA Canada's first FIFA game, an isometric Mega Drive football game with national teams and made-up players that started the best-selling series.
longDescription:
Where rivals such as Sensible Soccer and Kick Off looked down on the pitch from above, FIFA uses an isometric view. The player controls one of eleven footballers at a time and can switch between them, and up to four people can play together, on the same side or opposite sides, with the computer running everyone else. There are four modes: single Exhibition matches; a Tournament in the style of the World Cup, with three group games and up to four knockout rounds; Playoffs, which skips the groups; and an eight-team League played as a double round robin.

There are 48 national teams plus an EA All Stars side, each with 20 fictional players who look alike apart from darker skin for some teams; several are named after members of the development team, such as Tim Ansell of England. The PC CD-ROM version has commentary from Tony Gubba. A well-known oversight makes goals easy: standing a player in front of the opposing goalkeeper as he is about to clear the ball makes the computer keeper kick it straight to him.
trivia: EA's five-year deal with FIFA came with "minuscule" royalties because it covered no team names, logos, player names, likenesses or stadiums.
EA considered releasing it as Team USA Soccer in North America before deciding on one worldwide title.
It was rushed for Christmas 1993 to beat U.S. Gold's official World Cup game, due in spring 1994.
Footballers Les Ferdinand, Vinnie Jones and John Barnes played it against each other on the TV show GamesMaster in 1993.
Next Generation said the 3DO version "put 3DO on the map", and it was later a pack-in game for the Goldstar 3DO.
devStory:
After moving into sports with John Madden Football in 1988, EA's European arm concluded that a football game would sell best in Europe. A team of ten at EA's Canadian studios led by Bruce McMillan started it for the Mega Drive under the working title EA Soccer, with a budget of around $50,000 to $100,000, and added realism and an isometric view to stand apart from the top-down market leaders. Development finished in November 1993.

EA expected about 300,000 sales in Europe, but the Mega Drive version sold more than 500,000 and became the year's best-selling game in Europe despite its December release, including 400,000 copies in the UK in the last two weeks of December. Mean Machines Sega called it the "greatest soccer game yet seen", praising its animation and crowd sounds, while critics noted that the isometric view made it slower and the controls sometimes slow to respond. The 3DO version added multiple camera views and more detailed graphics. FIFA Soccer 95 followed in 1994, and the series had passed 100 million sales by 2010.

title: John Madden Football
description: John Madden Football (1988) is Electronic Arts' Apple II American football game, three years in the making as "Trip's Folly" because Madden insisted on eleven players a side, and the start of the Madden NFL series.
longDescription:
The game lets the player customise many aspects of a match, including conditions, the length of quarters, player fatigue, injuries and penalties. A quick, arcade-like mode sits alongside a deeper standard game with detailed player statistics and plays the player can design. There is no season play, only single games, and with no NFL or NFLPA licence it has no real teams, player names or stadiums, although some teams are based on real ones; players can also build a team from scratch.

It was ported to MS-DOS and the Commodore 64 in 1989. The 1990 Sega Genesis game of the same name grew into the yearly Madden NFL series, so the original is sometimes called Madden '88 or Madden '89 to tell it apart.
trivia: Joe Montana and Joe Kapp were approached first in 1982; Montana was working on a rival Atari football game and Kapp was beyond EA's budget.
EA first proposed teams of six or seven players, but Madden refused to endorse anything short of eleven a side.
Bethesda Softworks worked on parts of the game, and a legal issue with it added to the delays.
Madden was interested in the game as a teaching tool.
Its cover, by Chuck Styles, was reused for the All-Madden Edition of Madden NFL 23.
devStory: EA founder Trip Hawkins had long wanted a football game inspired by Strat-O-Matic's sports simulations. After Montana and Kapp turned him down, he approached John Madden two years later and reached an agreement. Fitting eleven players on each team was difficult with the technology of the time, and together with the Bethesda dispute this stretched development to three years. Inside EA the project became known as "Trip's Folly", and both staff and Madden himself assumed it would be cancelled. It came out in 1988 after EA's success with Earl Weaver Baseball, and Computer Gaming World reviewed it favourably for offering both its quick arcade mode and its detailed standard game.

title: Mario Golf
description: Mario Golf (1999) is Camelot's Nintendo 64 golf game, a pick-up-and-play take on the sport with Mario characters, made as a warm-up for the hardware and good enough that Nintendo cancelled its own golf game.
longDescription:
Players choose from Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Yoshi, Wario, Donkey Kong, Baby Mario, Metal Mario and five original characters, Plum, Charlie, Sonny, Harry and Maple, and play on courses themed after the Nintendo world. It strips away golf's complicated real-life aspects, but its engine still weighs many variables on each shot: the strength and direction of the wind, shown by a Boo, rain, each character's attributes, spin and the slope of the ground. Alongside stroke play there are speed golf, ring shots, mini golf and skins matches, and every character has voice samples for commenting on opponents' shots.
