A separate Game Boy Color version, also by Camelot, adds a story mode with role-playing elements. With the Transfer Pak the two versions can exchange characters and data, and a Game Boy Color character earns experience with each round.
trivia: Although the first game called Mario Golf, it is the second in the series after NES Open Tournament Golf.
Nintendo had recruited Camelot to make a role-playing game, but Camelot wanted to start with something simpler.
Its working title at Camelot was Mario Golf 64.
Famitsu gave both the Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions 30 out of 40.
It was re-released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console and on Nintendo Switch Online.
devStory: Nintendo had been making its own Nintendo 64 golf game, tentatively called Golf, when it recruited Camelot Software Planning for a role-playing game. Camelot preferred to make a simpler game first to get used to the hardware, and Nintendo was so impressed by its prototype that it cancelled the other golf game and assigned Camelot to Mario Golf 64. The game was announced in the February 1999 issue of The 64Dream. The Nintendo 64 version received universal acclaim on Metacritic, and the Game Boy Color version scored slightly higher, IGN calling it "an absolutely brilliant rendition of golf". Mario Golf: Toadstool Tour followed on the GameCube in 2003.

title: Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers
description: Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers (1993) is Jane Jensen's Sierra adventure in which a struggling New Orleans novelist researching the "Voodoo Murders" discovers his family's past as supernatural hunters, voiced on CD by Tim Curry, Leah Remini and Mark Hamill.
longDescription:
The story runs over a linear sequence of chapters, one day each, with a set of required actions to move on, but within a chapter play is largely non-linear and optional actions add background to the story. In Sierra fashion a running score tracks actions completed, and failing to escape a dangerous situation ends the game. Instead of a context-sensitive cursor, the player picks verbs from an icon bar, Walk, Look, Ask, Talk, Pick Up, Open/Close, Operate and Move, and inventory items can be selected as icons to use on the world. Talk gives brief exchanges, while Ask lets the player question main characters on general and specific topics, and a Recorder replays past conversations. An overhead map moves between locations, and a hint system points to where required actions remain.

Gabriel Knight, a horror novelist who runs a bookshop in New Orleans, is drawn by nightmares to investigate a string of killings dismissed by his childhood friend Detective Frank Mosely. With his assistant Grace Nakimura he learns of voodoo and a German great-uncle, Wolfgang Ritter, and finds the murders match those committed long before by Tetelo, a voodoo practitioner executed by his ancestor Gunter Ritter. The trail leads to Schloss Ritter in Germany, where he learns his family were Schattenjägers, "shadow hunters", and on to Benin before a final confrontation beneath the French Quarter.
trivia: Jensen said the film Angel Heart inspired its plot and atmosphere.
Virginia Capers, the narrator, won Computer Gaming World's Best Female Voice-Over Acting award; the editors said her performance alone made the CD version worth buying.
It shared Computer Gaming World's 1994 Adventure Game of the Year award with Day of the Tentacle.
Computer Gaming World listed a zombie ripping out the player's heart as seventh of "the 15 best ways to die in computer gaming".
The floppy version came on eleven disks, showing the CD version's video sequences as still images.
devStory:
Jane Jensen, who had worked on King's Quest VI, created, wrote and directed the game, and her husband Robert Holmes produced it and composed the music. She recalled that Ken Williams gave designers full freedom: "Nobody told you what to do with it. If it didn't sell, then you wouldn't do another game for him." Midway through, Sierra upgraded its engine to SCI32, and Jensen wrote that the team "fought bugs and snafus for six months" but still hit its Christmas date.

Sierra released it on CD-ROM and floppy disk on 17 December 1993, with a comic-book prequel in the box. Computer Gaming World's Johnny L. Wilson wrote that its opening "was the first time I've actually experienced fear when viewing a computer game", and critics praised its story, voice cast and graphics. It was not a big commercial hit: PC Gamer said Jensen's hope for King's Quest-sized success fell short, and it and its sequel had sold 300,000 copies together by December 1998. The Beast Within followed in 1995, Jensen novelised the game in 1997, and her studio Pinkerton Road remade it for its 20th anniversary in 2014.

sources.title: Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers

title: MechWarrior 2: 31st Century Combat
description: MechWarrior 2: 31st Century Combat (1995) is Activision's BattleTech mech simulator, in which the player fights the Refusal War of 3057 for Clan Wolf or Clan Jade Falcon, managing heat, armour and loadouts across 32 missions.
longDescription:
The player joins Clan Wolf or Clan Jade Falcon and fights on planets named in the BattleTech canon, on missions such as search and destroy, reconnaissance and base strikes, gaining squad commands in later ones. Between missions a mech lab lets the player change the weapons, armour, engine and heat sinks of any drivable mech. Control modes range from basic point-and-shoot to an advanced mode that steers the legs and torso separately. The on-board computer reports nearby forces, damage and ammunition, and heat has to be watched constantly: firing weapons repeatedly raises the temperature, which can set off ammunition, cost limbs and actuators or detonate the fusion engine. The computer tries an emergency shutdown when heat climbs too far, but the player can override it. A Windows 95 version added NetMech for battles over a network.

It is 3057, after the Clans' invasion of the Inner Sphere was halted by defeat at Tukayyid. Crusader factions accuse the Wolves' Ulric Kerensky, a Warden, of losing on purpose, and he answers by challenging them to settle it in combat. The Jade Falcons fight to resume the invasion, while the Wolves aim to weaken the Falcons for good.
trivia: It was planned for October 1994 but slipped after almost the entire development team turned over.
Its rendered introduction was produced by Digital Domain.
Its music, by Gregory Alper and Jeehun Hwang, was stored as standard CD audio and could be played on an ordinary CD player.
In the third quarter of 1995 Activision reported waits of up to an hour for its hint line, mostly because of MechWarrior 2 callers.
Gregory Fulton, later lead designer of Heroes of Might and Magic III, started his career as a tester on the game.
devStory:
Activision developed the game for MS-DOS and later ported it to Windows and the Mac, with enhanced versions for 3D accelerator cards. Quantum Factory built separate Saturn and PlayStation versions from scratch as MechWarrior 2: Arcade Combat Edition, with power-ups, more enemies, shortened missions and 16 new ones to make it faster and more action-led; a Panasonic M2 version was dropped when that console was cancelled. The Ghost Bear's Legacy expansion followed in November 1995 and the stand-alone Mercenaries in 1996.

It sold more than 500,000 copies within three months and was the 12th best-selling computer game in the US in 1996. Next Generation called it "the best 'mech simulator currently available", PC Gamer US named it the best action game of 1995, and it won the Origins Award for best science fiction computer game of the year. In 1996 Computer Gaming World ranked it the 27th best game of all time, and the console versions were also praised for how well they were adapted.

title: RollerCoaster Tycoon
description: RollerCoaster Tycoon (1999) is Chris Sawyer's theme park management game, written almost entirely in x86 assembly language, which became the best-selling PC game of 1999 and sold over four million copies by 2002.
longDescription:
The player completes a series of preset scenarios by building and running amusement parks. Dozens of roller coaster types are available, along with log flumes, carousels, bumper cars, haunted houses, go-karts, Ferris wheels and swinging ships. Handymen sweep paths, empty bins, water flowers and mow lawns, mechanics inspect and repair rides, security guards stop vandalism, and entertainers keep guests amused. Terrain can be raised, lowered and flooded to make the park more attractive and fit rides into the landscape, and food stalls, toilets and information kiosks have to be placed to meet visitors' needs. Players can also design their own coasters and rides piece by piece on a tile grid, setting direction, height and steepness and adding zero-g rolls, corkscrews, vertical loops and on-ride photos.

The game has 21 scenarios, each unlocking the next, and finishing them all opens Mega Park, a near-sandbox with nothing but a $50,000 loan and the objective "Have Fun!". Some parks are based on real ones: Katie's Dreamland is modelled on Lightwater Valley, complete with its coaster The Ultimate. The two expansions added 30 scenarios each.
trivia: Sawyer said he had hated roller coasters until he visited theme parks with money from Transport Tycoon; he has since ridden at least 700.
It was called White Knuckle for most of its development.
Sawyer wrote 99% of the code in x86 assembly language and the rest in C, in a small village near Dunblane.
Sawyer earned around $30 million in royalties.
Sawyer said "everyone is a bit stunned by the sales success", himself included.
devStory:
After Transport Tycoon in 1994, Sawyer chose a roller-coaster simulation as his next game, partly as an excuse to keep visiting theme parks for "research". He spent two years on it, with Simon Foster making the graphics in 3D modelling and paint programs and Allister Brimble writing the music; family and friends playtested it before Hasbro took over wider bug-testing. Hasbro Interactive released it under the MicroProse label in North America on 22 March 1999.

It was announced as the best-selling PC game of 1999, with 719,535 US sales that year, and was second only to The Sims in 2000 and 2001; GameSpot noted it had appeared in the weekly top ten almost continuously for two years. Critics praised its detail and coaster design, Computer Games Strategy Plus named it its 1999 strategy game of the year, and Entertainment Weekly called it "the thrill ride of the summer". The expansions Added Attractions (Corkscrew Follies in North America) and Loopy Landscapes followed in 1999 and 2000, Frontier ported it to the Xbox in 2003, and a series of sequels began with RollerCoaster Tycoon 2.

title: Outcast
description: Outcast (1999) is Belgian studio Appeal's open-world action-adventure on the alien world of Adelpha, drawn by a software "voxel" landscape engine and scored by an orchestra, two years before Grand Theft Auto III.
longDescription:
Former Navy SEAL Cutter Slade explores Adelpha in third or first person, using only two mouse buttons: one aims his weapon and the other is context-sensitive, starting a conversation in front of a character or making him jump when running. He can climb onto almost any ledge he can reach. After the tutorial, travel gates called daokas let him go to any region, teleport beacons speed movement within one, and a twon-ha, a beast of burden, can be bought or earned to ride. Much of the game is talking to the Talan natives, who respond according to a reputation system: help them and they become eager allies, harm them and they turn him away.

Weapons fire slow projectiles, so fights mean dodging and leading shots, though Cutter can also sneak past soldiers, who sound horns to alert each other and try to flank him. Completing tasks for each region's leader shuts down the food, mining and other production that supplies the soldiers, weakening them. Saving uses an in-world object, the Gaamsaav, which glows and makes a noise when squeezed that can draw enemies. The story sends Cutter to repair a damaged probe whose energy backlash has opened a black hole threatening Earth, and the natives hail him as their messiah, the Ulukai.
trivia: Its landscape is drawn by a ray-casting heightmap engine, often called a "voxel" engine, combined with polygons for objects, all in software without a 3D card.
Running at full speed at its maximum 512 × 384 resolution needed a top Pentium III and 128 MB of RAM.
Lennie Moore's score was performed by the Moscow Symphony Orchestra and choir and could be played by putting disc 2 in a CD player.
Its AI ran on a proprietary engine called GAIA, Game Artificial Intelligence with Agents.
A Dreamcast port was shelved when the Windows version failed commercially.
devStory:
Appeal combined its landscape engine with polygon, water and shadow engines for effects such as depth of field, bump mapping, translucent rippling water, bloom and lens flares, at the cost of very high CPU demands. Infogrames released it for Windows in 1999. It sold only 12,571 copies in the US by the end of the year, but did better in Germany, where it passed 50,000 by December, and reached 400,000 worldwide by 2002.

GameSpot and Computer Gaming World named it the best adventure game of 1999, and Next Generation urged players "tired of FPS madness" with "some serious horsepower" to try it. A sequel, Outcast II: The Lost Paradise, was abandoned when Appeal went bankrupt. Its founders reacquired the rights in 2013, released the remastered Outcast 1.1 in 2014, and followed it with the remake Second Contact in 2017 and Outcast: A New Beginning in 2024. In 2009 GamesRadar called it "revolutionary" for offering open-world 3D exploration two years before Grand Theft Auto III.

title: NetHack
description: NetHack (1987) is the open-source roguelike built over the internet by the DevTeam from the earlier Hack, a dungeon of permadeath, unidentified potions and absurd item interactions that is still being developed.
longDescription:
Players pick a race, role, sex and alignment, from traditional knights, wizards and priests to archaeologists, tourists and cavemen, and descend through the Mazes of Menace, about fifty levels mostly generated when first entered and then kept for the rest of the game. The goal is to retrieve the Amulet of Yendor from the bottom and offer it to the character's god, which grants immortality, "ascension". Along the way come sub-quests, including one for the character's role, the Wizard of Yendor, who keeps returning to harass the player, and finally the Riders, Death, Famine and Pestilence. A source-code comment says the player is the fourth horseman, War. Most characters start with a pet kitten or little dog; knights get a pony.

As in Rogue, items are unidentified: a potion may be only "pink", every scroll of one kind shares a nonsense label, and the descriptions are reshuffled each game. Items can be blessed, uncursed or cursed, and curses can twist effects, so a cursed potion of gain level lifts the player through the ceiling to the level above. Death is permanent, but the game sometimes saves the level where a character died as a "bones file" that another player may later stumble into. Experienced players add voluntary "conducts", such as playing vegetarian or killing nothing.
trivia: Hack, its ancestor, was written by high-school students who were refused Rogue's source code and wrote their own dungeon generator.
The DevTeam named its fork NetHack because the collaboration was done over the internet.
The tourist class came from Terry Pratchett's Discworld, and version 3.6.0 included a tribute to him.
Fans' saying "The DevTeam Thinks of Everything" (TDTTOE) reflects how many odd interactions were anticipated in the code.
Facebook's AI researchers posed NetHack as a grand challenge in 2021; no agent in the NeurIPS competition managed to ascend.
devStory:
Hack was created by Jay Fenlason, Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome and Jonathan Payne at Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School after they played Rogue at Berkeley. Fenlason gave the code to a USENIX conference, it spread on Usenet, and many forks followed. Mike Stephenson took over as maintainer and, with philosophy professor Izchak Miller and Janet Walz, started a new fork as the DevTeam, expanding the bestiary and items and drawing on sources beyond high fantasy. They released NetHack on 28 July 1987 and kept the main source restricted to a few members so that their release would remain the legitimate one, while Stephenson's 1989 NetHack General Public License allowed anyone to port or fork it.

Version 3.0 arrived in July 1989, and the team became known for its secrecy between releases. After 3.4.3 in December 2003 there was no major update until 3.6.0 in December 2015. Players gather on servers such as nethack.alt.org and in annual tournaments, and it has influenced games including ADOM, Spelunky, Diablo and Mystery Dungeon. Time included it in its 2012 list of the 100 greatest video games, and it was part of the Museum of Modern Art's "Never Alone" exhibition.

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
description: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (1984) is Infocom's text adventure written by Douglas Adams with Steve Meretzky, famous for its devious Babel Fish puzzle and one of the best-selling games of its time.
longDescription:
As Arthur Dent, the player types commands such as "look", "take screwdriver" or "put robe on hook" to solve puzzles and collect items. Most commands advance a turn counter, and some puzzles must be solved within a set number of turns or the game ends. Once Arthur has the Guide itself, he can look up a wide range of topics, some of which help with the puzzles.

The game loosely follows the first book. Arthur's house is about to be demolished for a bypass, and his friend Ford Prefect, secretly an alien, gets them aboard a Vogon ship just before the Earth is destroyed for a hyperspace bypass. After Vogon poetry and the airlock, they are rescued by the Heart of Gold, stolen by Galactic President Zaphod Beeblebrox, with Trillian aboard. While the others retire to the sauna, Arthur is left to get the ship to Magrathea, using the Infinite Improbability Drive to slip into the pasts of Ford, Zaphod and Trillian and bring back items that eventually let the Nutrimatic make real tea. The game ends as the crew is about to set foot on Magrathea.
trivia: Getting a Babel Fish out of a dispenser takes a chain of obscure actions within a turn limit; Infocom sold T-shirts reading "I got the Babel Fish!".
Failing the Babel Fish puzzle does not kill the player but makes the game unwinnable, since a later code needs Vogon translated.
Its feelies included a "Don't Panic!" badge, pocket fluff, Peril Sensitive Sunglasses, an empty bag of microscopic space fleet, and "no tea".
Computer Gaming World reported rumours that important people in the industry could not get out of the first room.
The BBC's 2004 20th Anniversary Edition, illustrated by Rod Lord, won an Interactive BAFTA.
devStory:
Series creator Douglas Adams designed the game with Infocom's Steve Meretzky, and it was released in 1984 for the Apple II, Mac, Commodore 64, CP/M, MS-DOS, Amiga, Atari 8-bit computers and Atari ST, Infocom's fourteenth game. Adams said the difficulty of the Babel Fish puzzle was intentional: "Just as the player gets comfortable in the narrow neck, the bottom drops out!" Jerry Pournelle warned that "even if you've memorized the book, these puzzles are hard".

It sold 59,000 copies in 1984, second only to Zork I among Infocom games, and 166,000 in 1985, the company's best seller that year; it passed 250,000 by November 1989 and ultimately sold 400,000. Compute! suggested it "may well be Infocom's best effort to date", and Computer Gaming World ranked it 42nd among the best games of all time in 1996. A sequel, Milliways: The Restaurant at the End of the Universe, was in trouble from its start in 1985 and was cancelled in 1989.

sources.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (video game)

title: Starflight
description: Starflight (1986) is Binary Systems' open-ended space exploration RPG for Electronic Arts, 270 star systems and 800 procedurally generated planets in which a captain from Arth slowly uncovers why stars are flaring.
longDescription:
The game begins at Starport, orbiting the planet Arth, where the player trades minerals, artifacts and Endurium, the crystal that fuels the ship, and hires a crew from five species for six posts: captain, navigator, science officer, engineer, communications officer and doctor. Skills improve through paid training, and a well-trained science officer, for instance, learns more about planets and spots aliens from further away. The ship starts with engines and a little fuel and is upgraded with weapons, armour and shields.

There is no set path: the player can mine, fight, trade or talk to aliens freely. Every one of the 800 planets in 270 systems can be scanned and landed on, though gravity above 8 g destroys the ship; on the surface a Terrain Vehicle drives across a Mercator map searching for minerals, lifeforms and ruins. The richest income comes from logging planets fit for colonisation. Continuum fluxes allow instant, fuel-free jumps. Aliens may be cautious, friendly or hostile, each race with its own speech, and the player's stance, such as arming weapons or choosing a tone of greeting, changes how they react. Gradually the story emerges of an Old Empire, a lost Earth and a Crystal Planet making stars flare and destroy all life.
trivia: It was written mostly in Forth, with some routines in x86 assembly, because the whole game had to fit in 128 KB of RAM.
A "fractal generator" that took six man-years let the team raise the number of planets from 50 to 800.
The alien names were made by combining random syllables, and the communication code was rewritten four times.
Archon designer Paul Reiche III, the lead designer's office-mate, suggested a "story network" to structure the plot, and later drew on Starflight for Star Control.
Mass Effect director Casey Hudson called Starflight "a key inspiration for the ME series".
devStory:
Rod McConnell and EA's Joe Ybarra conceived the project in 1983, and McConnell assembled Binary Systems: lead designer Greg Johnson, programmer Alec Kercso, Tim C. Lee on graphics and programming and Bob Gonsalves on sound, all first-time game designers. Dave Boulton, who had the idea of using fractals to generate a universe, quit early, calling it too ambitious. It took three years and "fifteen man-years", was nearly cancelled more than once and came out about a year late. Johnson said that "just by happenstance I ended up creating a very open ended system", and it is one of the earliest sandbox games and one of the first to generate its planets procedurally.

EA released it for PC on 15 August 1986, with later versions for the Amiga, Commodore 64, Atari ST, Mac and a revamped Genesis edition in 1991. It sold over 100,000 copies by December 1987 and eventually more than a million. Computer Gaming World named it Adventure Game of the Year for 1987, and Orson Scott Card called it "the standard against which all other space-exploration games must be measured". Starflight 2: Trade Routes of the Cloud Nebula followed in 1989.

title: Little Computer People
description: Little Computer People (1985) is Activision's social simulation in which a unique little man moves into a three-storey house inside the computer, a game with no way to win that is often called a forerunner of The Sims.
longDescription:
There is one setting, a cross-section of a three-storey house, and no win condition. Soon after starting, an animated character moves in and goes about his day, cooking, watching television and reading the newspaper. The player can type simple commands, play poker with him or give him presents, and now and then he makes contact himself, inviting the player to a game or writing a letter about his feelings and needs. Each copy generates its own character, named from a list of 256, with personality and mood settings that can lead him to ignore the player's commands, so no two copies play the same. His day runs on a six-hour real-time cycle. The manual keeps up the pretence that the little people are real and live inside the computer, with the player as their caretaker.

The Commodore 64 cassette version is cut down: the character is created afresh every time it loads, with no moving-in sequence and no memory, he does not communicate meaningfully, and the card games are missing.
trivia: Rich Gold conceived it as a "Pet Person" program like the Pet Rock toys of the 1970s.
David Crane, of Pitfall! and Ghostbusters, called it "one of the hardest programming challenges of my career".
The card games were nearly cut for time; Steve Cartwright added them near the end of development.
Activision's marketing played up a newspaper story about the discovery of people living inside computers.
The Famicom Disk System version, Apple Town Story, starred a girl and had a soundtrack by Nobuo Uematsu.
devStory:
Gold funded early work and hired James Wickstead Design Associates, which spent about a year refining the idea of a pet person living in a house. At that stage it was closer to a screensaver. Activision president Jim Levy showed it to David Crane, who took it on as a starting point for something interactive, arguing with Gold, who felt interactivity went against the Pet Rock concept. Crane said part of him wanted to make the character "the smartest thing in computing", but time made that impractical. Counting the earlier work, it took about two years when most games took four or five months.

Released in 1985 for the Commodore 64 and then the Apple II, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and Amiga, it won a Zzap!64 Gold Medal and best original game at the 1986 Golden Joystick Awards, and Jerry Pournelle wrote that it "sure has consumed all the game time we have around here". Retro Gamer said it sold well enough, but its development costs ruled out sequels. Will Wright has said he played it and received feedback on The Sims from Gold, while Crane said only that he took "the first baby steps toward the simulation genre".

title: EverQuest
description: EverQuest (1999) is Sony's 3D fantasy MMORPG set in Norrath, the first commercially successful online role-playing game with a 3D engine and still receiving expansions more than 25 years later.
longDescription:
Drawing heavily on text MUDs, especially DikuMUD, and through them on Dungeons & Dragons, EverQuest has players create a character from twelve races, from humans and three kinds of elf to dwarves, gnomes, ogres and trolls, then choose a class, a patron deity and a starting city. At launch there were fourteen classes in four broad groups: melee fighters such as the Warrior, Monk and Rogue; priests such as the Cleric, Druid and Shaman; casters such as the Wizard, Magician, Necromancer and Enchanter; and hybrids including the Paladin, Shadowknight, Bard and Ranger. Some armour and weapons can be used only by followers of a particular god, and a character's deity affects where they will be attacked on sight.

Players explore the medieval fantasy world of Norrath, eventually more than five hundred zones, fighting for treasure and experience, taking quests from non-player characters and learning trade skills. The design pushes co-operation, with each player filling a role in a group, and players can join guilds and role-play. Fighting other players is limited to a dedicated PvP server, arenas and agreed duels. Each server holds its own world and community, with peaks of more than 3,000 players per server.
trivia: Producer Brad McQuaid became a popular figure with fans through his in-game avatar, Aradune.
Some players jokingly nicknamed it "EverCrack".
GameSpot, naming it Game of the Year, said its editors spent weeks exploring Norrath instead of doing their jobs.
It had 10,000 subscribers 24 hours after launch.
In 2007 Sony Online Entertainment won a Technology & Engineering Emmy for it.
devStory:
Sony Interactive Studios America executive John Smedley secured funding in 1996 for a 3D game like the text MUDs, following the launch of Meridian 59, and hired programmers Brad McQuaid and Steve Clover; Bill Trost wrote Norrath's history and characters. The four credited creators said their shared play of MUDs such as Sojourn and TorilMUD inspired it. It had a budget of $15 million. When Sony's studio refocused on PlayStation games as 989 Studios, EverQuest was spun off into a new division, Verant Interactive.

Sony launched it on 16 March 1999 with modest expectations, and by the end of the year it had passed Ultima Online in subscriptions. Critics called it "the best game in its class", and GamePro wrote that the developers had "created the first true online killer app", while noting its slow early levels and poor documentation. It scored 85 on Metacritic and won the Interactive Achievement Award for online game of the year. Its surprising profits led Sony to reorganise Verant as Sony Online Entertainment in 2000. Subscriptions passed 500,000 in 2003, and EverQuest II followed in 2004.

title: Meridian 59
description: Meridian 59 (1996) is Archetype Interactive's online fantasy RPG for 3DO, the first 3D graphical MMORPG and one of the first games sold on a flat monthly subscription, launched about a year before Ultima Online.
longDescription:
There are no character levels or classes. Each skill and attribute develops on its own: hit points grow by killing monsters that challenge the player, and mana comes from finding mana nodes around the world. Characters learn skills from seven schools, weaponcraft and six schools of magic tied to the world's gods, from Shal'ille's healing and Qor's curses to Faren's elemental attacks, Riija's illusions and Jala's songs, and they can mix schools freely, limited only by intelligence.

The game is set in the 59th provincial colony of an ancient empire, cut off centuries ago when something went wrong with the magical nexus linking its worlds, and its six towns include the rebellious mining town of Jasper and the royal city of Barloque. Players can side with one of three political factions fighting for territory and tokens of power, join player-made guilds that vote on their leaders, display sigils on shields and win or lose guild halls, and read in-game bulletin boards and mail. The game came to focus on player-versus-player combat, with a player-run justice system to deal with player killing.
trivia: Looking Glass sent a cease and desist over the original name, Terranova, because of its own Terra Nova: Strike Force Centauri.
The "59" was added because "Meridian" was trademarked; the lore was later written to explain it.
Team member John Hanke later founded Niantic and co-developed Google Earth and Pokémon Go.
Characters' faces are drawn at higher resolution than their bodies to speed up loading.
The terms "massively multiplayer" and "MMPRPG" emerged in meetings at 3DO before its release.
devStory:
Mike and Steve Sellers founded the studio as Terra Nova Interactive in 1993, renaming it Archetype Interactive and the game Meridian after the legal letter. Run by the Sellers brothers and John Hanke, with Andrew and Chris Kirmse in key technical roles and a team of 22, it drew technical inspiration from Scepter of Goth. 3DO noticed it in early beta in April 1996, and Trip Hawkins bought Archetype that June. It went online in an early form on 15 December 1995, around 17,000 players joined the public beta, and it launched commercially on 7 October 1996 with a flat monthly fee, at a time when AOL still charged by the minute.

At the 1996 Online Game Developer's Conference, heads of online services called flat-rate pricing "naive", but Next Generation's Christian Svensson later wrote that a fair flat rate had proved the only way to win subscribers. CNET Gamecenter named it its role-playing game of the year. Retail sales were small, 14,359 in the US by June 1999. 3DO shut it down on 31 August 2000; Near Death Studios relaunched it in 2002, and in 2012 the Kirmse brothers released it as freeware with most of its source code open.

title: Street Fighter Alpha 2
description: Street Fighter Alpha 2 (1996), Street Fighter Zero 2 in Japan, is Capcom's arcade sequel that added Custom Combos, secret rival battles and Sakura, and was Japan's highest-grossing arcade game of 1996.
longDescription:
Alpha 2 keeps the first game's three-level Super Combo gauge, Alpha Counters, air blocking and fall breaking, but replaces Chain Combos with the Custom Combo. With at least one level of gauge, pressing two punches and a kick, or one punch and two kicks, starts a timed window in which the player can string any basic and special moves together until a timer gauge runs out. Only Guy and Gen can still chain, and to a lesser extent. Every character now has two Alpha Counters, one on punch and one on kick.

The single-player mode runs eight matches with a fixed final opponent for each character. Each character also has a secret rival who, if certain requirements are met, interrupts a match for a scripted exchange and a fight. With Akuma now a regular, a stronger Shin Akuma takes his place as the hidden challenger, appearing before the final opponent. All thirteen characters from Alpha return, with M. Bison, Akuma and Dan selectable from the start, joined by Dhalsim and Zangief, Gen from the original Street Fighter, Rolento from Final Fight and the newcomer Sakura, a schoolgirl who took up street fighting after seeing Ryu fight. A "classic" Chun-Li wears her Street Fighter II outfit.
trivia: Capcom USA chose three extra characters for the Western arcade release: Evil Ryu and "EX" versions of Dhalsim and Zangief using their Street Fighter II moves.
Shinji Mikami said normal hits were made to do more damage so the new characters would stay balanced.
Nintendo published the SNES version outside Japan; it used the S-DD1 chip to decompress graphics but still had loading times.
Capcom sold unsold SNES cartridges at a loss outside the US to clear its warehouses.
Gamest readers voted Dan and Sakura first and third in their top characters of 1996.
devStory:
Capcom unveiled the game at the AOU show in Tokyo in February 1996. Game Machine named it Japan's most successful arcade game of April 1996, ahead of Virtua Fighter 2, and it became the highest-grossing arcade game of the year in Japan; Gamest readers voted it Best Game of 1996. An update, Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha, added EX versions of more Street Fighter II characters, a survival mode and a two-on-one Dramatic Battle, and reached home consoles as Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold in the Street Fighter Collection.

The 1996 PlayStation and Saturn ports were praised for their faithfulness and for dropping the first game's easily exploited chain combos. EGM made the Saturn version, which kept more animation and the Western extra characters, a Game of the Month and later ranked it 36th among the best console games; it sold over 400,000 copies in Japan. Critics found the SNES version slow and choppy, though IGN later ranked it 96th among SNES games for how far it pushed the hardware. Street Fighter Alpha 3 followed in 1998.

title: Street Fighter Alpha 3
description: Street Fighter Alpha 3 (1998), Street Fighter Zero 3 in Japan, is the final Alpha game, a CP System II fighter with selectable "isms", a guard-crush gauge and a roster that kept growing across its many home versions.
longDescription:
In place of the earlier Manual and Auto modes, players choose one of three "isms". A-ism (Z-ism in Japan) plays like the earlier Alpha games, with a three-level Super Combo gauge and several Super Combos. X-ism, named after Super Street Fighter II X, gives a single gauge level and one powerful Super Combo, the most attack and the least defence, but no air blocking or Alpha Counters. V-ism has no Super Combos but allows Alpha 2-style Custom Combos, started by pressing punch and kick of the same strength. Every character's moves vary by ism. A new Guard Power Gauge drains as the player blocks; when it empties, the guard breaks and the bar shrinks. Throws now use two punch or kick buttons, and a Super Combo's level depends on which strength of button is pressed.

All eighteen Alpha 2 characters return, joined by Cammy, E. Honda, Blanka, Balrog and Vega, and by newcomers R. Mika, a wrestler who idolises Zangief, Sakura's rival Karin from the manga Sakura Ganbaru!, Cody from Final Fight, now an escaped convict, and the Shadaloo "Dolls" Juli and Juni.
trivia: The PlayStation version swapped hit sprites for polygons to save memory for animation and added a World Tour mode for building up a character.
In the Japanese PlayStation version a PocketStation could be used to train a character.
The Saturn version, released only in Japan, used Sega's 4 MB RAM cartridge to come close to arcade-perfect.
The Game Boy Advance version had so little room for voices that characters shared pitch-shifted samples, such as a higher Ken voice for Sakura.
The PlayStation version sold a million copies.
devStory:
Capcom released Alpha 3 in arcades in 1998 on the same CP System II hardware as the earlier Alpha games, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful arcade game of September 1998. The PlayStation port the same year added Dee Jay, Fei Long, T. Hawk, Guile, Evil Ryu and Shin Akuma. Next Generation called it possibly "the most playable and innovative fighting game since the original Street Fighter II", and the Official UK PlayStation Magazine said it would outlast Tekken 3, faulting only its graphics.

The Dreamcast's Saikyo Dojo version added online score display and downloadable weekly opponents, and in 2001 Street Fighter Zero 3 Upper brought the home characters back to arcades on Sega's NAOMI board. Later handheld versions added Yun, Maki, Eagle and Ingrid, for 39 characters on the PSP. Game Informer ranked it the 18th best fighting game of all time in 2019.

title: X-Men: Children of the Atom
description: X-Men: Children of the Atom (1994) is Capcom's first fighting game with Marvel characters, a fast CP System II fighter with air combos and crumbling multi-level stages that laid the groundwork for Marvel vs. Capcom.
longDescription:
The game follows the conventions of Street Fighter II and Darkstalkers, with ten selectable characters, six X-Men and four of their enemies, fighting best-of-three one-on-one matches. An X-Power gauge builds as the player attacks and powers X-Abilities and the more costly Hyper X moves, and breaking a throw or counter-throwing also uses some of it. New to Capcom's fighters were super jumps, long combos that can continue in the air, rolling away from or toward an opponent after falling, aiming projectiles such as Cyclops's optic blasts, and chasing a thrown opponent for follow-up attacks. Players can choose manual or automatic blocking, though automatic blocking disables some features. Some stages have floors that crumble, dropping the fighters to a lower level.

Loosely based on the comics' "Fatal Attractions" story, the plot has Magneto planning an electromagnetic pulse to plunge humanity into a dark age, with the X-Men's foes on his side. The single-player mode pits the player against six opponents and then the bosses Juggernaut and Magneto, and Akuma can appear as a secret opponent. The voice actors from the 1990s X-Men cartoon reprised their roles.
trivia: Capcom's contract with Marvel required a Street Fighter character, so Akuma was added as a secret opponent.
The arcade game used 32 MB for character data alone, while the Saturn, PlayStation and 3DO had 2 MB of RAM, so a third of the animation was cut for the Saturn.
Playing as Juggernaut in the Japanese Saturn version was left in by mistake, Capcom said.
Probe Entertainment struggled with the PlayStation version, which slipped from 1996 to 1998.
RePlay reported it as North America's most popular arcade game of March 1995.
devStory: Capcom released the game in Japan in December 1994 and in North America on 5 January 1995, building on its work on Super Street Fighter II Turbo and Darkstalkers. Next Generation praised its characters, mechanics, animation and voices while calling it "no better or worse than several others". The Saturn version, released in Japan in November 1995 and by Acclaim in the West in 1996, was hailed as near arcade-perfect; Sega Saturn Magazine called it "the first time comic book superheroes have been successfully translated to game format". By contrast, the MS-DOS version was mixed and the 1998 PlayStation version was panned for slowdown and missing frames, arriving after its own successors. Its fast pace, air combos and multi-level stages became the basis for X-Men vs. Street Fighter in 1996 and the Marvel vs. Capcom series that followed.

sources.title: X-Men: Children of the Atom (video game)

title: Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire
description: Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (1997) is the third Darkstalkers game, released at home as Darkstalkers 3, a Capcom fighter that replaced rounds with a single bout and two life bars.
longDescription:
Instead of rounds, each fight is a single bout. Every fighter has two life bars with markers, like Rare's Killer Instinct; when one bar empties, the fighters reset their positions as if a new round had started, but the winner keeps whatever health they had left. Part of the damage taken shows in white and can be recovered if the player avoids being hit again. The Dark Force System spends meter to give each character a unique special ability for a limited time.

The roster carries over from Night Warriors, minus Donovan, Huitzil and Pyron, and adds four newcomers: Jedah, Lilith, Q-Bee and B. B. Hood. Dark Talbain, an evil double of Jon Talbain, is his final opponent and a hidden playable character; Oboro Bishamon is a hidden boss; and Shadow lets the player take over the fighter just defeated for the next match. The story centres on Jedah Dohma, a noble of the demon world of Makai who has returned from the dead and creates a pocket dimension, Majigen, drawing in worthy souls to feed his new world.
trivia: It was going to be called Darkstalkers: Jedah's Damnation outside Japan; the US arcade title became Vampire Savior: World of Darkness.
Two Japan-only updates, Vampire Hunter 2 and Vampire Savior 2, came out simultaneously in September 1997 with different rosters.
The Japan-only Saturn version needed Capcom's 4 MB RAM cartridge and reproduced the arcade animation more faithfully than earlier home versions.
The PlayStation's Darkstalkers 3 compiled all three arcade versions and all 18 characters.
GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann called it "easily the best fighter Capcom has put out in years".
devStory: Capcom released Vampire Savior in Japanese arcades in 1997, and Game Machine listed it as the country's second most successful arcade game in its 15 June 1997 issue. Next Generation found it fun but "nothing special" next to Night Warriors, while GamePro said that despite being more of Capcom's 2D formula it "holds up beautifully"; both praised its animation and special moves. In 1998 it came to the Saturn in Japan and to the PlayStation as Vampire Savior: EX Edition, released in the West as Darkstalkers 3, which IGN called one of the best 2D fighters on the console. It was later remastered in Darkstalkers Resurrection and included in the 2022 Capcom Fighting Collection, and Eurogamer likened it to Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike as a second sequel in which Capcom "tends to go the full distance".

title: Rival Schools: United by Fate
description: Rival Schools: United by Fate (1997) is Capcom's comic 3D tag-team fighter about feuding students in a Japanese city, made for 60 frames per second on Sony ZN-2 hardware and later expanded on two PlayStation discs.
longDescription:
It plays like a polygonal Marvel vs. Capcom with Star Gladiator's four-button layout of two punches and two kicks. Each player picks a team of two, but the fights are one-on-one: the partner joins only for a Team Up attack, offensive or defensive, triggered by pressing punch and kick of the same strength when there is enough "vigor". The vigor meter stores up to nine levels; Team Ups cost two and solo super moves one. After each round, win or lose, the player can switch to the partner for the next. Every character has universal low and high launchers into air combos. Tardy Counters let a blocking player strike straight back with any hard normal, special or super move at no cost, and an Attack Cancel, timing a hit against an incoming one, cancels both and earns a level of vigor.

In Aoharu City, schools are suffering attacks and kidnappings, and students set out to find the culprit, which turns out to be the elite Justice High and its principal Raizo Imawano, with his nephew Hyo as the true mastermind. Choosing two characters from the same school gives a story mode with set fights and 2D cut-scenes; mixed teams play a standard arcade ladder. Sakura from Street Fighter is part of the cast.
trivia: Its working title was Justice Fist, about fighters from every country deciding who was strongest.
Director Hideaki Itsuno chose a school setting because he believed everyone had experience of school.
The two-character teams came from a programmer showing Itsuno three playable characters on one screen.
Sakura was included as "insurance" against poor sales.
The PlayStation's Evolution Disc had a dating-sim character creation mode that was dropped from the Western release as too long to translate.
devStory:
Itsuno wanted a polygon fighting game that ran at 60 frames per second; Capcom's earlier Star Gladiator ran at 30. His first design drew a muted response, so he reworked it around a school, at first imagining 40 characters fighting to be class representatives. Capcom artist Bengus drew all the character art. An unfinished version was Capcom's most popular game at the September 1997 JAMMA show, drawing bigger crowds than Street Fighter III: 2nd Impact, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's most successful arcade game in its 1 February 1998 issue.

The 1998 PlayStation version came on two discs, adding animated intros and endings, a voiced story mode and two characters, the PE teacher Hayato and gang leader Daigo, plus an Evolution Disc of minigames. Next Generation called the arcade game "good, clean button mashing" and the PlayStation version "one of the more enjoyable fighting games available". A Japan-only Nekketsu Seisyun Nikki 2 followed, then Project Justice in 2000; the band Rival Schools and its album United by Fate are named after the game.

title: Tekken 2
description: Tekken 2 (1995) is Namco's 3D fighting sequel with 25 fighters, a boxing kangaroo among them, whose PlayStation version introduced the series' Survival, Team Battle and Practice modes and sold 5.7 million copies.
longDescription:
The fighting system keeps Tekken's four buttons, one for each limb, 2D backgrounds and a playing field with no edges. New are attack reversals for some characters, back throws, chain throws and a sidestep for Kazuya and Heihachi, while Yoshimitsu gets a spinning sidestep that costs him health. Tackles do damage when made from a long run. Beating arcade mode with one of the ten starting characters unlocks that character's sub-boss.

There are 25 playable fighters, 17 returning and eight new. Characters who were clones in the first game became distinct, though they still share many moves, and Devil Kazuya, a palette swap in the first game's home version, is now a separate final boss. The newcomers include Jun Kazama, an animal-rights activist sent to arrest Kazuya; the Hong Kong police officer Lei Wulong; the taekwondo fighter Baek Doo San; the amnesiac kickboxer Bruce Irvin; and two genetically altered boxers, the kangaroo Roger and the dinosaur Alex. The story picks up two years after the first tournament: Kazuya, consumed by the Devil within him, runs the Mishima Zaibatsu, and Heihachi, who survived being thrown off a cliff, enters Kazuya's new tournament for revenge. The PlayStation version added CGI endings for every character.
trivia: Roger the kangaroo began as a team member's spare-time project, which colleagues pushed to put in the game.
Roger, Alex and the devil were added partly to break with the realism of Virtua Fighter.
Each character has roughly 800 polygons and took three days to a week to model.
The PlayStation has roughly half the memory used by the arcade game's data, so much of the conversion went into rewriting code to fit.
Footballer David James blamed his passion for the game for a decline in his performance.
devStory:
Development took about seven months before the arcade release in August 1995, with an updated Ver. B in October. It became Japan's most successful arcade game in Game Machine's 15 September 1995 issue and the country's highest-grossing arcade game of 1996, and sold about 40,000 arcade units worldwide. Yoshie Takayanagi and Yoshie Arakawa composed most of the music.

The 1996 PlayStation version sold over 1.2 million copies in Japan that year, making it the year's best-selling game there, and nearly a million in North America within four months; it reached 5.7 million worldwide. It holds a 93% GameRankings average. EGM's Crispin Boyer called it "the best 3-D fighting game you can find for any system", and critics singled out its practice mode as a feature that would become standard. Tekken 3 followed in 1997.

title: Samurai Shodown II
description: Samurai Shodown II (1994) is SNK's Neo Geo weapons fighter, rebuilt from the ground up after the first game's success, with weapon-breaking POW supers, rolls and hops, and an early form of the parry.
longDescription:
SNK rebuilt the sequel from scratch, bringing back almost all of the first game's cast, adding new fighters and making the controls more responsive. The POW meter now powers super special moves that do heavy damage and break the opponent's weapon, leaving them to fight unarmed until a replacement is thrown in. Fighters can roll forward and backward, duck high attacks and hop over low strikes. A last-second command lets a player deflect an incoming blow and leave the attacker briefly open, an offensive block later used in Namco's WeaponLord and popularised by Capcom's Street Fighter III. Cameos from other SNK characters, a hidden boss and many Easter eggs reward exploration.

A year after Amakusa's defeat, the vengeful spirit Mizuki Rashojin has possessed a shrine priestess to bring chaos in the name of the dark god Ambrosia. Tam Tam and Amakusa sit out; the new warriors are Haohmaru's merciless rival Genjuro Kibagami, Tam Tam's cat-like sister Cham Cham, the Prussian knight Neinhalt Sieger with his gun-filled gauntlet, the tiny old monk Nicotine Caffeine, the referee Kuroko as a hidden boss using moves from other SNK fighters, and Mizuki herself, the series' first female final boss, aided by the demon dog Maju.
trivia: Tam Tam was turned into Cham Cham's pet chimpanzee, Paku Paku, as divine punishment for losing his village's sacred stones.
The Neo Geo AES version hides the blood, but SNK handed out a code to restore it through magazines and its customer service line.
Its awkward English intro was not fixed because Neo Geo home sales were too small to justify paying for translation corrections.
It was the 12th most popular arcade game in North America in October 1994 while still in location tests.
Game Informer ranked it the ninth best fighting game of all time in 2019.
devStory:
SNK released the game for Neo Geo arcades and home systems in 1994. Game Machine listed it as Japan's most successful table arcade unit in its 1 December 1994 issue, and it was the country's eighth highest-grossing arcade game of 1995. The AES and CD home versions sold 335,505 copies in Japan. For years it reached no other Western platform except the PC; Xbox Live Arcade and Virtual Console versions followed in 2008.

EGM's four reviewers gave the home version 9/10 each and their Game of the Month. GamePro praised "the best graphics ever seen in a hand-drawn animated fighting game" while noting unbalanced combos, and suggested SNK was close to overtaking Capcom as the leading maker of fighting games. Retro Gamer called it "a fantastic two-fingered salute to Capcom", easily the best in the series for sheer fun and accessibility, though lacking the depth of later games.

title: Gradius III
description: Gradius III (1989) is Konami's third Gradius, a Japan-only arcade shooter with an Edit Mode for custom weapon sets, best known in the West as a reworked SNES launch game.
longDescription:
The player flies the Vic Viper against the Bacterion Empire across ten levels with the weapons, layouts and enemies familiar from the series. Stage 4 is a kind of bonus level seen from behind the ship, in which the player must avoid hitting walls while collecting floating power-ups, with no enemies at all. Two hidden levels are based on the early sections of Gradius and Salamander. Besides new preset weapon schemes, the new Edit Mode lets players build their own combination of missile, double, laser, shield and special power-ups, though some weapons are only available in the presets and others only in custom setups.

Like earlier Japanese versions in the series, it has no continues. The Japanese version includes a beginner mode covering the first three levels at an easier difficulty, after which the game invites the player to try the normal "technical" mode, which loops endlessly. The Asian release outside Japan lacks the beginner mode and the introduction but is easier overall.
trivia: It was released only in Japan, on 11 December 1989; the arcade version did not reach the West until the Gradius III & IV compilation on the PlayStation 2.
The SNES version is the only one that allows continues.
On the SNES, tapping A sixteen times within a second on the options screen unlocks a harder "Arcade" difficulty.
The PS2 version added an optional "wait level" to recreate the arcade slowdown that the faster hardware no longer produced.
Its music was composed and performed by Konami's Kukeiha Club with Miki Higashino.
devStory: Konami released the game in Japanese arcades in December 1989, and Game Machine listed it as the third most successful table arcade unit in its 15 January 1990 issue. The Super Famicom port came in December 1990 and the SNES version in North America in 1991, one of the system's launch games there. It kept the arcade slowdown and added an easier option and extra weapons, but dropped the pseudo-3D and crystal stages, moved and redesigned the cell stage as the finale and added a new high-speed stage with a boss called Beacon. GamePro called it "one of the most durable side-scrolling shooters", while Entertainment Weekly thought it too similar to earlier Gradius games to be worth $50. IGN later ranked it 45th among SNES games, and it was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and in Gradius Collection on the PSP.

title: Pac-Mania
description: Pac-Mania (1987) is Namco's scrolling, oblique-view Pac-Man directed by series creator Tōru Iwatani, which let Pac-Man jump over ghosts and was the last new Pac-Man arcade game for nearly a decade.
longDescription:
Seen from an oblique angle, the game plays much like the original: Pac-Man eats every pellet in a maze while avoiding the ghosts Blinky, Pinky, Inky, Clyde and a fifth, Sue, and Power Pellets turn them blue so he can eat them and send them home. The mazes now scroll both horizontally and vertically, and some wrap around at the sides. The big addition is a jump that carries Pac-Man over ghosts. Later rounds bring two new ghosts who can jump too: Funky, whom Pac-Man can only just clear, and Spunky, who cannot be jumped at all. Take too long over a stage and Pac-Man's jump steadily weakens until it is gone.

Bonus items appear after a set number of pellets, among them Red Power Pellets, which double the value of blue ghosts until Pac-Man loses a life, and Green Power Pellets, which make him faster for a while. There are four mazes, Block Town, Pac-Man's Park, Sandbox Land and Jungly Steps, cycled in order; the player can start in any of the first three, with a score bonus for starting in Pac-Man's Park or Sandbox Land and clearing its first round. Depending on the settings, the game ends after 11 rounds, 25 rounds or never.
trivia: It was the ninth Pac-Man game and the last made for arcades until Pac-Man Arrangement in 1996.
Atari sold 1,412 cabinets in North America in 1987, worth about $2.82 million.
It was runner-up for Best Coin-Op Conversion at the 1987 Golden Joystick Awards, behind Operation Wolf.
Westwood Studios made the NES version for Tengen.
Music from Pac-Man's Park and Block Town was later remixed for Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS and Wii U.
devStory: Namco developed the game under Pac-Man creator Tōru Iwatani and released it in 1987, with Atari Games handling North America; Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most successful table arcade unit of December 1987. Critics praised its originality and play. In 1988 Teque Software's Peter Harrap and Shaun Hollingworth converted it for the Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, MSX and ZX Spectrum for Grandslam, followed by X68000 and MSX2 versions in 1989, an Acorn Archimedes port and Tengen's NES and Genesis versions in 1990 and 1991. Entertainment Weekly gave the Genesis version a B−, and Poland's Top Secret gave the NES version full marks for its music, graphics, comic cut scenes and jumping. The arcade game has since appeared in Namco Museum collections, Pac-Man Museum+ and Hamster's Arcade Archives.

title: Galaga '88
description: Galaga '88 (1987) is Namco's fourth Galaxian game, a detailed update of Galaga with triple fighters, warps between dimensions and a soundtrack the enemies dance to.
longDescription:
As the Blast Fighter, the player shoots waves of Galaga aliens that fly into formation from the top and sides of the screen and then dive-bomb; touching an alien or its shots costs a life. Each formation is topped by four Boss Galaga, which take two hits and can capture the player's ship with a tractor beam. Shooting a Boss carrying a captured ship as it dives frees it to join the player's ship as a dual fighter, with more firepower and a bigger target. A dual fighter can be captured and rescued in turn to make a triple fighter, with wide, fast shots, which can also be gained from pink capsules.

The game is split into five worlds of up to four stages each, ending in a bonus stage. Defeating large enemies and destroying obstacles in a world yields up to two blue warp capsules, and finishing the bonus stage with both sends the player into a new dimension with different, harder enemies and formations. Two vertically scrolling stages each feature two enemy formations and a boss, and there are four endings depending on the dimension the player finishes in. Compared with earlier games, it has detailed backgrounds, larger enemies and more detailed ships.
trivia: Composer Hiroyuki Kawada wrote the music for the "Galactic Dancin'" bonus stages first, and programmers choreographed the enemies to it.
Kawada drew on orchestral music, tango, salsa and big band jazz for those stages.
On the TurboGrafx-16 in North America it was renamed Galaga '90.
The X68000 version adds a mode that replaces the aliens with characters from other Namco games, later called Galaga '88 Arrangement.
Atari sold only 986 units and boards in North America by the end of 1988.
devStory:
Namco showed a prototype at the JAMMA show in October 1987 alongside Pac-Mania, Bravoman and Assault, released it in Japan that December, and let Atari Games publish it in North America and Europe in 1988. Running on Namco's System 1 board, it let Kawada combine FM synthesis, Namco's wavetable sounds and PCM effects, and he wanted the music to convey entertainment rather than stoicism. It was Japan's sixth highest-grossing arcade conversion kit of 1988, its success there credited to its simplicity and additions, but it did poorly in North America.

Computer + Video Games liked its cute visuals and new ideas, Your Sinclair called it "one of the most enjoyable machines on offer this month", and ACE dismissed it as "nothing more than a prettified version of the original" while praising its looks and music. Allgame called the TurboGrafx-16 port the best shooter on the system, and Eurogamer described the Virtual Console release as a "pitch perfect dose of frenetic arcade blasting". Galaxian³: Project Dragoon followed in 1990.

title: Area 51
description: Area 51 (1995) is Mesa Logic's light-gun shooter for Atari Games, a last-ditch bid to save the struggling company that critics found dated but players made a 20,000-cabinet hit.
longDescription:
As a member of the STAAR team, alongside Lieutenant Stephanie Grant and Sergeant Major Marcus Bradley, the player fights through a warehouse, tunnels and other parts of the Area 51 facility to trigger its nuclear self-destruct, gunning down genetically altered zombie soldiers and the alien Kronn without hitting teammates. Shooting nothing but three STAAR members switches the game to Kronn Hunter mode, in which the player becomes a Kronn hunter sent to eliminate the rebels.

The player starts with a semi-automatic pistol and can shoot upgrade targets for a machine gun, a pump shotgun and finally an automatic shotgun; the shotguns give a wider margin for error and the automatics fire while the trigger is held, but any hit drops the player back to the pistol. Up to nine grenades, hidden in crates and bonus rooms, clear most enemies on screen, and flammable boxes and barrels can be shot to blow up nearby foes. Shooting certain objects in the right order opens shooting exercises, weapon stashes and bonus items, and other back doors warp ahead to later levels.
trivia: Designer Robert Weatherby got the idea from a Popular Science article, "Searching for the Secrets of Groom Lake".
It runs on the COJAG, a modified Atari Jaguar, with a hard drive, yet was never released for the Jaguar itself.
Atari's Silicon Graphics workstations were turned into an overnight render farm when other teams went home.
The STAAR members were motion-captured, while the enemies were made with stop-motion animation by Sneaky Pete Kleinow.
It topped RePlay's "Player's Choice" chart in December 1995.
devStory:
In 1994 Atari Games had gone years without a profitable game and lost many developers to Electronic Arts. It asked Ed Logg for a light-gun game, but he too left for EA with his game, Bounty Hunter, unfinished. Atari handed the project to Robert Weatherby's Mesa Logic, which found Bounty Hunter underwhelming and pitched its own concept instead. Lead programmer Charlie Grisafi dropped plans to stream video from CD, which could only produce a letterboxed picture, in favour of a hard drive and his own compression software.

Time Warner Interactive released it under the Atari Games label in 1995. Next Generation said it "provides shooters with what they want" but compared it with older games rather than the current crop, and critics often judged it inferior to Virtua Cop 2. Players disagreed: it sold over 20,000 cabinets and was cited as the first step in Atari Games' recovery from near collapse. Midway released PlayStation, Saturn and Windows versions in 1996, and Atari followed it with Maximum Force and Area 51: Site 4.

title: Point Blank
description: Point Blank (1994), Gun Bullet in Japan, is Namco's non-violent light-gun party game of quick shooting challenges, hosted by Dr. Dan and Dr. Don, that EGM ranked among the best arcade games of all time.
longDescription:
Two players with light guns take on short, non-violent shooting contests that test speed, judgement or pinpoint accuracy: hitting bullseyes in their own colour, gunning down cardboard criminals while sparing cardboard civilians, avoiding bombs, and protecting the hosts Dr. Dan and Dr. Don. The difficulty chosen, from Practice and Beginner to Advanced and Very Hard, sets how many stages must be cleared and how tough they are. Missions come in groups of four that can be tackled in any order. Players usually have three lives for the whole game, losing one for missing a stage's quota or shooting a forbidden target, and most stages give unlimited bullets.

The stages fall into six types. Accuracy rewards hitting the highest-scoring areas; Intelligence means counting to sixteen by shooting numbers; Memory is a card-matching game; Simulation has players shoot robbers but not civilians, or ninjas but not geishas in the Japanese theme; Visual Acuity asks for the target matching a picture; and Speed is a race to shoot targets of the player's colour. At the end the game ranks the player on points, lives left and continues used and suggests what to try next, from a harder difficulty to more practice.
trivia: Japan knows the series as Gun Bullet.
In the arcade both guns must be calibrated before the on-screen crosshairs will move.
The 1997 PlayStation version added an arrange mode, many new modes and an RPG-style quest mode, and supports the GunCon.
Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine called Dr. Dan and Dr. Don "an underrated dynamic duo".
EGM's Dan Hsu and John Ricciardi both called the PlayStation version the best light-gun game they had ever played.
devStory: Namco released Point Blank in arcades in 1994; like its first light-gun game, Steel Gunner, it penalises shooting bombs and cardboard civilians. It was Japan's seventh highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1995 and, according to EGM, a "cult favorite" in American arcades. The PlayStation version arrived in 1997 and was the third best-selling game in Japan in the week ending 10 August. Critics praised its variety: it tied with Resident Evil 2 for EGM's Game of the Month, GameSpot said it was "so enjoyable and difficult to put down you won't be bothered by the audiovisual shortcomings", and Next Generation found its quest mode forced but its two-player contests a highlight. EGM listed it as the seventh best arcade game of all time in 1997. Point Blank 2 followed in 1999 and then Point Blank 3, and a Nintendo DS collection used the stylus instead of a gun.

title: Crash Team Racing
description: Crash Team Racing (1999) is Naughty Dog's last Crash Bandicoot game, a PlayStation kart racer whose power-slide boosts led critics to rank it alongside, or above, Mario Kart.
longDescription:
Characters come in three types: large ones with slow acceleration and high top speed, balanced medium ones, and small ones with quick acceleration and sharp handling. The key technique is the power slide: holding a shoulder button to hop and steering before landing starts a slide, and pressing the opposite shoulder button when the Turbo Boost Meter turns red, as the exhaust turns black, gives a boost. Three boosts can be chained in one slide, the third the strongest, but waiting too long backfires and sliding too long spins the kart out. Hang time over jumps also earns boosts, and accelerating just before the start gives a head start. Question-mark crates hold weapons and boosts, and collecting ten Wumpa Fruit makes the kart faster and strengthens power-ups.

In Adventure mode the alien Nitros Oxide threatens to turn Earth into a concrete parking lot unless its best driver beats him. Winning trophies across a world's tracks opens a boss race for a key to the next, and side events award more: Relic Races against the clock with time-freezing crates, CTR Challenges to collect the letters C, T and R while winning, and Gem Cups. Arcade, Versus and Time Trial modes and a customisable four-player Battle mode round it out.
trivia: It began as an original game with block-headed characters before Naughty Dog agreed to make it a Crash game.
The team rebuilt Diddy Kong Racing's Crescent Island course in a prototype to test whether a track that size was possible on the PlayStation.
To avoid drawing up to 64 tyres in four-player split screen, programmer Greg Omi rendered them as camera-facing 2D sprites.
Nitros Oxide was first planned as a mad scientist trying to speed up the world, an idea referenced in a Disney Adventures comic.
Polar and Pura were originally going to share one kart as a single character.
devStory:
Naughty Dog pitched the game to Sony, which made a publishing deal with Crash owner Universal Interactive; the engine was built while Crash Bandicoot: Warped was in production. A team of 16 to 18 made it in eight months on a $2.4 million budget, with characters designed by Charles Zembillas and Joe Pearson, art direction by Bob Rafei and music by Josh Mancell of Mutato Muzika. The turbo system was meant to make it more involving than older kart games, and memory limits kept Oxide from being playable.

It was released in North America on 19 October 1999 and in Europe that December, promoted with a Crash-themed NASCAR car and a Pizza Hut demo disc. Critics called it the best kart racer on the PlayStation, and several, including EGM's reviewers, said it outshone Mario Kart for its controls, graphics and tracks, while noting how much it borrowed from Nintendo. It sold 1.9 million copies in the US and over 300,000 in Japan. Crash Nitro Kart followed in 2003, and Beenox remade it as Crash Team Racing Nitro-Fueled in 2019.

title: Gran Turismo 2
description: Gran Turismo 2 (1999) is Polyphony Digital's first game as a studio, a PlayStation racing simulation with nearly 650 cars and 27 tracks that shipped 9.37 million copies despite a rushed, buggy release.
longDescription:
The player races against computer-controlled drivers in two modes. Arcade Mode allows any available car and can enable damage. Simulation Mode, called Gran Turismo Mode in PAL and Japanese versions, is a career in which the player earns driving licences, buys cars and wins trophies to unlock new and returning courses. Nearly 650 cars and 27 tracks are included, among them rally stages.

The physics, handling and graphics are very close to the first Gran Turismo. The most noticeable change in driving is the brakes, which are much less likely to lock up and cause oversteer. The main differences are the greatly expanded number of cars, tracks and events in Simulation Mode. Players can now enter individual races without taking on a whole tournament, and there is no longer a separate qualifying session before each race.
trivia: Players found glitches soon after launch, and Sony of America offered replacement discs.
In the 30-lap Trial Mountain endurance race, a 680 bhp Vector M12 LM could appear despite a 295 hp limit, making it nearly unwinnable.
Full completion is impossible: the game expects 223 events but only 219 are available.
Its soundtrack includes The Cardigans' 1998 song "My Favourite Game".
It sold 815,430 copies in Japan in its first week.
devStory:
After the unexpected success of Gran Turismo, Polys Entertainment was spun off as Polyphony Digital, and lead developer Kazunori Yamauchi set out to make the sequel "an even better product". Sony's American executives expected it to "fly off the shelves faster than the original". In the UK it sold 130,000 copies in its first weekend, overtaking Ocarina of Time as the fastest-selling title, and about 250,000 in its first week, and it was a best seller for two months there and in Japan. In the US it passed a million within six weeks.

It received universal acclaim. Next Generation's Dan Egger wrote that "the rushed production of this game botched what could have been a near perfect sequel" but that it was "still the best racer ever made". Famitsu gave it 34 out of 40, and it was a finalist for console game of the year at the Interactive Achievement Awards. By April 2008 it had shipped 9.37 million copies: 3.96 million in North America, 3.68 million in Europe and 1.73 million in Asia.

title: Wipeout 2097
description: Wipeout 2097 (1996), Wipeout XL in North America and Japan, is Psygnosis's anti-gravity racing sequel with destructible craft, gentler wall collisions and a soundtrack from The Prodigy, The Chemical Brothers and Underworld.
longDescription:
Set more than four decades after the first game, it introduces the faster and more dangerous F5000 anti-gravity league. Players race hover craft that handle unlike cars, using air brakes to corner at high speed. Each craft now has a shield energy quota, and when weapons and impacts drain it to zero the craft is destroyed, though a pit stop can recharge it at the cost of a few seconds. New weapons include the Quake Disruptor, which sends a wave along the track that throws rivals into the air.

The classes Vector, Venom and Rapier rise in speed and track complexity. Gold medals on every track in the first three unlock a full season, which in turn reveals hidden options and new tracks, and Challenge mode advances only by winning, and finishing worse than third costs one of three lives. Four teams fly differently: FEISAR's balanced, well-shielded craft suits beginners; AG Systems is quicker than FEISAR but corners worse; Auricom is faster than both; and Qirex the fastest with the poorest steering. The PlayStation version supported analogue control through the NeGcon, while the Saturn port used Sega's 3D Control Pad.
trivia: It began as a tracks add-on for the first Wipeout, and the name 2097 was chosen so it would not seem a full sequel.
The North American title was going to be Wipeout XS, until someone pointed out that XS could mean "extra small".
Ghost vehicles appeared only in the European version because Atari held a US patent on them from Hard Drivin'.
Fluke wrote "Atom Bomb" for the game, with a music video set in the Wipeout universe.
The game disc also worked as an audio CD of the soundtrack.
devStory:
Psygnosis in Liverpool developed the game in seven months, with promotional art by Sheffield's The Designers Republic. Producer Andy Satterthwaite had asked to make a sequel and was given a tracks add-on instead, with a team of three coders, six artists and Nick Burcombe; work on the tracks began in January 1996, and he realised he could do more. Lead artist Nicky Westcott built on the original craft designs, and the team made the learning curve easier while keeping the top end hard. The biggest change was letting ships scrape along walls instead of stopping dead, which took longer than expected; months went into balancing the AI so that every ship could win. Westcott called it "a period of great energy and immense exhaustion at the same time".

Shown at E3 in May 1996, it sold around a million copies, and Saturn and Windows ports followed in 1997. GamePro gave it perfect scores, IGN said "It's games like this that make you proud to be a PlayStation owner", and EGM named it 1996's best music. It averaged 94.75% on GameRankings, third among PlayStation games there.

title: R4: Ridge Racer Type 4
description: R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 (1998) is Namco's fourth home Ridge Racer, a stylish PlayStation arcade racer with team stories, 321 cars and a mellower club soundtrack, often called the best in the series.
longDescription:
Racing centres on powersliding, in two styles depending on the manufacturer: Drift cars break into a smooth slide with a tap of the brake while turning, and Grip cars need the player to alternate brake and throttle. In the Grand Prix, Real Racing Roots '99, the player joins one of four teams of differing difficulty, R.C. Micro Mouse Mappy of France, Pac Racing Club of Japan, Racing Team Solvalou of Italy or the Dig Racing Team of the US, and picks one of four manufacturers, Age Solo, Lizard, Assoluto or Terrazi, which sets the car style and slide type. Each team has its own story, with a manager who talks to the player through the season.

Each race requires a qualifying position, rising through the season, and placing higher earns better new cars or upgrades. Racing every combination of team, manufacturer and finishing position yields 320 vehicles, and collecting them all unlocks a 321st modelled on Pac-Man. There is also Time Attack, the home series' first two-player split screen, an undocumented four-player link-cable mode, a decal editor and Extra Trials against powerful prototypes.
trivia: All 33 developers had also worked on the original Ridge Racer.
The art director looked to Ace Combat 2 for the sky effects.
The opening film starring Reiko Nagase took over six months to make, including planning.
Composer Hiroshi Okubo found singer Kimara Lovelace at a club event in Nishi-Azabu; Kohta Takahashi called him "the gatekeeper to club sound hell".
A bonus disc held a 60 fps version of the original Ridge Racer, and special editions came with the Jogcon controller.
devStory:
Development began in May 1997. It was the first PlayStation Ridge Racer to use Gouraud shading, and the staff said much "waste" was cut to allow it and high polygon counts; like Gran Turismo, the team used Sony's Performance Analyser development kit. Okubo led a soundtrack that moved from the rave sound of earlier games to funk, breakbeat, acid jazz, UK garage and neo soul, which he called "more mature, more fashionable", meant to suit the game's human drama.

Namco released it in Japan on 3 December 1998, with other regions following in 1999. Reviews were generally favourable; Famitsu gave it 35 out of 40, and some critics found its drifting too light compared with earlier games. It was Japan's 18th best-selling game of 1998 after less than a month on sale, and sold 759,527 copies there and 297,564 in the US. Time Extension ranked it the best Ridge Racer in 2023. Ridge Racer V followed in 2000.

title: Suikoden II
description: Suikoden II (1998) is Konami's PlayStation role-playing game of 108 Stars of Destiny and two friends split by the halves of one rune, a sprite-based sequel that sold poorly in the West and became a cult classic.
longDescription:
The silent protagonist and his best friend, Jowy Atreides, survive a false-flag massacre of their Highland youth brigade staged by the brutal Prince Luca Blight to justify invading the City-States of Jowston. Each of them receives half of the Rune of the Beginning, one of the 27 True Runes, which drives its two bearers to fight until one falls, much to the grief of the hero's adoptive sister Nanami. Over 100 characters can be recruited, often through a short side quest, and more than 40 fight; save data from the first Suikoden brings returning characters in stronger, and its hero can be recruited.

Combat comes in three forms. Ordinary turn-based battles field up to six characters, who can perform "unite attacks" that reflect their relationships. Duels are rock-paper-scissors contests of attack, wild attack and defend, with the opponent's dialogue as a hint. Army battles now play out on a grid like Romance of the Three Kingdoms or Fire Emblem: recruited characters lead or support units that add attack, defence and abilities, and a character killed there is gone for good. Experience depends on the level gap between party and enemies, so low-level characters catch up quickly. New features include three rune slots, a party inventory, a dash button and minigames, one reminiscent of Iron Chef.
trivia: Luca Blight hates Jowston after watching Jowstonian soldiers rape his mother in an earlier war.
Recruiting all 108 Stars of Destiny unlocks the best ending, in which Nanami turns out to have faked her death.
Writer Yoshitaka Murayama decided from fan letters that the first game's story was its selling point, and made story the sequel's focus.
Murayama has said he would have preferred to make a shoot 'em up, such as Taito's Metal Black.
Its limited Western print run was never reprinted, because the initial response was so lacklustre.
devStory:
