The series began when Konami assigned newcomers Murayama and Junko Kawano, with ten others, to its first PlayStation games; offered a baseball game, a racing game or an RPG, they revived an RPG project, aiming for a franchise to rival Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy. After the first Suikoden succeeded, Murayama wrote most of the sequel's story himself. Konami released it in Japan on 17 December 1998, in North America on 29 September 1999 and in Europe in July 2000.

It sold well in Japan, but in the West its 2D sprites looked dated at a time when 3D graphics were emphasised, and it met lacklustre sales and a modest reception, though Metacritic still records favourable reviews and Next Generation called it "one of the best RPGs to hit PlayStation this year". Since the 2010s critics have often named it the best Suikoden and one of the greatest RPGs. It was paired with the first game on the PSP in 2006 and remastered as Suikoden I & II HD Remaster in 2025.

title: SaGa Frontier
description: SaGa Frontier (1997) is Square's first PlayStation SaGa, a non-linear science-fantasy RPG with seven protagonists across the worlds of the Regions, a million-seller in Japan that divided Western critics.
longDescription:
Its Free Scenario System lets the player pick one of seven protagonists, all living in the same setting, the Regions, a group of worlds each with its own culture, level of technology and magic. From the start most characters can travel almost anywhere on regular inter-regional ships, explore pre-rendered field screens, talk to people to gather information, recruit allies and start quests. Each has a main quest plus optional ones, and a story changes depending on choices, events and who is in the party. The cast includes Asellus, a girl turned half-Mystic by a blood transfusion from the Mystic Lord Orlouge; the mage Blue, destined to fight his twin Rouge; Emilia, a former model framed for her fiancé's murder by the "Joker"; the bard Lute; Red, who becomes the superhero Alkaiser; Riki, a fox-like Lummox trying to save his world; and T260, an ancient Mec that has lost its memory.

Battles are turn-based, with 2D sprites against rotating 3D backgrounds. Most skills are learned in the middle of fights, spells are bought in shops, and party members can link combination attacks. Races include Humans, Mystics, Monsters and Mecs. Completing scenarios gives bonuses to the next, and finishing all seven opens the "2nd Division" room, where the player can fight every final boss and talk to the developers.
trivia: It was called Romancing SaGa 4 early in development, until the move from Super Famicom to PlayStation.
A ninth scenario, about a family of channellers squabbling over an inheritance, was dropped as too comedic.
The scenario of IRPO officer Fuse, cut from the original, was added in the 2021 remaster.
Blue's scenario was always meant to end in the middle of his final boss battle.
A hidden track in the pregap of the soundtrack's third disc was originally meant to be Riki's theme.
devStory:
Square Production Team 2 began work in December 1995, with Akitoshi Kawazu directing and producing, Koichi Ishii as planning chief, Kenji Ito composing and Tomomi Kobayashi illustrating. The team avoided 3D graphics because it did not yet know the hardware's capabilities, and Kawazu said time and disc space forced cuts, including parts of Asellus's story. It was the first game released abroad under the SaGa name rather than Final Fantasy.

It sold over 1.05 million copies in Japan in 1997, the year's fifth best seller there, and Famitsu's editors later voted it the 18th best PlayStation game. Western reviews were mixed, averaging 71% on GameRankings: critics admired the non-linearity in concept but said it made scenarios short and left players wandering without direction. IGN called it "the only bruised apple in Square's current collection of role-playing games", while GamePro gave perfect marks for graphics and fun. A remaster with the Fuse scenario was released in 2021.

title: Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain
description: Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain (1996) is Silicon Knights' top-down vampire action-adventure for Crystal Dynamics, in which the murdered nobleman Kain feeds on Nosgoth's living while hunting the corrupt Circle of Nine.
longDescription:
Seen from above, Kain crosses the land of Nosgoth and its dungeons, fighting with swords, a mace, axes and the two-handed Soul Reaver, solving puzzles and avoiding hazards. His blood meter drains over time and faster when he is hurt, so he must wound humans and animals and drink their red blood. Blue blood from ghostly foes restores the magic he spends on spells and shapeshifting, while undead black blood harms him and the green blood of demons and mutants poisons him. Spells come as tarot cards, from light to mind control and lightning, and he can become a bat to fly between checkpoints, a wolf, a cloud of mist that passes through gates or a human. Blood fountains, vials and rune pyramids raise his abilities, 100 secrets are hidden, and a day and night cycle makes him stronger at night and opens some doors under a full moon.

Kain is ambushed and killed, and the necromancer Mortanius raises him as a vampire. To avenge himself and find a cure, he must kill the nine sorcerer-guardians of the Pillars of Nosgoth, driven mad after one of them, Ariel, was murdered. Along the way he meets the elder vampire Vorador and fights the Legions of the Nemesis, and learns that he is himself the last guardian, so that the "cure" is his own death. The player chooses whether he sacrifices himself or dooms the world.
trivia: Kain was partly modelled on William Munny from the film Unforgiven.
The Soul Reaver sword was originally conceived for Silicon Knights' Too Human.
Writer Ken McCulloch called names like Mortanius "Names from Hell" because of the trouble getting them past marketing.
Cover art for the novel The Pillars of the Earth inspired the Pillars of Nosgoth.
Silicon Knights added an opening credit making clear that it created the game's concept, story and content, which it called "a first in the industry".
devStory:
It began as The Pillars of Nosgoth, proposed around 1993 by Silicon Knights president Denis Dyack and art director Ken McCulloch. Crystal Dynamics producer Lyle Hall saw it as "a Zelda-style take on a vampire action RPG" and helped persuade his company to choose the PlayStation over the 3DO and Saturn, with Amy Hennig as design manager. Dyack wanted "a game which adults would want to play", drawing on vampire myth, Shakespeare, Unforgiven, the Necroscope novels and The Wheel of Time. Development took three and a half years, Silicon Knights doubled its staff, and Crystal Dynamics sent employees to Canada for over six months. Simon Templeman voiced Kain, with Tony Jay as Mortanius.

Released in November 1996, it averaged 83% on GameRankings; critics praised its story, voice acting and scope but criticised long loading times and dark graphics, and EGM named it Role-Playing Game of the Year. A 2011 court filing showed at least 320,082 sales. A dispute over the rights left Crystal Dynamics with the series, and it made Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver without Silicon Knights.

title: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis
description: Resident Evil 3: Nemesis (1999) is Capcom's PlayStation survival horror game in which Jill Valentine escapes a zombie-overrun Raccoon City while hunted by Nemesis, a spin-off promoted to numbered sequel.
longDescription:
Jill explores the streets of Raccoon City, rather than the mostly indoor settings of earlier games, collecting weapons from pistols to a rocket launcher and managing a limited inventory with storage boxes. Herbs and first aid sprays restore health, gunpowders can be mixed into ammunition, and puzzles test logic. New to the series are a dodge and a quick 180-degree turn, explosive barrels that can be shot to damage nearby enemies, and up to nine enemies on screen at once. At certain perilous moments, the player must choose between two actions, and these choices change how the story unfolds and which ending is reached.

The Nemesis, a bio-weapon programmed to kill the surviving S.T.A.R.S. members, appears repeatedly as a boss. It is far stronger than Jill, fires a rocket launcher, dodges gunfire and follows her from area to area; in some encounters the player can choose to fight or flee, and even when beaten it keeps coming back. The story starts 24 hours before Resident Evil 2 and runs past it, as Jill teams up with members of Umbrella's U.B.C.S. unit, among them Carlos Oliveira and the treacherous Nikolai, before the government launches a missile at the city. Finishing the game unlocks The Mercenaries, a timed run across the city.
trivia: Nemesis was inspired by the liquid-metal T-1000 from Terminator 2.
Shinji Mikami said the idea was "to make you feel like you're being stalked".
It was first known as Biohazard 1.9 or 1.5, because it is set between the first two games.
Capcom chose Jill as "the only suitable character remaining" because Chris and Claire Redfield were taken for Code: Veronica.
The first 500,000 copies included a demo disc of Dino Crisis.
devStory:
After Resident Evil 2, Hideki Kamiya was directing the planned next game, set on a cruise ship, until Capcom dropped it as unlikely to finish before the PlayStation 2's launch. Not wanting fans to wait years for a PlayStation Resident Evil, Capcom promoted a side project by an inexperienced team under director Kazuhiro Aoyama to be the third main game; it then made Jill the lead and decided Raccoon City would be destroyed. Writer Yasuhisa Kawamura, new to the series, played the original to learn its world. Mikami produced, and the team grew from 20 to 40 or 50 people, developing it alongside Code: Veronica. Yoshiki Okamoto said full 3D would have meant "blocky, pixelated zombies", so it kept pre-rendered backgrounds.

It was released in Japan on 22 September 1999 and North America on 11 November, and sold a million copies by early October and 3.5 million by 2012. Critics praised its detailed city and Nemesis as an intimidating villain but found it short and its story simple. Windows and Dreamcast ports followed in 2000 and a GameCube version in 2003, and a remake was released in 2020.

title: Mega Man 8
description: Mega Man 8 (1996) is the series' first 32-bit game, a PlayStation and Saturn platformer with anime cutscenes, the alien robot Duo and some of the most mocked English voice acting in games.
longDescription:
The formula is that of the earlier games: Mega Man runs, jumps, slides, swims and charges his Mega Buster through side-scrolling stages, and each Robot Master he beats gives him its weapon, with weaknesses that reward choosing the order. As in Mega Man 7, an introductory stage leads to four Robot Masters, Tengu Man, Frost Man, Grenade Man and Clown Man, and four more, Aqua Man, Sword Man, Search Man and Astro Man, open after an intermission stage. New are the ability to use several weapons on screen at once, such as jumping into a Tornado Hold and swinging the Flame Sword while rising on its current, and to fire the Mega Buster even with a special weapon equipped. Bolts found in the stages buy upgrades from Roll in Dr. Light's lab, limited by the bolts and slots available, and mid-stage bosses award Rush items such as the Rush Bike.

Two alien robots crash to Earth after a battle in space. Dr. Wily steals a purple orb of "Evil Energy" from the crash site, while Dr. Light repairs the other robot, Duo, who has travelled the universe destroying that energy. Bass returns as a rival, empowered by Evil Energy.
trivia: Capcom received around 110,000 Robot Master ideas from fans in Japan; Tengu Man and Astro Man were designed in-house beforehand.
Duo was first designed as a creation of Mega Man 4's Dr. Cossack, which is why he still wears an ushanka.
Duo was first playable in the 1996 arcade game Mega Man 2: The Power Fighters.
Sony initially resisted a US PlayStation release of a 2D game, then approved it on condition it had content the Saturn lacked: a 12-page anniversary booklet.
The Saturn version adds two bosses from earlier games and a bonus art and sound mode.
devStory:
With Tokuro Fujiwara gone from Capcom, longtime series artist Keiji Inafune became producer and handed much of the work to director Hayato Kaji, an artist he considered his student, describing the approach as "seeing Mega Man from a distance". The team was often overwhelmed by releasing on two new systems and by anime cutscenes, made with the studio Xebec, which Inafune had wanted since the first game. Shusaku Uchiyama composed the score, his first lead project at Capcom.

It was released on the PlayStation in Japan on 17 December 1996 and on the Saturn in January 1997, reaching North America on both in March 1997. Retailers reported selling more than half their stock in three days, and the PlayStation version later sold at least 350,000 copies. Reviews were moderately positive: critics liked its looks but found little new and said it did not use 32-bit hardware fully, and EGM, IGN and others called its English dub among the worst in games. Mega Man & Bass reused its assets in 1998, and Mega Man 9 returned to 8-bit style in 2008.

title: Mega Man X4
description: Mega Man X4 (1997) is the first 32-bit Mega Man X, a PlayStation and Saturn platformer that let players take X's buster or Zero's sword through the whole game in a war against the Repliforce.
longDescription:
The eight main stages can be cleared in any order, past spikes, falling debris and enemy robots, with hover bikes called Ride Chasers and Ride Armor mechs in some. Heart Tanks raise maximum health and two Sub Tanks store energy for later. For the first time Zero is fully playable alongside X, chosen at the start and fixed for the playthrough. Both run the same stages but play very differently. X fires his chargeable X-Buster from range, gains a limited-ammo weapon from each boss and finds hidden capsules with armour upgrades. Zero fights up close with his Z-Saber and learns ammo-free techniques such as the Hienkyaku air dash and Kuuenbu double jump, but cannot be upgraded.

In the 22nd century, a floating city, Sky Lagoon, is brought down by a Maverick, killing countless humans and Reploids. Suspicion falls on the Repliforce, a Reploid army under General and his second-in-command Colonel, and when Colonel refuses to disarm, it declares independence for Reploids. The story differs by character: X's rookie partner Double turns out to be a spy, Zero is forced to fight Colonel's sister Iris, whom he loves, and Sigma is revealed to have staged the whole conflict.
trivia: To get Zero approved as playable, the developers gave him special moves based on Street Fighter.
Twice as many sprite animations were needed, so the team compressed character data and split stages into two sections.
Artist Haruki Suetsugu noticed that the X3 armour parts, attached a certain way, looked like an aeroplane, leading to X's secret Ultimate Armor.
Sony of America at first refused to let Capcom release it, reportedly over its policy against 2D games.
Zero shouting "What am I fighting for?!" over Iris's body is often cited as some of the worst voice acting in the franchise.
devStory:
The Mega Man X3 team had no sequel planned until Capcom wanted the series on new hardware. Inafune stepped back from artwork to produce and help write the story, in which the writers gave the Repliforce "moral leeway" instead of making them plainly evil, and left out human characters entirely. Xebec produced the animated cutscenes, and Toshihiko Horiyama composed the score. Planned as a Saturn exclusive for June 1997, it was delayed and made multi-platform.

Both versions were released in Japan on 1 August 1997, and in North America after Capcom persuaded Sony to allow the PlayStation version; Europe got only the PlayStation version that October. Critics praised the choice between X and Zero, the controls and the bosses, though some felt the 2D formula was worn out, with Next Generation suggesting players buy X3 used instead. EGM ranked it 78th in its 1997 list of the best games of all time. The PlayStation version sold 197,385 copies in Japan in 1997 and at least 350,000 in North America.

title: Lunar: The Silver Star
description: Lunar: The Silver Star (1992) is Game Arts' Mega-CD role-playing game, a "different kind of RPG" told with CD audio, animated scenes and voice acting, and the best-selling Mega-CD game in Japan.
longDescription:
In top-down 2D the player crosses towns, fields and harsh landscapes, completing story objectives and talking to people, with short animated interludes, full or quarter-screen, and CD-quality music carrying the story. Random encounters lead to turn-based battles in which characters act in order of speed. Characters must move close enough to strike unless they have a ranged attack, and they can also retreat into a corner, stand their ground or flee. The flying cat-like Nall, who does not fight, sizes up enemies before each battle. Progress is saved to the Sega CD's internal memory or a RAM cartridge.

Lunar is a small world orbiting the barren Blue Star, where humanity lived until war made it uninhabitable and the goddess Althena moved people to the Silver Star, setting four dragons to guard it. Fifteen-year-old Alex, from the mountain town of Burg, idolises the late Dragonmaster Dyne. An outing to a dragon's cave for a diamond leads the old white dragon Quark to urge him to pass the dragons' trials and become the next Dragonmaster. With his childhood friend Luna and companions such as Nash and Mia of the floating city of Vane, the bandit Kyle and the priestess-in-training Jessica, he confronts the sorcerer Ghaleon, who has become the Magic Emperor and kidnapped Luna. Locations were given a cool, "northern" feel, partly so that the characters could wear more clothes.
trivia: Game Arts founded Studio Alex, named after the hero, to oversee most of the game's development.
Nearly a third of the planned project was cut for time.
Working Designs translated the nearly four-megabyte English script in eight weeks.
The scene where Alex plays his harp to awaken Luna was added at Working Designs head Victor Ireland's request.
Mel's epithet "Hell" Mel became "Deadly" Mel in English for censorship reasons.
devStory:
Game Arts, known mostly for side-scrollers and shooters, wanted an RPG centred on animation and storytelling. Novelist Kei Shigema wrote a story meant to break from "hum-drum 'model'" games that "had stories, but had no story-telling", and Toshiyuki Kubooka designed the characters and planned the animated scenes. Noriyuki Iwadare, Hiroshi Fujioka, Isao Mizoguchi and Yoshiaki Kubodera composed the music. Working Designs, a small California publisher, made it its biggest project, working closely with the Japanese team, adding jokes and pop culture references and producing embossed manuals and seven different disc designs; its English cast included a young Ashley Parker Angel as Alex.

It sold out its Japanese production run in its first year, an estimated 100,000 copies, and Sega credited it with pushing Mega-CD sales; worldwide only Sonic CD sold more on the system. GameFan named it the best RPG of 1993 and GamePro called it "one of the best on any Sega system", though some found its battles dull. Lunar: Eternal Blue followed in 1994, and remakes began with Lunar: Silver Star Story Complete in 1996.

title: Lunar: Eternal Blue
description: Lunar: Eternal Blue (1994) is Game Arts' Sega CD sequel set a thousand years after The Silver Star, a larger role-playing game with nearly fifty minutes of voiced animation and twice the dialogue.
longDescription:
Play follows the first game: top-down 2D exploration, quests and conversations, and story told through text and animated cutscenes. Random battles are fought with attacks and magic, with characters moving into range, but the battle system now allows characters to be positioned in advance and has improved AI. Besides experience, battles award magic points used to strengthen spells and unlock skills. In the North American version, saving costs magic experience, a change Working Designs made so that players would "think about where and when to save", and the game remembers each character's last command.

A thousand years after The Silver Star, young explorer Hiro and his winged companion Ruby take a gem called the Dragon's Eye from a ruin and use it to enter the Blue Spire, where they meet Lucia, a girl from the Blue Star who must see the goddess Althena to stop the evil being Zophar. Hunted by Leo, captain of Althena's guard, who believes she is the prophesied Destroyer, they are joined by the gambler-priest Ronfar, the dancer Jean and Lemina, money-grubbing heiress to the magic guild, and discover that the Althena now ruling is false and that Ghaleon, the first game's villain, is her Dragonmaster.
trivia: Writer Kei Shigema took the idea of an oppressive god from the image of Sun Wukong unable to escape the Buddha's palm in Journey to the West.
It took three years and over $2.5 million to make.
The team first planned to set it a few years after the first game with an older cast, but feared the new characters would lose focus.
Its Japanese price of ¥9,900 was nearly $100 in 1994.
GameFan's preview called the translation "ingeniously written", a quote used in ads, then its review criticised the jokes, which Victor Ireland called "a complete about-face".
devStory:
Director Yoichi Miyagi returned to lead Game Arts and Studio Alex, with Kubooka directing the in-house animation and Noriyuki Iwadare composing the music, narrowing his range to give the score a unified feel. The game has over an hour and a half of recorded speech against the first game's fifteen minutes. Game Arts released it in Japan in December 1994, where it sold well and became the second best-selling Sega CD game there, though fewer copies than its predecessor. Working Designs released it in North America in September 1995, adding humour, fourth-wall breaks and balance fixes for battles found "near impossible".

US sales were low, which Ireland blamed on the arrival of 32-bit consoles and talk of the Sega CD's "death". Critics liked it: EGM praised its "great story and witty characters", named it the best Mega-CD game of 1995 and later ranked it 40th among console games, while Game Players and Next Generation felt something of the first game's charm had been lost. It was remade in 1998 as Lunar 2: Eternal Blue Complete for the Saturn and PlayStation.

title: Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom
description: Phantasy Star III: Generations of Doom (1990) is Sega's Genesis role-playing game whose story spans three generations, with marriage choices deciding the next hero and leading to four different endings.
longDescription:
The game keeps the series' turn-based formula, exploring 2D worlds, recruiting characters and fighting random encounters, but adds an auto-battle option and an icon-based menu, while "technique" magic plays a smaller role than before. Its distinguishing feature is that the story spans three generations. At key points the hero chooses which of two women he has met to marry, and the choice decides the next generation's lead: a child who may be Orakian or part Layan and Orakian, which changes their ability with techniques. Two paths in the second generation branch into four in the third, each with its own ending.

A thousand years earlier, the swordsman Orakio and the sorceress Laya led rival factions; both vanished during a truce, each side blamed the other, and travel between their worlds was banned. The game begins with Prince Rhys of the Orakian kingdom of Landen on his wedding day to Maia, an amnesiac who washed ashore two months before, when a Layan dragon snatches her away. Maia turns out to be a Layan princess whose people thought they were rescuing her. Later it emerges that both peoples descend from survivors of the planet Palm, destroyed in Phantasy Star II, and that their worlds are sections of a vast colony ship.
trivia: It was the first Phantasy Star made without series co-creator Yuji Naka, since most of the Phantasy Star II team had moved on to Sonic the Hedgehog.
Its team had never made a role-playing game before.
Composer Izuho Numata planned music that changed with who was in the party; memory limits meant it changes with how many are in it instead.
Its icon-based menus inspired those of Shining in the Darkness.
MegaTech's only complaint was that "it costs a massive £50!"
devStory:
Sega released the game in Japan in April 1990 and in North America in June 1991. Series veteran Rieko Kodama helped in early planning, and the new team chose branching paths to stand out in a crowded RPG market, but storage limits made the multiple endings hard to implement and forced cuts to the story. Designer Hirondo Saiki grew exhausted as the sole designer, though it was the first time designers and programmers worked as one team, and character designer Saru Miya recalled great hardship on what she called a "home-spun" project. Producer Kazunari Tsukamoto likened it to a collection of side stories compared with Phantasy Star II and IV.

Contemporary reviews were positive: Computer Gaming World called it "a rewarding epic tale which should be told on every Genesis system", and Dragon liked its marriage choices and endings while preferring Phantasy Star II. Later critics, averaging 68% on GameRankings, found its endings too similar and its style too different from the rest of the series, and it is now often seen as the series' black sheep.

title: Shining in the Darkness
description: Shining in the Darkness (1991) is Climax Entertainment's first-person Genesis dungeon crawler, made on Sega's minimum budget, that started the Shining series and sold over 300,000 copies in its first months.
longDescription:
The hero and two friends, Pyra and Milo, explore 3D first-person dungeon mazes, fighting random monsters and set boss battles in turn-based combat much like Dragon Quest or, more specifically, Wizardry. Between descents the party visits town to talk to people, buy equipment and visit priests, who save the game and revive fallen characters, all through an icon-based menu system that the game used for battles, equipment and conversations. Three characters are trapped in the dungeon, and rescuing any or all of them is optional, with the story changing depending on who is brought back.

In the Kingdom of Thornwood, the king's daughter and the hero's father have vanished, and the evil sorcerer Dark Sol threatens the land. The hero is charged with finding the Arms of Light, rescuing the princess and his father and stopping Dark Sol. A later game, Shining Force Gaiden: Final Conflict, revealed Dark Sol to be the son of Shining Force's villains Darksol and Mishaela, placing this game after Shining Force II in the series' timeline.
trivia: Producer Hiroyuki Takahashi said that apart from programming and graphics he did nearly all the work himself because the budget was so tight.
Takahashi said its core concept was "realism": the feeling of really moving through houses and dungeons.
Dragon described it as combining Phantasy Star III's icons and combat, the first Phantasy Star's first-person view and Phantasy Star II's close-up graphics.
Its success paved the way for Shining Force.
Spells, menus and the use of priests for saving carried through the series up to Shining Force III.
devStory: Sega gave Climax Entertainment the bare minimum budget it offered outside developers. Takahashi said the aim was a continuation of the excitement of moving through dungeons in older games such as Wizardry, making the player feel they were really in a fantasy world. Sega published it for the Genesis in 1991. Sega Pro gave it 93%, calling it "superior to all other RPGs of this style" and praising its scaling sprites, sound and icon menus, while Computer Gaming World called it a "hack-and-slash adventure" that was not the full CRPG many hoped for but "a decided step" towards one. It sold over 300,000 copies by late 1991. Historians see it as a pioneer of Japanese console RPGs, especially in Europe, which waited more than six more years for a Final Fantasy. It was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007.

title: Streets of Rage 3
description: Streets of Rage 3 (1994) is the last of Sega's original Genesis beat 'em up trilogy, with running, dodge rolls, branching stages and an experimental, semi-random techno score by Yuzo Koshiro and Motohiro Kawashima.
longDescription:
Up to two players fight waves of enemies as Axel, Blaze, Skate or the new Dr. Zan, a robot who turns every weapon he picks up into a ball of energy; meeting certain conditions unlocks Shiva and Roo the kangaroo, and in Japan a third bonus character, Ash. Every character can now run and dodge-roll vertically. Blitz attacks can be upgraded through successive play, and a recharging meter allows a special attack without losing health when it is full. Some weapons have their own special moves, but all weapons now break after a set number of uses, and the unlockable characters cannot hold them at all. Pits return from the first game, and some stages branch, for instance depending on whether players clear a room before a character dies from poison gas. Enemies are smarter, picking up weapons, blocking, attacking together and even stealing health-restoring food. A Battle mode pits two players against each other.

In the Western story, the Syndicate's Mr. X has set up the RoboCy Corporation and hired the roboticist Dr. Dahm to replace Wood Oak City's officials with robot duplicates, with bombs planted around the city to distract the police. Dr. Zan alerts Blaze, who calls in Axel and Skate. There are four endings depending on difficulty and timing.
trivia: The Japanese story is different: a new explosive called Raxine kills thousands and a general, Ivan Petrov, vanishes; the West made Petrov the police chief and dropped Raxine.
The Western release cut Ash, a gay stereotype, made female enemies' outfits less revealing and changed the heroes' colours.
The Western Normal setting is harder than the Japanese Hard, and the English version cannot be completed on Easy.
Koshiro created an "Automated Composing System" for the music, using heavily randomised sequences.
A section in which players ride motorcycles was cut but can be reached, unfinished, with a Game Genie code.
devStory:
Sega designed the sequel with a more complex plot, character dialogue, longer levels and faster play than the first two games, adding hidden characters and a few cut-scenes. Koshiro and Kawashima, both from Streets of Rage 2, drew on the Detroit hard techno popular in Tokyo clubs; Koshiro said his system generated sounds "you ordinarily never could imagine on your own". Critics were split on the music: Mean Machines called it "terrible", while Fact later called it the pair's "crowning achievement".

Reviewers praised the new moves, larger sprites and six-button pad support but felt it advanced the series little; Mega called it "uninspiring and easy to finish" before ranking it among the best Mega Drive games, and GameFan said the localisation "neutered" a fine game and urged readers to import the Japanese version. It was re-released in collections including Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection and the Genesis Mini 2, and Streets of Rage 4, which continues from its true ending, followed in 2020.

title: Alien Soldier
description: Alien Soldier (1995) is Treasure's late Mega Drive run-and-gun of 25 short stages and 26 bosses, built "for Mega Drivers custom" and released in North America only on the Sega Channel.
longDescription:
Compared heavily with Treasure's Gunstar Heroes, it puts far more weight on boss fights and has no two-player mode; the stages are short and filled with weak enemies, serving as breathers between 26 difficult bosses. Epsilon-Eagle can run, double jump, hover and carry four of six weapons, chosen before the game begins, each with its own ammunition bar. A dash across the screen becomes a damaging "Phoenix Force" attack when he is at full health, and a well-timed counter turns enemy bullets into health. He can fire in a fixed stance, standing still for quick aiming, or while moving, at the cost of directional accuracy. There are two difficulty settings, "supereasy" and "superhard"; the hard setting's enemies are only slightly tougher, but it has no passwords or unlimited continues.

The premise is given once, in an opening text scroll. In 2015 on A-Earth, Epsilon-Eagle, leader of the terrorist group Scarlet, is gravely wounded in an assassination attempt and lost in the space-time continuum. His successor Xi-Tiger proves too brutal even for Scarlet. When Xi attacks a laboratory and kills a girl, Epsilon, living as a parasite in a boy's body, reveals himself and sets out after him.
trivia: Director Hideyuki Suganami began as sole designer and programmer, when Mega Drive games usually had two of each.
The team planned 100 bosses; only about half of its ideas made it in.
The boss Seven Force first appeared in Gunstar Heroes.
Its title screen carries the slogan "Visualshock! Speedshock! Soundshock!"
By 2006 the scarce original cartridge sold for over 20,000 yen in Japanese used game shops.
devStory:
After Gunstar Heroes, Treasure split into four teams, making Dynamite Headdy, Light Crusader, a Yū Yū Hakusho fighter and Alien Soldier. Suganami led the two-year project and chose the Mega Drive despite 32-bit hardware being on sale, saying he may have been too captivated by making an "action shooting" game; Treasure aimed it explicitly at "hardcore" players, designing its difficulty and scoring for them. He cut most of a planned backstory to meet a 3 January 1995 deadline, and when he realised he could not finish alone, other staff joined and he worked through the New Year holidays.

Sega released it in Japan on 24 February 1995 and in Europe that May. Famitsu gave it 24 out of 40, but Mean Machines Sega called it "a real gameplayer's game" and a modern classic. Later reviewers praised its graphics, sound and intensity while warning of its steep learning curve; GameSpot said it made you feel like "an army of one". It was re-released on the PlayStation 2 in Japan in 2006, the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and Steam in 2011.

title: Earthworm Jim 2
description: Earthworm Jim 2 (1995) is Shiny Entertainment's sequel for the Genesis and SNES, which keeps the run-and-gun core but fills its levels with game shows, inflated heads and exploding sheep.
longDescription:
Jim again sets out to save Princess What's-Her-Name from Psy-Crow, but the levels vary far more than in the first game. Some, like the opening "Anything but Tangerines" and "Level Ate", play much like the original with more moves and guns, such as an auto-aiming gun and the "Barn Blaster", which wipes out every enemy on screen. A chip butty boosts Jim's suit power to 200%, and his friend Snott travels with him, letting him swing from slimy green surfaces or use Snott as a parachute.

Others break the mould. In "Villi People", Jim, disguised as a blind cave salamander, is guided through intestinal passages avoiding exploding sheep, before the level turns into a game show of nonsensical multiple-choice questions. "Inflated Head" has Jim floating upwards with a balloon for a head, dodging sharp objects and Evil the Cat. "The Flyin' King" is an isometric shooter in which Jim on his pocket rocket escorts a balloon-borne bomb to defeat Major Mucus. The finale is a race against Psy-Crow to the Princess, and in the end all three turn out to be cows in disguise.
trivia: The Genesis and SNES versions came out almost simultaneously; the SNES version has different backgrounds and lets players switch weapons.
In Japan the Genesis version was available only through the Sega Channel.
The MS-DOS version, packaged as The Whole Can 'O Worms, added CD audio and more voices but lacked the "Lorenzen's Soil" level.
David Perry said in 1994 that Shiny was considering a Jaguar version, which never appeared.
GameSpot nominated the 2002 Game Boy Advance port for worst Game Boy Advance game of the year, calling it "unplayable".
devStory: Like the first game, Earthworm Jim 2 was developed for the Genesis and ported to the SNES, and released in late 1995 and early 1996 depending on region and system; Screaming Pink later made Saturn and PlayStation versions. Reviews were very positive, and IGN and GameZone later judged it better than the original. GamePro wrote that it "manages to exceed the lofty standards of the first game", praising its new levels, varied soundtrack and animation, while one of EGM's four reviewers complained that "where the first had technique, this one just gets cheap". Sega Saturn Magazine gave the Genesis version 94%, but called the Saturn version "a great game – a year ago. On a different console." It was nominated for the Video Software Dealers Association's game of the year in 1995, losing to Donkey Kong Country 2. Later sequels, Earthworm Jim 3D and Menace 2 the Galaxy, were made by other developers and poorly received.

title: Yoshi's Story
description: Yoshi's Story (1997) is Nintendo's "2.5D" Nintendo 64 follow-up to Yoshi's Island, set in a pop-up storybook of cardboard and cloth, praised for its looks and criticised for being too short and easy.
longDescription:
Rather than reaching a goal, the aim in each course is to fill the Fruit Frame by eating 30 pieces of fruit, found lying about, in bubbles or carried by enemies. Scoring rewards strategy: eating the same fruit in a row earns more, and more still for each Yoshi's favourite fruit or the course's Lucky Fruit, while melons score most and exactly 30 are hidden in each course. The courses are spread over six pages of a storybook, four per page in rising difficulty. After the first page only one course is open on each, and collecting Special Hearts, three per course, opens more on the next page. Yoshis can run, duck, jump, ground-pound, hover briefly and throw eggs, though eggs no longer bounce and swallowed enemies become eggs at once. White and Black Yoshis can be found and unlocked.

Baby Bowser, jealous of the Yoshis' happiness, turns Yoshi Island into a pop-up book and steals the fruit-bearing Super Happy Tree. Six baby Yoshis hatch and set out to fight the gloom with cheer. The worlds are made of materials such as cardboard, fabric, plastic and wood, rendered in 3D but played in 2D.
trivia: It began as Yoshi's Island 64 for the 64DD before moving to cartridge.
After Japanese reviews called it too easy, Nintendo of America demanded more challenge, and the Western version gained changes and a Story Mode save.
Composer Kazumi Totaka also voiced Yoshi; those recordings became Yoshi's voice in later games, starting with Super Smash Bros.
Totaka's 19-note signature melody plays on the Trial Mode course select screen after the music loops eight times.
Its US soundtrack CD was cut in the shape of Yoshi's head, causing problems in many CD players.
devStory:
The Yoshi's Island team developed it, directed by Hideki Konno and produced by Takashi Tezuka, with Shigeru Miyamoto supervising and contributing ideas. Shown at Space World in November 1996, it demonstrated that the Nintendo 64 could run 2D games; Miyamoto said the 2D format was needed for the art style, and Nintendo called it "2.5D". Its cartridge was expanded from 96 to 128 megabits. Totaka's interactive score slows when Yoshi is unhappy and turns to rock when he is Super Happy.

It was released in Japan on 21 December 1997, where it sold 618,789 copies in 1998, and in North America in March 1998 after a delay Nintendo said was "based on us demanding A-plus quality", launched with an event in Lizard Lick, North Carolina. US sales of 679,219 by the end of 1998 were hurt by a late release and supply problems. It averages 65 on Metacritic: critics loved its graphics and music, but EGM's Crispin Boyer asked why there were not enough levels, bosses and secrets "to keep me busy longer than a weekend".

title: Turok 2: Seeds of Evil
description: Turok 2: Seeds of Evil (1998) is Iguana's Nintendo 64 first-person shooter sequel, a 32 MB cartridge of six huge levels, a skull-drilling Cerebral Bore and an optional high-resolution mode that sold 1.4 million copies in weeks.
longDescription:
As the new Turok, Joshua Fireseed, the player runs, jumps, climbs, swims and dives through six large levels linked by a hub, carrying an unlimited arsenal from bows to a flamethrower, a grenade launcher and the Cerebral Bore, which fires a homing projectile that latches onto an enemy's head, drills into the skull and explodes. Each level sets several objectives, such as destroying objects, rescuing hostages and killing enemies, before the exit portal leads to defending an energy totem, a boss fight or both. Keys found in levels open the hub's portals, so some levels can be tackled out of order, and an automap helps navigation. Losing all health costs a Life Force point and returns the player to a checkpoint; on the Nintendo 64 the game saves only at special portals.

Each level also hides a Primagen Key, reached with talismans that grant powers such as long jumps or walking on lava, so levels must be revisited to open the way to the final boss. The alien Primagen, trapped in his crashed Lightship, has roused the creatures of the Lost Land to destroy the totems that bind him. A split-screen multiplayer mode for up to four includes Frag Tag, in which one player is turned into a defenceless monkey.
trivia: The Cerebral Bore was inspired by the Tall Man's weapons in the 1979 film Phantasm; a proposed Leech gun was rejected.
Players can see five times as far as in the first game, with the remaining fog disguised as atmosphere.
Multiplayer was added, inspired by GoldenEye 007, once falling cartridge prices allowed more memory; the final 32 MB cartridge was the largest for a Nintendo 64 game at the time.
The enemies were not motion-captured because, project manager David Dienstbier said, they would look like a person in a lizard costume.
In Japan it was titled Violence Killer: Turok New Generation.
devStory:
Iguana Entertainment began the sequel before Dinosaur Hunter was released, with a team of about 18 that grew over its 21 months of development. An optimised version of the first game's engine allowed more complex geometry and real-time shadows, and early access to 64DD kits with the Expansion Pak led to a 640 × 480 high-resolution mode. Dienstbier said the team learned from Miyamoto to "start things off simple and gradually add to it", drawing on Mario and Zelda for the objectives and exploration. Over 10,000 hours of testing were reportedly done.

Backed by a $9 million marketing budget, with 1.75 million pre-orders from retailers, it slipped from Acclaim's "TurOctober" plans and was released in North America on 10 December 1998. It sold 1.4 million copies by January 1999. GameSpot called it "a landmark shooter and a must-buy" and its shooting game of the year, praising its graphics, deep levels and smart enemies, though critics faulted its uneven frame rate and fog. A Windows port followed in 1999, and Nightdive remastered it in 2017.

title: Beetle Adventure Racing!
description: Beetle Adventure Racing! (1999) is Paradigm and EA Canada's Nintendo 64 racer in which every car is a Volkswagen New Beetle, praised for its long, shortcut-filled tracks and four-player Beetle Battle mode.
longDescription:
The main game is a championship of Novice, Advanced and Professional circuits, with a secret Bonus Circuit unlocked after the rest, and completing each circuit unlocks new cars and tracks. Finishing the Professional and Bonus circuits awards two special cars: the Alien Beetle, whose horn says "We come in peace" in an alien voice, and the Police Beetle, whose siren makes computer racers pull over. Tracks hide four kinds of crates. Point crates, worth 2, 5 or 10, lie mostly off the track on shortcuts and earn continues, and finding all 100 points opens a new Beetle Battle arena. Nitro crates give a burst of speed, and three hidden Cheat crates per stage, announced with a "Groovy!", unlock a cheat menu, whose background hides the developers' faces.

Up to four can play. Two players can race on any unlocked track, and two to four can play Beetle Battle, a vehicular combat mode in which they collect six coloured ladybugs, try to destroy each other and race for the exit once the ladybugs are gathered. Single Race pits one player against computer cars on unlocked tracks. The play is similar to EA's own Need for Speed series.
trivia: It began as Need for Speed 64, cancelled when EA signed a deal with Volkswagen for a New Beetle game.
In Australia it was released as HSV Adventure Racing, with Holden Special Vehicles models in place of the Beetles.
A PlayStation port was planned but cancelled for technical reasons.
Its breakbeat soundtrack was composed by Phil Western, Scott Blackwood and Brenden Tennant.
A planned sequel, Adventure Racing 2, dropped the Beetle licence for unlicensed cars before being cancelled.
devStory:
In the late 1990s EA Canada and Paradigm were working on a Nintendo 64 Need for Speed with exclusive tracks, cars and Rumble Pak support. The designers wanted something to set it apart, and when Electronic Arts signed a deal with Volkswagen around the New Beetle, released the year before, the project became Beetle Adventure Racing. It was released in 1999 and in Japan, published by Electronic Arts Square, that November.

It received universal acclaim. Next Generation saw it as a rival to Top Gear and Need for Speed, The Electric Playground called its scenery "stunning" and it the first "truly addictive" Nintendo 64 game of 1999, and IGN's Peer Schneider named it one of the best racers on the system while regretting its few tracks and cars and "generic" drum and bass. It sold over 320,000 copies in the US, small by EA standards; senior producer Hanno Lemke blamed "terrible box art and a virtually non-existent marketing presence" and the many rival racers on the console.

title: Puyo Puyo
description: Puyo Puyo (1991) is Compile's falling-blob puzzle game starring the characters of Madō Monogatari, which Sega's arcade version turned into a competitive hit and the West first played as Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine and Kirby's Avalanche.
longDescription:
Players match coloured blobs called puyos to clear them, and chains of clears sends garbage into the opponent's grid, with the aim of filling it up. Compile's founder Masamitsu "Moo" Niitani produced the game, inspired by elements of Tetris and Dr. Mario, and it borrows its characters from Compile's 1990 role-playing game Madō Monogatari. The game has Single, Double and Endless modes. In Single mode, the player is Arle Nadja, a 16-year-old spellcaster who must beat 12 opponents, most of them just out for mischief, before facing the Dark Prince, who wants to take over the world. Double mode is a head-to-head contest between two players, and Endless mode is a chase for the highest score. A Mission mode sets 52 puzzles to clear with limited pieces.

Because sending so much garbage made matches short, Compile added "offsetting" from Puyo Puyo 2 onward, letting players cancel incoming garbage with chains of their own.
trivia: The Famicom Disk System version came out the same day as the MSX2 original, as part of Tokuma Shoten's Famimaga Disk series.
Sega's 1992 arcade version added the one-player story and two-player competition that defined the series.
The English arcade version renamed characters and removed the Harpies' wings, calling them Dark Elves.
The Game Gear version contains an English version, Puzlow Kids, shown on Western consoles.
Amiga Power commissioned a clone, Super Foul Egg, for one of its cover disks.
devStory: Compile released Puyo Puyo for the MSX2 in 1991, with Tokuma Shoten's Famicom Disk System version the same day. A year later Sega's arcade version greatly expanded it, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most successful table arcade unit of December 1992. Sega's Mega Drive version, released in Japan on 18 December 1992, was a best seller there for four months. Ports followed on the Game Gear, PC-9801, Famicom, Super Famicom as Super Puyo Puyo, Game Boy, PC Engine CD and FM Towns. In the West the Genesis version became Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine in 1993, with characters from the Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog cartoon, and two years later the SNES version appeared as Kirby's Avalanche in North America and Kirby's Ghost Trap in Europe. The series later reached the West under the name Puyo Pop, and the arcade original was re-released on Switch as Sega Ages Puyo Puyo in 2019.

title: Mr. Driller
description: Mr. Driller (1999) is Namco's arcade puzzle game, conceived as Dig Dug 3, in which Susumu Hori drills down through coloured blocks while racing his own dwindling air supply.
longDescription:
The player controls Susumu Hori, the Mr. Driller of the title, drilling through formations of coloured blocks to reach the bottom of a well, in a game described as a cross between Puyo Puyo and Dig Dug. Blocks of the same colour stick together, and when four of a kind connect they vanish, which can set off chain reactions; falling blocks can crush him. His oxygen meter drains constantly and is topped up by collecting blue air capsules, while brown blocks marked with an "x" take five hits to break and cost oxygen. The player has to balance speed, safety and air on the way down. The story has creatures called Undergrounders flooding the Earth with giant blocks.

Susumu was later connected to Namco's history: he is the son of Taizo Hori, the hero of Dig Dug, and the series' characters have become closely associated with the Namco brand in Japan.
trivia: Its creator Yasuhito Nagaoka had directed R4: Ridge Racer Type 4.
Nagaoka drafted it in 1998 as Dig Dug 3; co-creator Hideo Yoshizawa, formerly of Tecmo, renamed it Mr. Driller.
It ran on Namco's System 12 arcade hardware.
It won the first Arcadia Grand Prize from Japan's Monthly Arcadia magazine.
The Dreamcast port was criticised for looking technically inferior to Namco's earlier Dreamcast release, Soulcalibur.
devStory: Nagaoka designed the game to be more puzzle-based than the action-oriented Dig Dug and Dig Dug II, and Yoshizawa reworked his prototype before Namco released it in arcades in 1999 to critical and commercial success. Ports followed on the PlayStation, Dreamcast, Game Boy Color, WonderSwan Color, Windows and mobile phones, and Famitsu gave the Game Boy Color version its Silver Hall of Fame award. Western reaction was cooler; journalist Jeremy Parish suggested the backlash against the Dreamcast port contributed to the series' lukewarm reception outside Japan, though critics generally agreed its play was simple and addictive, and some found the home ports short of content. Yoshizawa and Nagaoka began Mr. Driller 2 in late 1999, and the dedicated team Project Driller made later sequels, including Mr. Driller G, which made Susumu the son of Dig Dug's Taizo Hori.

title: Ace Combat 2
description: Ace Combat 2 (1997) is Namco's arcade-style PlayStation combat flight game of 24 jets and 21 missions, made because its designer felt Air Combat was technically lacking, and a half-million seller in Japan.
longDescription:
Presented more like an arcade game than other flight simulators of the time, it has the player fly 21 missions in a choice of 24 fighter jets, with objectives such as intercepting enemy squadrons, sinking an aircraft carrier or defending a base. Missions pay money to spend on new aircraft for the player's hangar. From the fourth mission a wingman can be brought along for support. The campaign starts largely linear and later branches. A fuel meter acts as a time limit, ending the mission if it runs dry. New to the series are "aces", elite enemy pilots who can be shot down to earn medals and unlock their special aircraft.

There are two difficulty settings: Novice, and Expert, which allows realistic manoeuvres such as rolls and high-g turns. To keep things approachable, the planes do not use their real-world performance data, and a simplified physics model keeps a sense of realism while staying easy to handle. The game supports the PlayStation Analog Joystick, Namco's NeGcon and later the Dual Analog Controller.
trivia: The team wrote a program to find how many polygons the PlayStation could draw without strain, letting it push the graphics further than most games.
Developers photographed planes at an American armed forces airshow for reference.
A mission in which the player derails a train in a mountain valley was cut for technical reasons.
Its funk rock soundtrack was heavily inspired by Top Gun.
No soundtrack was released at the time; one finally came with Ace Combat: Joint Assault's Deluxe Pack in 2010.
devStory:
Designer Masanori Kato, who had worked on Air Combat, saw that game as incomplete from a technical point of view and set out with a small team to use the PlayStation's hardware as fully as possible, giving the player a real sense of flight. They drew on aviation books, magazines and films, wanted far more variety than Air Combat's two mission types, and checked whether each new fighter would make missions more interesting. The team hoped for advice from a real pilot but could not get it. Kohta Takahashi and Nobuhide Isayama composed the music.

Namco released it in Japan on 30 May 1997, in North America in August and in Europe in October. It sold over 500,000 copies in Japan by May 1998, earning a Gold Prize from Sony, and scored 83 on Metacritic. Computer and Video Games called it "the most intense flight experience to ever grace a console" and IGN "one of the best flight simulators ever to come to the PlayStation", while some critics missed multiplayer and found it monotonous or too hard. It was remade for the 3DS as Ace Combat: Assault Horizon Legacy in 2011.

title: Dragon Quest V: Hand of the Heavenly Bride
description: Dragon Quest V (1992) is Chunsoft and Enix's Super Famicom role-playing game spanning about thirty years of one hero's life, the first in the series to let defeated monsters join the party, and Japan's best-selling game of 1992.
longDescription:
The game uses the series' familiar systems, with experience levels, first-person turn-based battles and weapons and armour, but adds monster taming: after a battle, a defeated monster may ask to join the Hero if the party is strong enough, and recruited monsters fight and level up like human characters. Forty monsters can join in the Super Famicom version. A wagon from Dragon Quest IV holds party members not in the field, the tactics system returns with the option to control allies manually throughout, and up to three characters fight at once. After the ending, the series' first bonus dungeon opens.

The story follows the Hero for some thirty years, from his birth onwards. As a six-year-old he travels with his father Pankraz, until Pankraz is killed by Ladja of the Order of Zugzwang, a religious group serving dark forces, and the Hero and Prince Harry are sold into slavery to build a great temple. Escaping ten years later, he sets out to learn his father's secrets and find his mother, Madalena, said to have died after his birth. He must choose a bride, his childhood friend Bianca or the gentle Nera; becomes king of Gotha; is turned to stone for eight years; and discovers that the Legendary Hero his father sought is his own son.
trivia: Computer and Video Games reported release-day queues of up to three miles in places, and there were ten reported thefts.
It sold out over 1.3 million cartridges within a day in Japan, more than the Super Famicom Street Fighter II.
It was the first Dragon Quest not released in North America at the time, because of programming issues; it reached English only with the 2009 DS remake.
It is credited as the first known video game with a playable pregnancy.
Yuji Horii has called it his favourite in the series.
devStory:
As with the rest of the series, Yuji Horii wrote the scenario, Akira Toriyama drew the art, given outlined sprites for a manga look, and Koichi Sugiyama composed the music. As the first mainline Dragon Quest on the Super Famicom, it had much improved graphics and sound, and it was Chunsoft's last game in the series before the studio turned to its own projects. It was released in Japan in 1992 with 300,000 pre-orders.

It was Japan's top-selling game from October to November 1992 and the best-selling home game of the year, pushing up demand and prices for the Super Famicom, and by 1993 had sold 2.8 million cartridges in Japan. Famitsu gave it 36 out of 40, one of its three highest-rated games of 1992, and Gamasutra later praised its coming-of-age story as never "executed so magnificently". Its monster recruiting influenced later games and the Dragon Quest Monsters series. Remakes followed on the PlayStation 2 in 2004 and the DS in 2008, which added a third bride, Debora, whom Horii called a character "nobody in their right mind would pick!"

title: Dragon Quest VI: Realms of Revelation
description: Dragon Quest VI (1995) is Heartbeat's Super Famicom finale to the Zenithian Trilogy, a role-playing game of an amnesiac hero moving between a Real World and a Dream World, and Japan's best-selling game of 1995.
longDescription:
It is a traditional overhead role-playing game with random turn-based battles in first person, now with animated monster attacks. The party grows over the adventure, and progress depends on beating bosses and triggering story events. At Alltrades Abbey, characters can take one of several starting classes, each with eight levels earned by winning battles rather than by experience. Each level teaches spells or skills that are kept across class changes, and mastering certain combinations opens hybrid classes, such as Gladiator from Warrior and Martial Artist, and eventually the Hero class. It was the first in the series to give human characters special skills that are not spells. Other features include the wagon, a day and night cycle, mini medals, casinos, the new Slime Arena and Best Dresser Contest, and bonus dungeons.

The game opens with the Hero and two companions facing the demon king Murdaw and being overpowered, only for the Hero to wake in the mountain village of Weaver's Peak. He soon falls through a hole into a world where no one can see him. That world turns out to be the Real World, and the one he started in the Dream World, made of people's dreams. Many of the cast have lost their memories, and they must recover who they are while stopping the Archfiend Mortamor from merging both worlds.
trivia: Terry's design was Akira Toriyama's original design for the Hero, which Yuji Horii rejected.
It cost a steep ¥11,400, roughly over $100.
At 4 MB it was among the largest Super Famicom games, the biggest the console could support without extra bank-switching circuitry.
Nintendo Power reported it was planned for North America in spring 1996 as "Dragon Warrior V".
Its prequel, Dragon Warrior Monsters, starring young Terry and Milly, was released in North America though Dragon Quest VI was not.
devStory:
Heartbeat developed it in place of Chunsoft, with Horii writing, Toriyama drawing and Koichi Sugiyama composing as before. Enix delayed it by more than a year to develop it further, showed it at Shoshinkai in November 1995 and released it on 9 December. It launched with 1,274,857 sales, sold 2.5 million in December alone and reached 3.2 million in Japan, the year's best seller.

It was not localised at the time: translating it would have required bigger and more expensive cartridges, and by then Enix had dropped the Super NES and the American market. GamePro listed it among the best Japanese games never released in the US. Gamasutra's Kurt Kalata praised its dream-world scenario, suggesting it influenced Chrono Cross and Final Fantasy X, and its improved class system, calling it "still a fantastic game". The 2010 DS remake by ArtePiazza brought it to English for the first time in 2011.

title: Trials of Mana
description: Trials of Mana (1995), Seiken Densetsu 3 in Japan, is Square's Super Famicom sequel to Secret of Mana, an action RPG of six heroes, three intertwined plots and light-or-dark class changes that stayed in Japan until 2019.
longDescription:
From a top-down view, three party members fight monsters in real time; control can switch between them at any time, the others run by AI, and a second player can join. At the start the player picks three of six heroes and the one to lead, and the others appear as non-player characters. Each character uses one weapon type plus magic, and attacking fills a gauge for special moves. Spells, equipment and items are managed through the Ring Command, a circular menu that pauses the action. At each level up the player chooses which statistic to raise, and at level 18, at a Mana Stone, each character can take a Light or Dark class, with a second change at level 38 if the right rare item has been found. A fast calendar gives each weekday an elemental spirit that strengthens its magic, and day and night change enemies and events; Kevin becomes a werewolf when fighting at night, and a black market opens only after dark.

The three pairs of heroes, Duran and Angela, Hawkeye and Riesz, and Kevin and Charlotte, each have their own villains and storyline, chosen by the first character picked. As Mana fades, schemers try to unleash the Benevodons, eight monsters the Mana Goddess sealed in Mana Stones, and the heroes must claim the Sword of Mana from the sanctuary of the dying Mana Tree.
trivia: In the West it was known as "Secret of Mana 2" before Square's American branch cancelled it, citing bugs that could not be fixed in time.
Producer Masaru Oyamada said in 2020 that the cartridge had no spare capacity for localisation data.
A 1999 fan translation by Neill Corlett let English speakers play it two decades before the official release.
Director Hiromichi Tanaka recalled "fighting" Hironobu Sakaguchi for staff, who were being pulled onto Chrono Trigger and Romancing SaGa 3.
"Trials" was chosen because its "tri" honoured Koichi Ishii's wish for a word with "3" in it.
devStory:
Series creator Koichi Ishii designed the game, Tanaka directed it and Tetsuhisa Tsuruzono produced, with character art by manga artist Nobuteru Yūki and music by Hiroki Kikuta, who again worked almost around the clock and made his own instrument samples. Production began in 1993 with a long period of prototypes; the team scrapped what it had built for Secret of Mana to make a more action-oriented game, layered the graphics to get as close to 3D as it could and filled the cartridge to capacity, cutting a volcano boss for time. Ishii said its theme was "independence", and Tanaka kept the story light.

Square released it in Japan on 30 September 1995. Famitsu rated it highly, a little below Secret of Mana, and later reviewers praised graphics among the best on the Super Famicom and Kikuta's score, while finding the AI companions and Ring menu clumsy in combat and the stories clichéd. It finally reached the West officially in 2019 in Collection of Mana, and a 3D remake followed in 2020.

title: Romancing SaGa
description: Romancing SaGa (1992) is Square's Super Famicom role-playing game of eight protagonists exploring the world of Mardias in any order, the debut of Akitoshi Kawazu's Free Scenario System.
longDescription:
After choosing one of eight protagonists, the player roams the overworld freely, triggering events, fighting and taking on side activities, and recruits a party that can include the unchosen heroes. The main story advances according to how many events have been completed, the party's strength and who the player has talked to, an approach called the Free Scenario System. Battles begin on touching enemy sprites, and the party fights in a formation on a three-by-three grid that affects reach and defence. There are no experience points: statistics rise at random according to actions taken in battle, abilities spend Battle Points, and new skills come from using weapons repeatedly. Fallen party members recover at the end of a battle, but losing everyone ends the game.

A thousand years earlier, three evil gods, Death, Saruin and Schirach, fought the benevolent Elore; Saruin was imprisoned by ten Fatestones and the sacrifice of the hero Mirsa, and the stones have since scattered. The protagonists, including the noble heir Albert, the nomad Aisha, the thief Jamil, the witch-raised Claudia, the pirate Hawk, the warrior Sif, the adventurer Gray and the entertainer Barbara, are drawn into recovering the Fatestones before Saruin is freed.
trivia: The "Romancing" title was suggested by Nobuyuki Inoue, inspired by the film Romancing the Stone.
The eight protagonists drew on taiga dramas, with the number referencing the novel Nansō Satomi Hakkenden.
It was artist Tomomi Kobayashi's first video game; at her busiest she designed six characters a day, 40 in all.
Yoshinori Kitase designed its field maps, and Tetsuya Takahashi was on the graphics staff.
Composer Kenji Ito described its score as "rough" compared with Final Fantasy's "smooth" sound, and was left burnt out.
devStory:
Nintendo asked Square in 1990 for a new SaGa on the upcoming Super Famicom, after the Game Boy games' success. Series creator Akitoshi Kawazu directed, designed and wrote it, aiming to replace a single path with many stories, in direct contrast to the linear Final Fantasy; writing a central plot alongside eight separate stories proved hard, and Nintendo's cartridge limits forced cuts. Kazuko Shibuya made the sprites from Kobayashi's designs, and the text used extra-large kanji to save space.

Released on 28 January 1992, Square's second Super Famicom game after Final Fantasy IV, it topped Famitsu's sales charts from February to March 1992 and sold over 1.3 million copies worldwide by 2004. Famitsu's reviewers found its graphics weaker than Final Fantasy's but praised its freedom. GamePro reported a planned English release, but its complexity and amount of text kept it in Japan. Romancing SaGa 2 and 3 followed, and it was remade for the PlayStation 2 as Minstrel Song in 2005.

title: Legend of Mana
description: Legend of Mana (1999) is Square's hand-painted PlayStation action RPG in which the player builds the world of Fa'Diel by placing artifacts on a map, a beautiful but loosely plotted spin-off of the Mana series.
longDescription:
Fights happen in real time where enemies are met, with the hero helped by a support character tied to the current quest and a companion chosen from pets, monsters and golems, either of which a second player can control. Weapons such as swords and spears each teach a set of Special Techs, used when a meter filled by landing hits is full. Instead of a fixed world, the "Land Make" system has the player place Artifacts on empty plots of a map grid; each creates a Land to enter, usually holding a quest whose reward is another Artifact. Each Land's strength in the spirits of Mana depends on the Artifact, its position and its neighbours, changing the power of magic there. Around the hero's house, players can forge and combine equipment, grow fruit, raise pets and build golems.

Nine centuries after the Mana Tree burned and the lands of Fa'Diel were sealed into artifacts, an unnamed hero sets out to restore the world. The story is told through many quests in three main arcs: the persecuted, jewel-hearted Jumi race; the dragoon siblings Larc and Sierra serving rival dragons; and the tangled love story of the childhood friends Matilda, Irwin, Daena and Escad. Completing any one arc opens the final quest to the Mana Tree.
trivia: It was made in 2D because the PlayStation could not handle the fully interactive 3D world Koichi Ishii imagined.
Producer Akitoshi Kawazu persuaded Square's executives to delay it by two months, after it had been announced, so it could be finished.
Kawazu said the project taught him that his true skill lay in producing.
Yoko Shimomura flew to Sweden to record singer Annika Ljungberg for "Song of Mana", the series' first vocal track.
It won best graphics at the 4th Japan Game Awards.
devStory:
Series creator Koichi Ishii directed, with Chrono Trigger director Akihiko Matsui as designer, character art by Shinichi Kameoka and Kawazu, of the SaGa series, as producer; Retro Gamer later noted Kawazu's heavy influence on the design. Kawazu first gave Ishii a relaxed schedule and budget for his many ideas, then tightened it when the project ran out of time, and character sprites and item mechanics were cut to fit on one CD. Shimomura, new to the series, said in 2002 that it was the soundtrack that best expressed herself.

Square released it in Japan in July 1999 with demos of Vagrant Story, Chrono Cross, Front Mission 3 and Threads of Fate. It sold over 400,000 copies in its first week and 700,000 by the end of the year, and topped the PlayStation chart in its North American launch week in June 2000. Critics adored its art, EGM calling it "the most impressive 2D artwork ever seen on a console", and its music, but found it disjointed without a main story; GamePro said its focus was "obscured by the over-abundance of subplots". A remaster followed in 2021.

title: Vandal Hearts
description: Vandal Hearts (1996) is Konami's PlayStation tactical RPG, fought on rotatable 3D grid maps with 2D sprites, in which Ash Lambert uncovers a conspiracy in the young Republic of Ishtaria.
longDescription:
Battles take place on isometric grid maps whose three-dimensional terrain can be rotated, with characters drawn as 2D sprites. Water, trees and buildings block some cells, and terrain and positioning matter to strategy. A character can use its movement all at once or split it into several moves. Each side takes its whole turn in one go: the player moves every unit before the AI responds. Most stages are won by killing every enemy, but others ask the player to kill a particular enemy, reach a spot on the map or save certain characters while defeating others. The leader's death means instant defeat, and other fallen characters cost gold and sit out the rest of the stage.

Every character belongs to one of seven classes, Swordsman, Armor, Archer, Hawknight, Monk, Mage and Cleric, balanced like rock-paper-scissors: melee fighters beat Archers, Archers beat flying Hawknights, and Hawknights beat Swordsmen. The Monk mixes healing with fair strength, the Mage specialises in attack magic and is strong against Armor, and the Cleric heals. The story is set in Ishtaria, a republic formed after the sage Arris overthrew the Holy Ashah Dynasty, where Ash Lambert and his allies uncover a plot involving General Magnus Dunbar and a magical stone, and eventually the sword the Vandal Heart.
trivia: Its Japanese subtitle translates as "The Lost Ancient Civilization".
The 1997 Saturn version, released only in Japan, added a new rendered opening, animated cut-scenes, multiple endings, extra characters, weapons and spells.
A Windows version was released only in Japan and South Korea.
Konami announced a Vandal Hearts game for the Nintendo DS in 2004 but cancelled it.
EGM named it runner-up for strategy game of 1997, behind Command & Conquer: Red Alert.
devStory: Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo developed the game for the PlayStation, and it was released in Japan in 1996 and in North America and Europe in early 1997; Konami Computer Entertainment Nagoya made the Saturn conversion. Reviews were mixed. Critics praised its use of 3D terrain in combat, its sound and its spell effects, but disliked its linear story and progression. GameSpot and Next Generation both likened it to a stripped-down Shining Force without exploration or towns; Next Generation felt "the lack of exploration is offset by the extremely engaging combat sequences", while GameSpot called it a "fatal flaw". EGM's Dan Hsu complained that it spoiled its own twists by showing betrayals before the heroes learned of them, but its four reviewers gave it their Game of the Month. Vandal Hearts II followed on the PlayStation, and a prequel, Flames of Judgment, on PlayStation Network and Xbox Live Arcade.

title: Legend of Legaia
description: Legend of Legaia (1998) is Prokion's PlayStation role-playing game whose "Tactical Arts System" turns turn-based attacks into input combos, set in a world where a mysterious Mist has turned humanity's helpful Seru against it.
longDescription:
Random battles are turn-based, but attacking means building a sequence of directional strikes that the character then performs. Entering certain sequences in the right order unleashes powerful techniques called Arts, which can be chained by overlapping compatible inputs. Arts cost AP, regained by attacking, taking damage or using the Spirit command, which also greatly reduces damage taken and allows a longer sequence the next turn. Arts are found by experimenting in battle with enough AP or by talking to certain people, while stronger Hyper Arts must first be unlocked with items called Books. Equipping a weapon replaces one attack direction with Arms. The heroes also bond with Ra-Seru, rare companions who can capture the essence of enemy Seru to summon them with magic points, and who replace an attack direction and grow stronger as they level up.

In this world the magical Seru once helped people, alone or attached to them, until a Mist appeared and drove them wild, collapsing civilisation. On the eve of his first hunt, Vahn sees a giant Seru smash the wall of his village, Rim Elm, letting in the Mist. He bonds with a Ra-Seru named Meta, unaffected by the Mist, to awaken the village's Genesis Tree, then sets out across the world with the cavegirl Noa and the monk Gala to restore Genesis Trees and stop the Mist.
trivia: Contrail handled its production for Sony.
The Ra-Seru are immune to the Mist because, it is revealed, the Mist is made from Ra-Seru.
Next Generation said that if players could "deal with the trite, hackneyed story, the new fighting engine makes this worth checking out".
It was nominated for console RPG of the year at the 3rd Interactive Achievement Awards.
It was released in Europe only in May 2000, more than a year after North America.
devStory: Prokion developed the game for Sony Computer Entertainment, with Contrail as producer, and it was released in Japan in October 1998, North America in March 1999 and Europe in May 2000. Reviews recorded by GameRankings were favourable, and Next Generation felt its new fighting engine outweighed a trite story; Famitsu scored it 27 out of 40. The Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences nominated it for console adventure/role-playing game of the year. It had sold over 300,000 copies by January 2002, and a sequel, Legaia 2: Duel Saga, followed on the PlayStation 2.

title: Tales of Destiny
description: Tales of Destiny (1997) is the second main Tales game, Wolf Team's PlayStation action RPG about a stowaway who finds a talking sword, and for years the best-selling Tales game in Japan.
longDescription:
Battles use an enhanced version of Tales of Phantasia's Linear Motion Battle System, fought in real time on a 2D plane, playing more like a side-scrolling action game than a turn-based RPG. Melee and ranged attacks happen instantly, while spells need a chanting time that grows with their complexity, and when a spell goes off, the battle pauses for its animation. Special attacks hit harder or more often but cost technical points, and stringing together multi-hit combos earns extra experience. The player directly controls one character, with the rest run by AI following set strategies and formations, and can switch characters or order spells and specials for anyone through an in-battle menu. Spells and techniques can be assigned to button and direction combinations beforehand.

Long ago a comet darkened the world, and the Aetherians used Lens energy from its core to build cities in the sky, leaving the Erthers on the surface and dominating them with the superweapon Belcrant. Dissident Aetherian scientists helped the surface people forge sentient swords called Swordians, which won the Aeth'er Wars. Thousands of years later, country boy Stahn Aileron stows away on the flying ship Draconis, finds a "junk" sword that speaks to him as the Swordian Dymlos, and is drawn into a struggle over a giant Lens called the Eye of Atamoni.
trivia: Its North American producer said that because the 2D graphics were so "ordinary", the team focused on "an outstanding localization".
Namco America planned an English dub, but the final release kept the Japanese voices.
The Japanese opening theme, "Yume de Aruyouni" by Deen, was replaced in English for licensing reasons.
Its animated cut-scenes were made by Production I.G.
Tales of Eternia was released in North America as "Tales of Destiny II", though it is not this game's sequel.
devStory:
Many of Tales of Phantasia's staff at Telenet Japan's Wolf Team made the game, including composers Motoi Sakuraba and Shinji Tamura, with new character designer Mutsumi Inomata. Shown at the Tokyo Game Show in September 1997, it was released in Japan that December and in North America in September 1998. Famitsu gave it a Silver Award, and it sold over 450,000 copies in Japan by the end of 1997, earning a Gold Prize from Sony for passing 500,000; it reached about 1,139,000 worldwide by December 2007, the best-selling single-platform Tales game at the time.

Western reviews averaged 73% on GameRankings. IGN called it "highly recommended, as long as you're a fan of the classic Super NES", and RPGFan called its battles "a blast to play", while GameSpot gave it 4.9, criticising a "stale and exceedingly slow-moving story" and graphics that looked like an SNES game. A PlayStation 2 remake followed in Japan in 2006 and a Director's Cut in 2008.

title: Devil Summoner: Soul Hackers
description: Devil Summoner: Soul Hackers (1997) is Atlus's cyberpunk Megami Tensei role-playing game for the Saturn, in which a young hacker in a networked city negotiates with demons, recruits and fuses them, and fights alongside them.
longDescription:
Players explore dungeons in first person, solving puzzles and fighting demons in turn-based battles. The party always has one or two humans and can summon up to four demons. New demons are recruited by talking to enemies and negotiating, answering their questions, intimidating them or giving them items they want, and several allied demons can be fused into a single new one that inherits their abilities. Allied demons behave according to personality and alignment: friendly ones prefer healing and defence, while sly ones attack on their own, and a demon ordered to do something it dislikes may refuse or do nothing. Demons of clashing alignments may not co-operate. Raising their loyalty with gifts, or by letting them act freely, helps. Summoned demons consume magnetite, earned in battle or traded for, and take damage if it runs out.

The game is set in Amami City, a harbour town where the company Algon Soft has wired every home and business into a network as a demonstration of a "city of tomorrow", along with a virtual world called Paradigm X. The hero, a member of the hacker group the Spookies, gets into Paradigm X's closed beta and runs into supernatural forces, investigating demon attacks across the city with help from Nemissa, a demon possessing his friend Hitomi.
trivia: Its concept came from the internet boom around Windows 95, which made producer Kouji Okada and designer Kazuma Kaneko think about networks used as a means of control.
