Future Persona artist Shigenori Soejima designed sub-characters, items and the hero's portraits.
Composer Shoji Meguro blended jazz and techno to emphasise the cyberpunk setting.
Sony of America's content approval policy reportedly blocked a localisation of the PlayStation version.
It was first released in English only in 2013, on the Nintendo 3DS.
devStory:
After the success of the first Devil Summoner, development began in 1996 with Okada producing and Kaneko returning as character and demon designer. Kaneko created the world, writer Shogo Isogai the detailed story scenes, and the team experimented with showing different characters' points of view, drawing much of its antagonist Manitou and other elements from Native American folklore. Amami City was invented as a futuristic city on the opposite side of Japan from the first game's setting. Meguro wrote around fifty pieces, with less memory and freedom than he wanted, and found the project exhausting.

Atlus released it for the Saturn on 13 November 1997. It sold 160,850 copies in its first week and 258,679 by 2007, the 27th best-selling Saturn game in Japan. Its popularity led to a 1999 PlayStation port with new events and a Paradigm X casino, which sold 137,458 by the end of that year. The 2012 3DS version added full voice acting; critics liked its challenging battles and demon negotiation but found its dungeons bland. Soul Hackers 2 followed in 2022.

title: Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus
description: Oddworld: Abe's Exoddus (1998) is Oddworld Inhabitants' puzzle-platform sequel, made in nine months, in which Abe tries to stop the Glukkons brewing a drink from Mudokon bones and tears, now with quick saves and emotional Mudokons.
longDescription:
The game keeps Abe's Oddysee's flip-screen 2D design with no on-screen interface; touching hazards, being shot or falling usually means instant death, but lives are unlimited and the player restarts at the last checkpoint, and now can quick save anywhere. Puzzles use Abe's moves and abilities: GameSpeak phrases to command fellow Mudokons, chanting to possess enemies such as Sligs and Glukkons, throwing rocks, grenades and bones, and working mine cars and levers. A secondary goal is leading enslaved Mudokons to Bird Portals. This time Mudokons have moods: angry ones slap others, depressed ones may kill themselves if they see too much death, laughing gas makes them "wired", sick ones need a healing chant, and blind ones walk towards Abe's voice until told to wait. After drinking the Brew, Abe can even possess his own fart and use it as a flying explosive.

After destroying RuptureFarms, Abe learns from three Mudokon spirits that the Glukkons have turned the ancient burial grounds of Necrum into mines. His friends fall ill after drinking SoulStorm Brew, made from Mudokon bones, and later he discovers that the Brewery also extracts their tears by electrocuting slaves. Saving at least 150 of the 278 Mudokons earns the good ending.
trivia: Director Lorne Lanning said: "we killed ourselves getting Abe's Exoddus done in nine months. It was brutal."
The team added quick saves after reading forum complaints about Abe's Oddysee's saving and trial-and-error puzzles.
Its cinematics cost about $2 million, roughly half the budget, and were submitted as a short film for the 71st Academy Awards.
Killing all 278 Mudokons earns invincibility in an alternative "Maximum Casualties" ending.
It is considered a spin-off, not part of the planned Oddworld Quintology.
devStory:
After Abe's Oddysee's success, publisher GT Interactive pushed for a sequel by Christmas 1998, so Oddworld Inhabitants built it on the same engine. It was released for the PlayStation in November 1998 and Windows that December. CEO Sherry McKenna said the Academy Award submission was meant to improve the industry's reputation in animation: "If the game industry is ever going to have the reputation it deserves, we have to start somewhere."

Reviews were mostly positive and welcomed the quick save. Edge praised Abe's abilities but found it too similar to its predecessor, while GameSpot said that though it was "more of the same, it's more of a good thing", and IGN liked its improved graphics but disliked its trial and error. It won GamePro's E3 Showstopper award and was a finalist for console adventure and console game of the year, losing both to Ocarina of Time. In Germany it earned a Gold award for over 100,000 sales. A Game Boy Color version appeared as Oddworld Adventures 2, and it was reimagined as Oddworld: Soulstorm in 2021.

title: Twisted Metal 2
description: Twisted Metal 2 (1996) is SingleTrac's PlayStation vehicular combat sequel, a globe-trotting demolition derby with missiles that sold 1.74 million copies in the US and drew a lawsuit from an ice cream truck company.
longDescription:
In concept it is a demolition derby that allows ballistic projectiles. Players choose a vehicle and an arena, or a series of arenas in the story mode, and fight the other drivers using weapons collected from pick-ups scattered around the stage; the last one left wins. The two-player duel mode returns from the first game, and a new co-operative mode lets two players fight through the tournament as a team, though finishing it that way shows no ending.

A year after the first contest, held by the mysterious Calypso on Christmas Eve, Los Angeles is in ruins. Aboard his airship, its ticker reading "CALYPSO RULER OF THE EARTH", Calypso decides that the next Twisted Metal will use the whole world as its battleground, and fourteen of the world's best drivers gather to compete for whatever prize they desire. Besides the remains of Los Angeles, the arenas include Moscow, Paris, Amazonia, New York City, Antarctica, the Netherlands and Hong Kong. The player faces the boss Minion after Amazonia, and Dark Tooth after Hong Kong, before meeting Calypso in New York to claim the prize.
trivia: Frosty Treats, an ice cream truck company, sued Sony over the phrase "Frosty Treats" and similarities between Sweet Tooth and its safety clown; the appeals court rejected the claims.
SingleTrac was given 16 months to develop it, much longer than the first game.
The Windows version had cut-down graphics but did not need a 3D card and supported modem and internet multiplayer.
Its 1998 Greatest Hits re-release was published under 989 Studios.
GameSpot inducted it into its list of the greatest games of all time in 2003.
devStory: SingleTrac began brainstorming a sequel in late 1995 and, thanks to the first game's success, had 16 months to make it; Sony released it for the PlayStation and Windows in 1996. It was a financial and critical success, selling 1.74 million copies in the US alone, with the PlayStation version averaging 86.44% on GameRankings, though the PC version averaged under 50%. Critics saw it as an improvement over the original for its larger, more intricate levels and better characters, but were divided on its graphics: EGM's reviewers felt they had not improved, while Next Generation praised sharper textures, less clipping and a better frame rate. GamePro said "intense gameplay is what saves, and makes, the game", especially head to head. It was runner-up for EGM's action game of the year, and EGM later ranked it 64th among the best games of all time.

title: Primal Rage
description: Primal Rage (1994) is Atari Games' stop-motion dinosaur and ape fighting game set on a post-apocalyptic "Urth", whose gory finishing moves made it a hit, a merchandising success and a target of controversy.
longDescription:
Seven prehistoric beast-gods fight one-on-one: Blizzard, the ape god of good; Armadon, god of life; the raptor Talon, god of survival; the tyrannosaur Sauron, god of hunger; Chaos, the ape god of decay; Vertigo, the cobra goddess of insanity; and Diablo, the tyrannosaur god of evil. Each fights in its own domain, from the Cliff to the Inferno. Human worshippers wander the arenas and can be tossed about or eaten to regain health, scoring a bonus for eating the opponent's followers and a penalty for eating one's own. Before the final battle against every other monster, a minigame lets the player eat as many worshippers as possible to boost health for the endurance round. Two players can trigger hidden volleyball and bowling minigames played with humans.

Unusually, special moves are performed by holding buttons and then moving the joystick, though later arcade revisions also accepted the usual motion-then-button method. After a win, players can perform finishing moves, some of them comic, such as Vertigo turning her opponent into a cow. The setting is an Earth devastated by a meteor strike, its people reduced to Stone Age tribes and its continents shifted into the shape of a dinosaur skull.
trivia: Its fighters were clay models with metal armatures, animated in stop motion at about 400 frames each.
Animator Jason Leong pitched dinosaur gods at an annual brainstorm; someone else pitched only two T. rexes fighting.
Its unusual copy protection has prevented perfect emulation of the arcade original.
A parent's campaign over Chaos's urination fatality led Best Buy to pull the game from 251 stores; the ESRB re-rated it T.
Atari made more profit from its merchandise, such as action figures and comics, than from the game itself.
devStory: Production coordinator Stephen Riesenberger said it was designed to be accessible, with four buttons rather than six and special moves easy to pull off by button mashing. Time Warner Interactive released it in arcades in August 1994 in standard and deluxe cabinets, and RePlay reported it as the third most popular deluxe arcade game. Next Generation called it "an excellent show of graphics and sound design tarnished by unbalanced gameplay". It was ported to the Genesis, SNES, Game Boy, Game Gear, 3DO, 32X, Jaguar CD, PlayStation, Saturn, MS-DOS and Amiga, with reviews ranging from praise for the handheld versions to criticism of small sprites on the 16-bit consoles and dated play on the later ones. It sold more than 1.5 million copies and was nominated for the VSDA's game of the year. A sequel, Primal Rage II, was cancelled in development, its story later told in the novel Primal Rage: The Avatars.

title: Eternal Champions
description: Eternal Champions (1993) is Sega's own answer to Street Fighter II and Mortal Kombat on the Genesis, a story-driven fighter of nine souls plucked from history moments before their deaths, with stage-specific "Overkill" finishers.
longDescription:
Like Street Fighter II, it uses three punch and three kick buttons; players with the three-button Genesis pad press Start to switch between punches and kicks, and it also supports the Sega Activator motion ring. Each character's special moves, performed by pressing buttons together or charging, can reflect projectiles, scramble the opponent's controls or apply status effects, and they drain an "inner strength" meter that slowly recharges and can be depleted by taunts. Knocking a defeated opponent onto the right spot of a stage triggers an Overkill, in which part of the background kills them. Modes include an arcade ladder, practice, a Battle Room with extra hazards, and a training mode of mini-games.

The Eternal Champion foresees that mankind will fade because of the unjust deaths of key people throughout history, but has power to restore only one, so holds a tournament among them. The nine fighters include Larcen Tyler, a 1920s Chicago cat burglar killed in a hospital bombing; Jetta Maxx, a Russian aristocrat murdered on a tightrope in 1899; the ninja Shadow Yamato, thrown from a skyscraper in 1993; the cyber-kickboxer R.A.X. Coswell from 2345; and Xavier Pendragon, executed in the Salem witch trials. Winning reveals how the champion escaped death and changed their era.
trivia: Comic artist Ernie Chan drew much of the character design and art, credited only under "special thanks".
A player using the Sega Activator took 50% less damage and dealt 50% more than one using a pad.
It was promoted with a Sega Eternal Champions Cherry Slurpee at 7-Eleven.
IGN ranked its Overkills the best gore effects in video game history in 2006.
A Saturn sequel was cancelled because Sega of Japan felt Eternal Champions was holding back Virtua Fighter in the US.
devStory: Sega made the game after the success of Street Fighter II and Mortal Kombat, trying to stand apart with a stronger story, its own mechanics and elaborate finishing moves. It was released in North America in December 1993, with Europe and Japan following in early 1994. Reviews were mixed, averaging 62.5% on GameRankings: Mean Machines Sega gave it 97% and called it "at least as good" as Street Fighter II, while two of EGM's four reviewers found it a major disappointment with mediocre graphics and dull characters. It was the UK's best-selling Mega Drive game in February 1994 and sold over 1.6 million copies. The Sega CD's Eternal Champions: Challenge from the Dark Side followed in 1995, along with spin-offs Chicago Syndicate and X-Perts. Sega and Skydance announced a film adaptation in 2024.

title: ClayFighter
description: ClayFighter (1993) is Visual Concepts and Interplay's comic SNES fighting game, a parody of Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat with stop-motion clay fighters such as a snowman, an Elvis impersonator and an opera-singing Viking.
longDescription:
A meteor made entirely of clay crash-lands at an American circus, and its goo turns the circus attractions into bizarre caricatures with superpowers. The eight fighters, digitised from photographed clay models, are Bad Mr. Frosty, a snowman with an attitude who throws snowballs and rolls into opponents as a snow boulder; Blob, a master of "goojitsu" who morphs into objects such as a buzzsaw; Blue Suede Goo, an Elvis impersonator who throws musical notes and slashes with his hair; Bonker, a manic clown with pies and a big hammer; Helga, a Viking opera singer with a sonic scream; Ickybod Clay, a pumpkin-headed ghost who teleports; Taffy, whose stretchy body gives him some of the longest reach in the game; and Tiny, a posing wrestler who mostly punches.

Each fights on a themed stage, such as Frosty's icy lake with penguin spectators or Blue Suede Goo's flaming piano reading "Big Hunk O' Burnin' Clay". The final boss, N. Boss, a string of pearls whose name puns on M. Bison and "end boss", copies others' projectiles and is the only character not made of clay.
trivia: Artists at Danger Productions made about 70 clay models of Blob alone to capture his movements.
Thin Taffy was built from a stronger type of clay than simple Blob.
Interplay pitched it to parents who objected to "blood-and-guts games" as a non-violent alternative.
EGM named it Best Street Fighter Wannabee of 1993, and gave it awards for sound effects and its advert.
ClayFighter: Tournament Edition was first offered only as a Blockbuster rental.
devStory:
Visual Concepts president Greg Thomas conceived it as a "new" and "funny" alternative to violent fighting games, and took the idea to animators Ken Pontac and David Bleiman of Danger Productions in Brisbane, California. The two companies worked for nearly a year: Danger's artists spent months sculpting the fighters in different poses, and they were animated by stop-motion photography and digitised with a video camera linked to an Amiga, a process designer Jeremy Airey called long and tedious. Interplay spliced new animations and recorded the music, voices and sound effects.

It was released on the SNES in November 1993 and the Genesis in 1994, and had sold 200,000 copies by 1994. GamePro wrote that "fighting fans with a funny bone will enjoy ClayFighter", and EGM praised the Genesis version for keeping all the content, though it needed a six-button pad. Tournament Edition fixed glitches and added stages and modes in 1994, followed by ClayFighter 2: Judgment Clay and ClayFighter 63⅓.

title: Top Gear
description: Top Gear (1992) is Gremlin Graphics' early SNES racer from the makers of the Lotus games, a split-screen world tour with fuel to manage, three nitros per race and a Barry Leitch soundtrack that became a cult favourite in Brazil.
longDescription:
The aim is to become the world's fastest driver by racing across several countries, finishing in the top five to qualify for each next race. One player or two in split screen can take part, and players register a name and choose manual transmission, shifting with the shoulder buttons, or automatic. Four controller layouts remap acceleration, braking, gears and nitro. There are four cars with different handling, top speed and fuel use: the Cannibal is fast but has poor grip and drinks fuel, while the Sidewinder corners well and is economical.

Races come in regions of four courses, with points for finishing positions and a cumulative ranking deciding whether the player moves on to the next region. Each race allows three nitro boosts for bursts of speed. Running out of fuel ends a race, so players must judge when to make a pit stop to refuel at the cost of time. Races are held by day and night, and obstacles on the road slow the car badly on impact. Speed can be shown in miles or kilometres per hour.
trivia: Composer Barry Leitch reworked some tracks from his music for Lotus Turbo Challenge to meet a tight schedule.
The team reverse-engineered the SNES music driver, whose documentation was mostly in Japanese.
Memory limits meant the music's echo effect was set to one sixteenth note, the longest that would fit.
Brazilian studio Aquiris hired Leitch to score Horizon Chase, a spiritual successor.
It has been re-released under the name Top Racer.
devStory:
Gremlin Graphics, who had made the Lotus series on the Amiga and Mega Drive, developed the game for Kemco, and it was one of the first racing games on the SNES, released in 1992. The music was composed using the SNES ICE development kit with a sound card installed in a PC and custom software called MEDIT, which let the team take advantage of the SNES's eight-channel SPC700 sound chip and its real-time echo, uncommon on consoles of the time. Leitch said the "Vegas" track was one of the first pieces written for the game, built on his favourite chord progressions.

It received a positive reception, and readers of Super Famicom Magazine gave it 20.82 out of 30 in 1993. It became especially popular in Brazil in the early 1990s, helped by rental shops and widespread piracy, where it competed with F-Zero and Super Mario Kart, and its soundtrack, particularly the main theme, has since inspired thousands of fan covers online. It began the Top Gear series.

title: Mickey Mania: The Timeless Adventures of Mickey Mouse
description: Mickey Mania (1994) is Traveller's Tales' platformer for the SNES, Genesis and Sega CD in which Mickey travels through his own classic cartoons, from Steamboat Willie to The Prince and the Pauper.
longDescription:
Mickey visits levels based on his past cartoons: Steamboat Willie (1928), The Mad Doctor (1933), The Band Concert (1935), Moose Hunters and Lonesome Ghosts (1937), Mickey and the Beanstalk (1947) and The Prince and the Pauper (1990). He attacks by jumping on enemies or throwing a limited supply of marbles collected along the way. He can take five hits, shown by the fingers he holds up, restored by collecting stars, and Mickey hats give extra lives. Levels mix platforming with puzzles and set pieces such as escaping a rampaging moose and fleeing down a staircase as it bursts into flames.

The versions differ. The SNES version lacks the hidden Band Concert level and the Mad Doctor staircase and adds loading screens. The Sega CD version adds a CD soundtrack, extensive dialogue for Mickey and a finale in which he gathers pencils to summon the Mickeys from the other levels against Pete. The 1996 PlayStation version, Mickey's Wild Adventure, remade the sprites, rendered the staircase scenes in 3D and added a chase by Willie the Giant.
trivia: It was first meant for Mickey's 65th birthday in 1993, but that would have left only six months to make it.
It was designer David Jaffe's first design project.
Michael Giacchino contributed additional music to the CD versions.
A sequel was prototyped in 1994 but cancelled so Traveller's Tales could make a Toy Story game.
It won a 1994 Parents' Choice Award, and VideoGames named it the best Sega CD game.
devStory:
Traveller's Tales dropped the birthday tie-in in favour of the idea of Mickey travelling back into his own cartoons, recreating their events as a tribute to his early career. Sony Imagesoft published it in 1994 for the SNES, Genesis and Sega CD, with a CD soundtrack by Andy Blythe and Marten Joustra, and Psygnosis made the enhanced PlayStation port for Europe in 1996.

Critics praised its graphics and homage to the cartoons. GamePro found "the blend of past and present is magical" while calling the Genesis version too easy, although another GamePro reviewer thought the SNES version too hard for young players. Next Generation gave the Sega CD version four stars, saying "if you've got kids, I think it's the law", and Power Unlimited gave the SNES version 91%. Famitsu scored the SNES version 28 and the Genesis version 30 out of 40. Maximum gave the PlayStation version two stars for making no noticeable improvements, and in 2018 Complex ranked it 49th among SNES games.

title: The Lion King
description: The Lion King (1994) is Westwood Studios' SNES and Genesis platformer of the Disney film, drawn by Disney's own animators, famous for its beauty and for a difficulty its director later admitted was meant to beat rental periods.
longDescription:
Simba follows the events of the film, first as a cub and later as an adult. Young Simba mainly defeats enemies by jumping on them and has a roar, drawn from a refilling meter, that stuns enemies and solves puzzles. Grown-up Simba gains combat moves such as scratching, mauling and throwing. Lives are lost by running out of health, falling into pits, water or lava, or being hit by rolling boulders and falling stalactites, and checkpoints mark restart points. Continues, collected as Circle of Life icons, let the player restart the last stage reached.

Bugs restore health, rarer ones permanently extend the health and roar meters, and black spiders hurt. Hidden bugs open bonus stages: as Pumbaa, the player catches falling bugs until one hits the bottom or he eats a bad one, and as Timon, the player hunts bugs against the clock while avoiding spiders, earning extra lives and continues. Two levels, Hakuna Matata and Be Prepared, were adapted from scenes cut from the finished film.
trivia: Disney's own animators at Walt Disney Feature Animation drew its sprites and backgrounds.
Late in development the monkey puzzle in "Can't Wait to be King" was made harder to meet Disney's playtime requirements; there was no time to add levels.
Director Louis Castle said Disney wanted it hard so players could not finish it within a Blockbuster rental, and later apologised.
Dave Semmons wrote the Amiga version in assembly in two months, expecting Genesis code in 68000 assembly and finding it was written in C.
The 1995 European NES version was the last official NES release anywhere.
devStory:
Westwood developed the SNES and Genesis versions between January and July 1994 for Virgin Interactive, adapting the film's songs and orchestrations for the music, while other studios made the MS-DOS, Master System, Game Gear, NES and Game Boy versions. Of its $20 million budget, $8 million went on marketing. The SNES version sold 1.27 million copies in the US, it was the third best-selling game across formats in the UK at Christmas 1994, and Castle put total sales at about 4.5 million.

GamePro praised its "movie-quality graphics, animations, and sounds" but found the gameplay repetitive and the difficulty uneven, while Next Generation said that though much harder than Aladdin it was "never unfair or frustrating". Entertainment Weekly gave the SNES version an A, likening adult Simba's fights to "a PBS nature documentary", and EGM thought the Game Gear version controlled better than the 16-bit ones. It was re-released in Disney Classic Games: Aladdin and The Lion King in 2019.

title: Sonic 3D Blast
description: Sonic 3D Blast (1996), Sonic 3D: Flickies' Island outside North America, is the last Sonic game for the Genesis, an isometric platformer built mostly by Traveller's Tales in which Sonic rescues captive birds.
longDescription:
Seen from an isometric angle, with pre-rendered 3D models turned into sprites, Sonic keeps his jump, spin attack and spin-dash, collects rings as health and breaks monitors for shields, speed shoes and invincibility. Each zone has two acts in which he must free the Flickies, birds that Robotnik has trapped in robots, by destroying the robots, collecting all five birds in each section to move on, followed by a boss fight. Getting hit scatters both rings and Flickies; blue, pink and orange birds try to find Sonic again, while green and red ones wander and hop away. Ten Sonic medals give a continue.

Tails or Knuckles hide in each level, and standing next to one with at least 50 rings opens a special stage, viewed from behind Sonic as he runs a set path collecting rings and avoiding obstacles to win a Chaos Emerald. Gathering all seven unlocks the final fight and the true ending; otherwise Robotnik escapes with an Emerald. The story has Robotnik discover the Flickies on an island in another dimension and exploit their ability to travel through rings to hunt for the Emeralds.
trivia: It was originally titled Sonic Spindrift.
Lead programmer Jon Burton made errors open a secret level select instead of crashing, to help the game pass Sega's approval.
Burton squeezed a full-motion video intro into the 4 MB cartridge using compression.
The Saturn port, made in seven weeks, replaced the cancelled Sonic X-treme as Sega's Christmas 1996 Sonic game.
In 2017 Burton released an unofficial director's cut with better controls, a level editor and Super Sonic.
devStory:
Sonic Team conceived the idea during Sonic the Hedgehog 3, but was busy with Nights into Dreams, so Sega asked Traveller's Tales, impressed by its Toy Story and Mickey Mania games, to program it, with Sonic Team supplying designs. Development took eight months from July 1995. The isometric view drew on Sonic Labyrinth and Super Mario RPG, the bird collecting on the 1984 game Flicky, and the graphics on Donkey Kong Country. Jun Senoue and Tatsuyuki Maeda composed the Genesis music, while the Saturn version had a new CD score by Richard Jacques.

Both versions were released in November 1996, and the Genesis game sold over 700,000 copies, by one Sega employee's account. Contemporary reviews were positive: Computer and Video Games called it "the first essential Mega Drive game in years", praising the graphics and music, though some found the controls hard to adjust to. Critics thought the Saturn version too similar to the Genesis one, and later reviewers turned against the slow, isometric play, IGN calling it "a looping, lazy fetchquest", while still praising its visuals and soundtrack.

title: Golden Axe II
description: Golden Axe II (1991) is Sega's Genesis sequel to its fantasy beat 'em up, in which Ax Battler, Tyris Flare and Gilius Thunderhead retrieve the Golden Axe from the tyrant Dark Guld, with reworked magic and attacks.
longDescription:
The side-scrolling hack-and-slash play is almost identical to the first game. Players choose the barbarian Ax Battler with his two-handed sword, the amazon Tyris Flare with her longsword or the dwarf Gilius Thunderhead with his axe, each with their own elemental magic and a set of life bars. Several changes refine it. The back attack, triggered by pressing jump and attack together, now hits enemies on every side, and grabbed enemies can be thrown in either direction, including off cliffs. Rather than spending every magic pot at once, players hold the magic button and release it when the meter reaches the level they want. Ax Battler's explosive magic becomes wind, Gilius swaps lightning for rock, and Tyris keeps fire with new animations, while Ax Battler gains longer reach and stronger throws.

The main mode crosses seven stages, from a Ravaged Village and Ruins to Dragon's Throat Cave and Dark Guld's Chamber, each ending with a fight against a large group of enemies, collecting magic books along the way and riding three kinds of Bizarrian: Chicken Legs, green dragons and fire dragons. A rating follows each level. The Duel mode pits players against fifteen rounds of enemies in an arena. The story has Dark Guld, freed from ancient imprisonment a few years after Death Adder's defeat, seize the Golden Axe and lay waste to the land of Yuria.
trivia: It was also released in arcades on Sega's Mega-Tech cabinet, which played Genesis games.
Ax Battler gained a shoulder guard and Gilius black gauntlets.
Micom BASIC Magazine ranked it second in popularity in its March 1992 issue.
Mega placed it 14th in its Top Mega Drive Games of All Time.
The arcade follow-up Golden Axe: The Revenge of Death Adder indirectly addressed criticism of it.
devStory: Sega developed and published Golden Axe II for the Genesis in 1991 as the second game in the series, refining the original's mechanics rather than replacing them. It received generally favourable reviews, though many found it too close to its predecessor. Console XS thought it easier than the first game, Mega Action called it bigger and better but said "If you want more of the same, then this is for you", and AllGame's Scott Alan Marriott noted almost identical graphics, sound and options, concluding that "fans of the original probably won't mind that it's more of the same". In Japan readers of Mega Drive Fan gave it 20.95 out of 30. It has since been re-released in the Sega Genesis Collection, on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007, on Steam and in Sega Genesis Classics, and GamesRadar ranked it 34th among Mega Drive games in 2017.

title: Road Rash II
description: Road Rash II (1992) is EA's Genesis sequel to its brawling motorcycle racer, taking illegal races across the United States and adding split-screen two-player, nitro and chains, and the first game in which you could beat a cop.
longDescription:
The player races fourteen others and must finish third or better, winning a race on each of five tracks, set in Hawaii, Arizona, Tennessee, Alaska and Vermont, to advance through five levels. While riding, the player can punch, backhand or kick neighbouring racers and steal clubs and chains from opponents who swing them. Crashing into boulders, cars, deer or cows, or running out of stamina in fights, throws the rider from the bike to run back to it. Starting with $1,000, the player earns prize money to buy bikes of differing weight, speed and steering, some with nitrous charges fired by double-tapping the accelerator. A password saves progress.

Each crash wears down the bike's condition meter, and a wrecked bike or an arrest by the police ends the race with a repair bill or fine. Both grow, along with prize money, course length and aggression, at each level, and running out of money ends the game. Two players can take turns or race at once in split screen, either among the computer racers or alone in "Mano a Mano", choosing weapons before the start.
trivia: Artist Arthur Koch filmed himself swinging a chain as reference for the new weapon.
The cut-scenes' ten-pixel-tall characters were nicknamed "little dudes" by the team.
Letting players fight police officers caused uncertainty because of the recent beating of Rodney King.
The yellow Yamaha FZR1000 on the cover was producer Randy Breen's own bike.
It was Europe's second best-selling home game of 1992, behind Sonic the Hedgehog 2.
devStory:
EA decided on a sequel before the end of the 1991 Christmas season and set a deadline of the next Christmas, which the team thought tight, but the first game's framework let them concentrate on improvements. A team of three programmers, five artists and four track builders included returning producer and designer Randy Breen and programmer Dan Geisler. Breen expanded the races beyond California, saying they had "gradually expanded outward" from secret local races, "kind of a fight club thing". Moving from 5 to 8 megabits allowed the split-screen mode, which took Geisler about three months. Opponents were made less predictable, and police could now take damage and fight back. Rob Hubbard was among the audio team.

Released in December 1992, it outsold the first game. Critics praised the two-player mode and visuals, GamePro calling it "a noteworthy improvement on an already excellent game", while Mean Machines Sega and EGM felt the core play barely changed. A Game Boy Color version followed in 2000 as Road Rash.

title: NHL '94
description: NHL '94 (1993) is EA Sports' ice hockey game for the Genesis, SNES and PC, the first in its series with both NHL and players' union licences, and widely considered the greatest hockey game of all time.
longDescription:
The game keeps the series' vertical camera, which gave advantages over side-view hockey games, and NHLPA '93's 2D sprites with new animations. Its rosters reflect the 1992–93 season, including that year's expansion teams, the Mighty Ducks of Anaheim and the Florida Panthers. The key addition is the one-timer, shooting the puck straight off a pass, along with manual goalie control and the ability to save team and player records. Modes include exhibition games, single-game and best-of-seven Stanley Cup playoffs, a shootout and a demo, with both all-star teams but no international sides.

Team-specific organ songs play at the start of periods and after goals, such as the Hartford Whalers' "Brass Bonanza", "When the Saints Go Marching In" for the St. Louis Blues and the Chicago Blackhawks' "Here Come the Hawks", recorded by Los Angeles Kings organist Dieter Ruehle. Fighting, present in earlier games, was removed as part of the league licence.
trivia: It was planned as NHLPA Hockey '94 until EA sought permission to use NHL footage in the Sega CD version.
Programmer Mark Lesser, reassigned from John Madden Football '93, knew little about hockey.
Winnipeg Jets staffer Igor Kuperman rated the players in twelve categories, from zero to six.
A copy was placed in the Hockey Hall of Fame's archives in 2018.
Jeremy Roenick has credited his fame partly to being one of the game's best players.
devStory:
After NHLPA Hockey '93's success, EA planned a sequel with only the players' union licence, and producer Michael Brook meant to keep fighting, which the NHL had opposed. Lesser programmed the Genesis version, focusing on the camera, scrolling, puck control and speed, while EA's Canadian branch made the SNES and PC versions from his code. The team favoured accessible play over strict simulation, and Brook turned Kuperman's ratings into the game's numbers with extra statistics and a random factor; Kings coach Barry Melrose gave feedback on a development build. Late on, an agreement with the NHL brought official team names and logos in exchange for removing fighting.

It launched to acclaim in 1993. Computer Gaming World praised its "playing environment that is flush with realism, excitement and credibility", GamePro gave the Sega CD version a perfect score, and Lesser recalled it outselling the million-selling Madden '93. EGM ranked it 61st among the best games of all time in 1997, and it inspired leagues and tournaments such as Toronto's King of '94.

title: Virtua Cop 2
description: Virtua Cop 2 (1995) is Sega AM2's polygonal light-gun sequel, adding branching routes, car and subway chases and a third cop, Janet Marshall, and Japan's highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1996.
longDescription:
Players move automatically along a set path through three levels, but unlike the first game they choose between two routes at certain points. The job is to shoot criminals before they fire back, avoiding innocent bystanders, while breakable background objects can hide power-ups. As before, "justice shots" to an enemy's gun hand disarm them for extra points, and avoiding hits and hostages builds a score multiplier. Each level ends with a boss, followed by a final boss after all three. A Proving Ground mode sets players in hostile urban environments to fight through thugs and hunt down the rival player.

The Virtua City Police officers Michael "Rage" Hardy and James "Smarty" Cools, who brought down the E.V.I.L. Inc. criminal empire, are joined by Janet Marshall, an expert in criminal profiling. After a bank vice-president dies in suspicious circumstances and E.V.I.L.'s laundered accounts are emptied, a jewellery heist, a hostage-taking of the mayor on a ship and strange activity at a subway construction site lead back to terrorist Joe Fang, thought killed in a helicopter crash, whom players finally shoot down as he attacks on a jet pack.
trivia: In February 1995 AM2's Fumio Kurokawa said the team was "not sure if there will be [a] VC2".
It sold about 7,000 arcade cabinets by 1996, 4,000 of them in Japan.
Saturn development was slowed because AM2 prioritised the Saturn versions of Fighting Vipers and Virtua Fighter Kids.
A Saturn cheat code lets player one play as Janet.
The North American PC release was titled Virtua Squad 2.
devStory:
After the first Virtua Cop did well in arcades, Sega AM2 followed it with Virtua Cop 2 in 1995. Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful dedicated arcade game in its 1 November 1995 issue, and it became the highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1996 in Japan. Next Generation said that "no other laser-gun shooter comes close to it right now", praising its frame rate, level design and pacing.

The Saturn version, shown at E3 in May 1996 with only its first level playable, was praised as a close conversion and a considerable improvement on the original, with more interactive environments and intense chase scenes, though some again felt it too short for a home game while others pointed to the extra length of its branches. GameSpot said AM2 "delivered an incredible sequel that takes the concept to a whole new level", and EGM ranked it 98th among the best games of all time in 1997. Windows and Dreamcast versions followed, and Virtua Cop 3 succeeded it.

title: Fighters Megamix
description: Fighters Megamix (1996) is Sega AM2's Saturn-exclusive crossover of Virtua Fighter 2 and Fighting Vipers, with hidden fighters from other AM2 games including a Daytona USA racing car, and one of the Saturn's best sellers.
longDescription:
The full casts of Virtua Fighter 2 and Fighting Vipers meet, along with Kumachan, a bear mascot with no points of articulation. Players can switch between the two games' fighting systems, which differ in knockback and recovery, and fight in Virtua Fighter's open rings, without ring-outs, or Fighting Vipers' walled cages. The Vipers keep their breakable armour, so the Virtua Fighter characters gain moves to break it, along with some moves from Virtua Fighter 3, including a sidestep dodge. Both games' bosses are playable without cheats.

The one-player mode is split into nine courses, such as Girls, Muscle, Smart Guys and Dirty Fighters, each six fights followed by a hidden opponent, and completing them unlocks twelve secret characters. They include Bark and Bean from Sonic the Fighters, Janet from Virtua Cop 2, Kids Akira and Kids Sarah from Virtua Fighter Kids, Rent-A-Hero from a Mega Drive game, Siba, cut from Virtua Fighter's prototype, the new character Deku, a Mexican bean with a bird under his hat, and Hornet, the number 41 car from Daytona USA, which stands on its back wheels and boxes. There are also versus, team battle, survival and training modes.
trivia: It was never released in arcades, unusually for an AM2 game of the time.
AM2 said it always thought of "a festive game" for Saturn owners towards the end of the year.
It was kept secret until a press conference on 6 November 1996, less than two months before release.
The AM2 palm tree emblem becomes playable after 84 hours of play.
Digitiser ranked it third of 1997, below Super Mario 64 and Final Fantasy VII.
devStory:
Director Hiroshi Kataoka described it as a new fighting game with characters from both series rather than a simple combination, the hardest part being to reconcile their armour and defence systems while keeping each fighter's character. AM2 called it fairly easy to make, because compression techniques developed for squeezing Virtua Fighter 2 onto one disc made fitting its larger move list simple. It was intended as an introduction to Virtua Fighter 3, which never came to the Saturn, and borrowed The King of Fighters' idea of mixing characters from different games.

Critics hailed it as one of the Saturn's best games. Game Informer gave it 9.25, its highest score for any Saturn game, Next Generation called it "the best fighting game ever on a system that's already chock full of great fighting games", and Famitsu gave it 35 out of 40, though reviewers noted fewer polygons than Virtua Fighter 2 and easy AI. It sold over 600,000 copies in Japan and was the top Saturn rental in the US for three months of 1997. It has since been called a precursor of Super Smash Bros.

title: Bloody Roar
description: Bloody Roar (1997) is Raizing and Hudson Soft's 3D fighting game, released as Beastorizer in North American arcades, in which fighters transform mid-match into animal forms, praised on the PlayStation for its speed.
longDescription:
Eight fighters punch and kick in enclosed arenas, with combos, air juggles, counters, guard reversals and guard crushes. Opponents can be thrown against walls and fences for wall juggles, and a hard enough throw breaks the walls for a ring-out. Attacks fill a Beast meter, and when it is full a fighter can transform into an animal form with more speed and strength, new moves, longer reach and some recovered health, until enough damage forces them back. The PlayStation version added a Beast Rave mode, boosting speed by 25 percent and allowing rapid attack chains while draining the meter, and in North America a sidestep on the shoulder buttons. Modes include arcade, versus with handicaps, time attack, survival, practice and a spectator mode.

The story draws on the Gaia hypothesis: the Earth long ago planted animal genes in humanity as a dormant trigger, creating "zoanthropes" able to survive environmental collapse, but the Tyron Corporation discovered the code and began engineering them as biological weapons. The cast includes the wolf Yugo, searching for the truth about his father's death; the rabbit Alice, who escaped Tyron's experiments; the tiger Jin Long, a former Tyron assassin; and the lion Alan Gado, a one-eyed mercenary.
trivia: Director Kenji Fukuya found fights between ordinary humans dull and first wanted superpowered characters like Dragon Ball's Super Saiyans.
Eighting came up with the beast theme.
The PlayStation version had original music by Takayuki Negishi, while the arcade score's composers included Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata.
Its final boss is Uriko, an artificial chimera zoanthrope.
It lost the Interactive Achievement Award for console fighting game to WCW vs. nWo: World Tour.
devStory:
Raizing developed the game and Hudson Soft published it in July 1997 on Sony's ZN-1 arcade board, with character and visual design by Mitsuakira Tatsuta and Shinsuke Yamakawa. The PlayStation version followed in Japan on 6 November 1997, in Europe through Virgin in January 1998 and in North America through Sony in March 1998.

Reviews of the PlayStation version were generally positive. Critics praised its fast, fluid play, precise controls and transformation system, and said it blended Tekken, Virtua Fighter and Fighting Vipers, with an engine some found smoother than Tekken 2's. Its rock soundtrack was divisive, and its eight-character roster and generic characters drew repeated criticism; Next Generation dismissed the backstories as uninteresting. It was North America's 20th best-selling game in its first month. Bloody Roar 2 followed in 1998, and the series continued to Bloody Roar 4 in 2003.

title: Battle Arena Toshinden
description: Battle Arena Toshinden (1995) is Tamsoft and Takara's PlayStation weapons fighter, one of the first polygonal 3D fighting games after Virtua Fighter, whose sidestep is credited with taking the genre into "true 3D".
longDescription:
Eight anime-style fighters, designed by Tsukasa Kotobuki, battle with weapons. Each has basic moves, special attacks in the style of 2D fighters like Street Fighter, and a desperation attack usable only when their energy is around 10% or lower. The L and R shoulder buttons sidestep around the arena to dodge projectiles or escape danger, tapping forward makes the fighter run, and holding back blocks basic attacks and reduces damage from specials. A fighter wins by draining the opponent's health, having more health when time runs out or knocking them out of the unwalled arena; a mistimed run or special move can carry a fighter off the edge, which made for unique tactics. The main mode is a run of fights against every character and then the boss.

The tournament, broadcast as bloodsport for an elite audience, is run by the Secret Society, linked to the multinational Gerard Foundation. Its fighters include the Japanese swordsman Eiji Shinjo, searching for his lost brother Sho; his rival Kayin Amoh; Sofia, a whip-wielding Russian detective with lost memories; the miner Rungo Iron, trying to rescue his family; and Ellis, an orphaned dancer seeking her father, who turns out to be the sponsor, Gaia.
trivia: It was Takara's first original video game, made in under six months from the end of May 1994 by a team that reached 25.
Sony of America promoted it as a "Saturn killer", yet a Saturn version, Toshinden Remix, came out less than a year later.
Sony of America used Sofia as a mascot after dropping Polygon Man.
The DOS version added Earthworm Jim as a guest fighter, using Rungo Iron's moves.
In 2005 EGM named it the single most overrated game.
devStory:
Takara had been planning the game for another platform until Sony announced the PlayStation in late 1993. Tamsoft and Takara, who had ported Samurai Shodown and other SNK fighters to consoles, gave each character about 1,000 polygons and boasted that, unlike Virtua Fighter, attacks could come from the side or behind and players could circle opponents. It was released in Japan on 1 January 1995, weeks after the console, and as a launch title in the West that September, with re-done English voices.

It sold 696,851 copies in Japan, sold out in its first week in the US, and reached 532,724 there. Critics praised its Gouraud shading, transparencies, camera and sidestep, and EGM named it best fighting game of 1995, though Next Generation thought it lost to Virtua Fighter "by a hair" and GamePro said it relied "more on flash than fighting". The Saturn version sold poorly, and as Tekken and later Soul Edge arrived, the series faded despite sequels starting with Battle Arena Toshinden 2.

title: Rayman 2: The Great Escape
description: Rayman 2: The Great Escape (1999) is Ubi Soft's 3D platformer for the Nintendo 64, PC, Dreamcast and PlayStation, in which Rayman frees his world from robot pirates, rebuilt in 3D after starting life as a 2D sequel.
longDescription:
Rayman travels a mostly linear series of 3D levels, with a controllable camera, fighting robot pirates, solving puzzles and collecting lums, shards of magical energy. Enough lums open new parts of the world, and some are locked in cages along with imprisoned Teensies and freedom fighters. He begins with few abilities and gains more: firing energy orbs from his fist, later charged for more power, a strafing stance for aiming while dodging, swinging across gaps on purple lums, and using his helicopter hair to slow his fall and later to fly. He throws explosive barrels, rides giant plums across dangerous surfaces and rockets into new areas. Murfy, a "flying encyclopaedia", explains the mechanics, and collected lums reveal the world's back story.

Robot pirates under Admiral Razorbeard invade the Glade of Dreams and destroy its Primordial Core, stripping Rayman of his powers and capturing him. Freed by his friend Globox with a Silver Lum from the fairy Ly, Rayman must gather four magical masks to wake Polokus, the spirit of the world, and then take on Razorbeard aboard his ship, the Buccaneer. Collecting every lum and cage in a level unlocks a race in which one of Globox's children takes on a robot pirate.
trivia: Its art was inspired by Hayao Miyazaki, Tex Avery and Art Nouveau artists such as Alphonse Mucha.
Ubi Soft released Tonic Trouble first on the same engine, to avoid damaging Rayman's reputation.
The lead platform switched from PC to Nintendo 64 mid-development, so textures had to be reduced; the Dreamcast version uses the originals.
The PlayStation version includes a playable prototype of the original 2D version.
Tim Schafer named it, with Super Mario 64 and Skies of Arcadia, as an inspiration for Psychonauts.
devStory:
Development began in early 1996 as a side-scrolling 2D game with a team of six and a budget of 10 million francs, planned for release that year. With the rise of 3D games, the team rebuilt it as a 3D platformer inspired by Super Mario 64, and 70 to 80 developers, many inexperienced, worked on it for more than two years. The Dreamcast conversion, begun in March 1999 by about 25 people in Paris, prioritised 60 frames per second.

It was released for the Nintendo 64 and Windows in October and November 1999, the Dreamcast in March 2000 and the PlayStation that September, followed by the enhanced Rayman Revolution on PlayStation 2. Critics acclaimed it: Next Generation said it "can honestly claim to have something to offer any gamer of any age or skill", IGN called it "the most impressive feat of game design and execution the platforming genre has ever seen", and GameSpot judged the Dreamcast version the best. It was nominated for game of the year at the Interactive Achievement Awards, and Rayman 3 followed in 2003.

title: Harvest Moon 64
description: Harvest Moon 64 (1999), Bokujō Monogatari 2 in Japan, is Victor Interactive's Nintendo 64 farming game, in which the player restores a grandfather's abandoned farm, raises animals and courts one of five villagers through the seasons.
longDescription:
The player inherits an abandoned farm with an empty chicken coop and barn and five tools, a hammer, axe, sickle, hoe and watering can, which upgrade to silver and then gold with use. Unlike the SNES original, each day has limited time and stamina. Crops such as turnips, potatoes, corn and strawberries are bought in season, planted in tilled soil and watered, and some keep producing all season; everything withers when the season changes unless grown in a greenhouse. Wild herbs change with the seasons, some curing sickness and others causing it. Cows, sheep and chickens bought at the nearby ranch need feeding and shelter from rain, or they fall ill and die, while good care improves their produce.

The town has a church, bar, bakery, flower shop, library and tool shop, with characters' locations and opening hours changing by time and day, and festivals close the shops for events such as dancing and swimming. The player owns a dog, inherited from the grandfather, and can get a horse to ride or use as a portable shipping crate, and both can enter yearly races decided largely by their bond with the player. Five women can be courted, their affection shown by heart colours, and the player can marry and have a child; each also has a rival suitor. Photographs arrive in the mail to record milestones.
trivia: It is the third game in the Story of Seasons series, after Harvest Moon GB.
Natsume first said a Wii U Virtual Console release was technically impossible, then released it there in 2017.
The 2017 release was its first in PAL regions; the original European release had been cancelled for time.
It won the only Parent's Guide Choice Award given to a Nintendo 64 game by Mars Publishing's Parent's Guide to Nintendo Games.
Nintendo Power ranked it the 278th greatest Nintendo game.
devStory: Victor Interactive Software developed the game, publishing it in Japan on 5 February 1999, with Natsume releasing it in North America on 22 December 1999. Reviews were generally favourable, according to Metacritic, and Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40. Many reviewers found that its compelling, unusual play outweighed a repetitive soundtrack and glitchy visuals: IGN's Aaron Boulding forgave its "poor audio and visual elements" because he played it "for hours at a time", GameSpot's Joe Fielder called it "a strangely compelling, original little game that makes hours melt away incomprehensibly", and GamePro said it was not for "swashbucklers or diehard cityslickers". It was re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console in 2017 for the series' twentieth anniversary and on Nintendo Switch Online in 2023.

title: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber
description: Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber (1999) is Quest's real-time tactical RPG for the Nintendo 64, the third Ogre Battle game, in which young captain Magnus Gallant leads a revolution across Palatinus.
longDescription:
The protagonist, Magnus, commands a battalion of up to 50 troops divided into units of up to five, each needing a leader; most humans can lead, but not non-human creatures, soldiers or basic classes such as the Fighter and Amazon, with Gorgons and Saturos the main exceptions. The game is split into chapters, each a mission with objectives set out by the adviser Hugo, usually capturing an enemy stronghold or defeating a particularly strong unit, though his advice on how to deploy units need not be followed. When two units meet on the map, combat plays out automatically on an isometric, pre-rendered battlefield, with several characters acting at once and an array of attacks, critical hits and parries. A unit is disbanded when all its members die, and Magnus's death ends the game.

A class system defines each character's attacks, equipment and statistics, most characters can change class, and many classes work best in particular positions within a unit. Magnus, a recent graduate of the Ischka Military Academy, joins Frederick Raskin's revolution against Palatinus, then faces the Holy Lodis Empire and the Dark Hordes of the Netherworld. Three endings, chaotic, neutral or lawful, depend on the player's Chaos Frame.
trivia: It was announced in April 1997 as Ogre Battle 3, with completion planned for March 1998.
It was considered for the 64DD before settling on a cartridge, the second-largest N64 cartridge at 320 megabits.
It was the first Ogre Battle with 3D graphics.
Atlus kept some swearing in its translation to stay true to the original and aim at an older audience.
GameSpot named it best strategy game of 2000 and nominated it for "Best Game No One Played".
devStory:
After Tactics Ogre, series creator Yasumi Matsuno planned a third game balancing that game's "soft" concepts with the "niche" style of the original Ogre Battle, but he left Quest for Square, where he made Final Fantasy Tactics. Ogre Battle 64 was the first Ogre game Quest made without him. Characters were designed by Toshiaki Kato, and the team found realistic 3D models hard on the hardware. Hayato Matsuo, Masaharu Iwata and Hitoshi Sakimoto composed the music; Sakimoto found the N64's sound environment hard to work with.

Nintendo published it in Japan on 14 July 1999, and Atlus released it in North America on 5 October 2000, adding Controller Pak saves, in limited quantities attributed to a shortage of chips. Reviews were favourable, Famitsu giving it 33 out of 40; GamePro said that beneath its "intimidating interface and plodding pace lies a wealth of strategy". GameSpot noted its sales had "fallen prey" to the N64. It reached PAL regions only on the Wii Virtual Console in 2010.

title: Shadow Man
description: Shadow Man (1999) is Acclaim Studios Teesside's dark action-adventure based on the Valiant comic, in which voodoo warrior Michael LeRoi crosses between the living world and Deadside to stop serial killers and the demon Legion.
longDescription:
Sometimes described as a 3D metroidvania, the game follows conventions of the Metroid and Zelda series rather than role-playing mechanics: progress is non-linear, and new powers open access to new areas and paths forward. Michael LeRoi moves between Liveside, the world of the living, and Deadside, the land of the dead, using his dead brother Luke's teddy bear as the link between them.

In 1888 Jack the Ripper, frustrated that his ritual murders have not unlocked a mystical power, is promised it by a being called Legion in exchange for building an asylum for killers in Deadside. In the present day the voodoo priestess Mama Nettie bonds the Mask of Shadows to Michael, making him the latest Shadow Man, a line of voodoo warriors who guard the living from Deadside. Nettie dreams that Legion will bring the Apocalypse by gathering the Dark Souls of damned warriors to raise an immortal army, and that five serial killers, the Five, each carry a Dark Soul and are hiding in Liveside, where Michael's powers fail by day. Michael must collect Deadside's souls, assemble a knife called the Eclipser so Nettie can trigger an eclipse, and track the Five down.
trivia: The studio built its engine first, with no concept in mind, then chose Shadow Man from about eight comic series Acclaim offered.
Deadside's design drew heavily on the decaying industrial structures of Northeast England, where the studio was based.
The Asylum's headquarters was based on Pieter Bruegel the Elder's painting The Tower of Babel.
Its budget was more than $6 million.
Nightdive's 2021 remaster restored content cut from the original.
devStory: Announced in 1997 for a late 1998 release on the Nintendo 64, Shadow Man slipped to 1999 and was released on 31 August for the Nintendo 64, Windows and PlayStation, with a Dreamcast version on 1 December. The Dreamcast, PC and N64 versions received favourable reviews, while the PlayStation version was criticised for poor technical performance. N64 Magazine gave it 93%, calling it "a dark and glittering jewel in the N64's gaudy crown", Computer Games Strategy Plus praised it as "graphically rich and emotionally binding", and Edge called it "near-peerlessly expansive in size and demands on player time", though Next Generation thought it "a well-intentioned misfire". Nightdive Studios re-released it digitally in 2013 and remastered it in 2021, and a sequel, Shadow Man: 2econd Coming, followed on the PlayStation 2 in 2002.

title: San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing
description: San Francisco Rush: Extreme Racing (1996) is Atari Games' arcade racer through an exaggerated San Francisco, full of hidden shortcuts and huge jumps, which helped restore Atari's fortunes in arcades.
longDescription:
Races run through neighbourhoods modelled on real San Francisco locations, against a time limit extended at checkpoint gates. Each course has a fixed difficulty set by its obstacles and turns, and each car its own difficulty, speed and handling, the "Extreme" cars warning of a "full simulation" effect; transmission can be automatic or manual. Shortcuts hidden on each track, into sewers, off broken freeways and across rooftops, can gain time and places on the computer racers, or, if botched, send the player to the back. Hitting an obstacle hard enough or landing upside down makes the car explode, after which it reappears on the track, and an Abort button respawns it at will.

The original arcade game had three tracks and eight cars. San Francisco Rush: The Rock, a 1997 ROM update, added four tracks, including Alcatraz, four cars and a mirror option, and a later Wave Net version allowed online races between arcades. The Nintendo 64 port of 1997 added more tracks, hidden keys that unlock cars, a circuit mode and a Death Race in which wrecks stay on the track.
trivia: It was built on 3dfx Voodoo Graphics chips, cheaper to develop for than proprietary hardware, letting Atari sell it to operators for less.
Because cars hit 150–160 mph, the designers abandoned real maps for an alternate, more "fun" San Francisco.
It was the first game on Atari Games' Flagstaff engine.
The new tracks in The Rock, apart from Alcatraz, were designed for the Nintendo 64 version.
Its cabinet appears in the music video for Len's "Steal My Sunshine".
devStory: Atari Games unveiled Rush at the AMOA show in 1996. It was a major arcade hit and was credited as a comeback title for the company. Next Generation gave the arcade version four stars, saying its shortcuts add "a thrill of discovery not usually found in driving games". Midway ported it to the Nintendo 64 in 1997 and to the PlayStation and Windows in 1998; the PlayStation version had fewer tracks, no original music and heavier gravity. Reviews of the N64 port ranged from mixed to laudatory: critics enjoyed its shortcuts, outrageous jumps and smooth multiplayer, and GamePro joked that "the death-defying leaps will make you leave your stomach in San Francisco", but some found the brakes and analogue control weak and the soundtrack poor, while IGN said its extra modes made it feel like "a much better game designed for the home". Rush 2: Extreme Racing USA followed in 1998 and San Francisco Rush 2049 in 1999.

title: Cruis'n USA
description: Cruis'n USA (1994) is Eugene Jarvis's cross-country arcade racer for Midway and Nintendo, promoted as the first "Ultra 64" game though it ran on unrelated hardware, a big arcade hit with a poorly received Nintendo 64 port.
longDescription:
Players race along one-way courses loosely based on real places, avoiding oncoming traffic and roadworks, on a trip across the United States from San Francisco through California, Arizona, the Grand Canyon, Iowa, Chicago, Indiana and Appalachia to Washington, D.C., where finishing earns congratulations from President Bill Clinton. Each race must be won to move on, against a time limit extended at checkpoints, and the game ends when time runs out unless a continue is used. Players can switch the music with a dedicated button.

The cars are generic versions of real ones: a 1963 Corvette sold as the "1963 Muscle Car", a Ferrari 512 TR as the "Italia P69", a 1940 Ford as "La Bomba" and a Hyundai concept as the "Devastator IV", with an automatic or manual gearbox. Bonus vehicles include a police car, a school bus and a Jeep.
trivia: Lead developer Eugene Jarvis had created Defender and Robotron: 2084.
The cabinet shown as Ultra 64 hardware at the 1994 CES actually ran on a modified JAMMA board; the game uses Midway's V-Unit.
Nintendo pulled the N64 version from the console's launch line-up less than a month before release for not meeting its standards.
The N64 version cut the ability to run over animals and a scene of Bill and Hillary Clinton in a hot tub; Jarvis said "It seems like they don't have a sense of humor."
It was the first third-party Nintendo 64 game on the Wii Virtual Console.
devStory:
In early 1994 Nintendo signed a deal with Midway's parent WMS Industries for two arcade games billed as the first Ultra 64 hardware, wanting a racer to compete with Sega's Daytona USA and Namco's Ridge Racer. Jarvis pitched the concept, and the game was shown at the June 1994 CES alongside Rare's Killer Instinct; Nintendo of America's Howard Lincoln later admitted it was programmed before Nintendo 64 development tools existed. In arcades it was a success: one of America's five best-selling arcade games of 1994 and the highest-grossing dedicated cabinet of 1995, earning comparisons with Daytona USA.

Leland Interactive Media had to downgrade the graphics for the 1996 Nintendo 64 port, which reviewers panned for its jerky frame rate, poor collision detection and music, averaging 50.63% on GameRankings; IGN predicted it would be "the nadir of N64 racing games for many years to come". Even so, with few games yet available for the new console, it sold over a million copies by the end of 1997. It began the Cruis'n series.

title: Hydro Thunder
description: Hydro Thunder (1999) is Midway's arcade powerboat racer, with boost-fuelled jumps through settings from the Arctic to a flooded New York, which became a Dreamcast launch game and began Midway's Thunder series.
longDescription:
Similar in feel to Daytona USA, the game races high-tech speedboats through hazardous settings, from the cold seas of the Arctic Circle to a post-apocalyptic New York City. Blue and red boost icons, the red rarer and worth more, fill a boost tank; boosting increases speed and lets the player's boat knock rivals into the air, which the game calls the Mighty Hull. Braking while boosting performs a Hydro Jump, which with the many ramps reaches shortcuts and boosts that are otherwise out of reach.

Boats and tracks come in easy, medium, hard and bonus classes. Easy boats handle best but are slowest, hard boats are fast but difficult to control, and the four bonus boats mix qualities. Finishing in the top three on easy tracks unlocks medium ones, the top two on medium unlocks hard, and winning on hard tracks opens the bonus tracks, whose wins unlock the bonus boats. The arcade game had two bonus tracks, New York Disaster and Nile Adventure, plus a hidden Hydro Speedway; the home versions added Catacomb and Castle Von Dandy.
trivia: The arcade cabinet was built on Midway's earlier Hyperdrive cabinet and sold as a conversion kit for it.
It used San Francisco Rush's seat and Cruis'n USA's steering wheel, with a forward, neutral and reverse throttle instead of pedals.
Its normal volume was set below a subwoofer in the seat, to make players feel like a powerboat pilot.
The Nintendo 64 version allows four players with the Expansion Pak.
A planned Hydro Rush double pack with San Francisco Rush 2049 for the PlayStation 2 was cancelled.
devStory: Midway released Hydro Thunder in arcades in February 1999. Next Generation wrote that "Midway has finally created the boat-racing game that will bring this sub-genre to the forefront." It came to the Dreamcast as a launch title later that year, with graphics closest to the arcade version and "just shy of being a perfect conversion" according to Next Generation, and to the PlayStation, which added a career mode, and Nintendo 64 in early 2000. GameRankings recorded favourable reviews for the Dreamcast version and mixed ones for the others; GamePro praised its visuals and physics but noted two-player slowdown and limited replay value, and Edge called it "aggressive, surreal and compulsive" but "not Mario Kart on water". A sequel was cancelled, but the game spawned the Thunder series of Offroad Thunder and Arctic Thunder, and Microsoft released Hydro Thunder Hurricane on Xbox Live Arcade in 2010.

title: Silent Scope
description: Silent Scope (1999) is Konami's arcade sniper game, played with a rifle mounted on the cabinet whose scope shows a zoomed view, in which the player rescues the kidnapped First Family from terrorists.
longDescription:
A rifle is mounted on the cabinet, so players have to physically shift position to aim, and its scope shows a close-up of a small part of the screen, like a sniper's long-range view of where the rifle points. Some areas are dark and need night-vision scopes to spot opponents. Five shots can be fired before reloading. Time and health are limited: killing certain enemies adds time, while training the scope on an attractive woman awards health and bonus points. Each of the three stages, one for each member of the First Family, has sub-bosses and a large boss, who take more than one bullet unless hit with a precise headshot. Enemies shoot back if not killed fast enough, and civilians caught in the crossfire must be spared. At points the player chooses between two or three paths, easy, medium or hard, which change the boss and the next mission.

Scores depend on where an opponent is hit, multiplied by the number of successful shots in a row, with the most for headshots; on the practice range, shooting the guns of human-shaped targets earns bonuses. The story begins when terrorists ambush the President's convoy returning from Chicago and capture the First Family, demanding the release of their leader, the dictator, and ends with the player down to a single bullet after emptying a magazine into bulletproof glass as the dictator escapes.
trivia: In Japan, Game Machine listed it as the second most successful dedicated arcade game in its 1 September 1999 issue.
AllGame found its voice acting "unintentionally hilarious".
Home versions have a cheat to trade life for time and vice versa.
Other codes make it harder, for example by hiding the target indicators on enemies.
Famitsu gave the Game Boy Advance version 23 out of 40.
devStory: Konami developed and published Silent Scope for arcades in 1999, the first game in the Silent Scope series. AllGame's Brett Alan Weiss called the arcade version "a blast to play, though a few more realistic sniper missions would be nice", noting acceptable graphics but music that could not be heard during the action. The home ports on the PlayStation 2 and Dreamcast received moderately positive reviews, though Metacritic's average of 63% rests on few reviews. GamePro called the PS2 version "a picture-perfect arcade conversion" and "a must-rent title", and said the Dreamcast version's training courses "offer diverse fun". Edge gave the Dreamcast version seven out of ten, writing that it is "all about high scores through high accuracy" and that its "one shot, one kill moments of euphoria and despair" made it a success, and Next Generation called it "a solid shooting game with unique play mechanics". Sequels began with Silent Scope 2 in 2000.

title: Lords of Thunder
description: Lords of Thunder (1993), Winds of Thunder in Japan, is Red's fantasy shoot 'em up for the TurboDuo, made by former Thunder Force staff and known for its huge bosses and hard rock soundtrack.
longDescription:
The knight Landis, wearing the armour of his ancestor Drak, fights Zaggart of the Garuda Empire, who has revived the evil god Deoric, and his six dark generals across the land of Mistral. Unlike its predecessor Gate of Thunder, the player picks any of the first six stages in any order, as in Thunder Force III, with the last unlocked after the rest. Before each stage Landis chooses one of four armours, based on the classical elements, which change his shots and bombs and the difficulty, and buys extra bombs, shields and health elixirs in a shop with crystals. Four difficulty settings rearrange hazards and enemy patterns, and a cheat opens a hidden boss rush.

The screen scrolls constantly until a boss is reached. Landis fires long-range shots, swings a sword up close and uses bombs that clear enemies and bullets. Defeated enemies drop hearts that restore health, power crystals that raise firepower and blue and red crystals for the shop, also key to high scores. Getting hit or touching scenery costs health and firepower, and continues are limited, though more can be bought.
trivia: Its developers, Red Raimon, were former Technosoft staff who had worked on Thunder Force II and III and later founded CAProduction.
Satoshi Miyashita of T's Music composed the soundtrack under the alias "Groove King".
Manga artist Masamune Shirow drew the cover art.
A promotional recording edited by Tony Hawk was given away in a run of 10,000 copies.
EGM named it Game of the Month for March 1993.
devStory:
Red Raimon, the group within Red that had made Gate of Thunder, developed the game with Kazunori Nakazawa as planner and character designer, production co-led by Hudson Soft's Eiji Aoyama and Masaki Kobayashi, and Tomonori Matsunaga directing. Turbo Technologies released it for the TurboDuo in North America in March 1993, and Hudson Soft in Japan that April. Critics praised its sharp visuals, large bosses, lack of slowdown, frantic pace and soundtrack, VideoGames & Computer Entertainment calling it "the perfect game for players with fast reflexes", though some felt its play was less fierce or technical than Gate of Thunder's. GameFan rated it among the best shooters on the system.

A 1995 Sega CD port by Hudson Soft and Eleven was considered inferior, with washed-out colours, audio balancing problems and lower difficulty. Later reviewers rank it among the most important PC Engine shooters; Nintendo Life said its guitar rock soundtrack "fits like a chain mail glove". It has been re-released on the Virtual Console and the TurboGrafx-16 Mini.

title: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure
description: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure (1998), JOJO's Venture outside Japan, is Capcom's CP System III fighting game of Hirohiko Araki's manga, made by the Street Fighter III team, whose fighters summon guardian spirits called Stands.
longDescription:
Two fighters trade attacks and special moves, with a super meter that fills as they deal and take damage. The twist is the Stand, each fighter's own projection of energy. Most characters have an active Stand they bring in and out with a dedicated button: while it is out, attacks are stronger, new techniques and abilities such as double jumps open up, and the Stand can attack separately. But hits on a Stand hurt its user, doubly so if it is far away, and a Stand Gauge that drains under attack leads to a stunning "Stand Crash" if emptied. Clashing Stands start button-mashing "Blazing Fists" contests, and Stands can be programmed with attack sequences for long combos. Some characters have passive Stands built into their moves, and Young Joseph has none, fighting with Hamon.

Based on the Stardust Crusaders arc, the story follows Jotaro Kujo, who learns from his grandfather Joseph Joestar that his new Stand comes from the influence of the vampire Dio, and sets out to destroy Dio to save his mother. Story Mode loosely follows the manga with special stages, such as a side-scrolling hunt for the assassin N'Doul while dodging his water Stand.
trivia: Araki consulted on the game and designed Midler's full appearance from scratch, since the manga had shown her only from the waist down.
Some characters were renamed in English versions to avoid copyright problems.
The 1999 update, Heritage for the Future, was the sixth and last game on the CPS-3 board.
The PlayStation version's Super Story Mode covers the whole Stardust Crusaders arc, with minigames such as driving a car.
Edge called the Dreamcast version "a discourse for the devout" and a title "for fanatics alone".
devStory:
Capcom's Street Fighter III team developed the game, combining the anime-style art of Darkstalkers with Araki's characters for a highly stylised look. It was released in Japanese arcades in December 1998 and in North America in February 1999, and Heritage for the Future added eight more characters in September 1999. Game Machine named it Japan's most successful arcade game of January 1999, and it was the country's third highest-grossing arcade software of 1999. The PlayStation and Dreamcast versions sold more than 300,000 copies in Japan by March 2000.

The Dreamcast version received favourable reviews and the PlayStation one mixed ones. The Electric Playground called them "the most advanced (and strangest) of Capcom's 2D fighting games, but by no means the most addictive", GamePro said the PlayStation version was "best taken as an entertaining change of pace", and AllGame felt it lacked the fine-tuning to last. Famitsu gave both 31 out of 40. An HD version followed in 2012.

title: Star Gladiator - Episode 1: Final Crusade
description: Star Gladiator (1996) is Capcom's first in-house polygonal fighting game, a 3D weapons fighter of Plasma-powered duellists in the year 2348, which reportedly began life as a Star Wars game.
longDescription:
Instead of Capcom's usual six buttons, it uses four: two weapon attacks, a kick and a guard. Fighters duel on a hovering arena, and being knocked off loses the round. Two Plasma Reverses can be used at any time: a Plasma Reflect deflects an incoming move and stuns the attacker, while a Plasma Revenge counters with a fast strike. A Plasma Strike, usable once per round, does huge damage if it lands. The Plasma Combo System lets certain strings of attacks combo even through a block, and finishing a five-hit string with the right button triggers a damaging Plasma Final, a system dropped in the sequel. Arcade mode runs ten fights, ending with the sub-boss Gore and the final boss Bilstein, and beating Bilstein quickly enough leads to the true final boss, Super Bilstein.

In 2348, Nobel Prize-winning physicist Edward Bilstein discovers "Plasma Power", the energy of the human mind, but is exiled for experimenting on human bodies. Escaping in a cyborg body, he leads a rebel "Fourth Empire", and the Earth Federation turns to fighters able to wield Plasma Power. They include the bounty hunter Hayato Kanzaki with his Plasma Sword, the gymnast June with a Plasma Ring, the yo-yo-wielding alien street performer Saturn, the ape-like lumberjack Gamof and June's father Rimgal, turned into a velociraptor by Bilstein.
trivia: Capcom's Seth Killian said it was originally designed as a Star Wars game with Star Wars characters.
It was the second game on the PlayStation-based Sony ZN-1 arcade board, after Battle Arena Toshinden 2.
Black Hayato began as a palette swap before becoming a separate character in later games.
Hayato later appeared in Marvel vs. Capcom 2.
PlayStation Plus called the home version "the best fighting game available on any home system", for the moment.
devStory:
Capcom released Star Gladiator in arcades in July 1996, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixteenth most successful arcade game in its 1 September 1996 issue. Next Generation called it "a quirky, stylish game that is more subtle than obvious, with innovative gameplay and likeable character design", praising its three-dimensional movement and simple controls, and GamePro deemed it a satisfying first step into 3D for Capcom.

A PlayStation port, built on the same ZN-1 hardware, followed in October 1996 and averaged 82% on GameRankings. Critics praised its characters, variety of techniques and 3D backgrounds, though many found the single-player mode too easy; GamePro said its "visual appeal and outstanding control will put other 3D games on their backs", while IGN felt it was not as deep as Tekken 2. Its success led to a sequel, Plasma Sword: Nightmare of Bilstein, in 1998.

title: Cyberbots: Fullmetal Madness
description: Cyberbots: Fullmetal Madness (1995) is Capcom's CP System II mech fighting game, a spin-off of Armored Warriors in which pilots mix and match robot legs, arms and weapons, and the origin of Jin Saotome and Devilotte.
longDescription:
Players first pick a pilot, who decides the storyline, then a mech, or VA (Valiant Armor), which decides how the game plays. As in the Armored Core series, legs that change movement, arms that change reach and melee, and weapons can be mixed and matched between the available robots. Fights are one-on-one duels, with fewer characters on screen than the three of Armored Warriors, and each robot has a medium-sized list of attacks. A gauge charges with every hit or when the attack buttons are pressed together, and when full allows a "super special".

Near the end of the 21st century, an overcrowded Earth has sent many people to live in space colonies, and the army Earth Force has been conducting experiments.
