The pilots include Jin Saotome, who wants to become the best VA pilot to honour his father, killed in an accident a year earlier; Santana, a narcissistic former leader of the Mars Revolution; Mary Miyabi, Earth Force's only female captain; the retired captain Gawaine Murdock; Arieta, a girl escaping Earth Force's experiments on children; and the siblings Bao and Mao. Home versions added the space pirate princess Devilotte and the cyborg SHADE, among others.
trivia: The Saturn version required Sega's 1 MB RAM cartridge and has a code to play as an Akuma mech.
Its console ports were never released outside Japan, apart from an untranslated PlayStation Network release in 2011.
Jin Saotome later became a playable character in the Marvel vs. Capcom series.
Devilotte appears as a hidden character in Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo and an assist in Marvel vs. Capcom.
Next Generation said that "when the bots do attack, it looks like a bad disco contest".
devStory: Capcom built the game on its CP System II arcade board in 1995, and it saw only limited distribution in arcades outside Japan. Game Machine listed it as the thirteenth most popular arcade game in Japan in its 1 June 1995 issue, ahead of titles such as Virtua Fighter. Next Generation was unimpressed, writing that it "lacks the charm, craze - and gameplay - for which [Capcom] is known" and criticising the concept and limited combos. Saturn and PlayStation versions followed in Japan, the PlayStation one on 25 December 1997, both adding voices to the story mode and extra characters. The arcade game was later included in Capcom Arcade Stadium and Capcom Fighting Collection, and its successor was Tech Romancer in 1998.

title: Red Earth
description: Red Earth (1996), Warzard in Japan, is the first game on Capcom's CP System III board, a fantasy fighter with RPG growth in which four heroes battle giant boss monsters and level up, kept from home consoles until 2022.
longDescription:
In Quest Mode, the player picks one of four heroes and fights eight computer-controlled monsters one-on-one, each a boss with a huge health bar shown along the bottom of the screen and none of them playable. Hits knock out coins, which give experience to raise attack and defence and unlock new moves, and treasure chests with orbs for super moves and food to restore health, making it closer to Capcom's side-scrolling Dungeons & Dragons games than a standard fighter. A password saves the character's progress for later. Versus Mode lets two players fight as any of the heroes. It is one of the few Capcom games with fatalities, such as splitting opponents in half, and has multiple and hidden endings shaped by the player's choices, continues and the way enemies are killed.

Set in an alternate 14th century that never had a Renaissance, the evil wizard Scion sends monsters to conquer the world. The heroes are Leo, a king turned half-lion by a curse; the ninja Kenji; the "sorcerologist" Tessa, who studies the science of magic; and the martial artist Mai-Ling. The bosses include the dinosaur Hauzer, the oni Kongou, the harpy Lavia and Gi Gi, a robotic statue.
trivia: Takashi Sado said it was inspired by Capcom's Magic Sword and The King of Dragons.
Its stats and equipment were meant to let casual players keep up with experienced ones.
Gi Gi changes colour depending on which way it faces, inspiring Street Fighter III's boss Gill.
Scion can turn heroes into small creatures, such as Kenji into a beetle and Tessa into a penguin.
Its first home release came in 2022, in Capcom Fighting Collection.
devStory: According to Takashi Sado, Red Earth was made because of the growing popularity of fighting games in the 1990s, but with parameters and equipment to set it apart. It was the first game on Capcom's CP System III hardware, which Street Fighter III later used, and Takayuki Iwai composed its 72-track soundtrack with help from Ryoji Yamamoto and Wataru Hachisako. Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most popular arcade game in its 1 February 1997 issue, and Hyper rated it four out of five. Although it was never ported at the time, its characters lived on: Leo, Kenji and Hydron became playable in Capcom Fighting Evolution, Tessa in SNK vs. Capcom: SVC Chaos and Super Gem Fighter, and a Darkstalkers crossover manga, Maleficarum, was published in 1997.

title: Giga Wing
description: Giga Wing (1999) is Takumi's steampunk vertical shooter for Capcom, unusual for running on a horizontal monitor, built around a Reflect move that sends enemy bullets back at their owners.
longDescription:
Set during a fictional war in a steampunk world, the game has the player fly one of four futuristic aircraft through seven stages, destroying aircraft, tanks, ships and buildings, with a boss at the end of each. Every ship has three attacks: a normal spray of bullets, a Reflect that turns enemy bullets back to damage their ships, and a Force Bomb that cancels every bullet on screen. Ships start with two bombs and can carry up to seven, and bombs left after a boss fight earn a bonus. Destroyed enemies drop power-ups and medals that raise the score multiplier, and the game adjusts its difficulty according to the player's score at the end of each level. Three lives are given, and the seventh stage can be reached only without using a continue.

The four pilots, Sinnosuke, Ruby, Isha and Stuck, each have their own storyline, and two players together get a team storyline. The heroes are trying to destroy a powerful Medallion that many bosses use as a weapon, controlled by an evil man piloting a ship called the Stranger, revealed to have caused this war and earlier conflicts including the Second World War. In the bad endings a pilot sacrifices themselves in a kamikaze attack to destroy the Medallion.
trivia: Using a horizontally aligned monitor, like Treasure's Radiant Silvergun, is considered rare for a vertical shooter.
The Stranger appears to have been a friend of Stuck thirty years earlier.
Next Generation said the game "should be packaged with bottles of both Visine and Excedrin".
The Dreamcast version was delayed in the US from April to July 2000.
It was later included in Capcom Arcade Stadium.
devStory: Takumi Corporation developed Giga Wing, and Capcom published it in arcades in 1999, with a Dreamcast version following. Game Machine listed the arcade version as Japan's tenth most successful arcade game in its 1 May 1999 issue. The Dreamcast release, which reached the US on 18 July 2000 after a delay from April, received mixed reviews on GameRankings: Game Informer was favourable and EGM mixed while the game was still in development, and Famitsu gave it 28 out of 40. The arcade original was later re-released in Capcom Arcade Stadium.

title: Armed Police Batrider
description: Armed Police Batrider (1998) is Raizing's futuristic manic shooter in which teams of three "Zero-Cops" on jet bikes take on a criminal corporation, with up to eighteen bosses and characters from Battle Garegga and Mahou Daisakusen.
longDescription:
Players choose up to three of nine pilots, each on a flying jet bike called a Batrider, plus nine unlockable characters from Raizing's Mahou Daisakusen and Battle Garegga. Pressing A fires the main shot and, once collected, the Options; B fires a bomb; and pressing nothing charges an Aura, a small damaging field in front of the ship. Shot powerups, Options and medals fall often from small enemies, and extra lives come every 1,500,000 points. Four courses are offered. Training lasts three stages and spends any remaining bombs automatically when the player is hit. Normal runs five stages with a secret boss, Bashinet mk2. Advanced has seven stages and up to all eighteen bosses depending on the team and hidden tasks. Special is a boss rush. Many more secrets can be unlocked with codes or DIP switch settings.

In 2014 crime-ridden Manhattan's people flocked to Zenovia, an artificial island two kilometres south built by the GiganTech Cybertronics Corporation and patrolled by its robots. By 2019 it is a slum, and an investigation reveals that GiganTech's executives are among the country's most dangerous criminals, using Zenovia as a trap and testing ground for weapons. With police and armies unwilling to act, three police officers, three convicts and three psychics are drafted as Zero-Cops to stop the CEO and his ultimate weapon, "Discharge".
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixth most successful arcade game in its 15 March 1998 issue.
On the Advanced course a player may fight as few as seven or as many as eighteen bosses.
Its first appearance outside arcades was on the Sega Astro City Mini V in 2022.
Its Normal course plays three middle stages in random order unless Stage Edit is enabled.
In Japanese versions the Special boss rush must be enabled with a DIP switch.
devStory: Raizing developed Armed Police Batrider and Eighting published it in arcades in 1998, two years after Battle Garegga, many of whose characters and ideas it brought back as unlockable pilots alongside those of Mahou Daisakusen. Its many secrets and team-based character selection gave it unusual depth for the genre. It performed well in Japanese arcades, reaching sixth in Game Machine's chart for the first half of March 1998, but it was never ported to home consoles in its time. It finally reached a home system in 2022 as part of the Sega Astro City Mini V, a vertically oriented version of Sega's mini console, and in October 2026 the developer M2 announced a re-release, without confirming platforms or a date.

title: Twinkle Star Sprites
description: Twinkle Star Sprites (1996) is ADK's last Neo Geo game, a competitive shoot 'em up in which two players on side-by-side screens chain enemy kills to send attacks into each other's field.
longDescription:
Each player has a separate vertically scrolling field, divided by a bar, and shoots enemy formations arriving from the top. Destroying them in chains sends fireballs into the opponent's field. Shooting an incoming fireball enough times reflects it back as a glowing Reverse Attack, reflecting those summons indestructible Extra Attacks, and reflecting many at once can summon a boss, with the extra and boss attacks varying by character. Destroying one enemy in a formation and the rest with a combo scores a Perfect, which speeds up attacks and the countdown to special formations. A power gauge with three levels fires a character's charge shot, and at higher levels also launches Extra Attacks or a Boss Attack. When a countdown runs out, a special formation or a blue orb appears, and destroying the orb in a chain grants a few seconds of Fever with faster, more plentiful attacks.

Both players have five life points. Colliding with an enemy costs one but cannot kill; at the last point it halves it and stuns the player. Being hit by an attack or a boss costs three, and the opponent regains life whenever the player takes damage. If a round lasts over 102 seconds, or both players fail to make combos for too long, a Death enemy appears that kills on contact and can be volleyed to the other side.
trivia: Each character starts with two bombs that clear the screen and give brief invincibility.
The Saturn version added an anime-style intro, a new character and a bonus "Fan Disc".
SNK released an enhanced Dreamcast version in 2000 after buying ADK's properties.
Readers of Japan's Sega Saturn Magazine gave the Saturn port 8.85 out of 10.
A 2005 PlayStation 2 sequel, La Petite Princesse, was not released in North America because SNK judged it unmarketable there.
devStory: ADK developed Twinkle Star Sprites as its last Neo Geo production, and SNK released it in arcades in 1996, ported it to the Neo Geo AES in January 1997 and to the Neo Geo CD that February. Game Machine listed it as the fourteenth most popular arcade game in Japan in its 1 January 1997 issue. Critics were mixed, but fans were enthusiastic. AllGame's Kyle Knight called it "a refreshingly innovative title that manages to pull its seemingly incompatible elements together brilliantly" while noting slowdown, and IGN liked the Dreamcast version's extra options and multiplayer but found its graphics low-resolution and its single-player modes thin. It was included in the Japanese PlayStation 2 compilation ADK Damashii in 2008 and later re-released by Hamster and on PC.

title: Magical Drop
description: Magical Drop (1995), released as Chain Reaction in North American arcades, is Data East's fast competitive puzzle game in which a clown grabs and drops coloured bubbles, the start of a series best known on the Neo Geo.
longDescription:
A stack of randomly coloured bubbles descends from the top of the screen, and the player loses if a bubble reaches the bottom. The player's clown, at the foot of the screen, picks bubbles up and drops them back, and three or more of the same colour in a column vanish. Chains form when one drop sets off a chain reaction or when several groups are destroyed in quick succession, and chains make the opponent's stack descend faster. It is normally played by two, against a person or the computer. The series favours fast reflexes over careful planning; Next Generation said of the sequel that "there is no time to think, just time to do".

The characters are named after tarot cards, and each has a different attack pattern that makes the columns of the opponent's stack drop at different rates, breaking up the colours: with Devil all columns fall evenly, while with Sun the middle columns fall faster. The first game introduced the Fool, who always carries a cat, the narcissistic Magician, the bookish High Priestess, the fearless knight Chariot, the demonic boy Devil, the crybaby Star and the three-eyed goddess World, the final opponent.
trivia: It is based on Drop-Drop, a game by the Russian company Russ Ltd.
The home versions of the first game were never released outside Japan.
Next Generation called it "as addictive as sex after lunch... in a jester suit" while giving it two stars.
Mean Machines' reviewers disagreed about whether its Saturn version beat rival Baku Baku Animal.
G-mode now owns the series along with other Data East properties.
devStory: Data East released Magical Drop in arcades in 1995, titled Chain Reaction in North America, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's tenth most successful arcade game in its 1 September 1995 issue. Next Generation noted that it was "proving quite popular in Japan, despite the fact that this kind of game has been around now for at least five years", calling it neither brilliant nor new but fun. Mean Machines gave the Saturn version 84 out of 100, finding it addictive and full of options but frustratingly hard alone. Its Neo Geo sequels, Magical Drop II in 1996 and Magical Drop III in 1997, made the series better known, followed by versions for the PlayStation, WonderSwan, Neo Geo Pocket Color and Game Boy Color. The Super Famicom version of the original reached the Wii Virtual Console in Japan in 2007.

title: Baku Baku Animal
description: Baku Baku Animal (1995), released abroad as Baku Baku, is Sega's falling-block puzzle game in which animals eat their favourite foods, acclaimed on the Saturn and named Computer Gaming World's puzzle game of 1996.
longDescription:
Animal and food tiles fall into the playfield, and when an animal lands next to its favourite food, such as a monkey beside a banana, it eats it. The more connected food tiles an animal eats in one bite, the more points the player scores, and each meal drops random blocks into the opponent's field, after the piece they are currently placing. The aim is to leave the opponent unable to place any more blocks. Two-player competition was singled out by critics as the heart of the game.

The story has a king holding a competition to hire a royal zoo keeper for his daughter's many pets. The heroine, Polly, must beat the other applicants, each of whom trades a short exchange of dialogue with her before a match, with different responses depending on whether she wins or loses. The game's name is a Japanese onomatopoeia meaning roughly "chomp chomp".
trivia: Its Windows version was Sega's first network-compatible PC game.
A Sega NetLink version was announced but never released.
A white-label dance EP built from its sound effects circulated among DJs in 1996.
Jesper Juul's history of tile-matching games cites its "special objects to match" rule as distinguishing it from earlier games.
Sega Saturn Magazine described Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo as effectively a remake of Baku Baku Animal.
devStory: Sega developed the game for Japanese arcades in 1995, and Game Machine listed it as the eleventh most successful arcade game there in May 1995. It was then ported to the Saturn, Game Gear and Windows. The Saturn version was acclaimed: Maximum called it "the best 'next generation' puzzle game we've seen to date", Sega Saturn Magazine praised "some of the most addictive puzzle play since Tetris", and GamePro called it "undeniably the best puzzle game in the world so far". EGM's reviewers praised the Game Gear version as simple and accessible yet strategic. Computer Gaming World named it its 1996 classic/puzzle game of the year, warning that it "will eat up your time", EGM made it runner-up for handheld and puzzle game of the year behind Tetris Attack, and PC Gamer ranked it the 72nd best computer game ever in 1997.

title: Yoshi's Cookie
description: Yoshi's Cookie (1992) is Nintendo's NES and Game Boy tile-matching puzzle game in which rows and columns of cookies are rotated like a Rubik's Cube, adapted from an arcade game that failed its location test.
longDescription:
The playing field is a rectangular grid of several kinds of cookie, and the aim of each level is to clear it. The player moves a cursor to rotate individual rows and columns, in a manner similar to a Rubik's Cube, and whenever an entire row or column consists of one type of cookie it is cleared from the grid. New cookies keep entering from the top and right, and the game ends if the grid overflows. A sixth kind of cookie, shaped like Yoshi's head, occasionally appears as a wild card that helps clear a line of any other type.

In the single-player Action Mode, the levels grow steadily more complex. A VS Mode lets two players compete in split screen, and the Game Boy version allows up to four players, who cannot see each other's screens. The later SNES version adds a single-player VS Mode against the computer and a Puzzle Mode, in which each level starts from a set grid that must be cleared within a maximum number of moves.
trivia: It began as Hermetica, an arcade game by Home Data that did poorly in location testing.
The SNES version's Puzzle Mode levels were designed by Tetris creator Alexey Pajitnov.
Its soundtrack includes a rendition of "Csikós Post" by German composer Hermann Necke.
A promotional Super Famicom edition made for a Panasonic National microwave oven, limited to 500 copies, included recipes for the cookies.
One copy of that edition was valued at ¥157,500 in 2010.
devStory:
Home Data sold the rights to Hermetica to Bullet-Proof Software, whose SNES version, designed by David Nolte, was shown at the 1992 Consumer Electronics Show. Nintendo licensed the 8-bit versions and, with Tose developing, turned the game into Yoshi's Cookie with Mario characters; Bullet-Proof kept its SNES game but was allowed to use the Mario characters and the Yoshi's Cookie name. The NES and Game Boy versions came out in Japan on 21 November 1992 and in North America in April 1993, with the SNES version that June.

Famicom Tsūshin's reviewers called it addictive, though not as much as Tetris, and most fun with two players. The Washington Post called it "simple, but addictive, just like all puzzlers from the Big N", and Nintendo Power rated it the fifth best NES game of 1993. It was remade for the GameCube's Nintendo Puzzle Collection in 2003, and IGN later ranked it 50th among SNES games.

title: Wario's Woods
description: Wario's Woods (1994) is Nintendo's puzzle game in which Toad climbs among falling monsters and bombs to clear them, the last licensed NES game in North America and the only one rated by the ESRB.
longDescription:
Wario and his monsters have taken over the Peaceful Woods, and Toad sets out to return it to the sprites who lived there. To clear each round, the player matches monsters with bombs of the same colour, dropped from the top by a sprite: three or more objects in a horizontal, vertical or diagonal row, at least one of them a bomb, form a match, but three monsters alone do not. A Thwomp disguised as the ceiling can come down several rows, leaving less room. Each new round starts with more monsters, and some types can only be destroyed in particular ways, such as two matches in quick succession or a diagonal match.

Unlike Tetris or Puzzle League, the player does not move the pieces directly but controls Toad, who walks on top of the fallen objects, picks up single objects or whole stacks and puts them down elsewhere, kicks objects across the field and climbs the sides of stacks. He cannot reach everything, and if the field fills to the top it traps him and the game ends. A versus mode lets two players compete, with consecutive matches piling enemies into the opponent's field.
trivia: It was the final first-party NES game released in North America.
In Japan it was released alongside a re-release of The Legend of Zelda to coincide with the AV Famicom.
Two versions were broadcast in Japan for the Satellaview, one featuring the comedy duo Bakushō Mondai.
The NES version could be collected in the GameCube's Animal Crossing.
IGN ranked it 29th among SNES games.
devStory: Nintendo R&D1 and Intelligent Systems developed the game for the NES and Super NES, released in 1994 at the end of the NES's life, and its ESRB rating was given almost three months before its American release. Reviews were mixed. GamePro called the SNES version "a ho-hum puzzler" with difficult controls, Nintendo Power praised its fun two-player mode but found it harder to control than Tetris 2, and Next Generation thought its learning curve "too steep" for an action puzzle game. Later, AllGame's Christian Huey called the NES controls "both surprisingly complex and completely intuitive", while Scott Alan Marriott felt the SNES version did not match the addictiveness of Tetris or Dr. Mario. The NES version was one of the first Wii Virtual Console releases in 2006, and reviewers then praised its depth while wishing Nintendo had chosen the fuller Super NES version.

title: Light Crusader
description: Light Crusader (1995) is Treasure's last Genesis game, an isometric dungeon-crawling action-adventure in which the knight Sir David searches beneath the town of Green Row for its kidnapped people.
longDescription:
Seen from an isometric angle, Sir David explores a large multi-level dungeon beneath the graveyard of Green Row, fighting enemies, solving puzzles and finding the missing townsfolk. He can roam the town to talk to people and shop, and further down the dungeon are other settlements, including a guild of wizards and an entire town of goblins. Besides running and jumping, David attacks with his sword standing still, moving, jumping or lunging in mid-air. He commands four kinds of elemental magic based on the classical elements, which can be used alone or combined, up to all four at once, for attacks or buffs; water on its own heals him. The pause menu manages magic, items such as food and gear, and a map that the player fills in by exploring, without showing items or townspeople.

Invited by the king of Green Row, David learns that townspeople have been disappearing. The culprit is the wizard Ragno Roke, who, enraged when the queen rejected his marriage proposal, plans to sacrifice them to reawaken the demon Ramiah, sealed in the dungeon.
trivia: Its working title was Relayer.
Artist Hiroshi Iuchi said it was first planned as an action version of the RPG series Wizardry.
At one point the team started over from scratch, and Iuchi estimated the game was only 30% complete by the end of 1994.
It was one of four Genesis games in Treasure's deal with Sega, with Dynamite Headdy, Alien Soldier and a Yū Yū Hakusho fighter.
GamePro said David moves "with nowhere near the range or fluidity of movement of Ali in Beyond Oasis".
devStory:
Treasure's Kazuhiko Ishida programmed the game with Keiji Fujitake and president Masato Maekawa, with art by Iuchi and others and music by Aki Hata. The team wanted to improve the controls and enjoyment of pseudo-3D games with an isometric view, but Ishida found it hard to program multiple joints in 3D and Iuchi said the perspective strained the Genesis, delaying the game by over a year. Sega published it worldwide in 1995.

Mean Machines Sega called it "a superlative arcade adventure with great playability" despite finding it easy, and Next Generation said it was "one of the more exciting and graphically pleasing Genesis titles" but "by no means a RPG", criticising shallow puzzles and story and awkward controls. Three of EGM's four editors were negative, citing poor visibility, clunky combat and too many puzzles. Micom BASIC Magazine ranked it second in popularity in August 1995. It has since appeared on the Virtual Console, in Sega Genesis Classics and on the Genesis Mini.

title: Sword of Vermilion
description: Sword of Vermilion (1989) is Sega AM2's first console-exclusive game, an early Genesis action RPG that switches between several play styles, from top-down exploration to side-on boss fights, as an exiled prince gathers the rings of good.
longDescription:
The game mixes four styles of play that change with what the player is doing and where they are in the world. Most of the time the prince is controlled from a top-down view, but boss fights switch to a side-on perspective, and battles also occur when meeting enemies in the overworld or inside dungeons, where the prince fights with a sword and magic spells. More powerful swords and magic can be found in towns by talking to shopkeepers and other characters. Much of the game is spent fighting and exploring.

King Erik V of Excalabria and his friend King Tsarkon sought the eight rings of good and evil to bring peace and balance, but the rings of evil corrupted Tsarkon, who invaded Excalabria and destroyed Erik's castle. Before dying, Erik entrusted his infant son and the Ring of Wisdom to his most faithful knight, Blade, while Tsarkon scattered the remaining rings of good and turned the prince's mother to stone. Blade raised the boy in the village of Wyclif, and eighteen years later, on his deathbed, reveals the prince's true identity, sending him to collect the rings and save the realm of Vermilion.
trivia: It was the main RPG featured in Sega's "Genesis does what Nintendon't" advertising campaign.
It was one of the last Mega Drive RPGs to come with a hint book.
MegaTech called it "probably the best RPG on the Mega Drive".
Computer and Video Games preferred its action combat to Phantasy Star II's turn-based battles.
Mega ranked it 11th among Mega Drive games in 1992.
devStory: Sega's AM2 division developed Sword of Vermilion for the Genesis in 1989, its first game made exclusively for a console, and in North America it was promoted as the headline RPG of the "Genesis does what Nintendon't" campaign. Contemporary reviews were positive. Computer and Video Games called it an "excellent" and "highly compelling arcade/adventure RPG" offering "a vast, sprawling adventure", praising its engaging story, its music and sound, and its town graphics and detailed sprites, though it found the 3D screens "decidedly rough". MegaTech praised its "gripping plot" and user-friendly controls. Retrospective opinion has been more mixed: IGN's Lucas Thomas called it repetitive and formulaic, its play styles underdeveloped and held together like "a patchwork quilt". It was included in the Sega Genesis Collection for PlayStation 2 and PSP, on the Wii Virtual Console and on Nintendo Switch Online in 2021.

title: Knuckles' Chaotix
description: Knuckles' Chaotix (1995) is Sega's 32X Sonic spin-off in which Knuckles and the Chaotix are tied to a partner by a rubber-band tether, an ambitious oddity seen as the last of the classic 2D Sonic games.
longDescription:
It plays like earlier Sonic games, with rings, spin attacks, spin-dashes, shields and speed shoes, but the player is always tethered to a partner, human or computer-controlled, by a band that stretches like a rubber band and has to be used to move through stages. The partner can be called back for ten rings or thrown to distant platforms, and an anchored computer partner can be used to snap up to a ledge or catapult for speed. Five characters each have abilities: Knuckles glides and climbs, Mighty the Armadillo wall-jumps, Espio the Chameleon runs along walls and ceilings, Vector the Crocodile boosts through the air and Charmy Bee flies. Two more partners, the slow Heavy and the explosive Bomb, get in the way.

The six levels, called attractions, each have five acts set at different times of day, the fifth a boss fight with Robotnik. A hub world is used to choose partners and levels. Giant rings found with at least 20 rings lead to free-falling bonus stages, and finishing a level with 50 rings opens a 3D special stage to win one of the Chaos Rings that Robotnik and Metal Sonic want, needed for the good ending.
trivia: It began as Sonic Crackers, a 1994 Genesis prototype tethering Sonic and Tails, whose ROM leaked in 1995.
Tom Kalinske said it was once meant as a mainline Sonic game for the Saturn, but was "too big, it was taking too long, it was over budgeted, it was behind schedule".
Its working title was Knuckles' Ringstar.
Vector was created for the original Sonic the Hedgehog and scrapped; Charmy came from the Sonic manga; Espio was the only new character.
Apart from Mighty, the Chaotix returned as recurring characters from Sonic Heroes in 2003.
devStory:
Although Sonic Team is sometimes credited, the game was made by another internal Sega team including Sonic CD staff. Development began around April 1994 as an engine test, then moved to the 32X, and by December Sonic and Tails had been replaced by Knuckles, who had debuted in Sonic 3. The 32X allowed sprite scaling and polygon special stages, and Junko Shiratsu and Mariko Nanba composed the music. Sega released it in Japan on 21 April 1995 and in the West that May and June, rushed, according to Ken Horowitz, to help sluggish 32X sales.

It received mixed reviews and failed commercially along with the 32X. EGM's reviewers praised its graphics and called it one of the best 32X games, and GameFan rated it the best Sonic since Sonic 2, but critics widely found the tether clunky, GamePro likening it to being handcuffed, and the levels sparse and easy. IGN called it "a bad game with a good foundation". Fans have often asked for a re-release; apart from a spell on GameTap in 2005, it has never had one.

title: Heart of Darkness
description: Heart of Darkness (1998) is Amazing Studio's cinematic platformer, supervised by Another World creator Éric Chahi, in which a boy afraid of the dark travels to a shadow world to rescue his dog after six years of development.
longDescription:
In the vein of Chahi's Another World, it is a cinematic platformer with a linear story: the player guides Andy through hostile environments, solving puzzles and avoiding being killed by living shadows, hungry wildlife and deadly obstacles. Besides running, jumping and climbing, Andy at first has a plasma cannon that fires lightning to disintegrate shadows, though it is soon destroyed, and he then relies on magical powers that attack enemies and also grow and destroy trees from seeds. Lives are unlimited, and Andy restarts at the most recent checkpoint when killed. It has about half an hour of cinematic sequences, thousands of frames of 2D animation and pre-rendered backgrounds.

Andy, a boy with a fear of the dark, takes his dog Whisky to the park to watch a solar eclipse, and dark forces carry Whisky away. He follows in a homemade spaceship to the Darkland, crashing there, and crosses canyons, swamps, underwater caves and lava rivers, helped by a peaceful alien race, the Amigos, to confront the Master of Darkness and his treacherous servant.
trivia: It is unrelated to Joseph Conrad's novel of the same name.
Its orchestral score was written by film and television composer Bruce Broughton.
Versions were announced for the 3DO, Jaguar CD, Panasonic M2 and Game Boy Advance, and a Saturn exclusive was planned, but none appeared.
After Virgin dropped its funding in 1996, the team worked nine months unfunded before Interplay picked it up.
The Master of Darkness resembles Andy's teacher.
devStory:
Development began in 1992 with the PC as lead platform; the game was first shown in March 1995, said to be near completion, and then spent years in delays and platform changes, at one point signed as a Saturn exclusive before that console faded. Chahi called it one of his hardest projects because of the shift "from working alone to working with a team" while CD-ROM and 3D were changing the industry. When Virgin Interactive withdrew funding in December 1996, Frédéric Savoir said "we couldn't throw away four years of our life". The cut-scenes were rendered in 3D Studio, and the characters were rendered and scaled down as sprites animated in Deluxe Paint.

It was released for the PlayStation and Windows in 1998. The PlayStation version received favourable reviews: GamePro called it "just as clever as Out of This World", while Next Generation found the play unremarkable and said "the wait simply wasn't worth it". It was a finalist for an Interactive Achievement Award for sound and music. Chahi said the six years exhausted him, and he left games until From Dust in 2011.

title: Ehrgeiz: God Bless the Ring
description: Ehrgeiz: God Bless the Ring (1998) is DreamFactory's free-roaming 3D fighter for Square and Namco, with Final Fantasy VII's Cloud and Tifa in its cast and, on the PlayStation, a dungeon-crawling quest mode.
longDescription:
Drawing on wrestling games and DreamFactory's own Tobal series, Ehrgeiz allows full 360-degree movement and does not require fighters to face each other, so the camera stays mostly fixed, zooming in and out rather than circling the arena. Stages are three-dimensional, with interactive objects and changes in height, letting fighters leap onto crates or use them as weapons. There are four buttons: guard, high attack, low attack and a special weapon attack unique to each character. The original cast, designed by Tetsuya Nomura, includes the cyborg-armed mercenary Ken "Godhand" Mishima, the taekwondo film star Han Daehan, the kickboxer Prince Doza and the jujutsu student Yoko Kishibojin, fighting in a tournament for the legendary sword Ehrgeiz.

The PlayStation version adds Brand New Quest: The Forsaken Dungeon, a hack-and-slash dungeon crawl like Diablo with randomly generated floors. As the archaeologists Koji Masuda and Clair Andrews, the player descends for artefacts, levelling up through a five-point chart fed by eating protein, vitamins, minerals, carbohydrates and lipids from monster drops, while managing hunger. There are also minigames, including a race and a Reversi-like board game, and even wine trading that works like a stock market.
trivia: In the arcade version, Cloud, Tifa and Sephiroth appeared thirty, sixty and ninety days after the machine was first switched on.
The PlayStation version added Sephiroth, Yuffie, Vincent and Zack.
Square published the PlayStation version internationally while Sony published it in Japan, reversing their usual arrangement.
It was directed by Seiichi Ishii, designer of Virtua Fighter and Tekken.
Square EA ran an "Ehrgeiz Championship Tour" at Electronics Boutique and Babbage's stores from July 1999.
devStory:
DreamFactory, which had made Tobal for Square, developed the game, announced as the first project under an agreement letting Square develop for Namco's System 12 arcade board; it was shown at Namco's booth at the AOU Show in February 1998. Takayuki Nakamura, composer of Tobal 2, wrote the music. Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixth most successful arcade game in its 15 April 1998 issue.

The PlayStation version sold over 222,000 copies in Japan by the end of 1998 and 340,937 by December 2004, and Famitsu gave it 32 out of 40. Western reviews averaged 76% on GameRankings: IGN praised its graphics and presentation but found the play simplistic and the combinations hard to perform, GameSpot called the blocking "unintuitive" and the minigames disappointing, and Next Generation said it was "good to see developers straying from the accepted formula with new fighting designs that truly work".

title: Rage Racer
description: Rage Racer (1996) is Namco's third PlayStation Ridge Racer, a darker, more realistic entry that introduced buying and upgrading cars, a class-based Grand Prix and the series mascot Reiko Nagase.
longDescription:
Taking its visual cues from the arcade's Rave Racer, Rage Racer has a more realistic, darker colour scheme than the earlier games. For the first time in the series, the player earns credits by winning races and spends them buying and upgrading cars. Four manufacturers each favour a different attribute, such as handling, acceleration or speed, and each offers a standard car and a secret car locked until the top class is reached, along with an unlockable truck. Standard cars can be upgraded in several increasingly costly stages.

Racing is divided into five classes. The player has three attempts to finish in the top three of each class's events before moving on to the next. Completing the five Normal GP events unlocks the Extra GP, in which the same classes are raced on reversed courses, and awards the player 999,999,999 credits, more than enough to buy every car and upgrade them fully.
trivia: It was the first Ridge Racer with a CGI animated introduction.
Designer and director Nobuhisa Mikoda said it was "somewhat off series and aimed to pursue enjoyment in shift controlling".
It was unveiled, still untitled, at the Tokyo Game Show in August 1996.
Burnout creator Alex Ward called it the best Ridge Racer, saying Phantom Mile "doesn't beat the Extreme Oval from Rage Racer".
It was runner-up for EGM's racing game of 1997, behind Diddy Kong Racing.
devStory: Namco released Rage Racer in Japan on 3 December 1996, with other regions following in 1997. Its music by Tetsukazu Nakanishi and Hiroshi Okubo marked the start of Namco's new main sound team after earlier members left to work on games such as Street Fighter EX. Reviews were positive but mild. Critics approved of its more photo-realistic visuals, though some found them drab, and many felt it improved too little on its predecessors: Next Generation called it the best of the series but said it still lacked depth without more tracks, IGN said "we've just seen it all before", and GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann criticised its unrealistic crashes while calling it "an outstanding sequel". EGM's Kraig Kujawa and Dean Hager thought it a dramatic improvement on the original Ridge Racer. It sold well, and R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 followed in 1998.

title: Jungle Strike
description: Jungle Strike (1993) is EA's sequel to Desert Strike, an isometric helicopter shooter mixing action and strategy in which a lone pilot foils a drug lord and a terrorist's plot against Washington, D.C.
longDescription:
The player flies a Comanche attack helicopter over a slightly three-dimensional overhead view, and in some missions takes control of a motorbike, a hovercraft or an F-117, which has unlimited ammunition and variable height but crashes easily. Levels are made up of several missions to destroy weapons and installations, rescue hostages and prisoners of war, or capture enemy personnel, against armoured cars, artillery and tanks. The helicopter carries machine guns, Hydra rockets and Hellfire missiles, the more powerful weapons in smaller numbers, so the player must choose the right one for each situation. Armour drains under fire and is restored by power-ups or by airlifting rescued people to a landing zone. Fuel runs down steadily and is replenished from fuel barrels, and ammunition from ammo crates; running out of either armour or fuel costs a life.

Ibn Kilbaba, son of Desert Strike's villain, and the South American drug lord Carlos Ortega plan nuclear attacks on Washington, D.C. The first level defends the capital, including the President's limousine, before the campaign takes the fight to Ortega's jungle fortress, captures both men, and returns to Washington after they escape to stop four trucks carrying nuclear bombs from reaching the White House.
trivia: It was Electronic Arts' first 16-megabit cartridge.
Desert Strike's engine came from a failed flight simulator and was inspired by Matchbox toys and Choplifter.
The PC version adds a level in Alaska against a Russian defector threatening an oil spill.
Some Amiga magazines objected to its politics, Amiga Format calling the jingoism "rife".
Sega Force's Mat Yeo called it "the best shoot 'em up I've seen in a long time".
devStory:
After Desert Strike, then EA's best-selling game, director John Manley and associate producer Tony Barnes were given the sequel and, with project manager Susan Manley, expanded it with an opening movie and new vehicles and settings while keeping the core mechanics. EA released it for the Genesis in 1993, with SNES and enhanced MS-DOS versions by Gremlin, an Amiga version by Ocean and handheld versions by Black Pearl.

It was well received. Sega Force called it the "greatest game in the genre" and "twice as good" as Desert Strike, the Mega Drive version was a best seller for three months, and GamePro praised the SNES version for keeping the play while improving graphics and sound. Amiga Computing said it "could well be the best chopper title yet", though some found the difficulty steep. Mega ranked it 13th among Mega Drive games and IGN 71st among SNES games. Urban Strike, Soviet Strike and Nuclear Strike followed.

title: General Chaos
description: General Chaos (1993) is Game Refuge's satirical Genesis action-strategy game in which feuding brothers turned dictators send cartoon squads of gunners, launchers and flamethrowers against each other, for up to four players.
longDescription:
Two generals, Chaos and Havoc, fight either a single quick battle or a campaign of battles across a dynamic strategic map, with the aim of capturing the enemy's capital. Each player picks one of four teams: three of five soldiers with differing weapons, and one of two "commandos" with a control system that gives more direct control. The action is seen from an isometric view, balancing strategy with action: when opposing soldiers get close, they fight hand to hand, punching, kicking and blocking. A soldier who loses all his health falls, and the player can bring a medic to revive him a limited number of times, earning more medics by scoring points from items on the battlefield. A "boot camp" tutorial teaches the basics, and with a multiplayer adapter up to four people can play together against the computer.

The soldier classes include the Gunner, a well-rounded submachine gunner whose gun can jam; the Launcher, a slow but long-range rocketeer; the Chucker, who throws grenades over cover; the Scorcher, whose flamethrower has the shortest range but fires fastest and hits several soldiers at once; and the Blaster, who throws dynamite. The story has brothers Chaos and Havoc fall out over a torn comic book and grow up to rule the rival countries of Moronica and Viceria.
trivia: The Chucker, a bearded man in a Rambo-style headband, is a clear reference to Chuck Norris.
A Scorcher who walks into water fires bubbles instead of flames.
Launchers, Scorchers and Blasters can kill instantly, leaving a skeleton or ash that no medic can revive.
EGM called it "the ultimate one-on-one 'fighting' game!"
A 2013 Kickstarter by Brian F. Colin for a sequel fell more than $100,000 short.
devStory: Game Refuge developed General Chaos for the Sega Genesis, and Electronic Arts published it in 1993. It received generally positive reviews. Electronic Gaming Monthly gave it 8 out of 10, praising its humour, wealth of options and four-player mode. GamePro also praised the humour, multiplayer and enemy AI, summarising that it "combines brain-squeezing battlefield strategy, challenging squad tactics, and real-time button-pressing combat with humorous cartoon graphics". Its blend of real-time squad combat and strategy kept a following, and in 2017 GamesRadar listed it 48th among the best Sega Genesis/Mega Drive games of all time. In September 2013, Brian F. Colin launched a Kickstarter campaign to fund a sequel, but it fell well short of its goal.

title: Last Bronx
description: Last Bronx (1996) is Sega AM3's Model 2 weapons fighter about rival Tokyo street gangs, a hit in Japan that spawned a film, manga and radio drama but flopped in American arcades.
longDescription:
Matches are best of two rounds, won by knockout or by having more health when the 30-second timer ends. The stages are enclosed real Tokyo locations with no ring-outs, though fighters can jump onto the barriers and even backflip off them for a disqualifying ring-out. AM3 used the three-button punch, kick and guard layout of Virtua Fighter, with "punch" meaning the weapon; joystick and button combinations produce special and combination attacks, guard performs a feint called an Attack Cancel, and taunts are used even by the computer.

In an alternate post-bubble Tokyo, youth disillusionment has led to the All Tokyo Street Wars. The gang Soul Crew united the city's youth until its leader was murdered, and a mysterious group, Redrum, demands a tournament among the strongest gang bosses to decide who rules the streets, backing the threat with gang members found dead in Tokyo Bay. The fighters include Yusaku Kudo of Neo-Soul with a three-section staff, the nunchaku-wielding Joe Inagaki, the construction boss Saburo Zaimoku with a hammer, the skateboarder Tommy with a bō and Yoko Kono of the G-Troops, searching for her missing brother. Each has a joke alternative weapon, such as Zaimoku's frozen tuna.
trivia: Director Akinobu Abe said the characters wear clothes based on current Tokyo street fashion.
Weapons moved too fast to see, so the developers made them leave afterimages.
Sega kept its demo out of the February 1996 AOU show because AM2 was already showing several fighting games there.
Sega persuaded the British Board of Film Classification to let Joe's nunchaku appear uncensored in the PAL Saturn version.
Takashi Shimizu directed a live-action direct-to-video film of it.
devStory:
The team behind Virtual On developed Last Bronx on Sega's Model 2 board, using programming tricks to give metallic characters environmental mapping the hardware did not support. Released in 1996, it became a big hit and franchise in Japan, with a novel, manga and radio drama, but appeared in only a handful of American arcades. Next Generation called it "a grittier, and in some ways more inventive product than the sometimes overly smooth efforts of AM2".

The same team began the Saturn version on 8 November 1996, none of them having worked on the Saturn, prioritising the full animation and 60 frames per second; Abe found accurate weapon collision the hardest part. Released in Japan in August 1997 with a new story mode, it was praised for its smooth visuals, Sega Saturn Magazine calling them "virtually indistinguishable from the coin-op original", though critics found the cast small, combos cheap and the game weaker than Fighters Megamix. A Windows version followed in 1998 and a PlayStation 2 release in 2006.

title: Manx TT Super Bike
description: Manx TT Super Bike (1995) is Sega's Model 2 motorcycle racer set at the Isle of Man TT, whose tilting bike cabinet responded to the rider's body weight, and which supported up to eight linked players.
longDescription:
The game is set at the Isle of Man TT, the famously demanding motorcycle race. There are two courses: the Laxey Coast course for novices, a fictional track with scenery drawn from the island, and the harder TT Course, based on the real circuit. The bikes resemble the Castrol Honda RVF750 RC45. Up to eight players can race when enough cabinets are linked, as with Daytona USA.

Its cabinet set it apart. Earlier motorcycle games, starting with Sega's Hang-On, used a bike-shaped seat the player tilted by pushing their feet against the floor, but Manx TT's machine was sensitive enough to lean with the rider's shifting weight, so players could keep their feet on the bike and steer with their bodies. The Saturn version adds a Saturn mode with practice races and a challenge course of every track in order, split-screen two-player racing and analogue control, and the Saturn and PC versions keep the soundtrack as CD audio playable in any CD player.
trivia: Producer Tetsuya Mizuguchi got the idea after Sega Rally from a magazine article about the Isle of Man.
The team studied, with Castrol Honda, how a bike's sound travels to the rider's ear, and added a Model 1 sound board for four sound outputs.
Bikes need more polygons than cars, so they were kept simple to allow eight players without slowdown.
At about £15,000 a deluxe cabinet, it still sold out with its UK distributor after the January 1996 ATEI show.
Motor Raid was released as a conversion kit for its cabinet in 1997.
devStory:
Mizuguchi wanted "a game with a big graphic impact that used the player's body", combining the island's beauty with Japanese bikers' love of the open road. First shown at the 1995 JAMMA show at 20% complete, it became a worldwide arcade hit: the second most successful dedicated arcade game in Japan in Game Machine's 15 February 1996 issue and top-grossing in Australia that March. Next Generation called it "the next evolutionary step in bike racing sims".

Sega's Saturn conversion team was busy with Daytona USA: Championship Circuit Edition, so the port went via Psygnosis to Tantalus Interactive, an outside studio with no experience of arcade ports, which caused controversy. The result was praised as an exemplary conversion with excellent control, though critics found its extra content thin for a home game; Saturn Power thought it "the finest conversion of Manx TT onto the Saturn possible". It was the UK's third best-selling game across formats in April 1997. Perfect Entertainment made the PC version.

title: Scud Race
description: Scud Race (1996), Sega Super GT in North America, is Sega's first racing game on the Model 3 board, modelled on the BPR Global GT Series and hailed as the most gorgeous arcade driving game of its day.
longDescription:
Built in twin or deluxe cabinets that can be linked for up to eight players, the game is modelled on the BPR Global GT Series, featuring the cars of four prominent teams of the 1996 season. Every opponent car apart from the selectable ones is a Renault Alpine GTA/A610. There are four courses of varying difficulty, two of them beginner level in day and night versions, and as with Daytona USA, operators can switch on Grand Prix or Endurance modes for longer races. Its heads-up display and handling resemble Daytona's, but acceleration while drifting changes drifting strategy radically.

The 1997 update, Scud Race Plus, allowed every course to be raced in reverse and added a bizarre "Super-Beginner" course, an oval inside a giant children's playhouse with a rocking horse and bowling pins to hit, where players can race as a cat, a tank, an "AM2 crew" bus or a tin racing car. It was never marketed outside Japan, though switching the region setting gives "Sega Super GT Plus".
trivia: It was renamed Super GT in North America because "scud" recalled the Scud missiles of the then-recent Gulf War.
During testing, key members of the team raced the four real cars featured in the game.
AM2 head Yu Suzuki, though not on the team, advised on the drift handling and sound sampling.
A Dreamcast port was shown as a tech demo in 1998 but cancelled, and the game has never had a console release.
Its four tracks appear as an unlockable route in the Xbox version of OutRun 2.
devStory:
After Daytona USA, fans expected a sequel, and director Toshihiro Nagoshi said that with the same team many assumed one was automatic; instead, an arcade test game called Supercar evolved into Scud Race, which he felt had "a completely different look". Sega AM4 designed the cabinet. It was planned as the first Model 3 game but was pushed back for marketing reasons to follow Virtua Fighter 3, and made its world debut at the ATEI show in London on 21 January 1997 after a location test in California. A Saturn version was reported in April 1997, expected to need a proposed 64-bit upgrade cartridge, but never appeared.

Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful dedicated arcade game in its 1 March 1997 issue. Hyper gave it five stars, and Next Generation called it "the most gorgeous driving game ever to grace an arcade", a "visual masterpiece" with realistic speeds that players "have never ever experienced".

title: Prop Cycle
description: Prop Cycle (1996) is Namco's arcade flying game controlled by pedalling a bicycle-like cabinet, in which a pilot pops balloons to bring the floating islands of Solitar back to earth, inspired partly by Kiki's Delivery Service.
longDescription:
Prop Cycle is a 3D flying simulator in which the player pilots a human-powered aircraft, called a Lapperopter, by pedalling to spin its propeller and using handlebars to steer left and right and change altitude. The aim is to pop hot-air balloons. The player must first pass three test routes around their hometown, popping balloons that imitate the energy balls powering an ancient machine, to earn a single chance to fly to Solitar and destroy the real ones.

Two hundred years earlier, a war fought with a hyperspace magnetic weapon called the Tesla Bomb destroyed civilisation and carved the world into steep canyons. The survivors abandoned high technology for a simple life, using steam engines powered by fuel stones, and refined flight until people could fly with their own muscle power. When someone accidentally activates old technology hidden in a shrine, pieces of the town are torn from the ground and float into the sky as the islands of Solitar, rising ever higher with the townspeople trapped on them. Destroying the machine's energy balls brings the islands back down where they belong.
trivia: Designer Shigeki Toyama had worked on Xevious, Final Lap and Point Blank.
It grew from a 2D tech demo of a human-powered plane shooting enemies, whose sense of flight Toyama found intriguing.
The team spent a day hang gliding with a camera attached to the glider's wings.
To show programmer Naoyuki Koyama what "riding the wind" meant, Toyama attached a weight to an umbrella.
A planned "Sightseeing" free-flight mode was cut for time.
devStory:
Toyama wanted Prop Cycle to be highly interactive, with a reason to exist only in arcades, and distinct from other games, letting players feel the thrill of flight and the wind rather than simply defeat enemies. Development of the flying alone took three to four months. Jokingly calling himself the project's "movie director", Toyama designed the setting, story and characters and drew the art for the villages and levels, though he later regretted making players reach the last stage to understand the story. He was inspired by Studio Ghibli's Kiki's Delivery Service.

Game Machine reported it as Japan's second most popular arcade game of August 1996. Next Generation concluded that "in the final analysis, Prop Cycle's strengths win out over its weaknesses". Retro Gamer later called it one of the most unique arcade games ever made and more accessible than Namco's and Sega's other offerings, adding that there was "no question as to how it has stayed in so many locations after almost two decades".

title: Jet Moto
description: Jet Moto (1996), Jet Rider in Europe, is SingleTrac's PlayStation hoverbike racer over land and water, with magnetic grapples for slingshotting round corners, seen as Sony's answer to Wave Race 64.
longDescription:
Players race hoverbikes that float just above the ground and can ride over both land and water, and most courses are built around that ability, from beaches with debris-strewn water and ice-covered mountains to a track floating above a city. Alongside conventional circuits, it introduced "suicide" courses: the starting grid is in the middle, with checkpoints at either end, so riders race to one end, turn around and head for the other, repeatedly facing oncoming traffic. Riders belong to teams, and bikes carry logos of real products such as Mountain Dew and Butterfinger, like sponsored real-world racing.

The magnetic grapple lets a rider press a button near a red energy pole to attract the bike to it, slingshotting round tight turns without slowing down or swinging across gaps too wide to ride over. Each lap also gives four boosts. Twenty riders and three tracks are available at first, with seven more tracks unlocked by winning tournaments.
trivia: SingleTrac also made Twisted Metal and Twisted Metal 2.
Game Revolution likened its Dick Dale-style surf guitar to "spy tunes from James Bond movies".
The Electric Playground named its soundtrack one of the best of 1996.
It joined the PlayStation Greatest Hits range in August 1998.
It was re-released on PlayStation Network for the PSP and PS3 in 2007.
devStory: SingleTrac developed Jet Moto for Sony Computer Entertainment, which released it on the PlayStation in North America on 31 October 1996, in Europe in February 1997 and in Japan that August, with a PC version in November 1997. At the time it was seen as Sony's response to Nintendo's Wave Race 64. Reviews were mixed, averaging 78.9% on GameRankings for the PlayStation version and 75% for the PC: reviewers felt it had solid gameplay but was too difficult, and several praised its surf-rock soundtrack, GameSpot's Shane Mooney calling it "just the adrenaline pump [he] needed". It sold well enough to join the Greatest Hits line. SingleTrac made Jet Moto 2 in 1997 before leaving Sony, and Pacific Coast Power & Light developed Jet Moto 3 in 1999; later sequels, Jet Moto 2124 and a PS2 game, Jet Moto: SOLAR, were cancelled.

title: Koudelka
description: Koudelka (1999) is Sacnoth's gothic horror RPG for the PlayStation, created by former Square composer Hiroki Kikuta, in which a Romani psychic explores a haunted Welsh monastery in 1898, and the forerunner of Shadow Hearts.
longDescription:
Play moves between story scenes, exploration with puzzles, and battles. Exploration resembles early Resident Evil: Koudelka, a 3D model, moves through pre-rendered backgrounds seen from fixed camera angles, collecting a limited number of items and weapons. Random encounters lead to turn-based battles on a grid, where the three characters and their enemies move a square and act each turn with physical and magical attacks, status effects and healing. Weapons break after a number of uses, battles give experience and points to raise attributes, and weapons and abilities strengthen with use.

In 1898, near Aberystwyth, the Romani psychic Koudelka Iasant is drawn by a mysterious voice to Nemeton, a former monastery turned mansion now infested with monsters. With the adventurer Edward Plunkett and the Catholic bishop James O'Flaherty, sent by the Vatican to recover the Émigré Document, a book of Celtic rituals for immortality and raising the dead, she uncovers how Nemeton's owner used it to resurrect his murdered wife Elaine as a monster. The cast includes the caretakers Ogden and Bessy Hartman, who poison their guests, the ghost of an executed girl and a still-living Roger Bacon. Three endings depend on the player's actions.
trivia: All dialogue is spoken in English, with Japanese subtitles in Japan.
Motion capture for scenes of up to four people was recorded at FutureLight in Santa Monica, since the technology was not available in Japan.
Kikuta's inspirations included William Hope Hodgson's Carnacki, the Ghost-Finder and The Name of the Rose.
Koudelka's name comes from the photographer Josef Koudelka.
A twelve-year-old Sara Paxton voiced the ghost Charlotte.
devStory:
Kikuta, composer of Secret of Mana and Seiken Densetsu 3, wanted to direct but could not progress beyond composing at Square, so with SNK's funding he founded Sacnoth in 1997 with other Square staff and became the game's director, producer, writer and composer. He planned real-time battles with free movement, but staff who kept Square's traditional ideas built the turn-based grid instead, which he later regretted. The team researched British history and travelled to Pembrokeshire to study scenery and church architecture, and Yūji Iwahara drew over 100 character sketches. The score, arranged with Nick Ingman, used ambient sounds and church music influences.

SNK released it in Japan on 16 December 1999 and Infogrames in the West in 2000. It was "moderately successful" in Japan, and reviews were mixed: critics praised its atmosphere, cut-scenes and localisation but found the battles slow, the difficulty uneven and the weapon durability frustrating. Kikuta then left Sacnoth, and his planned sequels were never made; instead it led to Shadow Hearts, set after Koudelka's bad ending.

title: Brigandine: The Legend of Forsena
description: Brigandine (1998) is Hearty Robin's PlayStation turn-based strategy game of conquest on the continent of Forsena, in which Rune Knights lead troops of dragons, ghouls and pixies to take enemy castles.
longDescription:
The player rules one of six nations and aims to conquer the continent by capturing enemy castles while defending their own. Troops are led by Rune Knights, human or elven commanders, and made up of monsters such as dragons, ghouls and pixies, with RPG-style statistics; knights can change classes, and monsters can be promoted to stronger forms. A knight's Rune Power limits how many monsters can join their troop. In the preparation mode, each turn is a month: players reorganise troops, summon monsters with mana generated by their castles (monsters also cost mana in upkeep), equip items and send knights on quests, unplayable events that remove them for a few turns with good or bad results. They then send troops to attack adjacent enemy castles.

Battles are fought turn by turn on hexagonal grids, with up to three troops a side. The attacker has twelve turns to defeat every defending troop, and a troop is beaten when its leader falls or retreats; if a nation's ruler falls, its whole force withdraws. Monsters outside their leader's Rune Area grow weaker and are more likely to be captured, and slain monsters are lost for good. Units and spells carry elements, with red opposing blue and white opposing black. The war begins when General Zemeckis, accused of treason, overthrows King Henguist of Almekia and renames it the Esgares Empire.
trivia: Hearty Robin was known as Easlystaff when it showed the game at the September 1997 Tokyo Game Show.
Rulers have a unique class but cannot go on quests.
The 2000 Grand Edition added six-player multiplayer, a playable Esgares Empire, anime cut-scenes and Japanese voice acting.
Grand Edition switched its elements to a rock-paper-scissors system like Fire Emblem.
A sequel, Brigandine: The Legend of Runersia, came out on Switch in 2020.
devStory: Hearty Robin developed Brigandine for the PlayStation and released it in Japan in 1998, and Atlus published it in North America the same year as Brigandine: The Legend of Forsena. Primarily a strategy game, it also borrows the character growth of tactical role-playing games, with knights and monsters levelling up and changing class or form. In 2000 Hearty Robin released an expanded Brigandine: Grand Edition in Japan with multiplayer for up to six players, a playable Esgares Empire with its own story scenes, new knights, classes, items and monsters, simpler and faster 2D battle animations, a reworked soundtrack, an anime opening and a final boss once the continent is conquered. Twenty years later Matrix Software developed a sequel, The Legend of Runersia, published by Happinet for the Nintendo Switch in June 2020.

title: Robotrek
description: Robotrek (1994), Slapstick in Japan, is Quintet's comic SNES role-playing game in which a young inventor builds and programs up to three robots to fight for him, often cited as a forerunner of Pokémon.
longDescription:
Unlike most RPGs, the hero does not fight himself; the robots he invents do. Up to three can be built and customised in equipment, special attacks, colour and name. The player must invent their equipment, assign their attributes with Program Points rather than having them set automatically, and program special attacks as macro-like combinations of commands. Inventing is central: an invention machine combines items and Scrap into new equipment, more recipes come from the "Inventor's Friends" books, and weapons combined with others of the same type grow stronger, up to nine levels.

Battles start on contact with enemies on the map. One robot fights at a time, against up to three enemies, under a variation of the active-time system: it moves freely and attacks, then a gauge from E to F drains according to the action, and enemies act until it refills. Switching robots costs a turn. Experience comes as "Megs of Data", with bonuses for quick melee kills, and dropped items can be recycled for money. On the planet Quintenix, the hero, son of the inventor Dr. Akihabara, fights the Hackers, a gang led by Blackmore who want a time-travelling stone called the Tetron.
trivia: It was billed as a "comedy RPG", as its Japanese title Slapstick implies.
Designer Reiko Takebayashi first imagined the player building robots to help townspeople, who would rate the help to give experience.
Kōji Yokota designed the robots to look "retro" or "old fashioned".
It sold only 45,000 copies in Japan and 20,000 in North America.
Next Generation's Joe Keiser credited it as a predecessor of Pokémon's core play, with robots kept in capsules outside battle.
devStory:
Quintet, maker of ActRaiser, Soul Blazer and Illusion of Gaia, developed the game with sound by Yuzo Koshiro's Ancient and music by Ayako Yoda. Quintet president Masaya Hashimoto directed, Shinji Futami produced, Takebayashi was chief designer and writer and Shigemi Kita lead programmer, recoding the battle system several times. The concept was devised three years before release and development took a year and a half; an army of villains was later added to the original town-helping idea.

Enix released it in Japan on 8 July 1994 and North America that October, one of its last Western releases before a hiatus. Former Enix America producer Robert Jerauld blamed poor sales on little advertising and a crowded market. Reviews were mostly average: GameFan called it "a totally different and refreshing RPG experience" and critics liked inventing and robot-building, but GamePro said it "unsuccessfully attempts to push the envelope of its genre", and its graphics and rough translation drew criticism. Several writers have since noted its similarities to Pokémon and Robopon.

title: ActRaiser 2
description: ActRaiser 2 (1993) is Quintet's SNES sequel that drops the original's city-building for pure side-scrolling action, in which a winged Master fights the seven deadly sins in a story drawn from Paradise Lost and The Divine Comedy.
longDescription:
The game keeps only the platform action of the first ActRaiser, removing the city-building simulation. As the Master ("God" in the Japanese version), the player watches over the world from a floating palace, hears the people's plight and descends to fight the monsters. Each area has two acts: the first against minions of a lesser demon named after an unfavourable condition, the second against monsters of a greater evil named after one of the seven deadly sins. The Master now has working wings and must jump, fly, fall and float between platforms, armed with a sword and a shield that deflects some attacks. He relies heavily on magic, charged by holding a button and released to use up one of a limited number of scrolls, taking different forms depending on his position. Higher difficulty lengthens the charge time and toughens enemies, and the final area, Death Heim, cannot be reached on easy.

Tanzra ("Satan" in Japan), once the Master's servant, led a rebellion and was banished from the Sky Castle. Revived by his seven deadly sins, he unleashes them on the world. After defeating the sins and the mechanical false god Destruction in the Tower of Souls, the Master rams the Sky Castle into Death Heim to break Tanzra's barrier and faces him frozen in a lake of ice, like Satan in Dante's Inferno.
trivia: Quintet said it was made at Enix of America's request and designed to their specifications.
The prison for tax defaulters in the city of Leon is called Gratis.
The Tower of Babel was renamed the Tower of Souls in Western versions.
In the ending, the Master's statue slowly erodes, echoing the first game's suggestion that the world may one day forget him.
Quintet's later Saturn remake of both games, Act Remix, was reworked into Solo Crisis.
devStory: Quintet developed ActRaiser 2, and Enix released it for the Super Famicom in Japan on 29 October 1993, with Western releases following. It had no direct story link to the first game. Readers of Super Famicom Magazine gave it 20.3 out of 30, and critics were generally favourable. Quintet reported 180,000 copies sold worldwide: 100,000 in North America and 40,000 each in Japan and Europe. Total! ranked it 38th among SNES games in 1995, and in 2018 Complex placed it 81st, saying it was great despite being strictly a platformer without the first game's god elements. Quintet began a third ActRaiser for the Nintendo 64 but never finished it.

title: Hagane: The Final Conflict
description: Hagane: The Final Conflict (1994) is CAProduction and Red's SNES action-platformer starring a cyborg ninja on a mission of revenge, a demanding cult favourite compared with Shinobi and Ninja Gaiden.
longDescription:
The game blends traditional ninja and samurai imagery with a futuristic setting. Hagane switches between four weapons, a sword, a chain, shuriken and grenades, and has a limited supply of magic attacks that clear the screen. His moves include somersaults, flying jump kicks, wall jumps, slides and charge attacks. Three hits kill him, though health power-ups extend his meter beyond three until he dies. All the stages are platforming, except one in which he rides a hovercraft through a Mode 7 sequence. The stages are short but have very few checkpoints, there is no save feature, and running out of lives returns the player to the start of the chapter; the Japanese version allows only seven continues.

The Fuma and Koma ninja clans have mastered ninjutsu and black magic. The Fuma guard the Holy Grail, said to be powerful enough to destroy the world, until the evil Koma attack one of their factions and steal it. One man, Hagane, survives on the brink of death and is rebuilt by a mysterious old man, Momochi, with cyber-technology, only his brain remaining of his body. He sets out for revenge on the Koma clan; at the end, his purpose fulfilled, his eyes fade to black and time and nature reclaim his seated body.
trivia: GamePro called its music "techno Japanese rock at its most mundane".
Nintendo Power compared its graphics to "a good NES game".
Next Generation noted a striking resemblance to the Genesis Shinobi games.
Hardcore Gaming 101 called it a "cult classic" and "sleeper hit".
Total! ranked it 45th among SNES games in 1995.
devStory: CAProduction and Red Entertainment developed the game for Hudson Soft, which released it in Japan on 18 November 1994, in Europe in May 1995 and in North America in June 1995. Reviews were positive and compared it favourably with classic side-scrolling action games. Nintendo Power praised its challenge, non-stop action and controls, likening it to Ninja Gaiden, but faulted its lack of variety. GamePro liked the controls and the variety of special moves, recommending it to players wanting a nostalgic action game, but felt the repetitive enemies and settings and the waning 16-bit market stopped it being a classic. Next Generation praised its dark, detailed graphics and wide set of attacks while criticising its lack of originality. In a retrospective, Kurt Kalata found its play heavily influenced by Shinobi III and challenging, but thought its many mechanics underused and its environments too dark.

title: Cybernator
description: Cybernator (1992), Assault Suits Valken in Japan, is Masaya's SNES mecha action game in which soldier Jake Brain pilots an Assault Suit through a war over Earth's dwindling fuel, censored in its Western release.
longDescription:
Set in a future where Earth's fossil fuels are running out, the game follows a world war between the Axis and the Federation for the remaining resources and for territory on the Moon, fought with giant space stations and weapons of mass destruction. Jake, drafted into the Pacific States' Marine Corps, pilots a humanoid Federation Assault Suit with arms, legs, a torso and a head, a range of weapons and accessories, and full land and limited air capability. In the prologue he says he fights only because he is a soldier, not out of patriotism or politics.

From the warship Versis, Jake's platoon is tasked with destroying Bildvorg, the Axis's most powerful mech, piloted by Major Beldark, and the missions build towards that goal; in the fourth, the player saves an enemy suit entering the atmosphere while Beldark kills Jake's ally Apollo. The game has two endings. Failing any mission, such as not stopping the Arc Nova from falling or letting an enemy shuttle escape, leaves the Versis wrecked and Jake's partner Crea dead; succeeding in every mission ends the war with Jake and Crea reunited on the deck.
trivia: It is a prequel to Target Earth, set a century earlier, though released after it.
Designer Satoshi Nakai insisted on destructible environments.
The Western version removed the dialogue portraits and a scene in which the enemy president, under a banner like the EU's, kills himself.
The English manual is full of errors, including the Assault Suit's size and the laser's recharge time.
M2's 2023 Assault Suits Valken Declassified restored the uncensored content with a new translation.
devStory: Toshiro Tsuchida produced the game before joining G-Craft to work on Front Mission, Masanao Akahori composed the soundtrack, and Satoshi Urushihara drew the Japanese artwork. Masaya released it for the Super Famicom on 12 December 1992, and Konami published it in North America as Cybernator in April 1993. It sold only 10,782 copies in Japan, according to Famitsu, but reviews were generally favourable: GameFan called it one of the best SNES games, and EGM's reviewers all praised its graphics, two saying they showed off the SNES hardware, while disagreeing about whether it was too easy or too hard. In 1996 Next Generation said it "introduced many U.S. gamers to classically Japanese design values", and Super Play ranked it the 19th best Super NES game. It was later released on the PlayStation 2, the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console, and on Switch in Declassified form.

title: Pop'n TwinBee
description: Pop'n TwinBee (1993) is Konami's cheerful Super Famicom shoot 'em up, the sixth TwinBee game, in which two players can fly together, punch enemies and even throw each other, and which first reached North America in 2020.
longDescription:
Like Detana!! TwinBee, which it follows, up to two players can fly at once, player one as the blue TwinBee and player two as the pink WinBee. Players enter a name and choose one of three types of companion ships, which follow, engulf or surround their ship, and fly through seven stages, each ending with a boss. Instead of extra lives, each ship has a life meter, and a limited number of continues let players resume at the stage where they fell. As before, the guns shoot airborne enemies and bombs hit the ground, but ships can now also punch enemies at close range and launch tiny replicas of themselves at every enemy on screen, using a stock of charges. In a two-player game, one player can give the other some life energy or throw the partner's ship at the enemy. Bells, which change colour when shot, give different power-ups depending on their colour.

The options include a "couple" mode, which makes enemies aim mainly at player one, so that a less experienced player can enjoy the game alongside a stronger partner. The story begins when TwinBee and WinBee, patrolling Donburi Island, receive a distress call from Madoka, granddaughter of Dr. Mardock, a once-benevolent scientist driven mad by a bump on the head who now plans to conquer the world with an army of Acorn Men.
trivia: Its upbeat soundtrack, composed by Kazuhiko Uehara and others, draws on Japanese idol songs.
It was the first of three TwinBee games released in Europe, published by Konami's Palcom division.
It sold over 40,539 copies in its first week in Japan.
Readers of Super Famicom Magazine gave it 23.17 out of 30 in 1993.
North America first got it 27 years later, through Nintendo Switch Online in February 2020.
devStory: Konami developed and published Pop'n TwinBee for the Super Famicom in 1993 as the sixth game in the TwinBee series and a direct follow-up to the arcade Detana!! TwinBee, known in the West as Bells & Whistles. It was also released on the SNES in the PAL region, the first of three TwinBee games localised for Europe, followed by a Game Boy Pop'n TwinBee that was really the earlier TwinBee Da!! and the platform game Pop'n TwinBee: Rainbow Bell Adventures. According to Famitsu, it sold about 146,124 copies in Japan over its lifetime, and readers of Super Famicom Magazine ranked it 38th among Super Famicom titles in a 1993 poll. Critics' reviews were generally favourable. Its North American debut came only in February 2020, through an update to the Nintendo Switch Online SNES library.

title: Soldier Blade
description: Soldier Blade (1992) is Hudson Soft's fast vertical shoot 'em up for the TurboGrafx-16, the fourth Star Soldier game, rushed out in six months for the company's Caravan tournament and now seen as one of the system's best.
longDescription:
The player flies the starship Soldier Blade through seven "operations" to wipe out the Zeograd Army, an alien race bent on conquering Earth. It shares much with Super Star Soldier but puts heavy emphasis on speed. The ship starts with a Vulcan shot that kills most enemies in one hit, and coloured power capsules change it to a wave gun or a devastating laser, each also adding a pod that gives extra firepower. Collisions with enemies or bullets destroy the ship, but up to three capsules let it absorb three hits. Three power-ups can be kept in a storage box at the bottom of the screen and deployed at any time, and a weapon can be sacrificed for a screen-clearing superweapon. Each stage has a mid-boss and a boss, destroyed by hitting a weak point.

As in other Star Soldier games, two Caravan time-attack modes, of two and five minutes, challenge players to score as many points as possible. Finishing the main game unlocks a stage select.
trivia: It was first called Sonic Blaster F-92, after the player's ship, but was renamed for trademark reasons.
Development began on a 6-megabit HuCard, later cut to 4 megabits.
