Miscommunication made the first stage's large "Bay Wolf" battleships nearly defenceless and the sixth stage's missile pods fire spread shots instead of homing missiles.
A diagonally scrolling asteroid belt stage was cut for time and hardware reasons.
The tournament-only Soldier Blade Special Version, with just the Caravan modes, now fetches high prices.
devStory:
Designer Ukiuki Uribo conceived the game in conversations about what to use for Hudson's upcoming Caravan tournament; Hikaru Aoyama suggested a new shooter, and though Uribo hesitated with the event only six months away, executives pushed it forward. Uribo was also working on Game Boy games, and the team worked under constant time and memory pressure, adding ideas on the spot. Keita Hoshi and Makiko Tanifuji composed the music, Atsushi Kakutani designed the Caravan mode almost alone and Yuji Kaida painted the cover. Uribo wished they had had more time to refine it, and a planned Soldier Blade II never happened.

It was released on the PC Engine in Japan on 10 July 1992 and the TurboGrafx-16 in North America that September. Contemporary reviews were mixed: GameFan compared it favourably to Blazing Lazers, while one EGM reviewer called it "a hastily crafted title" and Player One found it too easy. The 2007 Wii Virtual Console release drew much more praise, Eurogamer calling it "twitch gaming in its purest, most basic form" and IGN singling out its speed.

title: Sonic Spinball
description: Sonic Spinball (1993) is Sega Technical Institute's Genesis pinball spin-off in which Sonic himself is the ball, made in nine months by American staff to fill the gap left by Sonic 3's delay.
longDescription:
Most of the game takes place inside Robotnik's "Pinball Defense System", four levels built like giant pinball machines in which Sonic is the ball. Flippers aim and launch him through each level, and he can be steered in the air with the directional pad after bouncing off bumpers or when falling towards the drain. The goal of each level is to collect every Chaos Emerald, some blocked until certain switches or bumpers are hit, and then defeat the boss that becomes accessible at the top, each needing its own strategy. A status strip gives hints and shows how many Emeralds remain. Beating a boss starts a bonus round on a regular pinball table with three balls, where the player can shake the table, though tilting too often locks the flippers.

Sonic starts with three lives, losing one each time he falls down a drain, and earns another at 20,000,000 points, scored from bumpers, loops, rings and enemies. Set in the world of the Sonic the Hedgehog TV series, the story has Robotnik build a fortress on a volcano, powered by magma and stabilised by the Chaos Emeralds, to turn the animals of Mobius into robot slaves.
trivia: Designer Peter Morawiec drew on Sonic 2's popular Casino Night Zone and the Amiga game Pinball Dreams.
To save time the team switched from assembly to C, unusual for Genesis games, which caused frame-rate problems.
Just before shipping, Sega learned it did not own the Sonic title theme, and composer Howard Drossin wrote a new one in two hours.
A Game Gear port replaced Sonic Drift worldwide after that game's poor reviews in Japan.
A Sonic Spinball spinning rollercoaster opened at Alton Towers in 2010.
devStory:
With Sonic 2 having boosted Genesis sales in 1992, Sega of America's management commissioned another Sonic game for the 1993 holidays when it realised Sonic 3 would not be ready, and the mostly American Sega Technical Institute made it while the Japanese team worked on Sonic 3. Morawiec and three colleagues pitched it with animations of Sonic as a pinball, and Sega sent veteran Japanese staff, including artist Katsuhiko Sato, to help; much of the game came together between June and August 1993. It was released in November 1993, followed by Game Gear and Master System versions in 1994 and 1995.

Morawiec expected "acceptance challenges" but was surprised it sold well, though he regretted the lack of time to polish it. Reviews were mixed: GamePro called it "fun, fast, and frenetic", and EGM's Ed Semrad praised its novelty and presentation, while Entertainment Weekly said Sonic moved like a "leaden marble" and critics widely faulted the controls. Sonic Pinball Party followed in 2003.

title: Thunder Force III
description: Thunder Force III (1990) is Technosoft's Genesis shoot 'em up, the first in the series to be purely horizontal, with a choice of starting planet and adjustable ship speed, ranked by EGM as the best shooter on the system.
longDescription:
The free-directional overhead stages of the first two games are gone, replaced entirely by horizontal scrolling, which became the series standard. The player chooses which of five planets, Hydra, Gorgon, Seiren, Haides and Ellis, to attack first, and after all five the game continues for three more stages into the ORN headquarters. The weapon system returns from Thunder Force II with changes: the enhanceable Twin shot and Back shot remain the defaults, some old weapons are reused or modified, and others are new. When the ship is destroyed on the default difficulty, only the weapon in use is lost, unless it is a default one; on higher difficulties every weapon is lost. Collecting the CLAW item now gives the full two CLAWs at once, and they fire the same weapon as the ship, like the Options in Gradius. The ship's speed can be raised or lowered across four levels at the press of a button.

Set about 100 years after Thunder Force and straight after Thunder Force II, the story has the Galaxy Federation struggling against the ORN Empire, which hides its base behind cloaking devices on five planets and defends itself with Cerberus, a system deadly to large ships and fleets. The Federation builds the FIRE LEO-03 Styx, small enough to slip past Cerberus but as powerful as a large starfighter, to destroy the cloaking devices and the ORN emperor, the bio-computer Cha Os.
trivia: Its success led Technosoft to retool it for arcades as Thunder Force AC.
Thunder Force AC was ported to the SNES in 1991 as Thunder Spirits by Toshiba EMI, without level selection.
Famitsu gave Thunder Force III 31 out of 40 but Thunder Spirits only 23.
Mega ranked it 17th among Mega Drive games in 1992.
After Sega bought the series' rights, Thunder Force AC came to Switch in 2020 as part of Sega Ages.
devStory: Technosoft developed and published Thunder Force III for the Mega Drive in Japan on 8 June 1990. The Genesis version was widely praised: GamePro called it "a straightforward flying shooter with gorgeous graphics", noting its large, detailed enemies and intricate backgrounds but warning that it was extremely difficult and best suited to hardcore fans, and MegaTech praised its parallax scrolling, sound and gameplay. In 1997 EGM listed it as the 59th best console game of all time and the best shooter on the Genesis. Its success brought it to arcades as Thunder Force AC on Sega's System C-2 board, nearly identical graphically but borrowing enemies and stages from Thunder Force II; Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixteenth most successful table arcade unit in its 1 February 1991 issue. Thunder Force III was re-released in Thunder Force Gold Pack 1 for the Saturn in 1996.

title: Gradius Gaiden
description: Gradius Gaiden (1997) is Konami's Japan-only PlayStation shoot 'em up, the fourth mainline Gradius, with four selectable ships, a rearrangeable power meter and the series' first two-player simultaneous play, seen as one of its best.
longDescription:
Players control one of four starships, the Vic Viper, Lord British, Jade Knight and Falchion β, to stop the Bacterian army destroying the planet Gradius. As before, they shoot down enemies while avoiding them, their projectiles and the terrain, and collect glowing Power Capsules dropped by some enemies to highlight weapons on the Power Meter, among them missiles, a double shot, lasers and the Options, glowing orbs that follow the ship and fight alongside it. Each ship has its own arsenal: the Vic Viper carries the standard Gradius weapons, the Lord British has Salamander's Ripple Laser and a pulsating "Disruptor" shot, the Jade Knight a "Circle Laser" that surrounds it with deadly rings, and the Falchion β a "Black Hole Bomb" that sucks in enemies.

At the start, players can rearrange the items on their Power Meter, for instance moving the Options to the front so they need only one capsule, an idea taken from the "meter edit" mode of Gradius III. Two new shields were added: the Guard, which makes the ship invulnerable to terrain, and the Limit, which gives three seconds of full invincibility. The levels were designed to stand apart from earlier games, from the snowy opening stage "Beyond the White Storm", the first snow level in the series, to a second stage among the remains of bosses, laser-reflecting crystals in the third and rotating Moai statues in the fourth.
trivia: The name Gradius IV was considered but dropped so the team would not stick only to established mechanics; "Gaiden" means "side-story".
The Guard shield came from programmer Isobe Neiichi always dying by colliding with the ground.
A "sea of mud" stage that slowed the ship was scrapped because it was not fun.
The second loop was added as fan service, to thank players who played it extensively.
It is one of twenty games on the Japanese PlayStation Classic, released in 2019.
devStory:
Directed by Seki Teisaku, with designers Kobayashi Takayuki and Chigasaki Kei and sound designer Miura Norikazu, it was made in under a year by staff who had worked on Gradius Deluxe Pack. Because earlier Gradius games were built for arcades and made purposely difficult, designing for a home console let the team make it more balanced and fair. It began as a single-player game; when multiplayer was added, Salamander's Lord British joined as the second player's ship, followed by the Jade Knight and Falchion β, and some effects were built to exploit the PlayStation's rotation and transparency.

Konami released it in Japan on 28 August 1997, but a planned US release bundled with Salamander Deluxe Pack Plus was cancelled, and it first reached the West in 2006's PSP Gradius Collection, without multiplayer. It sold 34,383 copies. Critics praised its visuals, soundtrack and creativity, though Famitsu felt it relied too heavily on fan service; Super Juegos compared it to Castlevania: Symphony of the Night, and Kurt Kalata later called it "the perfect example of how to evolve the series".

title: Neutopia
description: Neutopia (1989) is Hudson Soft's overhead action-adventure for the PC Engine and TurboGrafx-16, in which Jazeta recovers eight medallions to rescue Princess Aurora, widely seen as a close clone of The Legend of Zelda.
longDescription:
The land of Neutopia is divided into four spheres, land, subterrain, sea and sky, and its people prospered with the help of eight spiritual medallions controlled by Princess Aurora. One night the demon Dirth invades, captures the princess in the Climactic Castle and scatters the medallions in crypts across the spheres. The young warrior Jazeta receives a charmed compass at the Sacred Shrine that guides him to them, and must recover two from each sphere, each guarded by a boss, before reaching Dirth at the North Pole.

The top-down exploration resembles The Legend of Zelda. Non-player characters, many in caves revealed by burning objects, bombing walls or pushing rocks, give information. Besides his sword, Jazeta uses a fire rod whose fireballs grow in strength and range with his health, moonbeam moss to light dark rooms, a rainbow drop to cross gaps, falcon shoes for speed, magic rings that turn tough enemies into weaker ones, hourglasses that freeze enemies and wings that warp him back to where he last got a password. Swords, shields and armour upgrade from bronze to silver to "strongest", and his life meter grows with each medallion or monk he finds. Progress is kept by passwords or, with a TurboGrafx-CD or TurboBooster-Plus, in four save slots.
trivia: Enemies include spear-throwing goblins, fireball-throwing fish, fake rocks, ghosts and charging knights.
German magazine Power Play said the differences from Zelda "must be found with an electron microscope".
Its passwords run to 24 characters.
IGN called it "one of the most shameless Legend of Zelda clones ever created".
It was released on the Wii Virtual Console alongside Super Metroid and Shinobi III.
devStory: Hudson Soft developed Neutopia and released it for the PC Engine in Japan on 17 November 1989, and NEC released it for the TurboGrafx-16 in North America on 15 April 1990, after previews in Electronic Gaming Monthly and GamePro and a full walkthrough in the first issue of TurboPlay. Reviewers have widely regarded it as a Zelda clone, but many have praised its improvements over Nintendo's game: Nintendo Life's Marcel van Duyn singled out the fire rod, the warping wings and a lower difficulty, concluding it might be better than what it copied. Critics also faulted its long passwords, repetitive play and poor collision detection, and GameSpot found it more linear than Zelda, with grating music, though it praised the varied environments. Overall it is considered one of the better games of its type and of the TurboGrafx-16 library. It later came to the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console and PlayStation Network, and a sequel, Neutopia II, follows Jazeta's son searching for his missing father.

title: Air Zonk
description: Air Zonk (1992) is Red Company's TurboGrafx-16 shoot 'em up that reimagines the Bonk series in a punkish future, starring the sunglasses-wearing Zonk and a cast of absurd companions, and EGM's TurboGrafx-16 game of the year.
longDescription:
Air Zonk recasts the Bonk series as a scrolling shooter set in the future, with lighthearted, humorous designs for its environments and characters in the style sometimes called a "cute 'em up". Across five levels, play centres on shooting and bombing. Zonk can charge his shots for a more powerful attack, and a longer charge drops a bomb that damages every enemy on screen. Seven types of power-up can be collected, each with its own charged special attack; as in most shooters, picking up a new one replaces the current one, and if Zonk is hit while holding a power-up he loses it rather than his life, except with the Mini-Zonk, which cannot be charged and also drops from random enemies rather than only from florets.

Before play, the player chooses a companion, such as an anthropomorphic gumball machine or a mummy with a drill on its head, and can limit which friends are used on each level or play without them; each can only be used once. Zonk starts every stage alone and must collect eight smiley faces, the last appearing in giant form with sunglasses, to summon his friend, who first follows him like a Gradius-style option. Eight more smiley faces merge the two into a hybrid form with a new attack and 20 seconds of invulnerability. When it expires, a hit reverts Zonk to normal and the friend leaves, though he keeps any power-up he held before.
trivia: Zonk was designed to resemble Bonk, the TurboGrafx-16's caveman mascot, as part of an effort to update Hudson's image.
Bonk's antagonist King Drool appears, along with many other enemies from that series.
The three difficulty settings are sweet, spicy and bitter.
Readers of PC Engine Fan gave it 23.74 out of 30 in 1993, placing it 55th among PC Engine games.
Its 1993 sequel, Super Air Zonk: Rockabilly-Paradise, has a CD soundtrack of rockabilly music.
devStory: Red Company, the original creators of the Bonk series and also known for Gate of Thunder, developed Air Zonk with assistance from Naxat Soft, and Hudson Soft published it for the TurboGrafx-16 in 1992. The game was an attempt to modernise the company's image with a punkish new character who deliberately echoed its established mascot. It was well received: it holds 76.25% on GameRankings from four reviews, and Electronic Gaming Monthly named it TurboGrafx-16 Game of the Year in its 1992 awards. The sequel, Super Air Zonk: Rockabilly-Paradise, known in Japan as CD Denjin Rockabilly, followed in 1993 in the Super CD format for the TurboDuo, requiring the Super System Card on first-generation TurboGrafx-CD units, with all-new levels, assistants and enemies. Air Zonk came to the Wii Virtual Console in Japan in May 2007 and in North America and Europe that July, and to the Wii U Virtual Console in Japan in June 2014 and in the West in 2017.

title: Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams
description: Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams (1991) is Success's arcade shoot 'em up in which a sweet-obsessed young witch rides her broomstick through a dream world, the first Cotton game and a key title of the "cute 'em up" style.
longDescription:
Reminiscent of Parodius, the game follows the young witch Cotton and her fairy companion Silk through increasingly difficult levels of a fantasy, dream-like world. Players blast monsters and dodge their shots while collecting crystal power-ups that strengthen Cotton's firepower and unleash magic spells, and bombs can obliterate enemies. It adds role-playing elements, letting players level up their attack through 13 levels, but each of Cotton's three lives allows only one hit, and the game ends when all are lost unless more credits are inserted. It uses a main two-button configuration, runs on Sega's System 16 hardware and supports multiplayer.

The world of Filament has been wrapped in an evil mist that brings eternal night. Silk asks Cotton to defeat the monsters spreading the darkness, and Cotton refuses until Silk mentions Willow candy, which she will do anything to get, sending her off on her broomstick to save the world and claim her reward. Unusually for an arcade game of the time, it used hand-drawn animation.
trivia: Its working title was Kurumi-zaka Diary: Katsugeki-Hen.
Character designer Hideki Tamura had just quit the anime industry, and this was his first game job.
The Neo Geo Pocket Color version has become an expensive collector's item.
A 2007 mobile release was celebrated with a lottery for 50 Cotton-themed teacups.
Twinkle Star Sprites designer Yoshiyasu Matsushita named it as an influence.
devStory:
Success founder Takato Yoshinari produced the game, with Masaru Hatsuyama and Toshiyuki Kuwabara programming, Tamura and Shinobu Itō among the pixel artists, music by Kenichi Hirata and radio actress Takae Yoriguchi voicing Cotton. Sega published it in arcades in April 1991 and showed it at that year's AOU Show. It was popular in Japanese arcades: Game Machine listed it as the ninth most popular arcade game of May 1991, and it won awards at the 5th Gamest Grand Prize, including second place for Cotton herself among characters.

Hudson Soft brought it to the PC Engine Super CD-ROM² in February 1993, with CD audio and Tarako voicing Cotton in Japan, and Turbo Technologies released it in North America that April; critics praised its graphics and gameplay but some found the translation incoherent. An enhanced X68000 version followed in 1993, Cotton Original reached the PlayStation in 1999 to mixed reviews, Famitsu saying it was showing its age, and a Mega-CD port was never released. Cotton Reboot!, a remake based on the X68000 version, came out in 2021, and Retro Gamer counts the original among the key cute 'em ups.

title: WeaponLord
description: WeaponLord (1995) is Visual Concepts' gory weapons-based fighting game for the SNES and Genesis, designed by former Capcom staff for hardcore fans, with a deep counterattack system and early tuning for online play.
longDescription:
At its core WeaponLord is a standard 2D fighting game, but its mechanics set it apart. Thrust-blocking is an aggressive block similar to Street Fighter III's parry, every character has Deflect counterattacks, and special moves called "Take Downs" knock opponents onto their backs so the attacker can keep hitting them on the floor. Certain attacks landed on an opponent in mid-swing slice off a piece of clothing or hair, and matches can be finished with "Death Combos", gory Fatality-style combinations. Each fighter has between 9 and 12 special moves, performed with directional sweeps, two-second charges or by holding an attack button through a motion and releasing it. A password at the end of each match lets players return mid-game, a secret password makes the Demonlord Zarak playable in Story Mode, and endings change depending on which opponents were spared or killed with a Death Combo.

The story begins when a demon spirit enters a dying mercenary, who is reborn, defeats twenty rulers and becomes the Demonlord Raith. A shaman foretells that a child born on a violent night will rise to kill him, but Raith refuses his lieutenants' advice to kill that night's children. Years later the demon Zarak overthrows him, and twenty-five years after the prophecy he holds a tournament of champion warriors whose winner will face him in a final battle.
trivia: Making it weapons-based came from designer James Goddard's fascination with Conan the Barbarian.
Large sprites limited it to seven characters, so each was given an unusually large number of moves.
Comic artist Simon Bisley drew the cover art and logo.
It was the only game to display the XBAND logo on its box.
Only Zarak has a signature fatality; unique death combos were planned for everyone but cut in the rush to finish.
devStory:
Goddard had co-designed Street Fighter II: Champion Edition and Hyper Fighting and created Dee Jay, and Dave Winstead had worked on Super Street Fighter II Turbo. Both experienced tournament players, they left Capcom for Namco to gain creative control, taking over Ken Lobb's four-player brawler codenamed "Melee" and turning it into a one-on-one fighter designed for home consoles rather than arcades. They timed parry animations and turnaround for the lag of XBAND dial-up play, working closely with XBAND, which made it one of the first fighting games optimised for online play. Visual Concepts worked to a very tight schedule, adding the Genesis version late; chief programmer Steve Chiang wrote a tool called "Hero" to tune collisions frame by frame, the sprites were hand-pixelled and the painted backgrounds retouched in Photoshop. Before release it was tested in an arcade cabinet at Golfland in Sunnyvale, California.

It was not a large commercial success, which Goddard partly blamed on its arrival at the end of the 16-bit era. Reviews were mixed: critics faulted its choppy animation but praised the depth and innovation of its combat, while warning it was daunting for all but experienced players. It has been thought of as a basis for Namco's Soul Edge and Soulcalibur.

title: Treasure of the Rudras
description: Treasure of the Rudras (1996) is Square's last self-developed Super Famicom RPG, a Japan-only game set in humanity's final 15 days, in which players invent their own spells by typing magic words.
longDescription:
Every 4,000 years a Rudra appears with a new race, and the race before it is destroyed or driven to near extinction; the Danans, Merfolk, Reptiles and Giants have all come and gone, and fossilised Rudras survive as Lago Stones. With fifteen days left before humanity's turn, Sion, Surlent, Riza and Dune each come to hold a Jade found in the Lago Stones. The story is split into three scenarios, for the soldier Sion, the priestess Riza and the archaeologist Surlent, which can be played in any order and switched between, while the days ebb away in a fixed day-night cycle; actions in one can affect the others, so a relic left behind by one group may be found later by another. A fourth scenario brings in the thief Dune and all the heroes against the villains, including the evolutionary Gomorrah, the weapon Sodom on the Moon and the creator Mitra.

Exploration and turn-based battles follow the usual RPG pattern, but magic is unique. Players write spells of up to six katakana characters into a grimoire, called kotodama in Japanese. Most words do something, though most are useless; a full mantra combines a prefix, an elemental core and a suffix, with eight elements plus healing, and roots such as tou for lightning or aqu for water. Some unique words, many in English, skip the system entirely, and players can copy spells they see enemies cast.
trivia: Its plot borrows from Indian religions, with the name Rudra taken from an aspect of Shiva.
Battle planner Masahiro Kataoka imagined players swapping discovered words with friends.
Its engine was based on Final Fantasy V's technology, even though it was made alongside Final Fantasy VI.
The monster sprites were animated, unusual for Square's RPGs, to compete with rising 3D graphics.
Translating it means altering the game's code as well as its text, and it only reached English through a fan translation.
devStory:
Square's Osaka division made the game over three years from 1993, led by director Kouji Ide, whose staff had worked on Final Fantasy Legend III and Final Fantasy Mystic Quest. Ide's team started with the magic system, basing it on Japan's love of word play. Field planner Masato Yagi, hired in 1994, was given free rein over the maps, and programmer Shingo Tanaka tried to make long battles stress-free. Keita Amemiya, advertised from the start, only officially joined a year and a half before the end, revising existing designs with his studio Crowd, and Ryuji Sasai composed the music.

It was released on 5 April 1996, within four months of Bahamut Lagoon, Super Mario RPG and Treasure Hunter G, among Square's last Super Famicom games. Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40 and a place in its Silver Hall of Fame, praising how easy the complex magic was to understand, and Consoles+ rated it 92%. Retrospectively, Retro Gamer called it a "hidden gem" and HobbyConsolas one of the best Super NES games, while Destructoid likened its shifting perspectives to Game of Thrones. It came to the Japanese Wii and Wii U Virtual Console before those services closed.

title: Tail Concerto
description: Tail Concerto (1998) is CyberConnect's first game, a PlayStation 3D platformer in which a dog police officer pilots a robot to catch the cat sky pirates of the Black Cats Gang, in a steampunk world of floating islands.
longDescription:
Players control Waffle Ryebread, who pilots the semi-humanoid "Police Robo", which can run, jump, climb ledges and hover briefly. Its mechanical arms pick up and throw crates and bombs, and a long-range "bubble blaster" damages or immobilises enemies. Most levels involve catching enemy kittens by grabbing them with the robot's limbs, some end in boss battles, and others call for mine carts, a jet pack or heat-seeking missiles. The camera is mostly static but can be rotated in some action scenes. Players can also explore towns and talk to non-player characters, and each area hides whistles that give extra lives and boxes holding pieces of artwork for a gallery. It supports the DualShock's analogue sticks and vibration and has three difficulty settings.

The Kingdom of Prairie is a floating archipelago of anthropomorphic dogs and cats with a history of conflict, where dogs are the majority, people commute by airship and technology runs on steam and crystals from an ancient civilisation. Investigating the Black Cats Gang, Waffle recognises its leader Alicia as a childhood friend. The gang kidnap Princess Terria and gather five crystals for their backer Fool, unaware that they once powered the Iron Giant, which nearly destroyed the world centuries ago. Fool awakens it using Alicia's pendant, a childhood gift from Waffle, but the giant turns on him, and Waffle destroys its core.
trivia: Manga artist Nobuteru Yūki designed the characters.
Its Japanese theme song, "For Little Tail", was recorded by Kokia in 1997, a year before her debut.
Kokia called it an "illusion song" because it was not released until 2010, as a B-side.
It sold about 97,000 copies in Japan, short of its goal, and around 150,000 worldwide.
1Up.com's Jeremy Parish said the series felt like a combination of Laputa and Porco Rosso.
devStory:
CyberConnect began it in 1996, shortly after the company was founded, proposing to Bandai a PlayStation game in the vein of Super Mario 64 and Nights into Dreams. It took nearly two years, with almost 20 minutes of animation by Astrovision and music by Chikayo Fukuda and Seizo Nakata, and came out in Japan in April 1998 and France that December. Bandai of America worried that localisation would not finish in time, and the rights passed between US companies, including Activision, before Atlus USA released it in November 1999, replacing the theme song with an instrumental.

Famitsu gave it 30 out of 40, and Western reviews were above average: critics found it charming but too short and easy, and IGN noted an increasingly awkward translation. Company president Hiroshi Matsuyama pitched Tail Concerto 2 to Bandai in 1999, 2000, 2003 and 2004 and was turned down each time because of the low sales, so CyberConnect turned to .hack. The Little Tail Bronx world returned in Solatorobo: Red the Hunter in 2010 and Fuga: Melodies of Steel in 2021.

title: Wild 9
description: Wild 9 (1998) is Shiny Entertainment's 2.5D PlayStation platformer from the Earthworm Jim team, in which Wex Major uses an energy beam called the Rig to grab, bash and torture his enemies.
longDescription:
Wild 9 is a side-scrolling run and gun platformer with 3D polygonal graphics, played on a 2D plane, although the player can occasionally move into the foreground or background. Wex Major's main weapon is the "Rig", an electrical beam projecting from his back that latches on to enemies so they can be whipped around and thrashed, typically by bashing them into floors and walls or carrying them into pits and spikes.

Lost in an unfamiliar galaxy, Wex meets eight strange adventurers and becomes leader of the group they call the "Wild 9". They include Nitro, who explodes when he meets the things he is allergic to; Pokkit, whose jacket has endless pockets of endless things; Pilfer, a lizard with thousands of personalities; Volstagg, with gorilla and gazelle DNA; the solar-powered Crystal; Boomer McTwist, who draws powers from her Scottish superhero father's kilt; the hormonal mechanic MacSheen; Henry, made entirely of water; and B'Angus, a chihuahua-like creature living in the Rig who advises Wex. The 376-year-old Karn wants the Rig to enslave the universe, and kidnaps the rest of the crew, leaving Wex to rescue them.
trivia: Early ideas had a female hero with a glove that could vaporise enemies instantly.
Designer Kevin Munroe described it as if George Lucas had co-written Star Wars with Lewis Carroll and co-directed it with Tex Avery.
Its animation was done by hand rather than with motion capture.
In Japan, Sony released it in 2000 as Wildroid 9.
It was an AIAS finalist for Outstanding Achievement in Sound and Music, losing to Road Rash 3D.
devStory:
Designed by David Perry and Tom Tanaka, Wild 9 shared its developer, publisher and key staff with Earthworm Jim. Development began in 1996, shortly after Earthworm Jim 2, and lasted three years. A Saturn version was cancelled early, which was attributed to Perry's disillusionment with Sega of America's Saturn strategy, though he said work would resume if Sega made the Saturn commercially viable. By the end of 1997 Shiny was also looking at adding the tessellation technology built for Messiah. Interplay gave it a four-million-dollar marketing budget, large for the time, with commercials on ABC and Comedy Central and a spot on the demo disc packed with every new PlayStation.

Released in North America and Europe in September 1998, it received favourable reviews overall. IGN and GamePro enjoyed its Jim-like humour and inventive ways of torturing enemies, but EGM found it unforgivingly difficult, Edge criticised poorly placed checkpoints and scenery blocking the view, and Next Generation felt its rocky development showed in sloppy controls and a lack of variety. Famitsu gave the Japanese version 28 out of 40.

title: Kartia: The Word of Fate
description: Kartia: The Word of Fate (1998), Rebus in Japan, is Atlus's PlayStation tactical RPG in which magical cards create whatever is written on them, told across two intertwined campaigns and best known for Yoshitaka Amano's art.
longDescription:
The game is split into two volumes of 18 chapters each, one following the free knight Toxa Classico and the other Lacryma Christi of the Vigilance order. Each tells a complete story, but the two intertwine in one larger plot. Every chapter revolves around phantoms, beings summoned by certain humans using Kartia, magical cards that create whatever is written on them, such as Fire or Water. Players summon and command phantoms to fight for them, manage their supply of Kartia, cast magic with the cards and use them to make weapons for the human fighters, combining cards to create stronger spells and phantoms. Phantoms can die in battle, but if a human party member falls, the game is over and the chapter must be restarted.

In the world of Rebus, across Cross Land, Idorus, Nordia and Pentagram, Akueldo rebels smuggle the druid Mona, who carries a forbidden original Nothingness Kartia capable of destroying all existence. Toxa helps rescue her, while Lacryma, revealed as the daughter of the hero Kainas, is pressed to become an Inquirer, a Shrine warrior above the law. The rebels, led by Mona's half-elf twin Saradiart, seek the original Kartias needed to raise the floating paradise of Eden, and Lacryma learns that her supposedly dead father has joined them in the hope of reviving her mother.
trivia: Original Kartias kill anyone who uses them, except those with elven blood.
Shigenori Soejima, later known for Persona, worked on its item graphics.
Atlus USA first released it as a Blockbuster Video rental exclusive on 7 August 1998, with retail copies ten days later.
The rental version lacks the foil title lettering on its cover and has its own disc number.
It lost the 1998 OPM Editors' Award for Best Strategy to Final Fantasy Tactics.
devStory: Kartia was made by Atlus's internal R&D1 studio, the team behind Megami Tensei, with series veterans including producer Kouji Okada, scenarist Kazunori Sakai and designer Shirō Takashima, and with art by Yoshitaka Amano, known for his Final Fantasy work. It sold 117,594 copies in Japan and 60,000 in the United States. Reviews were favourable: Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40, and Next Generation praised its excellent soundtrack, competent translation and "immersive and innovative features", saying Atlus could go up against the competition in RPGs and win. GameSpot liked its presentation, music and range of options but found it too linear and its battles slightly monotonous, and GamePro judged it not quite as good as Final Fantasy Tactics or Tactics Ogre, though its two-player mode and unique features made it worthwhile for strategy fans. It was re-released on the Japanese PlayStation Network in 2011.

title: Threads of Fate
description: Threads of Fate (1999), Dewprism in Japan, is Square's light-hearted PlayStation action RPG with two playable heroes, a monster-transforming amnesiac and a banished princess who wants to conquer the world, made by former Xenogears staff.
longDescription:
At the start, players choose between Rue and Mint, and both campaigns play out around the hub town of Carona and the dungeons that open up during the story, all in 3D. Characters jump through minor platforming sections and use two action buttons for real-time attack combinations, under a mostly fixed overhead camera. Instead of experience levels, health rises with damage taken and magic points with the number of spells cast. Rue can collect up to five coins from defeated monsters and transform into them to use their abilities, while Mint fights with dual rings as melee and thrown weapons and combines elemental spells. Each has their own puzzles, with obstacles changed to suit them, and a New Game+ carries abilities over to unlock secret areas.

Rue sees his friend and caretaker Claire killed by an armoured man and wants to revive her; Mint, the selfish princess of the East Heaven Kingdom, is banished by her sister Maya and vows to take back her throne and conquer the world. Both seek the Relic left by the magical Aeon people, said to grant any wish, and cross paths repeatedly. The man who killed Claire, the Doll Master, wants it too, and it emerges that he and Rue are both Dolls, artificial beings made to resurrect the Aeon Valen, whose spirit is preserved in the relic, the Dewprism.
trivia: Mint was originally going to be the only protagonist, aimed at a female audience.
Writer Daisuke Watanabe split the story into two parallel scenarios, doubling his workload.
Staff slept in the office, and motion designer Yuichi Kikuchi had nightmares about the characters.
Monsters were designed mostly not to be scary, and the sound effects kept cartoonish, except for the Doll Master.
Watanabe said it gave him confidence writing female characters, which informed Yuna and Lightning in Final Fantasy.
devStory:
Director Koji Sugimoto, a programmer on Chrono Trigger and Xenogears, wanted something light, funny and accessible to follow Xenogears' mature themes, and to use his PlayStation experience to make a fully 3D game without pre-rendered cut-scenes. Square, which was encouraging smaller projects, approved his prototype, and a team of about twenty former Xenogears staff worked on it from March 1998 for a year and a half, with producer Hiromichi Tanaka, world design by Makoto Shimamoto, character designs by Tsutomu Terada and Tadahiro Usuda, and music by Junya Nakano, who said it shaped his style for Final Fantasy X.

It was released in Japan on 14 October 1999 and in North America on 18 July 2000 by Square Electronic Arts. It sold over 111,000 copies in Japan by the end of 1999, which Sugimoto considered poor, blaming competition. Critics generally praised its gameplay, graphics, story and localisation, though some found it shallow or too short and criticised the camera. Sugimoto said it became a favourite of Square staff including Yoshinori Kitase and Yasumi Matsuno, but a 2004 sequel pitch was rejected.

title: Body Harvest
description: Body Harvest (1998) is DMA Design's open-world Nintendo 64 action game in which a time-travelling soldier fights alien harvesters across a century, driving whatever vehicle he finds, a game Nintendo dropped over its violence.
longDescription:
Every 25 years, aliens from an artificial comet land on Earth, trap whole regions inside shields and harvest the population within a day before moving on. In 2016 they board Station Omega, home to humanity's last survivors, and the genetically engineered soldier Adam Drake escapes in the time machine Alpha I. He must fight through five areas over a hundred years: Greece in 1916, Java in 1941, the United States in 1966, Siberia in 1991 and the comet itself. Stopping the aliens in the first area they attack in each period saves the rest.

Levels are open worlds built around a series of missions. Aliens teleport in by land, air and sea to attack towns, and a meter tracks civilian casualties; if too many die, including from friendly fire or being run over, the area is destroyed and the mission fails. If Harvesters take eight people in one wave, they create a dangerous Mutant that hunts the player. Vehicles are central, from cars, trucks and motorcycles to tanks, armoured cars, boats, planes and helicopters, each with its own speed, armour and fuel, and often needed to progress. Buildings hide weapons, ammunition, fuel and weapon crystals that combine into a powerful laser. Destroying Alien Processors opens new areas and save points, and destroying the Shield Generator leads to each level's boss.
trivia: It was one of 13 games shown at the Nintendo 64's unveiling at Shoshinkai in 1995, and among the least complete.
Project leader John Whyte called the N64's drawing chip "a masterpiece of engineering".
Nintendo once asked the team to make the graphics "more materialistic", which left them puzzled.
A drop of Adam's blood in the opening hints at where his nemesis Tomegatherion is cloned from.
In 2025 it was re-released on a Polymega compilation, licensed by Piko Interactive.
devStory: Body Harvest was intended as a Nintendo 64 launch title. Unlike DMA's previous publisher Psygnosis, which took little interest in its games, Nintendo frequently directed major changes to the gameplay and visual style, and the language barrier made its wishes hard to understand. DMA head David Jones called the relationship "very hard" because Nintendo's quality was so high, saying the team implemented everything it asked for. Nintendo eventually dropped the game over its violent themes, leaving DMA to find a new publisher; Gremlin Interactive acquired the rights and released it in Europe, and Midway published it in North America. Reviews were average according to Metacritic, though Next Generation gave it four stars, calling it less clever and polished than DMA's Space Station Silicon Valley but an unsettling and enjoyable game with many original features.

title: Glover
description: Glover (1998) is Interactive Studios' Nintendo 64 puzzle-platformer starring a living four-fingered glove who must guide bouncing balls back to a castle to restore the Crystal Kingdom.
longDescription:
The aim of each stage is to move a ball to the goal. Six worlds each hold three stages, a boss stage and a bonus stage reached by collecting all its Garib cards, and clearing them restores a crystal to the castle. With the ball, Glover can roll, bounce, throw, slap and dribble it, walk on top of it, with reversed controls, and use it as a trampoline; without it, he can double jump, cartwheel, slam his fist and locate the ball and Garibs. The ball can be magically changed into a rubber ball, which floats and is the most versatile, a bowling ball that sinks and kills enemies, a magnetic ballbearing for precise control, or its fragile crystal form, which doubles Garib points. Potions give timed power-ups, and losing the ball or all three hearts costs a life.

In the Crystal Kingdom, a wizard's castle is surrounded by portals to worlds including Atlantis, a circus, a pirate domain, a horror fortress, a prehistoric era and outer space, and seven crystals on its spires keep the land alive. When the wizard mixes the wrong potions, the blast turns him to stone and throws his gloves away; Glover turns the falling crystals into rubber balls to save them, while the left glove, Glovel, falls in the cauldron and becomes the malevolent Cross-Stitch. A talking hat, Mr. Tip, offers hints.
trivia: The Garibs were named after a faxed bug report that read "There is a problem with the Garib", which nobody understood.
Shigeru Miyamoto reportedly suggested rebranding it as a Mario spin-off called "Mario's Glove".
Nintendo distributed the Nintendo 64 version in Europe.
The PlayStation version tells its story through FMV and changes the opening, with Glovel deliberately handing over the wrong potion.
Metacritic listed the 2025 PS5 re-release as the eighth worst game of that year.
devStory:
Interactive Studios developed Glover for Hasbro Interactive, announcing it at E3 1998, and it was released for the Nintendo 64 and Windows in 1998 and the PlayStation in 1999 under the Atari Interactive label. Nintendo showed interest in publishing it, but talks with Hasbro fell apart. The N64 version was generally well received: IGN praised its gameplay and music, Edge found it not very original but full of surprises, and Next Generation called it "a refreshing angle on typical platformers". The PlayStation port was panned, IGN giving it 2.6 and GameSpot saying it had "lost its soul".

A sequel, Glover 2, was announced in 1999 and reached around 80 to 85% completion before it was cancelled; former programmer James Steele later explained that a Hasbro employee had doubled the first game's cartridge order, leaving roughly half a million dollars of unsold stock. Piko Interactive acquired the rights from Atari SA in 2017, released a remaster on PC in 2022 and console ports in February 2025.

title: Bangai-O
description: Bangai-O (1999) is Treasure's frantic multidirectional shooter for the Nintendo 64, in which a hovering mech fills the screen with up to 100 missiles at once, released in only 10,000 copies before a Dreamcast port took it worldwide.
longDescription:
The player controls a weaponised mech piloted by Riki and his sister Mami, who are trying to stop criminals smuggling fruit contraband to fund their evil deeds. The mech flies freely around each of the game's 44 stages, and the boss must be found and destroyed to advance. It shoots in eight directions, and the pilots can be swapped instantly: Riki fires homing missiles and Mami shoots projectiles that bounce off walls. Stages are full of destructible buildings and obstacles, walls opened by switches, gun turrets and enemy mechs. There is a health meter but no invulnerability after a hit, so a barrage can kill instantly.

Destroyed enemies and objects release fruit that fills a meter powering the "scatter bomb", which can be charged to fire up to 100 shots in every direction at once; landing all 100 opens a portal to a shop selling upgrades. The Dreamcast version, released three months later, streamlined the game: bullets are stronger, destruction itself fills the bomb meter and fruit only adds to the score, the bomb fires up to 400 missiles depending on how close enemy fire is, and the shop is replaced by power-ups hidden in wreckage, with more enemy types.
trivia: Its obscure Japanese title is Bakuretsu Muteki Bangaioh.
Its story is based on typical Japanese yakuza revenge plays.
About ten people worked on it.
GameFan likened it to a mix of Sub-Terrania and Omega Boost, and another reviewer to Robotron.
In February 2026, two independent groups released separate fan translations of the Nintendo 64 version.
devStory:
Treasure programmer Mitsuru Yaida, known as "Yaiman", remembered being amazed by an old shooter that put huge numbers of bullets on screen, almost certainly the 1984 Japanese computer game Hover Attack, and set himself the challenge of handling the collision of that many bullets. Company president Masato Maegawa let him gather a team, with Yaiman as main programmer and "General Manager". They focused on fast, addictive play over graphics, using large, fast 2D effects and anime artwork; artist Koichi Kimura, fresh from Guardian Heroes, wanted to test the limits of 2D.

Announced in June 1999, it was released on 3 September, and ESP shipped only 10,000 copies, believing it a niche game. The Dreamcast version, with reworked sprites and CD-quality music, followed in Japan on 9 December 1999, and after rights passed between several publishers, Conspiracy Entertainment released it in North America in March 2001. Critics praised its manic, retro gameplay and varied level design, IGN calling it "a game that you either love, or just don't understand yet", though Dreamcast reviews were more critical of its graphics. Sequels followed on the DS in 2008 and Xbox 360 in 2011.

title: Shining the Holy Ark
description: Shining the Holy Ark (1996) is Sega's first-person Saturn RPG, a darker Shining game for adults that mixes polygons and sprites, sets up Shining Force III and lets pixies ambush enemies as battles begin.
longDescription:
Like Shining in the Darkness, it is explored in first person, using node-based movement rather than the free movement of most first-person games of the time, with battles almost entirely confined to dungeons. A party of up to four fights random, turn-based battles, still in first person but showing allies as they act, and reserve characters can be called in mid-battle. As in every Shining game, each menu has exactly four icon options. Characters grow through experience and equipment and learn spells automatically as they level up. Towns can be explored without battles and offer shops, saving and healing.

The game introduced a "pixie" system: the party befriends fairies, pixies, succubi, incubi and leprechauns, and when enemies appear the player has a few seconds to send the right type for the direction they come from, such as leprechauns for enemies from underground or fairies for those dropping from above. A correct choice damages the enemies and increases the gold and experience earned. The story follows mercenaries Arthur, Melody and Forte, hired by the King of Enrich to capture the renegade ninja Rodi. A craft crashes into the mine where they fight, and all four are healed by possessing spirits, though Forte's is evil, and the heroes set out to stop the revival of the legendary 1,000-year kingdom.
trivia: It is set ten years before Shining Force III, and its young Julian goes on to seek revenge in that game.
It began the saga of the Vandals and the Innovators, leaving behind the Devil Kings of earlier Shining games.
Motoi Sakuraba, later the composer of Shining Force III, wrote the soundtrack.
A 5% complete version was shown at the first Tokyo Game Show in August 1996.
In Germany it topped Karstadt's Saturn sales chart in July and August 1997.
devStory: Producer Hiroyuki Takahashi said that until Shining Wisdom the series had aimed for a broad audience, but that Japanese Saturn owners were mostly in their late teens or early twenties, so Holy Ark was redesigned around "fantasy that can be enjoyed by adults", producing a darker, deeper world. In contrast to Shining Wisdom's action-adventure format, it returned to first-person dungeon crawling and turn-based combat, and it had greater critical success. Though opinions varied, nearly every review ended by recommending it. Next Generation said that "SHA truly shines", praising how its mix of polygons and sprites gave it a visual uniqueness, Sega Saturn Magazine's Rich Leadbetter called it "the best RPG I've played in ages", and EGM's Crispin Boyer praised "some of the best animation ever seen in an RPG". Reviewers liked the pixie system and the variety of enemies, but some felt enemy animations dragged, and GameSpot found the story generic, saved by a solid translation.

title: Saturn Bomberman
description: Saturn Bomberman (1996) is Hudson Soft's eleventh Bomberman game, best known for battles of up to ten players on the Sega Saturn, and EGM's Saturn and multiplayer game of the year for 1997.
longDescription:
Alongside the usual battle and story modes, a master mode has the player race through a series of levels for a rank based on time, kept on a saved scoreboard, and there are several new power-ups. Dinosaur helpers hatch from eggs released by destroying soft blocks and come in three sizes, baby, adolescent and adult. Each can take only one hit, absorbing it in place of its rider, and a meter filled by collecting power-ups makes it grow; in battle mode it grows whenever its rider collects another egg. Players can jump off at any time.

The story mode, for one or two players, has Bomberman blow up poles topped with glowing red orbs, called Zarfs, while dodging or destroying enemies and collecting power-ups; once every Zarf is gone, an exit appears, followed by a short cut-scene leading to the next level. Battle mode supports two players without multitaps, six with one and ten with two, as well as computer opponents. With more than eight players, it switches to a widescreen arena with tiny characters and blocks and disables many power-ups, including the dinosaurs. The North American version also supports the Sega NetLink for four-player online play, two players per console.
trivia: It was released in Japan on 19 July 1996 but only reached Europe in May 1997 and North America that September, which critics complained about.
Most critics found the characters too small to make out in ten-player games on all but the largest televisions.
EGM's Dan Hsu called it "a mediocre one-player game" but "a fantastic multiplayer game".
It tied with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night for Game of the Month in EGM's 100th issue.
Pico Park developer Shunsuke Miyake named it, with Zelda: Four Swords, as an inspiration.
devStory: Hudson Soft developed and published Saturn Bomberman for the Sega Saturn, and it sold 129,616 copies in Japan. Critics were generally positive, especially about the ten-player mode and the range of modes and options: Sega Saturn Magazine's Matt Yeo praised how players could "simply pick up a joypad and leap straight into the thick of things", and Saturn Power's Dean Mortlock called it "probably the best multi-player game you'll ever play". Next Generation and GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann felt it did not escape the shadow of Super Bomberman 2, and the graphics and music were seen as failing to move the series on, while the story and master modes were faulted for difficult AI and unforgiving bosses, though Next Generation thought them its one advance on Super Bomberman 2. EGM named it 1997's Saturn Game of the Year and Multiplayer Game of the Year and ranked it the tenth best console game of all time. IGN later called it the best Bomberman alongside Bomberman '93, and GamesRadar placed it fourth among Saturn games.

title: Clockwork Knight
description: Clockwork Knight (1994) is Sega's early 2.5D Saturn platformer in which a clumsy toy soldier sets out to rescue a clockwork princess, a launch-era showcase that later helped inspire Grand Theft Auto.
longDescription:
In the vein of Mario and Sonic, it is a side-scrolling platformer, but it uses pre-rendered 2D sprites of high-resolution 3D models, like Donkey Kong Country, on top of fully 3D levels and bosses. Pepper attacks enemies and opens passages with his key: a quick tap thrusts it out and repeated taps twist it for a more powerful attack. He can also pick up stunned enemies and objects such as footballs and springs and throw them, including upwards. Each stage must be finished before the time limit or his hit points, usually three, run out, and with no checkpoints, dying sends him back to the start. The 13 levels span Betsy's Room, Kevin's Room, the Kitchen and the Attic, each with two normal levels and a fully polygonal boss, plus a final boss; between worlds, Soltia the perfume bottle runs a shell game where Imperial Crowns can win extra lives.

Sir Tongara de Pepperouchau III, "Pepper", is a clumsy toy soldier and something of a laughing stock, in love with Chelsea, the Clockwork Fairy Princess whose voice wakes the household's toys every midnight. When she is stolen and lesser toys are hypnotised into minions, Pepper and his rival Ginger set out to find her, since without her voice the toys will never live again.
trivia: The team first planned a darker sword-and-sorcery theme before switching to toys.
Designer Kats Sato cited Mickey Mania as an influence and Prince of Persia for its traps.
Western versions were made harder, with tougher bosses and costlier roulette games.
Traveller's Tales co-founder Jon Burton said it influenced the studio's Toy Story game.
DMA's Mike Dailly recreated its 3D side-scrolling effect on PC, and turning it overhead led to Grand Theft Auto.
devStory:
Producer Noriyoshi Oba said it took over a year to make, speeding up considerably once the toy setting was chosen, and freelance artist Masayuki Hasegawa designed its FMV. Sato kept a side-scrolling format because of the Saturn's limits on rendering many polygons. It came out in Japan on 9 December 1994 and as a launch title in North America and Europe in May and July 1995; producer Dante Anderson explained the harder Western versions by saying Japanese players like to finish games quickly, Americans want more challenge and Europeans tougher still.

Critics praised its graphics, responsive controls and scaling effects but found it unoriginal, too easy and too short; EGM's reviewers felt the 3D was "practically shoved down your throat", and Maximum said everything in it had been done before in 16-bit games. It sold an estimated 157,775 copies in Japan by November 1997, and about 36,000 in the US during 1995. Clockwork Knight 2 followed in 1995, but a puzzle spin-off and a GameCube continuation, Knight N' Knight, never appeared.

title: The Punisher
description: The Punisher (1993) is Capcom's violent arcade beat 'em up starring the Marvel vigilante and Nick Fury against the Kingpin, the start of Capcom's partnership with Marvel and widely ranked among the best comic-book games.
longDescription:
The game follows the formula Capcom set with Final Fight and Captain Commando: the heroes fight through waves of henchmen to the boss of each level. As with the limited roster of the first Street Fighter, the Punisher and Nick Fury are essentially interchangeable, sharing the same punches, kicks and throws, which chain into combos, and similar special attacks. The presentation imitates comic books, with on-screen sound effects such as "BLAM!" for gunshots. Players pick up melee weapons such as baseball bats and Japanese swords, thrown weapons such as knives and shuriken, and improvised ones from lead pipes and car tyres to a crude flamethrower, each with a durability meter shown beside the player's health. Food restores health, containers hold treasure, and hand grenades can be saved for the right moment. It stood out for its violence and frequent firearms, including an Ingram and an M16, and when gun-wielding enemies appear, the heroes draw their own handguns.

After his family are murdered for witnessing a mob killing in Central Park, Marine captain Frank Castle becomes the Punisher. He chases Mafia enforcer Bruno Costa from an illegal casino through New York to a Florida resort, where Bruno is killed by the Kingpin's robot Guardroid, then raids a drug ring, a poppy field in Arizona and a freight train before fighting through Jigsaw to the Kingpin in the King Building, which collapses at the end.
trivia: It runs on the CP System Dash, an enhanced CPS board that put more than ten enemies on screen without slowdown.
A pre-release version included rocket launchers that were cut.
The Genesis port removed Fury's cigar smoking and clothed the female ninja enemies.
The Genesis version's easy mode ends after only three stages.
Its first unchanged console release came in the 2024 Marvel vs. Capcom Fighting Collection.
devStory:
Capcom released The Punisher in Japanese arcades in May 1993 and in North America that July, beginning the partnership with Marvel that led to Marvel vs. Capcom. Play Meter listed it as one of the most popular arcade games of May 1993, and GamePro praised graphics that captured the comics' dark, sombre mood. A Genesis port by Sculptured Software followed in 1995 with downgraded graphics and sound, fewer enemies and objects, and censored violence; it was panned, Next Generation saying "not much good can be found" in it, and sold so poorly it became one of the rarest PAL Mega Drive games. A Capcom Power System Changer version and a PlayStation port by Crystal Dynamics were never released.

The arcade original has since gained cult status. Retro Gamer called it "a forgotten gem in Capcom's back catalogue", suggesting it was lost in a market flooded with beat 'em ups, IGN ranked it the tenth greatest superhero game in 2010, and WhatCulture! named it the best comics-based arcade game.

title: Dungeons & Dragons: Tower of Doom
description: Dungeons & Dragons: Tower of Doom (1994) is Capcom's first D&D arcade game, a four-player beat 'em up with role-playing elements and branching paths, set in the Mystara campaign world.
longDescription:
Up to four players choose a cleric, dwarf, elf or fighter and fight classic Dungeons & Dragons monsters, with bosses including a troll that regenerates unless burned, a black dragon, a Shadow Elf, a beholder, the optional superboss Flamewing, a great wyrm red dragon, and the archlich Deimos. At several points the party chooses between paths leading to different areas, so not every area can be seen in one playthrough. Play is more technical than most beat 'em ups, with blocking, strong, turning and dashing attacks, crouching and evading, and it demands careful tactics, since most enemies share the heroes' abilities and outrange them. Daggers, hammers, arrows and burning oil can be thrown, and spells are cast through magic rings or by the two spellcasters.

The fighter is balanced, with great range and power and the most health. The elf has a short sword and less power but seven arcane spells, from Magic Missile and Fireball to Polymorph Others and Cloudkill. The cleric can turn undead, cast five divine spells such as Sticks to Snakes and Cure Serious Wounds, and block vertical attacks others cannot. The dwarf has short reach but quick combos. The Republic of Darokin is besieged by monsters, and the adventurers, sent by the merchant lord Corwyn Linton, trace the attacks to Deimos and destroy him in his Tower of Doom.
trivia: As part of its D&D licence deal, Capcom also ported Eye of the Beholder to the SNES.
D&D enthusiast Alex Jimenez drew on Golden Axe for the action and Thayer's Quest for the branching paths.
Jimenez ran the design as a tabletop scenario for his San Jose gaming group, and Capcom revised it from their reactions.
It was planned with two buttons, but two more were needed for the inventory system.
The beaten Deimos turns out to be a pawn of an even bigger villain.
devStory:
Capcom acquired the D&D licence in the early 1990s, but its Japanese branch struggled to get TSR's approval and turned to Capcom USA to negotiate. Capcom and TSR met in January 1992 and agreed to write the story first and build the game around it. Few Capcom USA staff knew D&D, so assistant James Goddard brought in Jimenez to create a concept that Japanese developers could understand, supply character concept art and test the game; he also settled a debate with SSI over whether it should be Asian- or Western-themed.

Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit in its 1 March 1994 issue, and RePlay reported it as North America's most popular arcade game. GamePro praised its length, complexity, non-linearity and faithfulness to D&D, and GameSpy later called it as good as, though less remembered than, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and The Simpsons. It was paired with its sequel on the Japan-only Saturn Dungeons & Dragons Collection in 1999, limited to two players, and in Chronicles of Mystara in 2013.

title: Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow over Mystara
description: Dungeons & Dragons: Shadow over Mystara (1996) is Capcom's sequel to Tower of Doom, a deep arcade beat 'em up with six classes, equipment, Vancian magic, hidden items and multiple endings, and one of Capcom's last 2D side-scrollers.
longDescription:
To the cleric, dwarf, elf and fighter it adds a thief and a magic-user, and two sprite sets for each class let two players choose the same one, giving effectively 12 characters. Four buttons handle attack, jump, a select ring for items and use, with extra rings for spellcasters, and Street Fighter-style special moves include dashing and rising attacks for combos and juggles and a Megacrush that hits nearby enemies at the cost of the player's own health. Magic follows D&D's Vancian system, with a set number of each spell ready to cast, replenished by scrolls, and casting briefly pauses the game. Characters equip helmets, shields, boots, gauntlets and rings, magical items break after a few hits, and bosses drop rare items such as the Skin of the Displacer Beast that can be traded for magical equipment. Between stages, shops sell arrows, oil, daggers and potions.

Each class plays differently: the cleric heals and turns undead and cannot use bladed weapons, the dwarf has the most hit points and bashes open chests for extra treasure, the elf combines sword and spells, the fighter can dual-wield, the fragile magic-user teleports to dodge attacks, and the acrobatic thief picks locks, pickpockets and backstabs. After Deimos, the heroes cross the Broken Lands of Glantri to face his mistress Synn, who turns out to be a centuries-old red dragon trying to awaken a creature called The Fiend.
trivia: If a magic-user wields the hidden Staff of Wizardry against the final boss with at least three players and over a million combined experience points, the team can use the Final Strike attack.
Name entry allows six letters rather than the usual three, and swearing is replaced with a default name.
The Sword of Legends item is named after the top-ranking fighter in the high scores.
Its gnomes stand about a foot tall, unlike traditional D&D gnomes.
Only Battle Circuit (1997) came after it among Capcom's 2D arcade side-scrollers.
devStory: Capcom released Shadow over Mystara in arcades in 1996, with a guide and art book published by Shinseisha in the Gamest Mook series. Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixth most popular arcade game in its 1 April 1996 issue. Next Generation said it refined Tower of Doom, with animation at the level of X-Men: Children of the Atom, more characters, more branches and endings and abilities such as dual-wielding, though it gave only three stars, while VideoGames called it "Capcom's latest masterpiece". Its gear, secrets, forking paths and endings gave it high replay value and a cult following. It reached the Saturn in Japan's two-disc Dungeons & Dragons Collection in 1999, which used the 4MB RAM cartridge but limited play to two; Retro Gamer called it the system's best scrolling fighter despite long loading. Retro Gamer ranked it 16th among retro arcade games, GameSpy called it "one of the most purely entertaining titles ever released", and it was re-released in Chronicles of Mystara in 2013.

title: Marvel Super Heroes
description: Marvel Super Heroes (1995) is Capcom's CPS-2 fighting game loosely based on The Infinity Gauntlet, in which Marvel heroes and villains battle for the Infinity Gems, the step between X-Men: Children of the Atom and Marvel vs. Capcom.
longDescription:
Heroes and villains of the Marvel Universe fight one another for the Infinity Gems, while the main antagonist, Thanos, plans to use them to take over the universe. Players knock out the opponent, or finish the round with more life, using attacks and special abilities, and build a super meter for powerful Infinity Combo attacks.

The gems are its unique mechanic. The Power, Time, Space, Reality, Soul and Mind gems are won from opponents in arcade mode, or by meeting conditions such as landing the first hit in versus mode, and using one in battle gives a short-lived boost, such as more power or defence, health recovery or extra attacks. Certain fighters get special benefits from certain gems; Spider-Man with the Power Gem, for instance, creates a doppelganger on the far side of his opponent for extra damage. Capcom carried over the four characters from X-Men: Children of the Atom that its market research found most popular, Wolverine, Juggernaut, Magneto and Psylocke.
trivia: It is dedicated to Marvel artist Jack Kirby, who died in February 1994.
Stan Lee appeared at the booth when the home versions were unveiled at E3 1996.
The Saturn version uses the 1 MB RAM cartridge for extra animation frames and quicker loading.
Virgin delayed the European Saturn release to January 1998 so it could be bundled with the RAM cartridge.
Complex praised its gem-collecting as a "difference-maker" that keeps it feeling fresh.
devStory: Marvel Super Heroes was Capcom's second fighting game based on Marvel characters, after 1994's X-Men: Children of the Atom, and was followed in 1996 by X-Men vs. Street Fighter, the first Marvel vs. Capcom game. Game Machine listed it as Japan's eleventh most successful arcade game of December 1995. The arcade version was well received: Computer and Video Games gave it 5/5, and Next Generation, despite three stars, praised its "liquid-smooth animation" and said its 2D graphics were a "refreshing" change from polygon fighters. The 1997 Saturn port was widely praised for keeping the arcade's large, detailed sprites, Sega Saturn Magazine saying it "makes 2D graphics cool again", though some noted slowdown, and GameSpot found the home versions dull next to newer Capcom fighters. Critics generally rated the PlayStation version below the Saturn one, GamePro citing it as proof that the PlayStation could not handle 2D as well. It was re-released in Marvel vs. Capcom Origins in 2012 and the Fighting Collection in 2024.

title: Magician Lord
description: Magician Lord (1990) is Alpha Denshi's side-scrolling action game, one of the first four Neo Geo arcade releases and an AES pack-in, in which the wizard Elta transforms into six elemental beings to recover eight grimoires.
longDescription:
Centuries ago, a young man sealed the demon Gal Agiese and Az Atorse, the god of destruction, inside eight grimoires and was hailed as the "Magician Lord". When Gal Agiese breaks free and the grimoires vanish, his descendant Elta sets out across the land of Cadacis to recover them before Az Atorse is resurrected. Over eight stages, Elta jumps, climbs ladders, crouches and fires magic shots in four directions. Each stage has a main area with doors leading to trap-filled dungeons, and the goal is to find the door to the miniboss, whose defeat leads to the stage boss and a grimoire. Treasure chests hold extra lives, valuables, power orbs that raise his attack through three levels, and elemental orbs.

Collecting two fire, water or wind orbs transforms Elta, depending on the combination, into a dragon warrior that breathes fire, a waterman that throws bursting water balls, a poseidon that sends waves across the ground, a shinobi with spiralling magic, a samurai whose sword throws waves or a raijin that unleashes thunder. The first three move slowly, the last three jump high. Elta has two hit points in the arcade, three at home, rising to four or six when transformed, and reverts to normal when he drops back. Two players can take alternate turns, and progress can be saved to a Neo Geo memory card.
trivia: Gal Agiese's face is based on Colonel Cloud from Sky Adventure, though producer Akira Ushizawa said the two are unrelated.
It was the composers' first project using sampling, mixing R&B, heavy metal and jazz fusion.
It was easier in location tests, but the team made it harder because they felt the easy version was boring.
In North America it was packed with the AES Gold System.
A Metroidvania-style Neo Geo Pocket sequel, with transformations including a mummy, werewolf and golem, was cancelled when ADK went bankrupt.
devStory:
Alpha Denshi, which had worked with SNK on the hardware that became the Neo Geo, made Magician Lord as its first game for the system. Ushizawa, head of its second planning division and maker of Time Soldiers and Sky Soldiers, produced it and drew character sprites with Shinji Moriyama, while Hideki Yamamoto, Hiroaki Shimizu and Yuka Watanabe scored it. It was designed with home consoles in mind but was challenging as the team's first Neo Geo project. Shown at the 1990 AOU Show, it was released in arcades in April 1990 and on the AES in July 1991, followed by a Neo Geo CD version in 1994.

Former SNK staffer Chad Okada said it flopped in arcades but became the best-selling AES title of its time. Critics generally praised its graphics, sound and transformations, GameFan ranking it among the best action-platformers ever made, though many noted its difficulty and jerky animation; retrospectives have been mixed, Retro Gamer calling it a "dinosaur". Alpha Denshi later became ADK, the Neo Geo's most active third-party developer.

title: Baseball Stars
description: Baseball Stars (1989) is SNK's NES baseball game, the first baseball game with a battery save, letting players create teams and players, run a season and build their squads with prize money, features that became sports-game standards.
longDescription:
Battery backup let players create a team, set up a league, play a season and keep cumulative statistics, and it was also the first NES sports game to let players name their own players and teams. A role-playing element rewards each win with money based on the prestige of both teams' players, since prestige draws paying fans, and the money buys ability upgrades for players or pre-designed Rookie, Veteran and All-Star players; a hidden feature allows female players to be hired. Leagues of up to six teams can each play up to 25 games against every other team, for up to 125 games, with standings and top-ten leaders in batting average, home runs, RBIs, ERA, wins and saves.

Pitching offers curve balls, fast balls, off-speed pitches and sinkers, and batting is a level swing that comes down to timing. The fielding was revolutionary in its realism, helped by features such as off-screen fielders drifting towards fly balls, jumping and diving catches and infielders shifting with men on base. Eight fixed teams come with the game, including the American Dreams, whose players are named after legends such as Pete Rose, Hank Aaron and Babe Ruth, the Ninja BlackSox, Ghastly Monsters and the all-women Lovely Ladies, and six more can be created, each starting with about $30,000 and 18 players.
trivia: Some pitches drop unhittably over the plate, signalled only by a high-pitched squeak.
Games end under a 10-run mercy rule, and play stops instantly if a team leads by 100.
A game still tied after 18 innings is erased as if it never happened.
Nintendo also released it in arcades on its PlayChoice-10 system.
An EA producer on the NHL series said its GM mode was inspired by Baseball Stars.
devStory: SNK developed and published Baseball Stars for the NES in 1989. It was a critical success, often called the best baseball game on the system, and Nintendo Power readers once voted it the most popular baseball game. In 1997 Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it 87th among the best games of all time, saying it was "every bit as fun as it was eight years ago", and IGN later placed it 28th among NES games. Its create-a-player and create-a-team functions became standard features in sports games. It became an SNK franchise with five sequels: Baseball Stars 2 for the NES in 1991, which was far less popular because created teams and players could not be renamed and the graphics were not improved; Baseball Stars Professional, one of the first Neo Geo games, and Baseball Stars 2 on the Neo Geo; and two Neo Geo Pocket games. Its engine was also used in Little League Baseball: Championship Series.

title: Windjammers
description: Windjammers (1994) is Data East's Neo Geo flying-disc game, played like Pong or air hockey, which became a cult favourite decades later, winning Giant Bomb's Old Game of the Year and a side tournament at EVO.
longDescription:
The mechanics are essentially those of Pong or air hockey: players hurl a flying disc at the opponent's goal zone, against the computer or another player. Six characters each have their own speed and power ratings and a special throw, and move freely in eight directions around their half of the court, defending their goal and attacking the other. The disc generally gets faster with every throw until someone scores, when the referee serves it to the player who conceded. Yellow goal zones are worth three points and red ones five, and letting a lobbed disc drop is a "Miss" worth two points to the opponent. Each of the six courts sizes and positions its goal zones differently.

On defence, players stop the disc by touching it, usually by diving with a button press because of its speed, and when it is knocked into the air, a target shows where it will land. On offence, a player cannot move with the disc and can hold it for only a few seconds, aiming with the joystick to throw straight at the goal or bank it off walls and barriers. Matches have three sets of 30 seconds by default, up to 99 in the arcade, won by reaching 12 points or leading when time runs out, with a sudden-death round if the first two sets are both tied.
trivia: Unlike most sports, the timer does not stop when a point is scored.
Single-player mode is a ladder against each character in turn, getting harder each time.
Its rights passed to Paon DP, which hired former Data East staff, after Data East went bankrupt.
It was the only Neo Geo game delisted from the Wii Virtual Console, in 2013.
Giant Bomb began playing it regularly on camera in 2013.
devStory: Data East released Windjammers for the Neo Geo arcade system in 1994. RePlay listed it as North America's fourteenth most popular arcade game in April 1994, and Game Machine as Japan's twenty-second most successful table arcade unit in its 1 May 1994 issue, ahead of Samurai Shodown; the Neo Geo CD version sold 4,307 copies in its first week, according to Famitsu. It came to the Japanese Wii Virtual Console in 2010. Its reputation grew long after release: Giant Bomb gave it its "Old Game of the Year" award and made it a runner-up for 2017's, HobbyConsolas named it one of the twenty best Neo Geo AES games in 2014, and a growing competitive scene brought it to the Evolution Championship Series in Las Vegas as a side tournament in 2018. Dotemu released a port with online play for PlayStation 4 and Vita in August 2017 and Switch in 2018, then developed Windjammers 2, released in January 2022.

title: Magic Sword: Heroic Fantasy
description: Magic Sword (1990) is Capcom's arcade hack and slash game in which a hero climbs a 50-floor tower with rescued allies of different classes, choosing at the end whether to destroy the evil Black Orb or rule with it.
longDescription:
The dark lord Drokmar, called Dracmar in Japan, controls the Black Orb, an evil crystal that would let him rule the world. To stop him, the hero, the Brave One, or Alan in Japanese, must climb to the top of Dragon Keep, the 50-floor tower where Drokmar lives. Sharing much with Black Tiger, it is side-scrolling combat with some platforming. The player controls only the hero, while a computer-controlled ally follows him and attacks and jumps when he does. Allies are rescued along the way and include an Amazon archer, the axe-wielding Big Man, a Knight, Lizardman, Ninja, Priest, Thief and Wizard, and the player can carry one item to help the hero or ally.

A magic meter fills while the hero is not attacking and empties with each attack. Attacking when it is empty or blue gives only a melee attack, and magical allies such as the Priest and Wizard hold back; when it is red, the hero and magical allies add a weak ranged spell, and when it is full, a strong one. Health is shown in sets of five bars, the ally has up to four, and full-screen attacks come from collecting magic books or cost one full health bar. Eight of the 51 floors end in bosses, with Drokmar on the 50th, and seven secret doors let players skip levels.
trivia: Capcom planned to allow up to two allies per player, four in a two-player game.
Placing the enemies in each stage was the hardest part of development.
The secret doors were among the last features added.
A Capcom Power System Changer version was previewed but never released.
The SNES version sold only 6,637 copies in Japan.
devStory: Capcom developed Magic Sword for arcades, location-testing it in Japan by April 1990. Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most popular arcade game for the two weeks before its 1 September 1990 issue, and it ranked twelfth in a November 1990 Play Meter survey in North America. Gamest gave it several awards, including second place for both Best Action and Best Graphics, and Computer and Video Games' Julian Rignall said it would appeal to fans of slash 'em ups, while Your Sinclair found it unoriginal but highly playable.
