A single-player SNES port, announced at the 1992 Winter CES, followed that year to average reviews, Super Play criticising its animation, sound effects and slowdown. The arcade version was later included in Capcom Classics Collection Vol. 2 and Remixed, paired with Final Fight in Final Fight: Double Impact in 2010, and added to Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium.

title: Astal
description: Astal (1995) is Sega's hand-drawn Saturn platformer in which a boy made from a red jewel escapes his prison on the moon to rescue the girl he was created to protect, a largely ignored early Saturn game later remembered as a beautiful one.
longDescription:
Astal is a 2D side-scrolling platformer in which the hero runs and jumps through each level while avoiding or defeating obstacles and enemies. Different button combinations let him punch or throw enemies, punch the ground to stun those nearby, and inhale and exhale to charge a blowing attack that sweeps enemies or obstacles away. Parts of the scenery, such as trees and rocks, can be picked up and thrown. Defeating special glowing enemies fills a meter that calls in a bird to help, and in a limited asymmetrical co-op mode a second player controls the bird's wing attacks and dive-bombs. The graphics are hand-drawn, and Tokyo Movie Shinsha provided the animation for the cut-scenes.

The goddess Antowas created the world of Quartalia from a single jewel, then made two humans: from a green jewel, Leda, who has the power to make things live, and from a red jewel, Astal, made to protect her. While Antowas slept, the evil Jerado created the warrior Geist, who kidnapped Leda and held her beneath the ocean. Astal tore Quartalia apart to get her back, waking Antowas, who banished him to the moon, though Leda took pity and gave him her jewel. When Geist kidnaps Leda again, Astal breaks free and returns to a Quartalia transformed by Jerado, followed by a strange bird that will not leave him alone.
trivia: Sega of America cut Astal's default health from five points to three and allowed only one continue, against unlimited continues in Japan.
The Japanese opening theme, "Let Me Try Again", has vocals, while the American version is instrumental.
Ai Orikasa voiced Astal in Japan, and Lani Minella was credited for the English voices.
GamePro compared its graphics to "round-eyed-waif paintings".
Astal made cameos in Archie Comics' Sonic the Hedgehog, including the covers of issues 51 and 125.
devStory: Sega developed and published Astal early in the Saturn's life. It sold 23,919 copies in Japan, according to Famitsu, and reviews were average. GamePro's Lawrence Neves found it charming but too frustrating for children and too short, calling it "a good rental", and Next Generation said it was "a fine, side-scrolling action game" for Saturn owners but not a reason to buy a 32-bit machine. A contemporary IGN review dismissed it as "crappy" and "derivative", but in 2008 IGN listed it among the top Saturn games, writing that it had been largely ignored, "no thanks to the garish box art", but cherished by those who took it home as "this beautiful example of a fading genre". Reviewer Jennifer Diane Reitz called it "a rare, but slightly flawed gem", too short but "one hell of a ride while it lasts".

title: Hybrid Heaven
description: Hybrid Heaven (1999) is Konami Osaka's Nintendo 64 mix of action-adventure and RPG, set in an alien base beneath Manhattan, built as the studio's answer to Metal Gear Solid and one of the few N64 games with a widescreen mode.
longDescription:
Exploration borrows from 3D action-adventures such as Tomb Raider: the player moves freely, jumps, crawls, climbs and shoots, and solves puzzles by disabling electronic weapons or careful manoeuvring. Fights against monsters, called "biological weapons", switch to a different mode. Confined to a small room and unable to jump, crawl or climb, the player and the monster jostle for position in real time until one is close enough, with enough energy, to attack; time then freezes for a role-playing round in which the attacker picks an attack, the defender a defence, and the result is shown. Energy can be saved up to five times for combos, built one move at a time or chosen from presets. Using an attack or defence raises the statistics for that move, tracked separately for each limb, the torso and the head, and injured body parts make fights harder. A Vs. Battle Mode plays like a 3D fighting game with RPG elements.

The hero appears to be Mr. Diaz, a synthetic hybrid made by aliens, who turns on his masters by killing a clone meant to replace the President's bodyguard, Johnny Slater. In fact he is Slater, disguised as Diaz by the Gargatuans, three-foot aliens forced to help a traitor of their kind who plans to conquer Earth by replacing its leaders with clones, starting with the President.
trivia: Elements were inspired by the film Blade Runner.
The battle system took the most time of its roughly three years of development.
The team wanted fights to capture real fighting's combination of thought and action.
Johnny's motivation is to get back in time to meet his girlfriend under the Christmas tree on the White House lawn.
N64 Magazine gave it many multi-page previews and two covers.
devStory: Konami Computer Entertainment Osaka designed Hybrid Heaven as an answer to Konami Computer Entertainment Japan's Metal Gear Solid, trying to outdo its sister team's top title. It supports the Rumble Pak and Expansion Pak, and its enemies range from clones made for menial work and agents resembling secret servicemen in black suits and sunglasses to mutants, robots and hybrids of human and Gargatuan DNA; one hybrid, made to replace a cabinet secretary, pursues Johnny for much of the game. Because games of its kind were rare on the Nintendo 64, it carried a lot of hype, but reviews were mixed, from IGN's 7 out of 10 to GameSpot's 4.1. Next Generation said it was "certainly fun, but not quite excellent", arguing that with more variety, such as a city scene, it "could have been so much more than just an interesting hybrid with great graphics and sound".

title: Chameleon Twist
description: Chameleon Twist (1997) is Japan System Supply's Nintendo 64 3D platformer in which a chameleon uses his long tongue to swallow enemies, vault over gaps and swing round poles, a children's game panned by critics but followed by a sequel.
longDescription:
Players control one of four anthropomorphic chameleons across six themed worlds, mostly indoor environments that each end in a boss battle, collecting hearts to restore health. The tongue is central: once unrolled, it can be steered in any direction with the analogue stick until it reaches full length or hits a wall. It grabs power-ups from a distance and swallows enemies that stick to it, which can then be spat out at other enemies. Planting it lets the chameleon launch into the air to reach higher ground, with extra height when moving, like pole vaulting, and wrapping it round poles lets him pull himself across gaps or swing round them. A five-room training area teaches the controls.

The blue chameleon Davy follows a rabbit resembling the White Rabbit from Alice in Wonderland down a magical hole and finds he has taken a humanoid form. He, or his friends Jack, Fred or Linda, who share his powers, travel through the six lands beyond the portal, following the rabbit in search of a way home. A separate battle mode for two to four players offers Battle Royal, in which the last chameleon standing on a suspended platform wins, and Time Trial, which rewards whoever falls off the fewest times, with four difficulty settings, adjustable lengths and four stages.
trivia: It was originally planned only for Japan, but Sunsoft and Nintendo thought American children would enjoy it.
The music was almost universally criticised as overly saccharine and repetitive.
Critics split over the multiplayer: some called it worthless, others named Battle Royal a highlight.
It holds 59% on GameRankings from eight reviews.
Famitsu gave it 28 out of 40.
devStory: Japan System Supply developed Chameleon Twist and published it in Japan in 1997, and Sunsoft published it in North America and Europe. Reviews were mixed, with common complaints about awkward camera angles that cause mistakes, its short length and its low difficulty, though some critics noted in its defence that it was clearly aimed at young children. GameSpot called it "a pretty innocuous little game", worth a rental, adding that "kids though, they'll eat it up", and EGM's Sushi-X said that with beginners in mind he could see the appeal of its "overly cute graphics and sickeningly sweet background tunes". EGM and GameSpot both found it lacking in originality, and Nintendo Power said its innovative mechanics and puzzles wore thin until it became frustrating and dull. GamePro was more positive, calling it "straight-forward hop-n-bop stuff" with underlying entertainment value and even challenge, while IGN's Peer Schneider liked the tongue but not the graphics, sound or short quest. A sequel, Chameleon Twist 2, followed.

title: Viewpoint
description: Viewpoint (1992) is Aicom's isometric Neo Geo shoot 'em up, inspired by Zaxxon, with hand-drawn 3D graphics and a hip hop-influenced soundtrack that won EGM's awards for best graphics and music of 1992.
longDescription:
Viewpoint is an isometric scrolling shooter over six stages. Alongside the ship's main weapons, the player has three kinds of bomb: a wave of fire that starts behind the ship and rolls "up" the screen, a powerful circular nova-like blast, and a spread of mini-missiles that home in on several targets. By default, two players take turns, though simultaneous play can be switched on in the service mode. The isometric play was largely inspired by Sega's Zaxxon, and the overall look by Xevious and R-Type. Its 3D graphics were drawn entirely by hand rather than with pre-rendering software or 3D hardware.

The Neo Geo original was acclaimed for its cutting-edge visuals and funky soundtrack, while later ports were divisive. EGM's reviewers called the Genesis version a good conversion despite severe slowdown and weaker music, and Next Generation called it an exceptionally good port for a less powerful system on a much smaller cartridge, though it found the repetitive level design dull. The PlayStation version improved the visuals but drew complaints about an unsuitable new soundtrack, "gummy" controls and extreme difficulty, Next Generation writing: "We have no idea what kind of sadist converted this."
trivia: Aicom was a small studio also known for The Legendary Axe and Astyanax.
It was Sammy's first game in years and its only one for the Neo Geo MVS.
GameFan's two reviewers scored the Neo Geo version 99.5% and 99%, calling it "the best game on the system so far".
Saturn and Game Boy Color versions were cancelled.
A Nintendo 64 sequel, Viewpoint 2064, was cancelled, but a prototype surfaced in 2015 and an apparently final version in 2025.
devStory: Aicom developed Viewpoint and Sammy Corporation published it in November 1992, its first foray into the market since the early 1980s, with SNK also releasing it for the Neo Geo family. RePlay listed it as North America's fifteenth most popular arcade game in April 1993. Critics loved the Neo Geo version: it won both Best Graphics and Best Music in EGM's 1992 awards, Famicom Tsūshin scored it 30 out of 40, Computer and Video Games gave it 95% and Sinclair User 96%, and GamePro gave it full marks in every category, praising its animated backgrounds and "funky dance music" while noting its similarity to Zaxxon. It was later ported to the Genesis, PlayStation, X68000 and FM Towns, and the Genesis version made its international debut outside North America on the Genesis Mini 2 in October 2022.

title: Ninja Combat
description: Ninja Combat (1990) is Alpha Denshi's Neo Geo beat 'em up in which twin ninjas fight a shadow clan up a tower risen from the sea in New York, recruiting defeated bosses as playable characters, an arcade hit in North America.
longDescription:
In the year "199X", the twin ninjas Joe and Hayabusa battle the evil Kage Ichizoku, the "Shadow Family", whose Ninja Tower has risen from the ocean in the middle of New York City, to defeat the clan and its leader, the long-presumed-dead demon sorcerer Genyousai. Their journey runs over seven levels from an amusement park to the top of the tower. Shuriken are their main weapon, but they also pick up nunchaku, maces, ratchets, battle axes, spiked clubs and katana, and a somersault attack knocks down several enemies in a row. As an art of ninpo kairou, Joe can summon a fire dragon and Hayabusa a lightning strike to destroy every enemy on screen.

The heroes die if their life force runs out or time expires, and earn an extra life every 1,500 points or by picking up a gold capsule. Three of the minibosses, Musashi, Kagerow and Gembu, join the heroes when defeated and become optional playable characters, a feature several critics singled out. If the heroes win, Genyousai is destroyed and the Ninja Tower crumbles.
trivia: Joe and Hayabusa are not to be confused with Joe Musashi or Ryu Hayabusa.
Hayabusa means "falcon" and Kagerow "mayfly".
Its soundtrack was released on CD with The Super Spy's in November 1990.
ACE's Tony Dillon said the AES version's unlimited continues were a hardware design flaw in the first batch of systems.
It was one of five games in the 2008 PlayStation 2 compilation ADK Damashii.
devStory: Alpha Denshi developed Ninja Combat and SNK released it in Japanese arcades on 24 July 1990, followed by the Neo Geo home version in 1991 and a Japan-only Neo Geo CD version in 1994. Game Machine listed it as Japan's eighteenth most popular arcade game in its 15 December 1990 issue, but it did better in North America, where RePlay listed it as the top-grossing software conversion kit in January 1991. Reception has been mixed. EGM's reviewers praised its audiovisual presentation and distinct fighting styles but criticised the unlimited continues, short length, easy difficulty and repetitive play, while Joystick ranked it among the best console beat 'em ups alongside Double Dragon and Final Fight. Retrospective reviews were harsher: it holds 38% on GameRankings, Eurogamer called it a "rip-off" of Shinobi, Ninja Gaiden and Streets of Rage, and IGN called it "a profoundly unappealing gameplay experience". It came to the Virtual Console in 2007 and 2008 and to Hamster's ACA Neo Geo series.

title: Night Trap
description: Night Trap (1992) is Digital Pictures' full-motion video game for the Sega CD in which players watch surveillance cameras and spring traps on vampires stalking a teenage sleepover, a centrepiece of the 1993 Senate hearings that led to the ESRB.
longDescription:
A police squad, S.C.A.T., has the player watch live surveillance footage of the Martin household and trigger traps to catch anyone endangering the guests. Cameras cover eight locations, the entryway, living room, kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, driveway and two hallways, and a map shows how they connect. The player switches freely between them to follow events and eavesdrop for clues, helped by the undercover agent Kelli, and must avoid trapping her, other agents or the guests. A trap works only when a sensor bar moves into the red zone, and only with the correct access code, one of six colours; when the Martins change it, the player must overhear the new code and wait for the speaker to leave before switching. Counters show how many intruders have entered and how many have been caught.

Five teenage girls have vanished after staying at the Martin winery estate, and the family refused to let police search it. S.C.A.T. found traps, cameras and a control unit in the basement and spliced in an override. As five more girls, among them Kelli, arrive with Lisa's younger brother Danny, the house is invaded by Augers, vampiric beings that need blood, and the Martins themselves turn out to be vampires. Events and the ending vary widely depending on whom the player saves.
trivia: Its prototype, Scene of the Crime, was pitched to Hasbro's CEO and 22 executives in December 1986.
The surveillance idea came from the play Tamara, whose parallel stories run in 13 rooms.
Director of photography Don Burgess later shot Forrest Gump.
Hasbro, fearing "reproducible violence", did not want the Augers to bite or move too quickly.
Designer Rob Fulop reacted to the controversy by making the deliberately cute Dogz: Your Computer Pet.
devStory:
Fulop, James Riley and Tom Zito devised it for Axlon's VHS-based NEMO system, later called Control-Vision, which Hasbro backed. Zito hired Terry McDonell to write an original script after a Nightmare on Elm Street deal fell through, and Riley directed the 35 mm shoot over 16 days in Culver City in 1987, with Diff'rent Strokes star Dana Plato. With Sewer Shark, it shared a budget of about $4.5 million. Hasbro cancelled Control-Vision in 1989 over hardware costs, so Zito bought the footage, founded Digital Pictures and released Night Trap as the Sega CD's first interactive movie in November 1992.

Critics enjoyed its B-movie humour but found the gameplay shallow. At the December 1993 Senate hearing, Joe Lieberman said it promoted sexual aggression against women, and Toys "R" Us and Kay-Bee pulled it from shelves; Sega withdrew it in January 1994, calling it a misunderstood parody. The hearings led to the ESRB. It sold 400,000 copies by 1998 and was later ported to the 3DO, 32X and PC, and a 25th Anniversary Edition followed in 2017. It is often listed among the worst games ever but has become a camp cult classic.

title: Popful Mail
description: Popful Mail (1991) is Nihon Falcom's side-scrolling action RPG starring an unlucky elf bounty hunter, later remade for the Sega CD, where Sega almost turned it into a Sonic spin-off before fans objected.
longDescription:
Popful Mail is a 2D platform game with RPG elements, though without levelling up. Players jump, attack, open doors and chests and talk to characters, and a menu changes the active character, equips gear, uses items and saves. At first only Mail is playable, but the magician Tatt and the winged creature Gaw join later, and players can switch between them at any time. Mail is the fastest with the lowest jump, Tatt is balanced, and Gaw is slowest but jumps highest and usually hits hardest. Everyone, enemies included, has 100 health points, and ranged and magic attacks drain a blue-grey bar that refills when left alone. Each character can collect up to five weapons, from a sword, dagger and boomerang to a staff, fireball and claw, and items give effects such as invulnerability or footing in snow.

Long ago, three fallen gods, Morgal, Necros and Ulgar, were sealed in a floating tower after a great war survived only by an elf, a human and a dwarf. In the present, the elf bounty hunter Popful Mail beats the criminal golem maker Nuts Cracker, but his body escapes and his head turns out to be a decoy, so she goes after a 2,000,000-gold bounty on Muttonhead, a respected wizard turned criminal. Tatt is his former apprentice, hoping to turn him back.
trivia: Its play draws on Falcom's Ys games and Dragon Slayer IV and is now considered a Metroidvania.
Sega Falcom's Sega CD version was first planned as "Sister Sonic", starring a flirtatious female relative of Sonic as a bounty hunter.
Nuts Cracker speaks in a goofy Italian accent and throws his exploding head when beaten.
The theme for an unmade OVA became Megumi Hayashibara's "Hoshi o Tobikoete".
Mail's outfit is a costume for Tina Armstrong in Dead or Alive 5: Last Round.
devStory: Falcom released it for the PC-8801 on 20 December 1991 and the PC-9801 in 1992. Sega Falcom's Sega CD remake was announced as Sister Sonic in Beep! MegaDrive in November 1992, but Japanese fans wrote to Sega asking for a faithful remake, so it was cancelled in favour of one with Japanese voice acting, released on 1 April 1994. Working Designs localised that version for North America in early 1995, raising the difficulty and compressing the audio to fit the disc, and it remained the only version released outside Japan until a Switch release of the PC-8801 version in July 2024. A Super Famicom remake, Falcom's first game for the system, followed in June 1994, and a PC Engine Super CD-ROM² version by HuneX in August. Reviewers of the Sega CD version singled out its cinema scenes and voice acting, which GamePro said set its "quirky characters apart", Next Generation gave it three stars, and Retro Gamer later named it among the top ten Mega CD games.

title: Zanac
description: Zanac (1986) is Compile's fast vertical shoot 'em up for the MSX and Famicom Disk System, famous for an adaptive AI that raises or lowers the attack according to how well the player is doing.
longDescription:
The player flies the starfighter AFX-6502 Zanac over planets, space stations and open space through twelve levels of the System's defences, shooting enemies and bullets for points. Players start with three lives and lose all their power-ups when hit, reappearing briefly invincible, and can continue from the level where they ran out of lives. The rapid-fire main cannon is upgraded by power-ups in blue boxes that drift down the screen, adding more and faster shots, and a separate special weapon comes in eight numbered types, from directional shots to shields and indestructible projectiles; collecting a different number switches it and a matching one upgrades it. Enemies include meteors, aircraft, bullet-resistant disks, ground turrets and reconnaissance planes. Bosses are stationary fortresses of ground turrets that must be destroyed within a time limit for a bonus, and tough mini-boss ships change colour as they take damage.

Its defining feature is the "Automatic Level of Difficulty Control", or ALC, which adjusts the System's aggression to the player. Firing the cannon a lot, collecting power-ups and failing to destroy bosses in time raise it, bringing more and tougher enemies, while losing lives, starting a new level or destroying reconnaissance planes lower it. The System itself, an alien device like Pandora's box, holds boundless knowledge but unleashed destruction when mankind opened it wrongly.
trivia: It was made by core Compile developers including Masamitsu "Moo" Niitani, Koji "Janus" Teramoto and Takayuki "Jemini" Hirono.
Its makers went on to The Guardian Legend, Blazing Lazers and Puyo Puyo.
The MSX2 remake, Zanac EX, added smooth scrolling and extended music.
Allgame said its music came "as close as you can get to a Zen moment" in an NES shooter.
Zanac X Zanac for the PlayStation marked its 15th anniversary in 2001 with Zanac Neo and two-player co-op.
devStory: Compile first released Zanac for the MSX in 1986, published in Japan by Pony Canyon, and reworked it as Zanac EX for the MSX2 the same year. A heavily reworked version reached the Famicom Disk System on 11 November 1986, and FCI published it on the NES in North America in October 1987; the NES version came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and the Switch in 2021. In retrospect it has been seen as a unique shoot 'em up, combining Xevious-style air and ground targets with an extensive power-up system. GameSpot's Frank Provo praised its difficulty, its handling of many sprites without slowdown or glitches, and its adaptive AI, which he felt placed it in a subgenre of its own, and Allgame's Brett Alan Weiss called it extremely fast-paced, with the player almost surrounded by ships and bullets, though he felt the enemies did not "have much personality". Other criticisms included primitive sound, a steep learning curve and poor translation in the game and manual.

title: Valis: The Fantasm Soldier
description: Valis: The Fantasm Soldier (1986) is Wolf Team's action-platformer for Japanese computers, in which schoolgirl Yuko Asou wields the magic Valis sword to save three realms, the first game in Telenet's Valis series.
longDescription:
The demon lord Rogles extinguishes the light that powers the dream world Vecanti, and its queen, Valia, calls out for a hero. Yuko Asou, an ordinary Japanese schoolgirl, answers and is made the Valis warrior, wielder of the sword that can free Vecanti and protect the Earth and the land of spirits. Her classmate Reiko Kirishima is brainwashed by Rogles into trying to destroy her. In the original MSX, PC-8801 and X1 versions and their FM-7 and PC-9801 ports, Yuko fights through each level's enemies, jumps between ledges and searches for items and power-ups, and defeating the boss at the end raises her maximum health and attributes. At points the game pauses for cinematic cut-scenes that tell the story.

The versions differ. The Family Computer version is closer to a side-scrolling action RPG, harder, with large maze-like levels with multiple paths and no password or save. The 1991 Mega Drive remake plays like later Valis games, especially Valis III, with buttons to slide, jump and swing an upgradeable sword and magic spells won from bosses. The 1992 PC Engine Super CD-ROM² remake changed the jumping and sliding and added voiced cut-scenes, with Sumi Shimamoto as Yuko, and a mobile version added new stages and costumes.
trivia: It began as Shoujo Furyou Densetsu, a delinquent-heroine game inspired by Sukeban Deka, made secretly for a Login magazine contest.
When a Telenet superior disliked its graphics, writer Hiroki Hayashi was ordered to fix it and conceived Valis on the spot.
The story drew on an unfinished novel by Hayashi about the light and darkness of the human heart.
Hideaki Anno co-directed a three-minute Sunrise anime short promoting the Famicom version.
Designer Kouji Yokota regards the Famicom version as a remake rather than a port.
devStory:
Wolf Team, Telenet Japan's internal studio founded in 1986, made the game in about half a year. Hayashi and Yukio Mitsuhashi co-produced, designed and wrote it, Masahiro Akishino programmed the PC-8801 version and added scenario work, former Compile staffer Tomoki Anazawa programmed the MSX version, and Shinobu Ogawa composed the music. Akishino and Hayashi built their story and characters, Yuko and Reiko among them, on top of the project Osamu Ikegame had started before leaving Telenet.

Telenet published it for the MSX on 26 November 1986, followed by the PC-8801 and X1 that December and the FM-7 and PC-9801 in 1987; Tokuma Shoten published the Famicom version in 1987. It sold well and appeared among the best-selling games of 1987, though reviews of the MSX version were mixed, praising its graphics and music while criticising its difficulty. The Genesis remake drew average reviews, Sega Force summing it up as "High graphical content, low playability level", while the PC Engine remake was better liked, Retro Gamer calling it "arguably the best" in the series. Valis II, III and IV followed.

title: Gley Lancer
description: Gley Lancer (1992) is NCS's Japan-only Mega Drive shoot 'em up in which a young woman steals a starfighter to rescue her missing admiral father, notable for satellite gunners whose formation the player chooses.
longDescription:
Lucia Cabrock's father, Earth Federation Navy admiral Ken, has disappeared in a war between humanity and an alien race that can teleport. On hearing the news, Lucia and her friend Teim steal the Gley Lancer starfighter to save him. The player flies it through nine stages over constantly scrolling backgrounds full of enemies and obstacles, with the scenery stopping only when a boss is reached.

The key mechanic is a pair of satellite options called Gunners, activated by shooting silver and blue pods to collect weapons. Both Gunners always carry the same weapon, and each new power-up replaces it for both. At the start, the player picks one of seven formations for the Movers the Gunners are mounted on, determining how they position and aim, and during play the ship cycles through four speeds in a 1-2-3-4-3-2 order, with the starting speed set in the options. Hardcore Gaming 101's Kurt Kalata felt that the ability to aim its weapons opened new doors for shooters, making every other game seem "so strict".
trivia: Its title is engrish: the "r" in "grey" became an "l".
Producer Toshiro Tsuchida left Masaya in 1993 to found G-Craft, creator of Front Mission and Arc the Lad.
Noriyuki Iwadare, later known for Lunar and Grandia, was one of four composers.
A 2006 English fan translation by M.I.J.E.T. was later used, uncredited, in a 2023 Retro-Bit release.
A reimagining, Gley Lancer: Overdrive, was announced in 2026, including a Neo Geo version.
devStory: NCS Corporation, founded by Masaya Fujita in 1980 and known under its Masaya brand for Assault Suits, Langrisser and Cho Aniki, developed Gley Lancer, with Hikaru Satō as planner, Yukihiro Higuchi as main programmer and Hiroshi Aizawa drawing the characters. Masaya published it for the Mega Drive in Japan on 17 July 1992, and Samsung released it in South Korea. Reception was mixed, mostly from import reviews: critics praised its presentation, story introduction and cut-scenes, while views on its sprites, sound and length differed, and MegaTech recommended Thunder Force IV instead. It reached the Wii Virtual Console worldwide in 2008, which brought mostly positive reviews, though Eurogamer found little to set it apart. Kalata ranked it alongside Thunder Force IV and MUSHA among the Mega Drive's best shooters. Columbus Circle reissued the cartridge in 2019 and 2022, and Ratalaika Games' 2021 port with save states and stick aiming received generally favourable reviews.

title: Hydlide
description: Hydlide (1984) is T&E Soft's early open-world action RPG for Japanese computers, a two-million seller that introduced regenerating health, though its belated NES release was overshadowed by The Legend of Zelda.
longDescription:
In the kingdom of Fairyland, three magic jewels enshrined in the palace keep the peace. When an evil man steals one, the other two lose their sparkle, breaking the spell that sealed away Varalys, the most vicious demon in the kingdom, and in the turmoil the last two are stolen as well. Varalys turns Princess Ann into three fairies, hides her somewhere in the kingdom, releases a horde of monsters and makes himself ruler. The young knight Jim sets out in full armour into the wilderness to fight the monsters and restore peace.

It was one of the first action role-playing games, alongside Courageous Perseus and Dragon Slayer, and an early open-world game that rewarded exploration. Players can switch between attack and defence modes, save and load at any moment, and recover health by standing still, a regenerating health mechanic that decades later became common in games such as Halo. Ys used a similar regenerating health system.
trivia: Creator Tokihiro Naito was unaware of Ultima and Wizardry, never having used an Apple II.
It took The Tower of Druaga's formula into a colourful open world and borrowed The Black Onyx's health meter.
It was the first computer game to receive a Platinum award from Toshiba EMI for a million sales.
The NES version's music became notorious in the West for resembling the Indiana Jones theme and "It's a Small World".
Hideo Kojima designed Metal Gear Solid V to capture the open-world feel he had first felt playing Hydlide.
devStory:
Naito wanted to mix action and RPG elements into a new genre, inspired chiefly by The Tower of Druaga, so Hydlide leans more towards action than role-playing. Partway through development he read about Dragon Slayer and Courageous Perseus and was shocked to find he was not alone; he underestimated Dragon Slayer, which became Hydlide's biggest rival through its sequels. T&E Soft released it for the PC-6001 and PC-8801 in 1984, followed by MSX, MSX2, FM-7 and PC-9801 versions, and on the Famicom as Hydlide Special in 1986. It was well received and seen as an innovator in Japan, selling two million copies there, one million on computers and one million on the Famicom.

Fujisankei Communications International released Hydlide Special on the NES in 1989, essentially unaltered, where it compared poorly with Zelda, which had improved on it. EGM's reviewers gave it fives and sixes, and Western retrospectives have been generally negative. Sequels followed in Hydlide II, Hydlide 3 and the Saturn remake Virtual Hydlide, and Hideki Kamiya cited the series as an influence on Scalebound.

title: Silpheed
description: Silpheed (1986) is Game Arts' 3D polygon shoot 'em up for the PC-8801, brought to the US by Sierra On-Line and later remade for the Sega CD with pre-rendered video backgrounds that made it a showcase for the system.
longDescription:
Silpheed is a vertical shooter seen from an oblique angle, with enemies and objects shrinking as they move up the screen. The player flies the SA-08 Silpheed, deployed by the supercomputer Yggdrassil against the terrorist Xacalite, who has stolen "planetary buster" missiles and the battleship Gloire. With the fleet too far away to reach Earth in time, the experimental prototype must destroy Gloire. The ship moves freely around the screen, destroying enemies and dodging their fire, and shooting red orbs gives one of five weapon types, including homing missiles, an auto-aiming shot and a "phalanx" spread laser, which can be fitted to either side of the ship. The story is set after an alien ship discovered in 3032 led to rapid advances that let humans colonise space.

The 1986 original drew 3D polygon graphics over a tilted third-person backdrop. The 1993 Sega CD remake put polygon ships over pre-rendered full-motion video backgrounds, a technique Namco had used in Galaxian 3 and Starblade, and its story has Xacalite hack Earth's mother computer to seize the Solar System's space weapons, leaving a squadron of SA-77 Silpheeds as the last hope.
trivia: The ship's name most likely comes from the ballet La Sylphide.
Takeshi Miyaji designed it.
Sierra's 1989 DOS version 2.3 was bundled with Game Blaster sound cards.
Sierra's Apple IIGS port played the full Roland MT-32-based score on the Ensoniq chip.
Project Sylpheed, a 2006 Xbox 360 game by Square Enix, was billed as a spiritual successor.
devStory: Game Arts released Silpheed for the PC-8801 on 5 December 1986 and the FM-7 in March 1988, and Sierra On-Line brought it to the United States, releasing a DOS version in April 1989 and other ports. Dragon gave the DOS version five stars, calling it "highly addictive, extremely colorful", Computer Gaming World praised its music, and ACE scored it 905 out of 1000. A Sega CD prototype with fewer enemies was shown at the Winter CES in January 1993. The Sega CD version was a bestseller in Japan and a runner-up for GamePro's 1993 CD Game of the Year; Music Week rated it the system's second most technically impressive game after Thunderhawk, Consoles+ gave it 93% and Mega ranked it fifth among Mega-CD games. EGM's reviewers praised its backgrounds as "some of the most stunning visuals in a video game" but found it a "rather mundane" shooter, faulting its bosses, power-ups and the lack of interaction with the scenery. Game Arts and Treasure made a sequel, Silpheed: The Lost Planet, for the PlayStation 2 in 2000.

title: Kirby's Avalanche
description: Kirby's Avalanche (1995), Kirby's Ghost Trap in Europe, is the Western SNES version of Compile's Super Puyo Puyo, recast with Kirby characters, and the only Kirby game never released in Japan.
longDescription:
The play is the same as in Super Puyo Puyo. Pairs of coloured blobs fall from the top of the screen, and the player rotates and moves them before they land on the floor or the pile, so that blobs of the same colour touch above, below or to the side. When four or more of a colour touch, they disappear and the blobs above fall to fill the space. Setting off chain reactions drops rocks on the opponent's screen, filling it and leaving less room, with the number of rocks depending on how many blobs are popped and how many chains follow in a row. Rocks only vanish when a group of blobs touching them is popped, and a player loses when either of the middle columns of the top row fills up.

King Dedede challenges Kirby and the other residents of Dream Land to an Avalanche Competition at the Fountain of Dreams. Kirby battles through the forest in matches against old foes from Kirby's Dream Land and Kirby's Adventure, among them Whispy Woods, Kracko and Meta Knight, to a final showdown with Dedede for the Cup. Cut-scenes between rounds show Kirby and his opponents trash-talking in full sentences, and this Kirby is far more sarcastic and confrontational than the near-silent, friendly hero of other games, just as Arle and Carbuncle are in the Japanese version.
trivia: Kirby and friends replaced Super Puyo Puyo's Arle Nadja and Carbuncle to appeal to Western players.
Its music remixes tracks from Kirby's Adventure and Kirby's Dream Course, keeping only Puyo Puyo's panic music.
IGN compared it favourably to Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine, the Genesis's Puyo Puyo reskin.
EGM jointly ranked it and Mean Bean Machine 84th among the best games of all time in 1997.
It returned on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and Nintendo Classics in 2022.
devStory: Compile and HAL Laboratory developed Kirby's Avalanche and Nintendo published it for the SNES in North America and Europe in February 1995. Released late in the SNES's life, it has bright colours, advanced graphics for its time and several voice samples. Reviews were generally positive, averaging 74% on GameRankings from seven reviews. IGN gave it 7.5 out of 10, and GamePro wrote that "although Kirby's Avalanche is a rehash of an overdone puzzler theme, it's so well done that it's worth playing", singling out its graphics and cute digitised speech. Next Generation said that although it offered no improvements on what had come before, it was "still excellent fun", and EGM called it "one of the simplest, most addicting puzzle games around". Total! listed it ninth among SNES games in 1995, and IGN later placed it 68th in its top 100 SNES games.

title: Pokémon Trading Card Game
description: Pokémon Trading Card Game (1998), Pokémon Card GB in Japan, is Hudson Soft and Creatures' Game Boy Color adaptation of the card game, with RPG-style travel between Club Masters and 226 cards, including exclusives found nowhere else.
longDescription:
It simulates the tabletop collectible card game with role-playing elements like the main Pokémon series. The player, a young boy, travels the game world talking to non-player characters and challenging them to battles with 60-card decks. He must defeat eight Club Masters, each with a deck built around one of the game's elemental card types, and then four Grand Masters, whose defeat earns him the right to inherit four powerful Legendary Cards. At the start, he chooses one of three starter decks built around the three starting creatures of Pokémon Red and Blue, and each victory brings booster packs of random cards; up to four decks can be saved at once.

The 226 cards include those from the first three sets of the real game, plus exclusive cards unavailable elsewhere. Two real cards are missing, the base set's Electrode and Fossil's Ditto, because their effects were hard to translate into the game engine, and they are replaced by game-exclusive cards of the same Pokémon. Two players can battle or trade over the Game Boy's infrared port or Link Cable, and trading unlocks "Card Pop!", which gives cards otherwise inaccessible in the main game; the feature is absent from the 3DS version.
trivia: Card game designer and Creatures founder Tsunekazu Ishihara is a producer and appears in the game as "Mr. Ishihara".
Musician Tomoaki Imakuni has a cameo under his stage name Imakuni?.
Hudson is credited as developer only in the ending credits, not on the box, cartridge or title screen.
Copies came with an exclusive Meowth promotional card from Wizards of the Coast.
Saudi Arabia banned it over claims that its symbols promoted Zionism.
devStory: Hudson Soft and Creatures co-developed the game, Creatures handling planning, game design and card design. Revealed in November 1998, it came out in Japan on 18 December, a month before the tabletop game debuted in English. Nintendo of America announced an English version in September 1999, provisionally called Pokémon Card, but delayed it to April 2000, which IGN attributed to the company focusing on Pokémon Stadium. It sold 607,193 copies in Japan by the end of 1999 and 1.51 million in its first year in North America, and averaged 81.25% on GameRankings. GameSpot called it "a faithful and amusing adaptation" but found that collecting "226 pieces of paper" did not satisfy like "catching 'em all", while IGN called it "a blast to play", and in 2009 said it was the spin-off it would most like Nintendo to bring back. A Japan-only sequel, Pokémon Card GB2: Great Rocket-Dan Sanjō!, followed in 2001 with 445 cards, the first Pokémon game published by The Pokémon Company.

title: Mega Man V
description: Mega Man V (1994) is the last Game Boy Mega Man, the first with entirely original bosses, in which Mega Man fights the planet-named Stardroids from space with a new detachable Mega Arm and the robot cat Tango.
longDescription:
Months after Mega Man IV, Mega Man and his sister Roll are confronted in a field by Terra, a robot made of alien material that his Mega Buster cannot hurt. Defeated, Mega Man wakes in Dr. Light's lab while Terra and his eight Stardroids seize Earth's cities in hours. Dr. Light gives him the Mega Arm and a new companion, Tango the cat. After beating the Stardroids and Terra, he learns that Dr. Wily was behind them and storms the Wily Star, where he refights Enker, Quint, Punk and Ballade and the Stardroids. Wily then releases the ancient robot Sunstar, who turns on him; after Mega Man beats him, Sunstar, moved by Mega Man's ideal of peace between humans and robots but too damaged to be repaired, destroys himself and the Wily Star.

Stages are chosen in a non-linear order, and each boss's weapon is added to Mega Man's arsenal, with each boss weak to a particular weapon. Instead of charging a shot, charging the Mega Arm launches Mega Man's fist to strike an enemy and return. The Stardroids are named after the planets, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Pluto, with Terra named after the Latin for Earth. Rush's Coil and Jet modes help navigation, Tango turns into a buzzsaw that ricochets round the room, and Power Chips buy items from Dr. Light between stages.
trivia: Earlier Game Boy Mega Man games reused four bosses from one NES game and four from its sequel.
Keiji Inafune said it took the longest to make of the five Game Boy games.
Inafune, a cat lover, especially enjoyed designing Tango, whose name continues the series' musical theme.
The Wily Star is a reference to the Death Star.
It was the last game for an 8-bit console to use the classic Mega Man sprite until Mega Man 9 in 2008.
devStory: Minakuchi Engineering, which made three of the four previous Game Boy Mega Man games, developed it for Capcom, and Inafune designed the characters from initial concepts, saying that a theme "as vague as space" made things easier and harder at once and that he had "a lot of reservations" about the Stardroids. It was one of the first games with Super Game Boy support, adding a colour scheme and border on the SNES. Reviews were positive though critics noted little change: Famitsu's reviewers said only the stages, structure and enemies were new, and VideoGames called it a fun "rehash". Nintendo Power liked its gameplay and graphics but found it too short. In 2008 Nintendo Power named it the 14th best Game Boy game and the best of the portable Mega Man series. It is rare outside Japan; a planned 2004 Game Boy Advance compilation of all five was cancelled, but it came to the 3DS Virtual Console in 2013 and 2014 and Nintendo Classics in 2024.

title: Trip World
description: Trip World (1992) is Sunsoft's gentle Game Boy platformer, inspired by Gimmick!, in which the shapeshifting bunny-like Yakopoo recovers the stolen flower of peace, a rare collector's item never released in North America.
longDescription:
Yakopoo, a young member of the bunny-like Shabubu race, lives with his grandfather on the holy Mount Dubious, guarding the Maita Flower, the flower of peace. When shadowy creatures attack his grandfather and steal it, Trip World's inhabitants turn mad and quarrel endlessly, and Yakopoo sets out through five worlds, Mount Dubious, Savage Land, Ireland, Pudding Land and Mirror Land, each ending in a boss and some with a mid-boss. Most stages are linear, but some have several paths. The thief turns out to be the King of Mirror Land, a Shabubu possessed by a strange flower on his head, who fights Yakopoo in a robot.

Yakopoo can switch at any time between three forms: one that walks, jumps and kicks, one that turns his ears into wings to glide, and a fish form that swims and attacks with foam. Special fruit grants temporary forms such as Flower Yakopoo, which stuns enemies with seeds, and Tail Yakopoo, with a long-range tail attack. Unusually, most enemies do not hurt him on contact; they simply push him around unless provoked, though bosses attack freely. He starts with three lives, health pick-ups restore energy, and a level select on the title screen lets players continue.
trivia: Programmer Yuichi Ueda made items and characters slide down slopes.
Character designer Toshihiko Narita, who also worked on Gimmick!, drew Yakopoo as a chinchilla at Ueda's request.
Ueda recruited Mega Man composer Manami Matsumae to help with the music.
Nintendo disliked the team's box design, which left screenshots off the back.
Yakopoo appears as a mini-boss in Waku Waku 7 and can copy his opponent in Galaxy Fight.
devStory: Ueda conceived Trip World after being influenced by Gimmick! and, as programmer, had to learn the limits of the Game Boy; he also cut down on reused enemies and challenged the convention that touching enemies hurts. He said it was made in the spirit of a doujin game, and later counted it among the three games he felt most accomplished about. Sunsoft released it in Japan on 27 November 1992 and in the UK and Europe in 1993, but never in North America, and its limited run has made original cartridges expensive. Contemporary reviews were mixed: critics praised its graphics and music but found it short and easy, Video Games calling it ideal for inexperienced players. Retrospectives echoed this, Nintendo Life recommending Gimmick! instead, though many publications, including GameSpot and Polygon, have listed it among the best Game Boy games. It came to the 3DS Virtual Console in 2011 and 2012, and Limited Run Games' remaster Trip World DX was warmly received in 2023.

title: Mole Mania
description: Mole Mania (1996) is Nintendo's Game Boy puzzle game in which a mole digs above and below ground to steer a heavy black ball through each screen, rescuing his family from a bearded cabbage farmer.
longDescription:
On each screen, Muddy Mole must move a black ball to a gate to reach the next. He can push, pull and throw it, and dig into soft ground to travel underground around obstacles. Where to dig is the heart of the puzzles: holes in the wrong places can block his progress, a ball dropped into a hole returns to its starting point, and a bad hole can make reaching the gate impossible, forcing him to leave the screen and come back to try again. Obstacles include moving enemies, pipes, barrels, weights and bosses.

Muddy, called Mogurānya in Japan, is out to rescue his wife and seven children, kidnapped by Jinbe, a cabbage farmer and ruler of Jinbe Land. Muddy must cross Jinbe Land's seven worlds, avoiding enemies, solving puzzles, stealing cabbages and beating each world's boss, freeing his family one by one before facing Jinbe himself. Jinbe has a Mario-like look and build, with red overalls, a green shirt, a full beard hiding his face and a brimmed gardener's hat, and his enemies include dinosaurs and two unnamed "plumber sons".
trivia: It sold 11,830 copies in its first week in Japan and 89,407 in all.
Nintendo Power compared it to HAL's Eggerland series.
Total! called its above- and below-ground puzzles "not only new, but also surprisingly good".
1Up.com compared it to Adventures of Lolo.
It includes a two-player mode, bonus rounds and Super Game Boy enhancements.
devStory: Nintendo developed and published Mole Mania for the Game Boy, releasing it in Japan on 21 July 1996, North America in February 1997 and Europe in May 1997. Readers of Family Computer Magazine gave it 22.1 out of 30 in a 1998 poll. Nintendo Power's four writers praised its catchy music, challenge, multiplayer and Super Game Boy support but disliked levels that mixed simple and complex puzzles unevenly. Nintendo Magazine System's Dave McComb liked its simple but effective sprites, addictive puzzles, bosses and two-player mode, though he found the sound average, Mega Fun's Ulf Schneider stressed that each level needs careful planning and praised its battery backup, and IGN liked its presentation, non-linear structure and versus mode. Retrospective views have been equally favourable: Nintendo Life liked its crisp visuals, cut-scenes and soundtrack but found digging occasionally frustrating, and Hardcore Gaming 101 called it the result of "smart game developers" taking a simple premise and expanding it "in millions of smart ways". It came to the 3DS Virtual Console in 2012 and Nintendo Classics in 2026.

title: Final Fantasy Mystic Quest
description: Final Fantasy Mystic Quest (1992) is Square's simplified SNES role-playing game made for American beginners, with no random battles and action-adventure exploration, remembered as the "beginner's Final Fantasy" and for its rock-tinged music.
longDescription:
Players cannot roam the world map freely; instead they travel along set paths between icons for towns, dungeons and battlefields, with blocked routes opening as tasks are completed. It adds action-adventure elements: Benjamin can jump and use weapons outside battle, chopping trees with an axe, blowing open doors with bombs and crossing gaps with a grappling hook, and there are more puzzles than in earlier Final Fantasy games, such as moving ice pillars in the Falls Basin to use as platforms. There are no save points, since players can save at any time. Enemies stand visibly in dungeons instead of appearing at random, and turn-based battles offer attack, magic, items or defend, with an ally who can be controlled manually or by the computer. Armour cannot be equipped manually; new gear replaces or upgrades the old. Benjamin cycles through swords, axes, bombs and claws, each with its own use in the field, and finds spells in chests or as rewards for clearing battlefields of ten fights.

The world's four regions, Foresta, Aquaria, Fireburg and Windia, depend on four crystals of earth, water, fire and wind, which monsters stole from the Focus Tower. When his village is destroyed by an earthquake, the young Benjamin is charged by a mysterious old man with fulfilling a prophecy of a knight who will vanquish the darkness, and with allies Kaeli, Tristam, Phoebe and Reuben he defeats the four Vile Evils and the Dark King.
trivia: In Japan it was released as Final Fantasy USA: Mystic Quest.
Europe called it Mystic Quest Legend to avoid confusion with Final Fantasy Adventure, released there as Mystic Quest.
It was the first Final Fantasy game released in Europe.
The Dark King claims to have written and spread the prophecy himself.
The old man turns out to be the Crystal of Light in human form.
devStory: Designed by a Square team in Japan, it was aimed specifically at the US market, where console RPGs were not yet a major genre and Square's executives believed their difficulty put Americans off. Built in a graphic and gameplay style close to Final Fantasy Legend III, reusing much of its interface and sprites, it was marketed as a "simplified role-playing game... designed for the entry-level player" and sold for $39.99. Translator Ted Woolsey said action players tended to be younger and wanted to jump "straight into the action with a sword in their hands". Ryuji Sasai and Yasuhiro Kawakami composed the music, Sasai playing the guitar parts on the album's remixes. Square said it sold 800,000 copies, about half in Japan, but it failed to make console RPGs popular in North America and disappointed fans expecting a successor to Final Fantasy IV; Electronic Games called it "Final Fantasy with an identity crisis". Later reviews were largely negative, Kotaku dubbing it "The Worst Final Fantasy", though its music was widely praised, 1UP citing its "sweet sampled metal guitar licks".

title: Ken Griffey Jr. Presents Major League Baseball
description: Ken Griffey Jr. Presents Major League Baseball (1994) is Software Creations' SNES baseball game with real teams and stadiums but made-up players, a 1.2-million seller often ranked among the best baseball games ever.
longDescription:
The game had an MLB licence but not a players' association licence, so it has real teams and ballparks but fictional players, apart from Griffey himself, who carry the statistics of their real 1993 counterparts and can be renamed. Many stadiums are recreated in detail, from Fenway Park's Green Monster and the warehouse at Camden Yards to the waterfalls at Kauffman Stadium and the ivy at Wrigley Field, while cartridge limits put other teams in generic parks with green or blue walls. A battery-backed season mode runs for 26, 78 or 162 games, with a choice of four or six divisions, since the game appeared after MLB proposed six divisions but before the first such season. After each game, box scores appear in newspaper form with joke headlines, and a home run derby pits players against Griffey or fictional sluggers such as Barny Tater and Can O' Corn.

The invented rosters follow themes. The Braves are dance DJs, the Orioles honour John Waters films, the Red Sox include Cheers characters, the Dodgers, Mets and Padres are punk pioneers from Los Angeles, New York and England, the Expos are figures from the Manchester music scene, the Royals are US presidents and the Giants are Software Creations staff, among them the Pickford brothers.
trivia: Former umpire Steve Palermo voices the calls.
A batter's cry of "Oh come on!" was sampled from Jim Belushi in The Man With One Red Shoe.
A bug can reset players' home run totals after the All-Star game, which Nintendo customer service acknowledged.
The Cubs' names came from players director Brian Ullrich and his friends created in TV Sports: Football.
The SNES version came with a Griffey collector's card.
devStory: Software Creations developed the game and Nintendo published it for the SNES in 1994. By July 1994 it had sold 750,000 copies, and it ultimately sold 1.2 million. Reviews were mixed: GamePro criticised its lack of realism, from the fictional players and inaccurate parks to the ability to steer a pitch after release, but praised its music, its manual and its accessibility for beginners, while EGM found the computer too hard to beat alone but liked its digitised voices of Palermo and Jack Buck and scored it 6.6. It is nevertheless often rated by the public among the best baseball games of all time, and Complex ranked it 91st among SNES games in 2018. A 1997 Game Boy version, programmed by freelancer Brian Beuken, used only one stadium but was the first Nintendo Griffey game with both MLB and players' association licences. Nintendo followed it with three more Griffey games by Rare and Angel Studios, and MLB: The Show has included a retro mode emulating it.

sources.title: Ken Griffey Jr. Presents Major League Baseball

title: NBA Hangtime
description: NBA Hangtime (1996) is Midway's two-on-two arcade basketball game from the original NBA Jam team, renamed after Acclaim kept the Jam name, adding created players, alley-oops and double dunks.
longDescription:
Play is largely the same as Midway's NBA Jam games, keeping Tournament Edition's two-on-two match-ups, statistics tracking, legal shoving and "on fire" mode. New moves include spin moves, alley-oops and double dunks, in which one player passes mid-dunk to his teammate, and alley-oops and double dunks can trigger "team fire", setting both players alight. Each of the 29 teams has five players to choose from, with 1995-96 rosters in the arcade and 1996-97 rosters at home, and matches run four three-minute quarters.

The headline addition is "Create Player", which builds a custom player by spending a limited pool of points on height, weight, power, shooting and defence, with more points earned by winning. Using an ID and PIN, players work through every NBA team from the Vancouver Grizzlies to the Chicago Bulls, then face secret characters, though Michael Jordan does not appear because Midway did not pursue his image rights. A three-digit "combination lock" on the match-up screen, like Mortal Kombat 3's Kombat Kodes, unlocks changes to the game's look and play, and an NBA trivia quiz after each game once qualified arcade players for a prize draw.
trivia: Its theme song, "Whatcha Gonna Do?", was produced by rapper M-Doc.
Shaquille O'Neal is not licensed because he had been cleared for NBA Showtime.
Next Generation noted that created players are permanently saved in the arcade cabinet's memory.
NBA Maximum Hangtime, a late-1996 arcade update, added a hidden "hot spot" for each player.
EGM named it the fifth best arcade game of all time in 1997.
devStory: Hangtime was the third basketball game by the team behind NBA Jam; the name changed because Acclaim, the home publisher of the Jam games, had acquired it and released NBA Jam Extreme the same year. Computer and Video Games called the arcade version "the real, and quite worthy, successor to NBA Jam TE", and Next Generation said it had "all the playable qualities of NBA Jam, plus a slew of perks". Midway released home versions for the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation, with Funcom handling the Genesis and SNES ports and High Voltage Software a Windows version, while Saturn and Game.com versions were cancelled. The ports drew mixed reviews, most critics feeling they offered too little over NBA Jam: GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann said players had "seen it all before", while GamePro and IGN enjoyed the N64 version and its create-a-player mode. The PlayStation version was faulted for loading and slowdown. NBA Showtime: NBA on NBC followed in 1999, and Arcade1Up released a cabinet including it in 2020.

title: NFL Blitz
description: NFL Blitz (1997) is Midway's seven-a-side arcade football game from the NBA Jam team, with no penalties and late hits, dropkicks and dogpiles so violent that the NFL nearly handed back the licence fee.
longDescription:
Teams play seven-on-seven, and the traditional rules are thrown out: there are no penalties and no substitutions, and players can attack each other illegally, even with dropkicks. The game carries a full NFL licence, with the players and teams of the 1997 season. Its makers wanted to get players to the action faster than other football games, which they felt bogged players down in play-selection screens and setup menus.

AllGame's Brad Cook likened it to neighbourhood pick-up games "when every play was a pass and you needed two completions for a first down", adding that anyone who had treated opponents as a child the way the game allows was "probably reading this from prison right now". Next Generation called the arcade version "an unrealistic but adrenaline-packed experience", and later said the PlayStation version offered "the most intense game of football you're likely to find at home", though it found that the lack of play variety grew stale, especially alone. Computer Games Strategy Plus quoted the announcer's line after a late hit: "That was totally uncalled for, but awfully fun to watch."
trivia: It runs on Midway's Seattle System arcade board, based on a 3Dfx chipset.
Sal Divita said it supported two players rather than four because football lacked NBA Jam's teamwork.
It had an $8 million marketing budget.
Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Kordell Stewart was the cover athlete.
The PlayStation version won OPM's 1998 award for "Most Unrealistic Sports Game".
devStory:
The team, led by NBA Jam's Mark Turmell and Sal Divita, spent two years on it, aiming, in Turmell's words, to "do for the NFL franchise what we did for the NBA franchise". When NFL executives saw it at Midway's Chicago offices a week before launch, they reacted so badly to the violence that the league offered to return Midway's licence fee; it was approved only after compromises, including removing blood splatter and shortening the window for dogpiles and late tackles after plays. It was named Arcade Game of the Year in EGM's 1997 Editors' Choice Awards.

Ports followed in 1998 for PlayStation, Nintendo 64, Windows and Game Boy Color. The N64 and PlayStation versions received universal acclaim and ranked eighth and tenth among US home console games in their first month; N64 Magazine gave the N64 version 87%, and Hyper called it "the most satisfying quick-thrill game I can imagine". The PC version won IGN's Best Sports Game of 1998, and the N64 version was an AIAS nominee for Console Sports Game of the Year.

title: Tecmo Super Bowl
description: Tecmo Super Bowl (1991) is Tecmo's NES football game, the first licensed by both the NFL and its players' union, with every team and real players, and the subject of a lasting cult of tournaments and roster mods.
longDescription:
Earlier games used either real teams, real players or fictional substitutes, never real teams and players together. Tecmo Bowl had only a players' association licence, with twelve teams and short rosters, because LJN held an exclusive NFL team licence for its own NES game. For Tecmo Super Bowl, Tecmo secured both, making it the first and only NES game with real NFL teams and players. It offers the complete league of 28 teams, expanded rosters and playbooks, and statistics tracking including NFL records. Although released late in 1991, its rosters and attributes come from the 1990-91 season, so there are no 1991 rookies or off-season moves. Jim Kelly, Randall Cunningham and Bernie Kosar, not part of the players' union marketing deal, appear as QB Bills, QB Eagles and QB Browns.

Its Bo Jackson became infamous for speed and agility so extreme that players claimed he could run 1,000 yards in a game; TechTimes called him "absolutely, positively—and absurdly—unstoppable", and players regarded using him as close to cheating. Lawrence Taylor was used the same way on defence. ESPN and USA Today called Jackson the "greatest video game athlete of all-time", and two 2016 Kia Sorento commercials starring Jackson played on the joke.
trivia: At $54.99 it was the most expensive NES game released to that date.
It topped Babbage's NES sales chart from October to December 1992.
ESPN named it the greatest sports video game of all time.
PC Magazine ranked it tenth among the most influential video games of all time.
A 2016 Tecmo Madison tournament livestream drew 161,076 viewers.
devStory: Tecmo developed and published Tecmo Super Bowl in North America and Japan in 1991 as the sequel to 1987's Tecmo Bowl. It was a major success, and in 1997 EGM and IGN each named it among the top 100 games of all time; GamesRadar later noted it may be the only NES football game still widely played. Tecmo followed it with 16-bit versions for the SNES and Genesis in 1993, which fixed many bugs and added weather, punt blocks and in-game playbook changes, then Tecmo Super Bowl II and III and a 1996 PlayStation version, the last with both licences before EA's 2004 exclusive deal for Madden forced later Tecmo Bowl games to use generic players. With emulation, it has become one of the most modified NES games, with annual roster updates for college and professional football, online leagues and national tournaments, and an NFL Films Presents episode on the annual championship in Madison, Wisconsin, featured interviews with Emmitt Smith, Christian Okoye and Philip Rivers.

title: Blades of Steel
description: Blades of Steel (1987) is Konami's ice hockey game for arcades and the NES, known for its fast action and its fistfights, in which the loser goes to the penalty box, and a million-seller on Nintendo's console.
longDescription:
Players choose exhibition matches against the computer or a friend, or a playoff-style tournament for the Cup, at Junior, College or Pro difficulty. Eight fictional teams represent cities that had NHL teams at the time, Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and Edmonton in Canada and New York, Chicago, Los Angeles and Minnesota in the US, each with three forwards, two defencemen and a goaltender. Fights start when two players bump into each other three times in a row. In the stand-off, a player who punches rapidly may knock his opponent down with no penalty; if both throw punches, a voice yells "fight" and a fight screen appears, where players punch and block high and low with five hits of health. The loser goes to the penalty box, and up to four players can be sent off, for a 5-on-1 advantage, while a fight near a net may bring a penalty shot. Tied games go to a five-shot shoot-out and then sudden death.

There is no offside rule, and only two penalties are called besides icing: the two minutes for losing a fight and penalty shots, taken from the blue line like a football penalty. Voice samples, rare in NES games, announce "Blades of Steel!", "Faceoff", "Fight" and the garbled passing call, which the clearer arcade version confirms as "Get the pass".
trivia: In Japan it was later released as Konamic Ice Hockey.
The second intermission may show a mini-game advertising Contra and Jackal, in which a small ship attacks a huge one, referencing Gradius.
Otherwise, an ad shows a bear shooting the puck and mouthing "Nice Shot!"
EGM left it off its 1997 top 100 in favour of Nintendo's Ice Hockey, saying that was "clearly more fun".
It returned on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and the arcade version on Xbox Game Room in 2010.
devStory: Konami released Blades of Steel in North American arcades in 1987 and ported it to the Famicom Disk System and NES in 1988; the arcade version has more voice samples and commentary thanks to better speech hardware and more memory. It sold over a million copies and was well received, Allgame's Skyler Miller calling it "one of the most enjoyable sports games of its era". Reviews of the Virtual Console release were mostly positive, Nintendo Life finding it had aged better than Konami's other NES sports games such as Double Dribble, though Eurogamer's Dan Whitehead found the graphics poor even by 1987 standards, with the same player model repeated and garish colours to tell teams apart. Two sequels followed a decade later, NHL Blades of Steel '99 for the Nintendo 64 and NHL Blades of Steel 2000 for the PlayStation, with Game Boy Color versions by Climax Studios.

title: Urban Champion
description: Urban Champion (1984) is Nintendo's first 2D fighting game, a Famicom street brawl in which two men punch each other down the pavement into an open manhole, widely regarded as one of Nintendo's weakest NES releases.
longDescription:
Two fighters try to push each other off the sidewalk and past the edge of the screen. They stand in a defensive stance when not attacking and raise or lower their arms to block and strike high or low, so damage comes only from hitting the area the opponent is not guarding. Holding away dodges or retreats. A weak punch is fast and hard to defend but does little damage and knockback, while a strong punch hits harder but is slow and easier to block, dodge or interrupt. Each fighter starts a round with 200 stamina points; every punch costs one, a weak punch does four points of damage and a strong one ten, and an exhausted fighter takes full knockback from every blow.

A man occasionally drops flower pots from the windows, dazing whoever they hit, and a passing police car sends the fighters back to their starting positions. A fighter knocked off the edge falls into the street and the fight moves to the next block. Each round has a 99-second limit, after which the police arrest whoever is closest to the edge. Bouts are best of five, and after two lost rounds an open manhole appears behind the losing fighter; knocking him in wins the bout, and a woman showers the victor with confetti. In single-player Game A, the goal is 45 straight wins to become Champion.
trivia: It was inspired by the 1984 Game & Watch game Boxing, also known as Punch-Out!!.
Nintendo Power's 1990 Pak Source gave it scores as low as 1.5, one of only two games below 2 in a category.
1UP.com's Jeremy Parish said he would rather have nothing on the Virtual Console's debut week than Urban Champion.
IGN AU called it "worse than actually falling down a manhole".
Arika made a 3D Classics version for the Nintendo 3DS in 2011.
devStory: Nintendo released Urban Champion for the Famicom in Japan on 14 November 1984 and on the NES in North America and Europe in 1986, with an arcade version, Vs. Urban Champion, in 1985. It was eventually followed as a Nintendo fighting game by Joy Mech Fight in 1993. Reception was largely negative, and it has been regarded as one of the weaker Nintendo-published NES games. Retrospective reviews of its many re-releases, on e-Reader cards in 2002, the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console and Nintendo Classics, were similarly harsh: GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann said it was "about as boring as it can possibly be", Bob Mackey called it the "Bad Street Brawler of its day", and IGN's Lucas M. Thomas said it did not deserve the distinction of being Nintendo's first head-to-head fighter. Developer Ron Alpert was kinder, calling it one of the simplest games of its day but easy to pick up and play.

title: Wild Gunman
description: Wild Gunman (1984) is Nintendo's quick-draw light gun game for the Famicom and NES Zapper, adapted from Gunpei Yokoi's 1974 arcade machine that projected filmed gunslingers, and famously played by Marty McFly.
longDescription:
The player waits for an outlaw's eyes to flash, with a speech bubble reading "FIRE!!", and then shoots; firing too early makes the duel unwinnable and moves on to the next. The NES version has three modes: Game A pits the player against one outlaw, Game B against two, and Game C against an entire gang, with cartoon sprites in place of the original's filmed footage.

The 1974 original was one of Nintendo's electro-mechanical arcade games, built by Yokoi from the design of the company's Laser Clay Shooting System. A light gun was linked to a 16 mm projection screen showing full-motion footage of a Wild West gunslinger; if the player drew and fired fast enough when his eyes flashed, the film switched to the gunman falling, and otherwise to him drawing and shooting. Players faced five gunslingers in all, and a premature draw lit a "foul" light. Its four film scenes were each shot on two reels, one for each outcome, eight in total, filmed with uncredited local extras around Kyoto and at the Nara Dreamland amusement park.
trivia: The Famicom version came with the Beam Gun, a plastic revolver modelled on the Colt Single Action Army, with a holster belt.
Collector Benjamin Solovey discovered two of the original film reels in 2021.
The 1974 machine sold only around 100 units.
In Back to the Future Part II, Marty plays a fictional arcade version, and Part III shows it taught him to shoot a real revolver.
Nintendo re-released it on the Wii U Virtual Console on 21 October 2015, Back to the Future Day.
devStory: The 1974 machine, formerly known as Gun Fight, was released in North America by Sega in 1976. That year it was Japan's sixth highest-grossing electro-mechanical arcade game, behind Nintendo's own Sky Hawk and Mini Laser Clay, and one of the most popular machines at the AMOA show in North America. Nintendo adapted it into a video game for the Famicom in Japan in 1984, and in 1985 it was a North American launch game for the NES alongside the Zapper; the NES version was also published on the PlayChoice-10 arcade system. The original's footage has appeared in films: Craig Baldwin's 1978 experimental short Wild Gunman re-edited it to surreal effect, and in the 1981 film Gas the villain, played by western star Sterling Hayden, loses to the machine and shoots its screen with a real gun. In Super Smash Bros., the Duck Hunt duo can summon its gunmen, and their Final Smash traps opponents in a shoot-out with the gangsters from Hogan's Alley.

title: Hogan's Alley
description: Hogan's Alley (1984) is Nintendo's light gun game in which players shoot cardboard gangsters while sparing innocent civilians, named after the FBI's training range and, with Duck Hunt, one of the first hit light gun video games.
longDescription:
Each round begins with three cardboard cutouts sliding into position against a blank wall and turning to face the player, showing a mix of gangsters and innocent or friendly people, and the player must react quickly and shoot only the gangsters. In later rounds, the backdrop becomes a city block with five cutouts, some already exposed as they come into view. After five rounds of each, a bonus round gives a limited supply of ammunition to shoot up to ten tin cans thrown from one side, bouncing them onto ledges on the other side for points, with a bonus for unused shots; the game then returns to the wall at a faster speed. Shooting an innocent or failing to hit a gangster costs a life, and bonus lives come at set scores.

The NES version offers "Hogan's Alley A" with the blank wall, "Hogan's Alley B" with the town, and "Trick Shot", the can-shooting game with ten cans per round and unlimited ammunition. A "MISS" counter rises with each innocent shot, gangster missed or can dropped, and the game ends at ten.
trivia: Its namesake range was built at Camp Perry, Ohio, in the 1920s and redesigned for the FBI Academy at Quantico in 1954.
Three years after the game, the FBI built a new Hogan's Alley at Quantico resembling a small town.
Artist Cory Arcangel hacked it into "I Shot Andy Warhol", replacing the targets with Warhol.
Hogan's Alley-inspired games appear in the WarioWare series.
In Super Smash Bros., the Duck Hunt character kicks its tin can, which an off-screen Zapper keeps shooting until it explodes.
devStory: Nintendo released Hogan's Alley for the Famicom in 1984, then in 1985 as a Nintendo VS. System arcade Game Pak and as one of the 17 North American NES launch titles. The arcade version became popular in North America, popularising light gun games together with Duck Hunt, topped the RePlay arcade charts by November 1985, and was a very popular arcade game in Europe by 1986. Computer and Video Games called it "a pleasant change" from the space shooters then filling arcades, while noting its similarity to Sega's Bank Panic and that it might not appeal to everyone, and Computer Gamer praised its realistic gun controller. Computer Gaming World named it 1988's Best Target Game for the NES, calling it "an entertaining variation on the theme". A version using the Wii Remote in place of the Zapper came to the Wii U Virtual Console in North America on 7 January 2016.

title: Solar Jetman: Hunt for the Golden Warpship
description: Solar Jetman (1990) is Zippo Games and Rare's NES gravity shooter, the third Jetman game, in which a tiny pod hauls pieces of a legendary starship and fuel out of caverns on twelve planets, each with its own gravity.
longDescription:
Set after Lunar Jetman, it follows Jetman's quest for the pieces of the Golden Warpship, a mythical starship capable of interstellar travel. Viewed from the side, the player rotates Jetman's pod clockwise or anticlockwise and thrusts, subject to inertia but not drag, under a pull of gravity that changes from planet to planet and makes stable flight harder as the game goes on. Each of the twelve planets, plus a hidden one, has its own system of enemy-infested caverns explored in small pods launched from an immobile mothership, and the goal on each is to bring back a piece of the Warpship and enough fuel to reach the next.

Items are dragged with a tow cable that makes flying harder, and are dropped over the mothership or into small wormholes deeper in the caverns. Points from valuables and destroyed enemies buy power-ups for the pod after every other stage. If the pod is destroyed, Jetman ejects in an agile but vulnerable space suit and may be able to return to the mothership for a new pod, but dying outside the pod costs a life.
trivia: It began as Iota, an arcade shooter conceived by programmer Steve Hughes and inspired by the Atari ST game Oids.
Rare ordered it turned into a Jetman game halfway through development.
Ste Pickford drew on the ZX Spectrum game Scuba Diving for the pod's movement.
Finished Amiga, Atari ST and C64 ports were cancelled because the NES version sold poorly; the C64 version has since surfaced.
It is included in Rare Replay (2015) and on Nintendo Classics.
devStory: Zippo Games, founded by Ste and John Pickford and known for Ironsword, was bought by Rare after that game's success, which Ste Pickford disliked because he wanted to work independently. The brothers started Iota on 1 June 1989, and after the switch to Jetman they received little input from Rare, which Pickford took as a sign the Stamper brothers trusted them with their most "revered" series. Development took about a year, growing from two people to several. Tradewest released it in North America in September 1990 and Nintendo in Europe in September 1991, and Nintendo also put it on the PlayChoice-10. Despite poor sales, reviews were positive: Mean Machines called its playability "second-to-none" and its graphics "simply brilliant", Computer and Video Games' Richard Leadbetter compared it to Thrust, and Total! said exploring its twelve planets would "set the player at it for weeks", though its difficulty drew criticism.

title: Hard Drivin'
description: Hard Drivin' (1989) is Atari Games' arcade driving simulator, one of the first with 3D polygon environments, a force-feedback steering wheel and a stunt track with a loop and an open drawbridge.
longDescription:
The player test-drives a sports car in first person, covering one or two laps of a track for the best time while avoiding traffic and obstacles. The closed course splits into two joined circuits, a "speed" track and a "stunt" track with a vertical loop and an open drawbridge, and ordinary traffic drives at normal speed, causing a crash on contact. A manual transmission mode adds a clutch pedal and the chance of stalling, and the steering wheel vibrates. Invisible waypoints track progress, shown as flags on the course map when time runs out, and passing the halfway point grants extra time. Players who score in the top ten in certain modes race the computer's Phantom Photon car.

After a crash, whether into another car or from a missed landing, a ten-second instant replay shows an aerial view of the lead-up, and the car is returned to the last waypoint, which may be a long way back. Leaving the road starts a ten-second countdown to return before the car is moved back. The engine, transmission, suspension and tyre physics were modelled with Doug Milliken, co-author of Race Car Vehicle Dynamics, who is credited as a test driver.
trivia: Its 3D hardware grew from a prototype Atari and Namco began when Namco owned Atari Games; Namco's version became the System 21.
Its release was delayed by a vice president's doubts that anyone would buy a $10,000 cabinet.
It uses a 68010 CPU, two TMS34010 graphics processors and a DSP.
