Zzap!64 gave the C64 version 20%, and Commodore Force later gave it 9%.
Its home ports won Best Coin-Op Conversion at the 1989 Golden Joysticks.
devStory: Development began in 1988, and Atari had hoped to release it that year, but a vice president argued that nobody would buy a $10,000 arcade cabinet, recalling the cancelled Last Starfighter arcade game; weeks of research found the price acceptable. Doug Milliken's father William had led a team at Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory in the 1950s that adapted aircraft equations of motion to cars. Atari sold 3,318 cabinets. Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful upright or cockpit cabinet in its 1 June 1989 issue and it was Japan's sixth highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1990. Commodore User called it "a major first" that "really does put you in the driving seat", Your Sinclair named it the best arcade game of 1989, and Computer and Video Games the fourth best. It was ported to the Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum, whose version reached number 2 in the UK, Mega Drive and Lynx, though an NES version was unreleased. Race Drivin' followed in arcades in 1990.

title: APB
description: APB (1987) is Atari Games' comic arcade driving game in which rookie cop Officer Bob tickets litterbugs and chases wanted felons in a cabinet shaped like a police car, with flashing lights on top.
longDescription:
Seen from above, Officer Bob drives patrol car 54 with a wheel and gas pedal, trying to meet a daily quota of citations or arrests before time runs out. Day one is a closed course where he sirens traffic cones; from then on he pulls up behind offenders and hits the siren to make them pull over, some needing several taps. Each offence belongs to a particular vehicle, so only the pink convertibles litter, until speeding arrives, which anyone can commit, followed by road rage, drunk driving and "dopers". Doughnuts extend the time limit, filling stations refuel the car, and the daily "Speed Shop" upgrades it with brakes, guns, armour and radar. From day three, every other day brings an all-points bulletin for a felon such as "Bernie Gasman", wanted for arson, or "Buzz Geiger", wanted for stealing nuclear fuel.

Back at the station, Bob must shake a confession out of the suspect, filling the "Confess-O-Meter" by alternating fire and siren, before the Chief walks in; if he sees, the suspect walks free for police brutality and Bob gets demerits. Demerits also come from crashing without the siren, shooting innocent drivers, hitting pedestrians and doughnut huts and missing the quota, and too many ends with "TOO MANY DEMERITS. YOU ARE FIRED." as Bob is handcuffed and thrown in a paddy wagon or a garbage can.
trivia: The cabinet's red and blue roof lights flash when the siren button is pressed.
A detachable seat can turn the upright cabinet into a sit-down game.
Missing the quota earns a dressing-down, from "dragon breath" to having his nose honked.
Stranded motorists get a $75 ticket for Bob's trouble.
A Dragnet-like tune plays as convicts go behind bars.
devStory: Atari Games developed and published APB for arcades in 1987. Its team said it had an extended development in which new ideas such as the in-game shops kept being added, so the final game may have been overly complex. It enjoyed moderate success, its high-resolution graphics and novel cabinet adding to its appeal. Critics noted its rising difficulty, The Games Machine calling it at times "utterly frustrating", but praised its humour and cartoon look: Your Sinclair called it "one of the funniest games of the year", Computer and Video Games "hilarious", and Crash "refreshingly different". Allgame's Paul Biondich later wrote that its gameplay had "stood the test of time". Tengen developed home versions for the Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum, published by Domark in 1989, and a 1991 Atari Lynx version drew good reviews from CVG and Raze, though EGM's reviewers found it repetitive. It was later included in Midway Arcade Treasures 2 and Midway Arcade Origins.

title: I, Robot
description: I, Robot (1984) is Dave Theurer's arcade game for Atari, the first rendered entirely in real-time 3D polygons and the first with camera controls, in which a robot rebels against Big Brother; a financial flop now prized by collectors.
longDescription:
The player is "Unhappy Interface Robot #1984", a servant robot that has become self-aware and rebels against Big Brother. To clear each level, the robot must destroy Big Brother's giant blinking eye, first wearing down its shield by moving over red squares to turn them blue, then attacking the eye itself. It can jump, but is destroyed if it jumps while the eye is open, and birds, bombs and flying sharks add to the danger. Some levels end with a maze of gems to collect before facing the eye up close, and between levels the robot flies through space, shooting or dodging "tetras", meteors and a floating head that fires nails. The 26 levels repeat at higher difficulty with new colours, as in Theurer's Tempest, and after 126 the player is sent back to a random earlier level.

Players can move the camera closer to the robot or up for an overhead view; the closer the camera, the higher the score multiplier but the less of the level and Big Brother can be seen. Later "viewer killers" attack the camera directly, forcing a change of angle. A non-game drawing mode, Doodle City, which the game calls an "ungame", lets players move and rotate shapes leaving trails for up to three minutes per credit, at the cost of a life per minute.
trivia: Its working title was Ice Castles.
Dave Sherman's custom bit-slice 3D co-processor, nicknamed "pepperoni", handled about 2,000 polygons per second.
It used the same upright cabinet as Atari's Firefox laserdisc game.
A rumour that Atari dumped 500 unsold units in the ocean was called a "total myth" by employee Rusty Dawe.
Jeff Minter's Llamasoft released a remake in April 2025.
devStory: Earlier 3D games such as Theurer's Tempest used vector graphics, Interstellar used pre-rendered 3D and Cube Quest combined real-time 3D with laserdisc video, so I, Robot was the first arcade game drawn entirely in real-time filled polygons, a milestone recognised by Guinness. It ran on a Motorola 6809 with four POKEY sound chips and a Hall-effect joystick, and borrowed ideas from Galaga and Pac-Man. Technical problems delayed it and sent it back to the lab, and it was not fully released until June 1984. Only about 750 to 1,000 machines were made. Play Meter's Gene Lewin gave the dedicated cabinet 2 out of 10, saying it lacked the excitement of a top earner, while Roger C. Sharpe saw "sleeper" qualities, and Computer and Video Games called it "a cubist's delight". It was a financial flop but has been praised since for its innovation; Guinness's Gamer's Edition ranked it 90th among arcade games for impact. With Return of the Jedi, it was the last arcade game from Atari, Inc. before the company split, and it was first re-released in Atari 50 in 2022.

title: Haunted House
description: Haunted House (1982) is Atari's Atari 2600 adventure in which a pair of eyes in the dark explores a 24-room mansion by matchlight, hunting for the pieces of an urn, and is often cited as one of the earliest survival horror games.
longDescription:
The player, shown only as a pair of eyes peering in the dark, must find three pieces of a magic urn placed at random in the 24 rooms of a four-floor mansion and bring them back to the entrance. Matches, lit and blown out, reveal items and parts of the rooms. Only one object can be carried at a time, swapped by touching another, and stairways between floors work in only one direction. Vampire bats, tarantulas and a ghost roam the mansion and cost one of the player's nine lives on contact. Nine difficulty settings change the challenge: the easiest has one room whose walls are lit, while others add locked doors that need a hidden master key, more enemies, and bats that steal the item being carried and drop it elsewhere. A scepter stops most enemies chasing the player, though on higher settings the ghost keeps coming regardless.

Critics such as GameSpy's Christopher Buecheler and Allgame's Skyler Miller have called it one of the first survival horror games, for its creepy themes, limited item management and variety of monsters. Others, including Laurie N. Taylor and Bernard Perron, have argued that the genre began with Alone in the Dark and Resident Evil and that the 2600 could not create the mise-en-scène of fear later games did.
trivia: Its working titles were Mystery Mansion and Graves Manor.
The urn pieces' positions are generated by polynomial counters to save memory.
Programmer James Andreasen used the 2600's percussion sounds for the footsteps on the stairs.
Cover artist Steve Hendricks's first design was rejected by marketing because of where the eyes sat over a figure's chest.
Flux magazine ranked it 68th in its 1995 list of the top 100 video games.
devStory: Andreasen, a University of Colorado graduate, programmed it for the Atari VCS, whose TIA chip forced programmers to draw every frame themselves. Its rooms are hand-designed and loaded into the game, and it was among the first games to let the player scroll between large portions of the playing space. Released in February 1982, it was one of the top-selling games by July according to Cashbox. Electronic Games found it "much more atmospheric" than Atari's Adventure and "one of the most intriguing and novel video game cartridges to appear in some time", with "the spine-tingling sensation that something spooky is always about to happen", and The Space Gamer could find no drawbacks, while The Capital Times found its graphics blocky and How to Win at Video Games found it hard to understand at first. Game Informer later noted that it contained many elements of Silent Hill and Resident Evil. It has appeared in many Atari compilations, including Atari 50, and inspired new versions in 2010, 2014 and 2023.

title: Cyberball
description: Cyberball (1988) is Atari Games' seven-a-side robot football game set in 2022, played with an explosive ball instead of downs, whose four-player dual-monitor cabinet sparked tournaments across the United States.
longDescription:
Robots of different speeds, sizes and skills play a seven-man version of American football. Instead of downs, the ball heats up from "cool" to "warm", "hot" and "critical" as it is used, and can only be reset by crossing the 50-yard line or by a change of possession; a robot tackled with a critical ball is destroyed along with it. Robots also wear down as they are tackled, smoking and then catching fire, and a burning robot explodes when hit, fumbling the ball. Prize money buys faster, tougher units. On offence, players choose run, pass or option and then one of four plays; on defence, short, medium or long coverage and then a scheme.

The cabinet has two monitors, each with two sets of controls, allowing one player, two in co-op, or up to four head-to-head. Four-player games opened up new tactics: because several plays begin from identical formations, human receivers could run one route while pretending to run another, forcing defenders to read the play and race to the likely passing spot, often using their once-per-play turbo boost. That room to improvise built its popularity and led to tournaments across the US.
trivia: Tournament Cyberball 2072 (1989) moved the setting to 2072 and added 100 plays, a Rookie mode and new positions.
A two-player Cyberball 2072 cabinet and several conversion kits followed in 1989.
Converting an original cabinet to Tournament Cyberball 2072 required jumper wires and a ROM daughterboard.
Tengen planned an unlicensed NES version, but Jaleco bought the rights and released it in 1992.
Atari Corporation released Tournament Cyberball for the Lynx in 1991.
devStory: Atari Games developed and published Cyberball for arcades in 1988, and it was ported to the Sega Genesis, Atari ST, Amiga, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and NES. The NES version was less well received than the arcade original: GamePro faulted its poor controls, missing features such as player upgrades and "archaic" graphics, and VideoGames & Computer Entertainment's Chris Bieniek held it up as a definitive example of the NES's limits, while Allgame's Skyler Miller wrote that it ended up "feeling more like a primitive version of football than a futuristic one". MegaTech called the Genesis version a decent conversion with good graphics. In a retrospective, Allgame's Brett Alan Weiss called the arcade game "a highly influential futuristic sports game" with fast, hard-hitting action, finding it erratic but "undeniable fun for arcade-style sports enthusiasts".

title: Food Fight
description: Food Fight (1983) is General Computer Corporation's arcade game for Atari in which Charley Chuck dodges four chefs and a hail of pies, peas and watermelon to eat an ice cream cone before it melts.
longDescription:
Charley Chuck must reach and eat an ice cream cone on the far side of an open playfield before it melts completely, steering with an analogue joystick and throwing with a single button. In his way are four chefs, Oscar, Angelo, Jacques and Zorba, told apart by their hats, big and round, small and rectangular, tall and slender, and flat and limp. They climb out of holes in the floor, which also bring them back if they meet with an accident, and chase Charley. Piles of pies, peas, tomatoes and bananas lie around the screen, and both Charley and the chefs grab food from them to throw; most foods run out, but watermelon never does. A chef hit by food, from Charley or another chef, is knocked off screen. Charley loses a life if he touches a chef, is hit by thrown food, falls into an open hole or lets the cone melt.

Points come from hitting chefs and luring them into holes, and eating the cone ends the level with a bonus for every unused piece of food except watermelon. The cone's value rises until level 50, and food held when Charley eats it carries over to the next level. After a level with a close call, the game sometimes plays an instant replay of the whole level to music.
trivia: It is also known as Charley Chuck's Food Fight.
Atari sold 1,951 arcade cabinets.
The initials of its main creators appear in the high score table.
Eating the cone at the last possible moment in a level chosen for a replay resets the arcade machine.
Justin Emory set the default-settings world record of 107,778,200 points on 4 July 2021.
devStory: General Computer Corporation, which designed the Atari 7800's custom chips and produced Ms. Pac-Man, came to work with Atari after a dispute: it had made a kit to speed up Missile Command machines and claimed the copyright for the modified game, so Atari sued it for $15 million. They settled out of court, with Atari contracting GCC to make games including Food Fight and Quantum. Jonathan Hurd said everyone at GCC contributed. Food Fight was released for the Atari 7800 in 1986 and the same year on cartridge for the Atari 8-bit computers in the style of the XEGS, while a 2600 port was cancelled. In the 7800 version, if Charley is rarely hit during the replay, the game shows "ALMOST MADE IT" and restores the lost life. Clones called Foodwar and Mudpies appeared for the TRS-80 Color Computer in 1983, the arcade version came to Microsoft's Game Room, and a third-person shooter reimagining reached the Atari VCS in early access in December 2023.

title: Keystone Kapers
description: Keystone Kapers (1983) is Garry Kitchen's Activision platformer for the Atari 2600 in which Keystone Kelly chases the thief Harry Hooligan through a four-floor department store, dodging shopping carts, beach balls and toy biplanes.
longDescription:
Officer Keystone Kelly must catch the con artist Harry Hooligan, on the loose in Southwick's Emporium. The player moves Kelly left and right, jumping and ducking to avoid shopping carts, beach balls and toy biplanes, and rides the lifts and escalator between floors. A mini-map at the bottom of the screen shows Kelly as a black dot and Harry as a white one. Lives are lost by running out of time, colliding with a biplane or letting Harry escape to the roof. Catching him scores points, plus a bonus for the time left, and moneybags and suitcases lying around the store add more; an extra life comes every 10,000 points.

Kitchen began with a vertically scrolling design like Donkey Kong, with the cop climbing the building floor by floor after the crook, and had it presentable within a month. When he showed it to David Crane, Crane suggested making it extend horizontally like his Pitfall!, then in progress. Kitchen kept Donkey Kong's idea of objects thrown to slow the chase and borrowed the mini-map from Bob Whitehead's Chopper Command.
trivia: Its code name was Cop.
Kitchen said the Keystone Cops theme was his wife's idea, and their bowler hats, blue uniforms and billy clubs suited the 2600.
A Model T-like car outside the store was cut because it "cost too many bytes".
A television was removed as an anachronism.
A Western-themed sequel by his brother Dan, found in storage in 2018, was released as Casey's Gold in 2024.
devStory: It was Kitchen's third 2600 game after Space Jockey and a Donkey Kong port. He joined Activision in June 1982 and worked from a satellite office in Glen Rock, New Jersey, which Crane felt would protect the original team's chemistry; Kitchen described himself as still in "little man mode" after Donkey Kong. Code was written on a PDP-11 minicomputer, and the game had to fit 4 KB for financial reasons. Activision released it in May 1983, followed by ColecoVision and Atari 5200 versions, the latter adding music and a level select. Critics praised its graphics, Videogaming & Computergaming Illustrated calling Kelly's swinging arms and legs "an absolute delight", and Electronic Games called it "truly vintage Activision". It won a Certificate of Merit at the 1984 Arkie Awards. Allgame later found it "solid, yet forgettable", but Retro Gamer ranked it 11th among Atari 2600 games in 2008.

title: Megamania
description: Megamania (1982) is Steve Cartwright's Activision shooter for the Atari 2600 in which a space pilot's junk-food nightmare sends waves of hamburgers, steam irons and bow ties against his ship, named the best 2600 game by one magazine in 1984.
longDescription:
After a day of work, the pilot of an intergalactic space cruiser gorges himself on everything from ice cream to pizza and falls asleep into a nightmare in which his ship is attacked by food and household objects, among them hamburgers, steam irons, tyres, spinning dice and bow ties. One player or two taking turns fire the ship's missile launcher at the attackers before their fleet of three cruisers is destroyed, earning an extra cruiser every 10,000 points.

Eight waves move with different speeds and attack patterns, each worth more per hit, until the eighth wave of "Space Dice", after which every enemy is worth 90 points and the colours and patterns change. An energy bar at the bottom of the screen drains during each wave, costing a ship if it runs out, and leftover energy earns bonus points. The game options offer guided missiles, which follow the joystick, or straight missiles.
trivia: Cartwright was inspired by seeing the arcade game Astro Blaster at a Chuck E. Cheese restaurant.
His ship could use only eight bits and one colour.
Ideas for setting it apart included calling it Space Game; Tom Lopez suggested GadZooks!
Activision's ad agency came up with the junk-food nightmare.
Cartwright reused its code for Plaque Attack.
devStory: Cartwright had studied with David Crane at DeVry in Phoenix and joined Activision as it grew; Megamania was his second game after Barnstorming. Displaying objects moving horizontally past each other and missiles passing through rows of them took "months of late-night coding", and the game took over nine months to fit into 4 KB. Feeling the market was overloaded with space shooters, the team gave it a new theme. Released on 24 September 1982, it was among Activision's biggest hits of 1983, though Jim Levy did not list it among the company's million-sellers. Reviews were split: JoyStik called it "one of the most original variations of the bottom-shooter concept", while the Fort Worth Star-Telegram called it "Space Invaders with a vengeance". It won "Most Humorous Home Arcade Game" at the 4th Arkie Awards, and Video and Computer Gaming Illustrated named it the best Atari 2600 game in March 1984. Glyn Anderson adapted it for the Atari 5200 and 8-bit computers, and Cartwright later counted it, Seaquest and Frostbite among the best fast action 2600 games.

title: Demon Attack
description: Demon Attack (1982) is Rob Fulop's Atari 2600 shooter for Imagic in which a laser cannon fights waves of winged demons, Imagic's best-selling game and the subject of an Atari lawsuit over its Intellivision version.
longDescription:
From the surface of a planet, the player moves a laser cannon left and right, shooting winged creatures that hover above and attack in shifting patterns. Players start with three lives, called bunkers, shown at the bottom of the screen, and lose one each time they are hit. Waves grow more complex: in wave five, enemies split into two smaller ones when shot, and later demons dive at the cannon. A Tracer Shot mode lets players steer lasers after firing. Two players can compete, each with their own cannon, score and bunkers at the same time, or cooperate, swapping control of movement and firing every four seconds.

Fulop modelled it on Galaxian. The first complete version repeated one enemy pattern endlessly, so he worked on additional, more organic movements, and because the 2600 made horizontal movement smooth and easy, the demons move mostly horizontally. It was his first game with a graphic artist, Michael Becker, whose eight-phase animation for the demons Racing the Beam later said "broke the mold" for console development. Gary Kato's Intellivision version let demons move in any direction and added the flagship Pandemonium as a final boss, destroyed by eroding its shield and hitting a small rotating weak point.
trivia: Fulop left Atari after his Christmas bonus for Space Invaders turned out to be a voucher for a free turkey dinner.
He said he wanted to make something "so good, they'd cry when they saw it".
His working title was Death from Above.
Becker made the cover art from model toys painted silver and blue.
The Odyssey 2 version was the first cartridge for that system from an independent publisher.
devStory: Fulop co-founded Imagic on 17 July 1981, and Demon Attack took nine months; he had to fight marketing to keep it in the lab for a final month of polish. Released in March 1982 with Star Voyager and Trick Shot, it was the third best-selling console game of 1982 behind Pitfall! and Pac-Man. Atari, which held the home rights to Phoenix, sued over the Intellivision version's similar boss; Fulop, who disliked the boss, called the dispute "a silly hustling and political thing", and a January 1983 settlement let Imagic keep releasing it on many consoles and computers. Critics praised its graphics and unpredictable enemies, and it won Video Game of the Year at the 1983 Arcade Awards, while Billboard named Fulop designer of the year. Fulop said he knew it would do well but not that well, and regretted not making a sequel. GameSpy added it to its Hall of Fame in 2002.

title: Wonder Momo
description: Wonder Momo (1987) is Namco's Japan-only arcade beat 'em up, a loose parody of Ultraman-style superhero shows in which the player is an actress playing a transforming heroine on the stage of the Namco Theater.
longDescription:
The game opens with a parody of the MGM logo, Momo in place of the lion, before cutting to a theatre stage where a play begins. Rather than a hero saving the world, the player controls an actress playing the role of Momo, a young woman who gains super-powers, in a live show at the "Namco Theater", with Japanese voice samples. As Momo, she can only kick, which builds up her "Wonder" meter. Touching a tornado icon, or spinning on the spot, turns her into Wonder Momo, who can throw the Wonder Hoop, reusable but only after it bounces back to her. Crouching, she fires small energy waves, based on Ultraman's attacks, and her strongest move, the Wonder Typhoon, sprays waves to both sides of the screen while she spins.

It was unusual for its time in having a female lead, and it included some risqué fan service: photographers in the audience try to snap under her skirt, and if one succeeds she is stunned with embarrassment for a moment.
trivia: It was released in Japan on 24 February 1987.
Momo partners Bravoman in the Japan-only Namco x Capcom.
Her costume appears in Tales of the World: Radiant Mythology 2 and The Idolmaster.
Singer Haruko Momoi released an album titled WONDER MOMO-i.
A 2012 ShiftyLook webcomic, Wonder Momo: Battle Idol, led to a 2014 anime and a WayForward game, Typhoon Booster.
devStory: Namco developed and released Wonder Momo for Japanese arcades, and Game Machine listed it as the fourth most successful table arcade unit in its 1 April 1987 issue. NEC Avenue ported it to the PC Engine in 1989, and critics liked the conversion: Aktueller Software Markt praised its large sprites, soundtrack, special effects and easy-to-understand play, The Games Machine found it "great fun" for its bizarre premise, and Famitsu praised its detailed sprites, catchy music and faithfulness to the arcade. Both versions came to the Wii Virtual Console, the arcade version also appeared in Namco Museum Encore for the PlayStation, and Hamster added it to Arcade Archives in 2022. The ShiftyLook webcomic by Omar Dogan, Erik Ko and Jim Zub, set 25 years later, followed an idol named Momoko who gains Wonder Momo's powers and ran 200 pages until ShiftyLook closed in 2014; Graphinica's five-episode anime featured Momoi reprising the original Wonder Momo.

title: Genpei Tōma Den
description: Genpei Tōma Den (1986) is Namco's Japan-only arcade hack and slash game in which the resurrected samurai Taira no Kagekiyo fights through a demon-ridden Japan, acclaimed at home and later released abroad as The Genji and the Heike Clans.
longDescription:
The player is Taira no Kagekiyo, a samurai killed at the Battle of Dan-no-ura in the Genpei War. In this alternative history, he is resurrected to defeat his enemy Minamoto no Yoritomo and the heads of his clan, Minamoto no Yoshitsune and Saito Musashibo Benkei, whose tyranny has thrown Japan into turmoil and filled it with demons. He travels the Japanese countryside fighting enemies as they appear, in three styles of play: the standard side-scrolling Small Mode, Big Mode with huge characters, usually for boss fights, and Plain Mode, seen from overhead.

Most stages have torii gates that carry the player to another stage, and in Small and Plain Mode stages there are often several, leading to different routes across the map, while Big Mode stages have a single torii at the end. The journey also passes the Sanzu River, which in Japanese Buddhism separates this life from the afterlife and is often compared to the Styx, and mythological figures such as Emma-o, god of the underworld, appear.
trivia: It topped Gamest's chart as Japan's top-grossing arcade game in November and December 1986.
Kagekiyo placed third in Gamest's Best Character award.
GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann called it the worst game in any Namco Museum to that point: "a joke".
A 1988 Famicom spin-off, Genpei Tōma Den Computer Board Game, came with a cloth board, cards and metal Kagekiyo figures.
Kagekiyo's armour appears in Soulcalibur III's character creator.
devStory: Namco released Genpei Tōma Den in Japanese arcades in October 1986, and it was received in Japan as one of Namco's best arcade games. Game Machine reported it among the best-selling arcade games of November 1986, and it won several Gamest awards, including sixth place for the Grand Prize. Readers of Gamest's 1991 mook The Best Game voted it among the greatest arcade games, and the staff called it "an immortal masterpiece". An X68000 port followed in 1988, praised by Oh!X for new levels and secrets, and a PC Engine version in March 1990, which Famitsu inducted into its Gold Hall of Fame as "a port that does not spoil the taste of the original". Its first release outside Japan came in Namco Museum Vol. 4 in 1997, where reviews were mixed: IGN found it the strangest game in the set, and PlayStation Official Magazine – UK found it too hard. A sequel, Genpei Tōma Den: Kan no Ni, released in North America as Samurai-Ghost, followed on the PC Engine in 1992.

title: Alpine Racer
description: Alpine Racer (1995) is Namco's System 22 skiing arcade game, played by standing on swivelling foot pedals and gripping handlebars, a major hit in Japan and the US that set off a wave of arcade sports games.
longDescription:
Based on alpine skiing, it uses a handlebar controller with rotating foot pedals to simulate real skis. The player steers a skier down a snowy mountain course, avoiding trees and rocks and staying on the slope. Three courses grow harder with fast-moving obstacles and sharper turns, across Novice, Intermediate and Expert difficulty. In Race Mode, the skier takes on five computer opponents, and finishing first earns a replay; in Time Trial Mode, the skier goes solo against a countdown, restoring a second for each large gate passed. On one course, Pac-Man appears on a billboard wearing a Santa hat.

Critics praised the controls as unlike any other game: Next Generation gave it a perfect score, saying they gave a true sense of skiing and suggesting its premise could attract players of both genders, and GameFan called the graphics "nothing short of shocking". Spanish magazine Ultima Generacion found it far more original than Sega Rally and credited it with challenging the view that arcades held mostly violent games. Pac-Man creator Toru Iwatani said games like it drew players into the "heart" of arcades with distinctive controls, and historian Steve Kent cited it as an experience that could never be recreated at home.
trivia: Each cabinet cost $20,000, and an estimated 2,000 were sold in the US.
In March 1996 it was Japan's most successful arcade game, ahead of Tekken 2 and Virtua Cop 2.
It won Best New Equipment at the 1995 AMOA exposition.
Harvard sleep scientist Robert Stickgold found that people who played it before sleeping, including amnesiacs, dreamed of skiing.
Alpine Racer 3 on the PlayStation 2 added Klonoa as a guest skier.
devStory: Namco developed it for its System 22 hardware and gave it a limited release in December 1994 before a wide release in July 1995. Game Machine listed it as Japan's most popular dedicated arcade game in its 15 August 1995 issue, and in March 1996 Leisure Line reported it as the most successful arcade game in Japan, second in Australia behind Manx TT Super Bike and in the top three in the US. It was Japan's fourth highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1996 and among the top five in the US, and it was nominated for Most Innovative New Technology at the 1996 AMOA Awards. Its success led Sega, Namco, Konami and Innovative Concepts to release a wave of similar sports games in the late 1990s. Sequels followed: Alpine Racer 2 in 1996 with three skiers and linked multiplayer, the snowboarding spin-off Alpine Surfer the same year, Alpine Racer 3 in 2002, mobile versions, an iOS remake in 2009 and Super Alpine Racer in 2014.

title: Super Breakout
description: Super Breakout (1978) is Atari's sequel to Breakout, designed by Ed Rotberg and Ed Logg, which added multi-ball modes, ran on a 6502 processor and later came packed with the Atari 5200.
longDescription:
The basic play is unchanged from Breakout: the player uses a paddle to bounce a ball into a wall of destructible bricks. Super Breakout, though, offers three modes. "Double" gives the player two paddles at once, one above the other, with two balls in play. "Cavity" starts with one ball, but two more are trapped in pockets inside the wall and can be freed. "Progressive" moves the whole wall down step by step, speeding up the longer the ball stays in play. As with its predecessor, the arcade version is displayed in black and white, with overlays on the monitor to add colour.

Where the original Breakout was built from discrete logic, Super Breakout uses a MOS Technology 6502 CPU. Home versions came in colour and all include a version of the original Breakout: the 1979 Atari 8-bit cartridge supports up to eight players taking turns, and the VCS port, first sold by Sears under its Tele-Games brand in October 1981 and then by Atari in January 1982, adds two easier "Children's Version" games.
trivia: Namco and Esco Trading released it in Japan.
Logg helped after hearing Nolan Bushnell wanted Breakout updated, and went on to co-design Asteroids; Rotberg later designed Battlezone.
Atari sold 4,805 arcade cabinets.
A 1982 Kid Stuff record told the story of an astronaut breaking through a rainbow force field with bouncing missiles of light.
The Atari ST and Game Boy versions use sculpted bricks like Arkanoid.
devStory: Ed Rotberg wrote the game, with Ed Logg assisting on the design, and Atari released it in 1978. It was commercially successful in Japan, where it was the ninth highest-earning arcade video game of 1978, and in the US, where it was the eighth highest-earning of 1979. Atari published colour home versions for most of its consoles and computers, and it became the pack-in game for the Atari 5200 in 1982, which, unlike earlier versions with paddles, used the system's analogue joysticks. Creative Computing's David H. Ahl thought it a curious choice, since it hardly used the 5200's higher resolution and had the same number of bricks as the VCS version, though he preferred its lettering. An Atari ST version by Paradox followed in 1987, and Majesco released it for the Game Boy in 1998 and Game Boy Color in 1999. Flux magazine ranked it 93rd among the top 100 video games in 1995, and Atari brought it to the iPhone in 2008.

description: 720° (1986) is Atari Games' skateboarding arcade game in which a skater cruises Skate City between ramp, downhill, slalom and jump events, racing to reach a park before a swarm of killer bees arrives with the cry "SKATE OR DIE!"
longDescription:
The skater rides around a middle-class neighbourhood, Skate City, using everyday objects as ramps. Tickets grant entry to its four skate parks, called events, and each entry uses one; more tickets come from earning points, so the score is tied directly to how long the game lasts. Outside an event, a bar counts down to the arrival of a swarm of killer bees, captioned "SKATE OR DIE!" Once they arrive, the player has a little time left to reach a park, and the longer the delay, the faster the bees become until they cannot be escaped; being caught ends the game unless more money is inserted. Map icons on the ground show the roads, parks, shops and the player's position, and jumping over hazards earns points.

There are four levels of four events. Ramp has the skater gain height on a half-pipe and perform tricks until time runs out. Downhill is a course of slopes and banks where faster finishes score more. Slalom requires passing between pairs of yellow flags, each gate adding a little time. Jump launches the skater from ramps towards an off-screen bull's-eye, with cryptic marks on the ramp hinting at its position. Good results earn medals and cash to buy better equipment, and completing all sixteen events wins the game.
trivia: Its arcade program was written in the BLISS language.
It runs on Atari's System 2 hardware.
Sinclair User called Tiertex's ports "US Gold's finest hour".
An Atari Lynx port was never released.
Flux magazine ranked it 79th among the top 100 video games in 1995.
devStory: Atari Games developed and published 720° for arcades in 1986, and it received an overall positive reception from players and critics; Flux later called it "addicting" and completely unique for its time. It was ported widely. Tiertex Design Studios developed the Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and first Commodore 64 versions, published by U.S. Gold, and the Commodore 64 received two versions in 1987. The Amstrad and Spectrum versions followed in 1988, an NES version in 1989, and a Game Boy Color version, developed by Game Brains and published by Midway, in March 1999 in North America and Europe. Emulated versions of the arcade game are included in Midway Arcade Treasures, released in 2003 and 2004, and Midway Arcade Origins in 2012.

title: Clu Clu Land
description: Clu Clu Land (1984) is Nintendo's maze puzzle game for the Famicom and NES in which the balloonfish Bubbles swings around posts to uncover hidden gold ingots, while stunning the sea urchins that stole the kingdom's treasure.
longDescription:
The Unira, a kind of sea urchin, have stolen all the treasure of the underwater kingdom of Clu Clu Land, and the heroine Bubbles, a female balloonfish called Gloopy in Japan, sets out to recover it. In each stage she swims around a maze to uncover all the gold ingots, which usually form the shape of a heart or a mushroom, while avoiding the Unira and black holes. She can only change direction by grabbing the turning posts placed through the stages and swinging around them. A sound wave stuns the Unira, and stunned ones can be pushed into a wall for points. Bubbles loses a life if a Unira hurts her, if she falls into a black hole or if time runs out. In later levels, ingots flip between their uncovered and dull sides, so she must pass over them an odd number of times.

The title anglicises "Kuru Kuru", Japanese onomatopoeia for going "around and around", after Bubbles spinning round the posts; the same phrase gave its name to Kuru Kuru Kururin. The arcade VS. Clu Clu Land doubled the puzzles, added a Boss Unira and new level themes, and became the basis of the last Famicom Disk System game, Clu Clu Land: Welcome to New Clu Clu Land.
trivia: The Chicago Tribune singled it out with Ice Climber in 1986 for keeping its interest after repeated plays.
The Unira are an item in Super Smash Bros. from Brawl onwards.
Bubbles is an unlockable character in DK: King of Swing, whose play was inspired by Clu Clu Land.
Both the NES and FDS versions are unlockable in the first Animal Crossing.
A port was released for Sharp Zaurus PDAs in 2001.
devStory: Nintendo developed and published Clu Clu Land for the Famicom in Japan in 1984, released it in North America in 1985 as an NES launch title, and in Europe in 1987, with an arcade version on the Nintendo VS. System. A Famicom Disk System port added minor enhancements such as difficulty selection. In a June 1986 survey of the NES catalogue, the Chicago Tribune's Steven Kosek and Dennis Lynch picked out it and Ice Climber as the games that kept their interest. It returned on the Game Boy Advance in the 2004 Famicom Mini series, in the NES Remix series, on the Virtual Console for the 3DS and Wii U and on Nintendo Classics, and Hamster released the arcade version in Arcade Archives on the Switch in 2018. Its elements recur across Nintendo's games: Bubbles is a trophy in Super Smash Bros. Melee and a Spirit in Ultimate, the soundtrack appears as stage music, WarioWare: Smooth Moves and Twisted! include Clu Clu Land microgames, and Bubbles is a costume in Super Mario Maker.

title: Snowboard Kids
description: Snowboard Kids (1997) is Racdym's cartoon snowboarding racer for the Nintendo 64, with weapons, items and courses through amusement parks and deserts, widely compared to Mario Kart and a European million-seller.
longDescription:
Alongside the usual snowboarding, it adds "Shots", special weapons for attacking other riders, and items that help the player, hinder others or both. Riders have two item slots, one for a shooting item and one for a support item such as a rock or invisibility, and each item costs 100 gold during a race, earned by performing tricks or collecting coins on the course. Races run for several laps: at the bottom of the hill, riders pass through a lift gate that carries them back to the top, during which they cannot be attacked. Modes include a single-player adventure, head-to-head racing for up to four players, and time trials.

The nine main courses each have their own shape, obstacles, hazards and shortcuts, and many are snowy mountains, but others are unorthodox places to snowboard, including an amusement park, a desert, a vast valley, a dark highway and a Japanese village during the cherry blossom festival. Six characters, Slash, Nancy, Jam, Linda, Tommy and the unlockable Shinobin, available after all nine tracks are completed, differ in speed, cornering and trick ability, which determines their hang time for tricks that earn coins.
trivia: In Japan it is called Snobo Kids.
It was shown at the Tokyo Game Show on 5 to 7 September 1997.
EGM's Crispin Boyer liked that power-ups are bought rather than simply collected.
An enhanced port, Snowboard Kids Plus, came to the PlayStation in Japan in January 1999.
Its Player's Choice label in Europe indicates sales of at least a million.
devStory: Racdym developed Snowboard Kids and Atlus published it for the Nintendo 64. It was generally well received, though the most common criticism was a lack of originality, with most reviewers calling it a Mario Kart clone; most still concluded it was a good game, praising its smooth controls, inventive courses and the depth and replay value of its modes and minigames. IGN called it "a satisfyingly cute snow racer" for players wanting a simple ride rather than realism, and Next Generation said that despite its lack of originality it "does most things right". Computer and Video Games dismissed it as "very average", and GamePro warned of its "stifling kiddie atmosphere" while finding it fun, especially in multiplayer. EGM's reviewers were more enthusiastic, Dan Hsu calling it a "sleeper hit" that was "more than just a Mario Kart wanna-be", and Nintendo Life later found it "worthy of a place in anyone's collection". Snowboard Kids 2 followed in 1999 and SBK: Snowboard Kids on the DS in 2005.

title: Quest 64
description: Quest 64 (1998), Holy Magic Century in Europe, is Imagineer's elemental-magic RPG and the first role-playing game released for the Nintendo 64 in North America, praised for its graphics but faulted as shallow.
longDescription:
In Celtland, a medieval fantasy world resembling Ireland, the apprentice mage Brian sets out to find his father, who has left the monastery of the mages; Brian later learns that his father is hunting a thief who stole the Eletale Book. Along the way, Brian must recover elemental gems hoarded by powerful criminals before facing the final boss.

As in Chrono Trigger, battles take place where the enemy is met rather than on a separate screen, with Brian locked in place while the fight plays out. His spells work through elemental spirits, each of the controller's four C buttons matching one of the classic elements, wind, earth, water and fire. There is no traditional levelling: as in Final Fantasy II, statistics rise according to how the player fights, so being hit often raises defence, and white spirits found in the world let the player strengthen an element of choice, unlocking new attacks. Unusually, there is no money; every item is found in chests, dropped by monsters or given away. If Brian runs out of health he returns to the last inn where he saved, keeping his spells, items and experience. A compass and clock track the time of day, and some events happen only by day or by night.
trivia: It was announced in early 1997 as Eltale in Japan and Holy Magic Century elsewhere.
It was shown at Space World in 1997.
Konami published it in Europe.
Because Western versions were seen as too short and easy, the 1999 Japanese release, Eltale Monsters, added new events.
Imagineer's Game Boy Color follow-ups included Quest: Brian's Journey and a Mr. Do! clone, Quest: Fantasy Challenge.
devStory: Imagineer developed the game and THQ translated and published it in North America in June 1998, followed by Konami in Europe that September; despite its Japanese origin, it only reached Japan in July 1999. Expectations were high because it was the first true RPG on the Nintendo 64. Reviews were mixed, with a GameRankings average of 54%: critics praised its graphics, IGN writing that it proved "compelling RPG graphics are possible on a cart", and its inventive spell system, but faulted its lack of depth in gameplay, story and exploration. GameSpot mocked its formula: "Go to Town #1... Discover that there's a villain... he's stolen Unique Elemental Magic Item #1 from Lord #1." The consensus was that it could charm newcomers to RPGs but was too simple and trite for anyone else, and Next Generation, giving three stars, said it proved cartridges could work for RPGs but showed "the need for well-told stories and characters you care about". After moderate financial success, a sequel was considered and its story revealed, but it was cancelled.

title: Aero Fighters
description: Aero Fighters (1992), Sonic Wings in Japan, is Video System's vertical arcade shooter with an unusually large cast of national pilots, the first in its series and the game that accidentally named the Vlogbrothers' Nerdfighters.
longDescription:
Button one fires the main weapon, upgraded by P items or the rarer F items, though the top power level has a hidden ammunition count, after which the ship drops back a level. Button two launches a powerful special attack, limited by the number of B items collected, with two at the start of each life. Some ground enemies drop score items in the currency of the chosen pilot's nation. Players start with three lives and earn another at 200,000 points.

Its large cast of characters was unheard of in 1992, with pairs of pilots representing four nations; in two-player games only one nation can be chosen, and each side has four pilots to pick from. There are seven stages: the first three are drawn at random from four, one per nation, though pilots never visit their own nation's stage, and the last four are fixed. After the seventh, the player sees the pilot's ending and then plays much harder versions of the stages before the game truly ends. On the SNES, a code lets players fly the ship from Rabio Lepus.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit of April 1992.
It is the only Aero Fighters game released under the McO'River brand.
John Green misread its title as "Nerd Fighters" at Savannah Airport in a 2007 Vlogbrothers video, naming the channel's fan community.
Green was given an Aero Fighters cabinet in September 2013.
Original copies are rare and fetch astronomical prices at auction.
devStory: Video System developed Aero Fighters and Tecmo published it in arcades in 1992, and RePlay also reported it as the second most popular arcade game at the time. A solid game, it had little to set it apart in a crowded field; one critic called it "a thoroughly solid game" that "is also a game that is easy to forget". An SNES version followed in 1993 in Japan and 1994 in North America, which GamePro disliked for its slowdown, mediocre graphics and "monotonous" music. Main designer Shin Nakamura disliked Video System's plan to move to the Neo Geo, since vertical games were hard to make on its horizontal monitors, and left with like-minded staff to found Psikyo, whose first game was the similar Samurai Aces. The remaining team made Aero Fighters 2 and 3 for the Neo Geo, Sonic Wings Special and Limited, and Aero Fighters Assault, and a new game, Sonic Wings Reunion, launched in Japan in May 2025. Hamster added the original to Arcade Archives in 2023.

title: Sol-Feace
description: Sol-Feace (1990) is Wolf Team's horizontal shooter for the X68000 with angle-adjustable twin cannons and a Motoi Sakuraba score, later a Japanese Sega CD launch title and the add-on's North American pack-in game.
longDescription:
The player flies the starship Sol-Feace to stop a malfunctioning supercomputer before it enslaves all of mankind. Across each stage, it destroys incoming enemies while avoiding their fire. Its pair of dual cannons can be set to point forwards, backwards or diagonally, or arranged parallel to each other. Shooting small capsules leaves power-ups that add homing missiles, a piercing laser or a wide shot.

The six stages take in mechanical bases, wrecked star vessels and the planet Jupiter, each ending in a boss that must be hit in its weak point, and the last pits the player against the supercomputer itself. Animated cut-scenes between stages explain the story, with full voice acting in the Sega CD version. Reviews were mixed: Electronic Games called the Sega CD version a "solid side-scrolling shooter" and praised Sega for making it the pack-in, and GamePro liked the Genesis version's detailed visuals and pumping soundtrack, but Computer and Video Games found its ideas done better in Hellfire and Gynoug, and Retro Gamer called it a "below par" launch game with a CD soundtrack "tacked-on".
trivia: Composer Motoi Sakuraba later worked on Namco's Tales series.
It launched the Sega CD in Japan alongside Micronet's Heavy Nova.
The Genesis cartridge version was renamed Sol-Deace.
GamePro found its power-ups less impressive than Thunder Force III's.
Sunsoft has owned it since acquiring Telenet Japan's properties in 2009.
devStory: Wolf Team developed Sol-Feace and its parent company Telenet Japan published it for the X68000 on 22 November 1990. It was ported to the Sega CD in 1991 as one of the console's first Japanese launch titles, and Sega published that version internationally, making it the pack-in game for the North American release. Renovation Products released a Genesis cartridge version, renamed Sol-Deace, in 1992. Critics praised its fast action, graphics and soundtrack but criticised its lack of originality and found it below other shooters on the market; Wizard said it offered nothing new to the genre. Computer and Video Games said the Sega CD version was not a "total waste of money", praising its sound effects, speed, music and cut-scenes, while GamePro disliked the Genesis version's short length. In a retrospective review, Allgame found the sound effects mediocre and the music average but thought the dual-cannon mechanic an interesting idea and the frantic play and colourful visuals worth trying.

title: Mach Rider
description: Mach Rider (1985) is HAL Laboratory's vehicular combat racer for Nintendo, in which a superbike rider with a machine gun crosses a ruined Earth in 2112, with a track editor that only Japanese players could save from.
longDescription:
In the year 2112, Earth has been invaded by evil forces driving vehicles called Quadrunners. Mach Rider travels from sector to sector on a high-powered superbike, searching for survivors and destroying enemies in his path. The controls were more complex than most of the time: the pad steers, A accelerates, B fires a machine gun at enemies and obstacles, and up and down shift through four gears. Shifting to fourth at high speed gives an instant boost, while staying in a high gear after stopping slows acceleration. Ramming an attacking enemy into a hazard scores extra points and refills the bike's bullets.

Fighting Course is the main story, ten sectors with a choice of Track A or Track B in each, dodging oil drums and Quadrunners; when the bike is destroyed it breaks apart and reforms while energy remains. As in Ice Climber and Balloon Fight, there is no ending: after ten sectors comes a second quest of ten new ones, and then the original sectors again. Endurance Course sets a distance to cover within a time limit, where crashes cost time rather than lives, Solo Course is the same without enemies, and Design Mode lets players build their own sectors and race them in any mode.
trivia: Nintendo had sold a plastic toy race car called Mach Rider in 1972, with a jumping ramp and a stick shift.
Saving custom tracks required the Famicom Data Recorder, which was never released outside Japan.
Track saving was restored internationally in the Wii and Wii U Virtual Console versions, but not on the 3DS.
VS. Mach Rider in arcades is essentially a modified Endurance Course.
Each arcade level reveals more of an image of a woman with a dagger beside Mach Rider's bike.
devStory: HAL Laboratory developed Mach Rider and Nintendo published it for the Famicom and the Nintendo VS. System arcade board in Japan in 1985. The VS. System version reached North America the same year, the NES version followed in 1986, and the game came to the PAL region in 1987. Points are awarded according to the type of enemy or obstacle destroyed, and the Japanese Famicom release's Data Recorder support meant custom tracks could be saved, as in Excitebike. The game was later re-released on the Virtual Console for the Wii in 2007, the Nintendo 3DS in 2013 and the Wii U in 2014, and on the Nintendo Classics service for the Switch in 2024.

title: Red Baron
description: Red Baron (1981) is Atari's first-person vector-graphics biplane combat game, built alongside Battlezone on similar hardware, which flopped in arcades but inspired Sid Meier and Bill Stealey to found MicroProse's first game.
longDescription:
The player is a World War I ace flying a biplane for the Allies, in a game named after the nickname of German ace Manfred von Richthofen. It is divided into rounds, most split between air combat against one to three planes in formation and ground combat against two zeppelins and various ground targets, including pillboxes, turrets and buildings. Flight physics are not accurate, and the plane cannot be crashed directly into the ground, but the vector mountain ranges are solid, so flying into them costs a life, although shots pass straight through them in both directions.

The game adjusts its own difficulty, keeping a consistent average game time across the last 32 games played; its non-volatile memory stores the top three scores and the average game times, so that it adapts to the typical player at each location and avoids excessively long games. Like Battlezone, developed at the same time, it uses monochrome vector graphics, a first-person view and extra hardware for the 3D calculations.
trivia: Upright Red Baron and Battlezone machines share a cabinet, but Red Baron drops the mirror and mounts its monitor vertically.
The two games use the same Analog Vector Generator boards, interchangeable by swapping PROMs.
Their auxiliary boards are different and cannot be swapped.
MicroProse later obtained the very unit Meier and Stealey had played as a memento.
Its Atari Anthology version surrounds the screen with parts of the cabinet art.
devStory: Atari, Inc. developed Red Baron and released it in arcades in 1981. Electronic Games reported that it was not successful despite its "gorgeous quadra-scan graphics and magnificent audio frills", and hoped that "this marvelous flight simulator with a combat theme will re-emerge in home format some day". Its biggest influence came from a single session: while playing it in 1982, Bill Stealey and Sid Meier decided to create what became MicroProse's first game, Hellcat Ace. Red Baron was later included in Atari: 80 Classic Games in One! for Windows, Atari Anthology for the Xbox and PlayStation 2, and Atari Greatest Hits Volume 2 for the DS, and the arcade version is available on the AtGames Legends Ultimate cabinet.

title: Seaquest
description: Seaquest (1983) is Steve Cartwright's Activision underwater shooter for the Atari 2600, in which a submarine rescues divers from sharks and enemy subs while racing to surface before its oxygen runs out.
longDescription:
The player steers a submarine that fires an unlimited supply of torpedoes at sharks, which attack both divers and the player, and enemy submarines that fire torpedoes of their own, while rescuing divers swimming through the water. Enemies are worth 10 points at first, rising as the game goes on. The sub holds up to six divers, and each time it surfaces with fewer than six, one of the divers is taken away.

Oxygen is limited, so the player must surface often to refill it, but surfacing with no divers aboard costs a life, while surfacing with a full load earns a bonus for the oxygen remaining. Every trip to the surface makes the game harder, with more and faster enemies, until an enemy sub starts patrolling the surface itself and there is nowhere safe. Players begin with three extra lives and earn another every 10,000 points, alone or with two players taking turns.
trivia: Cartwright described it as a reskin of the arcade game Defender.
A salvage company with a similar name sued Activision over the title; the case was dismissed after Cartwright explained to its lawyers in Chicago that the game had nothing to do with sunken treasure.
Players who photographed a score of 50,000 could send it in for an Activision achievement patch.
The Video Game Update praised its "buoyant feeling", with air bubbles rising from the divers' kicking flippers.
Retro Gamer's Darran Jones said it was one of the few games to live up to its "fantastic box art".
devStory: Cartwright designed Seaquest for Activision, and it was released for the Atari 2600 in February 1983. He felt the 2600 adapted arcade games well, which was why most games of the era were "fast-paced arcade games". Contemporary reviewers in Video and Computer Gaming Illustrated, Micro & Video, Electronic Fun and Video Games Player praised its graphics as up to Activision's usual standard, and Games liked its sound, "a welcome change from the usual munch and crunch", while Micro & Video noted the warning sound when oxygen runs low. Jim Clark said it "splendidly creates an underwater environment", but his colleague E.C. Meade found it slow and not very hard, "too complex for kids and too slow for real enthusiasts", "good but nothing more". TeleMatch found the graphics "a little too abstract", and Electronic Fun concluded that once players got the hang of it, it was "a little like shooting fish in a barrel". Cartwright also made Megamania and Frostbite.

title: Frostbite
description: Frostbite (1983) is Steve Cartwright's last Atari 2600 game for Activision, in which Frostbite Bailey hops across drifting ice floes, turning them blue to build an igloo before the temperature drops to zero.
longDescription:
Frostbite Bailey must build igloos by jumping across four rows of ice floes, collecting a block of ice each time he lands on a white floe, which turns it blue, while avoiding falling into the sea. Killer clams, snow geese, king crabs and polar bears all threaten him, and passing fish can be caught for 200 bonus points. A falling temperature acts as the timer, and if it runs out he loses a life. Once the igloo is built and he goes inside, the remaining temperature and the number of rounds completed earn bonus points. Players start with three reserve lives, earn another every 5,000 points, and can choose Regular mode from level one or Advanced from level five, alone or with two players taking turns.

Cartwright had to stop players hopping back and forth between two floes forever, so blocks can only be added once all the floes are the same colour. He said Frostbite was one of the games most heavily tested before release, as it sped up until objects wrapped around the screen so fast that they sometimes seemed to move backwards, "like those old Westerns where the wagon wheels appears to be turning slowly in the opposite direction".
trivia: Its working title was Iceman.
Cartwright's first idea was jumping over rocks in a lava field, dropped because blue and white worked better on the 2600.
Critics compared it to Q*bert, but Cartwright said he based it on Frogger and had not played Q*bert until after finishing it.
Dan Gutman listed it among Q*bert clones but said it showed how to use an idea "without ripping off the original".
Retro Gamer ranked it 22nd among Atari 2600 games in 2008.
devStory: Cartwright joined Activision in 1982 and released Barnstorming and Megamania that year, then Plaque Attack, Seaquest and Frostbite in 1983. He found memory and screen timing difficult, something "extremely easy with higher programming languages, but" a real problem in 6502 code. Released in October 1983, it divided critics: The Video Game Update called it "cute, but kind of dumb" yet hard to stop playing, and Video and Computer Gaming Illustrated's Jim Clark said its design "is so well done, you feel the chill", while his colleague E.C. Meade called it "another step in the company's surprising decline", and Video Games found it a throwback next to Robot Tank and Enduro. Brett Weiss later found its arcade-style action very satisfying, though less colourful than most Activision games, and Retro Gamer said it would be wrong to call it a Frogger rip-off, praising its new mechanics and tight controls. It was re-released in Activision Anthology in 2002.

title: Robot Tank
description: Robot Tank (1983) is Alan Miller's first-person tank combat game for the Atari 2600, in the mould of Battlezone but with damageable systems, day and night battles and weather, hailed at the time as the best combat game on the system.
longDescription:
In 2019, the player remotely controls a robot tank, using radar to find and destroy enemy robot tanks heading for downtown Santa Clara, California. The enemy comes in squadrons of 12, and each squadron defeated adds a reserve tank to the starting three, up to a maximum of 12; the game ends when all the player's tanks are gone. Instead of exploding at the first hit, the tank suffers damage to individual systems, permanently weakening its firepower or its video display, until enough damage destroys it.

Battles happen at any time of day or night, shown on screen, and at night tanks must be tracked by radar alone. Each level's weather is announced at the start: clear, rain, which slows the tank, snow, which costs it traction, or fog, which limits its vision. When the player's tank is destroyed, the view dissolves into static, a touch young critic Rawson Stovall singled out.
trivia: Its development title was Robotank.
Miller produced about 200 pages of handwritten notes on computer printouts.
He had abandoned a racing game as "unworkable" before starting it.
Miller said that after finishing a game, "I really hate it and I don't want to see it again for months."
Answering comparisons with Battlezone, Activision said: "We don't steal any of our ideas."
devStory: Miller had made Surround, Hangman and Basketball at Atari before co-founding Activision with David Crane, where his games included Tennis, Ice Hockey and his most financially successful, Starmaster. He spent about two months writing code, two on graphics, sound and balancing the challenge, and two more having colleagues play it while he spent hundreds of hours debugging. Released in June 1983, it was among Activision's biggest hits of the year. Bill Kunkel called its graphics "non-parallel in the 2600 universe" and the game Miller's "masterpiece", "perhaps the finest target-arcade program ever developed for the 2600", and Computer Entertainer called it "the best combat game yet" for the system, though some found it unoriginal and critics regretted that damaged tanks cannot be repaired. Electronic Fun included it among the best video games ever in 1984. Allgame later called it "far ahead of its time" and "one of the most sophisticated Atari 2600 games", though it felt the weather gave only a false sense of variety.

title: Riddle of the Sphinx
description: Riddle of the Sphinx (1982) is Bob Smith's Atari 2600 adventure for Imagic in which an Egyptian prince gathers offerings to lift Anubis's curse, a puzzle-driven game inspired by San Jose's Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum.
longDescription:
Played from a top-down, vertically scrolling view, it casts the player as an Ancient Egyptian prince appeasing the gods with offerings found across the map. Anubis has cursed the land, filling it with scorpions and thieves, which the prince fends off with a rock sling. He grows thirsty, moving slower and throwing rocks shorter distances, until he refills at an oasis. Items in his inventory are selected and used with the second controller, and his inner strength, elapsed time, thirst and wounds are displayed using combinations of the 2600's colour and difficulty switches.

Nomad traders buy and sell items, temples of Anubis and Isis can help or harm, and landmarks include a sphinx, a phoenix, a pyramid and the Temple of Ra. On higher difficulties, landmarks only grant passage when given particular items, and riddles in the manual hint at what each requires. Solving a final riddle allows the last offering at the Temple of Ra, ending the game.
trivia: The Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum was three blocks from Smith's childhood home.
Smith said: "I didn't want to do another shooter so this is something more cerebral."
A contest winner presented his answer to the riddle on a 12-foot scroll of hieroglyphs and received $1,000 from Smith at the museum.
A UK contest offered £185 of Imagic products.
Smith estimates it sold about 750,000 copies.
devStory: Smith, who had made Video Pinball at Atari and worked on an unreleased Dungeons & Dragons 2600 game there, co-founded Imagic in 1981 with Rob Fulop and Dennis Koble. Riddle of the Sphinx was his second Imagic game after Star Voyager. He had written a kernel, the core code that feeds graphics to the 2600's TIA chip, that let enemies move down the screen while projectiles moved up, and built the game around it. It was released in the US in August 1982 alongside Fire Fighter, and in the UK before Christmas. Critics enjoyed its complexity and focus on puzzles over action: Electronic Games found the puzzles "challenging" though lacking replay value and gave it a certificate of merit for Best Adventure Videogame behind Pitfall!, The Space Gamer called it a "masterful" blend of strategy and arcade play, and JoyStik called it "one of the most elaborate quest/adventure games ever created". Vidiot, however, complained about its obtuse riddles.

title: Pinball Construction Set
description: Pinball Construction Set (1982) is Bill Budge's Apple II program for building and playing your own pinball tables with drag-and-drop parts, which created the construction set genre and which Steve Wozniak called the greatest program ever written for an 8-bit machine.
longDescription:
Users build their own virtual pinball machines by dropping bumpers, flippers, spinners and other parts onto a table, then play them. Attributes such as gravity and the physics model can be changed, and finished tables can be saved to floppy disk and freely traded, since Pinball Construction Set is not needed to play them. Its Lisa-like graphical interface, with representative icons and drag-and-drop table building, was for thousands of people their first experience of a GUI.

Computer Gaming World considered it revolutionary and said "there's something almost magical about the way this product works", noting that the nine-page manual was "overkill" since an eight-year-old had no trouble building tables. BYTE praised Budge's "marvelous sense of programming" and its encouragement of creativity, InfoWorld compared its importance to Scott Adams's Adventureland, and Compute! called it "a programming work of art". Orson Scott Card said his son used it as a graphics program.
trivia: Budge bought and took apart an old Gottlieb Target Alpha pinball machine to depict its parts accurately.
Budge does not enjoy video games and called months of playing pinball during development "sheer torture".
BudgeCo's box showed a photograph of the dismantled machine's parts.
EA's album-style box put Budge's name much larger than the game's.
In 2008 it was honoured at the Technology and Engineering Emmy Awards for user-generated content.
devStory: Budge, already a celebrity among Apple II owners for Raster Blaster, began it in July 1982 because he did not want to make another game ("all the current (arcade) games are either maze games or Pong") and was experimenting with his own tools. He was aware of the Apple Lisa and Xerox PARC's GUI research and modelled the interface on them. It was ambitious for the Apple's limited memory and graphics. BudgeCo published it in late 1982, but it sold poorly without a large distribution network, so Budge agreed when Trip Hawkins approached him in 1983, and Electronic Arts released it with Atari 8-bit and Commodore 64 versions, followed by IBM PC and Mac versions in 1985. It sold over 300,000 copies. Computer Gaming World ranked it the most innovative computer game in 1996, EA followed it with Music, Adventure and Racing Destruction sets, Will Wright cited it as an inspiration, and Budge released the Atari 8-bit source code on GitHub in 2013.

title: Swordquest: Earthworld
description: Swordquest: Earthworld (1982) is the first of Atari's Swordquest games for the Atari 2600, an action-adventure packaged with a DC comic hiding clues to a contest for $150,000 of jewelled treasure, cut short by the 1983 crash.
longDescription:
Each Swordquest game was themed on a classical element, and Earthworld's rooms follow the Western zodiac. The player moves through a maze of rooms, carrying objects from one and placing them in others, and passing between rooms sometimes requires a "twitch"-style minigame. Placing an item in the right room reveals numbers pointing to a page and panel of the packaged comic, where a hidden word can be found; submitting the right words in the right order to Atari entered players into the next phase of the contest. The game indicated more clues than were needed, and a second clue in the manual, pointing to prime-numbered pages, showed which to send in. With Fireworld, themed on the Kabbalah tree of life, and Waterworld, on the chakras, the series was among the first attempts to combine adventure-game logic with action, alongside Atari's Raiders of the Lost Ark.

The story follows the twins Tarra and Torr, whose parents were killed by King Tyrannus's guards after his wizard Konjuro prophesied that the twins would slay the king. Raised by thieves, they give themselves away while plundering Konjuro's sea keep and are told of the "Sword of Ultimate Sorcery" and the "Talisman of Penultimate Truth" before being transported to Earthworld, where they fight beasts of the zodiac and the thief Herminus.
trivia: It grew out of the interest generated by the Easter egg in Atari's Adventure.
The comics were written by Roy Thomas and Gerry Conway and drawn by George Pérez and Dick Giordano.
Earthworld's prize, the Talisman of Penultimate Truth, was an 18-karat gold disc set with 12 diamonds and the zodiac birthstones.
Winner Stephen Bell reportedly had the gold disc melted down, keeping the stones and small sword.
Flux magazine ranked Earthworld 71st among the top 100 video games in 1995.
devStory: Atari, then owned by Warner Communications, used two Warner subsidiaries for the project: DC Comics made the comics and the Franklin Mint crafted the prizes, each worth about $25,000, with a $50,000 "Sword of Ultimate Sorcery" for a final contest between the four winners. Tod Frye programmed the games, and in-house illustrator Warren Chang painted the box covers. For Earthworld, about 5,000 entries were received but only eight were correct, and Bell won the Talisman at Atari's Sunnyvale headquarters in May 1983. After the crash and a change of CEO, Atari cancelled the project; the Fireworld contest was held in January 1984, Waterworld was restricted to Atari Club members, and Airworld was never released, so Bell and Fireworld winner Michael Rideout each received $15,000 and an Atari 7800 instead of a final. The fate of the remaining prizes became an urban legend. The Space Gamer said the only reason to buy Earthworld was to try to win the prize, and Digital Eclipse completed the series with a new Airworld in Atari 50 in 2022.

title: Joust 2: Survival of the Fittest
description: Joust 2: Survival of the Fittest (1986) is Williams' sequel to Joust, with a vertical screen, distinct themed levels and a knight who can turn his ostrich into a pegasus, released after the golden age and now a rare cabinet.
longDescription:
As before, the player is a yellow knight on a flying ostrich, steered with a two-way joystick while a button flaps its wings; tapping faster climbs, steadily hovers and slowly sinks. Each wave is cleared by colliding with enemy knights on buzzards, and the rider whose lance is higher wins, while equal heights bounce both apart. A second player can cooperate or fight. Instead of the original's single evolving screen, each level has its own theme and gameplay, with backgrounds inspired by M. C. Escher, lead designer John Newcomer's favourite artist.

New elements include a transform button that turns the ostrich into a pegasus, stronger on the ground but a poor flyer, eggs that become mutant buzzards if they fall in the lava, a giant Shadow Lord riding scorpion-tailed buzzards, Crystal Bats that hatch from crystals in the ledges, and a Gold Egg that opens a rapidly changing box of random effects. Some events have synthesised speech, and buying in to continue keeps the current score.
trivia: Williams chose between sequels to Robotron: 2084 and Joust before picking Joust.
The staff added the Knight Lord to show a progression of villains.
Williams shipped only around 1,000 units, far fewer than Joust.
Newcomer later said its vertical monitor was a mistake that hurt the gameplay and home conversion.
Traveller's Tales included it unaltered in Lego Dimensions' 2016 Midway Arcade Level Pack.
devStory: With Williams' video game department shrunk by the industry's decline, the company wanted to sell a conversion kit for the then-popular vertical-monitor cabinets, and management felt a sequel would sell the kit better. Newcomer led development again on more advanced hardware than the original's, programmed like other Williams games in assembly language. Released after the golden age, it did not match Joust's critical or commercial success, which Allgame and Retro Gamer put down to the mid-1980s slump, and its cabinets have become fairly rare. It was never ported to home systems at the time, appearing only in compilations from Arcade's Greatest Hits: The Midway Collection 2 in 1997 to Midway Arcade Treasures and Midway Arcade Origins. IGN called its inclusion part of that collection's "real value" because of its rarity, and GamePro called it a substantial improvement on the original, while Allgame preferred Joust despite Joust 2's more detailed graphics and IGN's Craig Harris found it "slightly less imaginative".

title: Bubbles
description: Bubbles (1983) is Williams' offbeat arcade game in which a soap bubble cleans a kitchen sink, a non-violent take on Pac-Man by John Kotlarik and Python Anghelo, sold partly in a cylindrical plastic cabinet.
longDescription:
Seen from above, the player steers a soap bubble around a kitchen sink, absorbing ants, crumbs and grease spots before they slide down the drain. As it absorbs more, the bubble grows, gaining eyes and then a smiling mouth. Sponges and scrub brushes drift around cleaning the sink in competition, and touching one costs a life unless the bubble is at its largest, in which case the enemy is knocked away and the bubble shrinks; knocking sponges and brushes down the drain removes them for bonus points. Razor blades are always fatal, and roaches crawling from the drain can only be touched safely when carrying a broom, picked up from a cleaning lady who sometimes appears.

A level ends when all the point-scoring objects are gone; a bubble with a complete face moves on, otherwise a life is lost and the level replayed. Once the bubble has a face, the player can skip ahead by entering the drain when it flashes green, though going in too small costs a life. Kotlarik made the bubble accelerate in the joystick's direction and coast slowly to a stop when it is released, so the digital stick behaves almost like an analogue one, as though gliding on a slick surface.
trivia: Its plastic "Duramold" cabinet, rotationally moulded by Gary Berge, was used only for it, Blaster and Sinistar.
The plastic cabinets were durable but shrank over time, sometimes making the machine inoperable.
Cocktail and cabaret cabinets are the rarest versions.
Critics' most common complaint was its excess of blue.
Digital Eclipse could add it easily to compilations because its hardware is close to Defender's.
devStory: Kotlarik wanted a non-violent game with Pac-Man-like play in an open field rather than a maze, and Anghelo developed the concept with artwork, a scenario and the cabinet designs. It runs on Defender-like hardware with a 1 MHz Motorola 6809E and 48 KB of ROM. Williams showed it at the Amusement Operators Expo in Chicago in March 1983, where Electronic Fun called it a "goof-fest" with "superb" if monotonously blue graphics and Video Games called it a "nice change of pace", and Play Meter ranked it among the top fifteen arcade games by September. Computer and Video Games found its premise "pretty weird" and short-lived, and Video Games' John Holmstrom later saw it as evidence of Williams' decline. It had no sequel or home port until compilations from Williams Arcade's Greatest Hits in 1996 to Midway Arcade Origins, and a Shockwave web version appeared in 2000. Retrospective views have been mixed, Shacknews calling it "underrated" and Retro Gamer regretting how few remember it.

title: Jungle Hunt
description: Jungle Hunt (1982) is Taito's arcade platformer, first released as Jungle King until Edgar Rice Burroughs's estate objected to its Tarzan-like hero, in which an explorer swings on vines, swims with crocodiles and dodges boulders to save a woman from cannibals.
longDescription:
The game has four scenes scrolling from right to left. First, the explorer swings from vine to vine, pressing the button when two vines are close enough; missing one drops him to the jungle floor and costs a life. He then dives into a crocodile-infested river, stabbing crocodiles from below with his knife when their mouths are closed and surfacing for air, where he cannot attack, while rising bubbles can carry him upwards, sometimes into crocodiles. Next he runs up a hill, jumping or ducking boulders that bounce at varying speeds and heights. Finally, he must evade cannibals to reach a woman being lowered into a cauldron, and rescuing her brings "Congratulations!", "I Love You!!!" and a kiss. Later rounds repeat the scenes with monkeys on the vines and a spear-throwing cannibal in the tree.

Along with Moon Patrol, released a month earlier, Jungle King was one of the first video games with parallax scrolling. After the Burroughs estate's legal action, the hero became an explorer in a pith helmet and safari outfit, the vines were redrawn to pass as ropes, and the Tarzan yell at the start was replaced with music.
trivia: In Atari's home versions, the hero is Sir Dudley and the woman his wife, Lady Penelope.
Sierra On-Line developed the Apple II and IBM PC versions.
Taito's November 1982 rebrand, Pirate Pete, swapped vines for ship's ropes and crocodiles for sharks.
Taito's later re-releases include Pirate Pete rather than Jungle Hunt, for unknown reasons.
Milton Bradley published a board game version in 1983.
devStory: Taito developed and distributed it in arcades in 1982 as Jungle King, then quickly modified and re-released it as Jungle Hunt.
