Jungle King was the top-grossing upright cabinet on the RePlay charts by October 1982, Jungle Hunt topped them by January 1983, and by July 1983 it had sold an estimated 18,000 cabinets in the US. Bill Kunkel of Electronic Games predicted it could be Taito's "biggest hit since Space Invaders", following "the classic formula... easy to learn, difficult to master", though he called the vine graphics "downright hideous" and doubted its staying power. Atari published home versions for the 2600, 5200 and 8-bit computers in 1983, with Atarisoft releasing it for the Apple II, ColecoVision, Commodore 64, VIC-20, IBM PC and TI-99/4A. Video Games Player rated the 2600 version a B+, and Electronic Fun found the 5200 version a big improvement on the "disappointing" VCS one. It received a Certificate of Merit for Best Adventure Videogame at the 1984 Arkie Awards and is included in Taito Legends.

title: Elevator Action Returns
description: Elevator Action Returns (1994) is Taito's arcade sequel to Elevator Action, swapping the spy for a three-member counter-terrorist squad with four-way scrolling, two-player co-op and lavish, gory 2D animation.
longDescription:
With an eight-way joystick and shoot and jump buttons, players must enter every red door in each stage before heading for the exit; miss one and they cannot pass a certain point. A health gauge replaces one-hit deaths, and the original's vertical scrolling gives way to four-way scrolling, with new moves and weapons, three characters and two-player co-op. Smashing bins, garbage, sandbags and crates uncovers items, and blue doors spin a roulette for health, special guns, sub-weapons or points. The default handgun has unlimited ammunition, while missile launchers and automatic weapons revert to it when empty. Melee kills score double, and pressing both buttons throws each character's explosive. As before, lifts can crush enemies above or below, oil drums explode into fire trails, and electric barriers later hurt everyone, with bonus points for enemies killed by the scenery. Lives are lost to the health gauge, the timer, falling more than two storeys or being crushed by a lift.

In the late 1990s, the counter-terrorist unit DEF takes on a terrorist group led by Red Suit. Kart Bradfield is the fastest and most agile, with a Glock and floor-clearing grenades; Edie Burret fires fastest, with a Beretta and incendiary grenades but the least health; and Jad the Taff, the strongest and slowest, carries a Desert Eagle and proximity sensor bombs and tackles enemies in his way.
trivia: It is also known as Elevator Action II.
Ving ported it to the Saturn in a Japan-only 1997 release that also included the original Elevator Action.
Retro Gamer said its enemies looked like they had jumped from the frames of a 2000 AD comic strip.
Retro Gamer named it among ten essential Saturn imports.
An enhanced S-Tribute version with rewind and stage select was released in 2022.
devStory: Taito developed and published Elevator Action Returns for arcades, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's ninth most popular arcade game in its 1 May 1995 issue. Next Generation gave the arcade version three stars, saying it brought out "the impulsive, frenzied, shooting psychopath in you", and GameSpot's 1997 import review of the Saturn version gave it 5.2, calling it a "perfect rental" at best. Later opinion was much warmer: USgamer's Jeremy Parish called it "a game out of time" but "a lot of fun", Hardcore Gamer an "overlooked classic", and Retro Gamer's Darran Jones an "outstanding... fantastic sequel that totally blew away the original", praising its decaying, graffiti-covered buildings and "beautiful ballet of mayhem that would have made John Woo proud". IGN listed the arcade-perfect Saturn port among the best classic co-op games in 2005. It was included in Taito Legends 2 in 2006, though the PS2 and Xbox versions run at an upscaled resolution, and on the Taito Egret II Mini in 2022.

title: Psychic Force
description: Psychic Force (1996) is Taito's arcade fighting game in which floating psychics battle inside a force-field cube, slamming each other into its walls, popular in Japan but little noticed in the West.
longDescription:
Fights take place in a cube bounded by a magical force field, where the fighters float and move in every direction, although the game plays in 2D. The walls are central to its strategy: a character knocked into one takes damage, though not by moving into it voluntarily, and one hit again on the rebound is stunned and falls, invulnerable while falling. Matches go to the first to win two rounds, and if time runs out between human players, a sudden death round in a smaller space with empty gauges goes to whoever lands the first hit. An eight-way joystick and three buttons, guard, light attack and heavy attack, combine into combos, throws and special moves.

Special moves draw on the Psycho Gauge beneath the life bar; once it is empty, the fighter can only fire weak projectiles until it refills, slowly by itself or quickly by holding all three buttons. A Barrier Guard blocks physical and special attacks at a heavy cost to the gauge, an Evasion Barrier prevents a wall slam for 40% of it, and dashes move fighters quickly, the Quick Dash deflecting weak projectiles. In 2010, people with psychic powers, called "Psychiccers", are shunned until the organisation NOA, led by Keith Evans, offers them a utopia, opposed by his old friend Burn Griffiths of Anti-NOA.
trivia: It was first location-tested in October 1995.
Each Psychiccer uses an element such as fire, light, wind, electricity, gravity, time or ice.
Acclaim's localisation kept the Japanese voices and J-pop intro, adding only subtitles.
Triangle Staff animated a two-episode OVA in 1998.
A Puzzle Bobble-style spin-off, Psychic Force: Puzzle Taisen, came to the PlayStation in Japan in 1997.
devStory: Taito produced Psychic Force for arcades, releasing it in April 1996, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's third most successful arcade game in its 1 June 1996 issue. PlayStation versions followed in 1996 and 1997, published by Acclaim in North America and PAL regions, but it was released with little fanfare and was not a commercial success in the West, though it gained some popularity in Japan. Reviews of the PlayStation version were mediocre: Next Generation and EGM's four reviewers found the 3D movement a novelty that left fights dominated by cheap projectiles and characters sharing nearly the same move set, though EGM praised the anime sequences, and GamePro found it easy to master and boring in the long run. An arcade update, Psychic Force EX, made the boss playable and rebalanced the game, and a sequel, Psychic Force 2012, followed in 1998, reaching the Dreamcast and PlayStation. The original was re-released in Psychic Force Complete for the PlayStation 2 in 2006.

title: RayForce
description: RayForce (1994) is Taito's vertical shoot 'em up with a lock-on laser that hits up to eight enemies on a lower plane, made by a team told it was not allowed to make shooters, and later released as Layer Section and Galactic Attack.
longDescription:
The ship, the RVA-818 X-LAY, has two weapons. Its main gun fires straight lasers that grow stronger with power-ups, while a lock-on laser launcher, also upgradable, targets up to eight enemies at once with a reticle, hitting enemies on a lower plane than the ship that the main gun cannot reach. Unlike most shooters of the time, there are no screen-clearing bombs, a deliberate return to older designs.

In the distant future, a supercomputer called Con-Human, built to manage Earth's environment, becomes sentient and insane after a cloned human mind is linked to it. It exterminates 99.8% of humankind, makes corrupt clones of living things and turns the Earth itself into a planet-sized mobile fortress, its own body, to hunt down the survivors' space colonies. The X-LAY is one of the ships built to destroy it. At the end, the pilots destroy Con-Human and the fortress's core, and the badly damaged X-LAY drifts in space as the screen reads "Mission Complete" before the pilot's life ends.
trivia: Taito told the Kumagaya team it could not make shooters, so director Tatsuo Nakamura pitched design documents until management approved.
The lock-on laser grew from Xevious's bombing reticle; a programmer's objection to limiting it to four targets led to eight.
Graphic designer Hideyuki Katou chose a metallic Darius-like look despite management's displeasure.
Pre-rendered graphics were dropped because Namco's NebulasRay had already used them, to Katou's anger.
It was called Gunlock in European arcades, Layer Section on Japanese home systems and Galactic Attack on Acclaim's Saturn release.
devStory: Nakamura directed it with designer Tomohisa Yamashita and Katou, drawing on Taito's Master of Weapon for its top-down view and on Konami's Gradius for an "inorganic" world, and the team's experience on Darius II made balancing easy. The Taito F3 hardware's scaling limits pushed them towards simple geometric background shapes, as in Space Harrier, Metal Black inspired the dust clouds of the second stage, and Zuntata composed the music. Shown at the 1993 JAMMA show, it was released in Japan in February 1994, and Game Machine listed it as the third most popular arcade unit in its 1 April issue. The 1995 Saturn version drew mixed reviews: Sega Saturn Magazine and Maximum found it fun but outdated, while Next Generation praised its "quality development" and lack of slowdown and GamePro its "gorgeous" backgrounds. EGM ranked the Saturn version the 86th best console game in 1997. A planned sprite-based sequel, R-Gear, became the 3D RayStorm, and the prequel RayCrisis followed in 1998.

title: RayStorm
description: RayStorm (1996) is Taito's polygon follow-up to RayForce, a vertical shooter built around a multi-target lock-on laser, praised for its cutting-edge effects and the first game Working Designs released on the PlayStation.
longDescription:
Players choose one of two ships, with a third secret ship in home versions, and view them from a distance as they blast through vertically scrolling stages. The main weapon is a vulcan-like laser, and a missile weapon locks onto multiple targets, building a combo multiplier for points. Each ship has two special moves: a screen-wide Special Attack, unleashed once a bar fills through repeated lock-ons and followed by a moment of invincibility, and a Hyper Laser Assault unique to each ship, triggered by placing every available lock-on on a single target. Its plot, of the R-Gray's mission to destroy the Secilia Federation before it destroys Earth, is revealed mostly through the manual and Extra Mode and is unconnected to the Con-Human story of RayForce and RayCrisis.

Home versions add an "Extra Mode" with enhanced graphics, extra enemies, modified bosses, a tougher challenge, a different ending and scores kept on continuing. Clearing a mode unlocks a stage select, and clearing both unlocks "13 Players", in which the game must be completed with 13 ships from five groups, R-Gray 1 and 2 in manual and auto control and a single R-Gray 0 prototype, revealing an extra epilogue in Extra Mode.
trivia: It ran on Taito's FX-1 arcade board.
Its PlayStation demo at the August 1996 Tokyo Game Show was on a screen that dwarfed Taito's other demos.
Working Designs tried to license RayForce, but Acclaim had secured Taito's Western rights days earlier.
It was the first release on Working Designs' "SPAZ" shooter label, which ended with RayCrisis.
EGM's Dan Hsu compared it to "dating a gorgeous girl with zero brains".
devStory: Producer and director Yukio Abe, director Tatsuo Nakamura and Zuntata's Tamayo Kawamoto and Munehiro Nakanishi on music and sound returned from RayForce, and it is distinguished from its predecessor mainly by its polygon ships. Game Machine reported it among Japan's most popular arcade games of September 1996. The PlayStation version came out in Japan in January 1997, and Working Designs licensed it immediately on hearing it was available, making it their first PlayStation release; a playable demo was bundled with American PlayStations the month it came out. GameSpot called it "easily the best shooter currently available on the PlayStation", praising its lighting and explosions though finding it easier than RayForce, and Next Generation noted its debt to Xevious but said its design proved itself, with "powerful Macross-like mech bosses". Critics such as EGM and GamePro found the graphics cutting edge but the gameplay dated. EGM named it runner-up for Shooter of the Year behind Star Fox 64, and RayStorm HD followed in 2010.

title: G-Darius
description: G-Darius (1997) is Taito's fourth arcade Darius game and the first in 3D polygons, a branching horizontal shooter in which the Silver Hawk captures enemies and fights bosses in laser beam duels.
longDescription:
Though drawn in 3D polygons, it plays in two dimensions. The Silver Hawk is armed with forward missiles, small bombs and a force field, upgraded by large orbs dropped by specially coloured enemies. Each zone ends in a boss, after which the player picks the next zone along a branching path; there are 15 in all, lettered alpha to omicron, and five in a row lead to one of five endings, with two alternative routes halfway through each level as well. The "capture ball" seizes an enemy, which then follows and helps the ship as an extra turret or shield, can be detonated as a bomb, or can be absorbed for a special ability.

Absorbing a captured enemy fires a powerful laser beam for a short time, new to the series, and every major boss has its own. If both fire at once, a beam duel begins, and the player must hammer the fire button to overpower the boss's beam, which then dissipates as the player's grows in size and power and can devastate the boss; countering several boss beams multiplies it up to four times. A prequel, its story pits the people of Amnelia against the Thiima, biomechanical guardians awakened when Amnelia used the weapon A.N. to annihilate the world Blazer.
trivia: Some enemies and large bullets are immune to the beam, letting bosses shield themselves.
G-Darius Ver. 2 added a beginner mode that ends after three zones.
The PlayStation port, titled G Darius, is based on Ver. 2 and was published in the US by THQ.
Eurogamer called it "one of the greatest shooting games ever released" in 2014.
The 2021 Switch and PS4 version added an HD mode and later Ver. 2 and the Japanese PlayStation version.
devStory: Taito released G-Darius in arcades in 1997, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourth most successful arcade game in its 15 August 1997 issue, though it had fallen to tenth by 1 November. The PlayStation version followed on 9 April 1998 in Japan and that September in Europe and the US. It received favourable reviews according to GameRankings, Famitsu gave it 29 out of 40, and Next Generation said it was "fun for those fogies who can stomach it, but the average gamer will be bored to death". The arcade original was later included in Taito Legends 2 for the PlayStation 2, and a Windows version based on the PlayStation port was published in 2000 and 2001. A 2021 release for Switch and PlayStation 4 included a new HD version and was sold physically in Japan in the Darius Cozmic Revelation compilation, and G-Darius HD reached Steam in March 2022.

title: Hellfire
description: Hellfire (1989) is Toaplan's first horizontal shoot 'em up, developed alongside Truxton, in which a pilot switches between four fixed-direction weapons to attack a robot dictator's Black Nebula, and whose engine was reused for Zero Wing.
longDescription:
In 2998, as humanity spreads peacefully through space, a mysterious matter called the Black Nebula engulfs star after star, the work of Super Mech, a robot dictator from the far reaches of space. Space Federation member Captain Lancer launches a surprise attack in the only available fighter, the CNCS1, armed with Hellfire, the strongest weapon in the galaxy. Over six increasingly difficult levels, each with a boss, the background scrolls constantly until the boss is reached.

Its distinctive feature is the weapon system: four main weapons, upgraded with "P" icons, each firing in a fixed direction however the ship moves, switched with a change button. Speed-ups and "B" icons worth points, vital for extra lives, can also be collected. Depending on the arcade settings, a downed player restarts from a checkpoint or respawns on the spot, and losing a life resets the ship's firepower and speed. As in earlier Toaplan games, completing the last stage loops back to the first with denser bullet patterns. The Genesis version turned Hellfire itself into a screen-clearing bomb and added a shield and an option, while the PC Engine Hellfire S replaced Lancer with a heroine, Kaoru, whose ending sees her sacrifice herself to save Earth.
trivia: It was one of the first Toaplan releases to feature the company's name prominently.
Designer Tatsuya Uemura, a former composer, asked for a puzzle element to be included.
The team found terrain and collision detection frustrating, as their vertical shooter experience did not carry over.
Mega ranked the Genesis version fourth among the top Mega Drive games of all time.
Its rights belong to Tatsujin, a company named after Truxton's Japanese title.
devStory: Uemura, whose earlier Toaplan work included Tiger-Heli, Flying Shark and Twin Cobra, led it as an experiment in bringing Toaplan's style to a Gradius-like horizontal format, developed in parallel with Truxton. Its development was troubled by inexperience, and both single-player and co-op versions were planned from the start because of pressure to make two-player games; Kōetsu Iwabuchi drew the artwork. Taito released it in Japan and U.S.A. Games in North America in October 1989. Critics received it positively, though some compared it to R-Type. NCS Corporation ported it to the Genesis in 1990, with much the same staff, released by Masaya in Japan, Seismic in North America and Sega in Europe, and MegaTech called it "a slick and very good looking blaster which oozes playability". NEC Avenue's Hellfire S for the PC Engine Super CD-ROM² followed in April 1991 with an orchestral soundtrack and animated cut-scenes. Toaplan's second and last horizontal shooter, Zero Wing, used the same engine.

title: Fire Shark
description: Fire Shark (1989) is Toaplan's arcade sequel to Flying Shark, a 1942-style biplane shooter with a flamethrower weapon, popular in Western arcades but too hard for Japanese players.
longDescription:
Reminiscent of 1942, it sends the titular biplane through ten increasingly difficult levels against the tanks, battleships, kamikaze monoplanes and artillery of the mysterious Strange Fleet, over constantly scrolling scenery that stops only at an airport. The standard shot reaches half the screen's height, and bombs destroy everything in their blast. Destroying zeppelins releases coloured icons for a wide shot, a laser beam or a flamethrower, and other items include speed-ups, extra bombs, "P" icons, three of which raise firepower one level up to a maximum of three, and rare 1UPs. Lightning-shaped medals from destroyed containers add points, important since extra lives come at set scores. Depending on the arcade settings, players restart at a checkpoint or respawn where they fell, losing their firepower and speed, and finishing the tenth stage loops back to the first at a higher difficulty.

In the arcade story, the Strange Fleet arrives one summer night in 1991 at a small Mediterranean island and grows over two years until it attacks the whole world, to cries of "Fire Shark! Fire Shark! It's time to take-off!!" The Genesis version instead sets it in 19X9 against an industrial superpower called S Corps.
trivia: Its Japanese title uses "same", Japanese for shark, chosen for its strong animal sound.
Composer Masahiro Yuge said the flamethrower succeeded Truxton's blue laser.
Artist Shintarō Nakaoka drew the crowd at the take-off, which the team animated in their spare time.
Yuge regretted not balancing its difficulty for operators and players.
An X68000 version to be published by Kaneko was advertised but never released.
devStory: Yuge composed the music, Nakaoka drew the art and Sanae Nitō and Yuko Tataka designed it, though none were credited, and the team wanted it to carry "the same strengths" as Flying Shark. Toaplan released it in Japan on 2 November 1989 and in Europe later that year, with Romstar following in North America in March 1990, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most successful table arcade unit in its 1 January 1990 issue. According to Yuge, it did well in Western arcades but less so in Japan because of its difficulty. Toaplan's own Genesis port, faithful to the arcade with a harder setting, was released by DreamWorks, a division of Toy Soldiers, in North America in October 1990, by Toaplan in Japan and by Sega in Europe in 1992, and EGM gave it 33 out of 40. M2 included the arcade version in Hishou Same! Same! Same! in 2022, and artist Perry Sessions cited it as a main influence on Super XYX.

title: Out Zone
description: Out Zone (1990) is Toaplan's vertically scrolling arcade run and gun in which two cyborg mercenaries, hired with the UN's entire annual budget, fight off an alien invasion, an intense, well-regarded game that stayed out of homes for three decades.
longDescription:
Reminiscent of Commando and Ikari Warriors, it sends two cyborg mercenaries upward on foot through seven increasingly difficult levels, each ending in a boss. They start with bombs that destroy everything in their blast, though using one gives no invincibility. The distinctive weapon system offers two main guns, upgraded by "P" icons and swapped by collecting "C" icons: a forward gun that fires a three-shot spread straight ahead however the player moves, and an all-direction laser that fires the way the player is moving, sweeping bullets as they turn and firing rapidly when the button is tapped. Different enemy layouts call for constant switching, and "SP" icons give special weapons such as a flamethrower and a wall-piercing energy ball, along with 1UPs, speed-ups, shields and an energy extender.

As in Wonder Boy, an energy bar drains steadily and must be refilled with "E" icons, though it is not health; a single shot still kills. Lives are also lost to collisions, falls and running out of energy, sending players back to a checkpoint with their firepower and speed reset, and finishing the last stage loops back to the first at a higher difficulty. Hidden bonuses help reach the scores needed for extra lives, and characters from Flying Shark, Truxton and Zero Wing make cameos.
trivia: Its story sets the alien invasion from the planet Owagira in 2095.
Composer Tatsuya Uemura based the first stage's melody on the TV series Taiyō ni Hoero!.
Uemura called it "the most difficult product he worked on".
It first appeared outside arcades on the iiRcade console in December 2020.
It is in the book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
devStory: Uemura composed the music and created the sound effects, with Naoki Ogiwara as designer. Uemura found it hard because his experience with ship-based vertical shooters did not apply to an on-foot game without forced scrolling, where players could move or stop freely, and the team added puzzle elements that took time to plan, while the sound schedule kept being cut. Tecmo, Romstar and Toaplan released it worldwide in August 1990. Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most popular arcade game in its 15 August 1990 issue, and it charted in Australia, North America and the UK. Sinclair User called it "one hell of a challenge" that would "set the pulse racing", Your Sinclair compared it to Mercs, and Computer and Video Games gave it 80%. Unusually for Toaplan, it received no official home port at the time, which Retro Gamer and SHMUPS! lamented, until M2 announced a version and it appeared on the Astro City Mini V in 2022. A spiritual successor, FixEight, followed in 1992.

title: Dogyuun
description: Dogyuun (1992) is Toaplan's vertical shooter in which two pilots can merge their ships into one more powerful craft, a showcase of graphics that marked the game debut of artist Junya Inoue.
longDescription:
On the colonised planet Dino, contact with a police communication centre has been lost. Three pilots sent to investigate find it overrun by an alien race of metallic robots holding its staff hostage, and one of them, Kyle, is killed, so the other two counterattack in their Sylfers bomber fighters across ten stages. Ships start with a single laser that can be held on at close range for minor damage when not firing, and destroyed carriers release coloured weapon modules, from homing lasers to a lightning beam, with a 5,000-point bonus for collecting one of the same colour.

The "Unit Beam" system lets the two ships combine into one with far greater firepower, at the risk of losing both to a single shot or collision, and they can split at any time. When separate, each can capture a small enemy for continuous points or hold items. Two modules attach to the ships: a single-use bomb, which also triggers when hit, and a speed module that adds two satellite options to the default weapon. A spinning 1UP icon gives an extra life on one side and 100,000 points on the other, hidden bonuses help reach high scores, checkpoints save progress, and each loop of the game is harder than the last.
trivia: It began as a mecha game, whose leftover work was reused when tests of the robot concept failed.
Uemura suggested and approved the name.
Reaching the fifth loop triggers a kill screen that crashes the hardware, because nobody on the team could clear all the loops.
Inoue joined Toaplan in 1991 after seeing a recruitment ad in Gamest.
It first appeared outside arcades on the Astro City Mini V in 2022.
devStory: Producer Toshiaki Ōta, later founder of Tamsoft and producer of Battle Arena Toshinden, led a small team that had worked on Snow Bros., programming alongside Hiroaki Furukawa, with Tatsuya Uemura composing. Responding to players who felt Toaplan's earlier games did not impress visually, they put graphics before gameplay, and Uemura later said the gameplay suffered and development ran longer than usual. Inoue, who went on to design Knuckle Bash, drew the graphics. Shown at the 1992 AOU Show to positive reviews from seven Gamest writers, it was released in November 1992, and Game Machine listed it as the eleventh most successful table arcade unit in its 15 December issue. EGM praised its intensity and visuals, and GamesMaster noted its "fast and furious" action. Later critics such as Hardcore Gaming 101 and SHMUPS! praised its art, music and bosses and called it one of Toaplan's best lesser-known games, though some found its weapon system and mechanics underdeveloped. It was included in Toaplan Arcade Collection Vol. 1 in 2025.

title: Guwange
description: Guwange (1999) is Cave's arcade shooter set in Muromachi-era Japan, in which three people possessed by shikigami spirits fight their way to a malevolent god, steering their spirit to slow bullets and turn them into coins.
longDescription:
Unusually for the genre, the screen often scrolls horizontally or diagonally, following the path to the demon leader. Each character has a limited bomb, an energy blast that can be sent in any direction and dispels bullets. The other special attack sends the shikigami into the enemies: it can attack in a different direction from the player's shots and slip past obstacles, and enemy bullets that touch it turn pink and slow drastically, resuming full speed once past it, while bullets caught in an explosion are cancelled into coins. Scoring depends almost entirely on collecting coins without interruption. Damaging or destroying enemies keeps a countdown meter topped up, and if it empties, the coin count returns to zero; since a single chain can run through the whole game rather than stage by stage, the scoring is extremely unforgiving.

In the Muromachi period, more and more people are possessed by shikigami, which grant great powers but kill their hosts one year later. Legend says that a host who gathers the talismans of the five elements from five demons serving Guwange, the god trapped in Mt. Gokumon, and then slays him will be freed. The heroes are Shishin, a masked man kept alive beyond a year because his shikigami feeds on the humans he kills; Kamono Gensuke, a 15-year-old trainee pharmacist possessed by a vengeful tengu; and Hiiragi Kosame, a 17-year-old shrine maiden whose fox spirit is willing to die to save her.
trivia: Its stage 1 boss appears to be a dancer but is a man who accepted demonic power for revenge.
The stage 3 boss, Nekogumo, is part cat and part spider.
Shishin's lost daughter Mikoto is held captive in Gokumon for her spiritual power.
A harder "Blue Label" version was first a prize for Cave's top three players at an event.
Its arranged album features composers including Michiru Yamane and Michiko Naruke.
devStory: Cave developed Guwange and Atlus published it in arcades in 1999, and Game Machine listed it as the seventeenth most successful arcade game in its 1 September 1999 issue. Each character has their own introduction and ending. At its December 2007 Cave fest, the company unveiled the Blue Label special edition, with greater difficulty in later chapters, which later appeared in cabinet form. Cave released the soundtrack on a Guwange/ESP Ra.De. album, and in 2010 an arranged album featuring Masafumi Takada, Akari Kaida and Yoshitaka Hirota among others. Mobile versions were released in two parts for i-mode and Yahoo! Mobile phones and later combined into Guwange DX with enhanced graphics. 5pb. developed an Xbox 360 version released worldwide on Xbox Live Arcade in November 2010, adding the Blue mode and an Arrange 360 mode in which the player fires automatically and the right trigger controls the shikigami independently.

title: ESP Ra.De.
description: ESP Ra.De. (1998) is Cave's bullet hell shooter in which three psychics fight a syndicate trying to seize Tokyo in 2018, with a shield that turns bullets into gold, and the first game Junya Inoue art-directed at Cave.
longDescription:
In 2018, the ESPer Lady Garra and her Yaksa syndicate attack to remove all opposition and take over Tokyo, and players take one of three ESPers, Yūsuke Sagami, Jb-5th or Irori Mimasaka, through five increasingly difficult stages. Similar to DoDonPachi, it is a vertically scrolling bullet hell game, but unlike most Cave shooters the characters have only a shot, with the fire button held to slow movement. Its unique mechanic is the power gauge: holding the shield button raises a force field that makes the character invincible and turns enemy bullets into power-ups and gold blocks, draining the gauge, and releasing it unleashes a psychic blast that destroys enemies and bullets on screen.

Each character also has a piercing attack for extra damage, limited by its own gauge and central to scoring, since hitting enemies with regular and piercing shots raises a multiplier, hidden during normal play, that governs power-up drops. Once fully powered, defeated enemies drop gold blocks; collecting 200 starts a timer during which the multiplier produces energy tanks to refill the power gauge. Lives are hearts, and losing one resets firepower and gold, while continuing resets the score and locks the character choice.
trivia: It was made alongside Dangun Feveron by a crew of just nine.
Production began immediately after DoDonPachi.
Inoue wanted a visually attractive shooter with a realistic setting and human characters.
Nintendo Life compared its look to Akira and Ghost in the Shell.
M2's 2019 ESP Ra.De. Psi added a new character, Alice Master.
devStory: Inoue directed the art, with designers Akira Wakabayashi, Atsushi Aburano, Riichiro Nitta and Yūko Nakamura, programmers Ryuichi Yabuki, Satoshi Kōyama and Tsuneki Ikeda, and composer Masahiro Kusunoki. Atlus and Nihon System released it in arcades in April 1998, and Game Machine listed it as the fifth most popular arcade game in its 15 June 1998 issue. It proved popular with Japanese arcade players, and critics praised its power gauge, stylish presentation, Inoue's art and audio, though they found the scoring complex and confusing; Hardcore Gaming 101 called it "one of Cave's underrated classics" while finding Irori's voice annoying. Mobile versions followed in 2004 and 2005, but rights and publishing issues with Atlus kept it off home consoles until M2's ESP Ra.De. Psi for Switch and PlayStation 4 in December 2019, which Famitsu and Nintendo Life praised for its extra modes and fixes to the scoring. It spawned the spin-offs Espgaluda and Espgaluda II.

title: Sorcer Striker
description: Sorcer Striker (1993), Mahō Daisakusen in Japan, is Raizing's debut, a steampunk fantasy arcade shooter in which four bounty hunters hunt the goblin king, made in an apartment bedroom by former Aleste developers.
longDescription:
The goblins have built an empire of their own, and King Codwenna of the Violent Kingdom, after a disastrous attack by his knights, learns that they are ruled by a human and are mass-producing mana-powered magical weapons that nobody else can reproduce. Foreseeing his kingdom's doom, he puts a bounty on the head of King Gobligan. Players choose one of four bounty hunters, Gain, Chitta, Miyamoto or Bonum, through six increasingly difficult stages.

Borrowing from earlier Compile shooters such as Seirei Senshi Spriggan, each ship has a main gun powered up with coins from "P" bags and a sub-weapon swapped or upgraded with one of three magic books from destroyed carriers, giving homing, spread or straight shots that differ by character, plus screen-clearing bombs. As in MUSHA, some stages have mini-bosses. Losing a life respawns the player on the spot with their firepower reset, and finishing the first loop returns to the first stage, with the true ending reserved for completing the second.
trivia: Its working title was Haougekiden Saifuaa, a Chinese martial arts theme abandoned on Toaplan's advice that shooters need worldwide appeal.
Its power-up system was modelled on MUSHA because artist Kenichi Yokoo was a fan.
Ships were given hand-like extremities to give them personality.
Chitta is named after the Cinechitta cinema in Kawasaki near Raizing's offices, and Bonum after Bornnam in JoJo's Bizarre Adventure.
Its Japanese title was chosen from more than a hundred suggestions after Irem's In the Hunt made the first choice unusable.
devStory: Raizing, now Eighting, was founded by former Naxat Soft and Compile staff from the Aleste series, and Sorcer Striker was its first project, made by about four people: designer Kazuyuki Nakashima, Spriggan programmer Yuichi Toyama, artist Yokoo and 27-year-old freelance composer Atsuhiro Motoyama. Through the company president's former ties to Toaplan, Toaplan advised the team, supplied development tools and licensed its arcade board. Work began in March 1992 in an apartment bedroom, and the game was reworked into an accessible fantasy shooter to attract console RPG players, with mecha touches and a steampunk look to make shots and explosions flashier. Able released it in Japan and Europe in May 1993, and Game Machine listed it as the seventh most popular arcade game in its 1 August 1993 issue. X68000 and FM Towns ports followed, and M2 released it on PlayStation 4 in 2017. Hardcore Gaming 101 called it "an excellent game" often forgotten next to Raizing's later work. Kingdom Grand Prix and Dimahoo followed, and its heroes reappeared in Battle Garegga and Armed Police Batrider.

title: Gunbird
description: Gunbird (1994) is Psikyo's comic vertical shooter in which a cast of manga misfits race to collect the pieces of a magic mirror and make a wish, localised for the PlayStation as Mobile Light Force.
longDescription:
Players choose from manga-style characters who fly as their own craft, and a story told between levels and before boss fights follows their race to collect the pieces of a magic mirror. Ash is a 28-year-old German inventor with a jet pack; Marion a 13-year-old English witch on a broomstick, fun-loving and selfish, who mistreats her talking rabbit Pom-Pom; Valnus a Russian robot built six months earlier, with some of the game's best firepower, who secretly wishes to be human; Yuan Nang a courageous woman modelled on Sun Wukong from Journey to the West; and Tetsu a strong 60-year-old who flies a man-powered helicopter. Their rivals are the sky pirates of the Trump, Ace, Claud and their leader Rouge. Cut-scenes in co-op play are packed with comic dialogue, a recurring feature of Psikyo games.

Colliding with an enemy costs a level of shot power, which flies around the screen as a power-up until it reaches the edge, or a bomb if the shot is already at its lowest. Each of the two loops has seven stages, the first three picked at random from four; the second loop has denser, faster bullets and swaps in a stage unseen in the first. A solo player who clears the first loop chooses between two wishes with their own endings, and pairs get endings specific to their combination.
trivia: Mobile Light Force removed the whole story and ending and renamed the characters after XS Games employees.
Its US cover showed a Charlie's Angels-style picture unrelated to the game.
The fan art gallery was cut from Mobile Light Force, though its files remain on the disc.
It took fourth place for Best Shooting at the eighth Gamest Awards.
Gunbird 2 followed in 1998.
devStory: Psikyo developed Gunbird for arcades in 1994, with Jaleco publishing it in the US. Game Machine listed it as the ninth most popular arcade game in its 15 November 1994 issue, and Micom BASIC Magazine ranked it eighth in January 1995. PlayStation and Saturn versions came out in Japan on 15 December 1995, receiving mixed and average reception; Saturn Fan readers gave the Saturn version 22.2 out of 30. XS Games released the PlayStation version in North America as Mobile Light Force. Gunbird Special Edition, based on the arcade version and including Gunbird 2, came to the PlayStation 2 in 2004 and 2005, and it was included in Psikyo Collection Vol. 1 for Switch in 2018 with Strikers 1945, Samurai Aces and Sol Divide, which received mixed reviews. Hardcore Gaming 101 found it very enjoyable but less polished than later Psikyo games, and the mook Play This Retro Game! said its flashy power-ups made shooting fun.

title: Gokujō Parodius
description: Gokujō Parodius (1994), Fantastic Journey in Europe, is Konami's third Parodius game, a Gradius parody with eight absurd characters from a penguin to a stickman on a paper plane, made to bring shooters back to arcades full of fighting games.
longDescription:
Players choose from eight characters, each with weapons adapted from the standard Gradius arsenal: the Vic Viper, TwinBee, the penguin Pentarou, the hat-wearing octopus Takosuke, Hikaru, a bunny girl riding a rocket, Mambo the sunfish, Michael the stern angel pig and Koitsu, a stickman on a paper aeroplane. As in Gradius, power capsules highlight options on the power meter, and TwinBee's bells add more abilities, chosen by shooting them to change their colour. Seven stages grow harder through a UFO catcher machine, cookie castles and Las Vegas-style casinos, with bosses parodying Gradius, R-Type, Xevious, Galaga and Thunder Force, including a Big Core tribute whose core is a giant traffic light firing road signs. The soundtrack remixes classical music and Konami tunes.

The heroes fly through absurd places to grab a treasure and regain their past glory, only to find in a dance hall that the treasure is a talking bomb, "Mr. Past Glory", who apologises for not being treasure and blows the place up. It is harder than earlier Parodius games, with a "YOU LOSE" game over screen added just before the deadline to frustrate players, as in fighting games, and a "Semi-Auto" mode for newcomers.
trivia: Mambo is based on the MSX2 game Space Manbow.
Koitsu's shield was originally made of fire before being changed to a giant condom.
The pillow-like fifth stage boss attacks by firing power capsules, to help weak players.
The sixth stage's bunny-eared geisha pays homage to an enemy in Namco's Genpei Tōma Den.
Konami cited a lack of interest from US retailers for not releasing the Deluxe Pack in America.
devStory: Programmer and planner Tsukasa Tokuda, returning to Konami's arcade division after Parodius Da!, was asked to make an "anniversary" Parodius, and wanted a shooter to stand out in arcades crowded with fighting games; its subtitle, "Pursuing the Past Glory", expressed his wish for the industry to go back to its roots. Designer Shūjirō Hamakawa, a former anime character designer who had worked on Detana!! TwinBee, designed most bosses, and Kazuhiro Senoo, on his first game, gave the music the feel of an American variety show, choosing classical pieces with JASRAC. Tokuda planned six characters, but his boss pushed for eight, like fighting games' large rosters. It was a commercial success, Japan's fourth most successful arcade game of June 1994 according to Game Machine. A Super Famicom version in November 1994 added characters from Ganbare Goemon, Kid Dracula and Bio Miracle Bokutte Upa, and the Gokujō Parodius Da! Deluxe Pack came to PlayStation and Saturn. Maniac and Hardcore Gaming 101 praised its humour, variety and music.

title: Chack'n Pop
description: Chack'n Pop (1984) is Taito's single-screen arcade platformer starring a yellow creature with stretching legs who throws grenades to free hearts, the spiritual forerunner of Bubble Bobble with its Monstas and Mightas.
longDescription:
Chack'n, a yellow creature with extendable legs, makes his way through single-screen mazes, walking on floors or ceilings but not walls. He climbs steps and high walls by stretching his legs until he is tall enough to pass. He throws hand grenades to his left or right, with separate buttons for each direction, which explode after a moment into a cloud of smoke that kills Chack'n if he is caught in it. Solid walls block his way until he frees the hearts locked in cages with his grenades. Monstas hatch from eggs to obstruct him, with a bonus at the end of the level for destroying all of them or none, and each screen's time limit is marked by a Mighta pushing a boulder along the top of the screen.

It is considered a spiritual predecessor of Bubble Bobble because of its similar structure and shared characters, as the Monstas and Mightas became common enemies in that game. Chack'n and other characters have also made cameos in Taito's Ben Bero Beh, Bubble Memories and NY Captor.
trivia: It began at the University of Tokyo's Microcomputer Club as a Hitachi Basic Master Level 3 game by student Hiroshi Sakai, later of Game Arts.
Its working title was Chack'n Chack.
Hiroyuki Sakô redesigned the hero because he thought the original was not cute.
The team built a daughterboard to preview colours instead of burning an EEPROM for every check.
Its copyright notice says 1983, though it was released around April 1984.
devStory: Taito bought the rights to Sakai's game and developed the arcade version, with Sakô on character and level design and Jun Ishioka on programming, releasing it in Japan around April 1984. Sakô felt it flopped in Japanese arcades because of its difficulty, but the home ports, especially the Famicom and MSX versions, sold much better and made it one of Taito's "top IPs". Taito also ported it to the Sharp X1, PC-6001 and PC-8801, and Sega made an SG-1000 version. The arcade game is included in Taito Legends 2, Taito Memories and Taito Milestones, the Famicom version came to the Wii and 3DS Virtual Console, and Hamster added it to Arcade Archives. Retrospective views have been mostly negative: Retro Gamer said it "wasn't a great platformer" because of its complexity, PC Zone said it "isn't much fun", and HonestGamers called it "best forgotten", though Kotaku Australia recommended it to Bubble Bobble fans as a very different game.

title: Kangaroo
description: Kangaroo (1982) is Sun Electronics' arcade platformer, distributed in North America by Atari, in which a boxing-gloved mother kangaroo climbs to rescue her joey from fruit-throwing monkeys, one of the first Donkey Kong-like games that was not a clone.
longDescription:
Jumping is central, but there is no jump button: the player pushes the joystick up, or up and diagonally, to leap. On three of the four levels, the mother kangaroo starts on the bottom floor and must reach her joey, held by monkeys on the top floor, climbing between platforms or up ladders. Monkeys throw apples and apple cores, which she must jump, duck or punch, and she can punch any monkey she meets face to face with her boxing glove. Fruit hanging overhead can be jumped for points, and touching a bell replaces collected fruit with higher-value pieces. The big Ape occasionally appears to try to steal her gloves, and each level must be finished before time runs out.

On the third level, the joey hangs in a cage held up by a stack of monkeys, with a hoard of apples that will be released if five monkeys climb up to it. The kangaroo must punch each monkey in the stack several times to lower the cage, then climb up to the joey before it rises again. The music borrows classical and folk tunes: the "Turkish March" at the start, "American Patrol" during play, "Oh! Susanna" for completing a level and the "Westminster Quarters" when a bell is rung.
trivia: The arcade version has visible graphical glitches, such as briefly flickering sprites.
Jim Leiterman of Atari Research ported the 5200 version to the Atari 8-bit computers in a single day.
He submitted it to the Atari Program Exchange and asked for it to be published without credit, unusual for a service meant for user-written software.
In 1984 it replaced Pitfall Harry, Frogger and Donkey Kong Jr. as a cartoon in CBS's Saturday Supercade.
The cartoon, about kangaroos Katy and Joey in a zoo, has never been released on DVD or VHS.
devStory: Sun Electronics developed Kangaroo and released it in Japan in May 1982, and Atari, Inc. released it in North America that June. Arcade Express gave it 8 out of 10 in November 1982. Atari published ports for the Atari 2600 and Atari 5200 in 1983. Video magazine's "Arcade Alley" called the 5200 version "an excellent piece of work" but said it "fail[ed] to bowl [them] over", criticising "animation-quality graphics" used to dress up simple play; it nonetheless won "1984 Best Arcade-to-Home Video Game/Computer Game Translation" at the 5th Arkie Awards, where judges said it looked and played as a "virtual duplicate" of the arcade game. Reviewing the 2600 version for Electronic Fun, Charles Ardai wrote that despite its "horrible" graphics and sound, its gameplay was better than the arcade's. Hamster Corporation released the arcade game in its Arcade Archives series for Switch and PlayStation 4 in July 2020.

title: Omega Race
description: Omega Race (1981) is Midway's only vector-graphics arcade game, in which an Omegan Fighter circles a rectangular track blasting droid ships, a top earner that sold over 35,000 machines.
longDescription:
In the year 2003, the player pilots an Omegan Fighter around a rectangular "track", destroying enemy droid ships. The ship is rotated with a spinner, with one button for thrust and another for firing lasers. Enemies to destroy or avoid include drone ships, commander ships, two kinds of space mine and shooting star ships. The ship bounces off an invisible barrier at the edges of the screen, which briefly appears when hit, and by default extra ships come at 40,000 and 100,000 points.

Consumer Guide's How to Win at Video Games remarked in 1982 that "any unskilled player can pop a quarter into the machine and stay up there for up to 20,000 points", while Michael Blanchet's How to Beat the Video Games praised its "deceiving appearance", saying that despite looking easy it "develops a healthy level of frustration, which you'll find quite stimulating".
trivia: Consumer Guide reported the average machine took in $181 a week.
It was frequently among the top ten money-making arcade machines in a given week.
With Victory, it is one of only two ColecoVision games to support the Roller Controller trackball natively.
The Atari 2600 cartridge came with a "booster grip" adding separate thrust and fire buttons to the joystick.
It was cloned for the TRS-80 Color Computer as Space Race in 1982.
devStory: Midway Manufacturing developed and published Omega Race for arcades in 1981, and more than 35,000 machines were made. Commodore published ports for the Commodore 64 and VIC-20 in 1982, followed by ColecoVision and Atari 2600 versions from CBS Electronics in 1983. The 2600 version is one of a few CBS cartridges with an extra 256 bytes of RAM, promoted as "RAM Plus". The VIC-20 version was well reviewed: Compute! called it "a real winner for the VIC", BYTE said it "retains all the best characteristics of the arcade version" with fast pace, colourful graphics and good sound, and Ahoy! called it "fairly faithful to the arcade game, and very exciting"; it won a Certificate of Merit for Best Solitaire Computer Game at the 4th Arkie Awards. Temporary Sanity Designs later pitched an update for the Atari Jaguar to Atari Corporation, but it never went beyond the proposal stage.

title: Super Contra
description: Super Contra (1988) is Konami's arcade sequel to Contra, adding overhead stages and upgradable weapons as Bill and Lance fight an alien-possessed military base, ported to the NES as Super C and Probotector II.
longDescription:
A year after defeating the Red Falcon Organization, Bill Rizer and Lance Bean are sent back into action when alien forces take over an allied military base and possess most of its troops, forcing them to fight their former comrades as well as new, mutated forms of the aliens. Up to two players play at once, Bill in green and Lance in purple. The pseudo-3D and fixed-screen segments of the first game are gone, replaced by vertically scrolling overhead stages with eight-way movement, while side-scrolling stages now let players control jump height by holding the joystick up or down.

Flying capsules release a machine gun, spread gun, bomb gun or laser gun, now shown as the actual guns rather than Falcon letters, and picking up the same weapon twice upgrades it. In overhead stages, "hyper shell" items destroy everything on screen, can be stockpiled and carry over between those stages. Five stages cover a military base inside and out, a jungle and the alien lair, with stages 1, 3 and 4 side-on and 2 and 5 overhead. Depending on settings, up to four or six credits are allowed, and each player can now continue at any time. The English version ends after the final stage, while the Japanese version loops at maximum difficulty without continues.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Super Contra: The Alien Strikes Back.
The NES version was renamed Super C in North America to avoid association with the Iran–Contra affair.
The NES version replaced the Konami Code with a different code giving ten lives, thirty on Famicom.
Yuichi Sakakura altered the sound driver for Probotector II so its orchestra-hit samples would not play out of tune.
A 1996 bootleg hack, Super Contra 7, stole levels from other games and was reviewed by James Rolfe.
devStory: Konami location-tested Super Contra in December 1987 and released it widely in January 1988; unlike the first game's Gryzor, it kept its title in Europe. Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourth most successful table arcade unit in its 1 March 1988 issue, and in 1997 EGM named it the ninth best arcade game of all time. The NES port came out in Japan on 2 February 1990 and in North America that April, with three new vertically scrolling stages, new bosses and a chargeable fireball gun, and Hidenori Maezawa rearranged the soundtrack; it sold more than 500,000 copies, and Allgame called it "an excellent game that a lot of hardcore gamers will never forget", while Famitsu gave the Famicom version 25 out of 40. The PAL Probotector II, released in 1992, replaced the heroes with robots. Distinctive Software made Amiga and PC versions based on the arcade game, and the arcade original was re-released on Xbox Live Arcade in 2007, in the Contra Anniversary Collection in 2019 and in Arcade Archives in 2024.

title: Pac & Pal
description: Pac & Pal (1983) is Namco's third Pac-Man game, a reworking of Super Pac-Man in which Pac-Man flips cards to unlock items while his green companion Miru tries to carry them away, never released in North America.
longDescription:
Pac-Man moves through an enclosed maze in which items are locked behind doors. Running over the face-down cards scattered around the maze flips them to reveal items, which are then unlocked for Pac-Man to eat; items include a Galaxian flagship, a Rally-X car, a trumpet, a snowman and a miniature Pac-Man, all with the same effect. Two items in each maze, matching "S" cards, are power-ups that turn Pac-Man blue and larger, letting him fire a beam with the button to briefly stun the ghosts. Miru, a green creature with a pink bow, tries to pick up unlocked items and carry them to the centre box, and any she delivers before Pac-Man eats them are lost. Clearing the items ends the level, with a larger bonus if Miru takes none; an orange area below the centre box slows the ghosts and hides everything but their eyes. Touching a non-stunned ghost costs a life, but Pac-Man can pass through Miru safely.

The third level and every fourth thereafter is a bonus stage with ten cards and no ghosts: eight show dollar signs, one Miru, which doubles the total, and one Blinky, whose discovery ends the stage at once, though finding him last pays a bigger bonus.
trivia: Its soundtrack was composed by Yuriko Keino, known for Dig Dug and Xevious.
Midway planned to release it as Pac-Man & Chomp Chomp, replacing Miru with Pac-Man's dog from the Hanna-Barbera cartoon.
Chomp Chomp was limited to 300 machines for European countries.
It had no home release until Namco History Vol. 3 in Japan in 1998.
Paste wrote: "If you have no idea what's happening in this game, you're not alone."
devStory: Namco developed and released it in Japan in July 1983 as its third self-made Pac-Man game, since Midway had produced many sequels in North America with little Namco involvement. With the Pac-Man brand growing in Japan, Namco built it on Super Pac-Man, keeping its style and many mechanics while trying to fix its flaws after that game proved unsuccessful. North American release was abandoned because the market was oversaturated with Pac-Man games. After a few successful months it was a commercial failure and stayed obscure, which has been blamed on its departures from Pac-Man and its limited production. It later appeared in Namco Museum Remix, Virtual Arcade and Megamix, Pac-Man Museum and Pac-Man Museum+. Allgame called it "a travesty", the "worst and weirdest Pac-Man sequel ever", and USgamer's Jeremy Parish said it "hastened the series' demise" but was interesting in hindsight, while Hardcore Gaming 101 praised its experimentation, noting that the series would never experiment this much again.

title: Knuckle Bash
description: Knuckle Bash (1993) is Toaplan's rare beat 'em up in which renegade pro wrestlers, including a luchador and an Elvis lookalike, take down a corrupt wrestling organisation, one of the few Toaplan games never ported at the time.
longDescription:
A side-scrolling beat 'em up in the mould of Final Fight and Double Dragon, it sends wrestlers across ten stages in different locations to defeat the Mad Bull Group. At the start, players choose one of two scenarios, each with its own stages, and clearing certain scenarios unlocks an extra character. Unusually for the genre, stages consist mainly of waves of one or a few strong, boss-like enemies rather than long streams of weaker ones, and there are no weapons or objects to pick up at all. As in Streets of Rage 2, each character has a special attack that damages every enemy on screen, and between stages a minigame recalls Mortal Kombat's "Test Your Might".

The Mad Bull Group is a corrupt wrestling organisation tainting a sport whose wrestlers children look up to. Three former members, branded traitors for deserting, meet secretly at a Chicago hotel to contact a "Ninpow" master also wanted by the group, and venture into its Battle Kingdom headquarters. The roster is El Plancha, a luchador; Michael Sobut, an Elvis Presley lookalike; Jack Brow, a street fighter; Mr. Hayate, a ninja master of Ninpow; and Captain, an American football player who defects from the Mad Bull Group.
trivia: Toaplan originally commissioned the team to make a fighting game like Street Fighter II.
Junya Inoue designed it, with Nanpei Kaneko, who had worked on FixEight.
Masahiro Yuge and Osamu Ōta composed the music.
A bootleg, Knuckle Bash 2, appeared in 1999.
Its first official console release came on the Evercade's Toaplan Arcade 4 cartridge in December 2024.
devStory: It was made by largely the same Toaplan staff who would move to its offshoots after the company's 1994 bankruptcy, and Tatsuya Uemura, who said he was not involved, recounted that the planned fighting game drifted into a beat 'em up. Shown at the 1993 AOU Show, it was released in arcades worldwide that year by Toaplan and, in North America and Europe, Atari Games. Play Meter listed it as the 27th most popular arcade game of July 1993. Computer+Videogiochi noted its mix of Final Fight-style play and wrestling, Hardcore Gaming 101 said it "might not be fantastic, but it gets by on being an average beat em up that is just ridiculous enough to make it enjoyable", Retro Gamer was mixed and Wireframe called it "a rare foray into brawler territory" for Toaplan. Inoue went on to work at the offshoot Gazelle on 1995's Pretty Soldier Sailor Moon. Its rights now belong to Tatsujin, founded by Yuge in 2017.

title: Super Pac-Man
description: Super Pac-Man (1982) is Namco's own sequel to Pac-Man, designed by Toru Iwatani, in which Pac-Man eats keys to open doors and can grow into a giant, ghost-proof Super Pac-Man, a game its own designer called boring.
longDescription:
Sound and mechanics changed radically from the first two Pac-Man games. Instead of dots, Pac-Man eats keys to open doors to sections of the maze holding what were once bonus fruit, such as apples, bananas and Galaxian flagships, which become the items that must be cleared. Clearing all the food advances to the next level, where it is worth more. Early keys unlock nearby doors, but later ones often open doors far away, and Pac-Man can enter the ghost house at any time. Alongside ordinary power pellets, two "Super" pellets turn him into Super Pac-Man for a short time: much larger, faster with the "Super Speed" button, able to eat through doors and invulnerable to the ghosts, who look flattened as he flies over them, though he still needs a power pellet to eat them. He flashes white before reverting, and another pellet prolongs the effect.

A star appearing between the two centre boxes, while symbols flash inside them, gives a bonus: 2,000 points if two symbols match and 5,000 if they match the current level, or otherwise a ghost-like 200 to 1,600. Bonus levels fill the maze with food and no ghosts, with Pac-Man permanently Super, to clear against a countdown.
trivia: Bally Midway had separately commissioned General Computer Corporation to make Ms. Pac-Man.
Bally Midway projected US sales of 10,000 to 15,000 cabinets.
Japanese ports for the PV-2000 and Sord M5 were called Mr. Packn and Power Pac.
Atari 5200 and 8-bit versions were finished in 1984 but never released.
Pac-Man becomes Super Pac-Man in his Final Smash in Super Smash Bros. for 3DS and Wii U and Ultimate.
devStory: Namco developed Super Pac-Man and released it in Japan and Europe in 1982, with Bally Midway releasing it in North America in 1983. By May 1983 it was the top-earning arcade game of the month, and Arcade Express gave it 8 out of 10, calling its keys, locked doors and "Super Energy Dots" "the latest thrill for gobbler-lovers". Iwatani himself was critical, disliking Pac-Man's enlarged Super form and calling the game boring. Home versions came to the Commodore 64 in 1988 and IBM PC in 1989, and it appeared on the Game Boy Color in Ms. Pac-Man: Special Color Edition in 1999. It has since featured in many compilations, including Namco Museum Vol. 2, Namco Museum Virtual Arcade, Pac-Man Museum and Pac-Man Museum+, and Jakks Pacific plug-and-play joysticks. A 2006 Sprint mobile version was promoted with a sweepstakes for a Volkswagen New Beetle painted with Super Pac-Man art, shown at E3, and Hamster added the arcade game to Arcade Archives in 2022.

title: Rod Land
description: Rod Land (1990) is Jaleco's single-screen arcade platformer in which two fairies with magic rods stun monsters and slam them from side to side until they vanish, a Bubble Bobble-style game best known in Europe through its home ports.
longDescription:
One or two players control the fairies Tam and Rit, armed with magic wands. Following Bubble Bobble's lead, the rod does not kill monsters outright but leaves them immobilised and crying; it can then grab them in a magic force field so the player can smash them against the ground from side to side until they disappear, leaving a power-up. Each level is a single small screen of monsters, platforms, ladders and later tunnels. Unlike most games of its kind, the fairies can never jump and must use ladders, but they can conjure one ladder of their own above or below them to reach another platform. Only one such ladder can exist at a time, so summoning it again makes the old one vanish, which can also knock away a monster climbing it.

The fairies set out to rescue their mother, trapped in a tower. The arcade version also contains a completely different second story, with new graphics, levels, bosses and more robotic enemies, in which they enter a pyramid to stop a demon building a mobile fortress, guided at times by the spirit of their dead father, whose death the ending implies the demon caused. It can be started directly by moving the joystick down three times between inserting a coin and pressing start.
trivia: The Sales Curve's London office made the home versions, from the Amstrad CPC in 1990 to the Game Boy in 1993.
The NES version, released only in Italy, Spain, the Netherlands and Japan, adds stages and lets the fairies jump.
The Amiga port found unused enemy animations in the data and used them to show monsters switching to attack mode.
Programmers Ronald Pieket Weeserik and John Croudy fixed arcade bugs such as slamming enemies on thin air.
Amiga Power ranked the Amiga version the 16th best game of all time.
devStory: Jaleco developed Rod Land and released it only in Japan in April 1990, but it was ported widely and released internationally. Random Access began the Amiga port, published by Storm, in March 1991 and released it that September. Weeserik told The One the conversion was "easier" than others because the Amiga could reproduce everything in the coin-op at the correct frame rate, though Jaleco supplied around five hundred sprites "jumbled up and in the wrong colours". The 16-bit versions added hidden features, codes and extra levels, and replaced some of the arcade's less suitable synthesised sound effects; Weeserik said they wrote them the way the arcade version should have been written. The Commodore 64 version was coded by Steve Snake and the Spectrum version by Jason McGann and Shaun McClure, and in the Game Boy version players can strike enemies while on ladders. A puzzle spin-off, Soldam, followed in 1992, and Hamster released the arcade original in Arcade Archives in January 2021.

title: Sky Kid
description: Sky Kid (1985) is Namco's two-player biplane shooter in which the Sky Kids Red Baron and Blue Max must pick up a bomb en route to blowing up fortresses and ships, looping their planes past hidden Namco characters.
longDescription:
The players are the Sky Kids, "Red Baron" and "Blue Max", named after the World War I ace Manfred von Richthofen and the Pour le Mérite medal informally known as the Blue Max. Flying biplanes, they are assigned specific targets to bomb on each mission, using one button for the machine gun and the other to perform a loop. Their planes start without a bomb, which must be picked up on the way to the target, while ground and air units try to stop them and some missions demand flying through inhospitable terrain or around cities. Targets are fortress complexes or ships, and later in the 21 missions several targets appear in one mission. Points come from destroying air and ground targets, with an end-of-mission bonus for each, points for how much of the target is destroyed, and a further bonus only for its total destruction.

Looping over a billboard sometimes reveals one of four hidden Namco characters: Pac-Man, Inky, Rally-X's Special Flag or Dig Dug's Pooka. At the end of each mission, three dancing girls appear; looping in front of them makes them send hearts representing kisses, while shooting them turns the girls into pink powder puffs and the hearts into waving dogs.
trivia: Kitkorp released it in North American arcades in July 1986.
Sun Corporation, which absorbed Kitkorp, released the NES version in North America in 1987.
A VS. System arcade version, VS. Super Sky Kid, appeared in 1987.
In the ShiftyLook series Mappy: The Beat, Blue Max is a good-natured but unhelpful Nyamco employee with a Southern accent.
The Ace Combat series makes multiple references to Sky Kid.
devStory: Namco developed and published Sky Kid in Japan in December 1985, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit in its 15 January 1986 issue. An NES port came out in Japan on 22 August 1986 and in North America in September 1987, and at least one version was imported into the UK. The NES version later came to the Virtual Console on the Wii, 3DS and Wii U, the arcade version to the Wii Virtual Console, and Hamster released it in Arcade Archives in October 2021. A sequel, Sky Kid Deluxe, followed in 1986 as the first game on Namco's System 86 hardware, adding new enemies and targets, including the unkillable "Kaminari Kid"; its first worldwide console release came in Namco Museum Virtual Arcade for the Xbox 360, without Blue Max. Sky Kid was briefly revived as a ShiftyLook webcomic illustrated by Udon Entertainment, and a Sky Kid theme was released as DLC for Pac-Man 99.

title: Last Resort
description: Last Resort (1992) is SNK's dark, R-Type-like Neo Geo shoot 'em up, made by former Irem staff, with an indestructible drone that can lock in place or orbit the ship.
longDescription:
The player fights through five stages, twice, destroying each end boss by hitting its weak points. The ship is a cyber jet that, once it collects one, is accompanied by an indestructible robot drone. The drone shields the ship from small projectiles, much like the Dino 246 drone in Pulstar and Blazing Star, and doubles as an extra weapon with multi-directional fire that can be launched at enemies. It can be toggled between staying fixed in position and rotating around the cyber jet. Power-ups upgrade the jet through three levels of three types of firepower and increase its speed.

In the future, mankind has developed the technology to colonise space, but a mysterious computer virus infects the main computer running humanity's first space station, turning its automated defences against Earth and persuading other humans to join its side. Its attacks on Earth become so frequent that the planet's only hope lies in advanced spaceships with great firepower. Critics have compared the game to R-Type, and others its visuals to the 1988 film Akira.
trivia: It was developed by former Irem staff.
Seven Gamest reviewers responded positively when it was shown at the 1992 AOU Show.
Player One described its power-ups as a mix of R-Type and Forgotten Worlds.
Power Play called it the best classic-style shooter since R-Type and its sequel.
HobbyConsolas named it one of the twenty best Neo Geo CD games in 2014.
devStory: SNK developed and published Last Resort for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's thirteenth most popular arcade game of May 1992, while RePlay placed it sixteenth in North America that month. It was ported to the Neo Geo AES and Neo Geo CD and has generally been well received. Consoles Plus called it a reference shoot 'em up for the Neo Geo, and Hobby Consolas praised its graphics, music and two-player mode while missing an extra stage, but EGM's four reviewers panned the AES version, finding its impressive graphics and sound undone by crippling slowdown and a very short length, unforgivable given the console's power and the cartridge's price. Ultimate Future Games praised the Neo Geo CD version's "opera-style rave soundtrack" but found it short. Nintendo Life later compared its dark atmosphere to R-Type and Armed Police Unit Gallop and called it one of the best Neo Geo shooters, though it found the two-player mode broken. It was re-released in SNK Arcade Classics Vol. 1 and Hamster's ACA Neo Geo series.

title: Grobda
description: Grobda (1984) is Masanobu Endo's Xevious spin-off for Namco in which a defenceless enemy tank from that game is given lasers and a shield to fight 99 rounds of a deadly future sport, made in just three months.
longDescription:
Thousands of years in the future, humans pilot powerful laser-firing vehicles in a dangerous competitive sport called "battling". The player controls the Grobda, a screw-propelled tank, through 99 increasingly difficult rounds, each won by destroying all the enemies while dodging their fire as quickly as possible, in a multidirectional shooter similar to the Atari 2600's Combat. The laser destroys most enemies in one hit, though shielded ones need more. Each destroyed enemy explodes, taking out anything in its blast radius, Grobda included, and leaves wreckage that slows the tank down if it drives over it. Grobda's own shield briefly protects it from enemy fire, shown by a meter at the bottom of the screen, and once worn away it does not return until the next round.

The Grobda began as a defenceless enemy in Xevious, trying to dodge the player's air-to-surface bombs, and Endo thought arming it was a humorous idea that made for an interesting game. Composer Yuriko Keino wanted the background hum to speed up as the tank moved faster, and since the sound hardware could not do it, she wrote a custom program to make it possible.
trivia: It was one of the shortest developments at Namco, planned and completed in three months on a small budget.
Most of the team had worked on Xevious and The Tower of Druaga.
Namco's tagline was "Grobda has awakened its combat instinct".
It ran on the Super Pac-Man arcade board.
Wolf Team designer Kazuyoshi Inoue said it influenced Granada.
devStory: Endo, creator of Xevious and The Tower of Druaga, designed Grobda with a small Namco team. Namco released it in December 1984, and Game Machine reported it as Japan's top-grossing arcade game of that month; Magic Electronics distributed it in North America in September 1985. Dempa Software ported it to the PC-8801 in Japan the same year, and it has since appeared in Namco Museum Vol. 2, Battle Collection, Virtual Arcade and Megamix, the last adding a Grobda Remix minigame in which Pac-Man destroys enemies against the clock. It came to the Japanese Wii Virtual Console in 2009 and Hamster's Arcade Archives in 2023. In 1998 Allgame called it "a refreshing departure from slower, more methodical tank shooters such as Combat and Armor Ambush", praising its pace but criticising its high difficulty, and Hardcore Gaming 101 later found it much simpler than Xevious and was mixed on its difficulty.

title: Kingdom Grand Prix
description: Kingdom Grand Prix (1994) is Raizing's sequel to Sorcer Striker, an unusual hybrid of vertical shoot 'em up and race in which pilots blast enemies while trying to finish first in a kingdom-wide contest that ended a war.
longDescription:
On a vertically scrolling course, the player races seven rivals while shooting enemies and dodging bullets. Tapping the fire button shoots, while holding it gives a speed boost, and the ship's position on screen also sets its speed, the higher up the faster. Losing a life or reaching the next stage cuts overall speed. A limited stock of bombs destroys most enemies on screen and slows the rival racers. There are four power-ups, all adding to overall power apart from the bomb, which simply adds uses.

Twelve stages are arranged in branching paths, usually with a choice of two per level, one for the first and three for the sixth. Beating the first loop on one credit while finishing first overall unlocks a second loop made up of all the stages not chosen the first time. The story explains the race: after decades of war that cost countless innocent lives and legions of good men, the king decides to hold a great race across every part of the kingdom, open to all, and the wars stop as people look forward to the competition each year.
trivia: It is the second game in the Mahō Daisakusen series and the first to mix shooting with racing.
Its music had no album release until Wave Master published one on 24 April 2013.
The Saturn version adds a shooting-only mode without the race.
The Saturn version sold 7,441 copies in its first week, according to Famitsu.
In 2022 the arcade version was included on the Sega Astro City Mini V.
devStory: Raizing developed Kingdom Grand Prix, and Eighting released it in arcades across Japan and Europe in September 1994. GAGA Communications released a Sega Saturn version on 14 June 1996, which divided critics: three reviewers from the Japanese Sega Saturn Magazine rated it 5.33 out of 10 and Famitsu's four reviewers gave it 60 out of 100, while Consoles+ gave it 90% and Joypad three out of five. GameSetWatch's Todd Ciolek called it "a true curiosity, even if its one unique idea doesn't quite work", still worth trying "as both a solid twitch-game and a glimpse of one shooter developer's attempt at something different, if not necessarily better", and Hardcore Gaming 101's Kurt Kalata gave it a mostly positive retrospective. The series continued with Dimahoo, released by Capcom in 2000.

title: The Dig
description: The Dig (1995) is LucasArts' sombre science fiction adventure, based on an idea Steven Spielberg devised for Amazing Stories, in which astronauts sent to divert an asteroid are carried to a long-abandoned alien world.
longDescription:
A radio telescope spots an asteroid, dubbed Attila, on a collision course with Earth, and a five-person crew flies the shuttle Atlantis to plant explosives that will push it into a stable orbit: Commander Boston Low, voiced by Robert Patrick; German archaeologist and geologist Ludger Brink, voiced by Steve Blum; linguist and reporter Maggie Robbins; pilot Ken Borden; and NASA technician Cora Miles. The charges work, but Low, Brink and Robbins find the asteroid hollow, and when they enter its central chamber it turns into a dodecahedron pod and carries them to an alien planet. There they find signs of a vanished civilisation, life crystals that can raise the dead, and Brink's growing addiction to them, as they use xenoarchaeology to decipher alien text and find a way home.

It is a point-and-click adventure in which the player uses the mouse to look at and interact with people and objects, collect and use items and talk to characters, running on the SCUMM engine, the eleventh LucasArts game to do so and the last on MS-DOS. Unlike LucasArts' usual comedies, it takes a serious tone. Drawn 2D art is combined with limited pre-rendered 3D clips created by Industrial Light & Magic, and the communicator hides an "Asteroid Lander" minigame like Lunar Lander.
trivia: Its first design meeting, at Skywalker Ranch with Spielberg, George Lucas, Ron Gilbert and Noah Falstein, fell on the day of the 1989 San Francisco earthquake.
Orson Scott Card wrote the dialogue.
A cut character, Japanese tycoon Toshi Olema, would have died in an acid-dripping cavern.
Spielberg asked for the violence to be toned down after parents complained about taking young children to Jurassic Park.
It was the first LucasArts game with its soundtrack sold separately on CD.
devStory: Spielberg conceived it as an Amazing Stories episode and then a film, but it was too expensive to shoot, so it became a game. It had the longest development of any LucasArts adventure, passing through four project leaders, Falstein, Brian Moriarty, Dave Grossman and finally Sean Clark; Moriarty restarted it from scratch with a bloodier version for adults, and dropped ideas included survival mechanics with food and water and exploring alien cities. Announced for 1992, it was released in December 1995. Michael Land's score, a Kurzweil K2000 synthesiser enriched with samples of Wagner, was universally praised. The Dig sold 300,000 copies by early 1998, LucasArts' best-selling adventure at release, though Bill Tiller said management saw it as a letdown after the hype. Reviews were mixed to positive: critics found the puzzles harder than usual and the graphics and dialogue uneven, but praised its atmosphere and cut-scenes, PC Magazine saying it brought "a true cinematic style to your earthbound PC". Alan Dean Foster wrote a novelisation.

title: The Curse of Monkey Island
description: The Curse of Monkey Island (1997) is LucasArts' third Monkey Island game, in which Guybrush Threepwood accidentally turns Elaine into a gold statue, with cartoon art, a full voice cast and the last outing for the SCUMM engine.
longDescription:
After escaping LeChuck's Carnival of the Damned, Guybrush drifts to Plunder Island, where Elaine Marley is under siege by the zombie pirate. His escape sets off a voodoo cannonball that seemingly destroys LeChuck, but when he proposes to Elaine with a diamond ring from LeChuck's hold, the cursed ring turns her into a gold statue, which pirates promptly steal. The Voodoo Lady tells him to replace it with an uncursed ring of greater value on Blood Island. Along the way he assembles a crew of three pirate barbers, fights ship-to-ship battles, defeats the vain Captain Rottingham at rhyming insult sword fighting, meets the cannibals of Monkey Island, now volcano-worshipping vegetarians, and befriends Murray, a talking skull, before LeChuck returns as a fiery demon.

The verb and inventory menus of earlier games are replaced, as in Full Throttle, by a pop-up action menu shaped like a gold coin, with a hand for physical actions, a skull for looking and a parrot for talking or eating, and an inventory chest where items are dragged together, so scenes fill the whole screen. Players choose between a normal mode and a "Mega-Monkey" mode with more puzzles, and can let the crew handle sea combat or take full control.
trivia: Murray was meant to appear only in the first chapter but was so popular with testers that he was written into later scenes.
The song "A Pirate I Was Meant To Be" was cut from non-English versions because its puzzle relies on English rhymes, ending only when Guybrush rhymes with "orange".
Gary Coleman voices Kenny Falmouth.
A Monkey Island film was in the works afterwards, revealed when concept artist Tony Stacchi shared his art with a fan site.
Ron Gilbert said in 2008 that the team did "an excellent job of capturing the humor and feel of the game".
