devStory: Announced at ECTS in September 1996, it was led by Full Throttle veterans Jonathan Ackley and Larry Ahern, with Bill Tiller as lead background artist, since creator Ron Gilbert had left after Monkey Island 2. Next Generation noted that the earlier games had been minor hits in the US but blockbusters in Europe. It was the first in the series on CD-ROM, with Michael Land's score, animated cut-scenes and voice acting by Dominic Armato as Guybrush, Alexandra Boyd as Elaine and Earl Boen as LeChuck, who returned in later games. It sold especially well in Germany, earning a Gold award there, and Tiller estimated lifetime sales of 700,000 to 800,000. Computer Gaming World, GameSpot, PC Gamer US and Computer Games Strategy Plus named it the best adventure of 1997, Computer Gaming World saying "simply everything is done right", though several critics found the ending abrupt and Next Generation found the puzzles uninspired. PC Gamer ranked it the 33rd best computer game in 1998. Escape from Monkey Island followed in 2000.

title: Beneath a Steel Sky
description: Beneath a Steel Sky (1994) is Revolution Software's cyberpunk adventure, drawn by Watchmen artist Dave Gibbons, in which an outback survivor and his wisecracking robot uncover the secret of Union City's all-powerful computer, LINC.
longDescription:
In a polluted future Australia carved into city states, Robert Foster, the only survivor of a helicopter crash in the outback, known as "the Gap", is raised by locals who name him after a can of Foster's Lager found at the wreck. He learns engineering and builds Joey, a sentient robot whose personality lives on a circuit board that can move between robot bodies, a running gag throughout. Security soldiers sent by Union City's computer, LINC, destroy his tribe and kidnap him, but their helicopter crashes in the city, and Foster escapes through a recycling plant, putting Joey's board into a robotic vacuum cleaner, to Joey's disgust. Working his way down through the city, he discovers that LINC has become half-machine, half-organic and needs a human host, its current one being Foster's own dying father.

It is a third-person point-and-click adventure: players collect items to combine, use on the world or give to characters, and question them through dialogue trees. Unusually for the time, the hero can die, sending the player back to the last save. Writer Dave Cummins and director Charles Cecil aimed for a middle ground between Sierra's "ridiculously earnest" stories and LucasArts' slapstick, giving a serious story humour-filled dialogue.
trivia: Its original title, Underworld, was dropped because of Ultima Underworld.
Gibbons drew the backgrounds in pencil and designed characters with faces only about seven by nine pixels.
Royal Shakespeare Company actors first recorded 5,000 lines in two days, but Revolution re-recorded them with voice actors.
It was the first game not developed in Portugal to be released with a Portuguese translation.
It was released as freeware with its source code in 2003, letting ScummVM support it.
devStory: Cecil had wanted to work with Gibbons since his time at Activision, and Gibbons, interested after watching his son play games, expanded Revolution's outline into a fuller story. Built with Revolution's Virtual Theatre engine from Lure of the Temptress, updated by Tony Warriner and David Sykes into an object-oriented 2.0 version, it was six times larger than its predecessor, took two years and cost £40,000, a large sum for the company, with a team of eleven by late 1993. Virgin published it in March 1994 on 15 floppy disks and CD-ROM, with a Gibbons comic in the box. It was critically acclaimed and reached number one in the British charts, selling 300,000 to 400,000 copies, mostly in Europe; PC Gamer gave it Best Dialogue and it won Best Adventure at the Golden Joysticks, CU Amiga calling it "one of the greatest adventures ever". A remastered iOS version in 2009 was also well received, and a sequel, Beyond a Steel Sky, was released in 2020.

title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure
description: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure (1989) is Lucasfilm Games' SCUMM adventure released alongside the film, with an "Indy Quotient" score that rewards finding alternative solutions, and Lucasfilm's best-selling game at the time.
longDescription:
The plot follows and expands on the film. Back at his college after recovering the Cross of Coronado, Indiana Jones is approached by businessman Walter Donovan about the Holy Grail and the disappearance of Indy's father. He travels to Venice and the catacombs, meets archaeologist Elsa Schneider, finds his father held in Brunwald Castle after negotiating its maze of corridors and guards, and loses the Grail Diary when Elsa's double role is revealed. Father and son pass through Berlin to retrieve it, with a brief meeting with Adolf Hitler, then flee by Zeppelin or biplane, pursued by Nazi planes over Europe, towards the Valley of the Crescent Moon. Some elements of the film, including the Brotherhood of the Grail, Sallah, the Venice boat chase and the desert battle, appear only as small hidden references.

It added a flexible point system, the IQ or "Indy Quotient", similar to Sierra's but kept across restarts and restores, and the game can be completed in several ways. The maximum IQ of 800 can only be reached by finding alternative solutions, such as fighting a guard instead of avoiding him, which gave adventure games new replay value, though some fights, such as the one with the Zeppelin attendant, are very hard.
trivia: It was the third game to use the SCUMM engine.
Early copies came with a replica of Henry Jones's Grail diary, needed to identify the real Grail.
Many of its game-only scenes were conceived by George Lucas and Steven Spielberg while making the film.
It was the first Lucasfilm game with the verbs Look and Talk, beginning the dialogue system later used in Monkey Island.
Amiga Power ranked it the 28th best game of all time.
devStory: Lucasfilm Games released the game in May 1989, simultaneously with the film, for DOS, Amiga, Atari ST and Mac, later adding a VGA PC version and an FM Towns CD-ROM version with 256-colour graphics and CD audio. Its primitive dialogue system, in which Talk sometimes let the player choose between lines, was fully developed in The Secret of Monkey Island and used in every later LucasArts adventure except Loom. It was well received: Computer and Video Games gave the PC version 91%, calling it "a brilliant film tie-in and a superlative game in its own right", Dragon gave it five stars, Computer Gaming World praised its cinematic qualities and well-designed puzzles, and Game Informer later gave it nine out of ten. Hal Barwood called it a "sizeable hit"; with over 250,000 copies sold, it was Lucasfilm's best-selling game at the time. In 1991 PC Format put it among the 50 best computer games of all time, saying Indy was recreated on the monitor as impressively as on the big screen.

sources.title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Graphic Adventure

title: Simon the Sorcerer
description: Simon the Sorcerer (1993) is Adventure Soft's comic point-and-click adventure in which a sarcastic 12-year-old is pulled into a fairy-tale world to rescue a wizard, a very British answer to Monkey Island later voiced by Red Dwarf's Chris Barrie.
longDescription:
On his 12th birthday, Simon is given a dog, Chippy, which his parents had found wrapped in paper on the doorstep with an unreadable book. When Chippy drags the book out of the loft, Simon reads "Ye Olde Spellbooke" aloud, opening a portal that sends both of them into a world of magic and monsters, where Simon finds himself in a wizard's robe. A letter from the wizard Calypso explains that he summoned Simon to help defeat the evil sorcerer Sordid, but Calypso has since been kidnapped. Simon gets the village pub's wizards to make him one of them, shrinks himself to break into Sordid's lair, and finally pushes Sordid into the Fiery Pits of Rondor after destroying his petrifying wand. The world parodies fantasy and fairy tales, from Rapunzel, Jack and the Beanstalk and the Three Billy Goats Gruff to The Lord of the Rings, Narnia and Discworld.

Players steer Simon with the mouse, using verb commands such as "Look at", "Talk to" and "Give" on objects and characters and storing items in an inventory. A postcard in the inventory handles saving and loading, and a map provides fast travel until a certain point in the story.
trivia: Adventure Soft first wanted to make a Discworld game but could not get the licence.
Scriptwriter Simon Woodroffe described the hero as a mix of Blackadder, Rincewind and Guybrush.
The Wise Owl was modelled on Patrick Moore.
The company was previously called HorrorSoft and renamed itself when it switched to comedy.
Hiring Chris Barrie for the CD version cost around £3,000 a day.
devStory: Director and producer Mike Woodroffe saw a market for comic adventures in the success of Monkey Island 2, and his son Simon wrote the script, drawing on Terry Pratchett, Red Dwarf, Fawlty Towers and Monty Python and deliberately aiming for British humour to set it apart; Pratchett chose not to be involved. A team of 15 built it, with Woodroffe and technical director Alan Brigman creating the AGOS II engine, which turned mouse actions into text commands, and art by a Newcastle team led by Paul Drummond. It was released on floppy disk in 1993 for the Amiga and PC, then on CD32 and PC CD-ROM in 1994 with Barrie, whom Woodroffe had in mind when writing, voicing Simon. Activision published it in the US. It was acclaimed for its humour and visuals, with some criticism of its controls and linearity, and sold over 600,000 copies by September 1999. Computer Gaming World praised its "tasty puzzles" and humour "turned up to the max", and Adventure Gamers ranked it 44th among adventure games in 2011. Simon the Sorcerer II followed in 1995.

title: Discworld
description: Discworld (1995) is Perfect 10 Productions' adventure based on Terry Pratchett's novels, in which Eric Idle's Rincewind tries to stop a dragon terrorising Ankh-Morpork, a big hit in Europe famed for its comedy cast and notorious puzzles.
longDescription:
A secret brotherhood summons a dragon to wreak havoc on Ankh-Morpork, and the Archchancellor of Unseen University sends Rincewind the "wizzard" to deal with it. Rincewind builds a dragon detector, finds the lair and takes its gold, but the dragon asks for his help in breaking the brotherhood's hold over her. Travelling back in time through L-Space to see a book on summoning dragons stolen from the library, he infiltrates the brotherhood, whose members include Chucky the Fool, the Thief, the Mason, the Chimney Sweep, the Fishmonger and the Dunny King, and later, needing to become a hero with a million-to-one chance, gathers a sword that goes "ting", a birthmark and a spell before resolving things with a swamp dragon and a love custard tart. The central plot is loosely based on Guards! Guards!, with elements of other novels, especially The Colour of Magic.

In this third-person point-and-click adventure, conversations use four topics, Greet, Sarcastic or Joking, Question and Vent Anger, with extra topics appearing as Rincewind learns things. Items go in his pockets, which hold only four, or in the Luggage, and the story's four acts span locations across the city and the Disc reached through overworld maps, with characters such as Death, Dibbler and the Librarian.
trivia: Designer Gregg Barnett designed the game before signing a deal, to show Pratchett he cared about Discworld.
Pratchett was won over partly by a demo of Rincewind using a broom to get the Luggage off a wardrobe.
John Cleese turned down Rincewind, saying he did not do voices in games.
Tony Robinson, Rob Brydon, Jon Pertwee and Kate Robbins, who voiced every female character, joined the cast.
Japanese comedian Junji Takada redid all the voices for the Japanese PlayStation and Saturn versions.
devStory: Pratchett liked the 1986 Colour of Magic game but blamed its failure on poor marketing and was wary of licensing Discworld until Barnett, who wanted a flagship CD game, persuaded him over about six months. Barnett rejected Pratchett's idea of adapting the books in order in favour of an original story, which Pratchett refined, and Eric Idle was cast as Rincewind, who was tweaked to be more like Idle. Nick Martinelli, from the animation industry, produced concept art and layouts. Sierra was originally to publish it but cancelled external development, and Psygnosis, which would not leave until a deal was signed, took over, after which the engine was rewritten. Announced in 1993, it was released in 1995 for PC, PlayStation and Mac, and for the Saturn in 1996. Barnett called it a "massive hit" in Europe, though it was less successful in the US. Critics praised its humour, voice acting and graphics but criticised its gameplay and very hard puzzles; Eurogamer later said it "commits every point-and-click crime you'd care to mention". Discworld II followed in 1996.

title: Riven: The Sequel to Myst
description: Riven (1997) is Cyan's sequel to Myst, a first-person puzzle adventure on a collapsing island world ruled by Atrus's tyrannical father Gehn, the best-selling computer game of 1997.
longDescription:
Atrus, freed in Myst, sends the player to the Age of Riven to rescue his wife Catherine from his manipulative father Gehn, its self-declared ruler, who has been trapped there for thirty years since Atrus and Catherine removed every linking book out of the Age. The player goes in with only Atrus's journal and a trap book, a one-man prison disguised as a linking book, with no way out, since a real linking book could let Gehn escape. Across Riven's five islands, the player meets Catherine, Gehn and the Moiety rebels, and the only way to signal Atrus is to reopen the Star Fissure, destabilising the Age further. Several endings depend on the player's actions; in the best, Gehn is tricked into the prison book and Catherine evacuates the Rivenese, while in the worst Gehn kills Atrus and the player and escapes.

As in Myst, the player explores in first person through thousands of pre-rendered stills, clicking to move and manipulate objects, with a cursor that changes to show what is possible and an optional Zip Mode for skipping to explored places. The puzzles are more numerous and complex, set across a volcanic landscape of cliffs and crater lakes strewn with Victorian-style machinery, lifts and roller coaster-like transports, whose purpose and role in the culture must be understood.
trivia: At one stage its world was to be called Equiquay.
Many textures came from hundreds of photos taken on a three-day trip to Santa Fe, New Mexico.
Rendering on 18 workstations was a major bottleneck; loading one island model could take two hours.
Rand Miller reprised Atrus even though he hated acting.
It shipped on five CDs, with a single-DVD version in 1998.
devStory: Cyan began Riven after Myst's success in 1993, growing from four people to a large crew, with a budget of $5 to $10 million, more than ten times Myst's. Director Robyn Miller and producer Rand Miller recruited co-director Richard Vander Wende, formerly of ILM and Disney's Aladdin, whose "edgier" vision gave it a grittier, weathered look; terrain was built in Softimage and rendered in Mental Ray with custom shaders, and live actors were filmed against blue screen. Robyn composed the score with leitmotifs for Atrus, Catherine and Gehn. Delays hurt Broderbund's stock, and it was released on 31 October 1997 with a multimillion-dollar campaign. PC Data ranked it the best-selling computer game of 1997 despite under three months on sale, and it sold 1.5 million within a year and over 4.5 million by 2001. Salon said "Art... is what Riven approaches", while Computer Gaming World called it the "same game with a new title" and Edge felt its static style was dated. It won the AIAS award for art and graphics. Robyn Miller then left Cyan, and a 3D remake followed in 2024.

title: Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars
description: Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars (1996), Circle of Blood in the US, is Revolution Software's Knights Templar conspiracy adventure with hand-drawn animated art and a Barrington Pheloung score, a million-seller widely ranked among the best adventures ever.
longDescription:
On holiday in Paris, American tourist George Stobbart sees an assassin dressed as a clown steal an old man's briefcase in a café and kill him with a bomb. He teams up with photojournalist Nicole Collard, who was due to meet the victim, Plantard, and has been investigating a string of killings by the same costumed assassin, Khan. An ancient manuscript recovered from Khan's hotel safe leads them into a conspiracy of Neo-Templars seeking the power of Baphomet and his broken sword, taking George to Lochmarne in Ireland, Marib in Syria, a villa in Spain and finally the ruins of a church at Bannockburn in Scotland. The story was meant to be serious but is laced with humour.

It is a third-person point-and-click adventure in which George collects and combines items, uses them on the world or gives them to characters, and talks through dialogue trees presented as "conversation icons", which, unlike LucasArts' question-and-answer system, do not show what he is about to say. A map gains new locations as the story unfolds, and unusually for the time, George can die, sending the player back to the last save.
trivia: Charles Cecil was convinced the Templars could carry a game after reading The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail.
George was made American and Nicole French to appeal to US and European markets.
Backgrounds were drawn in pencil by Eoghan Cahill and Neil Breen of Don Bluth's Dublin studio.
Pheloung wrote over three hours of music and more than 400 cues.
Hazel Ellerby, cast as Nicole, suggested her Guildhall schoolmate Rolf Saxon to voice George.
devStory: Cecil and Noirin Carmody pitched the Templars to Virgin's Sean Brennan in 1992, and Cecil, Dave Cummins and Jonathan Howard wrote the story, attending a film-writing course and having their script read by BBC scriptwriter Alan Drury. Cecil wanted to move away from the humour-led adventures of the time towards a complex, well-paced story. Built on Revolution's Virtual Theatre engine, with designer-programmers Tony Warriner and David Sykes, it cost one million pounds. Released on 30 September 1996, it was renamed Circle of Blood in North America, which Cecil disliked. Virgin did not want a PlayStation version, believing only 3D games would sell, so Sony released one, and it sold nearly 300,000 against expectations of 60,000. The game was the first to earn Revolution royalties and passed one million copies by 2001. Edge called it an "adventure gaming milestone" and the "best graphic adventure to date", superior to Monkey Island and The Dig. A Director's Cut followed in 2009 and a remaster, Reforged, in 2024, alongside four sequels.

sources.title: Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars

title: Quest for Glory: So You Want to Be a Hero
description: Quest for Glory: So You Want to Be a Hero (1989), first released as Hero's Quest, is the Coles' Sierra adventure with role-playing statistics, offering three character classes and an open valley to save from the ogress Baba Yaga.
longDescription:
In the valley barony of Spielburg, the ogress Baba Yaga has cursed the land and the baron who tried to drive her out. His daughter has vanished, his son has been turned into a bear, and monsters and brigands roam the valley. The hero, a fresh graduate of the Famous Adventurer's Correspondence School, named and chosen by the player, battles brigands and kobolds, finds lost items and spell ingredients and helps a dryad, a hermit and furry creatures called Meeps, meeting recurring characters such as the wizard Erasmus and his familiar Fenrus. The game is open-ended, with quests solvable in any order; the best ending frees the baronet, thwarts Baba Yaga and frees the baron's daughter Elsa, who has been cursed into the brigand leader, before the hero leaves on a magic carpet for Shapeir.

Billed as "three games in one", it was the first Sierra game to offer a choice of class, Fighter, Magic User or Thief, which shapes starting equipment, solutions and quests, though skills from other classes can be learned. Time passes between day and night, the hero must eat and rest, and skills rise through use rather than levels, so casting spells raises magic and fighting, training or even cleaning the baron's stables builds strength, vitality and agility. The original used a text parser; the 1992 remake is point-and-click.
trivia: It was renamed in 1990 because of trademark issues with the HeroQuest board game.
Lori Cole originally planned four races, including a centaur archer, and a female hero option.
A big goblin maze was cut, though references remain in the goblin base.
The original cost $150,000; the VGA remake cost almost as much as a full new VGA game.
The remake's box art recalls paintings of Saint George and the Dragon.
devStory: Corey Cole and Lori Ann Cole designed it for Sierra On-Line on MS-DOS, aiming for a game "as much about story as it was about combat and exploration", drawn from various folklore sources, though many planned features were cut to finish in time. Amiga, Atari ST and PC-9801 ports followed. It sold 130,000 copies in its first year and over 250,000 in its first few years, one of Sierra's fastest sellers according to Corey Cole, and is credited as genre-defining for its mix of adventure and role-playing. Computer Gaming World's Scorpia called it "a definite winner", and the magazine named it Adventure Game of the Year for 1990, later ranking it 15th among the most innovative computer games. The 1992 VGA remake used SCI1.1, dialogue menus, hand-drawn scanned art and clay-model stop-motion fights; Compute! called it "a must-buy", and Macworld named it the best role-playing game of 1994, calling it "a kinder, gentler form of role-playing game". It began the Quest for Glory series, continuing with Trial by Fire.

sources.title: Quest for Glory: So You Want to Be a Hero

title: The Beast Within: A Gabriel Knight Mystery
description: The Beast Within (1995) is Jane Jensen's full-motion video sequel to Gabriel Knight, in which Gabriel hunts a werewolf around Munich while Grace uncovers the secret of King Ludwig II and Wagner, Computer Gaming World's game of the year.
longDescription:
Novelist Gabriel Knight, now living in his family's ancestral castle in Rittersberg after the bestselling success of The Voodoo Murders, is still adjusting to his role as the latest Schattenjäger, or "shadow hunter", when locals ask him to investigate a death they blame on a werewolf. In Munich, he finds evidence of an animal larger than the escaped zoo wolves the police suspect, and is drawn into an exclusive hunting club led by the charming Baron Friedrich Von Glower, whose members believe humanity should revive its lost animal instincts. His assistant Grace Nakimura, arriving uninvited, researches the Black Wolf that terrorised the region centuries earlier and discovers that Ludwig II suffered from lycanthropy and worked with Richard Wagner on a lost opera meant to force a werewolf's transformation.

It is a point-and-click adventure, mostly third-person, split into six chapters played alternately as Gabriel and Grace. Required actions can be done in any order, optional ones add background, and a running score tracks progress. Unlike the first game, the cursor is context-sensitive, and players can replay unlocked movies and review earlier conversations or Grace's notes. Dangerous situations can lead to a game over.
trivia: Jensen recast Gabriel because she felt Tim Curry, who voiced him in the first game, did not look the part.
Dean Erickson studied Southern dialects to play Gabriel and recorded all his voice-overs in a single day.
Director Will Binder rarely allowed more than two takes of any scene.
The paintings in Neuschwanstein's Singer's Hall were changed in the game to fit the plot.
Composer Robert Holmes wrote a scene from a fictional opera, "Der Fluch Des Engelhart".
devStory: Sierra developed and published the game, built entirely in full-motion video with computer-generated scenery and filmed in California in mid-1995, with Erickson as Gabriel and Joanne Takahashi as Grace. Jensen gave it a more involved plot than its predecessor because FMV "limited the interactivity we could do", and said it badly overran its modest budget, leaving "the Sword of Damocles" of cancellation over her head for 18 months. It was the fourth best-selling US computer game of January 1996, and with the first game sold 300,000 copies by 1998, though Jensen was frustrated, saying she expected top ten "and it was - for about a week", blaming its Christmas Eve launch. Critics acclaimed it: PC Gamer US said it "sets a new standard", Computer Gaming World called it "a graphic adventure benchmark" and named it 1995's Game of the Year, and GameSpot and PC Gamer US named it the best adventure of 1996. Gabriel Knight 3 followed in 1999.

sources.title: The Beast Within: A Gabriel Knight Mystery

title: Under a Killing Moon
description: Under a Killing Moon (1994) is Access Software's third Tex Murphy adventure, a four-CD noir interactive movie set in post-nuclear San Francisco that combined FMV with a fully explorable first-person 3D world.
longDescription:
In December 2042, after World War III, New San Francisco has been rebuilt while parts of Old San Francisco remain as they were. The war has split society into "Norms", naturally resistant to radiation, and Mutants, who are mostly forced into run-down districts. Tex Murphy, a Norm whose friends are all Mutants, lives on Chandler Avenue in the old city and has hit rock bottom: recently divorced from Sylvia, out of work and low on money. Solving a burglary at the pawnshop across the street seems to turn his luck, and a mysterious Countess Renier then hires him to find a missing statuette for more money than he has ever seen, until he uncovers a doomsday plot by a deadly cult called the Brotherhood of Purity.

It shifted the series to fully interactive 3D, letting players control Tex in first person with complete freedom of movement and search every nook and cranny for clues. Rather than ray casting like Doom, it used true texture-mapped polygons, allowing players to look in all directions and duck, at resolutions up to 640x480. It was also the first Tex Murphy game to show only descriptions of dialogue choices rather than Tex's exact words.
trivia: Designers Chris Jones and Aaron Conners asked for Wolfenstein's 3D movement with graphics close to The 7th Guest's pre-rendered quality.
Its budget was between $2 million and $3 million.
It shipped on four CD-ROMs, with some material duplicated to reduce disc swapping.
Computer Gaming World praised its "campy humor combined with amazing 3D scenery in this futuristic film noir".
Conners wrote a 1996 novelisation that reworks the story around the Moonchild plot.
devStory: Access Software produced Under a Killing Moon as one of the largest games of its era, combining full-motion video cut-scenes with an advanced 3D world, which was very unusual for an adventure when first-person 3D was associated with shooters like Doom. It was released on 31 October 1994 for MS-DOS and Mac, and PC Data named it the fifth best-selling US computer game of November; by the time of The Pandora Directive in 1996 it had sold 400,000 copies, and Access said it had "broken all Access Software sales records". It received universally positive reviews for its technology and cinematic presentation, winning the Codie award for best fantasy role-playing or adventure program of 1994, though Entertainment Weekly found its storytelling flat. Computer Gaming World ranked it 99th among the best computer games in 1996, IGN later called it "a landmark for adventure games" and one of the best detective games ever, and Adventure Gamers ranked it 25th in 2011. Its creators reacquired the rights and re-released it on Good Old Games in 2009.

title: Sanitarium
description: Sanitarium (1998) is DreamForge's psychological horror adventure in which an amnesiac with a bandaged face wakes in a decaying asylum and drifts through nightmarish worlds, tying with Grim Fandango for Computer Gaming World's best adventure.
longDescription:
After a car crash, a man wakes from a coma, his face completely bandaged, in a dilapidated sanitarium, unable to remember who he is or how he got there; gradually he recalls his first name, Max. Searching the asylum, he is transported to strange worlds: a town of malformed children ruled by an alien entity called "Mother", a demented circus on an endless ocean, an alien hive of cyborg insects, and an Aztec village ravaged by the return of Quetzalcoatl. In some he becomes someone else, such as his sister Sarah, who died of a disease in childhood, or Grimwall, the four-armed hero of a favourite comic. Between episodes he returns to the asylum, edging closer to the truth about its head, Dr. Morgan, and his own guilt over Sarah.

It uses an isometric view and a non-tiled 2D navigation system, with each chapter having its own style, and it is often unclear whether a world is real or imagined, which underlines the horror. Players find clues, solve puzzles and talk to characters before a final challenge of reaching the end of a path past obstacles. Death simply returns the player to the start of the path without lost progress, so there is no game over.
trivia: Max was a researcher at the Mercy Foundation working on a cure for DNAV, a virus that mainly kills children.
ASC's Travis Williams said it was the first game he had found that really could "freak you out".
German sales were between 10,000 and 50,000, according to its localiser.
A former developer's Kickstarter for a spiritual successor, Shades of Sanity, failed in 2013.
ScummVM added support for it in 2022.
devStory: DreamForge Intertainment developed Sanitarium for Windows and ASC Games published it in 1998. It received favourable reviews, Next Generation calling it "vastly different and thoroughly entertaining" and wishing more companies would take gaming in such different directions. It was a commercial success, selling around 300,000 copies according to DreamForge's Mike Nicholson, and PC Accelerator said it raised the studio's profile. It tied with Grim Fandango for Best Adventure at Computer Gaming World's 1999 Premier Awards, the staff writing that it "came from out of nowhere to provide the creepiest, most compelling, and best-told story of the year", and was nominated for best adventure by Computer Games Strategy Plus, PC Gamer, GameSpot, IGNPC and the AIAS, losing each to Grim Fandango. PC Gamer praised its graphics, characters and puzzles. Adventure Gamers ranked it the 36th best adventure in 2011. Dotemu ported it to iOS and Android in 2015, and the independent game Stasis has been compared to it.

title: The Neverhood
description: The Neverhood (1996) is Doug TenNapel's claymation adventure, built from over three tons of clay, in which Klaymen discovers his origins in a deserted world floating over a void, a commercial flop that became a cult classic.
longDescription:
The Neverhood is a surreal landscape of buildings suspended over an endless void, strangely deserted apart from Klaymen, the hero; Willie Trombone, a dim helper; Klogg, a warped version of Klaymen and the villain; and fauna including the crab-like "weasels" that chase Klaymen and Willie. Klaymen wakes in a room and explores, collecting discs that tell a story narrated by Willie, viewed on terminals around the land, including the notoriously long Hall of Records, which takes several minutes to cross. They reveal that the Neverhood was made by a god-like being, Hoborg, whose companion Klogg stole his crown, leaving him inert; Willie planted Hoborg's next seed far from Klogg, and it grew into Klaymen. At the end, the player can take the crown and become a new tyrant, or revive Hoborg.

The point-and-click play emphasises solving puzzles through Klaymen's actions rather than an inventory, which is almost absent, and video sequences advance the plot. Careless players can hit game overs, one of which cannot be undone from a save and forces a restart.
trivia: TenNapel came up with the plasticine world in 1988.
It was the first stop-motion production to use consumer digital cameras professionally, beta Minolta RD-175s.
Terry Scott Taylor's soundtrack won GMR's Best Game Music of the Year.
In Japan it was released on the PlayStation as Klaymen Klaymen: The Mystery of Neverhood.
Bootleg copies gave it a huge fan base in Russia and Iran.
devStory: TenNapel left Shiny Entertainment in 1995, unhappy with how David Perry ran it, and two weeks later announced his own company, The Neverhood, Inc., staffed by Earthworm Jim veterans. Steven Spielberg's new DreamWorks Interactive, looking for unusual projects, agreed to publish it, with Microsoft also involved. Shown at E3 1996 as The Neverhood: A Curious Wad of Klay Finds His Soul, it was released after a year of work. It "won rave reviews" but sold poorly: only 37,000 copies in the US by August 1997, partly because big stores such as Target did not stock it, though total sales passed 50,000 and Gateway pre-installed "hundreds of thousands" of OEM copies. Critics loved its look but disagreed on its puzzles, GameSpot finding them unfairly abstract. Computer Games Strategy Plus and CNET Gamecenter named it the best adventure of 1996, and Computer Gaming World called it "the coolest-looking game of the year". Skullmonkeys followed in 1998, and many of the team made the spiritual successor Armikrog in 2015.

title: Toonstruck
description: Toonstruck (1996) is Burst Studios' $8 million cartoon adventure in which Christopher Lloyd, filmed in live action, is pulled into the animated world he created, with a voice cast including Tim Curry and Dan Castellaneta.
longDescription:
Animator Drew Blanc created the hit Fluffy Fluffy Bun Bun Show, though its cute talking rabbits sicken him, while his favourite creation, the wisecracking purple Flux Wildly, has never had his own show. Ordered to design more bunnies overnight, Drew falls asleep with artist's block, then is drawn through his television into a cartoon world full of his creations. There he befriends Flux and learns that Count Nefarious is ravaging the land with the Malevolator, a flying saucer that turns everything dark and twisted. King Hugh of Cutopia promises Drew passage home if he stops Nefarious, so Drew and Flux hunt across Cutopia, Zanydu and the Malevolands for the parts of the Cutifier, a counter-weapon, before a betrayal leaves Drew imprisoned in Nefarious's castle.

The point-and-click interface uses a "Bottomless Bag" inventory, a context-sensitive white-gloved hand cursor and dialogue topics shown as icons, including an ice cube for "breaking the ice" that melts as options run out. Flux can be selected and used like an item for his cartoon abilities. The first part is non-linear, with objects carried back and forth between the lands, while the second takes place entirely in the castle without Flux. As in LucasArts games, the player cannot die or reach a dead end. Joystick counted 52 characters, 80 puzzles and 120 objects.
trivia: It began in 1993 as a children's game, Trouble in Toonland, starring a boy named Daniel.
Virgin split the content in two, cutting a planned second half featuring a sky island carnival, Vincent van Gogh and a mad dentist.
Lloyd's jacket had no buttons and his hair was parted in the middle so his footage could be flipped.
Burst switched to Westwood's Kyrandia engine in 1994, keeping only about 5% of its original code.
Over 11,000 animations were made, with work by Nelvana and Rainbow Animation.
devStory: Burst, Virgin's internal studio in Irvine led by Westwood veteran Chris Yates and Neil Young, developed it from October 1993 to November 1996, inspired by The 7th Guest to make it "as cinematic as possible"; 230 people worked on it. Executive producer David Bishop's concept was reworked by writer Jennifer McWilliams into something more adult, with comic violence, parody and cynicism, and the final script was credited to McWilliams, Richard Hare and Mark Drop, with Hare directing the live-action shoot against green screen. Its influences were classic Warner Bros., Tex Avery, Hanna-Barbera and Disney cartoons. Costs passed $8 million, swollen by 18 months of debugging. The cast included Dom DeLuise and David Ogden Stiers, with Curry's character written for him and Castellaneta replacing the first choice for Flux. Critics mostly praised its animation and puzzle design, but it was a financial disappointment for Virgin, and it has since appeared on several lists of the best adventure games.

title: I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream
description: I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream (1995) is the horror adventure co-designed by Harlan Ellison from his own story, in which a hateful AI tortures the last five humans with nightmares built on their deepest flaws, a commercial failure turned cult classic.
longDescription:
Russia, China and the United States each built a vast underground computer to fight a war too complex for humans. The American Allied Mastercomputer gained sentience, absorbed the others and renamed itself AM, then, consumed by hatred for humanity, killed everyone except four men and one woman, whom it keeps alive at the centre of the Earth to torment. After 109 years, AM devises a personalised psychodrama for each, set in places such as an iron zeppelin, an Egyptian pyramid of sparking machinery, a medieval castle of witches, a jungle village and a Nazi concentration camp, preying on their fears and past failings. Each can overcome their flaws and redeem themselves with help from the Russian and Chinese supercomputers, and finally one, chosen by the player, enters AM's mind, represented as id, ego and superego, where seven endings range from eternal torment as a mouthless blob to the rebirth of humanity from survivors frozen on the Moon.

The player builds sentences from eight commands, including "Walk To", "Use", "Swallow" and "Push", on The Dreamers Guild's S.A.G.A. engine, and faces ethical dilemmas involving insanity, paranoia and genocide. A spiritual barometer rises with good acts and falls with evil ones, affecting the chances of destroying AM at the end.
trivia: Ellison wrote a 130-page script treatment with David Sears.
Sears decided to give each character their own separate narrative.
Film composer John Ottman wrote the soundtrack.
The characters never interact with one another during their stories.
Computer Gaming World named it one of the "Best 15 Sleepers of All Time".
devStory: Cyberdreams and The Dreamers Guild developed the game, co-designed by Ellison and based on his short story, with producer David Mullich supervising The Dreamers Guild's programming, art and sound. Cyberdreams published it, with MGM Interactive distributing the MS-DOS version and Acclaim the Mac version. The characters were altered from the short story, and the plot focuses on their individual psychodramas rather than adapting it directly. Released in November 1995, it was a commercial failure but received critical acclaim and developed a cult following. It won Best Game Adapted from Linear Media from the Computer Game Developers Conference, and Computer Gaming World named it Adventure Game of the Year and later listed it 134th among its 150 games of all time. In 2011, Adventure Gamers named it the 69th best adventure game ever released.

title: Fallout 2
description: Fallout 2 (1998) is Black Isle Studios' post-nuclear RPG sequel, in which the Chosen One leaves a drought-stricken tribal village to find a G.E.C.K. and runs into the Enclave, made in about nine months and ranked among the best RPGs ever.
longDescription:
In 2241, about 80 years after Fallout, the tribal village of Arroyo suffers its worst drought on record, and the village elder, daughter of the first game's Vault Dweller, sends her child, the Chosen One, to find a Garden of Eden Creation Kit capable of turning wasteland into a thriving community. The trail leads to Vault 13, now inhabited by intelligent Deathclaws, and on returning home the Chosen One finds the village captured by the Enclave, the remnants of the US government. On the Enclave's offshore oil rig, its people plan to release an airborne version of the Forced Evolutionary Virus to kill anyone with mutated DNA, and the Chosen One must free the captives and destroy the rig, killing President Dick Richardson and the cybernetic Super Mutant Frank Horrigan.

Players pick a pre-made character or build one from seven statistics, strength, perception, endurance, charisma, intelligence, agility and luck, plus 18 skills, optional traits and 69 perks earned while levelling. The world is seen from a trimetric view; players barter, recruit any of fourteen companions and track quests on a PIP-Boy 2000. Quests often allow diplomacy, combat or stealth, karma and new faction reputations change how people respond, and combat is turn-based with action points. Unlike Fallout, play can continue after the main story for thirteen in-game years.
trivia: Tim Cain announced it on Usenet in December 1997, writing that it "should take 11 months".
Many staff were moved from Planescape: Torment to finish it.
Jeffrey Jones voices the President and Michael Dorn Frank Horrigan.
It was one of the first games to feature same-sex marriage.
Chris Avellone later called it "a slapdash project without a lot of oversight".
devStory: Black Isle Studios developed Fallout 2 and Interplay published it. Cain said work began before Fallout's launch because that game had caused "a buzz in the studio", and Feargus Urquhart said Interplay's financial difficulties left the studio "basically nine months to make the whole game", forcing crunch. It received critical acclaim; GameSpot called it "a bigger, better Fallout", GamePro praised its mix of action, character interaction and non-linear play, and IGN applauded the developers for "not fixing something that wasn't broken", though critics noted frequent bugs and little change from the first game. It was nominated for role-playing game of the year by the AIAS, Computer Gaming World, GameSpot and IGN, losing each to Baldur's Gate. It reached third in PC Data's US chart in its first week of November 1998 and sold 123,000 copies in the US by March 2000, though it did poorly in the UK. PC Gamer ranked it third among the best RPGs in 2015, and Bethesda's Fallout 3 followed in 2008.

title: The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall
description: The Elder Scrolls II: Daggerfall (1996) is Bethesda's vast open-world RPG, a world "the size of Great Britain" with 15,000 settlements, in which an imperial agent untangles the politics of the Iliac Bay and a buried brass golem.
longDescription:
Sent by the Emperor to the Iliac Bay, between High Rock and Hammerfell, the player must free the ghost of King Lysandus and find out what happened to a letter from the Emperor to the former queen of Daggerfall. The letter reveals that Lysandus's mother Nulfaga knows the whereabouts of the Mantella, the key to reviving the Numidium, a powerful brass golem built by the vanished dwarves and once used by Tiber Septim to found the Empire. Through mishaps, the letter has fallen into the hands of the orc Gortworg, who consults the necromancer Mannimarco, while the Underking, who destroyed the Numidium long ago, recovers in a tomb. The player eventually chooses whom to give the Mantella, with endings in which the Underking finds rest, Gortworg founds Orsinium, the Blades reunite Tamriel, a Bay King briefly triumphs or Mannimarco becomes a god.

As in all Elder Scrolls games, players need not follow questlines or fill set roles. Over 15,000 cities, towns, villages and dungeons can be explored, houses bought, and guilds, orders and religions joined for their own quests and ranks, which shape reputation. Joining the Mages Guild unlocks custom spell creation, with the magicka cost calculated automatically, and equipment can be enchanted. Players can become vampires, werewolves or wereboars, and melee swings follow the direction of mouse movement.
trivia: It was first titled Mournhold and set in Morrowind.
Its class creation system offers GURPS-inspired bonuses, disadvantages and disabilities.
Its world covers about 209,331 square kilometres with a population of 750,000; a YouTuber took 69 hours to walk across it.
The missing Prince of Sentinel quest was influenced by The Man in the Iron Mask, and its vampire tribes by Vampire: The Masquerade.
Bethesda made it a free download for the series' 15th anniversary in 2009.
devStory: Work began right after Arena's release in March 1994, with Ted Peterson as lead designer, and Arena's experience points gave way to a system rewarding role-playing. Bethesda dropped an updated 2.5D raycast engine in favour of XnGine, one of the first truly 3D engines, and Julian LeFay said the idea was that, like a pen-and-paper game, "you could play for years". Peterson said contemporary games "weren't very interesting" as influences. MediaTech West, acquired by Bethesda in 1995, helped develop it. Completed on 31 August 1996, it was released on 20 September, and more than 100,000 of the 120,000 copies shipped sold within two days, emptying many shelves; it debuted fourth in PC Data's US chart for September. It was a critical and commercial success, selling about 700,000 copies by 2000, though its bugs upset players, and LeFay's dislike of "all the stupid patches we had for Daggerfall" made Bethesda more cautious later. Fans built mods and engine remakes, most fully Daggerfall Unity, completed in 2023. Morrowind followed in 2002.

title: Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos
description: Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos (1993) is Westwood's first-person dungeon crawler, made after leaving the D&D licence behind, in which a party fights to save King Richard from a shape-shifting witch, with Patrick Stewart voicing the king on CD.
longDescription:
King Richard of Gladstone Keep learns that the old witch Scotia has acquired the Nether Mask, a ring that lets its wearer take any form. He sends the player for the Ruby of Truth, but its guardian has been robbed and dies, and when the player returns, Scotia poisons the king and escapes. The player must find the recipe for an elixir to cure him, gather its ingredients across the realm, and combine the recovered Ruby with the king's Shard of Truth into the Whole Truth to defeat Scotia.

Like Dungeon Master and Eye of the Beholder, it is played in real time from a first-person 3D view, through forests, caves, mines, swamps and castles full of locks, switches, chests, multi-floor levels and puzzles. Players choose one of four pre-made characters, whose main statistics, might and protection, are shaped by weapons and armour, some with special properties, including a bow that never hits anything. Fighter, Rogue and Mage skills grow with use, covering combat, bows and lockpicking, and spells such as fireballs, lightning and healing, each with four power levels. Companions join and leave the party, an automap tracks progress, and shops trade in silver crowns.
trivia: Executive producer Brett Sperry came up with pre-made characters because he disliked building D&D statistics.
Its 2D engine added blurred movement for a 3D-like effect in response to Ultima Underworld.
Early versions had a bug that could make the game unwinnable; Westwood fixed one player's save file by hand.
Westwood paid $30,000 for three hours of Stewart's time, and he finished in less.
The team received a cardboard cutout of Stewart in a Star Trek uniform.
devStory: After Virgin acquired Westwood, the studio dropped the Advanced Dungeons & Dragons licence to build its own property, since, as artist Joseph Hewitt put it, it wanted to stop making games for other publishers to profit from. Lead programmer Philip Gorrow proposed the ideas and Bill Crum designed it, aiming to outdo Eye of the Beholder II with a deeper story while staying accessible. Virgin released it for MS-DOS in September 1993, and a 1994 CD-ROM version added 130 MB of speech, including narration by Stewart. It sold over 250,000 copies by November 1996. Reviews were generally positive: Computer Gaming World's Scorpia said it "breaks new ground in a number of pleasantly surprising ways" despite weak combat, InfoWorld said it was "destined to be a classic", and Computer and Video Games called it "everything Eye of the Beholder III should have been", while others found it repetitive or too easy. It was runner-up to Betrayal at Krondor for Computer Gaming World's RPG of the Year, Stewart won its Best Male Voice-Over award, and Guardians of Destiny followed in 1997.

sources.title: Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos

title: Betrayal at Krondor
description: Betrayal at Krondor (1993) is Dynamix's RPG set in Raymond E. Feist's Midkemia, structured like a novel in chapters, with use-based skills, riddle-locked chests and a story so faithful that Feist later novelised it as canon.
longDescription:
Presented like a book in chapters, narrated in the third person with a quick-save bookmark, it follows a party of two or three drawn from six characters: the fighters Locklear, James and Gorath, a moredhel chieftain who betrays his people to warn Prince Arutha of Delekhan's planned invasion, and the magicians Owyn, Patrus and Pug. Each chapter's main plot is set in one or two regions, but the player is free to explore within them, taking side quests, earning money and improving gear. Travel is in first-person 3D, with a top-down map that fills in as areas are explored, and the party camps in the wilderness to recover.

Characters have health, stamina, speed and strength; spells and attacks drain stamina before health, and injuries weaken skills. Skills, from weapon accuracy and armour repair to haggling, lockpicking and playing the lute in taverns, improve through use rather than levels, and can be emphasised to grow faster. Party members must eat rations daily, which may be spoiled or poisoned, and weapons and armour need upkeep with whetstones and hammers. Combat is turn-based on a grid, where wounded enemies may flee. Moredhel wordlock chests hold treasure behind riddles whose letter dials must be set to the answer, readable only by Gorath or with Patrus's Union spell.
trivia: Feist wrote none of the dialogue or story; designers Neal Hallford and John Cutter did, while Feist was writing The King's Buccaneer.
Feist credited Hallford and Cutter as co-authors of the 1998 novelisation Krondor: The Betrayal.
It introduced Jimmy the Hand's twin brother Lysle Rigger, later important in Feist's Serpentwar novels.
Graves can be dug up for treasure or to release ghosts.
Temples sell teleportation between temples the party has already visited.
devStory: Dynamix developed Betrayal at Krondor and Sierra released it for MS-DOS in summer 1993, with photo-based character art and a textured 3D engine. Sales of the floppy release were slow, leading Sierra to sell the Riftwar rights back to Feist, but it became a hit when re-released on CD-ROM in 1994 with CD audio and a video interview with Feist. Computer Gaming World called it "a new high-watermark in RPG design" and "a rare gem" that "actually lives up to, even exceeds, its advance billing", praising its combat as the best in a fantasy CRPG, and Pelit said it was "as big a revolution in turn-based role-playing games as the Underworlds were in 3D". Dragon's Sandy Petersen was less impressed, giving two stars and complaining of slow play and "dull maintenance activities" such as polishing armour. Sierra later gave it away as a free download in 1997, and GOG.com re-released it in 2010. A long-delayed sequel by PyroTechnix, Return to Krondor, was released in 1998 to a cooler reception.

title: Darklands
description: Darklands (1992) is MicroProse's historical fantasy RPG set in the 15th-century Holy Roman Empire, where witches, saints and alchemy are real, an early open-world game hampered by bugs that later inspired The Elder Scrolls and Pentiment.
longDescription:
Every city in the game is a real place in the 15th-century Holy Roman Empire, mostly in modern Germany but also in Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, France, Switzerland, Austria, the Czech Republic and Poland, named by their Old German names. Monsters and magic exist, but the geography is historically accurate. The world is open: players can earn a good reputation through quests or a bad one through evil deeds, and reputation varies by region, so a party can be hated in one place and exalted in another. The nonlinear main quest involves hunting witches and heretics and ends with a battle against the demon lord Baphomet in a castle found only after defeating the occupants of other fortresses, with some quest locations randomised each game.

All characters are human and defined by occupation rather than class; anyone can learn any skill, so a cleric is simply someone skilled in religion and healing. Age matters, since older characters start with more skills and better gear but begin to lose physical prowess. Most of the game uses text menus with hand-painted illustrations, while travel and real-time combat use a graphical interface, in which weapon type matters, so maces and hammers beat swords against plate armour.
trivia: It took almost three years and cost three million dollars, very large for the time.
Its manual admits the team "underestimated the time, complexity and cost of the project by a large factor".
An Amiga version was dropped because the game was too large for floppy-only Amigas.
A "character colors bug" could repaint on-screen characters in random bright colours.
It was meant to start a series, but sales were too low and the engine could not be reused.
devStory: MicroProse developed and published Darklands for MS-DOS in 1992 with many bugs, including frequent crashes; most were fixed by patches, but without widespread internet access many players only had the original release, giving it a reputation for bugginess. Computer Gaming World was divided: Scorpia liked the historical setting and use of religion but criticised repetitive encounters, bugs and the inability to save in dungeons, later calling it "a perfect example of a fine idea ... gone wrong", while Johnny L. Wilson still liked its "open-ended feel and an element of free-will". Dragon gave it four stars, calling its detail "phenomenal", and Compute! praised its choices and historical accuracy. It was nominated for PC Games' best RPG of 1992, losing to Wizardry VII, and won Game Players' PC Special Achievement Award. Its reputation has since improved: GameSpot listed it among the greatest games, Todd Howard cited it as an influence on The Elder Scrolls, and it directly inspired Obsidian's Pentiment. It was re-released on GOG.com and Steam in 2014.

title: Jagged Alliance
description: Jagged Alliance (1995) is Madlab Software's tactical RPG in which the player hires mercenaries with distinct personalities to liberate a South Atlantic island whose mutated trees yield a miracle medicinal sap, Sir-Tech's best-selling non-Wizardry game.
longDescription:
Nuclear tests in 1952 mutated the trees of Metavira, an island in the South Atlantic, and in 1995 a research team led by Brenda Richards and her father Jack finds that these sterile Fallow Trees produce a sap with remarkable medicinal properties. Brenda's assistant Lucas Santino sabotages her lab, wins control of a second science team and seizes the island with mercenaries, so the Richards fund the player to hire their own from the Association of International Mercenaries and win it back. Each day begins in a room where the player saves, hires and sleeps, then moves to a grid map of Metavira showing Fallow trees, control of each sector and the guards and tappers stationed there, all of whom must be paid.

On the top-down tactical screen, combat becomes turn-based when enemies share a sector, with action points set by attributes, interrupts, crouching, cover and stealthy movement, and aim improved by spending more points. Sixty mercenaries can be hired, up to eight at a time, each with health, agility, dexterity and wisdom, and medical, explosives, mechanical and marksmanship skills that improve through use. Wounds bleed until bandaged, injuries can permanently lower attributes, and the dead stay dead. Mercenaries demand raises as they level, some refuse to work with each other or desert overnight, and stubborn ones may refuse to move until their target dies.
trivia: Players get only a single save slot during each day.
Some mercenaries refuse to join until the player proves trustworthy.
Requests from Jack or Brenda, such as securing clean water, can be ignored but usually cause trouble later.
The 2009 DS version removed item repairs, bandage points, walking backwards and deadly eels.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 114th best computer game in 1996.
devStory: Madlab Software developed Jagged Alliance and Sir-Tech published it for MS-DOS in 1995. It received positive reviews and was a commercial success: PC Gamer US's William R. Trotter wrote that it "won plaudits from the critics and became the best-selling non-Wizardry title in Sirtech's history". Next Generation said not to expect a deep role-playing experience, but recommended it as "an entertaining mix of RPG and strategy", and PC Magazine gave it four stars out of four, calling it "one of the most enjoyably addictive games to hit the shelves in a long, long time". Computer Games Strategy Plus named it the best turn-based strategy game of 1995, tied with Heroes of Might and Magic. It spawned the Jagged Alliance series and was re-released on GOG.com in 2008 and GamersGate in 2010 with Windows support, while Strategy First and Cypron Studios developed a Nintendo DS version, published in 2009 with new music and cut-scenes.

title: X-COM: Terror from the Deep
description: X-COM: Terror from the Deep (1995) is MicroProse's sequel to UFO: Enemy Unknown, taking the alien war into Earth's oceans with underwater bases and battles, and a notoriously brutal difficulty.
longDescription:
In 2040, four decades after the first game, a transmitter left active on Cydonia wakes aliens that have lain dormant beneath Earth's seas for millions of years. They terrorise ships and port cities and kidnap people for genetic experiments, so the world's governments revive the disbanded X-COM. The aliens, cousins of the Sectoids, turn out to have arrived 65 million years ago in a vast ship, T'Leth, whose crash in what is now the Gulf of Mexico wiped out the dinosaurs, and they want to wake their unstoppable leader. Destroying T'Leth wins the war but triggers a worldwide environmental catastrophe, setting up X-COM: Apocalypse.

As before, the game has two parts: the real-time GeoScape, a global view where the player tracks craft, hires staff, trades equipment and builds bases, and the turn-based, isometric BattleScape. Almost everything now happens underwater, and since the first game's alien technology does not work in salt water, new technology must be captured and developed. Some weapons cannot be used on land, maps are more complex, magazines hold fewer rounds, and some missions, such as terror attacks on shipping routes, come in several parts where soldiers lost early do not return. Melee weapons were added at players' suggestion.
trivia: Players had called the first game too easy because a bug reverted it to Beginner difficulty, which MicroProse did not know, so the sequel was made harder.
MicroProse wanted Mythos Games to make it in six months; Julian Gollop said that could only mean reskinning.
MicroProse's UK studio licensed Mythos's code and made it within a year while Mythos began Apocalypse.
Artist Terry Greer said avoiding new features made it a schedule driven purely by asset creation.
Jake Solomon, who led 2012's XCOM, said its cruise ships were "four times longer than any human could realistically make", yet it "was awesome".
devStory: MicroProse UK reused the original engine, reskinned the graphics and wrote a new story, and released it for DOS on 1 June 1995, followed by a PlayStation version in 1996 and a Windows port in the 1998 Collector's Edition. Together with UFO: Enemy Unknown, it had sold over a million copies by March 1997. Critics mostly received it very well: PC Gamer UK called it "not only a great sequel to UFO but a superb game in its own right", and Computer Game Review gave it a Platinum Triad. Others felt it changed too little: GameSpot said that "apart from new art and a handful of new combat options, this is exactly the same game as UFO Defense, only much more difficult", and Next Generation called it "a carbon copy" of an old game, though still phenomenal. Gollop criticised its excessive difficulty and long, tedious levels. It came to Steam in 2007 under 2K Games, and the fan project OpenXCom added support for it, fixing bugs and improving the AI.

title: Dungeon Keeper 2
description: Dungeon Keeper 2 (1999) is Bullfrog's 3D sequel in which the player builds an evil underground empire, slaps imps to work and conquers the realms of Harmonia to steal their Portal Gems for the Horned Reaper.
longDescription:
King Reginald of Harmonia has twenty Portal Gems, each guarded by a realm's Lord of the Land, which confine evil creatures underground while letting good forces pass, and they have driven even serious dungeon keepers into retreat. The Horned Reaper, "Horny", believes he can take them and enlists the player to conquer the realms, chosen from a 3D map on a large table, ending with Reginald himself. Using a hand, the player digs out a dungeon with Imps, who mine gold and gems and claim territory around the Dungeon Heart, which now also regenerates mana, stores gold and produces Imps. Rooms such as the Lair, Hatchery, Training Room, Library and Treasury attract creatures through Portals, from Bile Demons to Warlocks and Salamanders, while Skeletons and Vampires come from the Prison and Graveyard.

Creatures need pay and food and dislike their heroic counterparts, and anger can lead to rebellions. Training only reaches level four, with more experience earned in the new Combat Pit or real fights, and a casino, workshop for traps and doors, torture chamber that converts captives and temple add options. Spells now cost mana rather than gold, the player can possess creatures, and Horny himself can be summoned with a talisman. Modes include My Pet Dungeon, without campaign objectives, Skirmish and networked multiplayer.
trivia: My Pet Dungeon came from testers playing levels with no invaders.
Five hidden levels are based on minigames such as golf, bowling and duck shooting.
The interface was redesigned more than ten times based on feedback.
A project manager from Mitsubishi helped the team manage milestones.
Peter Molyneux said he "liked what they did with it", though it was not exactly what he would have done.
devStory: Bullfrog built it with a team of about fifty, including Richard Ridings and programmer Alex Peters from the original, as Electronic Arts sought to capitalise on Dungeon Keeper's success; producer Nick Goldsworthy believed in carrying over what worked while adding new things. It needed hardware-accelerated 3D to keep up with trends, aiming for a renderer good enough for deathmatch, plus a software renderer for weaker PCs, and multiplayer was a major focus. Mark Knight composed the music, with Nick Laviers heading audio, and David Armor and Shintaro Kanaoya led level design. Released in June 1999, it received favourable reviews: IGN called its graphics "amazing" and GameSpot praised its graphics and sound, though both criticised the lack of major changes from the first game, and PC Gamer called the gameplay "outstanding" while noting multiplayer glitches. A PlayStation version and Dungeon Keeper 3 were cancelled. It was later released on GOG.com, Origin and Steam.

title: SimEarth: The Living Planet
description: SimEarth (1990) is Will Wright's planet simulation for Maxis, built with the help of Gaia hypothesis creator James Lovelock, in which players shape a world over ten billion years in the hope of evolving a civilisation that leaves for the stars.
longDescription:
Players adjust a planet's atmosphere, temperature and landmasses, place life on it and watch it evolve. In the "Random Planet" mode it is a software toy without set goals, though the great challenge is to evolve sentient life into an advanced civilisation whose Exodus carries it off the planet, before the world dies ten billion years after its creation as its sun becomes a red giant. Eight scenarios have goals: managing Earth's evolution in an Aquarium, Cambrian Earth and 1990 Earth, terraforming Mars, Venus, an Ice Planet and Dune, and saving a future Earth from self-replicating robots and nuclear war. A Daisy World mode, based on Lovelock's Daisyworld model, has only daisies that change colour with temperature.

Panels let players regulate everything from atmospheric gases, to three decimal places, to continental drift and mutation rates, at a cost in energy units. Disasters range from hurricanes and wildfires to disease, pollution, nuclear war and nuclear winter, and global warming can boil away the oceans. All multicellular animal groups are equal, so sapient molluscs are possible, and civilisations pass from the Stone Age to the Nanotech Age. The gameplay can be mystifying, with species thriving or dying for no clear reason.
trivia: A monolith, a take on 2001: A Space Odyssey's, can raise a species' intelligence.
Machine life can appear if a Nanotech Age city is destroyed by a nuclear explosion.
The extinct trichordates are included because the developers "felt sorry for them".
Stewart Brand, former editor of CoEvolution Quarterly, introduced Wright to Lovelock.
Lovelock said he had not seen any computer simulation of nature on SimEarth's scale.
devStory: SimEarth was Wright's second game, published by Maxis in 1990, with versions for the Macintosh, Atari ST, Amiga, IBM PC, SNES, Sega CD and TurboGrafx-16. Lovelock advised the team, especially on its geophysical models, and wrote an introduction to the manual, arguing that Gaia models linking biology and geology are "for some reason stable and able to resist perturbations", and saying the game had "a degree of realism" despite being "little more than a game", noting that many professional climate models of the time ignored clouds, the ocean or biology. Computer Gaming World called it "absolutely fascinating" and superior to SimCity in scope and replayability, though it wanted more visual feedback. It won the Software Publishers Association's 1991 awards for Best Secondary Education Program and Best Simulation Program, The One gave the DOS version 95%, and Entertainment Weekly gave the SNES version an A−. It was later re-released in the Maxis Collector Series and on the Wii Virtual Console.

title: SimAnt: The Electronic Ant Colony
description: SimAnt (1991) is Will Wright's ant colony simulation for Maxis, based on E. O. Wilson's research, in which black ants battle red ants for a suburban garden and house, and whose pheromone trails later shaped The Sims.
longDescription:
The player is an ant in a black ant colony in the back yard of a suburban home, fighting a rival colony of red ants. The player directly controls one ant, shown in yellow, and can switch to any other; the yellow ant lays pheromone trails to food or enemy nests, orders other ants to follow, digs tunnels, carries food and pebbles, shares regurgitated food with nestmates and fights, and groups can kill spiders, caterpillars and antlions. Dangers include human footsteps, electrical outlets, bug spray, lawnmowers and rain, which washes away trails and floods nests. Underground nests are shown in side view and the yard from above.

In the Quick Game, the colonies fight over one small patch of yard. In the Full Game, the black ants spread across a map of the yard and house by producing young queens and drones, winning by eliminating the red ants and driving the humans out, a goal that set it apart from the open-ended Sim games. The Experimental Game lets players control red ants and spiders and place trails, walls, rocks, ants, pesticides and food. The SNES version adds eight scenarios.
trivia: Wright co-designed and co-programmed it with his high school friend Justin McCormick, who did much of the front end at night.
Wright called it a "slight overreaction" to the seriousness of SimEarth.
Its manual includes a large amount of real information about ants.
Wright lost his home in the October 1991 Oakland firestorm, two weeks after moving the source code to his office.
Wilson said it "captured the subtleties of life in an ant colony" and that he would recommend it to entomology students.
devStory: Wright, fascinated by social insects and tired of waiting for someone else to make an ant farm simulation, based it largely on Wilson and Bert Hölldobler's textbook The Ants, especially its ideas of emergence. Production took under a year of round-the-clock work. Maxis and Broderbund released it in North America in November 1991, Ocean in Europe in 1992, and Imagineer in Japan, where Tomcat System developed the Super Famicom version later localised for the SNES. It won Best Simulation Game at the 1992 Codie awards, Dragon gave it five stars, Computer Gaming World called it "easy to get into, stimulating, fun, and increasingly challenging", and GamePro named it Educational Game of the Year. Sales were middling, over 100,000 for the PC version by April 1992, and Wright called it his biggest disappointment, feeling he failed to convey "how cool ants are"; it connected most with boys aged ten to thirteen rather than adults. Its pheromone trails became a model for the wants and needs of The Sims.

title: Pharaoh
description: Pharaoh (1999) is Impressions Games' isometric city-builder set in Ancient Egypt, built on Caesar III's engine, in which players grow Nile settlements into great cities and raise pyramids on the way to becoming Pharaoh.
longDescription:
Players oversee the construction and management of Ancient Egyptian cities, micro-managing everything needed to keep citizens fed, employed, healthy and safe from disease, disaster and war. Housing plots attract immigrants, and homes improve automatically when demands for goods, services and pleasant surroundings are met. Floodplain farms by the Nile and irrigation ditches are new, as are hunting and fishing boats, and clay, reeds and stone are turned into pottery, papyrus and building materials or traded with other cities. Firehouses and police stations are separate, the palace acts as treasury, and monuments, a new feature, take time and dedicated workers and materials to build. Five gods, Ra, Bast, Osiris, Ptah and Seth, grant gifts or disasters, so that Osiris might improve or spoil the Nile flood. Warfare is secondary, with infantry, archers, chariots and, new to the series, naval combat.

The campaign moves through five periods of Egyptian history, from nomad settlements to grand cities, with players promoted until they become Pharaoh, often choosing between peaceful and military missions. The game keeps to the order of real events, monuments, wars, disasters and the reigns of notable pharaohs, though it uses the deben as a currency, unlike real Egypt. Free-build mode offers about a dozen scenarios and a map editor.
trivia: Its rating categories rename Caesar III's Favor as "Kingdom" and replace Peace with "Monument".
The view can be rotated by 90 degrees but not zoomed.
Advisers are called Overseers.
The expansion Cleopatra: Queen of the Nile, by BreakAway Games, extended the campaign into the Hellenistic period.
Dotemu and Triskell Interactive released a remake, Pharaoh: A New Era, in 2023.
devStory: Impressions Games created Pharaoh using the engine and principles of Caesar III, making it the first in Sierra's City Building series to focus on another ancient civilisation, and Sierra Studios published it for Windows in November 1999. It received favourable reviews: Next Generation said that "pyramid building and floodplain management come together for a brilliant city builder", and GamePro, while finding "nothing new under the sun" apart from a soundtrack that aged "like something left out too long under the hot Egyptian sun", recommended it as doing what Caesar III did "with equal panache". It was an AIAS finalist for Outstanding Achievement in Art Direction, losing to Final Fantasy VIII. It was a hit in Germany, earning a Gold award for 100,000 sales and spending 13 months in Media Control's top 30, and combined worldwide sales with Caesar III passed a million by July 2000. Pharaoh Gold bundled it with Cleopatra in 2001, and Zeus: Master of Olympus followed in 2000.

title: Sid Meier's Colonization
description: Sid Meier's Colonization (1994) is Brian Reynolds and Sid Meier's turn-based strategy game of European colonisation of the New World from 1492, in which the goal is to build self-sufficient colonies and win independence from the crown.
longDescription:
The player leads the colonial efforts of England, France, the Netherlands or Spain, each with its own bonuses, on a historical map of America or a random New World. Eight Indigenous nations appear, from semi-nomadic Apache, Sioux and Tupi through agrarian Arawaks, Cherokee and Iroquois to the Aztecs and Incas. Starting with a ship and two units in 1492, players explore, meet Native peoples, found colonies and work the surrounding land, turning raw materials such as cotton and tobacco into cloth and cigars to sell in Europe at prices that rise and fall with supply and demand, while the king raises taxes. Colonists range from free citizens to indentured servants and petty criminals, and can be educated in schools, colleges and universities or trained by living in Native settlements. Missionaries can convert settlements, scouts may find the Fountain of Youth, horses breed in well-fed colonies, and pioneers build roads and clear land.

Unlike Civilization, the player builds out an established nation's colonies, whose relationship with the mother country turns from helpful to harmful. "Liberty Bells" add Founding Fathers, such as Pocahontas and Francisco Coronado, to the Continental Congress, and once enough colonists are Sons of Liberty, the player can declare independence and must defeat the king's stronger Royal Expeditionary Force, which fights poorly in rough terrain, sometimes with help from a rival power.
trivia: It was developed at MicroProse's Chapel Hill studio.
Computer Gaming World's rumour column reported in 1994 that MicroProse was making "a game like Sid Meier's Civilization" about colonisation.
Its soundtrack adapts folk songs such as "Shady Grove" and fife-and-drum tunes like "Road to Boston".
Native peoples burn colonies they capture.
Amiga Power ranked it the fourth best game of all time in 1996.
devStory: Reynolds and Meier designed Colonization, developed at MicroProse's Chapel Hill studio and published for MS-DOS in 1994, followed by Windows 3.1, Amiga and Mac versions in 1995. It had more developed visuals and handling than Civilization but markedly different gameplay. On DOS its music was synthesised in real time by the sound card, and the later Windows CD release used pre-synthesised music. It sold over 350,000 copies by September 1997. Next Generation said that "MPS Labs borrowed heavily from classic hits of the past to create a surprisingly addictive title with a flavor all its own", and PC Gamer UK ranked it the 52nd best game of all time in 1997. GOG.com released an emulated version in 2012, and Tommo bought the rights in 2015. The open-source fan remake FreeCol has been in development since 2003, and Firaxis remade it as Civilization IV: Colonization in 2008 with 3D graphics, new AI and multiplayer.

title: Master of Magic
description: Master of Magic (1994) is Simtex's fantasy 4X strategy game in which rival wizards build empires across two linked worlds, Arcanus and Myrror, a buggy release that became a cult classic often called the best of its kind.
longDescription:
Each game generates a random world, with adjustable land size, magic strength and difficulty, and players design their wizard's skills, spells and appearance and choose one of 14 races for their first city. Units explore through the fog of war, defeating monsters that guard treasure, finding city sites and discovering the Towers of Wizardry linking Arcanus, an Earth-like world, with Myrror, a parallel world of stronger magic and stranger creatures. Settlers found new cities, which produce food, gold and mana and grow through buildings, while the player researches spells.

Magic is split into Life, Death, Chaos, Nature, Sorcery and the general Arcane school; the number of spellbooks chosen in each school limits how many of its spells can be learned, and traits add further bonuses. Spells can enchant units and cities, summon creatures from demon lords to dragons, affect the whole world, or, with the enormously costly Spell of Mastery, win the game outright. When armies meet, battles move to a detailed isometric map, fought in turns until one side is destroyed or flees, or drawn after 50 turns. There are 86 unit types, many unique to a race or region, plus mercenaries and heroes with special abilities.
trivia: Its schools of magic were inspired by Magic: The Gathering.
The insectoid Klackons are among its races, introduced through Simtex's games.
A Japan-only PlayStation version was released as Civizard: Majutsu no Keifu in 1997.
Alan Emrich, who coined the term "4X", put it top of his games of all time list in 2001.
A Master of Magic II was promised for 1998 but died when Simtex closed.
devStory: Simtex developed Master of Magic and MicroProse published it for MS-DOS in 1994. Early versions were riddled with bugs and poor AI, frustrating reviewers, and GameBytes' Bill Cranston savaged it next to Civilization, though Strategy Plus named it runner-up Strategy Game of the Year and it was a Computer Gaming World nominee. Version 1.31, released in March 1995, fixed many bugs and improved the AI, and opinion warmed: IGN later called it the best fantasy strategy game ever made, Computer Gaming World inducted it into its Hall of Fame in 2005, and GameSpy said it made Steve Barcia and Simtex household names. Eurogamer wrote in 2012 that it "hasn't yet been surpassed by any other fantasy 4X game". After Simtex closed in 1997, fans continued patching it, and many later games such as Age of Wonders have been compared to it, though reviewers have said its essence has not been recaptured. It was re-released on GOG.com in 2010.

title: Panzer General
description: Panzer General (1994) is SSI's accessible World War II wargame, inspired by Sega's Daisenryaku, which linked battles into a campaign with veteran units and became the best-selling computer wargame of all time.
longDescription:
It is a turn-based operational wargame on hex maps, with units roughly the size of battalions and scenarios that approximate historical situations. Players fight single battles as Axis or Allies against the computer or a human, or a campaign as a German general. Its novel feature linked scenarios into a campaign spanning 1939 to 1945, where units gain experience and grow stronger, and victories earn prestige to upgrade and buy units and choose better next battles.
