Combined-arms tactics are essential: artillery softens dug-in positions but needs protection, bombers can take out artillery but first air defences must go, fighters must both destroy enemy aircraft and escort bombers, and engineers bridge rivers, all rewarding a Blitzkrieg advance.

There are 38 scenarios, and the German campaign can start in Poland, North Africa, Barbarossa, Italy or Kharkov. Most missions demand capturing objective cities within a set number of turns, with a major victory for finishing at least five turns early, while later ones demand holding out. Major victories can change history: after beating France the player can invade Britain, and after taking Moscow early, even attack Washington, but failure ends with the general sacked or Germany driven back to Berlin.
trivia: SSI's team had played a Japanese Sega Genesis version of Daisenryaku extensively.
Designer Chuck Kroegel called its structure "diametrically opposed to the Gary Grigsby type of game that SSI was used to making".
It was particularly popular in Germany.
Computer Gaming World listed its game over scene eighth among "the 15 best ways to die in computer gaming".
60,000 of its first 250,000 sales came from the PlayStation version.
devStory: SSI was inspired by Daisenryaku's streamlined design, though founder Joel Billings was initially hesitant, and Graeme Bayless praised that game for boiling down "a highly complex subject... to the pertinent parts". Released in 1994, Panzer General was a major hit, selling over 250,000 copies at full price by August 1996 and many more afterwards, SSI's best-selling game in any genre; Retro Gamer called it the "greatest-selling true wargame of all time" in 2007. It won Computer Gaming World's Wargame of the Year and PC Gamer US's Best Wargame, finishing runner-up to X-COM for Game of the Year, and was the first wargame since 1987 to top CGW's reader poll; the magazine later ranked it the 15th best computer game ever, and it won the 1995 Origins Award. 3DO and PlayStation versions were also well reviewed. Computer Games Strategy Plus suggested wargamers might divide history into "Before Panzer General, and After", and GameSpot said it resurrected the genre. Allied General, Panzer General II and other sequels followed.

title: Wing Commander: Privateer
description: Wing Commander: Privateer (1993) is Origin Systems' open-ended space game in which freelancer Grayson Burrows trades, smuggles, hunts bounties or turns pirate across the Gemini Sector, while uncovering an ancient alien artefact.
longDescription:
Unlike the main Wing Commander games, the player is not a navy pilot but a freelancer who can be a pirate, merchant, mercenary or any mix of them, and can ignore the plot entirely or keep adventuring after finishing it. Play consists of flying and fighting in star systems, jumping between them, landing on bases and planets, talking to people and buying and selling equipment and goods across the quadrants of the Gemini Sector. Seven factions, merchants, bounty hunters, Retros, pirates, militia, the Terran Confederation and the Kilrathi, react according to their nature and the player's actions. Merchants profit from price differences between planets, while randomly generated missions from the mission computer pay for better weapons and equipment. Flight is seen from the cockpit, with combat like other Wing Commander games of the time, and bases use static first-person views.

In the story, a mysterious drone is attacking ships. On New Detroit, a man named Sandoval hires Burrows and gives him an artefact, then turns up dead. The xenoarchaeologist Dr. Monkhouse reveals it is half of a map left by the ancient Steltek, leading Burrows to a powerful weapon, a deadly drone and a Steltek scout come to remove the last traces of their technology.
trivia: Burrows's name was unknown for years, and fans called him "Brownhair" after "Bluehair", the series' Christopher Blair.
The Speech Pack added voices to in-flight communications, and the voice of the hero changed for the CD edition.
The Righteous Fire expansion pits Burrows against Retros, religious extremists led by Mordecai Jones.
Unlike the original, Righteous Fire cannot be lost by failing a mission.
A Privateer television series was planned to debut in 1997.
devStory: Origin Systems released Privateer in September 1993, with VGA pseudo-3D graphics at 320x200 in 256 colours. It was very popular, second in PC Data's DOS chart for September 1993 and first in Computer Gaming World's reader survey that November. The magazine liked its less structured story with Ultima-like "real moral choices" but called the writing "sophomoric" and recommended it to owners of high-end 486s, later noting unusual incompatibilities with sound cards and joysticks. It was runner-up for Computer Gaming World's Action Game of the Year, the editors saying it "introduced a free-wheeling open-endedness". White Wolf said it was "as close as you'll get to a true roleplaying experience". A 1994 CD-ROM edition included Righteous Fire and full speech. Privateer 2: The Darkening, led by Erin Roberts and featuring Clive Owen and Christopher Walken, was a self-contained spin-off in 1996, and Chris Roberts later made Freelancer with similar ideas. It was re-released on GOG.com in 2011.

title: Interstate '76
description: Interstate '76 (1997) is Activision's funk-soaked vehicular combat game set in an alternate 1976 where the oil crisis never ended, in which vigilantes in armed muscle cars fight to stop a plot against America's oil reserve.
longDescription:
In an alternate 1976, the 1973 oil crisis was never resolved, the American Southwest has fallen into lawlessness, and corrupt police can do nothing, so some civilians become vigilantes, arming and armouring their cars. When vigilante Jade Champion is found murdered in a junkyard, fellow vigilante Taurus persuades her reluctant brother Groove to join his investigation. Groove proves a talented driver and fighter, and the pair find a briefcase of money and plans for a nuclear device, leading them to a plot by Jade's killer, Antonio Malochio, who has been hired by OPEC to destroy North America's largest oil reserve and keep prices high.

Vehicles have a damage model affecting both looks and handling: weapons can be destroyed and tyres popped, and hitting buildings, signs or other cars causes damage. The "T.R.I.P." (Total Recreational Interactive Production) mode tells the story in episodes, alongside online "Multi Melee" deathmatch, "Auto Melee" against computer cars and standalone "Scenarios". Players choose weapons and accessories, tune engines, brakes and tyres, and balance weight and chassis between armour and stability. The cars faithfully reproduce real vehicles of the era, though under changed names for licensing reasons.
trivia: Lead designer Zack Norman got the 1970s idea while considering spending his MechWarrior 2 bonus on a muscle car.
Director Sean Vesce said the MechWarrior 2 engine was "held together with super glue and bubble gum".
Its soundtrack was played by a session band, Bullmark, with Primus drummer Brain and Third Eye Blind bassist Arion Salazar.
The team avoided more detailed models for cut-scenes to keep a consistent style.
20th Century Fox acquired film rights in 1998, but the film never happened.
devStory: Activision built Interstate '76 on a heavily modified version of its MechWarrior 2 engine, aiming, in Norman's words, for "a real action-simulation hybrid" with "a style and a soul that hadn't been exploited before". Released on 26 March 1997, it sold 74,028 copies in the US that year and received favourable reviews for its originality, style, music and characters, though critics faulted its graphics and the difficulty of driving and shooting at once. Next Generation said it "really is 'the funkiest PC game ever'", and GamePro said "every barb from Taurus is a treasure". It was runner-up to Quake II for action game of the year at Computer Gaming World and PC Gamer, winning Computer Gaming World's Artistic Achievement award and PC Gamer's music and cinematics awards. PC Gamer ranked it the 26th best computer game in 1998, calling it "the most original action game released in a decade". The Nitro Pack expansion followed in 1998, then the sequel Interstate '82 and the console spin-off Vigilante 8.

title: Rise of the Triad: Dark War
description: Rise of the Triad (1995) is Apogee's first-person shooter that began as a Wolfenstein 3D sequel, sending a UN special forces team against a cult on San Nicolas Island with jump pads, magic weapons and "Ludicrous Gibs".
longDescription:
A team of special operatives, the HUNT (High-risk United Nations Task-force), is sent to San Nicolas Island to investigate deadly cult activity in an ancient monastery, only for patrols to destroy their boat, their one way home. Learning that the cult plans to destroy nearby Los Angeles, they fight their way into the monastery. Players choose between five characters, Taradino Cassatt, Thi Barrett, Lorelei Ni, Doug Wendt and Ian Paul Freeley, who differ in hit points, speed and accuracy, and collect keys to progress through mostly linear levels, some with multiple exits. Enemies, played by digitised actors who were mostly Apogee staff and their families, may beg for their lives, fake death, dodge, ambush from the floor, fire nets or steal weapons.

Thirteen weapons fall into bullet weapons with infinite ammunition, missile weapons and magic weapons, and players carry the three bullet weapons plus one missile or magic weapon. Jump pads launch players upward or into long jumps, glass shatters, shooting lights dims rooms, and firing a missile at certain food warms it to restore more health. Sometimes kills produce extra gore with a "Ludicrous Gibs!" message, and gore can be set from bloodless to extreme. The COMM-BAT multiplayer supports up to eleven players across nine modes, including tag, a "Hunter" mode and capture the flag.
trivia: Its working titles were Wolfenstein II and Wolfenstein 3D: Rise of the Triad.
Scott Miller suspected id cancelled the Wolfenstein follow-up to keep attention on Doom.
The team called itself the Developers of Incredible Power; its planned second game, Prey, was later recycled by Human Head.
Female versions of some enemies were cut to save memory and shown in the credits as "actors who were cut from the game".
Its engine added elevation, panoramic skies, fog and floating "gravitational anomaly disks" for level-over-level areas.
devStory: It began as a follow-up to Wolfenstein 3D using that engine, and after id cancelled the project, Tom Hall wrote a new storyline so the team's assets would not go to waste, eventually moving away from Nazis to a cult reportedly inspired by the Californian legend of the Dark Watchers. Hall led the Developers of Incredible Power, including Mark Dochtermann, Jim Dosé, Joseph Selinske and Susan Singer, some of whom went on to Duke Nukem 3D. Apogee released the shareware episode, The HUNT Begins, in 1994 and the full game in 1995, and Miller estimated it sold around 110,000 copies. Next Generation called it an entertaining but undistinguished Doom replica that "never strays far enough from the Doom herd to fully break free", while Świat Gier Komputerowych gave it 85%, praising its presentation and features such as looking up and down, though it found the AI weak and the maps awkward. A remake by Interceptor Entertainment followed in 2013, and Nightdive's remaster, Ludicrous Edition, in 2023.

title: Starsiege: Tribes
description: Starsiege: Tribes (1998) is Dynamix's squad-based online shooter of jetpacks, vast outdoor maps and capture the flag, whose accidental "skiing" exploit became a defining technique and which won the AIAS online game of the year.
longDescription:
In the 40th century, humanity has spread across the galaxies through jumpgates, and factions fight for territory: the Children of the Phoenix, descended from people cut off from the Great Human Empire, the imperial knights of the Blood Eagle, and the lesser Diamond Sword and Starwolf, among countless splinter tribes. Players fight for one of the four major tribes across 40 levels, mostly outdoor environments in weather from sunshine to hail that stretch for several in-game kilometres, with bases scattered across them. Modes are capture the flag, run on 75 percent of servers, deathmatch, capture and hold, defend and destroy, the second most popular, and find and retrieve.

Light, medium and heavy armour determine armour, energy, ammunition and which weapons and equipment can be used, so only heavy armour carries the mortar and only light the sniper rifle. Inventory stations supply armour, vehicles, eight weapons and packs, and bases include generators, whose destruction shuts down turrets and stations, as well as sensors. Every player has a jetpack drawing on an energy cell, used for flight and evasive hops. By tapping jump with the right timing while descending a slope, players could "ski", building momentum to cross maps at high speed, an exploit of the physics that Dynamix made a proper feature in Tribes 2.
trivia: It follows the story of Metaltech: Earthsiege and Starsiege.
It was announced in May 1998.
A planned expansion, Tribes Extreme, with single-player missions and bots, was cancelled.
It sold 98,840 copies in 1999, against hopes of more than 250,000.
Vivendi gave it away free with Tribes 2 in 2004 to promote Tribes: Vengeance.
devStory: Dynamix developed Starsiege: Tribes and Sierra On-Line published it in 1998. It received favourable reviews: GameSpot found an almost perfect balance between gameplay, online connectivity and speedy performance, praising its seamless indoor-outdoor maps while noting weak training and queues at weapon consoles, and later named it among the greatest games of all time; Next Generation said it had "the design and the technology to be the next standard in Internet action gaming". It won the AIAS's Online Action/Strategy Game of the Year, losing PC Action Game and Computer Entertainment Title of the Year to Half-Life, as well as Online Game of the Year from Computer Games Strategy Plus and IGN. PC Gamer US gave it its 1999 Special Achievement in Innovation, saying "Tribes re-wrote the rules of online combat" with "airtight networking code". Tribes 2 followed in March 2001 and Irrational Games' Tribes: Vengeance in 2004.

title: Quake II
description: Quake II (1997) is id Software's science fiction shooter in which a lone marine fights through the alien Strogg's homeworld, a sequel in name only that shipped with native OpenGL and became one of the most widely licensed engines of its time.
longDescription:
Humanity's war against the Strogg, half-mutant, half-machine aliens who turn captured organisms into cyborgs, reaches their home planet, Stroggos, in "Operation Alien Overlord". Most of the invading marines are captured or killed as they near the landing zone, but Bitterman survives when another marine's capsule collides with his and sends him crashing far short. He fights alone through the industrial Strogg city, destroying strategic targets, and finally kills the Strogg leader, the Makron, in his orbital asteroid base. Unlike the first game's mix of science fiction and dark fantasy, it is purely science fiction.

Movement is slower than in Quake, and players can now crouch. Four of Quake's weapons return, redesigned, joined by the Blaster, Machine Gun, Chain Gun, Hyperblaster, Railgun and BFG10K, with power-ups including Quad Damage, Invulnerability, the Enviro-Suit and Silencer. Single-player now has mission objectives tied to the story, such as stealing a Tank Commander's head to open a door, much larger levels linked by a hub to travel back and forth, captured, insane comrades, and enemies that show visible wounds. Multiplayer offers deathmatch, co-op, one-on-one tournament play and capture the flag, with male, female and cyborg player models and customisable skins.
trivia: Names considered for a new property included "Strogg", "Lock and Load" and "Wor"; legal concerns led to the Quake name.
Tim Willits said its premise drew on The Guns of Navarone.
It was made by a 13-person team, and it was American McGee's last id game.
It was id's first game not released for MS-DOS, running natively on Windows 95.
GamePro praised the female multiplayer model as "an overdue nod to the growing number of QuakeGrrls".
devStory: It began as a new game, but after failed attempts id kept the Quake name while dropping the original's Lovecraftian horror for science fiction; with John Romero gone, Kevin Cloud led a more story-driven design, a decision that was controversial inside the company. Activision obtained worldwide distribution rights in May 1997, and it was released on 9 December after about a year of development, with music by Sonic Mayhem and Bill Brown. Its game code was published so modders could change it, and the full source was released under the GPL in 2001. The engine powered games including SiN, Heretic II, Daikatana, Soldier of Fortune, Kingpin and Anachronox, and Half-Life used it early on. It received very positive reviews: GamePro said it "lives up to its impossibly high hype", and GameSpot called it "the only first-person shooter to render the original Quake entirely obsolete". It won the AIAS's PC Action Game of the Year and Computer Gaming World's Action Game of the Year, and Nightdive released an enhanced version in 2023.

title: Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II
description: Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II (1997) is LucasArts' sequel to Dark Forces in which Kyle Katarn learns the ways of the Force and the lightsaber to stop his father's killers reaching the Valley of the Jedi, with light and dark side endings.
longDescription:
One year after Return of the Jedi, the Dark Jedi Jerec kills Jedi Master Qu Rahn while hunting for the sacred Valley of the Jedi, whose location was known to Morgan Katarn, Kyle's father, whom Jerec also murdered. Kyle, now a mercenary for the New Republic, learns the truth from the double-crossing droid 8t88, recovers his father's data disk and, guided by Rahn's spirit, finds a map to the Valley and Rahn's old lightsaber. With his partner Jan Ors, he battles Jerec's Dark Jedi, Yun, Pic, Gorc, Maw, Sariss and Boc, before facing Jerec himself in the Valley.

Primarily a first-person shooter with an optional third-person view, it has twenty-one levels with objectives. From level three, Kyle has a lightsaber, which also lights dark areas, deflects blaster fire and cuts through obstacles, and Force powers. Fourteen powers are split into light, such as healing and persuasion, dark, such as throwing objects and choking enemies, and neutral, such as jumping higher and running faster, upgraded with stars earned by completing levels and finding secrets. Sparing innocent characters and choosing light powers leads to the light side ending, while harming them and choosing dark powers leads to the dark. Multiplayer supports eight players on a LAN and 32 online through the MSN Gaming Zone.
trivia: Its cut-scenes included the first lightsaber footage filmed since Return of the Jedi in 1983.
The Force upgrade system was designed with role-playing games in mind.
Its Sith engine is a "true" 3D engine, replacing Dark Forces' 2.5D Jedi engine.
The 1998 expansion Mysteries of the Sith lets players control Mara Jade.
Next Generation said it was "to first-person shooters what sliced bread is to wheat products".
devStory: Justin Chin, who had worked on Dark Forces, led development, making the Force and the lightsaber its most significant additions. The Sith engine supported Direct3D 5.0 hardware acceleration, making it one of the early games to use 3D acceleration through Direct3D, and its 3D sound was extensively tuned for immersion, while full-motion video scenes used live actors over pre-rendered backgrounds. It debuted third on PC Data's US chart in October 1997 and sold 247,036 copies in the US by the end of the year. It received universal acclaim, averaging 91 on Metacritic: GamePro gave it perfect scores, calling it "probably the most fun you'll have with a corridor shooter this season", and Game Revolution said "the use of the lightsaber is just awesome", though IGN found some levels linear, with "bald key hunts", and opinions on the AI were mixed. It has been cited as one of the best games of all time. Mysteries of the Sith followed in February 1998 and Jedi Knight II: Jedi Outcast in 2002.

sources.title: Star Wars Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II

title: Grand Prix 2
description: Grand Prix 2 (1996) is Geoff Crammond's officially licensed simulation of the 1994 Formula One season, a near one-man project whose adjustable driving aids made it both a punishing sim and an accessible racer, selling 1.5 million copies.
longDescription:
It simulates the 1994 Formula One season with all 16 circuits and 28 drivers in 14 teams. Unlike the real season, where teams repeatedly changed drivers and liveries, it uses a single line-up and set of liveries from the 1994 German Grand Prix, where all teams ran without tobacco sponsors, so Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger, killed at the San Marino Grand Prix, are absent, as is Nigel Mansell. Some circuits show safety changes made during the season. Players take any of the 28 seats through practice, qualifying and races, a full championship or a customisable Quickrace, with hotseat and modem or LAN multiplayer; in turn-based multiplayer, the computer drives other players' cars while they wait.

Seven driving aids, including steering and braking help, automatic gears, traction control and indestructibility, can be switched on or off, with fewer allowed at higher difficulties. Cars can suffer engine, gearbox and electrical failures, trailing smoke or flames before parking at the roadside, the first game to show visual car failures. Setups can be tuned in great detail, a simulated TV view joins the cockpit camera, and a replay shows the last 30 seconds. There is no wet weather and no black flag system; cutting corners simply slows the car for a time.
trivia: It was released as Grand Prix II in North America.
It was the first serious racing sim with all three axes, letting cars get airborne, though they could not flip over.
In some cases the game crashed when a car was about to overturn.
A January 2025 fan "x86 mod" let it run natively on Windows for the first time.
A Steam re-release is planned as Geoff Crammond Racing 2, since EA holds the F1 licence.
devStory: Crammond developed it as the follow-up to 1991's Formula One Grand Prix, a rare one-man project in an industry dominated by teams, with SVGA graphics, 3D texture mapping, liveries mapped over 3D car models and an early 3D physics engine. MicroProse released it for DOS in July 1996 under an official FIA licence. Sales reached 500,000 by September, 750,000 by January 1997, driven largely by Europe, and 1.5 million by late 2000. Critics hailed it as the class of the field: GameSpot's Jim Varner praised how its aids made it both "a phenomenally complex and realistic driving sim" and one of the most fun arcade racers, calling it "unquestionably the best racing game yet made for the PC", and PC Zone gave it 95%. Next Generation named it the 46th best game of all time, and PC Gamer UK ranked it and its predecessor seventh in 1997. A large modding community has kept it updated with new seasons, and the modern MicroProse acquired the series rights in 2025.

title: Blade Runner
description: Blade Runner (1997) is Westwood Studios' "real-time 3D adventure", a sidequel to Ridley Scott's film in which rookie Blade Runner Ray McCoy hunts replicants in 2019 Los Angeles, with randomised suspects and thirteen endings.
longDescription:
Shortly after the film begins, McCoy is assigned to track down replicants suspected of slaughtering animals, a crime almost as serious as murder because most species are extinct. His investigation leads to a frame-up by the corrupt Lieutenant Guzza and into the underworld of Los Angeles. The story runs parallel to the film's, recreating its locations and some scenes and music; Deckard is mentioned and seen but never speaks, while Sean Young, Brion James, James Hong, Joe Turkel and William Sanderson reprise their roles. The supporting cast includes Lisa Edelstein as fellow Blade Runner Crystal Steele, Mark Rolston as the replicant leader Clovis and Pauley Perrette as fourteen-year-old Lucy Devlin.

Play centres on detective work: searching crime scenes, questioning suspects and analysing clues, which are filed automatically in McCoy's Knowledge Integration Assistant. The ESPER system enhances photographs to reveal hidden details, and the Voight-Kampff machine tests whether subjects are replicants by watching needles as the player chooses questions of low, medium or high intensity, after which the player can kill, arrest or release them. Which characters are replicants is randomised each game. McCoy's attitude in conversation can be set from Polite to Surly or Erratic, or chosen line by line, and the world runs in real time, with other characters pursuing their own aims, leading to one of thirteen endings.
trivia: Westwood used its own software voxel renderer rather than polygon-based 3D acceleration.
McCoy shares his apartment with his dog, Maggie.
Uploading data to the police mainframe brings in evidence found by other Blade Runners at random times.
A sequel was dropped because its production cost was thought commercially unviable.
Legal entanglements kept it off digital stores until GOG.com released it in December 2019.
devStory: Westwood Studios developed Blade Runner and Virgin Interactive published it for Windows in November 1997. Advertised as a "real-time 3D adventure game", it was one of the first adventures to combine 3D characters with a world that progressed in real time. It was a commercial success, selling over a million copies, and received generally positive reviews, averaging 77% on GameRankings. Next Generation gave it four stars, saying "all movie-licensed game publishers should take note", GamePro praised its faithfulness, cinematics and "riveting plot and slick style" while criticising the characters' "overwrought body language", and Science Fiction Weekly gave it an A+. It won the AIAS's PC Adventure Game of the Year and was nominated for PC Gamer's Best Adventure Game. Nightdive Studios and Alcon Entertainment released an Enhanced Edition for PC and consoles on 23 June 2022.

title: Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri
description: Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri (1999) is Firaxis Games' science fiction 4X game and spiritual sequel to Civilization, in which seven ideological factions colonise the planet Chiron as the world itself awakens to sentience.
longDescription:
Picking up where Civilization's space race ends, the UN colony ship Unity reaches Alpha Centauri in the 22nd century, but a reactor malfunction wakes the crew early, cuts contact with Earth and leads to the captain's assassination. The leaders on board form ideological factions, and as the ship breaks up, seven escape pods land on Planet: Deirdre Skye's environmentalist Gaia's Stepdaughters, Sheng-Ji Yang's Legalist Human Hive, Prokhor Zakharov's University of Planet, Nwabudike Morgan's capitalist Morgan Industries, Corazon Santiago's militarist Spartan Federation, Miriam Godwinson's Lord's Believers and Pravin Lal's Peacekeeping Forces. Planet's native xenofungus spawns mindworms that attack bases, and a voice begins invading the player's dreams, warning against pollution and terraforming, until it emerges that Planet is a dormant hive organism nearing a metamorphosis that would destroy humanity.

Played from an isometric view, it reworks Civilization II's bases, facilities, secret projects and research, but technology unlocks unit components so players design their own units. Players terraform the land, allocate energy between research and reserves, adjust their faction through social engineering, send probe teams to sabotage and steal, and negotiate in the Planetary Council. Victory comes through conquest, a three-quarter vote, cornering the Global Energy Market or the Ascent to Transcendence, as humanity joins Planet's metamorphosis.
trivia: Faction leaders are developed through monologues accompanying each scientific discovery.
Native life fights with psionic combat, which ignores weapons and armour.
Its E3 1998 showing won Best Turn Based Strategy in a vote of 27 journalists.
Critics compared its story to Kubrick, Frank Herbert, Arthur C. Clarke and Isaac Asimov.
Despite acclaim, it sold the fewest copies of any game in the Civilization series.
devStory: Sid Meier and Brian Reynolds, designers of Civilization and Civilization II, made it after leaving MicroProse to found Firaxis Games with Jeff Briggs. Electronic Arts released it and its expansion, Alien Crossfire, which added five human and two alien factions, in 1999, and Aspyr and Loki ported both to Mac and Linux the following year. It improved on Civilization II's engine with simultaneous multiplayer, social engineering, climate, customisable units, native life, more diplomatic and spy options, more ways to win and greater moddability. It received wide acclaim, scoring 92% on GameRankings and 89% on Metacritic, and was compared favourably to Civilization II, with praise for its writing, voice acting, custom units and deep technology tree, and it won several game of the year and strategy game of the year awards. It sold over 100,000 copies in its first two months, was the tenth best-selling US computer game of the first half of 1999 and reached 281,115 US sales by September 2000.

title: Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares
description: Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares (1996) is Simtex's space 4X sequel with multi-planet systems, custom races and the vengeful Antarans, an Origins Award winner regarded as a defining benchmark of the genre.
longDescription:
Long ago, the Orions and the Antarans fought a war that devastated most of the galaxy. The victorious Orions imprisoned the Antarans in a pocket dimension rather than exterminate them, then left, leaving the powerful robotic warship Guardian to protect their homeworld. Some time into each game, the escaped Antarans begin sending ever-stronger fleets to destroy colonies before vanishing. Victory comes from conquering every opponent, being elected supreme leader with two-thirds of the galaxy's population-based votes, or attacking the Antaran homeworld through a Dimensional Portal; taking Orion does not win outright but yields the Avenger starship and unresearchable technologies.

It is more complex than Master of Orion, borrowing mechanics from Master of Magic. Star systems hold up to five planets, shared with rivals, and food must be balanced, carried by freighters that a single enemy warship can blockade. Thirteen races, three new, can be joined by custom races built from ten "picks", and governments range from free dictatorships to democracy, unification and feudalism. Research spans eight areas, with miniaturisation shrinking components as technology advances, and leaders can be hired for colonies and ships. Players design warships, which can now turn in tactical combat, marines can board enemy ships, and planets can be destroyed outright. Multiplayer supports up to eight players.
trivia: It was designed by Steve Barcia and Ken Burd.
Fans regard race design as a crucial part of strategy, and reviewers called the "creative" trait overpowered.
Telepathic races can mind-control enemy colonies, which become instantly loyal.
Slow loading of artwork from CD led to advice to copy the whole disc to the hard drive.
MacSoft published a Mac version in partnership with MicroProse a year later.
devStory: Simtex, maker of Master of Orion and Master of Magic, developed it, and MicroProse published the PC version in 1996. It reached tenth on PC Data's chart in November 1996 and passed 200,000 global sales by mid-January 1997. Reviews were generally favourable, and it won the Origins Award for Best Fantasy or Science Fiction Computer Game of 1996, though reviewers disagreed about its added micromanagement: Bruce Geryk preferred the first game's simplicity, Tom Chick found it far more engaging, GameSpot's Trent Ward said its micromanagement was "everything that the hard-core veteran dreams of" but inaccessible to novices, and Next Generation felt it was "a little too stagnant". Reviewers praised the replay value of its many galaxies, races and options, Macworld saying its "countless strategy options will keep you coming back for more". It has since come to be regarded as a defining benchmark of space 4X games, with a large and active fan base.

sources.title: Master of Orion II: Battle at Antares

title: Myth: The Fallen Lords
description: Myth: The Fallen Lords (1997) is Bungie's dark fantasy real-time tactics game without bases or resources, where physics-driven arrows and bouncing grenades make friendly fire a constant danger, and whose success brought Bungie to Microsoft's attention.
longDescription:
For fifty years, the dark lord Balor and his lieutenants, the Fallen Lords, have been conquering the West, and in the seventeenth year of the war only one major city and a few towns remain in the hands of the Light, led by the Nine, powerful sorcerers known as Avatara, chief among them Alric. Players follow the Legion, an elite unit of the Light, as it tries to turn the tide and defeat Balor.

Unlike real-time strategy games, there is no base building, resource gathering or research; each level begins with the army already assembled, units do not heal, and new ones arrive only as scripted reinforcements. Players select units by clicking, double-clicking, shift-clicking or dragging a box, assign groups to keys, use nine formations and set facing with "gesture clicking", while the camera can be moved, orbited, panned and zoomed freely. A physics engine governs everything: severed heads bounce off units, a dwarf's missed Molotov cocktail can roll back downhill into his own side, and arrows drift with simulated aiming error or hit allies in melee. Each unit records its kills and battles survived, and while single-player uses only the Light, online multiplayer lets players command both Light and Dark.
trivia: It was the first game Bungie developed and released simultaneously for PC and Mac.
It sold over 350,000 copies, earning back roughly seven times its budget.
Bungie gave volunteer group MythDevelopers access to the source code to keep the games running.
GameSpot said the 1.1 patch fixed its "absurd level of difficulty" and unit-facing problems.
Microsoft bought Bungie in 2000 so Halo could launch with the Xbox.
devStory: Bungie, then known mainly as a Mac developer, released The Fallen Lords in North America in November 1997, and Eidos published it in Europe in February 1998. It received universal acclaim, averaging 91 on Metacritic, and was seen as a defining title of the emerging real-time strategy genre; reviewers praised its plot, graphics, level design, online multiplayer and difference from traditional RTS games, while criticising a single-player campaign many found far too hard even on the lowest setting, and awkward unit control. PC Zone praised its interface, camera, 3D physics and shadows but described "an overwhelming frustration" in play. It won Strategy Game of the Year from PC Gamer and Computer Gaming World and Game of the Year from Computer Games Strategy Plus and Macworld. At the time it was Bungie's most successful game, bringing the studio to the attention of PC gamers and Microsoft. Myth II: Soulblighter followed, and fan groups such as Project Magma have kept the series alive online for over a decade.

title: Dark Reign: The Future of War
description: Dark Reign: The Future of War (1997) is Auran's science fiction real-time strategy game for Activision, with two truly different sides, terrain-based line of sight and unusually customisable unit AI, which sold 685,000 copies.
longDescription:
Like Command & Conquer, players build structures for production, resource gathering, power and defence, paying in credits earned from shipments of water from fresh springs, while power comes from harvesting Taelon. Deposits regenerate but slow down when depleted, and the Water Contamination Unit can destroy enemy water supplies. The two sides have completely different units: the Freedom Guard are weaker but faster and better on rough terrain, suited to raids and ambushes, and can "phase" underground to hide, while the Imperium rely on armour, firepower and hover technology to overwhelm their enemies. An Infiltrator can sneak into an enemy headquarters to steal weapon designs, at increasing risk the longer it stays.

Line of sight depends on terrain height and shape, so forests suit ambushes and mountains limit recon. Buildings can be powered down to save energy, production queues are shared across factories, and named paths let units patrol or loop. Units can be told to search and destroy, harass or scout, and their pursuit range, damage tolerance and independence can each be set. In the story, the player is one of the last Tograns, whose world was destroyed in the war between the two sides, and must win simulations of famous battles before travelling back in time to Strata-7 to save the philosopher Alpheus Togra.
trivia: It began as Corporation: Offworld, shown to Activision in June 1996 alongside a sister game, Wild West.
Activision layered a new story over Auran's game to create Dark Reign.
It shipped with a mission construction kit for building maps and whole campaigns.
An expansion, Rise of the Shadowhand, was released on 26 March 1998.
A licensed Xbox Live Indie port, Dark Reign Redux, appeared in 2013 but was later taken down.
devStory: Auran co-founder Greg Lane led development of Corporation: Offworld, whose units, unit AI, tile-blending, map and production systems and real-time line of sight were already in place when Activision signed it in 1996. Auran kept building its Tactics Engine while Activision added a new story, and Dark Reign was released for Windows in 1997 with a large single-player campaign of thirteen missions, playable from either side, and online multiplayer. Edge praised its three-dimensional terrain for affecting how units moved. It was critically and commercially successful, with global sales of 685,000 by 2004, and a prequel, Dark Reign 2, followed on 3 July 2000.

sources.title: Dark Reign: The Future of War

title: Close Combat
description: Close Combat (1996) is Atomic Games' real-time World War II wargame, born as Beyond Squad Leader, in which every soldier has a simulated psyche and may refuse orders, freeze or go berserk under fire.
longDescription:
It simulates short-range battles between the US 29th Infantry Division and Germany's 352nd Infantry Division in the six weeks after the Normandy landings, seen from a top-down view rather than the isometric view of games like Warcraft II. Players control infantry, crew-served weapons and armour on either side with six commands, move, fire, move fast, defend, hide and smoke, and must use cover, suppression and positioning, since soldiers are vulnerable in groups and when charging. Battles take place among bocage, open plains and towns such as Saint-Lô, in 39 single battles or a campaign from the landings to Saint-Lô, which the Americans win by taking the town within 43 days. Two players can also fight each other.

Each soldier behaves according to a simulated psyche based on fatigue, preparedness, experience and past success, turned into probability tables that change during play. Stress and fear make squads reluctant to move or shoot, or inaccurate, and soldiers under severe stress may become shell-shocked or berserk. Units often disobey poor or dangerous orders, such as leaving cover unprotected, and the AI lets even unattended squads keep fighting with sensible tactics.
trivia: Atomic's president Keith Zabalaoui was inspired to make a real-time wargame by Dune II.
Military psychologist Dr. Steven Silver, a specialist in PTSD, helped build its psychological models.
Its early code name was Project X.
PC Gamer US called Beyond Squad Leader "perhaps the most eagerly awaited PC wargame ever".
The series grew to 17 titles selling over 5 million copies by 2018.
devStory: Atomic began it in 1992 under Three-Sixty Pacific, then moved to Avalon Hill in 1993, which rebranded it Beyond Squad Leader, a tie-in to its million-selling board game. Zabalaoui aimed to capture the spirit of Squad Leader rather than its rules, which polarised the board game's fans, and the relationship with Avalon Hill was troubled, with delays that made it look like vaporware. After a high-profile departure at Avalon Hill, Atomic broke away, renamed it Close Combat and finished it with Microsoft, releasing it in July 1996. It was the 13th best-selling US computer game that month and sold about 200,000 copies, ten times Atomic's earlier games, though Zabalaoui found it "frustrating" next to other RTS sales. Computer Games Strategy Plus likened it to SimCity 2000 and nominated it for wargame of the year, and Computer Gaming World said it "looks, sounds and plays like nothing else", while critics faulted its slow scrolling and some called its psychological modelling a mistake. Atomic made four sequels and Close Combat: Marines for the US Marine Corps.

title: Descent: FreeSpace – The Great War
description: Descent: FreeSpace – The Great War (1998) is Volition's space combat sim in which a Terran pilot fights a 14-year war against the alien Vasudans until a genocidal third race forces the two into an alliance, famed for its huge capital ships and explosions.
longDescription:
In the 24th century, a war between the human Terrans and the alien Vasudans is interrupted in its fourteenth year by the arrival of an enigmatic, militant alien race whose genocidal advance forces the two sides into a ceasefire to fight together. As a Terran pilot, the player flies a campaign of increasingly difficult missions with briefings, command briefings and training missions mixed in, meeting cruisers, destroyers, transports and space stations in orbit or asteroid belts. Some objectives are scripted to fail as part of the story, and the player chooses ships and weapons for themselves and their wingmen before most missions.

Fighters cover space superiority, assault, recon, interceptor and bomber roles, armed with energy guns aimed at shields, hulls or subsystems and dumb-fire, heat-seeking or aspect-seeking missiles and bombs. The HUD tracks shields, weapon and afterburner energy, damaged subsystems, targets, incoming missiles, wingmen and an escort list, with a flexible targeting system that can lock onto the nearest hostile and match its speed. Players balance energy between weapons, shields and engines, deploy countermeasures, call support ships to repair and re-arm, and order wingmen to attack, protect or depart. Its flight model is simple, with some Newtonian elements such as collision physics, but its controls go beyond an arcade game, and the main menu is set on a ship's deck.
trivia: Volition was formed when it split off from Parallax Software.
In Europe it was titled Conflict: FreeSpace – The Great War.
Hyperion Entertainment ported it to the Amiga in 2001.
Reviewers unanimously agreed its capital ship explosions were the most impressive they had seen.
The Silent Threat expansion has the player in an intelligence branch that later tries to overthrow the Terran government.
devStory: Volition developed it and Interplay published it in 1998. It was well received as a single-player space sim that brought together everything wanted in the genre, from capable AI wingmen to capital ships that dwarf the player's fighter and break up spectacularly, though its multiplayer suffered from lag and inaccurate statistics. Next Generation gave it four stars, saying it was too similar to other space sims to be "revolutionary" but "does take the space-combat simulation genre one step further". Reviewers were divided on its graphics, some admiring asteroids against glowing nebulae and others finding the 3D effects unconvincing and ship textures blurry, and it was compared with Wing Commander: Prophecy and X-Wing vs. TIE Fighter. PC Gamer UK placed it 20th in its 1999 Top 100. It sold around 100,000 copies and earned nearly $4 million by October 1999. The Silent Threat expansion was less well received, while FreeSpace 2 followed in 1999 to critical acclaim.

title: Hexen II
description: Hexen II (1997) is Raven Software's Quake-engine fantasy shooter, the end of the Serpent Riders trilogy, with four levelling character classes, destructible scenery and hub levels across four themed continents.
longDescription:
The world of Thyrion has been enslaved by the eldest and most powerful of the three Serpent Rider brothers, Eidolon, after the previous games freed two other worlds. He is supported by four generals modelled on the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, and to face each one the player must travel to a different continent: medieval European Blackmarsh, Mesoamerican Mazaera, Ancient Egyptian Thysis and Greco-Roman Septimus, before returning to Blackmarsh to confront Eidolon in his cathedral.

Instead of Hexen's three classes there are four, each with its own weapons and style: the "offensive" Paladin, the "defensive" Crusader, the spell-casting Necromancer and the stealthy Assassin. Role-playing elements give each character statistics that rise with experience, increasing their health and mana. Improvements over Hexen and Quake include destructible environments, mounted weapons and unique abilities gained on levelling up. As in its predecessor, levels are grouped into hubs of interconnected maps, where changes in one level affect another, and Heretic's Tome of Power returns.
trivia: It began as part of a planned trilogy finale, Hecatomb, abandoned after John Romero left id in 1996.
Activision pushed Raven to split Hecatomb into Hexen II and Heretic II.
Its OpenGL installer worked only with 3dfx cards, wrapping their Glide API.
Raven's 1998 Siege mod turned HexenWorld multiplayer into a castle siege with catapults and ballistae.
The Portal of Praevus expansion added a Demoness class and a Sino-Tibetan fifth continent.
devStory: Raven Software developed Hexen II on an enhanced Quake engine, and id Software published it for Windows in 1997. Much of its music remixes the Hexen and Heretic soundtracks to suit each hub. Activision acquired rights to PlayStation and Saturn versions, but neither was released. Reviews were generally positive: Edge praised its inventive, interactive levels, varied enemies and AI, and GamePro its fast multiplayer and class selection, saying "you could spend days playing through all four characters". GameSpot found its design superior to Hexen and its visuals "without equal in the action genre", calling it "one of the most beautiful games ever made", but said progress depended on actions so obscure that the result was "confusing and often frustratingly difficult". It was commercially unsuccessful, selling slightly over 30,000 copies according to Erik Bethke. Raven released the engine source under the GPL in November 2000, enabling ports to Linux and the Dreamcast, and it came to Steam in 2007.

title: Heretic II
description: Heretic II (1998) is Raven Software's third-person fantasy action game on the Quake II engine, in which the elf Corvus fights a plague of madness, a critically liked but commercially failed departure from the first-person series.
longDescription:
Corvus, hero of the first Heretic, returns from banishment to find that a mysterious plague has swept Parthoris, driving mad those it does not kill. Attacked and infected in his hometown of Silverspring, he is protected only because he carries one of the Tomes of Power, and must find a cure before he succumbs. His journey takes him through the city and swamps, a jungle palace, a desert canyon, an insect hive and dark mines to a mountain castle, where the ancient Seraph Morcalavin, seeking immortality with a false tome, has gone insane and created the plague; Corvus swaps in his real tome, curing Morcalavin and ending the plague.

Unlike the series' earlier first-person games, Corvus is controlled from a camera behind him. He combines melee and ranged attacks, with three weapons using their own ammunition and offensive and defensive spells drawing on green and blue mana; the Tome of Power is now a defensive spell that temporarily strengthens weapons and spells. His bladestaff can perform several attacks and sever enemies' limbs, magical shrines grant armour, health or permanent upgrades, and the 3D world allowed gymnastic moves such as climbing ledges, back-flipping off walls and pole vaulting.
trivia: Raven was inspired by Tomb Raider to make a third-person game on the Quake II engine.
Gerald Brom contributed concept art for its characters and creatures.
Corvus was given a backbone for realistic animation, with 1,600 frames in total.
Kevin Schilder composed the music.
Computer Gaming World said it proved "that a spell-casting, shirtless elf could actually kick ass".
devStory: A team of 20 began work in November 1997, programming the camera system within a month and, after Activision approved a demo, finishing just before Thanksgiving 1998. They kept the Quake II software renderer and enhanced it for 16-bit colour, animating Corvus mostly in Softimage and world objects in 3D Studio Max. Activision published it for Windows, and Loki, Hyperion and MacPlay ported it to Linux, Amiga and Mac. It is the only game in the Heretic and Hexen series unconnected to id beyond licensing the engine. Critics were positive: Next Generation gave it three stars, saying it "has a lot going for it", and Edge praised its mix of platforming and shooting, which set it apart from both id's shooters and Tomb Raider, and it was a finalist for Computer Gaming World's Best Action award. But it was a commercial failure, selling 28,994 copies in the US by April 1999, which Activision's Steve Felsen blamed on first-person shooter fans avoiding its third-person view.

title: Kingpin: Life of Crime
description: Kingpin: Life of Crime (1999) is Xatrix Entertainment's violent, foul-mouthed gangster shooter set in an art deco city that never was, with hireable gang members, weapon mods and a Cypress Hill soundtrack.
longDescription:
In a quasi-retro world mixing 1930s art deco with modern technology, from helicopters to monorails, a past the manual says never happened, the player is beaten and dumped in Skidrow by thugs working for Nikki Blanco, one of the Kingpin's lieutenants. Picking up a length of lead pipe, he sets out for revenge, rising through chemical plants, steel mills and train yards to Radio City, the Kingpin's headquarters. The game borrows heavily from Pulp Fiction and The Big Lebowski: the Kingpin is inspired by Marsellus Wallace, a boss called "The Jesus" shares John Turturro's character's name and personality, and much of the dialogue is lifted from both films.

It was noted for profanity-laden dialogue and graphic violence. Damage is area-specific, so headshots hurt more than leg wounds, characters' skins show where and how badly they are injured, and wounded enemies leave blood trails. Armour is split between helmet, body armour and leggings, and weapons can be upgraded with mods for firepower or rate of fire. Players talk to characters with positive or negative responses, which can reveal information, recruit gang members or provoke attacks, and characters react differently depending on whether the player's gun is holstered. Cash taken from bodies buys weapons at the Pawn-O-Matic or hires gang members, some needed for their skills.
trivia: Artist Viktor Antonov said it was first envisioned "like Blade Runner with a gangster touch".
Cypress Hill's involvement led the team to drop science fiction for a grittier, more realistic city.
Its soundtrack features three tracks from Cypress Hill's album IV, and the group provided voices.
The UK release came with a free Ministry of Sound album.
A remaster, Kingpin: Reloaded, was released in December 2023.
devStory: Xatrix developed Kingpin on the Quake II engine and Interplay published it in 1999. Released shortly after the Columbine High School massacre, as the first high-profile shooter since, it drew controversy: congressmen called for its cancellation, it was debated in the US Senate, and Best Buy, Wal-Mart and Toys "R" Us refused to stock it. Xatrix added a password-protected low-violence mode with bleeped swearing, and CEO Drew Markham included a message stressing that it "was never intended for children"; team member Greg Goodrich later said that without Electronics Boutique it "might have never seen the light of day in North America". It ranked 19th in PC Data's US chart for July 1999. Reviews were positive: GameSpot's Erik Wolpaw admired its "beautifully depicted metropolitan nightmare", PC Gamer UK called it "an incredible achievement in terms of graphics, AI and level design and a nasty, bloody swear-fest", and Computer and Video Games gave five stars, though PC Gamer US gave it 53%, finding it shallow and buggy. It was also ported to Linux.

title: Unreal Tournament
description: Unreal Tournament (1999) is Epic Games and Digital Extremes' multiplayer arena shooter, set in a future where "consensual murder" is a sport, with bots, mutators and modes from Assault to Domination, often counted among the greatest games ever made.
longDescription:
One of the first modern arena shooters, it focuses on head-to-head multiplayer deathmatch. The single-player campaign is a ladder of arena matches against bots, climbing towards a challenge for the title of Grand Champion against the mysterious Xan Kriegor. Game types include Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch for up to four teams, Capture the Flag, Domination, in which teams hold control points, Last Man Standing, where players start fully armed with limited lives, and Assault, in which one team attacks a base's objectives and then defends it for the same time. Bots fill out teams, can take orders, adjust their skill to the player and be customised. "Mutators" change the rules, such as "InstaGib", which arms everyone with instant-kill Shock Rifles.

Each weapon, from the Enforcer to the Rocket Launcher and the Ripper's ricocheting blades, has two fire modes, and the Redeemer fires a miniature nuke. Body armour, health packs and damage amplifiers lie across levels set in spaceships, outposts, castles and monasteries, with lifts, teleporters, water and lava. The story explains it all: losing a war against the Skaarj and facing riots in its mining colonies, the New Earth Government legalised "consensual murder" in 2291, and the Liandri Mining Corporation turned the fights into a profitable professional Grand Tournament.
trivia: It began as an expansion to fix Unreal's weak multiplayer network code.
It had a $2 million budget and about 350,000 lines of C++ and UnrealScript.
The PC version includes a level editor and works with most Unreal multiplayer maps.
Four free bonus packs added maps, characters and relics such as the Relic of Vengeance.
A 2014 Unreal Tournament reboot was halted when its team moved to Fortnite Battle Royale.
devStory: When Unreal came out in May 1998, its multiplayer was hampered by poor network code, so Epic made improving it a priority and began an expansion in summer 1998 that grew into Unreal Tournament, developed over about a year and a half with Digital Extremes. GT Interactive published it for Windows in 1999, followed by PlayStation 2 and Dreamcast versions from Infogrames. It received universal acclaim, scoring 92 on Metacritic and 94% on GameRankings, with praise for its graphics, level design and gameplay; Computer and Video Games called it "a technical and game-playing marvel", and GameSpy said it raised the bar for multiplayer shooters, though the console ports had limitations. It sold 100,998 copies in the US by the end of 1999, trailing Quake III Arena, and nearly 2 million worldwide by November 2001, and a Game of the Year Edition bundled the bonus packs in 2000. Unreal Tournament 2003, 2004 and 3 followed.

title: Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines
description: Commandos: Behind Enemy Lines (1998) is Pyro Studios' stealth-driven World War II tactics game in which six specialist commandos sabotage, assassinate and rescue behind enemy lines, a surprise million-seller and Spain's biggest game hit.
longDescription:
The player commands Allied commandos through twenty missions across wartime Europe and Africa, each preceded by a briefing on its background, objectives and escape route, with the whole map visible for planning. Each mission provides a set of commandos, and it fails if any is killed. The Green Beret moves barrels, climbs rough surfaces, uses a lure and kills with a knife; the Marine dives, uses a harpoon gun and pilots boats; the Driver drives vehicles and operates tanks and mounted guns and can heal; the Sapper handles grenades and explosives, cuts wire and sets traps; the Sniper takes out targets and can also heal; and the Spy wears enemy uniforms to distract soldiers and kills by lethal injection. All carry pistols, but the emphasis is on stealth and careful planning, since commandos cannot survive firefights.

Enemy soldiers, sergeants and officers man posts and patrol, sometimes with tanks and armoured cars. The player can view one enemy's line of sight at a time, a green cone with a light close range where commandos are spotted and a darker long range where only standing ones are. Spotted commandos are ordered to halt, enemies investigate footprints, bodies and noises, and an alarm brings out more troops from garrisons, sometimes failing the mission outright.
trivia: Designer Gonzalo Suarez said he made it because "there were hardly any tactical action games being developed".
Pyro hoped to sell around 15,000 copies.
Its custom engine avoided tiles for visual quality, so every map's layout and logic had to be built by hand.
It spent 16 weeks at number one in Germany and 15 in the UK.
A prequel, Commandos: Origins, was released in April 2025.
devStory: Pyro Studios made it over about 18 months in Madrid, the last 12 full-time, with a team of around 18 producing roughly 250,000 lines of C++ and assembly; lead programmer Jon Beltran de Heredia recalled ten-hour days, seven days a week, at the end. Co-designer Ignacio Pérez Dolset put the budget at about a million dollars, and David García-Morales composed the music. Eidos published it in 1998, and it received favourable reviews, Next Generation praising its "gorgeous" graphics and "tough" and "challenging" gameplay. It was a significant and unexpected success that Suarez credited to word of mouth, selling 706,000 copies by the end of 1998, winning a Gold prize at the 1999 Milia festival for EU revenues above €16 million, and passing 1.5 million worldwide. GameSpot Spain called it Spain's biggest game hit of all time by 2001. The standalone expansion Beyond the Call of Duty followed in 1999, then Commandos 2, 3 and Strike Force.

title: Heroes of Might and Magic II: The Succession Wars
description: Heroes of Might and Magic II (1996) is New World Computing's turn-based fantasy strategy game, the series' breakout, in which heroes lead armies for rival princes fighting over the throne of Enroth, voted the sixth best PC game of all time by PC Gamer in 1997.
longDescription:
After Lord Morglin Ironfist unifies the continent of Enroth and dies, his sons Archibald and Roland fight for the crown. Archibald engineers Roland's exile and takes the throne, and Roland leads a resistance. Each side has its own campaign: Archibald's uses the three "evil" factions, Necromancers, Warlocks and Barbarians, and Roland's the three "good" ones, Knights, Sorceresses and Wizards. Victories in campaign scenarios carry lasting bonuses forward, and players pick a starting bonus before each one. In the canonical ending Roland wins and Archibald is turned to stone by the court wizard Tanir.

Largely a graphical overhaul of the first game, it plays as a 4X-style strategy game: players secure resources, build towns, hire creatures and lead heroes across a world map, fighting creatures, heroes and castles on a separate battlefield. It added two factions, Necromancer and Wizard, each with its own creatures and themed town. Heroes keep primary skills but now also learn up to eight secondary skills, such as Wisdom for higher-level spells and Logistics for movement, each rising from Basic to Advanced and Expert. Magic moved from memorised spells to a spell point system, and units can be upgraded for better statistics and abilities. Only one building can be built or upgraded per town per turn.
trivia: It reused much of the first game's code, so it took less time to make than the original.
Paul Romero produced most of the soundtrack.
Archibald's petrification is referenced later in Might and Magic VI, when he is freed.
Computer Gaming World found it "nearly perfect", apart from the lack of a wait function.
The open-source fheroes2 project recreates its engine.
devStory: Jon Van Caneghem developed Heroes II through New World Computing, and The 3DO Company published it in 1996. PC Gamer reported that December that every 3DO retailer was reordering it, and combined series sales passed 500,000 by October 1997. Computer Gaming World called it a "strategy game that amaze[d] everyone with its surprising, addictive qualities and amazing ease of use", much better than the original, and PC Gamer US named it 1996's Best Turn-Based Strategy Game, "clearly a cut above". It was nominated for several other strategy awards but lost them to Civilization II and Red Alert, and Arcane found it more of the same but great fun. The Price of Loyalty expansion followed in 1997, and Heroes II Gold bundled both with 30 community maps in 1998. PC Gamer US ranked it the seventh best computer game ever in 1998, calling it "the most dangerously addictive turn-based strategy game in the history of PC gaming (with the possible exception of Civilization II)", and GameSpot inducted it into its greatest games in 2003.

sources.title: Heroes of Might and Magic II

title: Heroes of Might and Magic III: The Restoration of Erathia
description: Heroes of Might and Magic III (1999) is New World Computing's turn-based strategy classic in which Queen Catherine returns to reclaim her father's kingdom of Erathia, with eight factions, underground maps and a modding scene still active decades later.
longDescription:
With King Roland Ironfist missing, Queen Catherine rules Enroth until her father, King Nicholas Gryphonheart of Erathia, is assassinated, and Erathia falls to the Dungeon Overlords of Nighon and the Kreegans of Eeofol, who sack the capital Steadwick. Seven campaigns on the continent of Antagarich, told from alternating sides, follow Catherine as she rallies the wizards of Bracada and the elves of AvLee, retakes Steadwick and pushes into Nighon, while the necromancers of Deyja, who killed her father, raise him as a lich only to lose control of him. A final unlockable campaign follows separatists in the Contested Lands, a rising later implied to be Archibald Ironfist's work.

Heroes lead armies of mythical creatures across the world, gathering loot, resources for their towns and artefacts that boost them, and contesting mines for income, with combat on a hexagonal grid of moving, attacking and spellcasting units. It refines earlier mechanics and adds an underground layer, larger maps and more victory conditions, including hunting the Grail to build a powerful permanent structure. Eight factions are included, up from six, and heroes gain skills such as Diplomacy, which can persuade enemies to join rather than fight. It offers campaigns, cooperative and competitive multiplayer and 50 skirmish maps.
trivia: A Dreamcast port was cancelled in 2000; a collector bought a build in 2005 and released it in 2020.
A Game Boy Color port was oddly titled Heroes of Might and Magic 2.
The Armageddon's Blade expansion added a ninth town, the Conflux.
In 2025, the Complete edition became the first video game preserved on a 5D optical crystal.
The fan expansion Horn of the Abyss has new music from original composer Paul Romero.
devStory: Van Caneghem developed it through New World Computing, and 3DO released it for Windows on 28 February 1999, with Mac and Linux ports at the end of the year. It entered PC Data's weekly chart at third and was the second best-selling US computer game of March 1999, selling 185,553 copies in the US by September 2000. It received universal acclaim and became a defining turn-based strategy classic: Computer Gaming World said it "expands upon the insanely addictive play of the previous edition" and was "mind-boggling in its depth", despite uneven campaign pacing and sluggish online play, and Next Generation said it showed "turn-based play is alive and well". Armageddon's Blade and The Shadow of Death followed, bundled as Heroes III Complete in 2000, with the Heroes Chronicles episodes. Ubisoft's 2015 HD Edition, missing the expansions, was poorly received, while a large community, especially in Russian and Polish, has kept making mods, and a full remake was announced in 2026.

sources.title: Heroes of Might and Magic III

title: Might and Magic VI: The Mandate of Heaven
description: Might and Magic VI: The Mandate of Heaven (1998) is New World Computing's first-person RPG set in Heroes of Might and Magic's world of Enroth, with freely explorable 3D lands, real-time or turn-based combat and a flexible skill system.
longDescription:
Seven years after Heroes of Might and Magic II, on the Night of Shooting Stars, meteor-like spaceships full of Kreegans fall on Enroth, as the long war between the Ancients and the devil-like Kreegans spills onto nearby worlds, and King Roland Ironfist leaves for the north. The player guides four adventurers, all human, from humble beginnings to heroes who must save the land. Leaving grid-based maps behind, the world can be explored freely, mountains included, with full 360-degree turning and looking up and down, and battles fought in real time or a turn-based mode that limits movement. A calendar and day-night cycle govern events such as the solstices and the Circus of the Sun.

Characters choose one of six classes, Knight, Druid, Paladin, Cleric, Sorcerer or Archer, which set their starting skills and how health and magic grow, and distribute points across Might, Intellect, Personality, Endurance, Accuracy, Speed and Luck. They age as time passes, with penalties after fifty. Levels are gained only by training in towns, statistics rise through barrels, cauldrons, shrines and fountains, and class promotion quests, such as Paladin to Crusader, grant two further tiers. Skills have a Rank and an Expertise of Normal, Expert or Master, the latter taught by a single Master teacher per skill, and since advancement is not restricted by class, an archer can become as good with a sword as a knight.
trivia: It was the first Might and Magic game set on the same planet as Heroes of Might and Magic.
It has no character transfer from earlier or later games.
It is the only Might and Magic game without a choice of race.
A Limited Edition included a cloth map of Enroth, a strategy guide and the first five games on CD-ROM.
PC Gamer ranked it the 32nd best computer game ever in 1998.
devStory: New World Computing developed it and 3DO published it in 1998 as the sequel to Might and Magic V: Darkside of Xeen, continuing the story of Heroes II and running alongside Heroes III. It compared favourably with RPGs such as Daggerfall, and critics praised its non-linear, user-friendly design, detailed interactive world and polished, bug-free release. GameSpot called it "a standout game in what should be a great year for role-playing game fans" with "the best yet seen" graphics in a 3D first-person RPG, IGN said "any fan of role-playing games should already own this game", and RPGFan said its exploration and character development could keep players going for over 100 hours, though it could get tedious. It was nominated for RPG of the year by the AIAS, Computer Gaming World, PC Gamer, GameSpot and IGNPC. Three sequels followed, beginning with Might and Magic VII: For Blood and Honor, which continued its story and made the skill system considerably more restrictive.

sources.title: Might and Magic VI: The Mandate of Heaven

title: Wizardry VII: Crusaders of the Dark Savant
description: Wizardry VII: Crusaders of the Dark Savant (1992) is Sir-Tech's first-person party RPG on the planet Guardia, where rival factions race the player for the Astral Dominae and can beat them to vital quest items.
longDescription:
The story picks up where Wizardry VI: Bane of the Cosmic Forge left off. The theft of the Cosmic Forge, the pen the Cosmic Lords use to script the universe, has revealed the hidden planet Guardia and the Astral Dominae, an artefact with power over life itself. Multiple factions converge on Guardia to find it, among them the player's party and the Dark Savant. The setting mixes science fiction, with interplanetary travel and cybernetic androids, with high fantasy arms, armour and magic. Players can bribe, negotiate with or threaten the key characters of each faction, and as time passes those rivals may reach quest items first, forcing the player to change priorities. It was the first Wizardry with VGA colour graphics.

The game is played in the first person with tile-based movement and 90-degree turns, the party's portraits shown alongside the view. Up to six characters can be imported from Wizardry VI or created anew, choosing gender, portrait, race and profession; the first three fight on the front line while the back three rely on ranged weapons, spells or hiding. Besides humans, elves, dwarves, gnomes and hobbits there are lizardmen, faeries, half-dragon Dracons, dog-like Rawulf, cat-like Felpurr and the tall, hairy Mook. Characters may change profession later if they meet its requirements, at a cost. Combat is phased: the fastest act first, so an attack may hit a group already wiped out, or a healer may act too late.
trivia: The game has four different beginnings, one for each of Wizardry VI's three endings plus a fresh start.
Only faeries who become ninja can wield the Cane of Corpus.
Magic is split into four schools, Psionics, Alchemy, Theology and Thaumaturgy, across six elements.
A Japan-only PlayStation conversion by Sony Computer Entertainment followed in 1995.
An enhanced Wizardry Gold edition for Windows 95 and Mac OS appeared in 1996, distributed by Interplay.
devStory: Sir-Tech developed and published it in 1992 for MS-DOS as the seventh Wizardry and the second part of the Dark Savant trilogy. Scorpia of Computer Gaming World called it "the first Wizardry that has a real-world feel to it", with towns, ruins, wilderness, mountains and even a small sea, and approved of the improved inventory, though she criticised the small automap and the backtracking its open design demanded. She later said it "should not be missed" and named it Role-Playing Game of the Year. PC Magazine praised its humour, characterisation and documentation, PCGames and Computer Games Strategy Plus both named it the best role-playing game of 1992, and in 1996 Computer Gaming World ranked it the 105th best game ever.

sources.title: Wizardry VII: Crusaders of the Dark Savant

title: Ultima VII: The Black Gate
description: Ultima VII: The Black Gate (1992) is Origin's real-time, mouse-driven RPG in which the Avatar returns to an open, deeply interactive Britannia full of schemes, monsters and threats to the crown.
longDescription:
The player returns as the Avatar, a would-be paragon of virtue who must cleanse the medieval world of Britannia of plots, monster infestations and the undermining of royal authority. The world is no longer tile-based as far as the player is concerned: maps are layered, objects can be stacked, sometimes into makeshift stairs, and the game fills the whole screen at a pseudo-isometric angle. It was the series' first entirely mouse-driven game, with items simply dragged and dropped, and it introduced gumps, on-screen windows for containers, books, the spellbook and equipment. Play is real time, pausing only for inventory, menus and dialogue, and every companion is controlled by AI with a chosen behaviour, which spares micromanaging up to eight characters but occasionally fires a triple crossbow into a crowd of allies.

Almost anything not nailed down can be moved or used: the Avatar can bake bread, forge weapons, play instruments, paint a self-portrait or change a baby's swaddling, and the party must eat and drink or perish. Dialogue trees replace typed keywords, and topics appear only once they are learned in the story. Once free of the walled city of Trinsic the game is highly non-linear, and it puts less weight on virtue than earlier Ultimas: the Avatar may steal and murder without breaking the game, but witnesses react, companions may leave or even turn on him, and the Guardian appears to mock each crime.
trivia: Gumps, its on-screen container windows, were reused in Ultima VIII, Ultima IX and Ultima Online.
It was the first mainline Ultima to use dialogue trees.
Players must buy and carry a deed to board a horse-drawn carriage or ship.
A Super NES conversion was released in 1994.
Richard Garriott called it the most masterfully executed Ultima and, with Ultima IV, his favourite.
devStory: Origin Systems published it in April 1992 for MS-DOS. It was critically acclaimed and commercially successful, widely lauded as a high point of the series and regarded as one of the best video games ever made. Scorpia of Computer Gaming World praised its "first-class" graphics, sound and realism and its "engrossing" story, but criticised the slow performance, several serious bugs and the combat, estimating that the speed added about a week to her playing time. Charles Ardai argued it was "not more of the same" but "daring and unusual", calling the plot the best in the series and an allegory for real-world problems. Dragon magazine gave it four out of five stars.

title: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds
description: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds (1993) is LookingGlass Technologies' 3D first-person RPG in which the Avatar travels through eight parallel worlds to break the Guardian's hold on a sealed Castle British.
longDescription:
One year after Ultima VII, the Avatar and many familiar faces are celebrating at Lord British's castle when a dome of impenetrable blackrock seals it. The Guardian means to attack Britannia while they are trapped, and his spell has opened portals between eight parallel worlds, each a centre of his power. Freeing each world weakens his grip on the castle: a goblin-held prison tower in Fyrna, the floating fortress of Killorn Keep, ice caves ruled by a ghost, the energy beings of Talorus, the mage school Scintillus Academy, the Pits of Carnage and the Tomb of Praecor Loth. Meanwhile a traitor lurks among those trapped in the castle, and the Guardian taunts the Avatar in dreams.

The game is played from a character's eye view in 3D, with a free mouse cursor to examine objects, talk to characters and ready weapons. Built on its predecessor's engine, it keeps jumping, swimming and the automap. Players create a character with gender, class and skills from diplomacy and lockpicking to blacksmithing; attacks vary with where the screen is clicked, held clicks deal more damage, and spells come from combinations of collected runestones. Skills are now raised by training with characters rather than at shrines. Torches burn out, items wear and the character must eat, many puzzles have several solutions, and areas are revisited as the character grows stronger.
trivia: It was developed in nine months, starting in April 1992.
Its events follow Ultima VII: The Black Gate rather than the first Ultima Underworld.
According to Paul Neurath, it and its predecessor together sold half a million units.
Looking Glass streamlined the Underworld ideas to create System Shock.
Origin rejected several sequel pitches; Arkane's Arx Fatalis began as one.
devStory: Production began in April 1992, soon after Ultima Underworld was completed, and took nine months. The team aimed to make the world larger and more interactive and reused and improved the first game's engine, but insufficient staffing, extensive playtesting and the rapid schedule led to burnout. Most critics praised its graphics, design and non-linearity, while complaints focused on high system requirements and uneven pacing. PC Review called it "magnificent" and said it would take the sequel over the original any time, and PC Zone's David McCandless wrote that it was "about as close to Virtual Reality as you are ever likely to get from your mouse driver". The Toronto Star called it the best fantasy role-playing game "in this (or any parallel) world".

sources.title: Ultima Underworld II: Labyrinth of Worlds

title: Albion
description: Albion (1995) is Blue Byte's science-fantasy RPG in which a stranded space pilot discovers that the planet his corporation plans to mine is home to the feline Iskai and the descendants of ancient Celts.
longDescription:
In 2227 the DDT corporation sends the colony ship Toronto to a distant system for raw materials. Pilot Tom Driscoll and junior government agent Rainer Hofstedt survey a desert planet that the ship's AI, Ned, says is rich in ore, but their readings disagree with Ned's moments before their shuttle crashes. The planet, Albion, teems with life: the Iskai, a feline people who use plants for homes and transfer spirits between bodies, and Celts brought from Earth two thousand years earlier. Joined by the warrior Drirr, the mage Sira and the mute druid Mellthas, Tom learns that Ned has suppressed the truth and must stop the mining before it destroys the world.

The player leads a party of up to six, earning experience by fighting and solving puzzles and spending training points with trainers to raise skills. Most interiors use a 2D overhead view, with a smaller-scale map for the wider world, while dungeons, caves and the outsides of large cities switch to real-time first-person 3D with an automap. Combat is turn-based on a five-by-six grid: each turn the player picks attack, move, magic, item or flee for each character, actions resolve in order of speed, and because attacks target squares rather than enemies, a foe that moves first is simply missed. The party can only move in the bottom two rows, but an Advance Party option drags every enemy a row closer.
trivia: It is seen as a spiritual successor to the Amiga RPGs Amberstar and Ambermoon, by the same core team.
It was meant for the Amiga until Commodore's bankruptcy moved development to the PC.
It was released in German in 1995 and in English the following year.
It was a finalist for Computer Gaming World's 1996 Role-Playing Game of the Year, won by Daggerfall.
GOG.com re-released it with Windows support in 2015.
devStory: Blue Byte developed and published it for MS-DOS, with the core team of Thalion Software's Amberstar and Ambermoon, after Commodore's bankruptcy ended plans for an Amiga release. Reviews praised the originality of its combat, story and puzzles. PC Gamer US called it "a fun, engrossing, and involved roleplaying experience", Computer Gaming World recommended it to lovers of role-playing games "when another dry spell hits", and Next Generation called it a "bright spot in the desert" of computer RPGs at the time.
