Arcane rated it seven out of ten, praising its graphics and size, and Computer Games Strategy Plus called it "a breath of fresh air for the RPG crowd".

title: Stonekeep
description: Stonekeep (1995) is Interplay's first-person dungeon crawler with pre-rendered labyrinths, digitised characters and full-motion cut-scenes, planned as a nine-month project that took five years to finish.
longDescription:
Ten years ago the insane god Khull-Khuum, the Shadowking, destroyed the castle of Stonekeep, and the boy Drake was carried from its ruins by a mysterious figure. Returning as a man, Drake is visited by the goddess Thera, who sends his spirit into the ruins to find the orbs in which Khull-Khuum imprisoned the gods of the planets a thousand years before, during the Devastation. Along the way he gains the dwarves Farli, Karzak and Dombur, the dragon Vermatrix, the elf Enigma and Wahooka, King of the goblins, in a quest against Khull-Khuum and his consort the Ice Queen.

In the style of Eye of the Beholder and Dungeon Master, the player explores underground labyrinths full of monsters, treasure and traps, moving with the keyboard and using a mouse pointer that doubles as an aiming reticle and changes shape to examine, take or use things. Drake starts with a magic scroll that carries unlimited items and a magic mirror for equipping and feeding the party, and finds a six-part journal holding his statistics, clues, notes, items, runes and clickable level maps. Magic comes from inscribing Mannish, Fae, Throggish and Meta runes onto a spellcaster wand; the Meta runes boost the others, so double power turns one firebolt into two.
trivia: Its working titles were "Dungeon Game" and "Brian's Dungeon", after Interplay president Brian Fargo, who also chose the final name.
Planned with a $50,000 budget, it finally cost $5 million.
The intro sequence alone cost nearly half a million dollars, ten times the original budget for the whole game.
The original specification required no hard drive or mouse and ran from floppies on a 286; the final game needed a 386, mouse, hard drive and CD-ROM.
Interplay shipped 175,000 copies at launch, its biggest shipment ever at the time.
devStory: Brian Fargo and Todd Camasta first discussed the game in October 1988. Producer Peter Oliphant, who wrote the original story and programmed the graphics and AI engine, joined in 1990 and lead programmer Michael Quarles in 1991. Because the early stages looked good, the nine-month plan stretched to five years as PCs advanced from the 386 to the 486 and Pentium, and the crew grew to 200. Oliphant, a contractor, left in the fourth year, feeling his presence was causing constant feature creep, and Quarles saw it through to release a year later. Interplay spent $1.5 million on marketing, and the game placed fourth on PC Data's chart for November 1995, passing 300,000 sales by June 1998, though Erik Bethke later called its performance weak. Next Generation called it "well worth the wait", and Computer Games Strategy Plus named it the best computer role-playing game of 1995.

title: King's Quest VI: Heir Today, Gone Tomorrow
description: King's Quest VI: Heir Today, Gone Tomorrow (1992) is Sierra's point-and-click adventure, written by Roberta Williams and Jane Jensen, in which Prince Alexander seeks Princess Cassima across the Land of the Green Isles.
longDescription:
A few months after King Graham rescued his family from the wizard Mordack, Prince Alexander cannot stop thinking about Princess Cassima, whom Graham also freed. When the Magic Mirror shows her and a pattern of stars, Alexander sets sail, only to be shipwrecked on the Isle of the Crown. The vizier Abdul Alhazred tells him Cassima is mourning her dead parents and cannot be seen, then sets his genie on Alexander and spreads word that he is a foreign assassin. With the help of the jester Jollo, Alexander uses a magic map to travel between islands drawn from the Arabian Nights, Alice in Wonderland, classical myth, Beauty and the Beast and druid lore, and even descends into the land of the dead.

It was the second King's Quest with an icon toolbar, for walking, looking, acting and talking, in place of the text parser. Play revolves around logic puzzles, conversation and using collected items, and the island-hopping map is the only way to reach other islands. The boxed Guidebook to the Land of the Green Isles adds background and doubles as copy protection: the Cliffs of Logic guarding the Isle of the Sacred Mountain cannot be passed without it, and a poem in it encodes the solution to a puzzle in the island's labyrinth. A 1993 CD-ROM version added more voices, a slightly different opening and more detailed art and animation.
trivia: Its 3D introduction was made by Kronos Digital Entertainment, whose film work included Batman Returns and The Lawnmower Man.
Robby Benson voiced Prince Alexander.
It was the last King's Quest released on floppy disk, shipping on nine of them.
Revolution Software ported it to the Amiga after Sierra stopped releasing games for that platform.
Ken Williams said about 400,000 copies sold in its first week.
devStory: Roberta Williams met newcomer Jane Jensen, later the creator of Gabriel Knight, in May 1991, and the pair spent five months designing it, Williams writing the love story to make players connect emotionally. John Shroades painted 80 backgrounds, motion capture of costumed actors produced more than 2,000 character actions, Chris Braymen composed the MIDI music, and Jensen scripted over 6,000 lines of messages for the SCI1 engine. Williams put the budget at about US$700,000, with more than 20 people working for 14 months. Released in October 1992, it topped the DOS charts into December. Dragon gave it five stars, Computer Gaming World called it "Sierra's finest adventure to date", and it is widely seen as the high point of the series, though PC Format disliked its sudden deaths.

title: Space Quest IV: Roger Wilco and the Time Rippers
description: Space Quest IV: Roger Wilco and the Time Rippers (1991) is Sierra's comic adventure in which the janitor Roger Wilco leaps between past and future Space Quest games to stop the reborn Sludge Vohaul.
longDescription:
Heading home to Xenon after Space Quest III, Roger Wilco is cornered in a bar by androids working for Sludge Vohaul, the villain of Space Quest II, now reborn in the future and bent on revenge. Two soldiers save him and push him through a rift in time to a ruined future Xenon, which the game labels Space Quest XII: Vohaul's Revenge II, where Vohaul's digitised mind has infected the planet's supercomputer and enslaved its people. Roger steals a time machine and visits Space Quest X: Latex Babes of Estros, a parody of Infocom's Leather Goddesses of Phobos, where he meets his future ex-girlfriend, as well as a trip back to Space Quest I. Defeating Vohaul, he learns that the soldier who rescued him is his son from the future.

It was the first Space Quest with a point-and-click interface, like King's Quest V, offering icons to look, talk, use and, mostly for jokes, taste and smell. As in earlier Sierra games, deadly situations must be dealt with quickly to avoid a game over. Graphics were hand-painted in 256 colours and animated with motion capture. A mall arcade on Estros holds Ms. Astro Chicken: Flight of the Pullet, a sequel of sorts to Space Quest III's Astro Chicken and a nod to Ms. Pac-Man, in which a flying chicken drops eggs on squirrels, hunters and dogs until the cabinet explodes.
trivia: The time-travel plot parodies the series' own numbering.
Ms. Astro Chicken's theme is a variation on the Chicken Reel folk tune.
A December 1992 CD-ROM release added full speech.
Amiga and PC-98 versions followed in 1992, but an announced Atari ST version was cancelled.
Dragon gave both the PC and Macintosh versions five out of five stars.
devStory: Sierra released it on floppy disks in March 1991 for MS-DOS and Mac OS. Designers Scott Murphy and Mark Crowe preferred to keep the text parser, believing it added depth, but Ken Williams and creative director Bill Davis asked them to adopt point-and-click and management overruled them to keep Sierra's modern games consistent. It cost far more than earlier Space Quests but was a commercial success, praised for its humour, voice cast and presentation. Charles Ardai of Computer Gaming World wrote that "there are better adventure games than Space Quest IV [but] there are few games that are more entertaining", calling the CD version "the perfect multimedia game". The Amiga release was less well received. Space Quest V followed in 1993.

title: Freddy Pharkas: Frontier Pharmacist
description: Freddy Pharkas: Frontier Pharmacist (1993) is Al Lowe and Josh Mandel's comic Western adventure for Sierra, in which a former gunslinger turned pharmacist uncovers a plot to take over the town of Coarsegold.
longDescription:
In the 1880s, Freddy Pharkas gave up gunslinging after Kenny the Kid shot off one of his ears, and now runs the pharmacy in Coarsegold, California, the real town where Sierra had its headquarters. Businesses are being bought up or their owners scared away, and the slimy Sheriff Checkum P. Shift is no help. Narrated by the old-timer Whittlin' Willy, the cast includes Freddy's sidekick Srini, the drunken Doc Gillespie, cafe owner Helen Back, banker P.H. Balance, schoolmarm Penelope Primm and Madame Ovaree, while Kenny the Kid is a cartoon of Sierra president Ken Williams. Freddy must deal with horses with explosive flatulence, a snail stampede, a diarrhoea epidemic and a fire, before taking up his guns again.

The game runs on Sierra's SCI1.1 engine under both MS-DOS and Windows 3.1, with 256-colour hand-drawn art, scaling sprites and a point-and-click interface. Its manual, The Modern Day Book of Health and Hygiene, parodies 19th-century medical texts and acts as copy protection: Freddy must make up prescriptions from its recipes, measuring out chemicals with his lab equipment. A wrong prescription sends the customer back angry but does not end the game. The CD-ROM edition gave every character full speech, with Cam Clarke as Freddy.
trivia: Al Lowe coined the word "farmer-cist" by accident while brainstorming with Roberta Williams.
Lowe said that at the time "there wasn't a single Western computer game" on the market.
Lowe and Mandel also wrote the comic ballad that opens the game.
Game Informer named it one of the best adventure games of all time in 2006.
Adventure Gamers ranked it the 78th-best adventure game in 2011.
devStory: Al Lowe conceived it in 1992 as a spoof Western, citing Blazing Saddles as a major inspiration, and co-designed and wrote it with Space Quest writer Josh Mandel, who directed and produced the floppy release at Sierra's Oakhurst studio in mid-1993. Charles Ardai of Computer Gaming World called it "the Blazing Saddles of computer games", funnier than Leisure Suit Larry and able to "make a jaded player laugh out loud frequently". Lowe said it sold over 150,000 copies in roughly a year, which prompted the CD-ROM edition, and lifetime sales reached 500,000, though it had a reputation as a failure inside Sierra. He felt it deserved a sequel, but by the time the numbers came in Mandel had moved on.

title: Little Big Adventure 2
description: Little Big Adventure 2 (1997), released in North America as Twinsen's Odyssey, is Adeline Software's 3D action-adventure in which Twinsen uncovers an alien plot to kidnap the children and wizards of his planet.
longDescription:
Years after Twinsen defeated Dr. FunFrock, a storm over Citadel Island strikes his Dino-Fly from the sky. Once the weather wizard calms the storm, aliens called the Esmers land on Twinsun under a diplomatic guise, secretly kidnapping the wizards' children and inviting the wizards themselves to their home planet, Zeelich, as a trap. Newly graduated as a wizard, Twinsen accepts the invitation, is arrested on arrival, escapes, and returns to find Twinsun under Esmer martial law. Armed with a hovering prototype jetpack left by his friend Baldino, he travels between Twinsun, the Emerald Moon and the two-layered planet Zeelich.

Indoor scenes use an isometric 3D view like the first game, while outdoors switches to a 3D perspective view, and all characters and vehicles are polygon models that can turn and move freely. It is a real-time adventure mixing arcade-style sequences with role-playing elements, and once islands are unlocked they can be roamed freely, with many optional and non-linear tasks. Every line of text is spoken, nearly every character responds when Twinsen talks to them, and enemies go about tasks while the world is active. The world was considered extremely large and varied for its time, and completed tasks are rewarded with full-motion video, set to CD-quality music by Philippe Vachey.
trivia: Activision released it in North America in July 1997 as Twinsen's Odyssey, a month before its UK launch.
Planned Saturn and PlayStation versions were never released.
It was the third game made under the Adeline Software International label.
It was re-released on GOG.com in 2011 and Steam in 2015.
The source code for both Little Big Adventure engines was released under the GPL in October 2021.
devStory: Adeline Software International made it as the sequel to Little Big Adventure, revisiting only Citadel Island and Desert Island from the first game before moving most of the story to Zeelich. It sold more than 300,000 copies by August 1999, but GameSpot noted that weak sales of the first game had left Twinsen obscure in the United States, where it failed commercially, unlike France, and some English voice acting was criticised as corny next to the French. Computer Gaming World's Robert Coffey praised its unparalleled sense of marvel and imagination and its blend of action and adventure, GameSpot gave it 8.1 out of 10 and Next Generation four stars. It was runner-up for Computer Gaming World's 1997 Adventure Game of the Year, which went to The Curse of Monkey Island.

title: BioForge
description: BioForge (1995) is Origin's motion-captured interactive movie in which an amnesiac cyborg tries to escape the alien moon where mad scientists rebuilt him as a weapon.
longDescription:
In writer Jack Herman's distant future, scientists called the Mondites plot to overthrow the galactic government, the Reticulum, by blending man and machine into assassins. On Daedalus, a moon once home to the long-vanished Phyxx, the base commander Dr. Mastaba mutilates abducted prisoners for his ABA Project, and with technology borrowed from the Phyxx he finally succeeds. Then an alien is accidentally revived from its tomb, damaging the reactor and killing half the base. The player is Experimental Unit AP-127, a cyborg who wakes in a cell with no memories and must uncover the truth about himself, the station and the alien race, learning much of the backstory from diaries left by the crew.

Play mixes exploration, item puzzles, fighting and conversation, with full control over a character whose identity depends on the player's actions. Tank controls let him turn, walk, run, sidestep and enter a combat stance with punches, kicks and hand-to-hand weapons, in a system compared to Alone in the Dark. A replaceable, depletable battery inside his body powers a regeneration system that heals all damage and a built-in projectile weapon, the PFD Prototype, and upgrading or swapping it is key at certain points. An armoured suit lets him survive the harsh atmosphere outside and explore an archaeological dig.
trivia: Its working title was Interactive Movie 1.
Director Ken Demarest had the idea while programming Ultima VII, which he felt had too much freedom.
Origin reportedly paid $30,000 to $32,000 for the Flock of Birds motion-capture hardware.
A sequel was begun, re-scoped as an expansion pack and finally cancelled.
PC Gamer US nominated it as 1995's Best Adventure Game.
devStory: A core team of ten under Ken Demarest developed it at Origin from February 1993 to March 1995, in C++ and assembly, with a custom script language for the world and an HTML-style language for the interface. Models built in 3D Studio were animated from actors captured with the Flock of Birds system, using an in-house pose editor called S.A.L.S.A., and John Tipton created the music and effects. Richard Garriott, helping launch the interactive movie theme, argued that FMV alone did not make a game an interactive movie. Reviews were mixed: its "first-class" graphics, detail and interactivity were praised, and Next Generation found its characters moved in "a smooth, utterly convincing manner", but its system requirements, combat and controls drew criticism, and Edge called it "enjoyable, but ultimately uninvolving". GOG.com re-released it in 2012.

title: Crusader: No Remorse
description: Crusader: No Remorse (1995) is Origin's isometric action game in which a supersoldier deserts a tyrannical 22nd-century world government and fights for the Resistance in highly destructible levels.
longDescription:
Economic collapse has merged the world's nations into the World Economic Consortium, a dictatorship with taxes above 90 per cent that crushes all opposition. Returning from a mission in which they refused to fire on civilians, three of its elite Silencers are ambushed by a WEC mech, and the one survivor, a nameless captain, joins the outnumbered Resistance led by General Quentin Maxis. Distrusted and resented as a symbol of the regime, he earns respect through dangerous missions, often with poor equipment, until he uncovers the Vigilance Platform, a space station able to bombard any city on Earth, as a traitor betrays his cell from within.

The game is split into missions in factories, military bases, offices and space stations, full of soldiers, servomechs, traps, puzzles and civilians. Security cameras and secured doors trigger alarms that teleport in fresh soldiers or release robots until an alarm box is used, and keycards and switches do not work while it sounds. The environment was unusually interactive: most of it can be destroyed, and traps and defences can be turned on enemies, encouraging tactics that save resources. Weapons, ammunition, credits and healing stations are scattered through each level, and in the PC version the Silencer can carry only five firearms at once.
trivia: Director Tony Zurovec's chief inspiration was Castle Wolfenstein.
It runs on an advanced, SVGA version of the Ultima VIII: Pagan isometric engine.
Its Asylum Sound System used MOD files rather than General MIDI to sound good without expensive hardware.
A four-player co-operative mode was in the game until just before release.
It shipped with a fold-out propaganda poster, a newspaper and guides from both the WEC and the Resistance.
devStory: Loose Cannon Productions, a division of Origin Systems, developed it under Tony Zurovec, with live-action FMV cut-scenes in which the hero never speaks and music by Andrew Sega and Dan Grandpre of Straylight Productions. It was released for MS-DOS in 1995, with PlayStation and Saturn ports in 1997. Zurovec hoped for 100,000 sales, but it sold well over a quarter of a million and, according to Retro Gamer, earned a higher return on investment than any other standalone Origin product. GameSpot called it "so viscerally exciting that its shortcomings can be overlooked" despite cheesy cut-scenes and erratic controls, Next Generation praised its interface, graphics and sound, and Computer Games Magazine argued it was more than a mindless shooter. Crusader: No Regret followed in 1996.

title: System Shock 2
description: System Shock 2 (1999) is Irrational Games and Looking Glass Studios' first-person action RPG and survival horror game, in which an amnesiac soldier fights a genetic infection aboard the starship Von Braun.
longDescription:
In 2114 the rebuilt TriOptimum launches the experimental faster-than-light starship Von Braun, escorted by the military vessel Rickenbacker. A soldier wakes from a cryo-tube with amnesia and an illegal cybernetic implant to find the ship overrun by the Many, an infection that has turned the crew into hostile hosts and calls to him telepathically. Dr. Janice Polito guides him to safety, but when he reaches her she is dead: the voice was SHODAN, the AI of the first System Shock, whose bioengineering experiments created the Many and who now needs him to destroy them. The story unfolds through audio logs and ghostly apparitions.

It plays as a first-person shooter with a role-playing layer. Players begin by choosing a career in the Marines, Navy or OSA, which grant weapons, hacking and repair, or psionic powers, then develop freely using cyber-modules earned for objectives. Nanites buy supplies from vending machines and revive the player at Quantum Bio-Reconstruction Machines. Hacking is a minigame of connecting three nodes in a row. Weapons degrade and must be maintained, ammunition is scarce and suited to particular foes, from anti-personnel rounds for organic enemies to armour-piercing rounds for machines, and enemy organs can be researched to learn their weaknesses.
trivia: It began as a standalone game called Junction Point.
It was made in 18 months on a $1.7 million budget.
To meet a one-year deadline the team used Looking Glass's unfinished Dark Engine, also used for Thief.
Its character system was based on the methods of the pen-and-paper game Traveller.
Ken Levine wanted SHODAN's betrayal to deceive the player, not just the character, a controversial choice within the team.
devStory: Looking Glass approached Irrational Games in 1997 to co-develop a game, and the team, fans of System Shock, set out to push its dungeon-crawler roots further from the Doom comparisons that had hurt the original. Electronic Arts, which owned the System Shock rights, suggested it become a sequel, and the story was reworked. Horror rested on isolation, a fragile hero, moody sound and careful lighting. Released in August 1999 for Windows, it won over a dozen awards, including seven Game of the Year awards, and was praised for its hybrid play, sound and story, but sold only 58,671 copies by April 2000. GameSpot later called it "well ahead of its time", and Irrational's spiritual successor BioShock followed in 2007.

title: Jagged Alliance 2
description: Jagged Alliance 2 (1999) is Sir-Tech Canada's tactical RPG in which hired mercenaries and local rebels fight to free the Latin American country of Arulco from the ruthless Queen Deidranna.
longDescription:
The fictional country of Arulco has been ruled for years by the ruthless Queen Deidranna, and the player must overthrow her and restore peace. To do it they hire mercenaries and enlist local citizens, who can provide information or join the fight. A strategic map divides Arulco into sectors, where the player moves squads, controls the flow of time and uses a laptop to read email, buy equipment and hire or fire mercenaries. Mercenaries can be assigned to treat the wounded, repair gear, practise or teach skills, and train local militia to defend liberated sectors, and captured vehicles speed travel.

Sectors are explored on an isometric tactical screen in real time until someone spots an enemy, when play switches to turn-based combat. Each side spends action points to move and act, some unspent points carry over, and a character with points left can interrupt the enemy's turn. Mercenaries can run, crawl, swim and climb onto flat roofs, and there is no visual fog of war, though enemies appear only when someone can see them. The arsenal spans pistols, rifles, machine guns, knives, grenades, mortars, rocket launchers, mines and bombs, with hit chances depending on skill, obstacles and the action points spent aiming.
trivia: It is the third game in the Jagged Alliance series.
A 1998 magazine demo contained a unique map called Demoville.
It debuted at number one in Germany in April 1999 and passed 100,000 sales there by October.
GameSpot nominated it for 1999's Best Game No One Played.
An open-source AmigaOS 4 port was released in 2008.
devStory: Sir-Tech set out to keep the freedom of movement, character relationships and flexible story of the previous game while adding a real-time mode and character creation. Designer Ian Currie said multiplayer was left out because the non-linear story and role-playing elements did not suit it, and the engine was rewritten from the ground up several times, with much time spent on physics and ballistics, delaying it past October 1998. Released for Windows and later ported to Linux by Tribsoft, it was praised for its freedom, memorable cast, non-linearity and tactics, scoring 85 per cent on GameRankings. It was TalonSoft's second-largest hit and sold an estimated 300,000 copies by 2006, though only 24,000 in North America by the end of 1999. The Unfinished Business expansion followed in 2000.

title: X-COM: Apocalypse
description: X-COM: Apocalypse (1997) is Mythos Games' tactical strategy game, set in the megacity of Mega-Primus, that added real-time combat and a city of rival corporations to the X-COM formula.
longDescription:
Fifty years after Terror from the Deep, the battle of T'leth has ravaged Earth's biosphere and humanity lives in sealed megacities, the first being Mega-Primus, built over the ruins of Toronto. Run by 13 elected senators and the corporations that sustain it, the city is home to marginalised Sectoid hybrids and androids. When new organic, extradimensional aliens attack through tetrahedral gates, the government re-forms X-COM, and the player must eventually find a way to send craft and agents through the gates to take the war to the aliens' own dimension, where enslaved Sectoid survivors are discovered.

As before, there is a management layer, the Cityscape, and an isometric combat mode, the Battlescape, but this was the first X-COM to offer real-time combat alongside turns. Funding now depends on more than shooting down UFOs: X-COM must limit collateral damage, stop aliens infiltrating and taking over organisations, and keep good relations with groups that will demand compensation or attack if angered, such as Transtellar, which can stop agents travelling. The alien-worshipping Cult of Sirius is always hostile. X-COM can sell alien artefacts and its own manufactured goods, or raid other organisations. A self-adjusting system makes alien technology advance faster when the player does well and slower when they struggle.
trivia: Mega-Primus is built over the ruins of Toronto.
By 23 July 1997 it had shipped 120,000 copies worldwide.
It won Turn-based Strategy at PC PowerPlay's 1997 Game of the Year Awards.
GameSpot listed its ending among the most disappointing in 2000.
Fans began the open-source remake OpenApoc in 2014.
devStory: Mythos Games created the game while MicroProse wanted to produce the graphics, a relationship series creator Julian Gollop called "disastrous". He compared the experience to Francis Coppola's on Apocalypse Now: "Just about everything that could go wrong did go wrong", and it took three years and five different producers, with a design he admitted was too ambitious and complex. Artist Terry Greer recalled a painful mix of rendered and hand-drawn styles, including Tim White's intensely detailed character designs that did not shrink well to isometric scale. It still received favourable reviews; Next Generation called it "a step in the right direction, but a step with a wobble". It debuted at number six on PC Data's chart for July 1997 but sold less than the original.

title: Syndicate Wars
description: Syndicate Wars (1996) is Bullfrog's isometric real-time tactics sequel to Syndicate, in which cyborg agents of the EuroCorp megacorporation or the rival Church of the New Epoch fight for control of a world in revolt.
longDescription:
In 2191, 95 years after Syndicate, EuroCorp rules the world through military and economic power and mind-controlling CHIP implants, its decisions made by AIs linked through a global network. A virus called Harbinger, released by the Church of the New Epoch and its leaders The Nine, damages the implants and frees citizens, some of whom take up arms as the Unguided. From its London headquarters EuroCorp sends quartets of heavily armed agents to restore order, while also crushing sub-corporations that switch sides or bid for independence. The war ends on the Moon, reached by an orbital elevator, where The Nine plan to turn ionosphere equipment into a weapon to destroy all life on Earth. The game can also be played from the Church's side.

The isometric view of the original now rotates and tilts, so agents never vanish behind buildings. The player commands four agents, or acolytes, singly or in groups on missions around the globe, briefed through a fictional email system. Health, shields and weapon energy recharge over time, and research unlocks new weapons and cybernetic upgrades, from Uzis, miniguns and flamethrowers to the pulse laser, plasma lance, graviton gun and satellite-directed orbital strikes. The Persuadertron, or Indoctrinator for the Church, converts civilians and enemies into followers. Almost every structure can be destroyed, and money comes from robbing or destroying banks.
trivia: It runs on a modified version of the Magic Carpet engine.
It was first announced as a PlayStation exclusive for 1996, but the DOS version came first and the PlayStation one in 1997.
A Saturn version was cancelled because the market was too small to cover development costs.
Enemies were made to work as a team, unlike the original's, which acted as if unaware of each other.
Producer and lead programmer Mike Diskett later made the spiritual successor Satellite Reign.
devStory: Bullfrog built it on a modified Magic Carpet engine. Mike Diskett recalled that one of the biggest complaints about Syndicate was that agents disappeared behind buildings, and the team waited for the technology to allow a rotating map, while the AI was improved so enemies worked together. Next Generation found it "even more dark and menacing than the original", with stunning SVGA graphics, though the controls took getting used to, and GameSpot's Greg Kasavin said it "masterfully recaptures the dark, deadly emotion of the original" with a huge variety of weapons and scenarios, despite tiny characters and enemies getting free hits during rotation. It won Computer Games Strategy Plus's 1996 action game of the year, while critics judged the PlayStation version inferior.

title: Railroad Tycoon II
description: Railroad Tycoon II (1998) is PopTop Software's business simulation in which the player chairs a railway company across the whole history of the railroad, laying track, running trains and playing the stock market.
longDescription:
The game covers the history of railways from their beginnings to the present and beyond. The player picks a map and becomes chairman of a railroad company, trying to earn profits for investors and meet scenario objectives while rivals, breakdowns, train robbers, economic swings and scripted events get in the way. Most of the work is building track, stations and trains to carry passengers and freight. Revenue depends on time, distance, demand, cargo, the economy, station improvements and difficulty, while fuel, maintenance and overheads eat into it. Rival companies can share track and stations, splitting the revenue, and the view is now dimetric rather than the top-down view of the original.

Industries form production chains: coal and iron mines feed steel mills that turn one load of each into two loads of steel, so a well-planned line hauls raw materials one way and finished goods back. Locomotives differ in speed, fuel, preferred cargo and ability to climb grades, and grow more prone to breakdowns with age, while a wreck destroys engine and cargo alike. Players can also buy industries, though idle ones lose money. The financial side covers bonds, share buybacks, stock issues, dividends, mergers and bankruptcy, and the economy swings between booming, prosperity, normal, recession and depression, affecting revenue, share prices and interest rates.
trivia: Its soundtrack is mostly railroad blues and bluegrass, recorded in the studio rather than played as MIDI, some with vocals.
By August 2000 it existed in 39 different versions worldwide, eight of them English Windows editions.
The Dreamcast version of 2000 has remade 3D graphics.
A Platinum edition added over 50 community-made maps.
It was later ported to Linux.
devStory: In late 1997 Bruce Shelley said he would happily work on such a game but doubted it could sell in a blockbuster market. PopTop made it and Gathering of Developers published it, hoping for 250,000 sales in the 1998 holiday season; it passed 500,000 by February 1999, and the computer version sold more than 1.5 million copies by August 2001. PopTop's Franz J. Felsl said it did better in Europe than in the US, and Phil Steinmeyer credited its many editions, with the Gold edition and The Second Century expansion making up about a third of sales and the PlayStation version unsuccessful. It won Computer Games Strategy Plus's and CNET Gamecenter's 1998 Strategy Game of the Year awards, the former saying it captured almost everything gamers loved about the original.

title: SimCity 3000
description: SimCity 3000 (1999) is Maxis's third major SimCity, adding rubbish collection, farms, neighbour deals, named advisors and a greener, more varied landscape to the city-building formula.
longDescription:
The biggest change from SimCity 2000 is waste management: once a city reaches a medium size, rubbish piles up and must be disposed of at the city's expense. Farms appear on large light industrial zones with low land values and little pollution, a third zoning density joins the previous two, and power plants and now water facilities lose output with age before reaching the end of their lives. Neighbouring cities, introduced in SimCity 2000, become trading partners: mayors buy and sell water, electricity and waste services for a monthly charge, with penalties for cancelling a deal. Business deals let the player earn large sums by allowing structures such as a maximum security prison, at the cost of lower land values.

Land value is simulated much more realistically, producing distinct slums, middle-class districts and wealthy areas, with values highest near the city centre. The dimetric view remains, but the landscape turns from mostly brown to a realistic green that shifts with height from beach sand to bare ground and snow, with five steepnesses of slope and trees from small deciduous ones to towering redwoods. Seven named advisors give in-depth advice on finance, transport, environment, planning, safety, health and education, and utilities, while petitioners, from citizens to outside interests pushing harmful schemes like casinos, ask the player to change policies.
trivia: It was first developed as a fully 3D game, shown at E3 1997 in a demo later regarded as an embarrassment.
Lucy Bradshaw was brought in from EA in November 1997 to lead the project after the 3D version was scrapped.
It shipped a million copies in its first six months.
It was the best-selling computer game in the US in the first half of 1999.
Loki Games handled the Linux release.
devStory: In 1996, before Electronic Arts bought Maxis, management pushed for a fully 3D SimCity despite staff concerns that it was too graphically demanding, and it was developed for a year; its future release was even feared to be the fatal blow to a struggling Maxis. EA's new general manager Luc Barthelet questioned it, the 3D version was scrapped, and Lucy Bradshaw led a new version built on SimCity 2000's dimetric projection. Released in 1999, it sold 657,514 copies in the US that year, second only to RollerCoaster Tycoon, and the Unlimited edition sold another 1.1 million there by 2006. IGN gave it 9.0, GameSpot 8.5 while criticising the advisors, and Next Generation four stars, though the Mac OS version was poorly received.

title: SimTower: The Vertical Empire
description: SimTower: The Vertical Empire (1994), first released in Japan as The Tower, is Yoot Saito's skyscraper management simulation in which keeping the lifts moving is the key to a five-star tower.
longDescription:
The player builds and runs a modern multi-use skyscraper, deciding where to place restaurants, condominiums, offices, hotel rooms, shops and lifts. Tenants leave if their stress rises, so they must be given medical centres, car parks, recycling, clean hotel rooms with housekeepers and, above all, efficient transport. Built around an elevator simulation program, the game puts great weight on lift management: standard lifts span at most 30 floors, while express lifts can run the full height of a tower of up to 100 floors above ground and nine below. Attracting more tenants raises the tower from one star to five, unlocking new facilities.

The top rating, Tower, is awarded only for building a cathedral on top of a five-star building with every floor above ground developed. Random events keep the player busy: terrorists may phone to demand a ransom for a hidden bomb, which security must find before it explodes; workers digging underground may find gold treasure; and visiting VIPs judge the tower on things like a comfortable suite and easy navigation, their favourable rating being needed to reach the next star. At the end of each year Santa Claus and his reindeer fly past the tower. Graphics and sound resemble earlier Sim games, with background office buzz and lift bells.
trivia: Yoot Saito was inspired to make games by playing SimCity on the Macintosh at Waseda University.
An elevator company declined to share its scheduling information with Saito for research.
Saito's first mock-up was a monochrome tower made in HyperCard.
Japan's Nihon Keizai Shimbun named Saito Best Young Manager/Venture of the Year for the game.
The sequel, The Tower II, was released outside Japan as Yoot Tower.
devStory: After his first game, a simulation for a publishing house's media project, Saito's employer refused a second because it was not a video game company, so he left and built on his ideas of elevators and towers with freelance programmer Takumi Abe. Late in development he raised the palette from 16 to 256 colours and brought in a second designer for animation. The Tower was a profitable success in Japan, and after Will Wright told Maxis president Jeff Braun about it, Maxis localised it and renamed it to fit the Sim series, releasing it for Windows and Macintosh in November 1994; Saturn and 3DO ports followed in Japan in 1996. Reviews praised its open-ended, immersive formula but criticised its thin documentation and slow game speed, a real problem since time must pass to earn income.

title: Caesar III
description: Caesar III (1998) is Impressions Games' city builder in which a provincial governor raises Roman cities, keeping citizens fed, entertained and devout while facing disasters, angry gods and invaders.
longDescription:
In Career mode the player takes branching assignments set in historical Roman cities such as Brundisium and Londinium, each of growing size and complexity, and chooses whether to play a peaceful map, with stricter victory conditions plus earthquakes and fires, or a military one with the risk of invasion. The City Construction Kit offers open-ended building without victory conditions. Cities are built in an isometric view, and growth depends on interconnected supply chains for water, food, religion, entertainment, education and health. Terrain matters too, with river channels, fertile land and mining areas offering different resources and obstacles.

Unlike Caesar II, everything happens on a single map rather than separate province and city maps. Its signature mechanic is the walker: inhabitants deliver services to buildings by walking past them, so the layout of roads becomes a strategic question. Progress is judged on population and four ratings, Culture from temples, theatres and schools, Prosperity from jobs, housing and revenue, Peace from freedom from crime, riots and invasion, and Favor from meeting Caesar's requests for tribute and gifts on time. A chief advisor and specialists for labour, health, education, trade and religion help, and an Empire map shows trade routes and threats.
trivia: It began as a city-building game set in space before returning to Ancient Rome after six months.
It is part of Sierra's City Building series.
Sierra released a map editor with over twenty city locations as a free download.
It shipped 150,000 copies in its first month.
Global sales passed 400,000 by January 1999.
devStory: David Lester admitted Impressions hesitated over a third Caesar because Caesar II had been so well received that they did not know where to take it. After six months on a space setting, the team returned to Rome, which Simon Bradbury said offered a "wealth of material for a strategy game". Many features answered criticisms of Caesar II, including mission choice to reduce repetition and combat integrated into the city view, while walkers were meant to do something different from SimCity's simple coverage. Released on 30 September 1998 for Windows and Mac OS, it was praised for its presentation and complex design, though its military features drew criticism. It earned a German Gold award for 100,000 sales, and Sierra said the Caesar series had sold well over a million units by April 1999.

title: Sid Meier's Civilization II
description: Sid Meier's Civilization II (1996) is MicroProse's turn-based strategy sequel in which a tribe founded in 4000 BC grows into a civilisation that wins by conquest, by reaching Alpha Centauri or by surviving to 2020.
longDescription:
Players choose one of 21 historical civilisations, from the Americans, Aztecs and Babylonians to the Vikings and Zulus, or name their own, and compete against computer-controlled rivals, with barbarians as a further threat. The map is made of tiles with varied terrain, special resources and improvements such as irrigation, generated randomly to the player's specifications or pre-made. Starting in 4000 BC with a few units, including settlers to found the first cities, players explore the unknown world, and cities harvest food, trade and production from nearby tiles to build units, improvements and wonders of the world. Units, like chess pieces, mirror historical soldiers and occupations.

Once civilisations meet they open diplomatic relations, and in war one can conquer another's cities, eliminating a player who loses them all. Research is central, with advances grouped by era from ancient to modern. Victory comes from conquering every rival, launching a spaceship that reaches Alpha Centauri, or surviving until 2020 AD, after which a score is calculated. Compared with the original it adds and changes units, civilisations, wonders, tile specials and technologies, introduces diplomatic reputation and production waste, switches to an isometric map and improves the computer opponents. It also supports mods and scenarios that recreate historical, fictional and other situations.
trivia: Its working title was Civilization 2000.
Development was kept secret for years and announced only during final balancing.
Brian Reynolds added mod support, inspired by Doom, despite Sid Meier's fear that poor mods would be blamed on the company.
It was developed for Windows 3.1 using the WinG API.
It sold around three million copies by 2001.
devStory: Brian Reynolds, Douglas Caspian-Kaufman and Jeff Briggs designed it; asked about Sid Meier's involvement, Reynolds said, "We sat down and brainstormed about it and hashed out ideas, that's about it." Meier said the original "greatly favored the military approach to achieving victory" and the balance was adjusted to make trade and diplomacy more integral. Released in 1996, it was second on PC Data's chart for April and the fifth best-selling US computer game of the year, passing its predecessor's 850,000 sales by August 1997 and reaching 1.2 million by April 1998. It won numerous awards and appears on many lists of the best games of all time. Activision ported it to the PlayStation, and Civilization III followed.

title: Descent II
description: Descent II (1996) is Parallax Software's six-degrees-of-freedom shooter in which a pilot flies through robot-infested mines across six star systems, destroying each reactor and escaping before the meltdown.
longDescription:
As in the first Descent, the player pilots a fighter in zero gravity from a first-person view, free to move in any direction and rotate on all three axes, pitch, yaw and roll. Infected robots try to destroy the ship as it navigates extrasolar underground mines. In each level the reactor must be found and blown up, then the ship must escape through the exit before the mine self-destructs; every fourth level replaces the reactor with a boss robot. There are four levels in each of six themed star systems, plus six secret levels reached through hidden teleporters, full of power-ups but impossible to save in. Levels are made of rooms linked by doors, some needing blue, yellow or red keys, and new control panels open doors, remove walls or shut off force fields when shot.

To avoid getting lost the player can fire flares, use a headlight, consult a wireframe automap and drop markers on it. The big addition is the Guide-Bot, a scouting robot that, once freed, leads the ship to a chosen objective or power-up. Hostages earn bonus points if rescued, energy stations recharge the ship and generators spawn more robots. Weapons are split into energy-hungry primaries, from pulse lasers to plasma bolts plus two rotary cannons firing shells, and secondaries such as missiles and mines dropped behind the ship, with ten new weapons in all.
trivia: It began as a CD-based expansion pack for Descent before becoming a standalone game.
It cost $500,000 to make.
It was one of the earliest PC games to support force feedback, and officially supported virtual reality and stereoscopic graphics.
Its CD soundtrack featured industrial metal from artists including Type O Negative and Ogre of Skinny Puppy.
The PlayStation version was titled Descent Maximum.
devStory: Parallax Software spent about a year on it, upgrading the graphics to Super VGA with support for 3D accelerator cards. The portal engine was fundamentally unchanged: levels are built from adjacent convex cubes whose shared sides act as portals, so only visible areas are drawn, which kept it practical on inexpensive PCs. Dan Wentz composed the MIDI score. Reviews were very positive, praising the multiplayer and the Guide-Bot; GameSpot wrote that if you did not like Descent at least a little, "there is something wrong with you", and Next Generation praised its SVGA graphics, FMV story scenes and new items. PC Review felt the Guide-Bot undercut the series' disorientation, and the PlayStation version received mixed reviews over its frame rate. Descent 3 followed in 1999.

title: The Settlers II
description: The Settlers II (1996) is Blue Byte's city-building game with real-time strategy elements, in which shipwrecked Romans build supply chains and armies to find their way home through magical portals.
longDescription:
On each map the goal is to build a settlement with a working economy that produces enough soldiers to conquer rival territory, until the player controls the whole map or a set part of it. That means economic micromanagement: placing buildings, generating resources and keeping supply and demand in balance, all through a point-and-click interface with windows modelled on Windows 95. In the campaign, Roman sailors led by Captain Octavius are shipwrecked on an uncharted island and use a series of magical portals to try to return to the Empire, clashing with Nubians, Vikings and Japanese along the way across ten missions. In Free Game mode, players set their own rules and play with or against other people and the computer.

The core supply-and-demand play is broadly the same as in the first game, but much else changed. The graphics and sound were enhanced, with more movement on screen and more animations for the settlers themselves, and the four races look distinct. The economic system is more complex, and combat is more strategic, letting players use scouts and stationary offensive weapons, although soldiers still cannot be controlled directly in battle. The Mission CD added a nine-mission campaign in which Octavius's great-grandson sets out to conquer the world, along with new maps and a map editor.
trivia: It was originally released as The Settlers II: Veni, Vidi, Vici.
Volker Wertich, creator of the first game, sat it out, saying he didn't want to see "those little men for a while".
Lead designer Thomas Häuser had worked on quality assurance for the original.
A 2007 Nintendo DS port was panned for unresponsive controls and game-breaking bugs.
An Amiga version of the Gold Edition was released in October 2025.
devStory: Blue Byte always intended a sequel if the first game succeeded, and with The Settlers passing 215,000 sales by June 1996 a team of twelve began work immediately, seeking fan feedback and fixing aspects of the original they had been unhappy with. Thomas Häuser, who had compiled a list of problems while testing the first game, became project manager. Released in Germany in April 1996 and in Britain and North America that August, it earned 84 per cent on GameRankings. PC Games called it "world-class" and PC Gamer praised an economy "so sound that everything you do makes perfect sense", while common complaints were the lack of direct combat control and online multiplayer. It sold over 600,000 copies, far more than the original, and was remade for its tenth anniversary in 2006.

title: Falcon 4.0
description: Falcon 4.0 (1998) is MicroProse's highly realistic F-16 combat flight simulator, set in a full-scale war on the Korean Peninsula with a dynamic campaign that reacts to the player's actions.
longDescription:
The story begins in the early 1990s with North Korea invading the South and the United States sending aircraft, armour and ships in support; what follows depends on the player and may draw in China and Russia. The simulation models the Block 50/52 F-16 Fighting Falcon and parallels real fighter operations. More than 30 training scenarios teach manoeuvring, avionics and US Air Force procedures before the player enters the campaign, a dogfight mode for single engagements, or Tactical Engagements, effectively miniature campaigns. A logbook records flight hours, kills, decorations and rank, and good flying can earn medals and promotion while destroying friendly targets or ejecting needlessly can bring demotion or court-martial.

Campaigns split into briefings and missions. In briefings the player plans flights and packages, sets steerpoints and weapons loadouts, and can even command ground units directly, and ignoring the positions of enemy SAM sites or combat air patrols will almost certainly mean a short flight. Missions model flying, radar and weapons, threat evaluation, radio and navigation as closely as possible at the highest realism settings. Three campaigns shipped: Tiger Spirit, with the allies on the offensive, Rolling Fire, a closely matched fight, and Iron Fortress, with the South pushed back to its last line. Being dynamic, campaigns have no set path and evolve with the war.
trivia: It was banned in South Korea until 2003 because of its subject.
A developer leaked its source code in April 2000, and Kevin Klemmick later claimed responsibility.
Community work based on the leak became the officially licensed Falcon 4.0: Allied Force in 2005.
The community mod Falcon BMS adds DirectX 11 graphics, 3D cockpits and partial VR support.
The modern MicroProse reacquired the Falcon series copyright in May 2023.
devStory: In development from 1994, it was designed and produced by Steve Blankenship and Gilman Louie as the culmination of Spectrum HoloByte's Falcon series, begun in 1984; HoloByte had bought MicroProse and adopted its name. Slated for late 1996, it was finally rushed out on 12 December 1998 for Christmas, by which point Hasbro owned MicroProse and soon ended official development. It sold 209,000 copies in 1999 alone, and PC Gamer US named it the best simulation of 1998, while Computer Gaming World called it a sim of unprecedented detail. Thanks to the leaked code and its community, it is one of the longest-running PC game series built on a single code base.

title: Imperialism
description: Imperialism (1997) is Frog City Software's turn-based strategy game in which a 19th-century great power builds an industrial economy and empire to be voted, or fought, into ruling the world.
longDescription:
In a randomly generated world the player picks one of seven great powers and starts ruling in 1815. Once a decade every provincial governor in the world meets in the Council of Governors, and a two-thirds vote makes one power world ruler; minor nations favour powers that have treated them well in trade and diplomacy, while great powers back strong militaries. Without a majority, the power with most governors behind it wins in 1915. Historical scenarios let players lead Britain, France, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Russia and Prussia or Germany, Sardinia or Italy, starting in 1820, in the revolutionary year of 1848 or in 1882 as the arms race toward the First World War began.

Each turn decisions are made on five screens: the map, where specialists such as prospectors and engineers work and armies move; transport, industry, trade and diplomacy. The economy is the heart of the game. Timber from forests becomes lumber for transport, factories and ships, furniture to recruit workers or sell, and paper to train workers, educate soldiers and qualify specialists, while iron and coal make steel. Great powers often buy raw materials from minor nations and sell finished goods back, earning money and goodwill. Research boosts production or upgrades the military, battles can be fought by the player or the AI, and up to seven people can play over a network.
trivia: Its working titles included Sphere of Influence, Age of Industry and Sid Meier's Industrialization.
The 1820 historical start appears chosen so that France is not too weak at the outset.
Naval battles are always resolved by the computer.
Ubisoft has held its copyright since 2004.
It was followed by Imperialism II: Age of Exploration.
devStory: Frog City Software developed it for Windows and Macintosh, and Strategic Simulations published it in 1997, with a tutorial, five difficulty levels and later fan-made editors and mods such as a world map. According to former Frog City staff, its sales were unexpectedly strong: in December 1998 CNET Gamecenter's Barry Brenesal called it a "sleeper hit" and "extremely successful for a turn-based strategy title", still selling past 100,000 copies. It outsold its original sales goal more than seven times over and passed 300,000 copies by 2007. Macworld's Michael Gowan wrote that "while it lacks tactical realism, this sim provides strategy buffs some compelling management challenges".

title: Forsaken
description: Forsaken (1998) is Probe Entertainment's Descent-style 3D tunnel shooter, set on a dead future Earth and famed for coloured lighting so impressive it became a graphics card benchmark.
longDescription:
In 2113 a shockwave from a scientific accident has wiped out all life on Earth. In the PC and PlayStation versions the player is a scavenger hunting the planet's lost treasure, while in the Nintendo 64 release the goal is to kill the looters seeking it. In the style of Descent, the player steers a vehicle with full 3D movement through tunnels, with similar weapons and power-ups and missiles and mines counted as secondary weapons, plus elements borrowed from Quake. Its 22 missions ask the player to destroy every enemy ship in a maze of tunnels or hit targets such as a time limit or a percentage of enemies killed, and, as in Star Fox 64, different paths open depending on which targets are met.

There are four difficulty settings, easy, normal, hard and total mayhem, each with tougher enemies and less ammunition; the challenge was so severe that Acclaim released a patch that cut the difficulty dramatically. Multiplayer offers Free for All, Team Game, Capture the Flag, Flag Chase, Bounty Hunt and Team Bounty Hunt, each with sub-options, for up to 16 players on PC, four on Nintendo 64, where up to three computer players can join, and two on PlayStation. The PC version can also record demos. Every version's real-time coloured lighting drew praise, N64 Magazine likening heated battles to a lava lamp.
trivia: It was first titled ProjectX, then Condemned, before a possible naming conflict led to Forsaken.
It was often bundled with graphics cards and used as a benchmark for years.
Its drum and bass soundtrack was by The Swarm, Dominic Glynn and Stephen Root.
A Saturn version was cancelled when Acclaim withdrew support for the system.
Nightdive Studios released a high-definition remaster in 2018.
devStory: Probe Entertainment developed it between 1996 and 1998 under Fergus McGovern, as Probe was merged into its parent Acclaim and Microsoft's DirectX was starting to dominate PC development; the project was heavily driven by technology from the start. Iguana UK ported it to the Nintendo 64 as Forsaken 64 the same year. Reviews were favourable on all platforms. AllGame gave the PC version four and a half stars, calling its gameplay uninventive but praising "utterly impressive technical savvy", its lighting, frame rates, explosions and missile smoke trails, though the difficulty was sometimes considered excessive. Staff at Acclaim Studios Teesside planned a sequel that was scrapped when the studio closed in 2002.

title: Shogo: Mobile Armor Division
description: Shogo: Mobile Armor Division (1998) is Monolith's anime-inspired first-person shooter, mixing on-foot gunfights with battles in giant mechs, and the first game built on the LithTech engine.
longDescription:
In a war over the planet Cronus and its supply of kato, the liquid reactant that makes interstellar travel possible, the player is Sanjuro Makabe, a Mobile Combat Armor pilot and commander in the army of the United Corporate Authority. Founded as a joint venture of three organisations, the UCA is now independent and the dominant military power. Sanjuro's mission is to find and assassinate Gabriel, leader of the rebel group The Fallen. Before the game begins he has lost his brother Toshiro, his best friend Baku and his girlfriend Kura in the war, and he is driven by revenge and by his relationship with Kura's sister Kathryn; in his words, "It's kinda complicated." Most of the action takes place on Cronus or the spaceship Leviathan.

The game alternates standard on-foot shooting with combat in anime-style bipedal mechs, which, unlike in simulators such as MechWarrior, are controlled just like a first-person shooter. Its combat system includes critical hits: an attack will occasionally deal extra damage and give the player a health bonus, though enemies can score critical hits too. At two pivotal points the player makes a decision; the first is almost purely narrative, but the second determines who the player fights for the rest of the game and how it ends. The design draws heavily on Japanese animation, particularly Patlabor and Appleseed, and the real robot mecha genre.
trivia: It was originally called Riot: Mobile Armor.
Monolith shipped 100,000 copies to retailers in its debut week in November 1998.
It sold only about 20,000 copies in the US over Christmas 1998, and its planned expansion was cancelled.
Hyperion Entertainment ported it to the Macintosh, Linux and, in 2001, Amiga PowerPC.
Its critical success led Monolith on to The Operative: No One Lives Forever.
devStory: Lead designer Craig Hubbard later said that Shogo, "although critically successful", fell embarrassingly short of its goals, "a grim reminder of the perils of wild optimism and unchecked ambition" for a small team that struggled with planning, scope, staffing and inexperience. About six months before shipping they realised they could not make it great, "so we just focused on making it fun", putting their energy into making the weapons fun to use. Reviews were favourable, just short of universal acclaim on Metacritic, and Next Generation called it "an excellent game" able to stand up to Half-Life and SiN. CNET Gamecenter's Mark Asher called its sales disappointing, and with SiN and Blood II also failing he suggested the shooter market was smaller than believed.

title: The Nomad Soul
description: The Nomad Soul (1999), known in North America as Omikron: The Nomad Soul, is Quantic Dream's genre-mixing adventure in a domed alien city, with a soundtrack and cameo by David Bowie.
longDescription:
Omikron is a crowded metropolis on the world of Phaenon, sealed beneath a vast crystal dome since the planet's sun died and an ice age set in. Its sectors, Anekbah, Qalisar, Jaunpur, Jahangir and Lahoreh, have grown apart because citizens may not leave their own. A police officer, Kay'l 669, asks the player to leave their dimension and enter Omikron in his body to continue his investigation into serial killings. The trail reveals that the killer is a demon, that police commander Gandhar is a demon luring human souls into Omikron, and that Kay'l's request was a trap: if the character dies, the real player supposedly loses their soul forever. An underground movement, the Awakened, offers help.

Play mixes exploration, conversation and fighting, seen from third-person and side-on views in unarmed combat and first person with weapons. The player walks, runs, rides vehicles called Sliders and takes lifts to apartments and offices, and combat, speed and resilience improve with practice. Energy is restored with medikits, food and drink, and mana allows spells. On death, and eventually at will, the player is reincarnated in the body of the first character to touch them, with over forty people to inhabit. The SNEAK terminal holds character information, inventory and vital clues, magic rings save the game and buy advice, and seteks, the local currency, buy weapons and supplies.
trivia: David Bowie wrote ten original songs with Reeves Gabrels and spent two weeks in Paris on design sessions.
Bowie appears as Boz and as the singer of an in-game band playing gigs around the city.
David Cage's 200-page script was called "technically impossible" by his music-business contacts.
Cage added a first-person view at Eidos's request, despite it giving him headaches.
A planned sequel was cancelled.
devStory: Tired of 15 years as a composer, David Cage began writing it in 1994, set up a team of friends in one of his studio's isolation booths and gave them six months to build an engine and prototype before the money ran out. In the last week he called Eidos in London, which signed a publishing deal by noon the next day; a prototype was shown at E3 three months later, and the game took two and a half years. Cage wanted "a movie-like experience - with total immersion" mixing genres. Reviewers praised its graphics, soundtrack, story, reincarnation and combat but criticised its controls, loading times and mix of styles. Nominated as 1999's best PC adventure by several outlets, it sold over 600,000 copies, though few in North America. A Dreamcast version followed in 2000.

title: Gabriel Knight 3: Blood of the Sacred, Blood of the Damned
description: Gabriel Knight 3: Blood of the Sacred, Blood of the Damned (1999) is Jane Jensen's 3D adventure in which Gabriel Knight and Grace Nakimura search for a kidnapped baby in southern France and uncover vampires, Templars and the Grail.
longDescription:
Gabriel Knight, voiced again by Tim Curry, and Grace Nakimura, voiced by Charity James, take on a case to find a kidnapped infant and are drawn into a mystery involving vampires, the Knights Templar, the Holy Grail and Jesus in the Languedoc region of France. The story is inspired by the conspiracy theories surrounding Bérenger Saunière, a 19th-century priest said to have hidden a treasure around Rennes-le-Château. The game recreates a fictionalised version of the village, including the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene, alongside the real Rennes-les-Bains and Château de Blanchefort.

The story covers three days divided into time blocks; Gabriel handles the opening chapters, after which most alternate between him and Grace. Each block has required actions that can be done in any order, plus optional ones that add background, and a ticking clock signals when an action has changed things elsewhere. An overhead map with hints shows key locations, and a running score tracks progress. Moving the cursor over an object brings up a bar of verbs to examine, take or talk, and interviews offer topics to question people about, though conversations cannot be reviewed afterwards. Unlike earlier games in the series it is fully 3D, with the camera freely controlled except in cut-scenes and conversations. Its huge Le Serpent Rouge puzzle was called one of the best-designed in adventure history.
trivia: Jensen began designing it in December 1996, and the team already knew it would be the last Gabriel Knight.
A notorious puzzle has Gabriel use tape and cat hair to make a fake moustache; programmer Scott Bilas said none of the developers liked it.
It was announced in mid-August 1997.
It was the last game Sierra made before the adventure genre's collapse.
It was re-released on GOG.com in 2010 and Steam in 2016.
devStory: Sierra wanted the series in 3D to keep up with the times, but the team had little experience with it; programmer Scott Bilas joined mid-production to be told it was nearly finished, only to find features needed to make it playable were missing. Struggles with the engine caused delays, and some puzzles Jensen designed proved too complex and were replaced with ones she disliked. Jensen said "we were the last dinosaur on the block". Released for Windows in 1999, it was not a commercial success but received favourable reviews: IGN said it "proves that adventure games still have some life left in them", while IGN and GameSpot both criticised Curry's accent, some dialogue and the move to 3D.

sources.title: Gabriel Knight 3: Blood of the Sacred, Blood of the Damned

title: Shadow Warrior
description: Shadow Warrior (1997) is 3D Realms' Build-engine shooter in which the bodyguard Lo Wang turns on his employer's demonic plan to conquer a futuristic Japan, armed with a katana, shuriken and sticky bombs.
longDescription:
Lo Wang is a bodyguard and enforcer for Zilla Enterprises, a conglomerate that controls every major industry in a futuristic Japan. Well paid, he has long ignored its corruption, until company president Master Zilla allies with ancient deities to conquer Japan with creatures from the "dark side". Lo Wang quits, Zilla sends the creatures to kill him, and after learning that Zilla also had his old mentor Master Leep murdered, Lo Wang swears to end his schemes. The game ends with Zilla defeated in a giant samurai-styled war mech, though he escapes and promises they will meet again.

Like Duke Nukem 3D it runs on Ken Silverman's Build engine, but it pushed the engine further, with true room-over-room spaces, 3D voxels instead of flat sprites for weapons and items, transparent water, climbable ladders, turrets and drivable vehicles such as tanks, some of them armed. Levels mix combat with puzzles. The Japanese-themed arsenal includes shuriken and a katana alongside Uzis, a riot gun firing shotgun shells and an Eraser-inspired railgun, and the heads and hearts of certain enemies can be used as weapons. It marked the first appearance of a sticky bomb in a first-person shooter, an idea later popularised by Halo. Violent but humorous, the game also contains some sexual themes.
trivia: Development began in early 1994 as Shadow Warrior 3D, with screenshots released alongside Hocus Pocus.
Jim Norwood came up with the idea and George Broussard designed Lo Wang.
Lee Jackson's soundtrack played from CD audio rather than MIDI, allowing East Asian instruments and ambient tracks.
3D Realms released the source code in 2005, and the first source port appeared a day later.
Its depiction of East Asian cultures was criticised, notably by Elliot Chin in Computer Gaming World.
devStory: George Broussard said in 1996 that the team wanted it "to surpass Duke Nukem 3D in features and gameplay and that's a TALL order", and more tongue-in-cheek humour was added to match Duke's style. GT Interactive released the shareware version on 13 May 1997 and the full game that September, and Mark Adams ported it to Mac OS. Reviews ranged from average to positive: Computer Gaming World called it "an average action game" despite good engine enhancements, while GamePro praised its style, level design and soundtrack, and GameSpot found it "pretty fun despite its dated qualities". It sold 118,500 copies in the US by December 2002 and the shareware was downloaded 400,000 times. It was bundled with Duke Nukem 3D as East Meets West in 1998, later made free on Steam, and rebooted by Flying Wild Hog in 2013.

title: Strife: Quest for the Sigil
description: Strife (1996) is Rogue Entertainment's first-person shooter RPG, the last commercial standalone Doom-engine game, in which a mercenary joins a resistance fighting a plague-born religious tyranny.
longDescription:
A comet impact brought a deadly virus to the planet. Millions died, and some survivors mutated and began hearing the voice of a malevolent deity, forming The Order and enslaving everyone else. An unnamed mercenary, captured by Order troops near the town of Tarnhill, kills his guards, escapes and is recruited by Rowan into the resistance, The Front. Kept in touch by radio with a Front operative codenamed Blackbird, who offers help and commentary throughout, he takes missions from the rebel leader Macil and joins the assault on the Order's castle, where he kills the Programmer and discovers that the weapon he wielded is one of five fragments of the Sigil, a powerful weapon the Order worships.

Combat against the Order's infantry and war robots is standard first-person shooting, starting with just a dagger and finding weapons such as a crossbow and flamethrower, with an inventory for first aid kits, armour and gold. What set it apart were role-playing elements: friendly and neutral characters to talk and trade with, who hand out missions; alarms that bring guards running if the player opens fire outside combat, though the dagger and poison crossbow bolts allow stealthy kills; and two attributes, accuracy and stamina, that improve at certain points. Instead of linear levels, Tarnhill serves as a hub linking areas that stay as the player left them, and later the player must decide whom to trust, starting with whether to follow Macil's order to kill the Oracle.
trivia: It was the last commercially released standalone PC game built on id Software's Doom engine.
It began at Cygnus Studios, makers of Raptor: Call of the Shadows, who moved from Chicago to Texas to work with id.
After internal conflicts split Cygnus, the departing employees founded Rogue Entertainment and resumed work on it.
Blackbird's voice and personality were singled out for praise by reviewers.
Nightdive Studios released Strife: Veteran Edition in 2014.
devStory: Cygnus Studios had been making The Second Sword on id's older ShadowCaster engine when id asked it to build a Doom-engine game instead and relocate to Texas; the studio dropped The Second Sword for Strife, but conflicts soon split it, founder Scott Host returned to Chicago and the project was effectively cancelled until the breakaway staff formed Rogue Entertainment. The shareware version came out on 23 February 1996 and the full game that May, published by Velocity in North America and Studio 3DO in Europe. Reviews praised its novel play, in which killing everyone in sight ends badly, and its voice acting, but criticised the obsolete engine next to Duke Nukem 3D and Quake and its single save slot. It was later seen as underappreciated and a precursor to games such as Deus Ex.

title: Quake III Arena
description: Quake III Arena (1999) is id Software's multiplayer-focused first-person shooter, one of the first modern arena shooters and a long-standing fixture of esports tournaments.
longDescription:
Unlike earlier Quakes there is no story campaign. The setup is a single line: "the greatest warriors of all time fight for the amusement of a race called the Vadrigar in the Arena Eternal", and the intro shows one such warrior, Sarge, abducted while making a last stand. Single-player instead recreates multiplayer against bots, climbing tiers of maps from Crash at tier 0 to Xaero at tier 7, with duel-sized tournament maps acting as boss battles. Character models and biographies keep continuity with Quake and Doom, and the gothic-meets-technological architecture returns along with the Quad Damage, rocket launcher and BFG.

Weapons are balanced by role, such as the railgun at long range and the lightning gun up close, while the BFG becomes essentially a fast-firing rocket launcher hidden in hard-to-reach places. Weapons respawn at set points; on death a player loses everything and restarts with the map's spawn weapons, usually the gauntlet and machine gun, dropping their current gun for others to grab. Modes include Free for All, Team Deathmatch, one-on-one Tournament and Capture the Flag on symmetrical maps, all played over networks or the internet on a client-server model with a handicap system. Its minimalist design, deep customisation of settings such as field of view and advanced movement like strafe-jumping and rocket-jumping helped sustain a community still active in 2026.
trivia: It was made by nine people in 18 months.
Steve Jobs showed it publicly at Macworld in January 1999, and ATI leaked a hardware-vendor build that March.
A chainsaw and grappling hook in early builds did not make the final game.
John Carmack has called it his favourite of the games he worked on.
Its music is by Sonic Mayhem and Front Line Assembly founder Bill Leeb.
devStory: After the leak, id released a public beta, Quake III Arena Test, on 24 April 1999, first for Mac OS and later Windows, updating it through several versions with three maps from the final game. Activision published the finished game, which shipped to retailers on 2 December 1999. Reviews were very positive, describing it as fast and addictive, welcoming curved surfaces and finding it best played online; GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann called it outstanding, while Diehard GameFan named it the best "pure deathmatch" around but noted it needed a powerful graphics card. The Dreamcast port scored 93 on Metacritic. Often considered one of the greatest games ever made, it was played at QuakeCon, the Cyberathlete Professional League, DreamHack and the Electronic Sports World Cup.

title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six
description: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six (1998) is Red Storm Entertainment's tactical shooter in which careful planning matters more than firepower, since a single bullet can kill any operative.
longDescription:
Based on Tom Clancy's novel of the same name, it follows Rainbow, a secret international counter-terrorist organisation, as it investigates a seemingly random rise in terrorism and uncovers a conspiracy. Characters are affected by realistic factors and can die from one shot, so tactics and planning are rewarded over brute force. The PC campaign has 16 missions, with objectives such as killing enemies, rescuing hostages, defusing bombs, gathering intelligence and planting surveillance devices, and players can choose anything from stealthy infiltration to a frontal assault, except where stealth is required. Successful missions often last just minutes but may take dozens of attempts and changes of plan.

Before each mission the player is briefed, chooses operatives from five classes, Assault, Demolitions, Electronics, Recon and Sniper, organises them into colour-coded teams and picks weapons, equipment and uniforms. Most operatives are named characters with backstories and skills, but weaker generic reserves can be used to avoid risking them. On a map of the area the player sets each team's route, "go" codes to wait for, where to use flashbangs or breaching charges, and rules of engagement, or picks a preset plan instead. In the mission itself the player leads one operative while computer-controlled teammates follow the plan. Multiplayer offers co-operative missions and competitive matches.
trivia: The original concept, HRT, followed the FBI Hostage Rescue Team and was chosen from around 100 ideas.
It was renamed Black Ops, with settings from World War II to a dystopian story called Jackbooted Thugs considered.
It was developed in parallel with Clancy's novel, though Clancy's own involvement was minimal.
Mission counts differ by version, from 12 on Nintendo 64 to 21 on Dreamcast.
The Eagle Watch mission pack followed in January 1999 and Rogue Spear later that year.
devStory: The idea grew from concepts Red Storm drew up after its founding in 1996. CEO Doug Littlejohns, a former Royal Navy submarine commander and close friend of Clancy, wanted neither an arcade shooter with "mindless violence" nor a "boring" slow strategy game, so realism, action and planning guided the design, though setbacks forced the team to crunch. Released on 21 August 1998, it earned 85 on Metacritic; IGN called it "unlike any first-person shooter yet made" and PC Gamer US "undoubtedly one of the most original and best games of the year", while AI problems and glitches drew criticism and the console ports by other companies scored lower. It sold over 200,000 copies in its first year and is considered a milestone that shaped the tactical shooter genre.

title: Mega Turrican
description: Mega Turrican (1994) is Factor 5's Mega Drive run and gun, in which Bren McGuire dons the Turrican suit once more to destroy the returning Machine, now with a grappling hook.
longDescription:
Years after Bren McGuire, sole survivor of the starship Avalon 1, destroyed The Machine on the planet Landorin, its dark forces are gathering again, devastating planets and enslaving their people. Hearing a young girl's plea for help as her world is invaded, Bren, now leader of the United Planets Freedom Forces, puts on his Turrican assault suit and vows to finish The Machine for good. The player works through large levels, searching for secrets and shooting enemies along the way.

Three upgradeable weapons can be collected: the Multiple spread gun, a more powerful single-direction Laser, and the Rebound, which fires up and down along floors and ceilings while making the forward shot weaker. Pressing jump while holding down, provided there is enough special energy, turns Bren into a wheel, which is nearly invincible, can lay mines and can reach otherwise inaccessible places, a mechanic compared to Metroid's Morph Ball and Sonic's Spin Dash. For the first time in the series, Bren also has a grappling hook, and he can use a rope as well. Despite its long wait for a publisher, the Mega Drive version was later ranked 36th on GamesRadar+'s 2017 list of the best Mega Drive games.
trivia: The Amiga conversion, Turrican 3: Payment Day, was released first, in 1993.
Finished in spring 1993, the Mega Drive version waited a year for a publisher.
Data East released it in North America and contracted Sony Imagesoft for Europe.
German magazine Amiga Games ran a six-part development diary in 1992.
A Mega Turrican: Director's Cut cartridge with restored content appeared in 2022.
