devStory: Factor 5 began Turrican III for the Amiga right after Turrican II in 1991 and had a working demo, but with the Amiga market declining, it and Rainbow Arts moved the game to the Mega Drive. It was completely redesigned for the console and co-developed by Factor 5 and members of Kaiko. Work finished in spring 1993, but because Rainbow Arts did not operate directly in the console business, Factor 5 had to pitch the game to Mega Drive publishers, a process that ended a full year later when Data East signed it. Kaiko then converted the Mega Drive game back to the Amiga as Turrican 3, published by Rainbow Arts in Germany and Renegade elsewhere in Europe. Both versions were generally well received, and the Mega Drive version came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2008.

title: Kirby's Dream Land 3
description: Kirby's Dream Land 3 (1997) is HAL Laboratory's soft-focus Kirby platformer, the last SNES game Nintendo published in North America, with a hidden true final boss that shocked players with its violence.
longDescription:
Kirby is fishing with his friend Gooey on Planet Popstar when a mysterious dark cloud spreads across the sky, breaking the planet's rings. Warned by Coo, Kirby sets off to save Popstar once again. Like other traditional Kirby games, the aim is to reach the end of each stage, walking, swimming and flying through varied levels with the help of Animal Friends and Copy Abilities. Kirby can inhale enemies and often gains their powers, spit stars, fire air puffs and float, and some areas can only be reached with a particular ability, such as blocks that only break to the power shown on them.

There are two endings, depending on whether every Heart Star has been collected. Without them, Kirby defeats King Dedede, possessed by Dark Matter, then beats him a second time as Dark Matter reveals itself; after the credits a huge shadowed orb with a single red eye appears. With them all, Kirby chases Dark Matter into the sky with the Love-Love Stick, built from the Heart Stars, and faces Zero, leader of the Dark Matter army. Zero, a giant eye, fires blood from cuts in its own sclera, and when weakened its iris rips free in a spray of blood before ramming Kirby, a rare example of graphic violence in a first-party Nintendo game. It returned in Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards as 02.
trivia: It was the last SNES game published by Nintendo in North America.
Problems with its PAL conversion kept it out of Europe and Australia until a 2009 Virtual Console release.
It uses a pseudo-high-resolution SNES mode to blend dithered sprites.
The cartridge contains an SA-1 coprocessor.
It is the fifth Kirby game and the third under the Dream Land name.
devStory: HAL Laboratory developed it as the follow-up to Kirby's Dream Land 2, sharing many of that game's characters, and Nintendo released it on the SNES in 1997, late in the console's life. Its distinctive pastel look comes from the SNES's pseudo-high-resolution mode, which blends adjacent pixels, and the cartridge carries an SA-1 chip. Reception was mixed: GameRankings averaged 66 per cent, Nintendo Life criticised the low difficulty but praised the stylised graphics, and Nintendo World Report gave it nine out of ten for its graphics and music. IGN wrote, "It's not Super Star. But once you get past that, you can appreciate Dream Land 3 for what it is", and ranked it 62nd among SNES games. It reappeared in Kirby's Dream Collection in 2012.

title: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!
description: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble! (1996) is Rare's pre-rendered SNES platformer in which Dixie Kong and her baby cousin Kiddy search the Northern Kremisphere for the missing Donkey and Diddy.
longDescription:
Shortly after Diddy's Kong Quest, Donkey Kong and Diddy Kong vanish in the Northern Kremisphere, a fictional take on northern Europe and Canada. Dixie Kong sets out with her younger cousin Kiddy, using Funky Kong's vehicles to get around. At Kastle KAOS they destroy a robot thought to lead the Kremlings, only to find it was controlled by Baron K. Roolenstein, King K. Rool under a new name, with Donkey and Diddy inside powering it. Collecting bonus coins and cogs later reawakens the volcanic island of Krematoa and reveals his submarine, the Knautilus.

The pair cross 8 worlds and 48 levels of platforming, swimming and on-rails action, with returning barrels, bonus levels, DK coins, animal friends and multiplayer. Dixie slows her fall by spinning her ponytail, Kiddy bounces across water, and either can throw the other to break cracked floors or find secrets. Each level's DK coin is held as a shield by a Koin, beaten by bouncing a steel barrel off the wall behind it. The overworld is open to explore by speedboat and hovercraft, and thirteen Brothers Bear give hints, items and services in exchange for Bear Coins. New animal friends include Ellie the elephant, who sprays water from her trunk, and Parry the parallel bird, who flies above the Kongs collecting out-of-reach items.
trivia: Tim Stamper returned as director, with Andrew Collard and Paul Weaver designing.
Eveline Fischer composed most of the music, with extra tracks by David Wise.
Typing "Merry" on the file select screen turns the bonus levels Christmassy.
It sold over 3.5 million copies, though its release two months after the Nintendo 64's launch may have hurt sales.
EGM named it runner-up for SNES Game of the Year, behind Tetris Attack.
devStory: Rare began work shortly after Diddy's Kong Quest, again turning pre-rendered 3D animation from Silicon Graphics workstations into 2D sprites. It was released in North America on 18 November 1996, in Japan days later and in Europe that December, selling 1.7 million copies in Japan and 1.12 million in the US. It averaged 83 per cent on GameRankings: Nintendo Magazine System called it "king of the Kongs" with the "most detailed, beautifully animated Super NES graphics", GamePro saw it as a worthy swan song for the SNES, and Computer and Video Games called it the "pinnacle of achievement for the Super NES", while AllGame and Next Generation felt it offered "more of the same". It was ported to the Game Boy Advance in 2005.

sources.title: Donkey Kong Country 3: Dixie Kong's Double Trouble!

title: Mega Man X3
description: Mega Man X3 (1995) is the last SNES Mega Man X, in which X battles Dr. Doppler's Maverick utopia and Zero becomes playable for the first time.
longDescription:
In the 22nd century humans live alongside intelligent robots called Reploids, some of which turn to crime and are branded Mavericks. After twice defeating the Maverick leader Sigma, the Maverick Hunters X and Zero face the Reploid scientist Dr. Doppler and the utopia he has built for his Maverick followers. As in earlier games, X tackles eight stages in any order, each ending with a Maverick boss whose weapon he gains, and since every boss is weak to one weapon, the order can be planned to exploit those weaknesses. X can run, jump, dash, cling to and climb walls and fire his chargeable X-Buster.

Armour parts for the head, body, legs and X-Buster are hidden in capsules, and new chips add further abilities, though X can usually benefit from only one at a time. Heart Tanks extend life, Sub-Tanks store energy, and Ride Armor vehicles return, now summonable at any time once found. Zero can be called in to replace X in almost any stage, but he cannot collect armour or power-ups or fight bosses, with one exception that unlocks a secret weapon for X, and if he falls he cannot be used again. Like X2, the cartridge uses the Cx4 chip for basic 3D effects such as rotating and scaling wireframe objects.
trivia: It is known as Rockman X3 in Japan.
Keiji Inafune designed only X, Zero and Vile; other artists drew the remaining characters.
Inafune admitted being very "possessive" of Zero.
Later Saturn, PlayStation and Windows versions added animated cut-scenes and remixed music.
A planned 3DO version was cancelled.
devStory: Capcom produced the scenario, character designs and artwork, but much of the game design was sub-contracted to Minakuchi Engineering, which had made most of the Game Boy Mega Man games; Keiji Inafune, by now director, producer and writer, recalled "psychological turmoil" at letting outsiders develop it. Released in Japan on 1 December 1995 and in the West in 1996, it was well received for its gameplay, graphics, controls and playable Zero. GamePro enjoyed its difficulty and effects even though it brought little new, GameFan called it "a fitting 16-bit finale to a great series" and IGN ranked it the 67th-best SNES game, while Super Play found it far too similar to Mega Man X2. It later appeared in Mega Man X Legacy Collection in 2018.

title: The Firemen
description: The Firemen (1994) is Human Entertainment's overhead action game in which firefighters battle a blaze at a chemical company's Christmas party, rescuing civilians and racing to remove an explosive chemical.
longDescription:
When a large fire breaks out during a Christmas party at the chemical company Metrotech, firemen Pete Grey and Daniel McClean are sent in to rescue civilians, put out the flames and remove an explosive chemical called MDL from the building's basement, while another pair, Max and Walter, fight the fire elsewhere in the building. Winona radios advice and missions to the team, and Frank Weller, architect of the Metrotech building, also appears. The player controls Pete, while Daniel, who cannot be hurt, follows as backup.

Pete's hose can fire a direct stream or a wider close-range spray, and he can throw fire-extinguishing bombs. Water is unlimited, but continues are limited to three. Pete takes damage from fire and extreme heat, and the game ends when his life gauge empties with no continues left. Each level has a boss fire that must be put out in a particular way, and civilians trapped throughout the building can be rescued to partially restore his life. Critics praised its originality, controls, presentation, graphics and sound, and compared it with Jaleco's The Ignition Factor, finding it more action-focused and suited to beginners. Common criticisms were the lack of a two-player mode, low difficulty, short length and a single, repetitive setting.
trivia: It was released in Japan on 9 September 1994 and in Europe in mid-1995, but never in North America.
Famitsu gave it a Silver Hall of Fame award.
It sold 16,812 copies in its first week in Japan and about 30,137 in total.
Total! ranked it 76th in its top 100 SNES games, comparing its view to The Chaos Engine.
A PlayStation sequel, The Firemen 2: Pete & Danny, followed in Japan in 1995.
devStory: Human Entertainment developed and published it for the Super Famicom in Japan in 1994, with releases in Europe and Australia the following year. It received generally favourable reviews. Joypad praised its originality, controls and gripping play but criticised sprite flicker, Consoles+ commended its presentation, music and lack of slowdown while finding it easy, and Total! recommended it despite its short length and linearity. MAN!AC found the levels too similar, and Nintendo Acción liked its detailed sprites and simple controls but wanted it longer and harder. Última Generación summed it up as fun and playable, "a development that no one can escape".

title: QuackShot Starring Donald Duck
description: QuackShot Starring Donald Duck (1991) is Sega's Indiana Jones-inspired platformer in which Donald and his nephews follow a treasure map around the world, armed with a plunger gun.
longDescription:
Searching his uncle's library, Donald Duck finds an incomplete map to the treasure of King Garuzia, ruler of an ancient kingdom, who hid his most prized possession shortly before his death. Ignoring Daisy's concerns, Donald sets off with Huey, Dewey and Louie, while his rival Pete overhears and sends his own team after the prize. The trail leads to Count Dracula's castle in Transylvania for the full map, a Viking ship crewed by undead Vikings, and the South Pole for an old diary, which Pete takes by holding the nephews to ransom before Donald wins it back. The treasure turns out to be a plain stone statue, until the nephews break it and reveal a jewelled golden necklace.

Most levels have an overland section, which can be tackled in any order, and a dungeon such as the Maharajah's palace, which must be entered in a set sequence; clues found in some levels solve puzzles later on. Donald travels between areas by calling his nephews' biplane. His gun fires unlimited plungers that stun enemies, plus popcorn and bubble gum, the latter also supplied by Gyro Gearloose. Later the plunger can stick to walls as a temporary platform or to a passing bird to carry Donald further. In Duckburg, India and Egypt, chilli peppers raise his temper until he enters a "quack attack", charging forward invincibly and knocking out everything in his path.
trivia: In Japan it is called I Love Donald Duck: The Treasure of King Garuzia.
Sega showed it at the Consumer Electronics Show in May 1991.
It was the top-selling Mega Drive game in the UK on release.
Sega Pro gave it 95 per cent, calling its graphics "some of the best graphics around".
A Japan-only Saturn compilation, Sega Ages: I Love Mickey Mouse, paired it with Castle of Illusion in 1998.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Genesis, releasing it in North America in November 1991, in Europe a month later and in Japan on 20 December, drawing on the Indiana Jones films. Reviews were positive and universally praised its graphics, along with its music and puzzles. Computer and Video Games liked the graphics and gameplay but noted a slower pace than typical action games, MegaTech felt it lacked difficulty, and Console XS called it one of the best Mega Drive games. Sega Pro's Damian Butt criticised Donald's controls in places and the unlimited continues, but said that "QuackShot is everything a cartoon game should be". IGN later criticised its lack of speech samples. It was bundled with Castle of Illusion in The Disney Collection in 1996.

title: Bucky O'Hare
description: Bucky O'Hare (1992) is Konami's NES platform shooter based on the comic, in which the rabbit captain rescues his kidnapped crew from four planets, each joining the team with their own weapon and power.
longDescription:
In the parallel universe of the Aniverse, the robot K.O.M.P.L.E.X. orders the Toad Air Marshall to capture the crew of the Righteous Indignation. Captain Bucky O'Hare escapes, but the android Blinky, the cat Jenny, the duck Dead-Eye and the human Willy DeWitt are imprisoned on four planets that can be tackled almost in any order: the lush Green Planet, the volcanic Red Planet, the icy Blue Planet and the huge Yellow Planet of laser cannons and floating asteroids. Each is split into eight or more acts that vary in style and scrolling direction, from climbing a giant tree to riding a log down a waterfall. Once reunited, the crew is swallowed by a Toad tanker and must free one another and escape.

Every rescued crewmate becomes playable and can be swapped in with the select button. Bucky has a standard gun and a long jump, Willy fires a piercing beam, Jenny's third eye forms an energy ball, Dead-Eye shoots three ways and climbs walls, and Blinky's short-range bombs break the Blue Planet's ice while his jetpack lets him fly. Special abilities are charged by collecting power-up icons and unleashed by holding the B button, growing stronger the longer it is held. Enemies are androids and cyborgs modelled on toads, bosses appear mid-level as well as at the end, and continues are unlimited.
trivia: Director Masato Maegawa founded Treasure the year it was released.
Graphic designer Kaname Shindoh later worked on Treasure's Alien Soldier.
Hardcore Gaming 101 saw in it the "frantic rush approach to level design" of Treasure's 16-bit games.
Tomoko Sumiyama composed the music.
It was released in North America in February 1992 and in Europe a year later.
devStory: Masato Maegawa directed it and programmed it with H. Awai, with graphics by Kaname Shindoh, Madonna Taira and Toshiharu Furukawa; like other Konami staff, the team went on to work at Treasure. First announced in Nintendo Power in June 1991, it was previewed in Electronic Gaming Monthly and GamePro before release. Reviews were generally positive: Nintendo Game Zone and Poland's Top Secret called it one of the best NES games, and EGM felt its power-ups, variety and tight controls made up for its lack of new ideas. Reviewers highlighted the huge levels and speed, though Play Time found it scrolled so fast that small enemies hit unnoticed, and Nintendo Magazine System found it uninteresting after so many cartoon platformers.

title: Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos
description: Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos (1990) is Tecmo's NES sequel in which Ryu Hayabusa climbs walls, clones himself and fights the emperor Ashtar to stop him opening the Gate of Darkness.
longDescription:
A year after the first game, Ashtar, the evil lord who controlled Jaquio, plans to rule Earth by opening the Gate of Darkness with the Dark Sword of Chaos. US Army agent Robert T. Sturgeon recruits Ryu Hayabusa and tells him Irene Lew has been taken to the Tower of Lahja. Ryu rides a freight train, climbs the mountain and reaches Irene, only for Ashtar to escape with her into the Maze of Darkness and the World of Chaos. Ryu defeats Ashtar, but the sword vanishes, Irene is captured again, Robert is mortally wounded holding off demons, and Ryu must reach the altar before the Gate opens.

As before, Ryu fights through platforming Acts against a timer, leaping onto walls and ladders, but he can now climb up and down walls and use Power Boosting Items while clinging to them. Besides his Dragon Sword he can use ninja power for shuriken, boomerang-like Windmill Throwing Stars, fireballs aimed upward or downward, or the Invincible Fire Wheel, a ring of fireballs that destroys anything it touches. Crystal balls hold ninja power, score bottles, medicine, scrolls that raise maximum ninja power, and 1-ups. The big addition is an orange ninja symbol that lets Ryu "split his body": shadow clones follow him and copy every move, and can be positioned to take down enemies and bosses more easily. Each Act ends with a boss.
trivia: In Europe it was titled Shadow Warriors II: The Dark Sword of Chaos and released only in 1994.
Nintendo released an arcade version for its PlayChoice-10 system in 1990.
It debuted at number four on Nintendo Power's Top 30.
It was nominated in five Nintendo Power Awards '90 categories, including Best Bad Guy for Ashtar, but won none.
Game Players gave it an NES Excellence Award as one of the best games of 1990.
devStory: Tecmo developed and published it as the second of the NES Ninja Gaiden trilogy, releasing it in Japan on 6 April 1990 and in North America that May. Electronic Gaming Monthly previewed it from late 1989, noting its "explosive story", and Nintendo Power awarded four stars at the Winter 1990 CES for its cinema scenes and challenge. Reviewers found its visuals, controls and cut-scenes improved while keeping the high difficulty, though the plot was called more generic; EGM's Ed Semrad called it one of the best sequels ever released. One later reviewer called it "a challenging experience the likes of which gamers in the 8-bit era lived and died for". Ninja Gaiden III followed in 1991.

sources.title: Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos

title: Ninja Gaiden III: The Ancient Ship of Doom
description: Ninja Gaiden III: The Ancient Ship of Doom (1991) is Tecmo's final NES Ninja Gaiden, a science-fiction-tinged prequel in which Ryu Hayabusa, framed for Irene Lew's murder, uncovers a plot to breed superhuman bio-noids.
longDescription:
Set between the first two games, it opens with CIA agent Irene Lew chased off a cliff by a Ryu look-alike. To clear his name, Ryu investigates the laboratory where she died, and a stranger, Clancy, points him to the fortress of Castle Rock. There he learns that Clancy and agent Foster had been creating bio-noids, superhumans infused with life energy from an interdimensional rift that opened after the demon of the first game was defeated. Foster plans to make one from Ryu's corpse, Irene turns out to be alive, and Clancy reveals he has used them all to seize the ruins, which are a dimensional warship, the Ancient Ship of Doom.

Ryu can jump, cling to and climb walls, spring off them and use secondary weapons while clinging, and he can now also hang from pipes and ivy overhead, swinging up or dropping down. Ninja power fuels Windmill Throwing Stars, upward and downward fireballs, the Invincible Fire Wheel and the new Vacuum Wave Art, which fires blades above and below at once, while the new Dragon Spirit Sword extends the reach of his blade. Items such as Recovery Medicine are found in crystal balls. Each Act ends with a boss, the first four being elemental bio-noids of earth, wind, fire and water. The North American version allows only five continues before the game must be restarted.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Ninja Ryūkenden III: Yomi no Hakobune.
Masato Kato took over as designer from Hideo Yoshizawa.
The NES version doubled the damage Ryu takes compared with the Famicom original.
It was never released on the NES in Europe.
Atari ported it to the Lynx in 1993, but the small screen made characters and items hard to see.
devStory: Masato Kato said the series needed "to go into a new direction", swapping the Cthulhu-style motifs for science fiction and more robotic enemies. The team intended an easier game "a normal player can enjoy", but Tecmo made the American release much harder, with stronger enemies, limited continues and no password system. Finding it too hard to continue the story after Ninja Gaiden II, they set it between the first two games. It was released in Japan on 26 June 1991 and in North America that August. EGM called it the best Famicom game at a Tokyo trade show, saying "Ninja Gaiden gets better every time!", and early reviews praised its plot and challenge, though later ones criticised the plot, levels and difficulty. It joined the Ninja Gaiden Trilogy compilation on the Super NES in 1995.

sources.title: Ninja Gaiden III: The Ancient Ship of Doom

title: Double Dragon II: The Revenge
description: Double Dragon II: The Revenge (1988) is Technōs Japan's arcade sequel in which Billy and Jimmy Lee avenge Marian, shot dead by the leader of the Black Warriors, using new directional attack buttons.
longDescription:
The game opens with Marian, the damsel of the first Double Dragon, shot to death by Willy, leader of the Black Warriors, in revenge for his defeat. Brothers Billy and Jimmy Lee set out to avenge her across four missions: a heliport, a lumber storehouse, a farm and the gang's new hideout, each with sub-bosses along the way and a boss at the end. The arcade game is essentially an improved version of the original. Its biggest change replaces the punch and kick buttons with Left Attack and Right Attack, as in Renegade: pressing the button for the direction faced throws punches, while the opposite one delivers a back kick. New moves include a Hurricane Kick.

Many enemies return with new looks and attacks: Williams and Roper with knives and shovels, Linda with whips, knives and grenades, crew-cut Oharra and long-haired Bolo, the steel-masked Burnov, who vanishes leaving only his clothes and later rematerialises, Abore in his sunglasses, the kali-stick fighter Chin Taimei, and Willy with his machine gun. Crates, logs and steel balls can be thrown. After Willy falls, each player faces a shadowy doppelganger that copies their moves and drains their energy up close. A life is lost when the life meter or mission timer runs out, or on falling into a pit or spikes.
trivia: It began as an upgrade kit for the original Double Dragon before growing into a standalone game.
The NES version of 1990, published by Acclaim, is a very different game from the arcade original.
Binary Design made the 1989 home computer ports for Virgin Mastertronic.
The assembly source of the DOS version was put online by the Internet Archive in 2013.
An unrelated Game Boy game was released under the same name, adapted from the Kunio-kun series.
devStory: Technōs Japan first developed it as an upgrade kit for Double Dragon, but larger memory let it become a standalone game, with assets reused between the two. Game Machine listed it as Japan's seventh most successful table arcade unit of March 1989, and its Atari ST port was number three on the UK chart in early 1990. Technōs made its own very different NES version, Naxat Soft remade it for the PC Engine in 1993, and Palsoft's Japan-only 1991 Mega Drive version was a straight arcade port with smaller, less colourful characters. Arcade Sushi ranked it the ninth best retro beat 'em up in 2013, and it was re-released in Double Dragon Trilogy and Hamster's Arcade Archives.

title: Rad Racer
description: Rad Racer (1987), known in Japan as Highway Star, is Square's NES racer from coast to coast across America, programmed by Nasir Gebelli and playable in anaglyph 3D.
longDescription:
The player drives a "Transamerica" race from the West Coast to the East Coast, seen from behind the car. Two cars are on offer, a 328 Twin Turbo or an F1 Machine, though both perform exactly the same. Eight stages run through varied skylines and settings, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and Athens, and rival cars, from Volkswagen Beetles to Ferrari Testarossas, get faster as the race goes on. The car reaches 100 km/h before a turbo pushes it to a maximum of 255 km/h, and the player can brake, steer and even change the music while driving. Hitting obstacles or other cars can send the car flipping into a crash.

Each checkpoint, marked by a chequered flag, must be reached within a time limit, adding more time or ending the course. The dashboard shows a progress bar, speedometer, tachometer, score and remaining time. Unlike Out Run, when time runs out the car coasts down to a stop before the game ends, giving five to ten extra seconds to reach the next checkpoint. Pressing Select switches on a 3D mode for players wearing anaglyph glasses, and the game also works with the Power Glove and, in Japan, the Famicom 3D System's LCD shutter glasses. Reviewers widely compared it with Out Run but praised its sense of speed.
trivia: It was one of two Square games to use anaglyph 3D, after The 3-D Battles of WorldRunner.
Nasir Gebelli often drew the 3D-mode graphics by hand.
Gebelli stayed in Japan working out the scenery movement while the rest of Square holidayed in Hawaii.
It appeared in the 1989 film The Wizard.
It was one of three games in the 1990 Nintendo World Championships.
devStory: Square president Masafumi Miyamoto wanted to put the 3D skills of newly hired Nasir Gebelli, known for his Apple II games, to use; two programmers had just left, so Gebelli began programming it alone. Takashi Tokita, Hiromichi Tanaka and artist Kazuko Shibuya worked with him, and it was Akitoshi Kawazu's first Square game. It sold 1.96 million copies and placed eighth in Nintendo Power's player poll. Famitsu praised its speed but found it slightly monotonous, and Computer and Video Games called it "an extremely playable racing game". GameSpot's Skyler Miller later said it bore "more than a passing resemblance to Out Run" but was "more than just a clone", though its 3D effect suffered from flicker. It is considered one of the best racing games on the NES.

title: Metal Storm
description: Metal Storm (1991) is Tamtex's NES action platformer built entirely around flipping gravity, in which a combat mech storms a rogue laser cannon on Pluto.
longDescription:
In 2501 humanity has colonised the Solar System, and a robotic laser cannon on a Pluto outpost, built to defend Earth from aliens, malfunctions and turns on its makers, most recently destroying Neptune. With every attempt at triggering its self-destruct failing, the player pilots the M-308 Gunner, the most advanced combat mech available, to storm the base and set it off by hand. Pressing Up and Jump together flips the mech instantly between floor and ceiling. Other games, such as Mega Man 5 and Strider, had isolated reverse-gravity sections, but here every level layout, enemy pattern, hazard and boss is designed around it, turning corridors into puzzles of switching surfaces to dodge fire and get past barriers.

Six stages of two acts each lead to a seventh-stage boss rush. Hazards like laser emitters and crushing blocks switch on or off depending on which way up the mech is, and later stages wrap around the screen so that leaving one side brings the player back on the other. The arsenal is minimal: a Power Beam, a Shield and a Gravity Fireball that grants invincibility during a flip, only one held at a time, so movement and positioning matter more than firepower. Finishing the game unlocks Expert Mode, a complete reworking with most power-ups removed, new boss patterns and rearranged enemies and hazards, softened only by unlimited continues.
trivia: Tamtex was a Tokyo-based subsidiary of Irem.
It simulates parallax scrolling the NES did not natively support, using a custom mapper chip and bank switching.
It got a Nintendo Power cover feature.
The Japanese version came out over a year after the American one, in April 1992.
A 2019 re-release made the definitive Japanese version widely available for the first time.
devStory: Tamtex, which Irem often tasked with Famicom and NES games while it focused on arcades, developed it, and its steep but fair difficulty, pattern recognition and demand for precision reflect Irem arcade hits like R-Type. Released in North America in February 1991, it drew positive reviews: Computer and Video Games scored it 88 and called it a "slick, beautifully executed game", and Game Player's praised its large sprites and multi-scrolling backgrounds, calling it a "must-buy" for action fans. But as a new property on a waning console, with the Super NES about to launch, it was a commercial failure. Its reputation grew afterwards, first as an "unsung hero" in early-1990s magazines and later among internet-era retro gamers, who praised its innovation and technical feats.

title: Recca
description: Recca (1992) is KID's Famicom vertical shooter, made for a Naxat Soft competition, that pushed the hardware with relentless speed and sprites and is now one of the rarest Famicom games.
longDescription:
In 2302 an alien armada that has already obliterated the Andromeda galaxy, shortly after humans made peace with its inhabitants, sets out to destroy mankind. The player flies the Recca415 fighter in a fast-paced vertically scrolling shooter across four stages of enemies, obstacles and bosses. Five main weapons, each with strengths and weaknesses, and five sub-weapons that add two satellite options firing in several directions drop from destroyed enemies and are upgraded by collecting the same icon again, while clearing several waves can earn extra lives. Its signature feature is a charging shield: stop firing briefly and an energy shield forms in front of the ship, absorbing ordinary bullets and destroying anything in its blast when launched.

Being hit or crashing into scenery costs a life and resets firepower. Finishing the first loop of the Normal Game unlocks a harder second loop of seven rearranged stages. Score Attack challenges players to score as high as possible in two minutes, and Time Attack to clear two stages as fast as possible within five minutes. A hidden Zanki Attack mode, unlocked by cheat code, gives fifty lives but makes enemies release suicide bullets when destroyed, awarding bonus points for lives left at the end. Its sheer number of sprites and speed made it a showcase for what the Famicom could do.
trivia: It was made for Naxat Soft's Summer Carnival competition on 17 July 1992, alongside the PC Engine shooter Alzadick.
Programmer Shinobu Yagawa later made Battle Garegga, Ibara and Muchi Muchi Pork!.
Composer Nobuyuki Shioda tried eurobeat before settling on dark, heavy techno.
Few copies sold, making it one of the rarest and most valuable Famicom games.
Its first release outside Japan was on the 3DS Virtual Console in 2012 and 2013.
devStory: KID, a contract developer that had worked on American-focused games for Taxan, created it for Naxat Soft's Summer Carnival competition; Shinobu Yagawa programmed it, a designer known only as Etsuka drew the graphics, and Nobuyuki Shioda wrote the music after Yagawa asked for four-minute tracks, claiming they could "do the impossible on the Famicom". Released as attention was shifting to the Super Famicom, it sold few copies. Critics were mostly positive about its action, modes and music: Famitsu's reviewers warned it was unsuitable for beginners with too much on screen, while Poland's Top Secret gave it a perfect score in 1994, calling it "one of the best in its class". Retrospective commentary has been positive, and it is regarded as a precursor of modern bullet hell games.

title: Wizards & Warriors
description: Wizards & Warriors (1987) is Rare's NES action platformer in which the knight Kuros fights through the forests and caves of Elrond to defeat the wizard Malkil and rescue a princess.
longDescription:
Kuros, "Knight Warrior of the Books of Excalibur", sets out across the Kingdom of Elrond to defeat the evil wizard Malkil, who holds the princess captive in Castle IronSpire. He climbs through the trees of the Elrond forest to reach caves and tunnels, explores caverns of ice and lava, crosses a second forest and finally reaches the castle, a series of mazes where keys open doors and other captive damsels may be rescued before the final duel with Malkil. Kuros attacks with his Brightsword, in the air or by holding it in position, and with other weapons and magic.

The aim is to collect weapons, magic, gems and treasure to overcome enemies and hazards. Gems are needed to bribe the creature guarding the entrance to the next level, and each level ends with a boss empowered by Malkil's black magic, whose meter shows how tough it is, how many hits it needs and what kind of weapon will hurt it. Items hide inside acorns, torches and colour-coded chests that need matching keys, including the Boots of Force for kicking open chests and doors, potions of invulnerability, speed and jumping, a shield, the Potion of Levitation and the Dagger of Throwing. Kuros's life drains over time as well as from damage and is restored by meat, and continuing keeps items but resets the score.
trivia: In Japan it is titled Densetsu no Kishi Elrond (Legendary Knight: Elrond), published by Jaleco.
It was Acclaim's first game as a domestic publisher rather than localiser.
It was Rare's second NES game, after Slalom.
David Wise composed the soundtrack.
Nintendo Power called it the best game for the NES Advantage controller.
devStory: UK-based Rare developed it for the NES, and Acclaim released it in North America in December 1987, followed by Japan in July 1988 and Europe in January 1990. Magazines including Nintendo Fun Club News, Nintendo Power and VideoGames & Computer Entertainment praised its graphics, sound, challenge and arcade-style play; Nintendo Power nominated it for Best Graphics & Sound and Kuros for Best Character in its 1988 awards, though it won neither, while Power Play criticised its "stale gameplay". Computer Gaming World's Arnie Katz called it "engaging and well-programmed". Retro Gamer later called it "technically well ahead of other games for the console at the time" but felt unlimited continues made it easy. Three sequels followed, starting with Ironsword in 1989.

title: Ironsword: Wizards & Warriors II
description: Ironsword: Wizards & Warriors II (1989) is Zippo Games' NES sequel in which Kuros crosses four elemental domains to assemble the IronSword and face Malkil atop IceFire Mountain.
longDescription:
The wizard Malkil has taken the forms of the four Elementals, Earth, Wind, Fire and Water, to stop Kuros as he travels the land of Sindarin. Only the legendary IronSword can defeat him, so Kuros must gather its pieces and climb to the peak of IceFire Mountain. Each of the four domains is split in two: first Kuros must find a golden artefact belonging to the domain's Animal King and return it, opening the way to the second part, where he must find the magic spell needed to fight the Elemental. Without it the boss cannot be damaged, and Kuros cannot even stay in the room. Each Elemental destroyed yields a piece of the IronSword.

Kuros can jump, crouch, fight with his sword or cast spells chosen from a Magic Spell Screen. His life meter drops when he is hurt or falls too far and is restored by chicken and brew. Money from chests and enemies buys spells, stronger weapons, shields, helmets, keys and food, and inns in each domain sell supplies and offer a Bonus Chance game. Players may continue up to two times, though a bug removes the continue option as soon as Kuros sets foot in the earth domain rather than after completing it. Its size impressed reviewers: EGM's Steve Harris said "most of the competition pales by comparison".
trivia: It was the first game Ste and John Pickford's Zippo Games made for Rare.
Ste Pickford found the NES "sub-Commodore 64" but its games "ten times better" than home computer releases.
Its box art features Fabio.
It sold 500,000 copies in North America and 50,000 in Europe.
Zippo Games later became Rare Manchester.
devStory: Zippo Games had just finished Cosmic Pirate for home computers when the Pickford brothers visited Rare, were impressed by its NES library, and were asked to make the Wizards & Warriors sequel, with Rare largely leaving them to it. Acclaim released it in North America in December 1989 and in Europe in March 1991. Electronic Gaming Monthly's four reviewers praised its involving play and graphics, Ed Semrad calling it "a worthy sequel that fortunately is better than the original", though Donn Nauert warned that precise movements could frustrate; the magazine later made it Game of the Month and put its box art on the cover. Reviews praised its size, characters and bosses but criticised its lack of originality. Rare's satisfaction led to Zippo making Solar Jetman and Wizards & Warriors III.

title: Section Z
description: Section Z (1985) is Capcom's arcade shooter in which a jetpack-equipped astronaut fights through 26 alphabetical sections of an alien space station, later reworked into a non-linear NES maze.
longDescription:
In the third millennium, an astronaut is sent to infiltrate and destroy a space station orbiting near Earth that is secretly the base of the Balangool alien empire. In the arcade version the station is 26 corridors, or sections, from Section A to Section Z, grouped into five stages of five sections, with six in the last to fit the extra letter. Stages alternate between horizontal scrolling and upward vertical scrolling, each ends with a boss, and the final battle is against the L Brain at Section Z. One hit costs a life, extra lives come from score, and a continue is offered.

An eight-way joystick moves the astronaut, one button fires his rifle left or right while also dropping bombs, and the other turns him around, so he can shoot one way while retreating the other. Destroying dome-shaped containers releases S for speed and P for firepower, each upgradable three times and lost with a life, and B for bonus points. The 1987 NES version changed the design: three stages of 20 numbered sections each, where most sections end with a choice of two transporters, some leading back and some deadly until a condition is met. In each stage two power generators must be destroyed to open the final section and its boss, and one button now fires each way.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's eighth most successful table arcade unit in January 1986.
Hardcore Gaming 101 compared it to Namco's Baraduke, released earlier in 1985.
Not every NES section has to be visited to finish the game.
IGN ranked the NES version the 90th greatest NES game, praising its non-linear path.
The arcade original appeared in Capcom Classics Collection and Capcom Arcade Cabinet.
devStory: Capcom developed and released it in arcades in 1985 and published a home version for the NES in North America and Europe in 1987, altering its level design and controls. Hardcore Gaming 101's Federico Tiraboschi noted that, as in Baraduke, players control a free-roaming spaceman with a jetpack crossing sectors that scroll both horizontally and vertically, though without Baraduke's gravity and recoil. IGN wrote of the NES version that it "was unique, novel and also pretty confusing. But mastery of navigation in Section Z was a true badge of honor to hold in the NES age". The arcade game was later re-released on PlayStation 2, Xbox, PSP, Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 compilations.

title: Vice: Project Doom
description: Vice: Project Doom (1991) is Aicom's cinematic NES action game, mixing Ninja Gaiden-style platforming with driving and shooting stages as a detective uncovers an alien drug conspiracy.
longDescription:
In the distant future the B.E.D.A. Corporation, a maker of electronics and military weapons, is secretly a front for aliens who have lived hidden on Earth for centuries. Their substance Gel, meant as food for their species, is addictive to humans, with terrible side effects, and is being sold as an illegal drug. Detective Hart of the Vice unit is assigned to investigate B.E.D.A. after his partner Reese vanished on an earlier case, helped by his lover and fellow agent Christy and their acquaintance Sophia. Told through an unusually large number of cut-scenes for its time, the story blends anime, noir and biopunk, and opens with Hart chasing a maniac on the road only to find a monster behind the wheel.

The 11 stages run from Route 246 and Chinatown to a train, sewers, a power plant, a bio-tech laboratory and B.E.D.A.'s headquarters, each introduced by a movie-style sequence. The first and tenth stages are overhead driving sections in which Hart steers a red Ferrari F40 through three gears while shooting enemy cars, and two stages are first-person shooting galleries using a gun and grenades. The rest are side-scrolling platform levels with parallax scrolling, where Hart switches between an unlimited laser whip, a .44 Magnum and M-24 stick grenades, the latter two needing ammunition dropped by enemies. He can jump, crouch, climb ladders and run while crouching; meat restores health, every 100 coins earns a life, and continues are unlimited.
trivia: Its platforming has noticeable similarities to the NES Ninja Gaiden games.
It was released in Japan in April 1991 and in North America that November.
A Mega Drive conversion called Deep Scanner was developed but never released.
Sammy kept the rights, so Sega re-released it on Nintendo Classics in August 2019 after the two merged.
Nintendo Power rated it 3.8 out of 5.
devStory: Aicom developed it and Sammy Corporation published it for the NES, adding gun-shooting and driving segments to a side-scrolling action game in the Ninja Gaiden mould and telling its story through extensive cinematic scenes. Contemporary and later reviews were moderate: Nintendo Power gave it 3.8 out of 5 in 1991, and AllGame later awarded two and a half stars out of five. A planned Mega Drive version, Deep Scanner, was abandoned. Because Sammy retained the rights before merging with Sega, it was Sega that published the game's re-release on the Nintendo Switch's classic NES service on 21 August 2019.

title: Contra Force
description: Contra Force (1992) is Konami's North America-only NES run and gun, originally a separate Japanese game called Arc Hound, in which a four-person task force fights terrorists rather than aliens.
longDescription:
In 1992 C-Force, a task force of former military professionals, is formed to protect Neocity from terrorism. When their informant Fox warns leader Burns that the Head of Intelligence is being threatened by the criminal organisation D.N.M.E., Burns arranges to meet him at the harbour, only to find Fox dead. Unlike other Contra games, the villains are human terrorists rather than an alien menace. The player chooses between four characters: Burns, the leader; Iron, a heavy weapons expert; Smith, a sharpshooter; and Beans, a demolitions expert, who differ in weapons, speed and jumping ability.

Five stages, the Warehouse, Harbor, Mati Building, Aircraft Rumble and Blue Group Headquarters, alternate between side-view levels, where characters run, crouch and jump, and overhead levels with eight-way movement, all with shooting in eight directions. Instead of instant power-ups, a Gradius-style meter advances one step with each briefcase found in the destructible scenery, and the select button claims the highlighted upgrade, from each character's two special weapons to turbo fire and an invulnerable rolling attack. A pause menu lets players switch characters, assign one to a second player, or call a computer-controlled partner for five seconds with one of six strategies from defensive to offensive. Each character has three lives, so switching before one runs out keeps the game going, and continues are unlimited.
trivia: It was announced in Japan as Arc Hound, with no Contra connection, for an October 1991 release, then cancelled.
It was the third Contra game on the NES, after Contra and Super Contra.
Announced as the series' third console game, its delay to October 1992 led Contra IV to be renumbered Contra III: The Alien Wars.
Its overhead stages resemble those in Super Contra and Operation C.
AllGame criticised its slowdown and flicker but praised the choice of characters.
devStory: Konami first developed it as Arc Hound for Japan, announcing it in Famicom Tsūshin and in company brochures, but that version was cancelled. The game was still localised for North America as a Contra spin-off, at first scheduled for winter 1991 ahead of Contra III, then delayed until a few months after it, so the Super NES game, previously called Contra IV, was renumbered before release. Its plot and setting are unrelated to any other Contra. Reception was mixed: AllGame's Brett Alan Weiss criticised the slowdown and sprite flicker but praised the added strategy of choosing between characters with their own skills and weapons.

title: The Battle of Olympus
description: The Battle of Olympus (1988) is Infinity's Zelda II-inspired action RPG retelling the myth of Orpheus, who wins the favour of the gods to rescue his beloved from Hades.
longDescription:
Ancient Greece is terrorised by Hades, ruler of the underworld, who has kidnapped Helene, the lover of Orpheus. A top-down map of Greece links dungeons and city-states across eight regions, from the starting area of Arcadia to Argolis, Attica, Crete, Laconia, Peloponnes, Phrygia and Phthia. Orpheus must meet the gods and earn their favour, beginning with Zeus, who encourages the others to grant him weapons, a shield and special equipment, including a harp that summons Pegasus to fly him to distant places. Along the way he gathers the Harp of Apollo, the Sword of Hephaestus, the Staff of Prometheus and the Sandals of Hermes, plus three fragments of love that remind him of Helene.

Mostly a side-scroller with light platforming, it starts Orpheus with a wooden club and later gives him the fireball-throwing Staff of Fennel, the Nymph's Sword and the lightning-casting Divine Sword. Upgrades raise health, protection and speed. Compared with Zelda II, there is no downward stab or full-health sword beam, though one late sword fires beams at the cost of health unless a certain item is found. The game is somewhat non-linear, with optional side quests that earn secret items or powers from the gods. Foes include the Lamia, cyclops, centaurs, Talos, the Minotaur, the Graeae, Cerberus, the Stymphalian birds and the Nemean lion, and the final battle in the Temple of Hades begins against a shadow before Hades himself appears.
trivia: It was Infinity's first game, made by a team of three.
Designer and programmer Yukio Horimoto made it with his girlfriend and future wife Reiko Oshida, who did story and graphics.
Kazuo Sawa composed the music.
Brøderbund published it in North America in 1990 and Nintendo in Europe in 1991.
In 2026 the original team announced a new Steam version as their last game before retirement.
devStory: Horimoto and Oshida, who were dating, "wanted to make our game together" and chose Greek myths because Horimoto loved them. He openly drew on Zelda II: The Adventure of Link, saying the attacking, ducking and jumping motions were all influenced by The Legend of Zelda, and it became one of several NES games inspired by Zelda II. Imagineer released it in Japan as Olympus no Tatakai on 28 March 1988, and Radical Entertainment later ported it to the Game Boy for Europe. Famitsu scored it 28 out of 40 and reviewers noted the Zelda II likeness. Retrospectives were positive, with praise from Eurogamer in 2011 and Ars Technica in 2013, and in 2026 Polygon named it one of the ten best NES games missing from the Switch.

title: Shatterhand
description: Shatterhand (1991) is Natsume's side-scrolling NES action game in which a police officer with cybernetic fists fights a renegade cyborg army, helped by satellite robots built from collected letters.
longDescription:
In 2030 a band of military renegades called Metal Command, led by General Gus Grover, is building an army of cyborg soldiers to conquer the world. Steve Hermann, a young police officer from the Bronx, loses both arms in a clash with them and accepts two cybernetic replacements from the Law and Order Regulatory Division, becoming the agent Shatterhand. His main weapons are his fists, which can also punch away enemy bullets. Item containers release coins and Greek letter icons. Coins are spent by crouching on special platforms: 300 for health, 100 for more attack power, which turns his vest from green to brown, and 2,000 for an extra life.

The letters, α and β, can be switched by punching them, though too many punches turn one into a large gold coin. Collecting three summons a robotic satellite that fights beside him and lets him hover by crouching and holding A, with eight possible robots depending on the combination: ααβ fires lasers, for example, while αβα swings a sword. The robot can be destroyed by damage, and a new combination replaces it, but collecting the same combination twice merges Shatterhand with the robot for a short burst of extra power. After an introductory factory stage, Areas B to F can be played in any order before the final Area G opens, and continues are unlimited.
trivia: It began as a Famicom licensed game of the TV series Super Rescue Solbrain.
The Japanese version was published by Angel, a now-defunct Bandai subsidiary for licensed games.
Solbrain's carnival level, Area C, became a submarine level in Shatterhand.
Jaleco released it in North America in 1991 and Europe in 1992.
Most character and item graphics were changed for the Western version.
devStory: Natsume developed it, and in Japan Angel released it in 1991 as Tokkyū Shirei Solbrain, following the storyline of the live-action superhero series with its own opening sequence. For the Western release by Jaleco, the licence was removed: the story became Steve Hermann's fight against Metal Command, most characters and items were redrawn, and the carnival stage was replaced with an entirely different submarine level. The game follows many established conventions of side-scrolling action but stands out for its coin shops and letter-built robot companions. It received generally favourable reviews from critics.

title: Mighty Final Fight
description: Mighty Final Fight (1993) is Capcom's comic, super-deformed NES spin-off of Final Fight, with all three heroes, character levelling and new special moves.
longDescription:
The premise is that of the original Final Fight, retold as comedy. The Mad Gear Gang, Metro City's dominant street gang, has kidnapped Jessica, daughter of Mayor Haggar, and Haggar sets out to rescue her with Cody, her boyfriend, and Guy, Cody's training partner. In this version the gang's boss Belger kidnaps her because he is infatuated and wants to force her to marry him. The characters are drawn in a childlike "super deformed" style, in the spirit of Famicom games such as Konami's Kid Dracula and Namco's Splatterhouse: Wanpaku Graffiti, and the final boss is the mechanically enhanced Cyborg Belger.

Like the SNES ports it is single-player only, but unlike them it keeps all three arcade heroes: Cody, who mixes karate and boxing, the ninjutsu master Guy, and the former professional wrestler Haggar, each with almost all of their arcade abilities. Borrowing from the Famicom Double Dragon, it adds an experience system: defeating enemies earns points, more for stronger finishing moves, and each of six levels raises attack power and maximum vitality. Cody and Guy start at level 1 and Haggar at level 3, and at level 4 each learns a new special, Cody's Tornado Sweep projectile, Guy's Tornado Kick and Haggar's Running Clothesline. Weapons depend on the character, a knife, shuriken or oversized mallet, and five stages and two bonus rounds feature childlike versions of Mad Gear bosses such as Thrasher, Abigail and Murasame.
trivia: It is a spin-off of Capcom's 1989 arcade game Final Fight.
Power-ups include food, extra lives and even extra continues.
Belger's motive here is to force Jessica to marry him.
Arcade Sushi ranked it the sixth best retro beat 'em up in 2013.
It was re-released in Capcom Classics Mini-Mix for the Game Boy Advance in 2006.
devStory: Capcom developed and published it for the NES in 1993, by which time Final Fight had already been ported to the Super NES. Rather than attempt a straight conversion, Capcom reworked the arcade game into a comical, chibi-style retelling, keeping all three playable characters that the SNES versions had cut and adding features taken from Technōs Japan's Famicom Double Dragon, including experience points that unlock new moves. AllGame's Christian Huey was generally positive, writing that "while there are better titles to choose from in the genre, Mighty Final Fight has enough going for it to make it a guilty pleasure".

title: Ice Hockey
description: Ice Hockey (1988) is Nintendo's five-a-side NES hockey game, with three body types of player and brawls that send the loser to the penalty box, often cited as one of the system's best.
longDescription:
The play mirrors the real sport: two teams try to hit a black puck into the opposing goal over three periods, starting each with a face-off at the centre of the rink, and whoever has more goals at the end wins. Teams have five players including the goaltender, rather than six. The rink copies a real arena, with goal lines, attacking and defending zones, face-off spots and a neutral zone, both halves identical. The player picks from three body types for the team: a fast but weak player who excels at face-offs, an all-rounder, and a slow, powerful player who is poor at face-offs but strong at body checking and shooting.

When two opposing players tussle for the puck long enough, others pile in, and the player from the side that loses the fight goes to the penalty box for a time. Electronic Gaming Monthly praised it as having "some of the most hilarious gameplay of any sports game ever" while requiring real skill, noting how fights turn into brawls, crowd noise rises in close games with two minutes left, and varied team members make for strategic play. IGN's Mark Bozon called it the most addictive of Nintendo's early sports titles, saying it was in his NES as often as Super Mario Bros. 3.
trivia: Hideki Konno directed it, later going on to Super Mario Kart, Yoshi's Island and Luigi's Mansion.
Shigeru Miyamoto and Masayuki Uemura produced it, and Soyo Oka composed the music.
It was Hiroaki Hontani's last project for Nintendo before leaving Pax Softnica.
Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it 94th among the best console games of all time.
It was released for the Famicom Disk System as well as the NES.
devStory: Nintendo R&D4 developed it, with Narumi Nakajima and Hiroaki Hontani of Pax Softnica assisting on programming; Hontani had previously directed Volleyball for Nintendo, a remake of his own Attack Four. Released in 1988, it received positive reviews and is often cited as one of the best NES games. Nintendo Power ranked it 142nd in its Top 200 Nintendo games and IGN included it in its top 100 NES games. GameSpot's Aaron Thomas called the 2006 Wii Virtual Console release "one of those rare NES sports games that's almost as much fun to play today as it was when it was released", and it later returned on Nintendo Switch in 2018.

title: Journey to Silius
description: Journey to Silius (1990) is Sunsoft's NES run and gun, begun as a Terminator game, in which a scientist's son battles the terrorists who destroyed his father's space colony, set to a celebrated soundtrack.
longDescription:
In the year 373 of the new space age calendar, Earth's overpopulation has driven demand for space colonies. Jay McCray prepares to follow his scientist father to space colony #428 in the Silius Solar System, but the station is destroyed in an explosion that kills the research team and wipes its data. At his father's home Jay finds a floppy disk holding the complete colony plans and a message asking him to finish the project if terrorists succeed in destroying it. To protect the plans and avenge his father, Jay sets out after the terrorists.

Five stages take him through the ruins of a space colony, an underground concourse, the enemy hideout, a flying spaceship and a factory, fighting robots and security systems to reach each boss. Jay can lie down but only aim left and right. Besides his default handgun he can collect a shotgun, machine gun, homing gun, laser rifle and grenade launcher, all drawing on a Gun Energy gauge, and when it empties he falls back to the handgun. Enemies drop capsules that restore health and ammunition. After the final stage and credits, the game starts again from the first stage. Its music, by Naoki Kodaka, has been widely praised.
trivia: It began as a game of the 1984 film The Terminator until Sunsoft lost the licence.
In Japan it is called Rough World.
The American version, released first, shows the hero's face; the Japanese and European versions cover him in armour.
Kodaka used the NES's sample channel for a bassline and the triangle channel for a kick drum, reversing the usual approach.
It was re-released in Japan on PlayStation alongside Hebereke in Memorial Series: Sunsoft Vol. 5.
devStory: Sunsoft conceived it as an adaptation of The Terminator, but after losing the licence during development it changed the plot and graphics before release. Naoki Kodaka composed the soundtrack with programming help from Nobuyuki Hara, Shinichi Seya and Naohisa Morota; where most NES composers used the digital channel for sampled drums, Kodaka used it for a sampled bassline and the triangle channel for a kick drum. The game never won wide acclaim in the West, but its music has been widely praised. It was released on the Nintendo Switch's classic NES service in December 2019.

title: Delta Force
description: Delta Force (1998) is NovaLogic's tactical first-person shooter, loosely based on the US Army special operations unit, whose voxel terrain allowed long-range outdoor firefights few shooters could match.
longDescription:
Designed as a military simulation, it casts the player as a Delta Force operator, male or female, with a choice of faces, in operations across five campaigns in Peru, Chad, Indonesia, Uzbekistan and Novaya Zemlya. All five campaigns are open from the start, and completing missions unlocks more, sometimes several at once, for 40 missions in all. Objectives include wiping out hostile forces in an area, assassinating high-profile targets, destroying military equipment and escorting prisoners of war or civilians to extraction, often followed by reaching an extraction point. Enemy positions vary between play-throughs, and higher difficulties make the AI aim better, find the player faster and move in small groups that give each other covering fire.

Before each mission the player can freely change the default loadout across three slots: a main weapon, extra equipment and a sidearm. Unlike most shooters of the time, bullets are real objects with simulated ballistics, dropping and taking time to travel, so distant targets must be led. Optional ammunition and medical pickups are scattered across maps, though health is not shown on the HUD. Multiplayer over LAN or online supports up to 32 players, with every campaign mission playable co-operatively, human players replacing the AI operatives, alongside deathmatch, king of the hill and capture the flag, plus team versions of each.
trivia: It uses NovaLogic's Voxel Space engine, known from the Comanche series.
The engine did not support any form of 3D acceleration.
Combat could take place at distances of several hundred metres.
It helped popularise and define the tactical shooter genre.
Its series ran until Delta Force: Xtreme 2 in 2009, with a reboot released in 2025.
devStory: NovaLogic built it on its proprietary Voxel Space engine, which drew terrain with voxels and characters, vehicles and buildings with polygons, giving draw distances and terrain detail unseen in shooters of the time, at the cost of no 3D acceleration. Released for Windows in October 1998, it was a critical and commercial success. GameSpot called it "a very impressive game overall", praising its missions and sound but noting dated visuals and fewer planning options than Rainbow Six, PC Gamer called it "a surprising and welcome addition to the genre", and Next Generation found its solo play often uninspired but its multiplayer "one of the most satisfying gaming experiences available today". Delta Force 2 followed in 1999, and later Black Hawk Down in 2003.

title: Hidden & Dangerous
description: Hidden & Dangerous (1999) is Illusion Softworks' Second World War tactical shooter in which the player leads a four-man SAS team on missions behind enemy lines, where brief contact can be fatal.
longDescription:
The player commands a four-man British Special Air Service team on important missions during the Second World War, across six campaigns in Italy, Yugoslavia, Germany, Norway, the North Sea and Czechoslovakia. Before each mission the player selects soldiers and works through a comprehensive loadout of weapons and equipment, and briefings set out objectives, intelligence on enemy strength and recommended plans of advance. Missions include sabotage, search and destroy, rescuing prisoners of war and aiding the resistance.

In the field the player can take direct control by switching between the soldiers in the squad, issue voice commands, or use a tactical map that allows real-time control or planned manoeuvres carried out once the map is closed. The game can be played in first or third person, switching between the two at will. Although it takes liberties with real SAS missions and timelines, it keeps a degree of historical accuracy and an intense atmosphere, with realistic wounding: squad members can be badly hurt or killed by even brief contact with the enemy. Edge praised it as "challenging, deep, acutely atmospheric and an intense adventure", while AllGame called it "boxed potential". The Fight for Freedom expansion, known in the US as Devil's Bridge, added soldiers, weapons and missions in Poland, the Ardennes and post-war Greece.
trivia: It is regarded as a pioneering tactical shooter.
Tarantula Studios developed the PlayStation port.
It sold 350,000 copies by May 2000 and over a million by 2007.
It was particularly popular in the UK.
Hidden & Dangerous Deluxe was released free to promote the 2003 sequel and remains freeware.
devStory: Illusion Softworks developed it, and Take-Two Interactive and TalonSoft published it for Windows, Dreamcast and PlayStation. The PC and Dreamcast versions received average reviews overall: Edge gave the PC version nine out of ten, saying it "is such a sweeping success that it dwarfs any criticism" despite clunky controls and graphical glitches, NextGen praised the Dreamcast version's missions and options despite bugs, and GameZone wanted more patches and fixed online play. Most of its success came from Europe; PC Gamer US said it endured poor sales in the States because of competition from Rainbow Six, limited multiplayer and little marketing. The Fight for Freedom expansion was received less favourably, and Hidden & Dangerous 2 followed in 2003.

title: Silent Service
description: Silent Service (1985) is Sid Meier's Second World War submarine simulator for MicroProse, putting the player in command of a US submarine hunting Japanese shipping in the Pacific.
longDescription:
Set in the Pacific during the Second World War, it gives the player command of a US submarine on war patrols against Japanese shipping; "Silent Service" was the nickname of the US Navy's submarine force there. Players choose from realistic tactics, such as the End Around, or exploit near invisibility at night by keeping the submarine's profile low. Up to four projectiles can be in the water at once, a challenge when fighting several destroyers, and time runs faster when there is no combat. Navigation, damage repair and firing each have their own screen, giving access to a great deal of information while keeping attention on the task at hand.

Sid Meier identified the size of the theatre, the variety of tactical situations and evolving technology as key influences on the design: surface radar and wakeless torpedoes are only available in scenarios set after their real introduction. There are three kinds of mission. Torpedo/Gun Practice teaches the mechanics in a controlled setting, Convoy Actions are short missions based on individual historical submarine attacks, and War Patrols are longer missions based on real patrols but with freedom to plot one's own route. Computer Gaming World called it "easily the best [submarine simulator] for its simplicity of use and execution", praising its realism and criticising only the lack of saved games.
trivia: It was the first Sid Meier game for which he did not create the artwork; Michael O. Haire drew it.
It was developed in eight months, inspired by a fractal programming trick.
Rare developed an NES version, published by Konami in 1989.
It won the Charles S. Roberts Award for Best Adventure Game for Home Computer of 1985.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 86th best game of all time in 1996.
devStory: Sid Meier designed it over eight months for MicroProse, which released it in 1985 for the Apple II, Atari 8-bit, Commodore 64 and IBM PC before other ports. Co-founder Bill Stealey hired an illustrator whose work convinced Meier others' artistic talent was superior to his own. MicroProse sold 250,000 copies by March 1987 and about 400,000 overall, and it was the company's second best-selling Commodore game by late 1987. Info gave it four stars, Antic said Meier's team had "outdone themselves", and Compute! called it "both intriguing and addictive". Computer Gaming World credited it with introducing the control-room interface to submarine games, though by 1993 it considered it superseded by Silent Service II, released in 1990.

title: Shock Troopers
description: Shock Troopers (1997) is Saurus's overhead Neo Geo run and gun in which a squad of mercenaries, alone or as a switchable team of three, fights through branching routes to rescue a kidnapped scientist's granddaughter.
longDescription:
The terrorist group Bloody Scorpions has kidnapped scientist George Diamond and his granddaughter Cecilia to get hold of Alpha-301, a drug that turns ordinary people into superhuman soldiers. A special team of eight soldiers from different countries must fight through their ranks to reach the leader and save the granddaughter and the world, ending in a battle with the enemy commander atop an aircraft. At the start players pick Lonely Wolf, controlling one soldier with twenty units of life, or Team Battle, choosing three soldiers with ten each who can be switched on the fly, which offers a wider variety of special weapons.

Players also choose a Mountain, Jungle or Valley route and can switch to another halfway through, and the characters and paths chosen decide the life bonus received at each level. Each of the seven levels has a mid-boss as well as an end boss. Each soldier has strengths such as more life or more speed, plus a unique special weapon, or bomb, of varying range. An eight-way joystick moves and aims, while four buttons fire, dodge, use the special weapon and switch characters. Holding fire allows strafing, the dodge button avoids enemy fire, and attacking enemies at close range makes them drop items such as points, weapon power-ups and life.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's thirteenth most successful arcade game of December 1998.
Its sequel, Shock Troopers: 2nd Squad, followed in 1998 with an unrelated story and new characters.
M2 ported it to PlayStation 3 and PSP via NEOGEO Station in 2011.
Classic Game Room called the 2011 re-release the best game of that year.
Hardcore Gaming 101 hailed its "fantastic presentation that ranks among the best in the genre".
devStory: Saurus developed it for SNK's Neo Geo arcade platform in 1997. It has since been re-released many times, in SNK Arcade Classics Vol. 1 for PlayStation 2, PSP and Wii, on the Wii Virtual Console by D4 Enterprise in 2012, in DotEmu's PC version for the Humble NEOGEO 25th Anniversary Bundle in 2015, later on Steam and GOG.com, and in Hamster's ACA Neo Geo series. The game was very well received: Nintendo Life gave the Virtual Console release seven out of ten, saying it "succeeds in offering up an intense and explosive run-and-gun experience", Digitally Downloaded awarded four and a half stars, recommending it to newcomers to the genre, and Hardcore Gaming 101 noted the Virtual Console version "runs almost perfectly", unlike the one in SNK Arcade Classics.

title: Die Hard Arcade
description: Die Hard Arcade (1996), known in Japan as Dynamite Deka, is Sega's 3D beat 'em up in which John McClane fights through a skyscraper to rescue the President's daughter, with quick-time events and combinable weapons.
longDescription:
Terrorists have seized the President's daughter, Caroline Powell, and one or two players, as John McClane or Kris Thompsen, fight up through a skyscraper to save her. Bosses include a biker called Hog, the Mexican wrestler Jocko, the duo of sumo wrestler Mr. Oishi and army general Mr. Tubbs, a muscle-bound fire chief with tiny grenades and pairs of laser-shooting Spiderbots, all henchmen of Wolf "White Fang" Hongo. If both players survive, they fight each other on the roof for the daughter's sole appreciation, as at the end of Double Dragon. Like action films of the time, the violence is over the top, largely gore-free and played for laughs.

It was the first beat 'em up with texture-mapped 3D polygon graphics, and its sophisticated move set drew comparisons with fighting games. Players use fists, feet and weapons taken from enemies or the scenery, from brooms and pepper shakers to missile launchers, submachine guns and anti-tank rifles, and items can be combined, such as a spray and a lighter making a flamethrower. Most weapons are lost after each action scene, though handguns are kept while loaded. Quick-time events between scenes cost health or add an extra fight if failed, and two players can perform combined special moves and combos. The Saturn version includes Sega's 1979 arcade game Deep Scan for earning extra credits.
trivia: Sega lacked the Japanese video game rights to Die Hard, so it was released there as an original game, Dynamite Deka.
It began as a way to use surplus ST-V arcade boards and an unused Die Hard licence.
It was the last game made by Sega Technical Institute before the studio was dissolved.
Until shortly before release, previews showed movement on a single 2D plane.
It was Sega's most successful US-produced arcade game up to that time.
devStory: Sega AM1 and the US-based Sega Technical Institute created it at STI's facilities, AM1 providing engineering, design and art and STI art, design and animation, developing for the ST-V Titan arcade board and Saturn at the same time. Director Makoto Uchida said he was "personally a huge fan of Die Hard". Released in cooperation with Fox Interactive, it was Japan's second most successful arcade game in August 1996. Computer and Video Games compared it with Streets of Rage and Virtua Fighter 2, and Next Generation said it "breathes life into a dead-end genre" though attacks were hard to line up. The 1997 Saturn port was praised as a flawless conversion with satisfying weapons but criticised as short and easy. The sequel Dynamite Cop dropped the licence.

title: Zombie Revenge
description: Zombie Revenge (1999) is Sega's House of the Dead spin-off beat 'em up, in which three agents clear a zombie-infested city with fists, guns and other weapons.
longDescription:
U.D.S., or Undead Soldier, a top-secret government plan to use the dead for military purposes, is thrown into darkness by an unknown entity, and a year later the city is overrun by zombies. Three of the best AMS agents, Stick Breitling, Linda Rotta and Rikiya Busujima, are sent to wipe out the enemy and track down its mysterious leader, Zed. After fighting through the city they confront him; he reveals that Stick's father was involved in U.D.S. and that he wants revenge for his parents, murdered as part of the project. Despising all humans, Zed plans to spread the virus and unleashes a powerful U.D.S. inside himself, the God of Destruction, before the agents defeat him.

Players choose one of the three agents, who differ in their proficiency with hand-to-hand combat and guns, and fight zombies and bosses with fists, firearms and other weapons. As a spin-off of The House of the Dead, it is full of references: zombies look and sound as they did in the first game, the heroes of both series are AMS agents, icons of Thomas Rogan and G sit on Linda's computer desktop, and the Curien Mansion returns as a stage called The House of the Dead, with its original first-stage music. The final boss is Black Magician Type 01, and the credits replay the stages back to the start. The Dreamcast version adds a one-on-one Battle Mode for two players.
trivia: It was first titled Blood Bullet: The House of the Dead Side Story, then Zombies Nightmare.
A PlayStation 2 port by Acclaim Studios Teesside was cancelled.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's third most successful arcade game of April 1999.
Famitsu scored the Dreamcast version 32 out of 40.
GamePro pitched it at players who "didn't get enough beat-em-up action from Dynamite Cop".
devStory: Sega AM1 and Data East developed it, and Sega released it in arcades in 1999 with a Dreamcast port the same year. The Dreamcast version received mixed reviews. NextGen's Chris Charla wrote, "It looks great, it plays OK, but you'll be done with it forever in four hours", recommending a rental. GamePro's reviewers agreed it was worth renting but felt the "lobotomized hit-and-kick action" would bore players and that limited replay value, annoying sound and controls kept it from being a must-own, while Famitsu was more positive.

title: The House of the Dead 2
description: The House of the Dead 2 (1998) is Sega's light gun rail shooter in which AMS agents battle a zombie outbreak in Venice, with branching routes and multiple endings.
longDescription:
Investigating the 1998 Curien Mansion incident, AMS agent G disappears after finding the remains of Dr. Curien's work in Venice, where zombies break out. On 26 February 2000 the agency sends James Taylor, Gary Stewart, Harry Harris and British agent Amy Crystal to find him and evacuate civilians. James and Gary find an injured G, who gives them a journal on the enemies, and battle Judgment, the imp Zeal with his headless axe-wielding puppet Kuarl, the amphibious Hierophant, the serpents of the Tower and the chainsaw-wielding Strength. The culprit is Caleb Goldman, the businessman who financed Curien, who revives the bosses and the Magician to oversee the birth of the Emperor, a shapeshifting being meant to protect nature by destroying humanity.

Players shoot through hordes of zombies and monsters on rails while rescuing civilians, reloading by pointing the gun off-screen. Health is shown as torches, lost when hit or when shooting a civilian, and regained by rescuing civilians or finding first aid kits in crates and barrels. The first game's branching paths return with even more alternate layouts and locations, though they do not change the plot. Endings depend on whether one or both players beat the last boss, the number of continues and points: the good ending sees Thomas Rogan from the first game send the heroes to their next battle, while in the bad ending a zombified Goldman waits outside.
trivia: It ran on Sega's NAOMI arcade board.
Its intro's flashbacks to the first game were recorded in the game's own engine.
The Dreamcast version was a launch title and sold 339,721 copies in North America.
It became the basis for spin-offs, most notably The Typing of the Dead.
Game Informer ranked it 99th in its best games of all time in 2001.
devStory: Sega AM1 developed it as a direct sequel to the first House of the Dead. A very successful arcade release, it was Japan's third most successful dedicated arcade game of December 1998, and it was ported to the Dreamcast in 1999, Windows in 2001, Xbox as a bonus in The House of the Dead III, and Wii in The House of the Dead 2 & 3 Return. The Dreamcast version received favourable reviews and sold an estimated 234,756 copies in Japan; in Spain, its light gun bundle was the platform's best-selling game through December 1999. Famitsu praised its graphics and the replay value of its paths, IGN its level and enemy design but not its voice acting, and Game Informer its expanded gore and intensity.

title: Battle Circuit
description: Battle Circuit (1997) is Capcom's last arcade beat 'em up, a manga-styled science fiction brawler for up to four players in which super-powered bounty hunters chase a world-controlling computer program.
longDescription:
In the future year 20XX, super-powered bounty hunters capture wanted criminals, identified by serial numbers, in the city of Neo Koba. The game opens with the player arresting criminal 9696X, the scientist Doctor Saturn, and his blob-like sidekick aboard their spacecraft orbiting Earth. Back with their employer Harry, the hunters are sent after Johnny of the Delete Gang, who holds a floppy disk carrying the Shiva System, a malicious program able to control every computerised system in the world, and must fight through the gang to recover it and claim the bounty. Five characters are available, including Cyber Blue and Yellow Iris, each with their own attacks.

Up to four players fight through horizontally scrolling levels using two action buttons and the joystick. Coins collected from defeated enemies buy upgrade discs between levels that add new techniques to each character's arsenal. Pressing both buttons on the ground performs a life-draining super move, and when two players do so together they form a team-up attack.
