Pressing both in the air triggers a Battle Download, which grants the player and any allies a character-specific boost, such as Cyber Blue's Power Up for more damage or Yellow Iris's Speed Up for faster attacks; characters start each life with two and can collect up to five from capsules. Barrels and crates hide health and points, and reaching set scores earns extra lives.
trivia: It was first developed as an eight-player racing game, which was completed but never released.
Producers Noritaka Funamizu and Yoshiki Okamoto oversaw the beat 'em up version.
It was released in Japan and Europe on the same day, 19 March 1997, but not in North America.
Its North American and home console debut came in Capcom Beat 'Em Up Bundle.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's eighth most successful arcade game of June 1997, ahead of Street Fighter EX Plus.
devStory: Battle Circuit began life as a racing game for up to eight players with artwork by Haruki Suetsugu, which was finished but shelved. In 1997 Capcom's arcade production team, led by Noritaka Funamizu and Yoshiki Okamoto, made a new version. Structurally it resembles Capcom's earlier scrolling action games such as Final Fight and Alien vs. Predator, but it stands apart through a manga-style science fiction approach; Ikeno Metaka, overseen by Ohnishi Hiroki and Yamamoto Kouji, designed characters reminiscent of older Capcom heroes with comic-book flourishes. A speedy translation let it launch in Japan and parts of Europe simultaneously, with a few lines of Japanese dialogue omitted. It was Capcom's last beat 'em up made for arcades, and it later appeared in Capcom Arcade Stadium.

title: Puzzle Bobble 2
description: Puzzle Bobble 2 (1995), known in the West as Bust-A-Move Again, is Taito's bubble-shooting puzzle sequel, adding a branching single-player map and a tournament against Bubble Bobble characters.
longDescription:
The first sequel to Puzzle Bobble keeps its bubble-matching formula and builds on it. The one-player game now has a branching map, letting the player periodically choose between two groups of five levels, leading to different endings. A tournament-style variation of the two-player game pits the player against computer opponents, some based on Bubble Bobble characters, including versions of a Monsta and a Mighta. Some versions, including the PlayStation one, add time trials in which one player races previous records or two players race the records and each other.

Finishing the single-player game reveals a code that unlocks Another World, which subtly toughens the existing levels and redraws every backdrop to resemble Bubble Bobble, whose enemies also appear behind the credits. Next Generation called it "one of the most addictive puzzle games in the arcades right now", praising the "fascinating" trick of bouncing bubbles off the walls into the right spot, and Electronic Gaming Monthly's four reviewers applauded its amount of content, bank shots and fierce two-player competition. The North American Taito F3 arcade release differed greatly: Bub and Bob were replaced by a pair of disembodied hands, opponents by a generic computer, and backgrounds, audio and voices were changed, though the Neo Geo and console versions follow the Japanese original.
trivia: Home versions were called Bust-A-Move 2: Arcade Edition.
It was shown at JAMMA 95 alongside Dangerous Curves and Gekirindan.
The North American PlayStation and Saturn cover, with faces trapped in blue balls, made GameSpy's Top Ten Worst Covers.
Puzzle Bobble 2X added an alternative set of levels and holiday-themed attract animations.
It was among the nineteen best-selling PlayStation games of 1996 in the UK, according to HMV.
devStory: Taito developed and published it for arcades in 1995, where Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourth most successful arcade game of October, with the 2X update ninth in January 1996. Home versions followed for PlayStation, Saturn, Nintendo 64 and Windows, the MS-DOS and Saturn ports being based on 2X and adding a level editor. GameSpy's Kevin Bowen felt the disturbing North American cover was likely to frighten away young players, and Acclaim's later MS-DOS and Nintendo 64 releases used the European art. By the time the Nintendo 64 version arrived, the PlayStation and Saturn versions had been out nearly two years and Puzzle Bobble 3 was already available. It was later included in Taito Legends 2 and Hamster's ACA Neo Geo series.

title: Street Fighter EX
description: Street Fighter EX (1996) is Arika and Capcom's spin-off that brought Street Fighter into 3D polygons for the first time, keeping 2D-plane fighting and adding guard breaks and super cancels.
longDescription:
Released on Sony's ZN arcade hardware, it was the first Street Fighter with 3D polygon graphics, though play still largely follows a 2D plane, with the line of fighting shifting around a 3D arena. Its fighting system draws on Street Fighter II and Street Fighter Alpha with some original ideas. Special moves and super combos will be familiar, but the super meter is split into three separate sections rather than levels, unique to the EX series. Spending one section on a Guard Break smashes through an opponent's block and leaves them dizzy, more like a stun than Alpha's opening. Special moves can cancel out of regular moves or other specials, and Super Canceling chains one super combo into another for huge damage.

The original has 17 characters, two of them computer-controlled bosses, rising to 23 in the home version. Ryu, Ken, Chun-Li, Zangief and Guile appear alongside M. Bison as an unplayable boss and Akuma as a secret character, while new fighters include Allen Snider, a karate champion beaten by a young Ken who sets out to prove himself the world's best, and Blair Dame, daughter of a wealthy European family who trained in combat sports to defend her loved ones. Across the three EX games, 19 new characters made it the largest original roster introduced in any Street Fighter series, and several reappeared in Arika's later Fighting Layer and Fighting EX Layer.
trivia: Akira Nishitani, known for Street Fighter II, headed development.
Arika did not consult Capcom's Star Gladiator team, despite media assumptions.
The music was written by former Namco composers Takayuki Aihara, Shinji Hosoe and Ayako Saso.
A Nintendo 64 port was announced for 1997 but cancelled.
EGM's Dan Hsu said the PlayStation version was "what should've been called Street Fighter III".
devStory: Arika co-produced it with Capcom under Akira Nishitani. Arika vice president Ichiro Mihara stressed that it was "a different development line" from Star Gladiator, that Arika was not a Capcom subsidiary, and that "the concept is new and the know-how is new". Next Generation praised Capcom for taking the series into 3D but judged the arcade original a failed attempt that "plays more like a distant cousin to the Street Fighter series". An updated Plus arcade version and the PlayStation-only Street Fighter EX Plus α followed in 1997, and the latter, with new characters, modes and improved feel, was far better received: Next Generation called it "an outstanding title even non-SF devotees will enjoy". Street Fighter EX2 followed in 1998.

title: Plasma Sword: Nightmare of Bilstein
description: Plasma Sword: Nightmare of Bilstein (1998) is Capcom's 3D weapon-based fighting sequel to Star Gladiator, adding Plasma Fields that trap opponents with character-specific effects.
longDescription:
A year after Hayato Kanzaki of the Star Gladiators killed Fourth Empire leader Dr. Edward Bilstein on the planet Zeta, the Earth Federation enjoys peace, but the Empire is rebuilding amid rumours that Bilstein has been reborn, and Federation troopers sent to Zeta are wiped out by unknown forces. The reworked controls give four buttons: two weapon attacks, a kick, and a button for sidesteps and dashes. The Plasma Combo System is replaced by the Plasma Strike System, with a gauge of up to three levels powering super moves called Plasma Strikes. Fights now take place on an endless 3D field, so ring-outs are gone, and while set combos work as in other 3D fighters, special moves can be woven into them as in 2D games and the Street Fighter EX series.

Half a gauge level allows a Plasma Reflect or Plasma Revenge counter. The new Plasma Field costs one level: the character emits a sphere of energy, and if it hits, four invisible walls box in the arena, with effects that vary by fighter, from unlimited Plasma Strikes to growing to giant size or stopping time. Arcade Mode has eight stages, with a story mid-boss at the fifth and a character-specific final boss at the eighth. Earning enough Battle Ability points unlocks a fight against a "true" final boss and an extended ending; otherwise the player sees an abridged one.
trivia: It was shown at the February 1998 AOU Show under the title Star Gladiator.
It runs on Sony's ZN-2 board, an improved version of the PlayStation-based ZN-1.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's third most successful arcade game of June 1998.
The Dreamcast port followed in 2000.
It was re-released in Capcom Fighting Collection 2 in 2025.
devStory: Capcom developed it on the ZN-2 board as a sequel to 1996's Star Gladiator, reworking its control system and mechanics. Next Generation said in 1998 that Capcom had "taken few (if any) big steps forward" but had managed to "round out and deepen the gameplay essentials of its growing 3D library". The 2000 Dreamcast version received mixed reviews, praised for its refined play and visual style but criticised for a lack of originality: NextGen ranked it next to last among Dreamcast fighters, just ahead of Mortal Kombat Gold, while Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40 and GamePro called it "a good-looking game with lots of visual variety", if not in Soulcalibur's top tier.

title: Real Bout Fatal Fury
description: Real Bout Fatal Fury (1995) is SNK's fourth mainline Fatal Fury, adding a Power Gauge and breakable ring-out barriers, and marking Geese Howard's final fall.
longDescription:
Real Bout cuts the attack buttons from four to three: punch, kick and a Strong Attack that is a heavier punch or kick depending on the character. It keeps Fatal Fury 3's three-plane oversway system, with a main fighting lane plus foreground and background planes for dodging attacks or leaping at the opponent, now switched with a dedicated button. Chain combos, including in the air, resemble those of X-Men: Children of the Atom. Stages now allow ring-outs, a feature from 3D fighters such as Virtua Fighter, but the edges are guarded by barriers that must be broken by knocking the opponent into them enough times before a fighter can be sent out of bounds.

A new Power Gauge fills as players attack or defend. Half-full, it allows Guard Cancels, counterattacks after blocking that cost nothing. At maximum with more than half of the life bar left it enters S. Power, slowly draining while allowing one Super Special Move. At maximum with life flashing red it enters P. Power, allowing Guard Cancels and Super Specials freely until it empties, or one even stronger Hidden Ability. The roster carries over from Fatal Fury 3, with its bosses Ryuji Yamazaki and the Jin twins now regular fighters, and Duck King, Billy Kane and Kim Kaphwan return from Fatal Fury Special. Geese Howard is the final boss, and Terry's or Andy's ending shows him fall from the roof of his tower, refusing to be saved.
trivia: It was promoted with the tagline "So long, Geese!"
It was Geese Howard's final appearance in the Fatal Fury storyline.
Yasuyuki Oda later called it a masterpiece.
The Saturn port required the 1MB RAM cartridge.
The Neo Geo CD version sold 63,091 copies in its first week in Japan.
devStory: SNK redesigned the controls and battles for Real Bout, aiming for more exhilaration and ease of use with two health bars and flashy effects, and bringing much of the processing praised in Fatal Fury 3 to the foreground. Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourth most popular arcade game of January 1996. Electronic Gaming Monthly made the Neo Geo version its Game of the Month, praising its pits, characters, graphics and humour. GamePro called it a major improvement over Fatal Fury 3, "one of the best Fatal Fury games ever", though it disliked the lost button and the music, and Next Generation agreed. Maximum found it too similar to its predecessor but "a well-rounded and entertaining fighting title". Neo Geo CD, Saturn and PlayStation ports followed.

title: Detana!! TwinBee
description: Detana!! TwinBee (1991), released in Europe as Bells & Whistles, is Konami's colourful vertical shooter in which TwinBee and WinBee save planet Meru, with charge shots and bell-juggling power-ups.
longDescription:
Several years after the first TwinBee, Light and Pastel, making their debut, pilot TwinBee and WinBee across seven levels to defeat the evil alien Iva after Princess Melora sends an SOS from planet Meru. In the Japanese version one button shoots airborne enemies and the other drops bombs on ground targets, while the European version fires both at once. Holding the shot button fills a meter for a Big Shot released when the button is let go. Bells hidden in floating clouds can be shot to change colour, and alongside the original five colours come a purple bell that adds a tail shield and a black bell that slows the ship down. Mini-bells and the lucky star also return.

The ship GwinBee can be combined with to fire wider beams, and two players can line up side by side for the same effect or one above the other for a five-way spread; with GwinBee between them, he springs out and destroys everything on screen. After the first loop, a harder second loop follows, and inserting more credits after losing all lives continues the game with a free power-up. Japanese magazines Game Machine and Micom BASIC listed it among the most popular arcade games of spring 1991, and Gamest awarded it first place for Best Shooting in its 1991 Grand Prize, plus placings for graphics and music.
trivia: It was animator Shūjirō Hamakawa's debut as TwinBee character designer, credited as Shuzilow.Ha.
Michiru Yamane co-wrote the music to suit its "cute bee world".
Koji Igarashi programmed enemies for the PC Engine port, one of his earliest Konami jobs.
Light and Pastel's names come from the audio drama TwinBee Paradise.
Pop'n TwinBee followed on the Super NES in 1993.
devStory: Much of the Gradius team made it, with Masato Ohsawa directing, Toru Shimomura as sole programmer, Hiroshi Matsuura as engineer and Konami Kukeiha Club members Hidenori Maezawa, Masae Nakashima and Michiru Yamane on music. Released in Japanese arcades in February 1991 and in Europe that March, it was ported to the X68000, whose magazine Oh!X praised its arcade accuracy and nominated it for Game of the Year, and to the PC Engine in 1992, which readers of PC Engine Fan rated highly. Germany's Power Play called it a nice shooter with candy-coloured visuals. It has since appeared on Saturn, PlayStation, PSP, mobile phones, the Virtual Console and Hamster's Arcade Archives.

title: Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine
description: Dr. Robotnik's Mean Bean Machine (1993) is Compile's Puyo Puyo reworked for the West with Sonic the Hedgehog villains, a competitive falling-bean puzzler against Robotnik's henchbots.
longDescription:
On the planet Mobius, home to bean-like creatures, Doctor Robotnik plans to rid the world of fun by kidnapping the citizens of Beanville and turning them into robot slaves with his Mean Bean-Steaming Machine. His Henchbots round them up in dark dungeons, and the player, as Has Bean, breaks in to free them. Has Bean is Puyo Puyo's Carbuncle under a new name and reacts with different animations depending on how the player plays. Almost all of the other characters are replaced with ones from the Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog cartoon.

Pairs of beans fall onto each player's grid and can be moved and rotated until they land. Four beans of the same colour vanish, dropping any beans above them, which can set off further matches as chain combos. Chains send grey refugee beans to the opponent, which cannot be matched directly and only clear when a match is made next to them, and a player loses when beans spill over the top. Scenario Mode pits the player against 13 increasingly tough computer opponents, 1P vs 2P Mode lets two people battle, and Exercise Mode is for practice; the Game Gear and Master System versions add a Puzzle Mode of set bean layouts to clear. Critics praised the play, particularly in two-player competition, but criticised the difficulty and the genre's familiarity.
trivia: Sega replaced the Puyo Puyo characters fearing they would not appeal to Western players.
The 8-bit Game Gear and Master System versions were adapted from the Japanese Nazo Puyo.
Eurogamer called it a "fairly unapologetic reskin" of Puyo Puyo.
Mega Zone included it in its Top 50 Games in History in 1995.
Kirby's Avalanche was a similar Western reskin of Puyo Puyo for the SNES.
devStory: Compile developed it from its own Puyo Puyo, first released for the MSX2 in 1991, and Sega published it for the Genesis and Game Gear in 1993 and the Master System in 1994. Reviews were generally positive. Mega's Andy Dyer found it simple and not challenging enough, IGN and Nintendo Life liked that it was built for two-player competition, and Computer and Video Games found it as addictive as Tetris with more colourful visuals, while Gamezebo criticised its difficulty and "ancient" password system. The Game Gear version was also well received. It has been re-released in many compilations, including Sonic Mega Collection, Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection and Sega Genesis Classics, as well as on the Virtual Console and Steam.

title: Puyo Puyo 2
description: Puyo Puyo 2 (1994), or Puyo Puyo Tsū, is Compile's sequel that introduced offsetting, letting players cancel incoming garbage with their own chains, and became Japan's biggest arcade hit since Street Fighter II.
longDescription:
As before, Puyo fall in pairs that can be moved and rotated, and the game ends if the third column from the left fills to the top. The key new rule is offsetting, or sōsai: a player can counter and cancel incoming garbage Puyo with chains of their own, and even send the excess back to the opponent. Alongside standard garbage come Point Puyos, which add to the score and briefly strengthen chains when cleared beside other groups, and Hard Puyos, nicknamed Steelies, which are harder to clear. A custom rule, rensa shibari, can make chains below a set length score nothing and send no garbage. Chains were rebalanced to do less damage than in the first game, making comebacks more likely, and the rules created longer, better matches.

In the story mode, the Dark Prince builds a battle tower to steal both Arle Nadja's heart and Carbuncle, and Arle must beat an opponent on each floor, her bonus points working like experience. There are single, double and endless modes, five preset rule sets for versus play and custom rules. The Super Famicom version, Super Puyo Puyo 2, added a four-player mode with a multitap, Compile's first on a home console, and a later Remix edition allowed four players without one by filling in computer opponents. The name is an English pun: tsū, meaning expert, sounds like "two".
trivia: Sega released the arcade version in 1994.
It became the most widely known multiplatform game in Japan, on consoles, handhelds and computers.
It was Japan's fourth highest-grossing arcade software of 1995.
Its first international release was Puyo Pop for the Neo Geo Pocket Color.
The PC version alone included a separate Nazo Puyo puzzle quest.
devStory: Compile developed it, and Sega released it in arcades in 1994, where Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourth most successful table arcade unit that November; it became the biggest arcade game in Japan since Street Fighter II and the most prominent game in the series. Its success led Compile to port it to the Super Famicom, Mega Drive, PC Engine, Game Boy, Game Gear, Saturn, PlayStation, Windows 95, WonderSwan, Neo Geo Pocket Color and PlayStation 2, among others, with the CD versions adding voices and cut-scenes. Sega later paid tribute with Sega Ages 2500 Vol. 12: Puyo Puyo 2 Perfect Set, M2 included it in the 3DS Sega 3D Classics Collection, and it returned on Switch as Sega Ages Puyo Puyo 2 in 2019.

title: Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back
description: Crash Bandicoot 2: Cortex Strikes Back (1997) is Naughty Dog's PlayStation sequel in which Doctor Neo Cortex tricks Crash into gathering crystals, with new moves, Warp Room hubs and jetpack and surfboard levels.
longDescription:
On a group of fictional islands near Australia, Crash is abducted by Doctor Neo Cortex, who persuades him that the world needs saving: Crash must collect 25 crystals that will let Cortex harness the power of a coming planetary alignment and stop the planet being destroyed. Crash's sister Coco and Cortex's former assistant Doctor Nitrus Brio try to warn him, Brio urging him to gather gems instead. The crystals lie across 25 levels reached through Warp Rooms, hubs of five levels each; a level is cleared by grabbing its crystal and reaching the end, and clearing all five in a room leads to a boss before the next room opens.

Crash can jump on enemies, spin to knock them off screen, slide, and body slam to break objects, and jumping straight after a slide sends him higher. Enemies call for different attacks: those with dangerous tops cannot be jumped on, spiked ones must be jumped on or slammed, and frill-necked lizards and robots with heated rims must be slid into. Boxes hold Wumpa Fruit, 100 of which earn a life, and Witch Doctor's Masks that absorb a hit, with three in a row granting temporary invulnerability. Arrow boxes bounce Crash higher, and exclamation boxes make other boxes appear. Reviewers praised the variety added by new moves and the jetpack and rocket surfboard levels, though some criticised trial-and-error play and easy bosses.
trivia: It was made in 13 months on a $2 million budget, starting in October 1996.
Coco was created partly because Sony Computer Entertainment Japan was uncomfortable with the "super sexy" Tawna.
Ground fog was dropped from the jungle levels after critics accused developers of using fog to hide low polygon counts.
Andy Gavin wrote a new engine, GOOL 2, three times faster than the first game's.
It sold more than 800,000 copies in Japan by April 1998, then a record for a Western game there.
devStory: Naughty Dog began production in October 1996. Bob Rafei led concept art, art direction, level assembly and lighting with Eric Iwasaki, Erick Pangilinan, Charlotte Francis and Jason Rubin, adding sewer levels to work in some "dirty" locations, and Charles Zembillas drew the first sketches of Coco on 18 March 1997. Released by Sony Computer Entertainment, it averaged 89 per cent on GameRankings and is widely considered better than the original, praised for its graphics, controls and music; Game Informer and GamePro called it one of the PlayStation's best platformers. It became one of the best-selling PlayStation games of all time and was remastered in the Crash Bandicoot N. Sane Trilogy in 2017.

title: Crash Bandicoot: Warped
description: Crash Bandicoot: Warped (1998) is Naughty Dog's time-travelling third Crash game, in which Crash and Coco race Cortex, Uka Uka and N. Tropy for crystals across history, with plane, jet-ski and motorbike levels.
longDescription:
Immediately after the second game, the wreck of Cortex's space station crashes to Earth and frees Uka Uka, evil twin of Aku Aku. He joins Cortex and the time-obsessed Doctor Nefarious Tropy in a plan to gather crystals scattered across time and use their energy to enslave the planet, so Crash and Coco must travel through time and collect the 25 crystals first. The hub is the Time-Twisting Machine, split into five chambers with five level portals each; a sixth button appears after all five are cleared, opening a boss level, and beating the boss unlocks the next chamber.

Crystals may be at the end of a level or earned by completing a challenge, and Bonus Platforms lead to bonus areas that can be retried freely since no lives are lost there. Crash and Coco start with five lives, earning more from 100 Wumpa Fruit or special crates. Crash can jump on enemies, spin, slide and body slam, and defeating bosses grants upgrades such as stronger attacks and better jumping and running. A third of the game uses new engines: two 3D ones for aeroplane and jet-ski levels and a driving-style engine for motorcycle levels, while the rest keeps the classic Crash style. GameSpot called it "easily the best Crash yet", and Official U.S. PlayStation Magazine "the best 2.5D platformer ever released".
trivia: In Europe it was titled Crash Bandicoot 3: Warped.
Naughty Dog had only ten and a half months and just over $2 million to make it.
Crash got a real shadow because Sony America's producers were "sick of that little discus" following him.
It sold nearly 6 million copies.
It was the first non-Japanese PlayStation game to sell over a million copies in Japan.
devStory: Production began in January 1998. Programmers Andy Gavin, Stephen White and Greg Omi built three new engines, while Jason Rubin explained that the classic style was kept because abandoning it "would mean that we would be abandoning a significant proportion of gamers out there". An arbitrary-plane z-buffer and a sky-reflecting environment map gave the jet-ski and flooded Egyptian levels fluid-looking water. Released by Sony Computer Entertainment, it received universal acclaim: GamePro called it "a very strong contender for PlayStation game of the year", Game Revolution "a barrage of good things", and critics praised its gameplay, graphics and audio. It is considered one of the best games of all time, was remastered in the N. Sane Trilogy in 2017, and was followed by Crash Bandicoot 4 in 2020.

title: Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage!
description: Spyro 2: Ripto's Rage! (1999), known in PAL regions as Spyro 2: Gateway to Glimmer, is Insomniac's sequel in which Spyro is pulled into the realm of Avalar to stop the sorcerer Ripto, now able to swim, climb and headbash.
longDescription:
Spyro is planning a holiday when he is unexpectedly transported to the realm of Avalar, where the sorcerer Ripto has appeared and is causing havoc, and he joins the locals to stop him. Spyro fights with flame breath, a charge attack and gliding, while his dragonfly Sparx shows his health by colour and restores it by eating butterflies, obtained by flaming, charging or headbashing small creatures; bottled butterflies also grant an extra life. Avalar is split into three homeworlds, Summer Forest, Autumn Plains and Winter Tundra, with portals to realms. Reaching the end of a realm earns a talisman, and enough talismans open each homeworld's boss.

Realms also hold orbs earned through side tasks for characters, such as lighting lamps or protecting people, needed to open some portals and progress through the third homeworld. Gems pay the fees of Moneybags, a greedy bear who opens portals and teaches Spyro three new abilities: swimming to reach submerged treasure and tunnels, climbing certain surfaces, and a headbash that smashes rocks and cages. Each realm also has a power-up gate, activated by defeating enough enemies, that grants a temporary ability such as invulnerability, flight, supercharge, super flame, ice breath or a super jump. The first game's dragons are replaced by fauns, satyrs, animals and robotic businessmen, and Hunter the Cheetah, Moneybags and Ripto became recurring characters.
trivia: The name Ripto comes from the Japanese katakana spelling of Spyro.
Stewart Copeland composed the music.
Tom Kenny took over as Spyro's voice from Carlos Alazraqui.
It sold a million copies in North America by December 1999 and over 3.4 million by 2007.
It was remade in the Spyro Reignited Trilogy in 2018.
devStory: Insomniac president Ted Price said it was designed to offer a "greater challenge" for experienced players, with more depth and variety than Spyro the Dragon. Stewart Copeland's jungle-style score was engineered and co-produced by Jeff Seitz, and Universal Sound Studios created the sound effects. Sony Computer Entertainment published it in 1999, and it received favourable reviews for its colourful graphics, variety and amount of content. GamePro called it "an excellent platform action/adventure game ripe with the goods that make gaming great", NextGen said it had "more meat to it than the first", and Famitsu gave it 30 out of 40. It earned a Gold award for 200,000 UK sales, and Spyro: Year of the Dragon followed in 2000.

title: Star Ocean: The Second Story
description: Star Ocean: The Second Story (1998) is tri-Ace's science-fantasy action RPG, the first Star Ocean released abroad, with real-time battles, two protagonists and a sprawling crafting system.
longDescription:
Claude C. Kenny, an officer of a space-faring Earth organisation, is stranded on an undeveloped, medieval-level planet, where he meets Rena Lanford. Together they gather companions and must stop an evil group whose plot spans several worlds. The player chooses to play as Claude or Rena, and the journey and ending change with the choices made. Ten more characters can join, but only six fit into the eight-member party, and recruiting some rules others out. As in most RPGs, the party travels between towns and dungeons, following the story and taking side quests, and characters level up through battle.

Battles are fought in real time on a broad field: the player directly controls one character, free to trade blows head-on or circle round to flank, while up to three allies follow one of six AI strategies, such as "Spread out and attack" or "Save your Magic Points". Nine batches of skills bought in shops are learned with Skill Points, raising statistics, giving battle bonuses such as counterattacks, or unlocking Specialties like herbal medicine, cooking, writing, composing, pickpocketing and training. The whole party can combine on Super Specialties such as Master Chef, Blacksmithing, Publishing and Reverse Side, which counterfeits valuable items at the risk of allies thinking less of the character. Enix used sprites for the characters to achieve an anime look it felt polygons could not yet deliver.
trivia: It was released in North America in June 1999 and Europe in April 2000 by Sony Computer Entertainment.
It sold 1.094 million copies, 724,000 of them in Japan.
It was Japan's 13th best-selling game of 1998.
It inspired manga and anime adaptations.
The PSP remaster Second Evolution added animated scenes by Production I.G and 13 new endings.
devStory: tri-Ace developed it as the second Star Ocean, and Enix published it on the PlayStation, the first game in the series to leave Japan. It received favourable reviews and was lauded for innovative elements new to the genre while borrowing some of Final Fantasy VII's best features, though some critics found it mediocre; Next Generation's Jeff Lundrigan called it "average". It did not sell enough in North America to join the Greatest Hits range, but it has a cult following and is often considered the best Star Ocean. Tose's Star Ocean: Second Evolution remastered it for PSP in 2008, and Gemdrops' remake Star Ocean: The Second Story R followed in 2023.

title: Front Mission 3
description: Front Mission 3 (1999) is Square's tactical RPG of mechs called wanzers, the first in the series released in the West, with two separate story scenarios and pilots who can be shot out of their machines.
longDescription:
Like the rest of the series, it is part of a serialised storyline about characters and their struggles involving the mechs known as wanzers. It is a radical departure from the first two games, putting more weight on role-playing than strategy. Play is linear: watch story scenes, complete a mission, set up wanzers in towns and cities between missions, and sortie again, travelling on a world map that reveals new locations as the plot advances. New to the series is the Double Feature Scenario, two largely separate stories that share some events and places but are essentially full games in their own right.

Missions range from destroying every enemy to protecting a particular ally. The big change is that pilots themselves can be attacked: any hit may injure a pilot or force them to eject, and players can eject deliberately to fight on foot or hijack another machine on the battlefield. Skills are no longer learned through experience; instead, using wanzer parts in battle gives a random chance of learning a new skill from them, which can then be programmed into the wanzer's battle computer. Many of Front Mission 2's features are removed and missions are smaller, limiting strategic options, but Action Points, which govern how much each unit can do and grow with the pilot's combat rank, return along with Links, letting units with Link skills and suitable weapons support each other's attacks.
trivia: It was the first Front Mission released in North America, Europe and Australia.
In Japan it is also known as Front Mission Third.
It was the first Front Mission produced in-house after Square absorbed original developer G-Craft.
Koji Hayama, Hayato Matsuo and SHIGEKI composed the soundtrack.
A Nintendo Switch remake was released in June 2025.
devStory: Square's Development Division 6, led by Toshirou Tsuchida, spent two years on it, using their experience from Front Mission 2 to polish the play; Ko Sato designed the battle system, Akihiro Yamada worked on the art, and several characters went through multiple drafts or were dropped. As in other entries, the team deliberately drew inspiration from sources beyond traditional mecha anime and manga. Released in Japan in 1999 and in North America by Square Electronic Arts in 2000, it received favourable reviews and 32 out of 40 from Famitsu. IGN praised battle mechanics rarely seen in Square games since Final Fantasy Tactics, AllGame said its "deep, strategic gameplay makes up for most any of the flaws", and GameSpot and Edge criticised its graphics and limited tactics.

title: Wipeout 3
description: Wipeout 3 (1999) is Psygnosis's anti-gravity racer, styled by The Designers Republic, running in high resolution and widescreen to a soundtrack chosen by DJ Sasha.
longDescription:
Players race futuristic anti-gravity ships from eight racing corporations around eight circuits. Each craft has an energy shield that absorbs damage, and if it fails, the ship is knocked out of the race; shields recharge in a pit lane apart from the main course, more fully the longer the ship stays in it. Airbrakes help through tight corners, and Hyperthrust adds speed at the cost of shield energy, leaving the ship more vulnerable. Weapon grids across the tracks hand out random items, with new weapons joining the five carried over from earlier games, from rockets, missiles and mines to defensive shields.

There are six modes. Single races award medals to the top three, checkpoints must be reached in time or the racer is ejected, and consecutive gold medals unlock new tracks and craft. Time trials and challenges are joined by Eliminator, a deathmatch-style mode scoring points for destroying rivals and completing laps, and Tournament, which totals standings over several races, plus split-screen racing for two. The Designers Republic gave menus and courses a simple colour scheme to create what one Psygnosis staff member called "a believable future", and it is one of the few PlayStation games to run in 16:9 widescreen and high resolution. DJ Sasha selected the electronica soundtrack, including Orbital and The Chemical Brothers.
trivia: Psygnosis had just nine months and a small budget to finish it before the PlayStation 2 arrived.
An initial pool of 20 tracks was cut to 8 after playtesting.
It was the first Wipeout released only on a PlayStation console.
Wipeout 3: Special Edition, with extra tracks and content, followed in Europe in August 2000.
It was the last Wipeout on the original PlayStation, before Wipeout Fusion on PS2.
devStory: Psygnosis, by then owned by Sony and fresh from Wipeout 64, began work in 1999, three years after Wipeout 2097. Lead designer Wayne Imlach recalled that the tight schedule made the team conservative, refining what 2097 had established rather than changing the formula; many developers from the original were retained, early courses were kept easier for newcomers, and later ones toughened for experts. It averaged 87 on GameRankings and 89 on Metacritic, and GamePro called it "hands-down the best futuristic racing game to ever come on the PlayStation". Critics praised its graphics, music and minimalist design, with some calling it the series' best, but its high difficulty and lack of new content disappointed others, and The Times felt the programmers had focused "more with the overall look and feel".

title: R-Type Delta
description: R-Type Delta (1998) is Irem's first 3D R-Type, a PlayStation shoot 'em up with three distinct ships and a Dose System that powers devastating Delta Attacks.
longDescription:
Set in 2164, it is the fourth R-Type game and the first with 3D graphics. Players choose between fighters with different combinations of Force and Wave Cannon: the R-9 from the original R-Type, its updated version the R-X, with a tentacle-laced Force whose laser was revised several times, and the R-13, aimed at more hardcore, skilled players, its number chosen to feel sinister because of its link with superstition. Each ship was meant to feel like a different game while keeping the core R-Type play, and stages were designed around the R-9 before being adjusted for the other two.

The new Dose System lets the Force absorb energy as it collides with enemy projectiles and enemies, filling a Dose Gauge. At 100 per cent, the player can unleash the fighter's Delta Attack, a superweapon whose form depends on the ship. Programmer Takayasu Itou added the series' traditional Kid's Mode and Human Mode difficulty settings late in development, and the game was made much harder than earlier R-Types so that players would memorise stage patterns and learn from their mistakes. Critics highlighted the diversity, colour and detail of its graphics and complex polygon models, with unique explosions and attacks for each enemy, and its dynamic rock and techno soundtrack that changes with the surroundings.
trivia: Early planning documents called it R-Type EVE, after the novel Parasite Eve.
The name Delta came from the three ships and won a staff questionnaire; the symbol also stood for the fourth game.
Irem was inspired by the 3D visuals of Taito's RayStorm on PlayStation.
Famitsu scored it 34 out of 40.
EGM's Che Chou called it "the best R-Type ever".
devStory: Irem began work in early 1998, impressed by the fast action and polygon graphics of RayStorm's PlayStation conversion and hoping to rival it. It was the team's first 3D game, and early test versions were troublesome: many ideas did not work in 3D, terrain made the ship's hitbox hard to judge and caused unintended deaths, and Kita felt the polygonal Force looked "fake". Multiple ships were one of the team's most requested features, for replayability. It received favourable reviews: GameSpot said "If there's one PlayStation shooter to own, R-Type Delta is that shooter", GamePro called it "an excellent time-waster", and NextGen praised its looks but felt the genre's limits would soon relegate 2D shooters to classic collections.

title: Thunder Force V
description: Thunder Force V (1997) is Technosoft's final Thunder Force, a 2.5D Saturn shooter in which the Gauntlet fights a rogue supercomputer using CRAW options that combine into Over Weapons.
longDescription:
A combat unit is formed to fight the Guardian, a supercomputer that went rogue after deciphering the code of a space vessel, and the player pilots its starfighter, the Gauntlet. Environments are rendered in 3D while play takes place on a 2D plane, and unlike earlier Thunder Force games, polygons model the larger enemy ships and some scenery alongside sprites. There are seven levels, the first three playable in any order. Levels scroll automatically while the ship moves freely, and as in Thunder Force IV, players destroy constantly moving enemy formations and dodge their shots and obstacles, with a boss at the end of each stage.

The series' CRAW returns, an option that adds firepower and absorbs enemy bullets. Up to three can now be used at once instead of two, and they stay on screen for a while after being lost so they can be recollected. Combining the CRAWs with the current weapon creates a stronger Over Weapon for a limited time, draining the CRAWs' energy, shown by their change of colour, which recovers by collecting more CRAWs or waiting. Sega Saturn Magazine felt its mix of polygon ships and 2D parallax backgrounds looked "a little bit ropey" but that strong gameplay and better power-ups outweighed it, and Eurogamer later called it "a very solid shooter" with "perfectly-tuned" bosses.
trivia: Development began on the Mega Drive with pre-rendered 3D graphics, which the team thought looked cheap.
A special pack came with the remix CD Best of Thunder Force.
The Saturn version was never released outside Japan; Sega Europe considered it and declined.
The 1998 PlayStation port, Thunder Force V: Perfect System, added levels, CG movies and a time attack mode.
Working Designs released the PlayStation version in North America under its SPAZ label.
devStory: According to former Technosoft staff member Naosuke Arai, production began on the Mega Drive, but the team disliked the cheap look of pre-rendered 3D next to Thunder Force IV and moved to the Saturn, which could deliver the visuals they wanted. Technosoft released it in Japan on 11 July 1997; it was the last Thunder Force the company made. Electronic Gaming Monthly urged readers to ask Sega of America to release it, without success. The PlayStation version received average reviews, Next Generation calling its saving grace a return to "a time when games weren't as good as they are now". In 2007 Eurogamer's Rob Fahey judged it less refined than Einhänder or Radiant Silvergun but praised the CRAW as its "hook" and said it deserved far more credit than it received.

title: Silhouette Mirage
description: Silhouette Mirage (1997) is Treasure's 2D action game in which the heroine Shyna switches between two opposing attributes simply by turning left or right, throwing enemies around to hit them with the right one.
longDescription:
Everything revolves around two opposing attributes, Silhouette and Mirage. Silhouette enemies can only be destroyed with Mirage attacks and vice versa, and Shyna changes automatically depending on which way she faces: red and using Mirage when facing right, blue and using Silhouette when facing left. Both she and her enemies have health, reduced by attacks of the opposite attribute, and spirit, reduced by attacks of the same attribute, which governs how much damage a weapon deals. Getting enemies onto the correct side is therefore central, so Shyna can grapple, throw and slide into them, moves that do no damage themselves, and some bosses switch attribute mid-fight.

Shyna can also triple jump, crawl and dash, running up walls and along ceilings to dodge or reach hidden areas, and a reflector bounces enemy shots back. Extra weapons called parasites, such as Surosa single shots, Cavitas homing blasts and the powerful Grattoni laser, are bought with coins at the Hare Wares vendor; killing enemies yields a few coins, but mugging them with the Cash Bash yields more. There are seven levels, and alongside saving, the game uses arcade-style continues, with a single life and up to nine continues, its developers intending it to be played through in one sitting. Edge called it a "frantic, polished battle" but felt it could degenerate into button bashing.
trivia: Treasure announced it as its final Saturn game, but went on to make Radiant Silvergun.
Grabbing, throwing and the Cash Bash were added later because the team had many ideas it wanted to include.
It was ported to the PlayStation in 1998.
Working Designs' 2000 North American release raised weapon prices and enemy damage and drained spirit as weapons were used.
Next Generation's PlayStation review compared it to Richie Ashburn's line, "I know I've never seen it before".
devStory: Treasure, the maker of Gunstar Heroes and Mischief Makers, developed it as it shifted focus to the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation; producer Kōichi Kimura said the company aimed to make "fun games" and choose the best system for each. Director Masaki Ukyo said the original concept was an action game built on two attributes, with other ideas added later. ESP published it on the Saturn in Japan in 1997, where it was well received; Next Generation said it showed Treasure still innovating in an outdated genre, despite "too much" and unbalanced power-ups. The PlayStation version divided critics: Mega Fun found it slow, while IGN praised its "revolutionary new play mechanics and an insane amount of depth". Reactions to Working Designs' changes were split.

title: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon
description: Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon (1997) is Konami's surreal 3D action-adventure for the Nintendo 64, in which Goemon and friends stop a gang from turning feudal Japan into a Western theatre, with giant robot battles and musical numbers.
longDescription:
The Peach Mountain Shoguns gang plans to turn Japan into a Westernised fine arts theatre, and Goemon and his friends set out to stop them. The plot includes three cinematic musical numbers and battles between giant robots, and like other Ganbare Goemon games it is full of surreal humour and anachronisms. Players explore forests, fields, dungeons and towns modelled on feudal Japan, walking, running, jumping, attacking and using special abilities. Only one of the four characters is controlled at a time, but they can be swapped with a button press. Hearts show health, a Maneki-neko lucky cat adds an extra heart, and losing all hearts costs a life and returns the player to the entrance of the field map.

Towns and coffeehouses are safe from enemies, offering restaurants and inns to restore health, shops for armour and self-acting riceballs, and plenty of characters with plot clues or gossip. Progress is saved to a Controller Pak at inns and some dungeon entrances. Some routes need abilities earned through minigames; Ebisumaru, for instance, must hide in a giant's cupboard to learn shrinking magic. A status screen and a map of Japan help navigation, and the item Mr. Elly Fant reveals dungeon floorplans. Each dungeon ends with a boss, and some victories lead into battles where Goemon pilots the giant robot Impact, beginning with a music video and a high-speed race to smash structures and avoid hazards.
trivia: It was first titled Ganbare Goemon 5, then Legend of the Mystical Ninja.
A two-player mode was scrapped months before the Japanese release.
A 60 to 70 per cent complete build was shown at E3 in June 1997.
It was the second Ganbare Goemon game released in the West and the twelfth mainline entry.
Its cult following still makes mods for it.
devStory: Konami Computer Entertainment Osaka developed it, and the producers broke the series' numbered naming to stress how different it was. Early images showed Impact fighting a gun-toting foe in a modern city, later replaced by a battle over a forest and village with the Wartime Kabuki Robot Kashiwagi; the E3 build suffered clipping and camera problems before a mostly finished version appeared at the Tokyo Game Show in September 1997. It sold nearly 200,000 copies worldwide and received average reviews overall, with 28 out of 40 from Famitsu. Reviewers praised its graphics, gameplay and quirky story, while criticising the camera and slowdown and questioning whether its jokes would reach Western players. Edge gave it eight out of ten, urging Konami not to deny Western gamers "its charms".

title: Rocket: Robot on Wheels
description: Rocket: Robot on Wheels (1999) is Sucker Punch's debut, a Nintendo 64 platformer in which a maintenance robot saves a theme park using puzzles built on realistic physics.
longDescription:
Rocket is a maintenance robot built by Dr. Gavin, architect and owner of the Whoopie World theme park. On the night before opening day, Gavin leaves him in charge of the park and its two mascots, Whoopie the walrus and his envious raccoon sidekick Jojo. Jojo escapes his cage, clobbers Rocket with a mallet, steals the park's tickets and tokens, kidnaps Whoopie and sabotages the attractions so the park can be rebranded Jojo World. Rocket must recover the tickets and tokens, catch Jojo and rescue Whoopie before Gavin returns; finding every one sees the park renamed RocketLand, to Whoopie's dismay.

It was the first home console game whose play was driven by a realistic physics engine, with puzzles involving mass, inertia, friction and other physical properties. A hub world leads to six themed worlds, each with 12 tickets and 200 tokens. Tickets come from objectives such as helping characters, winning minigames, collecting every token or finding seven machine parts to reactivate a machine and open new areas, and enough tickets unlock new worlds. Tokens buy new abilities, and booster packs raise Rocket's maximum health. Every world has at least one vehicle for solving puzzles, such as the first world's hot-dog-shaped car. NextGen called it "an attractive, almost anti-violent 3D puzzler" with puzzles more suited to adults.
trivia: It was pitched as "Super Mario 64 meets The Incredible Machine".
Sucker Punch's founders came from Microsoft.
Nintendo supplied development kits but declined to publish it.
Sony liked it but turned it down, partly because it would first appear on a rival console.
Nintendo Power later named it the 18th best Nintendo 64 game of all time.
devStory: After leaving Microsoft to found Sucker Punch, the team built a prototype on a PC without development kits, pitched it to Nintendo, received kits but no publishing deal, and spent about a year of their own money building the first level. Sony was impressed but declined because the concept was not mascot-centric and would launch on the N64, and a deal with Electronic Arts would have meant cancelling it to start a PlayStation 2 game; the team kept pitching until Ubisoft published it in 1999. It received favourable reviews: GamePro said it "works so well precisely because it is so different from the typical platform game", though another GamePro reviewer found its interface tedious.

title: Kirby's Pinball Land
description: Kirby's Pinball Land (1993) is HAL Laboratory's Game Boy pinball game with Kirby as the ball, climbing three-floor tables owned by Whispy Woods, Kracko and the Poppy Bros. to face King Dedede.
longDescription:
Kirby is the ball, kept in play by two flippers as he bounces off walls, bumpers and enemies for points. Defeating certain enemies earns bonus points and multipliers that combine into a bonus at the end of each life, and Maxim Tomatoes block the drain for a short time. There are three tables, Whispy Woods, Kracko and Poppy Bros., each owned by a classic Kirby boss and made up of three floors, and the aim is to work Kirby up to the top floor to reach the boss. Each floor has gimmicks to help, such as characters that throw Kirby upward or summon a Warp Star.

Warp Stars lead somewhere different on each floor: on the bottom floor back to table selection, on the middle floor to a minigame for extra points and multipliers, and on the top floor to the boss fight, where the player must land a set number of hits without falling back. Beating all three bosses unlocks a fight against King Dedede, after which the tables can be replayed for a higher score. If Kirby drains on the bottom floor he lands on a springboard; a well-timed press of A bounces him back, even to the top floor, but the springboard shrinks with each use until Kirby is lost. Extra lives come from spelling EXTRA with letters that appear after bosses are beaten.
trivia: It was HAL Laboratory's third pinball game, after Rollerball and Revenge of the 'Gator.
It was the first Kirby spin-off and the second Kirby game on Game Boy.
It was the top-selling Game Boy game in the UK in March and April 1994.
Nintendo Power ranked it the fifth best Game Boy game of 1993.
It was re-released on the 3DS Virtual Console in July 2012.
devStory: HAL Laboratory developed it and Nintendo published it, its second pinball game after the NES title Pinball, releasing it in Japan on 27 November 1993. Famitsu's four reviewers praised its atmosphere, secrets and surprises, with one calling it "very-well rounded", though others found it too easy for the ball to fall between the flippers and one felt it had fewer features than Devil's Crush. Electronic Gaming Monthly's critics complained that the Game Boy screen's blurring made the action hard to follow, but deemed it "one of the better pinball games for any system" thanks to its ball-saving springboard, multi-table play and many hidden things to find.

title: Wetrix
description: Wetrix (1998) is Zed Two's 3D puzzle game, born from a water physics demo, in which players raise falling land pieces into walls to hold rain on an isometric landscape.
longDescription:
On a square isometric landscape, water bubbles fall from the sky, and the player must build mounds to hold it. Uppers, pieces shaped like rectangles, squares and Ts, raise parts of the land to form walls for lakes, falling much like Tetris blocks, while Downers lower it. Any water without a wall in its way spills off the edge into a drain shown as a water meter, and the game ends when the meter is full. Fireballs evaporate water for points depending on how much is vaporised, which also lowers the drain. Hazards wreck the player's work: Mines blast holes in the ground, Ice Cubes freeze the water, and earthquakes flatten the landscape once it rises too high.

Besides the standard Classic mode there is a faster Pro mode and a Practice mode that teaches the rules. Challenge modes end after one or five minutes or must be survived over a set number of pieces, such as 100 or 500, and Handicap modes start with a half-full drain, a layer of ice, raised or random land, or random holes. The only multiplayer is a two-player split-screen battle with a four-colour water meter: depending on the colour the water reaches, a player can launch an attack on the other, and evaporating a lake does not lower the meter. Critics applauded its addictiveness and originality but criticised the limited camera and were divided on its difficulty.
trivia: It was jokingly named Wetris before the title was changed to sound less like Tetris.
It began as a water-physics testbed for Zed Two's hack and slash game Vampire Circus.
Ocean only signed it after testers, and a receptionist between calls, kept playing the demo.
Famitsu gave it its highest rating for a Western-developed game in years.
Its success led to the PlayStation 2 launch sequel Aqua Aqua.
devStory: Ste and John Pickford left Software Creations to form Zed Two and "re-learn game design from the very basics". While Ste drew backgrounds and monsters for Vampire Circus, John built a demo of water flowing as a dynamic fluid over a shifting grid, which the brothers enjoyed so much they turned it into a puzzle game. Publishers wanted big, expensive games, but Ocean signed a two-game deal a week before merging with Infogrames, turning Vampire Circus into Taz Express while giving the brothers free rein on Wetrix. They made the PC version themselves from January to October 1997, and the Nintendo 64 port with three more programmers through Christmas 1997. The N64 version sold over 105,000 copies in the West and the PC version 30,000; Dreamcast and Game Boy Color versions followed in 1999.

title: Mega Man II (Game Boy)
description: Mega Man II (1991) is the second Game Boy Mega Man, made by Sokoban developer Thinking Rabbit, mixing bosses from Mega Man 2 and 3 as Dr. Wily uses a stolen time machine.
longDescription:
Dr. Wily steals an experimental Time Skimmer from the Chronos Institute and travels 37.426 years into the future. Alerted by the robot dog Rush's sense of smell, Dr. Light sends Mega Man into an underground passage full of Robot Masters from past adventures, then on to Wily's fortress with four more. There he meets Quint, a future version of himself that Wily captured and rebuilt; once beaten, Quint hands over his Sakugarne jackhammer, and Mega Man follows Wily to a space station to defeat him.

Like other Game Boy entries, it combines two consecutive NES games, here Mega Man 2 and Mega Man 3. Mega Man runs, jumps and shoots, and can now slide. The first four stages, home to Wood Man, Air Man, Crash Man and Metal Man from Mega Man 2, can be played in any order, and each defeated boss gives up its weapon, with limited ammunition refilled by enemy drops. After reaching Wily's fortress, a teleport room opens four more stages with Top Man, Hard Man, Magnet Man and Needle Man from Mega Man 3. Energy tanks fully restore health, and defeating some bosses unlocks Rush adaptors: Rush Coil for high jumps, Rush Marine for travelling underwater and Rush Jet for crossing long distances.
trivia: Capcom outsourced it to Thinking Rabbit instead of Minakuchi Engineering, which made the first Game Boy game.
Keiji Inafune said it felt different because the developer knew very little about the series.
It is considered the weakest of the five Game Boy Mega Man games.
Nintendo Power ranked it second in its top 10 Game Boy games of 1992.
Quint later appeared in Archie Comics' Mega Man series.
devStory: Capcom gave development to Thinking Rabbit, best known for Sokoban, rather than Minakuchi Engineering, which had made Mega Man: Dr. Wily's Revenge. Series artist Keiji Inafune admitted the different feel of its design came from the developer's limited knowledge of the series. It received mixed reviews, blamed partly on Thinking Rabbit's inexperience with this kind of game, with criticism of bland level design and a poorly optimised soundtrack; 1UP.com's Jeremy Parish dismissed it as "a random assortment of enemies and stages from Mega Man 2 and Mega Man 3 from NES, downsampled and downscaled for Game Boy". As a result Thinking Rabbit was not retained, and Minakuchi Engineering made the later Game Boy games. It has since been re-released on the 3DS Virtual Console and Nintendo Switch.

title: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters
description: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters (1991) is Nintendo's Game Boy sequel to Kid Icarus, in which the angel Pit trains to wield three sacred treasures against the demon Orcos.
longDescription:
Palutena, goddess of Angel Land, dreams of an invasion by the demon Orcos and his minions. She orders Pit, leader of her army, to undergo special training so he can use Angel Land's three sacred treasures, which she places under the protection of three fortress guardians. Pit explores the underworld tower, the overworld and the sky world tower, each of three areas and a labyrinthine fortress, armed with a bow and unlimited arrows. Saving is possible after each area, and Pit's health bar grows if he has defeated enough enemies. Beating the guardians earns the Wings of Pegasus, the Silver Armor and the Light Arrows, which give Pit new powers in the final sky palace, where Orcos turns Palutena to stone before Pit defeats him.

Unlike the NES original, levels scroll freely in all four directions, allowing backtracking, and Pit can flap his wings to slow his fall. Hidden doors lead to eight kinds of chamber: shops and black markets selling items such as healing potions for hearts dropped by monsters, information centres with hints, hot springs, bat chambers for earning hearts, treasuries with games of chance, Zeus's sacred chamber, which grants strength based on enemies defeated, and the sacred training centre, whose endurance test awards protective crystals, fire arrows or a long bow. In the ending, like the Icarus of myth, Pit flies too close to the sun and loses his wings.
trivia: It was never released in Japan until the 3DS Virtual Console in 2012.
Masafumi Sakashita designed it and Hideyo Kawaguchi programmed it.
Nintendo Power ranked it 18th among the 20 best Game Boy games.
It was the last Kid Icarus for 21 years, until Kid Icarus: Uprising in 2012.
GamePro gave its gameplay the maximum five points.
devStory: Nintendo developed it with the external company Tose, releasing it in North America in November 1991 and Europe in May 1992, making it one of few first-party Nintendo games not originally published in Japan. It drew generally favourable reviews for its gameplay, graphics and music. Nintendo Magazine System found it a "fairly jolly adaptation" but "rather long in the tooth", Joystiq said it "advances significantly beyond its predecessor", and IGN's Audrey Drake called it an "awesome sequel" and "a solid title that has undeservedly been all-but-forgotten". Its 2012 Japanese debut kept the English localisation and marked the release of Kid Icarus: Uprising, and Nintendo Life scored the re-release eight out of ten.

sources.title: Kid Icarus: Of Myths and Monsters

title: Game & Watch Gallery
description: Game & Watch Gallery (1997) is a Game Boy compilation of four Game & Watch classics, each playable in its original form or in a Modern version starring Mario characters.
longDescription:
Four games from Nintendo's Game & Watch handhelds of 1980 to 1982 are included, each in a Classic mode that recreates the original look and play and a Modern mode with extra mechanics, enhanced graphics and music, and Mario characters, all at Normal or Hard difficulty. In Fire, players move a tarp to catch people leaping from a burning building and bounce them to safety; in the Modern version, characters bounce for different lengths of time. In Manhole, players fill gaps in the street so pedestrians can cross; modern characters walk at different speeds, and Yoshi can set a manhole cover in advance that drops when stepped on.

In Octopus, players grab treasure from a sunken chest while dodging an octopus's tentacles, and in the Modern version Mario slows down the more treasure he carries. In Oil Panic, players catch falling oil and empty it without hitting bystanders or overflowing the bucket, and the modern Mario carries two buckets that can be swapped around. Every 200 points earns a star, up to five per mode and difficulty for 80 in all, and stars unlock a gallery of animations of other Game & Watch titles. On a Super Game Boy or Game Boy Color the games gain limited colour. IGN compared it favourably to Tetris and Dr. Mario as a strong "twitch" game.
trivia: It is the second Game & Watch Gallery, following Game Boy Gallery.
In Australia it was first released as Game Boy Gallery 2.
IGN readers voted it the best Game Boy action game of the century.
It averages 76.65 per cent on GameRankings.
Author James Newman cited it as an early example of the remastering trend.
devStory: Tose and Nintendo R&D1 designed it and Nintendo published it in 1997, in Japan on 1 February, the US on 5 May and Europe on 28 August. It received generally positive reviews: AllGame called each game "a simple yet dangerously addictive dose of pure unfettered and unvarnished fun", GamesRadar+ praised the updated versions but wished for more titles, and Eurogamer felt that without nostalgia it might be "little more than a curiosity". It was later released on the Nintendo Power cartridge service in Japan in 2000 and on the 3DS Virtual Console in 2011, where USgamer and Official Nintendo Magazine UK named it among the service's best.

title: Survival Kids
description: Survival Kids (1999), known in Europe as Stranded Kids, is Konami's open-ended Game Boy Color survival game, in which a shipwrecked child crafts tools from island materials to stay alive and perhaps escape.
longDescription:
After a storm capsizes their boat, the player character, a boy named Ken or a girl named Mery, is stranded on a deserted island and must work to survive and perhaps find a way back to civilisation. The backstory is minimal, and contact with other characters is scarce or absent depending on how the player proceeds. Seen from a 2D view like The Legend of Zelda and Pokémon, the game tracks hunger, thirst and fatigue alongside health, so the player must eat, drink and sleep, hunting, gathering and finding places to rest.

At its heart is merging, a crafting system: most objects are useless on their own, but two or three can be combined into tools, weapons and other items. A vine and a flexible piece of tree make a bow, a stick, bird feather and pointed rock make arrows, and a flexible piece of tree with fishing gut makes a rod. Kindling, arrows, torches and other items wear out and break, forcing players to make more, and meat rots within a day unless cooked and preserved with spices; around 15 kinds of plants exist, but their effects when eaten are shuffled each new game. The structure is non-linear, with no set goals beyond survival, and many endings depend on what the player discovers and crafts and the situation after a certain time.
trivia: It began the Survival Kids series, known as Lost in Blue in the West.
The heroes are called Kou and Nami in the Japanese version.
A sequel, Survival Kids 2: Escape the Twin Islands, followed in Japan in 2000.
Retro Gamer included it in its top ten Game Boy Color games.
Its first official re-release came on Nintendo Classics in May 2025.
devStory: Konami developed and published it for the Game Boy Color in 1999. It attracted more attention in retrospect than at release: Nintendo Power called it "inventive" and deserving of a "second look", Retro Gamer described it as "original", and Game Informer called it "innovative", a small-scale survival game made years before the genre became a popular standard. The series continued with Survival Kids 2, which added multiple openings and link cable support, then on the Nintendo DS as Lost in Blue, Lost in Blue 2 and Lost in Blue 3, on the Wii, and in a new Survival Kids for Nintendo Switch 2 in June 2025.

title: Tetris DX
description: Tetris DX (1998) is Nintendo's Game Boy Color launch version of Tetris, adding colour, new modes, saved player profiles and link-cable battles to the 1989 classic.
longDescription:
As in Tetris, players fit a falling series of blocks into complete rows that then disappear, and the game ends when blocks stack past the top of the play area. Marathon Mode is closest to the original, with blocks falling faster for every line cleared. Ultra Mode asks players to clear as many lines as possible in two minutes, and 40 Lines lets them choose a starting level and height before racing to clear 40 lines. Vs Mode offers battles against computer opponents on easy, normal or hard, or against another player with their own copy through the Game Link Cable.

Unlike the 1989 Game Boy version, it adds colour and saving: up to four players can store their names and high scores, and each is given a Power Rating that reflects their performance across the modes. Total Game Boy praised the colour for making blocks easier to tell apart, along with the convenience of saving, and felt it was "wise" of Nintendo to change so little of the core game since there was little to improve. Electronic Gaming Monthly found it easier than its predecessor, with a "less erratic" distribution of blocks, and some critics missed the original's background music. Reviewers broadly agreed it improved on Tetris but questioned whether owners of the original needed it.
trivia: It was a launch title for the Game Boy Color in October 1998.
Henk Rogers said Nintendo proposed it to The Tetris Company with the aim of keeping the original's design.
GameSpot said link play made it potentially one of the "best multiplayer [games] ever made".
Critics have listed it among the best Game Boy Color games.
It was added to Nintendo Classics in December 2024.
devStory: According to Tetris Company managing director Henk Rogers, Nintendo proposed the game for its new colour handheld, intending to keep the design of the original, and published it alongside the Game Boy Color's launch. It was well received for its additions: GameSpot's Cameron Davis praised its addictiveness and link-cable play, and another reviewer called it "more fun than the original", saying its new modes and colour justified buying it again. In retrospect, Digital Trends said its "vibrant color scheme made clearing lines and performing complex maneuvers more engaging", and The Escapist called it a strong remake that revamped "the classic with a dazzling display and additional game modes".

title: X
description: X (1992) is Argonaut and Nintendo's Japan-only 3D space combat game for the Game Boy, created by Dylan Cuthbert, who went on to program Star Fox.
longDescription:
The player commands the starship VIXIV, protecting the planet Tetamus II from a mysterious alien race by completing missions given by the Training Academy Coach. One of the few Game Boy games with 3D visuals, it offers full 360-degree movement through space in the style of Argonaut's Starglider 2, with much of the action taking place in long tunnels. Each of the ten stages, called objectives, must be completed against a time limit, with tasks ranging from protecting a base under attack and delivering cargo to shooting down enemy formations.

A radar at the bottom of the screen shows the ship's position, nearby enemies and objectives, and large openings in the ground let the VIXIV fast-travel to other parts of the map. Completing objectives earns up to ten stars, and missions require a certain number of stars, so falling short means restarting. All ten missions must be finished to complete the game. Dylan Cuthbert said it drew on the old 3D games he had played on the ZX Spectrum, "assembled rather haphazardly". Initial reviews were mixed, praising its technical achievement but criticising its high difficulty; in retrospect it has been acclaimed for its historical importance and gameplay, often compared to Star Luster.
trivia: It was released only in Japan; a North American version, Lunar Chase, was cancelled.
Argonaut reverse-engineered the Game Boy, filming a dismantled console running Tetris as a makeshift dev kit.
Cuthbert developed it on an Amiga 3000.
Gunpei Yokoi was reportedly "blown away" by its 3D wireframe graphics.
A DSiWare sequel, X-Scape, was released in 2010.
devStory: Argonaut president Jez San, intrigued by the Game Boy at the 1991 Consumer Electronics Show, commissioned Dylan Cuthbert to build a 3D engine for it. Official kits were hard to obtain, so the team reverse-engineered the hardware, and Cuthbert handled most of the design, some graphics and all of the programming. A Nintendo employee urged them to send a ROM to Kyoto, where Gunpei Yokoi and his engineers invited the team to Japan; Nintendo bought the rights from original publisher Mindscape, made Argonaut a licensee and published it in 1992. Nintendo of America cancelled the planned Lunar Chase release, feeling the game was too complicated for its audience. Alongside Faceball 2000, it remains one of the few attempts at 3D on the Game Boy.

title: Adventure Island II
description: Adventure Island II (1991) is Hudson Soft's NES platformer in which Master Higgins rescues Tina across eight islands, riding four dinosaur friends and managing an inventory of hammers and mounts.
longDescription:
Master Higgins' girlfriend Tina has been kidnapped by the followers of the Evil Witch Doctor, whose monster minions control eight perilous islands. Four friendly dinosaurs will ally with anyone brave enough to take on their common oppressors, and Higgins sets out to rescue her. The rules are those of the first Adventure Island, with an inventory system as the main addition: before each stage the player chooses which rescued dinosaur to bring and whether to take one of the stone hammers stored up. Because of this, collecting a second hammer no longer upgrades Higgins to fireballs but adds it to the inventory instead.

Checkpoints are gone, so dying means restarting a stage, but stages are much shorter than before. A different sound reveals where a hidden egg lies, and bonus areas are reached with keys found inside these eggs, some leading to item rooms or shortcuts to the next island. There are underwater and vertically scrolling stages, Higgins can backtrack a little, and finishing a stage lets him pick one of ten spinning eggs for points. Each island's boss waits on a set stage, but if Higgins loses to it, the boss moves elsewhere. The dinosaurs, summoned by playing-card suits inside eggs, are a blue camptosaurus that tail-whips and walks on ice, a red one that breathes fire and crosses lava, a pteranodon that flies and drops stones, and an elasmosaurus, the only one that survives underwater.
trivia: Unlike the first game, an adaptation of Sega's Wonder Boy, it is an original work.
It is the second Adventure Island on the NES.
Skateboards no longer carry over to the next stage.
A Game Boy version, known in the West simply as Adventure Island, followed in 1992.
It features in Nagai Noriaki's manga Cyber Boy.
devStory: Now Production developed it and Hudson Soft published it for the NES in 1991 as the sequel to Adventure Island. While the first game had adapted Sega's Wonder Boy, this one, like most later Adventure Island games, was an original design. Its main innovations were the inventory of hammers and dinosaur friends, keys hidden in eggs, and bosses that relocate after a defeat. AllGame's Skyler Miller preferred it to the original, praising its "improved graphics, a map screen, and most importantly, four dinosaur buddies for Master Higgins to ride, each with their own special ability". Cover artwork for the packaging was illustrated by Shelley L. Hunter.

title: Cruis'n World
description: Cruis'n World (1996) is Midway's arcade sequel to Cruis'n USA, racing around the globe from Hawaii to Florida, adding stunts and ending with a trip to the Moon.
longDescription:
The core play is the same as Cruis'n USA: race against a time limit to the goal, passing checkpoints that extend the clock. This time the route circles the globe, opening in Hawaii and continuing through Japan, Australia, China, Kenya, Egypt, Moscow, Germany, Italy, France, England, Mexico and New York City before finishing in Florida. There are more cars than in the first game, and Cruis'n World introduced stunts to the series: wheelies give short bursts of speed, while aerial flips knock seconds off the final race time, helping the player climb the records table, and stunts also help dodge obstacles and take tight curves.

Players who finish every stage including Florida see their car carried by a Space Shuttle to the Moon, where they are congratulated by then-President Bill Clinton. To build the tracks, the developers sent artists on a round-the-world trip to capture sights and major tourist attractions digitally. A Next Generation critic said that, like its predecessor, it had an unsurpassed sense of arcade driving, with fast driving, cars knocked off the road and chaotic multi-car collisions, and praised its more elaborate, skill-demanding tracks, but felt it was mastered very quickly and that pop-in remained as bad as before.
trivia: It won Most Innovative New Title at the 1996 AMOA show.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it a runner-up for Arcade Game of the Year.
The 1998 Nintendo 64 port by Eurocom adds a Moon track and a Championship mode with car upgrades.
The N64 version supports four players in split screen.
It was the best received of the Cruis'n home ports.
devStory: Midway Games developed it and Nintendo published it in 1996 as the sequel to the 1994 arcade racer Cruis'n USA. Development of the Nintendo 64 version began in 1996; Eugene Jarvis admitted that Williams Entertainment's port of Cruis'n USA had not been good, and an arcade-perfect conversion was promised. Eurocom took the licence and spent more time on it than on the earlier port. Nintendo announced it for autumn 1997, but it was quietly delayed until 1998. The port received mixed reviews, averaging 63 per cent on GameRankings, with Next Generation giving it two stars out of five for its minimal technique and difficulty.

title: Mystic Warriors: Wrath of the Ninjas
description: Mystic Warriors: Wrath of the Ninjas (1993) is Konami's ninja run and gun from the Sunset Riders team, in which five young ninja battle the Skull Enterprise across a dystopian future.
longDescription:
In a dystopian future New York, the evil Skull Enterprise has taken over the nation and plans to conquer the world. Five young ninja are targeted by its forces: Spyros, Keima, Kojiro, Brad and Yuri. Up to two or four players, depending on the cabinet, pick their characters, and one of the remaining members is kidnapped, prompting the others to set out. Crossing several regions of Japan, they find and free their friend, only for the rescued ninja to sacrifice themselves to release the others from an electric trap. The rest of the game is a quest for revenge, and after defeating Skull the survivors mourn their companion before returning home.

Controls use an eight-way joystick and buttons to attack and jump, and as in Sunset Riders, players can jump between upper and lower levels and slide. Characters throw unlimited shuriken or daggers and use their weapons up close. Improvements over Sunset Riders include switching characters after losing a credit and a life gauge that absorbs up to four hits. Box-carrying enemies drop power-ups: shuriken upgrades of up to two levels, food such as sushi, tempura, udon and sukiyaki to restore life, a blue shinobi orb that creates a temporary barrier, a yellow chikara orb that destroys every enemy on screen, and jewellery for points and brief invincibility. Each of the nine stages ends with a boss, and the player who hit it most earns bonus points.
trivia: It was made by the team behind Sunset Riders.
It adds hack-and-slash elements to Sunset Riders' formula.
The World Trade Center appears in some stages.
Its soundtrack appears on the album Konami Amusement Sounds '93: Summer Edition.
Hamster re-released it in Arcade Archives in December 2023.
devStory: Konami developed and published it for arcades in 1993, using the same team that produced Sunset Riders and keeping much of that game's play while adding close-range weapon attacks and a life gauge. Game Machine listed it as Japan's ninth most successful table arcade unit in April 1993. Its complete soundtrack was released in August 1993 on the two-CD album Konami Amusement Sounds '93: Summer Edition, and the game returned three decades later in Hamster Corporation's Arcade Archives series for Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4.

title: The King of Fighters '95
description: The King of Fighters '95 (1995) is SNK's team fighting sequel that introduced Team Edit and Kyo's rival Iori Yagami, as a resurrected Rugal Bernstein stages a new tournament for revenge.
longDescription:
A year after KOF '94, invitations to a new tournament arrive signed only "R". Rugal Bernstein, thought killed in an explosion, has survived and wants revenge on champion Kyo Kusanagi. The USA Team is replaced by the Rival Team, each with a vendetta: Iori Yagami wants to kill Kyo, Eiji Kisaragi wants to beat the Kyokugen Ryu fighters of the Art of Fighting Team, and Billy Kane wants to kill a Fatal Fury fighter in place of his boss Geese Howard.
