Kyo's father Saisyu appears as a fighter for the first time, having survived defeat by Rugal and been forced to serve him. After beating Saisyu, players face a stronger Rugal, whose powers consume and kill him.

Rules are mostly unchanged from KOF '94: players pick a team of three and fight rival teams until all three members are beaten, using taunts, special moves and combos, while revised dodge and counterattack mechanics make fighters react better. The big addition is Team Edit, which lets players build a custom team from any of the 24 characters instead of using the preset teams. Electronic Gaming Monthly named it Best Neo Geo Game of 1995, ahead of Fatal Fury 3 and Samurai Shodown III, and both EGM and GamePro singled out Team Edit as its best feature, though GamePro felt it brought few other improvements and Next Generation noted it was still always one-on-one fighting.
trivia: It marks the first appearance of Iori Yagami, who became Kyo's series-long rival.
It began the Orochi saga, which ended with KOF '97.
It was the first KOF ported beyond Neo Geo hardware, to PlayStation, Saturn and Game Boy.
It was originally meant to be a remake of KOF '94.
It sold over 700,000 copies.
devStory: Masanori Kuwasashi, director of KOF '94, led production at SNK's Osaka headquarters from shortly after the first game's release in winter 1994. The tired staff came up with more ambitious ideas, worked long days and cut back on sleep, but still had to drop many elements for time, and scheduling and balancing issues left it close to its predecessor. Kuwasashi used Saisyu's return, Iori's introduction and Rugal's stronger form to build a more coherent narrative, and bringing team editing to the forefront to give players more freedom was a key goal. It received positive reviews on arcade and consoles, Computer and Video Games calling it one of the best 2D fighting games, but the PlayStation version was criticised for its controls and long loading times.

title: The King of Fighters '96
description: The King of Fighters '96 (1996) is SNK's third KOF, shifting the focus to close combat with rolls, runs and short hops, as Chizuru Kagura's tournament leads to the Orochi servant Goenitz.
longDescription:
A new tournament is hosted by Chizuru Kagura, heir of the Yata Clan, who wants to find Kyo Kusanagi, conqueror of Rugal Bernstein, and ask him and his bitter rival Iori Yagami to help seal the Orochi demon as their ancestors did. The final boss is Goenitz, one of Orochi's servants. The cast was reshuffled, notably with a Boss Team of famous villains from Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting, and both Chizuru and Goenitz can be unlocked as playable characters. Unlike earlier games, the emphasis moved from projectiles to hand-to-hand combat.

Teams of three still fight through the tournament, but the old Dodge is replaced by an emergency evasion that rolls away from or towards the opponent, possibly ending up behind them. Players can choose short or high jumps, perform counter-techniques to cancel attacks, and run instead of hopping forward. Super Special Moves are available when the Power Gauge is full or life is flashing red, and with both at once an even stronger version can be used. It was also the first game with the Rush combo counter. Reviews were mixed: some praised the graphical improvements and new characters, while others felt new moves that failed to mesh projectiles with close combat left it unbalanced; Sega Saturn Magazine later called it a "disappointment".
trivia: Mature and Vice were missing from location tests because the staff had no time to finish them.
Its 362-megabit size made it the first game to break the technical limits of the MVS system.
It took a year to make, compared with two for the first KOF.
Yasuyuki Oda called it the most important game in the franchise, the basis for most of SNK's later work.
EGM named it Neo Geo Game of the Year, ahead of Metal Slug and Real Bout Fatal Fury.
devStory: SNK struggled to create the sprites and special moves of the new characters, and development ran right up to the scheduled release; staff found it hard to design new characters as appealing as the series' popular ones, and tight deadlines left balance problems and bugs. Game Machine listed it as Japan's most successful arcade game in September 1996, the AES version sold 33,323 copies in its first week, and GameSpot said it helped spark "a modest resurgence" in AES sales. The Saturn port sold 109,752 copies in its first week in Japan. PlayStation and Saturn versions were released only in Japan, and it later appeared in King of Fighters Collection: The Orochi Saga. Overall it sold over 188,000 copies.

title: The King of Fighters '97
description: The King of Fighters '97 (1997) is SNK's conclusion to the Orochi saga, letting players choose between Advanced and Extra fighting styles as the servants of Orochi try to revive their master.
longDescription:
The King of Fighters tournament has sparked a worldwide fighting craze, and the servants of the demon Yamata no Orochi, the "Will of Gaia", plan to revive their master with energy and sacrifices gathered from its fighters. The story focuses on Kyo Kusanagi, whose design was inspired by Japanese myth, notably the sword Kusanagi no Tsurugi won by the god Susanoo-no-Mikoto in his encounter with the mythical beast, and whose move Orochinagi was conceived to defeat it. The team behind it concentrated on creating bosses, above all Orochi, who faces the Sacred Treasures Team introduced in KOF '96.

Three-character teams return, and before choosing a team players select one of two styles. Advanced builds on KOF '96, with dodges, counterattacks and controllable jumps, but its Power Gauge fills when the player lands hits or performs special moves, storing up to three stocks; one stock powers a Super Special Move or activates MAX mode, boosting attack and defence, and a Super used in MAX mode becomes stronger still. Extra is based on KOF '94 and '95: the gauge is charged manually or filled by defending, entering MAX mode when full, Supers are available only in MAX mode or with life flashing red, and the side-step replaces the emergency roll. Hardcore Gaming 101 praised its new characters and seamless story but found it unbalanced.
trivia: It was the first KOF directed by battle system designer Toyohisa Tanabe.
It won Best Direction in Gamest's 1997 awards.
A later version, Global Match, added online features.
It inspired the first handheld KOF, King of Fighters R-1, in 1998.
Its ports sold over 336,000 copies combined in Japan.
devStory: Masanori Kuwasashi, under pressure from the yearly release schedule, stepped down after KOF '96, and battle designer Toyohisa Tanabe took over, balancing the characters with the main aim of ending the Orochi arc, planned since the series began, by revealing its title villain. KOF '97 set out to improve the experimental systems of the previous game and to give players many combos, which led to the Advanced and Extra styles. Released in arcades and on Neo Geo CD, with Japanese PlayStation and Saturn ports, it received positive reviews for its characters and narrative: AllGame called its presentation the series' best, and Sega Saturn Magazine called it a return to form. It sold well and was followed by KOF '98 and the visual novel The King of Fighters: Kyo.

title: Samurai Shodown III: Blades of Blood
description: Samurai Shodown III: Blades of Blood (1995) is SNK's darker weapon-fighting sequel, giving every character a Slash and a Bust version and a new three-slash button layout.
longDescription:
The third main Samurai Shodown is the first part of a two-chapter story set between the first and second games. Its aesthetic is darker: the light-hearted Earthquake, Cham Cham and Gen-an are gone, the kabuki master Kyoshiro Senryo is reimagined from a flamboyant performer into a grim, muscular man, and every character has been completely redrawn. Each fighter comes in two versions. Slash, known in Japan as Shura after the battle-loving asura, plays closest to Samurai Shodown II, while Bust, or Rasetsu after the rakshasa demon, is a more aggressive style with new moves, looking different only in colour, except for Nakoruru, whose Bust form fights with her wolf Shikuru instead of the hawk Mamahaha, and Galford, who fights without his dog Poppy for the first time.

The controls now give three of the four buttons to weak, medium and strong slashes and one to kicks, instead of two each. Many basic attacks can be cancelled into special moves, rare in earlier games, and special moves gain priority. Most of Samurai Shodown II's movement options are replaced by a dodge, pressing A and B together, which near an opponent becomes a quick switch to their back for follow-up attacks. Attacks can also be blocked in mid-air, and items are thrown onto the battlefield from off-screen rather than delivered by a man running in the background.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's most popular arcade game of the year.
The AES version sold 48,757 copies in its first week, according to Famitsu.
Takara made a Japan-only Game Boy version with a slightly different roster.
It was also released on Neo Geo CD, PlayStation and Saturn.
Shura and Rasetsu were sometimes mistranslated as "Chivalry" and "Treachery".
devStory: SNK developed it for the Neo Geo in 1995 as a substantial overhaul of the series, darker in look and with significant changes to play. It received moderately positive reviews. Electronic Gaming Monthly felt its graphics fell short of the first two games and that the Neo Geo controller made some moves hard, but praised the large roster and dual personas and rated the gameplay superior to its predecessors. GamePro's Major Mike felt that innovations like the personas and sidestep were offset by the loss of some of the best characters and weaker backgrounds, concluding that "while Shodown III won't disappoint fans of the series, it isn't the jump that Shodown II was over I." Samurai Shodown IV continued the story.

title: The Last Blade 2
description: The Last Blade 2 (1998) is SNK's darker sequel to its Bakumatsu-era sword fighter, adding an EX style and new characters including the evil spirit Setsuna and the swordsmith's daughter Hibiki.
longDescription:
The play is much as before, with minor adjustments, plus a new EX mode that combines the Speed and Power styles. The mood is grimmer from the introduction on, characters are coloured slightly darker, and cut-scenes are longer to emphasise the story. Characters are also less equal than before, with greater differences in strengths and weaknesses. Three newcomers join. Hibiki Takane is the 17-year-old daughter of the renowned swordsmith Genzō Takane, who was compelled by a silver-haired man radiating evil to forge the Yaso Magatsu Hi no Tachi over almost three months, work that left him bedridden; with his last cryptic words, she sets out after the man and the blade.

That man is Setsuna, a powerful spirit released when Kagami was defeated by Kaede, who possessed a dead baby on a battlefield, grew into an adult and now walks a path of destruction, hating humanity and wielding a black blade that trails dark energy. Kojiroh Sanada was captain of the fictional Shinsengumi Unit Zero, which investigated demonic forces; after he died investigating Hell's Gate, his sister Kaori took his identity to continue the work and restore faith in the Shinsengumi, a secret known only to Washizuka, with whom she shares moves without needing to charge them. Hibiki has two endings, one earned by defeating every Arcade mode opponent with super moves in every round.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most popular arcade game of December 1998.
The Neo Geo CD version adds a quiz mode, voiced cut-scenes and an art gallery.
The Neo Geo CD and Dreamcast versions add the first game's sub-boss Musashi Akatsuki.
The Dreamcast port was titled The Last Blade 2: Heart of the Samurai.
GamesRadar+ called it "one of the Neo Geo's prettiest, deepest fighters".
devStory: SNK developed and published it in 1998 for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms as the sequel to The Last Blade. It was released on the AES and Neo Geo CD, whose version sold 9,379 copies in its first week, and on Dreamcast in 2001. Next Generation gave the Dreamcast version three stars, calling it "a unique 2D fighter" and "a welcome break from the plethora of Street Fighter variants", though only available as an import. It was later paired with the first game in a Japan-only PlayStation 2 compilation, released by Code Mystics on PlayStation 4 and Vita in 2016, and included in Hamster's ACA Neo Geo series. In 2012 GamesRadar+ named it among little-known classic fighters deserving HD remakes.

title: Samurai Shodown IV: Amakusa's Revenge
description: Samurai Shodown IV: Amakusa's Revenge (1996) is SNK's fourth Samurai Shodown, concluding the story begun in III with ninja brothers Kazuki and Sogetsu, CD combos and Mortal Kombat-style fatalities.
longDescription:
Chronologically it is the second and final chapter of a story set between Samurai Shodown and Samurai Shodown II, following Samurai Shodown III. All twelve playable characters from III return, some retouched for a more cartoonish look, along with Charlotte, Tam Tam and Jubei Yagyu from earlier games. New are two ninja brothers of the Kazama clan: Kazuki, a fire-jutsu specialist who deserts to rescue their younger sister Hazuki from Amakusa, and the elder Sogetsu, who uses water jutsu, stays with the clan and is ordered to assassinate Kazuki for leaving.

The Slash and Bust versions of each character are retained, but aerial blocking is removed entirely, players can no longer charge their own POW gauge, and the off-screen item delivery is gone. A new CD combo, triggered by pressing C and D together, opens a strike that can be continued with a sequence of button taps. SNK also added a suicide move that forfeits the round in exchange for starting the next with a full POW gauge, and certain finishes allow a fatality in the vein of Mortal Kombat. GamePro felt it lacked the depth of Street Fighter Alpha 2 and Soul Edge but was easier to pick up and play, praising its "superb animation" and "outright beautiful" stages, and Electronic Gaming Monthly praised its large roster and big sprites.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's most popular arcade game in December 1996.
The AES version sold 9,253 copies in its first week.
The Japanese PlayStation version, released on 25 December 1997, adds Cham Cham.
Samurai Shodown! for the Neo Geo Pocket is a monochrome adaptation of it.
Nintendo Life gave the Virtual Console release eight out of ten.
devStory: SNK developed and published it for the Neo Geo in 1996 to complete the two-part story started in Samurai Shodown III, bringing back characters dropped from that game and reworking its systems. GamePro was unimpressed by the two new characters but pleased by the returning ones. Its PlayStation port, known in Japan as Samurai Spirits: Amakusa's Descent Special, followed at the end of 1997. Reviewing the later Virtual Console release, Nintendo Life praised its animation, heavy challenge and thrilling pace, noting that "a single slash [is] capable of turning the tide against any opponent."

title: Art of Fighting 3: The Path of the Warrior
description: Art of Fighting 3: The Path of the Warrior (1996) is SNK's motion-captured fighter, following Robert Garcia to Mexico with a nearly all-new cast and 3D-style juggle combos.
longDescription:
The story shifts from the Sakazakis to Robert Garcia, who disappears in search of his childhood friend Freia Lawrence and tracks her to Glasshill Valley, Mexico. The villain Tom Wyler wants her to complete a powerful elixir, begun by their fathers, that grants users supernatural strength, and Robert's wish to save her alone causes friction with Ryo and others. Ryo and Robert are the only returning fighters. Newcomers include Jin Fu-Ha, a traitorous former disciple of Eiji Kisaragi who tests himself against Ryo before going after Eiji; Karman Cole, the Garcia family's loyal employee sent to bring Robert home; Kasumi Todoh, who seeks to avenge her father Ryuhaku's defeat by Ryo; and private investigator Lenny Creston.

Desperation moves, taunts, dashes, back-dashes and ki meters remain, but holding a button for stronger punches and kicks is gone. The game emulates 3D fighters while staying 2D: characters can move forward while attacking to build combos, which are mostly juggles performed by pressing a few attack buttons in sequence, an unusual emphasis for a 2D game, and directional inputs change attacks. Desperation moves used against weakened opponents in the first round cause an Ultimate Knock Out that ends the match outright. Electronic Gaming Monthly gave it five out of ten, criticising the easy, unblockable, hugely damaging Ultra-Cool Attacks and its lack of originality, while Hardcore Gaming 101 compared its play to Virtua Fighter and Tekken.
trivia: It was the first SNK fighting game animated with motion capture.
Motion capture was recorded in the United States over one to two months, as SNK lacked the technology.
SNK developed it on Microsoft Windows instead of its own Artbox tool.
It is often noted for some of SNK's best sprite work.
An updated Art of Fighting 3 R adding King and Yuri Sakazaki is in development for Windows.
devStory: Produced by Hiroshi Matsumoto and Takashi Nishiyama like its predecessors, it was built around motion capture: each character's captured movements were turned into pixel art, and designer Nobuyuki Kuroki said that although the data lost its original form when refined, he still achieved smooth animation. The process brought several difficulties and limited the number of characters. The Neo Geo CD version sold 20,877 copies in its first week. Reviews were mixed, praising the visuals and mechanics but criticising the small cast and balance; Next Generation saw no balance problem but found it "too similar to every other 2D fighting game on the market", and Nintendo Life later gave it seven out of ten.

sources.title: Art of Fighting 3: The Path of the Warrior

title: Neo Turf Masters
description: Neo Turf Masters (1996) is Nazca's fast-paced arcade golf game for the Neo Geo, with a simple two-click swing, devious courses and wildly variable wind.
longDescription:
A fast-paced, arcade-style golf game, it offers stroke play for one or two players and match play for two. Players compete on four fictional courses in the United States, Japan, Australia and Germany, choosing one of six golfers with different attributes. Unlike many golf games of the time, which used a two-click swing to decide hook or slice, Neo Turf Masters uses one click to set the shot's power and a second to set its height, with hook and slice chosen beforehand using the B and C buttons.

That makes it much easier to pick up than its more technically demanding contemporaries, and it compensates with fiendish, if somewhat unrealistic, course layouts and highly variable wind. Although improved for the Neo Geo, it resembles Irem's Major Title 2: Tournament Leader in many ways, because it was programmed by former Irem staff who had worked on that game. The Neo Geo version mixes partially digitised sprites with realistic art, while a later Neo Geo Pocket Color version uses cartoonish, less detailed graphics. IGN gave the Virtual Console release 7.5 out of 10, recommending it to anyone who "appreciates SNK's arcade style and can jibe with the idea of juiced-up, high-speed golf".
trivia: It was one of Nazca's first two titles before SNK acquired it; the other was Metal Slug.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's twelfth most successful arcade game of March 1996.
Hamster's re-release is titled Big Tournament Golf because of a trademark conflict over "Masters".
A Neo Geo Pocket Color version was released in North America in 1999.
DotEmu ported it to iOS and Android in 2016.
devStory: Nazca Corporation, a team of former Irem employees who had worked on Major Title 2, developed it, and SNK published it in 1996 as an arcade MVS cartridge, a home AES cartridge and on Neo Geo CD. The Neo Geo version was later included in SNK Arcade Classics Vol. 1 for PlayStation 2, Wii and PSP and released on the Wii Virtual Console, while the Neo Geo Pocket Color version reappeared in Neo Geo Pocket Color Selection Vol. 1 in 2021.

title: Waku Waku 7
description: Waku Waku 7 (1996) is Sunsoft's comic Neo Geo fighter whose oddball cast parodies famous characters from games and anime, each with a chargeable, unblockable Harahara move.
longDescription:
Using features common to SNK fighters, such as four basic attacks and a zooming screen, Waku Waku 7 has an unusual feature set for its time. Its roster of nine characters, two of them only in the console ports' versus mode, each play very differently and parody a well-known character. Every fighter has a powerful Harahara move that must be charged, during which the character concentrates, speaks, strikes a pose or plays a fanfare while the game flashes a warning and sounds an alarm; once released it is unblockable and hard to dodge, but it can be interrupted while charging. Fighters can be launched through the screen into the other corner and attacked on the ground, though they can dodge or attack while getting up.

The characters chase the WakuWaku Balls for their own reasons. Rai Bakuoh is a cocky 13-year-old BMX rider with a double jump, parodying Sie Kensou. Arina Makihara is a 14-year-old bunny-eared girl seeking true love, spoofing half-animal shōjo heroines. Dandy-J is a whip-wielding treasure hunter in the mould of Indiana Jones and Joseph Joestar, aided by Natsumi and her cat. Mauru is a purple forest creature parodying Totoro, carrying a lost girl and fighting much like Darkstalkers' Sasquatch, while the slow but hard-hitting Politank-Z spoofs the police tanks of Dominion. Slash is a calm elf swordsman hoping to lift a curse from his laser sword.
trivia: The "7" refers to its seven main playable characters, not a sequel number.
"Waku waku" is a Japanese onomatopoeia for excitement.
It uses the same engine as Sunsoft's Galaxy Fight, with the mid-boss Bonus-Kun in common.
A Neo Geo CD version was cancelled and moved to the Saturn, which needs the 1 MB RAM cartridge.
The Switch re-release averages 76.25 per cent on GameRankings.
devStory: It was Sunsoft's third fighting game, after Sugoi Hebereke on the Super Famicom and Galaxy Fight. Released in arcades in 1996 and later on the Neo Geo AES with easy difficulty settings and limited credits, it was met with generally positive reviews; AllGame's Kyle Knight called its presentation among the best on the Neo Geo and praised its sound, fighting system and roster, while criticising its power gauge. The Japan-only Saturn conversion received a more mixed response for being a straight port, though readers of Sega Saturn Magazine rated it well. Hamster later included it in the ACA Neo Geo series, and Nintendo Life praised its cartoon presentation, frantic pace and varied cast.

title: Galaxy Fight: Universal Warriors
description: Galaxy Fight: Universal Warriors (1995) is Sunsoft's first side-view 2D fighter, a planet-hopping Neo Geo brawler with endlessly scrolling stages and no walls to be cornered against.
longDescription:
Players choose one of eight characters and travel across a solar system, defeating the opponents who inhabit each planet before facing the tyrant Felden to settle their personal scores. Alvan, the short, horned Prince of the Ruined Planet, survived when Felden destroyed his world Rozalis and murdered his family a thousand years ago, thanks to a magic crimson stone. Gunter is a gigantic, green, fire-breathing monster from Guljeff, the largest fighter in the game, and one of only two to sense the mystical nature of the mysterious G. Done, a brown-skinned thug from the planet Mani who wants only peace and freedom. Juri, a thief from Lezaar, is obsessed with becoming stronger and more beautiful and despises anyone she considers ugly.

The four-button layout gives three buttons to strikes of different speed and power, which depending on the character may be punches, kicks, tail whips or bites, while the fourth is purely for taunting. Pressing several buttons together can produce new attacks or special moves. The stages have no walls: instead of cornering opponents, the screen can scroll indefinitely. GameFan compared its zooming effect to Art of Fighting, while AllGame's Kyle Knight praised the presentation and controls but warned that its "odd borderless gameplay may be its worst enemy".
trivia: It followed Sunsoft's 1994 Super Famicom fighter Sugoi Hebereke.
The arcade version uses 32 four-megabit ROM chips, 16 megabytes in total.
Its engine was reused for Waku Waku 7.
The Neo Geo CD version sold 13,385 copies in its first week.
Saturn and PlayStation ports followed in 1996.
devStory: Sunsoft developed and published it for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms as its second fighting game and first side-view 2D fighter. Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourteenth most popular arcade game in March 1995. It received generally positive reviews, though some criticised its harsh difficulty and other design choices. Consoles Plus praised its visuals, speed, sound and playability, GameFan's reviewers liked its unusual roster and mechanics, and GamePro complimented its graphics and music. Hamster later re-released it in the ACA Neo Geo series.

title: Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo
description: Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo (1996) is Capcom's competitive gem-matching puzzler, in which super-deformed Street Fighter and Darkstalkers characters brawl as players trade crash gems and counter gems.
longDescription:
Similar to Sega's Baku Baku Animal, and like Capcom's earlier Pnickies, players guide falling pairs of gems into a pit twelve blocks tall and six wide. Gems only vanish when touched by a Crash Gem of the same colour, which clears every connected gem of that colour and can set off huge chains. Clearing gems drops Counter Gems onto the opponent's board, each counting down, usually from five, with every new pair until it becomes a normal gem; they can only be removed early by clearing an adjacent gem of the same colour with a Crash Gem. Same-coloured gems arranged in rectangles at least two by two fuse into a giant Power Gem, which sends more Counter Gems when cleared in a combo.

Every 25 pieces a diamond appears, wiping out every gem of the colour it lands on, though a bug lets players avoid its intended halving of Counter Gems sent. Borrowing Puyo Puyo 2's offsetting rule, players can cancel incoming garbage with chains of their own and send the excess back. Meanwhile super-deformed versions of Street Fighter and Darkstalkers characters act out a comic fight reflecting the match, performing fighting moves whenever their player sends Counter Gems. The title spoofs Super Street Fighter II Turbo, as there were no earlier Puzzle Fighter games, and its music and interface parody Street Fighter Alpha and Darkstalkers.
trivia: In Japan it was called Super Puzzle Fighter II X.
It was Capcom's response to Puyo Puyo 2, which was sweeping Japanese arcades.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixth most successful arcade game in August 1996, ahead of Tekken 2.
Its super-deformed characters were reused for Super Gem Fighter Mini Mix.
An HD Remix came to Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3, and a mobile successor in 2017.
devStory: Capcom developed and published it for arcades in 1996. It received positive reviews: Next Generation called it "ferociously competitive, unfairly addicting, and as intuitive as riding a bike", praising its cute art and Capcom in-jokes in four-star review, and Computer and Video Games compared it favourably with Tetris and Columns, highlighting the giant Power Gems and saying "when it's this much fun, it's well worth a go." Saturn and PlayStation ports also received generally positive reviews. It was later remade as Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo HD Remix and included in Capcom Fighting Collection and Capcom Arcade 2nd Stadium in 2022.

title: Super Gem Fighter Mini Mix
description: Super Gem Fighter Mini Mix (1997), known in Japan as Pocket Fighter, is Capcom's comic fighting game starring the super-deformed cast of Puzzle Fighter, who power up by knocking gems out of each other.
longDescription:
Using the super-deformed designs from Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo, it brings back most of that game's cast, from Street Fighter Alpha 2 and Night Warriors: Darkstalkers' Revenge, along with Ibuki from Street Fighter III and Tessa from Red Earth, with cameos from many Capcom games in the backgrounds. Every hit knocks gems out of the opponent, which can be collected to level up three special moves linked to coloured Gem gauges, a system based on Red Earth. Elemental orbs, visually based on Darkstalkers' elemental hits, can be thrown at angles to turn opponents to stone or freeze them, and each fighter starts with one, Tessa with ice and Ryu with lightning. Treasure chests and item carriers hold items, and food restores health.

The four buttons are Punch, Kick, Special and Taunt. The Special button performs a humorous unblockable move that makes the opponent drop gems, more if charged, and the direction held decides which colour falls, while holding back gives a character-specific defence. A super meter stores up to nine stocks for Mighty Combos of different levels. Mega Crushes, usable in mid-air, cost one stock and empty the Gem gauges to fire all collected gems at the enemy, and Counter Crushes roll the character across the screen attacking. Fighters start with three animated stock icons whose expressions change from happy to sad to surprised as the fight goes on.
trivia: It was ported to PlayStation in 1998, keeping the Pocket Fighter name in the West.
Saturn and WonderSwan versions were released only in Japan.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's ninth most successful arcade game of November 1997.
Complex ranked it the 42nd best fighting game of all time in 2011.
PS Extreme recommended it to fans uninterested in memorising long move lists.
devStory: Capcom developed and published it for arcades in 1997, reusing Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo's chibi character designs for a full fighting game. Next Generation gave the PlayStation version three stars, calling it "distracting fun for two players (although utterly mindless as a single-player game)" and "solid stuff, but only for the true cognoscenti", while PSM called it "a unique and humorous approach to the fighting game" that "really delivers".

title: Tobal 2
description: Tobal 2 (1997) is DreamFactory's Japan-only PlayStation fighter with Akira Toriyama designs, a dungeon-crawling Quest Mode and a record 200 playable characters.
longDescription:
The fighting system is unchanged from Tobal No. 1. Players move freely around 3D arenas as long as they face their opponent, with buttons for high, medium and low attacks and a grappling and blocking system offering many offensive and defensive options; each character also gains an unblockable fireball. The character models are higher resolution and Gouraud shaded, yet the game still runs at 60 frames per second, and it launched on the same day as Sony's Dual Analog Controller in Japan as the first game to support it.

The Quest Mode is greatly expanded, with six dungeons, from a Practice Dungeon to a Pyramid, a Desert Spaceship, the Molmoran Mine, a Castle and a Final Dungeon, plus a town where players can eat, sleep and shop and save at the church. Defeated monsters drop food, stones, potions, money or weapons, and characters gain experience separately for each arm, each leg, throws and guard, raising the damage they deal or reducing what they take; potions and stones can raise or lower these levels, and eating with a near-full stamina bar builds guard experience. Throwing a purple stone at a nearly beaten monster captures it for versus mode, bringing the roster to 200, among them a chocobo, though many are palette swaps. Quest characters can also be used in arcade and versus modes.
trivia: Akira Toriyama designed the characters, as in the first game.
As of 2010 it held the record for the largest fighting game roster, with 200 characters.
A North American release planned for 7 March 1998 was cancelled in favour of Einhänder.
Square cited Tobal No. 1's weak sales, which it believed were driven by its Final Fantasy VII demo.
Famitsu readers ranked it 50th among the best PlayStation games in 2000.
devStory: DreamFactory developed it and Square released it in Japan in 1997 as the sequel to Tobal No. 1. It would have been the last title in Square's publishing deal with Sony Computer Entertainment America, but the companies chose Einhänder instead; Square also said it lacked the time and resources to translate such a text-heavy game while localising Final Fantasy VII and Bushido Blade, and its deal with Sony barred outside translators. It sold over 318,000 copies in Japan in 1997, the year's 31st best-seller. Reviewing the import, GameSpot gave it 8.1 out of 10, finding it better than the first game but unlikely to compete with Tekken and Mortal Kombat. It was re-released under Square Enix's Legendary Hits label in 2007.

title: Battle Arena Toshinden 2
description: Battle Arena Toshinden 2 (1995) is Tamsoft's 3D weapon-fighting sequel, launched in arcades on Sony's ZN-1 board with an Overdrive meter, faster play and a deeper conspiracy story.
longDescription:
The final match of the last Toshinden tournament, between Eiji Shinjo and sponsor Gaia, was interrupted, and only the participants and the tournament's hosts, the Secret Society, knew why. Gaia, one of the Society's Divine Four, had used his tournament to try to recruit fighters against the Society's ruler, the Master, whose Gerard Foundation had turned from protecting the world to controlling it. He banned deliberate killing and invited martial artists from "the everyday world" to make the tournament more palatable and win sponsors, but failed to persuade any of the warriors to join him. Gaia returns demoted and without his armour, while Chaos and Tracy join the starting roster.

The core play is unchanged from the first Toshinden, but the sequel adds a simple combo system and an Overdrive gauge, along with mechanics tuned for faster play. The 3D movement was rebalanced: dodge-rolling no longer makes a character briefly immune, so it is no longer possible to roll straight through deadly attacks. Downed opponents can now be attacked, and ring-outs return, with the rule that when both fighters fall out at once, the one who lands last wins. Backgrounds were made more detailed by using layers of 2D parallax scrolling, as in Tekken 2, instead of the original's 3D backgrounds.
trivia: Unlike the home-only first game, it debuted in arcades in November 1995.
Capcom distributed the arcade version, its first 3D fighter, before Star Gladiator and Street Fighter EX on the same hardware.
The PlayStation version sold 435,712 copies in Japan and 133,491 in the US.
A Japanese PlayStation update, Toshinden 2 Plus, added tweaks and graphical improvements.
Kinesoft ported it to Windows.
devStory: Tamsoft developed it and Takara published it, planning an arcade-first release for October or November 1995 on Sony's ZN-1 hardware, followed shortly by a PlayStation port. Game Machine listed it as Japan's tenth most successful arcade game in February 1996. Critics generally found it good but too little improved over the original in play and graphics, falling short of Virtua Fighter 2 and Tekken 2; Electronic Gaming Monthly's reviewers were more positive, praising the graphics and new character Vermillion. The Saturn received its own spin-off, Battle Arena Toshinden URA, with a new story, arenas and four exclusive characters, and Battle Arena Toshinden 3 followed.

title: Bloody Roar 2
description: Bloody Roar 2 (1998) is Raizing's beast-transforming 3D fighter, adding cinematic Beast Drive super attacks as shapeshifting zoanthropes confront a militant supremacist group.
longDescription:
Five years after the first game, the zoanthropes who fought the fallen Tylon Corporation have returned to peaceful lives. But with their existence now public, hostility between humans and zoanthropes grows, giving rise to the Zoanthrope Liberation Front, which preaches zoanthrope supremacy and threatens humans and non-member zoanthropes alike. Meanwhile Alan Gado, known for promoting understanding between the two, becomes a fugitive. Rebels take on the ZLF and discover that its leader Shenlong is a puppet of Hajime Busuzima, who poses as his right-hand man; Busuzima escapes, but the ZLF is disbanded, and Gado asks the rebels to build a movement for reconciliation.

As in the first game, every character can transform into a beast form that unlocks new attacks, recovers some lost health and is generally faster or stronger. The sequel adds Beast Drives, super attacks that trigger a cut-scene and deal heavy damage, each unique to its character. Eleven fighters are playable, seven of them new. Bakuryu is a mole ninja once used as a weapon by Tylon and adopted by Yugo as his brother Kenji. Uriko, the first game's brainwashed final boss, can no longer fully transform because of the experiments. Stun is a former Tylon scientist turned into a man-made insect zoanthrope by Busuzima, and Shina is Gado's adopted daughter, a leopard and mercenary.
trivia: In Europe and Japan it is subtitled Bringer of the New Age, in the US The New Breed.
A PlayStation port followed in 1999.
Famitsu scored the PlayStation version 32 out of 40.
It was later re-released on PS3, Vita and PSP through PlayStation Network.
Bloody Roar 3 followed in 2000.
devStory: Raizing developed it and Hudson Soft published it in arcades in 1998 as the second Bloody Roar. The PlayStation version received mixed but broadly favourable reviews. Next Generation called it "a visually pretty and fun-to-play fighting game with just enough to set it apart from the rest of the 'me too' titles" despite minor balance issues, GamePro "a welcome addition to any fighter's library", and IGN said that what it lacked in originality it made up for "in a deep combo-laden fighting system, exquisite graphics, and layers of gameplay modes". GameRevolution was cooler, calling it fine "for a try or two and nothing more".

title: Mortal Kombat 3
description: Mortal Kombat 3 (1995) is Midway's third Mortal Kombat, a darker, more modern sequel in which Shao Kahn invades Earthrealm, adding running, chain combos, Animalities and Kombat Kodes.
longDescription:
Dropping the tournament of earlier games, it has warriors fight the returning Shao Kahn, who has resurrected his bride Sindel and launched an invasion of Earthrealm. A Run button with its own meter lets players dash at opponents, answering fans who felt earlier games favoured defenders; the meter drains when running, only forwards, and when performing combos. Pre-programmed chain combos, or "dial-a-combos", cannot be interrupted once the first hit lands, and some launch opponents into the air for further juggles. A "Choose Your Destiny" screen lets single players pick their difficulty, and some stages are interactive, letting an uppercut send both fighters through the ceiling into a different stage.

Fatalities, Babalities and Friendships all return, joined by Animalities, in which the winner turns into an animal to kill the opponent. To perform one, the winner must first grant Mercy, restoring a sliver of the loser's health in the third round, and then defeat them again. There are new Stage Fatalities in the Subway, the Bell Tower and the Pit 3, and Kombat Kodes, six-symbol codes entered before two-player matches, unlock extra features. The tone is darker, with a muted palette, heavily digitised characters and pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, and the imagery is Western and contemporary: highways, banks and rooftops, three cyborg characters, modern clothes in place of martial arts garb, and electronic music instead of Asian motifs.
trivia: It is the only main Mortal Kombat without Scorpion.
RePlay reported it as the most popular US arcade game of May 1995.
It was the highest-grossing arcade conversion kit of 1995 in the US.
The SNES version sold over a million copies by November 1995 and was the year's best-selling US home game.
Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 and Mortal Kombat Trilogy restored the omitted characters.
devStory: Midway considered making it in 3D but kept the sprite graphics of earlier games, and some returning characters were played by new actors. Released in arcades in 1995 as the sequel to Mortal Kombat II, it won an American Amusement Machine Association Diamond Award for sales alongside Daytona USA and the Neo Geo MVS. Williams Entertainment's Super NES and Genesis versions sold 250,000 copies in their first weekend, and the Mega Drive version became Brazil's best-selling Mega Drive game. It was nominated for the Video Software Dealers Association's 1995 Video Game of the Year, losing to Donkey Kong Country 2. Reviews were generally positive, though critics objected to the absence of several popular characters.

title: Mortal Kombat 4
description: Mortal Kombat 4 (1997) is Midway's first 3D Mortal Kombat and the series' last arcade release, adding weapons as the fallen Elder God Shinnok wages war on the realms.
longDescription:
Millennia before the first game, the Elder God Shinnok tried to conquer all six realms until the thunder god Raiden defeated him in a centuries-long war and imprisoned him in the Netherrealm. Now, with the sorcerer Quan Chi's help, Shinnok escapes, conquers Edenia with the aid of the traitor Tanya and prepares to strike the Elder Gods who banished him. Seventeen other playable characters take sides as the forces of light try to stop him and the forces of darkness seek to rule all the realms.

It plays much like earlier games, with running and combos retained, and despite its 3D graphics characters are mostly limited to a 2D path apart from sidestepping. New is a limited weapon system: each character can draw a special weapon with a button combination and swing, club or throw it with the punch buttons. Weapons can be dropped and picked up by the opponent, as can arena objects such as severed heads and rocks. A Maximum Damage cap automatically breaks combos that deal too much damage, preventing infinite combos unless disabled by a code. Each character has two standard Fatalities, plus two Stage Fatalities that throw the loser into a deadly part of the arena, and unlike the first three games there are no non-playable bosses except Goro in home versions. Next Generation called it "a fast-moving, dark, and disturbing fighter that retains many of the series' best qualities".
trivia: It was the first Mortal Kombat with 3D graphics and the last with an arcade release.
Animalities were dropped because animal transformations were hard to do in 3D.
Some Fatalities replay from different camera angles.
Ed Boon was joined by programmers Todd Allen and his brother Mike Boon.
Mortal Kombat Gold, an updated version, came to the Dreamcast in 1999.
devStory: Ed Boon, who had been the only programmer on the first Mortal Kombat, found the much larger team hard to lead and brought in Todd Allen and Mike Boon. Some staff had worked on Midway's first 3D fighter, War Gods, but dropped its "digital skin" technique, and with computer animation replacing filmed actors apart from some motion capture, Fatalities became easier to make. The team removed the series' comical finishing moves to make it more violent, and when news programmes raised concerns, Boon replied that more violent games already existed. Reviews were generally positive: Next Generation lamented the lack of real innovation but said "it's much better than War Gods", while GamePro noted bugs in version 1.0. It was ported to PlayStation, Nintendo 64, Windows and Game Boy Color in 1998, the last poorly received.

title: Killer Instinct 2
description: Killer Instinct 2 (1996) is Rare's arcade sequel that reworked its combo-driven fighting to reward aggression, adding throws, a super bar and parries.
longDescription:
As in the first Killer Instinct, fighters have two life bars, starting the second as soon as the first is emptied, and matches revolve around Quick, Medium and Fierce strengths and an automatic combo system. Pressing a strength button after an opener launches an auto-double and starts a combo, and openers are now safer, such as a close Fierce punch or kick. Combos can be extended with throws, super linkers, manual doubles and super end specials, and Super Moves can be placed inside combos, making them unbreakable and far more damaging. Normal moves lose priority and range and gain recovery time, characters are knocked down more easily, and throws are added to deal with blocking opponents.

Special moves no longer depend on priority but follow a three-way rock, paper, scissors system in which certain specials always beat others. A super bar fills as a fighter takes damage or has attacks blocked, enabling multi-hit Super Moves, usually extended versions of special moves. With combos more devastating, combo breakers became easier: punches now break kick doubles and kicks break punch doubles, rather than depending on strength. A new parry lets a defending player freeze an attacker and counter with a stunning technique or a three-hit special, and the finishing moves were reworked.
trivia: Midway released the arcade version.
A modified version, Killer Instinct Gold, came to the Nintendo 64 the same year.
A completed Super NES version was never released.
Programmer Martin Hollis left partway through to work on GoldenEye 007.
It returned as Killer Instinct 2 Classic on Xbox One in 2014.
devStory: A small Rare team led by Lee Schneuman and Ken Lobb began work soon after the first game, using the same hardware. Lobb said eliminating excessive defensive play "was the absolute highest priority" because it hurt beginners: "We now reward the aggressor big time." Kevin Bayliss redesigned every character to reflect the story's events, and Robin Beanland composed most of the music after Graeme Norgate left for Blast Corps and GoldenEye. Not as acclaimed as the original, it was still a commercial success with positive reviews for its combo system, graphics and sound, though Next Generation felt it largely recycled the original at a slower, choppier pace. Brazil's SuperGamePower gave the arcade version full marks, and Complex later named it among the 25 best 2D fighters.

title: Clock Tower
description: Clock Tower (1995) is Human Entertainment's Dario Argento-inspired point-and-click horror game, in which the orphan Jennifer flees the unstoppable Scissorman through the Barrows mansion.
longDescription:
In September 1995 Jennifer Simpson and fellow orphans Laura, Anne and Lotte, from the Granite Orphanage in Romsdalen, Norway, are adopted by the wealthy recluse Simon Barrows and taken to his mansion, known as the Clock Tower after its dominant feature. When Mary, the woman who brought them, takes too long to find Mr. Barrows, Jennifer goes looking, and one of the other children is killed by a stalker called Scissorman. Jennifer must explore the mansion to find a way out, heading for one of nine possible endings.

The player moves a cursor to direct Jennifer, investigating objects, opening doors and storing items, whose positions change with each playthrough. She can walk or run, but running drains stamina, recovered by sitting on the floor, and her portrait in the corner shows how she is coping. Jennifer cannot fight Scissorman: when he appears the game enters panic mode, and depending on her health she may trip, slow down and be killed. The only defence is to find hiding places or use traps in the environment, and if caught, rapidly pressing a button gives a chance to break free. Famitsu's reviewers stressed how frightening it was, one saying it would make players weep, and how the slightest mistake led to a game over. It is considered an influence on horror games and a pioneer of survival horror.
trivia: Jennifer's design was inspired by Jennifer Connelly's character in Phenomena.
Jennifer's movements were acted out by a woman from Human's planning division.
Character graphics were digitised from photographs of real people.
Clock Tower: The First Fear, an updated version, came to PlayStation, WonderSwan and Windows in 1997.
Its first official release outside Japan was Clock Tower: Rewind in October 2024.
devStory: Director Hifumi Kono wanted to pay homage to Dario Argento, especially Phenomena, borrowing its occult themes, distressed young women and bright colours in fog, and to make a game that felt like the old horror films he loved. It was an experimental project with a small budget and staff, and colleagues doubted a game about running from an enemy could work. Limited resources meant no mouse support and a much smaller map, though the 2D mansion was designed within a 3D space. Released for the Super Famicom in 1995, it sold well. Retrospective reviews praised its haunting atmosphere while finding the puzzles and exploration tedious; Hardcore Gaming 101 called it "one of the most thrilling experiences the [horror] genre can offer".

title: Armored Core
description: Armored Core (1997) is FromSoftware's third-person mecha shooter in which a mercenary Raven pilots a fully customisable robot for warring corporations on a ruined, underground Earth.
longDescription:
After a cataclysmic war called the Great Destruction wipes out most of humanity, survivors live underground for fifty years while corporations rise to power. The two largest, Chrome and Murakumo Millennium, fight constantly for supremacy, giving endless work to mercenaries called Ravens, who pilot powerful mechs known as Armored Cores for the highest bidder and are supplied by the neutral Ravens' Nest. The player passes the Raven Test, receives mail from the Nest's operator "R" and from a Murakumo agent, and takes corporate missions until both companies collapse; the final mission, requested by the Nest itself, is implied to be a trap to kill a Raven grown too powerful.

In single player, players choose missions on terrain from desert bases to space stations; levels are very open, with enemies appearing from all directions. Guns, rocket launchers, lasers, missiles and swords can all be fitted. Ammunition and repair costs come out of mission rewards, even on failure, and the money earned buys weapons and parts. Cores are highly modular, so that swapping leg units, for example, can make a mech faster, and Game Revolution put the possible combinations "in the very high millions". Pay rises with progress, and choosing some missions locks out others, creating branching paths that differ on replays. A two-player versus mode works through split screen or the PlayStation Link Cable.
trivia: Mecha designer Shōji Kawamori proposed the "armored core" concept that gave the game its name.
Kawamori's idea built modularity around a core block holding the cockpit, engine and limb joints.
It began the Armored Core series.
Its underground setting continued in the series until Armored Core 4.
It was re-released as a PSone Classic in 2007 in Japan and 2015 in North America.
devStory: FromSoftware developed it for the PlayStation, approaching Shōji Kawamori before the console's launch, when player-designed modular mechs were one of the only fixed ideas. Kawamori felt too much freedom would undermine a distinctive look, so he proposed modularity around a core block, which FromSoftware adopted as both the mech concept and the title. Sony Computer Entertainment released it outside Japan. It was favourably received, especially for customisation and multiplayer: GameSpot found the upgradable options "almost as charming as the gameplay", EGM called customisation its best aspect, GamePro said robot mechanics would enjoy "shopping through the detailed onscreen catalogs", and IGN called the multiplayer "the real meat of the game".

title: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere
description: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere (1999) is Namco's futuristic, story-driven combat flight game, whose branching two-disc Japanese campaign was cut down heavily for its Western release.
longDescription:
Like earlier Ace Combat games it is arcade-like next to other flight sims, but it puts more realism into energy management: tight turns and steep climbs bleed airspeed and cause stalls that are hard to recover from. Players fly 23 aircraft, and the setting moves from the modern day to a science-fiction future, with one mission flown in a spacecraft above Earth. In the Japanese release players can fight for four factions across 52 missions, with a branching story; the international release has only 36 missions, all on the UPEO side. Missions range from destroying enemy squadrons to defending bases, graded from A to D and charted on the title screen.

Instant replays show each mission's final moments, as in Ace Combat 2, and the camera can rotate fully around the player's plane. Between missions, an automatic search engine records information on organisations, places, characters and technology, and fully voiced, animated video messages arrive in a fictional email inbox. The Japanese version also has radio chatter from both the player's faction and opposing ones, with character portraits, while the international version keeps only friendly chatter. Famitsu praised its "overwhelming" graphics and deeper story, and Edge felt its branching storyline made it more involving than its predecessors.
trivia: It was released in Japan on 27 May 1999 and internationally the following year.
Financial constraints led Namco to cut the campaign down for North America and Europe.
R4: Ridge Racer Type 4 and TV dramas inspired its story-driven design.
Minoru Sashida of Techno Drive designed the menu interface.
It shipped over a million copies despite little promotion.
devStory: Development began in 1998 after the success of Air Combat and Ace Combat 2, with directors Takuya Iwasaki and Atsushi Shiozawa and producer Takashi Fukawa leading a team mostly from Ace Combat 2. They wanted it far more ambitious in content and presentation, making the story a mechanic that changed with the player's progress and decisions, and set out to make it visually distinct from other flight sims. The Japanese release was well received as ambitious, but the international versions drew confusion and disappointment over the missing missions and story and bland play. The Japanese version has since been re-evaluated, with critics praising its ambition, overarching story and additions to the series formula.

title: Nightmare Creatures
description: Nightmare Creatures (1997) is Kalisto's gothic action-horror game in which a priest or an immunologist's daughter fights monsters through an occult-plagued 1834 London.
longDescription:
In 1666 the devil-worshipping Brotherhood of Hecate experimented in London to create an elixir granting superhuman powers, but produced grotesque monsters instead; when they planned to use them as an army, member Samuel Pepys set their headquarters alight, causing the Great Fire of London. In 1834 London is again beset by evil: monsters are sighted, people mutate, and the dead rise, all part of the schemes of Adam Crowley, a mad scientist and occultist based on Aleister Crowley, aided by the Brotherhood. When Pepys's lost diary reaches priest and occult expert Ignatius Blackward, he sends it to New Orleans immunologist Dr. Jean Franciscus, who is killed and the book stolen. At the funeral, Ignatius and Jean's daughter Nadia receive a note pointing them to Crowley.

The single-player game lets players control Ignatius or Nadia. Besides each character's main weapon, they can use secondary weapons such as pistols, mines, fire bombs and magic spells. An adrenaline bar drains health when it runs out, so players must keep seeking out and winning fights to keep it full. The environments were modelled on 19th-century maps and blueprints. Critics almost uniformly praised its spooky atmosphere and monster designs but noted control problems and an occasionally frustrating camera, and they were split on whether the repetitive fighting outweighed its strengths.
trivia: Crowley is based on the occultist Aleister Crowley.
It was the first game made with Kalisto's own 3D tool, LibSys.
Mindscape was originally to publish it, but Activision won the rights just before E3 1997.
Sony Computer Entertainment published it in Europe.
The Nintendo 64 version replaced cut-scenes with text and let players switch off the adrenaline meter.
devStory: Kalisto Entertainment developed it for PlayStation, Windows and Nintendo 64, and bidding for the publishing rights was reportedly fierce. Activision released it in North America, promoting the PlayStation version with a TV advert voiced by Maurice LaMarche. It was a commercial hit, selling over 1.5 million copies by January 2000. The PlayStation version received favourable reviews and the Nintendo 64 and PC versions mixed ones. Next Generation wrote that "while the visuals are compelling enough to drive many players forward, the repetitive action is enough to make most wait for a level select code and a weekend rental". Nightmare Creatures II followed three years later, while a third game was cancelled in 2004.

title: SaGa Frontier 2
description: SaGa Frontier 2 (1999) is Square's watercolour-painted, non-linear RPG telling two intertwined stories, of an exiled prince and a young man investigating his parents' deaths, in a medieval Germanic world.
longDescription:
In the world of Sandail, whose plot, places and names draw heavily on medieval Germanic and Anglo-Saxon influences in a setting akin to the 13th century, players can follow Gustave XIII, an exiled would-be heir trying to reclaim his throne, or William Knights, a young man investigating his parents' deaths. The two scenarios eventually intertwine in a larger plot about the fate of the world. Hand-painted watercolour backgrounds and characters give it a storybook look unique in the series at the time. As in other SaGa games, progress is largely non-linear: within the story's basic flow, players complete missions, talk to characters and travel freely through the world and its harsh dungeons.

Battles are turn-based, with commands entered for each character at the start of a round and actions resolved by speed. Characters attack with weapons or cast magic to harm enemies or aid allies, and repeatedly fighting with weapons randomly teaches them special skills that hit harder and can combine with allies' attacks into combos. There are three kinds of battle, chosen by the player or set by the plot: one-on-one Duels, Team battles with up to four characters against an enemy group, and large Strategic battles. Each character can equip two kinds of weapon and specialise in particular fields. NextGen summed it up as: "If you thought FFVIII was unoriginal, this is the game for you. If you liked FFVIII, this is still the game for you."
trivia: It is the eighth original game in the SaGa series.
Its art was painted on canvas, then scanned and digitised for backgrounds and sprites.
It supports the DualShock controller and the PocketStation for extra content.
Famitsu scored it 35 out of 40.
SaGa Frontier 2 Remastered was released in March 2025.
devStory: Series creator Akitoshi Kawazu headed development, with music by Masashi Hamauzu. Announced in September 1998, it deliberately abandoned the CG videos and computer-style graphics of the first SaGa Frontier for a traditional, hand-drawn look. Released in Japan in April 1999, then by Square Electronic Arts in North America in February 2000 and in PAL regions that March, it received mixed to average reviews in the West but was reissued three times in Japan. GameSpot praised its art as "a pleasant breeze of creativity" amid CG and polygons, declaring "there is still a place for two-dimensional graphics", though it felt the game might alienate fans of the first SaGa Frontier.

title: Vandal Hearts II
description: Vandal Hearts II (1999) is Konami's tactical RPG following Joshua from childhood through a civil war in Natra, with simultaneous Dual-Turn battles and multiple endings.
longDescription:
Ten years ago King Zekras left Natra to his son Julius, but younger brother Lagore raised an army and took the throne. Lagore proved a fair king but was slowly poisoned by the Queen Mother Agatha and her lover Cardinal Ladorak, who made her young son Franz heir and now oppresses the peasantry with his secret police, the Blood Knights. In the northern village of Polata, Joshua and Rosaly, adopted children of the mayor, grow up with Clive, Yuri and the noble Adele. The childhood chapters introduce the hero and his friends before the story jumps to an adult Natra torn by a civil war between foreign-backed factions, where Joshua's band of outlaws is drawn into a plot to create a third faction and restore peace.

The game uses an overworld map of points of interest, town maps with taverns and shops, and battle maps, most revisitable. Over 120 weapon and armour combinations replace fixed classes, so a warrior can become a healer without penalty: skills are learned by equipping weapons and earning points to master them, while armour sets hit points, magic points, movement and defence. Combat uses a new Dual-Turn System, described as an Active Time Battle system for tactical RPGs, in which player and computer each move one unit at the same time. Three key choices determine the ending, with four distinctly different and three similar endings.
trivia: It is the sequel to 1996's Vandal Hearts.
Famitsu scored it 32 out of 40.
Gaming Intelligence Agency considered it vastly superior to its predecessor.
Its branching story is shaped by the player's dialogue choices.
Critics faulted its translation and lack of explanation of its systems.
devStory: Konami Computer Entertainment Nagoya developed it and Konami published it for the PlayStation in 1999. It received favourable reviews: NextGen's Francesca Reyes wrote that "with its steep learning curve, VH2 may not be ideal for novices, but because it has a strong story and clever battle features, it proves to be a great challenge for veterans". The story drew criticism elsewhere, with IGN finding it forgettable and GameSpot saying most players "won't care to follow" it, while Gaming Intelligence Agency missed the first game's variety of missions.

title: Gex: Enter the Gecko
description: Gex: Enter the Gecko (1998) is Crystal Dynamics' first 3D Gex, a TV-themed platformer in which the wisecracking gecko collects remotes to defeat his nemesis Rez.
longDescription:
Gex, a TV-binging, wisecracking gecko, must collect three kinds of remote to unlock TVs in the hub world and fight his arch-enemy Rez. He runs, jumps, tail-whips, tail-bounces and flying-karate-kicks his way through television-themed levels, and like a real gecko can climb certain walls and ceilings. Attacks defeat enemies, activate hint icons and break small TVs holding coloured flies that add health or lives, grant temporary upgrades, provide oxygen in outer space levels or mark checkpoints. Some stages require power-ups to progress, such as the cyber energy that activates jump pads and bridges in futuristic levels, and some enemies can only be beaten by using objects or machinery.

The hub world grows as Gex collects remotes and defeats bosses. Red remotes are earned by meeting level objectives, in any order, then standing on a green button before a TV. Each normal stage also holds two silver remotes, one hidden and one for collecting 120 items, and silver remotes unlock bonus levels that award gold remotes. Collecting every remote unlocks a special ending of concept art. Critics almost unanimously praised the level design: Electronic Gaming Monthly's Dan Hsu said it was ninety per cent of the fun, and GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann said its look and frame rate were "about as close to Mario 64 as you'll ever get on a PlayStation".
trivia: Much of its humour was inspired by The Simpsons; Simpsons writer Rob Cohen wrote Gex's one-liners.
It began as a 2D game until E3 convinced the team to go 3D.
Gex has a full skeleton, with more bones than a real gecko, so his mouth moves with his dialogue.
The Nintendo 64 version, Gex 64, cut levels, cut-scenes and voice lines.
Gex 3: Deep Cover Gecko followed in 1999.
devStory: Crystal Dynamics announced a Super Mario 64-style 3D sequel in early 1997. Lead programmer Adrian Longland recalled that it began as a 2D prototype with a hover mechanic until E3, when Crash Bandicoot and Mario 64 convinced the team to combine 3D graphics and an open world. Gex was rebuilt for the new perspective with a skeletal system and stretched skin to avoid tearing. Released on PlayStation in 1998, with Windows and Nintendo 64 versions, the latter by Realtime Associates, and a 2D Game Boy Color game of the same name, it received mostly positive reviews; the main complaints concerned the camera, low-polygon enemies and simplicity, and the N64 version was received less well.

title: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit
description: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit (1998) is Electronic Arts' exotic-car racer that made police chases a central part of the series, with knockout races, car tuning and a role-reversal cop mode on PC.
longDescription:
Racing exotic sports cars mostly through North American locations, from desert canyons and country villages to snowy mountain ranges, many with secret shortcuts, it splits play into two categories. Standard racing pits the player against one or seven rivals in circuit races, knockouts and tournaments that unlock bonus cars and a track. Hot Pursuit puts police on the track, as the player races a single opponent through a patrolled course, and police AI is improved, using several tactics to stop both racers. On PC, a role-reversal variant lets the player drive a police sports car and stop all six racers before they finish, unlocking extra police cars when every track is completed in both roles.

Knockout runs seven two-lap races of eight drivers on random tracks, eliminating the last-placed driver each time until one remains, while Tournament holds four-lap races against eight opponents. Two-player split screen arrives, and the PC version supports network play over serial, modem, IPX and TCP/IP. Car tuning lets players adjust engine and gear ratios, brake balance and speed, suspension, aerodynamics and tyres with sliders, trading acceleration for top speed or setting up wider, drifting turns. Next Generation called it "an excellent racer for both novice and expert enthusiasts", though its two-player mode suffered from frame rate drops.
trivia: EA Canada made the PlayStation version and EA Seattle the Windows version.
The PlayStation version came out on 25 March 1998 and the PC version on 23 September.
It is the third major Need for Speed.
Its PlayStation version scored just two points short of universal acclaim on Metacritic.
A direct sequel followed in 2002 and a reboot in 2010.
devStory: EA Canada developed the PlayStation version and EA Seattle the Windows version, with Electronic Arts publishing both in 1998, reintroducing police pursuits that became a defining feature of the series. It was a critical success, praised for its graphics and customisation. Next Generation praised the PC version's "fine 3D-accelerated graphics, lightning-fast response to the controller, incredible weather effects, and impressively valued terrain", while Official UK PlayStation Magazine called it "one of the most playable racing games released in the past year" but felt it could not compete head to head with Gran Turismo.

sources.title: Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit

title: Fighting Force
description: Fighting Force (1997) is Core Design's 3D beat 'em up, first pitched as Streets of Rage 4, in which four heroes fight through a doomsday cultist's army with soda cans, knives, car engines and guns.
longDescription:
Dr. Dex Zeng, a criminal mastermind with an army at his command, predicted the world would end in 2000. When New Year's Eve 1999 passes without the apocalypse, he decides there was an error and sets out to destroy the world himself. Four characters with their own reasons take him on, starting at a police cordon around his office skyscraper and moving through a shopping mall, a subway and a Coast Guard base to the top of his island headquarters. Players choose a route through some territories.

Hawk Manson and Mace Daniels are all-rounders, Hawk the stronger and Mace the faster. Ben "Smasher" Jackson is a big, slow bruiser who can lift and throw car engines, and Alana McKendricks is a fast but light-hitting teenager with an effective jump kick. Each has a special move that costs a portion of health. Waves of enemies are fought with fists and whatever comes to hand, from soda cans and knives to cars and guns, through urban and science fiction settings full of destructible scenery. Critics overwhelmingly enjoyed the large amount of scenery to smash and scavenge but felt that, despite the move to 3D, the play differed little from older 2D brawlers; GameSpot called it "basically a 3D version of Capcom's classic, Final Fight", while EGM's Shawn Smith asked, "when the 3-D works, why not go with it?"
trivia: Core Design first pitched it to Sega as Streets of Rage 4, but Sega declined.
Marc Silvestri created the story and character designs.
Dr. Zeng was inspired by the Heaven's Gate cult.
Ten coders from EA Japan collaborated on it.
A completed Saturn version was cancelled by Sega Europe, though French magazine Mega Force reviewed it.
devStory: In 1996 Core Design described it to Sega Magazin as a 3D game inspired by Streets of Rage, with up to five characters on screen, destructible environments and indoor and outdoor areas, then developed solely for the Saturn. When Sega declined, saying it had its own plans for the series, Core made it a standalone multi-platform game. Announced soon after Tomb Raider's success, it was highly anticipated and commercially successful, released by Eidos for PlayStation and Windows in 1997, with Crave publishing a Nintendo 64 version in 1999. Reviews were mixed; Next Generation found it "very fun" despite its derivative nature. A Battle Arena mode was cut, and Fighting Force 2 followed.

title: Thousand Arms
description: Thousand Arms (1998) is a steampunk RPG crossed with a dating sim, in which a womanising Spirit Blacksmith powers up magical weapons by dating the women he meets.
longDescription:
On a steampunk world, the Dark Acolytes, a mysterious organisation of cyborgs and robots, are hunting the five legendary Sacred Flames and spreading chaos. Meis Triumph, the stubborn, lazy 16-year-old heir to a family of Spirit Blacksmiths who learned womanising from his father, is driven from his comfortable home and chosen by the spirits of the Ancient Blacksmiths to find the flames first. His gift is reforging weapons to make them stronger and give them spells and special attacks, but to raise their power he needs a woman's help, increasing his intimacy level with her by going on dates.

His companions include Sodina, a brave 15-year-old whose Spirit Blacksmith brother was killed by the Acolytes and who is often enraged by Meis's lechery; Muza, a big, brave but dim knight who freezes around pretty girls; Wyna, the fight-loving daughter of the King of the Pirates, whose eyepatch is just for effect; Nelsha, a shy aspiring Dress Master whose personality and combat form change with her outfits; Kyleen, a cynical thief; and Soushi, a proud samurai in a pink kimono who first clashes with Meis. Meis can also date women met on his travels, from an inventor living on a giant train to a priestess obsessed with cleanliness, and he can summon Elemental Beasts in battle. The villain is Medeus, the Dark Emperor, who turned his body into a machine to live long enough to find the flames and become a god.
trivia: It mixes Japanese RPG and dating sim elements.
Medeus's servants, the Evil Mecha Five, are named after machine parts: Shaft, Bearing, Ratchet, Wire and Bolt.
Soushi's katana is called Masamune.
Famitsu scored it 28 out of 40.
GameSpot called it the first real example of a decent dating simulation in the US.
devStory: TOSE developed it and Atlus published it for the PlayStation in 1998. It received favourable reviews: NextGen's Jeff Lundrigan said it "straddles the line between being an enjoyable time-waster and a thoroughly engrossing game – either way, you can't miss", and GameFan gave it universal acclaim a month before its US release. GameSpot's Christian Nutt likened it to Sakura Taisen and Lunar, praising how its "solid RPG questing, graphics, dialogue, dubbing, and ambiance really push this game over the edge from standard to special", and predicted that anime fans would "get a big kick out of it".

title: Road Rash 3D
description: Road Rash 3D (1998) is Electronic Arts' PlayStation-only Road Rash, racing and brawling across a network of interconnected roads to a licensed soundtrack, with more focus on racing than fighting.
longDescription:
As in earlier Road Rash games, the player races motorcycles against other riders in an arcade style with little emphasis on realism, punching rivals or hitting them with weapons to slow them down. Winning earns money to upgrade the bike, while finishing last earns nothing and being stopped by the police costs money. Compared with its predecessors, it puts more emphasis on racing and less on combat. The courses are pieced together from a larger network of interconnected roads, so tracks may share segments but start or end in different places or turn down different routes; players can take a wrong turn, but going too far runs into invisible walls.

Through a licensing deal with Atlantic Records, the soundtrack features Sugar Ray, Kid Rock, CIV, The Mermen, Full on the Mouth and The Tea Party, with Sugar Ray contributing "Speed Home California", "Tap, Twist, Snap" and "Mean Machine". The riders were animated with motion capture, the actors perched on mock-up motorcycles. Edge praised the road network, "impressive" 3D engine and track design, but found the combat moves unresponsive and dependent on luck, and GamePro still considered it a worthy instalment despite its flaws.
trivia: It won Outstanding Achievement in Sound and Music at the AIAS Interactive Achievement Awards.
It was a GamePro Readers' Choice finalist for Best Racing Game, losing to Gran Turismo.
A planned PC version with LAN play and force feedback was never released.
EA said two-player mode was impossible because of how data streamed from the disc.
Road Rash 64, released a year later, reworked it with more combat and four-player modes.
devStory: Electronic Arts developed and published it exclusively for the PlayStation. Reviews were average, the commonest complaint being that it fell short of the Genesis and 3DO games, above all in lacking two-player play. GameSpot criticised graphical glitches and the reduced combat, IGN complained that after two to three years of development it controlled worse and played slower than the 3DO game, GameRevolution called it "one of the worst motorcycle games...ever", and Next Generation gave it two stars. Later games answered the criticism: Road Rash 64 put greater emphasis on combat with multiplayer for up to four, and Road Rash: Jailbreak added a two-player sidecar mode.

title: Aero Fighters 2
description: Aero Fighters 2 (1994), known in Japan as Sonic Wings 2, is Video System's Neo Geo vertical shooter with a varied roster of planes and pilots, ten stages and character-specific endings.
longDescription:
The game uses two buttons: A fires the plane's guns and B launches a special bomb from a limited stock. Destroying buildings and armoured enemy planes releases power-ups: a P raises firepower by one level, while an F jumps straight to maximum firepower for a limited number of shots. Some ground targets and buildings drop money bonuses whose value depends on how quickly the player destroys them and collects the reward. Each stage ends with a boss ship, and there are ten stages, after which each character has their own ending. The game then loops with palette changes, and only after the looped stages are cleared does it truly end.

Critics praised its variety of ships and backgrounds, its stage designs and its fun weapons and huge bosses. AllGame's Kyle Knight criticised its replay value, GamePro noted slowdown, a lack of sound effects for the player's jet and little originality but called it enjoyable with "crisp" controls, and Next Generation warned that skilled players would finish it on easy or normal in under an hour. Several European magazines compared it to Raiden II, Twin Eagle II, Last Resort and Viewpoint, praising its visuals while criticising slowdown and its music, and some found the Neo Geo CD version disappointing.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as Japan's seventh most popular arcade game of August 1994.
RePlay reported it as North America's fifth most popular arcade game of September 1994.
It averages 90 per cent on GameRankings.
HobbyConsolas named it one of the twenty best Neo Geo AES games in 2014.
Aero Fighters 3 followed in 1995 and the spin-off Aero Fighters Assault in 1997.
devStory: Video System developed it and SNK published it for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms in 1994 as the second Aero Fighters. It was popular in arcades on both sides of the Pacific and met generally positive reviews, with Superjuegos judging that it far exceeded its predecessor. Hamster Corporation later acquired the rights along with Video System's catalogue and re-released it in the ACA Neo Geo series, and Nintendo Life praised the Switch version's high score and caravan modes, choice of planes, enemy variety and multiple endings.

title: Devil Dice
description: Devil Dice (1998), known in Japan as XI, is Shift's million-selling PlayStation puzzle game in which a small devil rolls giant dice to match faces and set off chains.
longDescription:
The player controls a small devil running around a grid covered in large dice. It can walk on the ground beneath the towering dice or stand on top of them, moving from die to die or rolling a die in the direction it runs to turn up a different face. Making a group of adjacent dice showing the same number of pips, with at least as many dice as the number shown, makes them slowly sink into the field and vanish, and adding more matching dice to a sinking set creates chain reactions. Some modes add special types of dice with different properties for extra challenge.

Battle pits the player against a single computer opponent, each building chains and cancelling the other's. Puzzle mode asks players to clear all the dice within a limited number of moves, and completing a row of puzzles unlocks a picture to play on in Battle mode. Trial is the standard arcade-style mode, clearing as many dice as possible before the grid fills. Wars is a fast multiplayer mode for up to four computer opponents or five human players with a multitap, in which chains damage rivals until one remains. GamePro and Next Generation were both positive despite its high difficulty, and GamesTM later called it one of ten underrated PlayStation gems.
trivia: It was created through Game Yarōze, a Japanese competition giving amateurs access to PlayStation development.
Its first week in Japan brought 131,815 sales, rising to about 864,844.
It won Best Puzzle Game and Best Multiplayer Game at the 1998 OPM Editors' Awards.
THQ published it in North America.
