Sequels include XI Jumbo, the WonderSwan Color XI Little and Bombastic on PlayStation 2.
devStory: Lead designer Yuichi Sugiyama said it was made for Game Yarōze, a Japan-only programme run from 1995 to 1999 in which over 3,000 participants competed for a development environment to create commercial PlayStation games; over thirty titles reached market, including Devil Dice and the first Doko Demo Issyo. Programmer Shuichi Yano was one of the successful applicants. Shift developed it and Sony Computer Entertainment published it in Japan in 1998 and Europe in 1999. It received favourable reviews, with 30 out of 40 from Famitsu, became a million-seller, and returned as a PlayStation Classic demo on PS3 and PSP in 2007.

title: Top Hunter: Roddy & Cathy
description: Top Hunter: Roddy & Cathy (1994) is SNK's cartoonish two-lane beat 'em up in which galactic bounty hunters chase the Klapton space pirates across four elemental planets.
longDescription:
Roddy and Cathy, the galaxy's top bounty hunters, are sent to stop the Klaptons, a colony of galactic pirates plundering the cosmos. Four high-ranking Klaptons, Sly, Misty, Mr. Bigman and Dr. Burn, have seized four elemental planets, Forest, Ice, Wind and Fire, with big rewards on their heads. The hunters destroy their war machines, but each commander escapes, so in the Last Hunt aboard Captain Klapton's mothership Roddy and Cathy must beat all four again before taking on the captain. The order in which the planets are tackled changes their layouts: picking Ice before Forest, for example, alters the start of the Forest world.

Inspired by Double Dragon, The Combatribes, Joe & Mac and Spinmaster, it has players fight through areas collecting items and defeating a boss at the end of each stage, with Roddy for player one and Cathy for player two. Special moves are performed with joystick motions and the attack button, as in Street Fighter and The King of Fighters, and, as in Fatal Fury, the field is split into a background and foreground lane that players can jump between to attack enemies or avoid traps; the lanes are not always level and one may be blocked off. Its cartoonish graphics and robotic vehicles, much like the Slugs, have led it to be called a precursor to Metal Slug.
trivia: At just over 112 megabits it was branded a "100 mega shock" game, twice the size of the largest SNES cartridge.
Its development team was made up of former Irem staff.
EGM's reviewers felt it was far too easy, even on the hardest setting.
Spain's Superjuegos scored it 91 out of 100.
HobbyConsolas named it one of the twenty best Neo Geo AES games in 2014.
devStory: SNK developed and published it for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms in 1994 with a team of former Irem employees, and it was also released on Neo Geo CD. RePlay listed it as North America's sixteenth most popular arcade game, and Famitsu scored it 24 out of 40. Electronic Gaming Monthly's four reviewers averaged seven out of ten, criticising its low difficulty and short length given the price of Neo Geo cartridges, but all enjoyed its many techniques, outstanding graphics, bizarre bosses, orchestral music and lane-switching. It was later included in SNK Arcade Classics Vol. 1 in 2008, released on the Wii Virtual Console and re-released in Hamster's ACA Neo Geo series.

title: Shadow Tower
description: Shadow Tower (1998) is FromSoftware's bleak first-person dungeon crawler in which a mercenary descends into the underworld after his city and its tower are swallowed whole.
longDescription:
On the continent of Eclipse, the mercenary Ruus Hardy returns home to Zeptar in the Holy Land to find the entire city, and its central tower, sucked into the underworld. An old man gives him the Dark One's sword, the only weapon that can harm the demons responsible, and Ruus descends to rescue the old woman who raised him and the rest of Zeptar. Very similar to the King's Field series, it is an action-oriented first-person dungeon crawl of combat, hidden items, traps and encounters with characters.

There are no experience points. Instead, no creature respawns, and each type of enemy killed raises fixed statistics, so building up particular stats means hunting a variety of different foes, while a special item lets players raise any stat by a few points manually. Stat names can mislead players used to other RPGs: Strength, for example, governs hit points rather than attack power. Every piece of equipment has durability and wears down until it must be repaired or replaced, and there is no music and no automap. Unlike earlier King's Field games, the shield is an item that must be actively raised to block, and the equipment screen is more detailed.
trivia: Its aesthetics were inspired by Western fantasy.
It was made alongside Echo Night, sharing some sound staff.
Kota Hoshino's music went largely unused; some later appeared in Evergrace.
Agetec published it in North America in November 1999.
A Japan-only sequel, Shadow Tower Abyss, came to the PlayStation 2.
devStory: FromSoftware, known for King's Field, developed it with similar themes and mechanics but wanted to create an entirely new franchise, aiming for play that was difficult yet rewarding. It used a redesigned and polished version of the King's Field engine. FromSoftware published it in Japan on 25 June 1998, and Agetec, which had released several earlier FromSoftware games, localised and published it in North America on 23 November 1999. Reviews were poor, averaging 49 per cent on GameRankings, with Famitsu giving it 27 out of 40.

title: Blue's Journey
description: Blue's Journey (1990) is Alpha Denshi's colourful Neo Geo platformer in which the hero Blue saves the insect people of planet Raguy from the polluting Daruma Empire.
longDescription:
The peaceful planet of Raguy, home to insect people called Insectarians, has been invaded by the evil Daruma Empire, which plans to consume its resources and pollute it. Princess Fa, whom Blue loves, sends the heroic young man to save the planet. Blue can stun enemies, then pick them up and throw them as projectiles, and he can shrink himself to reach hidden areas. A second player can join as an unnamed green palette swap of Blue, and the game has several endings depending on events such as whether the player defeats their rival.

Its bright graphics were the most consistent point of praise. AllGame's Kyle Knight called them "cutesy" and colourful next to the NES and Genesis of the time and liked the multiple pathways, but rated the play as average and lacking difficulty. Consoles Plus praised the varied presentation, simple controls and multiple paths while finding the music repetitive, and Hobby Consolas praised its technical presentation, samba-style soundtrack, many secrets, bosses and two-player co-operative play. French magazine Tilt saw it as a cross between Marvel Land and Sonic the Hedgehog, an original and varied adventure platformer, and Génération 4 compared it to Super Mario Bros., while Consolemania found its graphics simplistic, its sound bland and its play frustrating.
trivia: RePlay reported it as the sixth most popular arcade game at the time.
It was ported to the Neo Geo CD in 1994.
It came to the Wii Virtual Console in November 2007.
Hamster re-released it in the ACA Neo Geo series.
HobbyConsolas named it one of the twenty best Neo Geo AES games in 2014.
devStory: Alpha Denshi developed it and SNK published it in 1990 for the Neo Geo arcade and home platforms, early in the system's life. Contemporary reviews were generally positive, though several critics, including Joypad and Joystick, noted its low difficulty and GameFan its short length. Later reception was more mixed: on the Virtual Console, Eurogamer's Dan Whitehead called its visuals "crude and blotchy" and recommended Super Mario Bros. 3 instead, GameSpot praised its sound but criticised its graphics and play, and IGN found it a passable platformer. The Neo Geo and Switch versions average around 50 per cent on GameRankings.

title: Turrican II: The Final Fight
description: Turrican II: The Final Fight (1991) is Factor 5's Amiga run and gun in which Bren McGuire, sole survivor of the Avalon 1, dons the Turrican suit to avenge his crew against The Machine.
longDescription:
In 3025 the United Planets Freedom Forces keep peace across the galaxy. The ship Avalon 1, commanded by Colonel Ardon C. Striker, is preparing to cross the galaxy's barrier when a huge battlecruiser appears and, with unknown technology, disables every defence. Mutants pour through a ruptured airlock and wipe out the crew in hand-to-hand fighting. The evil emperor The Machine, half-man and half-robot, steps on the body of soldier Bren McGuire and declares the crew no more, but Bren is alive. Alone, he reaches the equipment room, climbs into one of the new Turrican fighting suits and cries "Revenge!"

The game is described as a cross between Metroid, which inspired its huge, detailed labyrinth levels and morph-ball function, and Psycho-Nics Oscar, which inspired its graphics and weapons. Five distinct worlds are split across eleven levels, each with its own theme by Chris Huelsbeck, before a final showdown with The Machine. A music menu, reached with the space bar on the Amiga, lets players listen to every track. The soundtrack is widely regarded as one of Huelsbeck's best, and it was performed live by an orchestra at the second Symphonic Game Music Concert in 2004. Technically it boasts seven-layer parallax scrolling.
trivia: Manfred Trenz picked the name Turrican from a phone book, from the Italian name Turricano.
The Amiga version was finished first, but Trenz regards the C64 version as the original.
The Game Boy and Mega Drive versions were rebranded as Universal Soldier.
Amiga programmer Holger Schmidt said only the first game's scrolling routines were kept.
It was re-released in Turrican Flashback on PS4 and Switch in 2020.
devStory: The Amiga and Atari ST versions began development in May 1990 and were released by Rainbow Arts in February 1991. Like its predecessor it was originally coded on the Commodore 64, but most of the code was new: Holger Schmidt explained that "all we really kept were the scrolling routines. Everything else was optimized and rewritten because we needed more processing time for the sprites and animation." Trenz told The One that he always found titles in the phone book, since "there's loads of good material out there". It was also released for the CDTV, Amstrad CPC, ZX Spectrum and MS-DOS, and later for Mega Drive and Game Boy.

title: Lemmings 2: The Tribes
description: Lemmings 2: The Tribes (1993) is DMA Design's sequel that split the lemmings into twelve tribes, added over forty new skills and asked players to save at least one lemming per level.
longDescription:
Twelve themed worlds, each belonging to a tribe such as the Highland, Cavelem or Circus lemmings, contain ten levels of obstacles, traps and hazards. As before, the player guides lemmings from their entrance to an exit within a time limit by assigning a limited pool of skills to the autonomous creatures. But there is no longer a quota: delivering just one lemming opens the next level. Each tribe starts its world with sixty lemmings and survivors carry over between levels, so because some later levels need several lemmings working together, earlier ones may need replaying to save more. Gold, silver or bronze medals reward the number rescued.

Alongside the original eight skills come 43 new ones, either one-off commands or permanent abilities. Runner and Icarus Wings improve mobility, Builder and Planter add terrain, Miner and Bazooker remove it, and Blocker and Attractor affect nearby lemmings. A new, unlimited fan tool is controlled directly to blow lemmings using skills like Ballooner and Surfer and to power mechanisms. Players can pause, "nuke" all lemmings to restart a hopeless level, and now fast forward. The tribes differ in looks but not in play, with no skill exclusive to one tribe, except the Classic tribe, which keeps the original Blocker. Compute! called it "perfection improved upon".
trivia: It was the UK's top-selling Amiga game in February 1993 and top PC game that March.
The fast-forward feature came from an aborted arcade port.
Mike Dailly said that after fast forward, "it's now very hard to play the original Lemmings".
Computer Gaming World called it "twice the game its predecessor was".
It was ported to the Mega Drive, Super NES and Game Boy.
devStory: DMA Design developed it with Psygnosis, which programmer Brian Watson said played a more involved role in "helping with the game design and production". There was considerable pressure to repeat the original's crossover success, and lead programmer David Jones gave more thought to porting it to many platforms. Mike Dailly said the tribes were meant to create a more open-ended structure, giving players "at least some choice" when stuck and making the game last longer. It was a commercial success, though not as popular as the original nor ported as widely, and critics widely considered it better than the first game, praising its puzzles, animations, music for each tribe and friendly interface.

title: Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods
description: Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods (1991) is Bullfrog's god game sequel set in Greek myth, in which a demigod son of Zeus battles the Olympians with 29 divine powers and legendary heroes.
longDescription:
Like its predecessor, it is a god game in which the player guides their followers against those of an enemy god, but where Populous only alluded to undefined deities, the sequel is rooted in Greek mythology. The player is a demigod, one of Zeus's countless children by mortal women, and must defeat one Greek deity at a time before finally facing Zeus himself, who has promised a place in the Pantheon on Olympus to any child who survives. Instead of Populous's eight powers there are twenty-nine, thirty on PC, divided into earth, water, wind, fire, plants and people.

All are fed by a manna meter that fills as the population grows and drains as powers are used, so repeated devastating miracles empty it. Each category also offers a hero, transforming the player's leader into one of six legendary Greek figures who roams the map attacking enemies. When either side controls a set share of the map, usually 75 per cent, indestructible monsters such as the Colossus or Medusa rampage across it, a cue to finish quickly. Victories earn experience points to strengthen the six categories, improving accuracy and duration and lowering manna costs. There are 1,000 maps, and strong performances skip ahead several at once. One plant power spreads a deadly fungus whose growth follows the rules of Conway's Game of Life.
trivia: Its design began before Populous had finished playtesting.
Peter Molyneux said a sequel must be totally rewritten, or "it's really just a data disk".
The Challenge Games data disk moved the setting to Japanese mythology with 500 new maps.
The Mega Drive version was published by Virgin Games as Two Tribes: Populous II.
Computer Gaming World named it one of the best strategy games of 1992.
devStory: Bullfrog developed it for the Amiga, Atari ST and MS-DOS, with Electronic Arts publishing; keyboard work on the Amiga version began in March 1991 for a November release, though The One noted the game had effectively been in development for over two years. Designer Peter Molyneux reused no code or assets from Populous, though development began with the first game ported to newer hardware as a framework. Computer Gaming World called it "instantly absorbing and addictive", Super Gamer gave the SNES version 82 per cent as "an attractive update of the original with a much smoother control system", and Total! later ranked it 85th among SNES games.

sources.title: Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods

title: Treasure Island Dizzy
description: Treasure Island Dizzy (1989) is the Oliver Twins' second Dizzy game, a notoriously hard inventory puzzle adventure in which the egg hero escapes a desert island with just one life.
longDescription:
Dizzy is stranded and must solve a series of puzzles to obtain a boat and return to his friends and family, the Yolkfolk, journeying through haunted mines, tree villages and the sea bed. Compared with the first game it has a new inventory system and improved animations, fewer enemies and a stronger focus on inventory-based problem solving. A subquest, which turns out to be essential, asks Dizzy to collect thirty gold coins, a feature repeated in many sequels: on escaping the last island, the Shopkeeper appears and tells him he cannot leave without them, and since many coins are hidden behind scenery, this second task proved harder than the main game.

Critics consider it one of the hardest Dizzy games. There is no energy bar, and Dizzy has only one life, compared with five in the first game and three in Fantasy World Dizzy and most later titles. Uniquely, the player cannot choose which item to use: Dizzy simply drops whatever is at the top of his inventory, so if he is underwater with the snorkel at the top, picking up something else makes him drop it and drown instantly. It therefore demands more foresight and planning than any other game in the series. Commodore Format printed a "complete" solution and map which, like Codemasters' premium-rate hint line, left out the hidden coins.
trivia: It debuted at number ten in the Gallup Budget Top 10 and reached number one several times.
It reached number two in the All Formats chart, behind RoboCop.
It spent over two years in the Gallup All Formats Top 40.
The ZX Spectrum version alone sold over 100,000 copies.
The NES version was part of Camerica's Quattro Adventure compilation.
devStory: The Oliver Twins developed it and Codemasters published it in 1989 for the Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum, following it with Commodore 64, NES, Amiga, Atari ST and Atari Jaguar ports. It was a long-running budget hit and the sequel to Dizzy – The Ultimate Cartoon Adventure, introducing the inventory puzzles and coin hunts that later Dizzy games built on. Codemasters released a Windows version on its website in 2004, actually the Commodore 64 version bundled with an emulator, and the NES version returned on the Evercade's Oliver Twins Collection in 2020.

title: Pinball Fantasies
description: Pinball Fantasies (1992) is Digital Illusions' acclaimed Amiga sequel to Pinball Dreams, with four themed tables from an amusement park to a haunted house.
longDescription:
Like Pinball Dreams, it is an arcade-style pinball game with four tables, each with its own theme, objectives and mechanics, plus difficulty levels and options such as the number of balls. Party Land, the table in the shareware release, is set in an amusement park where lighting PARTY or CRAZY starts a high-scoring event. Speed Devils is about car racing, with players overtaking cars to take the lead. Billion Dollar Gameshow has players win prizes through combinations of ramp shots, and Stones 'N Bones is a haunted house where players light eight increasingly valuable modes by completing a bank of STONE-BONE targets, then cycle through them.

Every table awards an extra ball the moment the top score on the list is beaten, and another on a successful match at the end. Each has a special ramp, two on Speed Devils, that keeps a running total of Cyclones, Miles, Skills or Screams, with the first shot counting double and each worth 100,000 points in the bonus. Apart from Party Land, the tables award specials at set totals, and each has one or two high-scoring rounds started by meeting certain objectives, whose points are added to the bonus but lost if the player tilts. Some cartridge versions save high scores and settings to EEPROM.
trivia: Digital Illusions wanted to rewrite the ball physics, but Andrew Hewson persuaded them to reuse the engine.
Olof Gustafsson composed the soundtrack and Markus Nyström was the sole artist.
PC Gamer US ranked it the 33rd best computer game in 1994.
It was ported to CD32, Jaguar, Game Boy, MS-DOS, PlayStation and SNES.
Pinball Illusions followed in 1995.
devStory: The Pinball Dreams team made it, with producer Barry Simpson leading development, Fredrik Liljegren as manager and Andreas Axelsson and Ulf Mandorff programming. 21st Century Entertainment released it for the Amiga in Europe in October 1992, followed by a CD32 version based on the enhanced AGA release in 1993 and an MS-DOS port by FrontLine Design. It was a major commercial success and one of the best-selling games of its time, acclaimed for its presentation, visuals, audio and improvements over its predecessor. Console versions fared less well: GamePro found the SNES version's scrolling so jerky it was almost unplayable, and Next Generation complained that its partial view left players "shooting blind".

title: Lionheart
description: Lionheart (1993) is Thalion Software's lavish Amiga action-platformer in which the outlaw swordsman Valdyn sets out to recover the Cat People's holy relic from the evil Norka.
longDescription:
Valdyn, an outlaw swordsman called Lionheart, is arrested while gambling and summoned by the King of the Cat People. The Lionheart, the holiest relic of their religion, has been stolen by thieves sent by the evil Norka, and unless the King displays it at the coming Showing Festival he must abdicate in favour of his arch-chancellor Nargle. On the same night, Valdyn's beloved Ilene was turned to stone by a rare poison found only in Norka's country. Declared destined to reclaim the jewel, Valdyn is given a flying dragon, but a flying ship abducts him on the way and he must continue on foot.

Across 14 levels of monsters and hazards such as water, chasms, lava and fireballs, Valdyn runs, jumps, crouches, swings and climbs, gaining speed downhill to leap further, while slides and ropes can only be taken one way. Combat is central, with high, middle and reverse strikes, a low kick, a jump strike and a downward strike. He starts with four health points, three lives and two continues; hidden Energy Drinks restore health and Life Spheres add lives, while every hundred Energy Crystals unlocks an extra health point, up to eight, and stronger swords cut down tough foes faster. Harder difficulty levels change and greatly expand the stages. GamesMaster called it "a technical marvel which looks, sounds and plays like a dream".
trivia: Programmer Erwin Kloibhofer and artist Henk Nieborg joined Thalion after making Ghost Battle as freelancers.
They were inspired by Super Mario, Castlevania, Super Contra, Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts and Castle of Illusion.
Development began in November 1991.
GamesMaster rated it 90 per cent and The One 91 per cent.
Producer Eric Simon described it as a game "created out of passion".
devStory: After finishing Ghost Battle, Austrian programmer Erwin Kloibhofer and Dutch artist Henk Nieborg were hired in-house by Thalion, where producer Eric Simon "had bigger plans for us". Fans of Japanese action games, they wanted to make "a really outstanding action game for the Amiga", the kind they would buy on a console, and before joining Nieborg had already drawn a tileset and designed Valdyn on his Amiga 500. Thalion self-published it in 1993. GamesMaster praised the varied, useful moves, comparing them to a fighting game, and its "astounding" graphics, saying Thalion had "squeezed all the graphic power out of the Amiga", while The One called it "the finest example of its kind" for introducing some originality.

title: Superfrog
description: Superfrog (1993) is Team17's Amiga platformer in which a prince turned into a frog gains super powers from a bottle of Lucozade and sets out to rescue his princess from a witch.
longDescription:
In a nod to the Frog Prince fairy tale, an unnamed prince is turned into a frog by a jealous witch, who then abducts his princess. Sulking by the River O' Despair, he finds a floating bottle of Lucozade that gives him super powers, and he heads off to defeat the witch, completing smaller objectives such as finding a golden key in the castle or escaping captivity in a circus along the way. The story is told mostly through an animated introduction by Eric W. Schwartz.

There are 24 levels across six themed worlds: Magic Woods, Spooky Castle, Fun Park, Ancient Level, Ice World and Space Level. In each, Superfrog must collect a set number of coins before the exit will open, racing a countdown timer while managing health points, both restored by bottles of Lucozade. Coins, fruit and speed earn up to 15 credits per level, which can be banked for score or gambled on a slot machine minigame whose main prize is a level code for restarting later. Between the fifth and sixth worlds is a side-scrolling shoot 'em up, Project-F, an homage to Team17's Project-X complete with a remix of its theme, where the goal is simply to survive. The game ends with a boss fight against the witch in her castle.
trivia: Schwartz's intro originally included cameos by Sonic, Mario, Zool and Zooz, removed to avoid legal issues.
Allister Brimble composed the music.
The 1994 MS-DOS version by Bubball Systems dropped the animated intro and the shooting level.
A CD32 version followed on the Amiga.
Superfrog HD was released in 2013 and removed from stores in 2016.
devStory: Team17 developed and published it for the Amiga in 1993, and it was popular enough to spawn a CD32 version and, in 1994, an MS-DOS conversion by Bubball Systems. Islona Software re-released the CD32 version as a budget title in 1999, and the DOS version came to GOG.com in 2012. Although Team17's earlier games became relatively obscure after the huge success of Worms, Superfrog is remembered fondly for its solid play, smooth scrolling, cartoon-quality graphics and upbeat music, and despite being a small release next to blockbuster platformers like Sonic, it was well received and keeps a fan base that considers it an excellent example of the genre.

title: Walker
description: Walker (1993) is DMA Design's Amiga shooter in which a giant bipedal mech stomps from right to left through battles in 1944 Berlin, 2019 Los Angeles, the Middle East and a future Great War.
longDescription:
The player controls a bipedal mech through four stages of two levels each: 1944 Berlin, 2019 Los Angeles, the contemporary Middle East and Earth in 2420 during "The Great War". Its machine guns cut down waves of infantry, tanks and airships, and a level is finished when every enemy is dead, followed by a boss at its end. Firing raises a temperature gauge, and overheated guns must cool before firing again, while missiles can lock on to targets. The mech's shield is its health; when it is destroyed a life is lost, and losing all three ends the game. Unusually, the action scrolls from right to left.

The mouse aims the guns while the keyboard or joystick walks the mech, a split Ian Dunlop said kept the weapons free while moving and "gave the gameplay a bit more depth and interest". The huge mech meant enemies had to be small, partly inspired by the Lemmings characters, and the side-scrolling drew on DMA's own Menace. There are two difficulty levels, easy and arcade, with only the first two stages in easy mode, and on advanced Amigas the mech exchanges speech with its headquarters, recorded by Dunlop and Neill Glancy over walkie-talkie. Critics praised its graphics and sound: Amiga Force called it "one of the most satisfying shoot-'em-ups", though The One Amiga thought the mech looked "more like a mechanical chicken".
trivia: The mech originated in a sprite from Lemmings originally designed for Blood Money.
David Jones scrapped it in early 1990 before Dunlop and Glancy revived and redesigned it.
Neill Glancy's art was influenced by The Terminator and Akira.
An underground base linking the levels and a Prince of Persia-inspired level were cut.
Amiga Power ranked it 58th in its top 100 games of 1993.
devStory: David Jones began it after Blood Money in 1989, with graphics by Scott Johnston, but scrapped it in early 1990 when the design was not coming together. After the C64 and TurboGrafx-16 ports of Shadow of the Beast, he hired Ian Dunlop and Neill Glancy to continue, Glancy redesigning the game, and Raymond Usher wrote the soundtrack. Psygnosis cut some features for financial and time reasons and released it in February 1993. Reviews were positive for its animation and sound, with Amiga Action giving it an Accolade, though the repetitive play drew mixed reactions. A Mega Drive port and a 3DO sequel, Walker 2, were both cancelled.

title: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon
description: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon (1991) is Westwood's first-person Dungeons & Dragons sequel in which the heroes infiltrate a temple raising skeletal legions against Waterdeep.
longDescription:
After their first adventure, the heroes are resting at an inn when Khelben "Blackstaff" Arunsun, Archmage of Waterdeep, slips them a note: he sent a scout, Amber, to investigate evil brewing at the temple of Darkmoon, and she has not returned. Khelben transports the party to the temple, where they fight its clerics and other inhabitants and discover that the high priest, Dran Draggore, is assembling legions of skeletal warriors to attack Waterdeep. To reach the temple's inner sanctum the party must pass an acolytes' test, and in the final confrontation Draggore is revealed to be a red dragon.

The sequel adds outdoor areas, more interaction with the environment and more role-playing elements. Most of the game takes place in and around the temple, which can be roamed freely once inside: the catacombs beneath it, its upper levels and its three towers, silver, azure and crimson. Monsters attack in real time, even while the player is searching through spellbooks, a point Computer Gaming World's Scorpia criticised, while still calling it "a more substantial game" than the original, with "more to do, a bigger variety of critters to fight and a larger area to explore". GameSpy later said its completely original ending was badly needed given its "almost insane level of difficulty".
trivia: Its music was among Frank Klepacki's first work, written for the AdLib sound chip.
Paul Mudra, composer of the first game, worked only on sound effects.
SSI sold 73,109 copies.
Dragon gave it five out of five stars.
Eye of the Beholder III: Assault on Myth Drannor followed in 1993.
devStory: Westwood Associates developed it and Strategic Simulations published it for MS-DOS in 1991, with Amiga, FM Towns and PC-98 versions following; the PC-98 version added new songs for each main part of the game. Computer Gaming World named it one of the year's top role-playing games, following "the strong graphic and solid play-balance tradition of the original", and Scorpia called it "a definite must for all EOB fans" despite her interface complaints. The One gave the Amiga version 87 per cent, praising its "beautifully-drawn" graphics and atmospheric sound but calling it unoriginal next to Dungeon Master. The series as a whole passed 350,000 sales by 1996.

sources.title: Eye of the Beholder II: The Legend of Darkmoon

title: Captive
description: Captive (1990) is a science fiction Dungeon Master-style RPG in which an amnesiac prisoner remotely controls four droids to raid alien bases and break himself out of a space prison.
longDescription:
Trill is found guilty of a crime he did not commit and sentenced to 250 years in a cryogenic space prison. He wakes 248 years later with no memory of who or where he is, or why he was imprisoned, and in a corner of his cell finds a briefcase computer that controls four droids aboard a spaceship. Using them, he must find and free himself. The droids fly between planets in a vector-graphics space interface, land by capsule, find each base's entrance and explore its dungeons of puzzles and alien and robotic enemies. In each base they recover space probes that reveal the next base and destroy the generators powering the prison's force field, then escape before the base collapses.

A full mission is ten bases followed by the space station, where the player can free Trill and end the game or let him be recaptured and start a new mission. Shops sell, buy and repair weapons, ammunition and body parts, as each droid's head, chest, arms, hands, legs and feet can be upgraded individually, along with batteries, remote cameras, optics and devscapes. Front droids attack on the flanks while those behind fire projectiles down the middle. Played in real time from a first-person view, it grows fast enough to demand quick reflexes and clever use of the environment, such as trapping enemies in doors or flooding sections to paralyse robots.
trivia: Its planets and bases are generated from a single numerical seed, giving 65,535 levels.
It was called Federation War in development; an ACE magazine reader named it Captive in a competition.
Amiga Format and Zzap! both scored it 91 per cent.
Amiga Power ranked it the 31st best game of all time in May 1991.
A sequel, Liberation: Captive 2, followed.
devStory: Antony Crowther created it with a procedural algorithm that built each planet, base and inhabitants from a numerical seed, so only one base had to be active in a saved game. Mindscape published it for the Amiga and Atari ST in 1990 and MS-DOS in 1992. Zzap! felt it shared Dungeon Master's drawbacks, such as little interaction, but praised a "well designed" world, imaginative plot and opponents and challenging puzzles "with many thrills and spills to keep you on the edge of your chair", and PC Format named it one of the 50 best computer games of all time in 1991.

title: F/A-18 Interceptor
description: F/A-18 Interceptor (1988) is Intellisoft's Amiga combat flight simulator set over the San Francisco Bay Area, flying the F/A-18 Hornet against "terrorists" in six missions.
longDescription:
The player mostly flies the F/A-18 Hornet, with the F-16 Fighting Falcon available for aerobatics, free flight and the first mission, though in reality the F/A-18 is a multirole strike fighter rather than a true interceptor. The setting is the San Francisco Bay Area, with the Golden Gate and Bay bridges, Alcatraz and even Electronic Arts' San Mateo headquarters, and the player can operate from San Francisco and Oakland airports, Moffett Field and the USS Enterprise anchored offshore. Only air-to-air weapons are carried: Sidewinder and AMRAAM missiles and a Vulcan cannon with 500 rounds, plus chaff and flares.

After qualifying with a carrier landing, players take on six missions starting on 1 September 1994: visually identifying an unknown aircraft, sometimes MiG-29s and occasionally a Boeing 707; protecting Air Force One; intercepting two stolen F-16s; dropping a rescue pod to a downed pilot near the Farallon Islands; destroying a fast, low-flying cruise missile; and attacking a submersible aircraft carrier. Players long believed the last was impossible, and designer Bob Dinnerman said the carrier simply does not blow up when destroyed, so only the enemy planes need be shot down. There is no ending: the missions just loop. On Amigas with more than 512 KB, a theme reminiscent of Top Gun's anthem plays, at Dinnerman's request.
trivia: Pressing 0 at free-flight start places the player at an unimplemented Edwards Air Force Base.
Sound engineer Dave Warhol wrote the Top Gun-style theme.
Bugs let players land on water or upside down on the carrier.
Dragon gave it four out of five stars.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 87th best game of all time in 1996.
devStory: Intellisoft developed it, with Bob Dinnerman as designer and programmer, and Electronic Arts published it for the Amiga in 1988. It was well reviewed: Computer Gaming World gave it a positive review, and the Palm Beach Post called it "a pretty successful game", approving of the ability to fly the plane from any external view. In 1996 Computer Gaming World named it one of the best games ever, calling it a jet combat sim that set the state of the art for its era.

title: Falcon
description: Falcon (1987) is Spectrum HoloByte's acclaimed F-16 combat flight simulator, praised by a real F-16 pilot for its accuracy and the start of a long-running series.
longDescription:
The first official entry in Spectrum HoloByte's Falcon series of F-16 simulators, not counting 1984's F-16 Fighting Falcon, gives players a choice of 12 missions, with awards for flying at higher skill levels. Air-to-air and ground-attack weapons are limited in realistic ways. AIM-9J missiles, usually the only ones available, are less reliable than newer AIM-9Ls and useless head-on; guided AGM-65 missiles are easier to use than Mk 84 "iron" bombs but ineffective against hardened targets; and an ECM pod protects against missiles but takes up a hardpoint that could carry weapons or fuel. The enemy holds the western part of a square map divided into nine smaller squares.

Enemy targets are fixed ground sites, defended by MiG-21 interceptors, SA-2 missiles from known fixed sites and portable SA-7s that can appear anywhere. Compute! joked in 1989 that it "seemed harder to fly than the real plane", and an update that year reportedly made control and landings much easier. The Atari ST and Amiga versions add a semi-dynamic campaign in which the player roams the airspace hunting enemy aircraft and ground targets, destroyed buildings and SAM sites stay down for a time, and ground forces fight back and forth, along with two expansion sets, Operation: Counterstrike and Operation: Firefight.
trivia: An F-16 pilot with the 474th Tactical Fighter Wing gave it "good marks for accuracy".
It won three 1987 Software Publishers Association awards, including Best Simulation.
It was voted Best 16-bit Simulation Game at the 1989 Golden Joystick Awards.
Amiga Power ranked it the Amiga's eighth best game in 1991.
Genesis, SNES and Jaguar versions were planned but never released.
devStory: Sphere, Inc. developed it for the Macintosh and PC in 1987, and Rowan Software ported it to the Atari ST in 1988 and the Amiga in 1989; a CDTV version followed in 1992, along with a colour Macintosh update and a simplified TurboGrafx-16 version by Turbo Technologies. Computer Gaming World called it one of the most detailed and accurate flight simulators on the microcomputer market, Dragon gave it five stars, and Compute! praised its graphics, realism and documentation, while Atari ST User called it "one of the most polished flight sims that I've ever come across". Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the TurboGrafx-16 version 4.5 out of 10, finding the compromises made to fit a 4 MB cartridge left it awkward and dull.

title: Gunship
description: Gunship (1986) is MicroProse's AH-64 Apache helicopter simulator, flying primary and secondary missions across five theatres and earning medals and promotions for a persistent pilot.
longDescription:
Missions span five regions: a US training ground, Southeast Asia with the 1st Air Cavalry, Central America with the 82nd Airborne, the Middle East with the 101st Airborne and Western Europe with the 3rd Armored Division. After choosing region, style and enemies, the pilot receives a primary and secondary mission, such as destroying an enemy headquarters or supporting friendly troops, the latter easier because the fighting is closer to friendly lines. The Apache is usually armed with Hellfire missiles for hard targets such as bunkers and tanks, unguided FFAR rockets for soft targets, and high-explosive rounds for its 30 mm cannon, with Sidewinders as backup in some theatres.

Patient pilots can hop between hills to hide and pop up to attack, while aggressive ones fly fast, low and erratically for close cannon runs, risky against first-line enemies. Armour deflects most small-calibre fire, but damage can disable systems and eventually cause a power failure, forcing an autorotation landing; a badly injured pilot down in enemy territory goes missing in action. There is no time limit, and Forward Area Resupply Points rearm, refuel and repair, though the ideal is to finish both missions and return within 20 minutes. The game never ends: promotions stop at Colonel, but medals up to the Medal of Honor keep coming, even posthumously, until retirement as a Brigadier General.
trivia: MicroProse originally wanted an urban helicopter sim like Blue Thunder, but city graphics proved too difficult.
It reused tools developed for F-15 Strike Eagle.
Its sales passed 500,000 by 1989.
It won the Origins Award for Best Screen Graphics in a Home Computer Game of 1986.
U.S. Gold's 1993 Mega Drive version added arcade-style shoot 'em up stages.
devStory: MicroProse developed and published it in 1986 for MS-DOS, Atari ST, Amiga, Commodore 64, FM Towns, MSX, PC-98, X68000 and ZX Spectrum. It was MicroProse's third best-selling Commodore game by late 1987. Info gave the C64 version five stars, calling it "without qualification, the best combat flight simulator ever released for an 8-bit computer!", and Computer Gaming World said a five-star rating was "well-deserved", later recalling that "when initially released, this was THE helicopter simulation". Its success led to Gunship 2000 and Gunship!.

title: F-19 Stealth Fighter
description: F-19 Stealth Fighter (1988) is MicroProse's stealth flight simulator, built on an educated guess about America's secret stealth jet and released the same day the Air Force revealed the F-117.
longDescription:
The player flies missions of varying difficulty over four regions: Gaddafi's Libya, the Persian Gulf, the North Cape and Central Europe, under conditions of conventional war, limited war or cold war, in which merely being detected can cause a major diplomatic incident. A wide range of realistic ordnance can be chosen, and enemy aircraft, SAM sites and radar stations behave convincingly, patrolling at first and then searching aggressively once the player is detected. A realistic radar model compares the plane's changing radar signature with incoming pulses at different ranges and strengths.

Missions end in a variety of ways depending on the outcome, from rescue by a Sikorsky SH-3 Sea King to a Pravda headline announcing the pilot's capture, or an outraged ally or neutral nation protesting the destruction of its aircraft. A pilot roster tracks missions, rank, score and medals, and deaths are permanent, giving an extended campaign feel. The aircraft is based on the fictional F-19, inspired by a 1986 Testors model kit, though an option for the real F-117 was added, modelled on a deliberately vague 1988 press photo with wrongly stubby, wide proportions. The box included a thick manual on US and Soviet aircraft, keyboard overlays, a guide to stealth and fighter tactics and sketched maps of each war zone.
trivia: It is a 16-bit remake of the 1987 Commodore 64 game Project Stealth Fighter.
Sid Meier and Andy Hollis worked on the PC conversion.
Delayed from September to mid-November 1988, it sold out in two months.
Computer Gaming World named it Simulation Game of the Year.
Night Hawk: F-117A Stealth Fighter 2.0 replaced the fictional plane with an accurate F-117 in 1991.
devStory: After Jim Synoski and Arnold Hendrick finished Project Stealth Fighter for the C64, Sid Meier and Andy Hollis joined for the PC version, which Hendrick said borrowed only "the game scenario concepts, military equipment research data, and perhaps some flight dynamics algorithms". Before release, many had speculated about the missing F-19 designation, and MicroProse released the game the same day the US military first admitted the F-117A Nighthawk existed. Computer Gaming World praised its realism and documentation, with tutorials on aerodynamics, radar, stealth and tactics, and the Software Publishers Association named it Best Simulation. It came to the Amiga and Atari ST in 1990, the PC-98 in Japan, and Steam in 2015.

title: It Came from the Desert
description: It Came from the Desert (1989) is Cinemaware's 1950s monster movie game in which a geologist has 15 days to convince a desert town that radiation has created giant ants, and stop them.
longDescription:
On 1 June 1951 geologist Dr. Greg Bradley arrives in remote Lizard Breath, California, to study a meteor crash site in the desert south-west of town. He soon learns that the meteor's radiation has grown the local ants to enormous size, but few believe him. Racing the clock to stop the ants multiplying and spreading, he must visit mines, farms, a pub, an airfield, the local radio station and more to find evidence, convince townsfolk and authorities of the danger and contain the infestation, eventually calling on everything from workers to the National Guard's tanks and fighter jets.

Inspired by dozens of 1950s monster films, above all the giant-ant classic Them!, and titled after It Came from Outer Space, it mixes point-and-click dialogue with first-person and overhead action scenes in a non-linear structure typical of Cinemaware. It is mostly detective work, with time as the key resource: waiting, sleeping at home or in hospital and driving all use it, and Bradley has until 15 June. If he fails, the ants spread and the game ends gloomily; the good ending requires finding the colony and killing the queen. Games International praised its replay value, noting "there is no way that you will be able to discover all the subplots in one game", and called its sound "the best I've ever come across in any game".
trivia: An expansion, Antheads: It Came from the Desert II, followed in 1990.
Level 9 Computing ported it to MS-DOS in 1991 shortly before closing.
A 99 per cent complete Mega Drive version starring a teenage pest controller was cancelled.
Cinemaware later distributed the Mega Drive ROM from its website.
A full-motion video TurboGrafx-CD version was released in 1991.
devStory: Cinemaware released it for the Amiga in 1989, followed by an almost identical MS-DOS version in early 1991. A very different Genesis version by Black Pearl Software, an overhead shooter with craftable power-ups, was cancelled, and a TurboGrafx-CD version designed by David Riordan used full-motion video of live actors. Games International's John Scott rated both gameplay and graphics nine out of ten, saying "right from the opening sequence you know that this is something special", though he found the Antheads expansion too similar to the original. The game and its expansion were later released on Steam in a Cinemaware Anthology.

title: Wings
description: Wings (1990) is Cinemaware's First World War flying game, following a Royal Flying Corps pilot from 1916 to the Armistice through dogfights, bombing runs and a wartime diary.
longDescription:
The player is a rookie pilot who joins the Royal Flying Corps in 1916 and serves, later in the Royal Air Force, until the end of the war in 1918. Each mission is recorded in a daily diary, and objectives are tied to historical events, such as shooting down famous aces including Manfred von Richthofen. Inspired by the 1927 silent film Wings, the action is varied: dogfights with enemy planes, escorting bombers and bombing runs, flying the plane, firing its machine gun and dropping bombs.

Dogfights are flown from a first-person cockpit view showing instruments and landscape, and a range of aircraft can be chosen, some faster but more lightly armoured, others slower but tougher. Computer Gaming World called it "a whopping good arcade experience ... exciting, novel, and addicting" and the best choice for action gamers among World War I flight games. Retro Gamer later said that "the 3D sections looked absolutely incredible and far in advance of anything that had appeared on consoles, PC or even the arcades at the time", and that its story of a pilot's "eerily realistic wartime experiences" provoked a rare emotional response.
trivia: Magazine scores ranged from 78 per cent in Amiga Action to 94 per cent in CU Amiga and C+VG.
Amiga World ranked it third among all-time Amiga hits in 1993.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 65th best game of all time in 1996.
Wings Advance for the Game Boy Advance in 2002 added German missions.
A first Kickstarter for a remake failed; Wings! Remastered was funded on the second try.
devStory: Cinemaware developed and published it for the Amiga in 1990, and it was well received across the press. Computer Gaming World praised its "masterful combination of arcade action, flight simulation, and cinematic story", and GamesMaster ranked it 68th in its Top 100 Games of All Time in 1996. Raylight Games made Wings Advance in 2002, which averaged 80 on Metacritic. A 2012 Kickstarter for an HD remake raised only $51,740 of its $350,000 goal, but a second campaign in 2013 succeeded, and Kalypso Media released Wings! Remastered for Windows and macOS in October 2014.

title: Rocket Ranger
description: Rocket Ranger (1988) is Cinemaware's serial-inspired adventure in which a rocket-packed US Army scientist fights Nazi zeppelins dropping IQ-lowering lunarium to change the course of the war.
longDescription:
One night in a secret bunker, a US Army scientist receives artefacts teleported from a future where the Nazis won the Second World War and enslaved the world, along with a plea to change history. The Nazis' success rests on lunarium, a mineral found only on the Moon that drastically lowers the IQ of human males, dropped as bombs from zeppelins flying too high for anti-aircraft guns. With a rocket pack and a radium pistol, the player flies around the world, shoots down fighters, brawls with guards for rocket parts, raids lunarium depots for fuel and tries to win the trust of the kidnapped Dr. Barnstoff and his daughter Jane aboard a zeppelin, with digitised speech.

The goal is five rocket ship parts and 500 units of lunarium to reach the Moon and shut down the mines, where it emerges that an alien Interplanetary Union of Fascists has been helping the Nazis. A world-map strategy layer sends up to five agents to infiltrate countries, revealing key items, or organise resistance to delay the invasion of the US. Take-off is a timing minigame, and flights need exactly the right amount of fuel, chosen using a code-wheel copy protection system. Action scenes include third-person air combat against fighters, zeppelins and flak, assaults on bases from behind cover, and fistfights. Computer Gaming World said that "playing Rocket Ranger is like living the experience of the old serials".
trivia: It pays homage to 1950s science fiction serials and likely The Rocketeer comics.
A different Amiga version replaces the Nazis with alien invaders.
It was voted Best 16-bit Graphics of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards.
Computer Gaming World ranked it the 45th best computer game ever in 1996.
Its copy-protection penalty made Computer Gaming World's list of the best ways to die in games.
devStory: Cinemaware developed and published it in 1988, originally on the Amiga like most of its titles, drawing on Hollywood serials for its look, cut-scenes and clichés of a dashing hero and a damsel in distress. Computer Gaming World praised the Amiga version's graphics and sound but wished for saved games, given its difficulty and the chance of random events making it unwinnable. Compute! praised the MS-DOS version's EGA and Tandy graphics, and Orson Scott Card admired its variety of perspectives, interactive arcade scenes and "delightful hokum" such as the code wheel.

title: Sword of Sodan
description: Sword of Sodan (1988) is Discovery Software's Amiga hack and slash game in which royal twins Brodan and Shardan fight through eleven areas to destroy the necromancer Zoras.
longDescription:
Lordan, ruler of the northern kingdom, once survived the evil necromancer Zoras's attempt to overthrow him thanks to the hero Sodan. From his tower of human bones, Zoras learns forgotten spells from ancient parchments and conjures nightmarish creatures that march on Lordan's castle. Lordan sends his twin children, Brodan and Shardan, across the Cthol mountains to safety before he is killed, and they are raised and trained in swordsmanship by a bitter old man, who finally hands them the sword of Sodan. They fight their way to Castle Craggamoor and, after defeating Zoras, are accepted as the land's true rulers.

Players choose Brodan or Shardan, identical in play despite their looks, walking left to right through a horizontally scrolling world and fighting with their swords standing or kneeling; the shield is purely decorative. A map shows progress toward the castle between levels, with scrolls describing each location. The eleven areas run from the heroes' city gate through city streets, a forest and a graveyard, then six areas inside the castle's catacombs to the wizard's tower. Most levels are sword fights, though some have traps or puzzles. Players have five lives, an energy meter and a hit strength level raised by potions, which can also grant extra lives, brief invincibility or kill the current opponent outright. There are 13 enemy types and one ally, an ostrich-like creature called "the animal".
trivia: It was made by three Danish engineers at Discovery Software.
An Apple IIGS port by Visual Concepts was not made public until 2018.
Innerprise Software's 1990 Genesis version cut it to eight areas and eight enemies, attacking from both sides.
Electronic Arts published the Genesis version in the West and Sega in Japan.
Bethesda Softworks released a Macintosh version in 1993.
devStory: Three Danish engineers created it at Discovery Software in 1988, with Visual Concepts working on a simultaneous Apple IIGS conversion. Two years later Innerprise Software, which had bought the rights, made a scaled-down Sega Genesis port with reduced graphics and sound and notable gameplay changes: enemies attack from both directions, potions are more common and can be combined, and the forest and other areas were cut or merged. Electronic Arts published it in North America and Europe and Sega in Japan, and Bethesda Softworks later ported it to Macintosh System 7.

title: Impossible Mission II
description: Impossible Mission II (1988) is Novotrade's sequel to Epyx's Impossible Mission, in which the agent infiltrates Elvin Atombender's nine-tower fortress, cracking number puzzles and assembling a musical password.
longDescription:
Continuing directly from the first game, Elvin Atombender is seeking revenge and the player must stop him. His fortress has nine towers, eight of them themed around subjects such as computers, cars and furniture. Each tower's rooms are linked by two vertical corridors with lifts, while horizontal corridors to other towers are locked until a numerical puzzle is solved: each tower holds the numbers zero to nine in three colours, and a computer terminal lets the player test combinations. The lift to the central tower needs a password encoded in music, with a piece locked in a safe in each outer tower; the final password needs six distinct pieces, and because two are duplicates the player must rewind the tape to record over one.

The main additions are new robots and devices. Alongside security bots there are shovel bots that push the agent off platforms, suicide bots that jump off with him, mine bots that lay deadly mines, harmless pest bots that ride the lifts and get in the way, and squat bots that spring up and fling the player to a higher floor or crush him against the ceiling; the flying ball robot is gone. As well as snoozes that freeze robots and lift resets, players can now collect timed bombs and contact mines to blow holes in floors or open safes. Critics praised its challenging puzzles, impressive animation and tension against the clock.
trivia: It shares no code with the original; graphics were remade with an animation tool called Film Director.
The Atari ST was the lead platform.
Every room was redesigned for the ZX Spectrum version.
German magazine PowerPlay voted it the best skill game of 1988.
Impossible Mission III appeared for the C64 in 2026.
devStory: Novotrade developed it and Epyx published it in 1988 for the C64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Enterprise 128, NES, MS-DOS, Atari ST, Apple II, Apple IIGS and Amiga. Work on the C64 and Spectrum ports began once the Atari ST version was nearly done, and Spectrum programmer László Szenttornyai said the NES version "almost wasn't released because of the strict situation between Epyx and Nintendo." Reviews were mixed, criticising how little it changed from the original and its very limited sound. It was later followed by the Amiga-only Impossible Mission 2025 and included on the C64 Mini.

title: Ultima III: Exodus
description: Ultima III: Exodus (1983) is the first Ultima published by Origin Systems, introducing a four-character party and tactical combat as the heroes confront Exodus, spawn of Mondain and Minax.
longDescription:
Exodus, the offspring of Mondain and Minax, the villains of Ultima I and II, threatens the world of Sosaria, and the player travels there to defeat it and restore peace, concluding the Age of Darkness trilogy. Instead of a single hero, players now lead a party of four, built from eleven classes, Fighter, Paladin, Cleric, Wizard, Ranger, Thief, Barbarian, Lark, Illusionist, Druid and Alchemist, and five races, Human, Elf, Dwarf, Bobbit and Fuzzy, distributing points across Strength, Dexterity, Intelligence and Wisdom; race caps each statistic and so limits spellcasting. Classes balance fighting, magic and thieving differently, from Fighters who use every weapon and armour to Alchemists with daggers, half of the wizard spells and half the thieving skills.

On the map the party moves as one icon, but battles switch to a tactical screen where each character and enemy acts in turn, unlike the one-on-one blows of earlier Ultimas. Overworld enemies can be seen and avoided, while those in dungeons appear without warning, and the dungeons, now solid 3D rather than wireframe, are woven into the plot. Characters level up only by visiting Lord British. Townspeople can be bribed, robbed or attacked, though guards arrive in parties of eight; Lord British himself cannot be killed in a fight, though cannon fire from a ship in the moat can briefly topple him. It was one of the first computer RPGs with animated characters, and it added a musical score.
trivia: It was originally released as Exodus: Ultima III.
Richard Garriott credited Wizardry as the inspiration for its party-based combat.
It was ported to 13 other platforms, including a NES/Famicom remake.
It sold over 100,000 copies by August 1986.
It is credited with influencing Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy.
devStory: Released in 1983 for the Apple II, it was the first Ultima published by Richard Garriott's own company, Origin Systems, and ports followed on many systems. It sold over 120,000 copies by 1990 and ranked among the best-selling Apple II games. Softline said it "far surpasses" its predecessors, praising its "masterfully unified" plot and tactical combat and saying it "sets new standards for the fantasy gaming state of the art". Credited with laying foundations for the RPG genre, it was described by Computer Gaming World in 1994 as "the game that became known as Ultima to hundreds of thousands of cartridge gamers". Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar followed in 1985.

title: Curse of the Azure Bonds
description: Curse of the Azure Bonds (1989) is SSI's second Gold Box Forgotten Realms RPG, in which heroes wake with five magical tattoos that let evil factions control them, and must break each bond.
longDescription:
Renowned adventurers wake from a magical sleep in an inn in Tilverton, robbed of their possessions and with no memory of what happened. A passing landlord tells them they have been unconscious for over a month after an ambush on the road. On each character's arm are five azure markings, the bonds, each representing a separate evil faction that can possess and control them when it glows. The first bond forces them to attack a passing royal carriage, and after they defeat its faction, a band of assassins called the Fire Knives, they are banished from Tilverton for attempting to kill the King. The sage Filani explains the bonds, and the party must choose where to go next to remove the others.

A party of up to six player characters and two non-player characters is needed. Characters can be imported from Pool of Radiance or Hillsfar, or created from six races, nine alignments, two genders and six classes, now including the paladin and ranger, with multi-class options for demihumans; new characters start with 25,000 experience points, at level 5 for single-class heroes. Exploration uses Pool of Radiance's first-person view with a status panel and command menu, switching to an overhead view in combat, where spells and ranged weapons are aimed by lining up targets. An overland map of the Dalelands allows automatic travel between adjacent locations, with random encounters, and a new Fix command quickly heals the party if a conscious cleric or paladin is present.
trivia: It is a sequel to Kate Novak and Jeff Grubb's 1988 novel Azure Bonds.
A tabletop adventure module, FRC2, was written based on the game.
SSI sold 179,795 copies, more than a third on the Commodore 64.
CU Amiga-64 scored it 89 per cent.
It is the second of four Forgotten Realms Gold Box games, after Pool of Radiance.
devStory: Strategic Simulations developed and published it in 1989, continuing the events of Pool of Radiance in the Forgotten Realms setting and using the same Gold Box style, with slightly improved 16-colour graphics. It was almost as successful as Pool of Radiance, helped on the Commodore 64 by SSI being the last major American publisher still supporting the machine, and the series passed 800,000 sales by 1996. CU Amiga-64's Tony Dillon said the graphics were "more or less the same" as Pool of Radiance, "which is no bad thing", and that it was "still as entertaining and involving as the original", comparing its views to The Bard's Tale and Gauntlet.

title: Neuromancer
description: Neuromancer (1988) is Interplay's cyberpunk adventure loosely based on William Gibson's novel, moving between Chiba City and a 3D cyberspace of ICE and rogue AIs, set to music by Devo.
longDescription:
In 2058 in Chiba, Japan, the hero is trying to discover why his friends and other cyberspace cowboys are disappearing. Having fallen on hard times and pawned his cyberspace deck, he wakes face-down in a plate of Ratz's famous spaghetti, and his first task is to get the deck back from the pawnshop. Once upgraded for cyberspace, he finds Matrix users being flatlined by AIs led by the renegade Greystoke. After he destroys Greystoke, Neuromancer reveals that it manipulated him into killing the other AIs and traps him on a virtual island, from which he can escape to destroy Neuromancer and make the Matrix safe. Characters from the novel such as Armitage and Molly appear, sometimes as red herrings.

Play is split between a traditional adventure in Chiba City's "real world", where different locations open different grid sectors, and a 3D grid of cyberspace. There the player breaks through ICE to reach database nodes, trading damage with programs that hit once, over time or slow the ICE, until it cracks or the player is kicked out. AIs are fought mainly with skills, are invulnerable until hit with a specific skill or program, and losing to one means death, though a dead character can be revived for whatever money is on his credit chip. Skill chips bought for the brain jack implant give an edge, and skills improve with difficult successes. A code wheel is needed for PAX terminals.
trivia: It was meant to tie in with a 1988 film adaptation discussed with Ridley Scott and Mel Gibson.
Writer Timothy Leary sub-contracted the game rights and brought the project to Interplay.
Its soundtrack is based on Devo's "Some Things Never Change".
Computer Gaming World named it Adventure Game of the Year.
GameSpot inducted it into its greatest games of all time in 2004.
devStory: Interplay put most of its staff on the project to launch alongside the planned film; when the film was cancelled, Interplay considered dropping the game too but continued to avoid financial penalties. Mediagenic, a brand of Activision, published it in 1988 for the Amiga, Apple II, Apple IIGS, Commodore 64 and MS-DOS. Computer Gaming World's Douglas Seacat praised its pacing, wit, use of Gibson's setting and combat, complaining only about fixed conversation responses and disk swapping. Compute! praised its graphics, interface and Devo soundtrack, criticising only its "adolescent jokes", and named it one of nine great games for 1989.

title: Super Mario All-Stars
description: Super Mario All-Stars (1993) is Nintendo's SNES compilation remaking the first four Super Mario games with 16-bit graphics, new music and save files, and the first Western release of The Lost Levels.
longDescription:
The compilation contains faithful remakes of Super Mario Bros., Super Mario Bros.: The Lost Levels, Super Mario Bros. 2 and Super Mario Bros. 3, with their original premises and level designs intact, plus a two-player bonus game based on Mario Bros. reached from Super Mario Bros. 3. As in the originals, players guide Mario and Luigi through themed worlds, jumping between platforms, avoiding enemies and obstacles, finding secrets such as warp zones and vines, and collecting power-ups like the mushroom and the Invincibility Star. Three of the games are about rescuing Princess Toadstool from Bowser by stomping enemies and breaking bricks.

Super Mario Bros. 2 has a different story and style: Mario, Luigi, the Princess and Toad must defeat King Wart, who has cursed the land of dreams, by throwing vegetables and other objects, with the player choosing a character at the start of each life. The remakes add updated graphics, including parallax scrolling, new arrangements of the music, modified physics, the ability to save progress and bug fixes. Their designs were based on Super Mario World while trying to keep the feel of the originals. Critics considered it one of the best SNES games, Electronic Gaming Monthly calling it a "masterpiece from beginning to end" and Computer and Video Games a Super Mario director's cut, though some noted its lack of innovation.
trivia: Its working title was Mario Extravaganza.
Shigeru Miyamoto suggested the "value pack" partly so players could experience The Lost Levels.
It filled a gap in Nintendo's schedule while Yoshi's Island was still in production.
A 1994 re-release added Super Mario World.
It sold 10.55 million copies by 2015.
devStory: Nintendo Entertainment Analysis & Development made it after finishing Super Mario Kart, when Miyamoto proposed a value pack of all the Super Mario games; assistant director Tadashi Sugiyama said the aim was to let players try The Lost Levels, which Nintendo had once judged too difficult for the West. Freed from the NES's limits, the team rebuilt the games for the SNES. Released worldwide in late 1993, it was acclaimed as a must-have, Nintendo Magazine System estimating it could entertain players for up to a year. Famitsu described it as a model for video game remakes, and it was re-released for the 25th anniversary on Wii in 2010 and the 35th on Nintendo Switch in 2020.

title: Maui Mallard in Cold Shadow
description: Maui Mallard in Cold Shadow (1995) is Disney Interactive's platformer starring Donald Duck as a Magnum P.I.-style detective who switches into a staff-wielding ninja to recover a stolen island idol.
longDescription:
Donald Duck plays Maui Mallard, a "medium-boiled" detective spoofing Magnum P.I., visiting a tropical island when the Shabuhm Shabuhm idol, the island's guardian spirit, goes missing; unless it is recovered, the whole island will explode. His investigation leads through a creepy mansion, ancient ninja training grounds where he learns to become Cold Shadow, and a native village, where he is thrown into a volcano as a sacrifice, survives, and passes the "test of duckhood" to win the islanders' trust. In the North American versions all references to Donald are removed, because, according to composer Patrick Collins, marketing felt Donald Duck was not cool in the United States.

Its most distinctive feature is switching forms. Maui fights with a pistol that fires several kinds of bugs, some combinable for greater effect. From the second level he can become his ninja alter ego Cold Shadow, who fights up close with a bo staff and uses it to explore, for example climbing narrow tunnels. After that, the player can switch at will if they have enough ninja tokens, which on SNES also determine how many attacks Cold Shadow can chain, while the Mega Drive version uses separate red tokens for strength. Some levels force one form, since Cold Shadow cannot bungee jump on vines. Critics praised the large, non-linear levels, detailed graphics and the depth the two personas add.
trivia: It was originally released as Donald in Maui Mallard.
Inspirations included Hawaii Five-O, Magnum P.I., martial arts films, Earthworm Jim, Gunstar Heroes and Vectorman.
Creative Capers Entertainment helped with the animation.
A PlayStation sequel, Maui Mallard and the Lost City of Dread, was cancelled.
It was re-released on Steam and GOG in May 2019.
devStory: After Aladdin's success, Disney brought game development in-house rather than licensing to outside studios, and because its business model relied on existing characters, the detective was played by Donald Duck to give a clear brand identity; the design document was compiled in July 1994. It was released on the Mega Drive in Europe in November 1995, ported to the Super NES by Eurocom, to Windows in 1996 and to the Game Boy by Bonsai Entertainment in 1998. It received positive reviews: GameSpot called it "quite possibly the best low-tech title to come out this year" and GamePro "well-crafted entertainment for novice and veteran gamers", though critics noted control problems.

title: Crusader of Centy
description: Crusader of Centy (1994), known as Soleil in Europe, is Nextech's Zelda-style Genesis adventure in which a 14-year-old loses the ability to talk to humans but gains animal companions with special powers.
longDescription:
In Soleil Town, law requires every 14-year-old boy to train for battle, and Corona has just come of age, inheriting the sword and shield of his late father, a celebrated defender of the city. Monsters threaten humanity's existence. Early on, Corona loses the ability to speak to people but gains the power to talk to animals and plants. The story falls into two halves: first he explores and unlocks the world's regions, then, after defeating Dragon, he regains human speech and travels through time to build a better world and understand why the monsters are at war with humanity.

Seen from overhead, play centres on exploring, sword fighting and solving puzzles. Animals join Corona and lend him their abilities while "equipped", two at a time, from his dog, who pins enemies down for him to strike, to a penguin that adds an ice attack to his sword, with 16 animals to find, often opening paths to previously unreachable areas. Its look and mechanics were universally compared to The Legend of Zelda, especially A Link to the Past; Electronic Gaming Monthly called it a worthy Zelda clone, with two reviewers rating it as good as the Zelda games, while GamePro felt it had a too-familiar story and weak enemies.
trivia: It was commissioned under Sega's "Mega Roleplay Project" of seven RPGs from different developers.
Nextech was founded by former Wolf Team designers, who first made Ranger X as GAU Entertainment.
Sega of America passed on it, so Atlus USA published it in North America with its own translation.
The animals have different names in the US and UK versions.
It came to Nintendo Switch Online in June 2023.
devStory: Nextech developed it as its second game, conceived as an action RPG because the hero gains skills one after another. In the early 1990s Sega was losing Japan's RPG market to Nintendo despite Phantasy Star, Shining and Lunar, so in 1994 it announced the Mega Roleplay Project, of which this was part. Sega released it in Japan in 1994 and in PAL regions in 1995, and Atlus USA released it in North America in 1995. Reviews were largely positive for its gameplay, graphics and story, with some criticism of the controls and sound, and Japan's Micom BASIC Magazine ranked it fourth in popularity in September 1994.

title: Vectorman 2
description: Vectorman 2 (1996) is BlueSky Software's late Genesis sequel in which the orb-bodied robot fights a plague of mutant insects, morphing into the creatures he defeats.
longDescription:
After saving Earth in the first game, Vectorman's spaceship is shot down by a missile. He parachutes to the planet near an old research facility and finds it overrun by aggressive, destructive mutant insects, and sets out to wipe them out. Unlike the post-apocalyptic first game, he crosses a wide range of modern settings before reaching the source of the infestation, the evil Black Widow Queen.

It keeps the original's 2D action-platform play of running, jumping and shooting. There are 22 levels, more than the first game's 16 but generally shorter and smaller. His default shot fires in a straight line, but weapon upgrades found in levels change it and raise its damage. Vectorman can again morph into other forms, now by defeating particular enemies: beating a scorpion lets him walk on hot surfaces unharmed, while a rhinoceros beetle gives him a horned head for ramming foes. A bar of orbs shows his health, refilled by health orbs, and losing it all costs a life and restarts the level. Difficulty can be adjusted. GamePro praised its "cleaner graphics, more sound and voice effects, and faster, smoother gameplay" over the original.
trivia: Keith Freiheit, lead programmer of BlueSky's first Jurassic Park game, replaced original programmer Richard Karp.
Like the Genesis Sonic games, it reused its predecessor's engine.
It came out a year after the original, near the end of the Genesis's life.
Electronic Gaming Monthly gave it 7.25 out of 10.
Several Vectorman 3 proposals were made to Sega, but none came to fruition.
devStory: After its Jurassic Park games, BlueSky Software had made Vectorman under an exclusive Sega contract as a pre-rendered rival to Donkey Kong Country, and its success led to an immediate sequel. Development was rushed, since the Genesis was nearing its end and new releases were becoming rare in 1996. Sega published it that year. It was praised as one of the few late Genesis games that was not a cheap licensed cash-in and for pushing the hardware, but was generally viewed less favourably than the original and struggled to compete with the Donkey Kong Country sequels. EGM's reviewers liked its graphics and animation, though Sushi-X found its levels disappointingly small.

title: Golden Axe III
description: Golden Axe III (1993) is Sega's Japan-only Mega Drive sequel in which four new warriors battle Damud Hellstrike, who has stolen the Golden Axe and cursed the land's heroes.
longDescription:
Damud Hellstrike, the Prince of Darkness, has taken the Golden Axe, kidnapped the princess of Yuria, turned the king into a griffin minion called Eve and cursed all the warriors. The dwarf Gilius Thunderhead from the first game lifts the curse from one hero, who must free the others, defeat the villain and bring back the axe. The heroes are the giant Proud Cragger, the humanoid black panther Chronos "Evil" Rait, the swordsman Kain Grinder, who resembles Ax Battler, and the swordswoman Sarah Burn, who resembles Tyris Flare; Gilius appears only in cut-scenes.

Play is essentially that of the earlier games, side-scrolling through levels and fighting with weapons, fists, ridden Bizarrians and elemental magic, but with new moves: blocking, sweeps, projectiles, special attacks and improved grappling. Proud has a devastating air-slam throw, Chronos and Sarah can double jump and wall jump, and each character has a super move, a screen-crossing projectile or, for Chronos, an unstoppable lunge. In co-op, players can perform team attacks such as a human slingshot. Branching paths let players choose routes, freeing enough prisoners from barrels, crystal cells and guards earns extra lives, and the potion-carrying gnomes of the first game return, as does its all-at-once magic system.
trivia: It was released in Japan only, later reaching North America through the Sega Channel in 1995.
The Sega Channel version renamed Kain and Sarah as Ax Battler and Tyris Flare.
EGM told readers not to waste money importing it, calling its graphics plain.
IGN gave the Virtual Console release five out of ten.
It appears in Sega Genesis Collection and Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Mega Drive in 1993 as the sequel to Golden Axe II, bringing back features dropped from that game while adding new characters, moves and branching routes. Reception was mixed. Japanese readers of Mega Drive Fan and Sega Saturn Magazine rated it modestly, and Electronic Gaming Monthly said Sega of Japan was right not to release it in the US, calling its graphics "some of the most plain looking on the Mega Drive" and its magic effects unimpressive. IGN's Virtual Console review agreed that its quality was low. It was later re-released on PlayStation 2, PSP, Xbox 360, PlayStation 3, the Wii Virtual Console and Sega Genesis Classics.

title: Boogerman: A Pick and Flick Adventure
description: Boogerman: A Pick and Flick Adventure (1994) is Interplay's gross-out platformer in which millionaire Snotty Ragsdale becomes a booger-flicking, burping superhero to recover a stolen power source from Dimension X-Crement.
longDescription:
One stormy night, Professor Stinkbaum is building the Zap-o-Matic in his lab above Takey Dump, a machine to save the world from pollution by sending it to Dimension X-Crement. Eccentric millionaire Snotty Ragsdale, suspicious of the project, visits just as it is switched on, inhales a cloud of pepper and sneezes so hard he breaks the machine, opening a portal. A giant arm reaches out and steals its power source, Snotrium 357, so Snotty changes into his alter ego Boogerman in the men's room and jumps through the portal after it.

It is a straightforward side-scroller in which Boogerman attacks with burps, farts and flicked boogers across more than 20 levels and a final boss. Each level involves a light puzzle to reach the end and enemies unique to that level. His health is shown by his cape, which turns from red to yellow when hit; a second hit melts him away and costs a life, and collecting capes restores it. Huts act as checkpoints when touched, and after the final boss the credits scroll by in a playable sandbox where Boogerman can "fly-fart" with unlimited fuel. GamePro found that, gross as it was, it was fun to play, "almost a parody of last year's Disney's Aladdin" with extensive, challenging levels.
trivia: Interplay wanted a gross-out game for the Garbage Pail Kids audience.
Several bosses, including BoogerMiester, began as concept designs for Boogerman himself.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named Boogerman the Grossest Character of 1994.
Boogerman is a playable rival of Earthworm Jim in ClayFighter 63⅓.
A 2013 Kickstarter for an HD sequel fell short.
devStory: According to Chris Tremmel, Interplay asked Mike Stragey for a gross-out game, and Stragey came up with a gross superhero, the two never short of ideas for characters and locations; they worked closely with Little Gangster on the designs, going through dozens before settling on the final look. Interplay released it for the Genesis in 1994 and the Super NES in 1995, the latter with more colours, better voice clips, stronger bass and improved controls.
