Game Informer gave it 7.5 out of 10, saying "if you're looking for an action/platform game with a touch of the crass, look no further than Boogerman." It returned on the Wii Virtual Console in 2008.

sources.title: Boogerman: A Pick and Flick Adventure

title: Top Gear 2
description: Top Gear 2 (1993) is Gremlin's arcade racing sequel, more realistic than the first, with car damage, weather, upgrades and 64 tracks across 16 countries.
longDescription:
Like the first game, it reuses graphics and play from Gremlin's Lotus trilogy, but adds realism: a damage diagram on the left of the screen, slower and harder-handling cars, tougher, faster opponents and weather that forces switches between dry and wet tyres. There are 64 tracks in 16 countries of four races each, from Australasia to the United States, with a password after each country. Players must finish in the top ten to qualify, using six nitro boosts and road pickups for cash, extra nitro or an instant boost. If armour on part of the car is destroyed, further hits there cause a spin, and running out of fuel means disqualification.

With no pit stops, upgrading the gearbox becomes essential for the fuel economy needed in later, longer races, though the Genesis port has no fuel gauge. Prize money buys engine upgrades for acceleration and higher gears, stronger nitro, gearboxes for top speed and economy, more armour, better tyres for grip and new paint. Players can choose automatic or manual gears and configure the controls. Because of naming rights, Egypt's Giza Necropolis is renamed after Hugh Sitton, a Corbis photographer. Super Gamer gave the SNES version 83 per cent for its better graphics and more depth, and GamePro said that "for simple, straightforward fun, Top Gear 2 still qualifies".
trivia: In Japan it was released as Top Racer 2.
Kemco released it on the SNES in North America in September 1993.
Gremlin ported it to Amiga and CD32 in 1994.
Vic Tokai released the Genesis version.
IGN ranked it 95th in its top 100 SNES games.
devStory: Gremlin Interactive developed it as a direct sequel to 1992's Top Gear, and Kemco published it for the SNES in North America in September 1993 and in Japan that December, keeping the arcade-style play the series was known for while making it more realistic. Gremlin brought it to the Amiga and Amiga CD32 in September 1994, and Vic Tokai to the Genesis the same year. Nintendo Power gave the SNES version 3.55 out of 5, and GamePro felt the Genesis version had plenty of tracks and solid controls but seemed outdated next to newer racers because of its limited car configuration.

title: Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back
description: Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1993) is the SNES sequel to Super Star Wars, following the film with Luke, Han and Chewbacca, new Force powers and Mode 7 battles on Hoth.
longDescription:
Based on the 1980 film, it follows the formula of Super Star Wars with multiple playable characters and Mode 7 quasi-3D vehicle sequences, including an attack on the AT-ATs that Super Gamer called "absolutely stunning". Luke Skywalker, Han Solo and Chewbacca return, though the character select option is gone, and the controls add a double jump. Each character now has a primary and secondary weapon: Han can throw grenades, Chewbacca has a new spinning attack, and Luke can deflect blaster fire with his lightsaber. After a mission on the swamp planet Dagobah, Luke can also collect Force powers to use in later levels, and Darth Vader is the final boss.

Critics praised the graphics, sound and cinematic presentation faithful to the film, but criticised the controls, the hard difficulty, blind jumps and the large numbers of enemies, some hitting from off screen. AllGame gave it four and a half stars, valuing the password feature for making it less frustrating, and Power Unlimited gave it 92 per cent for its challenge and fun. Complex later ranked it the 20th best SNES game, calling it the best Star Wars game on the system though the hardest of the three.
trivia: A Mode 7 asteroid chase was cut for lack of cartridge space.
An EGM contest winner, Jeff Crosno, had his face put on a Rebel soldier in a Hoth cut-scene.
Unlike its predecessor, Nintendo was not involved in publishing it.
It was the UK's top-selling SNES game in February 1994.
GamePro named it the best SNES game of 1993.
devStory: LucasArts and Sculptured Software developed it and JVC Musical Industries published it for the Super NES in 1993, the sequel to Super Star Wars. It was well received: IGN gave it 7.5 for its enhanced Mode 7 graphics and ranked it 91st among SNES games, and Nintendo Power rated it the fourth best SNES game of 1993. In 1996 THQ announced a re-release for February 1997, alongside Super Return of the Jedi, to coincide with the Special Edition films, and it came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2009. Super Star Wars: Return of the Jedi followed in 1994.

sources.title: Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back

title: Super Star Wars: Return of the Jedi
description: Super Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (1994) is the final SNES Super Star Wars, adding Leia and Wicket to the playable heroes and the Endor speeder bike chase to the Mode 7 sequences.
longDescription:
Loosely following Return of the Jedi, with added scenes such as Luke fighting his way through the Death Star to reach the Emperor, it keeps the formula of the previous two games: selectable characters on certain levels, several playable heroes, Mode 7 vehicle sequences and the second game's controls and password saves. Luke, Han and Chewbacca are joined by Princess Leia and the Ewok Wicket. Bosses include Jabba the Hutt, the Rancor, Darth Vader and the Emperor, and vehicle sequences include the Endor speeder bike chase and a run in the Millennium Falcon.

Luke now has five Force powers rather than nine, recharges them more easily and can no longer use blasters. Leia changes look and fighting style with the plot, wielding a staff disguised as the bounty hunter Boushh at Jabba's palace, a broken chain as Jabba's escaped slave on his sail barge, and a blaster as a Rebel leader on Endor. Reaction was divided: GamePro praised the score but criticised frustrating controls, easy bosses and levels that felt like retreads of the previous games, while Electronic Gaming Monthly praised its "excellent" graphics and the need to move carefully through levels. IGN later ranked it 26th among SNES games for the variety its five characters bring.
trivia: LucasArts released it alongside Indiana Jones' Greatest Adventures.
Realtime Associates made Game Boy and Game Gear versions published by THQ in 1995.
EGM named it Best Movie-to-Game of 1994.
EGM and GamePro both named it Best Game Gear Game of 1995.
Complex ranked it 67th among the best SNES games in 2018.
devStory: LucasArts and Sculptured Software developed it and JVC Musical Industries published it for the Super NES in 1994, completing the Super Star Wars trilogy. GamePro rated the Game Boy version "one of the year's most fun and challenging handheld games" thanks to its five playable characters, and said the Game Gear version's graphics were nearly as good as the SNES's. THQ re-released it in February 1997 to coincide with the Special Edition films, and it came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2009 alongside the other Super Star Wars games. Complex felt it was almost as great as its predecessors but less difficult.

sources.title: Super Star Wars: Return of the Jedi

title: Last Ninja 2: Back with a Vengeance
description: Last Ninja 2: Back with a Vengeance (1988) is System 3's isometric action-adventure in which the ninja Armakuni is pulled into 20th-century New York to face the shogun Kunitoki again.
longDescription:
After the events of The Last Ninja, Armakuni holds the Koga scrolls and has begun training a new order of shadow warriors. During a training session he is mysteriously transported to New York City in the 20th century, and, torn from his own time, must defeat the evil shogun Kunitoki once more. Each level shows a different part of the city, divided into several screens and presented in an isometric view, in which the ninja can move in eight directions and jump.

Enemies armed with fists and ninja weapons wander the levels, and the ninja fights them bare-handed or with weapons found along the way, using a range of blows and attacks and the ability to block. Shuriken are thrown in a straight line rather than used in melee, killing or badly wounding any enemy they hit. Keys, a rope, a map and other items are scattered around, and collecting them and using them in the right place is essential to finishing the game, while hamburgers give an extra life when eaten. The Limited Edition of the original release came with a ninja mask and a rubber shuriken.
trivia: System 3's Mark Cale said the C64 version alone sold 5.5 million copies.
On that estimate, around one in four C64 owners bought it.
The NES version was simply titled The Last Ninja.
A 1990 Remix edition added an intro and a remixed soundtrack by Reyn Ouwehand.
It was runner-up for Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards.
devStory: System 3 developed and published it in 1988 for the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC as the sequel to The Last Ninja, with ports to the Acorn Electron, BBC Micro, Amiga, Atari ST, MS-DOS and NES following. It was an enormous commercial success, and in 2004 Retro Gamer readers voted it the 68th top retro game. Last Ninja 3 followed in 1991. The source code of a version for the Konix console was discovered in 2015, and City Connection re-released the NES version on Nintendo Switch in June 2025, the game's first release in Japan.

title: Magic Pockets
description: Magic Pockets (1991) is the Bitmap Brothers' first cute platformer, in which the Bitmap Kid chases the creatures who stole the toys from his bottomless trouser pockets.
longDescription:
The Bitmap Kid has magic trousers whose pockets hold an infinite amount, so he keeps all his toys in them. One day the creatures living in his pockets decide to keep the toys for themselves, and he sets out to get them back. He walks, jumps and hurls things at enemies across four areas, Cave, Jungle, River and Mountain, each split into stages, with a bonus stage tied to the toy being recovered: the bike, found in the caves, is won back in a bike race against the creatures.

The Kid's attack changes in each area and can be charged by holding fire; the biggest shot sucks enemies up instead of destroying them and turns them into pickups. Sweets add points, while silver and then gold stars produce helmets that grant temporary powers such as teleporting, laser beams or invincibility. Chewing gum from dispensers blows a bubble to float on, sometimes into secret areas. There is no timer, but dawdling brings a transparent bubble that chases the Kid ever faster, trapping him and stripping his power-ups, or on the last stage killing him. The title track is an instrumental of Betty Boo's "Doin' the Do".
trivia: Inspirations included Super Mario Bros., Rainbow Islands and Flood.
Renegade was part of the record label Rhythm King, which released Betty Boo's song.
Viewers of the TV show Motormouth played it by phoning in commands.
It was released for Atari ST, Amiga, Acorn Archimedes and MS-DOS.
A Game Boy Advance version announced in 2002 was never released.
devStory: The Bitmap Brothers developed it as their first attempt at a "cutesy platform game", and Renegade Software published it in October 1991. Because Renegade belonged to the music company Rhythm King, a remix of Betty Boo's "Doin' the Do" was used for the opening. It was played between cartoons on the Saturday morning show Motormouth, with callers giving the commands, and it received generally positive reviews from critics.

title: Splatterhouse 3
description: Splatterhouse 3 (1993) is Namco's gory Genesis beat 'em up in which Rick dons the Terror Mask a third time to save his family from monsters in their mansion, racing timers that change the story.
longDescription:
About five years after Splatterhouse 2, Rick and Jennifer have married and had a son, David, and Rick has made a fortune on Wall Street and bought a mansion in Connecticut, leaving the Terror Mask behind. But the Mask senses an ancient energy and speaks to him again, and Rick must put it on once more to fight the monsters that have invaded his home, beginning with saving Jennifer from an entity known as the Evil One. Unlike the earlier side-scrollers, its six levels, many set in the mansion, are explored non-linearly across rooms, often with backtracking, guided by a map of each level.

Each level has a time limit; running out does not end the game but changes the plot, leading to four possible endings. In the second level, for example, Rick must defeat a boreworm planted inside Jennifer before time runs out, or she is devoured from within. New is a Power Meter filled by Eldritch Orbs found in levels or dropped by enemies, which lets Rick transform into a hulking, more monstrous form with the Mask fused to his head, far stronger and able to launch pieces of flesh from his chest at nearby monsters, and to fling weapons rather than swing them. Weapons such as baseball bats and cleavers, extra lives, health items and passwords also appear.
trivia: In Japan it is called Splatterhouse Part 3.
It was one of the first games rated by Sega's Videogame Rating Council, receiving MA-13.
Unlike its predecessors, it was not originally released in Europe.
It was an unlockable extra in the 2010 Splatterhouse remake, with new art replacing its digitised photos.
AllGame said it "stands at the top of the beat-'em-up heap on Genesis".
devStory: Now Production developed it and Namco published it for the Sega Genesis in 1993 as the sequel to Splatterhouse 2, its graphic violence and gore earning an MA-13 rating in North America. Fangoria's Russ Ceccola wrote that the series' appeal was its bloody violence, "explicit and gross, but in an over-the-top way", and that the new map, time limits and multiple endings still boiled down to "cartoon violence taken to the extreme". AllGame's Geoffrey Douglas Smith called it "a fun and gory ride with plenty of enemies to pummel and a solid game engine".

title: Ecco: The Tides of Time
description: Ecco: The Tides of Time (1994) is Novotrade's sequel in which Ecco the dolphin travels to a future of flying dolphins and fights the returning Vortex Queen, gaining the power to transform into other creatures.
longDescription:
After saving his pod and the Earth from the Vortex aliens, Ecco is exploring a cave when an earthquake triggers an avalanche, and he finds the Asterite's powers have left him, along with his freedom from needing air. Something has killed the Asterite and is spreading fear through the ocean. Ecco meets Trellia, a long-finned descendant who takes him to a future where the ocean has its own mind, linked by waterways through the sky, and dolphins fly using helium sacs and telekinesis. There the future Asterite explains that the Vortex Queen survived, followed Ecco to Earth and killed the Asterite of his time, and that his trip in the Atlantean Time Machine split time in two: one future of flying dolphins, the other a dead, mechanical world drained by the Vortex.

Play is much as before: Ecco rams enemies at speed, uses sonar to talk to other cetaceans, activate crystal Glyphs and map his surroundings, combines charge and sonar for ranged attacks, and must surface for air. New puzzles include following dolphins through a maze and hunting for the Asterite's missing globes. The Pulsar power-up fires multi-directional sonar for a stage, and the Metasphere transforms Ecco into level-specific animals such as a seagull, jellyfish, shark, school of fish or Vortex drone. Some stages use a pseudo-3D effect in which Ecco swims through moving rings while dodging or attacking enemies.
trivia: In Japan it was titled Ecco the Dolphin 2.
It was released on most of Sega's then-supported consoles.
Ecco is called "the stone that split the stream of time in two".
Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the Genesis version 7.25 out of 10.
GamePro found it more accessible than the original, while two EGM reviewers found it harder.
devStory: Novotrade International developed it and Sega published it in 1994 as the second Ecco game, continuing the original's story with similar play and new additions. GamePro said it kept the best points of the first game, its concept and lifelike animation, praised Ecco's new transformations and called the audio "simple, soothing and effective", recommending it as an improvement. Electronic Gaming Monthly also called it an improvement and applauded its remarkably colourful graphics, and Next Generation gave it three stars, citing its "taxing puzzles, RPG elements, shooting stages, and some of the best Genesis graphics to date".

title: ToeJam & Earl in Panic on Funkotron
description: ToeJam & Earl in Panic on Funkotron (1993) is the funky aliens' platforming sequel, in which they jar up the Earthlings who stowed away to their home planet, a sharp break from the original's roguelike style.
longDescription:
Having escaped Earth in the first game, ToeJam and Earl return to their home planet of Funkotron only to discover that a bunch of Earthlings stowed away on their spaceship. The humans are spreading panic across the planet, even scaring Lamont the Funkapotomus, the source of all funk, away into another dimension, so the duo must clean up the mess they made and send every Earthling back home. Unlike its predecessor, a treasure hunt with randomly generated levels inspired by Rogue, it is a side-scrolling platformer for one or two players.

Players use a radar to locate nearby Earthlings, some hidden in the scenery, and throw jars at them to trap and collect them before sending them back to Earth. Contemporary critics praised its graphics, its Herbie Hancock-inspired soundtrack, fluid, non-violent action and two-player mode: the Chicago Tribune called it a "beautifully designed game", and The Washington Times "one of the funniest games we've ever seen", with superb graphics and "flawless" action and control. Fans of the original, however, were disappointed and confused by the move to a more generic format, and later reviewers felt the developers had followed the publisher's wishes rather than the fans'.
trivia: The developers' first sequel prototype kept the original's style, with ToeJam and Earl staging a rap concert on Earth.
Greg Johnson and Mark Voorsanger have said they regret abandoning that prototype.
Mega ranked it 14th among the best Mega Drive games.
GamesRadar ranked it the tenth best Genesis game in 2014.
Research suggests a significant minority of fans consider it the series' best.
devStory: After the original's success, Johnson Voorsanger Productions began a sequel in 1992, spending three to four months building on the first game's mechanics, with indoor areas, new terrain and fixed levels, before switching to a more generic platformer for lack of support from Sega. Sega published it for the Genesis in 1993, and it was well reviewed and commercially successful. Together with its predecessor it formed one of the Mega Drive's key exclusive franchises, but after Johnson and Voorsanger split with Sega the series went quiet until a commercially unsuccessful third game in 2002. It was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007, PlayStation Network and Xbox Live Arcade in 2012, and Nintendo Classics in 2024.

sources.title: ToeJam & Earl in Panic on Funkotron

title: Decap Attack
description: Decap Attack (1991) is Vic Tokai's Genesis platformer starring Chuck D. Head, a headless mummy who punches enemies with the face in his torso, a gothic Western makeover of Magical Hat.
longDescription:
Dr. Frank N. Stein and his assistant Igor create Chuck D. Head, a headless mummy with a face in his chest, and send him to defeat Max D. Cap, a demon from the Underworld whose monster army is conquering the surface and has split the skeleton-shaped island chain into pieces. Levels are named after parts of the skeleton, such as Abdomainland and Armington, and some require Chuck to collect an item for Dr. Stein. After reuniting the islands and defeating Max, Chuck trudges home, where Stein rewards him by turning him into a human.

Chuck attacks by thrusting his face out of his torso or jumping on enemies, and tapping jump slows his fall. A skull power-up sits on his shoulders like a head and can be thrown like a boomerang, always returning until Chuck is hit. Potions collected along the way can be used at will for effects such as invincibility or wiping out every enemy on screen, red totem poles restore health when landed on, and crouching to slide down a ramp knocks out an approaching enemy. Each area ends with a boss. Players choose up to three hearts per life in the options, rising to five with upgrades, whereas in the Japanese original a single hit was fatal. Sega Force praised its "big, bold, colourfully and beautifully animated" graphics but found it unoriginal.
trivia: It is a Westernised version of the 1990 Mega Drive game Magical Hat no Buttobi Tābo! Daibōken.
Art, plot, music and level designs were all changed from the Japanese original.
Both games descend from Kid Kool and Psycho Fox.
A comic strip based on it ran in the UK's Sonic the Comic.
Mega ranked it 22nd among the best Mega Drive games.
devStory: Vic Tokai developed it and Sega published it for the Genesis in 1991, reworking Magical Hat's play with new graphics, characters, music and levels for Western audiences; in Magical Hat, the flagpoles that restore health in Decap Attack award lives instead. Console XS noted it was the same game with gothic graphics and gory kills but found it big and very playable, and MegaTech called it "a fun-filled platform game". It has since appeared in several emulated compilations.

title: Ranger X
description: Ranger X (1993) is GAU Entertainment's Genesis run and gun in which a jet-packing exoskeleton pilot and his robot motorcycle fight off an invasion, with graphics that seemed to break the console's colour limits.
longDescription:
The player is Ranger X, pilot of a powered exoskeleton leading the fight to reclaim his home planet from the invading Rahuna forces. A jet pack allows short flights limited by its temperature, forcing a landing to cool down when it overheats. Alongside a standard pulse rifle, Ranger X has special weapons such as a flamethrower and homing attacks, which drain a power bar that only recharges under a bright light source, and more are added by collecting power-ups. On some levels he is joined by a support vehicle, an Ex-Up such as Indra, a futuristic motorcycle, a premise described as "RoboCop on a Harley", which moves and fires independently but can be ridden for its separate shielding.

Each level opens with a wireframe 3D cut-scene setting out the targets, and the player must fight through enemy forces, destroy every objective and then the stage boss to advance. Critics praised the tactics offered by the weapons and the need to manage the support vehicle; GamePro said "the unique dual action of flying and riding a motorcycle gives this game a step up against over other shooters". The graphics impressed most, with some reviews claiming it broke through the Mega Drive's colour limits and EGM calling them "some of the best graphics ever seen" on the system, though MegaTech noticed some sprite flicker.
trivia: It was the first game by GAU Entertainment, now Nex Entertainment, founded by former Wolf Team staff.
The team used no design documents, adding elements whenever memory allowed.
GAU built custom tools to push the Mega Drive to its limits.
Yoshinobu Hiraiwa composed the music and Noriyuki Iwadare made the sound effects.
GAU later renamed itself Nextech and made Crusader of Centy.
devStory: Designers Toshio Toyota and Toshio Yamamoto led development, with artist Ree Senfhu co-creating the pixel art. Yamamoto said the team relied on intuition rather than copying other games, aiming for a high-quality Mega Drive title, and that polish gave the visuals "a lot of shine too". Toyota, who had long wanted to make a side-scrolling robot action game, said they started by asking what makes a game fun and found the Mega Drive easy to work with, its colour problem being "a question of subtlety on the designer's part". Sega published it in 1993, and reception was generally positive, though some found its difficulty too high.

title: Sub-Terrania
description: Sub-Terrania (1994) is Zyrinx's gravity-bound Genesis shooter in which a lone pilot rescues miners from an alien invasion, fighting gravity, inertia and dwindling fuel in underground caverns.
longDescription:
On an off-world asteroid, aliens invade a vital subterranean mining colony, destroying its headquarters and leaving workers trapped in crevices as radioactive dust swirls toward them. The only weapon able to repel them is an experimental attack fighter, and a lone pilot must defeat the aliens and rescue the miners. Seen from the side underground, the ship is always pulled down by gravity, which can be used to save fuel. As in Gravitar and Thrust, the directional pad rotates the ship and a button thrusts in the direction it faces, but Sub-Terrania adds back thrusters for reversing away from enemy fire.

Each of the nine levels is an enclosed map that can be explored in any direction, with objectives set out beforehand except in the last three: rescuing miners, carrying and using special equipment, collecting sub modules that let the ship go underwater, and defeating alien bosses. Finding efficient routes is central. The ship's force field gives way after too much damage, and limited fuel must be topped up from strategically placed canisters, so refuelling has to be planned, while mining rails let the ship slide along and fire. Critics praised its "excellent" graphics, smooth parallax, physics and "superb" pseudo-industrial soundtrack, which Mean Machines Sega likened to Depeche Mode crossed with Martin Galway's C64 music.
trivia: Zyrinx was formed by Danish members of the demo groups Crionics and The Silents.
The Swedish members of those groups formed DICE instead.
Its style echoes the 1991 Amiga demo Hardwired.
Jesper Kyd was among Zyrinx's founders.
Edge noted there was never any slowdown, however busy the screen.
devStory: It was the first game from Zyrinx, a small Danish studio of demoscene veterans, David Guldbrandsen, Karsten Hvidberg, Jens Bo Albretsen, Michael Balle, Jesper Jørgensen and Jesper Kyd, who chose the Mega Drive partly because of how many sprites it could handle. Sega published it in 1994. It gained a reputation for being overly difficult and sold poorly, but critics were positive, describing it as an evolution of gravity shooters like Gravitar and Thrust and praising its originality, graphics and music, while noting its controls and physics took time to master. Zyrinx followed it with Red Zone.

title: Urban Strike
description: Urban Strike (1994) is the third Strike helicopter game, taking the fight across North America against a media mogul building a superweapon, and adding on-foot missions.
longDescription:
In 2001, H. R. Malone, a charismatic millionaire media mogul and failed presidential candidate, plans a superweapon to destabilise the US government. Strike C.O.R.E. spy Agent Ego, a former co-pilot from Jungle Strike, reports that components are being gathered in Hawaii, but Malone uncovers him and kills him with a car bomb. In Hawaii the player stops a theft of giant mirrors and saves a plastic surgeon who reveals that the man he once operated on, now Malone, was really Carlos Ortega, presumed killed in Jungle Strike. After missions in Mexico and San Francisco, Malone fires the weapon at New York, and its later shots lead Strike C.O.R.E. to a facility near Las Vegas, where Malone dies on his own weapon.

It keeps the series' helicopter mix of action and strategy while adding vehicles and settings across Hawaii, Mexico, San Francisco, New York and Las Vegas. The main helicopter is the fast, combat-ready Mohican; the heavier Blackhawke, built for large rescues, can be flown in the first two levels, and an experimental Ground Assault Vehicle can be stolen in the third. New on-foot missions take the player out of the helicopter and inside buildings with a rifle and missile launcher. Levels are made of missions to destroy weapons and installations and rescue hostages. GamePro called it "a top-notch helicopter-combat cart".
trivia: Its subtitle is The Sequel to Jungle Strike.
Co-designer Tony Barnes played Agent Ego.
It had a marketing budget of £500,000.
Black Pearl Software ported it to SNES, Game Gear and Game Boy, moving the story to 2006.
Mega gave it 88 per cent, saying EA had "taken the genre as far as it can go".
devStory: Electronic Arts developed and published it for the Genesis in 1994 as the third Strike game, after Desert Strike and Jungle Strike, followed by Black Pearl Software's ports in 1995 and 1996. GamePro praised its ten massive missions, mix of air and ground combat, new helicopter moves and techno soundtrack. Next Generation gave both the Genesis and SNES versions three stars, finding the SNES version more colourful but with less smooth controls and animation, and felt the formula was growing stale while still delivering for those wanting more of the same. Russia's Great Drakon found it too easy, the weakest of the series.

title: Skitchin'
description: Skitchin' (1994) is EA Canada's Road Rash-powered inline skating racer, in which skaters fight with chains and bats and hitch rides on car bumpers through twelve cities.
longDescription:
An inline skater competes in a tournament across twelve cities, including Vancouver, New York City and San Diego, needing fifth place or better to advance. Skaters can accelerate, jump, crouch, attack rivals and skitch, grabbing a moving vehicle's bumper for momentum, then launch off to slingshot to another vehicle or shake off an opponent trying to shove them away. Nunchaku, chains, pipes, crowbars, whips and baseball bats can be picked up from the road, often marked by traffic cones, or snatched from rivals mid-swing, and several can be carried at once. Ramps allow tricks scored by a trio of judges.

The skater starts with $100 and earns more by winning, skitching, performing tricks and knocking down opponents, while every race charges an entry fee. Between races, skates, wheels and protective gear wear out and can be replaced in a shop, whose owner refuses any purchase that would leave the skater unable to afford the next race; worn skates risk a blowout and crashing in worn gear means a hospital bill. Skitching on police cars pays more but risks arrest and a fine, and cars grow faster and rivals more aggressive as the tournament goes on. Critics praised its fluid scrolling, large, well-animated sprites and detailed settings, along with its two-player mode, but criticised its lack of level variety.
trivia: Its engine was repurposed from Road Rash.
Animations were rotoscoped from Troy Manering, reputed to be the best skater at Toronto's Skate Ranch.
The team toured Toronto photographing graffiti and recruited teenage graffiti artists.
EA included a disclaimer warning that skitching is dangerous.
Its soundtrack divided critics.
devStory: EA's Canadian division developed it, conceived by Dave Ralston, designed by Dave Warfield and directed by Tim Brengle, with programming by Lance Wall, Daniel Wesley and Lee Ingraham. Reusing the Road Rash engine to capitalise on that series' success, the team rented a warehouse with ramps for Jack Snowden to videotape Manering's moves. Released for the Genesis in 1994, it received generally positive reviews, with critics noting its similarity to Road Rash and finding the concept novel, though Mean Machines Sega and EGM felt the novelty wore off quickly, and GamePro found skitching tricky to master.

title: Pitfall: The Mayan Adventure
description: Pitfall: The Mayan Adventure (1994) is Activision's hand-animated revival of Pitfall!, in which Pitfall Harry Jr. searches the Mayan jungle for his kidnapped father.
longDescription:
After Pitfall II, Pitfall Harry settled down to raise his son, Harry Jr., becoming a legend for his exploits. Inheriting his father's love of exploration, Harry Jr. sets out through the Mayan jungles of Central America to rescue him from the evil Mayan warrior spirit Zakelua. In the style of Disney's Aladdin and The Lion King, it is a side-scrolling action platformer. Early stages are large and linear, full of obstacles, enemies and hazards to be overcome by running, jumping, climbing, swinging, shooting and dodging, while later ones are more maze-like, with different routes to the end, and some end with bosses.

Every stage hides items, ammunition, secrets and letters spelling "Pitfall". Harry Jr. moves in four directions, fights with his whip or with sling stones, boomerangs and explosives, and can charge a sling stone for a powerful shot or crouch to squeeze through tight spaces. Dying returns him to the last checkpoint, and continues or saved games, depending on version, resume progress. Kroyer Films provided hand-drawn animation, and GamePro called the SNES version's animation "some of the best character animations ever seen in an SNES game". The original Pitfall! is included as a bonus, though critics complained about losing control of Harry during certain animations.
trivia: It was first developed for the SNES as Pitfall Harry: The Mayan Adventure.
It was part of planned Activision revivals alongside Kaboom! and River Raid, both cancelled.
Kroyer Films had worked on FernGully: The Last Rainforest.
Early previews promised underwater and flying sections and 32 stages.
It sold over a million copies by June 1996.
devStory: Activision first showed it at the Summer CES in 1993 with sprite-based visuals as part of a string of Atari 2600 revivals. Slated for winter 1993, it slipped to 1994, and Kroyer Films was brought in to provide hand-drawn animation and graphics while the lead platform moved from the SNES to the Genesis. The Genesis and SNES versions launched for the 1994 holidays, followed in 1995 by 32X, Jaguar, PC and Sega CD versions by other developers, each with changes. Reviews were mostly positive for its presentation, visuals and sound, though GamePro noted that the split-second loss of control after jumps and turns could cost a life.

title: Aero the Acro-Bat
description: Aero the Acro-Bat (1993) is Iguana Entertainment's circus platformer starring a red bat who must rescue performers kidnapped by the vengeful industrialist Edgar Ektor.
longDescription:
As a spoiled rich kid, Edgar Ektor was banned from The World of Amusement Circus and Funpark after a prank nearly killed a lion. Twenty years later, now a powerful and evil industrialist, he sabotages the funpark with Zero the Kamikaze Squirrel and his Psycho Circus gang and kidnaps all the performers. Aero the Acro-Bat, the circus's greatest star, is the only hope of rescuing them, including his girlfriend Aeriel, and stopping Edgar.

In four worlds of five large levels each, Aero must complete tasks to reveal the exit warp, such as passing through hoops, stepping on platforms until they vanish and riding roller coasters, while avoiding awkwardly placed spikes that kill instantly. He attacks by throwing a limited supply of stars or with a diagonal aerial drill attack. Scoring enough points opens a bonus level in which Aero dives into a pool; on the Genesis this is a vertical platform level, while the SNES version uses Mode 7 for a dive above an overworld map. Electronic Gaming Monthly gave the SNES version 8.3 and the Genesis version 7.6, missing the SNES's music but praising the large, challenging levels, and named Aero the Best New Character of 1993.
trivia: David Siller created Aero, first sketching him in 1992.
Its mechanics were partly based on Namco's Mappy.
An NES version was planned but cancelled as 16-bit consoles took over.
A Game Boy Advance version in 2002 added battery saves and mission objectives.
It was followed by Aero the Acro-Bat 2 and the spin-off Zero the Kamikaze Squirrel.
devStory: Siller had carried the idea for years; although early designs looked like a human acrobat, he always meant Aero to be a bat. After he joined Sunsoft of America, his son Justin Siller designed the final concept, drawing on mixed themes from the 1970s and 1980s, and much of the work took place in Orange County, California. Iguana Entertainment developed it and Sunsoft published it for the Super NES and Genesis in 1993. Reviews were mixed: GameFan's reviewers scored the Genesis version highly and VideoGames gave both versions eight out of ten, but Digital Press gave it three out of ten. It returned on the Virtual Console in 2010 and on modern consoles in 2024.

title: Bubsy in Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind
description: Bubsy in Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind (1993) is Accolade's wisecracking bobcat platformer, built to be "as fast as Sonic and as deep as Mario", in which Bubsy defends Earth's yarn balls from alien Woolies.
longDescription:
The alien Woolies plan to steal Earth's entire supply of yarn balls, and since Bubsy owns the world's largest collection, he has the most at stake and sets out to stop them. The title is a pun on Close Encounters of the Third Kind. It is a 2D side-scrolling platformer of sixteen levels: Bubsy jumps on Woolies and collects stray yarn balls, earning an extra life for every 500, and starts with nine lives. GamePro praised its graphics and felt Bubsy had more personality than Sonic thanks to his animations and voice clips, and critics liked the non-linear levels, but several complained about his uncontrollable momentum and backgrounds that gave little sense of where a leap would land.

Director John Skeel wanted a game easy to play but hard to master. After weeks of listening to voice tapes he settled on a sped-up recording of Brian Silva, whose delivery drew on Looney Tunes characters such as Daffy Duck and Bugs Bunny, and Bubsy's catchphrase, "What could possibly go wrong?", came from a quip among the team. In December 1992 local children were invited for pizza and soda to playtest it, and their call for more secret paths led to underground tubes in the first level. On the SNES, a catnip hazard that drove Bubsy mad was replaced with banana peels because of Nintendo's censorship policies.
trivia: Designer Michael Berlyn played Sonic the Hedgehog 14 hours a day for a week for inspiration.
Development began on 6 December 1991.
Early sketches gave Bubsy shoes.
It won a Parents' Choice Award for being fun but non-violent.
A Windows port, Super Bubsy, followed in 1997, and Bubsy II in 1994.
devStory: Michael Berlyn, burned out on adventure games, designed it after studying Sonic. The Genesis version was worked on first and due in September 1992, but Accolade's legal troubles with Sega delayed it; artists Beckett Gladney and Ken Macklin created backgrounds and animations on a PC and a group called Solid Software programmed them for the Super NES. More than 20 people worked on the game, and the SNES and Genesis versions were developed and released almost identical, the SNES version first in 1993. Heavily marketed before release, it received generally favourable reviews, and Electronic Games listed it among the best SNES games.

sources.title: Bubsy in Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind

title: Wonder Boy in Monster World
description: Wonder Boy in Monster World (1991) is Westone's side-scrolling action RPG in which the young hero Shion answers a fairy queen's prayer and fights a monster invasion across interconnected lands.
longDescription:
Monster World was once peaceful until an army of monsters appeared from nowhere. The Fairy Queen Eleanora travels to Purapril to ask the Princess for help after her town of Alsedo is attacked, only to find the Princess missing and towns across the land under attack. Her prayer for a hero reaches Shion, a young man who vows to drive out the monsters, and on his travels he is often joined by a small companion who follows him. The quest takes him through many interconnected regions in search of the evil BioMeka.

It controls like a standard platformer, with running, jumping, crouching and attacking, but adds adventure elements: talking to townsfolk, collecting money to buy items, extending the life bar with hearts and equipping a wide range of armour, weapons and magic, as Shion acquires ever stronger swords, spears, shields, armour and boots. The Genesis version introduced a single save slot at inns. In the Japanese original, dying returned Shion to the last inn and charged him its fee, so returning to save could be as simple as dying, but the English versions show a Game Over instead, making early trips back to inns tedious until Return magic is found. The Master System version uses a 45-character password.
trivia: In Japan it is called Monster World III.
It is the fifth Wonder Boy game and third in the Monster World sub-series.
A Master System version was made for Europe in 1993.
Hudson Soft remade it for the TurboDuo as The Dynastic Hero, with a new theme and cast.
EGM gave The Dynastic Hero 7.2 out of 10, while GamePro called it "run of the mill".
devStory: Westone developed it and Sega published it for the Mega Drive in 1991, following Wonder Boy in Monster Land and Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap. In 1994 Hudson Soft remade it for the TurboDuo as The Dynastic Hero, recasting Monster World as the woodland of Tarron, invaded by the reptilian Drillkor Empire, with a hero named Dyna. Electronic Gaming Monthly praised that version's music, graphics and vast size, while GamePro mocked its "doe-eyed" characters but praised its emphasis on action. Both the Mega Drive and Turbo Duo versions came to the Wii Virtual Console in 2007.

title: Monster World IV
description: Monster World IV (1994) is Westone's final Sega-published Wonder Boy game, a Japan-only Mega Drive adventure in which the young warrior Asha and her flying pet Pepelogoo free the elemental spirits.
longDescription:
Asha, a green-haired girl in Arabian-influenced nomadic dress, is sensitive to spirits and hears the Elemental Spirits of Monster World pleading for help on the wind. She sets out to free them, becoming the master of a genie and adopting Pepelogoo, a small, round monster that flies by flapping its ears. The game mixes action-adventure, platforming and RPG elements across a 2D world of monsters and characters to talk to. Asha can swing her sword upward, downward and forward in mid-air depending on the direction pressed, and raise her shield by holding down.

Pepelogoo can be summoned to reach places Asha cannot: holding him slows her fall or gives a double jump, and he can shield her from falling rocks, serve as a platform over lava geysers and blow out fires blocking her path. Armour, bought in the hub town, extends her heart meter; shields raise defence and resist elements like fire and ice; and swords raise attack with special critical effects. Some items must be found in temples and caverns, including medicine that heals or, with Pepelogoo, revives her, and gold bars traded with a rich lady for money. 150 hidden life drops add a blue heart for every ten. Items can be missed for good, as each area becomes inaccessible once its boss is beaten.
trivia: It was released in Japan in April 1994.
Its first English release came on the Virtual Console in May 2012.
It appeared in Sega Ages 2500 Vol. 29: Monster World Complete Collection on PS2 in 2007.
It was the last Wonder Boy both published by Sega and developed by Westone.
Artdink remade it as Wonder Boy: Asha in Monster World in 2021.
devStory: Westone developed it and Sega released it for the Mega Drive in Japan in April 1994 as the sixth Wonder Boy game and the fourth Monster World game. It stayed in Japan for years, appearing on PlayStation 2 in 2007 and the Japanese Wii Virtual Console in 2008, before an English version finally reached the Virtual Console in North America and Europe in May 2012, followed by Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network. A full remake by Artdink followed in 2021.

title: Sonic R
description: Sonic R (1997) is the Saturn's only original Sonic game, a 3D on-foot racer by Traveller's Tales and Sonic Team that rewards exploration and is remembered for Richard Jacques's divisive vocal soundtrack.
longDescription:
Ten Sonic characters race to stop Doctor Robotnik from stealing the Chaos Emeralds and enslaving the world. Players choose a character and run footraces on five tracks, against the clock and the other racers, in single-player and multiplayer modes. Four characters are available at first and six more are unlocked by completing objectives. Although compared to kart racers like Mario Kart, it emphasises jumping and exploration, with multiple paths and hidden areas on every track. The original tracks are themed on classic Sonic stages such as Green Hill Zone and Chemical Plant Zone, and can be raced in reverse.

Rings can be spent on a temporary speed boost or to open doors to shortcuts and special items, and Item Panels give random advantages such as speed or shields that let a racer run on water or attract rings. Collecting five hidden Sonic tokens on a track and placing in the race allows a challenge against a secret character, who is unlocked if beaten, and Chaos Emeralds hidden on the tracks are won by finding them and finishing first. Its visuals were its strongest point: Next Generation called it "the most visually outstanding Saturn title" for its transparency and reflections, and critics praised its rarely faltering frame rate, while its controls, difficulty and short length were criticised.
trivia: It was originally known as Sonic TT, for Tourist Trophy.
Traveller's Tales rebuilt a Formula One game it was developing into Sonic R.
It was announced as "Phase Two of Project Sonic", after Sonic Jam.
Songs such as "Super Sonic Racing" and "Can You Feel The Sunshine?" were reused in later Sonic games.
Fan interest in it inspired Sega's later Sonic Riders.
devStory: After Sonic 3D Blast, Sega asked Traveller's Tales, which had a 3D engine without a clear purpose, to make a Sonic racer; development began in February 1997 as a joint project with Sonic Team and took nine months on a tight schedule. Sonic Team designed the tracks and the game's flow while Traveller's Tales implemented and programmed them with a custom engine built for the Saturn. Richard Jacques composed the soundtrack, which polarised players as either catchy and well produced or out of place. Released for the Saturn in late 1997 and Windows in 1998, it received mixed reviews, averaging 69 per cent, and retrospective views have been more negative. It reappeared in Sonic Gems Collection in 2005.

title: Sonic Blast
description: Sonic Blast (1996) is the last Game Gear Sonic platformer, in which Sonic and Knuckles chase Chaos Emerald shards through 15 zones rendered in Donkey Kong Country-style pre-rendered graphics.
longDescription:
Doctor Robotnik shatters a Chaos Emerald into five shards with a laser, and one strikes Sonic, who teams up with Knuckles to stop Robotnik collecting the rest and fortifying his island base. Both are playable: Sonic has his spin attacks plus a mid-air double jump, while Knuckles keeps his abilities from Sonic & Knuckles, gliding and climbing walls. There are 15 zones across five parts, from a traditional Green Hill Zone to underwater ruins, with loops, slides and teleporters, and every third zone ends in a fight with Robotnik and one of his larger robots.

Rings act as health, ten scattering when the player is hit, and lives are lost to crushing, drowning, pits or a hit with no rings. Monitors give rings, speed, shields, invincibility, extra lives or a mid-level save, though some show Robotnik's face and give nothing, and question-mark monitors grant a random power-up. A spinning signpost ends each act with a reward. As in Sonic the Hedgehog 3, giant rings hidden in levels lead to special stages in the style of Sonic 2's, where the player runs forward collecting rings to win an emerald shard. The pre-rendered visuals were meant to push the declining handheld, but they left Sonic and Knuckles with few animation frames and forced the removal of the timer.
trivia: It was the sixth and final Sonic platformer on the Game Gear.
Key staff from Aspect's earlier Sonic games did not work on it.
Despite the similar names, it has little in common with Sonic 3D Blast.
It was re-released on the Master System only in Brazil in 1997.
It came to the 3DS Virtual Console in 2012.
devStory: Aspect developed it and Sega published it alongside other outsourced Sonic games such as Sonic Labyrinth and Sonic 3D Blast, rendering the graphics in 3D and converting them to sprites in the manner of Donkey Kong Country and Mortal Kombat, and reusing elements from Sonic 3 and Sonic & Knuckles. Retrospective reviewers have deemed it one of the series' worst games. Nintendo World Report called it "a step back" from the other Game Gear Sonic titles because of "the attempt at aping Donkey Kong Country's pre-rendered sprites on a handheld", Nintendo Life criticised its "muddy colours and shaky animation", and others found the large character sprites too big for the small screen and the levels slow.

title: Sonic Drift
description: Sonic Drift (1994) is Sega's Japan-only Game Gear kart racer, the first Sonic racing game, with Sonic, Tails, Amy and Eggman drifting around 18 tracks based on the original game's zones.
longDescription:
Players race as one of four characters, Sonic, Miles "Tails" Prower, Amy Rose or Doctor Eggman, aiming to cross the finish line first. The 18 tracks are based on zones from the 1991 Sonic the Hedgehog, including Green Hill Zone. It was the first Sonic game with Amy as a playable character. The modes are Chaos GP, a grand prix of three six-track cups, green, yellow and red, scored by points; Free Run for practice; and Versus Mode for head-to-head races.

Inspired by Super Mario Kart but closer in feel to Sega's "Super Scaler" arcade racers such as Out Run and Super Monaco GP, it centres on drifting through corners at speed. Each character has strengths and weaknesses: Sonic accelerates quickly but handles poorly, while Eggman is slow to accelerate but fast. The top half of the screen shows the course map and the bottom the race. Monitors on the track give power-ups such as invincibility, and gold rings power a special move unique to each character, a speed boost for Sonic and a jump for Tails. Sega Pro's reviewers criticised its similar tracks, poor cornering and low difficulty, while Mega Fun found it fun and easy to master, if not as good as Super Mario Kart.
trivia: Flicky was originally planned as the fourth playable character, before being replaced by Amy.
A Western release was cancelled over quality concerns; Sega released a Game Gear Sonic Spinball instead.
It was released in Japan on 18 March 1994.
It first reached the West as an unlockable in Sonic Adventure DX: Director's Cut in 2003.
Sonic Drift 2 was released worldwide in 1995.
devStory: Sega developed it in-house, programmed by "Wa-Da" and "Shinchan", designed by Takako Kawaguchi, Gen Adachi, Shinichi Higashi and "K Dash", directed by Katsuhiro Hasegawa and produced by Hiroshi Aso, with music by Masayuki Nagao and box art by Yasushi Yamaguchi. Electronic Gaming Monthly's preview found it fast and enjoyable but hampered by flashing, choppy scrolling, and Sega Pro's Mark Hill wrote that "only a complete idiot would purchase a copy". Retrospective feedback has also been negative. It was later included in Sonic Mega Collection Plus in 2004 and Sonic Origins Plus in 2023.

title: Jurassic Park (Genesis)
description: Jurassic Park (1993) is BlueSky Software's Genesis film tie-in that lets players escape Isla Nublar as Dr. Alan Grant or hunt him down as a Velociraptor.
longDescription:
A side-scrolling action game with platform elements, it was unusual for offering two independent playable characters, chosen from the main menu. As paleontologist Dr. Alan Grant, the player crosses seven areas of Isla Nublar to reach the Visitors Center and escape by helicopter, facing dinosaurs freed from their enclosures. Grant uses a tranquilliser gun, stun gun, flash and gas grenades and a rocket launcher, all needing ammunition scattered around the island, sometimes in hard-to-reach places, and first-aid kits restore his health.

The Velociraptor jumps higher and runs much faster than Grant but can only attack up close with teeth and claws. Over five levels it must evade or kill the park's security guards, who carry grenades and missiles, and corner Grant at the Visitors Center, knocking out stray dinosaurs on the way and restoring health with meat or by eating a compy. Each character has three lives, losing one restarts the level, and passwords between levels allow continuing later; three difficulty levels change how fast and hard enemies attack. The Associated Press compared it favourably to Flashback, calling it "a winner" with great graphics, excellent control and "perfect" sound, while Rocky Mountain News found it boring and frustrating.
trivia: Acclaim and Activision both bid for the Genesis rights but lost to Sega.
Doug TenNapel was the lead artist.
Paleontologist Robert Bakker dissected a supermarket chicken to show the team dinosaur-bird similarities.
It was Sega's first game developed on Silicon Graphics computers.
About 250,000 copies sold in its first US week, a record $13.8 million.
devStory: BlueSky Software developed it as a tie-in to the 1993 film, drawing on elements from Michael Crichton's novel. The animators consulted experts who had worked on the film, and the team took field trips to natural history museums and zoos, studying ostriches and alligators, to reflect the latest dinosaur theories; Robert Bakker also appeared in a commercial for the game. Sega France reported 100,000 cartridges sold by May 1994. After the film's success, Sega released a sequel, Jurassic Park: Rampage Edition, in 1994, and both were re-released in Jurassic Park: Classic Games Collection in 2023.

title: Splatterhouse 2
description: Splatterhouse 2 (1992) is Namco's Genesis horror brawler in which Rick, tormented by guilt, puts the Terror Mask back on to rescue Jennifer from the land of the dead.
longDescription:
Three months after the first game, Rick is wracked with guilt at failing to save Jennifer and plagued by nightmares of her and the Terror Mask, which reformed after breaking at the end of the original. The Mask reappears and tempts him to find the house, promising that Jennifer can be saved and that it will give him power. In the Japanese version it tells him to find "the hidden house" and that Jennifer is in "the land of the dead", while the Western version simply says to "go back to the house", leading some players to mistake the intact mansion for the original West Mansion, whose charred ruins actually form the first stage. Rick rescues Jennifer, and the house sinks to the bottom of the river.

Play is very close to the first game: Rick fights through eight two-dimensional stages, punching, kicking, jump-kicking and slide-kicking and picking up weapons scattered through the levels, with a grotesque boss at the end of each. New are a difficulty setting and, in the English version, a password system taken from Splatterhouse: Wanpaku Graffiti. In the West the Terror Mask is skull-like, while in Japan it is white with black stripes over the eyes, loosely resembling a kabuki mask. GamePro invited players to "seek revenge on all those early childhood closet monsters".
trivia: In Japan it is called Splatterhouse Part 2.
It is the third Splatterhouse game, after Splatterhouse: Wanpaku Graffiti.
It was the first and only ESRB M-rated game released on the Wii Virtual Console.
It was an unlockable extra in the 2010 remake.
It was included on the Sega Genesis Mini 2 in 2022.
devStory: Now Production developed it and Namco published it for the Sega Genesis in 1992 as the sequel to the 1988 arcade Splatterhouse. Game Informer said it was "definitely one not to pass up", and Mega Action gave it 88 per cent as a "sick, slick scrolling beat-'em-up", while Mega Play's reviewers thought its gore would appeal to horror fans. Others felt the premise could not carry it: Sega Force called the controls "sluggish", VideoGames & Computer Entertainment said it did "nothing to advance the genre", and Mean Machines Sega noted poor graphics and a short campaign. Splatterhouse 3 followed in 1993.

title: Trouble Shooter
description: Trouble Shooter (1991), originally Battle Mania in Japan, is Vic Tokai's self-parodying Genesis shooter in which operatives Madison and Crystal fly to rescue a kidnapped prince.
longDescription:
Combat operative Madison is assigned to rescue a prince who has been taken hostage, accompanied throughout by her partner Crystal. Unlike Madison, Crystal can flip her firing direction to shoot behind them and is invulnerable to enemy fire. At the start of almost every stage, the player picks a special weapon, which must recharge after each use. Four kinds of power-up appear: speed-ups, life-ups, extra firepower and speed-downs. There is no lives system and only three continues, so collecting life-ups to raise Madison's hit points is essential.

The game has a distinctly self-parodying tone in its enemies, story and dialogue. Its concept came from an idea for a manga set between 1995 and 1997, and its influences included the book series The Gaming Magi, 1980s idol Noriko Sakai and locations near Sega's headquarters. One scene shows the heroine stomping on a Super Famicom, added because designer Fujito "Takayan" Takada was annoyed at how much bigger Super Famicom game budgets were; afterwards a fax went out to Sega's studios asking developers not to disparage other companies' characters and trademarks. Crystal's weapon-explaining role was originally given to a man named Fugu with a wheeled, pincered one-eyed cat, cut because Sega's quality assurance team disliked him.
trivia: It was released in North America in November 1991, before Japan in March 1992.
Development finished in 1990.
It was based on an arcade prototype made years earlier.
Takada speculated he got away with the Super Famicom scene because Sega disliked Nintendo.
A Japan and Korea-only sequel, Battle Mania Daiginjō, followed.
devStory: Fujito "Takayan" Takada fought to get it greenlit and, with little support from Vic Tokai at first, handled every aspect himself, from design, graphics, programming and music to PR, sales and scheduling, before more people joined and he moved into a supervisory role. Though finished in 1990, it was not released until 1991. It received generally favourable reviews; GamePro praised its humorous story, and Japanese readers of Mega Drive Fan and Sega Saturn Magazine rated it well.

title: Pulseman
description: Pulseman (1994) is Game Freak's Mega Drive platformer starring a half-human, half-digital hero who channels electricity to fight the Galaxy Gang led by his corrupted father.
longDescription:
In the 21st century, scientist Doc Yoshiyama creates the world's most advanced artificial intelligence, a thinking, feeling girl called C-Life. Falling in love with her, he digitises himself into his computer to be with her, and their union produces Pulseman, a boy who is half human and half C-Life. Unlike other C-Life, Pulseman can survive outside the computer, and he can channel electricity through his body, as a weapon and as a means of rapid travel through his Volteccer ability.

Living inside the computer twists Yoshiyama's mind and body, and he re-emerges as the evil Doc Waruyama. Using a system called EUREKA that lets C-Life beings manifest in the human world, he founds the Galaxy Gang and unleashes a wave of cyber-terrorism, and Pulseman must fight his own father and break up the gang. Released in Japan on 22 July 1994, it was ranked eighth in popularity by Micom BASIC Magazine that October. When it came to the Wii Virtual Console it received generally favourable reviews, averaging 80 per cent on GameRankings.
trivia: It was announced under the title Spark.
Ken Sugimori directed it.
Its staff included Satoshi Tajiri, Atsuko Nishida and Junichi Masuda, who later worked on Pokémon.
It reached North America in 1995 through the Sega Channel.
It joined Nintendo Classics in April 2023.
devStory: Game Freak developed it and Sega published it for the Mega Drive in Japan in 1994, with Ken Sugimori directing and much of the team, including Satoshi Tajiri, Atsuko Nishida and Junichi Masuda, going on to the Pokémon series. North America received it only through the Sega Channel in 1995. Japanese readers of Mega Drive Fan and Sega Saturn Magazine rated it moderately well. It was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in Japan in 2007 and in North America and Europe in 2009, and later on the Nintendo Classics service.

title: Goemon's Great Adventure
description: Goemon's Great Adventure (1998), known in Europe as Mystical Ninja 2 Starring Goemon, is Konami's 2.5D side-scrolling return for the series, with two-player co-op across a surreal Edo-period Japan.
longDescription:
The evil Bismaru has stolen Wise Man's resurrection machine and used it to revive Dochuki, prince of the underworld, and Goemon and his friends must cross five worlds to defeat him and destroy the device. Set in a fantastical Edo-period Japan of forests, mountains, towns and underworlds with touches of science fiction, it continues the series' offbeat, surreal humour. Abandoning the free roaming of Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon, it returns to the style of the Super Famicom games: movement is restricted to a 2D plane, but stages are rendered in 3D and wind along the z axis, giving it a 2.5D look like Yoshi's Story and Klonoa.

A world map links stages, with a town and a dungeon in each world. Entry passes, earned by clearing stages and doing tasks for townspeople, open the dungeons, and completing one opens the next world, with some non-linear touches such as a secret village and multiple routes. Players run, jump, attack and use special abilities as Goemon, Ebisumaru, Sasuke or Yae, swapped in towns or via portals to an interdimensional teahouse. Two players can play together, though both must stay on screen. Characters have three health bars, defeated monsters drop dumplings and lucky cats, and progress is saved to a Controller Pak. Critics praised its 16-bit-style side-scrolling, Castlevania overtones and varied levels, and GamePro said the 2.5D made it "more exciting than any old 2D scrollers".
trivia: It is the fourteenth mainline Ganbare Goemon game and the fourth released in the West.
It was released on 23 December 1998, the same day as a PlayStation Goemon game.
Children flocked to play it at the 1998 Tokyo Game Show.
It sold over 160,000 copies worldwide.
Reviewers have considered it one of the best side-scrollers on the Nintendo 64.
devStory: Konami developed and released it for the Nintendo 64 in 1998, promoting the Ganbare Goemon series heavily that Christmas alongside a PlayStation game and a Game Boy Color game. An English version was revealed in September 1998 and shown at E3 1999. It received favourable reviews: IGN gave it eight out of ten, praising non-linear puzzle elements and quests that took more than a day to finish, 1UP.com gave it an A, and critics welcomed the co-op mode as a huge improvement that recalled "classic Nintendo and Konami sidescrollers". The switch to side-scrolling also solved the camera issues of its predecessor, and its graphics and music earned high marks.

title: Doom 64
description: Doom 64 (1997) is Midway's darker Nintendo 64 Doom, with all-new monster and weapon art, coloured lighting, shape-shifting levels and the artefact-powered Unmaker.
longDescription:
After the Doom Marine's victories in Doom, Doom II and Final Doom, the UAC research installations are quarantined under apocalyptic radiation. Years later, a barely working satellite reports that a "single entity with vast rejuvenation powers" has been hidden by the radiation, and the Marine is sent back. Play follows earlier Doom games: across 28 story levels and four secret levels, the player fights demons, collects weapons and keys and hits switches to reach the exit while surviving ambushes and traps. Pressing switches often makes whole rooms rearrange and fold into new shapes.

All of Doom II's weapons return with new sprites and sounds: a two-bladed chainsaw, bloodstained gloves, a sparking plasma gun and a faster-reloading, kicking super shotgun. The new Unmaker, a hitscan weapon using cell ammunition, first imagined in the 1992 Doom Bible, can be upgraded by three hidden artefacts until it fires three independently aiming lasers. Most Doom monsters return with redesigns, though the revenant, arch-vile, spiderdemon and heavy weapon dude are missing; new are the nightmare imp and a final boss, the Mother Demon. Critics agreed it was by far the best-looking Doom yet, beyond even the PC version, with imaginative, more challenging levels, though IGN said players who had "played the PC, PSX, SNES, Mac, Saturn, etc versions to death" could do without it.
trivia: Its working title, The Absolution, became the name of the final level.
Development began in late 1994 under id Software's supervision.
Midway said it left out multiplayer because Nintendo lacked resources for multiplayer programming.
The Unmaker's only other official appearance is as the Unmaykr in Doom Eternal.
Nightdive Studios remastered it in 2020.
devStory: Midway's San Diego studio developed it from late 1994 under id Software's supervision, using a customised Doom engine with new kinds of level geometry and dynamic coloured lighting. Midway wanted every demon from the originals plus extra levels, but deadlines and cartridge space forced cuts. Released in 1997, it received positive reviews for its graphics, levels, soundtrack and atmosphere; Next Generation warned that "even the most skillful Doom fans will have their hands full", while some critics felt it added little new. It gained a cult following with fan source ports and mods, and Nightdive's remaster, published by Bethesda, came to Switch, PS4, Windows and Xbox One in March 2020.

title: Tetrisphere
description: Tetrisphere (1997) is H2O Entertainment's Nintendo 64 Tetris variant in which players drop and slide shapes onto a wrapped 3D sphere, chaining combos to dig through to its core.
longDescription:
Rather than completing lines on a flat field, players remove bricks on a three-dimensional grid wrapped around a sphere, generally aiming to dig through the layers to reach its core. Bricks are cleared when three pieces of the same shape touch as the result of a "drop", either when the player releases the held brick or when the brick beneath another is removed. This triggers a combo: the three bricks glow and implode, and any matching pieces in contact with them are removed in a chain reaction. Stacked pieces must sit exactly on top of each other, and O and I pieces must share a full side to count as touching, while other shapes only need to make contact.

Pieces already on the sphere can be moved by "sliding", lining up the shadow of the held piece with a matching shape; slid pieces can smash through crystal pieces but not other bricks. After a combo, random pieces begin to glow in proportion to its size, becoming power pieces, and a combo started with one lasts longer, letting the player start further combos while it runs. Its several modes and selectable funky soundtrack by Neil Voss were widely praised. GameSpot's Jer Horwitz called it "precisely the sort of game that the Nintendo 64 really needs", with "revolutionary gameplay, impressive long-term value" and effects beyond the PlayStation.
trivia: It began as an Atari Jaguar game called Phear, shown at the 1995 Winter CES.
Nintendo acquired it after seeing it at that show and announced it at Space World 1995.
H2O Entertainment was based in Calgary, Canada.
It was released in North America on 11 August 1997.
Despite limited advertising, it sold moderately well.
devStory: H2O Entertainment, founded by Steve Shatford, Christopher Bailey and Michael Tam, originally developed Phear for the Jaguar, whose levels required clearing a hole of a set size at the sphere's core. Nintendo, a Tetris Company licensee, reportedly acquired the rights after seeing it at the 1995 Winter CES, and H2O, which completed a reverse takeover with Entech Resources, then worked exclusively for Nintendo to rework it as a Tetris game. Released in North America in August 1997 and PAL regions in February 1998, it received generally favourable reviews for its originality, modes and music, and Horwitz noted big improvements over the Jaguar demo, though critics' experiences of the gameplay varied.

title: Top Gear Rally
description: Top Gear Rally (1997) is Boss Game Studios' Nintendo 64 rally racer with a working suspension model, changing weather and a six-season championship.
longDescription:
A follow-up to Kemco's original Top Gear, it mixes road and off-road surfaces on relatively open tracks with hidden shortcuts, raced in sun, night, fog, rain or snow. Before a race players can paint their car, choose tyres, set suspension stiffness and steering sensitivity and pick manual or automatic gears. Cars differ in acceleration, top speed, drivetrain and engine placement, which together with road and weather conditions change their handling: engine position affects how a car lands after a jump, and four-wheel drive cars grip better on gravel. Cars can be damaged, but without affecting performance.

Championship mode asks a single player to complete six seasons of two to four races, each against 19 computer opponents, scoring enough points to advance and unlocking cars and tracks; finishing first in every race of the last season reveals two bonus cars and a hidden track, and mirrored versions of each track can be unlocked. Arcade mode races an opponent against checkpoint time limits, Time Attack pits the player against a ghost of their best time, and Practice allows free driving, with Arcade and Practice supporting two players in split screen. Next Generation called it "a fabulous off-road racer with tons of bonus cars, courses, and replay value" that surpassed Sega Rally.
trivia: It began with a non-interactive Silicon Graphics demo that convinced Nintendo of America.
BMG Interactive was pitched the game first and passed on it.
Its fictional cars were modelled on real vehicles.
Two-player was kept to protect draw distance and a 30 frames per second target.
It was ported to Windows in 1999 as Boss Rally.
devStory: Boss Game Studios began work in July 1996 after its demo, built on workstations far more powerful than the N64 with 15,000-polygon cars, persuaded Nintendo of America it could make the game; Sega Rally was a major inspiration, though Boss wanted something that felt different. It spent two to three months building tools, including a physics engine with working suspension, and lead designer Colin Gordon said "no car [drives] like another". A planned level editor and a Mario Kart-style battle mode were dropped. Midway published it in North America on 30 September 1997. Reviews were generally positive, praising its crisp graphics and fluid but challenging play, while criticising weak sound effects and limited multiplayer.

title: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire
description: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire (1996) is LucasArts' Nintendo 64 action game in which mercenary Dash Rendar helps Luke Skywalker rescue Leia from Prince Xizor, opening with the Battle of Hoth.
longDescription:
Part of a multimedia project set between The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi, it casts the player as mercenary Dash Rendar, helping Luke Skywalker and rescuing Princess Leia from Prince Xizor across four chapters. Dash and his droid co-pilot Leebo deliver supplies to Echo Base just before the Battle of Hoth, and Han Solo gets him clearance to fly with Rogue Squadron. After defending the base in a snowspeeder, Dash fights wampas and an AT-ST to reach his ship, the Outrider, and escapes through an asteroid field. Later he hunts IG-88 and Boba Fett, who holds the carbon-frozen Han, while Xizor schemes to replace Darth Vader.

It is mainly a third-person shooter: Dash's blaster recharges after each shot and can be powered up, later levels give him a jetpack, usable even underwater in the sewers, and health packs and a limited stock of lives keep him going. Levels are timed, and challenge points for particular actions or hidden tokens unlock rewards. Other sequences vary the action: snowspeeder combat on Hoth, 360-degree turret battles and piloted space combat in the Outrider, and a high-speed swoop bike chase against a gang. The opening Battle of Hoth won praise, but critics found the other levels weaker and the shooting stages hampered by poor controls and a camera that limited the view or let Dash block the action.
trivia: Dash Rendar was a minor character from the book, built up as a Han Solo-like hero.
His ship, the Outrider, closely resembles the Millennium Falcon.
Senior artist Jon Knoles is credited with the idea of setting it between the two films.
It used the level editor from the Jedi engine of Dark Forces and Outlaws.
It was the third best-selling Nintendo 64 game of 1997, with over a million copies sold.
devStory: Work began in late 1994 on a side story to the films; rather than use the main characters, the developers built on Dash Rendar, which gave them more freedom. LucasArts developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 in 1996, with LucasArts releasing a Windows version in 1997. Its score uses tracks from the multimedia project's soundtrack. Reviews were mixed: critics praised its polygonal graphics as convincing enough to affect the mood, but Next Generation felt the cartridge format caused problems such as stiff sewer water and frequently looping music.

sources.title: Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire (video game)

title: Star Wars Episode I: Racer
description: Star Wars Episode I: Racer (1999) is LucasArts' podracing game based on The Phantom Menace, the best-selling science fiction racing game according to Guinness.
longDescription:
Based on the podracing sequence in Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace, it features all of the film's racers and its Tatooine course, plus additional competitors and tracks on Tatooine and other planets. Jake Lloyd and Lewis MacLeod reprise their film roles as Anakin Skywalker and Sebulba. Each podracer has an afterburner for a burst of speed, but its engine heats up as it is used, and pushing it too long starts a fire that destroys the pod and costs several seconds to respawn. Hitting too many walls or obstacles can also wreck one or both engines, and players can repair the pod while racing, though it slows down until the repairs are finished or stopped.

In Tournament mode, players compete in a championship, earning money for higher finishes to buy parts or repair droids and unlock tracks and racers. Free Race allows practice on unlocked courses with adjustable opponents but no rewards, and Time Attack races the clock, replaced on PC by a Free Play option with no opponents. Multiplayer differs by platform: the Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast versions offer two-player split screen, while the Windows and Macintosh versions allow up to eight players over a local network, using IPX on Windows and TCP/IP on Mac. It has appeared on many lists of the best Star Wars games, ranked fifth of all time by GMR in 2004 and third by PC Gamer in 2015.
trivia: It sold 3.12 million copies, a Guinness record for a sci-fi racing game.
Development took about two years, begun by two project leads from Shadows of the Empire.
The team built its physics from just a few short film clips.
Star Wars: Racer Arcade followed in 2000 and Racer Revenge in 2002.
An HD re-release came to Switch and PS4 in June 2020.
devStory: LucasArts developed and published it, releasing the Windows version in May 1999 alongside the film. The team tested several graphics APIs but shipped with only Direct3D because, according to project lead Brett Tosti, Glide and OpenGL showed no performance gain. With only a few short clips of the film's podrace to go on, they approximated its physics, and Tosti said they did not learn how close their estimates were until the very end. It received generally positive reviews, averaging about 76 per cent on GameRankings for the Nintendo 64 and Dreamcast versions.

title: Castlevania (Nintendo 64)
description: Castlevania (1999), often called Castlevania 64, is Konami's first 3D Castlevania, in which the Belmont heir Reinhardt or the magical orphan Carrie stop Dracula's return.
longDescription:
After a century of dormancy, Count Dracula is poised to return to power, and players choose between two heroes: Carrie Fernandez, a young orphan gifted with magic, or Reinhardt Schneider, whip-wielding heir to the Belmont clan. Each explores Dracula's grand estate to defeat him and his undead hordes. Combat adds a basic lock-on system, with a long-range attack, Reinhardt's whip or Carrie's homing energy balls, and a close-range one, a dagger or rings, each with strengths and weaknesses. The series' sub-weapons, axe, knife, cross and holy water, return, now powered by red jewels instead of hearts.

Much of the challenge comes from leaping between platforms that may rotate, glide along like a rail shooter, crumble underfoot or be invisible, while dodging enemies and traps. It also borrows from survival horror: players are locked into caged fights such as the battle with Cerberus hounds in a near-black Villa, timed duels where a ceiling descends, and fights with vampires who can bite the hero and turn their status to "vamp", blocking their main weapon and healing items unless cured. In the Villa's hedge maze, players must follow a boy named Malus while unbeatable enemies give chase. GameSpot praised it for capturing "the atmosphere and spirit of the series" with "some incredible bosses (just wait until you see Death... whew!)".
trivia: It was first shown as Castlevania 64 at the 1997 Tokyo Game Show and later called Dracula 3D.
Konami Computer Entertainment Kobe developed it.
Two of four planned characters were dropped, including the werewolf Cornell.
Its Japanese logo includes the English words "real action adventure".
It averages 78 on Metacritic.
devStory: Konami first showed it at the April 1997 Tokyo Game Show. It was about 10 per cent complete in September 1997 and 20 per cent in February 1998, and at the October 1998 Tokyo Game Show its playable levels were a hit. That month Konami Computer Entertainment Kobe cut two of the four planned characters, including Cornell, to focus the team and finish sooner. Released in 1999, it received generally positive reviews, most critics considering it a good transition to 3D despite the changes; IGN singled out its "outstanding sound effects with lots of bass". An expanded version, Castlevania: Legacy of Darkness, followed the same year.

title: Castlevania: Legacy of Darkness
description: Castlevania: Legacy of Darkness (1999) is Konami's expanded prequel to Castlevania 64, starring the man-beast Cornell as he races to save his sister from being sacrificed to Dracula.
longDescription:
In 1844 the man-beast Cornell returns home to find his village burned by Dracula's minions and his adoptive sister Ada taken to be sacrificed to resurrect the Count.
