Finding her pendant in a doorway, he follows her scent to Dracula's castle. On the way he reaches the Oldrey estate, where Gilles de Rais and Actrise have turned J.A. Oldrey into a vampire, and at his wife Mary's request Cornell guides their son Henry to safety. His rival, the man-beast Ortega, has allied with Dracula to finally beat him, becoming a chimera-like creature. Cornell defeats Dracula and saves Ada, but only by sacrificing his man-wolf powers, which were the dark lord's true aim.

It revises the first N64 game with improved graphics, extra villains and altered levels. Cornell's new story is the main focus, through new levels and redesigned ones navigated in new ways. Finishing it unlocks Henry's quest, set later in his life as he returns to Castlevania to rescue kidnapped children, and Carrie's and Reinhardt's original quests are unlockable bonuses. The platforming and survival horror elements remain: crumbling and invisible platforms, caged and timed fights, vampires whose bite leaves heroes in a "vamp" state, a hedge maze where Cornell must guide Henry while unbeatable enemies give chase, and a nerve-racking delivery of volatile "magic nitro" through the Castle Center, where a single fall or hit means death.
trivia: Cornell appeared in early media for Castlevania 64 but was cut before release.
It is both a prequel and an expanded remake of Castlevania 64.
Famitsu scored it 28 out of 40.
NextGen joked it was more like "Legacy of Mediocrity".
A planned Dreamcast follow-up, Castlevania Resurrection, was cancelled.
devStory: Konami developed it as a continuation of its first attempt at a 3D Castlevania, released earlier in 1999, restoring Cornell, who had been dropped from that game. Reception was mixed. NextGen's Blake Fischer found it merely "satisfactory" and hoped the Dreamcast game would be better, while GamePro's The Freshman called it "basically what the N64's Castlevania was meant to be... more of a remake than a sequel", and another GamePro reviewer felt that although it was bigger, it shared the original's problems.

title: International Superstar Soccer 64
description: International Superstar Soccer 64 (1997) is Konami's acclaimed Nintendo 64 football game, one of the console's best third-party titles, with 36 national teams and four-player matches.
longDescription:
Building on the Super NES's International Superstar Soccer Deluxe with 3D animation, it keeps largely the same squads, with near-authentic kits, though South Africa replaces Morocco. There are 36 international teams, and the Japanese version adds Bolivia, Yugoslavia, Iran, Australia, Canada and Saudi Arabia. Six modes include single matches, league battles and penalty shoot-outs. The International Cup is a round-robin tournament against teams from around the world, while the World League is a 70-match series against every other team. Scenario matches set specific goals, such as scoring within a time limit or keeping the opposition out.

Up to four players can play matches, and penalty shoot-outs also support four. Players can be created and traded, and individual opponents can be assigned a marker. Thousands of motion-captured animations portray a range of football techniques, matches have real-time commentary, and GameSpot praised its use of the analogue stick, with controls closely tuned to football's fast pace. Shigeru Miyamoto said at its Japanese release that "Konami's soccer game may be better than [Nintendo's N64] games", and GamePro called the Japanese version possibly one of the best soccer titles in Japan.
trivia: It was first released in Japan as Jikkyō J.League Perfect Striker, later adapted as Jikkyō World Soccer 3.
Turkey is listed as an Asian team.
The US team's home kit is its 1994 World Cup Adidas strip.
It sold over a million copies in Europe.
It was the UK's best-selling video game of July 1997.
devStory: Konami Computer Entertainment Osaka developed it as part of Konami's International Superstar Soccer series. It met with critical acclaim in Japan, with Famitsu scoring the two Japanese versions 32 and 31 out of 40, and in Europe, where Edge called the Japanese import remarkably versatile and entertaining. Next Generation said it went "farther than most titles in presenting a fantastic look and feel", advising players to have friends around. A commercial success, it topped the UK multi-format chart and is often called one of the best third-party releases on the Nintendo 64.

title: Mortal Kombat Mythologies: Sub-Zero
description: Mortal Kombat Mythologies: Sub-Zero (1997) is Midway's first non-fighting Mortal Kombat, a side-scrolling action-adventure following the elder Sub-Zero's hunt for Shinnok's amulet.
longDescription:
Set before the original Mortal Kombat, it follows Bi-Han, the elder Sub-Zero, a Lin Kuei assassin and thief hired by the sorcerer Quan Chi to steal a map of the elements from a Shaolin temple. Fighting through the temple's monks, he faces his rival Scorpion of the Shirai Ryu, also hired by Quan Chi, and kills him before delivering the map, setting him on the trail of Shinnok's amulet. It introduces characters and story elements later used in Mortal Kombat 4, released the same year, and is the last game in the series to use digitised actors.

Though an action-adventure, it plays much like the 2D fighting games, with four attack buttons, block and run buttons as in Mortal Kombat 3, and command-based special moves. A turn button changes Sub-Zero's facing and an action button picks up or uses items, and a status screen tracks inventory, experience and special moves. He starts with a small health bar and few lives, gaining experience from combos to grow stronger and unlock special moves powered by an ice meter that slowly refills. Key items must be found, and passwords record progress. Critics praised the move into a new genre and the PlayStation version's live-action cut-scenes but criticised its controls and punishing levels; GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann called it "a pretty amazing meld of fighting and platform jumping", while IGN called it "terrible".
trivia: It took about 14 months to make.
Designer and Sub-Zero co-creator John Tobias wanted to flesh out the character's backstory.
The core team at Midway Chicago was five artists, two programmers and a sound designer.
Its humanoid characters were digitised actors, while monsters and backgrounds were real-time 3D.
It was re-released in Mortal Kombat: Legacy Kollection in 2025.
devStory: Midway developed and published it for the PlayStation and Nintendo 64 in 1997, with news of it leaking in the third quarter of 1996. Reviews were divisive, with the PlayStation version considered the better of the two. Next Generation found its RPG elements a good feature but said that after "cookie-cutter enemies" and unpredictable traps, "even the most hard-core Mortal Kombat fans will find themselves frustrated and angry", while Spain's Superjuegos called it a delight for fans of beat 'em ups and Flashback-style adventures. Retrospective reviews have been more negative, some ranking it among the worst Mortal Kombat games.

title: Mortal Kombat Trilogy
description: Mortal Kombat Trilogy (1996) is Midway's final update to Mortal Kombat 3, gathering characters and arenas from the first three games and adding the Aggressor bar and Brutalities.
longDescription:
It shares the basic play and story of Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 but adds characters and stages restored from Mortal Kombat and Mortal Kombat II. The Ultimate MK3 roster is joined by Raiden and Baraka exactly as they appeared in MKII, given new running animations. A new Aggressor bar fills during a fight, twice as fast when the opponent is blocking, and when full grants faster movement and stronger attacks for a short time. Many fighters gain extra special moves, some simple variations and some unused animations from earlier games, such as Kano's knife spin, Kung Lao's air torpedo, Goro's spinning punch and Baraka's blade spin, while Shao Kahn and Motaro gain throws.

It introduced the Brutality, a finisher in which the winner pummels the opponent until they explode. Every arena from MKII, MK3 and UMK3 is included, along with four backgrounds from the original game, though each version drops a couple of stages, and the Stage Fatalities return except in the Pit II. Sub-Zero's famous Spine Rip is completely censored, the screen going black with only the word "Fatality", to avoid re-animating it. Electronic Gaming Monthly's reviewers all recommended the N64 version for its amount of content and lack of loading times, though two found its graphics disappointing for the hardware.
trivia: Several original actors had left Midway over royalty disputes, so their roles were recast.
Williams Entertainment initially said Johnny Cage would not appear because of the dispute.
It was released for PlayStation, Nintendo 64, Saturn and PC, plus Game.com and R-Zone.
Brazil's SuperGamePower called the N64 version the best Mortal Kombat.
France's Super Power gave the N64 version 91 per cent, preferring it to the PlayStation one.
devStory: Midway released it in 1996 as the second and last update to Mortal Kombat 3, after Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3. Because Ho Sung Pak, Philip Ahn, Elizabeth Malecki, Katalin Zamiar and Daniel Pesina had left over royalty disputes, their characters were played by new actors, while Carlos Pesina's sprites were kept for Raiden. Most of the background music from MKII and MK3 remained, especially on the CD versions. Reception varied widely by platform and publication: GamePro praised its content, faithful recreation of the arcade graphics and the Aggressor meter, and EGM's Crispin Boyer and Shawn Smith said it had converted them to Mortal Kombat fans.

title: ClayFighter 63⅓
description: ClayFighter 63⅓ (1997) is Interplay's claymation fighting parody for the Nintendo 64, spoofing Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat and Killer Instinct across multi-room arenas.
longDescription:
On the Isle of Klaymodo, a purple meteor called Bessie holds Bawk Choy, the key ingredient in Dr. Kiln's world-conquering mutagen. With the voodoo practitioner Happy Harry Houngan, Kiln has created henchmen such as Bonker, a clown gone bad, and Ickybod Clay. When Houngan bursts into the lab, a vial of the mutagen shatters on Kiln's hand, which he has to amputate; the severed hand scurries off into the jungle with Houngan in pursuit. Meanwhile a ship on a "three-hour tour" capsizes nearby, stranding Bad Mister Frosty, wok chef Kung Pow, Taffyman and Blob.

Like earlier ClayFighters, it uses stop-motion claymation rather than traditional computer animation. Most arenas have multiple rooms, 26 in all, and players can punch or kick each other into new rooms where the fight continues. It parodies other fighters throughout: a three-level super combo bar like Street Fighter Alpha, parries like Street Fighter III, super attacks that riff on Street Fighter moves, and a Killer Instinct-style combo system with mock names such as the "Itty Bitty Combo" and "Triple Brown Betty Combo". Next Generation found it "just so damn silly" that anyone who had played Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat or Killer Instinct would find it hilarious, but questioned paying $69.99 for "a good, albeit short-lived, chuckle".
trivia: The title parodies the "64" suffix of N64 games and The Naked Gun 33⅓.
It was initially titled ClayFighter 3.
Producer Jeremy Airey said "buckets of blood and gore get boring after a while".
An update, ClayFighter: Sculptor's Cut, was a 1998 Blockbuster rental exclusive.
Sculptor's Cut is one of the rarest and most valuable N64 games.
devStory: Interplay developed it as the third ClayFighter, produced by Jeremy Airey with designers Eric Hart and Rodney Relosa, aiming to make a legitimate fighting game that humorously parodied the genre's big franchises, replacing their extreme violence with gross or funny actions. Released for the Nintendo 64 in 1997, it was largely panned, averaging 48 per cent on GameRankings; reviewers found the humour and parody effective but criticised its gameplay, animation and AI, leaving it with little long-term appeal.

title: Rampage World Tour
description: Rampage World Tour (1997) is the arcade sequel to Rampage by its original designers, in which George, Lizzie and Ralph smash Scumlabs facilities around the world.
longDescription:
An accident at the corrupt Scumlabs unleashes three giant monsters, George, Lizzie and Ralph, who set about destroying Scumlabs bases around the world and its employees. In the final levels, CEO Eustace DeMonic turns himself into a monster to fight them, and is defeated in a battle on a lunar base. The sole surviving employee, Dr. Elizabeth Veronica, then tries to disintegrate the monsters with a ray gun on her spaceship, but only shrinks them, leaving them stranded aboard her ship.

As in the original, the aim of each stage is to destroy every building in a city while avoiding or destroying the military; take too long and jets fly in to bomb the rest, ending the stage with a lower score. In the opening city of Peoria, a tourism billboard cycles through regions of the country, and smashing it while it shows one sends the monsters there. Eating or ignoring World Tour power-ups controls which countries they visit, with foreign levels continuing until a Scumlabs plant is destroyed, and purple radioactive waste briefly turns a player into the super monster V.E.R.N. The game only ends when every Scumlabs city is flattened. The arcade version supports three players, as does the Nintendo 64 port, while the PlayStation and Saturn versions allow only two.
trivia: It was designed by Brian Colin and Jeff Nauman, who designed the 1986 original.
GT Interactive published the home ports in Europe.
It drew little interest at the JAMMA show in Japan.
A three-player mode was apparently cut from the PlayStation version at the last minute.
It appears in Midway Arcade Treasures 2 and Rampage: Total Destruction.
devStory: Game Refuge developed it and Midway Games published it in arcades in 1997, with ports for the PlayStation, Saturn, Nintendo 64, Game Boy Color and Windows. Next Generation criticised the decision to keep sprites rather than polygons, saying it would only make gamers "yearn for the original more than ever". Critics agreed the home ports were nearly arcade-perfect but were divided on the game itself: many welcomed it as a fun revival of an arcade classic, Electronic Gaming Monthly's Shawn Smith writing that "there's nothing like sitting down and playing a good old-time game".

title: Gauntlet Legends
description: Gauntlet Legends (1998) is Atari Games' 3D arcade sequel to Gauntlet, adding RPG-style character levelling saved by password as heroes chase runestones to banish the demon Skorne.
longDescription:
Long ago the corrupt mage Garm used a set of Runestones to summon the demon Skorne, who crushed him, imprisoned his soul in the Underworld and scattered the stones across four realms so they could never be used against him. Players must defeat the bosses of each realm to win the four keys to the desecrated temple and banish Skorne, while collecting the scattered Runestones, which let them pursue him into the Underworld to destroy him for good. The game continues as long as players keep their health up, and the first 500 arcade players to finish and send in a validation code won a free T-shirt.

New to the series is levelling: slaying enemies and gathering treasure earns experience that raises four attributes, Strength for physical damage, Speed for movement and attack rate, Armor against enemy attacks and Magic for the range and power of potions, and gold can buy further increases. The classic heroes return in new forms, the Warrior as a Minotaur, the Wizard as a Jackal, the Archer as a Tigress and the Valkyrie as a Falconess, each starting strong in one attribute. Unusually for an arcade game, progress is saved through passwords, letting players build characters up to level 99 with attributes of up to 999 over many sessions. GamePro said the 3D was "much more than a gimmick" and the legend "treated with befitting respect".
trivia: It is the sequel to 1985's Gauntlet and 1986's Gauntlet II.
It was the last Gauntlet produced by Atari Games.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixth most successful dedicated arcade game of 1998.
Home versions came to Nintendo 64, PlayStation and Dreamcast, starting in September 1999.
Gauntlet Dark Legacy followed in 2000.
devStory: Atari Games developed and published it for arcades in 1998, giving the series 3D graphics and long-term character saves. The Nintendo 64 port arrived first, in North America in September 1999, followed by PlayStation and Dreamcast versions. The arcade original received favourable reviews; the PlayStation version was mixed. NextGen said of the Dreamcast version that "four controllers and one Legends make for party-game excitement of the highest order", and GamePro called the N64 version an impressive port of a polished arcade game.

title: Buck Bumble
description: Buck Bumble (1998) is Argonaut's Nintendo 64 shooter in which a cyborg bumblebee battles an army of mutant insects born from a chemical spill in a London garden, set to a speed garage soundtrack.
longDescription:
A chemical spill at a factory in London mutates the local insects, and several kinds band together as the evil Herd, determined to take over the garden and then the world. The player is Buck Bumble, a volunteer bumblebee fitted with cyborg technology and a member of the Resistance. His nineteen missions include destroying Herd radar dishes, defending the Resistance base, raiding Herd supply lines through the sewers and finally fighting the mantis-like Queen. Completing an objective triggers a teleport to a mission summary and save screen.

The camera sits behind Buck as he flies freely, limited only by a height ceiling and level geometry, or walks on the ground. The screen shows a radar for enemies, a damage meter, the equipped weapon and the current objective, and Buck can carry up to eleven weapons, such as a stun gun, laser or rocket launcher. Flowers provide nectar to restore energy, some levels are split into areas linked by teleporters and gates, generators keep releasing beetles and wasps until destroyed, and water drowns Buck if he stays under for more than a few seconds. Two-player modes include Buck Battle, an aerial deathmatch, and Buzz Ball, a football game played with a zapper and rocket launcher.
trivia: It began as lead programmer Carl Graham's flight simulator test made for fun.
Justin Scharvona's soundtrack is entirely speed garage, chosen as "funkier than house and garage".
Joy Tech sold an unlicensed "Buck Bumble Pack" rumble accessory with it in UK shops.
Its main theme has enjoyed a modern resurgence in popularity.
It was designed with the rumble feature in mind to increase realism.
devStory: Argonaut Software developed it and Ubisoft published it for the Nintendo 64 in 1998. Carl Graham said his flight simulator test "evolved into a flying bee, and the horror we know as Buck Bumble today was born". Scharvona chose speed garage because techno and jungle seemed overdone and he wanted something futuristic and "not cutesy, something a bit harder". Reviews were lukewarm, with even positive ones noting technical shortcomings: critics such as IGN and N64 Gamer felt it fell below contemporary Nintendo 64 standards. The soundtrack was praised, though, and the game has since gained a following despite its relative obscurity.

title: Mace: The Dark Age
description: Mace: The Dark Age (1997) is Atari Games' violent 3D weapon-based fighter, built on 3dfx Voodoo hardware, in which warriors of the 12th century seek to destroy the sorcerer Asmodeus.
longDescription:
In the 12th century, the dark sorcerer Asmodeus wields the fabled Mace of Tanis, imbued with necropotic energy that promises eternal life and boundless power, and leads a Covenant of Seven nations. Leaders from East Asia and the remaining free nations of Europe send their chosen warriors to kill him before it is too late. Like many fighters of its time it is extremely violent: as in Mortal Kombat, a fighter who wins both rounds can perform an execution on the loser, and its play resembles Bio F.R.E.A.K.S. and Mortal Kombat.

Instead of ring-outs, arenas are bordered by dangerous terrain such as lava that damages anyone who strays out of bounds, similar to Dead or Alive, and stages feature interactive elements such as water. An evade button lets fighters step forward or back into the 3D environment. Critics widely agreed its graphics were excellent and its gameplay mediocre: Electronic Gaming Monthly called it "one of the most visually impressive fighting games around" but found the combos "don't flow smoothly" and the controls stuck in "a yesteryear-zone". GamePro, one of the few wholly positive reviewers, praised the "dynamic details that not only look great but add to the fun and playability" of its arenas.
trivia: It took about two years to make.
Thirty characters were created, then cut to eleven through teenage focus groups.
Its motion capture was performed by an Atari team member who belonged to the Society for Creative Anachronism.
Cheaper 3dfx hardware let Atari sell it to arcade operators at a lower price.
A PlayStation version was planned but never released.
devStory: Atari Games developed and published it for arcades using the 3dfx Voodoo graphics card, the technology behind San Francisco Rush, which was cheaper to develop for than proprietary hardware. It was a commercial success in arcades, turning Atari a profit, though reviews were average. Midway released a Nintendo 64 port, which critics judged the best fighter on the console only by default; Next Generation said it "would still get pounded into the ground by any PlayStation or Saturn fighter game", and GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann found it inferior to Dark Rift, saying it "looks fantastic but still plays poorly."

title: Rakugakids
description: Rakugakids (1998) is Konami's 2D Nintendo 64 fighter whose characters look like children's doodles, from a ray-gun astronaut to a sleeping tank bear.
longDescription:
The name joins the Japanese rakugaki, meaning doodle, with the English "kids", reflecting a visual style resembling children's drawings, with 2D fighters on 3D backgrounds. It plays like a toned-down Street Fighter with the standard six-button layout of three punches and three kicks, combined with directional commands for special moves. Every character has a one-button launcher that knocks the opponent into the air to be chased and attacked there, plus an extra jump in mid-air. Super combos, called Magic, use up to three levels shown as crayons, spent on offence for heavy damage, defence to knock opponents far away, or a counter while blocking.

Each fighter is credited to a child artist. Astronots, drawn by Andy, is a Buck Rogers-style astronaut with a ray gun and rocket boots; Captain. Cat. Kit is a hip-hop cat who fights with brass instruments, a basketball and breakdancing, and can burst into flames; Marsa is a witch with a chicken-like hat who can triple jump; Robot C.H.O is a grappler who transforms into objects such as a bin or a car; Beartank is a constantly sleeping green bear with tank guns; Cools. Roy is a cowboy aided by his cactus butler Alfred; and Mamezo, the villain, morphs into tools like forks and scissors. Hidden characters include the sub-boss Inuzo and the final boss Darkness, a ghost dog.
trivia: It was never released in the US.
The European version was criticised for being poorly converted, playing slower than the Japanese original.
Extra characters and options unlock based on total playtime.
Steve Merrett cited it among Konami's last gameplay-focused N64 games.
Its characters and music were later referenced in other Konami games.
devStory: Konami developed and released it for the Nintendo 64 in 1998. Its European release received mixed reviews, partly because the conversion ran slower than the original Japanese game. Journalist Steve Merrett cited Konami's Nintendo 64 library, including Rakugakids, International Superstar Soccer 98 and Castlevania, as its last set of games focused on gameplay, using the console's power to build on tropes from 2D gaming, and its 2D-fighters-on-3D-backgrounds formula is an example of how 2D fighting game makers tried to stay relevant in a market full of 3D games.

title: Extreme-G
description: Extreme-G (1997) is Probe Entertainment's futuristic Nintendo 64 combat racer, sending plasma bikes at over 750 km/h around rollercoaster-like tracks with missiles, mines and a trance soundtrack.
longDescription:
Pilots race plasma-powered bikes in an intergalactic Grand Prix at more than 750 km/h on tracks that loop like rollercoasters through hallucinogenic futuristic settings. Weapons found on the track include multi-homing and reverse missiles, magnetic and laser mines and shield boosts, along with specials such as invisibility, a phosphorus flash and the Wally-Warp, which sends any bike it catches to the back of the pack. Each round gives three nitro boosts that cannot be replenished, and falling off cliffs or the track costs only time, as the bike is teleported back and must rebuild its speed from a standstill.

Single players choose Novice, Intermediate or Extreme difficulty. The main Extreme Contest has three championships, Atomic with four tracks, Critical Mass with eight and Meltdown with all twelve, each requiring first place to progress, and wins at different difficulties unlock hidden bikes, levels and cheats for other modes. Multiplayer offers racing, flag capture and a battle mode. Critics praised its loops, jumps and corkscrews and its sense of speed, Electronic Gaming Monthly's Crispin Boyer saying no other game matched it, and compared the bike designs to Tron, while noting a steep learning curve, distance fog, slowdown with four players and dull battle arenas.
trivia: Its working title was Ultimate Racer.
Probe Entertainment was an internal Acclaim development team.
It was released in Japan on 29 May 1998.
Throwback Entertainment, which acquired the rights in 2006, re-released it on Nintendo Classics in 2024.
Sequels include Extreme-G 2, Extreme-G 3 and XGRA.
devStory: Probe Entertainment developed it and Acclaim Entertainment published it for the Nintendo 64 in 1997, with an original trance soundtrack. Despite strong competition among N64 racers, it received favourable reviews and was a commercial success. Reviewers unanimously called its graphics outstanding, GameRevolution praised its replay value from many tracks, weapons and multiplayer options, and most agreed the techno music, though unoriginal, suited the intense races, concluding that a handful of shortcomings kept it from the very top tier. Extreme-G 2 followed in 1998.

title: F-1 World Grand Prix
description: F-1 World Grand Prix (1998) is Paradigm Entertainment's Formula One simulation of the 1997 season, praised by N64 Magazine as the finest driving simulation ever made.
longDescription:
The Nintendo 64 version is based on the 1997 Formula One season, with all 17 circuits and all 22 drivers plus two unlockable bonus racers, except Jacques Villeneuve, who is replaced for licensing reasons by a silhouetted "Driver Williams" with a fictional helmet but his correct career statistics; the player can rename him, which also unlocks extras. The MasterCard Lola team is absent because it never took part in a race that season. Five modes are offered: Grand Prix, racing the 1997 season course by course; Exhibition, a single race; Time Trial; Challenge, recreating real scenarios such as trying to win the 1997 Hungarian Grand Prix as Damon Hill or beating Jean Alesi as David Coulthard at Monza; and two-player split-screen racing.

Before each race players can tune their car's tyres, fuel load and wing angle, and weather and its effects are simulated. N64 Magazine's James Ashton called it "the finest driving simulation the world has ever seen", Hyper gave it 86 per cent as "a great addition to any racing fan's game library", and Edge eight out of ten, while GamePro warned that only players wanting an extremely challenging F1 sim, or with enormous patience, would love it. Later versions moved to the 1998 season on Dreamcast and Game Boy Color, and to 1999 on PlayStation and Windows.
trivia: It used speech compression technology from Factor 5 to fit voice clips on the cartridge.
It was first developed as a Nintendo 64 exclusive.
It won a Gold award at the 1999 Milia festival for earning over €20 million in the EU.
It was nominated for Best Racing Game at The Electric Playground's 1998 Blister Awards.
F-1 World Grand Prix II followed in 1999.
devStory: Paradigm Entertainment developed it as a Nintendo 64 exclusive, and it was released in 1998 before versions followed for Dreamcast, Windows, PlayStation and Game Boy Color. The N64 and Dreamcast versions received favourable reviews; Famitsu gave them 29 and 30 out of 40. It was a success in Europe, and its sequel, F-1 World Grand Prix II, was published by Video System for the N64 in 1999. Eidos Interactive's later PlayStation and Windows versions received mixed reviews, though AllGame praised extras such as a fully customisable instant replay.

title: Dark Rift
description: Dark Rift (1997) is Kronos Digital's 3D fighter, the first Nintendo 64 game to run at 60 frames per second, pitting fighters from three dimensions against each other for pieces of a Master Key.
longDescription:
Set far in the future after Criticom, it spans three dimensions: the Neutral Dimension, home to Earth, the Dark Dimension of demons, and the Light Dimension of energy beings, who despite the name show no angelic qualities. The crystal sought in Criticom turns out to be the Core Prime Element of a Master Key holding the power to all the universe's secrets. Found long ago lodged in a spatial tear, the key burst into three pieces when retrieved, flinging two into other dimensions and widening the tear into the Dark Rift.

Players choose from eight fighters, with two hidden characters unlocked by finishing single-player mode, and fights default to three rounds out of five rather than the usual two out of three. Unlike Criticom, every animation was motion-captured, directed by Ted Warnock, whose background was traditional animation. Its graphics and animation were widely praised, with Electronic Gaming Monthly's Shawn Smith comparing them to Virtua Fighter 3, and IGN and Next Generation admired character designs such as Demonica and Morphix. But EGM's reviewers felt it was weak in every other respect, IGN and EGM found projectiles too slow to be useful, and Edge called it an average fighter that "fails to produce a single surprise".
trivia: It was first announced as Criticom II.
It began development as a Sega Saturn game.
The Windows version was announced to come out a month before the N64 one.
It was released in Japan as Space Dynamites on 27 March 1998.
It sits between Kronos's Criticom and Cardinal Syn.
devStory: Kronos Digital Entertainment, founded by Stan Liu, developed it and Vic Tokai published it for the Nintendo 64 and Windows in 1997. Liu said Kronos "got stuck doing fighting games for a while simply because we were one of the very few U.S. game developers that actually made a fighting game". Reviews were mixed, but many saw it as a big improvement on Criticom: IGN's Doug Perry said Kronos had "overcome its Criticom syndrome" and called it, for the time being, "the best fighter on Nintendo 64", while GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann said only its graphic effects saved it from falling below average.

title: Lands of Lore: Guardians of Destiny
description: Lands of Lore: Guardians of Destiny (1997) is Westwood's first-person adventure-RPG in which the cursed Luther shifts unpredictably between human, lizard and beast forms while uncovering the return of the god Belial.
longDescription:
Eons ago the god Belial was executed for fuelling a war between the Huline and the Dracoids by arming the latter, but before his death he arranged for a powerful creature to bring about his rebirth. Near Gladstone, the Draracle has a vision of a Huline girl cornered by a monster and sees it as a sign of Belial's return. In Gladstone, Luther, a young farmer and son of the late sorceress Scotia, is imprisoned on suspicion of belonging to the Dark Army, unaware himself of the curse that will drive his journey.

Like Realms of the Haunting, it is a first-person adventure with occasional combat, built around puzzles solved by clicking on objects and people, using inventory items, casting spells, attacking, or dragging objects and even corpses into place. Luther's curse makes him shift at random between three forms. The small lizard can enter tunnels, runs fast and casts spells easily but drowns in even shallow water; the tall, heavy beast jumps poorly but can step across gaps, wade through deep water, resist poison and hit hard, but cannot cast spells and must wait to change back; the human is a balance of the two and the only form that can use weapons and armour. Spells later let him change at will in human or lizard form. Most enemies leave him alone unless provoked, and he fights with melee, a bow, items and spells at four levels, with a fifth unlocked late in the game.
trivia: It is the sequel to Lands of Lore: The Throne of Chaos.
It abandoned the original's turn-based, D&D-style play for more action.
Westwood made it a flagship title for late 1997 after Daggerfall's success.
Its cut-scene monsters were made with 3D Studio, MeshPaint and Photoshop.
Lands of Lore III followed in 1999.
devStory: Westwood Studios developed it for MS-DOS and Windows, and Virgin Interactive published it in 1997, Next Generation reporting that Westwood made it a flagship title because RPGs like Daggerfall had become hits. It received above-average reviews. PC Gamer US called it a "very good game" but said its engine was dated next to Jedi Knight and Quake, and Computer Games Strategy Plus praised its "excellent" story and "rich" world but criticised its FMV, "awkward" controls and dated engine. PC PowerPlay hailed it as "perhaps the most complete game" its reviewer had played, and PC Zone called it "another Westwood masterpiece".

sources.title: Lands of Lore: Guardians of Destiny

title: An Elder Scrolls Legend: Battlespire
description: An Elder Scrolls Legend: Battlespire (1997) is Bethesda's linear Elder Scrolls spin-off, a first-person dungeon quest through a floating fortress and the planes of Oblivion to stop Mehrunes Dagon, with multiplayer.
longDescription:
On the edge of Oblivion floats the Battlespire, and the player must fight through it and the planes of Oblivion to find and defeat the daedric prince Mehrunes Dagon before his armies invade Tamriel. Unlike Daggerfall's open world, it is a linear game of seven dungeon levels completed by defeating enemies, solving puzzles and collecting objects. Players create a character from six races and eighteen classes, or a custom build spending limited points on hit points, skills, attributes, starting spells and equipment, and talk to characters through dialogue trees.

Combat is fought by clicking and dragging the mouse to swing a weapon in one of four directions, with a primary and secondary weapon swapped by a key. Spells come from character creation or scrolls in libraries and can be customised by type, area and range and bound to hotkeys. Skills improve with use, and finishing a level awards experience to raise skills and attributes. It was the first Elder Scrolls game with multiplayer: over a LAN or Mplayer.com, up to eight players can tackle the campaign co-operatively with extra monsters, compete in teams of up to four to finish levels first, or fight in deathmatch, though saving and dialogue are disabled in these modes.
trivia: It began as a Daggerfall expansion called Dungeon of Daggerfall.
It was announced at E3 1997 alongside Redguard.
Elder Scrolls developer Julian Le Fay led it.
PC Gamer UK called its animation "shockingly bad".
Its developers felt its failure, with Redguard's, began a decline at Bethesda that lasted until Morrowind.
devStory: After Daggerfall in 1996, Bethesda prepared several projects to capitalise on its success, turning a planned expansion into spin-offs that would tell more stories in Tamriel and fill the gap while Morrowind was delayed. Intended as simpler, more action-focused games reflecting player feedback, Battlespire was designed with smaller scope and linear levels. Released for MS-DOS in 1997, it received average reviews: Next Generation liked its focus and lack of "aimless wandering", but others missed Daggerfall's depth, found the XnGine graphics dated and criticised its many bugs. It is now seen as an unsuccessful spin-off.

title: The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard
description: The Elder Scrolls Adventures: Redguard (1998) is Bethesda's third-person action-adventure in which the mercenary Cyrus searches the island of Stros M'Kai for his missing sister amid rebellion and necromancy.
longDescription:
During the Tiber Wars, Tiber Septim's Third Empire has occupied Hammerfell after its king's death sparked a civil war between the Crowns and the Forebears. Septim backed the Forebears and drove Prince A'tor's Crowns back to the island of Stros M'Kai, where Admiral Richton and the mercenary dragon Nafaalilargus crushed them and A'tor apparently died from a poisoned arrow. Richton now rules the island ruthlessly. Cyrus, a Redguard mercenary working for a Khajiit crime boss, receives a letter from his mentor Tobias: his sister Iszara has vanished on Stros M'Kai. He uncovers that she was A'tor's lover and a member of the pirate Restless League, that A'tor's soul is trapped in a soul gem, and that the Sload necromancer N'Gasta has sent her soul to the daedric prince Clavicus Vile.

It is the only Elder Scrolls game with a predetermined character and a forced third-person view, a free-roaming action-adventure in which Cyrus has a set name, race and skills. Inspired by Tomb Raider, Prince of Persia and Ultima, it combines keyword conversations with characters, item puzzles and an epic story with dungeons, sword fights and chasms. The team focused its art on detailed real-time 3D environments of the island and its town using the XnGine, and Bethesda's subsidiary XL Translab created over thirty minutes of animation.
trivia: It is set at the end of the Second Era, between The Elder Scrolls Online and Arena.
It was in development for two and a half years.
It was released on 14 November 1998.
It was meant to start an Elder Scrolls Adventures series of action-adventures.
It was a finalist for Computer Gaming World's Best Adventure of 1998, losing to Grim Fandango and Sanitarium.
devStory: Bethesda Softworks developed and published it as the second of three projects following Daggerfall, released for MS-DOS in November 1998. It received favourable reviews; Next Generation said that "even with the faults... Redguard is an impressive addition to the Elder Scrolls series and deserves any true adventure fan's attention", and GameSpot and PC Gamer US nominated it as the year's best adventure, the latter noting its exploration and story despite action that might put off traditional adventure fans. Like Battlespire, though, it was a commercial flop, and Todd Howard later said it "didn't do well for the company", contributing to Bethesda's difficult years until 2000.

title: Space Quest V: Roger Wilco – The Next Mutation
description: Space Quest V: Roger Wilco – The Next Mutation (1993) is Dynamix's Star Trek spoof in which janitor Roger Wilco finally becomes a captain, of a garbage scow, and uncovers a mutagenic plot.
longDescription:
After Space Quest IV, janitor Roger Wilco enrols at StarCon Academy hoping to captain his own ship. He makes an enemy of the toupee-wearing Captain Raems T. Quirk, a blatant spoof of James T. Kirk, commander of StarCon's prize ship, the SCS Goliath, and cheats his way through an aptitude test. Ambassador Beatrice Wankmeister, the woman Roger's future son told him he would marry, arrives to investigate toxic dumping across the galaxy, and Quirk takes the job. Roger, meanwhile, gets his own command: the SCS Eureka, a garbage scow that works like a giant vacuum cleaner.

With his crew, including chief engineer Cliffy, a spoof of Scotty, Roger collects rubbish, adopts a facehugger as a pet, outwits WD40, a homicidal gynoid sent by the company that pursued him in Space Quest III, and captures her cloaking device. He breaks Cliffy out of a bar's brig after a brawl with the Goliath's crew, and on a barren planet finds colonists turned into mutants, with a canister from a genetics company dumped nearby. The game parodies Star Trek's ships, crews and episodes, along with films such as Alien and The Fly. Computer Gaming World's Charles Ardai found it both funny and suspenseful, praising its "first-rate" graphics and sound and dialogue "written with a dry wit and a sense of character".
trivia: It was the first Space Quest designed by Mark Crowe alone, without Scott Murphy.
It was the first Space Quest made outside Sierra, by sister company Dynamix.
It was sponsored by Sprint, whose logo appears after transmissions and on a billboard.
A character mocks MCI's "Friends & Aliens" plan.
Unlike Space Quest IV, it had no voiced version.
devStory: Mark Crowe had moved to Dynamix after Space Quest IV, so the fifth game was developed there and released by Sierra On-Line for MS-DOS on 5 February 1993. It was the only Space Quest, and Sierra's second game after Leisure Suit Larry 5, to carry real-world sponsorship, and Sierra gave it away to customers signing up with Sprint. Critics welcomed it as a fun addition to the series, Ardai concluding that "even the most demanding Wilcophiles will be pleased". Space Quest 6 followed in 1995.

title: Revenant
description: Revenant (1999) is Cinematix Studios' action RPG in which an undead warrior raised from hell hunts a kidnapped princess on the island of Ahkuilon and discovers he was once its king.
longDescription:
Locke D'Averam is a revenant, raised from Anserak, or hell, by the sorcerer Sardok, magical advisor to Lord Tendrick, ruler of the island of Ahkuilon. Bound to Sardok's will, Locke must rescue Tendrick's long-missing daughter, Princess Andria, from the Children of the Change, a cult led by the demon Yhagoro that has been taking over the island with mind-control magic, in exchange for his freedom. Gradually he learns that he was once king of an ancient empire centred on Ahkuilon, who made a pact with the demon god Kraxxus but refused to pay its price, his wife's soul, and was condemned to eternal suffering as his empire sank into the earth. Andria is his queen reborn, kidnapped to complete the sacrifice.

Combat changes with the control method. With the mouse, Locke attacks with minimal input, while the keyboard gives finer control over three basic attack types that chain into combos, some ending in enemy-specific kill moves, from stomping spiders to beheading swordsmen; a gamepad works similarly with almost any move mappable to buttons. Locke permanently raises attributes such as strength and agility and gains new fighting abilities at level thresholds. Talismans combine into spells, recipes for which are found on scrolls, from freezing and poisoning to holding foes in place for a magical attack followed by a special combat move. Based in the town of Misthaven, he allies with the Ogroks and frees the Druhg slaves along the way.
trivia: Locke is named after the House of Averam, which raised him from the dead.
His guide, the sorcerer Olihoot, helps him rediscover his past.
Sardok turns out to be a traitor with his own agenda.
Reviews from major outlets mostly scored it 7 to 8 out of 10.
It sold about 37,000 copies in the US by March 2000.
devStory: Cinematix Studios developed it and Eidos Interactive published it for Windows in 1999. It received above-average reviews, with major outlets generally scoring it between seven and eight out of ten, though its sales in the United States were modest, at around 37,000 copies by March 2000.

title: Realms of Arkania: Blade of Destiny
description: Realms of Arkania: Blade of Destiny (1992) is Attic's party RPG based on the German pen-and-paper game The Dark Eye, in which heroes race to find a legendary sword before an orc invasion.
longDescription:
An orc chief has united all the orc tribes and plans to attack the human lands. Hetman Tronde Torbensson, leader of the Thorwalians, hires the party to find the sword Grimring, the Blade of Destiny, lost since the death of its bearer, Hetman Hyggelik the Great, and stop the invasion of Thorwal. Recovering it means finding pieces of a treasure map, then defeating the orc chief and his minions; if the party fails within about two in-game years, the orcs attack and the game is lost.

It is a classic party RPG for up to six characters, plus an optional recruitable companion, moving through 3D towns and dungeons, with travel between them shown as a path on a 2D regional map. It uses the pseudo-3D engine of Attic's 1991 Spirit of Adventure at a higher resolution, borrowing Eye of the Beholder's inventory interface and Might and Magic III's screen layout. Monsters and characters are not shown in the 3D view; instead fights switch to an isometric view for turn-based tactical combat. White Wolf praised a world of over 70 towns, villages, dungeons and ruins and some original monsters, calling it "a solid roleplaying adventure that will challenge you without frustrating you".
trivia: It was the first game based on The Dark Eye by Schmidt Spiele.
The German original is Das Schwarze Auge: Die Schicksalsklinge.
Its success led Sir-Tech to release an English translation in 1993.
The three Realms of Arkania games sold over 2.4 million copies combined, according to Die Zeit.
Computer Gaming World's Scorpia found a bug that "won" the game by quitting during the final fight.
devStory: Attic Entertainment Software released it in German in 1992, and its success led to Sir-Tech's English version in 1993. Die Zeit reported that all three games in the series were commercial and critical successes. English-language reviews were mixed: Scorpia criticised its "awkward and confusing" magic system, punishing saves and high combat failure rates, and The One gave the Amiga version 73 per cent, calling its graphics poor and the game generic. Compute! felt it had "plenty of depth" for Wizardry and Might and Magic fans, and Pyramid recommended it for its graphics, story and background.

sources.title: Realms of Arkania: Blade of Destiny

title: Anvil of Dawn
description: Anvil of Dawn (1995) is DreamForge's pre-rendered first-person dungeon crawler, playable with just the left mouse button, named the best RPG of 1995 by Computer Gaming World.
longDescription:
The world of Tempest has been overrun by an evil warlord, and the last castle of the good is under siege. The player's hero is teleported into the occupied, devastated land to defeat the warlord and his minions. One of the last dungeon crawlers with step-by-step movement in a semi-3D world, it shows a real-time first-person view, with fully spoken dialogue and pre-rendered cut-scenes on CD. The player chooses one of five heroes at the start and controls only that character, meeting the others pursuing the same quest along the way. It is mostly action-oriented with some puzzles, has no experience points, as abilities and spells improve with use, and has several endings.

DreamForge focused on atmosphere and immersion, pre-rendering its 3D environments because real-time 3D dungeons of the day looked "flat and pixellated" to the team. Outdoor areas were lined with movement nodes and pre-recorded mini-cinematics to make travel seamless. The interface was simplified, with few on-screen icons and automatic quest logs, spellbooks and maps, and the whole game could be played with the left mouse button, which in turn led to a single hero instead of a party. Combat is pseudo-turn-based: enemies attack at set intervals but counter each of the player's blows, so attacking quickly speeds them up and attacking slowly slows them down.
trivia: Computer Game Review also named it the best RPG of 1995.
It was a nominee for Computer Games Strategy Plus's RPG of the Year, won by Stonekeep.
Chris Straka said the team tried to "bridge the gap between the novice and the expert player".
Several months went into designing its magic system.
Matt Barton called it "one of the best of the Dungeon Master-inspired games".
devStory: DreamForge Intertainment developed it and New World Computing published it for MS-DOS in 1995. It was critically acclaimed: Computer Gaming World singled out its "playability and balance", Computer Game Review called it "an excellent job all the way around", and Arcane described it as "hack-and-slash raised to an art form". PC Gamer US found it "attractive and enjoyable" though it did not stretch boundaries far, and Computer Games Strategy Plus argued faster and deeper games were available. Historian Matt Barton later praised its "careful pacing, splendid music, and ... superior interface".

title: Menzoberranzan
description: Menzoberranzan (1994) is SSI's Forgotten Realms RPG in which two adventurers descend into the Underdark to rescue kidnapped villagers, joining forces with the drow ranger Drizzt Do'Urden.
longDescription:
The only two survivors of a monster-hunting quest return to a village in Icewind Dale to celebrate, pass out after a night of heavy drinking and wake to find drow raiding the village and carrying off villagers. Sent into the Underdark to rescue them, they gather allies and eventually team up with Drizzt Do'Urden, who reveals the raid was ordered by his mother, Malice Do'Urden, to lure him back for punishment for abandoning his people. When they reach the drow city of Menzoberranzan, Drizzt is teleported away and captured, and the party must seek help from drow caught in a civil war between the two most powerful families, eventually defeating Malice, preventing Drizzt's sacrifice and freeing the villagers.

It runs on the engine of SSI's Ravenloft: Strahd's Possession, mixing Ultima Underworld's 3D world and real-time action with a concept similar to Westwood's Eye of the Beholder games. The player creates two characters and can gain non-player allies later. The setting comes from the 1992 tabletop box set Menzoberranzan: The Famed City of the Drow by Ed Greenwood, R. A. Salvatore and Douglas Niles. Reviews were divided: PC Gamer US called it the best Advanced Dungeons & Dragons game ever released, and Next Generation praised its painting-like high-resolution graphics, while Scorpia found it "a disappointment" and PC Zone said it "tries to be Ultima Underworld and fails miserably".
trivia: It was the last TSR-licensed game SSI published.
It was included in the 1996 AD&D Masterpiece Collection.
GOG.com released it in August 2015.
Computer Shopper called it a "must-have".
Dungeons and Desktops called it "infamously wretched (and hard to spell)".
devStory: Strategic Simulations and DreamForge Intertainment created it, and SSI published it in 1994. Al Giovetti of Electronic Entertainment summarised it as "high-quality role-playing meets fast-paced first-person exploration and spectacular real-time combat", and White Wolf Inphobia recommended it as an excellent introduction to SSI's newer AD&D games. Others were harsher: Quandaryland found it slower than Ravenloft with too many empty places, and GameSpy's Allen Rausch said that without a great plot and exciting monsters it was "less impressive than it was in players' imaginations".

title: Conquests of the Longbow: The Legend of Robin Hood
description: Conquests of the Longbow: The Legend of Robin Hood (1991) is Christy Marx's richly researched Sierra adventure in which Robin Hood raises King Richard's ransom while evading the Sheriff of Nottingham.
longDescription:
Robin Hood, a gallant, yellow-bearded woodsman and master of disguise, sets out to restore King Richard I to the throne by raising enough money to pay his ransom, while the Sheriff of Nottingham tries to capture and hang him and his men. Maid Marian leads a double life as a Nottingham noblewoman and a pagan forest priestess who equates the Virgin Queen of Heaven with the Virgin Mary, fearing she will be burned as a witch if caught; she is Robin's love interest and his link to the Queen Mother Eleanor of Aquitaine's network of spies and loyalists, also working to raise the ransom.

Most of the game is standard point-and-click adventuring with Sierra's icon interface from King's Quest V, travelling between areas via hotspots on a map, plus minigames of archery, combat and nine men's morris at adjustable difficulty. Play is divided into days, each ending with a cut-scene of Robin and his men discussing events, and vital tasks can be left undone, leading to a worse ending. Several puzzles are purely language-based, and the game is written in British English. Score is kept three ways: puzzle points, ransom money collected and outlaws still alive. There are four endings, from Robin being hanged to a pardon, a royal post without Marian's hand, or a noble title and marriage to Marian.
trivia: It is the second and final Conquests game, after Conquests of Camelot.
Its manual's bibliography lists twenty-eight volumes, including J. C. Holt's Robin Hood and Robert Graves's The White Goddess.
Marx's essays in the manual cover the legend's history, tree lore and video game piracy.
Computer Gaming World named it one of the top four adventure games of 1992.
Adventure Gamers ranked it the 42nd-best adventure game ever in 2011.
devStory: Designed by Christy Marx and published by Sierra On-Line in 1991 with VGA graphics, it involved considerable historical and cultural research for its setting and puzzles. Mark Seibert directed the music and sound effects, with synthesised score by Ken Allen, Christopher Braymen, Orpheus Hanley and Aubrey Hodges. Dragon gave it five out of five stars, and White Wolf found its "diversity" of combat, puzzles and arcade sequences most impressive. Adventure Gamers later gave it 4.5 out of 5, praising its puzzles, writing, research, branching plot and graphics while criticising unresponsive action controls, and called it a classic despite its relative obscurity.

sources.title: Conquests of the Longbow: The Legend of Robin Hood

title: Alone in the Dark 2
description: Alone in the Dark 2 (1993) is Infogrames' sequel in which detective Edward Carnby battles voodoo-possessed gangster pirates at the mansion Hell's Kitchen to rescue a kidnapped girl.
longDescription:
At Christmas 1924, three months before the first game, "supernatural private eye" Edward Carnby and his partner Ted Stryker investigate the kidnapping of young Grace Saunders. The clues lead to Hell's Kitchen, an old mansion belonging to an infamous gangster boss. When Ted disappears there, Carnby follows and learns that he has been murdered. The mobsters turn out to be the bodily forms of pirates who plundered the seas centuries ago and sold their souls for eternal life through voodoo, and Carnby must fight through the house and onto a pirate ship hidden in the cliff beneath it to uncover their secret, rescue Grace and learn why they want her.

The horror of the original is much reduced: there are supernatural elements, but the main enemies are gangsters and pirates who, though green and zombie-like, walk, talk and shoot like ordinary people. Carnby starts with a revolver and can pick up shotguns, Tommy guns, a Derringer, flintlock pistols and swords. The world is larger, spanning the mansion, its gardens and the ship in the caverns, but apart from the house it is explored in a strict linear sequence, a pattern later sequels followed. At times the player controls Grace, a child who cannot fight and is captured if spotted, so she must sneak around and turn household objects into booby traps.
trivia: A promotional mini-game, Jack in the Dark, starring Grace was given away at Christmas 1993.
It was ported to PC-98, FM Towns and 3DO.
Saturn and PlayStation versions were titled Jack Is Back in Europe and One-Eyed Jack's Revenge in North America.
Edge gave the PC version nine out of ten.
It is the second Alone in the Dark game.
devStory: Infogrames developed and published it in 1993 as the second Alone in the Dark. Computer Gaming World said it "looks rich enough to meet gamers' expectations for a solid sequel" and that, despite a weak ending, it was a good, solid challenge that would test players' reflexes as well as their minds, though not for the easily frustrated. Edge praised its more responsive controls, "nerve-tinglingly clear" audio and "movie-style production" values, as well as its far greater number of locations, warning that it was "gruesome" and frightening.

title: Lords of the Realm II
description: Lords of the Realm II (1996) is Impressions Games' medieval strategy game combining turn-based management of counties with real-time battles and castle sieges, as rival lords vie for a vacant throne.
longDescription:
In an alternate 1268, a king dies without an heir, and players compete with rival claimants to win the throne. Play alternates between a turn-based map, viewed isometrically and divided into up to ten counties held by two to five players, and real-time battles. Each county's economy is managed separately: food comes from grain or cows, and mining, smithing, forestry and farming produce resources that can be switched on or off, traded with travelling merchants or forged into weapons by blacksmiths. Labour is split between food and industry with a slider or managed in detail. Each county has a happiness level shaped by taxes and food supply; unhappy peasants riot, hungry ones die or emigrate, and events such as the Black Death or drought strike at random.

Armies are raised by conscripting peasants, who can become knights, archers or pikemen if the right weapons are available, and marched on the map to intercept enemy armies, towns or castles. Counties can be fortified with a palisade, motte and bailey, keep, stone castle or royal castle using stone and iron, and diplomacy allows gifts and alliances. Single players choose from 24 maps, difficulty and number of opponents. Critics praised the medieval theme and the blend of modes; Next Generation found its economic management "plausible" and "realistic" with a "sense of the dynamics of ruling", though some felt the two halves conflicted or lacked depth.
trivia: David Lester said it combined Civilization's turn-based play with Warcraft II and Command & Conquer's real-time battles.
The mix was also meant to make the series "more multiplayer friendly".
It was the 14th best-selling computer game of 1997 in the US and 19th of 1998.
Lester said it sold 2.5 million copies worldwide.
A Siege Pack expansion followed in June 1997.
devStory: Impressions Games developed it as the sequel to 1994's Lords of the Realm, and Sierra announced it after acquiring publishing rights to Impressions' games, releasing it for DOS, Windows and Mac in 1996. General manager and lead designer David Lester aimed to merge "visceral" combat with in-depth strategy and streamlined the economic simulation with slider bars to "reduce the learning curve of the game dramatically". It received generally favourable reviews, with PCMag calling the turn-based mode "very well-designed", while critics disagreed on its difficulty, AI and the strategic options in combat. It peaked at ninth on PC Data's charts in January 1997, and Lords of the Realm III followed in 2004.

title: Terminal Velocity
description: Terminal Velocity (1995) is Terminal Reality's fast, inertia-free flight shooter, likened to "Descent outdoors", in which the TV-202 starfighter fights an alien alliance that has turned on Earth.
longDescription:
In 2704 the Alliance of Space-Faring Alien Races, of which Earth is a member, suddenly turns on the planet and its fleet ravages it. Flying the powerful TV-202 starfighter, the player undertakes missions to defeat the enemy, learning in the third episode that a supercomputer called the Xenocidic Initiative on Proxima Seven is behind the war. A hidden mission in the CD-ROM version investigates the strange transformation of a nearby planet and reveals that the force behind it drove a man named Sy Wickens insane, his persona having been "accidentally" digitised by the supercomputer.

An action flight combat game with simpler controls and physics than flight simulators, it gives the craft no inertia, so it can change course instantly and fly slowly without falling. Seven weapons range from guns, blasters and rockets to homing missiles and a rare secret weapon, and powerful afterburners provide escapes at very high speed at the cost of being unable to fire. The ship can survive some hits and even collisions with terrain and tunnels. Each of the 27 missions has objectives such as enemies to destroy, tunnels, checkpoints and an extraction point, and every planet ends with a boss. Edge called it "the most convincing sensation of high-speed, low-level flight yet on the PC" and its eight-player mode "probably the best network game since Doom".
trivia: It was called Velocity Brawl during development.
Tom Hall co-produced it.
Lead programmer Mark Randel had been lead programmer of Microsoft Flight Simulator.
Its first episode was released as shareware.
Terminal Reality's Fury3, published by Microsoft, is essentially its Windows 95 version.
devStory: Terminal Reality developed it, and 3D Realms published it for MS-DOS and Windows 95 in 1995, with MacSoft releasing the Mac version. It has three episodes of three worlds each, apart from the two-stage Proxima Seven. It received generally favourable reviews, critics typically comparing it to Descent: GameSpot praised its immersive sense of speed as a "proverbial quick fix", and Computer Games Strategy Plus called it "Descent outdoors" with "impeccable" execution, though it felt point-to-point levels limited exploration, and some reviewers found the play lacking in depth.

title: Blood II: The Chosen
description: Blood II: The Chosen (1998) is Monolith's gory, darkly comic shooter sequel, set in a cyberpunk 2028 where the Cabal cult has become the mega-corporation CabalCo.
longDescription:
A century after Blood, Caleb has spent a hundred years searching for a way to resurrect his comrades, the Chosen, killed by the Cabal, a cult devoted to the demon Tchernobog. Since Caleb killed Tchernobog, the Cabal has become CabalCo, a global mega-corporation controlling the world's population through economic power, led by Gideon, raised to restore Tchernobog and destroy Caleb, now called the Great Betrayer. The game opens on a CabalCo subway train driven by Gideon, who rigs it to crash and escapes. Caleb chases him through New Town to a CabalCo museum, where a bodyguard's experimental weapon opens a dimensional rift that brings back Gabriella, one of the Chosen.

Set in 2028 instead of 1928, it mixes conventional weapons and magic items with cyberpunk technology and dystopian themes, along with heavy graphic violence and black humour. Single players choose one of the four Chosen, Caleb, Gabriella, Ishmael or Ophelia, who differ in marksmanship, maximum health and armour, though the story can only be completed as Caleb. Chapters unlock in order, and 17 weapons, some usable two at a time and most with a secondary fire mode, compete for just 10 slots. Power-ups grant temporary invulnerability, stealth or extra firepower. Multiplayer renames deathmatch "Bloodbath", with each Chosen starting with different weapons and four customisable stats.
trivia: Its deathmatch mode is called Bloodbath.
Multiplayer characters can be customised with ratings of 1 to 5 in four stats.
CNET Gamecenter reported disappointing US sales over Christmas 1998.
Mark Asher said it "went nowhere at the retail level" but did well in OEM deals.
Next Generation compared it to "the Sybil of video games".
devStory: Monolith Productions developed it and GT Interactive distributed it in 1998 as the sequel to Blood, keeping its predecessor's violence and humour but moving the setting a century forward. CNET Gamecenter's Mark Asher noted that, like SiN and Shogo, it sold disappointingly that Christmas, with only Half-Life doing really well, and speculated that the shooter market was smaller than believed. Next Generation gave it two stars out of five, saying "it mimics a lot of different shooter genres, but it has no personality of its own", and PC Gaming World also disliked it.

title: Requiem: Avenging Angel
description: Requiem: Avenging Angel (1999) is Cyclone Studios' first-person shooter in which the angel Malachi fights fallen angels on near-future Earth with divine powers, and the first game with bullet time.
longDescription:
Looking down on his creation, God is not entirely satisfied, and while most angels wait for his guidance, some descend to Earth to interpret his wishes themselves and become the Fallen. By the mid-21st century, led by Lilith, they control humanity's leaders, impose a totalitarian regime and drive the building of the Leviathan, humanity's first interstellar craft, which would let mankind reach Heaven itself and force God to bring about Armageddon, just as the Fallen want. The player is Malachi, a servant of God, who must leave Heaven, cross the limbo realm of Chaos and stop the Leviathan to avert the apocalypse.

The game opens in Chaos, where Malachi has no conventional weapons and relies on angelic powers that work much like the Force powers of Jedi Knight, each explained in the manual with a Biblical quote; one turns an enemy into a pillar of salt. It was the first game with a bullet time feature, slowing time to dodge bullets and kill several enemies. Alongside standard weapons such as a pistol, rocket launcher and railgun, Malachi can possess enemies to use weapons he cannot wield himself. Like Half-Life, it has no distinct levels but a seamless, interlinked world, mostly stylised everyday places on mid-21st-century Earth, such as a bar, a hospital and a power plant.
trivia: Its concept was heavily inspired by Milton's Paradise Lost.
Malachi is named after the Old Testament prophet; the name can mean "my messenger" or "my angel".
It was originally planned as three self-contained episodes set in different eras.
A rigid-body animation system stretched only the joints to save memory.
It was re-released on GOG.com and Steam in 2016.
devStory: Cyclone Studios developed it and 3DO published it in 1999. It received above-average reviews. PC Zone's Charlie Brooker praised its varied character models and advanced animation, "impressive character models that move in all kinds of unpleasantly believable ways". GameSpot commended its innovative angelic powers, comparing them favourably with Jedi Knight's Force powers, but felt it was ultimately a typical shooter without groundbreaking elements, and IGN found its level design boring and its multiplayer lacking.

title: Croc 2
description: Croc 2 (1999) is Argonaut's PlayStation platformer in which Croc searches for his long-lost parents and saves the Inventor Gobbo from the revived Baron Dante, across four Gobbo villages.
longDescription:
Croc sets out to find his missing parents and to rescue the Inventor Gobbo from a revived Baron Dante. Open-ended levels are spread across four Gobbo villages reached from an open hub world, and missions involve helping Gobbos, such as freeing one trapped in a steel cage or chasing down a Dantini who has stolen a sandwich. Completing enough levels in a village opens a boss level and then the next village. Some levels put Croc in a go-kart, speedboat, hang glider, hot air balloon or giant snowball.

Each level holds 100 crystals and five coloured crystals hidden behind platforming challenges or puzzles; finding all five reveals a golden trophy at the end of the level. Collecting every trophy in a village opens an extra level with a jigsaw piece, and the pieces unlock a fifth world of remixed level segments. In the hub, the cat Swap Meet Pete sells heart pots to raise Croc's life count, Gummi Savers Jumps to use as trampolines and a Clockwork Gobbo, a wind-up robot used to collect items. Croc runs, jumps, climbs and swims, with new triple and flip jumps for reaching higher. IGN praised its voice acting, graphics, soundtrack and size but criticised its difficulty and camera, and other critics shared those complaints.
trivia: It is the sequel to Croc: Legend of the Gobbos.
Fox cross-promoted it with Nabisco's Gummi Savers sweets.
A Windows version followed in 2000 and a 2D Game Boy Color version in 2001.
A Dreamcast version with new levels was planned but cancelled.
The original game's manual advertised it for PlayStation and Sega Saturn.
devStory: Argonaut Software developed it and Fox Interactive published it for the PlayStation in 1999, backed by a heavy advertising campaign. In May 2000 managing director Jez San said Argonaut was considering a Dreamcast version with new levels and worlds, pending Fox's approval, but it was cancelled when Argonaut stopped developing for the declining console. Reviews were mixed: GameSpot rated the PlayStation and PC versions poorly, GamePro's Nash Werner said he was "praying each new level would be Croc 2's last", while Scary Larry called it "an acquired taste".

title: Gex 3: Deep Cover Gecko
description: Gex 3: Deep Cover Gecko (1999) is Crystal Dynamics' third Gex game, in which the wisecracking gecko returns to the Media Dimension to rescue the live-action Agent Xtra from Rez.
longDescription:
Gex returns to the Media Dimension to rescue Agent Xtra, a government spy played in full-motion video by model Marliece Andrada, the only live-action character, kidnapped by his arch-enemy Rez. The hub is Mission Control, Gex's secret hideout, overseen by his butler Alfred the Turtle, and it expands as remotes from each level unlock new areas. Gex is voiced by Dana Gould in the US and by Danny John-Jules in the UK and Europe. Bigger levels, more on-screen characters and a retooled camera were made possible by better use of the hardware.

Play is similar to Gex: Enter the Gecko, adding vehicles such as a tank, a camel and a snowboard, plus swimming and gliding in some levels. Instead of the previous game's themed collectibles, Gex collects only bugs, as in the original, limited to 100 per level and kept only up to the last checkpoint on death, making the targets harder. Power-ups let him spit fire and ice, and collecting 100 footprints raises his energy permanently to eight hits. In bonus stages players can control Rex, Cuz and Alfred, and collecting all 50 remotes, including by beating Rez, unlocks a special ending featuring the development team. Side-scrolling minigames recall the series' 2D roots.
trivia: Several mechanics were ideas that could not fit into Gex: Enter the Gecko for lack of time.
Lead designer Chris Tremmel added side-scrolling minigames to vary the missions.
The development team ending is missing from the UK release because of its language selection screen.
A 2D Game Boy Color game, Gex 3: Deep Pocket Gecko, followed in 1999.
Next Generation called it "a passable game – barely".
devStory: Crystal Dynamics wanted the third Gex to focus more on story and on Gex's personality through "over-the-top animations", according to product marketing manager Chip Blundell, and Eidos Interactive published it on the PlayStation in 1999, followed by Nintendo 64 ports. The PlayStation version received favourable reviews, helped by impressive graphics and less platforming competition, while the N64 versions were criticised for stuttering frame rates, poor use of the analogue stick, with Gex running full speed however lightly it was pressed, and comparing badly with Super Mario 64.

title: Crusader: No Regret
description: Crusader: No Regret (1996) is Origin's isometric action follow-up in which the Silencer takes the Resistance fight to the WEC's lunar mines, with new weapons, gorier deaths and harder combat.
longDescription:
Forty-six hours after No Remorse, a WEC freighter bound for the Moon picks up the Silencer's escape pod. On the Moon, which the WEC uses as both a mine and a prison, dissidents and Resistance members are forced to dig Di-Corellium, the radioactive mineral behind almost all of Earth's energy, with about half the known reserves. Chairman Draygan is there to oversee lagging production, possibly hit by the Resistance cell at the hidden Dark Side base, and sends all his forces after the Silencer once he learns of him. Over ten missions the Silencer undermines the WEC, ending in a showdown with Draygan piloting a mech, after which the lunar headquarters are destroyed and the Resistance takes over the mines.

Mechanically it closely follows No Remorse, with teleportation pads for quick travel within and between levels. It adds new weapons and death animations, including freezing and shattering and two kinds of melting, and lifts the old limit of five firearms. Enemies no longer carry money, since there are no friendly merchants on the Moon, and the game is more combat-focused: where many obstacles in No Remorse could be bypassed or opened with passkeys, here brute force is usually the only option. Smarter enemies and trickier traps also raised the difficulty. The story is simpler and more straightforward than its predecessor's.
trivia: Critics and director Tony Zurovec regarded it as more of a standalone expansion than a true sequel.
It uses an advanced SVGA version of the Ultima VIII: Pagan engine.
Andrew Sega and Dan Grandpre of Straylight Productions composed the music.
It introduced higher-quality 16-bit audio samples.
GamePro gave it perfect scores for sound, control and fun factor.
devStory: Origin Systems developed it and Electronic Arts published it in 1996 as the PC-only follow-up to Crusader: No Remorse, again using the Asylum Sound System, which played MOD files for good audio without expensive hardware, and live-action FMV cut-scenes in which the hero never speaks. It was generally well received: GamePro's Major Mike said it "shows no remorse in outclassing its predecessor" with better graphics, more refined play and more mayhem, praising the new forward roll, GameSpot praised its graphical detail and PC Gamer welcomed controller support, though some critics disliked the FMV story and agreed it was more of a "level pack".

title: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans
description: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans (1994) is Blizzard's first Warcraft game, a fantasy real-time strategy game pitting the humans of Azeroth against invading orcs, which helped make multiplayer essential to the genre.
longDescription:
The player leads either the human inhabitants of Azeroth or the invading orcs. In the single-player campaign most missions involve building a small town, harvesting resources, raising an army and leading it to victory, while multiplayer games are always about destroying the enemy's forces. Both sides have melee units, ranged units and spellcasters, and some scenarios add wild monsters, which can sometimes be used as troops. It expands Dune II's "build base, build army, destroy enemy" formula with new mission types, such as putting down rebels of the player's own race, rescuing and rebuilding besieged towns, freeing friendly forces from an enemy camp, and limited-forces missions in which neither side can build more units.

Non-combatant workers carry gold dug from mines and wood chopped from forests back to the Town Hall; both are finite, so they must be gathered efficiently, and forests double as defensive walls early on when armies are small. Lower-level buildings work the same for both races but look different. Two players can compete by dial-up modem or local network, with DOS and Macintosh players able to face each other, and a random map generator supports skirmishes. It was not the first multiplayer RTS, but it persuaded a wider audience that multiplayer was essential, and its mission design and gameplay innovations were adopted by other developers.
trivia: Blizzard copied Dune II's artwork and redesigned every asset, but accidentally kept Dune II's font.
It was originally meant to be an RTS adaptation of Warhammer, but Blizzard could not get a licence from Games Workshop.
Bob Fitch said its theme combined The Lost Vikings with Lemmings-style masses of creatures.
The first game had no script, and its plot was improvised.
It ultimately sold 300,000 copies.
devStory: Inspired by Dune II and Herzog Zwei, Blizzard Entertainment was surprised that no further RTS games appeared in 1993 and early 1994 and seized on the lull, releasing it for MS-DOS in North America on 15 November 1994, with Interplay publishing in Europe and a Mac OS version in 1996. It made the company's finances secure for the first time, passing 100,000 sales within a year. It won PC Gamer's Editors' Choice Award, Computer Life's Critics' Pick and the Innovations Award at the Winter 1995 CES, and its sequel, Warcraft II, became the main rival to Command & Conquer.

title: Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger
description: Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger (1994) is Origin's space combat game that turned the series into an interactive movie, with Mark Hamill, Malcolm McDowell and John Rhys-Davies in over two hours of full-motion video.
longDescription:
In 2669 the Terran-Kilrathi War has raged for over thirty years. The hero of the first two games is now officially named Colonel Christopher Blair, played by Mark Hamill, and after the Kilrathi Crown Prince Thrakhath executes a group of Confederation prisoners, sparing only Blair's lover Angel Devereaux, Admiral Tolwyn, played by Malcolm McDowell, transfers Blair as Wing Commander to the TCS Victory, an ageing Ranger-class carrier. Old faces such as Hobbes and Maniac, played by Tom Wilson, serve alongside new pilots including Flint, and the arrogant test pilot Flash Dillon arrives with the prototype Excalibur heavy fighter. The Kilrathi soon deploy cloaked "Skipper" missiles and a bioweapon against the Locanda colonies.

Play alternates space combat missions against enemy craft with live-action cut-scenes, advertised with the slogan "Don't watch the game, play the movie!". Medals after missions were dropped in favour of cut-scenes that drive the story, and as commander Blair often chooses his ship, its missiles and his wingmen, some of whom can die permanently. Branching conversations let the player pick Blair's replies, which can change a character's attitude or the morale of the whole crew. The series moved from sprites to software-rendered, texture-mapped polygonal 3D, with a wholly new line of ships; Kilrathi craft became asymmetrical shapes with prongs, barbs and fangs, and the blockier forms suited the primitive polygon graphics of a time before 3D cards.
trivia: John Rhys-Davies plays both Paladin and Thrakhath.
The video was shot entirely against green screens, with every set created digitally.
It cost between $4 million and $5 million to develop.
A Sega Saturn version was announced and advertised but never released.
It sold over 700,000 copies in total.
devStory: Chris Roberts' third main Wing Commander was developed and released by Origin Systems in December 1994 for DOS and Mac OS, followed by 3DO in 1995 and PlayStation in 1996. It was another major hit, with the PC versions alone selling over 500,000 copies, and PC Data reported that the US computer version earned $15.9 million by October 1999.
