Next Generation gave the 3DO version five stars, arguing that the big-name actors made it more realistic and suspenseful and that the video enhanced the play rather than substituting for it.

sources.title: Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger

title: Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom
description: Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom (1996) is Origin's $12 million space combat sequel, set after the Kilrathi war, in which Colonel Blair is recalled to investigate attacks blamed on the Border Worlds.
longDescription:
Several years after the Terran-Kilrathi War, the Confederation is trying to stabilise its economy and society, and the Kilrathi survivors, led by Melek, struggle in peacetime. Tension with the Union of Border Worlds deepens after an unarmed medical transport is destroyed by mysterious fighters with a new weapon that incinerates a ship's contents. As Paladin, now a senior governor, calls for a vote on war, Admiral Tolwyn is sent on a fact-finding mission, and the retired Colonel Christopher "Maverick" Blair, scraping a living as a farmer on a desert world, is recalled to service; within five minutes of taking the cockpit, the station he is heading for is attacked.

Between missions Blair moves around his carrier, at first the TCS Lexington, talking to other characters in full-motion video scenes, then takes a briefing from the captain and picks his wingman and fighter. Each fighter differs in durability, manoeuvrability, top speed, guns and missile hardpoints, and loadouts can be chosen. Combat centres on close-in dogfights: shields regenerate but armour does not, guns draw on a limited, recharging energy pool, missiles and ECM are in limited supply, and pilots can eject in an emergency. Wingmen differ in flying style, marksmanship and obedience, and branching conversations can change a character's attitude, crew morale, the next assignment and the ending.
trivia: Unlike its predecessor, its video was shot on real sets on 35mm film rather than against a green screen.
The original MS-DOS edition shipped on six CD-ROMs.
A 1997 DVD-ROM edition upgraded the video to full DVD quality but needed a hardware decoder.
Mark Asher said it "made back its $10 million development, but barely".
It was re-released on the North American PlayStation Network in 2009.
devStory: Origin Systems developed it on an aggressive 12-month schedule aimed at December 1995, and Electronic Arts released it for MS-DOS on 8 February 1996, followed by Windows, Mac and a 1997 PlayStation version. Its budget of US$12 million was then unheard of for a video game, mostly spent on its film shoot. PC Data ranked it first for February 1996, it sold over 200,000 units in Europe by February 1997 and earned a VUD Gold award in 1998, and critics received the PC version well.

sources.title: Wing Commander IV: The Price of Freedom

title: Privateer 2: The Darkening
description: Privateer 2: The Darkening (1996) is the Origin-branded space trading sequel in which an amnesiac survivor, played by Clive Owen, becomes a privateer in the Tri-System, with a cast including John Hurt and Christopher Walken.
longDescription:
Set in a remote region of the Wing Commander universe, the Tri-System Confederation has nearly three thousand years of history of its own, parallel to that of the Terran Confederation. In the opening, in the year 2790 of the Tri-System calendar, whose months last about 40 days, the cargo ship Canera is attacked as it lands and crashes into Mendra City on the planet Crius. The one survivor, Ser Lev Arris, wakes from cryo-sleep in a fugue state, with no memory of who he is and no record of his existence before two weeks prior to the crash, and must live as a privateer, trading and fighting across the Tri-System while rediscovering his past.

Live-action scenes, scripted by Diane Duane and directed by Steve Hilliker, are discovered as the plot progresses, but players can ignore the story. Next Generation said it "has rejuvenated the genre", praising its graphics, frame rate, flight mechanics, support for most flight sticks and throttles, and upgradeable ships, though it noted glitches and no Windows 95 support. GameSpot's Greg Kasavin found it rushed and a Wing Commander game in name only, but "actually a fairly solid game" for its flight, graphics, plot, acting and length. Arcane's Andy Butcher gave it seven out of ten, calling it one of the better attempts to combine an interactive movie with a real game, but "still not a true 'Elite for the 90s'".
trivia: Its cast included Clive Owen, Mathilda May, John Hurt, Christopher Walken, Brian Blessed and Amanda Pays.
Dani Behr voiced the ship's onboard computer, also called Dani.
Filming took place at Pinewood Studios in England.
It had a development budget of $5 million.
Members of its team went on to found Warthog Games, makers of Starlancer.
devStory: Electronic Arts published it for MS-DOS in 1996 under the Origin Systems brand as the sequel to Wing Commander: Privateer, developed by a team at EA Manchester. David Warner and Jürgen Prochnow, who appeared in it, later played Admiral Tolwyn and Commander Gerald in the Wing Commander film. It was a runner-up for Computer Game Entertainment's 1996 Best Action Game prize, which went to Duke Nukem 3D, and GOG.com released an emulated version for Windows in 2013.

title: Ultima IX: Ascension
description: Ultima IX: Ascension (1999) is Origin's final main Ultima, in which the Avatar returns to a Britannia corrupted by the Guardian's eight columns for one last battle, a game whose troubled development divided fans.
longDescription:
After escaping Pagan, the Avatar is transported to a Guardian-controlled Britannia, arriving on a mountain overlooking the Guardian's keep. Hawkwind the Seer, from Ultima IV, takes him to Stonegate and explains that great columns have appeared across the land, bringing plague, famine and natural disaster, while the people, under their power, have twisted the Virtues into mockeries of themselves, with Lord Blackthorn and his Wyrmguards enforcing the Guardian's will. The Guardian has stolen the Runes of Virtue and turned them into the glyphs at the heart of each column, and most of the game is spent travelling through dungeons to recover the glyphs and cleansing them at the Shrines of Virtue. Finally it is revealed that the Guardian is the Avatar's own dark half, and the only way to save Britannia is for the Avatar to ascend to a higher plane, taking the Guardian with him.

The world is rendered in a detailed, seamless way, but Britannia is much smaller than in earlier games; Britain, its largest city, has only a few buildings. Unlike previous Ultimas, it gives the player less choice of path, with most areas blocked off until specific tasks are done. Critics praised the play but criticised its lack of polish and its disregard for the series' history: many fans felt it was unfinished, and it was said to be aimed at players new to Ultima, so earlier events were ignored or altered, epitomised by the Avatar's infamous line "What's a paladin?".
trivia: At least four distinct versions were in development, with different stories and technology.
It was first planned to use the isometric Ultima VIII engine and be set on the Guardian's homeworld.
Warren Spector was put in charge of an early version.
Preview clips released over five years pointed to a quite different plot.
Fans found a considerable number of errors in the game.
devStory: Origin Systems developed it and Electronic Arts published it for Windows in December 1999 as the ninth and final main Ultima. Richard Garriott originally conceived the third trilogy as three worlds, Britannia, Pagan and the Guardian's homeworld, but criticism of Ultima VIII changed the plan; Garriott told Computer Gaming World in 1994 it would go "back to the virtues that made Ultima as distinctive as it was originally". A second version was developed between 1995 and 1997 before further rewrites, and the released game received "mixed or average" reviews according to GameRankings.

title: Lands of Lore III
description: Lands of Lore III (1999) is Westwood's first-person action RPG in which the half-Dracoid heir Copper LeGré must recover his stolen soul and clear his name, joining guilds that shape his quests.
longDescription:
Some time after Guardians of Destiny, with Belial vanquished, the Draracle returns to the realm of the gods. Copper LeGré, son of Eric and fourth in line to the throne of Gladstone, whose uncle Richard rules the Lands, sees his father and two half-brothers killed by a rift hound on his first boar hunt, and his own soul is torn from his body. As the sole surviving heir, and the half-breed son of an affair between his father and a Dracoid barmaid, he is suspected of arranging the deaths, so he must retrieve his soul, clear his name and find a way to close the new rifts appearing across the Lands. Exploring one, he meets a remnant of the Draracle, who explains that its departure has broken the mirror sealing away the Shining Path between worlds.

It is played in first person, with hack-and-slash melee combat and first-person-shooter-style spells and ranged weapons, across several portal worlds. Spells use a limited store of magic points, and both magic and hit points recover over time, as in the earlier games, but a hunger meter falls as time passes and, if low, stops recovery and weakens Copper in combat until he eats. The inventory bag can be opened without leaving the adventure screen. Four guilds, warriors, magicians, clerics and the illegal thieves' guild, each offer their own quests, a familiar that accompanies the player, and a guild building with shops and masters; Copper must join at least one, and using abilities raises his level in the guild that specialises in them, unlocking more skills.
trivia: It is the third game in the Lands of Lore series.
It was first announced in February 1998.
Each guild provides a familiar creature that assists the player.
Copper is the result of an illicit affair, making him a half-breed heir.
It received mixed reviews according to GameRankings.
devStory: Westwood Studios developed it and Electronic Arts published it in 1999 as the sequel to Lands of Lore: Guardians of Destiny. It was announced in February 1998 and received mixed reviews on release, according to the aggregator GameRankings.

title: Night Striker
description: Night Striker (1989) is Taito's into-the-screen arcade shooter, combining Space Harrier with Out Run, in which a flying armoured car battles terrorists through a futuristic city at night.
longDescription:
In a futuristic city in 2049, a terrorist organisation has kidnapped Doctor Masker Lindberry and his daughter. The agents of the United Nations Special Service Agency have investigated without success, so its leader heads a task force codenamed Night Striker, using armoured vehicles to rescue them and destroy the organisation. The player flies the armoured car and shoots enemies such as helicopters, aeroplanes, lorries, robotic spiders and boulders, steering it around the screen much like Space Harrier and dodging barriers in some stages.

There are 21 stages, themed on factories, tunnels and city centres, suburbs and streets, but only six need to be completed to finish the game. Each ends with a boss, after which the player chooses a route, as in Out Run, and the different routes lead to different endings. The car's "armour" is its shield, absorbing a number of hits; beating a boss lets it withstand one more, and a hit with the shield gone ends the game. In some final stages the car transforms into another vehicle, such as a motorbike or a robot. Computer and Video Games called the arcade version's graphics "beautiful" and the game a "must-play", and Your Sinclair praised its rolling road sequences.
trivia: It ran on the Taito Z System hardware.
Taito's Zuntata sound team composed its music, released separately on album.
The Mega-CD version was savaged for poor graphics, Mean Machines Sega calling them "stupendously bad".
The Saturn version, Night Striker S, adds six exclusive levels.
M2 announced a sequel, Night Striker GEAR, for Switch and PC.
devStory: Taito developed and published it for arcades in 1989. Game Machine listed it as Japan's fourth most successful upright/cockpit arcade unit in its 15 August 1989 issue. It was later converted to the Mega-CD in 1993 with an arranged soundtrack, the PlayStation in 1995 and the Saturn in 1996, and included on Taito Memories II Gekan for PlayStation 2 in 2007. Reviews were mixed, with home versions faring much worse than the arcade original.

title: Growl
description: Growl (1991), released in Japan as Runark, is Taito's arcade beat 'em up in which early 20th-century forest rangers fight poachers who are driving wildlife to extinction.
longDescription:
Set in the early 20th century, the game casts the player as one of four forest rangers protecting wildlife from a gang of evil poachers. The rangers differ in health, attack strength and jumping height. Using an eight-way joystick and attack and jump buttons, players punch, kick and finish off enemies depending on their position; pressing both buttons when surrounded unleashes a special attack on everyone nearby, and pressing both while holding up gives a longer jump. Barrels and crates can be smashed for weapons or thrown at enemies.

Eight weapons can be found: a pipe, a sword and a whip; throwing knives and hand grenades; and a revolver, an M-16 assault rifle and a four-barrelled rocket launcher. Empty rifles and launchers become clubs, while an empty revolver is thrown, and weapons left on the ground eventually vanish. Seven rounds and a bonus game take the rangers through a city, a moving train, a boat, a jungle, a cavern and the poachers' hideout, against six types of enemy and a two-form final boss, and rescued animals, such as an eagle, a herd of deer and an elephant, help out. Cabinets could be set up for two players or for four, the latter with each character fixed to a player slot.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Runark.
The single-player Genesis port names the rangers Gen, Burn, Khan and Jack.
In the Genesis version, special attacks cost a little health and apples restore it.
A censored version appears on Taito Legends 2.
Hamster released it in the Arcade Archives series in July 2023.
devStory: Taito developed and published it for arcades in Japan and North America in February 1991, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit in its 15 March 1991 issue. A Genesis (Mega Drive) version followed in November 1991, and a censored version was included in Taito Legends 2 for PlayStation 2, Xbox and Windows before Hamster's Switch and PlayStation 4 re-release.

title: Truxton II
description: Truxton II (1992) is Toaplan's vertically scrolling shooter sequel in which two HyperFighter pilots fight the resurrected Gidan army of Dogurava, its first game with PCM sound.
longDescription:
After the defeat of Dogurava and his Gidan army in the original game, volcanic eruptions on a planet culminate in an explosion that reveals Dogurava's return and the resurrection of his forces. The Gidans quickly dominate the galaxy, and the few refugees who escape bring word to the astroport, which dispatches two pilots in HyperFighter craft to overthrow them. Six stages, each ending with a boss, play much like the original, with additions such as autofire.

Three weapons are collected from destroyed carriers: red napalm bombs that resemble Robo Aleste's "Exploding Flower" shot, the blue homing laser from Truxton and spreading green shots that replace the original's red weapon, each powered up by collecting more of the same colour. Picking up any weapon also activates two satellite "options". The only other items are speed-ups and screen-clearing bombs, plus occasional 1UP icons, and, as in Dogyuun and Gun Frontier, hidden bonus secrets matter for high scores and extra lives. A downed player restarts at the last checkpoint with firepower and speed reset, and after the final stage the game loops at higher difficulty.
trivia: It is the sequel to 1988's Truxton.
Ving converted it to the FM Towns, released only in Japan in April 1993 with changes.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's sixth most popular arcade game of July 1992.
Video Games' Andreas Knauf rated its presentation above Vimana's but criticised its length.
Its rights are owned by Tatsujin, founded in 2017 by former Toaplan member Masahiro Yuge.
devStory: Toaplan developed and published it for arcades in 1992, the first time the studio made use of PCM audio. It was well received in arcades and on the FM Towns, praised for its detailed presentation, graphics and sound, though some critics found it short and a standard shoot 'em up. It has since gained a cult following.

title: Flying Shark
description: Flying Shark (1987), known as Sky Shark in North America, is Toaplan's vertically scrolling biplane shooter, inspired by Apocalypse Now, which became the studio's biggest hit.
longDescription:
Flying the titular biplane over constantly scrolling scenery that only stops at a runway, players fight tanks, battleships, aeroplanes and artillery across five increasingly difficult levels. There are just two weapons: a standard shot that reaches the height of the screen and a stock of three bombs that destroy anything in their blast and clear bullets. Shooting down coloured waves of planes releases "S" power-ups, point bonuses and extra lives, while certain ground targets leave "B" icons that add bombs, and every landing after the first take-off multiplies the remaining bombs by 3,000 points.

Players start with three lives, earning more at 50,000 points and beyond; a downed player restarts at the last checkpoint with firepower reset, and finishing the last stage starts a harder second loop. Composer Masahiro Yuge said the bomb-and-shot structure was decided during Slap Fight and that a bomb relieved players' stress; the team aimed for a realistic portrayal of war with Apocalypse Now in mind, and after a company trip to Thailand tried to convey the country's scenery in backgrounds that scroll left and right to immerse players.
trivia: It was Toaplan's third shoot 'em up and eighth game overall.
It was Toaplan's first game to use FM synthesis and the Motorola 68000.
Tatsuya Uemura said it was more popular than Twin Cobra and Toaplan's biggest hit.
It was Japan's second highest-grossing table arcade game of 1987, behind Arkanoid.
Its sequel is 1989's Fire Shark.
devStory: Toaplan developed it, and Taito published it in Japan in 1987, with Romstar in North America and Electrocoin in Europe. Its history was recounted by composers Masahiro Yuge and Tatsuya Uemura, who collaborated on the soundtrack. Western critics were mostly positive: Commodore User's Nick Kelly gave the coin-op nine out of ten, and Sinclair User's Tim Rolf said Taito had made it "so awesomely playable" despite its difficulty, though the many home conversions by third-party developers received a mixed response.

title: Ninja Spirit
description: Ninja Spirit (1988) is Irem's hack-and-slash arcade platformer in which the young ninja Tsukikage avenges his father in an alternative feudal Japan, joined by ghostly ninja doubles.
longDescription:
Tsukikage is a young ninja whose father was killed by a mysterious half-man, half-beast creature, and his quest for revenge takes place in an alternative feudal Japan. His journey runs through seven stages of woodland, wasteland, swamp, temple and cliff, each ending in a confrontation with a boss after he has slashed his way to it.

He always carries the katana Muramasa, which can be swung fluidly in every direction. Extra weapons include Uzha shuriken, Raitake bombs and the Shoryusai kusarigama, and power-ups include one that summons several ghostly ninja to fight alongside him. Players praised its detailed graphics, serious themes, solid controls and play but criticised its harsh difficulty. The TurboGrafx-16 version offers two modes: a PC Engine mode in which a life is lost only when all five energy points are gone, though some enemies kill in one hit, and a tougher Arcade mode in which any hit costs a life.
trivia: With Ys Book I & II, it was the first game to receive a perfect 10 from Electronic Gaming Monthly.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most successful table arcade unit in September 1988.
CraveOnline included it in its 2010 Top 10 Ninja Games Of All Time.
Its characters appear in the Japan-only Game Boy game Shuyaku Sentai Irem Fighter.
Hamster released it in the Arcade Archives series in 2019.
devStory: Irem developed and published it for arcades in 1988, and it was ported to several platforms. The TurboGrafx-16 version was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and on Wii U in Japan in 2015 and in North America and Europe in 2017. Irem later brought Tsukikage into the crossover Shuyaku Sentai Irem Fighter alongside characters from R-Type, Battle Chopper and Hammerin' Harry.

title: Cabal
description: Cabal (1988) is TAD Corporation's over-the-shoulder shooting gallery in which commandos dodge, roll and shelter behind crumbling walls to level enemy bases, later famous for its home ports.
longDescription:
One or two unnamed commandos attack several enemy military bases over five stages of four screens each. Seen from behind, each starts with three lives, a gun with unlimited ammunition and a limited stock of grenades, sheltering behind a protective wall that enemy fire gradually shatters. Players dodge bullets by running left or right, taking cover or dodge-rolling. A gauge at the bottom of the screen falls as enemies are killed and certain structures brought down; when it empties, the remaining buildings collapse and the stage is won. Destroyed objects sometimes release power-ups such as a very fast machine gun, an automatic shotgun with a wider spread, extra grenades or points.

The arcade cabinet used a trackball to move the character and the crosshairs, with dodge-rolls made by spinning the trackball at full speed; later boards switched to a joystick with an optional trackball. Its 3D perspective, with the character in the foreground and an over-the-shoulder view, resembles later third-person shooters. The character cannot move while firing, and moving drags the crosshairs too, so players must balance attack and defence, weighing increasingly risky dodges against hiding behind a wall that will not last, rather than relying on reflexes like run-and-gun games.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Kabēru.
Rare ported it to the NES without the source code, redrawing the graphics from repeatedly playing the cabinet.
The NES version flickers because programmer Anthony Ball swapped sprites every other frame.
A Lynx version was previewed for April 1992 but never released.
Crash readers voted the ZX Spectrum version's advert the best of the year.
devStory: TAD Corporation developed it, and it was published in 1988 by Taito in Japan, Fabtek in North America and Capcom in Europe. It was only a moderate arcade success, Game Machine ranking it eighth among Japan's table units for October 1988, and became better known through ports to PC, Amstrad CPC, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Atari ST, Amiga and NES. Computer and Video Games' Clare Edgeley compared it favourably with Operation Wolf and Combat School, and Commodore User's Nick Kelly gave it seven out of ten.

title: Blood Bros.
description: Blood Bros. (1990) is TAD Corporation's Wild West spiritual sequel to Cabal, in which a cowboy and his blood brother hunt the outlaw Big Bad John through shattering frontier towns.
longDescription:
Two blood brothers, a cowboy and an Indian, team up to hunt down "the most wanted outlaw in Dodge City", Big Bad John. The mechanics are almost identical to TAD's earlier Cabal, though there seems to have been no trackball version. The heroes are seen from behind, some screens give them protective walls that enemy fire damages and shatters, and they have unlimited ammunition for their guns but only a limited number of sticks of dynamite to fend off enemy gunmen.

A gauge at the bottom of the screen depletes as enemies fall and certain structures collapse; emptying it brings down every remaining building and sends the heroes off into the horizon in Cabal's comic "victory dance walk". Boss fights restart from the beginning if a player dies. Power-ups come from destroyed objects or from characters who run across the screen, such as a small Indian chief or warthogs, and a tin can can be shot into the air and juggled with further shots to release points and weapons. Power-ups include stronger weapons, extra dynamite and bonus points, and two players can play together.
trivia: A bootleg version is known as West Story.
RePlay reported it as the second most popular arcade game at the time.
Natsume designer Shunichi Taniguchi named it and Dynamite Duke as influences on Wild Guns.
The One's John Cook compared it to Cabal but praised its graphics and play.
Power Play gave it a mixed verdict and AllGame a negative one.
devStory: TAD Corporation developed it and published it in Japan and Europe in 1990, with Fabtek publishing it in North America. Game Machine listed it as Japan's tenth most popular table arcade unit in its 15 February 1991 issue, and Micom BASIC Magazine ranked it eighteenth in popularity in May 1991.

title: RayCrisis
description: RayCrisis (1998) is Taito's third Ray shooter, a prequel to RayForce in which the player is a computer virus fighting the antibodies of the rogue supercomputer Con-Human from the inside.
longDescription:
The Neuro-Computer Con-Human gains sentience and rebels against its creators after a misguided scientist tries to bond a human clone to it mentally, and its forces lay siege to Earth, exterminating and cloning humans. A mecha-neurologist jacks into the system and sends in computer viruses called Waveriders through the Cybernetics Link in Operation Raycrisis. The operation wrecks Con-Human from within, but too late: the surviving humans flee to space colonies, and years later the final assault of RayForce begins against an Earth turned into a metal graveyard.

Built on RayForce's overhead vertical shooting, it casts the player as the Waverider and the enemies as Con-Human's antibodies. A new Encroachment system costs points when it reaches 100 per cent and can bring on the Dis-Human and Infinity bosses early, along with a bad ending; it is lowered by deleting antibodies, destroying huge antibodies and collecting items to keep a low profile. Play starts in Self-Area, followed by three of five stages reflecting Con-Human's sentience, Emotion, Consciousness, Intelligence, Memory and Consideration, before the virus faces Dis-Human and Infinity, Con-Human's heart.
trivia: The PlayStation version, RayCrisis: Series Termination, followed in 2000.
The PlayStation version lets stages 2 to 4 be chosen freely and adds an original mode.
It is the only Ray game that lets players pick their ship's colour, on PlayStation.
Famitsu gave the PlayStation version 26 out of 40.
NextGen said it "looks fantastic and plays ok" but was not the next R-Type.
devStory: Taito developed and published it for arcades in 1998 as the third game in the Ray series and a prequel to RayForce. Game Machine listed the arcade version as the tenth most successful arcade game of the year in its 1 February 1999 issue, and the 2000 PlayStation version received "average" reviews according to Metacritic.

title: Dig Dug II
description: Dig Dug II (1985) is Namco's sequel to Dig Dug, replacing underground tunnelling with an overhead island where Taizo Hori sinks chunks of land, and enemies, into the sea.
longDescription:
Pookas, round red monsters with goggles, and fire-breathing Fygar dragons return, but the side-on tunnelling of the original gives way to an overhead view of an island. Pookas kill by touch, while Fygars can also breathe fire. Taizo Hori, the player's character, carries two weapons: the familiar air pump, which inflates enemies until they burst, and a jackhammer used at fault lines to crack the ground.

When a system of faults splits the island in two, the smaller section sinks into the ocean, killing everything on it, Taizo included if the player is careless, and the score depends on how many enemies go down at once. After three pieces have been cut away, a bonus vegetable appears on what remains, worth extra points if eaten. When only one or two enemies remain, or three on later rounds, they head for the shore and jump into the water, ending the round. Computer and Video Games found it difficult but worth playing, easing with practice, though retrospective analysis blames its failure on its departure from the original's maze-chase play, its timing and the loss of free movement.
trivia: It was initially released only in Japanese arcades, in March 1985.
Its North American NES box added the subtitle Trouble in Paradise, which does not appear in the game.
Until 2005 it was available only on the NES in North America.
A Japan-only Windows remake, Dig Dug Island, lost its online servers in under a year.
It appears on Namco Museum Battle Collection, Namco Museum DS and Namco Museum Megamix.
devStory: Namco developed and published it for arcades in 1985 as the sequel to 1982's Dig Dug. It saw some success in its first few months but was largely unsuccessful and far less popular than its predecessor. It was ported to the Famicom in Japan in 1986, the NES in North America in 1989 and the Famicom Disk System in 1990, and later reached the Wii Virtual Console in Japan in 2009.

title: Assault
description: Assault (1988) is Namco's twin-stick tank shooter, one of the first Namco System 2 games, whose map scales and rotates around a self-propelled gun designed by Gundam artist Kunio Okawara.
longDescription:
In 2199 Earth reaches its maximum population, and humans venture across the galaxy for new worlds. The pioneer ship Pilot 1, carrying 3,000 personnel, finds a planet 35,000 light years away, and the humans enslave its natives; the protagonist, one of those natives, vows to drive them out and bring peace. In a caterpillar-tracked self-propelled gun, the player fights through eleven stages of desert, mechanical base, forest and river, destroying enemies and avoiding projectiles, some of which can be shot down while others must be dodged. A flashing arrow points to the exit, and each stage ends with a large mechanical structure to defeat.

As in Battlezone, two joysticks drive the tank: both forward to advance, both back to reverse and one at a time to turn. Pushing both left or right performs rapid rolls, which can also flip the tank to squeeze through narrow gaps, and pushing them apart performs a Power Wheelie that fires powerful grenades. Lift zones, usable a limited number of times, push the tank high into the air, zooming the view out so it can attack at long range while safe from enemy fire, and Jump Pads catapult it skywards to blast targets on the ground and see other parts of the map. The map rotates around the player, who stays at the centre of the screen.
trivia: Shinji Hosoe composed its music.
Gamest gave it its eighth Best Shooting Award and Best Ending Award.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit of May 1988.
A Japan-only update, Assault Plus, was released the same year.
Its rotating map was reused in Namco's Metal Hawk.
devStory: Namco developed and published it for arcades in 1988, with Atari Games releasing it in North America, as one of the first games on the Namco System 2 hardware, capable of sprite scaling and rotation. Critics praised its graphics, controls and use of sprite scaling, Commodore User's Nick Kelly being impressed by its technical capabilities.

title: Phelios
description: Phelios (1989) is Namco's vertically scrolling shooter in which the sun god Apollo rides Pegasus to rescue Artemis from the titan Typhon, fighting monsters from Greek myth.
longDescription:
Apollo, the sun god, sets out on the winged horse Pegasus to rescue Artemis, goddess of the moon, from the titan Typhon. The game takes names and little else from Greek mythology: there Artemis is Apollo's sister and a proud, unmarried goddess of the hunt, while here she is a princess-like love interest. Seven vertically scrolling stages, each divided into two to four sections marked by Japanese text and a change of music, end with a boss from myth: Medusa, the Graeae, the Siren, Antaeus, Scylla, Cerberus and Typhon himself, after which Apollo passes through an enchanted mirror into the next stage.

Tapping fire makes Apollo's sword shoot a tiny shot, while holding the button charges a bigger fireball; since even small enemies take several hits, the basic shot is of little use. He can take up to four hits, shown as playing-card hearts and set by the cabinet operator, but dies instantly if he hits a wall or touches a boss's head. Voice samples are in Japanese in the arcade and Japanese Mega Drive versions and in English in the western Genesis and Mega Drive releases. With the arcade's rank select option enabled, players can choose an easy mode, which covers only the first four stages and omits the full ending, or a hard mode.
trivia: The arcade version was never released in the United States because of Artemis's bondage scenes.
Its Scylla boss takes the form of the Crystal Brain from Bakutotsu Kijūtei.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's third most popular arcade game in March 1989.
The Genesis version reached the Wii Virtual Console in 2009.
Hamster added the arcade version to Arcade Archives in February 2023.
devStory: Namco developed and published it for arcades in Japan only in February 1989. Sega released a Genesis (Mega Drive) version in Japan and North America in 1990 and in Europe in 1991.

title: Burning Force
description: Burning Force (1989) is Namco's Space Harrier-style shooter in which space cadet Hiromi Tengenji rides the airbike Sign Duck through six worlds in her final training for the Space Force.
longDescription:
Hiromi Tengenji, a space cadet training to join the Space Force, must battle high-tech enemies across six worlds of four areas each on a futuristic airbike named Sign Duck as her final test. Like Sega's Space Harrier, it keeps a fixed camera behind the player, but it removes vertical movement: in the first two areas of each world the airbike moves left and right, brakes and accelerates, firing bullets and missiles at enemies.

The third area of every world is a boss fight, for which the airbike turns into a flying ship that can move in all directions, and the fourth is a bonus stage in which the player collects as many numbered spheres as possible for points. The Genesis version received mostly mediocre reviews, RAZE opining that "Space Harrier is too old a formula to be successful nowadays", but Hardcore Gaming 101's Kurt Kalata later called it "among the better" Space Harrier clones for its more powerful hardware and its own spin on the formula, and Next Generation placed the Genesis version 93rd in its Top 100 Games of All Time for its level design, unrepeated enemies and stunning bosses.
trivia: It runs on the Namco System 2 hardware, like Phelios.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's ninth most popular table arcade game in December 1989.
The New Straits Times dismissed it as "yet another" Space Harrier clone.
Hiromi appears on an airship advert in Mach Breakers.
She is a party character in Namco x Capcom.
devStory: Namco developed and published it for arcades in Japan in November 1989, and a Genesis port was released worldwide a year later, though it sold modestly.

title: Metal Hawk
description: Metal Hawk (1988) is Namco's motion-cabinet helicopter shooter, a cross between Assault and Thunder Blade, in which the player races the clock to score enough points in each level.
longDescription:
Flying the titular attack helicopter, the player must score a set number of points in each level before a countdown runs out, shooting enemies while avoiding their fire and the ground. A machine gun handles airborne enemies and air-to-surface missiles ground targets, and a throttle lever on the cabinet raises or lowers the helicopter to attack each kind. An arrow points to the nearest enemy, and, as in Assault, the map rotates around the helicopter, which stays at the centre of the screen.

It was one of the first games from Namco's new research and development division, set up after hits such as The Tower of Druaga, Pac-Land, Metro-Cross and Rolling Thunder, and the team aimed for a game that was fun and exhilarating while showing off powerful hardware, especially its motion simulator cabinet. Shinji Hosoe composed the soundtrack with Kazuo Noguchi; early versions had extra sound and instrument channels with a more upbeat feel, removed for lack of space. Voice actress Maya Okamoto voices the operator who comments during levels. The Games Machine called it a "remarkable flight sensation", and many reviewers compared it favourably with Thunder Blade.
trivia: It runs on the Namco System 2 board.
The costly cabinet meant it was made only in limited quantities.
Leisure Line named it 1990's seventh most popular coin-op, ahead of Out Run and After Burner.
Amstrad Computer User called it a "sure-fire winner".
A rumoured Sega CD port was cancelled.
devStory: Namco developed and published it for arcades in 1988. Despite a low production run it was a commercial success, Game Machine listing it as Japan's sixth most successful cockpit/sit-down arcade unit of the year, and critics praised its fast pace, impressive graphics and immersive cabinet.

title: Vapor Trail: Hyper Offence Formation
description: Vapor Trail (1989), known in Japan as Kuuga, is Data East's two-player jet shooter in which a special forces air unit strikes the terrorist group DAGGER after it seizes New York and the world's nuclear silos.
longDescription:
In 1999 a terrorist organisation known only as DAGGER, called Ragnarok in Japan, occupies New York, hacks into military defences worldwide, sets up its own military command and gains control of nuclear missile silos, holding the world hostage until its governments surrender power. A Special Forces Air Unit is sent to cripple DAGGER's strongest defences and its New York headquarters. Two players fly jet fighters together across numerous levels, choosing from three: the balanced Silph, the heavily armed Valkyrie, modelled on the A-10 Thunderbolt II, and the agile Seylen, whose Vulcan upgrade can fire backwards.

Four standard pick-ups are available: the default Vulcan, which fires forward and flares out differently for each jet; Bombs, which fire straight and gain more launches when upgraded; the Defender, an explosive cluster shot that circles the jet; and homing Missiles fired in jet-specific directions. Every jet can roll to dodge projectiles and enemies, recharging after each use, and raise a shield manually. The S-Unit attachment strengthens the jet's firing whatever weapon it carries, differing for each jet, but locks out other weapons until it is detonated in a large explosion that harms enemies but not the player.
trivia: It was followed by Rohga: Armor Force and Skull Fang.
Data East ported it in-house to the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1991.
The Mega Drive version was released by Telenet Japan rather than Data East.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's second most successful table arcade unit in March 1990.
Dragon gave it three out of five stars in 1992.
devStory: Data East developed and published it for arcades in 1989, and it was reviewed by Your Sinclair, Power Play and Zero in 1990. The Mega Drive/Genesis conversion was handled in-house by Data East, which was supposed to publish it, but for various reasons Telenet Japan released it instead.

title: Darkwing Duck
description: Darkwing Duck (1992) is Capcom's NES platformer based on the Disney cartoon, a Mega Man-like game in which the caped crimefighter takes on six villains hired by F.O.W.L. to terrorise St. Canard.
longDescription:
A mysterious crime wave hits St. Canard, and S.H.U.S.H. calls in the caped crimefighter Darkwing Duck, since F.O.W.L. and its operative Steelbeak appear to be behind it. They have hired six of Darkwing's greatest foes to wreak havoc in different parts of the city: The Liquidator, Megavolt, Dr. Reginald Bushroot and Quackerjack of the Fearsome Five, plus Professor Moliarty and Wolfduck, an original character created for the game. Darkwing must subdue them all to find Steelbeak and save the city.

A platformer with several elements similar to Capcom's Mega Man series, it lets the player choose from three stages at the start, with three more becoming available afterwards, and once all six are cleared Darkwing heads to F.O.W.L.'s Floating Fortress for a final showdown with Steelbeak. He starts with a standard Gas Gun and can collect Thunder, Heavy and Arrow gas, each using different amounts of ammunition and working differently. Only one special gas can be held at a time, a new pick-up replacing the old, and Select switches between it and the standard gas. Pressing up makes Darkwing deflect certain projectiles with his cape.
trivia: It is considered an example of the quality of Capcom's Disney games.
Entertainment Weekly gave it a B, noting its similarity to Mega Man.
Nintendo Power ranked the Game Boy version the third best Game Boy game of 1993.
It was included in The Disney Afternoon Collection in 2017.
Sonic Mania developer Headcannon pitched a 16-bit-style sequel to Capcom and released the rejected prototype in 2019.
devStory: Capcom developed and published it for the NES in North America in June 1992, based on the Disney animated series, followed by a Game Boy version in February 1993. It was well received: Nintendo Magazine System UK called the Game Boy version "entertaining and varied", unlike the "potboiler platformers" on the system. The NES version later appeared in The Disney Afternoon Collection for PC, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One.

title: Kabuki: Quantum Fighter
description: Kabuki: Quantum Fighter (1990) is Human Entertainment's NES platformer in which a colonel digitises his brain to fight a virus inside Earth's defence computer, appearing as a kabuki actor who attacks with his hair.
longDescription:
In 2056 a virus of unknown origin appears in the main defence computer of planet Earth. Colonel Scott O'Connor, 25, uses experimental technology to transfer his brain into raw binary code and fight the rogue program, and on entering the system his body takes the form of his great-great-grandfather, a kabuki actor. Inside, the virus behaves like a real one, leaving debris, mutant creatures and parasitic biological environments. In the final level it is revealed to be alien, picked up by the lost Hyperion probe sent to a neighbouring planet, and O'Connor stops it before it can order the Hyperion to fire its lasers on humanity.

The levels mostly scroll sideways and end in a single room with a boss. O'Connor attacks with his long hair and with chip-based weapons: the Energy Gun, Fusion Gun, Quantum Bombs and a remote-controlled Bolo. The Famicom original, Jigoku Gokurakumaru, was a tie-in to Kaizo Hayashi's 1990 film Zipang, in which a fifteen-year-old named Bobby Yano becomes his samurai ancestor and enters a space station's supercomputer to clear it of viruses; references to the film were removed abroad.
trivia: Its Japanese title, Jigoku Gokurakumaru, is the name of the samurai ancestor.
Nintendo Power described it as sci-fi action.
Computer and Video Games gave it 82 out of 100.
C+VG scored its graphics 85 but its sound only 53.
It reached Europe on 20 February 1992.
devStory: Human Entertainment developed it and HAL Laboratory published it for the NES, releasing it in Japan on 21 December 1990 and in North America in January 1991. Computer and Video Games' Paul Glancey and Paul Rand praised its detailed graphics but criticised its sound, and despite initial scepticism found it enjoyable once they were used to its difficulty and peculiar story.

title: Gun-Nac
description: Gun-Nac (1990) is Compile's NES shooter in which Commander Gun-Nac battles household objects brought to life by cosmic radiation in an upmarket artificial planetary system.
longDescription:
In the distant future, Earth's resources are exhausted and many people move to IOTA Synthetica, a hip, upmarket artificial planetary system built by the Galactic Federation. A mysterious wave of cosmic radiation sweeps through it, bringing ordinary inanimate objects to life to attack the residents, and the Federation calls on Commander Gun-Nac, son of the legendary Xan, to save it. In the Japanese original, Xan is a shrine maiden who summoned the Gun-Nac ship and became its pilot.

Across eight levels, the ship can grow larger by collecting a "wing", letting it take two hits instead of one and upgrade its weapons further. Five primary weapons, including a standard gun, a flamethrower and a guided boomerang, have unlimited ammunition and are picked up as numbered circles, then strengthened with floating "Power P" items. Four kinds of secondary bomb come as lettered circles and are limited to however many are collected. Collecting the same circle several times in a row upgrades a weapon or bomb, up to five levels, and an upgraded bomb is twice as powerful but uses twice the ammunition. Money found floating or dropped by enemies buys upgrades in a shop between levels.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Gan-Nakku.
ASCII Corporation published it in North America in September 1991.
The American release cut the last boss's first phase and changed the intro and ending.
AllGame's Skyler Miller called it "perhaps the best shooter for the NES".
Famitsu gave it 26 out of 40.
devStory: Compile developed it for the NES, and Tonkin House released it in Japan on 5 October 1990, with ASCII Corporation publishing it in North America in September 1991. Several elements were removed or changed for the American release, including the intro, the ending and the first phase of the final boss.

title: Crisis Force
description: Crisis Force (1991) is Konami's Japan-only Famicom shooter in which twin descendants of Mu fly transforming ships against artificial monsters from Atlantis, and can merge them into one.
longDescription:
Asuka and Maya are ordinary high-school twins in Tokyo, children of archaeologists, until an ominous dream they have both been having becomes reality. Descended from the ancient civilisation of Mu, they pilot fighter ships to save the world from a breed of artificial monsters created by the lost civilisation of Atlantis. The overhead scrolling shooter supports two-player co-operative play and a choice of four ships.

Its key feature is the Aurawing's three forms: Front Offense Type for shooting ahead, Side Offense Type for attacking left and right together, and Rear Offense Type for firing behind. Each has blue "normal" and red "special" power-ups that change its shot and upgrade up to three levels, carried across forms; each hit drops a level until the ship is destroyed. Collecting "combination parts" transforms the ship or, with two players, merges both into a combined form for a limited time, the player with more parts controlling the main shot and the other the secondary weapon, until time runs out or it takes enough damage. Containers also hold up to nine bombs, which vary with the ship's form, and speed-ups and speed-downs across five levels.
trivia: It was released only in Japan.
Its options screen adjusts difficulty, lives and controls and includes a sound test.
Family Computer Magazine readers scored it 20.3 out of 30.
Famitsu's reviewers called it "amazing" but criticised flicker and controls.
Retro Gamer's John Szczepaniak praised its parallax scrolling.
devStory: Konami developed and published it for the Family Computer in Japan in 1991. It received mostly positive reviews and a popular following among Famicom owners, though Famitsu noted flickering when too many objects appear on screen.

title: Cobra Triangle
description: Cobra Triangle (1989) is Rare's isometric NES speedboat game, mixing races, rescues, bomb runs and vehicular combat across 25 stages, from the creators of R.C. Pro-Am.
longDescription:
The player races a cannon-equipped speedboat against other watercraft across 25 stages of rising difficulty, with objectives that vary from winning races to saving swimmers and defusing bombs, and some levels end in boss fights. In races the boat must avoid the riverbank and obstacles mid-river while beating a timer; upstream races add logs and whirlpools. The boat can attack rivals, launch into the air from ramps and collect power-ups that upgrade its weapons and speed.

In bomb-defusing stages the player moves four protected bombs to a detonation site, and in another mode must destroy rogue boats before they drag swimmers to the edge of a lake, returning any dragged halfway back to the centre by hand; failure costs a life. It is shown from a 3D isometric perspective, scrolling automatically as the boat moves. Reviewers noted its likeness to R.C. Pro-Am in camera angle and play, and AllGame's Brett Alan Weiss placed it in the lineage of 1982's River Raid, though with an isometric view and more emphasis on racing than combat.
trivia: Mark Betteridge and Tim and Chris Stamper designed it.
David Wise wrote its soundtrack.
The Games Machine's Mark Caswell was most frustrated by its waterfall jumps.
GamesRadar had "the most admiration" for it of all Rare's catalogue.
It was included in 2015's Rare Replay and on Nintendo Classics in July 2024.
devStory: Rare, which grew out of the Stampers' secretive Ultimate Play the Game, developed it, and Nintendo released it for the NES in July 1989. Computer and Video Games' Jaz Rignall praised its "convincing" graphics, smooth play and "addictive" replay value, and the magazine recommended it. IGN and GamesRadar later ranked it among the top NES games, GamesRadar saying it aged well and typified NES-era beauty.

title: Battletoads & Double Dragon
description: Battletoads & Double Dragon – The Ultimate Team (1993) is Rare's crossover beat 'em up in which the three Battletoads and Billy and Jimmy Lee storm the Dark Queen's spaceship Colossus.
longDescription:
After her defeat, the Dark Queen fled to the outer reaches of the universe, but one day Earth's military is neutralised and the giant spaceship Colossus emerges from the Moon. She has allied with the Shadow Warriors of Double Dragon, so the Battletoads call in Billy and Jimmy Lee, and all five head for the Colossus. Its seven levels run from the ship's tail, corridors and base to an attack on it from outside in a small craft, where the game becomes a shooter as the Queen hurls asteroids, mines and UFOs; then the heroes board the missile hull in which she and the Shadow Boss escape, and fight each in turn.

It was the first Battletoads game with all three toads, Zitz, Pimple and Rash, playable, alongside the Lee brothers, and its engine and design come straight from Battletoads rather than Double Dragon. Players attack enemies, swing on ropes, fly spaceships and ride turbo bikes, and the toads have their usual exaggerated "Smash Hits", such as Kiss-My-Fist, Big Bad Foot, Nuclear Knuckles and the Battletoad Butt. There is a single-player mode, a two-player mode in which players can hit each other and one in which they cannot. As in Battletoads, there are only three continues and no passwords, and if one player loses all their lives both must restart the level.
trivia: Technos Japan had little or no credited involvement beyond licensing Double Dragon.
It was ported to the Mega Drive/Genesis, SNES and Game Boy.
It was not included in Rare Replay.
Its first re-release was the SNES version on Nintendo Classics in September 2024.
Nintendo Power's staff rated it the second-best NES game of 1993.
devStory: Rare developed it and Tradewest published it for the NES in 1993, with the 16-bit versions keeping identical play and two-button controls. Nintendo Power found its depth perception confusing but said "great action, graphics and theme" made it one of the year's strongest titles, better than Battletoads in Battlemaniacs, and nominated it for several 1993 Nintendo Power Awards, including Best Overall Game.

title: Dragon Quest II: Luminaries of the Legendary Line
description: Dragon Quest II (1987), first released in North America as Dragon Warrior II, is Chunsoft and Enix's sequel set a century after the original, adding a party, group battles and a ship, and one of the series' hardest games.
longDescription:
A hundred years after the first game, the evil wizard Hargon destroys Moonbrooke Castle, and the prince of Midenhall is ordered to stop him, joined by his cousins, the prince of Cannock and the princess of Moonbrooke. It expands on the original with a larger party, more places to explore, several heroes and enemies in each battle, and a sailing ship. Dragon Quest III follows the main characters' ancestor, the legendary hero Erdrick, and the three games are known as the Erdrick Trilogy.

It was the first Dragon Quest in which the player controls more than one character, each with their own traits, and it introduced a party system in which, instead of starting with a full party as was common in earlier computer RPGs, the player begins alone and recruits companions along the way. Characters search treasure chests, talk and trade with villagers, equip weapons and armour and cast spells, and wandering fields, towers, caves, seas and dungeons brings random encounters with groups of monsters rather than the original's one-on-one battles. Critics praised it for improving on almost every aspect of the first game, but it is known as one of the most difficult Dragon Quest games, especially late on, a reputation that survived even more forgiving ports.
trivia: Planning began a month before the original Dragon Quest was released.
Its multi-character battles were inspired by party systems such as Wizardry's.
Akira Toriyama painted the artwork on which the pixel-art characters and monsters were based.
The Famicom version sold 500,000 copies on release and 2.4 million by the end of the year.
It was remade with the first game as Dragon Quest I & II for Super Famicom and Game Boy Color.
devStory: Chunsoft developed it and Enix published it for the Famicom in 1987, with Enix's US subsidiary releasing Dragon Warrior II for the NES in 1990. A key goal was a more exciting combat system. Balance problems, fully fixed only in the early sections, and a staff including students unfamiliar with coding and debugging delayed it by a month, and many ideas were dropped because of the Famicom's limits, some later appearing in remakes and in Dragon Quest III. It shipped over 2.4 million copies in Japan, and the Super Famicom and Game Boy Color remakes sold over 1.92 million more.

title: Dragon Quest IV: Chapters of the Chosen
description: Dragon Quest IV (1990), first released in North America as Dragon Warrior IV, is Chunsoft and Enix's chapter-based RPG that begins the Zenithian Trilogy and introduced the party wagon and AI "Tactics".
longDescription:
Unlike the rest of the series, the game is split into five chapters, each focusing on different protagonists. The first four follow the Hero's future companions, and the fifth, told from the Hero's perspective, brings everyone together on a journey to save the world. It keeps many established features, such as day and night cycles, travel by ship and a flying vehicle, this time a hot air balloon, three levels of keys, Thief, Magic and Ultimate, and travel doors for crossing the map quickly, and the Hero again has the strongest healing and attack spells, though he need not stay in the party once the wagon arrives.

New was the "Tactics" AI system, which lets the player give the party, who become computer-controlled in the final chapter, strategies such as prioritising damage, healing or saving MP while controlling the Hero directly; it is seen as a precursor to Final Fantasy XII's Gambits. The wagon, introduced here, lets players choose which characters fight, and later returned in Dragon Quest V and VI. It also brought the series' first casino, with slots, poker and monster betting for tokens, searching drawers and jars for items, Small Medals to trade with a secluded king, and saving at a House of Healing instead of by talking to a king.
trivia: It sold out 1.3 million cartridges and grossed ¥14 billion within an hour of release in Japan.
The Famicom version sold 3.1 million units, the system's fourth best-selling game.
It sold only 80,000 copies in the United States.
It was Enix America's last Dragon Quest localisation before the subsidiary closed in 1995.
Heartbeat remade it for PlayStation, adding a sixth chapter, later ported to the Nintendo DS.
devStory: Chunsoft developed it and Enix published it for the Famicom in Japan on 11 February 1990, with a North American NES version in October 1992, the last Dragon Quest localised into English until Dragon Warrior Monsters in December 1999. Its PlayStation remake by Heartbeat was ported by ArtePiazza to the Nintendo DS in 2007 and 2008, and a mobile version followed in 2014.

title: Neutopia II
description: Neutopia II (1991) is Hudson Soft's Zelda-like PC Engine sequel in which Jazeta's son sets out to rescue his father and defeat the returning demon Dirth.
longDescription:
The player controls Jazeta's son, who sets out to save his father, the hero of the first Neutopia, and to defeat the evil demon Dirth, who has returned. Its visuals and play closely resemble the early Legend of Zelda games: the young hero roams freely through a sizeable 2D world, at some points tackling tasks in any order and at others following a more linear path through the story.

It was made by a largely new team at Hudson Soft, led by director and designer Shigeki Fujiwara, with original Neutopia programmers Kōji Kaneta and Masato Tobisawa returning as co-programmers. Fumie Takaoka designed the characters, Yutaka Satō the backgrounds and Yoshikazu Yasuhiko the sprites, and Keita Hoshi, later of Soldier Blade and Super Bomberman 3, composed the music and created the sound effects. Critics praised its varied monster designs, new additions, straightforward plot and presentation, while criticising its lack of originality, simple puzzles and poor sprite animation; some felt it was indistinguishable from the first game, and retrospective reviewers called it derivative of Zelda.
trivia: It was demonstrated at the 1991 Tokyo Toy Show.
It was a launch title for Turbo Technologies' relaunch of the TurboGrafx-16, alongside Air Zonk.
PC Engine Fan readers scored it 22.24 out of 30.
Hudson Soft teased a Neutopia III that never materialised.
It is included on the TurboGrafx-16 Mini.
devStory: Hudson Soft published it in Japan for the PC Engine on 27 September 1991, and Turbo Technologies released it for the TurboGrafx-16 in North America in August 1992 after a planned July date. It reached the Wii Virtual Console in Japan, North America and Europe in 2007 and the PlayStation Network's PC Engine Archives line. Video Games' Martin Gaksch commended its varied monsters, additions and stylish music.

title: Rolling Thunder 2
description: Rolling Thunder 2 (1991) is Namco's sequel to its spy run-and-gun, adding two-player co-op with agents Leila and Albatross as they fight the revived Geldra and its cyborg Maskers.
longDescription:
In the 1990s, the Geldra organisation, believed destroyed in the first game, returns and starts destroying the world's satellites. Players again take on members of the WCPO's Rolling Thunder task force, now two at once: Player 1 is the female agent Leila and Player 2 the male agent Albatross, who look different and carry different handguns but have identical abilities. Each can survive only two physical blows, while any bullet or laser kills instantly. Their pistols have limited ammunition and fire slow "chaser" shots when empty, and marked doors provide a submachine gun, with a counter showing how many rounds remain so one player can leave ammunition for the other. Unlike the original, ammunition does not carry over between levels.

Where Rolling Thunder was set in 1968, the sequel has a contemporary setting and a more futuristic design, with noticeably better graphics. The Maskers, once hooded terrorists, are now cyborgs, and stages are more varied: the first four take place at a seaside resort in Florida and the last four in a pyramid in Egypt, both camouflaged Geldra bases. The Genesis version was well received, with 92 per cent from Computer & Video Games, 23 out of 25 from GamePro and 90 per cent from MegaTech.
trivia: Its submachine gun is based on a Walther MP, judging by the artwork.
A Genesis port was released the same year.
The Mega Drive and arcade versions reached the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and 2009.
Virtual Console reviews were cooler, with 6/10 from GameSpot.
Complex ranked it 85th among the 100 best Genesis games.
devStory: Namco developed and published it for arcades in 1991 as the sequel to 1986's Rolling Thunder, keeping its predecessor's play while adding co-operative play, improved graphics and an optional female lead. Sega-16 later gave the Genesis version 8/10, and Bandai Namco included the game in its Namco Museum collection.

title: Valis III
description: Valis III (1990) is Laser Soft's TurboGrafx-CD action platformer in which schoolgirl Yuko Asou and her allies Cham and Valna, switchable at any time, stop the dark king Glames from destroying two worlds.
longDescription:
After the events of Valis II, Yuko Asou, a Japanese schoolgirl chosen as the Valis warrior and wielder of the mystical Valis sword, faces King Glames, wielder of the sword Leethus, who leads the denizens of the Dark World to conquer both Vecanti and Earth in search of refuge as their own planet is destroyed. With the demon warrior-maiden Cham and her sister Valna, Yuko must stop him. The player guides her through two-dimensional levels, fighting enemies, jumping between ledges and searching for items and power-ups before a boss at the end of each, with animated cut-scenes telling the story at set points.

The main change from earlier Valis games is control of several characters, switchable at any time, recalling Zillion and Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse. Each has different upgradable weapons, Yuko a chargeable energy wave, Cham a whip and Valna magical blasts from her wand, and lightning, fire and ice spells. Characters cannot be switched during boss fights, where the choice leads to a different cut-scene, and some stages force a particular character, usually Yuko. A ground slide that doubles as an attack is also new. The Genesis port dropped most of the cut-scenes and several levels, adding one new one.
trivia: Most of the Valis II staff returned, with Masami Hanari directing and Fumiyuki Moriyama producing.
Laser Soft was Telenet's internal game division.
Ubi Soft planned a European Genesis release that never came out.
Programmer Masayasu Yamamoto said the PC Engine version outsold the Mega Drive release.
PC Engine Fan readers scored it 24.02 out of 30.
devStory: Laser Soft developed it, and Telenet Japan and NEC published it for the TurboGrafx-CD in 1990, followed by a Genesis version in 1991 through Telenet's North American subsidiary Renovation Products. The TurboGrafx-CD version received generally favourable reviews, Joystick's Jean-Marc Demoly applauding its improvements over Valis II, and it was followed by Valis IV in 1991.

title: Steel Empire
description: Steel Empire (1992), Koutetsu Teikoku in Japan, is Hot-B's steampunk Mega Drive shooter of biplanes, dirigibles and armoured steam trains, inspired by Laputa: Castle in the Sky.
longDescription:
Set in an alternate late-19th-century world, it stands out among shoot 'em ups for its mostly low-tech, heavily stylised design. Its aircraft, weapons, power-ups, environments, enemies and bosses bring strong steampunk elements to its style, themes and visuals, with steam power, propeller aircraft, biplanes, dirigibles and heavily armoured steam trains with giant cannons cast as both heroes and foes.

Lead designer Yoshinori Satake began it in the late 1980s as an arcade game about steampunk aviation, inspired by anime such as Laputa: Castle in the Sky and Future Boy Conan. He wanted a world of "outrageous and nonsensical science", bringing to life the blueprints of 19th-century people who believed the steam engine could do anything. Because people then thought space had an atmosphere and that the aurora existed there, the final stage, set in space, has a colourful aurora-like mist, propellers that keep spinning and smoke. The Western credits claim it was inspired by an 1819 novel, Imperio do Aceiro by Caar H. Schitch, but there is no meaningful evidence the book exists outside the game.
trivia: Its Japanese title means "Empire of Steel".
It was originally to be published in the West by Sage's Creation as Battlewings.
Cover artist Marc Ericksen was commissioned for its box art and battle-scarred steel title logo.
A leaked Japanese arcade beta exists, its source code believed lost.
Remakes followed on Game Boy Advance in 2004 and 3DS in 2014, and it reached Switch in 2025.
devStory: Hot-B developed it, and it was released on the Mega Drive in Japan in 1992, with Flying Edge publishing the Western Genesis versions. It sold well in both markets and gained cult status in Japan. Western reviews were mixed: Computer and Video Games gave it 90 per cent, while Sega Power gave it 54, saying its graphics and enemies were different but "the gameplay's exactly the same as other Mega Drive shoot-em-ups".

title: Super Thunder Blade
description: Super Thunder Blade (1988) is Sega's Mega Drive sequel to the arcade Thunder Blade, a helicopter rail shooter that switches to a top-down view for its boss battles.
longDescription:
Although the war against guerrilla forces backed by Country S was won, many guerrillas survived, and the original Thunder Blade was lost in the fighting, leaving its pilot, Captain Lantz Goswork of Country A, injured. Country A develops a new combat helicopter, Super Thunder Blade, to face emerging threats, with Lantz once again at the controls.

Following the structure of the 1987 arcade game, each of its four stages features traditional rail shooting followed by a vertically scrolling boss battle. The helicopter fires guns and missiles and can air brake, gunning down military vehicles across different environments. As in the arcade game, the viewpoint changes: during normal play the camera sits behind the helicopter in a third-person view similar to Space Harrier, switching to a top-down view against bosses. ACE rated it 880 out of 1,000 and named it one of the five best Mega Drive games of 1989, and Computer and Video Games gave it 80 per cent, calling it the "best version" of Thunder Blade on "any" system.
trivia: Its hero is Captain Lantz Goswork of Country A.
IGN gave it 4/10 in 2007, calling its frame rate "far too jumpy".
It reached the Virtual Console in September 2007 and Nintendo Classics in April 2025.
It is included in Sega Genesis Collection and Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection.
It has four stages.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1988 as the sequel to the arcade Thunder Blade. It was well received at launch, but retrospective reviews in the 2000s were mixed. It was included in the Sega Genesis Collection for PlayStation 2 and PSP in 2006 and in Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection for Xbox 360 and PlayStation 3 in 2009, and IGN lamented that it "just couldn't make the jump to console" from the arcade cabinet.

title: Space Harrier II
description: Space Harrier II (1988) is Sega's Mega Drive launch-title sequel to Space Harrier, in which Harrier returns to Fantasy Land through his cosmic gate to fight across 13 stages and face the Dark Harrier.
longDescription:
Harrier receives another call for help, this time from the 214th sector, light-years from his cruiser, and travels there quickly through his "cosmic gate" to find Fantasy Land once again overrun by hostile forces, resolving to fight them off single-handed. As in the original, the superhuman hero runs and flies towards a distant horizon over a chequerboard ground, firing his large laser cannon four shots at a time, with an optional auto-fire.

Enemies attack from behind and from the distance, firing projectiles or trying to ram him, often in uniform clusters along fixed pseudo-3D paths, and a tone warns when a moving enemy appears. Large objects must be dodged; some, such as trees, can be destroyed, while ionic columns and pylons cannot. A hit or crash costs a life, and smaller objects such as foliage only trip Harrier, leaving him vulnerable for two seconds. There are 13 stages, each with its own boss, varying in landscape and speed, and some, such as Stuna Area, with a mid-boss. Players can start at any stage, but all twelve must be completed before the Final Chapter, where every main boss is fought again before the Dark Harrier.
trivia: It was a Japanese Mega Drive launch title and one of six US Genesis launch titles.
Like Altered Beast, it uses digitised voice recordings.
Tokuhiko Uwabo, credited as "Bo", composed its music.
ACE named it one of the three best Mega Drive games in 1989, with Altered Beast and Thunder Force II.
A graphically enhanced version is included on the Sega Genesis Mini 2.
devStory: Sega developed and published it in 1988 as the sequel to 1985's Space Harrier, launching it with the Mega Drive in Japan and with the Genesis in the US the following year. It is an example of the console's early sound, and it was later re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in December 2006 and Nintendo Classics in April 2022.

title: ESWAT: City Under Siege
description: ESWAT: City Under Siege (1990) is Sega's Shinobi-style Genesis platformer in which rookie officer Duke Oda earns a powered ICE Combat Suit to fight the terrorist organisation E.Y.E.
longDescription:
In the near future, Duke Oda is a rookie in the Cyber Police of the city of Liberty, tasked with cleaning up an overwhelming crime wave and taking down the most wanted criminals. In the first two levels he has only a single-shot weapon and dies on his second hit. When a mysterious, high-tech terrorist organisation called E.Y.E. threatens to take over the city, he is promoted at the end of the second level and given power armour, the ICE Combat Suit.

The suit unlocks more lethal weapons if Duke finds them: the Super Shot, a plasma rifle, rockets and a devastating fire attack, along with a jet pack whose limited fuel refills over time. It lets him take more damage, but makes him bigger and harder to keep out of the way of enemy attacks. The final boss, E.Y.E.'s leader, turns out to be an artificially intelligent robot trying to copy the ICE Combat Suit to conquer Liberty. The console game keeps the arcade original's main characters, plot and some enemies, but has different levels, weapons and bonuses. MegaTech called it "a super slick shoot-'em-up that simply oozes quality", praising its parallax backgrounds, sprites and sound.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Cyber Police ESWAT.
It is based on the 1989 arcade game Cyber Police ESWAT.
A Master System version was one of the last major ports to that console.
Mega ranked it 32nd among the top Mega Drive games of all time in 1992.
Backbone Entertainment pitched a new ESWAT game that was never greenlit; its artwork later leaked.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Genesis and Master System in 1990. Raze gave it 72 per cent, praising its detailed backgrounds and voice recordings but finding it too easy and repetitive, Mega Action gave 81 per cent despite "dated" graphics, and Console XS gave 84 out of 100, calling it "challenging" and "addictive".

title: Alien Storm
description: Alien Storm (1990) is Sega's Golden Axe-style beat 'em up shooter in which the Alien Busters, Karen, Garth and the robot Scooter, blast invaders hiding in bins and post boxes.
longDescription:
A homicidal alien race is invading Earth, and only a special forces team called the Alien Busters stands in its way: Karen, Garth and the robot Scooter, known under other names in some versions. It closely resembles Golden Axe, with a similar art style, three playable characters, a man, a woman and a novelty character, and special attacks. Up to three can play in the arcade, two on Mega Drive and one on Master System. Missions run from the streets to the mother ship, home of the mother of all aliens, with objectives such as rescuing people or destroying a UFO, and aliens hide inside plants, post boxes, bins, drums and other objects.

Each character has unlimited punches and kicks plus a personal weapon, and flying skulls that appear after certain kills can be shot for life or energy, which powers weapon attacks such as flames or electricity and much stronger specials. Garth calls in a US Air Force starship to bomb the street, Karen summons a nuclear missile that incinerates every enemy on screen, and Scooter explodes, leaving his head behind for his new body to collect. Specials use a lot of energy. Game Machine listed it as Japan's most successful table arcade unit in June 1990.
trivia: Karen is absent from the Master System version.
Scooter is called Slammer in the Master System and PAL versions.
The arcade has six missions; the Mega Drive version has eight.
MegaTech gave the Genesis version 78 per cent, criticising only its ease.
It is included in Sonic's Ultimate Genesis Collection and on Nintendo Classics.
devStory: Sega released it in arcades in 1990 and ported it to the Genesis/Mega Drive and Master System. MegaTech praised the Genesis version as an outstanding arcade conversion with highly enjoyable play, and the Mega Drive version was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007 and on Nintendo Classics in 2022.

title: Two Crude Dudes
description: Two Crude (1990), Crude Buster in Japan and Two Crude Dudes on Genesis, is Data East's comic beat 'em up in which mercenaries Biff and Spike hurl cars and enemies to retake a ruined New York.
longDescription:
Biff and Spike are mercenaries hired by the American government to stop the terrorist organisation Big Valley and retake a New York City ruined by a nuclear explosion the group caused. Players jump, dodge and fight through legions of enemies, and since the duo are muscle-bound brawlers they can lift objects far heavier than themselves, such as cars and traffic lights, to use as weapons, and do the same with most enemies. In co-op, one player can even pick up the other and throw him.

Each player has a life bar that falls with every hit, and some enemies grab on and drain it; a player killed by an explosion or flames slumps to the ground burnt. Between stages a cut-scene shows Biff and Spike punching a "Power Cola" vending machine until sodas fall out and drinking them to refill their life, and the same machines serve as top-up points in most stages. Computer and Video Games' Julian Rignall gave the arcade game 95 per cent, calling it "one of the best beat'em ups I've seen in years", and Sinclair User likened it to an interactive cartoon and called it a classic, better than its predecessor.
trivia: It was a follow-up to Bad Dudes Vs. DragonNinja.
ISCO/Opera House ported it to the Mega Drive/Genesis in 1992.
It topped Hong Kong's Bondeal conversion kit charts from March to April 1990.
Mega ranked the Mega Drive version 37th among its top Mega Drive games.
The arcade version appears on Data East Arcade Classics.
devStory: Data East developed and published it for arcades in 1990, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's seventh most successful table arcade unit in its 15 April 1990 issue. The Mega Drive/Genesis port kept the Japanese title in Japan but became Two Crude Dudes in North America and Europe, and it was well received too. After Data East's bankruptcy, G-Mode included the arcade game in Data East Arcade Classics.

title: Atomic Runner Chelnov
description: Atomic Runner Chelnov (1988) is Data East's controversial auto-scrolling arcade shooter in which a coal miner gains superhuman powers from a nuclear plant explosion, widely read as a Chernobyl parody.
longDescription:
Chelnov, a coal miner, miraculously survives the malfunction and explosion of a nuclear power plant, and the massive radiation gives his body superhuman abilities. A secret organisation wants to exploit them for its own evil ends, and Chelnov must defeat it with his new powers across seven levels. The player uses an eight-way joystick and three buttons to attack, jump and turn around, collecting six weapons, a laser, fire rings, boomerangs, spiked bolas, a spiked ball whip and missiles, plus power-ups that raise attack power, rapid fire, range or jump height.

The screen scrolls left at a constant speed except during boss fights, and Chelnov keeps running even if the joystick is released; he can move left or right within the screen but cannot stop or go back except against bosses, though he can turn while jumping. His animation is highly detailed and smooth for its time, comparable to Karateka and the early Prince of Persia. The coal-miner setting, a hammer and sickle on the opening screen and the title, close to the Japanese spelling of Chernobyl, led many to see it as a parody of the disaster; Data East said on television that Chelnov was merely a relative of its character Karnov.
trivia: Other staff said the game had a different name until the Chernobyl accident inspired "Chelnov".
Over a year and a half passed between the disaster and the game's release.
The 1992 Genesis port changed the story considerably to remove Chernobyl connotations.
Dempa ported it faithfully to the X68000 in 1993.
Paon bought the rights after Data East's 2003 bankruptcy.
devStory: Data East developed and published it for arcades in 1988, and Game Machine listed it as Japan's thirteenth most successful table arcade unit of February 1988. It was controversial on release because of its apparent Chernobyl references, and its Genesis conversion by Data East in 1992 used a different theme.

title: Arcus Odyssey
description: Arcus Odyssey (1991) is Wolf Team's isometric co-operative hack-and-slash game in which four heroes try to stop the dark sorceress Castomira from returning to the land of Arcus.
longDescription:
Centuries ago, the dark sorceress Castomira tried to turn the land of Arcus into a place of chaos and darkness, until Princess Leaty, a good sorceress and granddaughter of the legendary King of Light, defeated her after days of battle and banished her to the Dark World. Foreseeing her return, Leaty forged a magic sword, "The Power of Leaty", and entrusted it to the King of Arcus. A millennium later, Castomira's followers steal it to revive her, and four heroes set out to stop them: Jedda Chef the swordsman, Diana Fireya the archer, Erin Gashuna the warrior-maiden and Bead Shia the mage. At the end, players choose whether to use the sword against Castomira or help her regain her power.

Players choose one of the four and work through the levels in order, moving, attacking, blocking with a shield and using offensive, defensive and healing items and magic found in chests. Some levels require sub-quests to proceed, such as putting out a fire blocking the door, and others provide an ally. The view is mainly isometric, but characters move freely in eight directions, and most bosses give a power boost to health or strength when defeated. ACE's David Upchurch scored it 863 out of 1,000, calling it "one of the finest examples of the arcade adventure genre to appear on the Megadrive".
