trivia: It is part of the Arcus series, after Arcus, Arcus II: Silent Symphony and Arcus III.
It was also released for the X68000.
A 1993 SNES version was released only in Japan, as Arcus Spirits.
The North American SNES release was cancelled after Sega acquired Renovation Products.
Dragon gave it four out of five stars.
devStory: Wolf Team developed it, and Renovation Products released it for the Sega Genesis and X68000 in 1991. A North American SNES version was cancelled following Sega's acquisition of Renovation, the American publisher of Wolf Team and Telenet games, and a planned European release by Loriciels also fell through. Reviews were mostly mixed.

title: Granada
description: Granada (1990) is Wolf Team's free-roaming tank shooter, inspired by Namco's Grobda and Assault, in which mercenary Leon Todo pilots a Maneuver Cepter through a war over rare metals in a futuristic Africa.
longDescription:
In a futuristic Africa in 2016, a war over mining rights to rare metals has escalated quickly thanks to new weapons called Maneuver Cepters. Mercenary Leon Todo pilots the titular Maneuver Cepter tank to end the conflict once and for all. A multidirectional shooter similar to Thunder Force, it mixes action and shooting with mission-based exploration across eight themed stages, using a main two-button layout, with four difficulty levels that each add different conditions depending on the version.

Unlike most shooters, each level is a large field full of enemies, obstacles and enemy generators that can be roamed freely. The goal is to destroy every main target, marked as red dots on the HUD in the bottom right corner, and finally a boss, before the timer runs out, collecting items scattered around the stage along the way. It took two years to develop and was the first Wolf Team project to emphasise play over plot. It became briefly popular among X68000 owners and was nominated for Oh!X magazine's Game of the Year, losing to titles such as Dungeon Master, and the Genesis version was praised for its presentation, graphics, sound, controls, play and replay value.
trivia: It was Wolf Team's ninth X68000 game.
It was released for the X68000 in Japan on 20 April 1990.
Renovation Products published the Genesis version in North America.
The Genesis version has several changes from the original.
The X68000 version has been re-released only in Japan for Windows.
devStory: Wolf Team developed and published it exclusively for the X68000 in Japan in 1990, influenced by arcade games such as Namco's Grobda and Assault. A Sega Genesis port followed the same year, published by Wolf Team in Japan and Renovation Products in North America, and retrospective reviews of the Genesis version have been equally positive.

title: Slap Fight
description: Slap Fight (1986), Alcon in North America, is Toaplan's vertically scrolling shooter with a Gradius-style power-up menu, whose weapon system lived on in Truxton and Grind Stormer.
longDescription:
On the colonised planet of Theron, an alien race led by Gaudy has invaded, and the player, a pilot of the Allied League of Cosmic Nations (ALCON), counterattacks in the SW475 space fighter. Reminiscent of B-Wings, it seems standard at first, with constantly scrolling scenery that stops only for a boss, but apart from some stationary helicopters there are no flying enemies at all. Without power-ups the ship's shot reaches only half the height of the screen.

Its power-up system borrows from Gradius: some enemies drop star items that move a lit cursor along a menu of upgrades at the bottom of the screen. Every upgrade except the side shot also enlarges the ship's hitbox, making it an easier target and lives harder to keep, and a star lit when the ship is destroyed carries over to light the speed upgrade on the next life. Weapons affect enemies and terrain differently; some towers can only be destroyed by lasers or homing missiles, and other enemies fall faster to particular weapons. Hidden bonus secrets, revealed by shooting certain spots and scenery, are crucial for high scores and extra lives.
trivia: Tatsuya Uemura said few arcade boards were produced in Japan, but it was popular.
Game Machine ranked it Japan's seventh most successful table arcade unit of August 1986, above Ikari Warriors and Gradius.
It never received a direct sequel.
Grind Stormer is regarded as its spiritual successor.
Its rights are owned by Masahiro Yuge's company Tatsujin.
devStory: Toaplan developed it and Taito published it for arcades in 1986, and it was later ported to home systems by third-party developers. Western magazines gave it, and especially the home conversions, a mixed reception, though Den of Geek later noted its weapon system and the many ways to kill enemies, and its ideas were inherited by Truxton and Grind Stormer.

title: Demon's World
description: Demon's World (1989) is Toaplan's horror run-and-gun in which two Ghostbusters-style ghost hunters fight monsters unleashed by the demon king, from Japanese yōkai to Frankenstein's monster.
longDescription:
Two ghost hunters battle ghosts and monsters unleashed on Earth by the titular demon king across ten increasingly difficult auto-scrolling stages, some ending in bosses. Their guns come with energy packs reminiscent of Ghostbusters, and they can also defeat enemies by jumping on them and double-jump across platforms. Weapon power-ups switch the gun to lasers, bombs or a spread shot, collecting three "P" icons in a row grants a shield that absorbs an extra hit, hearts give points, and shooting certain spots reveals bonus secrets crucial for high scores and extra lives.

The better-known arcade version begins at a telephone box in a modern town before heading to a haunted American Old West. An alternative arcade version and the PC Engine version reorder the levels, starting in a fantasy China and then Japan, with creatures of Japanese folklore such as karakasa, chōchin-obake, kappa, hitotsume-kozō and rokurokubi, before moving on to a ghostly pirate ship and the haunted Old West, with a ghost town and a canyon full of Western monsters such as Frankenstein's monster, Dracula and Jason Voorhees-style masked killers.
trivia: Catalina Games published it in North America.
NEC Avenue ported it to the PC Engine Super CD-ROM², released only in Japan on 26 February 1993.
The PC Engine version was released as Horror Story.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's 22nd most popular arcade game of August 1989.
Its rights are held by Tatsujin, affiliated with exA-Arcadia.
devStory: Toaplan developed it, and Taito published it in Japan in 1989, with Catalina Games handling North America. The Japan-only PC Engine version added various changes and received a mixed response from critics who reviewed it as an import, Consoles + praising its graphics, music and play but criticising its presentation.

title: Zero Tolerance
description: Zero Tolerance (1994) is Technopop's rare Genesis first-person shooter in which an elite five-commando squad clears an alien-infested starship before its reactor blows.
longDescription:
In a future where mankind has colonised the Solar System, its settlements, outposts, mines, colonies, ships and stations are protected by the military Planet Defense Corps. When its flagship Europa-1 is attacked by a lethal alien aggressor, the Corps calls in Zero Tolerance, an elite strike squad of five specially trained commandos. Europa-1's last transmission shows heavy fire damage, nearly everyone aboard dead and strange creatures hunting the few survivors, and small-arms fire has damaged the nuclear cooling system, so an overheating core will destroy the ship within hours. The player must sneak aboard and eliminate the aliens and the "infected" crew to erase all evidence of the attack.

Its 40 levels span Europa-1, an abandoned merchant freighter, the Corps' fortified central command building and that building's sub-basements. The aim is to kill every enemy and reach the exit, a staircase or lift to the next level, though players can head straight for the exit at the cost of not receiving passwords until the area is finished. A killed commando is marked "deceased" and can no longer be used, and the game ends when all five are dead. Two Genesis consoles could be linked with a special cable through the second joypad port for multiplayer.
trivia: It is one of the few Genesis first-person shooters, alongside Bloodshot, Duke Nukem 3D and Corporation.
The link cable was meant to be included in the box, but a last-minute decision replaced it with a coupon for a free one.
GamePro praised its large, labyrinthine levels and co-operative multiplayer.
GamePro said the anxiety caused by an adversary round a corner was "severe".
The squad has five selectable commandos.
devStory: Technopop developed it and Accolade published it for the Sega Genesis in 1994. GamePro gave it a mostly positive review, noting that first-person games put pressure on a system's processor but that Accolade had done a good job, and praising its limited but effective sound effects.

title: Kolibri
description: Kolibri (1995) is Novotrade's 32X horizontal shooter in which a hummingbird, empowered by a life-giving crystal, defends the Earth against a destructive one, inspired by an angry real-life hummingbird.
longDescription:
Long ago a crystal from outer space embedded itself in the Earth and began creating life. Then a similar crystal crashed to Earth and began destroying that life and sapping the first crystal's strength, and before it was destroyed, the first crystal gave its power to a lone hummingbird, Kolibri, whose name means hummingbird in several European languages. It is up to the bird to save the Earth.

Numerous power-ups follow different patterns, some spreading shots and others homing in on enemies, and puzzles grow increasingly difficult from level to level. Producer Ed Annunziata was inspired after blowing cigarette smoke at a hummingbird that hovered in front of his face; days later it returned and he sensed its aggression, convinced "he was pissed that I second-hand smoked him, and he remembered me". Researching the birds, he was intrigued by their flight and built a shooter around one. Reviews were mostly middling: EGM praised its visuals and originality but criticised respawning in a vulnerable position, and GamePro's Lawrence Neves found it "just average", wanting something more like Gradius or R-Type.
trivia: Novotrade International is now known as Appaloosa.
Sega Saturn Magazine found "a certain dullness and insipidity" despite its size.
GamePro found turning the bird round to shoot behind "cumbersome and frustrating".
Next Generation mocked the "ultimate hummingbird simulation game".
Penny Arcade named it the "Best Hummingbird-based Shooter Available For The 32X" in 2001.
devStory: Novotrade International developed it and Sega published it in 1995 for the 32X add-on for the Genesis. Next Generation felt it offered nothing the standard Genesis could not do and that its play was "very monotonous", reserving most of its scorn for the "absurd" premise of a hummingbird toasting insects with a guided missile on its beak.

title: Wiz 'n' Liz: The Frantic Wabbit Wescue
description: Wiz 'n' Liz (1993) is Raising Hell Software's frantic, enemy-free Mega Drive platformer in which two wizards race the clock to rescue "wabbits" lost to a spell gone wrong on the planet Pum.
longDescription:
On the magical planet of Pum, a group of "wabbits" has been spirited away by a spell gone awry, and the wizards Wiz and Liz must rescue them. A humorous, cutesy platformer, it has no enemies apart from some end-of-level bosses. Levels are divided into eight worlds, each with its own graphical style and music. Wiz, Liz or both run through the landscape collecting wabbits against a strict time limit; each rescued wabbit releases a floating letter, and the player must spell out the magic word shown at the top of the screen, then rescue the rest, who now release fruit, stars and clocks that add time.

The time limit starts at three minutes and resets only when the character dies, though a glowing orange orb in the last ten seconds adds thirty seconds. At the end of each stage, collected fruit is mixed in a cauldron, producing bonus points, a minigame, a weird graphical effect, a change in the wabbits' colours, "Absolutely Nothing" or silliness such as a fake "Game Over" followed by a sheepish "Only joking...". Other Psygnosis characters, including Puggsy and the Lemmings, make cameo appearances. MegaZone called it "cute, original and very, very fast".
trivia: Lunatic Software developed the Amiga port.
Its bonus game was a challenge on the Sky One show Games World.
Amiga Action called it "a fast action platform extravaganza".
Amiga Power found it "absolutely lovely" but shallow.
Amiga Power praised its two-player mode and hidden minigames.
devStory: Raising Hell Software developed it for the Sega Mega Drive and Psygnosis published it in 1993, with an Amiga version by Lunatic Software following. Reviews of the Amiga version were generally positive.

title: Puggsy
description: Puggsy (1993) is Traveller's Tales' physics-driven puzzle platformer in which an orange space-hopper-like alien hunts for the spaceship stolen by the raccoon natives of The Planet.
longDescription:
Puggsy, an orange alien resembling a space hopper, lands his spaceship on The Planet intending to return home, but the planet's raccoon natives steal it. The game crosses a conventional platformer, with the usual enemies and various ways to kill them, with a puzzle game in which Puggsy often has to find objects and carry them to a particular place or use them to finish a level. Some objects act as power-ups, letting him survive a hit or two, speeding him up or making him briefly invincible, and others, such as guns with mostly unrefillable ammunition, help temporarily.

Objects follow a physics-based system that was innovative at the time: they can be thrown, each has its own weight, and careless stacks topple. Puggsy can carry a stack along flat ground, but on a slope everything except the bottom item tends to scatter. Items carried out of a level's exit are worth different scores, and a heart gives an extra life. Objects range from shells, weights, matches, keys and balloons to cups, barrels, clue-giving chests, knives and candles. There are 57 levels, 16 of them secret, six bosses, nine on Mega-CD, and five training levels under the "Junior" option, and not every level or boss must be beaten to finish.
trivia: Secret endings are triggered by goals such as spelling "HEROS" with blocks in a secret level.
The password to six special secret levels comes from "a silly maths" puzzle in the credits.
A Super NES version was cancelled.
MegaTech gave it 90 per cent and a Hyper Game Award but criticised its controls.
Puggsy cameos in Psygnosis's Wiz 'n' Liz.
devStory: Traveller's Tales developed it and Psygnosis published it for the Mega Drive, Mega-CD and Amiga in Europe in October 1993 and in North America on 6 January 1994. MegaTech called it "excellently designed and thought-out", and GamePro, reviewing the Mega-CD version, praised its controls, graphics, sound, challenge and detail, though it predicted veterans would tire of it faster than younger players.

title: Magic Knight Rayearth
description: Magic Knight Rayearth (1995) is Sega's Saturn action RPG based on the anime, in which three schoolgirls pulled into Cephiro tag-team to rescue Princess Emeraude, and the last Saturn game released in North America.
longDescription:
Eighth-grade girls Hikaru Shidou, Umi Ryuuzaki and Fuu Hououji are drawn from their school trips to Tokyo Tower into the world of Cephiro, where the Master Mage Clef tells them they must become the Magic Knights and rescue Cephiro's Pillar, Princess Emeraude, Princess Emerald in English, from the high priest Zagato to return home. The plot closely follows the first arc of the manga and anime, with every character from that arc plus the anime-only Inouva, but adds new locations and characters that considerably expand it, and, unlike the source, all of Zagato's minions die, including Ascot, Caldina and Rafarga. Each girl keeps a journal that gains entries after key events.

The player controls all three, but only one fights at a time; the other two follow, unable to attack and immune to enemies and hazards, and the active character can be switched instantly, so the girls tackle enemies and puzzles tag-team style. Unlike most RPGs, upgrades and spells mostly arrive at set points in the story rather than through independent achievements, except maximum HP and MP, raised by finding special items, and weapons and armour improve with general level-ups. Unlike in the anime, only Hikaru uses a sword.
trivia: It was one of the first games announced for the Saturn.
Working Designs released it in North America in 1998.
At least five other Rayearth games, all different, appeared on Game Boy, Super Famicom and Game Gear.
Famitsu scored it 26 out of 40.
GameSpot's Andrew Vestal considered localising a three-year-old game a wasted effort.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Saturn in Japan in 1995. Its prolonged localisation by Working Designs meant it did not reach North America until 1998, becoming the last Saturn game released there, where it received mild to positive reviews; it holds a 70.03 per cent average on GameRankings.

title: Sega Touring Car Championship
description: Sega Touring Car Championship (1996) is Tetsuya Mizuguchi's Model 2 arcade racer, inspired by German DTM footage, praised for its speed and realism but criticised for its difficulty.
longDescription:
Built for the Model 2 board, it was housed in a sit-down cabinet with speakers either side of the player's head and a subwoofer under the seat. It has four tracks, one of them secret and unlocked by reaching the season's final race. Critics generally praised its remarkable sense of speed and realism, but felt those same qualities made it excessively difficult; Next Generation called it "the most painstakingly realistic driving game yet", requiring extreme precision through corners and fractions of a second shaved off lap times.

Tetsuya Mizuguchi of Sega AM3 was inspired by a video of the Deutsche Tourenwagen Meisterschaft he saw while working on Manx TT Super Bike: the cars' interiors "looked just like F1 Grand Prix", the races were full of crashes, and the competing nations gave it a "nationalistic battle atmosphere". Development began in April 1996. The staff researched it through videos, magazines, books and races, some riding as passengers with championship drivers, and every engine sound was sampled from real cars. Securing the many sponsor decals took Mizuguchi to Europe and the US about three times. A techno soundtrack was chosen to match the acceleration, with tracks from Belgian and Italian artists produced through Avex Trax and four Japanese musicians picked by audition.
trivia: AM Annex was a new 15-person division hand-picked by Mizuguchi.
Mizuguchi said the small team was formed with AM3's and Sega's approval for better working conditions.
The Saturn version adds an unlockable fifth track.
The Saturn version lets players create and save custom cars.
It was also ported to Windows.
devStory: Sega AM Annex, a new internal division led by Tetsuya Mizuguchi and made up of transferred and newly hired staff, developed it, and Sega released it in arcades in 1996. Ports to the Sega Saturn, with split-screen multiplayer, and Microsoft Windows followed. Reviews were mixed.

title: Darius Gaiden
description: Darius Gaiden (1994) is Taito's acclaimed horizontal shooter for its F3 System, in which the Silver Hawk battles the aquatic machines of the Belsar empire across branching stages, with black hole bombs.
longDescription:
The Silver Hawk sets out to destroy the Belsar empire, which plans to wipe out the remnants of humanity on their new home, planet Darius; a second player can join at any time. After each stage players choose the next, so seven of its twenty-seven stages are played in one run. The ship must destroy constantly moving formations of enemies shaped like fish, crabs, seahorses and other sea creatures while dodging their fire and obstacles, and each level ends with a boss that must be hit in a weak spot such as its head or mouth.

The Silver Hawk starts with a forward shot; coloured emblems dropped by matching enemies add missiles (green), lengthen and strengthen shots (red) or give a shield (blue), and further emblems upgrade them, for example to missiles that fire forwards and backwards. New to the series are three black hole bombs, which open a swirling vortex that sucks in enemies and bullets before lightning deals massive damage, and the ability to capture mid-level bosses. Designer Hirokazu Kato insisted on dropping the earlier games' three-monitor display, feeling it had grown old, and the team focused on making it fun and unlike any other shooter.
trivia: It was originally titled Darius III; gaiden means "side story", as its plot falls between the first two games.
Producer Hidehiro Fujiwara had little exposure to the series beyond helping on the original Darius.
It was built to show off Taito's cartridge-based F3 System.
Gamest gave it awards including 2nd Best Graphic and 3rd Best Shooting.
The Saturn version sold over 70,000 copies in Japan.
devStory: Taito developed and published it for arcades in 1994 as the fifth Darius game, led by producer Hidehiro Fujiwara with designer Hirokazu Kato and programmer Akira Kurabayashi; Taito wanted big-name franchises on its new F3 board. It was critically acclaimed and commercially successful, and home versions for Saturn and PlayStation were well received, though some found its music bizarre. It is ranked among the greatest side-scrolling shooters and was followed by G-Darius in 1997.

title: Spyro: Year of the Dragon
description: Spyro: Year of the Dragon (2000) is Insomniac's acclaimed third Spyro game, in which the purple dragon chases a sorceress who has stolen the dragons' eggs into the Forgotten Realms.
longDescription:
An evil sorceress steals magical dragon eggs from the land of the dragons, and Spyro follows her to the "Forgotten Realms" to recover them. The eggs are spread across 37 levels, hidden or awarded for completing tasks, and the worlds are linked by hub "homeworlds" with gateways to other levels; moving on to the next hub requires finishing five worlds, collecting enough eggs and beating a boss. Not every egg is needed, and some can only be reached by returning later. Gems hidden in crates and jars are used to bribe the bear Moneybags into freeing captured characters and switching on things that help Spyro progress, and both count towards a completion percentage tracked in an atlas.

Spyro breathes fire, swims and dives, glides and headbutts his way past enemies, many of them creatures called Rhynocs. His health is shown by his dragonfly companion Sparx, who changes colour and then vanishes as he takes damage; without Sparx, the next hit costs a life and a return to the last checkpoint, and eating small creatures called fodder restores him. The game added new characters and minigames to the series, with improved graphics and music. Critics including NextGen and AllGame called it the best Spyro yet, and reviewers highlighted its high polish.
trivia: It was named for its release in the Chinese zodiac's Year of the Dragon.
Development took about ten and a half months, from November 1999 to September 2000.
The team was influenced by games including Doom and Crash Bandicoot.
It was Insomniac's last Spyro game, after Universal and Sony's relationship soured.
It was remade in the Spyro Reignited Trilogy in 2018.
devStory: Insomniac Games developed it and Sony Computer Entertainment published it for the PlayStation in 2000 as the third Spyro game and the last for the original PlayStation. It received "universal acclaim" according to Metacritic and sold more than 3 million copies worldwide, though GameSpot and IGN noted it brought only minor refinements. Spyro: Enter the Dragonfly followed in 2002.

title: MediEvil 2
description: MediEvil 2 (2000) is SCE Cambridge Studio's sequel in which the skeletal knight Sir Daniel Fortesque is revived in Victorian London to stop Lord Palethorn and Jack the Ripper from raising the dead.
longDescription:
In 1886, 500 years after Sir Daniel Fortesque's battle with the sorcerer Zarok, the wealthy industrialist and sorcerer Lord Palethorn of Kensington discovers Zarok's spellbook and casts its spell to raise the dead across London. The book's pages scatter across the city, Palethorn takes on a demon-like appearance, and the spell revives Dan, whose body has been on display in a museum. He is recruited by Professor Hamilton Kift and his ghostly sidekick Winston Chapelmount, a play on Winston Churchill, to stop Palethorn and Jack the Ripper from terrorising the city.

Alongside returning swords and shields, Dan can now use modern weapons such as a pistol, a blunderbuss and a Gatling gun, and a new feature lets the player pick two weapons to switch between in real time. Filling the Chalice of Souls in each level by defeating enemies earns more weapons, merchants called Spivs sell ammunition and services, and Winston gives hints and saves during long levels. Life Bottles extend Dan's health meter, refilled by Life Vials and Fountains. Midway through, Dan can place his head on a zombified hand to become Dan Hand, reaching areas his body cannot and alternating control between the two.
trivia: Its North American title is stylised MediEvil II.
First-game director Chris Sorrell was not involved; James Shepherd directed instead.
An early plot had Dan freeing Zarok from the Tower of London, dropped as a "B-movie twist ending".
Sony wanted it released before the end of the PlayStation's lifespan.
NextGen called it "a formulaic and agreeable way to pass the time".
devStory: After the first game's success, Sony Computer Entertainment commissioned its Cambridge studio to make a sequel, published for the PlayStation in 2000. The concept went through many transformations before the team settled on a Victorian Gothic revival setting. Reviews were favourable, if less so than for its predecessor: critics praised its detailed graphics and improved AI but criticised poor camera angles, low difficulty and its similarity to the original.

title: Parasite Eve II
description: Parasite Eve II (1999) is Square's survival horror sequel, directed by Resident Evil writer Kenichi Iwao, in which Aya Brea faces a new outbreak of Neo-Mitochondrial creatures in real-time combat.
longDescription:
Three years after the original, Aya Brea becomes caught up in another outbreak of Neo-Mitochondrial creatures. Play moves away from the first game towards traditional survival horror while keeping some role-playing elements. Aya uses tank controls, moving forwards and backwards and pivoting, and the camera is mostly fixed to a single view of each room. There is no Active Time Bar: battles are in real time, the first game's "range dome" is gone so she can hit off-screen targets from a safe distance, and there are no random battles, so enemies wander in plain view and can be avoided or planned for.

Aya's powers from the first game are locked, and she "rediscovers" her parasite energy abilities by spending experience earned from kills, choosing freely which to prioritise rather than unlocking them at set levels. They fall into four elements, fire for attacks, water for health, wind for status and earth for damage given or taken, with three abilities in each and three tiers per ability; the highest is the most powerful and the cheapest in MP. Its "bounty roster" lists 48 enemy types, each with its own attacks, strengths and weaknesses. Critics praised it but criticised its outdated controls.
trivia: It was originally planned as a spin-off starring Kyle, which explains the change of genre.
It became an official sequel, making Aya the lead and Kyle no longer playable.
Unlike the first game, it was released in PAL regions.
It reached North America and Europe in 2000.
Next Generation said "Eve II is scary good fun".
devStory: Square developed and published it for the PlayStation in Japan in 1999. Kenichi Iwao, who had directed and written Resident Evil, directed and wrote it, and Square chose to emulate that popular style. It received "generally favorable" reviews according to Metacritic, Next Generation giving it four stars and saying Square had taken most of the criticism of the original to heart.

title: Dino Crisis 2
description: Dino Crisis 2 (2000) is Capcom's action-focused sequel in which Regina and Dylan Morton fight hordes of dinosaurs through a jungle after a time-distorting event sends a research base into the past.
longDescription:
Special operative Regina returns to deal with the fallout of a time-distorting event that has sent a research base and its surroundings through time, and with team leader Dylan Morton she must battle dinosaurs to find a way back to the present. Designer Shu Takumi took over as director from Shinji Mikami, and the sequel trades its predecessor's survival horror for arcade-style action, with fixed camera angles, more open areas, more weapons and enemies and less emphasis on puzzles.

Killing dinosaurs in succession, countering attacks and avoiding damage earns "Extinction Points", which tally up between areas and are spent at computer stations, which also serve as save points, on new weapons, upgrades, health packs and ammunition; bandages stop bleeding. Many ideas abandoned from the first game were included, with more enemy types and more on screen at once for a claustrophobic feel, and pre-rendered backgrounds instead of 3D environments finally made a jungle setting possible, an idea dropped from the first game for technical reasons. Critics found it far less derivative of Resident Evil and praised its action, atmosphere and backgrounds, and still found it scary for the intensity of its dinosaur encounters.
trivia: It was Hiroyuki Kobayashi's debut as producer, after planning the first game.
Kobayashi said "it isn't all that interesting just killing dinosaurs", leading to points and sub-weapons.
It sold 1.19 million copies on PlayStation, fewer than its predecessor.
A PlayStation 2 version was announced but never released.
It was re-released on GOG.com in January 2025 and on Steam in February 2026.
devStory: Capcom Production Studio 4 developed it and Capcom published it for the PlayStation in 2000. Kobayashi said the hardest part was making a game "completely different" from Dino Crisis and Resident Evil. It was a critical and commercial success with "generally favorable reviews" on Metacritic, though some reviewers were mixed on the loss of survival horror, and a Windows port followed in 2002.

title: Fear Effect
description: Fear Effect (2000) is Kronos Digital's cinematic, four-disc action-adventure in which three mercenaries in a 2050 Hong Kong hunt a Triad boss's daughter and stumble into a pact with demons.
longDescription:
Around 2050, Wee Ming Lam, daughter of a powerful Hong Kong Triad boss, disappears, and three mercenaries, Hana Tsu-Vachel, Royce Glas and Jacob "Deke" DeCourt, set out to kidnap her before her father's men find her and hold her for ransom. She has vanished into the fictional Shan Xi protectorate, where Hana once worked in a brothel. What begins as a simple snatch-and-grab becomes a fiasco: Mr Lam owes his fortune and power to a pact with demons, and Wee Ming, a paper doll given life, is to be a sacrifice.

Its unshaded characters, textured to resemble cel-shading, made it one of the first games to attempt the technique, and instead of pre-rendered 2D backgrounds its environments are streaming or looping full-motion video, filling four discs. The player controls Hana, Deke or Glas through areas full of human and inhuman enemies with survival horror-style tank controls, but can run and shoot at the same time, fire two guns at separate targets and duck and roll away from fire, with puzzles between the action. The title refers to its life bar, a pulsing EKG that beats faster and turns red as the character is hurt, and calming acts, such as solving a puzzle or a stealth kill from behind, bring it back to green.
trivia: It contains elements of survival horror and stealth.
GameFan reviewed it favourably while it was still in development.
Edge said its controls made "the boss encounters absurdly difficult".
NextGen's Blake Fischer called it one of the most exciting and innovative adventures.
Fear Effect Sedna followed in 2018.
devStory: Kronos Digital Entertainment developed it and Eidos Interactive published it for the PlayStation in 2000. It received mainly positive reviews, praised for its cinematic presentation and unique visuals but criticised for its difficulty; Edge praised its tight script and distinctive graphics but found its play unbalanced. A prequel, Fear Effect 2: Retro Helix, followed a year later.

title: Fear Effect 2: Retro Helix
description: Fear Effect 2: Retro Helix (2001) is Kronos Digital's puzzle-driven prequel, showing how Hana, Rain Qin, Deke and Glas came together amid a global pandemic, from Hong Kong to the island of the immortals.
longDescription:
In Hong Kong in 2048, in the wake of a degenerative global pandemic called EINDS, Environmentally Induced Nucleotides Degeneration Syndrome, theft, murder and terrorism have become big business. Freelance operatives Hana Tsu-Vachel and newcomer Rain Qin, washed-up former soldier Royce Glas and cutthroat assassin Jacob "Deke" DeCourt each have their own motives, but become entangled in a sinister plot reaching far beyond politics, espionage or survival. The journey runs from a futuristic Hong Kong to the walled city of Xi'an, the lost tomb of China's first emperor and finally Penglai Shan, the mountain island of the immortals.

Like the original, it sets cel-shaded characters against pseudo-3D environments animated with looping full-motion video, and the player controls each of the four leads at different times for several perspectives on the story. It is mostly third-person, with controls mapped regardless of the character's facing, though a more traditional scheme is now an option. The arsenal includes pistols, shotguns and assault rifles, hand-held EMPs, a taser and a unique melee weapon for each character. It focuses on puzzles rather than combat, with few, statically placed enemies, aiming for tension over nonstop action; characters die easily, there are instant-death scenarios, and the fear gauge returns as the health meter.
trivia: It is a prequel to Fear Effect.
It was released in Japan as Helix: Fear Effect on 15 November 2001.
Rain Qin is a new character.
NextGen's Jeff Lundrigan ended his review: "Now, sequel please!"
The planned sequel was later cancelled.
devStory: Kronos Digital Entertainment developed it and Eidos Interactive published it for the PlayStation in 2001. It received "favorable" reviews according to Metacritic, NextGen saying everyone mature enough to appreciate it who owned a PlayStation should buy it.

title: Syphon Filter 2
description: Syphon Filter 2 (2000) is Eidetic's espionage shooter sequel in which Gabe Logan and Lian Xing, branded terrorists by the Agency, fight to expose the Syphon Filter virus conspiracy.
longDescription:
Hours after the first game, Gabriel Logan and Lian Xing have become enemies of the state to the Agency after uncovering its link to the Syphon Filter virus, and are labelled terrorists in public. Agency operative Dillon Morgan captures Lian at the PharCom warehouses, and as Gabe and his CBDC allies head to meet ex-Agency operative Teresa Lipan in Arizona, the Agency sends F-22 Raptors to shoot down their transport over the Colorado Rockies. Gabe and CBDC Lieutenant Jason Chance must make their way down the mountain to find their plane and a box of PharCom data disks, pursued by Agency operative Steven Archer.

Meanwhile, conspirators including Mara Aramov and Agency director Lyle Stevens plan to deliver the virus to a rogue Chinese general, Shi-Hao, while at an Air Force base Morgan and his men work with PharCom's Dr Elsa Weissinger to extract infected plasma from test subjects, including PharCom's CEO Jonathan Phagan, whose life support Morgan switches off to tie up a loose end. Lian escapes, kills Derek Falkan and rejoins Gabe, who kills Archer and recovers the data, and they kill Morgan at the PharCom Expo Center before he can find an encryption disk. The sequel also added multiplayer, with a choice of characters, including some killed in the first game, and maps not found in the single-player campaign.
trivia: John Garvin wrote the entire screenplay over a weekend.
Co-creator Richard Ham revised the second half, adding the Moscow sequences.
It was the last Syphon Filter released by 989 Studios in North America.
IGN compared its two-player mode favourably with Medal of Honor's.
It was added to PlayStation Plus Premium in 2022.
devStory: Eidetic developed it and Sony Computer Entertainment published it for the PlayStation in 2000. Unlike on the first game, Garvin and Ham had a complete vision before development started, and the team spent the next year building exactly what they had written. It received favourable reviews according to GameRankings, though many critics found it differed little from the original; GameRevolution said fans should "aim for the head and pull the trigger".

title: Colony Wars: Vengeance
description: Colony Wars: Vengeance (1998) is Psygnosis's branching space combat sequel set a century later, in which pilot Mertens joins the Earth Empire's Colonial Navy as it fights back against the League.
longDescription:
In 4671, a century after Colony Wars, the canonical ending saw the League of Free Worlds drive the Earth Empire's Colonial Navy into a last stand in the Sol system, where it held out; the League withdrew and closed the warp hole, cutting Sol off from the universe. Without fresh resources, the Empire collapsed into decades of civil war, held together only by a man named Kron and his anti-League propaganda. The player is Mertens, a pilot who enlists in the Navy and begins by eliminating rogue Navy forces.

Missions, mostly in space, are flown in one of four Colonial Navy fighters, each with a different mix of energy weapons, missiles or torpedoes, and some with non-lethal EMP cannons. Countermeasures shake off incoming missiles and a grapple gun captures important targets. New are upgrades to engine power, manoeuvrability, shields and afterburner duration using power pods earned after missions, and a lead-pursuit indicator for aiming cannon fire. For the first time in the series some missions take place in planetary atmospheres, flying the Navy's Spook drop ship, and some pit the player against giant League machines called Sentinels. The campaign is divided into Acts, with branching paths and outcomes that depend on performance, certain missions acting as turning points.
trivia: It was announced as Colony Wars: Codename Vendetta.
Its team was twice the size of the original's.
Its spaceships were modelled on real military weapons.
Producer Lol Scagg said rewritten code made it about 30 per cent faster.
PlayStation Official Magazine UK gave it 9/10: "A great game. Buy it Now".
devStory: Psygnosis developed and published it for the PlayStation in 1998 as the sequel to the previous year's Colony Wars. Scagg said the team had "totally rewritten the AI routines" and the collision routines. It averaged 86.67 per cent on GameRankings from 12 reviews.

title: Driver 2
description: Driver 2 (2000) is Reflections' undercover driving sequel in which Tanner can finally leave his car, chasing a Brazilian crime syndicate through Chicago, Havana, Las Vegas and Rio de Janeiro.
longDescription:
In Chicago, Pink Lenny meets a tattooed Brazilian man in a bar when two gangsters burst in and open fire; Lenny escapes but the Brazilian is killed. Examining the body at the morgue, police officers John Tanner and Tobias Jones find tattoos linking him to Alvaro Vasquez, leader of a Brazilian criminal organisation, and are sent undercover to investigate Lenny's part in Chicago's recent gang violence.

It expands Driver's structure and adds the ability for Tanner to step out of his car, explore on foot and commandeer other vehicles. Story missions, introduced by cut-scenes that make it play like a Hollywood car chase film, involve trailing witnesses, ramming cars and escaping gangsters or police, while all violence happens in pre-rendered scenes. A separate "Take a Ride" mode lets players explore at their own pace. Its four cities, Chicago, Havana, Las Vegas and Rio de Janeiro, are much larger than the original's, and every car, based on real Chevys, Fords, GMCs and more, can be driven, with hidden ones in each city and hubcaps that fly off as before. The PlayStation version offers two-player split screen.
trivia: In North America it was subtitled The Wheelman Is Back.
Its many FMVs meant it shipped on two discs, split by city.
Sennari Interactive's 2002 Game Boy Advance version keeps only Chicago and Rio.
The GBA version added four-player link play.
IGN called it possibly "the most disappointing game ... of 2000".
devStory: Reflections Interactive developed it and Infogrames published it for the PlayStation in 2000. Like Driver, it was a commercial success, though it received a less enthusiastic critical response, "mixed or average reviews" according to Metacritic; GameSpot's Ryan MacDonald called it "an extraordinary game". Driver 3 followed in 2004.

title: Wild Arms 2
description: Wild Arms 2 (1999) is Media.Vision's steampunk western RPG in which the anti-terrorist group ARMS recruits gunfighter Ashley, sorceress Lilka and war hero Brad to stop the organisation Odessa.
longDescription:
When the terrorist organisation Odessa tries to conquer the world, an international anti-terrorist group called ARMS is formed to fight it, recruiting heroes such as Ashley Winchester, a gunfighter, Lilka Eleniak, a teenage sorceress, and Brad Evans, a former war hero, alongside Tim Rhymeless, Kanon and Marivel Armitage, at a wealthy benefactor's call. The world of Filgaia mixes science fiction, steampunk and traditional fantasy: firearms called "ARMs", which unlike in the first game are not considered inherently dangerous, sit alongside cybernetic limbs, miniature robots, aircraft and radios, some powered by magic rather than science.

Players guide the party through environments, battles and puzzles in an isometric view, with 2D character sprites over 3D backgrounds and a camera that rotates through 360 degrees. Dungeons bring random encounters every few steps, signalled by an exclamation mark over the character's head and sometimes avoidable. Characters level up with experience, buy better weapons and armour in town shops and learn new skills. Each character also unlocks three "Tools" for exploring outside battle, opening hidden paths, destroying objects and solving puzzles: Brad's kick boots move large objects, and Lilka's fire wand lights torches and hits switches from a distance.
trivia: In Japan it is called Wild Arms: 2nd Ignition.
Ashley's tools include the Hurl Knife and the Flare Gun.
Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40.
NextGen felt it offered less than Vagrant Story or Alundra 2.
It reached PlayStation Network in Japan in 2007 and North America in 2009.
devStory: Media.Vision developed it and Sony Computer Entertainment published it for the PlayStation in 1999 as the second Wild Arms game. It received average reviews according to GameRankings; GamePro's Four-Eyed Dragon said it "returns to the classic role-playing style where story and character-building are at the heart of the gameplay".

title: Breath of Fire IV
description: Breath of Fire IV (2000) is Capcom's fourth Breath of Fire, in which the dragon-shifting Ryu and his allies try to stop an awakened immortal emperor from ascending to godhood.
longDescription:
As in earlier games, the hero is a young man named Ryu who can transform into powerful dragons, and here he joins other skilled warriors to stop an awakened immortal emperor from ascending to godhood and destroying the world of man. Like Breath of Fire III, it mixes 2D and 3D graphics: hand-drawn character sprites move through fully 3D environments seen from overhead, with a camera that can rotate up to 360 degrees in places but no longer tilt. Each playable character has a "field skill" for clearing obstacles or solving puzzles, and battles strike at random in hostile areas and dungeons.

Turn-based battles pit teams of three against any number of enemies, with characters acting in any order chosen by the player and reserves swapped in from the back row, where they cannot fight but recover health. The "Master System" from Breath of Fire III returns, letting characters apprentice under masters around the world and gain skills and stat increases by meeting conditions such as a number of battles fought or specific items found. The series' fishing minigame returns, as does Faerie Town, a village players build to open new features.
trivia: It was developed by Capcom Development Studio 3, with many Breath of Fire III staff.
Makoto Ikehara directed it, and Tatsuya Yoshikawa designed its hand-drawn sprites.
Rumours in 1999 suggested it would be a PlayStation 2 game.
It was Japan's best-seller in July 2000.
An enhanced PC port was released on GOG.com in 2025.
devStory: Capcom developed and published it for the PlayStation in Japan and North America in 2000 and Europe in 2001, with a Windows version in Europe and Japan in 2003. Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40, and it sold an estimated 334,000 copies in Japan in 2000, qualifying for a budget "PlayStation the Best" re-release in 2002. Its English release in North America and Europe was similarly well received.

title: Tomba! 2: The Evil Swine Return
description: Tomba! 2: The Evil Swine Return (1999) is Whoopee Camp's fully 3D platform-adventure sequel in which the feral boy Tomba rescues his friend Tabby from the Evil Pigs, using suits that grant new powers.
longDescription:
The pink-haired feral child Tomba sets out to defeat the Evil Pigs, a race of anthropomorphic pigs, and rescue his girlfriend Tabby. It keeps the first game's mechanics and "event" system, quests that are triggered and completed around the world, but moves to fully 3D environments. Movement follows set linear paths, with flashing arrows above Tomba's head where paths cross to show which ways he can go, and some areas can be explored from an isometric view. Signposts act as save points.

Tomba jumps onto enemies' backs, bites them and tosses them away, filling a magic meter in the corner of the screen, and can also find weapons such as flails, boomerangs and mallets. Collectable suits extend his abilities or protect him: the flying squirrel suit lets him glide long distances and the pig suit lets him talk to pigs. Critics praised its variety, controls and visuals, while reception of the audio was mixed and some criticised the many tedious events and simple, repetitive bosses; IGN's Jeremy Conrad called it an improvement on its predecessor, while GameRevolution and GameSpot saw it as a polished repackaging.
trivia: Whoopee Camp founder Tokuro Fujiwara handed direction to Kuniaki Kakuwa.
The move to polygons allowed dynamic camera movement in cut-scenes.
Famitsu gave it 31 out of 40.
Whoopee Camp disbanded after its lacklustre sales.
Limited Run Games released a Special Edition on 15 December 2025.
devStory: Whoopee Camp developed and published it in Japan in 1999, and Sony Computer Entertainment released it internationally the following year. It received favourable reviews according to GameRankings, but its weak commercial performance led Whoopee Camp to disband, left only to hold Fujiwara's assets. It was re-released on the PlayStation Network in Japan in 2011, Europe in 2012 and North America in 2015.

title: Pandemonium 2
description: Pandemonium 2 (1997) is Crystal Dynamics' psychedelic 2.5D platformer in which Nikki and Fargus race to reach the Comet of Infinite Possibilities, through levels inspired by Dalí, Escher and Picasso.
longDescription:
As the magic-infused Comet of Infinite Possibilities is about to pass over Lyr for the first time in 300 years, its inhabitants race to reach it and make a wish, and the sassy sorceress Nikki decides to steal the source of its power. It is a psychedelic 2.5D game, rendering characters and environments in polygons with a 3D camera while play stays on a 2D plane. Players choose Nikki or the jester Fargus, who have different specialities, and can switch for each level. Both can now climb ropes, crawl and pull themselves up ledges, and collecting treasure earns extra lives.

Powers collected along the way replace, extend or add to existing ones, and each character handles them differently: fire power lets Nikki shoot destructive fireballs, but makes Fargus invincible and deadly to touch while forcing him to keep moving forward. Machines and equipment appear in certain areas, and four boss stages follow blocks of levels, usually involving small puzzles, such as catapulting fireballs at a flying boss or surviving a giant mech while balanced on a speeding tank. Collecting over 80 per cent of a level's treasure unlocks the "Boarder Run" bonus, sliding along a course ahead of a pursuing vortex for at least one extra life, and hidden "life pieces" raise health from four hit points to as many as 16.
trivia: It is the sequel to Pandemonium!.
Deborah Ben-Eliezer voices Nikki.
Designer Zak Krefting described the level "Lick the Toad" as DNA from Dalí, Escher and Picasso.
It was still being finished in October 1997, the month of its release, after heavy crunch.
GameSpot called it "a fun and mostly unpredictable platform game".
devStory: Crystal Dynamics developed and published it for the PlayStation and Windows after more than a year of development. Krefting noted its increased difficulty, as the team "tend to build levels that are challenging for them to play". Reviews ranged from mixed to positive, the PlayStation version averaging 77.11 per cent on GameRankings, with most reviewers finding it more detailed and colourful than the original.

title: Mega Man Legends 2
description: Mega Man Legends 2 (2000) is Capcom's 3D action-adventure sequel in which Digger Mega Man Volnutt hunts for four keys hidden across the planet that lead to the legendary Mother Lode.
longDescription:
Mega Man Volnutt searches for four keys hidden around the planet to help find the Mother Lode, a legendary treasure thought to be an infinite source of energy. Play closely follows the first game, exploring ruins and fighting the robotic Reaverbots, but the ruins are now spread across several islands rather than mostly on Kattelox Island, reached aboard Roll's ship, the Flutter, with some islands opening only after certain missions.

Instead of needing a mayor's approval to enter ruins, Mega Man must pass tests to earn Digger licences of increasing class, which open ruins forbidden to lower-class Diggers; higher licences make Reaverbots tougher but they drop more refractor shards, the currency spent in shops. How he treats other characters, pleasing or angering them, affects how he is regarded, and he can pick up objects and people to complete missions. He can also suffer special damage from Reaverbots or hazards such as lava. Critics praised its improved graphics and play and its story, far more complex than the original series', but criticised its cliffhanger ending. GameSpot said it turned "what began as a mere spin-off into a worthy stand-alone franchise".
trivia: A demo with its own story was included in The Misadventures of Tron Bonne.
The demo was titled Rockman Dash 2 – Episode 1: Roll's Critical Moment.
In the demo, Tron has kidnapped Roll.
AllGame said it "trumps its predecessor in almost every way".
Unchanged Japanese ports came to PC in 2003 and PSP in 2005.
devStory: Capcom released it for the PlayStation in Japan and North America in 2000 and in Europe in 2001. In 1999 Capcom announced that The Misadventures of Tron Bonne would include a demo to show off its improved graphics and larger world. It was generally well received, more so than its predecessor.

title: Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins
description: Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins (2000) is Acquire's stealth prequel following the early lives of Azuma ninja Rikimaru and Ayame, with a celebrated Mission Editor.
longDescription:
In Sengoku-period Japan, four years before Tenchu: Stealth Assassins, the death of the elder Lord Gohda sparks a coup against his benevolent son Matsunoshin by his uncle Motohide. Each has a ninja clan behind him: Matsunoshin the Azuma ninja, the Gohdas' long-standing allies, while Motohide is manipulated by a neighbouring lord and the rogue ninja group the Burning Dawn. The young Rikimaru and Ayame, with their fellow Tatsumaru, must confront the Burning Dawn.

Played from a third-person view in 3D environments, missions ask the chosen protagonist to stay undetected and either avoid enemies or kill them silently, using a range of ninja tools and equipment. Missions take place at different times of day in rural farmland, bamboo forests, mountains, beaches, ships, villages and caverns. Afterwards the player is ranked on accomplishments such as kills and times spotted, and high ranks unlock special gadgets. One of its most acclaimed features was the Mission Editor, which let players build their own missions, choosing the layout, the characters placed in them and the objectives.
trivia: In Japan it was published as Rittai Ninja Katsugeki: Tenchu 2.
Director Takuma Endo wanted to make it for PlayStation 2 and regretted making it on PlayStation.
It had a budget of ¥200 million and a team of thirty.
Noriyuki Asakura returned as composer.
It sold over 101,000 units in Japan, according to Famitsu.
devStory: After Tenchu: Stealth Assassins sold a million copies, Activision requested a sequel; Acquire developed it for the PlayStation, published by Activision in the West and Acquire in Japan in 2000. Originally intended as a Western exclusive, it was adjusted to reduce niche Japanese elements while polishing play and graphics. It was the sixth best-selling title in its North American launch month, received "generally favorable" reviews and was seen as an improvement; Activision then acquired the series and moved it to K2 for Tenchu: Wrath of Heaven.

sources.title: Tenchu 2: Birth of the Stealth Assassins

title: Bushido Blade 2
description: Bushido Blade 2 (1998) is Lightweight's one-hit-kill sword-fighting sequel, pitting the rival assassin schools Narukagami and Shainto against each other and adding dual-sword attacks.
longDescription:
The story and characters now revolve around two rival schools of assassins: the Narukagami, mostly made up of characters from the first game, and the Shainto. Depending on the character, the player fights either to recover a legendary sword or to destroy the opposing school. The story mode changes from one large connected level to a series of skirmishes on different maps, each a run of generic ninja followed by a boss, one of the playable characters from the other school. Support characters appear along the way, and finishing a stage as one unlocks them for all modes.

Dual-sword attacks are new, and characters fight with swords or polearms of various types; weapons shared by both schools, such as the katana, look slightly different for each. Two exceptions are Tsubame and Katze, who carry guns and are sworn to opposing schools, offering a different challenge, though their shots can be parried with melee weapons. Most weapons return from the first game, but the yari and the M16 are gone, along with the rapier, sledgehammer, ninjato and the boss-only Double-Bladed Sword-Staff and Special Sabre, while the yugiri, wielded by the first game's final boss Hanzaki, becomes selectable only in the final battle against the unarmed "last member of the Kagami clan".
trivia: It is the sequel to 1997's Bushido Blade.
Famitsu gave it 29 out of 40.
Next Generation said it "isn't an easy game to classify".
Next Generation warned it might alienate fans wanting more of the same.
It was re-released on the PlayStation Network in 2008.
devStory: Lightweight developed it and Square published it for the PlayStation in 1998. It expanded some aspects of the original while limiting or removing others, and received favourable reviews according to GameRankings, Next Generation giving Square "kudos" for trying such a different approach.

title: Cardinal Syn
description: Cardinal Syn (1998) is Kronos Digital's dark-fantasy 3D weapons fighter with free-roaming arenas, in which clan champions fight in a tournament held by the sorceress Syn for the secrets of three swords.
longDescription:
War had consumed the Clans of the Bloodlands for generations until a mysterious being, later called the Wanderer, gathered them and read from his Book of Knowledge of the harmony they could achieve. Years of peace followed, until, as the land began to fade, he divided the Book into scrolls, gave one to each clan and vanished, and the clans went back to war over them. In the middle of a brutal battle, the powerful sorceress Syn appeared bearing the Wanderer's icon, took the scrolls, turned them into three inscribed swords holding the Book's knowledge and declared a tournament: each clan would send its greatest warrior to fight to the death for rule of the Bloodlands and the swords' secrets. The first tournament had no winner, as Syn secretly killed the final warrior.

A 3D fighter with free-roaming movement, it lets players move around small interactive stages during fights, much like Ehrgeiz and Bushido Blade. Leaving behind the science fiction of Kronos's Criticom, it is set in a dark, bloody medieval world, its fighters, many non-human, resembling Dungeons & Dragons characters armed with fitting melee weapons. It features combos, juggles, stage hazards, finishing moves, projectiles and power-ups, and crates in each stage can be smashed for items.
trivia: 989 Studios released it in North America.
It was showcased at E3 1997.
Next Generation called it "a pretty, if confusing, waste of time and effort".
GamePro joked that "the Syn committed in this game is syn-ple: Mediocrity".
Kronos also made Criticom and Fear Effect.
devStory: Kronos Digital Entertainment developed it and Sony Computer Entertainment published it for the PlayStation in 1998. It received "mixed or average" reviews according to GameRankings.

title: Spider-Man
description: Spider-Man (2000) is Neversoft's PlayStation game, built on the Tony Hawk engine and narrated by Stan Lee, in which a framed Spider-Man clears his name while foiling a symbiote invasion by Doctor Octopus and Carnage.
longDescription:
Framed by a doppelgänger and wanted as a criminal, Spider-Man must clear his name while foiling a symbiote invasion orchestrated by Doctor Octopus and Carnage. Villains from the comics appear as bosses, including Scorpion, Rhino, Venom, Mysterio, Carnage and Doctor Octopus, along with Monster-Ock, a Carnage-possessed Doctor Octopus created for the game, and co-creator Stan Lee narrates. Levels ask the player to reach the exit or complete an objective, and running out of health, falling off a building or failing an objective, such as rescuing a hostage, means retrying.

Spider-Man crawls on walls and ceilings, swings short distances and zips instantly between certain points. A limited supply of web cartridges lets him web up enemies to stall or defeat them, strengthen his punches or form an explosive barrier. Collectable comics unlock covers in the menu, and power-ups include Spider-Armor, which temporarily boosts strength and defence, and Fire Webbing, effective against symbiotes. Unlockable costumes have their own attributes, some helpful and some not: the Spider-Man 2099 costume adds strength, while the civilian Peter Parker outfit limits him to two web cartridges.
trivia: It uses the same engine as Tony Hawk's Pro Skater.
Spider-Man was a hidden character in Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2, referenced in the game.
The Nintendo 64 version uses comic-style captioned freeze-frames instead of video cut-scenes.
It was the first Spider-Man game from Activision, whose licence lasted until 2014.
The PlayStation version scored 87 on Metacritic.
devStory: Announced on 2 December 1998, it was developed by Neversoft and published by Activision for the PlayStation in 2000, with ports by other developers to Game Boy Color and Nintendo 64 that year, Dreamcast and Windows in 2001 and Mac OS in 2002. Reviews were generally positive, though they varied by system, and three sequels followed in 2001, including Spider-Man 2: Enter Electro on PlayStation.

title: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2
description: Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 (2000) is Neversoft's skateboarding sequel that added manuals, cash rewards and a level editor, and remains the best-reviewed PlayStation game of all time.
longDescription:
The player controls a professional or fictional skater in a third-person view with a fixed camera, performing tricks and completing level objectives in three-dimensional urban environments set to punk rock and hip-hop. Using the same engine as its predecessor with improved graphics and play, it introduced manuals, which let players link tricks along the ground, and cash rewards, which unlock new levels, raise the skater's statistics and buy better equipment. Its physics are loose for the sake of play, letting skaters jump to unrealistic heights.

Modes include a career mode, in which objectives earn money to develop the character, free skating with no objectives, multiplayer with a number of competitive games, and a level editor for building custom parks. Critics praised its addictive play, large environments, detailed graphics, fluid and precise controls, customisation and soundtrack, with only minor complaints, such as the lack of a first-person camera and the shortened soundtrack of the Nintendo 64 version. It is considered one of the greatest video games ever made and the highest-rated sports game.
trivia: Its 98/100 on Metacritic ties it with GTA IV and Soulcalibur, behind only Ocarina of Time.
Activision confirmed its acquisition of Neversoft on 4 October 1999.
It first appeared publicly at E3 2000 as a non-playable demonstration.
Natsume developed the Game Boy Color version.
Its Xbox version was part of Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2x.
devStory: Neversoft began hiring for a sequel by September 1999 and developed it for the PlayStation, published by Activision in 2000, with ports to Windows, Dreamcast and Game Boy Color the same year and to Mac, Nintendo 64, Xbox and Game Boy Advance in 2001. It was met with universal acclaim and remains the best-reviewed PlayStation game, and Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 followed in 2001.

title: Hogs of War
description: Hogs of War (2000) is Infogrames Sheffield House's comic 3D turn-based tactics game in which squads of anthropomorphic pigs fight a First World War-style conflict, voiced by Rik Mayall.
longDescription:
Teams of five pigs, loosely based on First World War nations, take turns in battle, much as in the Worms series. On each turn the player controls a single hog in third person, moving around the 3D map, jumping over terrain and swimming across water, but can only attack while standing still. Squad members can be given a class with its own weapons and abilities: heavy gunners with long-range weapons such as mortars, bazookas and rocket launchers; engineers who specialise in explosives such as grenades, land mines and TNT; espionage hogs who stay off the mini-map and use sniper rifles and camouflage; and medics who heal others at close or long range.

Beyond their inventories, hogs can use military vehicles such as tanks, turrets such as heavy artillery and pillboxes, and buildings such as bunkers and hospital tents. Modes include a standard deathmatch, single-player or multiplayer, and a single-player campaign. British comic actors Rik Mayall and Marc Silk voice the game, and its comedy was widely praised: IGN's Scott Steinberg enjoyed its "goofy sense of humour and endearing antics", and GameSpot's Frank Provo called it "drop-dead funny".
trivia: Gremlin founder Ian Stewart was inspired by the film Babe, Command & Conquer and Worms.
Developer Andrew Fox summed it up as "Worms, except in 3D and with pigs".
Early builds were so rough that cancellation was considered.
A sequel was announced but never released.
An official remaster is in production.
devStory: Development began at Gremlin Interactive in 1997 and took three years, lengthened by Infogrames' purchase of Gremlin in 1999, with two teams working on different versions. Infogrames published it for the PlayStation and Windows in 2000. It received "mixed or average" reviews on Metacritic and many comparisons with Worms Armageddon, but is considered a cult classic by some critics and has since inspired board and card games.

title: Worms Armageddon
description: Worms Armageddon (1999) is Team17's acclaimed turn-based artillery game in which teams of cartoon worms blast each other across destructible 2D landscapes with an arsenal of absurd weapons.
longDescription:
The player controls a team of up to eight earthworms trying to defeat opposing teams with a huge range of weapons on a destructible, customisable two-dimensional landscape, all in a cartoonish style with a distinctive brand of humour. Teams move in a randomly determined order, and on each turn only one worm can move, unless an item lets the team choose. Worms walk and jump, and with the right items can swing on a rope, parachute, teleport and bungee. A traditional match is won by killing every opposing worm, though some campaign missions have other goals, such as collecting a particular crate.

Begun as an expansion pack for Worms 2, it became a standalone game very similar to its predecessor, adding a new single-player mode and plenty of new content and reaching many more platforms. Critics praised its refined play and stylised graphics, and it has appeared on several lists of the greatest games of all time. GameSpot's Greg Kasavin noted that Worms 2 veterans would find it familiar but praised its ease of play, humour, graphics, physics, WormNet online service and deep customisation, likening the single-player missions to Lemmings.
trivia: It was originally titled Wormageddon, changed because it was too close to Carmageddon.
It was intended to be the last Worms game.
Creator Andy Davidson felt it needed more content, leading to Worms World Party.
The PC version was still being updated as recently as 2020.
Worms Armageddon: Anniversary Edition was announced in a Nintendo Direct in August 2024.
devStory: Team17 developed and published it for Windows in 1999 as the third Worms game, followed by ports to PlayStation, Dreamcast, Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color. It received favourable reviews on every platform and was succeeded by Worms World Party in 2001, the last 2D Worms before the series moved to 3D. The 2024 Anniversary Edition added a digital museum and emulated versions of other Worms games.

title: Thief II: The Metal Age
description: Thief II: The Metal Age (2000) is Looking Glass Studios' final game, a first-person stealth sequel in which master thief Garrett uncovers a conspiracy by the technology-worshipping Mechanist sect.
longDescription:
A year after Thief: The Dark Project, the steampunk metropolis known as the City, resembling both medieval and Victorian cities, is home to magic and steam technology alike, and to three factions: the enigmatic Keepers, the technology-minded Hammerites and the pagan worshippers of the Trickster. After the Trickster's defeat, a schism in the Hammerite religion has spawned the fanatical Mechanist sect, whose inventions are used by a resurgent police force to crack down on crime. Master thief Garrett unravels a conspiracy tied to the new sect through missions such as burglaries and frame-ups.

Played in first person, the aim is to complete objectives while evading guards and automated security. Garrett must keep out of sight and earshot, favouring shadows and quiet floors over lit areas and loud surfaces, with a light gem on the HUD showing how visible he is; he can fight, but is easily beaten. Responding to feedback on Thief, the team focused heavily on urban stealth and cut back on monsters and maze-like levels, and project director Steve Pearsall said the original had played it safe with "exploration ... or adventure oriented" missions.
trivia: Looking Glass began designing it in January 1999.
It uses the third version of the Dark Engine, also behind Thief and System Shock 2.
It was announced at E3 1999.
Slow royalty payments worsened Looking Glass's finances, and the studio closed in May 2000.
The fan expansion Thief 2X: Shadows of the Metal Age was released in 2005.
devStory: Looking Glass Studios developed it and Eidos Interactive published it for Windows in March 2000, with Eidos advances keeping the near-bankrupt studio running during development. It was well reviewed and initially outsold its predecessor, passing 220,000 copies worldwide by November 2000, but Looking Glass closed soon after release and plans for Thief III were cancelled; Ion Storm's Thief: Deadly Shadows followed in 2004.

title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear
description: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear (1999) is Red Storm's tactical shooter sequel in which the counterterrorist unit Rainbow investigates nuclear terrorism in Eastern Europe, one bullet at a time.
longDescription:
The secret international counterterrorist organisation Rainbow investigates nuclear terrorism in Eastern Europe. As in the original, characters are affected by realistic factors and can die from a single bullet, so planning and tactics matter more than force and firepower. It uses the same engine and play as Rainbow Six, heavily modified with better graphics and animation and improved AI, and adds new mechanics such as choosing camouflage and the return of Eagle Watch's hands-off "watch" mode. The campaign has 18 missions around the world, and multiplayer offers 20 maps.

Critics praised its significant improvements on the original formula but criticised AI that, while better, behaved inconsistently, and a cluttered planning stage made more burdensome by larger, more complex levels. It received generally positive reviews on PC, scoring 85.97 per cent on Metacritic, but mixed reviews on other platforms, from 75.77 per cent on Game Boy Advance to 60.07 per cent on PlayStation. It was nominated for numerous awards and is considered one of the best action games of 1999.
trivia: It was the last Rainbow Six game published by Red Storm before Ubi Soft acquired it in 2000.
A PlayStation 2 port was announced but cancelled.
Three expansion packs followed in 2000 and 2001.
The spin-off Take-Down – Missions in Korea used its engine.
In 2006 the US Department of Defense licensed its engine for training simulations.
devStory: Red Storm Entertainment developed and published it for Windows on 22 September 1999, with later ports for Dreamcast, Mac OS, PlayStation and Game Boy Advance. It sold over 200,000 copies in its first year and almost 500,000 by 2006, and was followed by Rainbow Six 3: Raven Shield in 2003.

sources.title: Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six: Rogue Spear

title: Outlaws
description: Outlaws (1997) is LucasArts' spaghetti western shooter in which retired Marshal James Anderson hunts the gang that killed his wife, credited as the first game with a sniper zoom.
longDescription:
Retired US Marshal James Anderson returns from the general store to find his wife Anna dying, his home burnt down and his daughter Sarah kidnapped by the outlaws Matt "Dr. Death" Jackson and "Slim" Sam Fulton, hired by the railroad baron Bob Graham to "enlighten" the county's people into selling him their land for a huge railroad; the psychotic Dr. Death took the instruction too far. After burying his wife, Anderson picks up his gun again and rides across the Old West, shooting his way through each of Graham's hired outlaws.

Anderson uses Old West weapons and items such as a rifle, shotgun, dynamite and revolver, lights dark areas with a lantern and digs with a shovel in certain spots, and some weapons have alternate fire. On the easier "Good" and "Bad" difficulties he can take several bullets, but on "Ugly" one or two shots kill him, forcing players to rely on stealth and cover. It is largely credited as the first shooter with a sniper zoom and one of the first with reloading. Cut-scenes rendered with LucasArts' INSANE engine are filtered to look hand-drawn. Inspired by The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, A Fistful of Dollars and other Clint Eastwood westerns, it features an orchestral score by Clint Bajakian.
trivia: It uses an enhanced version of the Jedi engine from Star Wars: Dark Forces.
Its voice cast includes Jeff Osterhage, Richard Moll and John de Lancie.
Twelve multiplayer characters were planned; six made the final game.
A free expansion, Handful of Missions, was released in 1998.
Nightdive's remaster was released by Atari on 20 November 2025.
devStory: LucasArts developed and published it for Windows on 7 April 1997. It received generally favourable reviews: its graphics were compared unfavourably with contemporaries such as Quake, but reviewers almost unanimously praised its play and soundtrack. It was not a major financial success but gained a cult following, and Complex included it among the 25 best LucasArts games.

title: Star Wars: X-Wing vs. TIE Fighter
description: Star Wars: X-Wing vs. TIE Fighter (1997) is Totally Games' third X-Wing game, the only one built primarily for multiplayer, with up to eight pilots in free-for-all, team and co-operative battles.
longDescription:
The third X-Wing game brought several technical advances over the original releases of its predecessors: it runs on Windows, requires a joystick, has a CD audio soundtrack, supports high-resolution graphics and adds texture mapping to the ship models in flight. Its multiplayer supports up to eight players in free-for-all, team-based and co-operative modes, and a pilot and mission selection system tracks each player's points and awards. As well as choosing a craft, players pick their squadron, and so their combat role, for each mission.

Everything could be played alone, but it is the only game in the series designed primarily for multiplayer, and it had no story-driven campaign. Delivering satisfying online play was a huge technical challenge: unlike Doom or Descent, set in closed rooms and corridors where players know little of each other unless they meet, its open deep-space setting required far more data to be tracked and sent between players. Edge gave it 90 out of 100, saying LucasArts had "finally listened to its legions of fans" and that it was "practically impossible" for such a game to fail, though it questioned what it offered players without a network.
trivia: The Balance of Power expansion added Rebel and Imperial campaigns of 15 missions each.
Both campaigns support eight-player co-op and cover the same events with different endings.
The Rebel campaign ends with an assault on the Super Star Destroyer Vengeance.
Balance of Power added the B-wing as a flyable craft.
A cut-down version, Flight School, was included in the X-Wing Collector Series.
devStory: Totally Games developed it for LucasArts, which released it for Windows in 1997. Criticism of its thin single-player content led Totally Games to create the Balance of Power expansion, which added story campaigns and further multiplayer features.

sources.title: Star Wars: X-Wing vs. TIE Fighter

title: Descent 3
description: Descent 3 (1999) is Outrage Entertainment's six-degrees-of-freedom shooter in which the Material Defender fights virus-infected robots across the Solar System, now inside and outside.
longDescription:
In a science-fiction Solar System, the player is the Material Defender, a mercenary helping the Red Acropolis Research Team stop robots infected by an alien virus. Like Descent and Descent II, it is a six-degrees-of-freedom shooter: the player flies a ship from a first-person view in zero gravity, free to move forwards and backwards, up and down and left and right, and to rotate in pitch, yaw and roll. The ship fires on enemies, uses afterburners for bursts of speed and lights dark areas with flares or a headlight.

For the first time, the game features outdoor as well as indoor environments, thanks to a hybrid engine combining a portal rendering engine with a flight simulator-style terrain engine. Alongside the single-player campaign, online multiplayer offers eight game types. Its graphics, enemy AI and outdoor areas were especially praised, GameSpot's Erik Wolpaw saying it "improves in almost every conceivable way on its predecessors and reestablishes the series as the premier example of the play style it single-handedly pioneered".
trivia: It was Outrage Entertainment's first project.
Parallax Software split into Outrage, which continued Descent, and Volition, which made FreeSpace.
Development began in November 1996 with a team of eight.
It scored 89 out of 100 on Metacritic.
The expansion Descent 3: Mercenary, with a level editor, followed on 3 December 1999.
devStory: Outrage Entertainment was founded when Parallax Software, creators of the earlier Descent games, split in two: Volition went on to make the FreeSpace space combat games, while Outrage continued the Descent series. Development began in November 1996 with a team of eight, and Interplay Entertainment published it for Windows in North America on 17 June 1999 as the sequel to Descent II, later porting it to Mac OS and Linux. It received positive reviews.

title: Incoming
description: Incoming (1998) is Rage Software's showcase 3D shooter in which the player takes the controls of aircraft, ground vehicles and gun turrets to repel an alien invasion of Earth in 2009.
longDescription:
In the near future of 2009, aliens invade Earth, and the player controls a range of vehicles and turrets to fight them. Mainly a vehicle simulation in an arcade style, with high scores and lives, it puts the player in aircraft, defence emplacements or surface craft, each with a primary weapon with unlimited ammunition and sometimes secondary weapons. Campaign missions to neutralise the alien threat include transporting cargo and defending allied convoys.

There are two campaigns: "campaign action", made up purely of simulation missions, and "campaign tactics", which adds sub-missions on a "tactical display" where the player commands several vehicles and gun emplacements much like a real-time strategy game. Each consists of ten "phases" in each of six locations, which can also be played in an arcade mode of fighting off aliens and collecting power-ups, and multiplayer uses the same mechanics with variations by game type. The PC version was praised for its then-advanced graphics, explosions, effects and cut-scenes made with the game engine, and its Dolby Surround sound; PC Zone called it "bloody good".
trivia: It used 3dfx technology and was bundled with some Voodoo2 graphics cards.
Rage considered a Nintendo 64 version at the 1997 ECTS, but none was released.
A Dreamcast version followed, released in Japan on 17 December 1998.
A sequel, Incoming Forces, came out for PC in 2002.
A 2003 arcade version ran on the Vortek V3 Global VR cabinet.
devStory: Rage Software, known for cutting-edge graphics and effects, developed and published it for Windows in mid-1998.
