The PC version was generally well received, while the Dreamcast version, released in North America on 15 September 1999 and Europe on 14 October 1999, met a less positive response.

title: Re-Volt
description: Re-Volt (1999) is Acclaim Studios London's racer of radio-controlled cars, tearing through museums, steamships, building sites and supermarkets armed with random weapons.
longDescription:
Players race radio-controlled cars around environments such as museums, steamships, construction sites and supermarkets, collecting random weapons during races to knock rivals aside. Cars and tracks are unlocked by succeeding in its tournament modes. Single Race pits the player against computer opponents, or up to four players against each other, and winning races in a cup unlocks a new car. Championship runs a four-race cup for points, in which finishing third or better is needed to advance; three failures end the championship, and winning a cup unlocks new levels and cars.

Time Trial challenges players to beat a target lap time, unlocking reversed, mirrored and reverse-mirrored tracks. Practice allows free exploration with no rivals or limit, with a star hidden on each track; collecting all the stars from a cup's tracks unlocks two more cars. Stunt Arena hides 20 stars around a loop, ramps and a half-pipe, some reachable only with faster cars, and collecting them all unlocks a new mode. Battle Tag is a multiplayer game of holding a hidden star until a timer runs down, and Clockwork Carnage swaps the usual eight RC cars for a race of 30 wind-up cars.
trivia: It was released for Windows, Nintendo 64, PlayStation and Dreamcast.
The PC and Dreamcast versions received favourable reviews.
The PlayStation version received unfavourable reviews.
Computer Gaming World praised the PC version's realistic RC-like handling.
A later Re-Volt Classic received mixed reviews.
devStory: Acclaim Studios London developed it and Acclaim Entertainment published it in 1999. Reception varied by version, according to GameRankings and Metacritic: favourable on PC and Dreamcast, mixed on Nintendo 64 and unfavourable on PlayStation. Computer Gaming World's Mark Clarkson praised the PC version's graphics and environments.

title: Midtown Madness
description: Midtown Madness (1999) is Angel Studios' open-world street racer set in a recreation of Chicago, offering "an unprecedented degree of freedom to drive around in a virtual city".
longDescription:
Instead of confining players to a track, it offers an open-world recreation of Chicago, where they win street races to earn new cars. Four single-player modes are available. Blitz requires passing three checkpoints and reaching the finish within a time limit; Circuit closes off most of the city to form race tracks against other cars; Checkpoint combines the two, racing rivals to a destination through traffic, police and pedestrians; and Cruise lets players explore at their own pace. Every mode except Cruise is split into missions, each unlocking the next.

Players set the weather, sunny, rainy, cloudy or snowy, the time of day from sunrise to night, and the density of pedestrians, traffic and police. The HUD shows race information and a detailed map, and can be switched off. Five vehicles are available at the start and five more can be unlocked by meeting goals such as top-three finishes, ranging from a Volkswagen New Beetle and a Ford F-350 to a city bus and a Freightliner Century truck. Races can also be played over a local network or the internet. IGN said it "doesn't rely heavily on driving authenticity; this game's all about fun".
trivia: It is also known as Midtown Madness: Chicago Edition.
The idea came to two Microsoft employees trying to cross a crowded Paris street.
It used Angel Studios' ARTS (Angel Real Time Simulation) technology.
Microsoft planned a family of Madness racers, including Motocross Madness and Monster Truck Madness.
Midtown Madness 2 followed in September 2000 and Midtown Madness 3 on Xbox in 2003.
devStory: Angel Studios developed it as one of its first PC games, and Microsoft published it for Windows in 1999 after a demo in August. It received favourable reviews according to GameRankings, and Angel Studios went on to make another open-world city racer, Midnight Club: Street Racing.

title: Need for Speed: High Stakes
description: Need for Speed: High Stakes (1999), Road Challenge in Europe, is EA's fourth Need for Speed, which added car damage, a career economy and a mode in which players can lose their cars.
longDescription:
Players race exotic cars on tracks across North America and Europe, alone against computer opponents or two at a time in split screen. Cars are grouped by class, from affordable performance models such as the BMW Z3 and Chevrolet Camaro to exotics such as the Ferrari F50 and McLaren F1. More realistic than its predecessors, it introduced a damage system in which collisions affect a car's appearance and performance, and economy-based tournaments whose cash prizes pay for repairs, new cars and upgrades for later races.

The Hot Pursuit mode from Need for Speed III was expanded with more options, including letting players drive the police trying to stop racers. The title was chosen to convey risk and consequence, embodied in High Stakes mode, where a player can lose a saved car, and the money spent upgrading it, in a race. Because its cars were licensed, Electronic Arts had to persuade manufacturers to let them be damaged, and it marked the return of the Porsche licence, absent from racing games since 1997's Porsche Challenge. Critics, who occasionally compared it with Gran Turismo, praised its graphics, AI and realism but criticised its inconsistent frame rate.
trivia: EA Seattle also worked on it.
The team brainstormed features such as damage and police play from fan feedback after Hot Pursuit.
Computer Gaming World named the Windows version Racing Game of the Year.
It was followed by Need for Speed: Porsche Unleashed in 2000.
Next Generation said it added enough to attract fans and newcomers alike.
devStory: EA Canada, with EA Seattle, developed it as the follow-up to Need for Speed III: Hot Pursuit, and Electronic Arts published it for the PlayStation and Windows in 1999. It received "generally favorable reviews" according to Metacritic, IGN remarking that it refined the series' formula while introducing new features.

title: Grand Prix Legends
description: Grand Prix Legends (1998) is Papyrus's demanding racing simulator of the 1967 Formula One season, with Brabham, Ferrari and Lotus cars on narrow, tree-lined circuits, some of them long gone.
longDescription:
Inspired by the 1967 Formula One season, it includes the Brabham, BRM, Eagle, Ferrari and Lotus teams, with drivers such as Jack Brabham, Denis Hulme, Jim Clark, Graham Hill, Dan Gurney, Jochen Rindt and Jacky Ickx, while two fictional teams, Murasama and Coventry, stand in for Honda and Cooper. Players can race alone or against computer opponents, adjusting many parameters for the skill and aggression of the AI drivers, or race others over a LAN.

Inspired by the 1966 film Grand Prix, the developers chose 1967 because the circuits of the time were narrow and lined with trees, houses and other features that, in a game, heighten the sense of speed, and because the cars' primitive suspension made their physics more visually dramatic. As some of the tracks no longer existed in their original form, the team visited town halls to obtain blueprints of defunct circuits, and Papyrus co-founder Dave Kaemmer said licensing was difficult, though people helped them along the way. GameSpot called it the most intense racing experience ever seen on a PC.
trivia: It was released under the Sierra Sports banner.
It took three years to develop with a team of 25 to 30.
John Surtees drives for the fictional Murasama team.
Coventry's drivers include Jochen Rindt and Pedro Rodríguez.
Next Generation praised its recreation of the 1967 season's cars and tracks.
devStory: Papyrus Design Group, co-founded by Dave Kaemmer, developed it over three years, and Sierra On-Line published it for PC in 1998 under its Sierra Sports banner. It received "favorable" reviews according to GameRankings: GameSpot said it offered the most intense racing experience yet seen on a personal computer, and Next Generation highly praised its graphics, its handling and its recreation of the 1967 season, with the cars and tracks of the era.

title: Zillion
description: Zillion (1987) is Sega's Master System tie-in to the Zillion anime, a code-cracking space adventure in which J.J. infiltrates the Nohza base to find five floppy disks and trigger its self-destruct.
longDescription:
The White Knights, a peacekeeping force of the Planetary System, set out to destroy the evil Nohza Empire's base on Planet X, misspelt "Norsa" in the North American version. J.J., hero of the Zillion anime, must infiltrate the labyrinthine underground base, fighting enemies, avoiding hazards and perhaps rescuing two captured allies, to collect five floppy disks that let him enter the self-destruct sequence into its mainframe. Starting outside the Mothership on the planet's surface, he spends almost the whole game underground, returning only to restore health or to leave once the mission is done.

The base is a maze of rooms guarded by tripwires, guards, laser turrets and force fields. Capsules hold key codes and power-ups, and rooms are unlocked with computer ID cards and the right four-digit code, found by searching capsules. Computers also allow other actions, such as switching off barriers, disabling traps or even committing suicide, and certain codes in certain rooms produce well-known "special messages". J.J.'s gun grows stronger to break tougher capsules, and once rescued, Apple, fast but weaker, and Champ, slower but stronger, become playable, each upgrading their gun, speed, jump and health. The Games Machine and GamesTM compared it to Epyx's Impossible Mission, and it has also been likened to Metroid.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Akai Koudan Zillion, "Red Photon Zillion".
It was a tie-in for Tatsunoko Production's Zillion anime.
J.J.'s gun was the design model for the Master System's Light Phaser.
Opa-Opa, the mascot of Fantasy Zone, features prominently in the Zillion series.
A sequel, Zillion II, followed in 1988.
devStory: Sega developed it for the Master System in 1987 as a companion to the Zillion anime series, and released a sequel, Zillion II, the following year.

title: Lord of the Sword
description: Lord of the Sword (1988) is Sega's side-scrolling Master System adventure in which would-be hero Landau must complete three tasks to become king of Baljinya and stop the demon Ra Goan's resurrection.
longDescription:
Followers of the Demon Lord Ra Goan kill the king and royal family of Baljinya, hoping to free Ra from a thousand years of imprisonment. The Elder Council decides that a new king must be crowned, or the kingdom will fall to Ra Goan when he returns, and that the rightful ruler will be a strong, brave man who completes three tasks. Landau, a would-be hero seeking the crown, accepts and sets out to save his homeland; by the end he becomes king, and five years later he is shown ushering in a new era of peace and prosperity.

The player explores a side-scrolling open world of flat lands, dark forests, mountains and swamps, each with its own monsters, armed with a sword for close combat and a bow for range. Towns and villages let Landau rest to restore health and gather information, and castles open only after certain tasks. Characters must be spoken to several times in a row to hear every message, or bosses and secret paths will not appear. Bosses must be struck at a weak point or moment, and each one beaten rewards a better sword or bow. There are up to ten continues but no password save. Computer and Video Games gave it 64 per cent, and The Games Machine 58 per cent, finding the play uninteresting and the game nearly impossible without its continues.
trivia: Its kingdom is called Baljinya.
Ra Goan has been imprisoned for a thousand years.
Failing to talk to characters repeatedly can hide bosses and secret paths.
The Games Machine felt its graphics did not stand out from other games of the time.
It has no password feature.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Master System in 1988. It received mixed reviews from critics.

title: Fantasy Zone II: The Tears of Opa-Opa
description: Fantasy Zone II: The Tears of Opa-Opa (1987) is Sega's colourful "cute 'em up" sequel in which the sentient spaceship Opa-Opa warps between zones to defeat an invasion led by his own dark double.
longDescription:
Opa-Opa once saved the Fantasy Zone from the invading Menon forces, at the price of fighting his own father, who led them. Ten years later, in Space Year 1432, the Nenon forces are spreading chaos, and Opa-Opa flies back in. The mastermind turns out to be an identical copy of himself; when his father appears, the sight brings Opa-Opa to tears and the double vanishes, revealed as the physical manifestation of his dark impulses, born of a war in his childhood. Reunited with his father, Opa-Opa purges the darkness and vows such a disaster will never happen again.

As in Defender, each level scrolls endlessly left or right, and the player travels freely to destroy the "bases" in each zone. New to the sequel are warps hidden behind certain bases that link the zones; each level has at least three, and once every base is cleared the warp leads to the boss. Bosses, large creatures that change colour as they are damaged, restrict movement, and the final stage is a boss rush before the last fight. Two buttons fire horizontal shots and bombs, the basic one dropping downwards, and stronger variants can be bought in shops. Its bright colours and whimsical designs set it apart from other shooters.
trivia: It is sometimes dubbed a "cute 'em up".
It was ported to arcades on the System E board, the Famicom and the MSX2.
The arcade version adds a radar of destroyed bases and a timer.
A System 16 remake was made for a 2008 PlayStation 2 compilation.
Computer and Video Games gave it 88 per cent and Console XS 90 per cent.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Master System in 1987. The Master System version was well received, and it was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in North America on 29 June 2009.

sources.title: Fantasy Zone II: The Tears of Opa-Opa

title: Ninja Gaiden (Master System)
description: Ninja Gaiden (1992) is SIMS's PAL-only Master System hack-and-slash platformer in which Ryu Hayabusa hunts the Shogun of Darkness after the massacre of the Dragon Village.
longDescription:
Ryu Hayabusa belongs to the Dragon Ninja clan, which has protected Japan for generations. While he is away, the Dragon Village is brutally massacred, and the last survivor tells him with his dying breath that the sacred Bushido scroll, powerful enough for its owner to control the world, has been stolen. As the last ninja of the clan, Ryu sets out to recover it from the evil Shogun of Darkness and his minions, among them the Sumo Wrestler, the Yakuza Oyabun, the Tsutenkaku Samurai, the Jetpack Soldier, the Ice Monster and the Stone Golem. Its story is unconnected to any other Ninja Gaiden game.

Play closely follows the NES Ninja Gaiden games: movement, attacks and jumps work the same way, and special ninja attacks are triggered by pressing up and attack together. Some features were replaced, though: instead of climbing hand over hand or clinging to walls, Ryu can jump from wall to wall, an ability that anticipates the 2004 Xbox game and later 3D entries. Two versions exist, one narrated by Ryu himself in great detail and one by an outside narrator with fewer plot details, with some dialogue and names differing between them.
trivia: Sega published it under licence from Tecmo.
It was released only in Europe, Australia and other PAL territories.
It used the Ninja Gaiden name rather than the Shadow Warriors title common in PAL regions.
Sega Force gave it 90 per cent.
Sega Force's Mat Yeo said he was "well impressed with this game".
devStory: SIMS developed it and Sega published it for the Master System in 1992. Because support for the console had ended in Japan and North America after poor sales, it was released only in PAL territories, where it was critically acclaimed.

title: Sonic the Hedgehog: Triple Trouble
description: Sonic the Hedgehog: Triple Trouble (1994) is Aspect's Game Gear sequel to Sonic Chaos, in which Sonic and Tails race Robotnik, Knuckles and newcomer Fang the Sniper for the Chaos Emeralds.
longDescription:
Sonic and Tails try to stop the powerful Chaos Emeralds falling into the hands of Doctor Robotnik, who has tricked Knuckles the Echidna into helping him, while treasure hunter Fang the Sniper, Nack the Weasel abroad, also hunts the Emeralds. Players choose Sonic or Tails across six themed zones of three levels each, the third ending in a boss. Both can spin dash; Sonic also has the peel-out from Sonic CD, while Tails can fly briefly. Many power-ups belong to one character, such as Sonic's jet board and Tails' Sea Fox, so routes through levels can differ slightly between them.

Rings are collected along the way; an enemy hit costs 30 and a spike 50, and 100 earns an extra life. Breaking a box with a Chaos Emerald icon while holding at least 50 rings sends the player to a special stage to win one of five Emeralds, some of them maze-like platforming levels and others flying a plane to collect rings. Critics enjoyed it and praised its graphics, but felt it lacked challenge and originality beyond its vehicles; Mean Machines Sega's Steve Merrett said it lacked "surprises and gameplay innovation". It has since been regarded as one of the best 8-bit Sonic games, closest to the quality of the 16-bit ones.
trivia: Fang was originally called Jet during development.
Early screenshots showed Fang with a gun, removed from the final game.
It was planned in the West as Sonic Chaos 2 for both Game Gear and Master System.
It was the first Sonic platformer exclusive to the Game Gear.
In Japan it was titled Sonic & Tails 2.
devStory: Aspect developed it and Sega published it for the Game Gear in November 1994 in the West and on 11 November in Japan, as the sequel to 1993's Sonic Chaos. It has been re-released in Sonic compilations, on the Coleco Sonic handheld and on the Nintendo 3DS.

title: Shining Force Gaiden
description: Shining Force Gaiden (1992) is Sonic! Software Planning's Japan-only Game Gear tactical RPG, set 20 years after Shining Force, in which Nick leads a new Shining Force into the Kingdom of Cypress.
longDescription:
Twenty years after Shining Force, the player controls Nick, a visitor to Guardiana chosen as the new leader of its Shining Force. The party travels to the Kingdom of Cypress to rescue Guardiana's captured soldiers and find a cure for Queen Anri, put under a sleeping spell by Cypress's ambassador, Woldol. In effect a story sequel to Shining Force, it continues Guardiana's history: Anri, Ken, Lug, called Luke in Shining Force, and Lowe are major characters, Lug is briefly playable, and Domingo appears as a hidden character. The starting party includes the sons of Lug, Ken and Hans, the sister of Tao and the nephew of Gong.

The game is a series of turn-based tactical battles separated by short cut-scenes, between which the player can save, promote characters, revive fallen allies and sometimes buy and sell weapons and healing items. Combat and levelling work exactly as in Shining Force. It begins the Cypress saga, continued directly in the Game Gear's Shining Force: The Sword of Hajya, set just two months later, which resolves the war between Cypress and the worshippers of Iom, and in Shining Force CD.
trivia: Its full Japanese title is Shining Force Gaiden: Ensei – Jashin no Kuni he.
It was released only in Japan.
It is the first game in the Shining Force Gaiden series.
The 1994 Sega CD remake Shining Force CD combined it with The Sword of Hajya.
Shining Force CD was released in Japan, North America and Europe and added two new scenarios.
devStory: Sonic! Software Planning developed it and Sega released it only in Japan for the Game Gear in 1992. Its story and that of its sequel later reached Western players through Shining Force CD, which remade both and added scenarios continuing their story.

title: GG Aleste
description: GG Aleste (1991) is Compile's Game Gear entry in the Aleste series, in which Ellinor Waizen pilots the Galvanic Gunner against the invading Moon Child army over seven stages.
longDescription:
In an alternative continuity, Ellinor Waizen, daughter of original Aleste hero Raymond Waizen, pilots the Galvanic Gunner space fighter against the invading Moon Child army to free the Earth. Following the conventions of earlier Aleste games, it sends the craft through seven increasingly difficult stages over constantly scrolling backgrounds full of enemies and obstacles, stopping only for a boss. Stages mostly scroll vertically but sometimes horizontally, and bonus rounds before the fourth and sixth stages send enemies past in preset formations without firing.

The main weapon is powered up by collecting "Power Chips", and eight special weapons can be found, upgraded by picking up the same one again. There is no bomb, but when the Galvanic Gunner is destroyed it detonates a powerful blast that damages everything on screen, and it respawns on the spot with reduced firepower. Unlimited continues are available. Graphic designer Hiroki Kodama co-designed it with programmer Yukinori Taniguchi, with Masamitsu Niitani producing; Kodama took over hurriedly from Kengo Morita, of Puyo Puyo, and made it out of pride as a Compile staffer.
trivia: Kodama's MSX experience let him develop for the Game Gear despite never making console software.
He did not know the Game Gear's hardware specifications at first.
Sega Saturn Magazine readers scored it 8.1232 out of 10 in 1995.
It is included in the Aleste Collection for Switch and PS4.
It was followed by GG Aleste II in 1993.
devStory: Compile developed and published it for the Game Gear in 1991. Critics, all reviewing it as an import, received it favourably, Joystick's Olivier Prézeau praising its smooth scrolling, set pieces, animation, controls and sound. A Game Gear Micro variant bundled it with the Aleste Collection's limited edition.

title: Citadel
description: Citadel (1985) is Michael Jakobsen's seminal BBC Micro platform-puzzle game set around a castle, in which the player hunts five hidden crystals, introduced by synthesised speech.
longDescription:
Centred on a castle, with outdoor areas including a wasteland, a pyramid, a sea and an island, the game asks players to find five hidden crystals and return them to their rightful place, then teleport to a separate set of locations to finish. Afterwards they can roam the castle freely to reach the maximum score, and only 99 points reveals the final congratulatory message. Unlike many platformers, touching fireballs, snakes and other hazards does not kill outright but drains a numbered energy supply, refilled by bottle-shaped objects; lose too much energy in one room and the screen turns red and returns the player to the room's entrance, stopping anyone simply walking through enemies.

Most enemies can only be avoided, except the monks, which can be destroyed. Players choose their character's sex, with a different sprite for each, unusual when memory was scarce. Rather than drawing the player over objects, the game combines the sprite's colours with what is behind it using an XOR operation, so the male hero's pink hair and yellow skin turn yellow and pink in front of the cyan stones of the Stonehenge screen, a distinctive effect reused in its two sequels. It was unusual for playing synthesised speech before loading, partly to advertise Superior's "Speech!" package, and for advanced effects such as splashing water.
trivia: It was also ported to the Acorn Electron.
Like most Superior Software games of the period, it came with a prize competition.
The prize went to the first player to find three crowns hidden around the map.
Reconstructed source code from the BBC Model B version was released in October 2018.
Many BBC Micro players regard it as seminal, with social media appreciation pages.
devStory: Michael Jakobsen developed it for the BBC Micro and Superior Software released it in 1985. It was widely acclaimed on release and remains one of the classic BBC Micro games; its author later made the Acorn Electron source and development versions of the BBC source available.

title: Castlevania II: Belmont's Revenge
description: Castlevania II: Belmont's Revenge (1991) is Konami's second Game Boy Castlevania, in which Christopher Belmont storms four themed castles to rescue his son Soleil from Dracula.
longDescription:
Fifteen years after Castlevania: The Adventure, Dracula returns and kidnaps Christopher Belmont's son Soleil at his coming-of-age feast, turning him into a demon. Using Soleil's mystical powers, Dracula regains human form and rebuilds his castle, and Christopher must face him again to save his son and Transylvania.

Unlike the first Game Boy game, it includes sub-weapons, holy water and the axe, or the cross in Japan. Four opening levels, each a separate castle themed on air, plants, earth or crystal, can be tackled in any order, much like Mega Man, and the levels contain large trap rooms. Progress is kept with passwords. The North American version replaced the cross, which flew in a long horizontal line like the fireball whip, with an axe that arcs upwards through walls and barriers. IGN felt it used the Game Boy's hardware better than its predecessor and praised its traditional Castlevania items and weapons and cleaner look, though it criticised the hero's lack of speed and short length. GameSpy called it one of the best action games on the original Game Boy.
trivia: It is a sequel to Castlevania: The Adventure.
It was released in Japan on 12 July 1991.
Tom Dubois created its North American and European box art.
The Konami GB Collection restored the cross and presented the game in colour.
Game Informer's Tim Turi considers it the best Castlevania on the original Game Boy.
devStory: Konami developed and published it for the Game Boy in 1991 as its second Castlevania for the handheld, releasing it in Japan on 12 July. The Konami GB Collection Vol. 4, released only in Japan and Europe, presented it in colour and restored the original cross sub-weapon, and it was re-released in the Castlevania Anniversary Collection in 2019.

title: Shantae
description: Shantae (2002) is WayForward's late Game Boy Color platform-adventure in which a half-genie whips foes with her hair and dances into animal forms to stop the pirate Risky Boots.
longDescription:
Sequin Land was once protected by Guardian Genies, whose children with humans became half-genies with limited powers; when the genies vanished, their children took their place. One of them, Shantae, guards the fishing village of Scuttle Town, though its mayor does not realise she is not a full genie. When the self-proclaimed "Queen of the Seven Seas", Risky Boots, and her Tinkerbat crew raid the town and steal a prototype steam engine from Shantae's adoptive uncle Mimic, he warns that four elemental stones could turn it into an unstoppable weapon, and Shantae sets off across Sequin Land.

Shantae attacks by whipping her hair, and gems from defeated enemies buy potions, items and new combat moves. Five towns are linked by areas full of enemies and obstacles, and characters open up dungeons, each with a guardian genie who teaches a new dance. Dances transform her into a monkey that climbs walls, an elephant that smashes boulders and stumps, a spider that crawls across webs and a harpy that flies, opening new areas and hidden items. A day and night cycle makes enemies stronger at night, when hidden fireflies can be collected; Warp Squids found in dungeons can be given to mother squids for instant travel to towns, and heart vessels raise her maximum health.
trivia: Matt Bozon heard that 20,000–25,000 copies were produced, which sold out without a second print run.
Bozon refused to blame Capcom for its poor sales.
It came out a year after the Game Boy Advance replaced the Game Boy Color.
Its 2013 3DS Virtual Console release was its European debut.
It reached Switch in 2021 and PS4 and PS5 in 2023.
devStory: WayForward developed it and Capcom published it for the Game Boy Color in 2002. It received favourable reviews but struggled to find an audience so late in the console's life; it has since been recognised as a cult classic, often listed among the best Game Boy Color games, and spawned a successful series of sequels.

title: Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble
description: Kirby Tilt 'n' Tumble (2000) is Nintendo's motion-controlled Game Boy Color puzzle game, played by tilting a special pink cartridge with a built-in accelerometer to roll Kirby through Dream Land.
longDescription:
Kirby is napping on a cloud when a Waddle Dee walks past carrying a round, pinball-like bumper, followed by King Dedede with a long one. Suspicious, Kirby follows on a Warp Star and discovers that Dream Land has lost its stars, so he sets out to get them back. Accelerometers in the cartridge control the game: the player tilts the Game Boy Color in the direction Kirby should roll to guide him to each level's goal in time, and quickly flicking the console towards themselves, like flipping a pancake, "pops" Kirby into the air.

Levels are strewn with stars, and collecting every level's red star unlocks bonus worlds with harder versions and less time. Time is extended by rolling over clock tiles, stopping a roulette on the timer, collecting 10-second clocks or passing checkpoints; below 50 seconds an alarm sounds and the music speeds up. The player has five lives, losing one when Kirby runs out of health, falls off the level, sinks into quicksand or water, or runs out of time, and can continue from the start of the current stage. Game Informer said the simple-sounding concept results in "one of the most dramatic, high-tension game scenarios seen on any system".
trivia: Development began in April 1999.
It was originally Koro Monkey, starring a monkey, until talks with Shigeru Miyamoto switched it to Kirby.
Its cartridge has a unique shape and translucent pink colour.
It debuted fourth on the NPD TRSTS chart for April 2001.
It was re-released on Nintendo Classics on 5 June 2023.
devStory: Nintendo developed and published it for the Game Boy Color, releasing it in Japan on 23 August 2000 and in North America on 9 April 2001; it was not released elsewhere. It received "favorable" reviews according to GameRankings.

title: Alex Kidd in Shinobi World
description: Alex Kidd in Shinobi World (1990) is Sega's Master System parody of Shinobi, in which Alex Kidd, fused with an ancient warrior's spirit, battles caricatures of Shinobi's enemies to save his girlfriend.
longDescription:
Hanzo the Dark Ninja escapes after 10,000 years of confinement and kidnaps Alex Kidd's new girlfriend while the couple are on a trip to the planet Shinobi. Powerless, Alex collapses in tears, until the ghost of the ancient warrior who first defeated the Dark Ninja finds him and explains that Hanzo plans to sacrifice her in a ritual to conquer the world. The warrior's spirit fuses with Alex, lending him strength, skill and courage, and together they set out to rescue her and destroy the Dark Ninja.

Despite the Alex Kidd name, it plays much more like the Master System Shinobi than Alex Kidd in Miracle World. Alex's basic sword slice defeats enemies and opens treasure chests holding extra health, throwing darts, a powered-up sword, extra lives and a magic ball that turns him into an invincible tornado; darts and the stronger sword last until the stage ends, a boss falls or a life is lost. He can jump between walls and spin around posts, ropes or bars to become a flying fireball. He starts each round with three hit points, up to six, and at full health heart chests hold extra lives instead. Four rounds loosely based on Shinobi's missions each have three stages, the third a boss battle, with Perfect and Secret bonuses for flawless play.
trivia: It began development as a Shinobi parody before becoming an Alex Kidd game.
It was released for North America, Europe and Brazil.
Computer and Video Games gave it 92 per cent.
C+VG's Robert Swan called it "brill! A combination of Alex Kidd in Miracle World and Shinobi".
It reached the Wii Virtual Console in Europe in December 2009 and North America in February 2010.
devStory: Sega developed it in Japan and released it for the Master System in overseas markets in 1990. It was critically acclaimed on release, Computer and Video Games praising playability that "becomes progressively more difficult as you go along".

title: Penguin Land
description: Penguin Land (1987) is Sega's puzzle-platformer in which a penguin guides a fragile egg down an icy cavern past polar bears, and the first home console game with battery-backed saving.
longDescription:
Three penguin eggs are lost on a distant planet, and Penguin Mission Commander Overbite must guide them down a frigid cavern full of traps, enemies and secret passages to the spaceship crew waiting at the bottom. The aim is to push and drop an egg to the bottom of a vertically scrolling ice cavern: Overbite pushes it left and right, drops it onto lower platforms and melts ice blocks to clear a path. The egg breaks if it falls more than three blocks, or if Overbite lands on it when it cannot roll aside.

Blocks include meltable ice, cracked ice that melts once the egg rests on it, rocks that can be dropped on enemies but crack the egg if they land on it, stone blocks that occasionally move by themselves, and tubes for the egg or the penguin. Polar-bear-like Gangows attack Overbite and the egg, breaking it if they corner it or land on it, and Cameel birds drop bricks if the egg is left unmoved too long. Egg shields, springs, point and time bonuses and control-inverting ghosts also appear. There are 50 stages and a level editor that can store up to 15 extra levels in battery-backed RAM.
trivia: Its Japanese title is Doki Doki Penguin Land Uchū Daibōken.
It is the second game in the Doki Doki Penguin Land series.
Its Japanese release came four days before The Legend of Zelda's US release.
Points are awarded for crushing Gangows, remaining time and round difficulty.
Dragon gave it three out of five stars in 1988.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Master System in 1987, the first home console game to include a battery backup save feature. It was reviewed by magazines including Computer and Video Games, The Games Machine and Power Play in 1988.

title: Psychic World
description: Psychic World (1991) is Hertz and Sanritsu's ESP-powered platformer, a version of the MSX2's Psycho World, in which Lucia uses elemental psychic weapons to rescue her twin sister from escaped lab monsters.
longDescription:
In 19XX, at a remote laboratory, Dr Knavik and his assistants, the twin sisters Cecile and Lucia, are researching the exploration and use of ESP. One day, as Lucia gets ready for work, an explosion rocks the lab; Dr Knavik is unharmed, but Cecile has vanished. He explains that his experiments involved testing a variety of monsters, which rebelled and carried her off, and as Lucia sets out on their trail he gives her the ESP Booster, a device that lets its user wield psychic powers.

Lucia runs through stages blasting monstrous enemies with the ESP Booster, collecting power-ups from them and from ledges and platforms. A gauge limits how often items and abilities can be used, refilled by power-ups like her health. Picking up the same item upgrades its weapon, and new weapons are won from mid-bosses and bosses. Weapons must be used strategically with the elements of each level: in the ice stage, rocks doused by falling water can be frozen with the ice shot into stable platforms, and the sonic wave destroys foreground objects blocking her path. RAZE gave the Master System version 70 per cent and Video Games 69, while Joystick gave the Game Gear version 83 per cent.
trivia: It was originally released in Japan for the MSX2 as Psycho World in 1988.
The Master System version was released only in Europe.
The Game Gear version was released worldwide.
Lucia's device is called the ESP Booster.
Her twin sister is named Cecile.
devStory: Hertz and Sanritsu co-developed it and Sega published it in 1991 for the Master System in Europe and the Game Gear worldwide, adapting the 1988 MSX2 game Psycho World. Reviews were mixed but mostly positive.

title: The Great Giana Sisters
description: The Great Giana Sisters (1987) is Time Warp's notorious Super Mario Bros.-inspired home computer platformer, pulled from shops after a notice from Nintendo but spread widely by piracy.
longDescription:
Giana dreams of a world of deserted castles full of monsters and can wake only by finding a giant diamond. Players control Giana alone, or alternate between her and her sister Maria in two-player mode, walking and jumping with a joystick across 33 horizontally scrolling levels while avoiding holes and hazards such as nails and fire. Each player has five lives and each level a 100-second limit. Most enemies are defeated by jumping on them, and power-ups grant lightning and strawberry projectiles, clocks that send every enemy on screen to sleep, magic bombs that wipe them out, and lollies worth an extra life.

Designed by Armin Gessert and Manfred Trenz, it was made at the request of Rainbow Arts' Marc Ulrich, who asked for a game like Nintendo's popular Super Mario Bros. but legally distinct. Time Warp was a label for Rainbow Arts' in-house team. After its West German launch it was released in the UK, where Zzap!64 and Computer and Video Games praised its play and secret levels despite its heavy debt to Mario, and Retro Gamer's Darran Jones noted its "fair amount of critical acclaim" on the Commodore 64.
trivia: It was released for the Commodore 64, Amiga and Atari ST, among others.
Rainbow Arts was founded in 1984 and bought by Soft-Gold in 1985.
Chris Huelsbeck's music has been performed by symphony orchestras.
Its C64 sequel, Hard'n'Heavy, played down the Nintendo inspiration.
New Giana Sisters games appeared from the early 2000s.
devStory: Time Warp developed it and Rainbow Arts published it in 1987. After its UK release Rainbow Arts received a notice from Nintendo and the game was pulled from shops, but it went on to become one of the most popular home computer games of its era through piracy and emulation.

title: Underwurlde
description: Underwurlde (1984) is Ultimate Play the Game's second Sabreman adventure, a vast platformer of nearly 600 flip screens in which enemies knock Sabreman back instead of killing him.
longDescription:
Sabreman, the pith-helmeted adventurer, jumps between platforms in a castle and its caverns seeking an escape past the exit guardians, each of which requires a specific weapon: a knife, a catapult or a torch. Seen from the side, the world is a series of 597 flip screens that change as he reaches the edge of the view, beginning in a castle decorated with clocks, birds and baskets and descending through vertical screens into the caverns. Walking off a ledge, Sabreman automatically attaches a rope to the ceiling and can swing across to another ledge, and at the bottom of a cavern he can ride a bubble back to the top.

Unlike Ultimate's earlier games, enemies do not hurt Sabreman but bounce him backwards, though being knocked off a precipice is fatal. He starts with seven lives, with a few more to find, and blue gemstones make him briefly immune to falls from any height. Harpies and gargoyles can be killed with his weapon, and after the first guardian eagles appear that can carry him off and drop him. There are three endings, each designed to lead into the plots of the three following Sabreman games. Computer and Video Games said it was likely the most expansive world on the Spectrum, and Retro Gamer called its flip screens "colossal".
trivia: It is the second Sabreman game, between Sabre Wulf and Knight Lore.
Firebird ported it to the Commodore 64 the following year.
One critic felt the C64 version had aged poorly in the year between releases.
Your Sinclair placed it in its top 20 Spectrum games, though readers ranked it near the bottom of their top 100.
It was included in Rare Replay in 2015.
devStory: Ultimate Play the Game released it for the ZX Spectrum in late 1984, shortly before Knight Lore. Reviewers recommended the original, praising its huge world and bubble-riding sections, though later critics noted its frustrating difficulty.

title: Deus Ex Machina
description: Deus Ex Machina (1984) is Mel Croucher's ZX Spectrum art game charting a "defect" in the machine from conception to death, the first game with a fully synchronised soundtrack, featuring Ian Dury and Jon Pertwee.
longDescription:
The game follows the life of a "defect" formed in "the machine", which takes the form of a human body, from conception through growth and evolution to death, from a single cell to a senile old being. Its progression is loosely based on the "Seven Ages of Man" speech from Shakespeare's As You Like It and is full of quotations from it and parodies of it.

The game itself has no sound; instead it comes with a 46-minute audio cassette, the same length as the game, to be played alongside it, making it the first game with a fully synchronised soundtrack of narration, celebrity performers and music. The cast included Ian Dury, Jon Pertwee, Donna Bailey, Frankie Howerd, historian E. P. Thompson and Croucher, who also composed the music. It could be played without the tape, and a full transcript was provided, but the soundtrack makes it easier to follow. Andrew Stagg coded the Spectrum original and Colin Jones the Commodore 64 version. It became the highest new entry in WHSmith's ZX Spectrum chart in November 1984 at number six, four places above Ultimate's Underwurlde, and later gained cult status as an underground art game.
trivia: It was later converted to MSX and Commodore 64.
Croucher said its £15 price, against the usual £8, kept sales low.
He blamed the lavish poster, packaging and "double vinyl gatefold".
It is included in the book 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die.
The original was re-released alongside a sequel/remake in 2015.
devStory: Mel Croucher designed and created it, and Automata UK published it for the ZX Spectrum in October 1984. Croucher later viewed it as a disappointment that only broke even, and in 2014 he released a book about its history and the making of the new game.

title: Spindizzy
description: Spindizzy (1986) is Paul Shirley's isometric action-puzzle game in which a shape-shifting probe called GERALD explores hundreds of floating stages against the clock, often compared with Marble Madness.
longDescription:
The player steers a probe called GERALD, the Gyroscopic Environmental Reconnaissance And Land-Mapping Device, through a world of interconnected stages of ramps and corridors suspended in space, using the keyboard or a joystick. GERALD can transform between a ball, an inverted square pyramid and a gyroscope, each handling the terrain slightly differently, and can move in eight directions and put on a burst of speed. The view can be rotated between four angles, with a compass arrow to help orientation.

The aim is to explore hundreds of stages before time runs out. Power jewels scattered around extend the limit, while falling off a stage, or from a great height, costs time. Ramps, corridors and other obstacles slow the probe, and a burst of speed up a ramp can launch it into other areas. Some tiles carry symbols that help, such as activating lifts to higher regions, and the game ends when time expires or the whole world has been mapped. Shirley, inspired by Ultimate Play the Game's isometric games, approached it as a mix of adventure and puzzle game, feeling the rolling-ball mechanic allowed creative puzzles. Reviewers praised its visuals and design but criticised its audio.
trivia: Electric Dreams was founded by Rod Cousens in 1985 as a British affiliate of Activision.
Shirley severed the US contract with Activision over late royalties and business practices.
It reached number one on the Amstrad charts in March 1986.
James Hague said it could have been an "all-time classic" with proper marketing.
A sequel, Spindizzy Worlds, followed in 1990.
devStory: Paul Shirley developed it and Electric Dreams Software published it in 1986 for several 8-bit home computers, partnering with Activision for the US release. It was successful in the UK and well received by the press, and later publications continued to praise it, though Shirley attributed its short marketing life to Activision.

title: Banjo-Tooie
description: Banjo-Tooie (2000) is Rare's sequel to Banjo-Kazooie, in which the bear and bird take on Gruntilda and her two sisters across larger, more puzzle-focused worlds, with four-player minigames.
longDescription:
Banjo and Kazooie return to stop the witch Gruntilda and two of her sisters, who plan to vaporise the inhabitants of the game's island. Like its predecessor it is a third-person 3D platformer that carries over most of Banjo-Kazooie's mechanics, but its worlds are much larger and place more emphasis on puzzle-solving, alongside jumping obstacles, collecting items and defeating opponents. Challenges and exploration reward collectables that open later challenges and worlds.

The golden jigsaw pieces called Jiggies still open new worlds, but instead of hunting for incomplete puzzle boards in the overworld, players bring them to a single board in a temple belonging to Master Jiggywiggy, which can be used once enough Jiggies have been collected, followed by a timed puzzle challenge. A multiplayer mode lets up to four players compete in minigames taken from the campaign, and the game supports a widescreen format. Critics praised its graphics and the size of its worlds but criticised its inconsistent frame rate. GameRevolution found it less repetitive than Donkey Kong 64 and a worthy successor, and Nintendo Power called it "the perfect cross between Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Kazooie".
trivia: Gregg Mayles and Steve Malpass designed it.
Development began in June 1998, straight after Banjo-Kazooie's release.
Worlds and a multiplayer mode cut from Banjo-Kazooie were used here.
A planned castle world was scrapped for lack of time.
It was the last Banjo game released by Nintendo before Microsoft bought Rare.
devStory: Rare developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 in 2000. Several new features were cut because of time and hardware limits. It sold 1.49 million copies worldwide by 2008, and later appeared on Xbox Live Arcade in 2009 via a 4J Studios port, in Rare Replay in 2015 and on Nintendo Classics in 2024, its first re-release on a Nintendo console.

title: Conker's Bad Fur Day
description: Conker's Bad Fur Day (2001) is Rare's adult-oriented Nintendo 64 platformer in which a greedy, hard-drinking red squirrel tries to get home to his girlfriend after a night at the pub.
longDescription:
Conker, a greedy, hard-drinking red squirrel, must find his way home to his girlfriend Berri after an evening of heavy drinking at the local pub. Though it looks much like Rare's Banjo-Kazooie, Donkey Kong 64 and Banjo-Tooie, it was made for mature audiences, with graphic violence, alcohol and tobacco use, profanity, dark and toilet humour, fourth-wall breaks and pop culture references. It is a 3D platformer whose later sections add shooter elements: an overworld links the levels, many of them blocked until Conker earns enough cash, and each enclosed level is explored freely to find tasks.

Most of the game involves helping other characters through linear sequences of challenges, such as beating bosses, solving puzzles and fighting enemies. Up to four players can compete in seven multiplayer game types. Development took four years, beginning as a family-friendly "generic 3D platform adventure" conceived after Super Mario 64 during work on Killer Instinct Gold in 1996; Tim Stamper planned from the start for it to star a cute squirrel. Announced as Twelve Tales: Conker 64 for late 1998, it was criticised at E3 1998 for its childish tone and resemblance to Banjo-Kazooie and was transformed into an adult game.
trivia: It follows Conker's Pocket Tales (1999).
Nintendo of Europe declined to publish it after a commercial appraisal.
Its advertising targeted male college students.
IGN's Matt Casamassina called it "quite possibly the most hilarious title ever created".
It was remade as Conker: Live & Reloaded for Xbox in 2005.
devStory: Rare developed it for the Nintendo 64, releasing it in North America on 5 March 2001; in Europe, THQ published it on 6 April 2001. It received critical acclaim, scoring 92 on Metacritic, but sold well below expectations because of limited advertising and its release late in the console's life, later gaining a cult following and inclusion in Rare Replay in 2015.

title: Perfect Dark
description: Perfect Dark (2000) is Rare's spiritual successor to GoldenEye 007, in which Carrington Institute agent Joanna Dark uncovers dataDyne's alien conspiracy, one of the N64's most technically advanced games.
longDescription:
Joanna Dark, an agent of the Carrington Institute research centre, tries to stop an extraterrestrial conspiracy by rival corporation dataDyne. A campaign of levels tells the story, while multiplayer offers a co-operative mode and traditional deathmatch with computer-controlled bots. Players can lean left and right, look up and down, crouch, crawl and drop from most ledges, though there is no jump, and a single button operates computers, lifts and doors.

As a spiritual successor to GoldenEye 007, it shares many of its features and runs on an upgraded version of its engine. One of the most technically advanced Nintendo 64 games, it requires an Expansion Pak for the campaign and most multiplayer features. Shortly before release, a feature letting players put a photograph of their choice on their multiplayer character's face was cut because of sensitivities about attacking images of real people. Critics widely praised its graphics, AI and range of multiplayer options, but some criticised its inconsistent frame rate. GameSpot called it "unparalleled" as a console first-person shooter, and it is occasionally cited among the greatest games of all time.
trivia: GoldenEye director Martin Hollis led its first fourteen months before leaving Rare.
Rare had planned a Tomorrow Never Dies game but was outbid by Electronic Arts.
It won the BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Moving Images Award for 2000.
A Game Boy Color counterpart unlocks options via the Transfer Pak.
An Xbox 360 remaster with online multiplayer was released in 2010.
devStory: Rare developed and published it for the Nintendo 64 in 2000 after a development cycle of nearly three years. It was critically acclaimed and sold relatively well, joining Nintendo's Player's Choice line, and won the Golden Satellite Award for Best Interactive Product in 2001. It was re-released on Nintendo Classics in 2024.

title: Excitebike 64
description: Excitebike 64 (2000) is Left Field Productions' 3D motocross sequel to the NES Excitebike, with tricks, extreme jumps, a track editor and the original game hidden inside.
longDescription:
Players choose one of six riders with preset handling and use the stick or D-pad to accelerate, brake, slide and boost. As in the original, pulling back gives more air on jumps and pushing forward drops the front wheel to land on slopes; riders can also tilt the bike in mid-air to set the angle for turns and sideswipe opponents. Many tracks hide shortcuts that require slowing down and changing direction, or boosting across chasms, between hills and over vehicles and buildings, following the original's "extreme" jumps and physics.

The main mode is a 20-track season, with races unlocking more tracks and features, plus a tutorial, exhibitions and time trials. A major feature is the track editor, which lets players build and save fully working tracks. The announcer, Limua, calls out tricks and crashes. Extras include an emulated version of the original Excitebike, a 3D remake called Excite 3D with the same obstacles, a Stunt Course, a Hill Climb, a football game with a giant human-sized ball and an "infinite, randomly generated" desert track. Real dirt bike gear brands such as Bell Helmets, Alpinestars and No Fear feature throughout.
trivia: It is the first 3D game in the Excite series.
The developers used inverse kinematics to animate riders' movements and tricks.
The team took inspiration from Wave Race 64.
Re-releases removed every Fox Racing logo.
Famitsu gave it 29 out of 40.
devStory: Left Field Productions developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 in 2000, focusing on speed, jumps and tricks like the original. It received "generally favorable reviews" on Metacritic, two points short of "universal acclaim", and was re-released on Wii U in 2016 and Nintendo Classics in 2023; Excite Truck followed on Wii in 2006.

title: Mario Tennis
description: Mario Tennis (2000) is Camelot's acclaimed Nintendo 64 tennis game, with an easy-to-learn but deep two-button shot system, and the debut of Waluigi.
longDescription:
Its control system differs from most tennis games: shots are played with one or both of the two main buttons, which spin the ball in different ways. Pressing a button twice hits harder with more spin, pressing the two in different orders produces other shots such as lobs and drop shots, and pressing both together unleashes a powerful smash. Holding a button longer before contact makes the shot stronger. Seven types of shot are possible with just two buttons, letting newcomers learn quickly while encouraging experienced players to develop strategies, and these mechanics carried into later Mario Tennis games.

Matches can be singles or doubles. Exhibition offers a single match, and Tournament mode runs singles or doubles elimination tournaments against computer opponents, with higher difficulties unlocked as cups are won. The game is known for the debut of Luigi's rival Waluigi and the return of Princess Daisy and Birdo. At Nintendo's suggestion, Daisy, previously seen only in Super Mario Land and NES Open Tournament Golf, was brought back to give Peach a doubles partner as Mario had Luigi; Camelot also asked to include girlfriends for Wario and Waluigi, but Shigeru Miyamoto said he "didn't even want to see" them.
trivia: It follows Mario's Tennis on the Virtual Boy.
A Game Boy Color version with RPG elements was released as Mario Tennis GB in Japan.
It was a runner-up for GameSpot's annual Best Nintendo 64 game award.
It was followed by Mario Power Tennis on GameCube.
The N64 version reached Nintendo Classics in 2021.
devStory: Camelot Software Planning developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 in 2000. It received critical acclaim and "universal acclaim" on Metacritic for its accessible yet deep controls, physics and amount of content, and was re-released on the Wii and Wii U Virtual Consoles.

title: Paper Mario
description: Paper Mario (2000) is Intelligent Systems' papercraft-styled RPG in which Mario and his partners rescue the seven Star Spirits after Bowser steals the Star Rod and lifts Peach's castle into the sky.
longDescription:
Bowser steals the Star Rod from Star Haven, imprisons the seven Star Spirits, makes himself invincible, defeats Mario and lifts Princess Peach's castle into the sky. To save the Mushroom Kingdom, Mario must free the Star Spirits, whose power can cancel the stolen Star Rod, by defeating the minions guarding them. The game combines traditional role-playing with Mario series ideas: in the overworld Mario jumps and swings his hammer to overcome obstacles, and many puzzles and barriers depend on the abilities of his partners, each with a speciality needed to progress. Partners join as he reaches new places, and one accompanies him at a time, interchangeable at will.

Partners also help in turn-based battles, where they have no HP of their own and damage only stuns them for a while. Battles are distinctive for "action commands", timed button inputs that make attacks more effective. Nintendo first approached Square, maker of Super Mario RPG, but it was busy with Final Fantasy VII, so Intelligent Systems developed it, with Shigeru Miyamoto producing, Kumiko Takeda and Kaori Aoki writing the script and Naohiko Aoyama as art director responsible for its distinctive look. It was praised for its concept, battle system and graphics.
trivia: It was released in Japan in 2000 and internationally in 2001.
It was Japan's top-selling game in its launch week, selling over 276,000 copies.
It scored 93 on Metacritic.
Nintendo Power ranked it the 63rd best game on a Nintendo system in 2006.
Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door followed on GameCube in 2004.
devStory: Intelligent Systems developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 as the first Paper Mario game. It received critical acclaim and topped the charts for two weeks in other regions, and was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2007, Wii U in 2015 and Nintendo Classics on 10 December 2021.

title: Pokémon Stadium
description: Pokémon Stadium (1999) is Nintendo's 3D turn-based battle game for all 151 original Pokémon, which used the Transfer Pak to bring players' own teams in from Red, Blue and Yellow.
longDescription:
Built around 3D turn-based battles using the 151 Pokémon of the Game Boy's Red, Blue and Yellow, it has no story. Players pick a party of six, using either Pokémon uploaded from the Game Boy games through the bundled Transfer Pak or rental Pokémon with set movesets, and choose three for each battle. The Pokémon are shown in 3D with their own battle animations, and an announcer comments on the action.

The Stadium consists of four Cups, tournaments of three-on-three battles against set line-ups, eighty battles in all, each with its own rules and restrictions. Gym Leader Castle pits the player against the eight Kanto Gym Leaders, the Elite Four and the Champion. Minigames add variety, and the Transfer Pak also lets players view, organise, store, trade and battle with their Game Boy Pokémon. Critics praised its visuals and its connectivity with the Game Boy games, GameSpot's Jeff Gerstmann calling the latter its "main hook", but criticised its audio and repetitive play.
trivia: It was the first Stadium game released in the West.
It succeeded the Japan-only 1998 Pocket Monsters Stadium.
Pocket Monsters Stadium was initially planned for the cancelled 64DD.
It sold a million copies before the end of 2000.
It was re-released on Nintendo Classics on 12 April 2023.
devStory: Nintendo EAD developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 in Japan in 1999 and in Australia, Europe and North America in 2000. It became one of the best-selling N64 games, scoring 78.60 per cent on GameRankings, and was followed by Pokémon Stadium 2 in 2000. IGN, like GameSpot, considered the Game Boy connectivity a highlight, while the game's audio quality and repetitive battles drew criticism.

title: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards
description: Kirby 64: The Crystal Shards (2000) is HAL Laboratory's first 3D-rendered Kirby, a 2.5D platformer in which Kirby gathers the shards of a fairy crystal shattered by Dark Matter, mixing copied powers into combos.
longDescription:
Dark Matter invades Ripple Star, a planet of fairies, and when the fairy Ribbon flees with a sacred crystal, Dark Matter shatters it into 100 shards and scatters them across the galaxy. Ribbon, clutching one shard, falls onto Pop Star and befriends Kirby, who agrees to recover the remaining shards across six planets and defeat Dark Matter. Along the way the artist Adeleine, King Dedede and his minion Waddle Dee each stumble on a shard and are possessed by Dark Matter, so Kirby must fight them to free them, after which they join him.

Like Pandemonium! and Klonoa: Door to Phantomile, it is a 2.5D platformer, with 3D characters and environments but play on a 2D plane. As in earlier Kirby games, Kirby crosses levels and gains powers by swallowing enemies, and new Power Combos let him mix two powers into stronger ones. Up to four players can compete in three multiplayer minigames. Critics praised its colourful visuals and classic play but found it too easy and short, and likened it to other 2.5D N64 platformers such as Goemon's Great Adventure and Yoshi's Story.
trivia: It was the first Kirby game with 3D computer graphics.
Development began in September 1997.
It was planned for the 64DD add-on before becoming a standard N64 cartridge.
HAL switched from the analogue stick to the D-pad about a year before release.
It was the last traditional home console Kirby until Kirby's Return to Dream Land in 2011.
devStory: HAL Laboratory developed it and Nintendo published it for the Nintendo 64 in 2000. It received "generally favorable reviews" according to Metacritic and was re-released on the Wii Virtual Console in 2008, Wii U in 2015 and Nintendo Classics in 2022, as well as in Kirby's Dream Collection in 2012.

title: Aidyn Chronicles: The First Mage
description: Aidyn Chronicles: The First Mage (2001) is H2O Entertainment's 3D Nintendo 64 RPG in which a poisoned young squire, Alaron, seeks a cure, with turn-based tactical battles and permanent party deaths.
longDescription:
While searching for a missing farmer named Kendall, the young squire Alaron meets a strange spirit and is poisoned by goblins. He wakes from a terrifying vision of monsters in the hut of Oriana, a healer, who tells him the poison is beyond ordinary medicine. Back at Castle Gwernia, King Phelan sends him to seek help from the Mirari people. The player moves Alaron around a 3D world, indoors and out, from a mostly overhead third-person view, with real-time day and night affecting visibility and combat; neither his speed nor the camera can be changed, and other party members can only be controlled in battle. A menu handles equipment, abilities, stats, items and the world map.

Combat is turn-based, with turn order influenced by characters' and monsters' stats. The party is moved to a separate battlefield of varied terrain, where each member can move a limited distance shown by transparent borders. Height and attacks from behind affect damage, and each character's solar or lunar aspect makes them stronger or weaker depending on the time of day. Spells and talents show their area of effect with a red flame border that grows with skill level. Party members who die in battle are removed from the game permanently, and if Alaron dies the game ends.
trivia: H2O Entertainment was a Canadian studio.
It was released in North America on 20 March 2001.
It reached Europe on 3 August 2001.
It held a 47.36 per cent rating on GameRankings.
IGN's Jon Griffith called it "a really -- and I mean really -- tedious experience".
devStory: H2O Entertainment developed it and THQ published it for the Nintendo 64 in 2001. It received "mixed or average reviews" according to Metacritic, IGN feeling its scope was too large and that it had no way of drawing players into its story or play.

title: Duke Nukem: Zero Hour
description: Duke Nukem: Zero Hour (1999) is Eurocom's third-person Nintendo 64 shooter in which Duke travels through time, from Victorian London to the Old West, to stop aliens killing his ancestors.
longDescription:
Aliens land again, and the government calls in Duke, who fights through New York with the Marines to the Statue of Liberty, where he discovers their plan: to travel back in time and change history so Earth becomes easy to conquer. During the fight he is thrown into a future where the aliens have won and humanity is near extinction, battling new alien breeds and zombified fallout victims until he meets resistance fighters in the ruins of the US Army's New York headquarters. They send him back through time to restore history, first to the Old West, where the aliens plan to detonate a bomb in the Earth's core and technical problems force him to rely mostly on period weapons, though allies send back some modern ones.

Locations, weapons, items and clothing match each period Duke visits. Compared with the series' usual over-the-top comedy, it includes more mature elements, such as meeting Jack the Ripper near the fresh murder scene of Mary Jane Kelly in Victorian England and a serious depiction of a New York devastated by atomic war. It uses a large 32-megabyte cartridge and can use the Expansion Pak for better graphics at the cost of frame rate, and its four-player split-screen multiplayer switches to a first-person view.
trivia: It is a third-person entry in the usually first-person Duke Nukem series.
The aliens try to eliminate Duke's ancestors.
Its GameRankings score of 67 per cent was based on an unrepresentative sample.
Nintendo Power, IGN, Game Informer and GamePro gave it favourable reviews.
Reviewers commended its controls, environments and multiplayer.
devStory: Eurocom developed it and GT Interactive published it for the Nintendo 64 in 1999. It received moderate scores on release.

title: Albert Odyssey: Legend of Eldean
description: Albert Odyssey: Legend of Eldean (1996) is Sunsoft's Saturn RPG in which Pike, raised by harpies, travels with a talking sword to cure his petrified sister and stop the revival of the god Vlag.
longDescription:
Pike's family was murdered by monsters when he was an infant, and he was raised by a family of winged humanoids known as Harpies. Twenty years later, an evil mage turns his adoptive sister to stone, and with Cirrus, a talking sword holding the spirit of one of the legendary Eldean siblings, Pike sets out to find a cure. He uncovers a plot by evil magicians to turn the world's races against each other and revive the ancient god Vlag, and with friends met on the way must stop its resurrection. Companions include Eka, a withdrawn singer who wields throwing weapons and powerful spells; Leos, a priestess and martial artist with healing abilities; and Gryzz, a dragonman, the eldest and strongest of the party, who fights with two katana and breath weapons.

It is a traditional RPG with an overhead view and menu-driven combat. Originally made for the Super NES and moved to the Saturn late in development, it was conceived as a "gaiden", or side story, with backstory, characters and plot independent of earlier Albert Odyssey games, and it is the first in the series with traditional turn-based RPG play rather than tactical strategy. EGM's Dan Hsu called it "not only beautiful (both musically and graphically)" but one of the most involving RPG stories, with "witty" dialogue.
trivia: It was released in Japan in August 1996.
Working Designs released it in North America in July 1997.
It was the first Albert Odyssey game released in English.
It was re-released in Japan on 20 June 1997 in the budget Saturn Collection line for ¥2,800.
Pike inherited the sword Cirrus from his father.
devStory: Sunsoft produced it for the Sega Saturn, porting it from the Super NES late in development, and released it in Japan in 1996. The North American version, released by Working Designs, received mixed reviews, though EGM's Dan Hsu gave it an Editors' Choice award.

title: Cotton 2: Magical Night Dreams
description: Cotton 2: Magical Night Dreams (1997) is Success's arcade shooter sequel in which the witch Cotton or her rival Appli flies through a dream world to recover the stolen "Bluewater Willow" candy.
longDescription:
The young witch Cotton, or her rival Appli, travels with the fairy Silk and the hat Needle across seven increasingly difficult stages of a magical, dream-like world, defeating monsters to return the missing "Bluewater Willow" candy to the Pumpkin Kingdom. Like Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams, it mixes shooting with fighting and role-playing elements on a three-button layout.

Players blast monsters and dodge fire while collecting elemental crystals that strengthen their weapons, much as in Soldier Blade, and unleash powerful magic spells. Shooting a crystal changes its colour, which decides the primary weapon, and using crystals for a spell lowers firepower. Attacks can be improved through five levels, a role-playing element kept from the original, though its charge attacks and fairy abilities are gone. New are life bars that let each character survive several hits, and fighting game elements. Headed by Takato Yoshinari, it was made by Success staff who had worked on the original Cotton, and ran on Sega's ST-V hardware.
trivia: It is the fourth game in the Cotton series.
It was ported to the Sega Saturn.
Its Saturn version sold over 8,907 copies in its first week, according to Famitsu.
Tecmo released a remixed edition, Cotton Boomerang, in 1998.
Cotton Boomerang added characters, new scoring systems and altered stages.
devStory: Success developed it and Tecmo published it in arcades in 1997 as the arcade sequel to Cotton: Fantastic Night Dreams. Both it and Cotton Boomerang were well received on the Saturn, mostly by critics reviewing them as imports, for being faithful conversions of the arcade originals. Readers of the Japanese Sega Saturn Magazine also voted on both Saturn versions in the magazine's public polls, and the remixed Cotton Boomerang was likewise praised as a faithful conversion.

title: Deep Fear
description: Deep Fear (1998) is Sega's Saturn survival horror game set in an underwater research base, where John Mayor fights mutated staff while managing a dwindling air supply.
longDescription:
On the Big Table, an underwater research facility in the Pacific Ocean, an unknown infection begins turning the staff into hostile mutants, and John Mayor must explore the base, gathering items and resources, fighting enemies and seeking a way out. Characters and enemies are 3D models set against pre-rendered environments seen through fixed camera angles, and John can be moved with traditional tank controls or with full analogue control on the Saturn's 3D Pad. Missions involve finding certain characters and items while managing ammunition and first aid kits.

Combat relies on guns, and John's movement is limited while his weapon is drawn. Lockers around the base supply new weapons and ammunition, and he can carry one powerful "Special" weapon at a time. Its key mechanic is air: each area has a limited supply that runs down over time, faster with gunfire, and must be recharged at Air System terminals, which also serve as save points, while underwater areas require a breathing mask with its own limited air. The game ends if John's health or breath runs out, or if an area's air is exhausted. It was designed as a science-fiction take on the Japanese "mansion mystery" genre, aiming to create fear from its environments and monsters.
trivia: Rieko Kodama co-produced it.
Kenji Kawai composed the music.
Artist Yasushi Nirasawa designed the monsters.
Reviewers frequently compared it to Resident Evil.
A rumoured North American release never happened.
devStory: System Sacom and Sega CS2 co-developed it and Sega published it for the Sega Saturn in 1998. Japanese and European publications reviewed it positively, while English-language reviews were more mixed: its music and play were praised, its graphics divided opinion and its voice acting was panned.

title: Mr. Bones
description: Mr. Bones (1996) is Zono's genre-hopping Saturn game in which a good-hearted reanimated skeleton, held together by "skeletal magnetism", battles the mad philosopher who raised the dead.
longDescription:
DaGoulian, a mad philosopher who believes one can only "ensure the survival of good by making evil thrive", sets out to purify the world with evil. Playing a special set of drums powered by science and alchemy, he taps a primal power he calls "skeletal magnetism" and summons the dead from their graves as skeletal soldiers. One cemetery inmate, though, is pure of heart and is raised with blue, good skeletism rather than red, keeping his free will. DaGoulian orders his army to destroy the rebel, who calls himself Mr. Bones and resolves to stop him.

Much of the play depends on managing the skeletal magnetism holding Mr. Bones together, and the game allows, and sometimes requires, him to carry on with less than a full skeleton. Its most distinctive quality is that hardly any two levels play alike: some just change the camera, while others become a different genre entirely, from music and rhythm games to a Breakout-style game and a memory test, though most remain action-platforming with variations in play and viewpoint. Beaten levels can be replayed directly from the main menu. Reviewers sharply disagreed over whether it was bizarre and extraordinarily original or mundane "hop n bop" platforming.
trivia: It was conceived by Ed Annunziata.
Ronnie Montrose composed and performed the soundtrack.
Angel Studios produced its cut-scenes and art assets.
GameSpot's Tom Ham gave it a modest score but a relentlessly positive review.
Ham praised its blues-rock soundtrack and eerie visuals.
devStory: Zono developed it and Sega published it for the Sega Saturn in 1996. It met with divisive reviews, some hailing it as strikingly original and others dismissing it as a hackneyed, generic platformer.

title: Three Dirty Dwarves
description: Three Dirty Dwarves (1996) is Appaloosa's comic Saturn beat 'em up in which three dim but heroic dwarves from a children's role-playing game crash into the real world, armed with sporting goods.
longDescription:
Four children genetically engineered by the army grow up to be child geniuses rather than perfect soldiers, so General Briggs puts them to work making weapons. To escape, they play their favourite role-playing game and lead its party, a trio of slow-witted but heroic dwarves, through a gateway into the real world. The dwarves' equipment burns up on entry, and they land in a sporting goods store, arming themselves with what they find. Monsters from the game world follow them, and the dwarves must fight through them to find the children and confront Briggs.

Most levels play as a typical beat 'em up, advancing to the end of the stage and defeating enemies on the way. Up to three players each control one dwarf, and with fewer players they can switch between dwarves at any time. A single hit knocks a dwarf unconscious, but another active dwarf can revive him by attacking him, effectively slapping him awake. Each dwarf has short- and long-range attacks of differing speed, and skulls taken from fallen enemies or boxes can be spent on special team attacks, such as starting a fight among themselves or merging into one of three huge combined dwarves.
trivia: It was later ported to Windows.
SegaSoft announced it would be its first PlayStation game once it had a licence, but this never happened.
Briggs eventually offers the dwarves army jobs with generous benefits.
EGM praised the "comic weirdness" of its cut-scenes.
Next Generation felt the side-scrolling beat 'em up genre was getting tired.
devStory: Appaloosa Interactive developed it and Sega published it for the Sega Saturn in 1996. The Saturn version received moderately positive reviews, most critics praising its humour and personality.

title: Clockwork Knight 2
description: Clockwork Knight 2 (1995) is Sega's Saturn platformer sequel in which the toy soldier Pepper sets out again after the sleeping Chelsea is kidnapped once more, adding cards, races and a donkey ride.
longDescription:
Picking up from the first game's cliffhanger, Chelsea is safe but will not wake, and while the toys not under the spell wonder what to do, she is kidnapped again, sending the wind-up knight Pepper off to rescue her once more. Play is identical to its predecessor, using the same items and the same structure of four rooms with two levels each plus a final boss: the Kid's Room, Study Room, Bath Room and Clock Tower, each with its own household environments and obstacles.

New are collectable playing cards, automatically scrolling stages and hidden races. Four cards are hidden in each main level, and finding all four earns a gold key; all 32 unlock a level-select code. In some stages Pepper rides his donkey Barobaro, whose detachable head can be launched at enemies, and hidden obstacle races against Le Bon and Prunchau offer extra rewards. The North American release, based on a Japanese compilation, adds a "Bosses Galore" mode in which players control Pepper or his rival Ginger against the bosses of both games, with a ranking that unlocks bonus content at Expert or above. Maximum found it as short as the original but with far more replay value, and called its graphics "far in advance of any other comparable next generation product".
trivia: It began as the second half of a project first conceived as a single game.
It was released in Japan on 28 July 1995 and Europe on 27 October 1995.
The Japanese compilation Clockwork Knight: Pepperouchau no Fukubukuro followed on 15 December 1995.
The US release, on 17 February 1996, was based on that compilation but locked out the first game.
Many critics considered it a dramatic improvement over the first game.
devStory: Sega developed and published it for the Sega Saturn in 1995 as the direct sequel to Clockwork Knight; designer Kats Sato later explained that Sega had divided the original project into two games. It was well received, critics citing its improved replay value and pacing.

title: Puyo Puyo Sun
description: Puyo Puyo Sun (1996) is Compile's third Puyo Puyo, set on a tropical beach where Satan has enlarged the Sun, adding Sun Puyo to the series' competitive falling-blob puzzles.
longDescription:
Satan, the Dark Prince of English versions, uses special magic to make the Sun bigger over a remote island, hoping to create a paradise where he can relax surrounded by girls in bikinis. On Easy, Draco Centauros takes the chance to find a tanning spot and ends up sunburnt, while Arle Nadja and Schezo take the lead on Normal and Hard. After the great success of Puyo Puyo 2, Compile took a slightly more retro approach so the game would feel closer to the original.

As before, Puyo fall in pairs from the top of the screen and can be moved left and right and rotated 90 degrees either way, and the game is lost if the third column from the left fills to the top. The offset (Sousai) and all-clear (Zenkeshi) rules from Puyo Puyo 2 remain, but every counter now drops special garbage in a preset pattern, random in the Game Boy version, and since the all-clear bonus is gone, clearing the screen drops Sun Puyo instead. The title is a pun: "san" means three in Japanese, it is the third game, it is set on a tropical beach and it introduces Sun Puyo.
trivia: It is the sequel to Puyo Puyo 2.
Game Machine listed it as Japan's fifth most successful arcade game in February 1997.
A PC version was also translated into Korean.
Game Boy Color artwork could be unlocked and viewed in the N64's Puyo Puyo~n via the Transfer Pak.
A versus-only Genesis port, VS Puyo Puyo Sun, appeared on the Sega Genesis Mini 2 in 2022.
devStory: Compile developed and published it as an arcade game in 1996, the third main Puyo Puyo. Home ports followed, including PC, with music slightly different from the arcade original.

title: Sakura Wars
