description: Sakura Wars (1996) is Sega and Red Company's "dramatic adventure" mixing tactical RPG, dating sim and visual novel, in which Ensign Ichiro Ogami leads a theatre troupe of steam-armoured heroines defending 1920s Tokyo.
longDescription:
In a fictionalised Taishō-era 1923, the Imperial Combat Revue is a military unit that fights supernatural threats to Tokyo while posing as a theatre troupe. Imperial Japanese Navy Ensign Ichiro Ogami is made leader of its all-female Flower Division, women with magical abilities who defend the city against demons in steam-powered armour called Kobus, and he becomes caught up in its conflict with the Hive of Darkness and in the personal lives of its members.

Dubbed a "dramatic adventure" game by Sega and told across ten episodes, it combines tactical role-playing, dating sim and visual novel elements in two modes. In adventure mode Ogami explores the Grand Imperial Theater and talks with its characters, and in battle mode the Flower Division fights on a turn-based grid. Creator Oji Hiroi conceived it in 1990, and his small team in Red Company's planning department developed the idea from 1993, with full production beginning a year later after Sega's approval. Writer Satoru Akahori, composer Kohei Tanaka and character designer Kōsuke Fujishima joined the project.
trivia: It was released only in Japan.
An English fan translation was released in 2019.
It was ported to the Dreamcast and remade for PlayStation 2.
Most English-language reviews appeared years after release, though GameFan reviewed it as an import in 1996.
Its direct sequel, Sakura Wars 2: Thou Shalt Not Die, followed in 1998.
devStory: Sega and Red Company developed it and Sega published it for the Sega Saturn in 1996. It was a critical and commercial success, one of the Saturn's best-selling games, and launched the Sakura Wars series of sequels and spin-offs. Famitsu and Sega Saturn Magazine reviewed the original Saturn release, and a 2000 English-language review rated the later Dreamcast port highly.

title: Tonic Trouble
description: Tonic Trouble (1999) is Ubi Soft Montreal's 3D action-adventure, conceived by Michel Ancel, in which alien janitor Ed must undo the chaos caused when he dropped a mutating fluid onto Earth.
longDescription:
Ed, an alien janitor aboard the Mothership Albatros, drops a container of unidentified fluid onto Earth, turning the planet into a mutated version of itself. The drunkard Grögh drinks from it, gains powers and conquers the Earth, and as Ed the player must solve puzzles and defeat enemies to gather the tools needed to beat Grögh and recover the container to make an antidote.

Played from a third-person view, Ed explores 3D environments through platforming and portals, armed with a peashooter used in first person. A mad doctor builds new gadgets as levels are completed: the peashooter, a bow tie that lets Ed fly, a diving helmet for underwater exploration, a belt that disguises him as an enemy, and a pogo stick for crossing lava and stomping open trapdoors. Ed jumps, climbs, flies, swims and crawls, and eating popcorn turns him into Super Ed, unlocking kicks and slaps. Thermometers extend his health bar, and a stick beats enemies, flips switches and prises open doors to bonus areas. Fetch quests involve collecting red orbs and other items, and collecting bonus spheres unlocks a secret level.
trivia: It was conceptualised by Michel Ancel.
Around 120 people worked on it, with pre-production starting in June 1996.
The N64 and Windows versions have twelve levels; RFX Interactive's Game Boy Color version has six.
It sold 1.1 million copies by 2001.
It was re-released on Nintendo Classics in 2025.
devStory: Ubi Soft Montreal developed it and Ubi Soft published it for the Nintendo 64 in August 1999 after several delays, followed by Windows that December. Reviews were mixed, averaging 53 per cent for the N64 and 70 per cent for Windows on GameRankings: critics approved of its controls, music, level design and graphics but criticised its camera and derivative nature, though EGM called it "a tightly developed platformer".

title: Wipeout 64
description: Wipeout 64 (1998) is Psygnosis's anti-gravity racer for the Nintendo 64, the only Wipeout released on a Nintendo console, adding analogue control, team weapons and four-player split screen.
longDescription:
Set in 2098, a year after Wipeout 2097, it keeps the series' futuristic anti-gravity racing against human or AI rivals. Inspired by Formula One, but instead of downforce for grip, its craft use fictional air brakes for ever sharper turns. It introduced analogue control suited to the Nintendo 64 pad, along with new weapons, teams and tracks; most tracks are mirrored layouts of circuits from Wipeout and Wipeout 2097.

Alongside returning homing missiles, machine guns and electro-bolts, each team has its own unique weapon, and new options include firing three rockets at once and rear-locking missiles. An unlockable "Cyclone" power-up, exclusive to this game, strengthens weapons, and an elimination counter tracking opponents destroyed paved the way for Wipeout 3's Eliminator mode. Where earlier games linked two screens for multiplayer, it introduced four-player split screen, and a new Challenge Mode sets goals in fixed classes and tracks: the fastest time trial, the highest race finish or the most eliminations in a weapons-based deathmatch.
trivia: It is the third game in the Wipeout series.
Psygnosis had been owned by Sony Computer Entertainment for five years when it was released.
All later Wipeout games were released only on Sony hardware.
It scored 84/100 on Metacritic.
Critics debated whether it was a "true sequel" to Wipeout 2097.
devStory: Psygnosis developed it and Midway Games published it for the Nintendo 64 in 1998. It received generally positive reviews, critics praising its individuality within the series, graphics, larger choice of tracks and craft, atmosphere and "superior track design", with "everything a futuristic racer needs". At the time Psygnosis was owned by Sony Computer Entertainment, and every later Wipeout game appeared only on Sony hardware, leaving Wipeout 64 the series' sole Nintendo release.

title: Ready 2 Rumble Boxing
description: Ready 2 Rumble Boxing (1999) is Midway's comic 3D boxing game for the Dreamcast, with larger-than-life fighters such as Afro Thunder, bruising faces and a special "Rumble Flurry".
longDescription:
Like Nintendo's Punch-Out!!, it features boxers with colourful personalities, such as Afro Thunder and Boris "The Bear" Knokimov, but it is in 3D, giving more control over the fighter in the ring, and players can choose any boxer from a large roster. Ring announcer Michael Buffer appears as himself.

During fights a RUMBLE meter fills a letter or two at a time as hard blows land, with especially strong punches earning more. Once "RUMBLE" is spelt out, the player can power up and trigger a "Rumble Flurry", a unique, heavily damaging combination for each character. Fighters gradually show bruises and swelling as a bout goes on; the idea had appeared in SNK's Art of Fighting in 1992, but reviewers widely praised the fun it added. The Dreamcast, PlayStation and Nintendo 64 versions each have an exclusive boxer, Jimmy Blood, Gino Stiletto and J.R. Flurry respectively. It was developed on PCs with 3dfx graphics cards, and lead programmer Dave Wagner said the team separated the graphics layer from the rest of the code to keep it portable, rewriting and optimising the renderer specifically for the Dreamcast.
trivia: Point of View developed the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation ports.
Crawfish Interactive made a separate Game Boy Color version.
The Game Boy Color version was one of the few on the system with built-in rumble.
NextGen said "Midway once again proves it's untouchable".
Sequels followed in 2000 and 2009.
devStory: Midway Studios San Diego developed it and Midway published it for the Dreamcast in September 1999, with N64, PlayStation and Game Boy Color versions that November. It received "favorable" reviews on every platform except Game Boy Color, which was "mixed", and was followed by Ready 2 Rumble Boxing: Round 2 and Ready 2 Rumble: Revolution.
